name: !’Khwa (Rain Bull)
description: The !’Khwa (Rain Bull) is a powerful water and rain spirit in San mythology of Namibia and southern Africa. Depicted as a semi-mythical bull-like creature associated with rainfall, waterholes, and the生命-giving rains of the Kalahari. The Rain Bull is both feared and respected as a source of life and destruction. In San cosmology, the Rain Bull dwells in waterholes and can be harnessed by rain shamans (!ǁgi:ten) who enter trance to guide it across the land, bringing life-giving rain. If angered or mishandled, the Rain Bull can cause destructive floods or devastating storms. The creature is depicted in the famous rock art of the Drakensberg and Namibian mountains

name: 'Umi-a-Liloa
description: A legendary Hawaiian chief of the island of Hawaii, known for his justice, wisdom, and military prowess. 'Umi-a-Liloa was the son of the great chief Liloa, born to a commoner woman. Despite his humble maternal lineage, 'Umi was recognized by his father and eventually became one of the greatest rulers of ancient Hawaii. He unified the island of Hawaii, reorganized the land divisions, established just laws, and protected the common people. 'Umi is remembered as the model of the wise and just ali'i (chief), who ruled with concern for the welfare of his people. His story is one of the most detailed chiefly histories preserved in Hawaiian oral tradition

name: //Gaunab
description: //Gaunab (Gaunab) is the Khoikhoi malevolent deity of death, sickness, and misfortune, personifying darkness and the west. He eternally battles the creator Tsui-//Goab, who wounded his knees in their wrestling match. The lunar cycle reflects their conflict: waning moon is //Gaunab's temporary victory, new crescent marks Tsui-//Goab's return. Documented by Theophilus Hahn (1881) and later scholars.

name: A-Men (Rainbow Serpent)
description: The A-Men, also known as the Rainbow Serpent, is one of the most powerful ancestral beings in Australian Aboriginal mythology, particularly among the Yolngu and Lardil peoples of Arnhem Land. This immense serpentine creator deity emerged from beneath the earth during the Dreamtime, carving out huge ridges, mountains, and gorges as it pushed upward across the landscape. The Rainbow Serpent is closely associated with water sources such as permanent waterholes, springs, and rivers, and is believed to control the most precious resource of life itself. It is both a benevolent giver of life and a destructive force when angered, capable of summoning powerful storms and cyclones

name: Aapisowaahs
description: Aapisowaahs (Apisowaahs, Iipisowaahs) is the Morning Star of Blackfoot tradition, not a Crow figure as the entry claims. He is the son of Nato'si (Sun) and Ko'komiki'somm (Moon); his story, connected to Poia/Star Boy and the Star Bride, is central to Blackfoot star-lore and the Sun Dance. The Crow people have their own cosmology (Old Man Coyote, Akbaatatdia), distinct from this Blackfoot being.

name: Aarni
description: Not a folklore creature — Aarni is a Finnish avant-garde metal band (1998–present) by Master Warjomaa. The name was likely chosen for its mythological resonance (cf. 'aarni' as treasure guardian in Ganander), but no such entity exists in Finnish mythology. Ganander's Mythologia Fennica mentions 'aarni' as a treasure-guarding spirit (haltija), but the band is the primary modern referent.

name: Aasik
description: Aasik is a grotesque creature of Greenlandic Inuit legend said to live around the dog-pens, feeding on scraps and waste and growing monstrously large until the people are forced to destroy it. The being is recorded in Greenlandic oral tradition and appears in retellings of Inuit folklore.

name: Aataentsic
description: Aataentsic is the Huron (Wyandot) version of the Sky Woman, the first mother of creation. According to Huron tradition, she lived in the Sky Land until the chief's daughter (also called Aataentsic in some versions) fell through a hole created when the wild apple tree was uprooted. Swans caught her and placed her on the Great Turtle's back. The animals dove for earth, and Old Toad succeeded where larger animals failed, bringing up grains of earth in her mouth. Aataentsic gave birth to twin daughters, one of whom became the mother of the twin brothers Ioskeha and Tawescaron who completed the creation

name: Abaasy
description: Abaasy are the malevolent lower-world spirits of Yakut (Sakha) cosmology: grotesque multi-headed monsters with iron teeth, bodies blending human and animal traits, some one-eyed or one-limbed. Sadistic and destructive, they bring disease, death, and misfortune, steal souls, and devour humans, and can only be defeated temporarily. Their eternal conflict with the Aiyy drives the Olonkho epics.

name: Abada
description: In Kongo tradition, the Abada (also Nillekma or Arase) is a unicorn-like creature the size of a small donkey with a boar's tail and two crooked horns that hang limp when relaxed but harden when threatened. Its horns act as antidotes to poison and disease. Father Balthazar Tellez (17th c.) distinguished it from the unicorn: 'The Abada has two crooked horns... serving as antidotes against poison.

name: Abai Geser
description: Abai Geser ('the Mighty') is the great hero of the Buryat Epic of Gesar, a mighty warrior in celestial armor who rides a magical horse and radiates divine power as a son of the sky gods. Brave, cunning, relentless, he battles ever-stronger demonic foes, from giant rats to sun-devouring monsters, using trickery and disguise. The Geser epic is shared across Tibet, Mongolia, and Buryatia.

name: Abaia
description: Abaia is a gigantic magical eel from Melanesian mythology that dwells at the bottom of deep freshwater lakes in Fiji, the Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu. The beast considers all creatures in the lake its children and protects them furiously against anyone who would harm or disturb them. Those foolish enough to catch fish from a lake containing Abaia are overwhelmed by a great wave caused by the thrashing of its powerful tail. If someone harms a creature living in Abaia's home, it causes a great rain storm that floods the land and drowns those who caused the harm. Abaia's magical powers may stem from encounters with an undiscovered species of giant eel living in remote lakes

name: Abchanchu
description: The Abchanchu is a legendary vampiric creature from the Aymara region of Bolivia, considered the most feared evil being among the Aymara people. This shapeshifting vampire dwells in desolate caves and grottoes of the altiplano, the high plateau of the Andes Mountains. According to tradition, the Abchanchu is the bastard brother of Ekeko, born from an extramarital affair of the Mallku of Chakamita with his concubines. The creature preys upon human compassion by disguising itself as a helpless traveler in need, then attacks and drains the blood of anyone who offers assistance, causing death through blood loss or strange diseases

name: Abiku
description: Àbíkú are Yoruba spirits believed to die in childhood, return to their mothers, and be reborn repeatedly, embodying the cycle between the ancestral realm and earthly life. Families respond with protective rituals, iron ornaments, and names that flatter or mock the child, hoping to break the cycle of death and return in West African cosmology.

name: Abonsam
description: Abonsam is a malevolent spirit from the traditional beliefs of the Akan people of Ghana and the Gold Coast region of West Africa. The name derives from Akan terms denoting evil thrown about in disorder, referring to a malevolent force that embodies fundamental opposition to moral and social harmony. Unlike physical forest monsters such as the Sasabonsam, Abonsam is an intangible, spectral presence that manifests through subtle yet ominous phenomena. When accidents, disease, or misfortune afflict an area and shamans determine that Abonsam is to blame, elaborate rituals are performed to drive the spirit into the sea and restore communal balance

name: Abram Moos Kara Taaci
description: Abram Moos Kara Taaci is a powerful female shamanic figure of Altai epic tradition, linked to the underworld and called a daughter of Erlik. Capable of shapeshifting and wielding dark magic, she knows the lower world deeply and acts as both guide and challenger to epic heroes; in the Maadai-Kara epic she confronts Kögüdei Mergen. Her role reflects female shamanic power in Altai epic.

name: Abu Al-Salasil
description: Abu al-Salasil ('Father of Chains') is a terrifying figure of Gulf Arab folklore — a towering, dark-skinned being wrapped in heavy iron chains whose clatter fills coastal settlements at night. Parents invoke him to keep children indoors, and he is repelled by reciting Quranic verses such as Ayat al-Kursi. One tale traces him to a shackled slave who fled mad into the wilderness.

name: Abuk
description: Abuk is the first woman of Dinka mythology, the one well-known female deity among the Dinka and Nuer (where she is called Buk or Acol). According to the creation myth, Nhialic made Abuk and Garang from clay; Abuk's wish to plant more than the single daily grain led to the separation of heaven and earth. She is the mother of Deng and patroness of women and gardens.

name: Abumi-guchi
description: The Abumi-guchi is a strange furry yokai from Japanese folklore, specifically a type of tsukumogami formed from a traditional stirrup that once belonged to a mounted warrior who fell in battle. First illustrated in Sekien Toriyamas Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro from 1784, this spirit is born from the lingering attachment between a fallen soldier and his equipment. Unlike aggressive tsukumogami that punish neglectful owners, the Abumi-guchi embodies quiet mournful loyalty, waiting eternally in the fields where its master died. The stirrup was left behind on the battlefield, and unable to fulfill its purpose of supporting the rider, it transforms into a living creature

name: Acalica
description: The Acalica are mythological weather-controlling spirits from Bolivian folklore, sometimes called weather-fairies, with origins in indigenous Quechua and Aymara traditions of the Andean region. These elusive beings inhabit high-altitude underground caves and mountaintops, where they remain largely hidden from human sight in the rugged terrain of the Andes. The Acalica serve as subordinate guardians to Pachamama, the revered Mother Earth deity, acting as localized enforcers of her will by regulating weather patterns to maintain ecological balance and fertility. They are generally benevolent spirits associated with natural elements like rain, wind, hail, and frost

name: Acqua Che Canta
description: Acqua Che Canta, meaning singing water in Italian, is a water spirit from the folklore of northern Italy, particularly the Alpine and pre-Alpine regions including Veneto, Friuli, and the Dolomites. These creatures are known by many names including anguane, agane, vivane, subiane, and aquane. They are nature spirits akin to the nymphs of Roman mythology, blending characteristics of Germanic undines and Slavic rusalki. The Acqua Che Canta are guardians of springs, streams, and water sources, and are central to the ancient Saga of the Fanes, a mythological tale of the Dolomites. They can be benevolent protectors or dangerous seducers depending on how they are treated

name: Adaro
description: The Adaro are among the most fearsome sea-spirits of Melanesian mythology, originating from the Arosi people of Makira, Solomon Islands. They are described as human-headed fish-men with gills behind the ears, a long tail-fin, a dorsal horn, and a spear-like projection emerging from the head. Adaro are malevolent beings who prey upon fishermen who venture too far or violate cultural taboos. They have the power to launch poisonous flying fish at victims and can traverse rainbows and waterspouts, symbolic pathways between ocean and sky. The term adaro carries dual meaning: it refers to the monstrous fish-man but also signifies a bad soul, contrasting with aunga, the good soul

name: Adbar Spirits
description: Adbar are ancient guardian spirits in Ethiopian folk belief who inhabit every mountain, river, forest, crossroads, and natural feature of the landscape. These pre-human spirits serve as intermediaries between God (Egziabher) and the natural world, each with a specific territory and responsibility. Some Adbar protect travelers on dangerous roads, others guard the fertility of farmlands, and still others watch over water sources and springs. Before a journey or harvest, Ethiopians traditionally offer coffee beans, incense, or bread to the local Adbar, asking for safe passage or bountiful yield. The Adbar are neither good nor evil -- they are ancient forces of nature who demand respect. Offending an Adbar brings misfortune, while honoring it brings protection

name: Adinkra
description: Adinkra refers to a collection of West African symbols created by the Bono people of Gyaman, now Ghana, named after their original creator King Nana Kwadwo Agyemang Adinkra. Each Adinkra symbol represents concepts related to traditional wisdom, aspects of life, the environment, and philosophical ideas. One significant Adinkra symbol is Funtunfunefu Denkyemfunefu, representing Siamese crocodiles, which symbolizes democracy, cooperation, and unity among different groups. Another is Ananse Ntontan, meaning spiders web, which represents wisdom, creativity, and the complexities of life, associated with Anansi the spider trickster of West African folklore

name: Adlet
description: The Adlet (Erqigdlit) are the half-human, dog-legged people of Inuit mythology in Greenland, Labrador and the Hudson Bay coasts. In the story of 'The Girl and the Dogs', a girl marries the dog Ijirqang and their children become the adlet. Rink and Boas recorded the tradition in 1889; on the east Greenland coast it is told as the origin of the Qavdlunait and Irqigdlit, cannibals in some versions.

name: Adonis
description: Adonis is a Phoenician god of beauty, desire, and vegetation whose worship was centered at Byblos in ancient Lebanon. His name derives from the Semitic word 'Adon' meaning 'Lord,' and he represents the archetypal dying-and-rising deity whose death and rebirth symbolized the annual cycle of seasons. According to myth, Adonis was born from a myrrh tree. The goddess Aphrodite fell deeply in love with his extraordinary beauty, but Persephone also claimed him. Zeus decreed Adonis would spend part of the year with each goddess. Adonis died after being gored by a wild boar, and from his blood Aphrodite caused anemone flowers to spring forth. The Adonis River (Nahr Ibrahim) flows from Afqa where the myth places his death and was said to run red with his blood each spring due to red soil runoff

name: Adroanzi
description: Adroanzi is a guardian spirit from the mythology of the Lugbara people of Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo. In Lugbara cosmology, Adroanzi are nature spirits associated with specific locations such as rivers, rocks, trees, and forests, serving as protective entities of the natural landscape. They are considered lesser spirits compared to the supreme creator god Adroa, but they play an essential role in mediating between the human world and the divine realm. These spirits are deeply connected to the land and are believed to inhabit sacred sites where they watch over the community and maintain the balance between the natural and supernatural worlds

name: Adtjis-ietnie
description: Adtjis-ietnie is the Sami goddess of disease, a malevolent figure from southern Sami (Swedish Sapmi) tradition. According to the myth of the Golden Time, she was the wife of Adtjis (the greedy brother) who came from the underworld carrying a sack of diseases. When Adtjis murdered his good brother Naevie over land jealousy, Adtjis-ietnie released all the diseases from her sack into the world, ending the Golden Age when there was no sickness, cold, night, or sorrow. She represents the Sami explanation for the origin of disease and suffering — not as punishment but as something brought into the world through human greed and violence. Unlike Jábmiidáhkká who governs death as a natural process, Adtjis-ietnie is specifically a bringer of sickness — an active, malevolent force. The myth draws a connection between human moral failure (murder, greed, jealousy) and the introduction of suffering into a formerly perfect world

name: Adze
description: The Adze is a vampiric spirit from Ewe folklore, told by the people of Togo and Ghana. In the wild, the Adze takes the form of a firefly, allowing it to travel through keyholes and cracks at night. Once inside a home, it drinks the blood of sleeping victims, causing sickness and death. If captured, the Adze transforms into human shape, revealing either a possessed witch or a grotesque diminutive humanoid. People possessed by an Adze are viewed as witches (abasom). The legend likely originated as an explanation for mosquito-borne illnesses like malaria

name: Adze
description: Adze is a vampire from Ghana mythology. In the wild, the Adze takes the form of a firefly, allowing it to travel through keyholes and cracks at night. Once inside a home, it drinks the blood of sleeping victims, causing sickness and death. If captured, the Adze transforms into human shape, revealing either a possessed witch or a grotesque diminutive humanoid. People possessed by an Adze are viewed as witches (abasom). The legend likely originated as an explanation for mosquito-borne illnesses like malaria

name: Adze
description: Adze is a vampire from Ewe mythology. In the wild, the Adze takes the form of a firefly, allowing it to travel through keyholes and cracks at night. Once inside a home, it drinks the blood of sleeping victims, causing sickness and death. If captured, the Adze transforms into human shape, revealing either a possessed witch or a grotesque diminutive humanoid. People possessed by an Adze are viewed as witches (abasom). The legend likely originated as an explanation for mosquito-borne illnesses like malaria

name: Afriq (Berber Demon of Destruction)
description: Afriq is a malevolent demon or nature spirit in Berber (Amazigh) folklore, particularly in the mythology of ancient Numidia (modern Algeria and Tunisia). The name Afriq is etymologically linked to the name of the continent Africa itself, as the Romans named the province Africa after the Berber tribe of the Afri and their local deity. Afriq is described as a dark, shadow-like being that emerges from the desert wastes, bringing destruction, drought, and plague. Unlike the more subtle jinn of Islamic tradition, Afriq is purely destructive. He is said to ride the desert winds and be visible as a dust devil or sandstorm. In Berber mythology before the Islamic period, he was a figure of chaos and sterility, counterposed to the life-giving forces of nature

name: Agaýunus Peri
description: Agaýunus Peri is a supernatural fairy-woman of the Turkmen epic, wife of the legendary hero Göroglu, a woman of luminous beauty in ethereal clothing who can appear and disappear at will, moving between human and spirit worlds. Loving and graceful, she reflects the Turkmen belief in peris as intermediaries between mortals and the unseen.

name: Agbé
description: Agbé is the powerful sea deity of the Fon people of Benin, ruling the ocean and all marine life within the Vodun pantheon. As the third-born son of the creator pair Mawu and Lisa, Agbé occupies a crucial position in the divine hierarchy, governing the vast, unpredictable, and life-sustaining waters that border the Fon homeland. For the coastal communities of Benin whose survival depended on fishing and maritime trade, Agbé's presence was immediate and essential. He maintains the delicate balance between water and land, ensuring that the ocean remains a source of nourishment rather than destruction. In Fon cosmology, the earth rests upon primordial waters, making Agbé not just a sea god but a stabilizing force beneath the world itself. His role extends to controlling tides, currents, storms, and marine life. Agbé's worship has been carried across the Atlantic through the slave trade, where he became Agwé in Haitian Vodou, retaining his identity as lord of the sea depicted as a regal figure associated with ships and ocean travel

name: Agogwe
description: The Agogwe is a purported small human-like biped reported in East African folklore and cryptozoology, primarily from Tanzania and Mozambique. These creatures are described as diminutive hominids standing approximately four feet tall, covered in russet or brown hair, walking upright like humans. The most famous account comes from Captain William Hichens, who reported seeing two such creatures in the Ussure and Simibit forests while on a lion-hunting expedition around 1900. The local hunter with him identified them as agogwe, little furry men rarely seen. A second account from Cuthbert Burgoyne in 1927 described similar beings walking among baboons on the coast of Portuguese East Africa

name: Agokoli
description: Agokoli (Unknown). is a human. Agokoli is a legendary tyrannical king of Notsé (in present-day Togo) from Ewe oral tradition. His oppressive rule drove the Ewe people to escape through a hole in the city wall, leading to their dias. Source: Ewe oral tradition; Ghanaian/Togolese historical narratives

name: Agwe
description: Agwe (also called Agbe) is the Fon vodun of the sea and the ruler of the ocean realm. One of the children of Mawu and Lisa, Agwe was born as part of a pair of twins (both named Agbe) who were given dominion over the sea pantheon. Agwe commands the oceans, seas, and all marine life. He is the protector of sailors, fishermen, and those who travel by water. He is also the master of Aido Hwedo, the cosmic rainbow serpent who now rests coiled in the ocean depths — when the serpent shifts, Agwe's domain is disturbed, causing earthquakes and tidal waves. Agwe demands offerings for safe voyages and abundant fishing. He is associated with the color blue and with conch shells. His worship is central to coastal communities in Benin and Togo

name: Ah Puch
description: Ah Puch is the Mayan god of death, darkness, and disaster, also known as Cizin, Kisin, Yum Cimil, or Hunhau among various Maya groups. He rules over Mitnal, the lowest and most terrifying level of the Mayan underworld, a place of fear where souls of the wicked are tortured. Mayans were notably more fearful of death than other Mesoamerican cultures, and Ah Puch was envisioned as a hunting figure that stalked the houses of people who were injured or sick. He is associated with owls, dogs, bats, vultures, scorpions, and spiders, and is closely allied with the gods of war, disease, and sacrifice, working against the gods of fertility

name: Ahayuta (Twin War Gods)
description: Ahayuta (Ahayu'da), the Zuni twin war gods, were created by the Sun Father Awonawilona to protect the first people and are second only to him in power. They led the people from the fourth underworld, shaped the earth, and destroyed the monsters of the new world. Effigies carved from lightning-struck cottonwood are placed in open-air shrines to weather away.

name: Ahoeitu
description: Ahoeitu is the legendary first Tu'i Tonga (sacred king of Tonga), founder of the dynasty that ruled Tonga for over a thousand years. Born to a Tongan chiefess and the god Eitumatupua, who descended from heaven on a great tree, Ahoeitu was of both divine and mortal parentage. His jealous half-brothers murdered him and cut his body into pieces. When Eitumatupua discovered the crime, he restored Ahoeitu to life and punished the treacherous brothers. Ahoeitu became the first of the Tu'i Tonga line, establishing the sacred kingship with divine authority. His story reinforces the sacred nature of Tongan kingship and the consequences of defying divinely ordained rule

name: Ahuizotl
description: The Ahuizotl (from Classical Nahuatl āhuitzotl, 'spiny aquatic thing') is a legendary creature in Aztec mythology, described as the guardian of lakes and a servant of the rain god Tlaloc and his consort Chalchiuhtlicue. It is described as the size of a small dog with waterproof, spiky black fur, pointed ears, and hands like a monkey's on both its limbs and the tip of its prehensile tail. The creature lures people to their deaths by crying like a human baby or by causing fish to jump to the surface, drawing fishermen to the water's edge. It uses the hand on its tail to snatch its prey, then feasts on their eyes, nails, and teeth. Victims of the ahuizotl were believed to be chosen by the water gods and destined for Tlaloc's paradise. The conquistador Hernán Cortés once reported to the King of Castile that one of his men had been killed by an ahuizotl. The creature was also taken as an emblem by the Aztec ruler Ahuitzotl. The revolutionary anti-porfirist periodical 'El Hijo del Ahuizote' was named after the creature. The ahuizotl is most likely based on the water opossum, which possesses a prehensile tail and water-repellent fur

name: Aino
description: Aino is a human heroine in the Kalevala (Finnish national epic), not a folklore creature. She is Joukahainen's sister, promised to Väinämöinen after he wins a singing contest. Refusing to marry the old sage, she drowns herself and transforms into a water spirit (nixie/perch), later taunting Väinämöinen. Her story is a literary creation by Elias Lönnrot (19th c.

name: Airavata
description: Airavata is the divine white elephant of Hindu myth, mount of Indra, born from the churning of the ocean of milk. Described with four tusks, seven trunks (or three heads/six tusks), pristine white skin. Guards Svarga's entrance, controls rain clouds. Appears in Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavad Gita (10.27), Puranas. Known as Erawan in Thai/Lao tradition, on royal flags.

name: Aisha Kandisha
description: Aisha Kandisha is the most feared jinn in Algerian and North African folklore, a beautiful but deadly female water spirit of Berber origin. She is described as a stunningly beautiful woman from the waist up but with goat or camel legs, carrion hands, and poultry claws. Her skin is said to be extremely white, with long black or red hair that flows down to her hips. Aisha Kandisha is associated with water sources including rivers, springs, wells, and the sea, and emerges at night to seduce and kill men who disrespect women or venture alone into desolate areas. According to historical accounts, the legend may be based on a real 16th-century resistance fighter named Aisha who led attacks against Portuguese occupiers before being killed, her story gradually transforming into supernatural legend. In Berber tradition, she is considered the queen of the jinn, a figure of immense power who can both bless and curse. The only way to escape her is to surprise her with fire, which is considered her weakness. Moroccans and Algerians traditionally burn incense or recite Quranic verses to ward off her presence

name: Aisha Kandisha
description: Aisha Qandisha (Aisha Kandisha) is a female spirit of the Maghreb, most strongly documented in Moroccan folklore but known across the region including Tunisia. Described as a beautiful woman with long hair and lower limbs that end in hooves, she haunts rivers and springs and is said to seduce and harm those who stray; she is invoked in protective rituals and possession practices in North Africa.

name: Aisha Qandisha
description: Aisha Qandisha is a female mythological figure in Moroccan folklore, a jinn-like entity with a distinct personality who is both feared and revered. She is associated with bodies of water such as rivers, lakes, and the sea, and is known to use her beauty to seduce men before driving them mad or killing them. Her origins trace back to ancient Canaanite religion through the goddess Qetesh, and some theories suggest she was derived from a real historical figure, a Moroccan countess from El Jadida who helped resist Portuguese colonization by seducing soldiers who were then killed by Moroccan fighters lying in wait

name: Aitu
description: Aitu is a term found throughout Polynesian languages referring to ghosts, spirits, or demons, often malevolent in nature. The word appears across Tongan, Samoan, Maori, Tahitian, Cook Islands, and other Polynesian mythologies with varying specific meanings. In Tongan mythology, ʻaitu or ʻeitu are lesser gods, many being patrons of specific villages and families, often taking the form of plants or animals and regarded as more cruel than other gods. In Maori mythology, aitu refers to sickness, calamity, or demons, while the related word aituā means misfortune or accident. In the Cook Islands, Aitu is also the name of ancient tribes who came from the east

name: Aitvaras
description: The Aitvaras is a nature spirit in Lithuanian mythology, also known as Atvaras, Damavykus, Pukis, Sparyzius, Koklikas, Gausinelis, Zaltviksas, and Spirukas. It is identical to the Latvian Pukis. This creature is a household spirit that hatches from an egg laid by a nine-to-fifteen-year-old rooster. Once an Aitvaras lodges itself in a house, it most often refuses to leave and becomes a permanent resident. It brings both good and bad luck to the inhabitants, providing its adopted home with stolen gold and grain from neighbors, though this often gets the household into trouble when the thefts are discovered

name: Aiyy
description: Aiyy are the benevolent celestial deities of Yakut (Sakha) cosmology, radiant beings of light often pictured as majestic humanoid figures in white robes, though some appear as horses, eagles, or swans. Benevolent yet distant, they respond to prayers and sacrifice rather than intervening directly, guiding chosen heroes to preserve cosmic balance against the chaotic Abaasy.

name: Ajalamo
description: Ajalamo is the Yoruba orisha associated with the creation of the earth and the molding of physical land. In some Yoruba traditions, Ajalamo is the potter deity who shaped the physical earth from clay before humans were created. Ajalamo is sometimes depicted as a divine potter at the cosmic wheel, forming the hills, valleys, and continents. The name relates to the idea of the one who spreads or flattens the earth. While less widely known than Obatala or Oduduwa, Ajalamo holds an important place in specific Yoruba creation narratives as the craftsman of the terrestrial realm. Ajalamo's work made the earth habitable for the humans that Obatala would later mold

name: Ajatar
description: Ajatar (also Ajattara, Aijotar) is an evil female forest spirit in Finnish folklore, described with hair reaching her heels and breasts to her knees (like Swedish Skogsrå). Connected to Hiisi and Lempo, she spreads disease and pestilence. Closely associated with serpents — in runic songs, the snake originates as 'a twig in Aattara's fence'.

name: Aje
description: Aje is the Yoruba orisha of wealth, prosperity, and economic success. Also known as Ajé Shaluga or Aje Olokun (associated with the deity of the ocean, Olokun), Aje represents the spiritual force behind financial abundance and commercial success. Aje is particularly associated with the marketplace, trade, and business acumen. Those who honor Aje through proper rituals and ethical business practices are blessed with prosperity. Aje is not merely material wealth but the spiritual principle of abundance itself — the concept that wealth flows through proper spiritual alignment. Markets in Yorubaland often have shrines to Aje where traders make offerings for successful commerce

name: Ajisali
description: Ajisali is a type of ogre or oni from Japanese folklore, belonging to the category of large, fearsome humanoid monsters that feature prominently in Japanese mythology and folk tales. Oni like the Ajisali are typically depicted as brutish, horned giants with wild hair and fierce expressions, known for their great strength and terrifying demeanor. They are said to inhabit remote mountainous regions or isolated areas where they may prey upon travelers and villagers who venture too far from civilization. In Japanese tradition, oni are complex figures that can be both malevolent and, in some cases, protective when properly appeased

name: Ak-Kaan (White Khan)
description: Ak-Kaan, the White Khan, is a divine hero of Altai tradition, his body shining with divine radiance, wearing white robes and riding an argamak winged steed. He seeks truth and justice, defeats dark shamans and demons, and establishes a new faith blending shamanism with Buddhist and Tibetan influences—read as the mythological reflection of the Altai shift toward Burkhanism (Ak Jang) around 1900.

name: Ak-Kula
description: Ak-Kula is the magical white stallion of Manas, greatest hero of the Kyrgyz epic, a white horse whose coat glows like moonlight and whose eyes betray human understanding. Born from the sea, it speaks with a human voice, giving prophetic warnings and fighting beside him, untameable by the unworthy. It is as iconic as Manas, embodying the bond between heroes and steeds.

name: Akbaatatdia
description: Akbaatatdia (One Who Has Made Everything), also known as Iichíkbaalee (First Doer) and Isáahkawuattee (Old Man Coyote), is the supreme Creator in Crow religion. This singular omnipotent god created the entire universe. The Crow believe the universe consists of three worlds: the physical world (the smallest), the spirit world (the intermediate realm), and the third world where God alone dwells. Akbaatatdia is omnipresent and omnipotent. Because God created everything, all of nature is sacred, and all religions are considered valid paths to the same Creator

name: Akhal-Teke Horse Spirit
description: The Akhal-Teke horse spirit embodies Turkmenistan's national horse, a breed some 3,000 years old: metallic golden coat, serpentine neck, lean build. Traditionally spiritually bonded to its rider, it can cross 300 miles of Karakum Desert without water, guided by ancestral spirits, and is treated as a family member. Chinese records called them 'Heavenly Horses' said to 'sweat blood' from thin skin.

name: Akkarmora
description: 'Akkarmora' is not attested in Norwegian folklore. Web research and Norwegian folk-belief records show no sea-guardian of this name; the entry appears invented from 'akkar' (Norwegian for squid/octopus) plus 'mora' (mother). Genuine Nordic sea beliefs include the Kraken and the hafgufa, and the draug of the sea, but no Måsøy 'squid mother' legend is documented.

name: Akkedem
description: Akkedem is a nature spirit from the folklore of the Philippines, belonging to the rich tradition of diwata and nature spirits in Filipino mythology. These spirits are believed to inhabit natural features such as trees, rivers, mountains, and forests, acting as guardians of the natural world. In Filipino indigenous belief systems, nature spirits like Akkedem are respected and appeased through offerings and rituals to ensure harmony between humans and the environment. They are part of a complex spiritual ecosystem where every natural element has its own guardian spirit that must be treated with proper respect

name: Aku-Aku
description: The ancestral spirits of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) who inhabit the island's caves, cliffs, and sacred sites. Aku-Aku are the spirits of the dead who remain connected to the land of the living. They could be both protectors and tricksters, guiding the living toward prosperity or leading them astray. Aku-Aku are deeply connected to the moai statues - each moai was believed to embody an ancestor's spirit, channeling their mana to protect the community. Oral traditions tell of spirit encounters in caves, where Aku-Aku would offer knowledge in exchange for offerings. The most powerful Aku-Aku was Ure, who taught the islanders the art of moai carving. Belief in Aku-Aku persists today

name: Al
description: Al (also called Alk in Armenian) is a dwarfish, half-human half-animal evil spirit that preys specifically on pregnant women and newborn infants in Armenian folklore. Described with iron teeth, brass or copper fingernails, fiery eyes, a clay nose, disheveled hair, tusks of a wild boar, and sagging breasts resembling a crone's form, the Al wears a pointed hat covered with small bells and can become invisible. It steals the lungs, liver, and heart of women in childbirth, destroys embryos causing miscarriages, and steals babies up to forty days after delivery, replacing them with imps. After stealing a woman's organs, the Al attempts to cross the first source of water, after which the woman cannot be saved. According to Near Eastern tradition, God created an Al for Adam's first consort Lilith, but since the Al was made of fire and Adam of earth, they were incompatible, birthing the eternal enmity between the Al and Eve's daughters

name: Al (Childbirth Demoness)
description: The Al is a demonic being in Persian folklore that personifies puerperal fever, targeting women during and after childbirth. The name derives from Iranian 'al' meaning red. Described as a red-haired, stunted female creature with a clay nose, red face, and a straw basket hanging from her shoulder containing the liver or lung of a young mother. She attacks mothers within the first six days after birth, causing sickness (al-zadagi) and death. Belief in the Al is widespread across Iran, the Caucasus, and Central Asia. According to tradition, God created an Al for Adam's first consort, but the earth-born Adam could not adapt to the Al's fiery nature, establishing eternal enmity between the Al and Eve's daughters

name: Al Basty
description: Al Basty, also known as Albasty or Al Karisi, is an ancient female spirit found in the folklore of Turkic peoples across the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Middle East, with origins dating back to Sumerian mythology. The name derives from Turkic words where al means red and basti means pressing. She is the personification of guilt who visits those with guilty souls or who come from families that have committed unpunished bloody crimes. In Turkic folklore she is known as Al Karisi and is believed to haunt women in their postpartum period, causing psychological problems. Traditional practices are applied for forty days after childbirth to protect new mothers

name: Al Ghoula
description: Al Ghoula is the female form of a ghoul from Arabic and Islamic folklore, a type of jinn-like demon that dwells in cemeteries, deserted places, and wilderness areas. The ghoul concept originated in pre-Islamic Arabian religion and the female ghoul is sometimes called umm ghulah or mother ghoul. In Arabian folklore, Al Ghoula appears to men as a long-lost female relative or an unassuming old woman, using glamour to lure hapless victims into her home where she can eat them. The male characters female relatives can often see through the illusion and warn them of the danger. The word ghoul entered English literature through William Beckfords novel Vathek in 1786

name: Al-Khidr
description: Al-Khidr, meaning 'The Green One,' is an immortal prophet and mystic figure deeply revered in Jordanian and Levantine folklore. He is described in the Quran (Surah Al-Kahf) as a righteous servant of God possessing divine wisdom and secret knowledge. In Jordanian tradition, Al-Khidr is believed to be a wandering immortal who appears to those in distress, particularly travelers, sailors, and seekers of spiritual wisdom. He symbolizes renewal, greenery, and life, and is associated with springs, rivers, and fertile lands. His shrines are found throughout Jordan and the Levant, making him a bridge between Islamic mysticism and local folklore traditions

description: Al-Khidr, meaning 'The Green One,' is an immortal prophet and mystic figure deeply revered in Jordanian and Levantine folklore. name: Al-Khidr
description: Al-Khidr ('the Green One') is a mysterious, immortal guide of Islamic tradition, celebrated in the Quran (Surah al-Kahf 18:60-82) for the journey he shares with Moses. Veiled in green, he appears at springs, seashores, deserts and crossroads to teach hidden wisdom through acts that seem unjust but serve divine mercy. In Jordan and the Levant, shrines and green-marked sites mark his presence.

name: Al-Mahrouq
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Arabic name means 'the Burned One', but no Tunisian source records a jinn by this name and the cited references do not mention it. Jinn are genuine figures of Tunisian and Islamic belief, beings created from smokeless fire, but they are unnamed or bear attested names such as Aisha Kandisha of Maghrebi tradition.

name: Al-Mi'raj
description: Al-Mi'raj is a bizarre and fearsome creature from Arabian folklore — a giant yellow rabbit with a foot-long black spiraled unicorn horn growing from its forehead. Despite its rabbit-like form, Al-Mi'raj is a ferocious carnivore that uses its horn to impale much larger victims before devouring them. According to al-Qazwini's Wonders of Creation, Al-Mi'raj lived on a mythical island in the Indian Ocean called Jazira al-Tennyn (Dragon Island). One legend claims that after Alexander the Great defeated a fearsome dragon that terrorized the island by feeding it bulls filled with poison, the grateful islanders presented the giant horned rabbit to him as a gift. The only way to ward off Al-Mi'raj is through a trusted witch's spell. This creature represents the Arabian tradition of combining familiar animals with supernatural traits to create unsettling hybrids

name: Al-Ruhban
description: Al-Ruhban is a unique creature from eastern Algerian folklore — the product of a marriage between a human and a jinn. According to Algerian oral tradition, when a jinn and a human produce offspring, that child is an Al-Ruhban. Raised initially in the jinn world among his or her jinn parent, Al-Ruhban inherits human qualities from the human parent that allow it to take human form and live among people undetected. Unlike pure jinn, who must take animal shapes (cats, dogs) to appear in the human world, Al-Ruhban can pass as completely human. It prefers cooked human food (rejecting the bones, leftovers, and waste that jinn favor) and loves human gatherings. You might sit next to one on a bus or share a road with one without knowing. Al-Ruhban is distinguished by average height, long hands, very white (Caucasian-like) skin, blue eyes, and yellow eyelashes. It always hides its hands in its pockets to conceal identifying marks. If its true identity is discovered, it flees immediately — because sorcerers seek to capture it and force it to reveal hidden treasure locations guarded by jinn. Al-Ruhban is highly respected in Algerian folklore as one of the best-natured supernatural beings

name: Ala
description: Ala is the supreme earth goddess of the Igbo people, the highest alusi in the Igbo pantheon. Her name literally means "earth" or "land." Ala is the goddess of fertility, morality, death, and creativity. She holds the deceased ancestors in her womb, rules over the underworld, and enforces Igbo law and customs (omenala). Crimes and taboos are called "nso Ala" — desecration of the earth. Her sacred messenger is the python (eke), which is so revered that killing one requires full human burial rites. Every Igbo village maintains an Ala shrine (ihu Ala) where community decisions are made. Ala is responsible for the fertility of the land and women, and the annual yam festival honors her. Her consort is Amadioha, the god of thunder

name: Aldar Qose
description: Aldar Qose is the beloved trickster of Kazakh folklore, a poor wanderer in threadbare clothing whose unassuming look hides a sharp mind. Never resorting to violence, he relies on elaborate verbal tricks to outsmart the wealthy and powerful, exposing greed and hypocrisy. His tales are social satire championing wit over wealth and power across the Kazakh steppe.

name: Alfvor
description: Alfvor (Unknown). is a elf. Álvor (elves) are nature spirits in Swedish folklore, beautiful but dangerous beings who dwell in forests and meadows. They are known for their enchanting music and dance, which can lure humans.. Source: Swedish folklore; Nordic ballad tradition

name: Alhkw Ntam Creator Nuxalk
description: Alhkw'ntam is the creator of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola), who made the world and set the sun and moon in their boxes in the sky house Nusmata. With the Four Carpenters, his helpers Masmasalanicw, he shaped the land, gave the people their arts, and established the order of the seasons and ceremonial life.

name: Alhkw Ntam Nuxalk
description: Alhkw'ntam is the supreme creator of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition, the 'heavenly father' who keeps the sun in a box in Nusmata, the land above. In the Smayusta of the Four Carpenters he is served by four supernatural carpenters who carve the first ancestors, and his light is stolen by the charcoal-made Raven Qwaxw, who brings day to the world.

name: Alhkw'ntam (Creator)
description: Alhkw'ntam is the Creator of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) cosmology, the supreme being who holds the sun in a box in his long-house in Nusmata, the land above the world. With the Four Carpenters (Masmasalanicw) he shaped the earth and its first ancestors, while Raven (Qwaxw) released the light. The account is preserved on the official Nuxalk smayusta site and in Boas' Bella Coola texts.

name: Ali
description: Ali is a demonic figure from Persian and Central Asian folklore, belonging to the same class of spirits as the Al and Albasty traditions found across the Caucasus and Turkic regions. These spirits are specifically associated with harming pregnant women, causing miscarriages, and interfering with childbirth. The concept of Ali is deeply rooted in pre-Islamic Persian beliefs and has parallels throughout the Middle East and Central Asia. In Persian tradition, Ali is described as a demon that preys on women during the vulnerable period of pregnancy and childbirth, reflecting ancient explanations for maternal and infant mortality

name: Alicanto
description: Alicanto is a legendary bird of Chilean mining folklore, especially the Norte Chico region. It is said to feed on gold and silver, and its metallic plumage glows with an eerie light that attracts miners hoping to follow it to hidden ore deposits. Miners who look away or grow greedy are said to lose the bird and their way in the mountains.

name: Almas
description: Almas is the wildman or ape-man of Mongolian legend, reported chiefly from the western aimags and the Altai. It is described as a large man-like biped of five to six and a half feet, covered in thick dark brown, reddish, yellowish, or black hair except on hands and face, often with a heavy beard. Shy and reclusive, it is treated both as legend and as a possibly real primate.

name: Aloja
description: Aloja is a type of siren or water spirit from Slavic folklore, particularly found in Polish, Czech, and Slovak traditions. Like the Greek sirens, Alojas are beautiful female water spirits who use their enchanting voices to lure men to their doom. They are associated with rivers, lakes, and other bodies of water where they sing to passing travelers, captivating them with their ethereal voices. The men who fall under their spell are drawn into the water where they drown. These spirits are part of the broader Slavic tradition of rusalki and water nymphs, embodying the dangerous allure of untamed waters

name: Alp
description: The Alp is the quintessential nightmare demon of German folklore, a shapeshifting malevolent spirit that sits upon the chest of sleeping people, causing the crushing sensation, paralysis, and horrifying visions now understood as sleep paralysis. The word itself is the German form of 'elf' — both derive from Common Germanic — and the Alp represents the earlier, darker aspect of elf folklore before Victorian literature romanticized elves into beneficent beings. Unlike the general 'elf' of modern fantasy, the Alp is a distinctly malefic creature that torments sleepers, rides horses to exhaustion, and tangles hair into 'elflocks.' It wears a magical Tarnkappe (cloak of invisibility), which grants it powers and must be retrieved if lost. Alp attacks were blamed for symptoms now recognized as sleep apnea, night terrors, and hypnagogic hallucinations. A child born with a caul (amniotic membrane on the head) or with a full head of hair was traditionally believed to be destined to become an Alp after death

name: Alpamysh (Uzbek)
description: Alpamysh (Alpomish) is the national heroic epic of Uzbekistan and its hero, a mighty warrior of the Kongrat tribe who rides the magical horse Baychibar. He defends his people against usurpers, fights for justice, and restores order to a divided tribe. The Uzbek version recorded from bard Fazil Yuldash-oghli exceeds 14,000 verses, performed by bakhshi singers.

name: Alpamysh Batyr
description: Alpamysh Batyr is the central hero of the Kazakh version of the Alpamysh epic, a mighty batyr in traditional warrior attire who rides his magical horse Baychibar. Defender of his people, loyal husband, and wise leader, he represents the ideals of Turkic warrior culture. Recorded versions reach some 14,000 verses, performed by bakhshi singers to dombra accompaniment.

name: Alpomish
description: Alpomish is a legendary hero from Turkic folklore, particularly prominent in Uzbek, Kazakh, and other Central Asian epic traditions. He is the central figure of the Alpomish epic, one of the most important examples of Turkic oral literature, dating back to ancient times and passed down through generations of storytellers. The epic tells the story of Alpomish, a heroic warrior who overcomes numerous challenges, battles monsters and enemies, rescues his beloved, and proves his worth through courage, strength, and cunning. The epic belongs to the broader tradition of Central Asian heroic poetry similar to the Kyrgyz Manas or the Oghuz Book of Dede Korkut

name: Alux
description: Aluxes are small, elf-like trickster spirits of the Yucatec Maya. They haunt ruins, cenotes, forests, and cornfields, hiding tools, leading travelers astray, and stealing food. Given corn, honey, or balché, they become protective guardians; farmers build small stone 'kahtal alux' houses at field corners to guard crops. An alux lives seven years unless regularly 'fed.'

name: Am Fear Liath Mòr
description: Am Fear Liath Mor, meaning the Big Grey Man in Scottish Gaelic, is a legendary cryptid said to inhabit the summit and slopes of Ben Macdui, the second-highest mountain in the British Isles, located in the Cairngorms range of Scotland. This mysterious entity has been reported by climbers and hikers since the late 19th century, with the most famous account coming from renowned physician and mountaineer Professor Norman Collie in 1891. The creature is associated with feelings of extreme fear and dread, footsteps following behind climbers in the mist, and occasional sightings of a tall grey figure looming in the fog. It is considered one of Scotlands most famous unsolved mysteries

name: Amadioha
description: Amadioha (Unknown). is a deity. Amadioha is the god of thunder and lightning in the Igbo pantheon of Nigeria. He is considered one of the most powerful deities, serving as the arbiter of justice who punishes wrongdoers with thunderb. Source: Igbo mythology; Nigerian oral tradition

name: Amaguq
description: Amaguq is the Iñupiaq word for wolf and the name of a wolf-spirit in Inuit tradition, a trickster able to shape-shift between wolf and human form. Reference works on mythological animals record him among Arctic trickster figures, related to the great wolf Amarok. Sources: Yowann Byghan's 'Sacred and Mythological Animals' (2020) and Mary Ellen Snodgrass's 'Encyclopedia of Fable' (1998).

name: Amalvipik
description: Amalvipik is a monstrous creature from Armenian folklore, a type of demonic entity that dwells in remote mountainous regions and abandoned places. Armenian mythology is rich with various supernatural beings that reflect the countrys ancient history and its position at the crossroads of Eastern and Western traditions. Amalvipik represents a class of monsters that threaten travelers and those who venture into wild, uninhabited areas. These beings serve as cautionary figures in Armenian folk tales, warning against straying from the community and the safety of civilized life into the dangerous wilderness where supernatural threats await the unwary

name: Aman Doger
description: Aman Doger is a sea monster from Javanese and Indonesian mythology, specifically from the folklore of Java, Indonesia. The name combines aman meaning safe or peaceful and doger referring to a type of mythical creature. This sea monster is said to inhabit the waters around the Indonesian archipelago, particularly the Java Sea. In Indonesian maritime folklore, sea monsters like Aman Doger represent the dangers of the ocean and serve as explanations for shipwrecks, disappearances at sea, and the mysterious forces that sailors must contend with. The creature reflects the deep connection between Indonesian cultures and the surrounding seas that have been central to trade and communication for millennia

name: Amarok
description: Amarok (Amaroq) is the gigantic solitary wolf of Greenlandic Inuit legend, which hunts alone unlike the pack and devours anyone foolish enough to hunt alone at night. According to H.J. Rink, Greenlanders used the word only for this legendary wolf. It appears both as a dangerous predator and as a tester of strength that picks off the sick caribou, in some tales a benevolent guardian.

name: Amaru
description: Amaru (or katari in Aymara) is the cosmic serpent/dragon of Andean mythology (Inca, pre-Inca). A double-headed serpent dwelling in lakes and rivers, connecting the earthly world (kay pacha) with the underworld (uku pacha) and upper world (hanan pacha). Represents infinity, wisdom, water, lightning, and the Milky Way.

name: Amaterasu
description: Amaterasu is the Japanese sun goddess, one of the most important deities in the Shinto religion of Japan. However, in the context of this bestiary Amaterasu is categorized as a monster, likely referring to the wilder aspects of her nature or a lesser-known monstrous manifestation. Amaterasu Omikami, meaning the Great Divinity Illuminating Heaven, is the goddess of the sun and the universe. According to Japanese mythology, she was born from the left eye of the primordial god Izanagi when he purified himself after visiting the underworld. She is the legendary ancestor of the Japanese imperial family, who claim descent from her grandson Ninigi-no-Mikoto

name: Amenokal (Tuareg Ancestral Spirit of Leadership)
description: Not an ancestral spirit but a real political office: the amenokal (amenukal) is the supreme traditional chief of a Tuareg confederation, head of an 'ettebel' (drum) chiefship among groups such as the Kel Ahaggar, Kel Adagh and Kel Air. Succession passes among the kin of a deceased holder, and authority rests on prestige and consensus rather than force.

name: Amikiri
description: Amikiri is a yokai or supernatural creature from Japanese folklore, specifically a type of tsukumogami that appears as a bizarre hybrid creature. Its name literally means net cutter, and it is said to use its specialized claws or pincers to cut fishing nets and mosquito nets. According to Japanese folklore, Amikiri is found in coastal areas and near rivers where fishermen set their nets. It is considered a nuisance spirit that damages fishing equipment, causing frustration for fishermen. The creature appears in the Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro, a collection of yokai illustrations by the famous 18th-century artist Sekien Toriyama

name: Amirani
description: Amirani is a culture hero and demigod from Georgian mythology, comparable to the Greek Prometheus or the Armenian Mher. He is the son of a hunter and a goddess, blessed with superhuman strength from birth. The Amirani epic is one of the most important cycles in Georgian mythology, telling the story of a hero who challenged the gods and suffered eternal punishment. According to the myth, Amirani was chained to a rock in the Caucasus Mountains as punishment for stealing divine fire and revealing its secrets to humanity. An eagle or raven eternally pecks at his liver, but the chain is said to weaken each year when the smith who forged it visits him

name: Amma
description: Amma is the supreme creator god of the Dogon people of Mali, who created the universe from a cosmic egg called aduno tal which contained all future matter and motion. Alone at the beginning of time, Amma created the world but the first being, Ogo (Yurugu the Pale Fox), was born prematurely and without a twin, embodying incompleteness and disorder. To restore balance, Amma created the Nommo, twin amphibious fish-beings who represent water, speech, and cosmic order. Amma is a sky god who governs the cosmos from afar, accessible through ritual and divination

name: Ammit (Devourer)
description: Ammit, also known as the Devourer or Eater of the Dead, is a female demon from ancient Egyptian mythology who played a crucial role in the afterlife judgment of souls. She sits beneath the Scales of Justice in the Hall of Maat during the Weighing of the Heart ceremony, where the heart of the deceased is weighed against the feather of Maat representing truth and justice. If the heart is found to be heavier than the feather indicating a life of sin Ammit devours the heart, condemning the soul to eternal oblivion rather than the paradise of the Field of Reeds. She represents the ultimate consequence of living an unjust life

name: Amur Tiger Spirit
description: The Amur tiger spirit, called Amba, is the most sacred animal in Nanai tradition, appearing as a giant Amur (Siberian) tiger with luminous eyes and glowing stripes that can stand on its hind legs and speak, sometimes as a tiger-human hybrid. Noble and powerful, it protects the forest and enforces natural law, rewarding respect for nature and punishing poachers and desecrators.

name: Anansi
description: Anansi, called Kwaku Ananse, is the spider trickster of the Akan and Ashanti peoples of Ghana, a small creature who overcomes mighty foes by wit. In the best-known tale he wins the sky god Nyame's stories by capturing the python Onini, the hornets Mmoboro, the leopard Osebo, and the dwarf Mmoatia, after which all tales are called anansesem.

name: Anansi
description: Anansi (Kwaku Anansi) is the Jamaican trickster spider, brought from Akan/Ashanti Ghana via the slave trade. Acquired all stories from sky god Nyame by capturing python, hornets, leopard, and fairy Mmoatia. Shape-shifts between spider and human; wife Aso, sons Ntikuma et al. Symbol of slave resistance and cultural survival. Tales end with proverbs ('If yuh cyaan ketch Kwaku, yuh ketch him shut').

name: Anansi
description: In the Ivory Coast, the spider trickster of the Akan appears as Kacou Ananzè among the Baoule and other Akan peoples, who carry the same story cycle across the border from Ghana. Kacou, like Kwaku, is the day-name of a boy born on Wednesday, and his tales of outwitting larger beasts, gods, and neighbours belong to the shared anansesem tradition.

name: Anansi
description: Anansi (Ananse), the spider trickster of Akan folklore, is celebrated across the forest belt of Ghana and the eastern Ivory Coast, where his tales traveled with trade and migration. In Ivorian versions he outwits larger beasts through cunning. His story tradition crossed the Atlantic with the slave trade and survives as Aunt Nancy in the Caribbean and southern United States.

name: Anarteq
description: Anarteq is a figure of Greenlandic Inuit legend, a hunter taken into the sea by a sea spirit who adopted him and taught him to live beneath the waves, granting him power over the sea animals. On returning to his village he shares knowledge of hunting and of the sea. The tale is recorded in Knud Rasmussen's Eskimo Folk-Tales.

name: Anaye (monsters)
description: The Anaye are the monstrous beings that roamed the Fourth World of Navajo tradition, terrorizing the people after the emergence from the lower worlds. These monsters were born from the unnatural acts during the separation of men and women. The greatest of the Anaye was Yé'iitsoh the Big Giant, who wore armor of flint knives. Others included Déélgééd the Horned Monster, giant birds, cliff-throwing monsters, and beings who caused hunger, poverty, cold, and old age. The Hero Twins Monster Slayer an

name: Ancestral Spirits Iceland
description: Ancestral Spirits Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. Ancestral spirits from Icelandic folklore watch over their descendants through generations.. Source: Icelandic folklore — ancestral spirits documented in Icelandic folk belief.

name: Andaokut Nuu Chah Nulth
description: Andaokut is the hero of a Nuu-chah-nulth myth cycle who frees the children stolen by Malahas, the Woman of the Woods. He is born from the mucus or tears of the grieving mother, grows swiftly, finds the children in the forest, kills Malahas, and restores them to their families, ending the terror the ogre-woman had brought to the villages.

name: Angano
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. In Malagasy, 'angano' means 'tale' or 'story' and is the word for the folk narratives themselves, not a creature; no source records a man-eating ogre named Angano. Giants and ogres do appear in Malagasy oral tales, but no attested name corresponds to this entry.

name: Angara (River Spirit)
description: Angara is the personified river spirit of Buryat folklore, a beautiful maiden whose flowing hair becomes the river's current and whose robes are woven of blue-green water, moving swiftly forward without looking back. Determined and rebellious, she defies her father, the lake spirit Baikal, for love; her escape represents the unstoppable force of the river flowing from Baikal to the Yenisei.

name: Angatra
description: Angatra are malevolent spirits of the dead in Malagasy belief: restless shades of people whose bodies were never properly buried or whose memory the living failed to preserve. They haunt tombs and places of death, feared as dangerous unlike the benevolent razana (ancestors). In some accounts neglected angatra become kinoly, murderous wraiths that roam at night.

name: Angel Denmark
description: Angel Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. The Angel is a character from Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale who carries a dead child through heaven's gardens.. Source: Danish folklore — angel/spirit figure documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Angelo Custode
description: The Angelo Custode (guardian angel) is the personal angel believed to protect and guide each individual, a tenet of Catholic teaching and popular piety. Rooted in scripture (Matthew 18:10, Acts 12:15) and elaborated by Aquinas, it holds that every person receives an angel at birth. Devotion includes the 'Angel of God' prayer and the 2 October feast of the Guardian Angels.

name: Anghir
description: Anghir is a giant water bird of Buryat creation mythology, an immense diving bird able to reach the depths of the primordial ocean. As the obedient servant of the creator god, it ventures bravely into the unknown and brings up the first earth, the act through which the world and humanity come into being. Anghir is the Buryat Earth-Diver figure found across Siberian and Central Asian traditions.

name: Aningaut
description: Anningan is the Moon god of the Greenland Inuit, brother of Malina, the Sun goddess. He chases his sister across the sky and forgets to eat during the pursuit, which is why he grows thin in phases and disappears for three days at the new moon; his endless chase explains the alternation of day and night and the changing moon.

name: Anjana
description: The Anjana is a protective nature spirit from the folklore of Cantabria and surrounding regions of northern Spain, deeply woven into the rural traditions of the Iberian Peninsula. These benevolent supernatural beings are considered guardians of the natural world, particularly forests, meadows, and mountain passes. They belong to a class of mythological creatures that served as intermediaries between the human and natural realms in pre-Christian Celtic-Iberian belief systems. Unlike the more dangerous creatures of Spanish folklore, Anjanas are fundamentally kind and helpful toward humans, though they can be mischievous when disrespected. Their legends share similarities with other European nature spirits such as nymphs, fairies, and dryads, reflecting the universal human impulse to personify the forces of nature. The Anjana tradition remains alive in rural Cantabria, where locals still tell stories of encounters with these gentle guardians of the wilderness

name: Ankou
description: The Ankou is the death-cart driver of Breton tradition, a gaunt, skeletal figure who collects the souls of the dying in a creaking wagon (karrig an Ankou); the sound of its wheels is an omen of death. By custom, the last person to die in a parish becomes the Ankou for the following year. Parallels appear in Cornish (Ankow) and Welsh (Angau) tradition.

name: Ankou
description: The Ankou is the death-messenger of Breton folklore, a skeletal or shrouded figure who rides or drives a cart, gathering the souls of the dying; the last person to die in a parish becomes the Ankou for the following year, and the creaking of his wheels is a mortal omen.

name: Anpo
description: Anpo (Anpao) is the spirit of dawn in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan to bring light to Maka when she complained of cold and darkness. Anpo's red light illuminated the world, but it was not enough for Maka, leading to the creation of Wi the Sun. Later, when Maka complained of being too hot, Skan decreed that Han (darkness) and Anpo should follow each other around the world, creating the cycle of day and night. Anpo represents the first light of creation, the transition from darkness to illumination

name: Anqa (Mythical Bird of Arabia)
description: The Anqa is a golden, fabulous female bird in pre-Islamic Arab mythology, described as immensely beautiful and colorful with a long neck, a human-like face, four pairs of wings, and a whiteness in its neck. Created by God with all perfections, she lives alone on Mount Qaf, flies far away, and only appears once in ages. According to Zakariya al-Qazwini's 'Wonders of Creation', the Anqa lives for 1,700 years, mates at 500 years of age, and its chick remains in the egg for 125 years. Her diet consists exclusively of elephants and large fish. She became a scourge upon humanity (the word 'anqa also means calamity) and was eventually exterminated by a prophet. Often identified with the Persian Simurgh and the phoenix; in Turkish she is called Zumrudu Anka (the Emerald Anqa)

name: Ant Ancestor-Spirit (Nepali)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Nepali tradition records an 'ant ancestor-spirit', and the claimed desert-borderlands framing does not match Nepal's geography. Nepali folk religion venerates ancestors and local deities, and genuine Himalayan figures include the yeti and the masked demon-dancer Lakhe, but the ant plays no documented spiritual role.

name: Ant Spirit ( Maori)
description: No ant spirit or ant atua is attested in Maori tradition; the entry's narrative of a forest-guardian ant is invented. Maori supernatural beings include the patupaiarehe, pale-skinned fairy folk of forest and mountain, the maero, and the taniwha, water guardians — none of which is an ant.

name: Antaeus (Anti)
description: Antaeus (known to the Berbers as Anti) is a giant figure from ancient Berber and Greek mythology, associated with Libya. According to the myths, Antaeus was the son of Poseidon (god of the sea) and Gaia (goddess of the earth), and he lived in the interior deserts of Libya. He would challenge all passers-by to wrestling matches and remained invincible as long as he remained in contact with his mother, the earth, from whom he drew his strength. He always won his matches and killed his opponents, using their skulls to build a temple to his father Poseidon. The Greek hero Heracles (Hercules) encountered Antaeus as part of his 11th labor. Realizing he could not defeat Antaeus through conventional wrestling, Heracles held him aloft—cutting him off from the earth—and crushed him to death. This iconic battle came to symbolize the Greek colonization of Libya. The Antaeus myth reflects the historical conflicts between the Berbers and Greek colonists in Cyrenaica. The giant was also associated with the city of Tangier (through his wife Tinjis), showing how the myth spread across North Africa. Antaeus was considered a protector of Libyan land by the Berbers

name: Antelope Spirit
description: The Antelope Spirit is a messenger and omen spirit in Comanche mythology. In the story of Hotuiyi, a Comanche hunting party pursuing antelope encountered a strange antelope with glowing eyes—a spirit messenger. The antelope led the hunters to a hidden spring and traced a path around a canyon where enemies lay in ambush, saving them from both thirst and attack. Thereafter, the Comanche considered antelope sightings as omens: if the antelope runs east, good fortune follows; if west, danger approaches

name: Anubis
description: Anubis, the jackal-headed god of the necropolis, is the guardian of mummification and the guide of souls into the afterlife. He presides over the Weighing of the Heart, balancing each soul against the feather of Ma'at. Son of Osiris, he embalmed the first corpse and has since opened the way for the dead, his black jackal form pacing the desert tombs.

name: Anulap
description: Anulap is the god of knowledge and magic in the mythology of Chuuk (Truk) in the Federated States of Micronesia, husband of the creator goddess Ligobubfanu and grandfather of the trickster Olifat. He taught humanity navigation, medicine, and sacred arts, and his wisdom was essential to voyagers reading stars, currents, and winds between the islands.

name: Anyanwu
description: Anyanwu is the sun deity in Igbo cosmology, representing the supreme solar force. As the embodiment of the sun, Anyanwu is associated with light, life, and the divine eye that watches over humanity

name: Anzar
description: Anzar is the ancient Amazigh (Berber) god of rain, particularly revered in the Kabyle and Aurès regions of Algeria. According to the myth, Anzar is a powerful and capricious deity who controls the life-giving rains. One day, he fell in love with a beautiful mortal woman. When she refused his advances, Anzar withdrew all rain from the land, causing a devastating drought. Crops withered, animals died, and the people suffered until the woman finally relented and agreed to marry him. Their union brought the rains back, making the land fertile once more. This myth is still enacted through the Taghonja/Tislit n'Anzar ritual during drought periods — women create a doll-bride from a ladle and parade it through villages singing for rain. Anzar's story explains both the origin of rain and the capricious nature of weather. He represents the untamed power of nature that must be respected and, through ritual, propitiated. The cult of Anzar survived Islamization and remains one of the most persistent pre-Islamic beliefs in North Africa

name: Anzar (Berber Rain God)
description: Anzar is the ancient Berber rain god, one of the most important deities in pre-Islamic Berber mythology of Algeria. He is a powerful figure associated with rainfall, fertility, and agricultural prosperity. The name Anzar (also spelled Anẓar) is derived from the Berber root meaning 'to see' or 'to foresee,' relating to his ability to see the needs of his people and send rain accordingly. In Kabyle and Chaoui traditions of Algeria, Anzar was venerated through specific ceremonies and rituals designed to invoke his favor during times of drought. The most famous ritual involved a procession where a young girl would be led through the village singing special rain-invoking songs, a practice that survived into the Islamic period in a modified form. Anzar is associated with the rainbow (called 'the belt of Anzar' in some Berber dialects) as a sign of his promise of rain. With the Islamization of North Africa, the figure of Anzar was integrated into Islamic cosmology, and his role was often assimilated into the figure of certain saints (marabouts) who were believed to have the power to bring rain

name: Apep
description: Apep, the great serpent of chaos, is the eternal enemy of the sun god Ra in Egyptian mythology. Each night he coils in the underworld to swallow the solar barque, and each dawn Ra's crew, aided by Seth and the magic of Isis, repels him. Storms were read as his writhing, and his name, written with the cut-hieroglyph, was ritually destroyed.

name: Apistotoke
description: Apistotoke (also known as Ihtsipatapiyohpa, 'Source of Life') is the great creator god of the Blackfoot people. A divine spirit with no human form or attributes, Apistotoke is entirely gender-neutral and never personified in traditional folklore. He created the Sky Beings (Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the stars), then Ksahkomitapi (Earth) as mother to all creation. Na'pi (Old Man) was created as the first man and demigod who shaped the world. Apistotoke takes a minimal role in folklore, with Na'pi and Kipitaakii performing the hands-on work of creation and teaching

name: Apophis
description: The giant serpent of Egyptian chaos, known as Apophis or Apep, who represents the primal forces of darkness, disorder, and non-being that constantly threaten the cosmic order established by the sun god Ra. This immense entity dwells in the Duat, the Egyptian underworld, and is the eternal enemy of Ma'at, the principle of truth, balance, and cosmic order. According to myth, Apophis existed before creation in the primeval waters of Nun and was born from Ra's umbilical cord or from the saliva of the goddess Neith. Unlike most Egyptian deities who could be appeased through worship, Apophis was purely destructive and could never be fully destroyed, only temporarily repelled. The Egyptians performed elaborate rituals called the Books of Overthrowing Apep, in which wax effigies of the serpent were spat upon, mutilated, and burned to aid Ra in his nightly battle. Every sunrise represented Ra's victory over chaos, reaffirming the triumph of order over the endless darkness

name: Apsara (Celestial Dancer)
description: The Apsara (Khmer: អប្សរា) is a celestial dancer goddess from Khmer mythology, born from the churning of the Ocean of Milk — the Hindu creation myth deeply embedded in Cambodian culture. According to legend, when the devas (gods) and asuras (demons) churned the cosmic ocean using Mount Mandara and the serpent Vasuki, the Apsaras emerged as exquisitely beautiful celestial maidens whose purpose was to entertain the gods with heavenly dance. The most important Apsara in Khmer tradition is Mera, from whom the name 'Khmer' is derived — combining 'Kambu' (the legendary hermit-founder) and 'Mera' to form Kambuja (Cambodia). The Apsara dance was considered so sacred that only the royal court could perform it. The bas-reliefs of Angkor Wat depict over 1,800 distinct Apsara carvings, each with unique hairstyles, jewelry, and gestures. The Royal Ballet of Cambodia continues this tradition, with Apsara dance remaining a symbol of Khmer cultural identity and spiritual devotion

name: Apwoyo (Hare)
description: Apwoyo is the clever hare trickster of Luo folklore, a small but extraordinarily cunning creature who constantly outsmarts larger and stronger animals through pure wit. In one famous story, Apwoyo tricked a mighty elephant and a huge python into a tug-of-war, pitting them against each other. In another tale, he escaped being eaten by the lion by claiming to be Were's messenger, sent to inspect the animals' behavior. When the hyena tried to copy Apwoyo's tricks, disaster always followed. Apwoyo stories teach Luo children that intelligence and quick thinking are more valuable than brute strength

name: Aqrabuamelu
description: Aqrabuamelu (also known as Girtablilu) is a hybrid creature from Mesopotamian mythology combining the torso, arms, and head of a human with the lower body, legs, and tail of a scorpion. These scorpion-people appear most famously in the Epic of Gilgamesh, where a pair of them, a male and a female, guard the entrance to the Mashu Mountains—the gateway through which the sun god Shamash passes each day and the threshold to the underworld realm of Kurnugi. According to the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, Tiamat created these scorpion-beings as part of her monstrous army to wage war against the younger gods. In Akkadian mythology, they were believed to have the power to see beyond the horizon and warn travelers of impending danger

name: Aral
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Aral' is a Turkic word meaning 'sea' or 'island', best known from the Aral Sea, and no tradition records a water spirit by this name. Water spirits are genuine in Turkic and Central Asian belief, such as the Turkic su iyesi or the su perisi, but they are not called 'Aral'.

name: Arash
description: Arash (Unknown). is a human. Āraš the Archer is a legendary figure from Persian mythology who shot an arrow marking the border between Iran and Turan. His heroic sacrifice made him a national symbol of selflessness.. Source: Shahnameh (Ferdowsi); Persian mythological tradition

name: Areop-Enap
description: Areop-Enap is the primordial spider creator in Nauruan creation mythology. In the beginning, Areop-Enap existed alone in darkness on an endless sea. Searching for food, he found an enormous clam that swallowed him. Inside the darkness, he discovered two snails. He slept three days transferring his power to each snail, then sent the smaller snail to open the clam, leaving a phosphorescent trail. In the light, he found a white worm called Rigi. Areop-Enap cast a strength spell on Rigi to pry open the clam. The clam died from the effort, and Areop-Enap made the lower shell into Earth and the upper into the sky. He placed the smaller snail in the west to become the Moon and the larger snail in the east to become the Sun. Rigi drowned in his own sweat and was hung in the sky as the Milky Way. Humans were created from stones to support the sky

name: Argamak
description: The argamak is the winged steed of Altai epic tradition, a magnificent white horse swift as the wind with glowing eyes and powerful wings. A loyal companion rather than mere transport, it travels between the three cosmic worlds, carrying heroes to the sky court of Bai-Ülgen and down to Erlik's underworld while advising and protecting its master.

name: Arsu and Azizos
description: Arsu and Azizos are twin guardian deities from ancient Syrian (Palmyrene) mythology, worshipped as protectors of caravans and travelers crossing the dangerous Syrian desert. Azizos personifies the morning star (Venus as the morning star) and is depicted as a camel rider or a warrior on horseback, while Arsu personifies the evening star (Venus as the evening star). Together they represent the cycle of day and night, and are associated with the twin stars that guide travelers. They were particularly revered in the caravan city of Palmyra, where their temples stood near the famous Temple of Bel. These twin gods embody the duality of protection and guidance, watching over travelers in both day and night. Their worship spread across Syria and northern Arabia, and they are sometimes identified with the Greek Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux) and the Arab deities Allat and Manat

name: Arwe
