description: Arwe (Unknown). is a serpent. Arwe (also known as Wainaba) is a serpent-king from Ethiopian mythology who ruled for four hundred years before being destroyed by the founder of the Solomonic dynasty. He is a giant serpent who deman. Source: Ethiopian mythology; Book of Aksum; Ge'ez manuscripts

name: Arọ̀ni
description: Arọ̀ni is a Yoruba forest spirit known as "one having a withered limb," credited with teaching herbal medicine while guarding the secrets of Osain, the orisha of healing and herbs. Often shown as a small bird or animal, Arọ̀ni is a powerful and mysterious presence who aids only those who show proper respect to the forest and its pharmacopoeia.

name: Asanbosam
description: Vampiric tree-dweller of the Akan peoples of southern Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Togo and 18th-century Jamaica. It has iron teeth, pink skin, long red hair and iron hooks for feet, hangs in tall forest trees and drops on passers-by to drink blood and flesh. It punishes hunters who break forest rules; the Akan read it as a warning against over-hunting and sacred groves.

name: Asasabonsam
description: The Asasabonsam is a fearsome forest vampire from Akan folklore, closely related to the Asanbosam and Sasabonsam traditions found across Ghana, Ivory Coast, and Togo. This malevolent being dwells in the deepest, most inaccessible parts of the forest, particularly in ancient trees with sprawling canopies. The Asasabonsam is considered one of the most dangerous supernatural entities in West African folklore because it actively hunts humans for their blood rather than simply protecting territory. Unlike ghosts or spirits, the Asasabonsam is a physical, corporeal being that leaves tangible evidence of its attacks. European slave traders and colonial administrators recorded accounts of the Asasabonsam during their encounters with Akan peoples, and the creature appears in Edward Long's 1774 History of Jamaica, brought to the Caribbean by enslaved Akan people. The legend reinforces traditional prohibitions against entering forbidden forest areas and teaches respect for the boundaries between human settlements and the wild

name: Asasbasu
description: Not independently attested in documented Akan folklore or academic sources: no source records a creature named 'Asasbasu'. The entry appears to conflate two documented Akan figures — the Asasabonsam, a forest ogre-vampire with iron teeth and iron hooks, and the Obayifo, a night-witch that leaves its body to drain children's blood. The name itself is not recorded.

name: Asase Yaa
description: Asase Yaa is the great earth goddess of the Akan people, second only to Nyame in the pantheon. As the wife of Nyame (or Nyankopon), she is the mother of all life and the foundation of the material world. Asase Yaa has two aspects: Asase Yaa (the elder, representing the dry/barren earth and the realm of the dead) and Asase Afua (the younger, representing the fertile earth and agricultural abundance). Thursday is her sacred day — farmers do not work the land on Thursday in her honor. She is also the mother of Anansi the trickster in some traditions. As the goddess of truth, oaths sworn upon her earth are considered unbreakable. She is worshipped in the fields rather than in temples

name: Asdiwal Tsimshian
description: Asdiwal is the hero of a celebrated Tsimshian myth studied by Claude Lévi-Strauss. Son of Ho, who made him magic snowshoes, Asdiwal chases a white bear up a ladder into the sky and finds it is the daughter of the Sun; he wins her through impossible trials and marries her, before his boastfulness brings him ruin.

name: Asema
description: The asema is a vampire-witch of Afro-Surinamese legend: an old man or woman by day who sheds the skin at night and flies as a blue ball of light to suck blood from sleeping victims. Householders ward it off with garlic, bitter herbs, or seeds scattered on the floor, which the asema must stop and count; it must reclaim its skin before sunrise or it is destroyed.

name: Asiman
description: The asiman is the living vampire-witch of Fon and Ewe tradition, documented in Dahomey (now Benin) and shared with neighboring West African peoples. An ordinary-looking woman by day, at night she leaves her body to fly as a corpse-candle or ball of light, drains the blood of sleeping victims, and takes animal form after feeding. She is destroyed only in that animal form.

name: Asiman
description: The asiman is the vampire-witch figure known to the Akan of Côte d'Ivoire and, above all, documented among the Fon of Dahomey: a woman who seems ordinary by day but at night sheds her body to fly as a corpse-candle or ball of light, drinking blood from the sleeping, then turning to animal shape. Regional Akan equivalents include the obayifo and the Ewe adze.

name: Asiman
description: The asiman is the vampire-witch of Fon (Dahomey) tradition in Benin: an ordinary woman by day who, at night, leaves her body and flies as a corpse-candle or ball of light. She drains blood from sleeping victims, especially children, then shapeshifts into an animal; only in that animal form can she be destroyed. She is kin to the Ashanti obayifo and the Ewe adze.

name: Asura
description: In Indian religions, asuras are power-seeking beings locked in eternal conflict with the more benevolent devas. Originally, in the Rig Veda, the term asura referred to a class of powerful beings that included both gods and demons, but over time it came to exclusively denote demonic forces opposing the divine order. In Hinduism, asuras dwell in the subterranean realms of Patala and wage constant war against the devas for control of the cosmos. They embody the qualities of pride, envy, wrath, and insatiable ambition, often serving as moral foils to the gods in epic narratives such as the Mahabharata and the Puranas. In Buddhism, asuras are one of the six realms of samsara, occupied by titanic beings consumed by jealousy and conflict

name: Aswang
description: Umbrella term for various vampiric, shapeshifting creatures in Philippine folklore - one of the most feared supernatural beings in Filipino culture. Combines traits of vampires, werewolves, ghouls, and witches. The term itself means 'to devour.' Different regional types include: the manananggal (half-bodied viscera-sucker that separates at the waist), the tik-tik/wak-wak (winged creature with extendable tongue), and the bal-bal (grave-robbing corpse eater). All types share preference for pregnant women, unborn fetuses, children, and the sick

name: Atabey (Taino Mother Goddess of Fresh Water)
description: Atabey (also called Atabex) is the supreme mother goddess of the Taino people, the goddess of fresh water, fertility, and the moon. She is the feminine counterpart to her son Yocahu -- and in Taino belief, she conceived Yocahu without a male partner (Maorocoti), making him a virgin-born god. Atabey is the primordial mother who represents the nurturing, life-giving forces of nature: freshwater springs, rivers, rain, the moon, childbirth, and fertility. She was one of the most widely worshipped Taino deities, consulted by women during pregnancy and childbirth. In Taino art, Atabey is often depicted as a frog-like figure (associated with the Coqui) or as a woman giving birth in a squatting position -- known as the Voyant pose -- with her hands on her hips and her legs open. These figures were carved into stone zemis and placed in caves and sacred sites. Spanish chroniclers noted that the Taino believed Atabey was the mother of the sea (Bagua) as well as fresh water, showing her dominion over all waters

name: Atai Ulan
description: Atai Ulan is the leader of the eastern, malevolent Tenger sky-gods in Buryat tradition, lifelong antagonist of Abai Geser in the Epic of Gesar. A gigantic dark figure, his body parts retain monstrous power even in death: dismembered, his scattered remains spawn the demons that plague the world. In one account, disease-spirits from his impaled toe give the mythological origin of gout.

name: Atargatis
description: Atargatis is an ancient goddess from Phoenician and Syrian mythology, primarily worshipped in the Levantine coastal region including what is now Lebanon. She is considered the first mermaid in recorded history. According to legend, Atargatis was a beautiful goddess who accidentally killed her mortal lover, the shepherd Hadad. Overcome with shame and grief, she cast herself into a lake near Hierapolis (modern Manbij), intending to transform entirely into a fish. However, the waters only transformed her lower half, leaving her upper body human, creating the first mermaid. She is associated with fertility, protection, and social order, often depicted wearing a mural crown symbolizing her role as founder of city life. Her primary sanctuary was at Hierapolis in Syria, but her worship spread throughout the Levant, including Phoenician cities in Lebanon. She is often shown holding a fish or with fish symbolism

name: Atira
description: Atira is the Pawnee goddess of the Earth and wife of Tirawa, the creator god. Her name literally means 'Mother Corn,' and she is associated with the corn that sustained the Pawnee people. Atira is a nurturing figure who provides food and life from the earth. In the Hako (Calumet) ceremony, a symbol representing Atira was created, showing corn painted to represent the Rainstorm, Thunder, Lightning, and Wind. The South Bands of the Pawnee particularly honored Atira through agricultural ceremonies, giving thanks for the harvest and praying for continued fertility of the soil

name: Atum (Primordial Creator God)
description: Atum is the primordial creator god of Egyptian mythology, the first deity of the Heliopolitan Ennead. He created himself from the primordial waters of Nun, then masturbated to create Shu (air) and Tefnut (moisture). His tears created humanity. Atum is both male and female (the Great He-She), representing the totality of creation. He is associated with the setting sun (as Atum-Ra). In later periods, he merged with Ra as the sun god. Atum is the father of the gods and the king of the gods before the reigns of Shu, Geb, and Osiris. He is the embodiment of completeness and the source of all existence

name: Aumakua
description: Hawaiian family guardian spirits - ancestors who have died and returned in spiritual form to watch over and protect their descendants. The word combines 'au' (period of time/with) and 'makua' (parent/ancestor). Unlike Western spirit animals, aumakua are NOT the entire species - only a specific individual animal or object possessed by an ancestral spirit. Each family has its own specific aumakua, passed down through generations. They are 'ano lani (heavenly nature) and 'ano honua (earthly nature) - beings of both realms

name: Aunt Ganga
description: Aunt Ganga of Cape Verde appears either as a giant bird with sharp talons or stern bird-like woman, punishing taboo-breakers and protecting the innocent.

name: Aunt Nancy
description: Aunt Nancy is the African American adaptation of Anansi the Spider, the famous trickster figure of West African Akan folklore. In the transatlantic journey, the male spider Anansi became feminized as 'Aunt Nancy' (a pun on 'Anansi'). Aunt Nancy retained the spider's core trickster qualities — cleverness, greed, and the ability to outwit larger and more powerful beings — but was reimagined within the context of African American plantation life. Like Br'er Rabbit (who shares many Anansi story plots), Aunt Nancy represents the triumph of wit over strength. Stories of Aunt Nancy were passed down through oral tradition, particularly in Gullah Geechee communities, and she remains a beloved figure in African American storytelling, embodying the cleverness that enabled survival under oppression

name: Aurora Spirits
description: In Inuit tradition, the aurora borealis is not merely a natural phenomenon but the manifestation of spirits playing in the sky. Known as aqsarniit or arsanit in Inuktitut, the dancing lights are believed to be the souls of the dead playing a celestial game of ball with a walrus skull, or the torches of spirits guiding the recently deceased to the afterlife. Different Inuit groups hold varying beliefs: some see the lights as the spirits of ancestors engaged in joyful celebration, while others regard them with fear, believing they can descend and snatch away the living. The lights are also thought to be the result of the sky-watching sedna spirits, or the reflecting light off the armor of celestial beings. In Greenlandic tradition, the aurora was believed to be the souls of stillborn children dancing through the cosmos

name: Awang Semaun (The Legendary Hero)
description: Awang Semaun is the legendary culture hero and founding father of Brunei, celebrated in the Brunei Darussalam national epic. According to the Silsilah Raja-Raja Brunei (Genealogy of Brunei Kings), Awang Semaun was a figure of superhuman strength and wisdom who helped establish the Brunei Sultanate. He was one of 14 brothers born from a magical womb, each with extraordinary abilities. Awang Semaun was renowned for his physical strength, seafaring skills, and ability to communicate with animals and spirits. He served as the chief minister to the first Sultan of Brunei and is credited with expanding Brunei's territory, defeating sea monsters that plagued the coast, and establishing the foundations of Malay civilization in Borneo. His exploits include moving mountains, damming rivers, and slaying a giant serpent that terrorized the Brunei River

name: Awi Usdi
description: Awi Usdi, or Little Deer, is the chief of the deer people in Cherokee mythology and the spirit guardian of all deer. When the animals held councils to decide how to protect themselves from overhunting by humans, Awi Usdi led the Deer council and decreed that any hunter who kills a deer without first asking pardon for the offense would be afflicted with rheumatism, a painful disease of the joints and muscles. Awi Usdi himself would run to the site of each killing and ask the deer's spirit if it heard the hunter's prayer of apology. If the spirit had not heard a prayer, Awi Usdi would follow the hunter home by the drops of blood and strike him down with disease

name: Awonawilona
description: Awonawilona is the supreme creator deity of the Zuni people of New Mexico, whose name translates to "All Container" or "He Who Contains Everything." In Zuni creation mythology, Awonawilona existed before all things as a formless, self-created being containing within itself the potential for all existence. From this primordial state, Awonawilona initiated creation by becoming the mist and clouds that filled the void, then transformed into the sun-father to bring light and warmth to the world. The deity then created the Earth Mother (Awitelin Tsita) and Sky Father (Apoyan Tachu) from the green scum that formed upon the primordial waters. From this divine pair, all life, land, and the nine layers of the universe emerged, with each layer becoming home to different creatures and spirits

name: Ay-Chürök
description: Ay-Chürök ('Moon Swan') is a swan maiden of the Kyrgyz epic, the fairy wife of Semetey in the Manas cycle. As a human she is stunningly beautiful and luminous; as a swan, pure white and graceful, able to fly between human and celestial realms. Loyal and wise, she links the human and spirit worlds, a swan-maiden motif common across Central Asian folklore.

name: Ayida Weddo (Rainbow Serpent)
description: Ayida Weddo is the lwa of rainbows, serpents, wind, and water in Haitian Vodou, and the beloved wife of Damballa, the great serpent lwa. Together they form the primordial cosmic couple -- Damballa is the sky father, Ayida Weddo is the rainbow mother. She is depicted as a iridescent serpent, a beautiful woman entwined with a serpent, or as the rainbow itself arching across the sky. Ayida Weddo represents the bridge between heaven and earth, the promise after storms, and the continuous cycle of life. Her origins are in the Fon and Yoruba traditions of Dahomey (Benin), where she is known as Aido-Hwedo, the cosmic serpent who supports the sky. In Haitian Vodou, she is gentler than the African version, a protective maternal figure who brings hope, renewal, and the beauty of divine promise. She is syncretized with Our Lady of the Rosary or the Virgin of the Immaculate Conception. Her colors are white, blue, and rainbow hues. Offerings include white eggs, coconut, sweet rice, milk, and white flowers

name: Ayida-Weddo
description: Ayida-Weddo (also known as Aido Hwedo) is the cosmic rainbow serpent of Fon/Dahomey mythology who supports the entire world. According to the Fon creation myth, Ayida-Weddo served as Mawu's mount during creation — his winding body shaped the mountains, valleys, and rivers of the earth. After creation, he coiled beneath the earth to support its immense weight, holding his own tail in his mouth (forming an ouroboros). When the serpent shifts or readjusts his position, earthquakes occur, and when he moves beneath the ocean, tidal waves are caused. Ayida-Weddo rests in the cool of the seas, protected from the sun's heat. He represents cosmic order, eternity, and the cyclical nature of time. In Haitian Vodou, Ayida-Weddo is known as Damballa, the most important lwa, worshipped as the serpent of wisdom and the connection between heaven and earth

name: Azarakhsh (Persian Lightning Horse)
description: Azarakhsh is a mythical fire-breathing horse from Persian mythology, whose name means 'lightning' or 'fire' in Middle Persian. It appears in the Persian epic tradition, particularly associated with the great hero Rostam. The Azarakhsh is a fiery, untamable steed of immense speed and power, its hooves striking sparks from the earth. Unlike the more domesticated Rakhsh (Rostam's famous horse), the Azarakhsh represents the wild, untamed power of nature. It is sometimes described as a horse of the Zoroastrian fire divinity (Atar), embodying the sacred element of fire. In some traditions, it is associated with the star Sirius (Tishtrya) and the rains

name: Aziza
description: The Aziza are benevolent forest spirits in Fon and Dahomean mythology of Benin. Described as diminutive 'little people,' these beings inhabit anthills, hollow trees, and sacred groves within the deep forests. Unlike many spirits in West African folklore that are feared, the Aziza are known for their wisdom and generosity toward humans who respect the forest. They are credited with teaching humanity essential survival skills including the use of fire, knowledge of medicinal herbs, hunting techniques, and tracking of animals. The Aziza serve as moral arbiters of the forest, providing guidance and assistance to those who show proper respect for nature while withholding help from those who violate ethical or ecological boundaries. In their original pre-contact form, the Aziza were wingless little people; later European-influenced accounts sometimes depict them with butterfly-like wings, though this is considered a syncretic addition. They represent the Fon worldview that wisdom and survival knowledge originate from respectful engagement with the natural world

name: Azuki arai
description: Azuki arai, meaning "bean washer," is a mysterious yokai from Japanese folklore that inhabits mountainous regions across the country. Known also as azuki togi ("bean grinder"), this peculiar spirit spends its time near remote forest streams obsessively washing red azuki beans while singing an eerie, dreadful song. The azuki arai is more often heard than seen, and its presence is announced by the distinctive "shoki shoki" sound of beans being rhythmically washed in a bamboo basket. The yokai's song poses a sinister question to any who hear it: "Azuki araou ka? Hito totte kuou ka?" ("Shall I wash my red beans, or shall I catch a human to eat?"). Despite this menacing invitation, the azuki arai is notoriously shy and will flee at the slightest disturbance, making actual sightings extremely rare

name: B Gg
description: B Gg (Unknown). is a spirit. Der Boogg is a snowman-like effigy figure from Swiss folklore, symbolically burned at the Sechselauten spring festival to predict the coming summer weather.. Source: Norwegian folklore — spirit documented in Norwegian oral tradition.

name: Baal
description: Baal is the chief Canaanite-Phoenician storm god, a divine warrior who defeated the chaos monster Yamm to establish cosmic order. His cult centers included Byblos, Tyre, and Sidon in modern Lebanon. In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Baal first defeats Yamm using the divine maces Yagrush and Ayamur, establishing himself as king of the gods. He is then challenged by Mot who defeats him and sends him to the underworld. His sister Anat retrieves his body and Baal returns to life, defeating Mot and restoring fertility to the land. This cycle of death and rebirth reflects the agricultural seasons of the Levant. Baal is depicted as a young, bearded warrior wielding a thunderbolt-spear and standing on a bull

name: Baba Dariah
description: Baba Dariah, Father of the Tide, is a water jinn of Emirati tradition who rules the deep waters and coral reefs of the Gulf. He commands the tides and speaks to the creatures of the sea, shielding honest boatmen while dragging the arrogant to the depths. The Gulf coast still respects his power, and his legend warns against taking the sea for granted.

name: Baba Djenka
description: Not independently attested in documented Ghanaian folklore or academic sources: no collection records a forest spirit named 'Baba Djenka'. The description's traits — a spirit that steals items, twists paths and makes travelers lose their way — resemble the documented Akan mmoatia, small forest dwarfs with backward-turned feet, but no figure bears this name.

name: Baba Roga
description: Baba Roga, meaning "Horned Grandmother," is a fearsome witch-bogeyman figure from Bulgarian and broader Balkan folklore, used for centuries by parents to frighten misbehaving children into obedience. While the figure shares etymological and thematic roots with the more famous Baba Yaga of Russian folklore, Baba Roga has distinct characteristics that reflect specifically Bulgarian and South Slavic traditions. This horned crone is said to dwell in the deep forests and mountain caves of the Balkan peninsula, emerging at night to search for children who have disobeyed their parents. Unlike some bogeyman figures that are purely malevolent, Baba Roga occupies an ambiguous space in folklore; she is primarily a disciplinary tool rather than a genuinely evil entity, and stories emphasize that good behavior provides complete protection from her attention. The figure likely descends from pre-Christian Slavic deities associated with winter, darkness, and the wild forces of nature

name: Baba Yaga
description: Baba Yaga is the iconic East Slavic witch: a gaunt crone with iron teeth who dwells in a hut on chicken legs deep in the forest. Flies in a mortar, steers with a pestle, sweeps tracks with a broom. Tests visitors with three impossible tasks; rewards cleverness with magical gifts, devours the failures. Commands forest creatures.

name: Baba Yaga
description: Baba Yaga (Polish Baba Jaga, Czech Ježibaba) is the West Slavic forest witch, closely related to the Russian figure. Dwells in a hut on chicken legs in dense Masovian oak forests. Same mortar/pestle/broom attributes, same three-task tests. May reflect Finno-Ugric influence (stilt-storehouse huts). Ježibaba differs in appearance and tale types.

name: Babi Ngepet
description: Babi Ngepet is a boar-shaped demon of Javanese and Balinese folklore, a man transformed into a wild pig through pesugihan, dark magic traded for wealth. The transformed man raids villages at night as a boar to drain or steal their money while an assistant guards a floating candle, its flame the link to his human body. The tale warns against enriching oneself through pact-making and greed.

name: Bacab
description: Four aged sky-bearing brothers in Mayan cosmology - the ultimate sky pillars. Like Atlas but Four. Each holds one corner: Hobnil (East/red), Cantzicnal (North/white), Saccimi (West/black), Hosanek (South/yellow). Placed by the creator at four points to hold up sky so it doesn't fall. Escaped when world was destroyed in the deluge. Later became connected to the four Chaacs (rain deities) and Pauahtuns (wind deities). Also linked to the four Year Bearer patron deities for divination. Can cause earthquakes if they shift position. Originally associated with four animals (iguana, opossum, turtle, snail) or insects in earlier periods

name: Baccoo
description: The Baccoo is a mischievous dwarf-like spirit from Barbadian (and Guyanese) folklore that is captured and kept by humans to bring wealth and prosperity. Usually contained in a corked rum bottle or kept in the attic, the Baccoo must be fed a steady diet of milk and bananas to remain cooperative. If starved or neglected, it becomes a violent poltergeist, throwing objects and causing mayhem throughout the home. The Baccoo reflects West African spiritual concepts (the Akan mmoatia and Yoruba Abiku) merged with European bottle-imp legends brought by Dutch and English colonizers. The creature represents the moral ambiguity of sudden wealth and the dangers of making deals with supernatural forces

name: Backoo
description: The Backoo is a unique entity from Guyanese folklore, blending African, Indigenous, and colonial influences into a singularly strange creature. This spirit is described as having a body that is half wood and half flesh, with an abnormally large head and missing kneecaps. The Backoo is bound to serve those who know the correct rituals to summon and control it, typically through a contract or pact that exchanges lifelong servitude for some form of payment, often the owner's soul. The creature subsists on a diet of milk and bananas, and will carry out any task assigned by its master, from domestic chores to supernatural errands. However, the Backoo is also notoriously unreliable and mischievous; if not constantly supervised and given clear instructions, it will deliberately misinterpret commands or perform its duties in the most destructive way possible. The legend likely originated from the various "servant spirit" traditions brought to the Caribbean by African slaves and adapted to the Guyanese context

name: Bacul
description: Not independently attested: no Romanian forest spirit named Bacul appears in folklore sources, and searches return only Hoia-Baciu, the 'Haunted Forest' near Cluj associated with paranormal claims and UFO reports.

name: Badger Deity of Apache
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No documented Apache tradition features a badger deity; the badger is neither a prominent Apache animal figure nor a clan or ceremonial spirit. Genuine Apache spirit beings include the Gan (Mountain Spirits) of the Crown Dance, Coyote, and the owl, which carries death associations.

name: Badger Deity of Creek
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is not a documented Muscogee (Creek) deity or clan animal; Muscogee clans include Bear, Deer, Wind, and Bird. Genuine Muscogee spirit figures include the Master of Breath, the Tie-Snake, and the Little People, and the Green Corn ceremony opens the ceremonial year.

name: Badger Ghost of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No documented Blackfoot badger ghost exists. Blackfoot religion centres on Napi (Old Man), the Sun, and vision-quest guardian animals such as the buffalo and eagle; the badger appears in no attested Blackfoot source.

name: Badger Ghost of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Blackfoot tradition records a badger ghost. Blackfoot spiritual life centres on Napi (Old Man) the trickster-transformer, the buffalo, and vision quests in which animals may appear as guardians, but the badger is not a documented vision figure.

name: Badger Ghost of Miwok
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Miwok tradition records a badger ghost. Miwok creation is led by Coyote and his grandson, the falcon Wek-Wek, with other animals playing supporting roles; Miwok beliefs about the dead do not single out any badger spirit.

name: Badger Ghost of Passamaquoddy
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is not native to Passamaquoddy territory, and no badger ghost appears in their tradition. Documented Passamaquoddy spirits include the culture hero Glooskap, the storm-bird Pamola, and Kiwahq, the wild twin brother of Glooskap; guardian spirits are sought in dreams but never as a badger.

name: Badger Ghost of Uzbek
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Uzbek tradition records a badger ghost. Uzbek folk belief includes jinn, devs, and paris, along with Turkic nature spirits, but the badger plays no documented spirit role; the wolf and eagle are the culturally prominent Turkic animals.

name: Badger Ghost of Zulu
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Zulu tradition records a badger ghost, although the honey badger (ratel) is respected for its ferocity in African animal lore. Genuine Zulu spiritual beings include the amadlozi (ancestral spirits), the trickster Hlakanyana, and the impundulu (lightning bird); no badger figure appears in the record.

name: Badger Giant of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No documented Blackfoot badger giant exists. Blackfoot tradition tells of powerful beings and earlier races, but the badger plays no attested role; the claim is a generic extension of giant stories with no source.

name: Badger Giant of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Blackfoot source records a badger giant. Blackfoot tradition does include stories of earlier races and giant beings, but the badger has no documented role in them; attested Blackfoot spirit focus falls on Napi, the buffalo, and vision quests.

name: Badger Giant of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Tlingit source records a badger giant; the badger is not a crest animal, and the documented giant-spirit category 'Nah' includes no badger figure. Tlingit crest animals are the Raven, Eagle, Wolf, Bear, and Killer Whale.

name: Badger Giant of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is not a Tlingit crest animal, and no Tlingit badger giant is documented. Tlingit clan crests belong to the Raven and Eagle moieties (Wolf, Bear, Killer Whale), and 'Nah' refers to giant spirits, but no source connects these to a badger.

name: Badger Giant of Ute
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No documented Ute tradition features a Badger Giant. Ute stories centre on Coyote the trickster and include earlier races of animal and giant beings, but the badger plays no attested role in them; the American badger is native to the region but absent from Ute myth.

name: Badger Guardian of Ashanti
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is not a traditional Ashanti (Akan) spirit animal. Genuine Ashanti forest beings include the sasabonsam, the mmoatia dwarfs, the abosom (lesser deities), and Anansi the spider; the leopard, python, and crocodile carry royal symbolism, but no badger guardian is documented.

name: Badger Nature-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: No Blackfoot source documents a 'badger nature-spirit.' Blackfoot tradition knows Napi (Old Man) and spirit-helpers acquired through vision quests, but the badger is not attested as a named nature-spirit. This entry is the same template fabrication as the Canada variant and adds no independent tradition; the Blackfoot homeland spans Montana and Alberta.

name: Badger Nature-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: No Blackfoot source documents a 'badger nature-spirit.' Blackfoot tradition centers on figures such as Napi (Old Man) and on personal spirit-helpers gained through vision quests, but the badger does not appear as a named nature-spirit in the record. The entry is a template fabrication ('X nature-spirit of Y'), and its 'Canada people' framing is invented.

name: Badger Nature-Spirit of Haida
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is not a Haida crest or spirit figure; Haida lineages belong to the Raven and Eagle moieties, and crests include the bear, killer whale (Sgaana), and wolf. No Haida source records a badger nature-spirit; the genuine supernatural beings of Haida tradition are the beings of these crests and their stories.

name: Badger Nature-Spirit of Passamaquoddy
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is not native to Passamaquoddy territory, and no such nature-spirit is documented. Passamaquoddy tradition instead features the culture hero Glooskap, the storm-bird Pamola, and wilderness spirits such as Kiwahq; the wild-spirit twin is the closest attested analogue.

name: Badger Spirit of Aztec
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger appears in no Aztec source and is absent from the tonalpohualli day signs; tlazolteotl is a goddess of filth and purification, not a badger spirit. Genuine Aztec animal-spirit concepts, the tonal and the nagual, attach to attested animals such as the jaguar, eagle, dog, and monkey.

name: Badger Spirit of Creek
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is not among the documented Muscogee (Creek) animal clans or spirit figures. Muscogee tradition instead honours the Master of Breath, clan animals such as Bear and Deer, and beings like the Tie-Snake and Little People; no badger spirit is attested.

name: Badger Spirit of Paiute
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No documented Paiute tradition features a badger spirit, though badgers are native to the Great Basin. Paiute stories centre on Coyote the creator-trickster and, in some groups, Wolf; the badger has no attested role in Paiute cosmology or storytelling.

name: Badger Spirit of Passamaquoddy
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is not native to Passamaquoddy territory and is not a documented spirit being. Passamaquoddy tradition centres on Glooskap, Pamola, and wilderness spirits such as Kiwahq; no badger totem or guardian spirit appears in the ethnographic record.

name: Badger Spirit of Pomo
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Pomo source records a badger spirit, despite badgers being native to Pomo territory. Pomo ceremonial life centres on the Kuksu (Guksu) dance cult and figures such as Coyote and Bear; the badger plays no documented role in Pomo ritual or cosmology.

name: Badger Trickster of Aymara
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The badger is absent from the high Andes and plays no role in Aymara tradition, whose trickster is the fox. Andean cosmology's three worlds, hanan pacha, kay pacha, and ukhu pacha, structure Aymara belief, but no badger figure appears in it.

name: Badger Trickster of Cree
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Cree tradition features a badger trickster. The Cree culture-hero and trickster is Wisakedjak (Whiskey Jack), with the hare and, further west, Coyote in some regional variants; the badger has no documented place in Cree storytelling.

name: Badger Water-Spirit of Creek
description: No Creek (Muscogee) tradition documents a badger water-spirit; the input itself concedes the badger is not water-associated in Creek belief. The genuine water-beings of Creek cosmology are the great serpents and water panthers said to inhabit rivers, springs, and swamps. The 'badger water-spirit' is a template fabrication combining an animal with an element and a nation.

name: Bahamut (Cosmic Fish)
description: Bahamut is a colossal cosmic fish in Arabic mythology that supports the entire structure of the world. According to medieval Islamic cosmology, Bahamut is so vast that all the oceans of the world placed in one of its nostrils would be like a mustard seed in the desert. Upon Bahamut's head stands a giant bull named Kuyutha (or Kiyuban) with 40,000 horns and legs, upon whose back rests a mountain of ruby, atop which stands an angel who supports the seven heavens and the earth. Below Bahamut lies a fathomless sea, beneath that a realm of air, then a realm of fire, and finally the great serpent Falak. The fish causes earthquakes when it stirs. Bahamut appears in the 496th night of the Thousand and One Nights, witnessed by Prophet Isa (Jesus)

name: Bahri Spirits (Moroccan Sea Jinn)
description: Bahri spirits (from Arabic 'bahr' meaning sea) are a class of water-dwelling jinn in Moroccan folklore that inhabit the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea along the Moroccan coast. They are considered the most dangerous of all jinn in Moroccan belief, as they are completely alien to human nature and do not share the terrestrial realm with humans. They appear as half-fish, half-human creatures with green eyes, scaled skin, and webbed hands and feet. Bahri spirits are blamed for shipwrecks, drownings, and disappearing fishermen. They enchant sailors with beautiful songs (like the Greek Sirens) or drag swimmers underwater. They are most active during storms and at sunset. Some traditions say they are led by a king named Sakhr or reside under the sea in crystal palaces. They are unique among jinn for being unable to cross fresh water

name: Bai Ze
description: Bai Ze is a legendary chimeric creature from Chinese mythology, first recorded during the Tang Dynasty, known for its extraordinary wisdom and supernatural perception. According to ancient Chinese texts, Bai Ze appeared to the Yellow Emperor, Huangdi, during his reign around 2600 BCE, revealing the secrets of all the supernatural beings in the world. This encounter resulted in the creation of an encyclopedia of spirits and demons, a text that became foundational for Chinese demonology and exorcism practices. Bai Ze is said to possess complete knowledge of every creature, spirit, and demon that exists, including their names, appearances, and methods for warding them off. The creature's name translates literally to hundred marsh or hundred languages, reflecting its comprehensive knowledge of all beings. In Chinese folk religion, Bai Ze is venerated as a protective oracle who can reveal hidden dangers and provide the knowledge needed to counter malevolent spirits. The legend of Bai Ze has influenced Chinese literature, art, and religious practice for over a thousand years, with its image appearing on protective talismans and temple murals throughout China

name: Bai-Ulgan
description: Bai-Ulgan, also known as Bai Ülgen or simply Ülgen, is a prominent deity in the traditional shamanic religion of the Mongolian and Turkic peoples of Central Asia. He is the chief of the good deities, a creator god who dwells in the upper world, associated with the sky, light, and cosmic order. In Mongolian shamanism, the universe is divided into three realms: the upper world of the deities, the middle world of humans, and the lower world of dark spirits. Bai-Ulgan presides over the upper world, sitting on a golden throne at the summit of a cosmic mountain, where he judges human actions and maintains the balance of the universe. He is particularly associated with hunting, mountains, and wildlife, serving as the protector of animals and the enforcer of ethical hunting practices. Bai-Ulgan is not merely a passive deity but an active force in human affairs, rewarding those who respect nature and punishing those who take more than they need. His worship involves offerings, prayers, and the guidance of shamans who can ascend to his realm through ritual journeys to seek his blessing for hunting expeditions or to petition for the well-being of their communities

name: Baiame
description: Baiame is the supreme creator god and sky father in the mythology of several Aboriginal Australian peoples of southeastern Australia, including the Kamilaroi, Wiradjuri, and Eora nations. In the Dreamtime, Baiame descended from the sky world to create the land, plants, animals, and humans. He gave the people their laws, customs, and ceremonies before returning to the sky, where he remains watching over the world from his home in the Milky Way. Baiame established the rules of marriage, the totem system, and the proper relationships between people and land. His wives include Birrahgnooloo (associated with fertility and floods) and Cunnembeillee. Baiame is portrayed in rock art as an enormous figure with radiating headgear suggesting divine power. His son Daramulum acts as an intermediary between Baiame and humans

name: Baikal (Lake Spirit)
description: Baikal, 'Old Man Baikal,' is the personified spirit of the world's deepest lake and a founding father in Buryat lore. Stern and possessive, he raised his daughter Angara until she fled him for the hero Yenisei; enraged, he hurled the Shaman Stone after her, yet she escaped to the sea. The lake remains a sacred, living entity honored with offerings.

name: Bajlozi
description: Baloz, recorded in the database as 'Bajlozi,' is a monstrous giant or sea-monster of Albanian heroic poetry, an antagonist fought by the Kreshnik heroes, especially Muji and Halili, in the Songs of the Frontier Warriors. Epic heroes overcome him through courage and guile. The input's 'shadow giant fond of riddles' is inaccurate; the figure belongs to the martial oral epics.

name: Bajrak (Orang Bati)
description: Bajrak, also known as Orang Bati, is a fearsome flying demon from the folklore of Seram Island in the Maluku archipelago of eastern Indonesia. The creature's name Orang Bati translates to bat man in the local Malay dialect, describing its batlike humanoid form. According to local legends, the Bajrak is a nocturnal predator that emerges from the caves and dense forests of Seram's interior mountains to hunt at night. The creature is particularly feared because of its reported taste for human flesh, especially that of children. Bajrak legends are most common in the traditional communities around Mount Binaiya, Seram's highest peak, where locals tell stories of babies and small children being snatched from their homes during the night. The creature has been reported for generations, with accounts dating back to the period of Dutch colonial presence in the region, when European observers recorded local testimonies about the flying demon. In contemporary times, the Bajrak has attracted the attention of cryptozoologists who speculate that the legend might be based on sightings of large fruit bats or unknown flying creatures inhabiting the island's remote interior

name: Bakai
description: Bakai is the wise elder and counselor of the Kyrgyz epic of Manas, the voice of reason among the heroes. In the episode of his meeting with Manas, he advises the young leader to unite the Kyrgyz clans and return to their homeland of Ala-Too, restoring the people's strength and power; his counsel shapes the destiny of the epic's hero.

name: Bakh
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No source records a Sudanese 'Bakh' forest spirit. The Nuba peoples of South Kordofan do keep traditions of ancestral and nature spirits, including kujur rainmaker-mediums, but no forest being by this name appears in the ethnographic record.

name: Bakru
description: Bakru, also called Backoo or Bacro, is a malevolent forest spirit from the folklore of Suriname and the surrounding Guiana region of South America, rooted in the Afro-Caribbean traditions brought by enslaved Africans and adapted in the context of the Surinamese rainforest. According to traditional belief, Bakru are created by evil sorcerers using dark magic derived from Winti, the Afro-Surinamese spiritual tradition. The sorcerer creates a wooden doll or statue in human form and, through a ritual involving the sacrifice of a child or the use of a deceased child's soul, animates it with a corrupted spirit. The resulting Bakru is bound to serve its creator, performing evil deeds and accumulating wealth for the sorcerer. However, the Bakru is perpetually hungry and must be fed regularly, often with blood or milk. If not properly controlled, the Bakru will turn against its creator, causing destruction and death. Belief in Bakru remains strong in Suriname and among the Surinamese diaspora, with the creature representing the dangers of black magic and the moral consequences of dealing with dark forces for personal gain

name: Baktan
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No source records a Senegambian giant named 'Baktan'. Local legends do attribute the Senegambian stone circles (Wassu, Sine Ngayène, Kerbatch) to ancient giants, but the named figure appears to be an invention; the closest genuine analogue is the anonymous giant-builders of these megalith traditions.

name: Baku
description: Baku is the dream-devouring yōkai of Japanese tradition, a chimera with a bear's body, elephant's head and tusks, rhinoceros ears, ox tail, and tiger paws. Children call 'Baku-san, come eat my dream' three times after nightmares, and baku talismans guard beds. A hungry baku may devour good dreams too, taking hopes away; the name also became the Japanese word for tapir.

name: Bakunawa (The Moon-Eating Serpent)
description: The Bakunawa is a massive sea serpent or dragon in Visayan and Bicolano mythology believed to cause eclipses by attempting to swallow the moon. Originally a beautiful sea goddess transformed into a serpent as punishment for loving a mortal, the Bakunawa rises from the ocean depths to chase the moon across the sky. According to legend, the supreme god Bathala created seven moons to illuminate the night, but the Bakunawa, amazed by their beauty, swallowed six of them. To prevent the loss of the final moon, people make loud noises with pots, pans, and drums during eclipses to frighten the serpent into releasing the moon. The Bakunawa's movements served as a geomantic calendar system for ancient Filipinos and were part of babaylan (shaman) rituals. It is usually depicted with a characteristic looped tail and a single horn on the nose

name: Bakwa
description: Bakwa is the legendary Snake King of the Kalinago people of Dominica — a great diamond-crested serpent with magical powers that slithered out of the sea and took residence in a cave in the mountains. According to the ancient Kalinago legend retold by children of Atkinson School, Bakwa used his powers to grant wishes to those who approached him with respect. Maruka, a Kalinago farmer, was the first to discover Bakwa and receive his blessings. The legend is associated with L'Escalier Tete Chien (Staircase of the Snake), a natural rock formation resembling a staircase rising from the Atlantic Ocean on Dominica's southern coast in the Sineku area of the Carib Territory. According to Kalinago tradition, this formation is the pathway made by the enormous boa constrictor when it emerged from the ocean

name: Bakwas
description: Bakwas (Bukwus), the Wild Man of the Woods, is a dangerous forest spirit in Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) tradition and counterpart of Dzonokwa, the Wild Woman of the Woods. He lurks in the deep forest and lures wanderers with ghostly food that turns eaters into spirits like himself; prepared encounters may bring spiritual power, careless ones death or madness. He features in winter ceremonial dances.

name: Bama Dat
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Burmese source records a ghost named 'Bama Dat'; Burmese terms for the dead are thaye (ghosts/corpses) and the nat cult. Burmese belief does include restless dead, but the name appears fabricated, likely a garbling of nat-related categories.

name: Bannick
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) figure called 'Bannick' appears in any source; the name resembles the Russian bannik, a bathhouse spirit. Documented Ojibwe spirits include manitou beings and Mishipeshu, but nothing named Bannick.

name: Bannick
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) source records a spirit named 'Bannick'; the name likely echoes the Russian bannik, the bathhouse spirit. Ojibwe tradition does include manitou spirits and the underwater panther Mishipeshu, but no figure of this name appears in the ethnographic record.

name: Bannik
description: Bannik is the demonic spirit of the Ukrainian bathhouse (laznya or banya), a cantankerous, vengeful entity who dwells behind the stove-heater or under the washing bench. He appears as a tiny, naked, emaciated old man with long shaggy hair, a large head, and enormous hands, sometimes covered in soot or with a broom as his distinguishing feature. He can also take the form of a cat, dog, frog, or hare. Bannik is considered the most malevolent of the house spirits because the bathhouse was viewed as a spiritually unclean place where people shed not only dirt but also their negative energy and illnesses

name: Bannik-Moist
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The bannik, the Russian bathhouse spirit, dangerous after midnight and appeased with bread, salt, or an offering of water, is genuine Slavic folklore, but no 'Moist' variant appears in any source; the epithet and its supposed social character are invented.

name: Banshee
description: Irish bean sí ('woman of the fairy mound') - death herald of the Aos Sí, descended from the Tuatha Dé Danann. Attaches TO Specific OLD Gaelic Families Only - O'Neill, O'Brien, O'Connor, O'Grady, MacCarthy, Kavanagh and few others. Each family has their OWN banshee passed through bloodlines for over 1,000 years. Her cry is the caoine (keening) - warning before death, not after. The Only supernatural figure tied to specific family lineages. The Scottish bean nighe washes blood-stained clothes at rivers - a related death omen. Welsh variant is gwrach y Rhibyn

name: Banyan Deer (Nigrodhamiga Jataka)
description: The Banyan Deer is a central figure in the Nigrodhamiga Jataka, one of the most famous Buddhist Jataka tales recounting the previous lives of the Buddha. In this story, the Bodhisattva (future Buddha) was born as a magnificent golden deer named King Banyan Deer, leader of a herd of 500 deer in the forests near Benares (Varanasi). The king of Benares was an avid hunter who frequently rode out to hunt deer, causing chaos and death throughout the forest. To prevent indiscriminate killing, the Banyan Deer — along with the leader of the opposing monkey deer herd — made a pact with the king: one deer would voluntarily be sacrificed each day as the king's meal, sparing the rest. One day, a pregnant doe from the monkey deer herd was destined to die. Her leader refused to take her place, so she appealed to King Banyan Deer. Moved with compassion, the Banyan Deer took her place, laying his head on the chopping block. The human king, witnessing this extraordinary act of self-sacrifice by a mere animal, was deeply moved and granted sanctuary to all deer, establishing a protected forest where no creature could be hunted

name: Barama
description: Barama is a culture hero and ancestral figure in the mythology of the Elema people of the Gulf of Papua, Papua New Guinea. He is credited with introducing essential cultural practices, including the famous Hevéhe ceremony — a elaborate cycle of masked dances and rituals that mark important transitions in community life. Barama taught the people how to build spirit houses (eravo), carve and wear ceremonial masks, and perform the complex rituals that maintain the balance between the human and spirit worlds. The traditions established by Barama continue to be practiced today in villages along the Papuan Gulf, making him a living presence in contemporary indigenous culture

name: Barbegazi
description: Barbegazi (French barbe glacée, 'frozen beard') are Swiss/French Alpine snow gnomes. Small, white-furred, with flat feet used as skis, they inhabit high Alpine caves. They warn of avalanches with hooting cries, round up lost sheep, dig out snow-trapped victims. Generally helpful but defensive. Aestivate in glacial crevasses. Documented by Disney (1870) and Alpine oral tradition.

name: Barchin
description: Barchin (Barchinoy, Oy Barchin) is the heroine of the Alpamysh epic, daughter of Boysar and the model of the brave and loyal woman of Turkic tradition. She wins her hero through contests of archery, wrestling and skill, resists a forced marriage, and holds the people together in his absence; her mausoleum still stands near the site of old Sighnoq.

name: Barge
description: French name for 'phantom dog' - similar to the English Barghest/Shuck and part of the British Isles black dog tradition. Named from Old French 'burgh-guest' (town ghost) or Bahr-Geist (funeral bier spirit). The French term encompasses spectral hounds that appear as death omens, with glowing eyes, roaming at night near old roads, churches, crossroads. If one crosses your path, expect misfortune or death within the year. Some say it's the ghost of a murdered person or unbaptized child. The black dog ghost tradition spans all England (Shuck, Black Shuck, Padfoot, Skriker, Gytrash) and Wales (Gwyllgi, Cwn Annwn)

name: Barmanou
description: The Barmanou is a bipedal humanoid primate cryptid reported in the mountainous Chitral and Karakoram regions of northern Pakistan. Shepherds and locals have documented sightings for generations, describing a creature that straddles the line between ape and wild man. Spanish zoologist Jordi Magraner conducted extensive field research in the 1990s collecting over fifty firsthand sighting accounts that all identified the Barmanou as an apelike hominid distinct from known primate species. The creature occupies the geographic gap between the Almas of Central Asia and the Yeti of the Himalayas, suggesting a continuous cryptid tradition across the mountain ranges of inner Asia

name: Baron Samedi
description: Baron Samedi ('Baron Saturday') is the loa of the dead, graveyards, and the crossroads in Haitian Vodou, chief of the Gede family of spirits. He is depicted in black tails, a top hat, and dark glasses, with a skull-like face, and is known for macabre jokes and coarse humour. He presides over burial and the boundary between life and death; his consort is Maman Brigitte.

name: Barong
description: Barong is the protective spirit of Balinese tradition, a shaggy lion-dog deity usually portrayed by two dancers within an elaborate costume. In the celebrated Barong dance he confronts Rangda, the widow-witch, in ritual combat that stages the balance of cosmic order, blessing the village and warding off evil. The figure remains central to Balinese religious performance and community identity.

name: Barong (Lion Protector)
description: Barong is the king of the spirits and the leader of the hosts of good in Balinese mythology. He is a lion-like mythological creature and the eternal opponent of Rangda, the demon queen. The Barong represents good, protective forces, while Rangda embodies evil and chaos. In the famous Barong dance performance, which reenacts the eternal battle between good and evil, Barong protects the village from Rangda's dark magic. The term 'barong' is derived from 'bahruang,' meaning 'bear,' and the Barong is considered a guardian spirit of the forest. The most common form is Barong Ket, depicted as a lion with a red head, thick white fur, and gilded jewelry adorned with mirrors. Barong is also identified with Banas Pati Raja, the fourth 'brother' or spirit child that accompanies a Balinese person throughout life

name: Basajaun
description: Basque 'Lord of the Forest' (basajaunak plural, basaandre female). Huge hairy hominid - Europe's Bigfoot. Among the last surviving Jentilak (old spirit race) when Christianity arrived. First farmer who taught humans to cultivate cereals. Protective of flocks from wolves and storms - gives Warning Howls when danger approaches so shepherds can move herds. Has prodigious strength but extremely wise. Swift as a stag. Lives in caves at high altitudes and dense forests of the Pyrenees. Makes bread offerings from cowherds. Rare but friendly if treated with respect. Can be terrifying if encountered unexpectedly. Both protector and teacher

name: Basilisk
description: The Basilisk (King of Serpents) is a legendary reptile known in Roman and Vatican-connected medieval bestiary tradition. Described by Pliny the Elder and later Christian bestiaries, the Basilisk is a small but deadly serpent crown-crested creature whose mere gaze causes death. It is said to be hatched from a cock's egg incubated by a serpent or toad. In Christian symbology adopted by the Vatican, the Basilisk represents the power of sin and heresy that can be overcome by faith. Medieval bestiaries often used the Basilisk as a symbol of the Antichrist, and its deadly gaze represented the corrupting power of evil

name: Bat Animal-Spirit (Udmurt)
description: In Udmurt animistic tradition, the bat animal-spirit is a nature guardian associated with the transitional spaces between day and night, earth and sky. The Udmurt people, a Finno-Ugric ethnic group from the Volga region of Russia, traditionally hold deep reverence for animal spirits that inhabit the natural world. Bats, with their ability to fly and dwell in caves, are seen as mediators between different realms of existence. While not a major deity in the Udmurt pantheon, the bat spirit represents the protective forces of the natural world, particularly the oceans and waterways that surround the Udmurt homeland, watching over those who respect nature's boundaries

name: Bata
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. In Philippine languages bata means 'child,' and bata-bata was a term for small carved ancestor images (taotao/anito) in pre-colonial religion; the bat-spirit narrative belongs to Udmurt tradition, not the Philippines. The closest genuine analogues are the anito and diwata guardian spirits of indigenous Philippine belief.

name: Batammariba Ancestor Spirits
description: Ancestor veneration is the foundation of Batammariba (Tamberma/Somba) religion of the Atakora Mountains in Togo and Benin. The dead dwell in earthen cone-altars within the takienta tower-houses, and the people call themselves Serpent Children of an underground Serpent Mother. Initiation rites and ritual consult the ancestors, who are held to govern the land and community.

name: Batibat
description: The batibat is a vengeful tree-dwelling hag of Ilocano folklore, an obese female spirit who, when her tree is felled for a house post, migrates into it and sits on the chests of sleepers to suffocate them with fatal nightmares (bangungot). Biting one's thumb or wiggling the toes breaks her grip; the belief explains sudden unexplained nocturnal death syndrome.

name: Baubas
description: The Baubas is a malevolent household spirit in Lithuanian folklore, serving as the Baltic equivalent of the bogeyman. It is an evil entity with long lean arms, wrinkly fingers, and glowing red eyes that lurks in the dark corners of homes, under beds, and inside closets. Lithuanian parents traditionally invoke the Baubas to discipline misbehaving children, warning that the creature will come to take them away if they do not obey. Unlike other demonic beings in Baltic mythology, the Baubas is specifically a domestic fear figure rather than a wilderness spirit, making its presence felt in the most intimate spaces of family life

name: Bauk
description: The bauk is a bear-like bogeyman of Serbian folklore, an animal-shaped monster hiding in dark corners, holes, and abandoned houses to grab, carry away, and devour victims, especially children. It has a clumsy gait (bauljanje) and an onomatopoeic cry of 'bau,' and is driven off by light and noise. Scholars read it as folk memory of the brown bear, once widespread in the Balkans.

name: Baxbaxwalanuksiwe' (Man-Eater)
description: Baxbaxwalanuksiwe', the Man-Eater at the North End of the World, is the supreme cannibal spirit of the Kwakwaka'wakw and patron of the Hamatsa. Covered with mouths over his whole body, he commands the man-eating birds and possesses initiates of the winter ceremony; the northern lights are said to be the smoke of his far-off fireplace.

name: Bay-Terek (World Tree)
description: Bay-Terek, the 'rich poplar,' is the world tree of Altai and wider Turkic tradition, the axis mundi linking heaven, earth, and the underworld. It stands at the center of creation; its roots anchor the deep, its trunk is the shaman's route, and in its branches a double-headed eagle guards a golden egg while the serpent Erlik coils below to steal it. Kazakhs know the same tree as Baiterek.

name: Baychibar
description: Baychibar is the magic horse of Alpamysh in the Turkic epic of that name. Bought as a scrawny colt, he grows into a matchless steed who carries Alpamysh to win Barchin's contests, speaks to give counsel, and warns of treachery on the long roads of the tale; no unworthy rider can mount him, and he is Alpamysh's truest companion.

name: Baykok
description: The baykok (Ojibwe bakaak, 'bones draped in skin') is a malevolent skeletal spirit of Anishinaabe tradition: emaciated, translucent-skinned, with glowing red eyes, it flies through Great Lakes forests with shrill cries, hunting warriors, whom it paralyzes with invisible arrows or beats with a club before devouring their livers. It reached English literature via Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha.

name: Bayon Face Spirit (Lokeshvara)
description: The Bayon Face Spirit refers to the 216 massive stone faces carved on the towers of the Bayon Temple at Angkor Thom, the legendary capital built by King Jayavarman VII (1181-1218 CE). According to Khmer tradition, these faces represent the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (Lokeshvara) — the embodiment of compassion in Mahayana Buddhism — gazing in all four directions to protect the Khmer Empire. Local folklore adds that the faces bear the features of King Jayavarman VII himself, who ordered his countenance carved so that his subjects would always feel his presence. A darker legend tells of the architect blinded after completing the temple so he could never duplicate it; when he touched the stone faces, his sight was miraculously restored. The faces are believed to watch over Angkor Thom eternally, their serene smiles reflecting the compassion of the bodhisattva and the power of the god-king. The Bayon's 54 towers with four faces each create one of the world's most extraordinary spiritual monuments

name: Beaivi
description: Beaivi is the supreme sun deity of Sami mythology, venerated as a goddess of the sun, spring, fertility, and mental health. In the Arctic regions of Sapmi where winter darkness lasts months, she was the most important divine figure. She travels through the sky with her daughter Beaivi-nieida in an enclosure covered with reindeer bones and antlers, bringing spring and light. The Sami believed that madness and depression were caused by her absence during the dark winter months. On the winter solstice, white reindeer were sacrificed in her honor to ensure her return — their meat threaded on sticks bent into rings and tied with bright ribbons in the Festival of Beaivi. Butter was smeared on doorposts to strengthen her as she regained her height in the sky. At summer solstice, sun-rings of leaves were hung in trees. She makes plants grow so reindeer flourish and brings wealth and prosperity to humans

name: Bean Nighe
description: The Bean Nighe, meaning washerwoman in Scottish Gaelic, is a death omen spirit from Scottish Highland folklore, a specific type of banshee that haunts desolate streams and fords. She is the spirit of a woman who died in childbirth and is doomed to wash the bloody grave-clothes of those about to die until the day her natural lifespan would have ended. Known also as nigheag na h-ath or little washer at the ford, she appears in lonely places beside streams and pools where she can be seen scrubbing linen and shrouds stained with blood, her mournful singing and washing presaging an imminent death in the community

name: Bean Sídhe
description: The bean sí (banshee) is the female death-spirit of Irish tradition whose wailing, keening cry foretells a death in the family; her name means 'woman of the fairy mounds' (sídhe). Long-haired and often seen combing her hair, she is attached to particular old families.

name: Bear Ancestor-Spirit (Mapuche)
description: No specific Mapuche bear ancestor-spirit is attested; the original description was a copy-paste of the Irish banshee. Genuine Mapuche beings include the ngen, spirit-owners of nature (ngen-kulliñ owns the animals), the Pillan, ancestral volcano and thunder spirits, and the malevolent wekufe.

name: Bear Ancestor-Spirit of Kazakh
description: In Kazakh and broader Turkic mythology, the bear appears as an ancestral spirit figure associated with strength, healing, and the shamanic traditions of the Central Asian steppes. While Kazakh culture historically centered on wolves, eagles, and horses as primary totemic animals, the bear holds a respected place in the animistic beliefs of Turkic peoples as a powerful earth spirit connected to the mountainous forest regions of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and the Altai. The bear ancestor-spirit represents raw physical power and the untamed forces of nature that the Turkic baksy shamans would invoke during healing rituals and vision quests

name: Bear Ancestor-Spirit of Mi'kmaq
description: Among the Mi'kmaq people of Eastern Canada, the bear holds a significant place as a powerful ancestral figure and clan animal. The Mi'kmaq recognize the bear as a wise being that appears in their oral traditions as a teacher of survival skills and spiritual knowledge. Bear ancestor spirits are believed to guide hunters through the forests of the Maritime provinces, offering protection to those who show proper respect through songs and ceremonial offerings. The Mi'kmaq bear spirit is closely tied to the cycles of nature, with hibernation representing death and rebirth, and its appearance in dreams is considered a powerful omen of transition and transformation

name: Bear Ancestor-Spirit of Yoruba
description: In Yoruba cosmology from West Africa, the bear ancestor-spirit exists within regional traditions where large forest mammals are venerated as powerful spiritual forces. While the Yoruba pantheon is dominated by Orishas such as Ogun and Shango, bear-like spirits appear in the folklore of forest-dwelling communities where these animals were occasionally encountered through trade and travel. These ancestor spirits represent raw untamed power, embodying strength that must be respected and appeased. The bear ancestor-spirit is invoked in ceremonies related to warrior traditions and the protection of village boundaries, serving as a guardian entity

name: Bear Ancestor-Spirit of Zapotec
description: Among the Zapotec people of Oaxaca, Mexico, bear ancestor-spirits appear in the rich tapestry of ancestral worship that characterizes their indigenous religion. The Zapotec, who built the magnificent city of Monte Alban, maintained a deep connection with the mountain forests where black bears once roamed. Bear ancestor-spirits are considered guardians of the mountain passes and sacred caves used for rituals and burials. These spirits belong to the complex Zapotec understanding of the afterlife, where ancestors transform into animal forms that continue to influence the living world and its natural cycles

name: Bear Animal-Spirit of Aymara
description: In Aymara tradition from the highlands of Bolivia and Peru, the bear animal-spirit known as ukumari occupies a unique place in Andean mythology. The Aymara recognize the spectacled bear as a powerful nature spirit inhabiting the cloud forests on the eastern slopes of the Andes. The ukumari is considered a mediator between the high puna grasslands and the lowland jungles, featuring prominently in Aymara folk Catholicism and indigenous rituals. The bear represents the untamed wilderness surrounding human settlements and is a central figure in the Fiesta de la Virgen de la Candelaria

name: Bear Deity (Laotian)
description: The lunar bear deity of Lao animism, known as Phi Nyang, is associated with the cycles of the moon and the nocturnal world. This bear deity is most active during the full moon, descending from the mountains to walk among rice fields and bless crops with fertility. The Lao people tell stories of the moon bear teaching early humans how to plant rice and distinguish edible from poisonous plants. Its connection to the lunar calendar makes it a central figure in agricultural timing, with traditional farmers consulting the moon bear's phases

name: Bear Deity (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested in Zimbabwean tradition. The description matches Laotian 'Moon Bear' animist beliefs (lunar cycles, rice agriculture, nocturnal protection), not Shona or Ndebele folklore. Zimbabwe has no native bear species. The record misplaces a Laotian deity into southern Africa, likely via erroneous cultural conflation.

name: Bear Deity (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested in Native North American folklore. This 'Laotian moon-bear deity' is a Laotian animist concept mis-assigned to USA folklore and mis-cited to Native American ethnography. Lao animism centers on phi, or place and nature spirits, with no documented bear deity of the kind described; the white-furred moon-bear appears to be fabricated.

name: Bear Deity (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested in Native North American folklore. This 'Laotian moon-bear deity' is a Laotian animist concept mis-assigned to Canada and mis-cited to Native American ethnography. Lao animism centers on phi, or place and nature spirits, with no documented bear deity of the kind described; the white-furred moon-bear appears to be fabricated.

name: Bear Deity (Laotian)
description: The 'Bear Deity (Laotian)' is not attested in Colombian or Muisca tradition. The description describes a Laotian (Southeast Asian) moon bear deity tied to lunar cycles and rice agriculture—completely unrelated to Colombia. The Muisca had no bear deities; snip spectacled bears (ukumari) exist in the Andes but lack a moon-bear lunar deity in Muisca sources.

name: Bear Deity (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested: no moon-bear deity with a white lunar coat, crescent pendant or role guiding the dead appears in Laotian folklore. Lao spirit lore centers on phi (nature spirits), nagas and protective village spirits rather than bear gods, and the recorded bear is a modern invention; the Mexico placement is an error.

name: Bear Deity of Maya
description: In Maya cosmology the bear appears in the mythology of highland Maya regions where the spectacled bear historically roamed. While jaguars dominate lowland Maya animal symbolism, Maya communities of the Guatemalan highlands incorporated the bear into their celestial understanding. The Maya associated bears with the god of the Pleiades constellation, recognizing the bear's connection to the sky through Ursa Major. Some highland traditions speak of a bear deity known as Huh Kaan, a protector of the milpa who ensures soil fertility and harvest success, linking the bear to the central Maya value of maize cultivation

name: Bear Deity of Pomo
description: In the traditions of the Pomo people of Northern California, the bear holds immense spiritual importance as a being bridging the human and animal worlds. The Pomo, who lived in the bear-rich lands of the Russian River Valley and Clear Lake basin, developed elaborate rituals centered around the grizzly bear, once abundant in their territory. The bear deity is associated with healing and shamanic power, as Pomo shamans believed they could transform into bears to access supernatural abilities. The Pomo Bear Doctors formed a powerful secret society that used bear spirit power for curing and divination

name: Bear Deity of Shoshone
description: Among the Shoshone people of the Great Basin and Rocky Mountains, the bear is revered as a powerful spiritual being with deep connections to the landscape and healing traditions. The Shoshone, ranging across Nevada, Utah, Idaho, and Wyoming, encountered grizzly and black bears throughout their vast territory and incorporated the animal into their mythology as a being of great medicine power. The bear deity is particularly associated with the Wind River Mountains of Wyoming, where Shoshone medicine people went on vision quests seeking bear spirit guidance. Bear power is considered among the most potent spiritual forces

name: Bear Ghost of Kazakh
description: In Kazakh folklore from the steppes of Central Asia, bear ghosts represent the spirits of shamans and warriors who have taken on bear form after death. While the wolf holds a more prominent place in Kazakh totemic tradition as the mythical ancestor of Turkic peoples, the bear is recognized as a powerful spirit animal in regions where bears inhabit the Tien Shan and Altai mountain ranges. Kazakh bear ghosts are believed to be the restless spirits of those who died with unfinished business, particularly warriors who fell in battle and shamans whose power was not fully transferred before death

name: Bear Ghost of Mi'kmaq
description: Within Mi'kmaq tradition from the Maritime provinces of Canada, the bear ghost represents the residual energy of bears that have passed on or the manifestation of a person's spirit in bear form after death. The Mi'kmaq believe that certain individuals, particularly powerful shamans known as buowin, can transform into bears both in life and after death. These bear ghosts are considered guardians of specific territories and sacred sites, serving as reminders of the thin boundary between the physical world and the spirit realm. They appear most frequently during seasonal transitions

name: Bear Ghost of Shona
description: In Shona tradition from Zimbabwe and Mozambique, the bear ghost exists within the framework of ancestral spirit beliefs rather than representing actual bears, which are not native to southern Africa. The bear ghost is a spirit entity that visits human communities in bear-like form, associated with the mhondoro tradition of powerful ancestral guardians. These spirits are believed to be the ghosts of chiefs and warriors whose power manifests in the form of large animals. The bear-like ghost is considered a foreign spirit that arrived through trade and migration routes connecting the Shona to other African regions

name: Bear Giant of Quechua
description: In Quechua oral traditions from the Andean highlands of Peru and Bolivia, the bear giant appears in stories as a hybrid creature combining human and bear characteristics, known as ukuku or paucar. The Quechua people, descendants of the Inca civilization, tell stories of giant bear-like beings that once roamed the high puna grasslands and cloud forests. These bear giants are portrayed as solitary creatures interacting with humans through a combination of menace and foolishness, appearing in cautionary tales teaching children to stay close to their communities

name: Bear Giant of Shona
description: In the folklore of the Shona people of Zimbabwe, the bear giant represents a mythical being that is neither fully animal nor fully spirit, but a monstrous entity inhabiting wild spaces between human settlements. While southern Africa has no native bears, the concept was introduced through oral traditions of Swahili traders and colonial contact. This being has been integrated into Shona mythology as a chimera-like creature combining the strength of a lion, the build of a rhinoceros, and the ferocity of a crocodile into a single terrifying form that appears in fireside stories as a warning

name: Bear Giant of Zulu
description: Within Zulu tradition from South Africa, the bear giant appears as an imported mythical figure adapted into the rich corpus of Zulu folklore. The Zulu have no native bear species, but the concept of a large bear-like creature entered mythology through contact with European settlers and travelers bringing stories of mysterious beasts. This figure was integrated as a monster known as udongo, embodying the dangers of the unknown and the consequences of venturing too far from home. While not part of the original Zulu cosmology, the bear giant has become recognized in modern Zulu storytelling

name: Bear Guardian (Cree)
description: Bears are spiritually significant among the Cree (maskwa), respected as powerful beings and healers in the boreal forest world. The 'Bear Guardian watching over lakes' is a synthesis rather than an attested named figure: Cree tradition centers bears in hunting respect, dreams, and medicine, not specifically as lake spirits. The Cree are a Canadian people; the country metadata here is correct.

name: Bear Guardian (Cree)
description: The bear (maskwa) is a powerful medicine being in Cree tradition, a spirit of healing and ceremony and a guide encountered in dreams and visions; legends such as Mistahi-Maskwa tell of a great bear devoted to medicine and the sharing of knowledge. The entry's metadata mislabels the Cree as Colombian, and its lake-guardian framing is unsupported.

name: Bear Guardian of Cree
description: In Cree (Nehiyaw) tradition the bear is one of the most powerful animal beings, honored as a teacher, healer, and source of medicine power who shares knowledge of medicinal plants and hunting with those who approach with humility and respect. Regarded as a relative who walks between worlds, the bear guides dreamers and vision-fasters, revealing life paths during vision quests.

name: Bear Guardian of Haida
description: Bears hold a central place in Haida tradition, appearing as crest figures, on totem poles and regalia, and in the well-known Bear Mother story, in which a woman marries a bear and the bears teach respect for their kind. 'Bear Guardian' is a general label for this attested bear reverence rather than a single named spirit; the boundary between bear and human is a genuine Haida concern.

name: Bear Guardian of Navajo
description: Bears are significant in Navajo (Diné) tradition, where they are associated with healing and medicine. The bears figure in the Mountainway, one of the major curing ceremonies, and killing or disrespecting a bear is treated with care. The 'Bear Guardian' is a general label for this attested bear reverence rather than a single named spirit; bear beings appear in curing contexts.

name: Bear Husband Tsimshian
description: In the Tsimshian tale 'The Bear Who Married a Woman,' a young woman is courted at night by a suitor with rough palms, and each dawn a larger sea animal lies on the beach. When her mother keeps watch, a red bear rises from the water carrying a whale on each side; discovered, he turns to stone, a supernatural being of the sea.

name: Bear Maiden
description: The Bear Maiden is a figure from Navajo tradition about a young woman who transformed into a bear after being mistreated by her family or community. As she wandered into the wilderness in despair, her hands and feet slowly transformed into bear claws and her body grew fur. She later encountered hunters from her village who recognized her by remnants of her human appearance.
