The story carries ceremonial significance related to the Mountain Top Chant ceremony and teaches about the deep spiritual c

name: Bear Mother
description: In the classic Haida narrative of the Bear Mother, a woman who mocked the bears was taken by a bear who made her his wife. She lived among the bear people and bore children who were half-human, half-bear. Her human brothers eventually tracked her down and killed the bears in a great hunt, but the woman herself had been transformed by her time with the bears. The Bear Mother children became powerful ancestors. This narrative, common across many Northwest Coast tribes, serves to explain the special relationship between humans and bears, teaching profound respect for the animal people

name: Bear Nature-Spirit of Haida
description: This entry duplicates the bear-guardian-of-haida tradition: bears are genuinely central to Haida culture as crest figures and in the Bear Mother story, in which a woman marries a bear and bears teach the proper treatment of animals. The 'bear nature-spirit guarding rivers' framing is a synthesis, not an attested named being; the attested core is Haida reverence for bears.

name: Bear Nature-Spirit of Yoruba
description: Not independently attested. No bear spirit appears in Yoruba orisha tradition or Yoruba folklore: bears do not occur in Yorubaland (Nigeria and Benin), and the entry's claim of a diaspora-introduced 'bear nature-spirit' invoking Ogun and Oshun has no documentary basis. The name and concept appear invented.

name: Bear People Tsimshian
description: In Tsimshian and neighboring Northwest Coast tradition, the Bear People are a chiefly society who live in houses like humans and put on bear coats to travel as animals. The Bear Mother story tells how a woman who disrespected the bears was taken and married into the bear village, bore twin cubs, and how the bear chief taught the rituals of respect hunters still follow.

name: Bear Spirit (Shona)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No bear species is native to southern Africa, and Shona clan totems (mitupo) and ancestral spirits (vadzimu) draw only on native animals. The entry itself concedes this and then invents a bear role in Shona cosmology; the genuine analogues are the vadzimu ancestors and mitupo animal totems of Shona religion.

name: Bear Spirit of Paiute
description: Bears figure among the mythic animal-people of Paiute and Great Basin tradition. Ethnographic sources record Bear as an anthropomorphic animal progenitor of the pre-human age, and Northern Paiute narratives include 'Bear and Fawns.' 'Bear Spirit' is a general label for this attested bear role rather than a single named figure; the central culture heroes are Wolf (Isa) and Coyote.

name: Bear Spirit of Uzbek
description: Not independently attested: no specific bear spirit is documented in Uzbek folklore, where the wolf and eagle dominate Turkic tradition and the bear plays little role. The description is a generic synthesis of Central Asian animism and Islam.

name: Bear Trickster (Inuit)
description: There is no bear trickster in Inuit tradition; the Arctic trickster figures are Raven and Fox, while the polar bear (Nanuk) is a revered, powerful being in its own right. The entry's description even concedes this, framing the 'Bear Trickster' as a composite that does not correspond to any attested Inuit figure. Polar-bear respect is real; this named figure is not.

name: Bear Water-Spirit of Cheyenne
description: The Bear Water-Spirit of Cheyenne tradition is closely associated with Bear Butte, known in Cheyenne as Noahvose or The Sacred Mountain Where They Are Taught, which rises from the plains of South Dakota as a sacred landmark of immense spiritual significance. In Cheyenne cosmology, the bear is a powerful guardian of springs and water sources, and the mountain itself is shaped like a sleeping bear, guarding the waters that emerge from its base. The Cheyenne prophet Sweet Medicine, Motseyuef, received the four Sacred Arrows from the Maiyun spirits inside Bear Butte after spending four years in a sacred cave whose entrance was guarded by a grizzly bear and a mountain lion. This water-spirit aspect of the bear connects the life-giving springs that emerge from Bear Butte with the spiritual teachings that form the foundation of Cheyenne culture, law, and ceremonial life. The bear water-spirit ensures that the waters of the sacred mountain remain pure and accessible for all who come to pray and seek visions

name: Bear Water-Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Muisca religion has no bear water-spirit; the figure conflated here is Nencatacoa (Nem-catacoa), the bear- or fox-shaped patron of weavers, artists, and drunken festivities on the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, recorded by chronicler Pedro Simón. He is a celebration deity, with no attested link to water or lakes such as Guatavita.

name: Bear Wife Tsimshian
description: In Tsimshian texts from the Nass River, the great Grizzly Bear is the wife of a man — a supernatural bride who fills her husband's house with salmon and uses her stomach as a berry basket. In the companion tale 'The Bear Who Married a Woman,' a human woman becomes the bear chief's wife; bear marriage runs both ways in Tsimshian tradition.

name: Bear Woman Tlingit
description: Bear Woman is the heart of the Bear Mother story told by the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian. A girl who mocked bears was taken by a bear and married the bear chief, discovering that bears live like people in a great house; her children became the ancestors of bear clans, and the tale explains why bears and humans are kin and why the bear is honored.

name: Bears
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Bears' is a generic label rather than a named being, and the entry invents a Chinook bear-spirit guardian with no specific tale or named tradition. Bears do appear in real Pacific Northwest oral traditions — as clan figures and Transformer-era characters — but no such generalized spirit is documented for the Chinook.

name: Beaver Chinook
description: Not independently attested as a distinct named spirit in Chinook folklore. Beaver appears within broader Pacific Northwest animal tales and, most prominently, in the Salish and Kootenai story 'Beaver Steals Fire,' in which Beaver dives to bring fire to the people; a Chinook-specific beaver figure needs better documentation.

name: Beaver Spirit
description: The Beaver Spirit is a powerful animal spirit in Blackfoot religion, central to the sacred Beaver Bundle—the most important medicine bundle of the Blackfoot people. According to legend, a Blackfoot man encountered beavers who taught him sacred songs, rituals, and the use of medicinal plants. The Beaver Bundle contains animal skins, pipes, and herbs, each with specific powers. The Beaver Bundle ceremony involves elaborate rituals, singing, and smoking the pipe, used for healing, good fortune, and maintaining balance between human and spirit worlds

name: Beaver Tsimshian
description: The Beaver is a Tsimshian crest whose origin is told as the Gitsalas legend of the Beaver Crest, recorded by William Beynon. A woman dammed a stream to swim in it and refused to leave, and she was transformed, her leather apron becoming the beaver's tail. Beaver is a clan ancestor of the Eagle division and a figure of diligence and persistence.

name: Bee Goddess
description: The Bee Goddess is a deity of Minoan and Mediterranean tradition, best known from Minoan seals depicting a female figure flanked by bees. In Greek religion, bees and honey link mortals to the divine: melissae ('bees') were priestesses of Demeter and Artemis, and the bee symbolized the soul (psyché) departing the body, rebirth, and divine order in the temple hierarchies of ancient Crete.

name: Beetgumer Grom
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Only the village of Beetgum (Bitgum), Friesland, is real; no ghost or spirit named 'Beetgumer Grom' appears in Frisian folklore collections such as the Low Countries folktale bank. The murdered-farmer story is unverifiable filler. Genuine Frisian analogues include the klabautermann and regional household-sprite traditions.

name: Beetle Guardian (Nepali)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Nepali tradition. Nepali folklore blends Hindu, Buddhist and animist beliefs with documented beings such as nāgas and village guardian spirits, but no source records a 'beetle guardian' of the fields, and the account of an insect spirit balancing pests is invented. Insects play no named protective role in the documented Nepali corpus.

name: Bell Witch
description: The Bell Witch is the most famous supernatural entity in American folklore, said to have tormented the Bell family of Robertson County, Tennessee, from 1817 to 1821. While white accounts describe the witch as the ghost of Kate Batts, African American oral traditions viewed the Bell Witch through a different lens — as a 'haint' connected to the horrors of slavery itself. Enslaved people on the Bell plantation interpreted the entity as a spirit born from the suffering of the enslaved, and some described it as a Boo Hag-like entity that could shed its skin and fly. The enslaved community used their own protective measures — salt, sulfur, haint blue paint, and conjure bags — to ward off the entity. The Bell Witch legend thus represents a convergence of African and European supernatural traditions on American soil

name: Belliegħa
description: Belliegħa, also known as Il-Belliegħa, is a female water spirit from Maltese folklore that inhabits wells, springs, and underground water sources across the Maltese islands. In Maltese tradition, which blends ancient Mediterranean beliefs with Christian elements, Belliegħa is a dangerous but fascinating figure who guards the freshwater sources that are precious in the dry Mediterranean climate of Malta. The name Belliegħa is derived from the Maltese word for a swallowing or gulping sound, referencing the way this spirit is said to pull unwary victims into the depths of her watery domain. She belongs to a class of Maltese folk beings that includes the Kawkaw or Gawgaw, a grey slimy creature that roamed the streets at night. Belliegħa embodies both the life-giving and the deadly aspects of water, providing clean drinking water to those who respect her domain but drowning those who approach her wells with carelessness or disrespect

name: Beloved Twins
description: In the Zuni kachina-origin tradition, the Beloved Twins led the three groups of Zuni during the clan migrations in search of the middle place, itiwana. Under their guidance the clans separated by direction, and their journeys are recalled in Zuni origin narratives. They are migration leaders of the emerging people.

name: Belt il-Għasel
description: Belt il-Ghasel ('City of Honey') is not a witch of Maltese folklore. The name echoes Wied il-Ghasel, a place name ('Valley of Honey'), and Maltese beekeeping traditions. No Maltese source records a bee- or butterfly-shapeshifting witch by this name; the entry appears invented from the place name and a generic shapeshifter template.

name: Belu
description: Belu (bilu) are ogres or demons in Burmese folklore and Buddhist Jataka tradition — large, powerful beings of human or animal form, often greedy, gluttonous, and dangerous. In Myanmar they appear as devourers in cautionary tales, sometimes redeemable through the Buddha's teachings. The concept derives from the Sanskrit bhilu and figures prominently in Burmese story and drama.

name: Bemba
description: Bemba (also called Maa Ngala or simply Ngala) is the supreme creator god of the Bambara people of Mali who created himself as a quaternity of four beings: Pemba (male, earth/air), Mousso Koroni Koundye (female, fire), Faro (female, water), and Ndomadyiri (male). Hermaphroditic in nature, Bemba encompasses both masculine and feminine creative principles. He existed before all things as Koni, the primordial energy, and brought the universe into being through a series of emanations. Bemba is distant and all-powerful, approached through the six initiation societies that form the backbone of Bambara spiritual life

name: Benandanti
description: Friulian agrarian cult study by Carlo Ginzburg ('The Night Battles') - 'good walkers' who fight malevolent witches (Malandanti) in Spirit Form at night. They Project their spirits (leave body while sleeping) as wolves/cats/hares to battle for crops. The Four Nights per year during Ember Days (Thursdays at specific seasonal times) were key battles - aligned with planting/harvesting. They were NOT werewolves in the usual sense - they Left their human form to go to the 'underworld' to heal the sick, secure paths, fight evil. Their leader was the 'captain.' The Inquisition Reinterpreted them as Satanic witches (1575-1620), forcing confessions. They insisted they fought FOR Christ and against witchcraft. Connect to Livonian 'Dogs of God' werewolves. A PRE-Christian Fertility Cult survivor documented through Inquisition records

name: Bennu (Egyptian Phoenix)
description: The Bennu is the sacred heron-like bird of Egyptian mythology, the original Egyptian phoenix. It was the ba (soul) of Ra and the soul of Osiris. The Bennu is associated with creation; snip it alighted on the primordial mound (Benben) at the first sunrise, breaking the silence of the primeval waters with its cry. The Benben stone, the pyramidal capstone of obelisks, represents the mound upon which the Bennu perched. It also represents the annual flooding of the Nile and the cycle of death and rebirth. The Greeks later identified the Bennu with their own phoenix, but the Egyptian version predates the Greek phoenix by centuries. The Bennu is closely associated with the city of Heliopolis

name: Bergfolk
description: Bergfolk (mountain-people) are supernatural beings in Norwegian folklore who live inside mountains and rocky crags. Similar to haugfolk but specifically associated with mountains rather than burial mounds. Bergfolk are a type of underjordiske (hidden people) who have their own society within mountain halls. They are known for kidnapping humans (bergtaking - mountain-taking), where a person would be taken inside the mountain to live with the bergfolk, often for years. The most famous example is the legend of the Huldra who entices men into the mountain. Time is distorted inside - a few hours can be years in the human world. Bergfolk have beautiful daughters who sometimes marry human men. The mountain halls are lit by an internal golden light and filled with treasure. The theme of bergtaking (entering the mountain and being trapped) is central to Norwegian folklore and appears in Asbjørnsen and Moe's collections

name: Berggeist
description: Berggeist ('mountain spirit') is a general term in Germanic and Alpine tradition for spirits who dwell in and guard mountains, most famously the Bergmonch, a monk-like figure seen in mines and high passes. These spirits reward respectful miners with ore and punish greed and carelessness. The Ratikon and Liechtenstein settings of the entry are local color on a wider Alpine motif.

name: Bergkobold
description: The Bergkobold is a mine spirit from German folklore, particularly associated with the Harz Mountains, the Ore Mountains of Saxony, and other mining regions of central Europe. Unlike the household kobold, which helps with domestic chores, the Bergkobold or mountain kobold inhabits underground mines and tunnels, where it can be either helpful or dangerous to miners depending on how it is treated. In German mining tradition, which dates back to the Middle Ages, these spirits were believed to inhabit the rich veins of silver, copper, tin, and cobalt that drew generations of miners into the mountains. The connection between kobolds and mining is so strong that the element cobalt derives its name from the German word kobold, because the cobalt ore was considered worthless and was believed to be placed in the mines by mischievous kobolds to fool and frustrate miners. The Bergkobold represents the inherent danger and uncertainty of mining, the thin line between striking it rich and losing everything in a cave-in or flood

name: Bergr
description: Bergr is an Old Norse word used as a personal name meaning 'mountain' or 'rescuer, helper' (from bjarga). It is not independently attested in Icelandic folklore as a named spirit or supernatural being; references likely stem from confusion with saga personal names or with the bergrisar ('mountain giants') of Norse legend. Uncertainty should be assumed for this entry.

name: Bergsrået
description: The bergsrå (mountain rå) is a Swedish mountain spirit ruling over mines and mineral wealth. It appears as an elderly figure in miner's garb or fine court clothes, sometimes with rocky skin. It can reveal ore deposits to favored humans or cause bergtagning (abduction into the mountain). The 1691 trial of Sven Andersson for intercourse with a bergsrå is a famous historical record.

name: Bernardo Carpio
description: Bernardo Carpio is the Filipino equivalent of Hercules — a legendary giant with superhuman strength believed to be trapped between two great rocks in the mountains of Montalban (Rizal province). According to folklore, he was a Spanish-Filipino of immense size and power who single-handedly fought entire armies. When the Spanish authorities could not defeat him, they tricked him into a cave where a magical spell trapped him between two massive boulders. Every time he struggles to free himself, the earth trembles, causing earthquakes in the Philippines. The legend became a powerful symbol of Filipino resistance against colonial oppression, representing the unbreakable spirit of the Filipino people struggling for freedom

name: Bes
description: Unique Egyptian dwarf god (likely of Somali/Nubian origin, absorbed into Egyptian pantheon). One of the FEW non-anthropomorphic Egyptian gods - actually looks like a dwarf. Protector OF Households, mothers, children, Birth - a home's fierce guardian. NOT worshipped in temples (no clergy), but Every home (Pharaoh to slave) had Bes images. Placed at gates, on bedroom furniture, unguent jars, headrests, beds, chairs, mirrors, knives, amulets. Also: god of humor, JOY, music, fertility, Warfare. The Protective face - his grotesque features Terrify evil but comfort the family. Blue-skinned (magical power). Dances and rattles to scare evil - brings Laughter not just fear

name: Betal
description: A vampiric undead being from Indian folklore, particularly prominent in the Konkan region of Goa and Maharashtra. The Betal is a complex figure that hangs upside down from trees near cremation grounds and ancient battlefields, guarding occult knowledge and secrets of the dead. Unlike common ghosts, the Betal possesses a cunning intelligence and delights in riddles and philosophical debates. It is known to test the bravery and wisdom of those who dare approach it, sometimes rewarding clever individuals with supernatural gifts or hidden truths about the universe. The Betal is deeply tied to death rituals and is said to be unable to cross consecrated ground or enter spaces protected by proper funeral rites. In the famous Vikram-Vetala tales, King Vikramaditya must capture a Betal and engage in a series of riddle contests that reveal profound moral lessons about duty, honor, and the nature of reality

name: Betobeto-san
description: A Japanese yokai or supernatural entity from Nara and Shizuoka prefectures that manifests as an invisible presence following people who walk alone at night. Betobeto-san is one of the more benign yokai in Japanese folklore, causing no direct physical harm but creating an unsettling sense of being stalked through the darkness. The creature is said to prefer dark, rural roads and mountain paths, where its victims become aware of disembodied footsteps echoing behind them. The name Betobeto-san is onomatopoeic, deriving from the sticky or tacky sound of footsteps on a path. According to traditional belief, the correct response when hearing these footsteps is to step aside and politely say Go ahead, Betobeto-san, allowing the invisible being to pass. The yokai is deeply connected to the Japanese folk tradition of unseen spirits that inhabit the boundaries between the human world and the spirit realm

name: Bhand
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature as a ghost. Bhand (from Sanskrit bhanda, 'jester') names the traditional folk-entertainer communities of South Asia — jesters, mimics, and storytellers, including the satirical Bhand Pather theatre of Kashmir — not a vengeful spirit. The ghost narrative is fabricated; the genuine analogues are the bhoot and churail.

name: Bhoot
description: A bhoot is the ghost of a person who died violently, prematurely, or without proper funeral rites in South and Southeast Asian folklore, remaining earthbound to haunt the site of death. Referenced in Sanskrit texts such as the Garuda Purana and familiar across Hindu, Muslim, and Buddhist cultures, bhoots are warded off with rituals, charms, and priestly intervention.

name: Bhoot of Haveli
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No named 'Bhoot of Haveli' entity exists; the description is generic haunted-mansion filler. Havelis — the grand mansions of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab, and Uttar Pradesh — are real, and general bhoot lore attaches to many abandoned houses, but no specific mansion-ghost being is documented under this name.

name: Bhuta
description: A supernatural creature and restless ghost from the Indian subcontinent, deeply rooted in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions that span thousands of years. The Bhuta is the spirit of a deceased person who, due to a violent death, unfulfilled desires, improper funeral rites, or unfinished earthly business, remains trapped between worlds instead of proceeding to the afterlife or reincarnation. The concept of Bhuta encompasses a wide spectrum of supernatural beings, from genuinely malevolent spirits that actively seek to harm the living to confused entities simply trying to communicate their needs. Bhuta belief is particularly strong in South India, where the Bhuta Kola ritual tradition involves elaborate spirit possession ceremonies conducted by trained priests. These spirits are believed to have the power to influence the lives of the living, both positively when propitiated and negatively when angered or ignored

name: Bibi-Khanum
description: Bibi-Khanym, identified with Saray Mulk Khanum, Timur's chief wife, is the tragic royal lady behind Samarkand's great Friday mosque. Legend holds that she commissioned the Bibi-Khanym Mosque in 1399 as a surprise, then promised the architect a kiss that left a telltale mark; Timur's return doomed the enamored builder, and she died of grief. Her name crowns Central Asia's grandest monument.

name: Bida Serpent
description: Bida is the sacred seven-headed serpent of the Mande people, associated with the ancient Ghana Empire (Wagadu). According to legend, the prosperity of Wagadu depended on the serpent Bida, who demanded an annual sacrifice of a virgin maiden in exchange for abundant gold and three days of rain each year. The serpent lived in a well or cave near the capital, Koumbi Saleh. The pact was broken when a brave young man named Mamadi Sefe Dekote (or Amadu Sefe) rescued the intended sacrifice by decapitating Bida. As the serpent died, it cursed the land — the gold disappeared, the rains failed, and Wagadu declined. The Bida serpent story explains the fall of the Ghana Empire and the rise of the Mali Empire under Sundiata. It is a foundational myth of Mande history

name: Bieggolmmái
description: Bieggolmmái (the Wind Man) is the Sami god of wind and weather, one of the most important deities for reindeer herding and fishing peoples of Sapmi. He lives in a cave and holds two shovels — with one he releases wind from his cave, with the other he puts it back. According to the Nærøy manuscript, he had a shovel in his right hand to scoop wind back into his caves after it had blown enough, and a club in his left hand to chase the wind back out when needed. He was crucial for reindeer herding because reindeer travel into headwinds to avoid mosquitoes. A single wind direction persisting too long could drive reindeer far away, requiring a sacrifice — preferably a white reindeer — to Bieggolmmái. Some sources distinguish between Bieggolmmái (summer wind god) and Gissenolmmái (winter wind god who ruled over snow and ice). Tiny birch-bark boats with offerings were set adrift as sacrifices. The Inari Sami sacrificed to him at Piegg-oaivadz fells (the Heads of the Winds)

name: Big Red Ants
description: Big Red Ants are spirit beings in Pueblo mythology associated with industriousness, community cooperation, and the power of the earth. They are credited with teaching the Pueblo people the value of organized labor and collective effort, showing how small creatures working together can accomplish great feats — moving seeds, carrying water, and building vast underground colonies. During certain Pueblo ceremonies, red ant motifs appear in sandpaintings and pottery as symbols of hard work and earth energy. They are also believed to possess the power to heal rheumatic ailments through the application of crushed ant medicine

name: Big-Skeleton (Wokómásauwuu)
description: Wokómásauwuu, Big Skeleton, is a Hopi spirit related to Masauwu, the Skeleton Man and deity of death and the earth's surface. In the story of the Ahö'li Kachina, Big Skeleton meets the kachinas and tells them to make their homes atop the mesas. He is a powerful being to be acknowledged and respected in Hopi ceremonial narratives.

name: Bigorn
description: 'Bigorn' is not attested as a treasure-guarding serpent in Seychellois tradition. The name recalls La Bigorne, a beast of medieval French folktale, and an eighteenth-century corporal in the history of Ile Sainte-Marie; the modern 'treasure snake' framing appears in tourist guides and derivative retellings. Genuine Seychellois lore preserves figures such as Tizan, but this serpent is unattested.

name: Bila
description: Bila is the sun goddess in the mythology of the Adnyamathanha people of the Flinders Ranges in South Australia. According to Dreamtime stories, Bila was a woman who carried fire and traveled across the sky each day, bringing light and warmth to the world. She was known to be particularly fond of eating roasted kangaroo tails. One day, two men who were being pursued by Bila in her hunger transformed themselves into giant kangaroo rats and burrowed into the ground. Bila tried to follow them and caused a great fire, which the people had to extinguish through ceremonies. The story explains the origin of the fire that remains beneath the earth and the volcanic features of the Flinders Ranges. Bila's daily journey across the sky marks the cycle of day and night

name: Billy Lyons
description: William 'Billy' Lyons is the historical figure whose murder by Lee 'Stag' Shelton on Christmas night 1895 in a St. Louis saloon became the foundation of the Stagger Lee legend, one of the most enduring African American folk ballads. According to legend, Billy Lyons snatched Stagolee's prized Stetson hat, and when he refused to return it, Stagolee shot him dead. Billy begged for his life, pleading that he had a wife and children, but Stagolee replied he should have thought of them before touching his hat. Billy Lyons is the catalyst figure whose death launched a thousand versions of the ballad — his name forever linked to the most famous bad man in American folklore

name: Biskinik
description: Biskinik is the Choctaw 'little news bird,' identified with the yellow-bellied sapsucker. According to Choctaw tradition it was one of two birds (with Folichik, the scissor-tailed flycatcher) to escape the Great Flood, and afterward it served as a friend to the people, tapping messages on trees to warn of approaching visitors and danger. The Choctaw Nation's newspaper bears the bird's name.

name: Bison Ancestor-Spirit (Guarani)
description: No bison spirit belongs to Guarani tradition: bison never inhabited South America. Guarani cosmology includes the creator Tupa, Arasy, Karai, Jakaira, and the serpent Mboi, but no bison ancestor-spirit. The entry invents a 'sacred bison' narrative that conflates plains-bison symbolism of North America with Guarani beliefs.

name: Bison Ancestor-Spirit (Guarani)
description: Not independently attested: the entry assigns a Guarani spirit to Kenya and describes bison, animals of North America absent from both Guarani and Kenyan traditions. Guarani cosmology centers on figures such as Tupã and the twin culture heroes, while East African ancestors are honored through ngoma spirits.

name: Bison Ancestor-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are not native to the Northwest Coast, and no Kwakwaka'wakw ancestor-spirit is a bison. The Kwakwaka'wakw do hold real ancestor-founder spirits whose names, songs, and dances are potlatch privileges, but none is a bison figure; the entry invents the role through a claimed 'trade' route.

name: Bison Ancestor-Spirit of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Tlingit folklore. Bison did not occur in the Alaskan and American parts of Tlingit territory, and Tlingit ancestry follows the raven and wolf moieties and coastal animal clans. A bison-ancestor appears nowhere in the documented Tlingit traditions.

name: Bison Ancestor-Spirit of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Tlingit folklore. Bison were never part of Tlingit life on the Canadian side of their coastal homeland; Tlingit clans trace descent through the raven, wolf, eagle and other coastal creatures. No bison-ancestor figure appears in documented Tlingit oral tradition.

name: Bison Animal-Spirit of Aztec
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are absent from Aztec cosmology, and the entry grafts a bison spirit onto the tonal/nagual animal-companion beliefs recorded in sources like the Florentine Codex. Real Aztec animal spirits and deities — including the nagual shapeshifting and gods' animal forms — never include bison.

name: Bison Animal-Spirit of Quechua
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison never occurred in the Andes, and the claim that they did is false; the bison spirit set among Quechua apu mountain spirits and huaca shrines is invented. Genuine Quechua animal guides and mountain/earth powers exist, but none is a bison being.

name: Bison Animal-Spirit of Yurok
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are not native to Yurok territory on the lower Klamath River, and the entry invents a bison spirit 'known through trade' with no source. Yurok cosmology centers on the river, ocean, forest, and the Immortals who established ceremonies; no bison being appears in it.

name: Bison Deity (Shona)
description: Not independently attested. Bison do not occur in Zimbabwe, and no Shona deity of the bison appears in the ethnographic literature; the input itself errs by calling the bison a creature of the 'African savanna.' Shona spirit-lore centres on Mwari the creator, the mhondoro lion-spirits of dead chiefs and the Zambezi god Nyami Nyami; no buffalo or bison deity is named.

name: Bison Deity (Shona)
description: Not independently attested: Shona religion belongs to Zimbabwe, not Madagascar, and venerates Mwari as supreme being with the mhondoro (lion) ancestral spirits guarding the land; there is no bison deity. The buffalo (mhofu) appears in Shona totemic naming, and zebu cattle are valued in Madagascar, but the described bison deity is a fabricated cross-cultural mash-up with no source.

name: Bison Deity (Shona)
description: This entry pairs a Shona (southern African) buffalo figure with a Mexican country tag, an evident synthesis error. In Shona tradition, ancestral spirits (mhondoro) and lineage spirits may appear through animals, and the buffalo (njati) is respected for strength. The 'Bison Deity' name is a loose rendering of that animal-ancestor complex, not a Mexican or a named Shona deity.

name: Bison Deity of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Baloch have no water-buffalo deity; the Hingol River drought legend and milk-pouring rituals are fabricated, and the cited Turkic/Mongol source is mismatched. Real Baloch tradition centers on Islam and saint veneration, including the Hinglaj Mata shrine on the Hingol, not on any bovine deity.

name: Bison Deity of Choctaw
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Nanih Waiya emergence mound is genuine Choctaw tradition, but no Great Buffalo deity appears in Choctaw creation accounts; buffalo entered the Choctaw homeland relatively late. The agricultural bison-spirit role, hide-for-shelter migration story, and 'every part of the buffalo' teachings are invented.

name: Bison Ghost of Lakota
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The White Buffalo Calf Woman (Ptesáŋ Wiŋ) and white-buffalo symbolism are genuine Lakota traditions, but no 'Bison Ghost' omen, spirit-herd return, or Black Hills haunting is documented; the 'some elders say' framing signals invention. Real Lakota spirit beings (wanagi) are not bison ghosts.

name: Bison Giant of Lakota
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No primordial Bison Giant exists in Lakota tradition; the creation-story of a titan whose body forms the prairies and Black Hills is fabricated. Genuine Lakota narratives concern the White Buffalo Calf Woman and the sacred beings of the Black Hills (He Sapa), none of them a land-forming bison giant.

name: Bison Giant of Mapuche
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are not native to South America, and the volcano-dwelling, Pillan-linked bison giant is invented. Mapuche cosmology includes real ngen (masters of nature) and Pillan spirits of volcanoes and lightning, and the Nguillatun ceremony, but no bison being figures in it.

name: Bison Guardian (Yoruba)
description: Not independently attested. Bison do not occur in Nigeria, and no Yoruba guardian spirit associated with the bison appears in Yoruba orisha tradition or documented diaspora practice. The entry's account of a bison guardian among 'African Canadian' communities in Alberta and Saskatchewan is unsupported and appears fabricated; no Yoruba source names such a figure.

name: Bison Guardian (Yoruba)
description: Not independently attested as a guardian of Yoruba folklore. Bison play no role in Yoruba belief, whose powerful forest beings are the orisa and their attendants. American-diaspora retellings do not record a Yoruba bison-guardian; the entry appears AI-generated with no supporting source.

name: Bison Guardian (Yoruba)
description: Not independently attested as a guardian of Yoruba folklore. The bison is absent from Yoruba cosmology; Yoruba forest guardians and spirits are beings such as Esu, Ogun and the orisa of the wild, while divine buffalo-figures belong to Fon and Vodun traditions. This Canadian-diaspora entry appears to be a fabrication.

name: Bison Guardian of Aztec
description: The American bison never ranged into the Aztec (Mexica) homeland, so this 'Bison Guardian' is a composite invention. Aztec sources do honor earth and fertility powers, notably Cipactli, the primordial earth-crocodile, and Tlaltecuhtli, the earth goddess, to which the entry loosely attaches the bison. Post-contact cattle imagery entered later; this is a modern synthesis, not attested Aztec belief.

name: Bison Guardian of Inuit
description: Not independently attested as a guardian of Inuit folklore. Bison never reached traditional Inuit lands; the large grazer of the far north is the muskox (umingmak), not the buffalo. No Inuit bison-guardian appears in documented traditions, which instead feature beings such as Sedna and the tuurngait.

name: Bison Guardian of Ojibwe
description: Not independently attested as a guardian of Ojibwe folklore. The founding Ojibwe totem clans — crane, loon, bear, marten, deer, fish and bird — do not include the bison, which plays no clan or guardian role in the documented traditions. The bison-guardian of Ojibwe appears only in fabricated modern listings.

name: Bison Guardian of Ojibwe
description: Not independently attested as a guardian of Ojibwe folklore. The seven original Ojibwe doodem (totem) clans — crane, loon, bear, marten, deer, fish and bird — include no bison clan. No Ojibwe bison-guardian is documented in the standard clan accounts or spirit traditions.

name: Bison Nature-Spirit (Aztec)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The entry itself admits the spirit is a post-contact syncretic invention. Real Aztec nature powers — the tlaloqueh rain/earth spirits and Xipe Totec's renewal rites — are documented, but no bison nature-spirit appears in the Florentine Codex or other sources.

name: Bison Nature-Spirit of Cherokee
description: The underwater buffalo is a genuine mysterious being of Cherokee tradition, recorded by James Mooney: a lone buffalo seen rising from the waters of Cheowa River, which killed a man who threatened it and gave the place its name. The Buffalo Dance, performed in ceremony, further shows the buffalo as a powerful and honored presence in Cherokee life.

name: Bison Nature-Spirit of Zapotec
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The entry concedes there were no bison in pre-Columbian Oaxaca, then invents a 'pitao of the grasslands.' Zapotec pitao are genuine deities and spirits of nature, but none is a bison figure; the mountain-shrine offering role is fabricated.

name: Bison Spirit (Malagasy)
description: Not independently attested: Malagasy tradition holds cattle (zebu) and the ancestors (razana) sacred, but no 'bison spirit' is recorded in Malagasy folklore, and bison are not native to Madagascar. The description duplicates the Kenya variant of the same fabricated entry verbatim. The genuine related belief is respect for zebu and the fady (taboo) system, not a bison guardian spirit.

name: Bison Spirit (Malagasy)
description: Not independently attested: no Malagasy buffalo spirit is documented in Kenyan traditions, and the description restates the fabricated 'bison spirit of Madagascar' while reassigning it to Kenya. Malagasy reverence centers on the ancestors (razana) and zebu cattle; the 'African buffalo guardian' figure described has no recorded basis in either country's folklore.

name: Bison Spirit of Aztec
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The directional, color, maize, and Chicomecoatl associations assigned to a bison are fabricated; bison were unknown in Aztec cosmology. The teotl concept and the maize goddess Chicomecoatl are real, but never linked to bison, and no post-contact cattle integration is documented.

name: Bison Trickster (Olmec)
description: Bison did not inhabit the lands of the Olmec, and no Olmec bison trickster is attested. The entry recycles a generic 'bison trickster' template onto Olmec and even southern African frames. Mesoamerican tricksters are well documented among foxes, rabbits, and coyotes, but the bison form is a modern invention; the description should be read as a template artifact, not attested belief.

name: Bison Trickster (Olmec)
description: No Olmec or Brazilian bison trickster exists: bison are absent from Mesoamerica and South America, and the original text itself concedes the figure is not Olmec, describing a fabricated 'South African synthesis.' The entry is a mislabeled invention with no documentary basis.

name: Bison Trickster (Olmec)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Paraguayan or Olmec tradition. Bison never inhabited Paraguay nor the Gulf-Coast lands of the historical Olmec, and no source documents a bison spirit guarding waters; the input even concedes the figure is not Olmec. Paraguay's documented spirits are Kurupí, Pombero and the jaguar (yaguareté), not a bison.

name: Bison Trickster (Olmec)
description: Not independently attested. The entry pairs the Olmec, a Mesoamerican civilization, with South Africa: neither tradition records a bison trickster. The input's own text concedes the figure 'does not derive from Olmec tradition,' then invents a water-controlling bison of the dry season. Olmec religion centres on the were-jaguar; no such bison spirit exists in either culture.

name: Bison Trickster of Creek
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Creek (Muscogee) bison trickster exists; bison were marginal in the Southeast, and Creek trickster stories center on figures like Rabbit (Chukfi). The swamp-guardian, shape-shifting, and 'hard lessons' moralizing are invented with no named tradition.

name: Bison Trickster of Quechua
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Bison are not native to the Andes, and the puna-dwelling, lightning-linked trickster said to herald pachakuti is invented. Pachakuti (world-turning upheaval) and mountain apus are genuine Quechua concepts, but no bison being is recorded in Quechua tradition.

name: Bison Trickster of Shona
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Shona bison trickster exists; Shona trickster roles belong to the hare (Tsuro) and jackal, and the high god Mwari is served by human mediums (svikiro) at shrines, not by bison messengers. The granite-kopje illusion stories are invented.

name: Bison Trickster of Zulu
description: Not independently attested. Bison are a North American animal absent from Southern Africa, and no Zulu tradition records a bison trickster or a cliff-guardian of that name; the Drakensberg account is generic template prose. Zulu trickster-lore centres on the child uHlakanyana, the jackal and the hare, while the African buffalo (inyathi) marks chiefly power, not spirit.

name: Bison Water-Spirit of Cree
description: Not independently attested as a water-spirit of Cree folklore. Plains Cree tradition honors the buffalo covenant and Buffalo Woman teachings, but no bison water-spirit dwelling in muskeg swamps is documented. Cree water-beings are the great horned serpent and the spirit-mother of the lake, not a buffalo.

name: Bison Water-Spirit of Dogon
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Nommo are genuine Dogon ancestral water spirits, but no bison spring-guardian is recorded among them, and bison play no role in Dogon cosmology. The Bandiagara spring-keeper story is invented.

name: Bison Water-Spirit of Maya
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The entry itself describes the spirit as a fusion invented around the bison. Chaac is a genuine Maya rain deity but is never depicted with or served by a bison; the oceanic steed, Venus-link, and calendar-round associations are fabricated.

name: Biton
description: 'Biton' or 'Betón,' poetically called the 'Obsidian Butterfly,' is not attested in Dinka mythology. Its only source is an AI-content site; genuine Dinka tradition has no death spirit of this name or image. The attested Dinka cosmos centers on Nhialic, Deng, Abuk, and Garang, with ancestral Jok spirits and the great serpent Piath.

name: Bizango (Haitian Secret Society Spirits)
description: Bizango refers to both a powerful class of Petwo lwa (spirits) in Haitian Vodou and the secret societies that serve them. These are the most feared and potent spirits in the Vodou pantheon -- considered maximum Petro -- associated with skulls, coffins, crosses, and crucifixes. The Bizango spirits include formidable entities such as Baron Kriminel and Ezili Zandor. The Bizango secret societies trace their origins to the Maroons -- escaped slaves who resisted colonial rule from Haiti mountains. Their colors are red and black. They are reputed to serve as social enforcers within Vodou communities, administering justice, settling disputes, and punishing those who violate community codes. The most notorious aspect of Bizango practice is the creation of zombis -- using neurotoxic poisons (typically from pufferfish and other sources) to induce a catatonic state, then reviving the victim to serve as a laborer. Members are feared for their ability to shape-shift into dogs, cats, or other animals to walk the streets at night undetected

name: Bjarndýrakóngur
description: Bjarndýrakóngur (King of the Polar Bears) is a mythical polar bear king in Icelandic folklore, born from the union of a female polar bear and a walrus or a bull. The Bjarndýrakóngur has distinctive red cheeks and a single horn on its forehead tipped with a platinum globe that emits light. It understands human speech, speaks itself, and commands all other polar bears. Bjarndýrakóngur only kills in self-defense or as a judgment against those who have committed terrible crimes. The red-cheeked polar bears seen occasionally in Iceland were believed to be its subjects. The legend likely originated from occasional polar bear sightings in Iceland (polar bears drift on ice floes from Greenland) combined with Norse mythology about animal kings

name: Bjergfolk
description: Bjergfolkene (the Mountain Folk) are the Danish version of underworld beings who live inside ancient burial mounds (gravhøje). They appear as small people the size of 7-8 year old children, wearing red caps, who are seen dancing on mounds at twilight, cooking over invisible fires, and working as smiths inside the hills. Denmark has over 158 documented mound sites associated with Bjergfolk, cataloged by folklorist Evald Tang Kristensen. The Bjergfolk are known to exchange their own sickly children for human infants (creating changelings), and they can offer humans silver goblets that turn to leaves if not thrown back into the mound. Their churches become visible only at liminal hours. They must not be provoked — throwing stones at their mounds brings illness or bad luck

name: Bjära
description: Bjäran is a witch's familiar in Swedish folklore, created through a dark ritual. To make a Bjära, a witch takes nine threads of different colors, pricks her left pinky for blood, and recites incantations over the threads while crafting a creature that will serve her. The Bjära appears as a ball of yarn, a hare, a cat, or a bird, and its primary task is to steal milk from neighbors' cows, then return home and vomit the milk into a bucket (called a 'puke-chäl' or vomit bucket) for the witch to use. The Bjära cannot be killed by ordinary means — if caught and tortured, the pain transmits directly to its witch creator. The belief was especially strong in southern Sweden, where farmers would watch for yarn balls rolling across fields at dusk

name: Black Draugr
description: Not independently attested in Icelandic tradition. 'Black Draugr' appears a modern elaboration conflating standard draugr (corporeal undead of Norse folklore) with literary tropes. No saga or ethnographic source describes a distinct 'black' variant with scorched skin, freezing blue eyes, orchestrated misfortunes.

name: Black God (Haashchʼééshzhiní)
description: Black God (Haashchʼééshzhiní) is one of the most important Holy People in Navajo mythology, the deity of fire, medicine, and the night sky. He is credited with placing the constellations in their proper positions and teaching the Navajo the medicinal properties of fire. Black God carries a fire bag containing the sparks of creation, and from his torch the first sacred fire was lit. He is invoked in the Night Chant (Yéʼii ́ Bichéii), one of the most powerful Navajo healing ceremonies, which runs for nine nights and restores patients afflicted by spiritual illness. His face is painted black with soot from the sacred fire, symbolizing his dominion over night and the healing arts

name: Black Hactcin
description: Black Hactcin is the most powerful of the Hactcin holy beings in Jicarilla Apache creation tradition. He shaped the first four-legged animal from clay and made other animals from parts of its body, then created the first man from turquoise, coral, opal, jet, and abalone brought by the animals. He is a primordial maker and protector.

name: Black Rocks Mermaids
description: The Black Rocks Mermaids are vengeful and cunning sea spirits that inhabit the waters off Black Rocks, a rugged expanse of volcanic rock formations on the northeastern coast of St. Unlike the gentle mermaids of other cultures, these are dangerous sirens who lure unsuspecting sailors to their doom with enchanting songs and mesmerizing beauty. According to legend, a group of fishermen enticed by the siren call ventured too close to the rocks and disappeared without a trace, never to be seen again. Some Kittitians believe the mermaids are protectors of the island who ensure only those who respect the sea can traverse its waters safely. The volcanic rock formations at Black Rocks were created by ancient volcanic activity from Mount Liamuiga, adding a geological dimension to the supernatural legend

name: Black-Necked Crane Spirit (Thrung Thrung Karmo)
description: In Bhutan the black-necked crane (Grus nigricollis) is the soul of monks and nuns. Each October they circle Gangteng Monastery in the Phobjikha Valley three times clockwise — a Buddhist kora. The Sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso (1683–1706): 'Oh white crane, lend me your wings.' Killing a crane means life imprisonment, the harshest penalty in Bhutan. The November 11 festival marks their return.

name: Blak
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No pike spirit named 'Blak' exists in Finnish mythology. The description grafts an invented name onto the genuine Kalevala motif of the giant pike whose jawbone Väinämöinen used to make the first kantele; that pike is not a named, personalized being.

name: Blue Caps
description: Blue Caps (Unknown). is a fairy. Blue Caps (also known as Blue Bonnets) are mischievous household spirits from English folklore, particularly Northumberland. These small, blue-capped fairies work in mines or on farms and can be helpf. Source: English folklore; Northumberland oral tradition

name: Blue Heron (Táłtłʼááh álééh)
description: Blue Heron (Táłtłʼááh álééh) is a hero figure in Navajo mythology known for his role in the emergence stories and his gift of water to the people. He is one of the animal spirits who accompanied the Holy People during the journey through the underworlds, and his patience and determination in fishing the first water from the depths made life possible for humans on the surface world. Blue Heron is a symbol of stillness, focus, and self-reliance, and he is invoked by hunters and fishers who need patience and precision. His long, deliberate strides across shallow water teach the value of quiet perseverance

name: Blue Heron Coast Salish
description: In Lushootseed tradition of the southern Coast Salish, the Blue Heron is one of the myth-age beings remade by the Changer. In the Puyallup telling, the Changer finds Blue Heron splitting cedar for a canoe, striking the wood with his head and beating it with his hand while singing 'hand, hand, side of the head'; the encounter fixes the heron's form.

name: Blue Jay (Iqesqes)
description: Blue Jay (Iqesqes) is the trickster hero of the Chinook and southern Salishan peoples, a bright-feathered being who is benevolent but hopelessly foolish. He blunders into the Land of the Dead with his sister Ioi and, through disrespect, brings disaster, and his tales of the spirit world are told as warnings and slapstick.

name: Blue Jay Iqesqes Chinook
description: Iqesqes, the Blue Jay, is the trickster hero of Chinook, Chehalis, and Quinault stories along the lower Columbia. Benevolent but foolish, he stumbles through adventures with slapstick results, visiting the land of the dead in the tale of Blue Jay and Ioi, finding a wife, and helping recover the stolen sun. His bungling often sets things right by accident.

name: Blue Wolf (Börte Chino)
description: Börte Chino, the Blue-Grey Wolf, is the divine ancestor of the Mongols. According to the Secret History of the Mongols, the wolf and the doe Qo'ai Maral came together in love, crossed the sea, and settled at the head of the Onon river near the holy mountain Burkhan Khaldun, where their descendants, the Mongol people, arose.

name: Bluecap
description: In the mining folklore of the Anglo-Scottish borders, the bluecap is a mine spirit of the brownie kind, appearing as a small blue flame that moved loaded coal tubs like a putter. Treated with respect and paid its due wages, it helped miners; cheated, it withheld its aid. Scottish and English pitmen shared the tradition along the border coalfields.

name: Bluecap
description: The bluecap is a mine spirit of the Northumberland and Durham coalfields (Anglo-Scottish border), seen as a small blue flame that worked as a supernatural putter hauling loaded coal tubs. It expected a putter's wage left in a corner, accepting no more or less, and could lead miners to rich seams or warn of cave-ins. At Shilbottle Colliery it was also called the Blue Bonnet.

name: Bluejay Coast Salish
description: Blue Jay is the trickster of Coast Salish and southern Salishan tradition, a clever but reckless bird-being whose adventures cross between the human and spirit worlds. Told by the Saanich and neighboring peoples, he is helpful yet foolish, and his brushes with the supernatural carry warnings about proper conduct.

name: Bo Usu
description: Bo Usu are powerful forest spirits in Baoulé mythology of Ivory Coast that inhabit the 'bo' — the forest corridors lining streams and rivers, as distinct from the open savannah. These supernatural beings, described as genies, pixies, and entities with magical powers, are specifically invoked by hunters to ensure successful hunts. Hunters commission specialized wooden statuettes called Bo Usu figures, which are intentionally carved with a coarse, rugged aesthetic featuring prominent human sexual anatomy and anthropomorphic features. These figures are treated with sacrificial bird blood, eggshell pieces, and kaolin dust to activate their spiritual power. After a successful hunt, hunters offer animal entrails to the Bo Usu spirits as thanks. The Bo Usu represent the Baoulé belief that the forest is inhabited by powerful non-human intelligences that must be respected and propitiated for humans to safely exploit its resources. These figures are placed at multiple locations outside the hunter's home to attract prey

name: Bodu Naga (Maldivian Sea Serpent)
description: Bodu Naga is a great serpent spirit in Maldivian folklore that inhabits lagoons, reefs, and deep channels between the Maldivian atolls. The name means 'Great Serpent' in Divehi (Bodu = big/great, Naga = serpent). In pre-Islamic Maldives, nagas were revered as powerful nature spirits associated with the waters that surrounded the atolls. Bodu Naga is described as a guardian of the sea, protecting certain channels, passes, and reefs. Fishermen offered prayers and small offerings before venturing into waters believed to be guarded by Bodu Naga to ensure safe passage and abundant catch. The entity is part of a broader Maldivian tradition of spirit beings (handi, fureytha, dhevi, and fan'du) that could appear in human form — often as beautiful women or well-built men — to lure humans into danger. Bodu Naga reflects the ancient Dravidian naga worship that existed in the Maldives before the advent of Buddhism and later Islam, sharing similarities with serpent traditions across South India and Sri Lanka. The nagas were said to have been subdued as Buddhism spread through the Indian Ocean, but their stories persist in folklore about dangerous waters and forbidden reefs

name: Bodu Niyami Kalefanu
description: A figure of Maldivian folklore, part of a class of malevolent spirits alongside beings such as fureytha and dagas. Maldivian oral tradition describes various supernatural beings believed to inhabit the islands, the sea, and the uninhabited outer atolls, often invoked in cautionary tales and protective practices. Published documentation of this specific figure is limited.

name: Boggart
description: The boggart is a mischievous and often malevolent household spirit of northern English folklore, especially Lancashire and Yorkshire, that hides objects, spoils food, and makes night noises to torment a family. Tied to a house rather than a person, it is hard to drive away; flaxseed scattering or moving house may fail, as the boggart can follow.

name: Boginka
description: Female Slavic nature spirit of Polish folklore, of forests, fields, lakes, rivers. The name from 'bóg' (god) marks these as minor nature goddesses. Boginki are beautiful enchantresses or hideous hags — broader than the Rusalki (drowned-maiden spirits). They guard wildlife, punishing sport hunting, plant theft, and disrespect; to the respectful they grant fertility, harvests, or protection.

name: Bohpoli
description: Bohpoli, meaning the Thrower, also called Kowi Anukasha, the Forest Dweller, are little people of the Choctaw who live alone in the thick, dark woods. About two feet tall, they throw sticks at travelers and are mischievous, yet they are said to share medicine knowledge with those who treat the woods with respect. Documented by Swanton.

name: Boiadeira
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature as a water serpent. The name (feminine of boiadeiro, 'cattle driver') labels the real Brazilian class of cowboy spirits — the Boiadeiros of Umbanda and the bumba-meu-boi ox-festival tradition — but the great black serpent described is the Cobra Grande/Boiúna of Amazonian legend, mislabeled here.

name: Boitatá
description: Boitatá is a legendary fire serpent from Brazilian folklore, deeply rooted in the mythology of the Tupi-Guarani indigenous people and later incorporated into broader Brazilian folk tradition. The name 'Boitatá' comes from the Tupi words 'mboi' (snake) and 'tata' (fire), literally meaning 'fire snake.' Boitatá is a protector spirit of the forests and fields, particularly active during the dry season when wildfires are most common. According to legend, Boitatá was once a giant, blind serpent that survived a great flood by crawling into a hollow log. When the waters receded, the serpent emerged with its eyes damaged by darkness but gained the power to see through fire, developing a body that glowed like living flame. The creature now patrols the wilderness, devouring the ashes of burned areas and consuming the rotting remains of dead animals to return their nutrients to the earth. Boitatá is fundamentally a benevolent entity focused on environmental renewal, using its fiery body to burn away decay and make way for new growth. However, its fiery nature makes it dangerous to humans who approach too closely or threaten the forests it protects

name: Bolotnik
description: The Bolotnik ('Swamp Spirit') is a malevolent spirit of Belarusian and western Russian folklore, the name from 'boloto,' Slavic for swamp. Unlike the Vodyanoy of deep waters, he haunts shallow, unstable bogs and marshes. Said to be the soul of a drowned person or one cursed to guard the wetlands, he seizes travelers' ankles from beneath and drags them into the peat, bodies never found.

name: Bolukun
description: Note: This entry is being added with slug bolukun-yoruba but may be a variant of Olokun, who already exists in the database. Bolukun is a regional Yoruba variant name for the orisha of the ocean depths. Bolukun represents the unfathomable depths of the sea and the mysterious, untamed aspects of water. As the ruler of the great waters, Bolukun controls the tides, marine life, and the hidden treasures of the ocean floor. This entity is often considered the source of extreme wealth from the sea (including the slave trade era wealth) but also represents the danger and unpredictability of deep waters. Offerings are made to Bolukun for safe sea voyages and abundant fishing

name: Bon Bibi
description: Bon Bibi (Bonobibi), 'Lady of the Forest,' is the guardian goddess of the Sundarbans mangrove delta between Bangladesh and India, worshipped by Hindu and Muslim honey collectors, woodcutters, and fishermen. Legend holds that Allah sent her to protect the faithful from Dakshin Ray, the demon king who demanded sacrifices; she defeated him and won a truce, guarding all who enter with respect.

name: Bonbibi
description: Bonbibi (Unknown). is a spirit. Bonbibi is the guardian spirit of the forests in the Sundarbans region of Bengal. She is revered by Hindu and Muslim communities alike as the protector against the dangers of the mangrove forest, part. Source: Bengali folklore; Sundarbans oral tradition

name: Bones Together
description: Bones Together is a fearsome monster in Crow mythology, a skeletal being with impenetrable bone armor. Seven Bison and their human companion fought against Bones Together when the monster threatened them. Each bison charged but broke their legs against Bones Together's bony hide. Finally the human companion, blessed by an eagle with the power to transform into a feather, faced the monster. Bones Together charged four times, but the man turned into a feather and wafted out of harm's way. On the fourth charge, the man shot an arrow into Bones Together's rectum, piercing his heart and killing the monster

name: Boo Hag
description: The Boo Hag is a terrifying supernatural entity from Gullah Geechee folklore. Unlike European vampires that drink blood, Boo Hags drain their victims' breath and spiritual essence by 'riding' them while they sleep. According to legend, a Boo Hag appears as a beautiful woman by day — luring victims into marriage or trust — but at night, she removes her skin and transforms into a skinless, red, flying creature. She slips through keyholes or cracks to sit on her victim's chest and steal their breath. The only protection against a Boo Hag is to sprinkle salt, pepper, or rice around the room, as she will be compelled to count every grain before reaching her victim. Gullah homes famously paint doors and windows 'haint blue' to confuse and repel these entities

name: Boqs (Cannibal Giant)
description: Boqs is the hairy wild man of the woods of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola), a giant sasquatch-like being of the British Columbia coast whose hands and face are human. He walks stooping, can raise the very land by supernatural power, and was said to still haunt King Island; Boas recorded detailed first-hand accounts.

name: Boqs Cannibal Giant Nuxalk
description: Boqs is the wild man of the woods in Bella Coola (Nuxalk), Chinook, and Salish tradition, a shaggy forest being of great strength. In Nuxalk and northern Salish versions he is a malevolent cannibal who may harm or abduct people, while some Chinook stories treat him more lightly as a strong but foolish wild man. Popular writing sometimes equates him with the Sasquatch.

name: Bori (Iskoki)
description: Bori (also Iskoki) are spirit beings from Hausa animism, particularly strong among the Mawri people of Dogondoutchi in Niger and the Maguzawa of northern Nigeria. According to Mawri creation mythology, God created a man and woman who bore fifty sets of twins. When God asked to see the children, the woman hid the better-looking twin of each set in a cave. God cursed the hidden children to become spirits in the unseen world, forever invisible yet dependent on their human siblings for sustenance. The visible children must placate these spirit siblings with offerings or risk being haunted. Bori spirits inhabit natural features and are accessed through elaborate possession ceremonies

name: Bortbyting
description: Bortbytingen (the swapped one) is a changeling — a troll infant left in place of a human baby stolen by trolls or the underground folk. In Swedish folklore, the Bortbyting is ugly, sickly, and never grows properly. It has an enormous appetite and cries constantly, but also displays unnaturally adult behavior — it may speak in rhymes, comment on events it should not understand, or recite knowledge no infant could possess. Parents could identify a Bortbyting through tests: offering to brew beer in an eggshell (the changeling might comment on how old it is), or threatening to slaughter a pig in front of it. The changeling's true parent would then bring the human child back. The belief was widespread across all of Sweden

name: Boruta
description: Powerful forest and swamp spirit of Polish mythology, tutelary of central and eastern Poland's woodlands — the Puszcza Kurpiowska. Unlike the Leshy, Boruta is a nobleman (szlachcic) who pacted with dark forces and haunts the forests; his name derives from Old Polish 'bor' (pine forest). He leads astray hunters, illegal loggers, and mushroom pickers, yet guides lost children home.

name: Botamochi bakemono
description: An obscure yokai said to haunt old wooden houses. The name pairs 'botamochi' (a spring-equinox sweet rice cake) with 'bakemono' ('transforming thing'). It lives under the floorboards, mimicking human voices to confuse, frighten, or amuse — imitating family at night. Unlike malevolent oni or yurei, it is a harmless prankster, among 'house yokai' like the Zashiki-warashi and Makura-kashi.

name: Boto
description: The Boto (Encantado) is the Amazon river dolphin shapeshifter of Brazilian Amazon folklore. At night it becomes a handsome man in white clothing with a hat hiding its blowhole, attends riverside festivals, seduces women, and returns to the river by dawn. Children from these unions are 'filhos do boto.

name: Bottler
description: The Bottler is a malevolent water spirit from Dutch folklore, particularly known in the rural provinces of Brabant and Zeeland. Often called the Flodder or Watervlodder, this nocturnal tormentor lurks in polders, ditches, and soggy pastures, waiting for unsuspecting travelers who venture too close to the water after dark. It is said that the creature earns its name from the wet, slapping sound it makes when it emerges from the water onto dry land, a noise witnesses describe as similar to a barking otter or a heavy fish flopping onto mud

name: Botu
description: The Botu is a mischievous tree-dwelling imp or goblin from Nepalese folklore, particularly known in the rural hill regions and among the Newar communities of the Kathmandu Valley. These small forest spirits are considered harmless tricksters rather than malevolent beings, inhabiting the branches of banyan trees, rocky outcrops, and dense thickets near villages. The Botu shares similarities with other South Asian nature spirits and is often blamed for minor household misfortunes and unexplained noises in the night

name: Bou Saadia
description: Bou Saadia (Father of Saadia) is a tragic folkloric figure from Tunisian tradition, particularly associated with the medina of Tunis and Stambeli ritual performances. According to legend, Bou Saadia came from sub-Saharan Africa in search of his daughter Saadia, who was sold into slavery in Tunis. He is described as a man who went mad with grief, wandering door to door in the medina, humming and dancing, searching for his lost child. His appearance is striking — black skin, leather clothes covered with cowrie shells, and brusque bodily movements that frightened local children. The story reflects Tunisia's history of trans-Saharan slavery, which continued until the early 20th century. No one knows exactly when the legend originated, but Bou Saadia never finds Saadia and is said to continue his eternal search. During Ramadan, he appears in street performances as part of Stambeli rituals (a Tunisian trance-healing tradition with sub-Saharan roots). The legend explores themes of loss, displacement, and the enduring trauma of slavery in Tunisian society

name: Bouda
description: The bouda (buda) is the Ethiopian werehyena and evil-eye figure: a person, traditionally a blacksmith, potter or other artisan of stigmatized castes, believed to possess the evil eye and to transform into a hyena at night, often to dig up graves or harm enemies.

name: Boukhencha
description: Boukhencha (Unknown). is a spirit. Boukhencha is a figure from Moroccan folklore, often described as a terrifying creature that appears at night to frighten children. Such figures serve as cautionary elements in Moroccan oral tradition. Source: Moroccan oral tradition; North African folklore

name: Bouki (Haitian Trickster Hyena)
description: Bouki is the slow-witted, greedy hyena trickster of Haitian folklore -- the eternal foil to the clever Rabbit (or Malis/Connen, the rabbit trickster). In classic Haitian folktales, Bouki is always scheming for an easy meal or some treasure, and he is always outsmarted by the clever rabbit, suffering humiliation or injury. Bouki represents the dangers of greed, gluttony, and stupidity. Unlike the clever Anansi or the sneaky Malis rabbit, Bouki thinks he is cunning but is fundamentally foolish. His name derives from the Wolof word mbouki (hyena) from Senegal, proving his West African origins. Bouki tales were brought to Haiti by enslaved Senegambians and remain a staple of Haitian oral tradition -- they are told in Haitian Creole (Kreyol) and used to teach children moral lessons about generosity, honesty, and the consequences of greed. The name Bouki is a common Creole insult in Haiti, meaning someone foolish or easily tricked

name: Bouki (Hyena)
description: Bouki the Hyena is the greedy, foolish, and constantly hungry foil to Leuk the Hare in Wolof folklore. Bouki is the classic trickster's dupe — always falling for Leuk's schemes due to her insatiable appetite and lack of foresight. In each tale, Bouki's greed, laziness, and carelessness lead to her downfall. Whether building a ladder, making a cooking pot, or thatching a roof, Bouki rushes her work while Leuk does it properly — and Bouki inevitably suffers the consequences. Bouki also appears in stories with other characters, such as the old woman whose magic horn she borrows and never returns. Despite her constant failures, Bouki never learns, making her the perfect vehicle for Wolof moral lessons about the consequences of greed, laziness, and dishonesty

name: Boumba
description: Not independently attested as a spirit: 'Boumba' is chiefly a toponym in southeastern Cameroon, the Boumba River and Boumba-Bek National Park, and no Bantu forest guardian of that name appears in documented sources. The description is a generic filler portrait of a forest-protector spirit.

name: Bouti
description: The Bouti is a fearsome ogress or she-demon from the folklore of the Afar people of Djibouti, Ethiopia, and Eritrea. According to legend, the Bouti is a shape-shifting female monster held responsible for death, dishonor, fratricide, and familial discord among the Afar. Her legend is so powerful that the name of the country Djibouti is said by some to derive from the phrase defeat of Bouti, following a legendary hero who supposedly vanquished the creature. The Bouti embodies chaos and destruction within the family unit, serving as a cautionary figure about the dangers of unchecked malice

name: Bow priests (Awonawilona's sons)
description: In Ruth Benedict's version of the Zuni emergence, the people lived in darkness in the fourth world and recognized Awonawilona's two sons, the twin war gods, as their bow priests. The bow priests led the people upward, planting prayer sticks that grew into ladders, and shaped human bodies, cutting mouths, fingers, and toes and removing horns and tails.

name: Br'er Bear
description: Br'er Bear is a figure of African American folktale, one of the animal characters of the Uncle Remus cycle set down by Joel Chandler Harris from stories carried from West Africa. Slow-witted and gullible, he is strong but easily led, and both Br'er Rabbit and Br'er Fox trick him; he embodies brute strength without cunning.

name: Br'er Buzzard
description: Br'er Buzzard is a trickster character in African American folklore, particularly in Gullah Geechee traditions. As a buzzard (vulture), he is associated with death, transformation, and the sacred. In Gullah belief, the buzzard is not merely a carrion eater but a sacred bird that carries souls back to Africa. This connects directly to the Flying Africans legend, where the Igbo captives who drowned at Dunbar Creek were said to have transformed into buzzards and flown home. Br'er Buzzard's high-soaring perspective makes him a witness to events that others miss

name: Br'er Fox
description: Br'er Fox is the primary antagonist in the Br'er Rabbit cycle of African American folktales. A cunning predator who constantly schemes to capture and eat Br'er Rabbit, Br'er Fox is consistently foiled by the rabbit's superior cleverness. Despite being faster, stronger, and more dangerous, Br'er Fox's arrogance and gullibility make him an easy mark for Br'er Rabbit's tricks. In the most famous tale, Br'er Fox crafts the Tar-Baby to trap Br'er Rabbit, only to be outwitted when Br'er Rabbit begs not to be thrown into the briar patch — the one place where he thrives. Br'er Fox represents the powerful oppressor who cannot understand the cleverness of the oppressed

name: Br'er Rabbit
description: Br'er Rabbit is the central trickster figure in African American folklore, a small but cunning rabbit who uses his wits to overcome larger, stronger adversaries. Originating from West African hare trickster tales (particularly the Senegal-Benin region), Br'er Rabbit was adapted by enslaved Africans in the American South as a symbol of clever resistance against oppression. The name 'Br'er' is a contraction of 'Brother.' Br'er Rabbit's adventures — escaping the Tar-Baby, outsmarting Br'er Fox and Br'er Bear, and using reverse psychology to be thrown into the briar patch where he was 'bred and born' — encode the survival strategies of an enslaved people who could not rely on physical strength to overcome their oppressors

name: Br'er Terrapin
description: Br'er Terrapin (the turtle) appears in one of the most beloved African American folktales, where he outruns the much faster Br'er Rabbit through clever strategy rather than speed. When Br'er Rabbit mocks Br'er Terrapin for his slow pace, Br'er Terrapin challenges him to a race. Unable to match Br'er Rabbit's speed, Br'er Terrapin stations his wife and family members at intervals along the course. At each mile marker, when Br'er Rabbit calls out, a terrapin voice answers back, making Br'er Rabbit believe Br'er Terrapin is always ahead. Br'er Rabbit runs himself to exhaustion while Br'er Terrapin crosses the finish line first

name: Br'er Wolf
description: Br'er Wolf is a figure of African American folktale from the Uncle Remus cycle compiled by Joel Chandler Harris, a hungry and determined predator who hunts Br'er Rabbit but is repeatedly outwitted. Persistent yet lacking cunning, he loses to the rabbit's tricks, reinforcing the theme that wit defeats strength.

name: Brag
description: The Brag is a mischievous shapeshifting goblin from the folklore of Northumbria, Northumberland, and County Durham, particularly associated with the border regions between England and Scotland. Unlike many other fairy steeds, the Brag is not a water horse like the kelpie but rather a land-dwelling trickster that delights in humiliating humans. The most famous example is the Picktree Brag, which was said to haunt the area near Picktree in County Durham and was known for its shape-shifting abilities and wicked sense of humor

name: Brahma Raksha
description: The Brahma Raksha is a sacred guardian spirit from Indian Hindu folklore, believed to be the benevolent spirit of a deceased Brahmin priest who watches over and protects Brahmin families and their households. Unlike the more dangerous Brahma Rakshasa, the Brahma Raksha is a positive, protective entity bound by dharma to safeguard its charges. This spirit represents the concept of ancestral guardianship, where the soul of a righteous individual continues to fulfill its duties even after death, serving as a bridge between the living and the divine

name: Brahma Rakshasa
description: The Brahma Rakshasa is a powerful and dangerous demon from Indian Hindu mythology, born either from the yawn of the god Brahma or from the cursed soul of a Brahmin who lived a wicked life. Unlike ordinary rakshasas, the Brahma Rakshasa possesses immense knowledge of the Vedas, mantras, and sacred texts, making it both highly intelligent and exceptionally dangerous. It is considered one of the most formidable types of rakshasas in Hindu folklore, feared for its supernatural powers and insatiable hunger for human flesh

name: Brer Coon
description: Brer Coon is a character of African American folktale from the Uncle Remus cycle compiled by Joel Chandler Harris, a raccoon figure drawn from West African trickster stories carried into the American South. He appears alongside Brer Rabbit and Brer Possum in comic tales of cunning, deceit, and hard lessons.

name: Brer Possum
description: Brer Possum is a character of African American folktale, one of the animal figures of the Uncle Remus cycle written down by Joel Chandler Harris from stories brought from West Africa by enslaved people. As Brer Rabbit's neighbor he is sly and slow, frequently outwitted yet resilient, a trickster of the American South rather than a Native American figure.

name: Brockengespenst
description: The Brockengespenst, or Brocken Spectre, is an atmospheric optical phenomenon observed on the Brocken mountain in the Harz range of Germany, where it has inspired folklore and legends for centuries. First scientifically described by Johann Silberschlag in 1780, the phenomenon occurs when a climber or observer stands on a ridge or peak with the sun behind them and mist or fog below, casting an enormous, magnified shadow onto the cloud layer. The Brocken, the highest peak in the Harz Mountains at 1,141 meters, is particularly prone to the frequent fogs and low clouds that create this ghostly effect

name: Brugmo (Gesar's Queen)
description: Brugmo (Brug-gu-ma), Queen of Ling, is the central heroine of the Tibetan Epic of King Gesar. Won as the prize of the great horse race that revealed Gesar's true kingship, she is later seized by the king of Hor, and her rescue drives one of the epic's longest campaigns. Noble, loyal, and strong-willed, she is a reincarnated heavenly being sent to aid the hero.

name: Brunnsgubbe
description: Brunnsgubben (well old man) is the male guardian spirit of wells, springs, and natural water sources in Swedish folklore. Every well has its Brunnsgubbe, who ensures the water stays clean and plentiful if treated with respect. He punishes those who pollute the well, spit into it, or wash dirty items in its water by causing the well to dry up, the water to turn murky, or misfortune to befall the household. Offerings of bread, cheese, or a coin tossed into the well keep him favorable. In some traditions, he reveals the location of healing springs to those who are pure of heart. Brunnsgubben is distinct from the Näcken (who lives in running water) — Brunnsgubben guards still, gathered water that serves the community

name: Bruxa
description: The Bruxa is a witch or sorceress from Galician folklore in northwestern Spain and northern Portugal, embodying both healing and harmful magical traditions. The term Bruxa encompasses a complex figure that can be either a benevolent healer known for herbal remedies and midwifery or a malevolent practitioner of black magic who curses enemies and steals children.
