This dual nature reflects the ambivalent position of wise women and folk healers in Galician rural society, where they were both respected for their knowledge and feared for their potential to cause harm

name: Bu Darya
description: Bu Darya, meaning Father of the Sea in Arabic, is a malevolent water demon from Kuwaiti and Persian Gulf maritime folklore. This sea-dwelling entity is feared by sailors and fishermen across the Gulf region, blamed for shipwrecks, drownings, and the mysterious disappearance of those who venture too far from shore. The legend of Bu Darya reflects the dangers of life at sea for Gulf pearl divers and fishermen, serving as a supernatural explanation for the many lives lost to the waters of the Arabian Gulf

name: Bu Draeyah
description: Bu Draeyah is a giant sea serpent of Qatari legend, deep blue of scale with glowing golden eyes, who guards the pearl beds of the Persian Gulf. He is a water spirit of harsh judgement: generous to honest divers, destructive to the greedy who strip his reefs. Sacred chants are said to soothe him, and his name is still spoken in pearl-diving households.

name: Bu Draya
description: Bu Draya (also Bu Daryā, meaning 'Father of the Sea' from Persian) is a terrifying sea jinn from Bahraini and Arabian Gulf folklore. Believed to be a malevolent water spirit, Bu Draya appears in the darkest nights to prey on pearl divers and sailors. Described as a huge half-human, half-amphibious creature, it summons winds and controls waters to capsize boats. Its most notorious trick is mimicking drowning cries at night — when a sailor jumps in to rescue what sounds like a comrade, Bu Draya seizes and devours them. According to Bahraini tradition, if sailors recognize Bu Draya aboard their vessel, they must shout for axes and saws (al-jadum wal-minshar), which frightens the creature back into the sea. The legend is intimately tied to Bahrain's pearling heritage, serving as both a cautionary tale and an explanation for the dangers of the sea

name: Bucca
description: The Cornish Bucca is a male sea-spirit merman specific to the folklore of Cornwall, particularly associated with Lamorna Cove and the coastal mining communities of West Cornwall. This version of the Bucca is believed to once have been a human prince cursed by a witch to live as a sea creature, making him a tragic figure torn between two worlds. The Cornish Bucca inhabits both the coastal waters and the flooded tin mines that run beneath the sea, serving as a guardian of miners as well as fishermen

name: Buda
description: Buda (Ge'ez: ቡዳ) is a powerful and feared figure in Eritrean and Ethiopian folk religion, representing the supernatural power of the evil eye combined with the ability to shapeshift into a hyena. The belief is deeply rooted in the highland cultures of Eritrea, particularly among Tigrinya-speaking communities. Buda is believed to be a power held and wielded by specific individuals, often associated with marginalized social groups such as metalworkers (täbbäb), potters, tanners, and weavers. The power is thought to be hereditary, transmitted through family lines, and can be either conscious or unconscious. Those with Buda can harm others through their gaze, causing illness, misfortune, or even death. By night, they are believed to transform into hyenas to attack livestock, desecrate graves, or harm enemies. Protective measures including amulets (kitab), holy water, and invocations of God's name are used to ward against Buda's effects

name: Buda
description: Buda (Ge'ez: ቡዳ) is the Eritrean-Ethiopian belief in the evil eye wielded by hereditary social groups, often metalworkers, potters, and tanners, who harm others through their gaze and are said to shapeshift into hyenas at night. Protective amulets (kitab), holy water, and invocations of God's name ward off its effects.

name: Buda
description: Buda (Tigrinya). is a shapeshifter. Buda is a shapeshifter from Tigrinya folklore in Eritrea, believed to embody the spiritual traditions of the region.. Source: Tigrinya oral tradition

name: Buffalo People
description: The Buffalo People are significant spirit beings in Cheyenne mythology and oral traditions, representing the deep spiritual connection between the Cheyenne people and the American bison, which was central to their way of life on the Great Plains. These sacred beings are not merely animals but intelligent, spiritual entities with their own society, customs, and medicine power. The Buffalo People taught the Cheyenne important ceremonies and hunting practices, and their stories emphasize the reciprocal relationship between humans and buffalo, where respect and gratitude must be shown for the buffalo's sacrifice in providing food, shelter, and tools

name: Buffalo Spirit
description: The Buffalo Spirit (Tatanka) is one of the most powerful and revered animal spirits in Lakota mythology. The buffalo is considered a relative of the Lakota people and a source of life, providing food, clothing, shelter, and tools. Buffalo spirits appear in many stories—as the buffalo people who intermarry with humans, as spirit guides in vision quests, and as the ultimate gift from the Creator. The White Buffalo Calf Woman is the most sacred manifestation of the buffalo spirit. The buffalo also appears as one of the Wakan Kuya (lesser sacred beings)

name: Buffalo Woman
description: Buffalo Woman is a revered figure in Kiowa mythology, serving as a powerful symbol of the sacred relationship between the Kiowa people and the buffalo herds that sustained them on the southern Great Plains. In Kiowa oral tradition, Buffalo Woman appears as a liminal being who bridges the human and animal worlds, often bringing important teachings, prophecies, or warnings to the people. Her stories reinforce the Kiowa understanding that buffalo are not merely resources but relatives with their own intelligence, spirituality, and agency in the cosmic order

name: Bukavac
description: The Bukavac is a demonic aquatic monster from Serbian and broader Slavic mythology, particularly associated with the region of Syrmia in modern-day Serbia. The creature's name derives from the Serbian word buka, meaning noise, referring to the terrifying sounds it makes as it emerges from its watery lair at night. The Bukavac is one of several lake-dwelling monsters in Slavic folklore, feared by those living near isolated lakes and ponds, where it was blamed for unexplained drownings and the mysterious disappearance of livestock near water's edge

name: Bukha Noyon
description: Bukha Noyon is the celestial bull of Buryat tradition, a totemic progenitor who descended from the sky to create and defend the western Buryat clans. Fought and beloved, he is said to have shaped the land with his body and to have become the ancestor of the Bulagat tribe. Sacred sites in Buryatia still receive offerings to this powerful bull-god.

name: Bukit Timah Monkey Man
description: The Bukit Timah Monkey Man (BTM) is Singapore's most famous cryptid, said to inhabit the Bukit Timah Nature Reserve. Described as an upright-walking monkey-faced hominid standing 1-2 meters tall, the creature has been reportedly sighted since 1805, with the most recent report in 2020. During World War II, Japanese soldiers claimed to have seen the creature. Despite extensive folklore and media coverage, expeditions have failed to produce conclusive evidence. The reserve suggests misidentified macaques, but believers point to the creature's size and upright posture as distinguishing features

name: Buku Spirits
description: Buku spirits are powerful and volatile forest-dwelling supernatural beings in the mythology of the Jola (Diola) people of Senegal, particularly in the Casamance region. These spirits inhabit the sacred forests, groves, and wilderness areas that surround Jola villages, acting as both guardians and potential threats. The Buku are deeply feared and revered for their unpredictable nature and for their intimate connection to the mysteries of the bush — the untamed wilderness that exists beyond human settlements. They are associated with initiation rituals, traditional healing, and the maintenance of social order. When properly propitiated, Buku spirits can offer protection, guidance, and fertility to the community. However, if offended through violations of taboos or disrespect to sacred spaces, they can bring illness, misfortune, or even death. The Buku embody the Jola worldview that the natural world is filled with powerful, sentient forces that demand respect and careful negotiation. Their worship involves secret society ceremonies, offerings at sacred groves, and the guidance of ritual specialists who serve as intermediaries

name: Bukwus (Wild Man of the Woods)
description: Bukwus (Bakwas) is the wild man of the woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a small green spirit with a skeletal face and long curving nose. He prowls the deep forests, whistling to lure the living toward the realm of the dead; some accounts name him the husband of Dzunukwa, the Cannibal Woman, and his masked figure appears in the winter ceremonial.

name: Bukwus Wild Man Of The Woods Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Bukwus (Bakwas) is the wild man of the woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a small, green-skinned ghost-king with a skeletal face and long curving nose. He prowls the forests, whistling to lure the living toward the realm of the dead; some accounts name him the husband of Dzunukwa, the Cannibal Woman.

name: Bulgasari
description: Bulgasari is the iron-eating monster of Korean folklore, blending elephant, bear, and tiger traits with iron skin and ember eyes. It devours metal to grow ever larger, destroying weapons and armor, and can be controlled by whoever knows its secret name. A symbol of insatiable destruction and growth, it inspired the 1985 North Korean film Pulgasari.

name: Bull Snake
description: Bull Snake is a character in the Hopi tale of Coyote and Bull Snake exchanging visits, recorded in the Traditions of the Hopi. Coyote finds Bull Snake's burrow beautiful and comfortable; the pair's exchange frames a homely lesson about envy and contentment. He is a narrative figure of a folktale, not a ceremonial spirit.

name: Bultungin
description: The Bultungin is a werehyena from the folklore of the Kanuri people of Nigeria and the former Bornu Empire around Lake Chad. The name Bultungin comes from the Kanuri language and translates literally to I change myself into a hyena, reflecting the creature's nature as a shapeshifter. Belief in the Bultungin was so strong that certain villages in the Bornu region were traditionally believed to be populated entirely by werehyenas, with the village of Kabultiloa being particularly associated with these creatures

name: Bulyit
description: Bulyit is a Noongar (southwestern Australian) name for small, hairy, malevolent spirit-beings — grouped with Gnardi and Mumari — that lurk in shadows and are said to carry off children who stray from camp, especially near sundown. The entry misattributes them to the Wurundjeri and Kulin nations of Victoria; the term is genuinely Noongar.

name: Bunian
description: The Bunian are invisible human-like spirits in Bruneian and Malay folklore, often described as 'hidden people' who dwell in forests, jungles, and remote natural areas near human settlements. They are believed to lead parallel lives to humans, with their own villages, markets, and social structures that exist in an unseen realm overlapping the physical world. The Bunian can be helpful or harmful depending on how they are treated, and they are known to interact with humans through subtle signs, sounds, and mysterious occurrences. Some traditions hold that certain gifted individuals or those born with spiritual sight can perceive the Bunian, and that they occasionally marry humans or take human children

name: Bunjil (The Eagle)
description: Bunjil is the great creator deity and ancestral spirit of the Kulin Nation, the collective of Aboriginal Australian peoples including the Wurundjeri, Boonwurrung, Taungurung, Djadjawurrung, and Wathaurung who inhabit the Port Phillip region of Victoria. Represented as a wedge-tailed eagle, Bunjil is revered as the supreme being who created the earth, carved out waterways, shaped the mountains and valleys, and brought forth animals, plants, and the first humans. He is a benevolent and wise figure who established the laws, social structures, and ceremonial traditions that govern Kulin life, serving as the ultimate source of moral and spiritual authority. Bunjil's creative acts during the Dreamtime continue to resonate through the landscape and cultural practices of his people

name: Bunyip
description: Aboriginal Australian water spirit ('bunyip' = devil/spirit) from southeastern Australia (Yorta Yorta, Ngarrindjeru, Wonnarua, Kurnai). Lives in waterholes, billabongs, swamps, rivers. Spiritual Guardian of water - not just monster. The word today means 'devil' but represents deep spiritual significance. Different descriptions: dog-like face, flippers/webbed feet, round head + elongated neck (like diprotodon), body like ox/hippo/manatee. Some say Manatee-like, others emu-neck with folds of skin. First written description 1845: pale blue eggs, deadly claws, brightly colored chest. Makes booming/roaring noises that may be bittern bird. Eats women and children - Warned to avoid deep water. Connected to Dreamtime and sacred waterways. Ngarrindjeri: 'Mulyawonk' - punishes those who take too much fish, takes children who go too close

name: Bura
description: Bura is a malevolent wind spirit from Azerbaijani and Caspian Sea folklore, known for its sudden and devastating appearances that sweep away everything in its path. This destructive elemental entity is particularly feared by shepherds, nomads, and maritime communities whose livelihoods depend on calm weather and stable conditions. Bura is associated with violent storms, tornadoes, and dust devils that arise without warning, tearing through settlements, flattening tents, uprooting trees, and churning the Caspian Sea into lethal waves. Despite its reputation for destruction, some legends suggest that powerful sorcerers or those with esoteric knowledge can command Bura, directing its fury against enemies or using it to protect sacred sites from intruders

name: Buraq (Celestial Steed)
description: Buraq is the fabulous celestial steed that carried the Prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem and through the seven heavens during the Night Journey (Isra and Mi'raj) in 621 CE. Described as a wingèd creature, white and luminous like lightning, larger than a donkey but smaller than a mule. Its step stretches as far as the eye can see, covering impossible distances in moments. In Near Eastern and Persian art, Buraq is depicted with the head of a beautiful woman, the body of a horse, and the tail of a peacock. The name Buraq derives from the Arabic root for 'lightning', reflecting its phenomenal speed. The creature is also associated with other prophets before Muhammad, including Ibrahim (Abraham)

name: Burkhan Khaldun Spirit
description: Burkhan Khaldun, in the Khentii mountains of northeastern Mongolia, is the holiest mountain of the Mongols, the birthplace and reputed burial place of Genghis Khan and one of four sacred peaks of the land. Spirits are said to dwell upon it, their presence marked by ovoo cairns, and pilgrims approach it with reverence after rites begun on the banks of the Kherlen river.

name: Butterfly Nature-Spirit (Tongan)
description: No butterfly spirit or guardian of sacred mountains is attested in Tongan tradition; Tongan mythology centers on Maui, the sky and sea god Tangaloa, and the divine descent of the royal lineage. The entry's description is an invented nature-spirit narrative with no documentary basis.

name: Butterfly Spirit (Hausa)
description: Not independently attested. No Hausa spirit of the butterfly appears in documented Hausa tradition; the entry's framing — a 'desert-guarding butterfly spirit' adapted 'within Russian folkloric interpretation' and carried along trade routes — is internally contradictory and unsupported by any source. The name and concept appear fabricated.

name: Butterfly Spirit (Hausa)
description: No butterfly spirit is attested in Hausa tradition, and the entry is mislabeled as Russian: the Hausa are a West African people. The genuine Hausa spirit world is the bori system of iskoki, organized in the twelve houses of Jangare, but no butterfly iskoki is documented. The description mixes an invented desert-guardian narrative with garbled text.

name: Butu
description: Butu is a masked spirit figure from the RaGbenle secret society of Sierra Leone, representing the ancestral spirits and supernatural forces that underpin traditional social order. The RaGbenle society is a powerful regulatory institution among the Mende and related peoples, responsible for maintaining law, conducting initiations, and acting as intermediaries between the living and the spirit world. Butu appears during crucial community ceremonies—initiations, funerals, harvest festivals, and judicial proceedings—embodying the authority of the ancestors and enforcing societal norms. The spirit's presence brings both awe and fear, as it represents the consequences of violating sacred laws and the power of the hidden forces that shape human destiny

name: Buundheex
description: Buundheex is a shape-shifting spirit in Somali folklore that can transform into any human or animal form to deceive and prey upon victims. Unlike the purely monstrous Dhegdheer, Buundheex is more subtle and insidious, using deception rather than force. The spirit typically appears as a beautiful woman or trusted friend to lure travelers from the path, then reveals its true nature when the victim is isolated. It is particularly active at crossroads, watering holes, and isolated desert stretches. Somali elders say Buundheex can be identified by its eyes -- which never quite match the borrowed face -- and by imperfect mimicry of human speech. Protective amulets (xirsi) and prayers ward off Buundheex

name: Buuti
description: The name 'Buuti' does not occur in attested Somali tales of Dhegdheer, the cannibal ogress. In the genuine cycle the daughter is left unnamed, though versions do contrast her kindness with her mother's cruelty. The elaborate 'Buuti' biography, including a cursed goddess lineage, appears only on modern fiction and content sites and is not part of Somali oral tradition.

name: Buzz Buzz
description: Not independently attested. 'Buzz Buzz' is a placeholder entry with no known tradition, origin or culture: its own source field admits 'unknown origin — likely a placeholder or minor spirit reference, no confirmed traditional sources.' The account of an 'electricity spirit' inventing a modern folkloric category appears AI-generated; no folklore collection records a being of this name.

name: Bwiti
description: Bwiti is a complex spiritual discipline from Gabon and surrounding regions of Central Africa, centered on the ritual use of iboga (Tabernanthe iboga), a psychoactive plant root that induces profound visionary states. As one of Gabon's three official religions alongside Christianity and Islam, Bwiti represents a sophisticated system of spiritual knowledge, healing practices, and cosmological understanding that has survived centuries of colonial disruption. The Bwiti tradition involves elaborate initiation ceremonies lasting several days, during which initiates consume iboga under the guidance of experienced practitioners called Nganga. These ceremonies are designed to facilitate direct contact with ancestral spirits, reveal the root causes of illness or misfortune, and provide transformative spiritual insights that reshape the initiate's understanding of existence

name: Bynesånden
description: Bynesånden (the Byneset Spirit) is a local ghost from the Byneset area of Trondheim, a rural district on the west side of the Trondheimsfjord. The spirit is believed to be the ghost of a woman who died of a broken heart after her lover was lost at sea. She is said to appear at the Byneset church (one of the oldest stone churches in Norway, dating to around 1180) and along the Byneset shoreline. The Bynesånden appears as a woman in traditional Norwegian folk dress, walking silently along the road or standing at the churchyard gate, waiting for her lost love to return. She is considered a gentle ghost — she does not frighten people deliberately but is a melancholy presence. Some versions say she appears before major storms to warn fishermen not to go out. The legend is recorded in the Norsk Folkeminnesamling's archives from Byneset, confirming it as an established part of local Trøndelag folklore

name: Bysen
description: The Bysen is a Gotland-specific forest gnome condemned to wander for moving boundary markers. He carries an axe, appears as a grey little man or a stump, and wears a red cap. He misleads travelers, delays timber transports, and tips loads. Turning one's garment inside out breaks his enchantment. Mainland Sweden has the similar skälvrängare (unholy land-surveyor).

name: Bytting
description: Bytting (also known as skifting, from bytte = to swap) is a changeling in Norwegian folklore - a troll or hulder child secretly exchanged for a human infant. The underjordiske (hidden people) were believed to envy human babies for their health and strength, and would swap their own sickly, ugly offspring for robust human infants. A bytting was identified by unusual behavior: constant crying, insatiable appetite, physical deformities, or developmental delays. Traditional remedies included beating the child, placing it on a dung heap, threatening it with fire, or leaving it outside on three consecutive Thursday nights - causing the huldra mother to retrieve her own child and return the human baby

name: Bà Chúa
description: Bà Chúa ('Lady') is an honorific for Vietnamese female deities of trade and prosperity, above all Bà Chúa Kho ('Lady of the Storehouse') of Bắc Ninh, whose devotees borrow money from her and repay with interest, and Bà Chúa Xứ ('Lady of the Realm') of Núi Sam, Châu Đốc, honoured by a major festival in the first lunar month.

name: Bà Triệu
description: Bà Triệu, known as Lady Triệu or Triệu Thị Trinh, is a legendary Vietnamese warrior heroine who led a rebellion against the Wu Chinese occupation in the 3rd century AD. According to folklore, she possessed supernatural strength and the ability to grow to giant size in battle, making her an invincible force against enemy armies. Born in Quan Yên village (present-day Thanh Hóa province), she gathered a force of over 1,000 warriors, including many women, and fought numerous battles against the occupying forces. Though ultimately defeated, Bà Triệu became one of Vietnam's most enduring symbols of resistance against foreign domination and women's empowerment, and she is venerated as a protective spirit at temples throughout northern and central Vietnam

name: Bái Zhúrén (White Snake)
description: Bái Zhúrén (White Snake), known as Bai Suzhen in Chinese, is the central figure of one of China's most beloved folktales, 'The Legend of the White Snake' (Bai She Zhuan). She is a thousand-year-old white snake spirit who transforms herself into a beautiful woman to experience human love, eventually marrying the mortal scholar Xu Xian. Their relationship faces relentless persecution from the Buddhist monk Fahai, who recognizes Bai Suzhen's true nature and believes the union between human and spirit is an abomination. The story explores profound themes of love conquering boundaries, the conflict between spiritual law and human emotion, and the question of whether beings of different natures can truly understand one another. The legend has been adapted countless times in Chinese opera, film, television, and literature over the centuries

name: Bäckahästen
description: The bäckahästen (brook horse) is a Swedish manifestation of the näcken water spirit. It appears as a magnificent white or dappled horse near streams and fords. When mounted, it lengthens to accommodate more riders, then dashes into deep water to drown them. It can be controlled by carving a cross on its back or knowing its true name. Closely parallels the Scottish kelpie and Norwegian nøkken.

name: Bärbel
description: 'Barel' is not attested as the name of a Swiss forest or game spirit. The closest documented figures are the dwarfs and Fanggen of Alpine belief who tend chamois and punish wasteful hunters, as in the 'Fairy Mythology' collections. No Swiss source names such a guardian 'Barel,' so the entry appears to be an invented personification built from a generic forest-spirit template.

name: Bækhest
description: Bækhesten (the Brook Horse) is a water spirit in Danish folklore that appears as a beautiful, majestic white horse emerging from streams and rivers, especially in foggy weather. It lures children and unwary travelers onto its back with its gentle appearance, but once mounted, the rider cannot dismount — the horse's back lengthens to accommodate more riders, and it gallops into the deepest part of the water to drown them. It is most dangerous at twilight and during fog. The Bækhest can be foiled by placing a piece of steel between the horse and the water, or by calling its true name. In some traditions, the Bækhest is an aspect of Nøkken, the water spirit, who takes equine form to lure victims. The belief was especially strong in Jylland, where over 40 specific stream locations were recorded by Evald Tang Kristensen

name: Bøygen
description: Bøygen (also written Bøyg, Bøygen) is a monstrous serpentine creature in Norwegian folklore, most famously featured in Henrik Ibsen's Peer Gynt where it is described as a huge, invisible worm that smothers its victims. In authentic folk tradition, bøygen is a shape-shifting dragon-like being that coils around its prey and crushes them. Particularly associated with the Gudbrandsdalen and Østlandet regions. The bøygen could be invisible, making it impossible to fight - one could only walk through it, a terrifying experience. The creature was known to block paths and roads, demanding that travelers solve riddles or turn back. The name bøyg means curve or arch - referring to the creature's curved, coiling shape. Related to the Swedish bäckahästen (brook horse)

name: Bøylefosstrollet
description: Bøylefosstrollet is the troll associated with Bøylefossen, a dramatic waterfall in the Setesdal valley. According to local legend, the Bøylefosstroll lived behind the waterfall and guarded a treasure hidden in a cave in the cliff. The troll would emerge on misty days to sit on the rocks beside the waterfall, washing its clothes in the spray. It was said to be a solitary female troll who had been turned to stone by the sunrise but still moved during fog and mist. The mist from the waterfall provided enough cover for the troll to move — it was neither fully stone nor fully alive. Local farm children were warned not to play near the waterfall for fear the troll would snatch them. The Bøylefoss waterfall is a real landmark in Setesdal, one of the region's most dramatic natural features

name: Búp
description: Not independently attested as a fruit spirit of Vietnamese folklore. 'Búp' is an ordinary Vietnamese word meaning a bud or sprout, and the Lĩnh Nam chích quái, the medieval collection cited, records no spirit of jackfruit or durian under this name.

name: Caanaba
description: Caanaba (also spelled Canaba) is a cosmic serpent in Fulani mythology, designated by Gueno (the eternal creator) to be the guardian of cattle. Usually taking the form of a great serpent, Caanaba protects the sacred herds under the care of Koumen, the primordial shepherd. The serpent represents the primordial, earth-bound aspect of pastoral divinities — the chthonic guardian that complements Koumen's child-like innocence. Caanaba's serpent form connects the Fulani cattle tradition to the broader West African motif of the cosmic snake that guards treasure, knowledge, or sacred animals

name: Cadejo
description: El Cadejo is a legendary spirit from Salvadoran folklore that manifests as two spectral dogs — a White Cadejo and a Black Cadejo — representing the eternal struggle between good and evil. The legend has pre-Columbian indigenous origins, where dogs were believed to help humans pass into the afterlife. With the arrival of Christianity, the story evolved into a dualistic tale. The White Cadejo, with blue eyes, is a protective spirit that guards drunkards, lost travelers, and innocent children from harm. The Black Cadejo, with burning red eyes, is a malevolent entity that preys on evildoers, drunks, and those with impure intentions — stalking them through village streets and stealing their souls. The Salvadoran writer Manlio Argueta immortalized these creatures in his children's book 'Magic Dogs of the Volcanoes' (Los Perros Mágicos de Los Volcanes). The Cadejo legend is so important that Salvadorans dress up as the dogs in Independence Day parades

name: Cadejo
description: Cadejo is a spirit from Central American mythology. The legend has pre-Columbian indigenous origins, where dogs were believed to help humans pass into the afterlife. With the arrival of Christianity, the story evolved into a dualistic tale. The White Cadejo, with blue eyes, is a protective spirit that guards drunkards, lost travelers, and innocent children from harm. The Black Cadejo, with burning red eyes, is a malevolent entity that preys on evildoers, drunks, and those with impure intentions — stalking them through village streets and stealing their souls. The Salvadoran writer Manlio Argueta immortalized these creatures in his children's book 'Magic Dogs of the Volcanoes' (Los Perros Mágicos de Los Volcanes). The Cadejo legend is so important that Salvadorans dress up as the dogs in Independence Day parades

name: Cadejo
description: Cadejo is a spirit from Mesoamerican mythology. The legend has pre-Columbian indigenous origins, where dogs were believed to help humans pass into the afterlife. With the arrival of Christianity, the story evolved into a dualistic tale. The White Cadejo, with blue eyes, is a protective spirit that guards drunkards, lost travelers, and innocent children from harm. The Black Cadejo, with burning red eyes, is a malevolent entity that preys on evildoers, drunks, and those with impure intentions — stalking them through village streets and stealing their souls. The Salvadoran writer Manlio Argueta immortalized these creatures in his children's book 'Magic Dogs of the Volcanoes' (Los Perros Mágicos de Los Volcanes). The Cadejo legend is so important that Salvadorans dress up as the dogs in Independence Day parades

name: Cadejo Chico
description: Cadejo Chico is the smaller, more mischievous counterpart to the Cadejo Grande in Central American folklore, particularly prevalent in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Costa Rica. Unlike its larger, malevolent relative, the Cadejo Chico is known for its playful and sometimes helpful nature, though it can still be dangerous to those who mistreat it. Rooted in Maya and Nahua mythology, the cadejo legend stems from ancient beliefs in animal spirit companions known as naguals. The Cadejo Chico specifically represents the trickster aspect of these traditions, a supernatural dog spirit that delights in testing humans and revealing their true character through its pranks and tests

name: Cadejo Grande
description: Cadejo Grande is the larger, malevolent manifestation of the supernatural dog spirit in Central American folklore, particularly prominent in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua. Unlike its smaller, mischievous counterpart the Cadejo Chico, the Cadejo Grande is a fearsome hellhound-like creature that actively seeks to harm or kill travelers who wander alone at night. The legend has deep roots in Maya and Nahua mythology, where dogs served as companions to the dead on their journey to the afterlife, and shamans known as naguals could take animal form. The Cadejo Grande represents the dark aspect of this spiritual tradition, sometimes described as an incarnation of the devil himself that preys on the wicked and unwary

name: Cagüeiro
description: Cagüeiro is a shape-shifting outlaw figure from Cuban folklore, particularly associated with the rural countryside and Afro-Cuban folk traditions. Unlike many supernatural creatures that are inherently magical or mythological in origin, the Cagüeiro is a human who has gained the power to transform into any animal or object through the use of magical incantations and pacts with dark forces. This figure is deeply rooted in the syncretic blend of Spanish, African, and indigenous Caribbean beliefs that characterize Cuban folk magic, where outlaws and renegades were often attributed with supernatural abilities as a reflection of their status outside the boundaries of normal society and the law

name: Caipora
description: Caipora is a powerful forest spirit from Brazilian folklore, considered the guardian of wildlife and game animals throughout the vast Amazon rainforest and beyond. The name comes from the Tupi language, meaning 'inhabitant of the forest,' and this entity is deeply embedded in the indigenous Tupi-Guarani mythological tradition. The Caipora is variously depicted as male or female, dwarf or giant, and is known to be both a protector of animals and a punisher of hunters who violate traditional hunting codes. It is closely related to the Curupira, another forest guardian, and the two are sometimes conflated or considered different aspects of the same spiritual force that regulates the relationship between humans and the natural world

name: Caleuche
description: El Caleuche, also known as the Buque de Arte or Magic Ship, is a legendary ghost ship from Chilote mythology in southern Chile, specifically the Chiloé Archipelago. This supernatural vessel is one of the most enduring and complex legends in South American folklore, blending elements of Mapuche mythology with Spanish colonial influences and maritime superstition. The Caleuche appears as a brilliantly illuminated ship that sails the channels and fjords of Chiloé, crewed by witches, drowned sailors, and supernatural beings. Its name may derive from the Mapudungun words caleutun, meaning to transform, and che, meaning people, reflecting the ship's ability to change shape and its connection to shape-shifting witches

name: Calon Arang
description: Calon Arang (Unknown). is a witch. Calon Arang is a legendary witch from Balinese folklore, a widow skilled in black magic who terrorized a kingdom after her daughter was rejected in marriage. The tale is performed in the traditional B. Source: Balinese folklore; traditional dance-drama

name: Calèche de Lallmatie
description: Calèche de Lallmatie is a Mauritian ghost legend: a luminous white carriage drawn by two white horses, bearing two women in white, seen at midnight near Lallmatie village. A passive omen of the French colonial past, it haunts roads without attacking. Documented in Mauritian folklore collections and 'Culture of Mauritius' folklore section. Pre-dates Touni Minwi hysteria.

name: Camahueto
description: Camahueto is a Chilote aquatic bull from Chiloé Archipelago, Chile. Born in rivers with a single spiral horn like a unicorn, it grows massive and migrates to the sea. Destructive on land: destroys crops, creates valleys and floods. Only a machi can lasso it with kelp and return it to the ocean. Its horn shavings are prized medicine.

name: Camazotz
description: Camazotz (meaning 'Death Bat' in K'iche' Maya) is a bat spirit and death god in Late Post-Classic Maya mythology from the Popol Vuh. He serves the lords of the underworld, Xibalba. In the Maya Hero Twins myth, Camazotz appears in the 'House of Bats' trial, where Hunahpu and Xbalanque must spend the night surrounded by circling bats. When Hunahpu sticks his head out of his blowgun to check if the sun has risen, Camazotz immediately snatches off his head and carries it to the ballcourt to be used as a ball by the death gods. In Classic Maya iconography, the leaf-nosed bat is depicted as a person's nahual or way-spirit bringing disease over enemies. The bat is associated with night, death, and sacrifice throughout Mesoamerica. Camazotz remains one of the most recognizable figures from the Popol Vuh and has appeared in popular culture including Dungeons & snip Dragons, Stranger Things, the Monsterverse graphic novels, and Fate/Grand Order

name: Cannibal Giants
description: Cannibal Giants are fearsome creatures from the oral traditions of various First Nations peoples across Canada, particularly among the Algonquian and Athabaskan-speaking tribes of the Subarctic and northern woodlands. Known by different names in different languages, these beings share a common archetype: giant humanoid monsters driven by an insatiable hunger for human flesh that embody the harsh and unforgiving nature of the northern wilderness. Unlike the spirits and animal guides that feature prominently in many Indigenous traditions, these giants are unequivocally malevolent, representing the dangers that await those who venture alone into the deep forest or who violate the sacred balance between humans and the natural world

name: Cannibal Giants
description: Cannibal giants are man-eating monsters of the oral traditions of Algonquian and Athabaskan peoples of Canada's Subarctic and northern woodlands — known as wihtikow (windigo) among Cree, Ojibwe, and related nations. Frozen, famine-driven giants born of isolation and starvation, they embody the dangers of the deep winter bush; related beings include the Mi'kmaq chenoo.

name: Canyon People
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature as spirit beings. 'Canyon People' (Tseyi Ndee) is the name of an Apache band, not a class of guardian spirits; the entry invents deep-gorge inhabitants and ancestor-mediator roles with no named narrative. Genuine Apache place-spirits exist in oral tradition, but none is recorded under this name.

name: Cap-a-Taille
description: Cap-a-Taille is a malevolent nocturnal spirit from French folklore, particularly associated with the forested regions of medieval and early modern France. Known as a cauchemar or nightmare spirit, this entity is closely related to the Germanic Alp and the English mare traditions, part of a widespread European belief in beings that torment sleepers by sitting on their chests and causing terrifying dreams. The name Cap-a-Taille likely derives from Old French words suggesting a head or hooded figure that cuts or oppresses. In French peasant tradition, this spirit was blamed for sleep paralysis, night terrors, and the mysterious feeling of being watched or restrained during the night, especially for those who slept alone or in isolated dwellings near forests

name: Capelobo
description: Capelobo is a therianthropic vampire-like monster from Brazilian mythology, particularly prevalent in the northern states of Pará and Maranhão. Its name fuses the Guarani word capê, meaning broken or crooked leg, with the Portuguese lobo, meaning wolf, describing both its appearance and its lupine nature. The Capelobo is closely related to other Brazilian monsters such as the Mapinguari and the Lobisomem, representing a distinct regional variant of the werewolf archetype that incorporates elements of Amazonian wildlife. Unlike European werewolves that are typically humans who transform into wolves, the Capelobo is a permanent monster that takes features from local animals including the tapir, peccary, and giant anteater, making it a uniquely Brazilian adaptation of the shapeshifter legend deeply rooted in indigenous folklore

name: Capotona
description: Capotona is a mournful coastal ghost in Cape Verdean folklore, haunting shorelines and abandoned lighthouses. It manifests as a spectral figure emitting mournful sounds, countered by sunrise. Represents the perils of the sea and lost sailors. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tradition alongside Catchorrona.

name: Carival
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Trinidadian spirit named 'Carival' exists; the entry is a fabricated personification of Carnival. Trinidad's real folk entities include the douen, La Diablesse, the soucouyant, and Papa Bois, none of which is a personification of the festival.

name: Cat Sidhe
description: Cat Sidhe (Unknown). is a fairy. The Cat Sidhe is a fairy creature from Irish and Scottish folklore, appearing as a large black cat with a white spot on its chest. It was believed to be a witch transformed into feline form.. Source: Scottish and Irish folkloric sources; Celtic mythology

name: Cat Sídhe
description: The Cat Sídhe, also known as Cat-sìth in Scottish Gaelic, is a fairy creature from Celtic mythology that resembles a large spectral black cat with a distinctive white spot on its chest. This being spans both Scottish and Irish folklore, though it is more prominent in Scottish Highland traditions. Unlike ordinary fairy creatures, the Cat Sídhe occupies an ambiguous space between fairy, witch, and omen of death, reflecting the complex relationship between the Celtic otherworld and the mundane realm. The legend may have been inspired by actual encounters with the Scottish wildcat, which is larger and more ferocious than domestic cats, or by the Kellas cat, a hybrid between wildcats and domestic cats found only in Scotland. The Cat Sídhe is one of several supernatural felines in Celtic lore, alongside the Cù-sìth (fairy dog) and the Ceffyl Dŵr (water horse)

name: Catchorrona
description: Catchorrona ('black dog') is an ominous spectral hound in Cape Verdean folklore, appearing at moonlit crossroads to warn or terrify night wanderers. It induces fear and stealth, repelled by silver bells. Represents dangers of nocturnal travel. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tradition.

name: Celestial Deer
description: The celestial deer of Mongolia is the leaping, antlered stag carved on the Bronze Age deer stones that stand across the northern steppe, monuments some three thousand years old. Scholars such as William Fitzhugh interpret these 'flying deer' as spirit beings that carry the souls of warriors and leaders toward the heavens, making the deer a creature of the upper world.

name: Celestial Moose
description: The celestial moose is the great elk of Evenki star-lore, read in the constellation of the Big Dipper. In the best-known telling the heavenly hunter Mangi pursues the elk across the sky, the Milky Way is his ski track, and the turning of the northern heavens retells their endless chase, a story of the hunt that shaped the world above.

name: Celestial Reindeer (Seven Reindeer)
description: Among the Nenets of Siberia the bright northern stars are read as a celestial reindeer or elk pursued across the sky, a tale told by forest Nenets reindeer herders to mark the turning of the seasons. Because the reindeer stands at the heart of Nenets life, its image in the heavens carries both practical and sacred meaning.

name: Cemi (Taino Spirit Being and Sacred Object)
description: Cemi (also spelled Zemi) refers to both the spirit beings in Taino mythology and the sacred objects that housed them. In Taino belief, the world was populated by countless zemis -- spirits that inhabited natural features (mountains, rivers, caves, trees) and could be invoked through carved stone, wood, shell, or bone objects. The most distinctive form of zemi is the three-pointed stone (trigonolito), usually carved from limestone or guayacan wood, representing the connection between the three layers of the Taino universe: the heavens (turei), the earth, and the watery underworld (coaybay). Major zemis included Yocahu (supreme god), Atabey (mother goddess), Guabancex (goddess of chaos), and Baibrama (god of cassava). Chief zemis were kept in sacred houses (bohio del cemi) and consulted for divination using the cohoba ritual -- an inhalation of hallucinogenic powder that allowed the behike (shaman-priest) to communicate with the spirits

name: Cerberus
description: Cerberus, often called the Hound of Hades, is the most fearsome canine in Greek mythology, serving as the guardian of the underworld's gates to prevent the dead from escaping and the living from entering without permission. Born from the union of the monsters Echidna and Typhon, Cerberus is sibling to other multi-headed terrors including the Lernaean Hydra, Orthrus, and the Chimera. According to Hesiod's Theogony, Cerberus originally had fifty heads, while Pindar gave him one hundred, though later literary and artistic traditions universally settled on three. The creature's primary mythological role is as the object of Heracles' twelfth and final labor, the most challenging of all, which required the hero to descend into Hades and bring the beast back alive to King Eurystheus

name: Chaac (Chaahk)
description: Chaac, the Maya rain god (Chaahk), is a humanoid deity with a long curling trunk-like nose, fangs and shell ear ornaments who hurls his lightning axe (K'awiil). He brings rain to the crops and dwells in clouds, mountains and cenotes; his four directional aspects wear red, white, black and yellow, and neglect provokes storms or drought.

name: Chaac (Chaahk)
description: Chaahk, the Maya thunder-and-rain deity of lowland Guatemala, snorts rain through his long curling nose, wields a lightning axe and wears fangs and shell ear ornaments. He lives in clouds, mountain caves and cenotes and must be appeased with offerings, for his four colored directional aspects can unleash destructive storms or withhold the rain that the cornfields need.

name: Chameleon (Messenger of God)
description: In Yao creation tradition of Malawi the chameleon, messenger of the god Mulungu, sets fish traps in the primordial waters and one day draws up the first man and woman, whom God bids him release to grow to maturity. Among the Chewa the chameleon bears the message of immortality, delayed by the lizard that brings death instead — a motif shared across Bantu and Kikuyu traditions.

name: Chang Er
description: Chang'e, also originally known as Heng'e, is the revered Chinese goddess of the Moon and one of the most prominent figures in Chinese mythology, folk religion, and cultural tradition. Her story is intimately connected with the myth of Hou Yi, the legendary archer who shot down nine of the ten suns that once scorched the earth. According to the ancient divination text Guicang from the Zhou Dynasty, Chang'e ascended to the Moon after consuming an elixir of immortality. Over millennia, her story has evolved through countless poems, paintings, and festivals, making her a symbol of nostalgia, solitude, feminine beauty, and the eternal human longing for the unreachable. She is celebrated annually during the Mid-Autumn Festival, one of the most important holidays in Chinese culture, when families gather under the full moon to eat mooncakes and honor her myth

name: Chang Pheuak (White Elephant)
description: The White Elephant (Thai: ช้างเผือก, chang pheuak) is the most sacred animal in Thai mythology and a direct symbol of royal power connected to Buddhist cosmology. According to legend, Queen Maya, the mother of the Buddha, dreamt of a white elephant offering her a lotus flower before she conceived — establishing the white elephant as a symbol of spiritual purity and royal legitimacy. The discovery of a white elephant was considered a divine sign that the reigning king ruled with righteousness (dharma). The legend of Phra Phutthabat (the Buddha's footprint) tells of a white elephant that knelt to show the sacred footprint at Saraburi province. White elephants were so revered they received royal titles, were never forced to work, and were considered members of the royal family. The Thai national flag historically featured a white elephant on a red background

name: Changing Woman
description: White-painted Woman, the Apache counterpart of Changing Woman, is the mother of the hero twins Child of the Water and Killer of Enemies, whom she bore on White Mountain. She is the ideal of Apache womanhood and the model for the girls' puberty ceremony, which re-enacts her power to age and then grow young again with the seasons.

name: Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé)
description: Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé), also called White Shell Woman, is the central deity of Navajo religion. Born from the darkness, she lives in the west beside the ocean, aging and renewing herself with the seasons, and she bore the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer and Child of the Water, fathered by the Sun. She gave the Navajo their clans and the Blessingway ceremonies.

name: Changó
description: Changó, also spelled Shangó or Xangô, is one of the most powerful and revered orishas in the Yoruba religion and its Afro-Caribbean derivatives including Santería, Candomblé, and Lukumí. As the orisha of thunder, lightning, fire, war, dance, and justice, Changó embodies masculine power, passion, and royal authority. Originally a historical king of the Oyo Empire in what is now Nigeria, he was deified after death and became the第四 king of the Yoruba pantheon. During the transatlantic slave trade, his worship was carried to Cuba, Brazil, Trinidad, and other parts of the Americas, where he was syncretized with Saint Barbara in Catholic tradition due to the shared symbolism of lightning and thunder. Changó remains one of the most widely worshipped orishas in the Afro-American diaspora, representing the indomitable spirit of resistance and the power of righteous anger

name: Charonda
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Cypriot vampire called 'Charonda' is recorded. The name speculatively conflates Charos (Charon), the Greek folk personification of death prominent in Cypriot laments, with the vrykolakas vampire tradition; no blood-drinking being of this name is documented in Cypriot sources.

name: Chase Vault
description: The Chase Vault mystery is one of the most famous and enduring paranormal legends of the Caribbean, centered on a family tomb in the Christ Church cemetery of Barbados. Between 1812 and 1820, the heavy lead-lined coffins interred in the Chase family vault were repeatedly found disturbed, moved from their original positions, and in some cases overturned, despite the vault being sealed with a marble slab and showing no signs of forced entry. This bizarre phenomenon attracted widespread attention, including official investigations by colonial authorities including Lord Combermere, the Governor of Barbados. The mystery has inspired countless theories ranging from natural causes like flooding and earthquake tremors to supernatural explanations involving spirits, curses, and malevolent entities, making it one of the most famous haunted vault cases in paranormal history

name: Chenoo
description: The Chenoo is a cannibalistic ice monster of Mi'kmaq and Wabanaki mythology. A Chenoo was originally human, but was transformed through an act of cannibalism or extreme trauma into a monster with a heart of ice and an insatiable hunger for human flesh. Chenoos are enormous, with claws and fangs, and their heart is visible through their translucent ice chest. Unlike the windigo of the northern Algonquian tribes, the Chenoo can potentially be healed and restored to human form through love, prayer, and traditional ceremonies

name: Cherruves
description: Cherufe is a being of Mapuche tradition said to dwell in the lava pools of southern Chilean volcanoes, a creature of molten rock and sharp crystals with a man-eater's appetite. Its stirrings are blamed for eruptions and earthquakes, and communities historically offered sacrifices to appease it. The input mislabels it a water serpent; it belongs to volcanic fire, not to lakes and rivers.

name: Cheval Mal Fet
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The name 'Cheval Mal Fet' garbles 'Le Chevaler Mal Fet' — 'the ill-made knight' — the epithet of Lancelot in Arthurian romance, popularized by T. H. White's novel 'The Ill-Made Knight.' No phantom horse or Haitian or Belgian ghost-horse tradition by this name is documented.

name: Chhinnamasta (Self-Decapitated Goddess)
description: Chhinnamasta ('the Self-Decapitated One') is a powerful Tantric goddess, one of the ten Mahavidyas (great wisdom goddesses) in Shaktism. The legend tells that once, while bathing in the Mandakini River with her attendants Dakini and Varnini, Parvati (in her form as Chhinnamasta) was overcome by a ravenous hunger that her attendants also felt. When asked to satisfy their hunger, Parvati severed her own head with a sword and held it in her hand. Three jets of blood spurted from her severed neck — one feeding her own mouth, and two feeding her attendants. The iconography shows her standing in a battlefield or cremation ground, holding her severed head, drinking her own blood. Her name literally means 'she whose head is severed.' The myth symbolizes the goddess's power to transcend death and her role as both destroyer and sustainer of cosmic energy (Shakti). Chhinnamasta represents the realization that the true self is beyond the body, and that life and death are two aspects of the same divine reality. She is associated with self-sacrifice, spiritual awakening, and the transcendence of ego

name: Chichkhan
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Kazakh mountain-dwarf spirit named 'Chichkhan' appears in any collection of Kazakh or Central Asian Turkic folklore. Kazakh animistic tradition does describe yer-su earth-water spirits, divs, and witch-figures such as Zheztyrnak, but none matches this name.

name: Chickcharney
description: The Chickcharney is a legendary bird-like creature from the folklore of Andros Island in the Bahamas, one of the most distinctive mythological beings in Caribbean oral tradition. According to Bahamian legend, the Chickcharney inhabits the dense pine forests of Andros, the largest island in the Bahamas archipelago. The creature has been part of local folklore for centuries, with stories passed down through generations. A notable legend connects the Chickcharney to Neville Chamberlain, the former British Prime Minister, who allegedly angered Chickcharnies by cutting down their trees while working on a sisal plantation in the Bahamas, causing his political career to be cursed. Modern researchers, including paleontologist Lisa G. Buckley, suggest that the Chickcharney legend may be based on the prehistoric barn owl species Tyto pollens, which coexisted with ancient humans in the Bahamas

name: Chickcharnies
description: Chickcharnies, a variant spelling of Chickcharney, are mischievous feathered spirits from the folklore of Andros Island in the Bahamas, deeply woven into Bahamian oral tradition. These creatures are considered omens of either great fortune or terrible misfortune, depending on how they are treated. The legend of the Chickcharnies is concentrated in the dense pine forests of Andros, where they are believed to be guardians of the natural order. The most famous story involving Chickcharnies concerns British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, who worked on his father's sisal plantation on Andros in his youth. According to local legend, Chamberlain cut down trees inhabited by Chickcharnies, bringing a curse that doomed his political career and contributed to the failure of the Munich Agreement decades later, serving as a powerful cautionary tale about respecting nature

name: Chief No Vitals
description: Chief No Vitals (also known as No Vitals) is a Crow culture hero who discovered tobacco and established the Tobacco Society (Bacu'sua). According to tradition, he was instructed by the Creator Akbaatatdia to seek the sacred plant at Devils Lake in eastern North Dakota. The Creator told him that the worship of tobacco would help the Crow honor God and maintain their connection to the spirit world. Chief No Vitals found the plant and brought it back, establishing the Tobacco Society to ensure all rites and rituals for cultivating tobacco are performed correctly. Smoking tobacco carries prayers directly to God as smoke ascends to the heavens

name: Chil-kuyz
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Uzbek cave spirit named 'Chil-kuyz' is recorded. Uzbek and broader Turkic tradition instead names harmful spirits such as albasti and the iye (yeys) household and nature guardians; 'Chil-kuyz' appears to be an invented blend of these figures.

name: Child of the Water
description: Child of the Water is the Apache culture hero, one of the twins born to White-painted Woman. With his brother Killer of Enemies he rid the world of monsters, slaying the Owl-Man Giant, the Buffalo Monster, and the Eagle Monster, and he remains the model of the Apache warrior, told of across the Chiricahua and other Apache oral traditions.

name: Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní)
description: Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní) is one of the Navajo Hero Twins, younger brother of Monster Slayer. Born to Changing Woman and fathered by the Sun, he accompanied his brother on the quest to rid the world of the Anaye (monsters). Together they journeyed to their father the Sun, passing deadly tests. Child of the Water assisted in killing the great monsters including Yé'iitsoh and Déélgééd, shooting the giant's head alongside his brother. He represents the protective, nurturing aspect of the w

name: Chimera
description: The Chimera is one of the most famous monsters in Greek mythology, a fire-breathing hybrid creature from Lycia in Asia Minor that has become the archetype for all composite mythical beings. First described by Homer in the Iliad, the Chimera was the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, sibling to Cerberus, the Lernaean Hydra, and Orthrus. According to Hesiod's Theogony, the Chimera had three heads: a lion in front, a fire-breathing goat in the middle, and a serpent in the rear. The hero Bellerophon, riding the winged horse Pegasus, was tasked by King Iobates of Lycia to slay the Chimera. Bellerophon succeeded by flying above the creature and shooting it with arrows, or according to some accounts, by dropping a block of lead into its fiery throat that melted and suffocated the beast from within

name: Chindi
description: Chindi (Navajo: ch'ijidii) is a concept in Navajo religious belief referring to the negative spiritual residue left behind after a person dies. Unlike a ghost in the Western sense, the Chindi is not the soul of the deceased but an accumulation of everything negative about their life including pain, fear, anger, disappointment, resentment, and rejection. According to Navajo tradition, the Chindi leaves the body with the person's last breath and lingers in the vicinity of the death site and the deceased's possessions. Traditional Navajo practices surrounding death are deeply shaped by the need to manage, disperse, or avoid contact with the Chindi, which is believed to cause illness, misfortune, and even death. The concept reflects the Navajo emphasis on harmony and balance known as hozho, where negative energy must be carefully managed to maintain spiritual health

name: Chinthe
description: The chinthe is the stylized lion-guardian of Burmese Buddhism, a heraldic rendering of the Asiatic lion that flanks the entrances of pagodas, stupas and kyaung monasteries throughout Myanmar. Tradition derives it from the Mahavamsa tale of a Vanga princess wed to a lion whose son Sihabahu slew his father and raised a lion statue in atonement; the chinthe also marks Tuesday in the Burmese zodiac.

name: Chiruwi
description: Chiruwi is a duel-challenging creature of Central African folklore: a one-sided being said to confront passers-by in combat. A traveller who wins earns the Chiruwi's mercy and a gift of great medical knowledge, becoming a successful medicine man; one who loses is killed. The figure tests strength and courage and appears in obscure folklore collections, sometimes placed in Malawi.

name: Chitapo (Lake Spirit)
description: Chitapo (also spelled Kitapo) is a female lake spirit from the mythology of the Lamba and Bemba people of Zambia. She resides at the bottom of lakes, where she hoards vast treasures of diamonds and emeralds. Chitapo is a malicious spirit who lures people to a watery grave, not unlike sirens and mermaids in European legends. She is sometimes described as a mermaid, with the upper body of an attractive woman and the lower body of a fish. However, this mermaid-like imagery may have resulted from conflation with the Funkwe, a giant water snake with the tail of a fish that is said to inhabit the same lakes and serve as Chitapo's guardian. In some variations, the lake spirit takes the form of a small diamond that sits in the mouth of the giant snake, protecting it. Chitapo is also associated with children born under ill omens, whom she is said to dispose of. Lakes Nakamwale, Kashiba, and Namulolobwe in Zambia are particularly associated with the Chitapo legend. Offerings are sometimes made to appease her before fishing or swimming

name: Chiuta (The Spider Creator)
description: Chiuta, meaning 'Great Bow' (a reference to the rainbow as his symbol), is the supreme creator deity in Chewa and Tumbuka mythology of Malawi. Unlike many creator gods who are remote and uninvolved, Chiuta is depicted as intimately connected to creation through the powerful image of a spider descending from the sky on a silk thread. According to the Chewa creation myth, in the beginning there was only Chiuta and the barren earth. Chiuta lived above in the sky, and below him the earth was desolate. One day, clouds began to cover the sky, lightning flared, and thunder rumbled. The sky opened, and Chiuta, in the form of a spider, descended on a silk thread from the heavens to the earth, bringing life and fertility. The rainbow is considered Chiuta's visible manifestation, bridging the heavens and the earth. Chiuta is omnipresent but shapeless, and while prayers can be made directly to him, ancestors and spirits play a large intermediary role. The deity is associated with natural phenomena from the sky, such as rain and thunderstorms

name: Chiwara
description: Chiwara is a mythical half-human, half-antelope being who taught the Bambara people the fundamentals of agriculture. Using its antlers and a pointed stick to dig the earth, Chiwara demonstrated how to cultivate the land, making it possible for farmers to grow crops. The people followed its example and became expert farmers, but their harvests grew so bountiful that they began wasting grain. Disappointed by human ingratitude, Chiwara buried itself deep into the earth and disappeared. To honor their lost teacher, the Bambara created the iconic Chiwara headdresses — carved wooden antelope masks worn by dancers in agricultural ceremonies, leaping and turning like antelopes to keep the teaching alive

name: Cholula
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Cholula' is the name of a city in Puebla, Mexico, not a folkloric being. The giant tradition attached to its great pyramid belongs to Xelhua, a Nahua survivor of the Fourth-Sun flood who climbed Mount Tlaloc and, in early colonial accounts, raised the pyramid of Tlachihualtepetl.

name: Chonchón
description: The Chonchon is a terrifying creature from Mapuche folklore of Chile and Argentina, described as the detached flying head of a kalku, a Mapuche sorcerer who has transformed through black magic. The Chonchon is one of the most feared beings in Mapuche mythology, representing the dark side of shamanic power and the ultimate expression of malevolent abilities. According to Mapuche tradition, a kalku who has reached the pinnacle of dark arts can separate their head from their body at night and fly through the air to spy on enemies, cast curses, or drink the blood of sleeping victims. The Chonchon is closely associated with the Pewenche and Huilliche peoples of southern Chile and Argentina, where stories of night-flying sorcerers have been told for centuries

name: Chort
description: Chort is an anthropomorphic malevolent spirit or demon in Slavic folk tradition, found across Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Polish, Czech, Slovak, and other Slavic cultures. The term chort represents a complex figure that evolved from pre-Christian Slavic mythology into Christian folk demonology. In Slavic paganism, chort was associated with Chernobog, the god of darkness, and considered a son of the dark deity and the goddess Mara. With Christianization, the chort was syncretized with the Christian devil. However, in many folk traditions, particularly Ukrainian and Czech, the chort retained a distinct identity as a trickster and tempter rather than an embodiment of absolute evil, often portrayed as surprisingly foolish and easily outwitted by clever peasants who manage to turn the demon's own schemes against him

name: Chufi (Rabbit)
description: Chufi, the Rabbit, is the trickster of the Muscogee (Creek) people, a small, quick animal whose cleverness and mischief animate many Creek stories. In one well-known tale he stole fire from those who kept it hidden and brought it to the people; in others he outwits larger animals, and his escapades teach the limits of cunning.

name: Chuhayster
description: Chuhayster (Unknown). is a forest-spirit. Chuhayster (also spelled Chuhaister) is a tutelary forest deity from Ukrainian Carpathian folklore, unknown in any other mythology. He is described as a giant, shaggy humanoid with bright blue eyes wh. Source: Hutsul folklore; Ukrainian Carpathian oral tradition

name: Chukfi (Rabbit)
description: Chukfi (Chokfi), the Rabbit, is the trickster of the Chickasaw people. Clever, mischievous, and sometimes selfish, he uses his wits to outsmart larger animals and to explain how things came to be; stories tell why Rabbit has a short tail, why the possum's tail is bare, and how deer gained their antlers.

name: Chukwu
description: Chukwu (also known as Chineke or Chi Ukwu, meaning "The Great Spirit") is the supreme god of the Igbo people. Chukwu created the cosmos, all lesser deities (alusi), and humanity. Associated with the sun, which is considered the "Eye of God on Earth," Chukwu is all-powerful, all-knowing, and transcendent. The name Chukwu is used in countless Igbo names reflecting divine attributes: Chukwudi ("God lives"), Chukwuma ("God knows"), and Chukwuemeka ("God has been very kind"). Chukwu is considered too great for direct worship; instead, the Igbo venerate the alusi who serve as intermediaries. Every person's chi (personal spirit) is a fractal representation of Chukwu residing within the individual

name: Chullachaqui
description: Chullachaqui, also known as Shapishico, is a mythical forest creature from the Peruvian and Brazilian Amazon jungle, prominent in the folklore of the Quechua, Shipibo, and other indigenous peoples of the Amazon Basin. The name derives from the Quechua words chulla meaning one or odd and chaki meaning foot, referring to the creature's most distinctive physical trait of mismatched feet. The Chullachaqui is a guardian spirit of the rainforest, protector of trees and animals, and punisher of those who break taboos in the forest. According to Amazonian tradition, the Chullachaqui belongs to an older species that lived in the rainforest long before humans. Most of the time these beings dwell in remote forest spots far from human habitation where they tend their own gardens, uninterested in human affairs

name: Chulyen Crow Nuu Chah Nulth
description: The name Chulyen belongs to the Dena'ina, an Athabaskan people of south-central Alaska, where Chulyen is the raven trickster and transformer of the Kenai Peninsula, not a Nuu-chah-nulth figure. Nuu-chah-nulth tradition gives the raven's role to its own culture hero, while the Dena'ina raven cycle tells how Chulyen stole fire and shaped the land.

name: Chupacabra
description: First reported in Puerto Rico, 1995, preceded by the 1975 'vampiro de Moca'. The name — 'chupa' (sucks) + 'cabra' (goat) = 'Goat-Sucker' — coined by Silverio Pérez. The Canóvanas sighting set the classic image: 4-5 feet, gray, wraparound eyes, spines. Types: bipedal reptilian kangaroo; quadrupedal hairless dog-like (mangy coyotes). Radford's 2011 study found predators and disease, not a vampire.

name: Chupacabras Boricua
description: Chupacabras Boricua is the Puerto Rican regional variant of the legendary Chupacabra cryptid, distinguished by its specific origin in the island's folklore and unique description compared to mainland versions. The name Boricua refers to the Taino name for Puerto Rico, Boriken, making this the original version of the Chupacabra legend that emerged in 1995. The first reported attack occurred in March 1995 in Moca, Puerto Rico, where eight sheep were found dead with puncture wounds and reportedly drained of blood. The name chupacabras meaning goat-sucker was coined by Puerto Rican comedian Silverio Perez. The most famous eyewitness Madelyne Tolentino of Canovanas reported seeing the creature in August 1995, and her description became the template for the Puerto Rican version, later investigated extensively by skeptic Benjamin Radford

name: Chupacora
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Chupacora' is an unattested variant of the chupacabra, a livestock-killing cryptid first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995 and since reported across Latin America. No distinct Guatemalan 'Chupacora' with its own characteristics is documented.

name: Chura-Batyr
description: Chura-Batyr is the epic hero of the Tatar people, rooted in the historical figure Chura Narykov of the sixteenth-century Kazan Khanate. Tales present him as a defender of the Tatar lands, a warrior of great strength and loyalty whose downfall through betrayal became a byword for resistance and lament in Tatar oral tradition.

name: Churail
description: The churail (also churel or chudail) is a feared female revenant of South Asian folklore — Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Nepal — the spirit of a woman who died in childbirth or an unnatural death. She haunts peepul trees, crossroads, cremation grounds and wells, appearing as a beautiful young woman in white whose feet are often turned backward, to seduce and destroy men, especially male kin.

name: Churel
description: South Asian female ghost/witch ('Churel,' 'Chudail,' 'Churail' - also called 'Pichal Peri' = backward feet). Origins: woman who died in pregnancy, childbirth, or wronged by men. Most common: died during childbirth (considered 'impure' death). OR died as bride with husband/family mistreating her - Returns for vengeance. Connected to 'Peri' (Persian supernatural). Mixes Hindu concepts + Islamic jinn beliefs. ONE OF THE Most Feared - drains life force (not just blood): victims wither, age Rapidly - decades in one night. Lures young men by shapeshifting into beauty, then embrace drains life. MEN Killing is her signature - but also targets infants, children

name: Chut
description: Chut is a spectral entity from Scottish Highland folklore, particularly associated with the Orkney and Shetland Islands as well as parts of the northern Scottish mainland. This mysterious being is classified among the many nature spirits and apparitions that populate the rich Celtic and Norse-influenced folklore of northern Scotland. The Chut is considered a harbinger of misfortune, often appearing before storms, accidents, or deaths in fishing communities. The folklore of the Orkney and Shetland Islands represents a unique blend of Pictish, Celtic, and Norse traditions, and the Chut belongs to a class of supernatural beings that reflect the harsh maritime environment and the precarious lives of coastal communities who depended on the sea for their survival

name: Chyskhaan
description: Chyskhaan is the Lord of Cold in Sakha (Yakut) belief, a spirit who rules the fierce frosts of Siberia and dwells in an ice palace said to stand near Oymyakon, one of the coldest inhabited places on earth. When his breath thickens and his horns gather frost, the deepest cold of winter is said to be drawing near.

name: Ciguapa
description: The Ciguapa is a nocturnal mythical creature from Dominican folklore, described as a wild woman who inhabits the high mountain regions of the island. Her most distinctive feature is that her feet are turned backward, making it nearly impossible for hunters or trackers to follow her footprints. She is deeply tied to the natural world, possessing expert knowledge of medicinal herbs and plants found in the dense tropical forests. The first written account of the Ciguapa appeared in 1866 in the story 'La Ciguapa' by Francisco Javier Angulo Guridi. Some scholars debate whether the legend has Taíno origins or was introduced through European influences, drawing comparisons to mermaid myths and the Hindu churel

name: Ciguapa
description: The Ciguapa is a nocturnal wild woman of Dominican mountain folklore whose backward-turned feet baffle trackers. The earliest written account is Francisco Javier Angulo Guridi's 1866 story 'La Ciguapa.' Scholars debate a possible Taíno origin against European parallels such as mermaids and the churel.

name: Cikavac
description: The Cikavac is a mythical winged creature from Serbian folklore, born from an egg laid by a black hen that must be carried under a woman's armpit for forty days. During this gestation period, the woman must not confess, cut her nails, wash her face, or pray, adhering to strict taboos that imbue the egg with magical properties. The resulting creature serves its owner by stealing milk from neighbors' cattle and honey from their beehives, bringing these goods back to its master. The Cikavac also grants its owner the ability to understand the language of animals, a gift that provides insight into the hidden workings of the natural world. This creature appears in the Serbian mythological dictionary compiled by Kulisic, Petrovic, and Pantelic

name: Cipactli
description: Cipactli is a primeval sea monster from Aztec mythology, often described as a gigantic crocodilian-fish-toad hybrid that existed before the creation of the world. In Aztec cosmology, the gods Tezcatlipoca and Quetzalcoatl created the earth from Cipactli's body after Tezcatlipoca sacrificed his foot using the monster as bait. The name Cipactli means 'crocodile' or 'caiman' in Classical Nahuatl, and it also represents the first day of the Aztec divinatory calendar, the tonalpohualli, which consists of 260 days. This creature is closely related to Tlaltecuhtli, the earth monster deity, and to Zipacna, the earthquake demon of Mayan mythology who appears in the Popol Vuh. Karl Taube has identified connections between Cipactli and Olmec crocodilian iconography dating back to the Formative period

name: Cipitío
description: Cipitío is a beloved legendary character from Salvadoran folklore, the illegitimate son of La Siguanaba and Lucero de la Mañana (Lucifer). Cursed by the god Teotl as a result of his mother's infidelity, he was condemned to remain a child forever, with his feet set backward as a reminder of the twisted affair of his parents. He is generally portrayed as an 8 to 10-year-old boy with a large conical hat and a pot belly. His name derives from the Nahuatl word 'cipit' or 'cipote' meaning child. Cipitío is a mischievous trickster who wanders into farmers' fields, throws pebbles at beautiful women, hides in bushes to scare people, and eats ashes leftover in rural kitchens. Farmers would find child's footprints in their fields and blame Cipitío. Despite his mischief, he is generally regarded as benevolent and is even associated with bringing good luck. He is so beloved that he has his own television show on Salvadoran Educational Television, where he teaches morals and values to children

name: Coblynau
description: The Coblynau are mythical gnome-like creatures from Welsh folklore that haunt mines and quarries throughout Wales and areas of Welsh settlement in America. The name is related to the English word 'goblin' and may derive from the German 'kobold' via French. First documented extensively by Wirt Sikes in his 1880 book 'British Goblins', the Coblynau are considered friendly fairies despite their grotesque appearance. They are closely related to the Knockers of Cornish folklore, mining spirits that share similar behaviors. Unlike the more malicious goblins of other traditions, the Coblynau are generally helpful to miners who treat them with respect, using distinctive knocking sounds to guide workers toward the richest veins of ore deep underground

name: Coca
description: The Coca is a legendary female dragon from Portuguese and Galician folklore, feared for lurking in dark places to snatch unwary children. Unlike many male dragons in European mythology, the Coca is distinctly female and plays a central role in traditional Corpus Christi celebrations in northern Portugal, particularly in the town of Monção. During these festivities, the Coca engages in a symbolic medieval tournament with Saint George, reenacting the famous dragon-slaying legend. The creature is also related to the Coco or Cuca, a bogeyman figure used to frighten children across the Portuguese-speaking world and Latin America, where it is sometimes depicted as an anthropomorphic alligator in children's books

name: Cogaz
description: Cogaz is the eldest son of Kaang (Cagn), the supreme creator god in San (Bushman) mythology of southern Africa. As a great chief alongside his father and Qwanciqutshaa, Cogaz appears in numerous San creation myths and tales

name: Coleando
description: Not independently attested as a monster of Chilean folklore. 'Coleando' is the Spanish gerund for swishing or wriggling a tail (as in the idiom 'vivito y coleando'), not the name of a being, and no source documents a 'Coleando' water monster. The genuine Chilean aquatic figures are El Cuero, the Nguruvilu and the Camahueto, which the entry's own list confuses with this invention.

name: Comorian Dragon
description: Comorian Dragon (Comorian). is a dragon. A winged serpentine dragon from Comorian folklore, associated with volcanic rock formations and storms in the Indian Ocean archipelago. Source: Atlas Obscura; Comorian oral traditions

name: Comorian Jinn (Mashetani)
description: In the Comoros Islands, belief in jinn (locally called mashetani) is deeply ingrained in the culture, representing a syncretic blend of Islamic theology with indigenous African and Malagasy spirit beliefs. Comorian jinn are invisible spirits created from smokeless fire who inhabit a parallel world to humans. They are believed to dwell in specific locations such as ancient baobab trees, volcanic craters, coral reefs, and abandoned wells. Unlike the purely malevolent spirits found in some traditions, Comorian jinn are morally complex beings capable of both good and evil actions. They are particularly associated with illness and strange behavior, and traditional healers (fundi or mganga) perform rituals to diagnose and treat jinn-related afflictions. The belief system reflects the islands' history as a crossroads of Swahili-Arabic culture, where maritime trade brought not only goods but also spiritual concepts from across the Indian Ocean. Respect for jinn involves specific protocols: avoiding whistling at night, seeking permission before entering certain areas, and leaving offerings of food or incense

name: Conjure Doctor
