description: The Conjure Doctor (also known as a root doctor, hoodoo doctor, or two-headed doctor) is a powerful figure in African American folk belief — a practitioner of conjure, hoodoo, and rootwork who possesses supernatural knowledge and the ability to influence events through magical means. Conjure Doctors serve as community healers, spiritual advisors, and protectors against evil. They use herbs, roots, bones, and personal items to create mojo bags, cast spells, or provide protection. Essential tools include John the Conqueror root (for luck and protection), goofer dust (for cursing), black cat bones (for invisibility and luck), and candles. The Conjure Doctor occupies an ambiguous position — feared for their power to curse, respected for their power to heal, and essential to the spiritual life of the community

name: Coqui (Sacred Frog Spirit of Puerto Rico)
description: The Coqui is a tiny tree frog (Eleutherodactylus coqui) native to Puerto Rico that has transcended biology to become a sacred cultural and mythological symbol. In Taino mythology, the Coqui distinctive two-note nocturnal call Co-kee! has a divine origin. According to legend, a beautiful Taino goddess fell in love with Coqui, the chief son. They met in secret, but the evil god Juracan (the spirit of chaos and hurricanes) snatched Coqui away. Heartbroken, the goddess transformed her lover into a tiny frog that would forever call his own name into the night. The Taino people depicted the Coqui extensively in petroglyphs, pottery, and stone carvings, with its wide-eyed frog symbol representing fertility, femaleness, and the spirit world. Today, the Coqui is an unofficial national symbol of Puerto Rico -- the saying Soy de aqui, como el coqui (I am from here, like the coqui) expresses deep-rooted cultural identity

name: Corn Girl
description: Corn Girl is a Navajo Holy Person associated with the sacred mountain Tsoodził (Mount Taylor), the southern boundary mountain of the Navajo world set with turquoise and female rain. She dwells there with Turquoise Boy, guarding corn and its growth, and stands with them as an emblem of fertility and the Navajo corn-growing cycle.

name: Corn Maidens
description: The Corn Maidens are the sacred corn spirits of the Pueblo peoples, especially the Zuni and Hopi, who embody the growth and life of maize. In origin accounts the maidens brought corn up from the underworld, sang and danced it into being, and when they were neglected the harvest withered until the people and their kachina priests called the maidens back.

name: Corn Maidens (various colors)
description: The Zuni Corn Maidens are seven sisters who personify the different colors of corn, fostered and guarded by Paiyatuma, the God of Dew and Dawn and flute-playing patron of spring. When they left the Zuni in anger the harvest withered, and Paiyatuma with the Kachina Fathers brought them home with magic wands and flute songs, restoring the crops.

name: Corn Mother
description: Corn Mother (also known as Iatiku among the Acoma) is the central female deity in Pueblo mythology who gave corn to the people. After emergence into the light, when people had no food, Corn Mother scraped her skin and from the scrapings produced corn of all colors — white, yellow, blue, red, and black. She taught how to plant, tend, harvest, and prepare corn. In Pueblo tradition, corn is not merely a crop but a sacred being with a spirit. The health of the corn crop reflects the people's relatio

name: Corn Woman
description: Corn Woman is the corn-giving spirit of the Muscogee (Creek) people, honored at the busk, the Green Corn Ceremony that begins the Creek new year. In origin accounts corn was a gift that came through a woman, and the ceremony renews the world with new fire, thanksgiving, and the first fruits of the harvest.

name: Cosmic Elk
description: The Cosmic Elk (also called the Golden-antlered Deer or Celestial Elk) is a central figure in Sami astral mythology — the great elk or reindeer that lives in the sky and is hunted by the thunder god Horagalles (Tiermes/Dierpmis). This cosmic hunt is reflected in the constellations: Orion is the hunter, the Pleiades are the deer/elk, and the Milky Way is the tracks of the mythic elk-hunter's skis. When the thunder god shoots the celestial elk with his fiery arrow, an apocalypse ensues — fire envelops the earth, mountains boil, ice boils, stars fall, the moon goes out, and the sun sinks. The myth is described in Kola Sami tradition: 'But on earth it becomes dust.' Petroglyphs from the last millennium BC depict this cosmic hunt myth, showing its ancient origins. The golden-antlered deer is sometimes identified with Meandash-pyyrre, the celestial form of the mythic reindeer who is also described as a sun symbol, the snow-covered golden-horned reindeer who flies from one side of the land to the other

name: Cougar Ancestor-Spirit (Muisca)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Muisca tradition. Muisca cosmology of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense is documented around Sué, Chía, Bachué, Bochica and Chiminigagua; no cougar ancestor-spirit appears in colonial sources or ethnography. The only tangential echo is the sixteenth-century epithet of Bochica as 'father of a tiger', which does not constitute a cougar cult.

name: Cougar Ancestor-Spirit (Muisca)
description: The Muisca of the Colombian highlands (not Mexico) revered animal forms and ancestral powers, with deities such as Bachue and Bochica central to their cosmology. The puma, native to the Andes, could carry such symbolic weight, but a specific Muisca 'cougar ancestor-spirit' is not directly attested in colonial sources. The entry misplaces the culture in Mexico.

name: Cougar Ancestor-Spirit of Aymara
description: The Cougar Ancestor-Spirit of the Aymara people is a powerful guardian being from the Andean highlands of Bolivia, Peru, and Chile. In Aymara cosmology, the puma or cougar was one of the most sacred animals, representing strength, courage, and the earthly realm known as Kay Pacha. The Aymara believed that powerful ancestral spirits known as Achachilas, who dwell in the highest mountain peaks, could manifest as cougars to protect their descendants and the natural world. These spirits served as intermediaries between the human world and the greater deities such as Pachamama and Inti, ensuring the balance of nature was maintained and that communities prospered

name: Cougar Ancestor-Spirit of Baloch
description: The Cougar Ancestor-Spirit from Baloch tradition represents the powerful guardian spirits of the Baloch people of Balochistan, a region spanning parts of Iran, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. In Baloch folklore, big cats such as leopards and cougars are regarded as powerful spirit animals that carry the souls of revered ancestors. The harsh, arid mountains and deserts of Balochistan are believed to be patrolled by these guardian spirits, who watch over nomadic herders and their livestock. Baloch oral tradition preserves stories of these cougar spirits protecting travelers through dangerous mountain passes and appearing to warriors before important battles. The legend reflects the deep connection between the Baloch people and the rugged landscape they inhabit

name: Cougar Ancestor-Spirit of Cheyenne
description: The Cougar Ancestor-Spirit from Cheyenne tradition is a revered guardian being in the spiritual beliefs of the Cheyenne people of the Great Plains. In Cheyenne cosmology, the mountain lion is respected as a powerful animal spirit associated with hunting prowess, stealth, and protection. The Cheyenne believe that the Great Creator Ma'heo'o imbued certain animals with special spiritual powers to assist humanity. Cougar ancestor-spirits serve as guides for warriors and hunters, teaching them patience and the importance of moving through the world with awareness and purpose. The Cheyenne hold the cougar in high regard alongside other sacred animals such as the buffalo and the wolf

name: Cougar Ancestor-Spirit of Maya
description: The Cougar Ancestor-Spirit from Maya tradition represents the sacred jaguar-cougar deity figures central to Maya cosmology. In Maya mythology, large felines were associated with the underworld Xibalba, the night sun, and the spiritual power of rulers. Although the jaguar was more prominent in Maya iconography, the cougar or puma also held significant spiritual meaning, particularly in the highland Maya regions where jaguars were less common. Maya kings and queens often incorporated feline imagery into their royal regalia to signify their connection to the underworld and their authority to rule. The cougar spirit was believed to guide the souls of the dead through the nine levels of Xibalba

name: Cougar Ancestor-Spirit of Uzbek
description: The Cougar Ancestor-Spirit from Uzbek tradition reflects the ancient nature worship and animal reverence found in Central Asian folklore. Although cougars are not native to Uzbekistan, the concept of powerful feline ancestor-spirits blends with local traditions of snow leopard and tiger spirits found across Turkic mythology. In Uzbek folk belief, ancestors could reincarnate as powerful animals or manifest as guardian spirits to protect their descendants. These spirits are associated with the mountains and forests of the Tian Shan range, where they watch over villages and herds. The tradition incorporates elements of pre-Islamic Tengriism mixed with Sufi mysticism

name: Cougar Ancestor-Spirit of Zulu
description: Not independently attested. The cougar is not native to South Africa, and the input's own text concedes this, substituting the leopard (ingwe), whose skin marks Zulu royalty and regiments. No Zulu ancestor-spirit is recorded in cougar form: ancestral veneration centres on the amadlozi and amathongo, whose animal manifestations are documented creatures such as the python, not New World cats.

name: Cougar Animal-Spirit of Apache
description: The Cougar Animal-Spirit of the Apache people is a powerful guardian being in Apache spiritual traditions of the American Southwest. In Apache cosmology, the mountain lion or cougar is respected as a spirit animal associated with hunting prowess, leadership, and protection. Apache warriors sought the cougar's power through vision quests and ceremonies, believing that the spirit would grant them stealth, courage, and strategic wisdom. The Apache recognize the Gaan, or mountain spirits, as powerful protectors who dwell in sacred mountains, and the cougar spirit is closely associated with these traditions. The cougar's ability to move silently and strike with precision makes it a powerful ally

name: Cougar Animal-Spirit of Haida
description: The Cougar Animal-Spirit from Haida tradition represents the powerful guardian spirits found in the rich animistic mythology of the Haida people of Haida Gwaii (formerly the Queen Charlotte Islands). In Haida cosmology, the natural world is filled with supernatural beings known as Sga'na qeda's, powerful spirits that can appear in animal forms and interact with humans. Although cougars are not native to Haida Gwaii, the Haida recognized mountain lions from mainland interactions and incorporated feline spirit power into their complex totemic system. The Haida believe that animals can transform between animal and human forms, and that powerful ancestor-spirits often manifest through animal manifestations to guide and protect their descendants

name: Cougar Animal-Spirit of Inuit
description: The Cougar Animal-Spirit from Inuit tradition represents the powerful animal guardian spirits that form the foundation of Inuit spiritual beliefs across the Arctic regions of Canada, Alaska, and Greenland. While cougars are not found in the far north, Inuit mythology includes the concept of powerful predator spirits such as the Amarok, a giant wolf spirit that hunts alone. This cougar spirit should be understood within the broader context of Inuit animism, where all animals possess souls and powerful spirits can manifest in forms appropriate to their purpose. The Inuit believe in numerous nature spirits known as tuurngait and inua, the spirits that inhabit all living things, and powerful feline spirits from more southern regions are incorporated into this rich spiritual framework

name: Cougar Animal-Spirit of Maliseet
description: The Cougar Animal-Spirit of the Maliseet people is a guardian figure from the Wabanaki Confederacy traditions of the northeastern United States and eastern Canada. The Maliseet, also known as Wolastoqiyik, have a rich oral tradition that includes powerful animal spirits who act as intermediaries between the human world and the Great Spirit. Cougars, also called eastern mountain lions, once roamed the forests of Maliseet territory along the Saint John River valley and were respected as powerful hunting spirits. Maliseet mythology emphasizes the interconnectedness of all living beings and the importance of showing respect to the spirits of animals that give their lives to sustain the people

name: Cougar Animal-Spirit of Pomo
description: The Cougar Animal-Spirit from Pomo tradition is a powerful guardian being in the spiritual beliefs of the Pomo people of northern California. The Pomo, who lived in the region north of San Francisco Bay, traditionally inhabited areas where mountain lions were common and respected as powerful spirits. In Pomo cosmology, the world is filled with spirit-beings known as Xa'nis, and powerful animals like the cougar were believed to possess especially strong spiritual power. Pomo shamans and medicine people called upon animal spirits for healing, protection, and guidance. The cougar spirit is associated with the hilly oak woodlands and redwood forests that characterize the Pomo ancestral homeland

name: Cougar Animal-Spirit of Ute
description: The Cougar Animal-Spirit from Ute tradition is a revered guardian figure in the spiritual beliefs of the Ute people of the Rocky Mountain region, spanning parts of present-day Colorado, Utah, and New Mexico. The Ute, who have inhabited the Southern Rocky Mountains for centuries, hold the mountain lion in high regard as a powerful spirit animal representing leadership, courage, and strategic thinking. In Ute tradition, animal-spirits serve as teachers and protectors, guiding individuals through the challenges of life. The cougar spirit is particularly associated with warriors, chiefs, and those who carry responsibility for the welfare of others, reflecting the mountain lion's position as an apex predator in the Rocky Mountain ecosystem

name: Cougar Deity (Muisca)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No cougar or puma deity appears in the documented Muisca pantheon of the Colombian Altiplano. Colonial records of the 1563 Ubaque ceremony mention a 'tiger' — perhaps a puma or jaguar — tied to the culture-hero Bochica, but no cave-guardian cougar deity is attested.

name: Cougar Deity of Cheyenne
description: No cougar deity is attested in Cheyenne tradition. In the Cheyenne story of 'The Woodpecker's Mother-in-Law' the mountain lion stands for courage, but it is a story figure, not a god. Cheyenne divine power belongs to Maheo and the Sacred Powers; the mountain lion never held deity status in documented Cheyenne religion.

name: Cougar Deity of Maliseet
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No cougar deity is recorded in Maliseet (Wolastoqiyik) tradition, and cougars were not established in Wabanaki territory. The Maliseet culture hero is Koluskap (Glooscap), the transformer of Wabanaki myth; the cougar sky-guardian role described is fabricated.

name: Cougar Deity of Paiute
description: In the Numic traditions of the Great Basin, the legend 'The Wolf, the Fox, the Bobcat and the Cougar' tells how these four animal spirits helped the Shoshone-Bannock and related Paiute peoples defeat the Nimerigar, cannibalistic little people who shot poisoned arrows. The cougar appears as a heroic spirit ally, not a deity.

name: Cougar Deity of Yoruba
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Cougars are not native to West Africa and no cougar deity exists in Yoruba cosmology. The genuine feline symbol is ekun, the leopard, totem of royalty and of the thunder god Shango, who is depicted wearing leopard skin; the entry conflates a cougar with this leopard symbolism.

name: Cougar Ghost of Choctaw
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Choctaw tradition does include the panther (koi) as a clan animal and the horned serpent Sint Holo as a water spirit, but no 'cougar ghost' guarding river crossings is documented. The river-threshold guardian role is invented.

name: Cougar Ghost of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested: cougars (mountain lions) do not occur in Kazakhstan, and no 'cougar ghost' appears in Kazakh sources; the figure is likely a mislabeled big-cat spirit. Genuine Kazakh great-cat traditions concern the snow leopard (ilbirs) and the extinct Caspian tiger (qaplan, yulbars), both revered in steppe and mountain lore as powerful guardian beings.

name: Cougar Ghost of Lakota
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Lakota tradition describes a cougar 'ghost' or a 'lone warrior' mountain-lion spirit as narrated here. Lakota oral tradition features animal powers sought in vision quests, but this specific cougar-spirit figure and its symbolism have no documented source.

name: Cougar Giant of Choctaw
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Choctaw emergence tradition holds that the people came from the underworld through the mound of Nanih Waiya, but no 'cougar giant' dwelling beneath it or causing earthquakes appears in any recorded tradition. The being is fabricated.

name: Cougar Giant of Kikuyu
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Cougars are not native to Africa, and no Kikuyu tradition describes giant spirit-cats guarding the lakes of Mount Kenya. Kikuyu cosmology centers on Ngai, the supreme god of Kirinyaga; the marozi, a spotted-lion cryptid of the Aberdares, is a separate and unverified notion.

name: Cougar Giant of Kwakiutl
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) cosmology includes Dzunukwa the wild woman, Bakwas the ghost king, and Sisiutl the sea serpent, but no cougar giant figures among the transformation beings of the winter ceremonials. The cougar-giant role is invented.

name: Cougar Giant of Shoshone
description: In Shoshone oral tradition, the legend 'The Wolf, the Fox, the Bobcat and the Cougar' recounts how four animal spirits helped the Shoshone-Bannock defeat the Nimerigar, warlike little people of the Rocky Mountains who shot poisoned arrows. The cougar here is a heroic spirit ally, not a giant or mountain guardian.

name: Cougar Giant of Ute
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Ute tradition records a cougar giant or a mountain-lion spirit with fixed color and season attributes. Ute mythology centers on Sinawav the creator and a circle of major animal spirits, but no cougar being matching this entry is documented.

name: Cougar Guardian (Guarani)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. No source records a protective cougar guardian among the Guarani, and the input's claim that Guarani-speaking peoples of Mexico preserved such a being is unfounded. Genuine Guarani forest spirits are Pombero, Jasy Jatere and Kurupí, while the tree-guarding Curupira belongs to Brazilian Tupi folklore, not to a Paraguayan cougar.

name: Cougar Guardian (Guarani)
description: The Guarani and Tupi peoples of Paraguay, Brazil, and Argentina revere forest spirits who protect the wilderness and punish those who overexploit it, including the Curupira and jaguar-related guardians of the forest. The puma, called yaguarundi in the region, fits this protective role. The entry mislabels the culture as Mexican; the Guarani homeland lies in South America.

name: Cougar Guardian of Aymara
description: In Aymara cosmology from the Andean highlands of Bolivia, Peru, and Chile, the cougar guardian (puma) is a sacred animal spirit associated with mountain springs, water sources, and the pastoral economy that sustains Aymara communities. The Aymara people, who have inhabited the altiplano around Lake Titicaca for millennia, consider the puma one of the most spiritually significant animals in their religious system. In Aymara tradition, the puma belongs to a group of eight sacred emblematic animals known as sallka (wild animals that are loved), each associated with specific productive functions in the Andean world. The puma and the chullumpe bird are emblems of pastoralism, serving as spiritual pastors for llamas and alpacas. The Aymara believe that mountain spirits (mallkus) appointed the puma as their awatiri (pastor), the supernatural shepherd of the wild herds that belong to the mountain gods

name: Cougar Guardian of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Cougars are not native to Balochistan. The genuine feline of Iranian-plateau tradition is the palang (leopard), a term rich in Persian literary symbolism (Rustam's leopard-skin), along with babr (tiger); the cave-guardian 'cougar' is invented.

name: Cougar Guardian of Creek
description: In Creek (Muscogee) tradition the panther is honored through the Panther Clan, Katsalgi, one of the principal matrilineal clans of the Creek Confederacy. Panther hunting medicine was highly regarded, and among the related Seminole the Panther clan is the premier medicinal clan.

name: Cougar Guardian of Mapuche
description: In Mapuche tradition from Chile and Argentina, the cougar guardian (pangui in Mapudungun) is a powerful spirit-being associated with the underworld and the protection of sacred mountains and underground passages. The Mapuche people, who have inhabited the southern Andes for millennia, regard the puma as one of their most significant spiritual animals. The puma is called futamaye meaning great uncle in Mapudungun, reflecting the close relationship between the Mapuche people and this powerful feline. Mapuche warriors traditionally incorporated particles of puma bone into their bodies during initiation ceremonies to gain the cats strength and courage. The cougar guardian protects the entrances to the underworld (Minche Mapu), the realm beneath the earth where Mapuche spirits reside after death. The Mapuche believe that the puma spirit acts as an intermediary between the human world and the spirits of the ancestors who dwell below

name: Cougar Nature-Spirit (Kikuyu)
description: Within Kikuyu oral traditions the cougar nature-spirit represents one of many territorial guardians assigned by Ngai to protect specific ecological zones across the central Kenyan highlands. These spirits belong to a complex hierarchy of supernatural beings including ancestral spirits, nature deities, and the distant high god. The cougar spirit specifically oversees transition zones where cultivated fields meet wild forests, acting as a regulator of the relationship between human settlement and untamed nature. Kikuyu folklore teaches these spirits were placed during the age of origins when the first parents Gikuyu and Mumbi established the nine clans and received the land as a sacred trust from Ngai himself

name: Cougar Nature-Spirit (Kikuyu)
description: Cougar Nature-Spirit (Kikuyu) is a nature-spirit from Guatemala mythology. These spirits belong to a complex hierarchy of supernatural beings including ancestral spirits, nature deities, and the distant high god. The cougar spirit specifically oversees transition zones where cultivated fields meet wild forests, acting as a regulator of the relationship between human settlement and untamed nature. Kikuyu folklore teaches these spirits were placed during the age of origins when the first parents Gikuyu and Mumbi established the nine clans and received the land as a sacred trust from Ngai himself

name: Cougar Nature-Spirit (Kikuyu)
description: Cougar Nature-Spirit (Kikuyu) is a nature-spirit from USA mythology. These spirits belong to a complex hierarchy of supernatural beings including ancestral spirits, nature deities, and the distant high god. The cougar spirit specifically oversees transition zones where cultivated fields meet wild forests, acting as a regulator of the relationship between human settlement and untamed nature. Kikuyu folklore teaches these spirits were placed during the age of origins when the first parents Gikuyu and Mumbi established the nine clans and received the land as a sacred trust from Ngai himself

name: Cougar Nature-Spirit of Haida
description: Among the Haida people of Haida Gwaii the cougar nature-spirit occupies a distinctive place in the pantheon of supernatural beings known as Sgaana qedas. The Pacific Northwest coastal forests and mountainous islands provide the backdrop for this powerful spirit, which the Haida associate with remote peaks and dense cedar groves of their archipelago. In Haida cosmology all animals possess spirit counterparts in the invisible world, and the cougar spirit is particularly respected for its solitary nature and connection to the mysteries of the deep forest. It appears in oral histories as one of the animal crest spirits that certain Haida lineages claim as ancestral guardians and totemic symbols of their clan identity

name: Cougar Nature-Spirit of Inuit
description: Inuit oral traditions include nature spirits associated with various animals that inhabit or pass through northern territories. While the cougar is not a typical Arctic dweller, Inuit cosmology recognizes spirits that travel between worlds and may appear in forms unfamiliar to the physical landscape. These cave-dwelling spirits belong to the broader category of tuurngait, helping spirits that angakkuit call upon for guidance and protection. The cougar nature-spirit represents mysterious forces dwelling within limestone caves and ice-carved grottoes found along Arctic coastlines and river valleys, places where the boundary between the human world and the spirit realm grows thin and permeable

name: Cougar Nature-Spirit of Maliseet
description: The Maliseet people of the Maritime provinces and Quebec tell of a cougar nature-spirit dwelling in underground chambers and root systems of vast Acadian forests. This spirit belongs to the rich animistic tradition of the Wabanaki Confederacy, where all natural features possess spiritual essence and guardian beings oversee specific territories. The Maliseet traditionally inhabited the Saint John River watershed, and their oral literature describes the underground world beneath the forest floor as a complex realm inhabited by spirits regulating the growth of medicinal plants, movements of game animals, and seasonal cycles governing traditional sustenance practices

name: Cougar Spirit (Mixtec)
description: In the rich mythological landscape of the Mixtec people the cougar spirit embodies transformation and the liminal space between earthly existence and celestial power. Mixtec religion recorded in surviving pre-Columbian codices describes a universe created through the sacrifice of primordial beings and maintained by interactions between humans, nature spirits, and gods like Dzahui and Nine Wind. The cougar spirit belongs to this intricate web of relationships, serving as a psychopomp guiding souls of Mixtec nobles through the nine levels of the underworld into the presence of ancestors. Its association with wind and breath connects it to the fundamental life force animating all creation in Mixtec thought

name: Cougar Spirit (Mixtec)
description: In the rich mythological landscape of the Mixtec people the cougar spirit embodies transformation and the liminal space between earthly existence and celestial power. Mixtec religion recorded in surviving pre-Columbian codices describes a universe created through the sacrifice of primordial beings and maintained by interactions between humans, nature spirits, and gods like Dzahui and Nine Wind. The cougar spirit belongs to this intricate web of relationships, serving as a psychopomp guiding souls of Mixtec nobles through the nine levels of the underworld into the presence of ancestors. Its association with wind and breath connects it to the fundamental life force animating all creation in Mixtec thought In South Africa folklore, this figure is known among the South Africa people.

name: Cougar Trickster (Mapuche)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Mapuche tradition. The puma (pangui, trapial) is genuinely significant as a sacred animal in Mapuche culture, but no source records a 'cougar trickster' called trapial wekufe who assisted the sun during creation; Antu is the Mapuche sun, not a creation hero. The trickster role is invented rather than drawn from Mapuche oral tradition.

name: Cougar Trickster (Mapuche)
description: Not independently attested. No documented tradition records a 'cougar trickster' among the Mapuche, and none connects such a figure to Myanmar: the entry crosses a South American people (Mapuche) with a Southeast Asian country, and its 'trapial wekufe' name and Antu culture-hero narrative are unsupported. Cougars do not occur in Myanmar, and no Burmese source names this being.

name: Cougar Trickster of Guarani
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. The seven monstrous sons of Tau and Kerana are fixed in the corpus recorded by Cadogán and Colmán: Teju Jagua, Mbói Tu'i, Moñái, Jasy Jatere, Kurupí, Ao Ao and Luisón; no cougar is among them. The claim that a feline underworld trickster ranks among these siblings is a fabrication.

name: Cougar Trickster of Guarani
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. This Brazilian variant repeats the Paraguay entry's fabrication that a cougar ranks among the seven monstrous sons of Tau and Kerana; the documented sons are Teju Jagua, Mbói Tu'i, Moñái, Jasy Jatere, Kurupí, Ao Ao and Luisón, none a cougar.

name: Cougar Trickster of Kwakiutl
description: Among the Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka_wakw) people of coastal British Columbia, the cougar trickster belongs to the rich tradition of forest spirits and supernatural beings that inhabit the temperate rainforests of Vancouver Island and the mainland coast. Kwakwaka_wakw cosmology recognizes four distinct spirit realms: sky spirits, sea spirits, earth spirits, and otherworldly spirits. The cougar trickster operates primarily as an earth spirit associated with the dense cedar and hemlock forests, occupying a role similar to but distinct from the better-known Dzunukwa. Its stories are told during winter ceremonies when the boundary between the human world and the spirit world thins, and supernatural beings walk among the villages

name: Cougar Trickster of Pomo
description: The Pomo people of northern California speak of a cougar trickster that inhabits the dense redwood and oak forests of their ancestral territory. In Pomo cosmology animal spirits play central roles in creation stories and continue to influence daily life through their presence in the landscape. The cougar trickster is particularly associated with the transition zones between the coastal mountain ranges and the interior valleys, areas where different ecological communities meet and where spiritual energy is believed to concentrate. Pomo oral tradition includes the cougar among the first animals created by the Maker, assigning it the role of both guardian and provocateur in the balance of natural forces

name: Cougar Trickster of Zulu
description: Among the Zulu people of South Africa the cougar trickster represents a spirit that inhabits swampy lowlands and transitional wetlands that the Zulu call amaxhaphozi. While the cougar is not native to southern Africa, in Zulu spiritual cosmology the term refers to a big-cat spirit entity with similar characteristics to the ingwe leopard spirit but with distinct trickster qualities. This being belongs to the complex Zulu spirit world that includes the ancestors, nature spirits, and the creator god uMvelinqangi. The cougar trickster operates in liminal wetland environments where water, earth, and air meet, making it a being of transitions and boundary-crossing in both physical and metaphorical senses

name: Cougar Water-Spirit of Apache
description: Not independently attested as a water-spirit of Apache folklore. Cougars are honored among Western Apache as powerful medicine animals and directional guardians, but no Apache cougar water-spirit is documented. Apache water-beings include the horned serpent; a cougar of the desert springs is not attested in the sources.

name: Cougar Water-Spirit of Paiute
description: The Paiute people of the Great Basin region honor a cougar water-spirit that watches over the rivers and streams flowing from the Sierra Nevada mountains into the desert valleys. In Paiute cosmology water spirits occupy an essential role as providers of life in an environment where water is scarce and precious. The cougar spirit specifically guards the smaller flowing waters such as creeks and streams rather than lakes, reflecting the Paiute's deep knowledge of their arid homeland's hydrology. Paiute oral traditions describe this spirit as one of several animal guardians appointed during the creation period by the Wolf, the Paiute culture hero, to watch over different aspects of the natural world

name: Cougar Water-Spirit of Zapotec
description: In Zapotec cosmology from Oaxaca, Mexico, the cougar water-spirit is associated with underground water sources and cavern systems that characterize the region's karst topography. The Zapotec people, whose civilization flourished at Monte Alban and Mitla, believed that underground water was controlled by powerful spirits connected to the earth deity Cocijo, the god of rain and lightning. This cougar water-spirit operates in the liminal space between the surface world and the subterranean water systems, serving as a guardian of the hidden rivers that flow beneath the valleys of Oaxaca. Zapotec codices and funerary urns sometimes depict feline figures in association with water symbols and the underworld

name: Cougar Water-Spirit of Zulu
description: Not independently attested. No Zulu water-spirit is recorded as a cougar, an animal absent from South Africa; the 'cougar of the cliffs' that carries prayers skyward is invented template prose. Zulu aquatic spirit-lore centres on the inkanyamba, a great serpent of rivers and storms, and the mamlambo river-creature; neither has a cougar form.

name: Covered in Mud
description: In the traditions of the Muscogee Creek people of the Southeastern United States, the being known as Covered in Mud appears in stories about the creation and ordering of the world. The Muscogee believe that in the beginning the earth was covered entirely by water, and the only land was a single muddy hill that grew from the depths. Covered in Mud is one of the primordial beings that emerged from this original mud, carrying with it the creative potential of the fertile earth. This being features in the Muscogee migration narratives and ceremonial cycles, representing the connection between the people and the land from which they emerged. The Muscogee town square and ceremonial grounds are physical representations of this original emergence

name: Coyote
description: While coyote as a trickster figure is most famously associated with Navajo, Hopi, and other Southwestern tribes, this entry appears to conflate Inuit tradition with elements of Coyote and Raven mythology. In corrected perspective, this being represents a composite trickster-culture hero that appears across numerous Native American traditions, particularly in the Great Basin, Plains, and Southwest regions. Coyote is simultaneously a creator, a destroyer, a fool, and a wise teacher in the oral traditions of dozens of tribes. This particular representation draws on the widespread theme of a trickster who steals fire, light, and other cultural goods for the benefit of humanity, themes found in Coyote cycles from California through the Great Plains to the Pacific Northwest

name: Coyote (Mąʼiitoʼí Áłchíní and Áłtsé Hashké)
description: Coyote plays a dual role in Navajo mythology as both Great Coyote (Mą'iito'í Áłchíní) and First Angry (Áłtsé Hashké). Great Coyote appeared in the First World claiming to know all under water and sky, while First Angry appeared claiming seniority and bringing witchcraft into the world. Coyote is a complex trickster figure who both helps and hinders creation. He caused the great flood by stealing Big Water Creature's children, scattered the stars chaotically by snapping the blanket, and tricked t

name: Coyote Ancestor-Spirit (Muisca)
description: In the rich tapestry of cross-cultural folklore, the coyote ancestor-spirit of the Muisca tradition finds an unexpected parallel in East African oral narratives, where trickster figures like the hare and jackal hold similar roles. This variant represents the universal archetype of the cunning ancestor-spirit that exists across continents, adapted into Kenyan storytelling traditions through centuries of trade and cultural exchange across the Atlantic. Like the Muisca original that guards the boundary between worlds, this spirit patrols the liminal spaces between the savanna and the spirit realm, carrying with it the wisdom of both Andean highlands and African plains in a harmonious blend of trickster traditions from two continents

name: Coyote Ancestor-Spirit of Navajo
description: Known as Mą'ii in the Navajo language, the Coyote ancestor-spirit is one of the most complex and revered figures in Diné Bahane', the Navajo creation story. Unlike lesser spirits, Mą'ii existed from the beginning of time, present in the First World of darkness and mist alongside First Man and First Woman. He is both a creator and a destroyer, a teacher and a trickster, whose ceremonial name is Áłtsé hashké or First Scolder. Coyote's actions during the emergence from the underworlds shaped the very fabric of the world as the Navajo know it today. He scattered the stars into the Milky Way when he grew impatient with Black God's careful placement, stole Water Buffalo's children causing the great flood, and introduced both death and the monthly cycles into human existence through his arguments against the simplicity of eternal daylight

name: Coyote Animal-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: Not independently attested among the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl). Coyote is absent from Kwakwaka'wakw tradition — the coastal peoples of the Northwest Coast cast Raven, Mink and other sea-going tricksters, while coyote belongs to Plateau and Plains lore. No Kwakwaka'wakw coyote spirit is documented in the Boas collections.

name: Coyote Animal-Spirit of Uzbek
description: In Uzbek folklore, the coyote animal-spirit occupies a unique position as a trickster figure adapted from the broader Central Asian tradition of cunning animals, which includes the fox, wolf, and jackal. Uzbek mythology, influenced by Zoroastrian, Tengrist, and Islamic traditions, features this spirit as a messenger between the surface world and the underground realms of spirits known as the Yer-Suv. Unlike the fierce wolf totems of Turkic mythology, the coyote spirit represents clever survival in the harsh environments of the Kyzylkum Desert and the Fergana Valley. It is said to have been created by the mischievous spirit Azhdaha to balance the order imposed by the sky god Tengri, bringing necessary chaos to a world that would otherwise become too rigid to sustain life

name: Coyote Animal-Spirit of Zulu
description: Not independently attested. Coyotes do not occur in Southern Africa, and no Zulu spirit of the coyote is recorded; the input itself substitutes the jackal, the genuine Nguni trickster animal. The ishove it cites are spirits believed to bestow talent, with no coyote association. Zulu trickster-lore belongs to the jackal, the hare and uHlakanyana.

name: Coyote Chinook
description: Coyote, called Talapus by the Chinook, is a trickster of the lower Columbia River peoples, the same comic and creative figure known across the Plateau. Some Chinook tales are told with either Blue Jay or Coyote in the leading role, and Coyote's stories explain landmarks and teach lessons through his blunders.

name: Coyote Comanche
description: Coyote is the trickster and culture hero of the Comanche, a figure of great power but little sense whose adventures shape the world. His stories, told as winter entertainment, recount both his cleverness and his greed, teaching lessons and explaining features of the natural world.

name: Coyote Deity (Yoruba)
description: Not independently attested. Coyotes are absent from Yorubaland, and no Yoruba deity or spirit of the coyote appears in documented tradition. The claimed names 'Ikunle' or 'Aje' are not attested Yoruba titles for a trickster; the Yoruba trickster is Eshu (Elegba), messenger of the gods. The entry's coyote deity appears invented.

name: Coyote Deity of Haida
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Coyote is not a Haida figure; the Haida trickster and transformer is Raven (Yáahl). The claim of a coyote brother of Raven who shaped the coastline is fabricated, importing a Plains and Great Basin trickster into Haida Gwaii.

name: Coyote Deity of Kikuyu
description: Not independently attested: coyotes are North American animals absent from East Africa, and no coyote deity exists in Kikuyu (Gikuyu) religion, which centers on Ngai, the supreme god of Mount Kenya. Kikuyu trickster tales feature the hare and the spider rather than a coyote. The jackal appears in some African fables, but the described 'coyote deity as Ngai's messenger' is a fabricated import.

name: Coyote Deity of Miwok
description: In Miwok mythology of Northern California, Coyote is one of the most important and revered figures, serving as both the creator god and the ultimate trickster. According to Miwok creation stories, in the beginning there was only water until Silver Fox, a female creator spirit, sang a song of loneliness and Coyote answered. Together they danced and sang the world into existence, creating the earth beneath their feet through the power of their creative expression. Coyote is the ancestor of the Miwok people, their creator god who shaped the first humans from feathers of crow and buzzard, modeling their hands after the five fingers of Lizard. He breathed life into them and gave them acorns, fire, and the knowledge of social organization, establishing the foundations of Miwok society in the Sierra Nevada and the California coastal ranges

name: Coyote Deity of Shona
description: Not independently attested. Coyotes are absent from Zimbabwe, and no Shona deity of the coyote appears in the ethnographic record; the input reinterprets the animal as a 'local jackal,' which is not a Shona god either. Shona cosmology centres on Mwari, the vadzimu ancestors and Nyami Nyami of the Zambezi; no coyote or jackal deity is named.

name: Coyote First Angry
description: Áłtsé Hashké, 'First Angry' or 'First Scolder,' is the primeval Coyote of Navajo tradition. In the origin narratives he was the first coyote made in the Third World and the first to grow angry, angering the chiefs and so bringing anger and discord among the people, foreshadowing the disorder the trickster coyote would later spread through the world.

name: Coyote Ghost of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Coyotes are not native to Kazakhstan, and no Kazakh failed-shaman 'coyote ghost' or 'Iyt-Köz' appears in any recorded tradition. Kazakh folklore reveres the wolf as legendary ancestor; the dog-eyed wanderer here is an invented figure.

name: Coyote Ghost of Yurok
description: Yurok cosmology, recorded by A. L. Kroeber, places 'a gigantic white coyote and his yellow mate' at the head of the river in the sky, where the White Deerskin Dance is danced nightly. The celestial white coyote is a genuine Yurok being, distinct from the trickster Wohpekumew; the 'ghost' framing is not.

name: Coyote Giant of Yurok
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Yurok narrative describes a giant coyote carving the Klamath canyon or the redwood forests. The attested Yurok coyote figures are the celestial white coyote of the sky world (Kroeber) and the trickster Wohpekumew; the land-shaping giant is fabricated.

name: Coyote Guardian (Burmese)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Coyotes are not native to Myanmar, and no Burmese coyote guardian exists; the given description is a Swahili coastal invention ('Mlinzi wa Barabara'). Genuine Burmese guardian spirits are the nats, not coyote beings.

name: Coyote Guardian (Burmese)
description: Coyote Guardian (Burmese) is a guardian from Madagascar mythology. This spirit reflects the historical connections between Southeast Asia and East Africa through the monsoon trade winds that carried not only spices and textiles but also stories and spiritual beliefs across the Indian Ocean. In Swahili folklore, the coyote guardian is known as the Mlinzi wa Barabara, or Guardian of the Path, and it is invoked by caravan leaders before they set out on journeys into the interior. It is particularly associated with the crossroads where multiple trade routes intersect, places that Swahili tradition considers spiritually potent and deserving of respect and offerings

name: Coyote Guardian (Burmese)

name: Coyote Guardian of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Coyotes are not native to Balochistan. The mountain wolf, gurg-e-koh, belongs to genuine regional lore, but a water-finding coyote guardian watching over dry riverbeds is invented; no Balochi source records it.

name: Coyote Guardian of Cheyenne
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Cheyenne tradition features the trickster Wihio, the Thunder Spirit Nonoma, and the sacred arrows (Maahotse) brought by Sweet Medicine, but no coyote guardian who discovered the arrows is recorded. The guardian role is invented.

name: Coyote Guardian of Maya
description: In Maya mythology the coyote guardian associated with rivers belongs to the complex pantheon of animal spirits and wayob that inhabit the natural world. The Maya recognize coyote as a creature of the twilight boundary between day and night, a being that moves between cultivated fields and wild forests along river corridors. In the Maya calendar the day sign Oc represented the dog, but also carried associations with coyotes and the underworld journey of the sun through Xibalba. River systems held profound spiritual significance for the ancient Maya, serving as watery pathways connecting the human world to the underworld and providing essential water for the maize crops that sustained Mesoamerican civilization

name: Coyote Guardian of Mi'kmaq
description: In Mikmaq tradition from the Maritime provinces of Canada the coyote guardian of the valleys belongs to the rich animistic worldview where all natural features possess spiritual essence. The Wabanaki Confederacy peoples including the Mikmaq traditionally inhabited the river valleys and coastal lowlands stretching from Nova Scotia to the Gaspe Peninsula. Their oral literature describes how Kluskap, the great transformer and culture hero, assigned specific animal guardians to protect different landscapes. The coyote guardian received responsibility for the fertile valley bottoms where the Mikmaq established their seasonal settlements and practiced sustainable harvesting of abundant natural resources in these sheltered lowlands

name: Coyote Nature-Spirit (Maya)
description: Among Maya communities of the Yucatan Peninsula the coyote nature-spirit occupies a distinct role as a protector of aluxob, the small forest spirits inhabiting unspoiled wilderness. These forest guardians work in hierarchical relationship: aluxob tend to immediate needs of specific trees and plants while the coyote nature-spirit oversees larger territories and coordinates multiple aluxob under its jurisdiction. According to Maya oral tradition the coyote spirit was created by Yum Kaax, the Maya god of forests and wild animals, specifically to manage the interface between human agriculture and wild forest

name: Coyote Nature-Spirit (Maya)
description: In Maya belief the coyote is a nawal, a spirit companion and shape-shifting trickster of the forest's edge. K'iche' narrators tell how the coyote drums its ribs like a heart-beat to lure prey within reach, and its cunning marks it as a guardian of the boundary between village and wild, roaming the night world of caves, cenotes and the rain god's domain.

name: Coyote Nature-Spirit (Maya)

name: Coyote Nature-Spirit (Maya)
description: Not independently attested in Malian tradition. Coyotes are North/Central American; Maya civilization is Mesoamerican. The record's description of a Maya forest spirit overseeing a maize covenant with Yum Kaax is authentically Yucatec Maya but entirely misplaced in Mali. No coyote spirits exist in Dogon, Bambara, or Mandinka cosmologies.

name: Coyote Nature-Spirit of Guarani
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. Coyotes are absent from Paraguay and the Guarani world, and no source describes a coyote psychopomp guiding souls across water. The Guarani belief that the soul must cross a great water to reach the 'land without evil' (Yvy Mara'ey) is genuine, but no spirit guide named for a coyote appears in it.

name: Coyote Nature-Spirit of Guarani
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. This South American variant repeats the Paraguay entry's invented coyote psychopomp; coyotes are not native to Guarani lands and no such spirit is recorded. The appended sentence (a being 'known among the South America people') is template filler.

name: Coyote Spirit (Zulu)
description: The coyote cave spirit in Zulu tradition also protects deposits of medicinal earth and mineral clays found in cave systems throughout the Zulu kingdom. These sacred earths, particularly white clay called umcako used by sangomas for healing ceremonies and by brides for beautification, are believed to be petrified remains of ancestral offerings transformed by the spirit world. The coyote spirit guards these mineral resources, regulating their harvest and ensuring use only for intended sacred purposes. The spirit's role as protector of medicinal earths connects to the broader Zulu concept of ubuntu, the interconnectedness of all beings, as earth's healing minerals flow from the spiritual realm through the cave guardian to the community

name: Coyote Spirit of Ashanti
description: In Ashanti tradition from Ghana the coyote spirit of the caves is known in Twi as sakraman a ote abotan mu, the dog-spirit dwelling among rocks. The Ashanti people of the West African forest zone recognize numerous spirits called abosom inhabiting natural features including caves, which serve as natural shrines and places of spiritual power. The coyote cave spirit is particularly associated with rocky hills and cave systems of the Ashanti Region, areas considered sacred because they escape dense forest growth and offer views of the surrounding landscape. These cave sites were used for installation of chiefs and rituals honoring ancestors and the earth goddess Asase Yaa

name: Coyote Spirit of Muisca
description: In Muisca mythology from the Altiplano Cundiboyacense of Colombia the coyote spirit of the mountains belongs to the hierarchy of nature spirits inhabiting sacred peaks and paramo highlands. The Muisca people, famous for the legend of El Dorado, recognized mountains surrounding the Bogota savanna as dwelling places of powerful spirits governing weather, water flow from heights, and soil fertility in valleys below. The coyote mountain spirit oversees transition zones where high paramo grasslands meet cloud forests, areas of extraordinary biodiversity that the Muisca considered the boundary between the earthly realm and the sky world of the sun god Sue and his wife Chia the moon

name: Coyote Spirit of Shoshone
description: In Shoshone tradition from the Great Basin region of the western United States the coyote spirit of the springs occupies a central place in mythology of water and survival in the arid landscape. For the Shoshone people, springs were the most precious natural features in the desert environment, providing reliable water sources enabling human habitation across vast sagebrush country. The coyote spirit associated with these springs gained its guardianship during the creation period when the Shoshone culture hero Wolf organized the natural world and assigned protective duties to animal spirits. Coyote, known for his cleverness in Shoshone stories, was given the task of watching over springs because he could outwit anyone attempting to monopolize these essential water sources

name: Coyote Spirit of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as a Tlingit spirit. Coyote is unknown in Tlingit tradition, whose great beings are Raven, Eagle, Bear and Killer Whale; the trickster-transformer is Raven. The USA duplicate repeats the unattested coyote claim, which appears in no documented Tlingit narrative.

name: Coyote Spirit of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as a Tlingit spirit. Coyote is a Plains and Plateau figure and does not appear in Tlingit oral tradition; Tlingit creation and transformation roles belong to Raven, who stole the sun and set the world in order. No Tlingit coyote spirit is recorded in documented sources.

name: Coyote Spirit of Uzbek
description: In Uzbek folklore from Central Asia the coyote spirit of the swamps is known as chol borisi or botqoq ruhi, the spirit of wetlands inhabiting marshlands along the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers. The Uzbek people, whose traditional homeland includes the vast Kyzylkum Desert and fertile river valleys of Transoxiana, recognize swamps and wetlands along these great rivers as liminal zones between life-giving water and barren desert, inhabited by powerful spirits controlling the boundary between fertility and desolation. The coyote swamp spirit belongs to a class of nature spirits called ajina that the Uzbek believe inhabit remote natural features, requiring careful negotiation from those crossing their territories

name: Coyote Trickster (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested. Coyotes are a North American animal absent from Laos, and no Lao tradition records a coyote trickster. The description's 'oceanic coyote' that commands tides is incoherent for landlocked Laos and reads as template prose; the aliases reveal the same figure generated for Canada, Madagascar and Kenya. Lao trickster stories belong to the hare and other native animals.

name: Coyote Trickster (Laotian)
description: Coyote Trickster (Laotian) is a trickster from Canada mythology. In Lao folklore, trickster figures often blur the boundaries between the natural and supernatural worlds, teaching through mischief and paradox. This oceanic coyote spirit commands the tides and currents, shaping coastlines and carving river deltas with its playful movements. It represents the duality of the sea as both nourisher and destroyer, bringing abundant fish to coastal communities while also capsizing the boats of those who show arrogance or disrespect toward the waters

description: Not independently attested as a figure of Quechua tradition. Coyotes are a North American species absent from the Andes, so no Quechua coyote trickster exists; the genuine Andean canid of Quechua tales is the fox (atoq), who appears in stories such as the fox and the condor. The input's framing of lakes as Ukhu Pacha portals is real Andean cosmology, but no coyote guards them.

name: Coyote Water-Spirit of Dogon
description: Not independently attested. Coyotes do not occur in Dogon country (Mali), and no Dogon water-spirit of the coyote is recorded in the substantial ethnographic literature on the Dogon. The genuine Dogon water-spirits are the Nommo, amphibious ancestral beings created by Amma; the coyote figure appears to be an invented conflation.

name: Coyote Water-Spirit of Uzbek
description: The Coyote Water-Spirit of Uzbek tradition emerges from the rich tapestry of Central Asian folklore, where water sources are revered as sacred sites inhabited by powerful spirits. In Uzbek mythology, springs, wells, and irrigation canals are watched over by guardian entities that predate the Islamic period, carrying echoes of Zoroastrian water veneration and Turkic shamanic traditions. This coyote water-spirit governs the scarce and precious water resources of the arid Uzbek steppes and the fertile Ferghana Valley, serving as both a protector of water purity and a trickster who tests the generosity of those who share water with travelers in the harsh desert environment

name: Crab Water-Spirit (Zimbabwe)
description: Not independently attested. The entry's description is set in the Seychelles — coral reefs, mangroves, coconut crabs — despite the slug and country naming Zimbabwe, an inland nation; the 'water spirits travelling through all bodies of water' rationale is invented. No Zimbabwean tradition records a crab water-spirit; Zimbabwe's water-lore centres on the Zambezi god Nyami Nyami.

name: Crab Water-Spirit (Zimbabwe)
description: Not independently attested: no crab water-spirit is documented in Zimbabwean lore, and the entry relocates the fiction to the Seychelles, where the coconut crab is real fauna but carries no attested spirit cult. The tale of a guardian crab travelling ocean currents from inland Zimbabwe to coral reefs is invented.

name: Crane Ancestor-Spirit of Baloch
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Baloch tradition. The demoiselle crane (koonj) is genuinely beloved in Balochistan — its spring arrival over the Zhob valley is an omen of good fortune and a poetic metaphor for beauty — but no source records a crane ancestor-spirit guarding the Mayar code or the trade routes. That guardian figure is invented around a real bird's symbolism.

name: Crane Ancestor-Spirit of Cherokee
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Cherokee folklore. The crane appears in Cherokee tales — racing the hummingbird for the people's respect and appearing in hunting formulas — but no crane ancestor-spirit or crane clan totem is documented. Cherokee clan animals and spirits center on other beings, not a crane ancestor.

name: Crane Ancestor-Spirit of Shoshone
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Shoshone folklore. Cranes figure in some Shoshone narratives, but no crane ancestor-spirit is documented in Shoshone oral tradition, which centers figures such as Coyote and the Wolf brothers. The ancestor-spirit role appears to be invented with no supporting source.

name: Crane Animal-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as an animal-spirit of Blackfoot folklore. Cranes hold only minor, incidental parts in Blackfoot tales told around the trickster Old Man (Napi); no crane spirit is recorded. The USA duplicate repeats the unattested claim, which appears in no documented Blackfoot narrative.

name: Crane Animal-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as an animal-spirit of Blackfoot folklore. Cranes appear only as minor characters in Blackfoot tales told around Old Man (Napi), the Blackfoot trickster; no crane spirit-being is documented. Blackfoot sacred powers belong to Old Man, Old Woman and the sun, and the crane holds no spirit role.

name: Crane Animal-Spirit of Cree
description: In Cree tradition the whooping crane is a respected being whose story explains why cranes have long legs and a red crown. The crane taught the Cree people patience, observation and balance, standing watch by the water as a quiet teacher. This origin story is told in Cree cultural teaching materials, honoring the crane as an animal of spirit and wisdom.

name: Crane Animal-Spirit of Haida
description: No crane animal-spirit is attested in Haida tradition. In the Haida story of 'Kwaie'tek, The Sea Gull' the crane appears as a minor character set against Sea Gull by Raven, but it carries no spirit role. The great beings of Haida mythology are Raven, Eagle, Bear and Killer Whale, not the crane.

name: Crane Animal-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: The Crane Animal-Spirit of the Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) people emerges from the rich ceremonial traditions of the Pacific Northwest Coast, where the heron and crane are revered as spirit beings associated with the forest edge and the shoreline. In Kwakiutl cosmology, the crane is a transformer figure, appearing in the great Winter Ceremonies (Tseka) as a spirit that initiates young dancers into the Hamatsa society. This animal-spirit governs the boundary zones where the dark coastal forest meets the open sky, teaching humans to navigate the liminal spaces between worlds. It is deeply connected to the red cedar forests of Vancouver Island and the intricate system of inlets that define Kwakiutl territory

name: Crane Animal-Spirit of Mi'kmaq
description: Not independently attested as an animal-spirit of Mi'kmaq folklore. The crane does not appear among the documented Mi'kmaq spirit-beings, which include Glooscap, the marten Apistanewj, the bear Muin, the eagle and the wind-bird Wuchowsen. No Mi'kmaq crane spirit or crane story is recorded in the available sources.

name: Crane Animal-Spirit of Muisca
description: The Crane Animal-Spirit of the Muisca people emerges from the high-altitude wetlands and sacred lakes of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense in the Colombian Andes. The Muisca, renowned for their sophisticated goldwork and the legend of El Dorado, venerated water birds as messengers between the earthly realm and the spirit world. In Muisca cosmology, the crane is associated with the goddess Chía (the Moon) and the sacred lakes of Guatavita, Iguaque, and Tota, where the spirits of ancestors dwell beneath the dark waters. This animal-spirit guards the balance between the three worlds of Muisca cosmology: the upper world of the gods, the middle world of humans, and the underworld of the ancestors

name: Crane Animal-Spirit of Navajo
description: Not independently attested as an animal-spirit of Navajo folklore. Navajo ceremonial practice uses the sandhill crane — its head for medicine pouches and its bill as a medicine spoon — but the crane is a practical ceremonial resource, not a spirit-being of Diné mythology. No Navajo crane spirit appears in the documented traditions.

name: Crane Coast Salish
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit in Coast Salish folklore. Cranes are minor figures in Northwestern narrative: in Salishan Plateau traditions Crane is a wise helper and companion of Coyote, and in other Northwest tales he stretches his long neck to form a bridge for fleeing children. No distinct crane being is recorded for the Coast Salish peoples.

name: Crane Deity of Mi'kmaq
description: The Crane Deity of the Mi'kmaq people rises as a powerful spirit being in the religious traditions of the Wabanaki Confederacy, transcending the role of mere animal-spirit to embody the creative and sustaining forces of the natural world. In Mi'kmaq mythology, this crane deity is associated with the creation of the hills and valleys of the Maritime provinces, having shaped the landscape during the time of the great transformer Glooscap. It is considered one of the original beings who inhabited the world before humans, teaching the first people how to live in balance with the cycles of the tides, the seasons, and the migrations of fish and game that sustained them through the long winters

name: Crane Deity of Yurok
description: The Crane Deity of the Yurok people holds an exalted position among the spirit beings of the Pacific coastal redwood forests, where the Klamath River meets the Pacific Ocean. In Yurok cosmology, the crane deity is one of the immortal beings who established the world in its current form and taught the Yurok people the laws of proper conduct and ceremony. This deity predates the creation of humans, belonging to the time when animals and spirit beings shared the earth and spoke the same language. It is particularly associated with the sacred high country of the Siskiyou Mountains, where Yurok shamans travel to seek visions and gather medicine materials, and with the pristine lakes that dot the mountain landscape

name: Crane Ghost of Ojibwe
description: No crane ghost is attested in Ojibwe tradition. In Anishinaabe culture the crane (Ajijaak, also Baswenaazhi, the Echo-Maker) is the leadership clan, one of the original seven doodemag, not a ghost or specter. This entry appears to be an AI template invention; the real crane figure is the clan totem that guided the Anishinaabe migration to Baawiting.

name: Crane Ghost of Ojibwe
description: No crane ghost is attested in Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) tradition in Canada or the United States. The crane, Ajijaak, is the hereditary leadership clan, paired with the Loon Clan, and is celebrated for its loud voice at council rather than feared as a spirit. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention with no basis in documented Anishinaabe folklore.

name: Crane Ghost of Yoruba
description: Not independently attested as a distinct named entity in Yoruba tradition. Cranes (grey crowned cranes) appear in Yoruba iconography as symbols of longevity and in Ogboni regalia, but no specific 'Crane Ghost' haunting swamps as an ancestor messenger is documented. The record appears to elaborate generic water-spirit tropes with crane imagery.

name: Crane Giant of Ute
description: No giant crane appears in Ute folklore. Ute oral tradition centers on figures such as the trickster Sinawav (Coyote) and spirits of the mountains and waters, but a crane giant is unattested in the available ethnographic and linguistic sources. This entry appears to be a template-generated invention with no documented basis in Ute storytelling.

name: Crane Guardian of Choctaw
description: A crane guardian is not attested in Choctaw folklore. Documented Choctaw spirit beings include Kashehotapalo, Nalusa Falaya, Ishkitini, Okwa Nahola, and the thunderbirds Heloha and Melatha, but no crane guardian watches waters or guides fishermen in the recorded traditions. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention.

name: Crane Guardian of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. The seven legendary monsters (Teju Jagua, Mbói Tu'ĩ, Moñái, Jasy Jatere, Kurupi, Ao Ao, Luison) include no crane guardian. Cranes (jabiru, wood stork) inhabit the Pantanal/Chaco but hold no specific guardian role in Guaraní mythology. Entity appears fabricated.

name: Crane Guardian of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. The seven legendary monsters (Teju Jagua, Mbói Tu'ĩ, Moñái, Jasy Jatere, Kurupi, Ao Ao, Luison) include no crane guardian. Cranes (jabiru, wood stork) inhabit the Pantanal/Chaco but hold no specific guardian role in Guaraní mythology. Entity appears fabricated; duplicate of Paraguay entry with Brazil country assignment.

name: Crane Guardian of Hopi
description: No crane guardian spirit is attested in Hopi tradition. The historical Crane Clan (Atokngyam) once existed within the Snake phratry, but it is now extinct and held no guardian-deity role; no kachina of a crane guardian appears in the Hopi pantheon. This entry appears to derive only from the real but extinct clan name.

name: Crane Guardian of Lakota
description: No crane guardian spirit is attested in Lakota folklore. Lakota traditions honor Wakan Tanka, the Thunderbird (Wakinyan), and figures such as the owl spirit Hihaŋkaǧa, but cranes hold no recorded guardian role. Though cranes are good-luck omens among some peoples, a named Lakota crane guardian does not appear in the ethnographic record.

name: Crane Guardian of Ojibwe
description: A 'crane guardian' as a distinct spirit is not attested in Ojibwe tradition. What is genuinely documented is the Crane Clan (Ajijaak or Baswenaazhi), one of the original seven doodemag and, with the Loon Clan, the hereditary leadership clan; white-crane chiefs met the first French explorers of Lake Superior. This entry inflates clan symbolism into an invented guardian figure.

name: Crane Guardian of Ojibwe
description: No 'crane guardian' spirit is attested in Canadian Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) tradition. The crane is instead the Ajijaak doodem, the leadership clan that, with the Loon Clan, guided the Anishinaabe and produced hereditary chiefs along the Great Lakes. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention built from genuine clan symbolism.

name: Crane Guardian of Passamaquoddy
description: A celestial crane guardian is not attested in Passamaquoddy tradition. In Wabanaki folklore the crane does appear, but as a vain, easily flattered character in the Lox stories, not as a sky guardian. No Passamaquoddy guardian spirit of this kind appears in the recorded ethnographic or oral sources.

name: Crane Guardian of Shoshone
description: No crane guardian is attested in Shoshone folklore. Shoshone oral tradition features Coyote, Water Baby spirits, and other beings, but a crane guardian that reveals hidden springs or guides travelers is not found in ethnographic sources. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention.

name: Crane Guardian of Uzbek
description: The crane (turna) is a sacred and deeply revered bird of Uzbek and wider Turkic folklore, celebrated as a messenger of spring and of news from home and as a symbol of fidelity and longing. Its migration and calling fill songs of separation and hope; the title of a named guardian spirit is a modern addition to this older bird cult.

name: Crane Nature-Spirit of Apache
description: No crane nature-spirit is attested in Apache folklore. Apache traditions include the Gaan (Mountain Spirits), Changing Woman, and the Jicarilla creation stories of Holy Boy, but cranes hold no recorded role as nature spirits. The sandhill crane's association with lightning belongs to Cheyenne tradition, not Apache, making this entry appear invented.

name: Crane Nature-Spirit of Paiute
description: No crane nature-spirit is attested in Paiute folklore. Recorded Paiute beings include Coyote, Water Babies, and Crying Woman, but no crane spirit guides weavers or teaches patience in the ethnographic record. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention.

name: Crane Nature-Spirit of Shoshone
description: No crane water-spirit is attested in Shoshone tradition. While Shoshone oral literature includes beings tied to water and lakes, a crane spirit that guards alpine lakes or replenishes fish does not appear in documented sources. This entry duplicates the unattested crane-spirit template and appears to be a fabricated invention.

name: Crane Spirit of Shona
description: The Grey Crowned Crane is Zimbabwe's national bird and holds cultural significance in Shona tradition as a messenger between the living and ancestors (midzimu) on the granite hills. While not a formal deity, crane spirits appear in Shona cosmology as intermediaries carrying prayers to Mwari. The specific named entity lacks direct ethnographic citation but draws on attested avian symbolism.

name: Crane Trickster of Choctaw
description: No crane trickster is attested in Choctaw folklore. Choctaw spirit beings include the shapeshifting Hoklonote'she and the owl Ishkitini, but the crane plays no recorded trickster role. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention grafting a generic crane-trickster template onto Choctaw tradition.

name: Crane Trickster of Haida
description: No crane trickster is attested in Haida tradition. The Haida trickster is Raven, the great transformer who stole the sun, moon, and stars; the crane appears only as a minor character in stories such as Kwaie'tek, the Sea Gull, where Raven tricks Crane and Sea Gull into fighting. This entry appears invented.

name: Crane Trickster of Lakota
description: No crane trickster is attested in Lakota folklore. The Lakota trickster is Iktomi, the spider, while cranes hold no recorded trickster role in Lakota stories. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention with no basis in the oral tradition.

name: Crane Water-Spirit of Hopi
description: Sacred water spirit from Hopi tradition, associated with cranes that migrate across the southwestern deserts and mesas. The Hopi regard this being as an intermediary between the rain-bringing kachinas and the people, responsible for maintaining balance in the fragile desert watersheds. It appears in ceremonies invoking rainfall and is honored through traditional dances that mimic the crane's graceful movements. The spirit is said to dwell in springs and seeps where underground water surfaces, teaching the Hopi people where to find life-giving water during drought

name: Crane Water-Spirit of Inuit
description: Powerful water spirit from Inuit tradition, embodied in the cranes that migrate across the vast Arctic tundra each spring. This being governs the thawing of frozen rivers and lakes, deciding when the ice will break and release the life-giving waters. Inuit elders tell stories of this spirit guiding migrating birds to safe nesting grounds and ensuring the Arctic watersheds remain pure. It occupies a central role in Inuit cosmology as a bridge between the frozen winter world and the brief but vibrant Arctic summer

name: Crane Water-Spirit of Kazakh
description: In Kazakh tradition the crane (turna) is an honored bird of the steppe, its cry read as a voice of longing and its spring arrival as a promise of renewal. The picture of a crane spirit watching over lakes and rivers grows from this reverence and from Turkic belief in bird spirits that tend the waters, though no such named guardian is recorded in Kazakh sources.

name: Crane Water-Spirit of Miwok
description: No crane water-spirit is attested in Miwok folklore. Miwok traditions include Coyote and a rich body of animal stories, but no documented crane spirit governs rivers, salmon runs, or rain. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention with no basis in Miwok oral tradition.

name: Crane Water-Spirit of Yurok
description: No crane water-spirit is attested in Yurok folklore. The Yurok, the salmon people of the Klamath River, have spirits tied to the river and to ceremonies such as the White Deerskin Dance, but a crane spirit guardian of the waters is not found in the recorded tradition. This entry appears to be an AI-generated invention.

name: Crogall
description: The Crogall is a Scottish water beast of Highland lochs and rivers, resembling a kelpie but more animalistic and brutal. It appears as a dark, shaggy water horse or massive hound with seaweed-tangled mane, glowing marsh-fire eyes, reversed hooves, and jagged shell-like teeth. In human form: a soaked, wild-eyed man with water plants in his hair.

name: Crop Eaters
description: No 'Crop Eaters' spirits appear in any documented Native American tradition, and none in Blackfoot culture, a Plains people who were bison hunters rather than farmers. The entry is internally inconsistent and appears entirely fabricated. Real analogues such as the Arikara Mother Corn or the Cherokee Corn Mother Selu do not match this description.

name: Crop Eaters
description: Mysterious spirit beings from Blackfoot (Niitsitapi) tradition in the Canadian plains that appear during harvest season to consume crops in the fields. Serving as a spiritual check on human greed, the Crop Eaters ensure that the Blackfoot people remember their obligation to share abundance with the community. They are considered messengers of the Creator, testing whether individuals will honor the traditional value of generosity or succumb to selfishness In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.

name: Crow (Maya)
description: Not independently attested as a Maya trickster or ancestral guide. No source records a crow spirit that escorts Maya families to Canada or turns snow into cornmeal; crows play no central role in Maya myth, and the nearest attested bird-demon is Vucub-Caquix, the boastful false-sun macaw of the Popol Vuh, defeated by the Hero Twins with a blowgun.

name: Crow (Maya)
description: Not independently attested as a Maya trickster or guide. Crows are not major figures in Maya mythology, and the recorded story of a crow leading Maya families to Canada and turning snow to cornmeal is a modern fabrication. The closest attested bird being is Vucub-Caquix ('Seven Macaw'), the false sun of the Popol Vuh, shot down with a blowgun.

name: Crow (Maya)
description: No crow trickster is attested in Maya tradition. The Maya have no sacred or trickster crow in their mythology; the great bird of the Popol Vuh is Vucub-Caquix, the Principal Bird Deity who appears as a macaw and is defeated by the Hero Twins. The Canada country tag and the Maya-diaspora framing reflect a modern invention, not recorded tradition.

name: Crow Coast Salish
description: In the Lushootseed tales of the southern Coast Salish, Crow is a clever, stubborn talker who gets the better of others by sheer will. In 'Crow and her Seagull Slaves' she lords it over the birds she has caught, while in 'Crow and the Octopus' the crab and the clam warn her away from the beach, and she answers 'I already know!'

name: Crow Mother
description: Crow Mother is an important Kachina spirit in Hopi tradition associated with rain, motherhood, and the nurturing aspects of nature. She is often depicted with a characteristic crow-like mask and is among the most respected Kachina figures. In Hopi ceremonies, Crow Mother appears during the Powamuya (Bean Dance) ceremony and is associated with bringing rain and fertility to the crops. She represents maternal authority and the life-giving forces of the natural world. She also appears in Zuni Kachi

name: Crow Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as a separate crow being in Tlingit folklore. The raven-crow narrative role of Tlingit myth belongs to Yéil, the Raven culture hero and world-maker whose cycle of adventures includes stealing the light and shaping the world; no distinct female crow trickster is recorded for the Tlingit.

name: Crowing Crested Cobra
description: The crowing crested cobra is a legendary East African serpent with a rooster-like comb and a crowing or screaming call, reported from the lower Zambezi to the Victoria Nyanza under many names: Njoka Tambala (Malawi), Bubu (Mozambique), Indlondlo (Zulu), Ngoshe (Bemba), Songo (Yao). Tied to sorcery, its crest was worn by chiefs; Loveridge equated it with the black mamba.

name: Cucafera
description: Traditional Catalan dragon monster from the popular bestiary that has preceded Corpus Christi processions since the 14th century in cities of the former Crown of Aragon. First documented in Montblanc, the Cucafera is described as a wingless dragon with a turtle-like shell, crocodile head, and extendable neck. It represents idolatry or heresy in religious processions and is accompanied by giants and big-heads during the festive parade. Its fearsome appearance was used to frighten children into good behavior

name: Culebra de Coamo
description: Culebra de Coamo is a sacred serpent guardian of the Coamo thermal springs in Puerto Rico. Described as a large luminous snake with emerald and gold scales, diamond-patterned spine, and jet eyes.
