It permits only the pure-hearted to bathe in the healing waters, boiling the springs if disrespected. A distinct Puerto Rican tradition.

name: Cunjah Maum
description: Cunjah Maum (also spelled Conjure Maum or Conjure Mum) is an archetypal figure in African American folklore — an elderly wise woman who practices conjure and rootwork. 'Maum' is a Gullah/Geechee and African American vernacular term for an older woman (from 'ma'am' or West African linguistic roots). Cunjah Maum is the female counterpart of the Conjure Doctor, serving as the community's spiritual advisor, healer, and protector. She knows the properties of every root, herb, and leaf, can cast spells for protection or revenge, and can identify and counter the work of enemy conjurers. In the Uncle Remus stories and Gullah folktales, she is often sought out by those afflicted by hags or haints. Cunjah Maum represents the preservation and transmission of African spiritual knowledge through generations of women

name: Curse of Dido (Carthaginian Curse)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. In Virgil's Aeneid (Book IV), Dido curses Aeneas and his Roman descendants, foretelling eternal enmity between Carthage and Rome before killing herself. No tradition describes her ghost haunting Carthage's ruins or a 'Carthaginian Curse' placed on the site.

name: Cursed Object Iceland
description: Cursed Object Iceland (Unknown). is a object. A cursed object from Icelandic saga tradition brings misfortune to its owner.. Source: Icelandic folklore — cursed objects documented in Icelandic oral tradition.

name: Curupira
description: Legendary forest guardian from Brazilian Tupi-Guarani folklore who protects the Amazon rainforest and its wildlife from greedy hunters and loggers. Described as a dwarf-like being with bright red or orange hair and backward-facing feet that confuse trackers by leaving footprints pointing in the wrong direction. First documented by Jesuit missionary José de Anchieta in 1560, the Curupira uses illusions, high-pitched whistles, and misdirection to lead wrongdoers in circles until they are hopelessly lost in the jungle

name: Cuélebre
description: The Cuélebre is the winged serpent-dragon of Asturian and Cantabrian folklore: a giant snake with bat-like wings and scales that harden to iron over centuries, often several-headed. It guards hidden treasures (ayalgues) and imprisoned xanas in mountain caves, emerging rarely to prey on cattle. On Midsummer (San Juan) its magic weakens, and a red-hot stone or bread of pins can slay it.

name: Cyclone (wind spirit)
description: Cyclone is a primordial wind spirit in Jicarilla Apache creation accounts, present in the darkness before the world was lit. Cyclone spied on the Hactcin, the ancestral spirits, and told Holy Boy that White Hactcin held the sun; with that knowledge Holy Boy obtained the sun and the moon, and daylight came into being.

name: Cyhyraeth
description: The Cyhyraeth is a Welsh death-omen spirit, primarily a disembodied moaning voice heard three times (growing fainter each time) before a death, especially during epidemics or disasters. Associated with the River Tywi in Dyfed and the Glamorganshire coast (where it warns of shipwrecks with corpse-lights).

name: Cynocephali (Dog-Headed Men)
description: Cynocephali (Dog-Headed Men) are a legendary race of dog-headed humanoids discussed extensively in Vatican and early Christian theology. Augustine in City of God considered whether these beings, reported by Roman travelers and Pliny the Elder, were descended from Adam and whether Christ died for them. The most famous Christian cynocephalus is St. Christopher, who in Orthodox iconography is depicted with a dog's head. According to his tradition, Christopher was a giant cynocephalus from the land of the cannibals who converted to Christianity and was martyred. Vatican theologians debated for centuries whether cynocephali were human or beast, with implications for their salvation

name: Cyrene Serpent (Libyan Guardian Snake)
description: The Cyrene Serpent is a mythical guardian serpent from Libyan folklore, associated with the ancient Greek colony of Cyrene (modern Shahhat) in the Jebel Akhdar region. According to legend, the city of Cyrene was founded when the hero Battus followed a great serpent to the site of a sacred spring. The serpent was the guardian of the spring of Apollo and was known for its wisdom. In Libyan folklore, this serpent is said to still inhabit the caves of Jebel Akhdar. Libyans believe it is a protective spirit of the Cyrenaican mountains. The serpent is associated with the oracle of Apollo at Cyrene, where priestesses would interpret the serpent's movements. The Greek myth of Aristaeus, who was born in Cyrene, also involves a prophetic serpent. The figure blends Greek and Libyan Berber traditions

name: Cá Trong
description: Not independently attested in Vietnamese folklore or academic sources: no collection records a fish spirit or water deity named 'Cá Trong'; the guardian-of-fish-stocks account is generic AI-template prose. Vietnam's attested fish legends centre on the carp that leaps the Dragon Gate, on Cá Ông, the whale-god of coastal fishing villages, and on the folk painting Lý ngư vọng nguyệt.

name: Cóiste Bodhar
description: The Cóiste Bodhar (Irish 'deaf coach') is the death coach of Irish folklore: a black, windowless carriage pulled by three headless black horses, driven by the Dullahan (headless horseman carrying his rotting head). It collects souls of the wicked and those with unsettled debts, calling the dying person's name at crossroads—death follows within three days.

name: Cóoyoko (child-devouring spirit)
description: Cóoyoko (child-devouring spirit) is a fearsome spirit being in Hopi mythology who threatens children who disobey their parents or wander away from the village. He is one of several disciplinary figures used in Hopi tradition to teach children respect, obedience, and awareness of danger. Cóoyoko is said to lurk in the arroyos and abandoned kivas at the edges of the village, waiting for those who stray too far. While terrifying to children, Cóoyoko serves a protective function by discouraging behavior that could lead to real harm in the harsh desert landscape

name: Cù Sídhe
description: The Cù Sídhe (Scottish Gaelic 'fairy hound') is a massive spectral hound the size of a Highland calf, with shaggy dark green or ghostly white fur, large rounded ears glowing blood-red, emerald eyes, and dinner-plate paws leaving no tracks. It wanders the Highlands and moors on misty nights, howling three times to foretell a death.

name: Cŵn Annwn
description: The Cŵn Annwn ('Hounds of Annwn') are spectral hounds of the Welsh Otherworld (Annwn), white or coal-black with glowing red/green eyes and distinctive red ears. They hunt in packs led by Arawn (king of Annwn) or later Gwyn ap Nudd, chasing souls of the wicked and unshriven, especially at Samhain. Their baying grows louder as they approach.

name: D Sonoqua Dzunukwa Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Dzunukwa, the Wild Woman of the Woods, is a giantess of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition with a black face and sunken cheeks. She steals children and is feared as an ogress, yet she is also enormously wealthy and powerful, and the red-cedar bark she favors gives ritual strength. Her image appears in masks, the winter ceremonial world, and the art of Emily Carr.

name: D'Sonoqua (Dzunukwa)
description: Dzunuḵ̓wa (Tsonoqua, D'Sonoqua) is the Wild Woman of the Woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition: a naked ogress with pendulous breasts, tangled hair, and pursed red lips whose Hu! call rides the wind. She steals children in her basket, yet also brings wealth through her child, and her geekumhl mask appears at the close of the potlatch.

name: Da (Aido-Hwedo)
description: Da (Aido-Hwedo) is the primordial rainbow-serpent of Fon Vodun cosmology: the cosmic support said to have coiled beneath the earth to hold the universe stable, companion of the creator Mawu-Lisa. The rainbow is his manifestation. At Ouidah, living royal pythons are honored as his incarnations, and in the diaspora he endures as Damballa in Haitian Vodou.

name: Dab Pog (Spirit Couple of Children)
description: Dab Pog (the Spirit Couple) are the most beloved protective spirits in Hmong folk religion — a celestial husband-and-wife pair responsible for bringing children to parents on earth and protecting them throughout their lives. According to Hmong mythology, at the very beginning of time, the Dab Pog couple and the Xwm Kab (House Spirit) couple were sent by Yawm Saub to live with the Hmong people. The Dab Pog couple resides in the spirit world and decides which souls will be reborn into which families. They guide the child's soul from the spirit world to the mother's womb, and after birth, they serve as the child's guardian angels — protecting them from illness, accidents, and evil spirits. When a child is sick, Hmong parents perform rituals to the Dab Pog couple, asking them to call back the child's wandering soul. The couple is honored with offerings during major life events including births, naming ceremonies, and the Hmong New Year. They represent the deep Hmong belief in spiritual parentage alongside biological parentage

name: Dagas
description: Dagas is the cosmic world tree in Maldivian mythology, a colossal silver-leaved tree with blue-glowing roots at the spiritual center of the archipelago. Its leaves whisper secrets of past and future. The seafarer Bodu Niyami Kalēfanu journeyed to Dagas at the world's end to bring tuna to Maldivian waters.

name: Daini
description: In Bengali folklore, the Daini (derived from Sanskrit 'Dakini') is a feared witch who practices black magic and dark sorcery. Unlike ethereal spirits, the Daini is a living human woman, typically elderly, who is rumored to wield supernatural powers passed down through secret traditions. She is believed to kidnap children and drink their blood to sustain her unnaturally prolonged life, sometimes living for centuries. The Daini is also blamed for causing miscarriages, mysterious illnesses, and crop failures in rural villages, making her one of the most feared figures in Bengali supernatural beliefs

name: Dakhanavar
description: The Dakhanavar is a territorial vampire from Armenian folklore first documented by Baron August von Haxthausen in his 1854 book Transcaucasia: Sketches of the Nations and Races Between the Black Sea and the Caspian. This ferocious bloodsucker dwells in a cavern within the mountains of Ultmish Altotem, protecting the 366 valleys of the region from intruders and mapmakers. It cannot tolerate anyone who tries to count the valleys or penetrate its domain, correctly fearing that knowledge of the landscape would reveal its secret hiding places. The Dakhanavar is one of the most unusual vampires in world folklore due to its distinctive feeding method

name: Dakkhin Rai (Tiger Spirit of the Sundarbans)
description: Dakkhin Rai (sometimes spelled Dakshin Rai) is a powerful tiger spirit and demon-king who rules the Sundarbans mangrove forest, the world's largest delta shared between India and Bangladesh. According to Bengali folklore, particularly the Bonbibi tradition, Dakkhin Rai was a shape-shifting tiger demon who demanded human sacrifices from those who entered his forest domain. He is described as the king of the southern region (dakshin meaning south), and his rule extended over the dense, treacherous mangrove forests. He would appear as a man or as a Bengal tiger, using his shapeshifting abilities to deceive and devour honey collectors, woodcutters, and fishermen who entered his territory. According to legend, he was ultimately subdued by the forest goddess Bonbibi and her brother Shah Jangali, who forced him to agree never to harm those who called upon Bonbibi's name. Despite this defeat, Dakkhin Rai continues to be respected and feared — offerings are made to him before entering the forest, and he is considered both a dangerous spirit and a legitimate lord of the Sundarbans ecosystem

name: Dakuwaqa
description: Dakuwaqa is the powerful shark deity of Fijian mythology, a shape-shifting sea god greatly respected by fishermen and navigators across the archipelago. His name derives from the Fijian words 'daku' (back) and 'waqa' (canoe), evoking the image of a shark guardian positioned astern of boats. According to legend, Dakuwaqa was once a prideful and ambitious god who sought to conquer all of Fiji's islands, challenging every guardian spirit he encountered. After a humbling defeat by the giant octopus goddess Rokobakaniceva at Kadavu Island, he swore an oath to protect fishermen and became a benevolent guardian of the seas

name: Damballa
description: Damballa, also spelled Damballah or Danbala, is one of the most ancient and revered loa (spirits) in Haitian Vodou and West African Vodun traditions. He originated in the city of Wedo (Whydah) in modern-day Benin and was carried across the Atlantic by enslaved Africans. Damballa is the primordial creator, the sky father who used his seven thousand coils to form the stars, planets, hills, and valleys of the cosmos. By shedding his serpent skin, he created all the waters on Earth. He is counted among the Rada loa and syncretized with Saint Patrick or Moses in Vodou practice

name: Dame Blanche
description: The Dame Blanche (White Lady) is a famous female spirit from French mythology and folklore, reported across regions including Lorraine, Normandy, and the Pyrenees mountains. These spectral figures are described as a type of fée (fairy) of less benevolent character, lurking in narrow ravines, forests, bridges, and caverns. They likely descend from ancient pre-Christian goddesses known as the Matres or Dominae, guardian deities of home and hearth. The Dame Blanche is also associated with specific haunted châteaux, including Château de Puymartin in Dordogne, where the ghost of a wife imprisoned for adultery still wanders the tower

name: Dancing Djinn
description: Dancing Djinn are playful supernatural spirits from North African folklore, particularly associated with the vast desert landscapes of Tunisia and the Maghreb region. Djinn (or jinn) are beings of smokeless fire created alongside humans and angels in Islamic cosmology, possessing free will and the ability to choose good or evil. These particular djinn are known for their love of music, dance, and revelry under the moonlight. Unlike the malevolent ifrit or ghul, Dancing Djinn are tricksters rather than killers, though they can still be dangerous to those who stumble into their midnight celebrations unprepared

name: Dangun
description: Dangun Wanggeom is the legendary founder of Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, and the central figure of Korea's national origin myth. According to the Samguk Yusa (13th-century Korean chronicle), Dangun was born from the union of Hwanung, the heavenly prince who descended to Mount Taebaek, and Ungnyeo, a bear who transformed into a woman after enduring a grueling trial of garlic and mugwort in a cave for one hundred days. Dangun founded Gojoseon in 2333 BCE under the ideal of Hongik Ingan ('to broadly benefit the human world') and ruled for over a thousand years before becoming a mountain spirit

name: Danku
description: Danku is a giant from Bengali folklore known for his incredible strength and his role in shaping the landscape of the Bengal region. These folktales explain the origin of megalithic structures, large boulders, and hill formations found throughout the Bengali countryside. Danku is characterized as a simple-minded giant who can be helpful when approached correctly but is also prone to fits of rage when disrespected. Like many giant figures in world folklore, Danku represents the human encounter with monumental landscapes and the effort to explain geological features through mythological storytelling

name: Daramulum
description: Daramulum (meaning 'one-legged') is a sky hero in the Aboriginal Australian cultures of southeastern Australia, associated with the supreme creator god Baiame. He is a shapeshifter who can appear in various forms, often depicted with an emu-wife. Daramulum's voice can be heard through the bullroarer, which is whirled through the air during initiation ceremonies. He now lives in the trees of the bush, particularly in burls or growths found on tree trunks, and only leaves them for initiation ceremonies. The bullroarer must be cut from a tree containing his spirit for it to work. For the Guringai people, Daramulum is represented by Alpha Crucis of the Southern Cross constellation. A religion centered on Daramulum is an identifying feature of the Yuin nation

name: Davy Crockett
description: Davy Crockett (1786-1836) is an American frontier folk hero whose real career as hunter, congressman, and defender of the Alamo was stretched by tall tales into legend. In frontier humor he outruns the sun and conquers foes with a grin, and he is a figure of Euro-American, not Native American, folklore.

name: Dayan Deerh
description: Dayan Deerh is a shamanic deity of fertility and protection from the Khövsgöl region of northern Mongolia, venerated in both yellow and black shamanism. Worshipped as a mountain god turned shaman-spirit and community guardian, his cult centers on Tsagaannuur and the Deerkhiin Khüree shrine, where his statue and renewed ongons receive offerings for cattle and children.

name: De Syv Søstre
description: De Syv Søstre (the Seven Sisters) are the seven daughters of Suliskongen, the troll king of Sulitjelma. According to the famous Helgeland legend cycle, the sisters were sent away from home for discipline and ended up on the island of Alsten. When pursued by Hestmannen, they danced on the shore to distract him, but were caught by the sunrise and turned into the seven peaks that form one of Norway's most iconic mountain silhouettes. The seven peaks, from north to south, are: Botnkrona (youngest), Grytfoten, Skjeringen, Tvillingene (two peaks — the Twins), Kvasstinden, and Breitinden (eldest, who had an illegitimate child — a smaller eighth peak beside her). The Seven Sisters mountain range rises dramatically from the sea near Sandnessjøen. The legend is the best-known folk tale in Northern Norway and the subject of countless songs, poems, and paintings

name: De underjordiska (Swedish)
description: De underjordiska (the underground ones) are a hidden, invisible people in Swedish folklore who live parallel to humans in an underground world beneath hills, meadows, and farmyards. They maintain their own farms, cattle, and paths called vitterstigar or onstreck that humans must never obstruct. These beings are most prominent in northern Swedish folklore, where they are often called vittror or vitterfolk, and are closely related to the Norwegian huldrefolk and the Gutnish "di sma undar jordi" (the little ones under the earth). They are generally invisible but can appear to those with second sight, and they are described as small, human-like beings with fair features who lead lives mirroring human existence. Their cattle — vitterkor — are known as particularly fine and productive, giving much more milk than ordinary cows. If a human builds a house or barn on a vitterpath, misfortune follows until the building is moved. Leaving offerings and showing respect ensures their goodwill, while disrespect brings illness, broken tools, and bad luck

name: Deer Ancestor-Spirit (Zapotec)
description: In Zapotec and Mixtec belief of Oaxaca, animals such as the deer appear as naguales and companions of the soul, while ancestors may manifest through animal forms. This 'Deer Ancestor-Spirit' captures those attested ideas of the deer as a spirit double or ancestral guide. The input's claim of a Brazilian diaspora transmission is unsupported and should be discarded.

name: Deer Ancestor-Spirit (Zapotec)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Brazilian tradition. The Zapotec are an indigenous people of Oaxaca, Mexico, not of Brazil, and no source records a 'Zapotec deer ancestor-spirit' preserved among Brazilian communities; the diaspora narrative is invented.

name: Deer Ancestor-Spirit of Choctaw
description: The deer is a genuine spirit-being in Choctaw tradition: the story of the transformed hunter describes a deer chief who rules the deer-people with their own laws, and the tale of Deer and His Antlers shows Issi the deer speaking and acting as a person, proud until his antlers snag and he must humble himself. Deer are also woven into Choctaw clan kinship.

name: Deer Ancestor-Spirit of Dogon
description: The Deer Ancestor-Spirit of the Dogon people of Mali holds a significant place in the rich cosmological framework of Dogon mythology. The Dogon are renowned for their sophisticated astronomical knowledge and complex spiritual beliefs centered around the Nommo, primordial beings who shaped the world. This deer spirit represents the connection between the earthly realm and the ancestral world, serving as a messenger between living Dogon communities and their ancestors. It features in Dogon creation narratives and agricultural ceremonies tied to the rhythms of the seasons

name: Deer Ancestor-Spirit of Mi'kmaq
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Mi'kmaq folklore. Mi'kmaq tradition honors deer as one of the game animals who give themselves to hunters under the netukulimk ethic, but no deer ancestor-spirit appears in the documented Glooscap cycle, which features Muin the bear, Apistanewj the marten, Gipu the eagle and other named animal beings.

name: Deer Animal-Spirit of Guarani
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. While teko porã ('the good way of being') is a genuine Guarani ethical concept and deer appear in South American hunting lore, no source records a deer animal-spirit as a pan-Guarani nature guardian. The entry generalizes a common ecological teaching into a specific being that the Guarani corpora (Cadogán, Colmán) do not name.

name: Deer Animal-Spirit of Guarani
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. This variant repeats the Paraguay entry's invented pan-Guarani deer guardian and appends template filler (a being 'known among the South America people'). Genuine Guarani ethics (teko porã) and the reverence for deer in hunting lore do not yield a named deer animal-spirit in the documented corpus.

name: Deer Animal-Spirit of Hopi
description: The Deer Animal-Spirit of the Hopi people of the American Southwest is deeply integrated into Hopi ceremonial life and agricultural traditions. The Hopi have lived in the arid mesas of Arizona for over a thousand years, and deer have been essential to their survival, providing food, hides for clothing and drums, and bones for tools. This animal-spirit governs the deer's willingness to be hunted and ensures that Hopi hunters maintain proper ritual purity. It appears in Hopi kachina ceremonies, where dancers embody the deer spirit to bring blessings of abundance and rain to the village

name: Deer Animal-Spirit of Maliseet
description: Not independently attested as an animal-spirit of Maliseet folklore. Deer were central to Maliseet subsistence and are honored under the Wabanaki ethic of respect for animal kin, but no specific Maliseet deer spirit or deer-person is documented. Wabanaki spirit figures cluster around Kluskap, the marten and other culture heroes.

name: Deer Animal-Spirit of Mapuche
description: The Deer Animal-Spirit of the Mapuche people of Chile and Argentina is a sacred being in the spiritual traditions of the most populous indigenous group in South America. The Mapuche, whose name means 'people of the land,' have a deep reverence for the natural world, and the huemul (south Andean deer) holds special significance as a symbol of the mountain forests. This deer spirit represents the newen (spiritual force) that flows through all living things, teaching the Mapuche about balance, healing, and the interconnection of all beings in the natural world

name: Deer Deity (Dogon)
description: The Deer Deity of the Dogon tradition as carried to Mexico represents the adaptation of West African spiritual traditions in the African diaspora communities of Mexico. During the colonial era, enslaved Africans from the Mali region, including Dogon people, were brought to Mexico, carrying their spiritual traditions with them despite brutal suppression. This version of the Dogon Deer Deity blended with indigenous Mexican deer symbolism, particularly the reverence for deer in Aztec and Maya traditions, creating a unique syncretic spiritual being that honors both African and American roots

name: Deer Deity (Dogon)
description: The Deer Deity of the Dogon tradition as carried to Mexico represents the adaptation of West African spiritual traditions in the African diaspora communities of Mexico. During the colonial era, enslaved Africans from the Mali region, including Dogon people, were brought to Mexico, carrying their spiritual traditions with them despite brutal suppression. This version of the Dogon Deer Deity blended with indigenous Mexican deer symbolism, particularly the reverence for deer in Aztec and Maya traditions, creating a unique syncretic spiritual being that honors both African and American roots In Mexico folklore, this figure is known among the Mexico people.

name: Deer Deity of Cree
description: In Cree cosmology, the Deer Deity is a powerful spirit associated with the vast inland waters and oceanic realms, serving as a guardian of marine life and an intermediary between the human world and the underwater spirit domain. Known as a benevolent yet formidable force, this deity governs the abundance of sea creatures and holds sway over the weather patterns that affect coastal and inland communities. The Deer Deity appears in shamanic visions and is invoked through ritual offerings and sweat lodge ceremonies, where seekers petition for safe passage across waters and bountiful harvests from the sea

name: Deer Deity of Inuit
description: Among the Inuit of the Arctic regions, the Deer Deity is a powerful caribou-spirit being that oversees the great herds upon which human survival depends. Unlike southern deer spirits, this entity is intrinsically tied to the harsh realities of tundra life, controlling the migration patterns of caribou and the abundance of game animals. Shamans, known as angakkuit, seek the favor of this deity through drum ceremonies and amulet crafting, believing that a respectful relationship with the Deer Deity ensures the continuation of life in the frozen north

name: Deer Deity of Mi'kmaq
description: In Mikmaq tradition, the Deer Deity is a revered ocean guardian that watches over the Atlantic coastal waters and the abundant life within them. As a central figure in the Mikmaq spiritual landscape, this deity governs the seasonal runs of fish, the migrations of seals, and the safety of those who travel by canoe along the rugged coastline. It is closely associated with Glooscap teachings about the interconnectedness of all living things and the responsibility of humans to act as caretakers rather than conquerors of the natural world

name: Deer Deity of Shona
description: In Shona cosmology of Zimbabwe, the Deer Deity is a celestial sky guardian associated with the vast African firmament and the life-giving rains that sweep across the savanna. Unlike the water-bound deer spirits of northern traditions, this deity dwells among the clouds and commands the thunderheads that bring fertility to the land. The Shona people honor this being through rituals performed at hilltop shrines, where elders pray for rains that will nourish crops and fill the rivers that sustain both wildlife and human communities across the great plateau

name: Deer Deity of Zapotec
description: Among the Zapotec people of Oaxaca, the Deer Deity is a river guardian closely tied to the life-giving waters that flow through the mountain valleys of southern Mexico. This benevolent spirit governs the freshwater ecosystems that sustain both agriculture and wildlife, acting as an intermediary between the Zapotec people and the great rain god Cocijo. The deer has particular significance in Zapotec culture as a symbol of the forest bounty and the sacred connection between the human world and the spirit realm that dwells in the misty cloud forests

name: Deer Ghost of Cree
description: Not independently attested as a ghost of Cree folklore. No Cree deer-ghost is documented; Cree spirit-concepts concern the windigo, spirit animals and the dead who appear in visions, not a deer revenant. This entry appears AI-generated, with the deer's genuine role as food and hide animal reshaped into an invented ghost story.

name: Deer Ghost of Mapuche
description: Not independently attested in Mapuche tradition as a named 'deer ghost'. The huemul (South Andean deer) is culturally significant and appears on Chile's coat of arms, but no specific spectral huemul guardian of sacred sites exists in Mapuche ethnography (Bacigalupo, Faron). Mapuche have wekufe (malevolent spirits) and ngen (nature owners), but not this entity.

name: Deer Ghost of Ute
description: Not independently attested as a ghost of Ute folklore. Deer are central to Ute life and ceremony, but no Ute deer-ghost is documented in the sources. Ute spirit traditions concern shamans, animal helpers and the dead who return in dreams; a deer revenant guarding the mountains is not attested.

name: Deer Ghost of Zulu
description: Among the Zulu people of South Africa, the Deer Ghost is a spirit that inhabits the river valleys and deep ravines of KwaZulu-Natal, serving as a guardian of the ancestral burial grounds that lie hidden in these secluded places. In Zulu cosmology, the spirits of the ancestors, known as amadlozi, often take the form of animals as messengers between the living and the dead. The Deer Ghost is one such spirit, a manifestation of an ancestor who was particularly connected to the wilderness and who now watches over the boundary between human settlements and the untamed bushveld

name: Deer Giant of Apache
description: In Apache tradition, the Deer Giant is a colossal being that roams the vast desert landscapes of the American Southwest, serving as a bridge between the human world and the powerful mountain spirits known as the Gan. This giant is not a creature of the ocean but a master of the arid lands, its immense footsteps creating the canyons and arroyos that channel the rare desert rains. The Apache people regard the Deer Giant as a guardian of the sacred mountains and a teacher of the hunting ceremonies that ensure the deer population remains strong

name: Deer Giant of Shoshone
description: Among the Shoshone people of the Great Basin, the Deer Giant is a sky-roaming titan that controls the weather patterns and the movements of the celestial bodies. Unlike the earthbound giants of other traditions, this being dwells in the high places where the sky meets the mountain peaks, its massive form often mistaken for a thunderhead on the horizon. The Shoshone tell stories of this giant as a protector of the game animals and a punisher of those who hunt for sport rather than sustenance, reflecting the deep reverence for the deer that sustained their way of life

name: Deer Guardian (Mixtec)
description: In Chilean interpretations, the deer guardian spirit draws from both Mapuche and coastal traditions, embodying the protective energy of the pudu, the worlds smallest deer species that inhabits the dense bamboo forests of southern Chile. This guardian is associated with the sky through its connection to the condor, the great bird that carries prayers to the heavens. The spirit represents the delicate balance between the lush forests of the Lake District and the immense Andes mountains, serving as a bridge between the coastal realms and the high alpine zones

name: Deer Guardian (Mixtec)
description: Not independently attested in South African tradition. The Mixtec are an Indigenous people of Oaxaca, Mexico. The description explicitly describes a Chilean pudu deer guardian of alerce forests in the Andes, copied from a Chilean/Mapuche context and mislabeled as South African/Mixtec. Fabricated cross-continental misattribution.

name: Deer Guardian (Mixtec)
description: Not independently attested in Ghanaian tradition. 'Mixtec' refers to a Mesoamerican people of Oaxaca, Mexico; the record's description details a Chilean pudu deer guardian of Nothofagus forests with volcanoes and lapis lazuli — entirely South American. No deer guardian exists in Ghanaian Akan, Ewe, or Ga folklore.

name: Deer Guardian (Mixtec)
description: Not independently attested in Chilean tradition. MISATTRIBUTION: The Mixtec are an Indigenous people of Oaxaca, Puebla, and Guerrero in MEXICO, not Chile. Mixtec culture includes Eight Deer Jaguar Claw and deer imagery in codices, but no 'Deer Guardian' exists in Chile. The pudú (small Andean deer) is native to southern Chile, but its guardian is a Mapuche ngen, not a Mixtec figure.

name: Deer Guardian of Apache
description: In Apache tradition, the Deer Guardian is a spirit that watches over the vast desert expanses of the American Southwest, protecting the hidden water sources and the hardy wildlife that survives in these harsh conditions. Unlike the ocean guardians of northern traditions, this being commands the dry arroyos and the scarce desert springs that emerge from beneath the sun-baked earth. It is closely linked to the Apache Crown Dancers and the Mountain Spirit ceremonies, where its power is invoked to heal the sick and to guide young people through the trials of coming of age

name: Deer Nature-Spirit (Zapotec)
description: Zapotec tradition of Oaxaca treats caves and underground chambers as portals to the underworld (Lyobaa), places where spirits of nature and rain are addressed. The deer, a principal game animal of the mountains, is linked to these sacred spaces in ritual and oral accounts. The entry's cave-dwelling 'Deer Nature-Spirit' is a synthesis consistent with attested Zapotec cave and animal beliefs.

name: Deer Nature-Spirit of Maya
description: The deer is a central figure in Maya religion and art, linked to the maize cycle, the forest, and the hunt, and appearing throughout the Popol Vuh and on painted ceramics. Deer spirits guard the forest and its water sources such as cenotes and aguadas. The entry's 'Deer Nature-Spirit' is a fair synthesis of these attested associations, though no single named deer deity underlies it.

name: Deer Nature-Spirit of Tlingit
description: In Canadian Tlingit communities of British Columbia, the Deer Nature-Spirit guards the coastal hills and inlets where the deer migrate between the mainland and the islands. This version of the spirit is particularly associated with the misty fjords and the dense temperate rainforest that blankets the Inside Passage. The Tlingit people of Canada maintain that this spirit is the keeper of the boundary between the saltwater shores and the dark forest interior, two fundamental realms in Tlingit cosmology that represent the known and the mysterious

name: Deer Nature-Spirit of Tlingit
description: In Canadian Tlingit communities of British Columbia, the Deer Nature-Spirit guards the coastal hills and inlets where the deer migrate between the mainland and the islands. This version of the spirit is particularly associated with the misty fjords and the dense temperate rainforest that blankets the Inside Passage. The Tlingit people of Canada maintain that this spirit is the keeper of the boundary between the saltwater shores and the dark forest interior, two fundamental realms in Tlingit cosmology that represent the known and the mysterious In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.

name: Deer Nature-Spirit of Uzbek
description: In Uzbek folklore, deer nature-spirits are revered as sacred guardians of the natural world, embodying the delicate balance between the human realm and the wild. Central Asian Turkic and Mongol traditions hold the deer as a mystical messenger between earth and sky, often associated with shamanic journeys and ancestral wisdom. These spirits are believed to inhabit remote wetlands and springs, where they watch over the purity of water sources and the creatures that depend on them. Hunters and travelers who enter their domains must show respect through offerings and ritual gestures, or risk losing their way in the marshes forever

name: Deer Spirit (Khmer)
description: In Khmer tradition, deer spirits are forest guardians that embody the life-giving force of springs and water sources. Cambodian animist beliefs recognize nature spirits known as Neak Ta that inhabit trees, rocks, streams, and springs, with deer spirits being among the most revered for their gentle yet powerful presence. These spirits are considered intermediaries between the human world and the realm of ancestral spirits, often appearing in times of environmental distress to remind communities of their duty to protect the forests and waters that sustain them

name: Deer Spirit of Aymara
description: In Aymara and Andean tradition the taruka, the Andean deer (Hippocamelus antisensis), is a sacred wild (sallqa) animal whose non-human 'owners' are the mountain spirits (mallku, apu), for whom deer are herds, in places called the cows of the ancestors. Ritual hunting requires offerings to that owner and forbids taking breeding males; the deer also appears as the celestial topa taruka.

name: Deer Spirit of Cherokee
description: In Cherokee tradition, the deer spirit known as Awi Usdi (Little Deer) is one of the most revered animal spirits, serving as the protector of all deer and the enforcer of hunting ethics. Cherokee spiritual beliefs teach that Awi Usdi was appointed by the Deer Clan to ensure that humans hunt respectfully and never kill more than they need. This spirit plays a central role in Cherokee animal mythology, where it established the rules of the hunt after humans began killing animals wastefully. The story of Awi Usdi remains a powerful lesson in ecological balance and respect for all living things

name: Deer Spirit of Dogon
description: In Dogon tradition from Mali, deer spirits are associated with the sacred springs and water sources that sustain life in the arid Bandiagara Escarpment region. The Dogon people, renowned for their complex cosmology and astronomical knowledge, recognize animal spirits as intermediaries between the creator god Amma and the human world. Deer spirits specifically guard water sources, which are precious in the dry Sahel, and are linked to the Nommo water spirits that feature prominently in Dogon creation mythology. These spirits ensure that springs remain pure and that those who approach them do so with proper reverence

name: Deer Trickster (Mixtec)
description: In Mixtec tradition from Oaxaca, Mexico, the deer trickster is a complex figure that embodies both the sacred and the mischievous aspects of the forest. Mixtec codices, which were painted on deer hide in an accordion-like format, frequently depict deer in mythological scenes alongside gods, rulers, and supernatural events. The deer trickster uses its intelligence and knowledge of the forest to outwit larger, stronger opponents, teaching lessons about cunning over brute force. It is associated with the wind that moves through the trees, carrying secrets and whispers between the worlds of humans and gods

name: Deer Trickster of Shona
description: In Shona mythology from Zimbabwe, the deer trickster is a swift and clever figure that inhabits the granite kopjes and cliff faces of the Zimbabwean plateau. Shona folklore is rich with trickster animals that teach moral lessons through their cunning adventures, and the deer trickster stands out for its ability to use speed and intelligence to overcome challenges. Unlike the more common hare or tortoise tricksters of African folklore, the deer trickster represents the union of physical grace and mental agility. It is associated with the restless wind that sweeps across the savanna, carrying the whispers of ancestors

name: Deer Trickster of Uzbek
description: In Uzbek folklore, the deer trickster is a cunning cave-dwelling spirit that uses its knowledge of the underground world to outwit larger and more powerful beings. Central Asian Turkic mythology features many trickster figures, and the deer variant combines the sacred status of the deer in shamanic tradition with the clever, unpredictable nature of the trickster archetype. It is said to guard hidden entrances to the underworld and the treasures within, testing those who seek them with riddles and illusions. The deer trickster represents the border between the known world and the mysteries of the earth's depths

name: Deer Water-Spirit of Ashanti
description: In Ashanti mythology from Ghana, the deer water-spirit is an aquatic guardian that inhabits the cave springs and hidden water sources of the forest. The Ashanti people, part of the larger Akan ethnic group, have a rich pantheon of water spirits that protect rivers, lakes, and springs. The deer water-spirit specifically guards the underground water systems that feed the sacred rivers, including the Tano River which is itself personified as a deity. These spirits are seen as intermediaries between the human world and the powerful forces of the earth's waters, ensuring that communities have access to clean water and that the water spirits are properly respected

name: Deer Water-Spirit of Maliseet
description: In Maliseet tradition from the Maritime provinces of Canada, the deer water-spirit is a guardian of mountain springs and highland lakes. The Maliseet (Wolastoqiyik) people of the Wabanaki Confederacy hold deep spiritual connections to the waterways that define their traditional territory, including the Saint John River watershed. Deer water-spirits are believed to inhabit the mountain sources of these rivers, protecting the purity of the water that flows downstream to the villages. The Maliseet people consider these spirits essential allies in maintaining the health of the ecosystem and perform ceremonies to honor them during the spring thaw

name: Deer Water-Spirit of Ojibwe
description: In Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) tradition from Canada, the deer water-spirit similarly protects mountain waters but with specific connection to the Canadian Shield watersheds that feed Hudson Bay. This variant of the spirit is closely tied to the rugged terrain of northern Ontario and Manitoba, where countless lakes and rivers are born from ancient bedrock. The Canadian Ojibwe traditions emphasize different aspects of the deer water-spirit, particularly its role in winter survival and its connection to the northern lights. It shares the same essential nature as the southern variant but with adaptations to the harsher northern climate and the specific geography of the Canadian boreal forest

name: Deer Water-Spirit of Ojibwe
description: In Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) tradition from Canada, the deer water-spirit similarly protects mountain waters but with specific connection to the Canadian Shield watersheds that feed Hudson Bay. This variant of the spirit is closely tied to the rugged terrain of northern Ontario and Manitoba, where countless lakes and rivers are born from ancient bedrock. The Canadian Ojibwe traditions emphasize different aspects of the deer water-spirit, particularly its role in winter survival and its connection to the northern lights. It shares the same essential nature as the southern variant but with adaptations to the harsher northern climate and the specific geography of the Canadian boreal forest In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.

name: Deer Water-Spirit of Yurok
description: In Yurok tradition from the Pacific Northwest coast, the deer water-spirit is a guardian of the springs and streams that flow through the redwood forests of northern California. The Yurok people have a deep spiritual relationship with the Klamath River and its tributaries, which they consider the center of their world. Water spirits in Yurok tradition are powerful beings that must be treated with great respect, as they control the salmon runs, the health of the forest, and the prosperity of the villages. The deer water-spirit specifically protects the spring sources of these vital waterways, ensuring they flow year-round even through the driest California summers

name: Degei
description: Degei is the supreme creator god and serpent deity in Fijian mythology, revered as the primordial being who created the islands of Fiji and all life upon them. Unlike the creator gods of many other Pacific cultures, Degei is not a distant sky god but an immanent presence who dwells within the earth itself, particularly in the Nakauvadra Mountains on Viti Levu. According to Fijian oral traditions, Degei is both a creator and a judge of souls, determining the fate of humans after death. The name Degei is sometimes spelled Ndengei, and the deity represents one of the most important figures in the Fijian spiritual pantheon

name: Degei (Ndengei)
description: Degei (also spelled Ndengei) is the great serpent god of Fiji, specifically venerated as the ancestor spirit who led the first humans from the Nakauvadra Mountains down to the coastal regions. This manifestation of Degei focuses on the god's role as an ancestral figure rather than the supreme creator. Fijian mythology is unique in the Pacific islands for featuring snake deities despite the complete absence of native snakes in Fiji's ecosystems, making Degei a remarkable cultural anomaly. The most detailed accounts of this tradition were documented by British colonial administrator Basil H. Thomson in the late 19th century, who recorded elaborate oral traditions about the serpent god's role in Fijian history

name: Deildegast
description: Deildegast (from Norwegian: deil meaning boundary + gast meaning ghost) is a restless undead spirit in Norwegian folklore. The deildegast is the ghost of a person who moved boundary markers or stole land during their lifetime. As punishment, the spirit is condemned to eternally wander the boundary lines, endlessly trying to lift or replace the boundary stones. This ghost is bound to the earth until the stone is returned to its rightful place. The deildegast is closely associated with Telemark, Agder, and Østlandet regions. Similar to the Greek myth of Sisyphus. Can only be freed if a living person listens to their confession and helps move the stone back. Arne Garborg's Haugtussa features a deildegast

name: Dekki H'd'rtna
description: Dekki H'd'rtna (Various). is a spirit. Dekki H'd'rtna is a spirit from Various folklore in Eritrea, believed to embody the spiritual traditions of the region.. Source: Eritrean oral tradition

name: Delal a Ngibtal
description: Delal a Ngibtal ('Mother of Ngibtal') is the reef serpent of Palauan tradition, a benevolent water spirit dwelling among coral reefs and shallow lagoons. Her name links her to Ngibtal, the mythic giant clam whose tears are said to move the ocean's tides, and she is credited with commanding the waters and speaking with the fish. She represents the sacred bond between the Palauan people and the sea.

name: Demon
description: Demon (Generic). is a demon. Malevolent supernatural entities who seek to corrupt, tempt, or torment humanity. Source: Religious texts, global demonology

name: Demoni
description: In Vatican collections and Christian demonological traditions, Demoni is a category of demonic entities documented in the extensive grimoires and bestiaries preserved in the Vatican Library. The Vatican Mythographers, medieval scholars who compiled and commented on classical mythology, created comprehensive catalogs of supernatural beings that merged pagan mythological creatures with Christian demonology. These texts, including influential works like the Liber Monstrorum and various bestiaries, documented creatures such as the basilisk, cockatrice, griffin, and manticore within a Christian moral framework, interpreting them as symbols of sin, temptation, and the eternal struggle between good and evil

name: Den Grå Dame
description: Den Grå Dame (the Grey Lady) is a famous ghost of Arendal, haunting the Det Kallevigske palé (Kallevig Palace), the old town hall of Arendal. The Grey Lady is the ghost of Cathrine Kitty Kallevig (1783-1840s), a wealthy shipowner's wife who lived in the mansion. Dressed in a grey 1800s silk dress, she has been seen by numerous employees since the 1980s — appearing in the upper-floor hallways, near the grand staircase, and in the council chamber. Her appearances reportedly increased during the 1992 municipal merger when the building was used for contentious political meetings. The Grey Lady is said to be a protective spirit who watches over the building. Local historians note that the tradition contains elements from international castle ghost traditions adapted to the Sørlandet setting. Academic studies have compared her to the Grey Lady of Glamis and other European grey lady traditions

name: Den Vilde Jæger
description: Den Vilde Jæger (the Wild Huntsman) is the Danish version of the Wild Hunt, led by King Valdemar Atterdag (reigned 1340–1375). According to legend, Valdemar loved his castle Gurre Slot so much that when God offered him Heaven, he replied: 'Keep Your Heaven — I want to stay at Gurre!' As punishment, he was condemned to hunt across Sjælland for eternity with black horses and dogs with flaming mouths. The hunt rides at midnight during storms, between Vordingborg in the south and Gurre in the north. At Tokkekøb, a farm's gates burst open every night for the hunt to pass through. At Gurre Lake, the sound of Valdemar's hunting horn still echoes on stormy nights. Finding his dropped glove brings either great blessing or terrible doom, depending on which version of the legend you hear

name: Desert Jinn
description: Desert Jinn (Somali/Islamic). is a spirit. Luminous, invisible spirits of the Somali desert capable of illusions and shape-shifting. Source: Somali-Islamic Folklore

name: Destroyer (Guarani)
description: The Destroyer is a fearsome demonic entity from Guarani mythology, representing the destructive forces that threaten the balance of the natural and spiritual worlds. The Guarani people of Paraguay and surrounding regions believe in a complex cosmology where spirits of destruction test the faith and resilience of humanity. These entities are not inherently evil in the Christian sense but represent necessary forces of chaos that challenge creation and force growth through adversity. The Destroyer inhabits the wastelands and underworld regions of Guarani cosmology, emerging when the natural order is disrupted or when humans forget their sacred duties to the earth

name: Detora
description: Detora is the guardian hero of Nauruan tradition, a brave, protective spirit celebrated for superhuman strength and mastery of the outer reefs and coastal caves. His feats, passed down in Nauruan oral narrative, cast him as the defender of the homeland against the sea. He embodies Nauruan ideals of courage, resilience, and communal protection.

name: Dev
description: Dev is a type of giant or ogre in Armenian folklore, derived from the Persian word 'div' meaning demon or monster. These creatures appear throughout Armenian folktales and epic poetry, including the national epic 'Daredevils of Sassoun,' where they serve as formidable opponents for heroes. Armenian devs are characterized by their immense physical strength, limited intelligence, and generally brutish nature. Unlike the truly evil demons of other traditions, Armenian devs are often portrayed as stupid rather than malicious, capable of being outwitted by clever humans. They are associated with the construction of megalithic structures, as their immense strength explains the presence of ancient stone monuments across the Armenian landscape

name: Devatha
description: Devatha refers to a class of divine beings in Sri Lankan Buddhist and animist traditions, encompassing nature spirits, guardian deities, and ancestral spirits that protect villages, forests, and waterways. The concept blends pre-Buddhist animist beliefs with Theravada Buddhist cosmology, where devathas are benevolent beings who have achieved a favorable rebirth through merit but remain within the cycle of samsara. In Sri Lankan folk Buddhism, devathas are actively worshipped and propitiated, with rituals seeking their protection for crops, journeys, and daily life. Unlike the fully enlightened Buddhas, devathas are approachable beings who can directly intervene in human affairs

name: Devi
description: Devi is the great goddess in Hinduism, embodying the supreme feminine divine energy known as Shakti. Worshipped across India for millennia, she manifests in both benevolent and fearsome forms. As the mother goddess Mahadevi, she is the source of all creation, preservation, and destruction. Her gentle aspect appears as Parvati, Uma, and Gauri — the loving consort of Shiva. Her fierce aspect manifests as Durga, the ten-armed warrior goddess who rides a lion into battle against demons, and Kali, the black goddess of time and destruction who wears a garland of skulls. The Devi Mahatmya, a sacred text from the Markandeya Purana, recounts her epic battles against the buffalo demon Mahishasura and the demon lords Shumbha and Nishumbha, establishing her as the supreme protectress of cosmic order

name: Devi
description: Devi, the Great Goddess of Hinduism, is the supreme feminine power, Shakti. Her gentle forms include Parvati, Uma, and Gauri; her fierce forms include Durga, the ten-armed warrior who slays the buffalo demon Mahishasura, and Kali. The Devi Mahatmya of the Markandeya Purana recounts these victories.

name: Devil (Stagolee)
description: The Devil appears in African American folklore as a complex figure — sometimes a fearsome adversary, sometimes a comic figure who meets his match. In the Stagolee legend, the Devil is challenged by the bad man himself: after Stagolee is hanged for murder, he arrives in Hell and pulls his pistol on the Devil, kicks him off his throne, and takes over the underworld. The Devil finds he cannot control Stagolee and must beg God to let him into Heaven. In High John the Conqueror tales, the Devil sets impossible tasks for John but is outwitted by John and his daughter's cleverness. The Devil in African American folklore is often a figure who can be overcome through wit and courage — a reflection of a worldview in which even the most powerful adversary can be defeated by a clever mind

name: Devil's Tower
description: Devil's Tower, known as Mato Tipila or Bear Lodge to the Lakota and Tso-aa to the Kiowa, is a sacred geological formation in northeastern Wyoming and the first declared United States National Monument. In the oral traditions of over twenty Native American tribes including the Lakota, Cheyenne, Kiowa, Crow, and Arapaho, this 1,267-foot monolith of striated igneous rock is a living spiritual being central to creation narratives. The most widespread legend tells of seven young girls chased by a giant bear who climbed onto a low rock and prayed for deliverance. The Great Spirit caused the rock to grow skyward, carrying the girls beyond the bear's reach. The bear's claws scored the rock's sides, creating the distinctive vertical columns visible today. The girls became the constellation Pleiades. The Tower remains a site of vision quests, prayer offerings, and ceremonial bundles left among its crevices

name: Dewi Sri (Rice Goddess)
description: Dewi Sri is the revered Javanese, Sundanese, and Balinese Hindu goddess of rice and fertility, still widely worshipped across Indonesia. According to Sundanese myth, she was born from a miraculous egg laid by the naga god Antaboga. She grew into a princess of such beauty that the supreme god Batara Guru became dangerously attracted to her. To prevent scandal in heaven, the gods poisoned her, and her innocent body was buried. From her grave sprouted all the useful plants essential to humanity: from her head grew coconuts, from her eyes grew rice (white from the right, red from the left), from her hair grew grasses, from her arms grew teak trees, and from her body grew all fruits, vegetables, and tubers. She is equated with the Hindu goddess Lakshmi and remains the most important agricultural deity in Indonesia

name: Dhanvantari (Physician of the Gods)
description: Dhanvantari is the Hindu god of medicine and the physician of the gods (devas), revered as the originator of Ayurveda, the ancient Indian system of medicine. He emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra Manthana) holding a pot of amrita (the nectar of immortality) in his hands. According to the Bhagavata Purana and Vishnu Purana, Dhanvantari rose from the ocean as the last of the fourteen treasures (ratnas), carrying the pot of nectar that the devas and asuras had been churning for. He is considered an avatar of Vishnu, appearing to restore health and longevity to the world. The name Dhanvantari means 'moving like a bow' or 'one who travels through the arc of a bow,' referring to the swift and direct nature of his healing. He is credited with compiling the Ayurvedic text the Charaka Samhita in some traditions, though Charaka is more commonly identified as the primary author. Dhanvantari is worshipped by physicians, surgeons, and those seeking healing

name: Dhegdheer
description: Dhegdheer, meaning 'Long Ear' in Somali, is a fearsome cannibalistic demon from Somali folklore who hunts in forests and preys primarily on lost or wandering children. Once a mortal woman whose selfishness and greed led a curse to transform her into a monster, Dhegdheer possesses supernatural hearing that allows her to detect even the faintest sounds from great distances. She is closely associated with the Hargega Valley and the Caves of Xargega in the Sanaag region of northern Somalia. Her legend is so deeply embedded in Somali culture that children are warned not to wander far from home lest Dhegdheer snatch them. Her daughter Buuti features in stories as a heroic figure who defies her cannibalistic mother's nature to save innocent villagers. Dhegdheer eventually meets her end when the forces of natural justice drown her in a river, returning peace to the land

name: Diablada
description: The Diablada ('dance of the devils') is the famous mask dance of the Carnaval de Oruro, Bolivia, rooted in the Uru people's Llama-Llama ritual and reshaped under Spanish Catholic influence. Dancers in baroque devil (Supay) masks and armor enact the battle of good against evil, with the archangel Michael triumphant; Oruro's carnival became a UNESCO Masterpiece of Intangible Heritage in 2001.

name: Didibri
description: Didibri are dragon-like creatures from Surinamese folklore, derived from the Sranan Tongo word for devil or dragon. These fearsome beings appear in the oral traditions of Suriname's diverse population, including Creole, Maroon, and Indigenous communities. The most famous tale, documented by folklorists Melville and Frances Herskovits in the early 20th century, tells of a twelve-tailed dragon named Didibri who transforms himself into a handsome human — calling himself Je Man — to woo a human woman. His twelve dragon brothers await to devour her. The story features magical objects called obia that the woman's brother uses to create obstacles — a great lake, a sea of fire, a field of cutting grass, and a mountain — that the dragons must overcome. Didibri represents the boundary between the human world and the dangerous spiritual realm in Surinamese cosmology

name: Dievas
description: Dievas is the primordial supreme sky god in Baltic mythology, worshipped by ancient Lithuanians, Latvians, and Old Prussians as the creator of the universe and ruler of all deities. His name derives from the Proto-Indo-European sky father *Dyēus, making him cognate with the Vedic Dyaus Pita, Greek Zeus, and Roman Jupiter. Dievas is the god of light, sky, prosperity, and wealth, and alongside Perkūnas (thunder god) and Potrimpo, forms the supreme triad of Baltic deities. According to creation myths, Dievas and his twin brother Velns, the trickster god, created the universe by wrestling upon a rock in the primordial ocean, which became the center of the world. He is also known as Praamžius, the god of time, sky, peace, and friendship. His two sons, the Ašvieniai, are the divine twins who pull the sun goddess Saulė's chariot across the sky

name: Dilyéhé (Mountain Sheep People)
description: Dilyéhé, known as the Mountain Sheep People, are sacred animal-spirit beings in Navajo (Diné) tradition who serve as the guardians of the mountains. They are among the Holy People who taught the Navajo people how to live in harmony with the natural world. The Mountain Sheep People possess deep knowledge of the high country — its plants, waters, and paths — and they share this wisdom with humans who approach them with proper respect and offerings. They grant blessings of health, hunting success, and protection during mountain travel. In Navajo cosmology, the Dilyéhé inhabit a realm between the physical and spiritual worlds, appearing in visions and ceremonies to those who seek their guidance. They are closely associated with the sacred mountains that define the four cardinal boundaries of Dinétah, the traditional Navajo homeland

name: Dimo
description: Dimo is a cannibal giant in Sotho (Basotho) folklore who terrorizes villages, devouring anyone he catches. In the beloved tale of Tselane, Dimo tricks the young girl into opening her door by mimicking her mother's secret call-and-response song. He consulted a medicine woman who told him to thrust a red-hot iron rod down his throat to clear his voice, which succeeded. He captured Tselane and put her in a bag, but local children discovered her and replaced her with a swarm of bees. When Dimo opened the bag at home, the bees attacked and stung him to death. Dimo represents the dangers that threaten the vulnerable and the triumph of cleverness over brute force

name: Diser
description: The Diser (singular: Dis, from Old Norse dís meaning "lady") are a collective of powerful female spirits in Norse mythology and Germanic tradition who act as protective guardians of individuals, families, and clans. They are intimately associated with fate, fertility, and death, occupying a mysterious space between deities, ancestral spirits, and supernatural guardians. The Disir encompass a broad range of female supernatural figures including valkyries (called "Odin's Disir"), norns, and certain goddesses like Freyja. They could be either benevolent protectors who guided their charges through life or harbingers of doom whose appearance foretold death. The dísablót, a major sacrificial festival held at the beginning of winter, was dedicated to the Disir, and the Disting fair in Uppsala still carries their name today. In Swedish folklore, they were believed to be the spirits of female ancestors who watched over their descendants, and offerings were made to them at births, weddings, and funerals

name: Ditaolane
description: Ditaolane is the great hero and deity of the Basotho people who saved humanity from the all-devouring monster Khanyapa (also called Kholumodumo or Kammapa). Only one pregnant woman survived the monster's rampage by hiding in a stable. She gave birth to Ditaolane, who emerged from the womb wearing a necklace of divination bones and instantly grew into a full-grown man. Taking a knife, he confronted Khanyapa and was swallowed, but inside its belly he slashed the monster's entrails, killing it. Thousands of humans and animals emerged alive. The people he rescued grew to fear him and plotted his death. Ditaolane turned himself into a stone, escaping their treachery, or in another version his heart became a bird and flew to the sky

name: Div
description: Divs are malevolent giant-demons of Azerbaijani and broader Turkic mythology, derived from the Zoroastrian daeva tradition. They appear in countless Azerbaijani fairy tales and in the Kitabi-Dede Korkut epic as the primary antagonists of human heroes. Divs live in deep wells, underground caves with three chambers, and mountain caverns across Azerbaijan, from the Talysh Mountains in the southeast to the Greater Caucasus range. They possess magical powers including shapeshifting, and are known for kidnapping beautiful women, hoarding treasure, and devouring humans. Some Divs have multiple heads, horns, and enormous teeth. Despite their fearsome reputations, a few folktales show sympathetic Divs who befriend humans

name: Div
description: Divs are malevolent giant-demons of Azerbaijani and broader Turkic mythology, derived from the Zoroastrian daeva tradition. They appear in countless Azerbaijani fairy tales and in the Kitabi-Dede Korkut epic as the primary antagonists of human heroes. Divs live in deep wells, underground caves with three chambers, and mountain caverns across Azerbaijan, from the Talysh Mountains in the southeast to the Greater Caucasus range. They possess magical powers including shapeshifting, and are known for kidnapping beautiful women, hoarding treasure, and devouring humans. Some Divs have multiple heads, horns, and enormous teeth. Despite their fearsome reputations, a few folktales show sympathetic Divs who befriend humans In Azerbaijan folklore, this figure is known among the Azerbaijan people.

name: Div (Daeva)
description: In Persian epic and folk tradition, divs are monstrous, night-active demons of inverted nature, descendants of Zoroastrian daevas. The Shahnameh portrays them as adversaries of the hero Rostam, most famously Div-e Sepid, whose blood restores the blinded king's sight. Folklore warns of divs lurking near villages after dark.

name: Div (Daeva)
description: Divs (Persian: dīv, from Avestan daeva) are demonic beings of Iranian tradition, demonized in Zoroastrianism from older Indo-Iranian deities. In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh they are the chief antagonists of Rostam, including Div-e Sepid, the White Div who blinded King Kay Kavus, and Akvan-e Div.

name: Div (Daeva)
description: Divs are demonic beings of Afghan folk tradition, part of the wider Persianate belief descended from Zoroastrian daevas. In Dari and Pashto tales divs dwell in remote mountains and caves, guard treasure, and abduct travelers, and heroes must outwit or overpower them. The Afghan div tradition is real, though details vary locally.

name: Div-e Sepid
description: Div-e Sepid, the White Demon, is a legendary creature from Persian and Afghan mythology, best known as the chieftain of the divs of Mazandaran and the penultimate adversary in Rostam's Seven Labors from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. The White Demon is a being of colossal size and power, commanding armies of lesser divs from his cave fortress in the mountains. He is described as having white skin or fur, a black face, and immense strength. His most devastating power is his ability to blind entire armies through sorcery — he destroys Kay Kavus's forces by conjuring a dark storm of hail, boulders, and tree trunks, then captures the king and his paladins, blinds them, and imprisons them in a dungeon. Only Rostam can defeat him, extracting the White Demon's liver to restore sight to the blinded heroes. Some scholars interpret the White Demon as a symbolic representation of Zal, Rostam's albino father, making their battle an Oedipal struggle

name: Diwata (Nature Spirit/Deity)
description: Diwata are a broad class of nature spirits, goddesses, and guardian deities in pre-colonial Philippine mythology. The term encompasses a wide range of spiritual beings who inhabit natural features such as mountains, forests, rivers, seas, and trees. Diwata are similar to the concept of anito (ancestral spirits) but generally refer to higher nature deities. They are benevolent when respected but can be vengeful when their domains are desecrated. Each natural feature was believed to have its own diwata guardian — Mount Makiling has Maria Makiling, Mount Arayat has Maria Sinukuan, and Mount Mayon has Daragang Magayon. The diwata concept reflects the deep animist spirituality of pre-colonial Filipinos, who saw the natural world as alive with sacred presences

name: Diwata 0534
description: Diwata 0534 (Unknown). is a spirit. Diwata are nature spirits from Philippine folklore who guard mountains, forests, and waters like fairies.. Source: Philippine indigenous religion — Diwata are nature spirits/goddesses documented in Visayan and Tagalog oral tradition.

name: Diyin Dineʼé (Holy People)
description: Diyin Dineʼé (Holy People) are the sacred beings who shaped the world and established the laws of the Navajo people during the long emergence through four underworlds. They include First Man, First Woman, Changing Woman, Monster Slayer, Born for Water, and many others, each responsible for different aspects of creation — from placing the stars to teaching the people how to weave. The Diyin Dineʼé gave the Navajo their ceremonies, songs, and the concept of hózhó (beauty, balance, and harmony). Their stories are not merely myths but living prescriptions for correct living, healing, and maintaining right relationship with the natural world

name: Djibo
description: A Malian hyena-shapeshifter figure: a being said to pass between hyena and human form in the service of sorcerers, aligned with the Bambara (Bamana) Korè initiation society, whose suruku hyena masks are danced in ritual and whose members 'become' hyenas by roleplay.

name: Djinn
description: Djinn are invisible, shapeshifting spirits of Islamic folklore widely believed in the Gambia, where they can influence human fate, possess the unwary, or act as moral enforcers in desert and ruin contexts. Their power is invoked through charms, amulets, and the guidance of marabouts in Gambian Islamic folk practice.

name: Djinn
description: In Wolof and broader Senegalese folklore, jinn (djinn) are supernatural beings of smokeless fire, integrated from Islamic tradition into pre-existing spirit beliefs. They shapeshift (often as snakes), inhabit ruins and deserts, and can be mischievous or helpful. Iron and Qur'anic verses repel them. Not merely tricksters — they occupy a parallel moral universe accountable to God.

name: Djura (Berber Wandering Spirit of the Atlas)
description: Djura (or Idjura) is a wandering spirit figure from Berber folklore of the Middle Atlas Mountains of Morocco. Djura is said to be the spirit of a holy person (wali) who was cursed to wander eternally for a transgression committed in life. Unlike settled saints (murabitun), Djura has no tomb or shrine; snip his presence is felt as a sudden cold wind on a hot day, the sound of unseen footsteps, or a fleeting shadow in the corner of vision. He is both a guardian and a warning: he protects travelers lost in the mountains, guiding them back to safety, but also tests people's generosity and faith by appearing as a beggar. Those who are cruel to beggars will be led astray by Djura; snip those who are generous will find their way. He is accompanied by a ghostly dog or ram

name: Dodo
description: The Dodo is the great bush-spirit and bogeyman of Hausa tradition in Niger and northern Nigeria, an ancient deity of the dry season whose wife Damina brings the rains. A giant, cannibalistic being of forests, swamps and baobab trees, he seizes those who stray from home; his tales enforce obedience, community and respect for boundaries.

name: Dogs of Metal (Metalhunde)
description: The three metal dogs — eyes like teacups, water wheels, and the Round Tower — are literary creations from Andersen's 1835 tale "The Tinderbox," summoned by a magic tinderbox. No independent Danish folk tradition attests these constructs; they belong to Andersen's invention, drawing on ATU 562 (Spirit in the Blue Light).

name: Dogs Of Metal Denmark
description: Dogs Of Metal Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. Three giant metal guard dogs from Hans Christian Andersen's The Tinderbox with eyes as large as round towers.. Source: Danish folklore — spirit figures documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Dokkaebi
description: Dokkaebi are legendary goblin-like creatures from Korean mythology and folklore, deeply embedded in both North and South Korean cultural traditions. Unlike ghosts (gwishin), dokkaebi are nature deities or spirits born from inanimate objects that have been imbued with spiritual energy over time — old discarded household tools like brooms, farming implements, or objects stained with human blood and emotions. They possess extraordinary supernatural powers and are known for their mischievous and unpredictable interactions with humans. Dokkaebi are neither purely good nor evil; they reward kindness and punish greed, often testing human morality through games and challenges. They are famously associated with the dokkaebi bangmangi, a magical club that can grant wishes and summon objects, though it cannot create life. Dokkaebi are skilled at ssireum (Korean wrestling) and cannot be beaten unless their right side is exploited. They are strongly attracted to buckwheat products and can be warded off by horse blood or sieves hung outside doors

name: Dokkaebi
description: Dokkaebi are goblin-like spirits of Korean folklore, born from old household objects imbued with spiritual energy. Neither wholly good nor evil, they reward kindness and punish greed, wield the wish-granting bangmangi club, excel at ssireum wrestling, and can be warded off by horse blood or a hanging sieve.

name: Dokkaebi
description: Dokkaebi (도깨비) are the goblins of Korean folklore: mischievous spirits said to form from objects stained with human blood or from old discarded household tools. They appear as horned, ugly beings who play pranks, trade using barley-straw or wooden money that turns back to leaves, and can be driven away with fire, pork, or red beans. Their magic club (dokkaebi bangmangi) is said to summon treasure.

name: Dokkaebi Gam
description: Korean folklore knows the dokkaebi, a horned goblin of ambiguous character, and its bangmangi (magic club) is central to a famous tale cycle: a kind woodcutter who aids a dokkaebi receives a club that yields gold, while his greedy rival is beaten or left poor. The 'Dokkaebi Gam' entry garbles this motif: the club rewards virtue and punishes greed, it does not spawn goblins.

name: Domen-heksene
description: Domen-heksene (the Witches of Mount Domen) are the spirits of witches who gathered at Mount Domen near Vardø in Finnmark, the site of Norway's most infamous witch trials. Between 1621 and 1663, 91 people were executed for witchcraft in Vardø — more than anywhere else in Norway. According to local folklore, the witches gathered at Domen to meet Satan, flying as cats, dogs, birds, or sea monsters. The mount itself is said to be haunted by their spirits, and strange lights and sounds are still reported there. The Vardø witch trials were unique in their focus on Sami magic and the use of the devil's mark as evidence. Domen-heksene represent the tragic intersection of Sami shamanic traditions and Christian persecution

name: Domovoi
description: The Domovoi is a household spirit in Russian and Slavic folklore, deeply rooted in pre-Christian ancestor worship traditions. The name comes from the Russian 'dom' meaning house — the Domovoi is literally 'the one of the household.' This spirit lives behind the stove, under the threshold, or in the attic of traditional Slavic homes, serving as the guardian of the family. Belief in the Domovoi has persisted for centuries, surviving Christianization and continuing into modern times, particularly in rural areas. The Domovoi is considered the personification of the family's founder or a deceased male ancestor, making it an integral part of ancestor veneration. When a family moves to a new home, they perform a ritual to invite the Domovoi to join them, often by leaving bread and salt as offerings. The spirit ensures domestic harmony, protects children and livestock, and maintains the moral order of the household. Neglecting the Domovoi or behaving immorally causes it to become angry and potentially abandon the home, leaving the family vulnerable to misfortune

name: Domovoy
description: The Domovoy is the protective household spirit of Slavic mythology, worshipped across Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Serbia, and other Slavic nations. Derived from the Proto-Slavic root 'dom' meaning house, the Domovoy is the master and guardian of the home who protects the family from harm, oversees domestic harmony, and ensures the prosperity of the household. According to folklorist E. Kagarov, the Domovoy is a personification of the supreme god Rod in the microcosm of the family. The Domovoy is closely linked to ancestor worship — many traditions identify the spirit as the soul of the family's founder or a deceased male relative. The Domovoy has a female counterpart called Domania, Kikimora, or Domovikha who handles the domestic sphere. Unlike many European household spirits, the Domovoy is deeply integrated into the religious and moral life of the family, not merely a mischievous sprite but a guardian of the kin's spiritual and physical well-being

name: Domovoy (Slavic House Spirit)
description: The Domovoy, known as Domovoi or Domovik in various Slavic languages, is a household spirit deeply rooted in Slavic mythology across Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Serbia, and other Eastern European nations. The name derives from the Proto-Slavic root 'dom' meaning house, establishing this entity as the master and guardian of the home who protects the family and oversees domestic harmony. According to folklorist E. Kagarov, the Domovoy represents a personification of the supreme god Rod within the microcosm of the family, linking it directly to ancestral worship traditions where the soul of the family's founder continues to watch over the living. The Domovoy is deeply integrated into the moral framework of the household, not merely as a mischievous sprite but as a guardian of the kin's physical and spiritual well-being across all aspects of domestic life

name: Douen
description: The Douen is a forest spirit of Trinidad and Tobagonian folklore, the soul of an unbaptized child who died and now wanders the woods. Its backward-turned feet confuse trackers, and it lures children away by mimicking the voices of parents and loved ones. Parents use Douen tales to keep children from wandering alone.

name: Dovregubben
description: Dovregubben (The Dovre King/Old Man of Dovre) is the king of the trolls who lives in the Dovre Mountains, created by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen for his 1867 play Peer Gynt. Dovregubben is a huge, ugly troll king with a nose like a club and a scepter made of a cow's tail. In Peer Gynt, he presides over his troll court in the Dovre Hall and gives Peer the infamous ultimatum: "Be true to yourself, enough for yourself" (the troll's motto, contrasting with the human ideal of "be yourself"). The phrase "I Dovregubbens hall" (In the Hall of the Mountain King) was immortalized by Edvard Grieg's famous musical composition. Though created by Ibsen, Dovregubben has become deeply embedded in Norwegian folklore as the quintessential troll king. The Dovre Mountains themselves have been associated with trolls since medieval times

name: Doña Sebastiana
description: Doña Sebastiana is a New Mexican Hispano death figure — a skeletal woman with bow and arrows in a wooden cart, whose rattling is heard before a death.
