Carved as bultos in the santero tradition, she is identified with Santa Muerte in some stories and in others a separate figure who grants sinners a final confession.

name: Drac
description: The Drac is a shapeshifting water spirit of southern French folklore, bound to the Rhône and neighboring rivers. Described by Gervase of Tilbury in the Otia Imperialia (c. 1213), dracs float gold rings or cups to lure people, drag nursing women below to raise their young, and can be repelled by the sign of the cross.

name: Drache
description: Drache is the German word for dragon. In Germanic folklore the Drache is a fire-breathing serpent or reptile guarding treasure in mountains, caves, and forests, with regional forms such as the Lindwurm. In the Nibelungenlied, Siegfried slays the dragon and bathes in its blood to become invulnerable.

name: Dradokke
description: A dradokke (dra-doll, dragedokke) is a doll-like object of Norwegian folk belief that 'draws' wealth to its owner. Sources in the Norsk Folkeminnesamling record that it was sent out at night to bring back milk, grain, clothes, gold, and silver, sometimes from drowned men at the seabed; recipes for making one could call for stolen cloth or a dead thief's right thumb.

name: Dragon
description: Dragon (Generic). is a dragon. Legendary reptilian creatures of immense power, typically associated with fire, wealth, and wisdom. Source: Global mythology, comparative folklore studies

name: Dragon (Drage)
description: Drage is the Danish dragon: gigantic winged serpent with fire/poison breath, impenetrable scales, hoarding gold in mountain caverns or ruined castles. Sleeps ages; fiercely territorial when awakened. Vulnerable at underbelly, to hubris, strong heroes. Appears in Danish folktales ('Treasure in Sabro Creek', 'Lord Peter'). Represents heroic challenge and greed's danger. Cognate with Norse linnormr.

name: Dragon Denmark
description: Dragon Denmark (Unknown). is a dragon. Dragons appear in Danish folklore and legend, often guarding treasures or terrorizing villages. The Danish flag (Dannebrog) is traditionally said to have fallen from the sky during the Battle of Lynda. Source: Danish folklore and ballad tradition

name: Drakaina
description: The Drakaina is the feminine form of the drakon in Greek mythology — a serpent or serpent-woman of chthonic power. Notable drakainai include Echidna, mother of monsters; Campe, guardian of Tartarus slain by Zeus; and Delphyne, the serpent who guarded Zeus' umbilical cord and was killed by Apollo.

name: Drake (Swedish)
description: In Swedish folklore, the drake is a wingless, serpentine dragon that guards treasure hoards deep in the forest. Unlike the fire-breathing dragons of continental European legend, the Swedish drake is primarily a giant serpent with a horse-like mane or fish-like dorsal fin along its spine. It is often called lindorm (lindworm) and is distinguished by its ability to make treasure grow: anything lying beneath a drake increases in value at the same rate the serpent grows. The drake can spit a foul milk-like substance that blinds its enemies, and when threatened it may swallow its own tail to form a wheel and roll away at high speed, earning it the nickname hjulorm (wheel snake). Drake eggs are said to be laid under linden trees, and once hatched the young slither away to make homes in piles of rocks. The belief in drakes survived long after Christianization and persisted well into the 19th century in rural Sweden

name: Drakos
description: In modern Greek folk tradition, drakos (pl. drakoi) are monstrous, ogre-like giants, distinct from the classical drakon. Dragon-slayer tales, including the Akritas cycles, recount heroes battling drakoi and their wives. This folk meaning of drakos as a giant or ogre is well attested in Greek oral tradition.

name: Draugar
description: Draugar are the undead revenants of Icelandic saga and folklore, animated corpses that rise from graves and burial mounds. Corporeal and supernaturally strong, they swell to a huge size, bring disease and death to nearby farms, and can be fought but not easily killed. The best-known are Glámr in Grettis Saga and the mound-dweller Kárr the Old.

name: Draugen
description: Draugen is the sea-revenant of Danish and Norwegian coastal folklore, the ghost of a fisherman or sailor drowned at sea. He appears as a drenched figure rising half from the water, sometimes rowing a half-boat, and his appearance or cry foretells drowning and shipwreck. Belief was strongest in Norwegian fishing communities, where the draug warned of storms.

name: Draugr
description: Draugr (ON draugr, Norw. draug, Sw. drög) is a corporeal undead revenant in Norse/Nordic folklore. Guards burial mound (haugbúi) and treasure with superhuman strength, shapeshifts (seal, bull, cat), curses intruders. Skin hel-blár ('death-blue') or nár-fölr ('corpse-pale'), reeks of decay. Kárr inn gamli in Grettis saga explicitly called draugr.

name: Draugr
description: Draugr (Icelandic). is a undead. A corporeal undead creature that guards its burial mound with superhuman strength. Source: Norse mythology; draugar are corporeal undead, documented in the Sagas and Norse ethnographic studies.

name: Draugr (Swedish variant)
description: The Swedish variant of the Draugr shares many characteristics with its Norse cousins but has developed distinct features shaped by Sweden's unique coastal geography and maritime traditions. In Swedish folklore, the Draugr, also known regionally as drög or draug, is specifically associated with the Baltic Sea coast and the archipelagoes of Sweden, where it appears as the undead spirit of sailors and fishermen who died at sea. The Swedish Draugr tradition emphasizes the creature's role as both a guardian of sunken treasure and a bringer of storms, reflecting the dual nature of the Baltic Sea as both a source of livelihood and a cause of death for coastal communities. Unlike the more varied Draugr of Icelandic sagas, the Swedish variant is almost exclusively maritime in nature, with strong connections to shipwrecks, fishing disasters, and the treasures that lie beneath the waves

name: Draugr (Swedish variant)
description: Along Sweden's Baltic coast and archipelagoes, the draugr is the revenant of a fisherman or sailor lost at sea. This maritime variant guards sunken treasure, raises storms, and harries living boatmen, reflecting the sea as both livelihood and grave. It is distinct from the mound-dwelling draugar of the Icelandic sagas.

name: Draugur
description: Draugur (Faroese dreygur) is the Faroese form of the Norse draugr, a walking dead being of island tradition. Draugar in the Faroes were often described as large figures in grey clothes who guarded burial mounds and treasure or, in sea lore, as the drowned dead who rose to drag the living down. The sign of the cross and naming them aloud were said to ward them off.

name: Drekavac
description: The Drekavac, meaning 'the screamer' or 'the screecher,' is a terrifying mythical creature from South Slavic mythology, with particularly strong belief in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is most commonly described as the restless spirit of an unbaptized child that rises from its grave at night to haunt the living, emitting horrifying wails that blend animal cries with human sobs. In Maglaj, Bosnia, it takes the form of ghostly fallen soldiers unable to find peace, while in Kozarska Dubica it resembles a vampire-like undead man. The creature appears variably as a dappled, spindle-thin being with an oversized head, a humanoid canine, or a formless apparition. Its defining trait is its agonizing scream, which foretells death when appearing as a child or cattle disease when in animal form. The Drekavac is visible mainly at night, especially during the twelve days of Christmas (called 'unbaptized days') and early spring, and is repelled by dogs and bright light

name: Drekavac
description: The Drekavac ('screamer') of South Slavic belief is the restless spirit of an unbaptized child that wails horribly at night, blending animal cries with human sobs. In parts of Bosnia it appears as a dappled, spindle-thin being or a spectral soldier, and its scream is said to foretell death or cattle disease. It shows itself at night, especially during the twelve 'unbaptized days' of Christmas.

name: Dreq
description: Dreq, from Latin draco, is a dragon-demon of Albanian folk belief that rises from lakes and freshwater to attack livestock and people. Closely related to the multi-headed kulshedra, it takes a more draconic, vampiric form. Albanian tradition ties the dreq to dangerous waters, explaining drownings and mysterious deaths near lakes and rivers.

name: Druk (Thunder Dragon of Bhutan)
description: The Druk (Thunder Dragon) is Bhutan's national symbol, giving the country its name Druk Yul ('Land of the Thunder Dragon'). The 12th-century Tibetan master Tsangpa Gyare heard thunder thrice while founding Ralung Monastery and named his Drukpa Kagyu lineage after it; the dragon later became Bhutan's emblem. The Druk commands storms — its roar is thunder, its serpentine body lightning.

name: Dsonoqua
description: Dsonoqua, also known as Dzunukwa or Tsonoqua, is a powerful and complex figure from the mythology of the Kwakwaka'wakw people of the Pacific Northwest Coast of Canada. Unlike many North American spirit figures, Dsonoqua is neither purely benevolent nor malevolent but embodies a wild, untamed power that demands respect and caution. She is often described as a giantess or wild woman of the forest who possesses both dangerous and beneficial aspects, capable of devouring children who disobey while also granting supernatural powers to those who prove worthy. The Dsonoqua tradition is an integral part of Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial life, appearing in the hamatsa ceremony where initiates are symbolically captured by Dsonoqua and transformed into supernatural beings

name: Duende
description: Small, mischievous humanoid beings in Portuguese folklore, similar to goblins, elves, or leprechauns. Duendes are described as small-statured creatures wearing big hats who whistle an enchanting song through the forest to lure young children away from home, causing them to lose their way. The name derives from 'dueño de casa' (master of the house), suggesting they were originally household spirits. In Portuguese tradition, duendes inhabit forests, caves, and abandoned places. They are known to move objects, hide belongings, and create noises in cupboards. Some legends describe them as guardians of nature who punish those who harm the forest

name: Duende
description: Small, mischievous humanoid beings in Portuguese folklore, similar to goblins, elves, or leprechauns. Duendes are described as small-statured creatures wearing big hats who whistle an enchanting song through the forest to lure young children away from home, causing them to lose their way. The name derives from 'dueño de casa' (master of the house), suggesting they were originally household spirits. In Portuguese tradition, duendes inhabit forests, caves, and abandoned places. They are known to move objects, hide belongings, and create noises in cupboards. Some legends describe them as guardians of nature who punish those who harm the forest In Portugal folklore, this figure is known among the Portugal people.

name: Duende (Forest Guardian)
description: El Duende of Ecuadorian folklore is a small forest spirit, a wrinkled little man in a broad hat and pointed shoes who guards forests and highlands while playing tricks, stealing food, and leading animals astray. He is said to lure disobedient children into the woods, where offending him can make one lose one's way forever, and he collects children's nail clippings as a protective charm.

name: Duende (Forest Guardian)
description: Peruvian duende belief blends Quechua and Aymara tradition with Spanish colonial influence. In the Amazon the duende is close to the chullachaqui, a shapeshifting jungle spirit that guards the forest and misleads hunters; in the highlands it takes on mountain-spirit traits, watching over fields and communities. Parents use the figure to keep children from wandering alone in the bush.

name: Duende (Forest Guardian)
description: In Belize the duende is Tata Duende (Nukuch Tat to the Yucatec Maya), a small forest guardian with backward-turned feet and no thumbs who whistles to lure or punish the unwary and protects animals and the bush. Parents warn children against the forest, for Tata Duende is said to steal the thumbs of careless children. He is a well-known figure of Belizean Maya and Creole folklore.

name: Duizendpoot
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Duizendpoot is simply the modern Dutch word for a centipede (literally 'thousand-foot') and names no mythological being in Dutch tradition, where the nearest domestic or forest spirits are the kabouter and the klabauterman. The present description is a copy-pasted Belize duende text.

name: Duk Ib The Changer Coast Salish
description: Dukʷibəɫ, the Changer, is the transformer of Lushootseed and Coast Salish tradition who travelled the myth-age world remaking its beings. He met Blue Heron splitting cedar with his head, straightened out the chaotic creatures of that age, and left animals, rocks, and landmarks in their present forms. In other Salish languages he appears as Xelas or the Transformer Brothers.

name: Dullahan
description: Headless Rider - Irish 'Dubhlachan' (from dubh 'black'). Also called 'Colainn Gan Cheann' (body without head). NOT related to the Banshee (her lineage): the Dullahan is a solitary death Bringer, NOT a herald. The Banshee Warnings before death, but the Dullahan Brings the death himself. No parents, no family - he's a force, not a person. Rides the 'Coiste Bodhar' (Soundless Death Coach) made from Coffins, Bones, Funerary remnants. The coach axle is Spine, wheel-spokes are thigh bones. He carries his own Severed Head under his arm as a lantern - the dead eyes glow like coals, the grin has razor's teeth. The head calls out names - wherever he Stops is where death occurs. He rides at night with Black Horse. Some versions: he rides headless horses, carries a whip made from human spine. NOT benevolent - he's 'Unseelie fairy' (malevolent). One name: 'Gan Ceann' = without head. Unlike the Banshee, sees Your death rather than announcing it - he is death itself, riding to collect souls

name: Duppy
description: Duppy is the Bahamian term, shared across the English-speaking Caribbean, for the spirit of a dead person. Duppies are usually malevolent and wander at night, haunting the places they knew in life, and obeah practitioners may summon them or set them on others. Bahamians take precautions against duppies, reflecting an African-descended view of the dead lingering among the living.

name: Duppy
description: Duppy is the Kittitian word for a restless ghost, from the Akan-derived vocabulary of the African diaspora. Duppies linger where they lived, especially plantations and lonely places, making noises, moving objects, and playing tricks, and can be vengeful if wronged in life. Kittitians avoid shouting a name at night lest a duppy answer, and the tall Mocko Jumbie stilt-walker wards them off.

name: Durga
description: Durga is the supreme warrior goddess of Hinduism, the invincible divine mother who rides a lion into battle against demonic forces that threaten cosmic order. Created by the combined energies of the gods Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, she was granted their most powerful weapons to defeat the buffalo demon Mahishasura, who could not be killed by any man or god. Durga represents the concept of Shakti, the primordial feminine creative energy that both creates and sustains the universe. Her mythology is primarily recorded in the Devi Mahatmya, a sacred text that describes her epic nine-day battle culminating in the slaying of Mahishasura on the tenth day. She is a central figure in Shaktism and is widely worshipped across India, Bangladesh, and Nepal during the festival of Navratri

name: Dutchman
description: The Dutchman is one of the most feared jumbies in Guyanese folklore, a malevolent spirit associated with the silk cotton trees (Ceiba pentandra) known throughout the country as "Dutchman trees." These massive trees are believed to be haunted by the spirits of Dutch colonizers from the 17th and 18th centuries who were cruel to their slaves and were condemned to guard the treasures they buried beneath the roots. The legend holds that any person who climbs, cuts, or damages a silk cotton tree will suffer terrible consequences, including violent falls, broken necks, severe illness, or even death. The Dutchman jumbie is considered second only to the Ole Higue in the hierarchy of Guyanese supernatural beings and continues to be a deeply held belief in many rural communities

name: Duwende (Dwarf/Goblin)
description: Duwende are dwarf-like goblins or earth spirits in Philippine folklore, closely related to the Nuno sa Punso (dweller of the anthill). These small, mischievous beings are believed to inhabit ant hills, termite mounds, old trees, and underground places. They are generally invisible but can choose to reveal themselves to humans. Duwende come in two types: white duwende (good, helpful spirits) and black duwende (mischievous or malevolent spirits). They are known to play tricks on humans — hiding objects, leading travelers astray, or causing minor illnesses if their homes are disturbed. To appease them, Filipinos leave food offerings or ask permission ('tabi po, nuno') when passing by anthills. Despite their small stature, duwende are powerful spirits that demand respect

name: Dvärg (Swedish)
description: Dvärgar (dwarves) are master smiths and craftspeople of Norse mythology and Swedish folklore, born from the blood of the primordial giant Ymir. In the Norse creation myth, maggots from Ymir's flesh were transformed into dwarves by the gods, and they dwell underground in Svartálfheim (also called Niðavellir, the Dark Fields). Four dwarves — Austri, Vestri, Norðri, and Suðri — hold up the four corners of the sky. Dwarves are renowned across the Nine Worlds for their unparalleled skill in metallurgy and magic, having forged the most powerful artifacts in Norse myth: Thor's hammer Mjölnir, Odin's spear Gungnir, Freyr's ship Skíðblaðnir, the golden boar Gullinbursti, and the multiplying ring Draupnir. In later Swedish folk belief, dvärgar merged with the broader category of underjordiska (underground dwellers), described as small, quiet people living under boulders or near ancient burial mounds, deeply connected to nature and highly territorial. They are described as pitch-black in appearance and turn to stone if exposed to daylight

name: Dwarf
description: Dwarfs (cannibal dwarfs) are small but dangerous humanoid beings in Arapaho folklore. In the Nihancan story, a small dwarf armed with a bow and arrow was mocked by Nihancan the trickster for his small size and tiny weapon. The dwarf challenged Nihancan to shoot his bow—when Nihancan tried, he found it impossibly heavy. The dwarf then shot an arrow with incredible power, splitting a boulder in half. Nihancan was humbled, learning that size does not determine power. The Arapaho tradition includes stories of cannibal dwarfs who are powerful and dangerous despite their small stature

name: Dwarf
description: Dwarfs (cannibal dwarfs) are small but dangerous humanoid beings in Arapaho folklore. In the Nihancan story, a small dwarf armed with a bow and arrow was mocked by Nihancan the trickster for his small size and tiny weapon. The dwarf challenged Nihancan to shoot his bow—when Nihancan tried, he found it impossibly heavy. The dwarf then shot an arrow with incredible power, splitting a boulder in half. Nihancan was humbled, learning that size does not determine power. The Arapaho tradition includes stories of cannibal dwarfs who are powerful and dangerous despite their small stature In Unknown folklore, this figure is known among the European people.

name: Dwarf (Dvergr)
description: The Dvergr, or Norse dwarf, is a master craftsman and smith from the underground realm of Svartalfheim or Nidavellir in Norse mythology. These ancient beings were originally maggots that emerged from the decaying flesh of the primordial giant Ymir, later transformed by the gods into humanoid form with great intelligence and skill. Dwarves are renowned across the nine realms for their unparalleled metalwork and magical craftsmanship, having forged the most powerful artifacts in Norse myth including Thor hammer Mjolnir, Odin spear Gungnir, the golden boar Gullinbursti, the magical ring Draupnir, and Freyr ship Skidbladnir. They are associated with the earth, rocks, caves, and underground forges, and are known for their wisdom, greed, and cunning nature

name: Dwen
description: The Dwen is a haunting figure in Saint Lucian folklore — the spirit of a child who died before baptism, condemned to wander the earth. Called Dwen in Saint Lucia (Douen in Trinidad and Dwenn in Grenada), these entities are characterized by backward-facing feet with heels to the front and knees also reversed. They have no faces — only a smooth surface where features should be, except for a small mouth to speak with. They wear large floppy straw hats to hide their facelessness. The Dwen is said to wait near forest edges and call to children by name, mimicking a parent's voice, trying to lure them into the woods. In Saint Lucian tradition, the Dwen is sometimes associated with Papa Bois and is considered a protector of the natural world. The legend reflects the historical importance of baptism in Saint Lucian society — dying unbaptized meant eternal restlessness

name: Dwenn
description: The douen (dwen) is a spirit of Grenadian and wider Trinidadian folklore: the soul of a child who died unbaptized, appearing as a faceless child under a wide straw hat, with feet turned backwards. It lures living children into the forest by calling or asking for help, and its reversed footprints make it impossible to track.

name: Dybbuk
description: A dybbuk is a malicious possessing spirit in Jewish folklore, believed to be the disembodied soul of a dead person that wanders restlessly due to its former sins and unresolved earthly attachments. The name comes from the Hebrew word "davak," meaning "to cling" or "to cleave," describing how the spirit clings to and inhabits the body of a living person. Belief in dybbuks was especially prevalent in 16th and 17th century Eastern Europe among Ashkenazi Jewish communities, and the concept draws from Kabbalistic teachings about reincarnation and the journey of the soul. A dybbuk possession is typically non-consensual, involves a male spirit entering a female host, and causes a range of physical and mental afflictions that require a formal exorcism ritual to expel

name: Dze-temi
description: Dze-temi is a guardian spirit from Georgian folklore that protects cattle and sheep, watching over flocks in the high mountain pastures of the Caucasus. This pastoral deity is deeply connected to the traditional Georgian way of life, where livestock herding has been a central occupation for thousands of years. Dze-temi is believed to appear either as a gigantic ram with golden fleece or as an old shepherd with a crook, testing the diligence and care of shepherds who tend their flocks in the remote alpine meadows. The spirit demands respect and occasional offerings of bread and salt in exchange for its protection, and it will drive away wolves, thieves, and other threats that endanger the livestock under its watchful gaze

name: Dzudzerume
description: Dzudzerume is a powerful witch from Georgian folklore, a shapeshifting female practitioner of dark magic who lives in remote mountain villages and wields formidable supernatural abilities. Unlike the typical European witch figure, Dzudzerume is deeply rooted in the unique mythology of the Caucasus region, combining elements of pre-Christian pagan beliefs with later folk traditions. She is known to ride bulls or wolves through the night sky, attending secret gatherings of witches on Mount Kazbek, one of Georgia highest peaks. The Dzudzerume specializes in love spells, curses, and causing illness, and she can be identified by her lack of a shadow, a common trait among supernatural beings in many folk traditions

name: Dzunukwa Cannibal Woman Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Dzunukwa (Dzunuk'wa) is the Cannibal Woman of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a giant wild woman of the deep woods with black tangled hair, a puckered mouth, and a huge cedar-bark basket on her back. She carries off children to eat them but is clumsy and easily outwitted, and her masked figure is a dramatic presence of the winter ceremonial.

name: Dâyuni'Sï
description: Dâyuni'sï, 'Beaver's Grandchild,' is the water-beetle who plays the decisive role in the Cherokee creation story of how the world was made. When all was water, the animals sent divers down to find earth; each failed until Dâyuni'sï dove to the bottom and returned with a little mud, which spread and grew into the land.

name: Déélgééd (Horned Monster)
description: Déélgééd is the Horned Monster, a fearsome creature in Navajo tradition that lived in the water and had one horn. After defeating Yé'iitsoh, the Hero Twins tracked this monster to its lair. Monster Slayer shot the creature multiple times; its blood gushed out and it plunged into the ocean. As it floated on the surface, both twins shot arrows into it until it was dead. The head of Déélgééd floated to shore where people later used its horn for ceremonies. This victory was one of several that clear

name: Dödning
description: Dödning (Swedish 'dead one') is a revenant returning from the grave between midnight and dawn. Appears as at death but darker, grave-dirtied, glowing/missing eyes. Returns for unfinished business, grudges, improper burial; spreads illness by touch. Knocks, calls names, attacks. Repelled by holy symbols, iron, sunlight, decapitation.

name: Dønnamannen
description: Dønnamannen ('the Man of Dønna') is a troll of Norwegian legend tied to the reclining rock formation on the island of Dønna in Nordland. The story connects him to the Seven Sisters, the famous mountain range on nearby Alstenøya: as a troll he is said to have been turned to stone, and his rock silhouette lies on its back with hands folded across its chest, visible from the sea.

name: Džambas
description: Džambas is a fierce demon from Macedonian folklore, a terrifying creature that haunts the dark forests of North Macedonia armed with iron teeth and copper claws. This malevolent entity is one of the lesser-known but deeply feared figures in Slavic Balkan mythology, representing the dangers that lurk in the wilderness beyond the safety of human settlements. The Džambas specifically targets lone travelers who venture into its forest domain, attacking with brutal ferocity and showing no mercy to its victims. According to traditional beliefs, this demon is vulnerable to iron, a common weakness among supernatural beings in Slavic folklore, and those who must travel through haunted forests carry iron tools or weapons for protection

name: Džin
description: Džin is the Bosnian variant of the jinn, supernatural beings in Islamic and pre-Islamic folklore that were created from smokeless fire and inhabit a parallel world alongside humans. In Bosnian tradition, heavily influenced by Ottoman-era Islamic culture, džins are powerful spirits that live in ruins, caves, abandoned wells, and other wild, desolate places. Unlike Western ghosts, džins are not spirits of the dead but distinct created beings with their own societies, hierarchies, and free will. They can be either Muslim or non-Muslim, good or evil, and are known to interact with humans in various ways, sometimes offering help, sometimes causing harm. Džins can be trapped in bottles or bound to service through magical means, a concept that spread into Western folklore

name: Each-Uisge
description: The Each-Uisge (Gaelic 'water horse') is the deadliest water horse of Scottish and Irish folklore, inhabiting sea lochs and freshwater lochs. It shape-shifts into a fine horse, pony, handsome man, or enormous bird (boobrie). If mounted, the rider's skin adheres and the each-uisge drags them to the deepest water, devouring the whole body except the liver.

name: Eagentci
description: Eagentci, meaning "ancient-bodied one" or "old woman" in the Seneca language, is the earth mother and primordial sky woman of Iroquois and Seneca mythology. Also known as Atahensic or Sky Woman, she is the central female creative force who fell from the Sky World through a hole created when she uprooted a sacred tree. As she fell, birds caught her and gently lowered her onto the back of a giant turtle that emerged from the cosmic waters, forming what became Turtle Island (North America). She is the grandmother of the twin gods Hahgwehdiyu (Sapling, the good creator) and Hahgwehdaetgah (Flint, the evil destroyer), and her body became the source of the earth plants that sustain humanity. She is associated with marriage, childbirth, and the cycle of life

name: Eagle Ancestor-Spirit of Ute
description: The Eagle Ancestor-Spirit is a sacred guardian figure in Ute mythology, representing the deep spiritual connection between the Ute people of the Great Basin and Rocky Mountains region and the natural world around them. As an ancestor spirit taking the form of an eagle, this powerful being is the guardian of remote springs and water sources in the mountainous Ute homeland, protecting these vital water supplies that sustain life in the arid landscape. The eagle is one of the most significant animal spirits in Ute tradition, symbolizing wisdom, courage, and connection to the creator Sinawav. Ute oral tradition tells of this spirit teaching humans to respect nature and live in harmony with the land through visions, dreams, and ceremonial encounters in the high country

name: Eagle Animal-Spirit of Cree
description: The Eagle Animal-Spirit holds a position of profound importance in Cree mythology as the sacred guardian of remote cliff faces and high rocky outcrops across the traditional Cree territories of what is now Canada. In Cree spiritual tradition, the eagle is the most revered of all birds, serving as a messenger between humans and the Great Spirit (Kise Manito). The Eagle Animal-Spirit is specifically tasked with protecting cliff habitats and teaching humans the wisdom of living in balance with nature. It appears to Cree hunters, shamans, and vision seekers, offering guidance and protection. The eagle is one of the primary animal spirits invoked during ceremonial practices including shaking tent ceremonies, sweat lodges, and vision quests

name: Eagle Animal-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: The Eagle Animal-Spirit is a revered figure in Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka-wakw) mythology of the Pacific Northwest Coast, serving as a guardian of hills and elevated places within the traditional territories of Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland of British Columbia. In Kwakiutl culture, the eagle is one of the four primary clans, alongside the Killer Whale, Raven, and Wolf, and holds significant ceremonial importance. Eagles are believed to be powerful ancestral spirits that can transform between human and animal forms, appearing in the intricate transformation masks used during potlatch ceremonies. The Eagle Animal-Spirit is associated with the Sky World, spiritual vision, and inherited family crest privileges that are passed down through generations within specific numaym (lineage groups)

name: Eagle Animal-Spirit of Lakota
description: The Eagle Animal-Spirit, known as Waŋblí in the Lakota language, is one of the most sacred beings in Lakota mythology and spirituality of the Great Plains. The eagle is considered the strongest and bravest of all creatures, serving as the primary messenger between humans and Wakan Tanka, the Great Spirit or Great Mystery that pervades all of creation. In Lakota tradition, eagle feathers are given as the highest honor, representing bravery, wisdom, and spiritual attainment. The Waŋblí carries prayers from the earth up to Wakan Tanka on its powerful wings, and its feathers adorn the sacred pipe that is central to Lakota religious practice. The eagle spirit teaches courage, vision, and connection to the divine

name: Eagle Animal-Spirit of Ute
description: The eagle holds a dominant sacred position in Ute cosmology, considered the most powerful animal spirit with the ability to cure afflictions and carry prayers to the Creator. Among the Ute people, eagle feathers are used in ceremonies such as the Bear Dance, Sun Dance, and Worship Dance to fan participants and brush away spiritual problems. The eagle is believed to have more power than any other creature, capable of seeing and hearing things that other beings cannot, making it the ultimate messenger between the human world and the divine

name: Eagle Deity (Khmer)
description: In Khmer mythology, the eagle deity is known as Garuda (Krŭd in Khmer), a divine being that is half-man and half-bird, serving as both a protective guardian and a symbol of royal power. Garuda's roots stretch back to Hindu epics where he hatches after centuries in an egg to liberate his mother from captivity. Khmer kings adopted Garuda as a symbol of sovereignty, adorning thrones and ceremonial regalia with his image. Across Cambodia's sacred landscape, Garuda appears on lintels and pediments at Angkor Wat, Preah Khan, and other temples, locked in eternal battle with the serpentine Nagas

name: Eagle Deity of Kikuyu
description: Not independently attested as a deity: Kikuyu religion honors Ngai (Mwene Nyaga), the supreme god of Mount Kenya, and 'Nyaga' in his name refers to the whiteness of the ostrich, not an eagle. Hawks and eagles appear in general East African omen lore, but no eagle deity is documented among the Kikuyu, and the description is a generic 'eagle as divine messenger' template.

name: Eagle Deity of Passamaquoddy
description: In Passamaquoddy mythology, the eagle is a revered bird of great spiritual significance, serving as a messenger between humans and the Creator. The Passamaquoddy people of Maine and the Maritime provinces regard the eagle as a guardian figure associated with the sky world and the upper realms. Eagles are seen as wise beings who taught humans important lessons about respect for nature and balance in life. The eagle's feathers are used in ceremonies and are considered gifts from the spirit world, carrying prayers upward and blessings downward. The eagle deity watches over the community and protects sacred spaces

name: Eagle Deity of Yoruba
description: In Yoruba mythology, the eagle is associated with the orisha (deity) Ogun and with the concept of ase (divine authority and power). The eagle's ability to soar to great heights and see with clarity makes it a symbol of vision, leadership, and spiritual insight. Among the Yoruba people of Nigeria, the eagle is considered a royal bird, associated with kingship and the authority of the oba (ruler). Eagle feathers are used in the crowns and regalia of Yoruba chiefs, signifying their connection to the divine realm and their role as intermediaries between the people and the orishas

name: Eagle Deity of Zapotec
description: In Zapotec mythology, the eagle is a powerful symbol associated with the sky, the sun, and warfare. The Zapotec civilization of Oaxaca, Mexico, regarded the eagle as a creature of great spiritual significance, often linked to their most important deity Cocijo, the lightning and rain god. Eagles were seen as messengers of the gods and guardians of the celestial realm. In Zapotec iconography, the eagle appears in ceramic art, sculpture, and architectural decoration, representing the warrior class and the nobility. The bird's association with height and vision made it a natural symbol for rulers and priests who needed to see beyond ordinary perception

name: Eagle feathers
description: In many Native American traditions, particularly among Plains and Woodland tribes, eagle feathers are considered the most sacred of ceremonial objects, embodying the spirit and power of the eagle itself. Eagle feathers are not merely decorative items but are living objects that carry prayers to the Creator, witness truth, and confer honor upon those who earn them. The feathers are used in a wide variety of ceremonies including healing rituals, dances, peace ceremonies, and vision quests. Among the Lakota, Cheyenne, and other Plains nations, eagle feathers are given as the highest honors for acts of bravery in battle or for exceptional service to the community

name: Eagle Ghost of Mi'kmaq
description: In Mi'kmaq mythology, the eagle is a powerful spirit being associated with the sky realm and the Great Spirit (Glooscap/Klu skap). The Mi'kmaq people of eastern Canada regard the eagle as a messenger and protector who carries prayers to the Creator. The eagle ghost specifically refers to the spirit of an eagle that has passed into the spirit world but continues to watch over and guide the living. In Mi'kmaq tradition, the eagle is considered the chief of the birds and is deeply respected for its wisdom, strength, and connection to the upper world. Eagle feathers and bones are used in sacred bundles and healing ceremonies

name: Eagle Ghost of Ute
description: Not independently attested as a ghost of Ute folklore. The eagle is deeply sacred to the Ute — eagle feathers carry prayer and eagle spirits are honored in ceremony — but no Ute eagle-ghost is documented. Ute traditions of the dead involve the spirits of ancestors, not a supernatural eagle revenant.

name: Eagle Giant of Mapuche
description: In Mapuche mythology of Chile, the eagle giant is a formidable sky being associated with Pillan, the powerful spirit of thunder, fire, and volcanoes. The Mapuche people regard eagles as sacred messengers of the upper world (Wenumapu), where gods, spirits, and ancestors reside. The eagle giant differs from ordinary eagles in its immense size and supernatural power, serving as a guardian of the celestial realm and a servant of the creator god Nguenechèn. In Mapuche cosmology, the eagle giant is both feared and respected for its ability to control the weather and communicate the will of the gods to humanity

name: Eagle Guardian (Zulu)
description: In Zulu-influenced traditions of Myanmar, the eagle guardian reflects the syncretism of African and Southeast Asian spiritual beliefs about raptors as divine messengers. The eagle is revered as the king of birds, a symbol of royal authority, courage, and spiritual vision. Eagle feathers are reserved for leaders and warriors, conferring the bird's power of clear sight and connection to the divine. The eagle guardian watches over communities, carries prayers to the spirit realm, and protects against evil forces. Its image appears in ceremonial regalia and is invoked during important rituals and community gatherings

name: Eagle Guardian (Zulu)
description: Eagle Guardian (Zulu) is a guardian from Guatemala mythology. The eagle is revered as the king of birds, a symbol of royal authority, courage, and spiritual vision. Eagle feathers are reserved for leaders and warriors, conferring the bird's power of clear sight and connection to the divine. The eagle guardian watches over communities, carries prayers to the spirit realm, and protects against evil forces. Its image appears in ceremonial regalia and is invoked during important rituals and community gatherings

Eagle feathers are reserved for leaders and warriors, conferring the bird's power of clear sight and connection to the divine. name: Eagle Guardian of Aymara
description: In Aymara mythology of Bolivia and the Andean highlands, the eagle is a sacred bird associated with the upper world (hanaq pacha) and the sun god Inti. The Aymara people regard the eagle as a messenger of the gods, capable of flying higher than any other creature and thus closest to the divine realm. Eagles are associated with Mallku, the Andean concept of spiritual authority and ancestral power, and their feathers are used in ceremonies by amautas (spiritual leaders). The eagle guardian watches over the highland communities from its nests on inaccessible cliff faces and mountain peaks

name: Eagle Guardian of Quechua
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Quechua tradition. In Quechua cosmology the sacred bird of the upper world, messenger to Inti and the apus, is the condor (kuntur), not an eagle, and no eagle guardian-spirit is recorded. Eagles do appear among the sacred animals of Aymara Isluga, but the entry transfers that role to Quechua Peru without evidence.

name: Eagle Nature-Spirit of Ute
description: In Ute cosmology, the eagle nature-spirit is a powerful embodiment of the natural world's sacred intelligence, representing the highest spiritual authority among the animal beings. The Ute people believe that all living things possess supernatural power, and the eagle sits at the apex of this spiritual hierarchy. The eagle nature-spirit is not merely a supernatural bird but the living embodiment of the sky's power manifest in the natural world. It governs the relationship between the Ute people and their mountain environment, serving as both a teacher and a guardian of the ecological balance that sustains life in the Colorado Plateau

name: Eagle Spirit
description: Eagle Spirit is a powerful guardian and teacher in Crow mythology. In the Bones Together story, the Eagle blessed the human companion with the power to transform into a feather, which allowed him to evade the monster's charges and defeat Bones Together. Eagles are considered sacred birds in Crow culture, associated with the sky, the sun, and divine power. Eagle feathers are used in ceremonies and headdresses as symbols of spiritual authority. Eagle Spirit guides warriors and vision seekers, granting them the power of keen sight and spiritual elevation

name: Eagle Spirit (Guarani)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. This Paraguay variant repeats the misassigned Aztec founding myth of Tenochtitlan and adds the unfounded claim of 'Guarani-influenced traditions of Mexico' exchanging eagle beliefs; no Guarani eagle spirit is documented in Paraguay. The entry is a Mesoamerican legend mislabeled as Guarani.

name: Eagle Spirit (Guarani)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Guarani tradition. The input's description is wholly about the Aztec founding myth of Tenochtitlan (the eagle on a cactus), which belongs to Mesoamerica, not to Guarani-speaking Brazil. No source documents an eagle spirit among the Guarani, and the conflation of Guarani with Mexican eagle symbolism is unfounded.

name: Eagle Spirit (Guarani)
description: The eagle is a defining symbol of Mexican tradition, above all in the Mexica founding legend of Tenochtitlan, where an eagle perched on a cactus devouring a serpent marked the city's site, and in the eagle-knight (cuauhtli) warrior order. Guarani belief belongs to South America, so the entry mismatches culture and country; the substance is the well-attested Mesoamerican eagle.

name: Eagle Spirit of Cherokee
description: In Cherokee mythology, the eagle spirit is the most sacred of all birds, revered as the messenger between the Cherokee people and the Creator (Unetlvnv/Galvladi). Among the Cherokee of the Southeastern United States, the eagle is known as Awohali and is considered the chief of all birds because it flies the highest and can see all things. The eagle spirit plays a central role in Cherokee ceremonies, particularly those related to war, healing, and community purification. The killing of an eagle was a sacred act performed only by designated Eagle-Killers during the winter season, followed by elaborate rituals of apology and thanksgiving to appease the eagle's spirit

name: Eagle Spirit of Cree
description: In Cree tradition the eagle is among the most sacred beings: its feathers are a strong spiritual power, gifted to young men in ceremony with tobacco and prayer, and the eagle carries the people's prayers up to the Creator. Eagle whistles are sung with the breath of the Creator during Cree drum ceremonies, honoring the eagle as a spirit of strength and vision.

name: Eagle Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Muisca tradition. The Temple of the Sun at Sogamoso and the deities Sué and Chía are genuine elements of Muisca cosmology, but no source records an 'Eagle Spirit' presiding over that sanctuary or serving as a celestial messenger. The entry grafts a generic Andean eagle figure onto documented Muisca institutions.

name: Eagle Spirit of Zapotec
description: The Eagle Spirit from Zapotec tradition is a sacred guardian of mountain springs and water sources across the Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, Mexico. In Zapotec cosmology, this spirit presides over the life-giving waters that flow from the highlands down to the valleys where maize grows. The Zapotec people, descendants of the ancient civilization that built Monte Albán, revere this spirit as one of the nahuales (animal spirit companions) that protect the natural balance of the region. It is particularly associated with the mountain springs used in purification ceremonies

name: Eagle Trickster (Malagasy)
description: Not independently attested: no eagle trickster is recorded in Malagasy folklore, and the description invents a diaspora tradition of the eagle watching over the North American Great Lakes, which has no documented basis.

name: Eagle Trickster (Malagasy)
description: Not independently attested as a trickster of Malagasy folklore. In Malagasy tradition the eagle (voromahery) is a royal messenger of God, not a trickster; Malagasy trickster roles belong to the hare or the tortoise. The 'USA' framing also signals a fabricated diaspora entry with no documented source.

name: Eagle Trickster of Blackfoot
description: The Eagle Trickster from Blackfoot (Niitsitapi) tradition in the Canadian plains is a complex spirit entity that governs the ocean waters and the seasonal cycles affecting both the Pacific coast and inland waterways. In Canadian Blackfoot oral traditions, this being is closely associated with Napi, the creator-trickster, who transforms into an eagle to observe human activities from above. It plays a vital role in teaching the Blackfoot people about the interconnectedness of all waters, from the Rocky Mountain streams to the Pacific Ocean

name: Eagle Trickster of Blackfoot
description: The Eagle Trickster from Blackfoot (Niitsitapi) tradition in the Canadian plains is a complex spirit entity that governs the ocean waters and the seasonal cycles affecting both the Pacific coast and inland waterways. In Canadian Blackfoot oral traditions, this being is closely associated with Napi, the creator-trickster, who transforms into an eagle to observe human activities from above. It plays a vital role in teaching the Blackfoot people about the interconnectedness of all waters, from the Rocky Mountain streams to the Pacific Ocean In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.

name: Eagle Trickster of Kazakh
description: The Eagle Trickster from Kazakh tradition is a revered spirit that guards the mountain valleys and highland pastures of the Tien Shan and Altai mountains. In Kazakh folklore, this being is deeply connected to the ancient tradition of golden eagle falconry (bürkütchilik), which has been practiced by Kazakh nomads for thousands of years. The spirit tests the worthiness of hunters and teaches the sacred bond between humans and eagles. It is said to have taught the first Kazakh falconer how to train eagles for hunting

name: Eagle Trickster of Uzbek
description: The Eagle Trickster from Uzbek tradition is a guardian spirit of the Pamir and Tian Shan mountain ranges that form the backbone of Uzbekistan's landscape. In Uzbek folklore, this sky spirit oversees the remote mountain passes and high-altitude pastures where shepherds graze their flocks. It is associated with both creation and destruction, as it controls avalanches and rockfalls that reshape the mountains. Elders say that the Eagle Trickster was once a human shaman who was transformed into an eagle by the spirits of the mountains for his wisdom and cunning

name: Eagle Water-Spirit of Hopi
description: The Eagle Water-Spirit from Hopi tradition is a sacred being that governs the marshlands and springs on the Hopi mesas of northeastern Arizona. In Hopi cosmology, this spirit bridges the realm of the sky (eagle) and the realm of water (essential for life in the arid Southwest). It is invoked during rain ceremonies and the Niman (Home Dance) kachina ceremony, where eagle feathers are used to draw moisture from the clouds. The Hopi believe this spirit controls the precious water sources that allow their dryland farming to succeed

name: Eagle Water-Spirit of Mapuche
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Mapuche tradition. Mapuche cosmology includes the ngen, spirits that own natural places, and water spirits associated with rivers and lakes, but no source describes an eagle owning the waters, controlling fish spawning, or assisting machi healing rituals. The entry composes a hybrid being from unrelated Mapuche elements.

name: Eahpáraš
description: Eahpáraš is a restless, wandering spirit in Sami folklore — the soul of someone who died improperly, particularly children who died before being named, baptized, or properly integrated into the community. These spirits cannot transition to Jábmiidaibmu (the underworld) and are condemned to wander the earth, causing trouble for the living. They can cause illness, misfortune, or simply wail in the wilderness. The most tragic cases are murdered children whose spirits return to haunt their parents. The only remedy is to perform proper burial rites, even long after death, to allow the soul to find peace. The concept reflects the Sami belief that a proper death includes not only physical death but also proper social and spiritual transition. An eahpáraš is not inherently evil but is displaced and miserable — its mischief stems from its unresolved state. The phenomenon is extensively documented in Emilie Demant Hatt's By the Fire (1922) collection of Sami stories

name: Earth Mother (Blackfoot)
description: Earth Mother (Komatoskia) in Blackfoot (Niitsitapi) tradition is the primordial female deity who created the land, plants, and all living things. She is the wife of the Sun (Natosi) and mother of the Morning Star. In Blackfoot creation stories, Earth Mother molded the mountains and valleys from her own flesh and covered them with grass and forests. She taught the first women how to gather roots, prepare hides, and perform the sacred ceremonies that maintain the balance between humans and nature. She represents fertility, nourishment, and the cyclical renewal of life

name: Earth Spirit
description: Earth Spirit is a powerful nature spirit in Arapaho mythology. In the story of How Medicine Man Resurrected Buffalo, when all buffalo had disappeared during a terrible famine and the Arapaho were starving, a powerful medicine man went into the mountains to seek a vision. After four days of fasting, the spirit of the Earth came to him and told him the buffalo had gone underground because the people had been wasteful. Following the Earth spirit's instructions, the medicine man gathered the tribe and opened a passage to the underground buffalo world, releasing the buffalo to save the people. The Earth spirit also taught them never to waste the buffalo's gift

name: Ebigane
description: Ebigane is a predatory hybrid monster from Equatorial Guinean (various groups) folklore. It haunts dense rainforests, combining stealth and versatile attacks. Described as a composite earth-creature, it represents primal wilderness dangers. Fire is its weakness. The legend encodes wisdom about natural and spiritual worlds.

name: Egbe
description: Egbe is the collective spirit of unborn children and the celestial society of souls in Yoruba cosmology. Before birth, every person belongs to a spiritual "club" or society called Egbe in the spirit world (Orun). Members of Egbe make a covenant to support each other in the earthly realm. Those who are born into the world carry their Egbe connection as a spiritual bond. Egbe is also known as the "Heavenly Society" or "Spiritual Playmates." People who feel a strong connection to their Egbe can communicate with them through offerings and prayers. Egbe represents the cosmic community of souls that transcends the boundary between the spirit world and the physical world

name: Egbere
description: Egbere are malevolent nocturnal goblins in Yoruba (not Igbo) folklore. Short-statured forest/grave dwellers who emerge at midnight weeping and riding sheep. They guard a mat of wealth; seizing it grants riches, though their tears are feigned. Documented by Crowther (1852) and Taylor (1898) in Yoruba accounts.

name: Egungun
description: Egungun are the collective spirits of the ancestors in Yoruba religion, manifested through masked masquerades in Nigeria and the African diaspora. During egungun festivals, costumed performers channel ancestral presence, offering blessings, guidance, and judgment to the living. The tradition preserves genealogical memory and honors the continuing role of the dead in community life.

name: Eigigu
description: Eigigu, 'the moon bride,' is the luminous woman of Nauruan mythology who dwells on the moon, governing its cycles and the tides of the surrounding lagoon. Said to weave baskets of light, she appears radiant in the full moon and is regarded as a benevolent, rhythmic figure in Nauruan cosmology, embodying feminine divinity and the cyclical nature of time.

name: Eintal
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Norwegian water-spirit named 'eintal' appears in folklore collections, and the proposed ein plus tal ('lone song') etymology is invented. The genuine lake-dwelling musician who enchants listeners with fiddle music is the nokken, and Telemark accounts of such a being belong to that figure.

name: Ekong
description: Ekong is a colossal serpent guardian in Fang mythology (Equatorial Guinea). It inhabits deep rivers and underwater caverns, manipulating water and using hypnosis to protect sacred places. Sacred rhythms known to Fang elders can counter it. Ekong symbolizes the boundary between physical and spiritual worlds and reinforces respect for water sources.

name: El Aro
description: El Aro is a terrifying phantom from Honduran folklore, described as a misty, wheel-shaped apparition that roams the countryside at night. Its name derives from the Spanish word for 'hoop' or 'ring,' referencing its distinctive shape. According to legends from the departments of Comayagua and Francisco Morazán, El Aro is a tormented spirit that appears to solitary travelers on dark roads. Some versions say it is the soul of a man who committed terrible sins, condemned to roll endlessly through the night until it frightens enough sinners to repentance. Parents use the tale to keep children from wandering after dark

name: El Añá
description: El Añá is a legendary lake serpent from the folklore of the Andean lakes region of Argentina, particularly in the provinces of Neuquén and Río Negro. The name derives from Mapuche and Guarani mythologies, where it refers to malevolent water spirits. Unlike the more famous Nahuelito, El Añá is described as a hybrid creature combining serpentine and cervine features. Indigenous Mapuche and Tehuelche peoples told stories of this creature to explain disappearances near deep, cold lakes, warning children and careless shepherds away from treacherous shorelines where the water drops suddenly into abyssal depths

name: El Boyo
description: El Boyo is a malevolent water spirit from Nicaraguan folklore, specifically associated with Lake Nicaragua (Cocibolca) and the surrounding rivers. Described as the ghost of a drowned man, it rises from the depths to drag the living down to join it in the watery abyss. The legend is particularly strong in the cities of Granada and Rivas, where lake drownings were historically common. The tale served as a cautionary story to warn children and young people about the dangers of swimming alone or at night in the lake's unpredictable currents and the bull sharks that inhabit its waters

name: El Cadejo
description: El Cadejo is a supernatural dog-shaped spirit from Central American folklore, well-known in Panama. Unlike the dual white/good and black/evil Cadejos of other Central American countries, Panama's Cadejo is a single black creature. It is described as a large black dog with glowing red eyes, dragging heavy chains. Though monstrous in appearance, the Panamanian Cadejo is generally harmless and acts as a spectral companion on lonely roads. The legends trace back to Maya mythology and Nahua shamanistic traditions where dogs served as companions to the dead on their journey to the afterlife. The Cadejo represents the ancient belief that every human possesses a spiritual animal companion

description: El Cadejo is a spirit from Panama mythology. Unlike the dual white/good and black/evil Cadejos of other Central American countries, Panama's Cadejo is a single black creature. It is described as a large black dog with glowing red eyes, dragging heavy chains. Though monstrous in appearance, the Panamanian Cadejo is generally harmless and acts as a spectral companion on lonely roads. The Cadejo represents the ancient belief that every human possesses a spiritual animal companion
