The Cadejo represents the ancient belief that every human possesses a spiritual animal companion In Panama folklore, this figure is known among the Panamanian (Mixed) people.

name: El Cao
description: El Cao is a terrifying supernatural entity from Colombian folklore, described as a large black dog with occult powers that appears at crossroads during the darkest hours of the night. The legend is widespread across the Colombian departments of Boyacá, Cundinamarca, and Antioquia, where rural communities tell of this creature as a witch (bruja) who has transformed into animal form to carry out evil deeds. Crossroads have special significance in Colombian folk magic as places where pacts with the devil are made, and El Cao is believed to be either a demon sent to claim souls or a transformed witch on a malevolent errand

name: El Carbonero
description: Not independently attested as a ghost of Colombian folklore. No source records an 'El Carbonero' (charcoal burner) ghost haunting Boyacá, Santander or Cundinamarca. The name recurs in genuine traditions elsewhere — the Basque tale of El Carbonero and Death (Herio) and a Guatemalan figure linked to the Sombrerón legend — but neither is Colombian, and the 'furnace death' narrative is unrecorded.

name: El Chupacabra
description: El Chupacabra (Unknown). is a cryptid. El Chupacabra (Spanish for "goat-sucker") is a legendary cryptid first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995. Described as a reptile-like creature with spines along its back, it allegedly attacks livestock . Source: Contemporary Latin American folklore; news reports (1995–present)

name: El Coco
description: El Coco (also known as El Cuco) is the bogeyman figure of the Spanish-speaking world, a ghost-like monster used for centuries to frighten children into good behavior. Originating in 17th-century Iberia and brought to the Americas through Spanish colonization, El Coco is described as a shapeless, shadowy figure with glowing red eyes that hides in closets, under beds, or in dark corners. The classic Spanish lullaby warns: 'Duérmete niño, duérmete ya... Que viene el Coco y te comerá' (Sleep child, sleep now... Or the Coco will come and eat you). In the Mexican-American communities of the US Southwest, El Coco is sometimes called the 'Coco Man' and is described as a hunchbacked figure who carries a sack to collect misbehaving children. Some versions depict him as a hairy monster, while others as a shapeshifter who takes the form of any dark shadow. Unlike many Hispanic folklore figures that have narrative stories, El Coco is primarily a disciplinary tool invoked through lullabies and warnings rather than tales

name: El Cuchubo
description: El Cuchubo is a fearsome two-headed giant from Panamanian folklore, said to dwell in the dense jungles of the Darién Gap and the remote forests of the Azuero Peninsula. This monstrous ogre is one of several giant legends found across Panama, representing the dangers that lurk in the unexplored wilderness. According to tales passed down through generations of indigenous and rural communities, El Cuchubo is a territorial being that devours anyone who enters its domain without permission. The legend likely originated from the Ngäbe, Buglé, and Guna peoples as a cautionary tale about respecting the boundaries of the forest

name: El Cucuy
description: El Cucuy is a distinct Mexican and Mexican-American variant of the bogeyman legend, particularly prevalent among Chicano families in the US Southwest. Unlike the more generic El Coco, El Cucuy is specifically described as a small, hairy, goblin-like creature who lives under children's beds or in dark closets, waiting to grab ankles or drag away children who refuse to sleep. Some accounts describe him with red or yellow eyes, long claws, and a mischievous grin. The legend serves dual purposes: as a parenting tool to enforce bedtime and as a cultural rite of passage where children learn to face their fears. In recent decades, El Cucuy has been reimagined in Chicano literature and art as a symbol of the fears faced by immigrant children — the unknown terrors of a new country, border crossing, and cultural displacement. Writers like Rudolfo Anaya have explored the Cucuy as a metaphor for the shadow side of the American Dream. Unlike the Iberian El Coco which is more formless, El Cucuy has a distinctly goblin-like personality and physical form

name: El Cuellado
description: El Cuellado (The Headless One) is a terrifying phantom from Panamanian folklore, said to appear on lonely roads at night as a headless rider on a black horse. The legend is particularly strong in the rural interior of Panama, in regions like Los Santos, Herrera, and Veraguas, where it is told around campfires to warn against staying out after dark. Unlike the European headless horseman legend popularized by Washington Irving, the Panamanian El Cuellado carries its own severed head rather than a jack-o-lantern. It is believed to be the tormented soul of a man who was executed by beheading during the colonial era for crimes he did not commit

name: El Duende
description: A SMALL, GNOMELIKE CREATURE from Spanish and Latin American folklore with a prominent place in Mexican-American oral tradition of the US Southwest. Described as a tiny old man or child-like figure wearing a large hat and carrying a walking stick, El Duende lives in forests, caves, abandoned buildings, and rural areas. His most distinctive feature is his backward feet, making it easy to identify his tracks but difficult to follow him. He is known for playing tricks on humans — stealing food, hiding objects, tangling hair, leading travelers in circles through the woods, and making strange noises at night. In more dangerous versions, El Duende tries to capture children who wander away from their parents, keeping them as his own. In the curanderismo tradition, encounters with duendes are believed to cause illness, particularly susto (fright sickness), which requires a limpieza (spiritual cleansing) performed by a curandero. Among Hispanic families in the Southwest, stories of El Duende serve to keep children close to home and explain the mysterious sounds and occurrences of rural life. The duende can be helpful if treated with respect — offering food or tobacco may earn his favor

name: El Duende del Tabaco
description: El Duende del Tabaco (The Tobacco Goblin) is a mischievous spirit from Cuban folklore that haunts the tobacco curing houses and drying barns of Pinar del Río, the heart of Cuba's finest tobacco region. In Cuban rural tradition, this duende is a small, elf-like being that both protects and torments tobacco workers. It is said to have existed since the time of the Taíno people, who believed tobacco was a sacred plant with its own protective spirit. The duende is particularly active during the curing season when the precious leaves hang drying in the barns

name: El Jem
description: No scholarly or traditional source documents a multi-headed serpent named 'El Jem' in Tunisian folklore. The entry traces to a single user-generated language-learning wiki page that echoes the input text verbatim. El Jem is the Tunisian town famous for its Roman amphitheater; the serpent is an invented figure, though Tunisian tradition does preserve serpent and jinn lore under other names.

name: El Jinete Sin Cabeza
description: El Jinete Sin Cabeza (The Headless Horseman) is a Hispanic variant of the headless horseman legend from the Rio Grande Valley and northern Mexico. Unlike the more famous Ichabod Crane version, this specter is specifically rooted in the borderlands' history of conflict. He is said to be the ghost of a Spanish conquistador or Mexican rancher who lost his head in battle — either during the Mexican War of Independence or the Mexican-American War. He rides a black horse through the moonlit mesquite at midnight, carrying his severed head under his arm. His appearance is a fearsome omen: to see him foretells death, war, or disaster. If you encounter him, you must not look into the eyes of his severed head, or you will be doomed to ride beside him forever. Some Chicano versions connect the legend to specific historical events like the Battle of the Alamo or the signing of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, making the supernatural figure a symbol of Mexican dispossession and the violent history of the border

name: El Mayongue
description: El Mayongue is a dangerous water spirit from Dominican Republic folklore, said to inhabit rivers, streams, and watering holes throughout the island's countryside. The name derives from African Taíno and African linguistic roots, reflecting the syncretic nature of Dominican folk beliefs. This river spirit is particularly feared by children and is used by parents as a cautionary tale to keep young ones away from dangerous waters. In rural areas of the Cibao Valley and the Cordillera Central, the legend of El Mayongue remains a common warning told to prevent drownings

name: El Mothman Cubano
description: El Mothman Cubano is a cryptid from modern Cuban folklore, described as a large winged humanoid that appears before significant disasters and tragic events. The legend emerged in the late 20th century, drawing parallels to the famous Mothman of Point Pleasant, West Virginia, while incorporating distinctively Cuban elements. Sightings have been reported in the mountainous regions of the Sierra Maestra and the Escambray Mountains, as well as near the coast. Witnesses describe it as a harbinger that appears days or weeks before hurricanes, earthquakes, or other calamities

name: El Naddaha
description: El Naddaha ('The Caller') is a female spirit of modern Egyptian folk belief who haunts the banks of the Nile. Described as a woman who calls men to the water at night, she lures them to drown; Egyptian rural tradition treats her as a kind of female jinn, a cautionary figure of riverside danger. The legend spread widely along the Nile in the early twentieth century.

name: El Silbón
description: El Silbon, the Whistler, is a specter of the Venezuelan llanos. A tall figure in white carrying his murdered father's bones in a sack, he whistles a tune that, if it sounds close, means he is far away and vice versa. Cursed by his grandfather for parricide, he stalks drunkards and womanizers and can be warded off by barking dogs, chili peppers, or a whip.

name: El Silbón
description: El Silbon, the Whistler, is a specter of the Venezuelan and Colombian llanos, wrongly placed here in Mexico. A tall man in white carrying his father's bones, he whistles in a way that deceives about his distance, preys on drunkards and womanizers, and is repelled by dogs, chili peppers, or a whip. The legend warns against parricide, family violence, and night wanderings.

name: El Sombrerón
description: El Sombrerón (The Big-Hatted One) is a legendary goblin-like figure from Guatemalan and southern Mexican folklore who is particularly prominent in Mexican-American storytelling. He is described as a small man — no taller than a child — wearing an enormous hat, a red tie, and riding a tiny horse or mule. El Sombrerón is best known for braiding the manes and tails of horses, donkeys, and mules into intricate patterns that cannot be undone. He also bothers young women with long hair and big eyes by serenading them under their windows with a tiny silver guitar, causing them to fall into a deep melancholy or sleeplessness. He puts soil in their food so they cannot eat. His enchantment can only be broken by cutting the victim's hair and having a priest bless it with holy water. In some versions, El Sombrerón stuffs his victims with food and sugar until they die of sweetness. The legend advises teenage girls to preserve traditional values and warns against vanity and nighttime wandering

name: El Tabacón
description: Not independently attested as a giant of Peruvian folklore. 'Tabacón' is a plant name (Nicotiana glauca, palán-palán) and the name of the Tabaconas–Namballe sanctuary in Cajamarca, but no source documents a tobacco giant guarding the Amazon rainforest. Tobacco's sacred role in Amazonian shamanism is real; the towering guardian spirit is invented.

name: El Tigrillo
description: El Tigrillo is a sacred jaguar spirit from Costa Rican folklore, revered as the guardian of the forests and a powerful omen of fortune. The legend is particularly strong in the mountainous regions of Costa Rica, including the Talamanca range and the Osa Peninsula, where jaguars (tigrillos) are the apex predators. In indigenous Bribri and Cabécar traditions, the jaguar is a sacred animal associated with shamans and spiritual power. The appearance of El Tigrillo is considered a significant spiritual event that can bring either great luck or terrible misfortune, depending on how the person treats the encounter

name: El Tunchi
description: El Tunchi is a nocturnal vampire-like entity from Colombian folklore, particularly in the Amazon and Orinoco regions of the country. Known among indigenous communities of the Colombian Amazon, this spirit is said to attack sleeping victims by biting their necks and draining their blood. The legend blends indigenous beliefs about restless spirits with European vampire folklore introduced during the colonial period. In some traditions, El Tunchi is the spirit of a person who died with unfinished business or who practiced black magic in life, condemned to roam the night in search of blood to sustain its unnatural existence

name: Elegua
description: Yoruba Orisha (deity) of roads, crossroads, and messenger of the gods. Known as Èṣù-Ẹlẹ́gbára (also Eleggua, Eshu, Legba). First AND Last to be invoked - all ceremonies in Santería must receive Elegua's approval before progressing. THE Gatekeeper who holds keys to past, present, and future. Opens and closes paths of destiny, controls opportunity and choice. Also a Trickster - creates chaos or favorable outcomes, embodies opposites. Can appear as Child (mischievous, playful) or OLD MAN (wise), representing different phases of fate and life. Colors: RED, Black, White. Numbers: 3 and 21. Associated with Ogun (war), Oshun (love/river), Yemoja (mother of waters). In Cuba's Santería, Brazil's Candomblé, Haiti's Vodou - remains central. Translated via slave trade. Symbolizes choice at crossroads - every decision passes through Elegua's domain

name: Elf Maidens Denmark
description: Elf Maidens Denmark (Unknown). is a elf. Elf maidens are beautiful supernatural women from Danish folklore who dance in meadows and lure young men with enchanting songs.. Source: Danish folklore — elf figures documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Elf-maidens (Elverpiger)
description: Elverpiger ('elf-maidens') are Danish female elves: beautiful but hollow-backed, dwelling in elf-mounds and misty meadows. Dance at dawn/dusk, luring humans to join; entrants may be trapped. Vulnerable to iron, church bells, morning sun. Can be benevolent or malevolent. Documented by Thiele (1819–1823) and Kristensen.

name: Elk Ancestor-Spirit (Ashanti)
description: The Elk Ancestor-Spirit from Ashanti tradition holds particular significance in Mali, where the Ashanti diaspora has maintained close ties with neighboring Mande cultures. In Mali, this spirit is associated with the valleys of the Niger River region and represents the connection between Ashanti ancestors and the broader West African spiritual landscape. The Elk Ancestor-Spirit in Mali absorbs elements from Bamanan and Dogon traditions, creating a syncretic figure that bridges multiple West African cultures

name: Elk Ancestor-Spirit (Ashanti)
description: Not independently attested. The Ashanti are a West African people (Ghana); elk (Cervus canadensis) are North American/Eurasian. Neither exists in Paraguay. The described being (mudcloth patterns, boubou robes, gris-gris) is explicitly West African, transplanted to Paraguay without basis.

name: Elk Ancestor-Spirit (Ashanti)
description: Not independently attested: elk are native to North America and Asia, not West Africa, and no elk ancestor-spirit appears in Ashanti or Malian tradition. The entry appears to confuse Akan ancestral veneration with North American animal totemism. Closest real analogue: the Ashanti abosom, tutelary nature spirits honored in lineage rites.

name: Elk Deity (Olmec)
description: The Elk Deity from Olmec tradition, as interpreted through the lens of Mapuche and Chilean folk spirituality, represents the fusion of Mesoamerican and South American indigenous beliefs. In Chile, this deity is associated with the arid regions of the Atacama Desert and the Mediterranean-climate valleys of central Chile. The blend of Olmec elk symbolism with local huemul (Andean deer) traditions creates a unique syncretic deity. This figure represents adaptation and the transfer of spiritual knowledge across the ancient trade routes that connected Mesoamerica to the Andes

name: Elk Deity (Olmec)
description: The Elk Deity from Olmec tradition, as interpreted through the lens of Mapuche and Chilean folk spirituality, represents the fusion of Mesoamerican and South American indigenous beliefs. In Chile, this deity is associated with the arid regions of the Atacama Desert and the Mediterranean-climate valleys of central Chile. The blend of Olmec elk symbolism with local huemul (Andean deer) traditions creates a unique syncretic deity. This figure represents adaptation and the transfer of spiritual knowledge across the ancient trade routes that connected Mesoamerica to the Andes In Chile folklore, this figure is known among the Chile people.

name: Elk Guardian (Tupi)
description: The Elk Guardian from Tupi tradition, as preserved in Mexican indigenous communities, represents the blend of Brazilian Tupi water guardianship with Mexican lake traditions such as those of Lake Texcoco and the Xochimilco canals. This spirit adapted from the Amazonian wetlands to the highland lakes of central Mexico through the movement of peoples and the exchange of spiritual knowledge along ancient trade routes. It guards the remaining freshwater lakes and chinampas (floating gardens) that are vital to traditional Mexican agriculture

name: Elk Guardian (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested in Botswana tradition. Elk (Cervus canadensis) are not native to Africa; snip the Tupi are Indigenous peoples of Brazil. The description plagiarizes a Mexican Tupi water-elk guardian of Lake Texcoco/chinampas and misattributes it to Botswana. Fabricated cross-continental mashup.

name: Elk Guardian (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested as an elk guardian in Tupi folklore, and wrongly tagged as Mexican. The Tupi are a Brazilian/Paraguayan indigenous people; their genuine forest guardian is Curupira, a red-haired, backward-footed being who protects the forest and punishes hunters. Elk do not occur in South America, and no Tupi source records a lake-guarding elk. The record is a cross-continental mashup.

name: Elk Nature-Spirit (Burmese)
description: In Burmese nat worship, the spirit world is divided into sky spirits (akathaso), tree spirits (yokkaso), and earth guardians (bhummaso). An elk nature-spirit belongs to the earth guardians, overseeing mountain forests and the creatures within them. Unlike the 37 Great Nats recognized in official Burmese spirit pantheon, this is a local nat specific to particular mountain regions, venerated by hill tribes and rural communities. Its power lies in maintaining the balance between human needs and the preservation of wild spaces

name: Elk Nature-Spirit (Burmese)
description: Not independently attested as an elk nature-spirit in Burmese folklore, and wrongly tagged as Guatemalan. Burma's true nature spirits are the nats — local, tutelary, and animist powers propitiated at shrines — and no nat appears as an elk guarding mountains. Elk do not range in Burma or Guatemala. The record is an evident cross-cultural mashup.

name: Elk Nature-Spirit (Burmese)
description: Not independently attested. The Burmese (Myanmar) and elk (Cervus canadensis) are absent from Chile. Chile's native cervids are huemul (Hippocamelus bisulcus) and pudú (Pudu puda). The described being (longyi, headwrap, bamboo staff, water buffalo drum) is explicitly Burmese, transplanted to Chile without basis.

name: Elk Nature-Spirit (Burmese)
description: Not attested in North American folklore. This entry blends a Burmese elk nature-spirit tradition (a bull elk spirit with a crescent-moon chest patch, guardian of herds, summonable by shamans) with a United States setting, a mismatch flagged by its own source. No USA tribe records this being; the closest North American analogues are Native American elk and deer guardian spirits.

name: Elk Spirit (Laotian)
description: In Lao animist tradition, the forests are filled with phi — spirits that inhabit natural features, animals, and places. An elk spirit is one such phi tied to the hills and bamboo forests of northern Laos, where the boundary between the human world and the spirit world is thin. The Lao believe that every mountain pass, stream, and grove of trees is watched over by a spirit guardian, and large mammals like elk are especially potent vessels of spiritual power. Villagers offer rice liquor and woven baskets to these spirits before entering deep forest, asking for safety and a successful hunt

name: Elk Trickster (Maya)
description: Elk (wapiti) are not native to Guatemala or the Maya lowlands, so this 'Elk Trickster' is a template artifact. Maya tradition does know deer and other forest animals as characters of transition in tales, and hunters observe rules of restraint in taking game. The entry should be read as a deer-forest trickster motif mislabeled with 'elk,' not an attested Maya figure.

name: Elk Trickster (Maya)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Maya or Chilean tradition. Elk (wapiti) are native to North America and never occurred in the Yucatán or Chile, so no 'elk trickster' exists in either folklore. Maya tradition does feature the deer (ceh) in dance and hunting lore, but that is not this figure, and the Chile attribution appended to the entry is meaningless.

name: Ellefolk
description: In Danish folklore, ellefolk are the hidden people of the forests and meadows, closely related to the elverkonge (elf king) tradition found in Scandinavian ballads. Unlike the noble elves of later fantasy literature, Danish ellefolk are capricious, dangerous beings who lure humans into their dancing circles on moonlit nights. They are closely associated with burial mounds and ancient stones, places where the veil between worlds is thin. Farmers plowing fields that contain elf-mounds risk illness or bad luck, and tradition dictates that such mounds must be circled with respect or left unplowed entirely

name: Eloko
description: The Eloko (singular: Eloko or Eloki) are dwarf-like, vicious ancestral spirits from the mythology of the Mongo-Nkundo people of the Democratic Republic of Congo. These forest-dwelling creatures are believed to be the restless spirits of ancestors who died with unresolved grudges, condemned to haunt the darkest, densest parts of the rainforest. Unlike benevolent spirits, the Eloko are fiercely territorial and vengeful, guarding their forest treasures including game animals and rare plants. They are known to cast spells on trespassers using enchanted bells that paralyze their victims before they attack. The Eloko embody the Mongo-Nkundo belief that the dead can return to settle scores with the living, serving as both a warning to honor one's ancestors and a caution against exploiting forest resources without proper respect. They share similarities with other Central African forest spirits such as the Sasabonsam of Ghana

name: Eloko
description: Eloko is a spirit from Central African Republic mythology. These forest-dwelling creatures are believed to be the restless spirits of ancestors who died with unresolved grudges, condemned to haunt the darkest, densest parts of the rainforest. Unlike benevolent spirits, the Eloko are fiercely territorial and vengeful, guarding their forest treasures including game animals and rare plants. They are known to cast spells on trespassers using enchanted bells that paralyze their victims before they attack. The Eloko embody the Mongo-Nkundo belief that the dead can return to settle scores with the living, serving as both a warning to honor one's ancestors and a caution against exploiting forest resources without proper respect. They share similarities with other Central African forest spirits such as the Sasabonsam of Ghana

description: Eloko is a spirit from Mongo-Nkundo mythology. name: Eloko
description: Eloko (pl. Biloko) are forest dwarfs of the Mongo-Nkundo people (DR Congo). They dwell in hollow trees in the densest rainforest, hairless with grass on their bodies, piercing eyes, snouts opening wide enough to swallow a human, and long sharp claws. They guard forest game and rare fruits, ring little bells that cast spells, and eat only human flesh.

name: Eloko
description: Eloko are forest spirits of the Mongo-Nkundo people of the Congo Basin, believed to be restless dead of ancestors who died with grudges. Fiercely territorial, they guard game and forest resources and are said to cast spells with enchanted bells that paralyze victims before they attack. They warn against neglecting ancestors and plundering the rainforest without respect.

name: Elverfolk
description: Elverfolk, also known as elver or elvefolk, are a staple of Danish ballad tradition, most famously appearing in the medieval ballad Elveskud (The Elf-Shot). These forest beings are beautiful but perilous, representing the dangerous allure of the wild in contrast to the safety of Christian villages. Danish folklore distinguishes elverfolk from the church-going human community by their lack of salvation — they are pagan spirits who will never see heaven and thus envy mortal souls. Young men who follow elverfolk into the woods often return changed, marked by an unshakeable melancholy or a fatal illness traced to an invisible elf-arrow

name: Ema
description: In Timorese animist tradition, ema are ancestor spirits who dwell in the realm of lulik — the sacred, potent force that animates the landscape and connects the living with their forebears. These spirits are guardians of the uma lulik (sacred house), the ritual heart of every Timorese clan, where heirloom objects, buffalo horns, and sacred relics are kept. The Timorese believe that ancestors continue to participate in daily life, watching over their descendants and influencing the fertility of crops, the health of livestock, and the outcome of important endeavors. Communication with ema occurs through ritual speech, betel nut offerings, and animal sacrifice led by the lulik nain (lord of the sacred)

name: Emadloti
description: The emadloti are the ancestral spirits of Swazi traditional religion, the most active forces in daily life. Unlike the remote creator Mvelincanti, they watch over descendants and shape fortune; neglect brings illness or misfortune until offerings restore harmony. Offerings include beer libations, prayer and animal sacrifice at life events, the king as chief intermediary to the royal ancestors.

name: Emandwa
description: Among the Baganda people of Uganda, emandwa are clan spirits that serve as divine messengers and intermediaries between the human world and the supreme creator Katonda. The term emandwa also refers to the traditional healers who are possessed by these spirits — literally the man who has a spirit sit on his head. Each Baganda clan maintains its own emandwa spirits, which are believed to be the spirits of notable ancestors, warriors, or clan founders who were elevated to spiritual status after death. The emandwa system is central to Baganda healing practices, where spirit mediums enter trance states to diagnose illness, resolve disputes, and prescribe sacrifices. The most famous emandwa shrine is on the Ssese Islands of Lake Victoria, dedicated to the python spirit Luwala

name: Encantada
description: Encantadas are fairy spirits of the Pyrenees mountains, found in Catalan, Aragonese, and Basque folklore. Unlike the winged fairies of northern European tradition, encantadas are enchanted women bound to specific natural features — caves, waterfalls, mountain lakes called ibones, and deep forest pools. They are most active on the Nit de Sant Joan (St. John's Eve, June 23), the summer solstice, when they emerge from their watery hiding places to wash clothes in moonlight and comb their long hair with golden combs. Catalan legend holds that whoever captures a piece of clothing or a golden comb from an encantada will be blessed with good fortune and freedom from poverty for life

name: Enkai (Engai)
description: Enkai, also known as Engai, is the supreme god of the Maasai people of Kenya and Tanzania. Enkai is neither male nor female but manifests in two distinct aspects: Enkai Narok (the Black God), who is benevolent and brings rain, grass, and prosperity, and Enkai Na-nyokie (the Red God), who is vengeful and brings drought, lightning, and famine. According to Maasai cosmology, Enkai once lived on earth with humanity but withdrew into the sky after being displeased. Before leaving, Enkai lowered cattle from heaven on a leather thong through a sacred fig tree, entrusting them to the Maasai as their sacred guardians. Enkai's dual nature reflects the balance of the Maasai world -- the life-giving rains and destructive droughts. Prayers to Enkai are offered at the sacred mountain Oldoinyo Lengai (Mountain of God) and beneath wild fig trees (oreteti). Enkai is associated with black (good disposition) and red (anger), visible in the clouds

name: Eototo
description: Eototo is the chief of the Hopi katsinam, the spiritual counterpart of the Hopi village chief and 'father' of all katsinam. He knows all the ceremonies and appears at the Powamu ceremony in February, when he draws cloud symbols in cornmeal and pours sacred water into the kiva to bring rain for Hopi agriculture. Shabby in appearance, his power is not to be judged by looks.

name: Epilsen
description: In Yurok cosmology of northwestern California, the world is inhabited by wo'gey — powerful spirit-beings who shaped the landscape before humans arrived and who still dwell in sacred places: high mountain peaks, remote springs, old-growth redwood groves, and stone enclosures called tsekteya. An Epilsen belongs to this class of spirit-beings, a resident of the high country where Yurok medicine-makers and pilgrims travel to cry and shout for help, seeking visions and spiritual power. The Yurok believe that all features of nature — trails, rocks, trees, springs — possess consciousness and power, and the Epilsen spirit mediates between humans and these living forces of the natural world

name: Er Sogotokh
description: Er Sogotokh, 'the Lonely Man,' is the first human and ancestor-hero of Sakha (Yakut) oral epic, the olonkho. The earliest olonkho printed in the West, published by Otto von Böhtlingk in 1851, tells how the solitary first man struggles against hostile spirits and secures fire, horses and a family line for his descendants, founding the human lineage of the Sakha people.

name: Erdlaveersissok
description: Erdlaveersissok, 'the Entrail-Seizer,' is a terrifying being of Greenlandic Inuit tradition who haunts the celestial path to the moon. Travelers who laugh or lose their composure on that journey have their entrails torn out by it; the tale teaches the value of discipline, mental strength and restraint on the spiritual journey.

name: Erect Horns
description: Erect Horns (Tomȯsévėséhe) was the prophet of the Só'taeo'o people who later merged with the Cheyenne. He received the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat) at Tȯhóonévose (Stone Hammer Mountain) near the Great Lakes. The sacred hat represents female power, complementing the male power of the Sacred Arrows—together they form the two great covenants of the Cheyenne Nation. Erect Horns gave the people the Sun Dance ceremony and convinced the tribe to abandon their sedentary agricultural lifestyle, adopt the nomadic Plains horse culture, and rely on buffalo for survival

name: Erik Munks Gjenferd
description: Erik Munks gjenferd is the ghost of Erik Munk (1530s-1590s), a ruthless 16th-century mine owner who operated the Barbu silver and copper mines near Arendal. According to legend, Munk acquired land through fraud — he tricked a man named Benkestok into swearing an oath on what the man thought was his own land, while Munk had secretly placed soil from that land in the man's shoes. After his death, Munk was condemned to become a deildegast (boundary ghost), endlessly wandering the boundaries of his ill-gotten lands. However, unlike the typical deildegast who carries a boundary stone, Erik Munk's ghost haunts specifically the mining district of Barbu outside Arendal. His ghost is said to appear at the old mine entrances and along the paths between Arendal and Barbu. He represents the shadow side of Arendal's mining prosperity, reflecting the harsh conditions and exploitative practices of early Norwegian mining

name: Erlig Khan
description: Erlig Khan (Erlik, Erleg) is the lord of death and judge of the underworld in Mongolian and Turkic belief: he reigns in the copper palace of Tamag, weighs the souls of the dead, and looses sickness upon the living. Powerful and implacable yet bound by cosmic law, he is equated with Yama and, among Mongols, called Erleg or Yerleg.

name: Erlik (Altai)
description: Erlik (Erlik Khan) is the god of death and the underworld of Altai and Turkic tradition: the creator's firstborn who fell for pride and was banished to the ninth layer of the earth, where he reigns in a palace of copper and gold and judges the dead. From below he sends plague and evil spirits, demanding animal sacrifice from fearful shamans.

name: Erlik Khan
description: Erlik Khan (Erlik) is the great god of death and the underworld, Tamag, in Turkic and Mongolian belief. Brother of the creator Ülgen, he rules the dead below the earth, sends plague and evil spirits against the living, and is propitiated by Buryat, Khakas and Mongolian shamans who seek to travel safely between the worlds of the living and the dead.

name: Erlking
description: Malevolent ELF-King from Germanic folklore. Name: German 'Erlkönig' = 'Alder-King' (NOT 'elf' - mistranslation from Danish 'elverkonge' = 'elf-king'). Origin: Johann Gottfried Herder adapted Danish folk ballad 'Elveskud' (Elves' Shot) into German as 'Erlkönigs Tochter' (Erl-King's Daughter). Goethe then created his famous 1782 ballad where the antagonist IS the Erlking himself (changed from original daughter). Danish Original: elverkongens datter (elf-king's daughter) - female spirit who tempts nobleman, strikes him when refused. Goethe'S Version: Father rides with feverish son at night. Child sees Erlking and his 'daughters' (golden robes, dancing, games). Father sees only mist/willow trees. Erlking threatens 'Gewalt' (force) if boy won't come willingly. Boy dies - father finds him dead on arrival. IN Scandinavia: ellekonge - king of the elves, lives in forests, stalks children. Touch Kills immediately. Lures with promises of joy, golden clothes, his daughters' companionship. Connected to 'Alveskud' ballad (woman rejects elf-lover, elf shoots her)

name: Erlkönig
description: The Erlkönig (Erl-King) is a sinister figure from German and Danish folklore, most famously immortalized in Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's 1782 ballad Erlkönig and later set to music by Franz Schubert. The name is a mistranslation of the Danish ellerkonge (elf-king), which German translators confused with Erle (alder tree), literally creating king of the alders. In the ballad, the Erlkönig is a supernatural entity who appears to a dying child, offering him beautiful games, flowers, and the company of his daughters. The father, riding desperately through the night with his sick son in his arms, cannot see the Erlkönig but hears his voice coaxing the child toward death. In Danish tradition, the ellerkonge is the king of the ellefolk (elves), who lives in an elf-hill and presides over the nightly dances of the hidden people

name: Erzulie Freda (Goddess of Love and Beauty)
description: Erzulie Freda is the lwa of love, beauty, luxury and feminine charm in Haitian Vodou, portrayed as a light-skinned woman in pink, blue, white and gold finery, adorned with jewelry and surrounded by mirrors, lace and perfume. Syncretized with Our Lady of Sorrows, she is both radiant and melancholy, weeping for the world's suffering.

name: Eshu
description: Yoruba Orisha (deity) of Trickery, Crossroads, Duality, and Languages. Differs From Elegua but Closely Related - some say they are brothers, some same being (256 paths for Elegua vs 101 for Eshu in Santería). Primary Trickster - causes mischief to teach lessons, plays jokes, creates chaos. Messenger between Ajogun (malevolent spirits), Orishas (benevolent), and humans. Speaks ALL languages. Dual Nature: both good and evil, right and wrong, cleverness and vanity, violence and lust. In Cuba: 'Eleguá moves silently, Echu breaks through forcefully.' In Palo Mayombe (Colombia): 'Exu.' In Haitian Vodou: 'Papa Legba' - wise old man with cane, opens gate between worlds. In Candomblé: 'Exu de Candomblé.' Creator of mischief and teacher - his trickery exposes human folly. Carries sacrifices to Orishas. In Ifá divination: 256 paths to Elegua are all Eshu manifestations. Participated in world creation alongside Obatalá, Olorum, Odudua. 'Eshu Bi' = stern/forceful avatar - old man AND young boy. 'Eshu Ayé' works with all Orishas including Olokun, walks beach shores. 'Father who gave birth to Ogboni' (secret society)

name: Estsanatlehi
description: Estsanatlehi, also known as Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé or Changing Woman, is the most revered deity in Navajo (Diné) mythology, associated with the cyclical renewal of life, the changing seasons, and female puberty. According to Diné Bahaneʼ (the Navajo creation story), she was created from a turquoise figure placed on a buckskin at the sacred mountain Chʼóolʼį́ʼí, brought to life by the Wind and the songs of the Holy People. She grew from infant to womanhood in four days. Her parents are Long Life Boy and Happiness Girl, who represent the means by which all life passes through time. She is the mother of the Hero Twins Monster Slayer and Born for Water, who rid the earth of monsters. She later created the first four Navajo clans from skin rubbed from her own body

name: Etiäinen
description: Etiäinen is a Finnish fetch/doppelgänger spirit: an image that goes ahead of a person, performing actions the person later repeats (door closing, shadow seen). Also a premonitory feeling of impending events, often death. Spontaneous and involuntary unlike clairvoyance. Ganander (1789), Krohn documented it. Cognate with Norwegian vardøger, Swedish vörðr. Modern Finnish 'etiäinen' means premonition.

name: Etügen
description: Etügen Eke ("Mother Earth") is the supreme earth goddess in Mongolian and Turkic Tengrist mythology. She is the second highest deity after Kök-Tengri (the Eternal Blue Sky) and is considered perpetually virginal. Etügen governs all natural forces and all living beings are subordinate to her. She is the patroness of homeland, nature, fertility, and the cycle of seasons. The name Etügen may derive from Ötüken, the sacred mountain of the ancient Turks. Medieval sources sometimes confused her with a male counterpart named Natigai, but this is believed to be a mispronunciation. Etügen existed in the middle of the universe and together with Tengri she maintains cosmic balance. Sacrifices were made to appease her every spring before cattle-breeding and planting, and every autumn after the harvest. A reddish horse was typically sacrificed near rivers and lakes to appeal for fertility and well-being

name: Evening Star
description: Evening Star is a female deity in Pawnee mythology, placed in the West by Tirawa. She initially resisted the divine plan to create humankind when Morning Star was sent to mate with her. Morning Star had to fight and defeat forces in the western sky to overcome her resistance. Their union produced the first human, a girl. Evening Star represents the feminine principle of creation, the western direction, and the mysteries of the night. In the Morning Star sacrifice ceremony, a captive girl was symbolically transformed into the Evening Star before her sacrifice

name: Evening Star Tsimshian
description: Evening Star is the celestial daughter of the Sun in the Tsimshian myth of Asdiwal. Appearing on earth as a white bear pursued by the hunter Asdiwal, she carries him into the sky, where he wins her through impossible trials; their union and Asdiwal's later boastfulness are central to the story analyzed by Levi-Strauss.

name: Evil One (Cheyenne)
description: In Cheyenne tradition, the Evil One represents the malevolent forces that threaten the harmony of the community and the natural world. Cheyenne cosmology recognizes various evil or harmful spirits that can cause sickness, misfortune, and death. The most feared of these is the Two-Face (Hestovatohkeo'o), a monster with a second face on the back of its head that kills anyone who makes eye contact with it. Other malevolent beings include the Rolling Head, a disembodied vampiric head that seeks revenge for betrayal; the Ma'xemestaa'e, a hairy humanoid with birdlike feet; and various water monsters (Mehne or Axxea) that lurk in springs and menace travelers. The Cheyenne believe that humans who commit grave wrongs or die unnaturally may also return as wandering evil spirits, traveling the Short Fork of the Milky Way (the "suicide road") and returning to plague the living

name: Evus
description: Evus are mischievous trickster spirits in Equatorial Guinean folklore (various groups). They dwell at village borders and forest edges, using illusion and shapeshifting to teach moral lessons. Strong-willed determination counters them. Evus appears in tales like 'The Bewitchment of Angutisugsuk' and 'The Spirit of the Great River.

name: Eynhallow Monk
description: Eynhallow Monk (Unknown). is a human. The Eynhallow Monk is a figure from Orcadian folklore associated with the island of Eynhallow in Orkney, Scotland. The abandoned church on the island is said to be haunted by a spectral monk.. Source: Orcadian folklore; Scottish island traditions

name: Fairy
description: Fairies are supernatural beings of European folk belief, spanning Celtic (aes sídhe, Tuatha Dé Danann), Germanic (elves, dwarves), Slavic, and Romance traditions. The term derives from Old French faerie, from fae, from Latin fata ('fate'). Origins include demoted angels, spirits of the dead, nature spirits, or a hidden earlier race; in tales they act as helpers, abductors, or amoral tricksters.

name: Fairy
description: English fairy tradition encompasses diverse beings: the trooping fairies of hills and mounds, solitary spirits like the brownie (household helper), boggart (malevolent house spirit), pixie (Southwest), and the Lincolnshire/Fenland Tiddy Mun. Not a single entity but a class.

name: Fairy
description: Scottish fairy tradition encompasses the Seelie and Unseelie Courts, trooping fairies (Sídhe), and solitary spirits like the brownie, glaistig, and each-uisge. Not a single being but a class of nature spirits inhabiting knolls (sídhe), lochs, and glens.

name: Fairy
description: In Italian folklore the fata is a fairy or fate-like woman whose name descends from Latin fata, the goddesses of destiny, and who appears in the Pentamerone and other collections as a magical benefactress or enchantress. Italian fairies blend the classical Parcae with medieval enchantresses such as Morgan le Fay, and regional figures from the Befana to water spirits are classed among them.

name: Fairy
description: The input record's description details Polish fairies (rusałka, boginka, dziwożona, południca, świtezianka, nożnica) — a complete misattribution. Norwegian fairy tradition features huldra (skogsrå), vetter, nisser, tusser, and bergfolk — nature spirits of forests, mountains, and farms. No Polish fairy beings belong to Norwegian folklore. This record appears to be a data contamination error.

name: Fairy
description: The vila (víla) is the Czech and West Slavic woodland spirit, a beautiful maiden who dwells in forests, mountains, and waters, dances at night, and can help or harm travelers. Villagers left her gifts, avoided her groves, and told of men who followed her song only to be lost; she belongs to the wider Slavic vila family.

name: Fairy
description: German folklore has no generic 'fairy.' Specific beings include Elfen (light elves), Feen (fate-women), Holda's retinue, kobolds, Heinzelmännchen, Puks, and wood-wives (Moosfrauen). Jacob Grimm traced Weiße Frauen to Norse Ljósálfar. This entry conflates distinct beings; no single 'German fairy' exists.

name: Fairy
description: In French tradition the fée is a supernatural woman who grants gifts to newborns and shapes the destiny of mortals, dwelling in forests, springs, and castles of the Otherworld. Two archetypes dominate medieval literature: the fairy godmother and the fairy lover (Morgane, Viviane, Melusine). Regional forms such as the dames blanches and the fées des houles preserve older, more ambivalent beliefs.

name: Fairy
description: The input record's description again details Polish fairies (rusałka, boginka, dziwożona, etc.), not Danish beings. Danish fairy tradition includes elverfolk (elves), älvor, and the ballads' 'ellepiger' (elf-maidens) who dance in mist and abduct humans. No Polish fairy beings belong to Danish folklore. This is the same data contamination as fairy-norway.

name: Fairy
description: Not attested in Canadian folklore. The input's description is purely Polish-Slavic material — rusałka, boginka, dziwożona, południca and świtezianka — mistakenly filed under 'Canada.' Indigenous Canada has genuine 'Little People' figures (Wabanaki mikumwess, Ojibwe/Cree memegwesi, Mi'kmaq puglatmu'j), but no generic European fairy belongs to Canadian tradition.

name: Fairy
description: Polish folklore describes a range of fairy-like spirits, including the wila (vila) of the woods and fields, the dziwożona, and the boginki who watch over infants. These beings are beautiful but unpredictable, rewarding the kind and punishing the careless, and their tales survive in rural custom, stories of changelings, and seasonal rituals.

name: Fairy
description: Fairy (European). is a nature-spirit. General term for magical nature spirits in European folklore. Source: European folklore, Celtic and Germanic oral traditions

name: Fakse
description: Fakse is a type of carved wooden cult idol from the Setesdal region of Sørlandet, representing a rare survival of pre-Christian worship practices into the 19th century. The most famous fakse figures were Fakse-Brokke (from Brokke farm in Valle) and another from Rygnestad — male wooden figures about one meter tall, carved from pine. Farmers offered beer, butter, and food to the fakse, believing it would bring prosperity, protect livestock, and ensure good harvests. If the fakse was moved or disrespected, it would cause cattle disease and misfortune. The fakse tradition persisted in Setesdal until the mid-1800s when Christian authorities destroyed or removed the figures. The fakse represents the survival of Norse cult practices (similar to the worship of the Norse gods through idols) in the isolated mountain valley of Setesdal, where Christianity arrived later and blended with older traditions

name: Falak
description: Falak is a colossal fiery serpent from Arabian cosmology, believed to lie dormant in the depths of hell, waiting to swallow the heavens, the earth, and hell itself at the apocalypse. In the cosmic hierarchy, Falak rests beneath Bahamut (the great world fish), who carries a bull named Kuyuta, who supports a gemstone slab upon which stands an angel shouldering the earth. Falak is bigger and arguably more gruesome than the Basilisk of European legend. Its name means 'daybreak' in Arabic, an ironic reference to its role as an agent of cosmic destruction. According to some traditions, Falak refrains from devouring creation only out of fear of God. It represents the raw destructive potential of chaos held in check by divine will, and the ultimate end of all things in Islamic eschatology

name: Falcone
description: The peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) is the national bird of San Marino, a native raptor of the cliffs of Mount Titano celebrated as a symbol of freedom and honored in recent state coin issues. This entry inflates it into a folkloric 'monster' and an omen of a Captain Regent's death, a framing found in no Sammarinese source. The bird is real and emblematic, not a supernatural creature.

name: Fallow Doe (Ghoa Maral)
description: Gua Maral (the Fallow Doe) is an ancestress of the Mongols in the Secret History of the Mongols: with the wolf Börte Chino she forms the legendary progenitor pair who crossed a lake to found the lineage of Chinggis Khan. Gentle and divine, she symbolizes blessing, fertility, and the mythic origins of Mongol royalty.

name: Famadihana
description: The Famadihana is not a creature but the honored ancestor spirit at the center of the Malagasy "turning of the bones" ceremony, a funerary tradition practiced primarily by the Merina and Betsileo peoples of Madagascar's central highlands. Known as razana (ancestors), these spirits remain intimately involved in the daily lives of their descendants long after death. The famadihana ceremony occurs roughly every five to seven years, when families exhume the bodies of their ancestors from family crypts, rewrap them in fresh silk shrouds (lambamena), and dance with the corpses while carrying them over their heads. The ceremony reaffirms the bond between the living and the dead. The razana are believed to become cold and uncomfortable in their old wrappings, and the famadihana warms them both literally and symbolically while rewriting their names on the new shrouds so they will never be forgotten

name: Fanahy
description: The fanahy is a core concept in Malagasy spirituality, referring to the spirit or essence that determines an individual's character, behavior, and moral nature. Unlike the European concept of a singular soul, Malagasy tradition recognizes multiple spiritual components within a person, with fanahy being the moral and spiritual force that shapes personality. A person can have a "good fanahy" (generous, kind, socially harmonious) or a "bad fanahy" (stingy, angry, antisocial). When a person dies, the fanahy departs permanently from the body. If the deceased receives proper burial rites and famadihana ceremonies, the fanahy becomes a benevolent razana (ancestor spirit). If neglected, it may become an angatra (malevolent ghost) that haunts graves and brings misfortune. The fanahy represents the ongoing moral presence of the dead within the community of the living

name: Fara Makan
description: Fara Makan is a legendary hunter-hero in Mande mythology credited with creating the Niger River — the lifeblood of West Africa. According to tradition, Fara Makan tracked a wounded antelope for seven days across the parched savanna. Dying of thirst, he shot an arrow deep into the ground, and water burst forth, creating the Djoliba (Niger River). The river wound across the Sahel, bringing life to the lands of Mali, Niger, and Nigeria. The great river enabled agriculture, trade, and eventually the rise of the Mali Empire. Fara Makan is remembered as a master hunter who sacrificed his own comfort to bring water to his people. His story is part of the Mande hunters' tradition, and he is considered a founding figure of the Mande hunter fraternity

name: Faraa Kankurang (Wuleng Wuleng)
description: Faraa Kankurang, also known as Wuleng Wuleng (meaning 'red, red') or Ifangbodi, is one of the three original Kankurang masquerade forms in Mandinka tradition of The Gambia, distinguished by its powerful mystical identity and connection to the spirit world. Unlike other Kankurang forms primarily associated with social discipline, Faraa Kankurang carries a more deeply spiritual and supernatural character. Elders describe it as one of the original forms brought from the ancient Manding Empire, with costumes and performance styles that emphasize otherworldly power and transformation. The Faraa Kankurang's costume is made entirely of jaffo (bark) covering the whole body, and the performer carries two machetes. Known as 'The Flying Kankurang' because of its rapid, supernatural movements, it is traditionally heard at night and seen high up in tall trees, where it protects circumcised boys from evil spirits. In 2008, UNESCO recognized the Kankurang tradition as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, acknowledging its cultural significance to Mandinka identity

name: Faro
description: Faro is a powerful water deity in Mandinka and Bambara (Mandé) mythology, revered across Senegal, Mali, and The Gambia as a purifying force that brings cosmic order, speech, and fertility to the world. In Mandé creation narratives, Faro sacrificed himself to atone for the sins of his twin brother Pemba, being cut into sixty pieces that fell to earth and became trees. The supreme creator Mangala restored Faro to life in human form, sending him to earth in an ark made from his placenta carrying the first ancestors, animals, and plants. Faro then caused a great flood to wash away the impurity created by Pemba, saving only the righteous in his ark. Faro is associated with water purification, spiritual justice, rebirth, and the Niger River, which is considered his physical manifestation. He also granted humanity the gift of speech and language, establishing the foundation of culture and social order. Faro represents the Mandinka concept that true creation requires sacrifice, purification, and the establishment of balance between opposing forces

name: Farsakh
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Farsakh is a Persianate unit of distance (the parasang, roughly five to six kilometers), not a Pamiri giant, and the 'giant builder of terraces and fortresses' account is fabricated. The genuine giants of Iranian-influenced Central Asian tradition are the divs of Persian mythology.

name: Fata
description: The Fata is the fairy-fate figure of Italian tradition, descended from the Latin Fatae and the Roman Parcae. A beautiful woman in courtly gown with a magic wand, she acts as godmother and fate-weaver, bestowing gifts at a child's birth; vain and proud, she punishes slights with curses. She inhabits forests, wells and crossroads, surviving today in the Fata Turchina of Pinocchio.

name: Fenghuang
description: Fenghuang (鳳凰) is the Chinese phoenix, a composite celestial bird often described with the head of a golden pheasant, the back of a tortoise, the neck of a snake, and the tail of a fish, its five colors carrying cosmic significance. It is said to appear only in times of peace and virtuous rule, and it pairs with the dragon as a symbol of yin, the empress, and marital harmony.

name: Fenrir
description: Monstrous wolf - son of Loki + giantess Angrboða. Siblings: Jörmungandr (Midgard Serpent) + Hel (underworld). Old Norse: 'Fen-dweller' or 'Fenrisúlfr.' Prophecy foretold he would destroy gods. The gods tried Three fetters: (1) Laeding (broke), (2) Dromi (broke), (3) Gleipnir - made by dwarves from Impossible things: sound of cat's footsteps, woman's beard, mountain roots, fish's breath, bird's spit, bear's nerves. Looks like silk ribbon but unbreakable. The gods Tricked him - said 'test your strength.' Fenrir knew if he couldn't break it, they'd never free him. He agreed Only if Tyr put his hand in his mouth as pledge. When Fenrir couldn't break Gleipnir, Tyr lost his hand. Fenrir BIT OFF TYR'S Hand. Now bound to rock Gleipnir until Ragnarök. A sword is stuck in his jaw to gag him. At Ragnarök: Breaks Free, Swallows Odin. Odin's son Vidar kills him by stabbing heart or tearing jaws apart

name: Fetch
description: The Fetch is a spectral double or apparition of a living person in Irish and Northern English folklore, regarded as an omen of impending death. The term likely derives from Hiberno-English adaptation of Old Irish faith meaning seer, or from Old English faecce found in medieval glossaries. In 19th-century collections by John and Michael Banim, the fetch appears as an exact duplicate whose sighting carries profound significance. If seen in the evening, the fetch portends imminent death; snip snip if seen in the morning it may signal a long life ahead. The concept shares similarities with the Germanic doppelganger, the Norse fylgja, and the Scottish wraith. Francis Grose associated the term with Northern England in his 1787 Provincial Glossary. Patrick Kennedy's 1866 Legendary Fiction of the Irish Celts includes The Doctor's Fetch, where a physician's double appears to his wife the night before his sudden death

name: Finnur hin Fróði
description: Finnur hin Fróði (Finn the Wise) is the most renowned figure in Faroese wizard folklore, a legendary wise man and magic-worker associated with the 'Black Book' (Cyprianus/Svarteboken) tradition that spread across Scandinavia. In Faroese folk belief, wizards and cunning folk possessed books of black magic that could only be passed on to a willing successor. These practitioners could control weather, heal the sick, find lost objects, ward off trolls and hidden people, and counter malevolent magic. The island of Svínoy and the village of Sumba are particularly associated with wizard lore. The tradition blends pre-Norse pagan elements with later Christian mysticism — wizards were known as 'readers' (lesarar) who could read from the Black Book to achieve supernatural results. Finnur hin Fróði is celebrated in Faroese kvæði (ballads), notably in 'Finnur hin Fríði' (CCF 26), preserved in multiple transcriptions by Svabo, Hammershaimb, and others

name: Fire Keeper
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No 'Fire Keeper' spirit appears in recorded Charrua tradition; the account is a modern AI-style retelling of an unwritten 'gratitude to fire' lesson. Surviving records of Charrua belief are sparse, and no named fire spirit is documented for them.

name: Firebird
description: Legendary Slavic magical bird - Zhar-Ptitsa (Russian: жар-птица, 'fire-bird'). PAN-Slavic: Ukrainian 'zhar-ptytsia,' Czech 'Pták Ohnivák,' Polish 'Żar-ptak,' Slovenian 'Rajska/zlata-ptica.' Etymology: 'zhar' = fire/glow. Feathers Shine Continuously even when plucked - like embers, like the sun. Symbol of Hope and unattainable beauty. Associated with golden apples granting Eternal Youth. In tales: tries to steal apples from royal orchards before dawn. Prophetic - feather can predict the future. Capturing triggers the quest. In 'Ivan Tsarevich and the Gray Wolf': quest to capture Firebird's tail feather. In 'Maryushka': gentle orphan girl receives magic. Connected to Adam/Eve: only creature who didn't taste Forbidden Fruit, rewarded with immortality through death and rebirth (like Phoenix). Symbolizes: transformation, renewal, the danger of greed

name: First Angry (Áłtsé Hashké)
description: First Angry (Áłtsé Hashké) is a genuine Coyote Holy Person of Diné creation accounts. In the Diné Bahane' he emerged with the first beings, declared that he existed before they were formed, and is named as the one who brought witchcraft into the world, so that his power must be guarded against in Navajo ritual.

name: First Angry Coyote
description: Átsé hashké, 'First Angry,' is the Navajo personification of anger and witchcraft, called into being in the primordial world. In the Origin Myths of the Navaho he stole the children of Water Buffalo by stretching a rainbow across the waters, an act that introduced evil and witchcraft into the world and made him the source of malevolence among the Holy People.

name: First Man (Áłtsé Hastiin)
description: First Man (Áłtsé Hastiin) is a primordial figure in Navajo creation mythology. In the First World, he was formed from the breath of Black Cloud and White Cloud, carrying white corn and crystal. He made a fire with crystal and joined with First Woman after seeing her light from across the darkness, establishing the pattern of life. He led the people through the four worlds, created the sacred mountains, and helped plan the creation of the Sun and Moon. He drew a plan in the dirt to arrange the st

name: First Woman (Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́)
description: First Woman (Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́) is a primordial figure in Navajo creation mythology. She was formed from Blue Cloud and Yellow Cloud in the West, carrying yellow corn, white shell, turquoise, and yucca. She made a fire with turquoise and joined with First Man. She caused a great conflict by boasting that women could live without men, leading to the Separation of the Sexes which lasted four years and resulted in the birth of monsters. She helped rescue children taken by Big Water Creature and partic

name: Fisaga
description: Fisaga is a gentle wind spirit from Samoan mythology, personifying the light and pleasant breeze associated with fine weather. In the Samoan language, fisaga refers specifically to a gentle, pleasant wind that brings good conditions. The most famous legend involving Fisaga comes from the tale of Ti'iti'i who imprisoned the winds one by one in his canoe or calabash to control their power over the land. Ti'iti'i captured all the fierce and destructive winds, leaving only Fisaga free to roam the islands. This myth explains why the gentlest breeze remains at liberty while stronger winds must be summoned when needed. In some versions the demigod Maui is credited with the capture of the winds rather than Ti'iti'i. Fisaga represents the benevolent aspect of nature, a force that brings comfort rather than destruction. Samoan navigators traditionally called upon Fisaga for safe passage through chants and offerings

name: Fish Hawk Tlingit
description: In the Tlingit Raven cycle, Fish Hawk (the osprey) appears in a folk-etymological tale of how the osprey gained its white head. Raven, in the shape of a woman, marries a chief, and supernatural power from a shaman turns Fish Hawk's head white; the episode also frames Raven's theft of the sun. The bird's keen sight and pale head are thus explained.

name: Fjeldvīg
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. Fjeldvig is a Norwegian place-name and surname, not a Danish folklore being, and the description grafts generic bjergfolk (hill-folk) lore onto the name. Genuine Danish mound-folk belong to the bjergfolk complex related to the nisse and trold; no being called Fjeldvig is recorded.

name: Fjellvette
description: Fjellvette (mountain wight) is a nature spirit specific to the mountains of Vestlandet. The fjellvette is a type of vette (nature spirit) that guards specific peaks, mountain passes, high pastures, and rocky crags. Each mountain in Vestlandet had its own fjellvette who protected the wildlife and punished humans who showed disrespect — killing too many reindeer, scarring the mountain with mining, or building without permission. The fjellvette could create rockfalls, avalanches, and sudden storms to drive people away. However, it could also guide lost travelers to safety, reveal hidden routes over mountain passes, and grant good hunting to respectful hunters. Offerings of food or coins were left at mountain cairns to appease the fjellvette. The tradition was strongest in the high mountain areas of Jotunheimen, Hardangervidda, and the Jostedalsbreen glacier region. The fjellvette is distinct from the bergfolk (mountain people) who live inside mountains — the fjellvette is the spirit of the mountain itself, not a resident

name: Fjörulalli
description: Fjörulalli (Beach Walker) is a smaller variant of the skeljaskrímsli in Icelandic folklore, about the size of a medium dog to a calf. Fjörulalli is covered with shells or lava fragments and has a small rounded head. It is generally considered harmless to humans but has a nasty habit of tearing the udders off sheep it encounters on the beach. Pregnant women were warned to avoid fjörulalli sightings. The creature walks along beaches at night, its shell coating making a distinctive rattling sound. Fjörulalli has been sighted on all Icelandic coasts, with particularly common reports from the Westfjords and the Reykjanes peninsula. The name means beach-walker. Unlike the larger skeljaskrímsli, fjörulalli does not approach houses or seek human contact — it stays on the shoreline

name: Fjøsnisse
description: Fjøsnisse (barn nisse) is a specialized type of Norwegian nisse that lives specifically in the cowshed (fjøs) and cares for the cattle. While the general nisse protects the entire farm, the fjøsnisse is devoted exclusively to the welfare of the cows, goats, and other barn animals. In Norwegian folk tradition, a well-kept barn with healthy, productive cows was a sign that the fjøsnisse was content. The fjøsnisse was known to braid the tails and manes of cattle, keep the barn clean, and help during calving. If offended, he would spoil the milk, tangle the cows' tails into impossible knots, or cause the animals to fall ill. The fjøsnisse expected offerings of the first milk from a new cow or extra portions of Christmas porridge. This specialized barn spirit reflects the central importance of dairy farming in traditional Norwegian agriculture

name: Fladså Trolden
description: Fladså Trolden (the Fladså Troll) is a giant troll from local folklore in Sydsjælland who once decided to bury the town of Næstved in sand out of spite. He filled a huge sack with sand from the Øresund beach and began carrying it inland toward Næstved. On the way, he stopped at Mogenstrup Kro (Mogenstrup Inn) for a drink. While the troll drank, a clever Nisse crept up to the sack and pricked holes in it with a pin. As the troll continued his journey, sand trickled steadily from the holes, creating a trail of hills across the landscape. By the time the troll reached his destination, the sack was empty, and Næstved was saved. The sand hills he left behind are still called Fladså Bakker (Fladså Hills) today, visible on the road between Næstved and the coast of Fakse Bugt

name: Flat Pipe
description: The Flat Pipe is the most sacred ceremonial object of the Arapaho people, central to their creation story and spiritual life. In the beginning, a man carrying a Flat Pipe walked on the primordial waters—the pipe itself was integral to creation. The Flat Pipe was used by the Flat Pipe Creator to summon trees and animals, and was transformed into a Red-headed Duck to help dive for mud. In historical times, the Flat Pipe bundle was kept by a designated keeper and brought out for the Sun Dance and other major ceremonies. The pipe represents the covenant between the Arapaho people and their Creator

name: Flat Pipe Creator
description: The Flat Pipe Creator is the supreme being in Arapaho creation mythology. In the beginning there was only water covering everything. A man carrying a Flat Pipe walked on the water for six days, weeping and fasting, searching for a safe place to rest his pipe. On the seventh day he summoned seven cottonwood trees and all the creatures. Various animals dove for mud—Grebe, Kingfisher, Otter, Beaver, Garter Snake, and others—all failed. On the seventh dive, Turtle and the Man (who transformed his Flat Pipe into a Red-headed Duck) succeeded. The Man cast the mud in four directions, creating the Earth. This Creator is identified with the sacred Flat Pipe itself, the most sacred Arapaho object

name: Floghamen
description: Floghamen (the flying shape) is a shape-shifting spirit from Setesdal folklore in Sørlandet. The floghamen is the spirit-form of a witch or sorcerer that flies through the air while the person's body sleeps. The term comes from flog (flight/flying) and ham (shape/form). In Setesdal tradition, certain people could send their ham (soul-form) out of their body to travel as a bird, a ball of light, or a flying shadow. The floghamen would travel vast distances — to other farms, across the mountains, or to gatherings of other floghamen. If the sleeping body was disturbed or turned around, the floghamen could not return and the person would die or go mad. The floghamen tradition is related to the Norse concept of hamfarir (shape-traveling) and shows how pre-Christian beliefs about the soul persisted in Setesdal well into the 19th century. Johannes Skar documented multiple floghamen accounts in Gamalt or Setesdal

name: Flower-people (Blomsterfolk)
description: Not independently attested in Danish tradition as a named being. Danish folklore has generic nature spirits (ellefolk, huldrefolk) and flower-associated beliefs (e.g., elder tree mother), but 'Blomsterfolk' as tiny flower-born guardians appears to be a modern literary invention or conflation. The closest analogue is the general Scandinavian vättar/huldrefolk who inhabit natural features.

name: Flying African
description: The myth of the Flying Africans tells how enslaved Igbo captives, landing at Ebos Landing on St. Simons Island in Georgia in 1803, turned and walked back across the water to fly home to Africa rather than live in bondage. Collected by the Federal Writers' Project in the 1930s, the tale of flight became a lasting symbol of resistance and freedom.

name: Flying Africans
description: The Flying Africans are a central figure in African American legend, born from the historical tragedy of Igbo Landing in 1803. When 75 Igbo captives from Nigeria were brought to St. Simons Island, Georgia, they rose up against their captors, grounded the ship at Dunbar Creek, and walked deliberately into the water singing — choosing death over slavery. From this tragedy arose the legend that the Igbo did not drown but transformed into buzzards and flew back across the Atlantic to Africa. The story evolved into the broader 'People Could Fly' tradition collected by Virginia Hamilton, in which enslaved Africans secretly retained the magical ability to fly — a power brought from their homeland — and when the conditions became unbearable, they would soar into the sky and return to Africa

name: Flying Dutchman
description: Flying Dutchman (Unknown). is a ghost. The Flying Dutchman is a legendary ghost ship condemned to sail the oceans forever, never able to make port. Sightings of the phantom vessel are considered an omen of doom by sailors.. Source: The Phantom Ship (Marryat, 1839); Naval folklore

name: Flying Head
description: The Flying Head is a terrifying cannibalistic spirit from Iroquois and Wyandot mythology. It appears as a giant disembodied head as tall as a man, covered in thick black hair with bat-like wings and long sharp claws. It preys on humans, especially widows and orphans, visiting their homes at night and beating its wings on the walls. Its appearance portends death within days. Its skin is impervious to weapons. The Flying Head is associated with whirlwinds and is feared as a bringer of disease and death

name: Flying Troll
description: Not independently attested in Swedish folklore. Trolls in Nordic tradition are earth-bound (mountain, forest, sea); snip flight is not a traditional attribute. The 'flying troll' appears in the literary fairy tale 'Dag and Daga and the Flying Troll of Sky Mountain' but this is a modern fairy-tale construction, not oral tradition.

name: Fog Woman
description: Fog Woman is a Tlingit supernatural being who, in Swanton's 'Raven and Fog Woman' (myth #108), was Raven's wife. Washing her hands in a basket, she summoned the first salmon into the world; when Raven grew jealous and cruel, she and the salmon departed to the sea. The story explains the origin of salmon runs and the seasons.

name: Folletto
description: The folletto is a mischievous house-sprite of Italian folklore, a generic term covering regional imps such as the salvanello (Veneto), monacello (Calabria) and mazapégul (Romagna). Small, agile and often invisible, it can fly and disappear at will, tangling hair and manes or hiding objects by night, yet helps households that treat it well. As a folletto di vento it rides whirlwinds.

name: Forest Person
description: The Forest Person, known in Tlingit as Kooshdaa kaa or Kushtaka (land otter man), is a shape-shifting spirit from Pacific Northwest indigenous mythology, particularly among the Tlingit people whose territory extends from southeastern Alaska into Canada. These powerful supernatural beings straddle the boundary between human and animal, living where forest meets shore. According to Tlingit creation stories, the Great Raven granted the Land Otter the gift of duality, illusion, and disguise, charging them with preserving the souls of those who drowned, as drowning was considered the most horrible death preventing reincarnation. The Kushtaka serve as both rescuers and predators, saving souls from eternal dissolution while transforming them into boundary-world beings. Similar spirits appear among the Tsimshian as Watsa and the Dena'ina as Nat'ina in South Central Alaska. They are particularly associated with Thomas Bay in Alaska

name: Forest Person
description: The Forest Person of Pacific Northwest tradition is Kushtaka (Kooshdaa kaa), the 'land otter man' of the Tlingit and neighboring peoples whose range extends from southeast Alaska into Canada. A shapeshifter straddling human and animal, it is tied to drowning: Kushtaka may rescue or transform the souls of the drowned. Similar beings appear among the Tsimshian and Dena'ina.

name: Forest Sprite
description: Forest Sprite (Icelandic). is a spirit. A forest spirit who uses a magical flute to cast an enchanted sleep upon travelers. Source: Icelandic folklore

name: Fosen-Sjøtrollet
description: Fosen-Sjøtrollet (the Fosen Sea Troll) is a sea troll said to inhabit the waters off the Fosen peninsula in Trøndelag. Unlike the mountain trolls of inland Norway, this sjøtroll (sea troll) lives in the ocean and comes ashore only at night to raid farms. The Fosen-Sjøtrollet is described as a massive, ugly creature that lives in a cave on a remote Fosen skerry, emerging at low tide to hunt for fish and seals. It has the characteristic troll aversion to sunlight — if caught above water at sunrise, it turns to stone. The many small skerries and islands along the Fosen coast are said to be sjøtroll that were caught by daylight. Unlike mountain trolls who throw boulders, the Fosen-Sjøtrollet is associated with creating dangerous tidal currents and whirlpools. Local fishermen traditionally poured iron nails into the sea before passing certain skerries to ward off the sjøtroll

name: Fossegrim
description: Norwegian water spirit - 'Fossegrim' = 'waterfall lord/grim' (from 'fosse' waterfall + 'grim' supernatural/masked). Also: Swedish 'Strömkarlen' (stream-carol player). Supernatural Musician - plays fiddle (Hardanger fiddle) with such mastery that trees dance and waterfalls stop to listen. Plays the sounds of forest, wind, water over strings. Related to nøkken (water spirit), kvernknurr (mill spirit). Explains exceptional Norwegian fiddling tradition. Legend: musician Myllarguten (1801-1872) and Ole Bull learned from Fossegrim. Swedish 'Strömkarl's lay has 11 variations - corresponds to 11-note Hardanger tuning

name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Aztec
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No sacred fox ancestor-spirit occurs in Aztec religion; the description conflates the fox with coyote figures such as Huehuecoyotl, the aged coyote trickster god, and invents messenger and calendar associations. The fox is not a significant figure in recorded Mexica mythology.

name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Lakota
description: In Lakota tradition the fox (sungila) is a notable animal in medicine and storytelling, and the Kit Fox Society (sungila okolakiciye) was a warrior order that policed the home camp and supplied food. The fox appears in tales as a clever figure valued for sharp wits and survival in dangerous country.

name: Fox Ancestor-Spirit of Passamaquoddy
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No named Passamaquoddy fox ancestor-spirit or 'protective fox tracks' appears in Wabanaki collections; the description is generic woodland moralizing. The central culture hero of Passamaquoddy tradition is Gluskabe, and no developed fox spirit figure is documented.

name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Ashanti
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox figure appears in Akan anansesem (spider-story) tradition, whose trickster is Ananse, and the hunting-omen claims are invented. The fox does not hold a developed role in recorded Ashanti animal tales.

name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No named Baloch fox spirit or fox trickster tale is recorded; the description is generic desert-animal moralizing. Genuine Baloch folklore preserves named tales and characters, but no attested fox tradition supports this entry.

name: Fox Animal-Spirit of Kikuyu
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox spirit or omen belief is recorded in Kikuyu oral collections, and the claimed meaning for the fox in Ngai's cosmos is invented. Kikuyu animal tales center on other creatures; no developed fox figure is documented.

name: Fox Deity (Ashanti)
description: Not independently attested. No fox deity appears in documented Ashanti (Akan) cosmology or folklore; the Ashanti trickster is Anansi the spider, and the fox plays no recorded role in Akan religion. The entry's account of offerings made to a 'fox deity' for discretion and careful planning is unsupported and appears invented.

name: Fox Deity of Cree
description: In Cree oral tradition the fox appears as a shrewd, adaptable figure of the northern forests and plains, admired by hunters for thriving in harsh winters. Beyond general respect for the animal's cleverness, no named Cree fox deity is documented; the fox's role is that of a wise animal in tales rather than a formal spirit.

name: Fox Deity of Maya
description: The fox (chomak in Yucatec Maya) appears in Maya folk tales as a clever, cunning figure who outwits larger animals, and some accounts link the fox to night and trickster themes. Beyond general folk-tale use, no formal Maya fox deity is recorded in the codices or Popol Vuh.

name: Fox Deity of Ojibwe
description: In Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition of the Great Lakes, the fox is a clan animal (doodem) linked to cleverness and diplomacy and appears in tales as a shrewd trickster. The fox is a respected minor spirit figure in medicine practice, not a formal deity; no dedicated fox deity is documented.

name: Fox Deity of Ojibwe
description: In Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition, the fox is one of the animal clan figures (doodem), representing cleverness and diplomacy, and appears in storytelling as a shrewd helper or trickster. Animal powers are respected in Anishinaabe medicine practice, and the fox is a real but minor spirit figure rather than a named deity.

name: Fox Ghost of Inuit
description: Not independently attested as a ghost of Inuit folklore. Inuit tradition knows the fox-woman, a fox who takes human form and marries a hunter — a shape-shifter tale, not a ghost story. No Inuit fox-ghost is documented; the fox's roles are those of trickster and spirit-wife, not revenant.

name: Fox Giant of Apache
