description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The Apache fire-stealing culture hero is Coyote, not a fox; the 'Fox Giant' is an invented conflation, and no such being appears in recorded Apache creation stories.

name: Fox Giant of Aztec
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox giant exists in Aztec (Mexica) myth; the text itself conflates the fox with the tlacuache (opossum) and invents Tezcatlipoca associations and underworld-guide roles. These claims trace to AI content farms, not to Mesoamerican sources.

name: Fox Giant of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested: while the fox (tülki) is a familiar trickster in Kazakh tales, such as those of Aldar Köse and in the Korkut-ata tradition, no 'giant fox' being is recorded in Kazakh folklore. The description inflates the fox's attested trickster role into a fabricated primordial giant. The closest genuine figure is the cunning fox of the folktales, not a supernatural giant.

name: Fox Guardian (Lakota)
description: In Lakota tradition the fox (šunğíla) is a genuine medicine animal: it is said to reveal the locations of healing herbs to medicine people and to teach swift escape and courage under fire. The Tokala, the Kit Fox warrior society, took its name and its ideals of bravery, generosity and selfless service from the fox, honoring it as a protector and guide.

name: Fox Guardian of Inuit
description: Not independently attested as a guardian of Inuit folklore. The documented Inuit fox figures are the fox-woman of the Labrador legend, who becomes a hunter's wife, and the trickster fox of northern tales; neither acts as a guardian spirit. No Inuit fox-guardian is recorded in the available sources.

name: Fox Guardian of Ute
description: Not independently attested as a guardian of Ute folklore. The fox appears in some Ute tales as a clever figure, but no Ute fox-guardian or fox-spirit is documented in the sources. Ute spirit-helpers center on shamans and animal powers such as the bear and the eagle, not a guardian fox.

name: Fox Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested as a named Tupi entity. Tupi-Guarani mythology includes fox tricksters (e.g., Aguara in Guarani) but no specific 'Fox Nature-Spirit' with the described crystalline, celestial attributes. The elaborate description appears to be a modern literary invention.

name: Fox Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
description: Not attested in USA or Tupi folklore. The fox trickster Aguara belongs to the Guarani and Chané peoples of Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil, not the Tupi, and not to North America. In Guarani stories Aguara stole algarroba seeds from Viscacha, outwitted the jaguar, and captured the vulture to obtain its rubber. The North American framing is a misattribution.

name: Fox Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
description: Not attested in Canadian or Tupi folklore. The fox trickster Aguara belongs to the Guarani and Chané peoples of Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil, not the Tupi, and not to North America. In Guarani stories Aguara stole algarroba seeds from Viscacha, outwitted the jaguar, and captured the vulture to obtain its rubber. The Canadian framing is a misattribution.

name: Fox Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested. Duplicate of the Brazil entry with identical fabricated description. Guarani fox figures (Aguara) are tricksters, not celestial guardians with stardust tails. No Paraguayan ethnography supports this specific entity.

name: Fox Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested in Malagasy tradition. Tupi are Indigenous people of coastal Brazil—not Madagascar. The 'celestial fox spirit of Atlantic rainforests' describes a Brazilian Tupi-Guaraní figure misassigned to Madagascar. Malagasy fox-like spirits don't exist (no native foxes). Cross-regional error placing a Brazilian Amazonian figure in the Indian Ocean.

name: Fox Nature-Spirit of Creek
description: No fox nature-spirit is attested in Creek tradition. The fox appears in the Creek story of 'The Fox and the Fry Bread' as a clever character, but it carries no spirit role. Creek spiritual beings are tied to fire, the Green Corn Ceremony and beings such as the tie-snakes; a fox nature-spirit is not documented.

name: Fox Nature-Spirit of Haida
description: No genuine fox nature-spirit is documented in Haida tradition; this entry is an unverifiable composite. Haida cosmology centers on Raven as trickster and creator, the Bear Mother, the supernatural killer-whale beings Sgaana, and the culture hero Nanasimget, none of which includes a fox spirit.

name: Fox Spirit (Zulu)
description: In the rich oral traditions of the Zulu people, this fox spirit is an embodiment of the duality of nature—simultaneously a playful trickster and a solemn guardian of the ancestral lands. It is believed to inhabit the intersection of the physical world and the realm of the Amadlozi (ancestors), acting as a mediator that carries the whispers of the living to the ears of the departed. Its influence is most felt during the transition of seasons, where it is credited with steering the winds that bring the necessary rains to the parched savannahs

name: Fox Spirit (Zulu)
description: In the rich oral traditions of the Zulu people, this fox spirit is an embodiment of the duality of nature—simultaneously a playful trickster and a solemn guardian of the ancestral lands. It is believed to inhabit the intersection of the physical world and the realm of the Amadlozi (ancestors), acting as a mediator that carries the whispers of the living to the ears of the departed. Its influence is most felt during the transition of seasons, where it is credited with steering the winds that bring the necessary rains to the parched savannahs In Mexico folklore, this figure is known among the Mexico people.

name: Fox Spirit of Ashanti
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox spirit acts as messenger of Asase Yaa or keeper of sacred groves in Akan belief; those claims are invented. The Akan spirit world centers on figures such as Asase Yaa, Nyame, and the trickster Ananse, with no attested fox spirit.

name: Fox Spirit of Creek
description: No fox messenger spirit is attested in Creek (Muscogee) tradition. Documented Muscogee supernatural beings include Chufi, the Rabbit trickster; Kolowa, a hairy man-eating ogre; the underwater Tie-snakes; and Isti Papa, the 'man-eater' giant. The entry invents a messenger role with no support in ethnography.

name: Fox Spirit of Maya
description: The Maya fox (chomak/ch'amak) is a folk-tale figure of cunning and transformation, and contemporary Maya communities tell stories of the clever fox. Claims that the fox aided the Hero Twins in the Popol Vuh or guarded sacred fire are not supported by the text; the fox is best attested as an everyday trickster of oral tradition.

name: Fox Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No fox messenger or divination figure appears in recorded Muisca mythology; the claimed role as messenger of Sue and Chia and the links to Lake Guatavita and El Dorado are invented. Muisca tradition preserves no named fox spirit.

name: Fox Spirit of Zapotec
description: The fox is a significant animal in Oaxacan Zapotec belief, where naguales and soul-companions may take animal form, and where caves and the underworld (Lyobaa) belong to the spirit world. The entry presents the Zapotec fox as a solemn guide of souls and helper of shamans, a plausible but generalized synthesis; specific 'psychopomp fox' tales are not widely recorded.

name: Fox Trickster (Mixtec)
description: The fox figures in Mixtec and wider Mesoamerican oral tradition as a clever, deceptive animal, though the specific 'Mixtec fox trickster' of this entry is a synthesis. The input's claim of codex illustrations showing a fox-headed, staff-carrying figure is unverified. What is attested is the fox as a wily trickster animal across the region's folktales.

name: Fox Trickster of Creek
description: The Fox Trickster of the Creek (Muskogee) nation is a revered figure in Southeastern Native American folklore, known for his clever schemes and transformative encounters with humans. In Creek tradition, the fox is considered one of the most intelligent beings in the animal world, possessing knowledge of hidden springs, medicinal roots, and the language of birds. This trickster figure appears in stories told during winter months, teaching children and adults alike about the consequences of greed, dishonesty, and disrespect toward nature. Unlike the more dangerous water spirits of Creek lore, the fox trickster is seen as a mischievous but ultimately helpful teacher who reveals the interconnectedness of all living things

name: Fox Trickster of Lakota
description: The Fox Trickster of the Lakota people is a venerated spirit being that roams the hills and prairies of the Great Plains, serving as both a teacher and a cautionary figure. In Lakota cosmology, the fox is associated with keen observation, strategic thinking, and the ability to adapt to changing circumstances. This trickster appears in oral traditions passed down through generations, often in stories that explain natural phenomena or reinforce community values. While the Lakota have Iktomi the spider as their primary trickster figure, the fox trickster occupies a distinct role as a more subtle, observational being who reveals truth through indirect means and challenges humans to look beyond surface appearances

name: Fox Trickster of Ojibwe
description: This Canadian variant of the Ojibwe fox trickster reflects the distinct traditions of Ojibwe communities living north of the Great Lakes in Ontario and Manitoba. While sharing many characteristics with its American counterpart, this northern manifestation is more closely tied to the extensive network of Canadian Shield waterways and the long, harsh winters that define the region. The trickster appears in stories from Ojibwe elders in communities along the shores of Lake Superior and Lake Huron, where the relationship between humans and the spirit world is mediated through the seasonal rhythms of ice and open water

name: Fox Trickster of Ojibwe
description: This Canadian variant of the Ojibwe fox trickster reflects the distinct traditions of Ojibwe communities living north of the Great Lakes in Ontario and Manitoba. While sharing many characteristics with its American counterpart, this northern manifestation is more closely tied to the extensive network of Canadian Shield waterways and the long, harsh winters that define the region. The trickster appears in stories from Ojibwe elders in communities along the shores of Lake Superior and Lake Huron, where the relationship between humans and the spirit world is mediated through the seasonal rhythms of ice and open water In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.

name: Fox Trickster of Zapotec
description: Zapotec oral tradition of Oaxaca includes humorous tales of clever animals, among them the fox, told at community gatherings as warnings against vanity and greed. The entry contrasts a playful fox trickster with a solemn fox spirit; while both moods exist in regional tales, the specific division and the cave-dwelling framing are the editor's synthesis, not a fixed figure.

name: Frog (Chʼał)
description: Frog (Chʼał) is a water spirit in Navajo mythology associated with healing, rain, and the power of speech. Frog is one of the Holy People who taught the Navajo the importance of articulating prayers clearly, because Frog's croaking was the first form of sacred speech. He is closely linked to the Water Chant (Tóee ́ Hózhǫ́ǫ́jí), one of the most powerful healing ceremonies, and his image appears in sandpaintings used during this rite. Frog is believed to bring rain by singing, and his presence near a dwelling signals abundant water and good fortune

name: Frog Guardian (Bhutanese)
description: The Frog Guardian of Bhutanese tradition is a protective nature spirit associated with the kingdom's pristine valleys and mountain streams. In Bhutanese Buddhism, which blends Mahayana Buddhist teachings with ancient Bon animist beliefs, the frog is considered an auspicious creature symbolizing fertility, abundance, and the cleansing power of water. This guardian deity watches over specific valleys and watersheds, ensuring that villagers maintain harmony with the natural world. Local legends tell of the Frog Guardian appearing to lamas and village elders to deliver warnings about impending floods or to bless new agricultural cycles. Its worship is integrated into annual village rituals that celebrate the changing seasons

name: Frost Giant (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Tupi tradition. Tupi-Guarani cosmology of tropical Brazil records beings such as Tupã, Anhangá and the Curupira, but no source mentions a frost giant or attributes unseasonable cold to one; frost is rare in the lowlands and is not personified in Tupi mythology. The entry is a generic giant archetype misassigned to the Tupi.

name: Frost Giant Iceland
description: Frost Giant Iceland (Unknown). is a giant. A frost giant from Icelandic folklore is a being of ice who dwells in frozen wastelands.. Source: Norse/Icelandic folklore — frost giant documented in Icelandic oral tradition.

name: Fuath
description: The Fuath is a class of malevolent water spirits from Scottish Highland folklore, whose name literally translates to 'hate' or 'hatred' in Gaelic. These dangerous entities inhabit the lochs, rivers, and coastal waters of Scotland, particularly in the remote regions of the Highlands and the Hebrides. The Fuath is considered an umbrella classification that includes several specific types of water spirits, such as the Each-Uisge (water horse) and the Tarbh-Uisge (water bull). Unlike the more familiar kelpie, which primarily targets children, the Fuath is known to attack adults without discrimination, representing the most dangerous aspects of Scotland's cold, dark waters

name: Funkwe (Giant Water Snake)
description: The Funkwe is a giant hybrid water snake of Lamba tradition in Zambia, guardian of the lakes Nakamwale, Kashiba and Namulolobwe and of their mistress the Chitapo, a female lake spirit sometimes shown as a mermaid or as a diamond the serpent holds in its mouth. It protects treasure, governs rainfall and fertility, and some scholars read it and the Chitapo as a single myth that later diverged.

name: Fureytha
description: Fureytha are shimmering reef spirits in Maldivian folklore — luminous, protective water beings inhabiting coral reefs and lagoons. They embody the fragile beauty of the marine ecosystem and guide or warn fishermen. Playful and protective, they emphasize reef preservation. Part of pre-Islamic Maldivian animist tradition, later syncretized. Documented in Maldivian oral narratives.

name: Futakuchi-Onna Variant
description: This Cameroonian variant of the two-mouthed woman draws from Central African witchcraft traditions, where the concept of hidden bodily anomalies as markers of supernatural power is common. Unlike the Japanese Futakuchi-onna, which typically results from a miserly husband starving his wife, the Cameroonian variant is associated with the deliberate acquisition of occult power through black magic. In Cameroon's diverse spiritual traditions, witches are believed to gain extraordinary abilities through pacts with malevolent spirits, often marked by physical transformations. This variant reflects both indigenous beliefs about witchcraft and the universal folklore motif of hidden hunger and insatiable appetite

name: Fylgja
description: The Fylgja is a guardian spirit that accompanies a person throughout their life, acting as a mirror of their soul and a harbinger of their fate. In Swedish folklore, every person is born with a Fylgja, usually in the form of an animal that matches the person's temperament (e.g., a bear for a strong leader, a fox for a cunning trickster). The Fylgja is not always seen, but it often appears in dreams or as a fleeting glimpse in the corner of the eye. Its most critical role is appearing shortly before a person's death, warning them of the coming end

name: Fylgje
description: Fylgje (also fylgja, from Old Norse fylgja meaning to follow) is a guardian or following spirit in Norwegian folklore with roots in Old Norse religion. The fylgje is a spirit that accompanies a person from birth, usually appearing in animal form — a bird, fish, bear, wolf, or horse. It is normally invisible but can appear in dreams or in critical moments. The fylgje's actions reflect the fate of the person: if the fylgje is seen by others, it foretells the person's death. In Vestlandet tradition, the fylgje was particularly associated with specific families — each family had its own fylgje animal (often a bear for powerful families, a seal for coastal families). The fylgje could also appear as a woman (in which case she was called a fylgjukona) who acted as a protective matron for the family line. The concept bridges Old Norse pagan belief and later Norwegian folklore

name: Fänggen
description: Fänggen (singular: Fängge) are gigantic female wood sprites or wild women from Alpine German folklore, particularly found in Bavarian and Tyrolean traditions. They are described as hairy, ugly giantesses as tall as trees, often considered the female counterpart of the wild man or moss-grown mountain giant. In the Bavarian Upper Palatinate, smaller dwarf-like variants called Fankerl or Waldfänken also exist, with shaggy beards and glowing red eyes. Fänggen are man-eating creatures who live in the deep forests and prey on travelers who lose their way

name: Fänggen
description: Fänggen (singular: Fängge) are gigantic female wood sprites or wild women from Alpine German folklore, particularly found in Bavarian and Tyrolean traditions. They are described as hairy, ugly giantesses as tall as trees, often considered the female counterpart of the wild man or moss-grown mountain giant. In the Bavarian Upper Palatinate, smaller dwarf-like variants called Fankerl or Waldfänken also exist, with shaggy beards and glowing red eyes. Fänggen are man-eating creatures who live in the deep forests and prey on travelers who lose their way In Germany folklore, this figure is known among the Germany people.

name: Fée
description: The Fée (French fairy) tradition represents one of Europe's most sophisticated and influential fairy lore systems, deeply interwoven with French literature, court culture, and folk magic. Unlike the diminutive winged fairies of Victorian England, the French Fée are powerful supernatural women—often of noble stature and immense magical ability—who intervene directly in human affairs. This tradition reached its literary zenith in the 17th century salon culture, where writers like Charles Perrault and Madame d'Aulnoy codified tales of fairy godmothers, enchanted objects, and magical transformations. The word 'fairy' itself derives from the Old French 'faerie,' meaning enchantment or magical realm

name: Ga-Gorib
description: Ga-Gorib is a fearsome monster from Khoikhoi mythology who sat at the edge of a deep hole, challenging passersby to throw a stone at his forehead. The stone would bounce back and kill the thrower, who would then fall into the pit. The trickster hero Heitsi-Eibib refused the challenge and instead distracted Ga-Gorib before striking him behind the ear. Ga-Gorib lost his balance and fell into his own pit, dying in the hole he had prepared for others. Ga-Gorib represents the cosmic obstacle that must be overcome through cleverness rather than direct confrontation

name: GaayhllGa Jaad (Flood-Tide-Woman)
description: In Haida tradition the woman whose rising caused the great flood is a tide-controlling figure: mocked for her seaweed-like backbone, she sat at the water's edge and the tide rose with her until the whole island flooded, scattering the people on rafts to different lands. The episode appears in Swanton's Haida Texts and Myths and has been linked to post-glacial sea-level rise.

name: Gaayhllga Jaad Flood Tide Woman Haida
description: Gaayhllga Jaad, the Flood Tide Woman, belongs to the Haida tradition of a great deluge. In the story told by Chief Young of Haida Gwaii, a woman wrapped in an unfamiliar fur cape was mocked by children; as she sat by the shore the water rose, sweeping away villages and scattering the survivors on crude rafts. Geologists read the tale as a distant memory of post-glacial sea-level rise.

name: Gadyucha
description: The Gadyucha is a death-omen spirit from Turkmen folklore, taking the form of a gigantic owl that foretells mortality and misfortune. In Turkmen and broader Central Asian traditions, owls are considered potent omens associated with cemeteries, ruins, and the boundary between the living and the dead. The Gadyucha is most often described as female, reflecting the Central Asian belief that female spirits are particularly attuned to matters of life and death. This spirit plays a significant role in Turkmen folk medicine and spiritual practice, as its feathers and bones are sometimes used in protective amulets, and its appearance is taken seriously as a warning to prepare for impending transitions

name: Gahe (Mountain Spirits)
description: The Gahe (Gaan in Western Apache) are the Mountain Spirits, powerful supernatural beings in Apache tradition who live inside sacred mountains. They appear as masked dancers wearing distinctive tall wooden-slat headdresses with black-and-white body paint and black buckskin kilts. The Gahe ceremony is central to the Girls' Puberty Ceremony (Sunrise Ceremony), the longest and richest Apache ritual. Four Mountain Spirits typically dance together with a clown figure, moving in syncopated rhythm to si

name: Galamani
description: Galamani is the sacred serpent of the Fulani epic of Silamaka and Pullori, the legendary heroes of the Macina region of Mali. When Silamaka consulted a geomancer to gain invulnerability against the Bambara king Da Monzon Diarra, he was told he must first capture the sacred serpent Galamani alive. With his companion Pullori's help, Silamaka succeeded where many had failed, capturing the serpent and fashioning a protective belt from it. Galamani represents the invulnerability charm and the magical power inherent in the natural world that heroes must master before they can achieve greatness

name: Galone
description: Galone, the Burmese garuda, is a golden bird-king of Myanmar's Buddhist-influenced cosmology who eternally wars with the nāga serpents. Revered as a protective divinity, his image was mass-tattooed during the 1930 Saya San uprising, when followers believed the galone sigil would shield them from bullets, and he remains a symbol of royal and resistant power.

name: Galuxwadzuwus (Crooked-Beak)
description: Galuxwadzuwus, the Crooked-Beak of Heaven, is a man-eating bird of the Kwakwaka'wakw winter ceremonial, one of the cannibal attendants of the great devourer Baxbaxwalanuksiwe at the North End of the World. Dancers who wear his long, downward-curving beak mask in the Hamatsa ceremony tame his uncontrolled hunger through ritual.

name: Gamlingene oppi Steinberget
description: Gamlingene oppi Steinberget (the Old Men in Steinberget) is a Trøndelag legend about a group of ancient spirits who live inside Steinberget (Stone Mountain), a prominent rock formation in Trøndelag. According to tradition documented in Birger Sivertsen's 'Eventyr og sagn fra Trøndelag', these 'gamlinger' are the spirits of wise old men from ancient times who were taken into the mountain rather than dying. They live inside Steinberget in a great hall lit by subterranean fires, where they sit around a stone table discussing ancient wisdom, the weather, and the affairs of the local community. At night, their voices can sometimes be heard murmuring from cracks in the rock. They are generally benevolent, occasionally helping lost travelers or warning the community of coming disasters, but they dislike loud noises and disrespectful behavior near their mountain

name: Gan
description: The Gan (also spelled Gaan or Ga'an) are sacred mountain spirit beings in Apache tradition, central to the spiritual and ceremonial life of the Western Apache, Chiricahua, and other Apache groups. The Creator, known as Usen, sent these powerful spirit beings to teach the Apache people how to live in harmony with the land, each other, and the spirit world. The Gan are ancient messengers and teachers whose wisdom is preserved in over a thousand years of ceremonial songs. They are primarily channeled during the Apache Crown Dance (Gaan Dance), a healing and protection ceremony where masked dancers become the living embodiment of these mountain spirits

name: Gandharva (Celestial Musician)
description: Gandharvas are a class of celestial beings in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions who serve as divine musicians and singers in the courts of the gods. Originating in the Rigveda as a singular celestial being who watches over Soma, they evolved into a class of minor deities numbering 6,333 according to the Atharvaveda. They are described as handsome beings who wear fragrant attire and have exceptional musical skills. In Hindu cosmology, they are the musicians of Indra's court and the husbands of the Apsaras (celestial dancers). Gandharvas guard the sacred Soma drink and play beautiful music for the devas in their palaces. Some are part-animal, usually with bird or horse features. They are associated with fertility and virility, and in Hindu law, a 'gandharva marriage' is one contracted by mutual consent without formal rituals. In Buddhism, gandharvas are among the lowest-ranking devas who dwell in scents and fragrances, and the term also refers to beings in the intermediate state between death and rebirth

name: Ganesha
description: Ganesha (Unknown). is a deity. Ganesha is the elephant-headed god of wisdom, prosperity, and obstacle removal in Hinduism. He is one of the most widely worshipped deities in the Hindu pantheon.. Source: Hindu scripture; widespread living tradition

name: Gangikozō
description: Gangikozō is a yokai from Japanese folklore, known as a riverbank-dwelling water spirit that belongs to the broader kappa family of aquatic creatures. Its name combines 'gangi' (riverbank or stepped pier) and 'kozō' (young boy or priest), suggesting its youthful appearance and riverside habitat. According to folklorists, Gangikozō may represent a transitional form of kappa, existing between the fully aquatic water spirit and a hairy mountain spirit. This yokai was first catalogued by the famous Edo-period artist Toriyama Sekien in his supernatural bestiary, though local legends of similar creatures predate his compilation by centuries

name: Gangsi
description: The Gangsi is a river spirit from Korean folklore, particularly associated with the southern regions of the Korean Peninsula. Described as a merman-like being, the Gangsi controls the movements of fish and the bounty of freshwater fisheries, making it a figure of great importance to fishing communities. In Korean folk religion, water spirits like the Gangsi are classified as 'sin' (deities) of intermediate rank, capable of both blessing and punishing humans depending on how they are treated. The Gangsi tradition reflects Korea's deep cultural connection to its rivers and the importance of maintaining proper relationships with the spirit world through rituals and offerings

name: Gara Yakka (Sinhalese Demon of Disease)
description: Gara Yakka is a prominent demon in Sinhalese folklore, part of the Daha Ata Sanniya (the eighteen maladies) — a group of eighteen diseases believed to be caused by demonic possession. He is portrayed as a fearsome Yaksha (demon) who was once a mortal wrongdoer transformed into a malevolent spirit. Gara Yakka is particularly associated with causing childhood illnesses, fevers, convulsions, and nightmares. According to Sinhalese demonology, he is one of the most feared disease-bringers, capable of inflicting severe suffering on his victims. The traditional exorcism rituals to counter Gara Yakka involve the Yak Deshiya or Devil Dance, a complex performance where masked dancers embody the demon and enact his subjugation through drumming, chanting, and dance. These rituals blend Buddhist, Hindu, and indigenous animist traditions and are performed by specialist exorcist-priests (adura or kattadiya). Gara Yakka is neither purely evil nor good — like many Sinhalese yakshas, he can be both a disease-bringer and a protector when properly propitiated

name: Garamantes (Ancient Desert Giants)
description: The Garamantes are a legendary people of ancient Libya, described by Greco-Roman sources and Berber oral tradition as powerful desert warriors, often attributed with giant stature or superhuman abilities. According to the Greek historian Herodotus (5th century BC), the Garamantes were a great people who inhabited the interior of Libya, herding cattle and driving four-horse chariots across the Sahara. In Berber mythology, the Garamantes are remembered as powerful ancestral figures who built an elaborate underground irrigation system (foggara) and ruled over a desert kingdom in the Fezzan region of southwestern Libya. Archaeology has confirmed that the Garamantes were a real civilization (c. 1000 BC - 500 AD) with a sophisticated society, but their legendary depiction often exaggerates their size, strength, and magical abilities. The Garamantes are said to have possessed knowledge of the spirit world, could communicate with desert jinn, and built their capital city Garama using techniques taught by supernatural beings. Their kingdom was called 'a legend of wealth and power' by ancient writers

name: Garang
description: Garang is the first man in Dinka mythology of South Sudan, created alongside Abuk, the first woman, by the supreme creator Nhialic. According to Dinka creation tradition, Nhialic formed Garang and Abuk from the rich clay of Sudan, then placed them in a huge pot. When the creator opened the pot, Garang and Abuk emerged as fully formed human beings. Nhialic gave them only one grain of corn each per day for sustenance, which left them perpetually hungry. When Abuk began hoarding and planting grain for agriculture, the creator was displeased, but this act of innovation ultimately shaped human civilization. Garang represents the first human male in Dinka cosmology and, together with Abuk, establishes the foundation of Dinka lineage and society. Unlike Abuk who has specific symbols and continued worship, Garang is primarily significant as the male half of the primordial pair. Their children included Deng, the powerful god of rain and fertility, making Garang the ancestor of a divine lineage as well as humanity

name: Garcis (or Gartis)
description: Garcis (also known as Gartis) is a giant from Latvian mythology, sharing characteristics with giants found throughout Baltic and Slavic folklore. These beings are described as incredibly strong but not particularly intelligent, often creating landscape features accidentally through their clumsy actions. In Latvian folk songs (dainas), which preserve much of the pre-Christian Baltic mythological tradition, Garcis appears as a semi-comic figure whose enormous strength is matched only by his naivety. He is the Latvian cognate of the Lithuanian Gigantis and shares similarities with the Norse jotunn and Slavic velikany, representing the raw, untamed forces of nature that shaped the Baltic landscape

name: Gardvord
description: Gardvord (farm guardian) is the older, original Norwegian farm guardian spirit, predating the nisse in Norwegian folk tradition. The gardvord was believed to be the first person buried on a farm or the founding ancestor whose spirit remained to protect the farmstead. Unlike the bearded nisse, the gardvord was often described as a small, naked child or a tiny old man who lived in a tree on the farm, usually an ash or elm. Offerings were made at this tree. The gardvord tradition was strongest in western and northern Norway, distinct from the nisse tradition of Østlandet. The name comes from gard (farm) + vord (guardian). Closely related to the Swedish tomte and Danish husnisse

name: Garuda
description: Hindu divine eagle - King OF Birds, mount (vahana) of Vishnu. Sanskrit: 'Garuḍa' from 'gṛ' (to swallow/devour). Half-Brother of Aruna (sun's charioteer). Birth: from egg of Vinata (Kaśyapa's wife). Her sister Kadru mothered Nagas (serpents). Rivalry: Kadru tricked Vinata into slavery. VOW: Garuda would free her by earning Amrita (nectar of immortality) for the serpents. HE Stole it from gods, waged war on Indra and all devas, Defeated them. Vishnu impressed, granted Immortality before he even got the nectar. In gratitude, became Vishnu's eternal mount. Enmity with serpents lasted - he ate them to sustain himself on journey. Symbolizes triumph of good over evil. Carried mountain Mandara during Samudra Manthan (churning of ocean)

name: Gashadokuro
description: Gashadokuro is a colossal skeletal yokai from Japanese folklore formed from the vengeful bones of people who died of starvation or in battle without proper burial rites. The name derives from the onomatopoeic gachi gachi meaning the rattling sound of bones, and dokuro meaning skull. These towering spirits stand between fifty and one hundred feet tall, emerging only during the darkest hours of night near ancient battlefields and mass grave sites. Their creation stems from the accumulated grudges of the unburied dead whose anger ferments into a supernatural force. The earliest recorded legend dates back over one thousand years to the rebellion of Taira no Masakado, whose sorceress daughter Takiyasha-hime summoned a great skeleton from fallen soldiers using black magic to attack Kyoto

name: Gast
description: Gast is the general Swedish term for a ghost or returning dead person (gengångare), not a specific water spirit. The input record misclassifies it as a 'water spirit' with 'storm calling' abilities. In Swedish folk belief, gast/gengångare are restless dead who haunt specific places, cause cold spots, and can be laid to rest through proper burial rites or exorcism.

name: Gatekeeper (Maya)
description: In Maya mythology and folklore, Gatekeepers are powerful guardian spirits known as Balam or Balaam, which means jaguar in the Maya language. These tutelary beings serve as protectors of villages, agricultural fields, and sacred spaces throughout the Maya region spanning modern-day Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and Honduras. The balam are considered spiritual guardians who defend their communities from evil spirits and natural threats, most active during the night hours in reflection of the jaguar's nocturnal nature. In Maya cosmology, four principal balam spirits are associated with the four cardinal directions, each protecting their specific territory and warding off storms, floods, and disasters. These directional guardians maintain harmony between the physical and spiritual worlds, and their worship was integral to pre-Columbian Maya religion that continues in modified form today

name: Gazar-bichig
description: Not independently attested: the name combines Mongolian 'gazar' (land, place) and 'bichig' (script, document), meaning a land document or map, not a spirit. No household or forest spirit called Gazar-bichig is documented in Mongolian folk religion. The real vertical script Mongol Bichig and the lamaist reverence for texts are factual, but the personified 'spirit of sacred manuscripts' is invented.

name: Gbahali
description: The gbahali is a giant crocodile-like cryptid reported from the rivers, swamps and waterways of Liberia, part of local oral tradition and popular cryptozoology. Witnesses describe a short-snouted, lizard-headed beast with more erect limbs than a crocodile, reaching up to about a hundred feet; some link it to a surviving prehistoric reptile or a misidentified monitor lizard.

name: Gbekre
description: Gbekre is a powerful spirit-deity of the Baoulé people of Ivory Coast, often depicted as a baboon-like figure serving as a judge of souls and protector against evil forces. Unlike the refined, polished ancestor statues typical of Baoulé art, Gbekre figures are intentionally rough-hewn and coarse, combining human and animal features in a deliberately unsettling manner. This crudeness is symbolic of Gbekre's role as a 'humbler' deity who judges the dead and protects the living against sorcerers and malevolent spirits. Gbekre figures, also known as bowl-bearing monkey figures, are used in various cult practices including trance divination, the Mbra society rituals, and as protective talismans against witchcraft. The name 'gbekre' actually means 'mouse' in the Baoulé language, though early French ethnographers mistakenly identified these figures as 'baboon gods.' Despite this etymological confusion, Gbekre remains an important spirit in Baoulé cosmology, associated with judgment, protection, and the enforcement of moral order

name: Geb (Earth God of Egypt)
description: Geb is the Egyptian god of the earth, lying beneath his wife-sister Nut (sky). He was separated from her by their father Shu (air), who holds Nut aloft. Geb is the father of Osiris, Isis, Set, Nephthys, and Horus the Elder. He was considered a benevolent king of the gods in early times. Earthquakes are the laughter of Geb. He is often depicted with green skin, representing vegetation, lying on his back with one knee raised. The dead were said to be 'embraced by Geb' and he judged souls alongside Osiris. He was associated with agriculture (crops grow from his body), healing (as a healer of snake bites), and also as a weigher of the dead's hearts

name: Gesar of Ling
description: Gesar of Ling is the culture-hero of the Tibetan epic: a warrior-prince born in humble guise who grows to unite the kingdom of Ling and slay demons across the Himalayan world. Superhumanly strong and able to shape-shift, he battles evil kings and monsters; his epic is among the longest in the world and is still performed by bards.

name: Geser Khan
description: Geser Khan (Geser Bumba Khan) is the heroic ruler of Mongolian legend: an epic warrior descended from the gods who descends to the earth to destroy the demons oppressing the human world. Divine-born, shape-changing, and demon-slaying, he represents the ideal of protective, righteous heroism in the pan-Mongolian Geser epic cycle.

name: Gewi
description: Gewi (Unknown). is a deity. Gewi (also spelled Gcwi) is the second son of Kaang (Cagn), the supreme creator god in San (Bushman) mythology. He appears alongside his elder brother Cogaz in the creation myths of the Maluti Bushmen. Source: San (Bushman) mythology; Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd, 1911)

name: Ghost
description: Ghost (Generic). is a spirit. The spirit of a deceased person that remains in the physical world, often due to unfinished business. Source: Global folklore, paranormal studies

name: Ghost Iceland
description: Ghost Iceland (Unknown). is a ghost. Icelandic ghosts (draugar) are revenants from Norse and Icelandic folklore. Unlike the transparent spirits of modern depictions, Icelandic draugar are physical, corporeal undead beings that can cause . Source: Icelandic sagas; Nordic folklore traditions

name: Ghostly Chieftain Iceland
description: Ghostly Chieftain Iceland (Unknown). is a human. A ghostly chieftain from Icelandic saga tradition returns after death to guide or terrorize the living.. Source: Icelandic folklore — ghost documented in Icelandic sagas and folk belief.

name: Ghosts Chinook
description: In the Chinook texts recorded by Franz Boas, the dead live in a shadowy town where they appear as skeletons and whisper in the dark. The tale of Blue-Jay and Ioi tells how Blue-Jay's dead sister Ioi is taken as a ghost bride at night, and how Blue-Jay travels to the afterworld to bring her back, only to see the dead fall to pieces at dawn.

name: Ghosts Iceland
description: Ghosts Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. Ghosts draugar from Icelandic folklore are the restless dead who rise from graves to haunt the living.. Source: Icelandic folklore — ghosts documented in Icelandic folk belief.

name: Ghoul
description: In Palestinian folklore, the Ghoul (Ghul) is a terrifying female shapeshifting monster that preys on travelers, especially at night. The ghoul is one of the most feared entities in Palestinian oral tradition, second only to jinn in prevalence. Unlike the Western concept of ghouls as male undead, the Arabic ghul is always female (grammatically feminine in Arabic) and is classified as a type of evil jinn. Palestinian stories describe ghouls dwelling in desolate areas, graveyards, and ruins where they wait to lure passing humans. The ghoul's primary method is deception — it transforms into an attractive woman, a familiar relative, or even a child in distress to lure victims close before devouring them. The ghoul appears prominently in Palestinian versions of One Thousand and One Nights tales

name: Ghoul
description: Ghoul is a demon from Iraq mythology. The ghoul is one of the most feared entities in Palestinian oral tradition, second only to jinn in prevalence. Unlike the Western concept of ghouls as male undead, the Arabic ghul is always female (grammatically feminine in Arabic) and is classified as a type of evil jinn. The ghoul appears prominently in Palestinian versions of One Thousand and One Nights tales

name: Ghoul
description: The ghoul is a flesh-eating desert demon of Arab and Jordanian folklore, classed among the diabolical jinn and said to be offspring of Iblis. It haunts graveyards, ruins, and empty wastes, shifting shape freely but betrayed by its unalterable ass's hooves. Usually female, it lures travellers as an old woman or lost relative, then devours them; a single blow kills it, a second restores it to life.

name: Ghul
description: The Ghul is one of the most feared creatures in pre-Islamic and Arabian folklore, originating from the Bedouin traditions of the Arabian Peninsula including Saudi Arabia. Ghuls are shapeshifting demons belonging to the jinn, inhabiting deserts, cemeteries, and abandoned places. They lure unwary travelers by appearing as trusted figures, especially beautiful women, then devour them. Ghuls have ass-like feet that they cannot hide, the only way to identify them. A famous pre-Islamic poem recounts the warrior-poet Ta'abbata Sharra's fight with a ghul. According to Islamic tradition, ghuls are rebellious jinn struck by comets when trying to eavesdrop on heaven, deformed into insane desert demons

name: Gia Lâm
description: Not independently attested. No Vietnamese source records a forest spirit named 'Gia Lâm': the name is a district of Hanoi, birthplace of the hero Saint Giong, while 'già làng' denotes a Central Highlands village elder, a human role rather than a supernatural being. The 'old man of the trees' guardian account is generic template prose with no documentary basis.

name: Giant
description: Giant (European). is a giant. Humanoids of colossal size and strength, often depicted as primordial beings who helped shape the geography of the world. Source: European mythology, Greek and Norse oral traditions

name: Giant Cat Iceland
description: Giant Cat Iceland (Unknown). is a giant. The giant Yule Cat Jolakotturinn from Icelandic folklore devours those without new Christmas clothes.. Source: Icelandic folklore — the giant cat of Icelandic oral tradition.

name: Giant Cloud-swallower
description: Häki Suto, the Giant Cloud-Swallower, is a Zuni ogre who brought drought by drinking the clouds from the sky, so the rains failed and the people starved. In Zuni folk tales the War Twins pursued and slew him, freeing the clouds so the waters returned to the land, explaining drought and the restoration of rain through the twins' heroism.

name: Giant Iceland
description: Giant Iceland (Unknown). is a giant. A giant from Icelandic folklore is a massive being living in the highlands often hostile to humans.. Source: Icelandic folklore — giant figures documented in Icelandic oral tradition.

name: Giant monster
description: In the Origin Myth of Acoma, the hero twins Masewi and Oyoyewi, born from the piñon nuts of Sun Youth, destroyed the monsters that terrorized the emerging Pueblo people. The record's 'giant monster so large it could consume entire villages' condenses this Acoma cycle, in which the twins hunted and slew giant beings across the land.

name: Giant Wolf
description: Giant Wolf (Icelandic). is a beast. A massive white wolf that guards a hidden paradise in the Icelandic highlands. Source: Icelandic folklore Found in The entrances to the Hidden Valley in the Icelandic highlands. Documented in ethnographic records.

name: Giantress (Old Woman Giant)
description: In the Chinook origin account, an old giantess, wise in the protocols of the spirit world, gave tools and guidance as the South Wind hatched Thunderbird's egg on Saddleback Mountain; the children that emerged became the first Chinook people. The tale also explains why salmon are sliced in a particular way, following the giantess's instructions.

name: Giants (Jætter)
description: Jætter (ON jötnar) are a primordial race in Norse/Danish tradition, not mere giants. Descend from Ymir, dwell in Jötunheimr, ancestors of Odin and Thor. Terms: risi, þurs, troll (male), gýgr (female). Embody chaotic nature and wisdom; gods seek them for secret knowledge. Later folklore demonised them as dim-witted mountain-dwellers turned to stone by sun.

name: Giants Denmark
description: Giants Denmark (Unknown). is a giant. Giants are massive humanoid beings from Danish folklore who dwell in the mountains and often interact with human heroes.. Source: Danish folklore — giant figures documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Gikuyu
description: Gikuyu is the first man and founding ancestor of the Kikuyu people. According to tradition, Ngai (the supreme god) created Gikuyu and took him to the summit of Mount Kenya (Kirinyaga). From this sacred vantage point, Ngai showed Gikuyu the beautiful highlands below and instructed him to build his homestead at Mukurwe wa Gathanga, where many mugumo (wild fig) trees grew. Ngai gave Gikuyu the land with its rivers, forests, and animals, establishing a covenant. At Mukurwe wa Gathanga, Gikuyu found Mumbi, the first woman, who became his wife. Together they had nine daughters who became the founders of the nine Kikuyu clans. When it was time for them to marry, Gikuyu prayed to Ngai beneath the fig tree, and nine young men appeared. Gikuyu represents the ideal relationship between humans and the divine

name: Giltinė
description: Giltinė is the goddess of death in Lithuanian mythology, one of the oldest and most feared deities in the Baltic pantheon. Her name derives from Lithuanian words gelti meaning to sting or to pierce, and geltonis meaning yellow, both referring to her venomous killing method and pale complexion. Giltinė is considered the sister of Laima, the goddess of fate and childbirth, representing the complementary forces of birth and death in Baltic cosmology. In Lithuanian tradition, Giltinė does not act as a malevolent force but rather as a necessary aspect of the natural cycle of existence. She is accompanied by her sacred bird, the owl, whose hooting is considered an omen of death. Giltinė evolved from earlier beliefs where death was personified by the owl itself before taking human form. She has various alternative names including Kaulinyčia meaning bony one, Maras associated with plague, and Kapinių žmogus meaning graveyard person. Her mythology reflects the Baltic understanding of death as an inevitable transition rather than an end

name: Gizo
description: Gizo is the spider trickster of Hausa folklore, a clever but overconfident schemer whose plans often backfire spectacularly. In one well-known tale, Gizo tries to outwit the Wisdom Bird but fails, teaching that intelligence without humility leads to ruin. Another story tells of him building a luxury lagoon home through trickery by convincing other animals to build it for him, claiming a magical competition. Gizo embodies both the cleverness and the folly of human nature, serving as a moral compass for Hausa communities. His tales, told by griots across Nigeria and Niger with drumming and call-and-response, teach the dangers of greed and the value of community

name: Glacial Nykur
description: The nykur (or nennir) is a water horse from Icelandic folklore, documented by Jón Árnason. It appears as a beautiful grey horse near lakes and rivers, but its hooves are reversed. Anyone who mounts it becomes stuck fast and is dragged into the water to drown. The creature can be defeated by calling its true name, causing it to lose power and vanish.

name: Glaistig
description: The Glaistig is a haunting spirit from Scottish mythology, classified as a type of fuath or supernatural being that haunts the Scottish Highlands and islands. Also known as Maighdean Uaine or the Green Maiden, this ambivalent creature appears in legends across Scotland with both benevolent and malevolent traits. The name derives from Scottish Gaelic glas meaning gray, wan, or pale green, reflecting her characteristic coloring. The glaistig is deeply connected to specific locations such as castles, farms, and grazing lands where she forms attachments lasting for generations. Her mythology shows clear influence from Norse folklore, particularly the hulder or hidden folk of Scandinavian tradition. In the Highlands, she is sometimes associated with particular clan histories, acting as a tutelary spirit for certain families. The glaistig represents the ambiguous nature of Celtic fairy beings who could be helpful or harmful depending on how they were treated, embodying the capricious relationship between humans and the supernatural world in Scottish tradition

name: Glooscap
description: Glooscap is the great culture hero and transformer of the Mi'kmaq and Wabanaki peoples. According to the Mi'kmaq creation story, he was created when lightning struck the earth three times, and he lay for 365 nights with his head to the rising sun. Huge in size and powers, he created natural features such as the Annapolis Valley, the Five Islands of Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island (Abegweit). He defeated monsters like the giant frog who swallowed all the water, the Wind Eagle who caused too much wind, and the evil frost giants. He gave the people tobacco and taught them the sacred ceremonies

name: Gloson
description: Gloson (Glo-so, 'Glowing Sow') is a Swedish spectral boar with glowing eyes and a saw-toothed ridge along its back, charging at travelers on roads and running between their legs to split them open. A death omen in Swedish folk belief, documented by Hyltén-Cavallius and Ebbe Schön. Related to the Germanic tradition of spectral beasts. The name derives from 'glo' (glow) + 'so' (sow).

name: Gluskabe
description: Gluskabe is the Abenaki version of the Wabanaki culture hero, created from the dust of the Great Spirit Tabaldak's hands after he finished creating humans. According to Abenaki tradition, Gluskabe and his evil twin brother Malsumis were born together — Gluskabe given the power to create a good world full of kind animals, sweet fruits, and gentle rivers. He captured the Wind Eagle to stop the constant wind, stole tobacco from Grasshopper for the people, founded the First Mother's corn sacrifice, and taught the people how to live. His grandmother Nokomes advised him through all his adventures

name: Gnefro
description: The Gnefro is a legendary household spirit from the folklore of the Umbria region of central Italy, particularly associated with the Valnerina valley, the Marmore Falls area, Lake Piediluco, and the territory between Terni and Rieti. These diminutive creatures are deeply rooted in Italian rural folk tradition, representing a local variation of the widespread European belief in domestic spirits. The gnefro shares characteristics with Roman lares and penates, Slavic domovoi, and Germanic kobolds, suggesting a common Indo-European origin for household spirit beliefs. In Umbrian tradition, gnefri live in small groups near waterfalls, rivers, and forests, particularly around the spectacular Cascata delle Marmore, one of Italy's tallest waterfalls. They are considered protectors of households and homes, though their capricious nature means they can cause as much mischief as they provide help. The belief in gnefri reflects the Roman Catholic influence on pre-Christian Italian folk beliefs, where ancient pagan household spirits were transformed into folklore figures rather than fully suppressed

name: Goblin
description: A goblin is a small, grotesque, mischievous spirit of English folklore, from the family of household and wilderness spirits that includes hobgoblins and boggarts. Goblins are chiefly pranksters who cause annoyance rather than real harm. The word likely comes from the French gobelin or medieval Latin gobelinus, and the figure has spread widely through literature and fantasy.

name: Goblin
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature as a Danish being. The description is the English goblin entry copy-pasted with a filler line; 'goblin' names no Danish tradition, whose household spirit is the nisse and whose wilderness beings are the trold and elverfolk.

name: Golden Frog
description: The Golden Frog is a being of Mongolian creation myth: the earth rests on a giant golden frog, and when the frog stirs, the land shakes. Sometimes shown with arrows or bolts pinning it in place, it symbolizes the fixed foundation of the world in Mongol and regional Central Asian cosmology.

name: Golem
description: The Golem is an animated anthropomorphic being from Jewish folklore created entirely from inanimate matter, typically clay or mud, brought to life through Kabbalistic rituals and the invocation of divine names. The most famous golem legend is that of the Golem of Prague, created by Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel, known as the Maharal of Prague, in the late sixteenth century to protect the Jewish community from blood libel accusations and persecution. The word golem appears in the Hebrew Bible in Psalm 139:16, where it means unformed substance or embryo, later evolving to mean an unfinished or shapeless being. The concept of golem-making was part of Jewish mystical tradition, where creating a golem was seen as a way for medieval Jewish mystics to come closer to understanding God's creation of Adam. The golem legend represents themes of artificial life, the limits of human power, and the dangers of creating beings that cannot be controlled. The story has inspired countless literary and artistic works, establishing the golem as a foundational figure in the mythology of artificial beings

name: Golem-Bakku
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Sri Lankan folklore. No source documents a water-spirit named 'Golem-Bakku' protecting wells or springs; the name is neither Sinhala nor Tamil and resembles the Japanese baku (dream-eater), not a Sri Lankan being. Genuine Sri Lankan guardian spirits are the devata, yaka and nāga figures invoked around water and shrines.

name: Gondol
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Setesdal source, including Johannes Skar's Gamalt or Sætesdal, records a lake spirit named 'gondol', and the name is best known as a Norwegian cable-car brand. Genuine Setesdal water-lore centers on the nøkk (näk); 'gondol' appears in no ethnographic record.

name: Goreu
description: Goreu fab Custennin is not a shapeshifting spirit but a hero of the Welsh tale Culhwch ac Olwen in the Mabinogion: son of Custennin the giant and cousin to Arthur, he joins Culhwch's quest and, at the story's end, beheads the giant chieftain Ysbaddaden, whose fortress and lands he receives. His name means 'best'.

name: Goubet Monster
description: Ghoubbet al-Kharab, a cliff-ringed cove on the Gulf of Tadjoura in Djibouti, is locally known as the 'Gulf of Demons'; the enclosed basin, nearly 200 m deep with violent currents, has long been linked in Afar and Somali coastal belief to sheytan and other supernatural beings. Occasional cryptid-monster claims circulate, but no such creature has been documented.

name: Gramya Devata
description: Gramya Devata or Gramadevata are village deities from Bengali and wider Hindu folk tradition, serving as local guardian spirits that protect specific hamlets, fields, water sources, and communities across the Indian subcontinent. The Sanskrit term combines grama meaning village and devata meaning deity, referring to the localized nature of these gods whose authority is tied to particular geographic areas. In Bengal, these deities form a crucial layer of popular Hinduism that coexists with the greater pantheon of Puranic gods, representing the grassroots expression of religious devotion. Gramya devatas are among the most ancient forms of worship in South Asia, with archaeological evidence suggesting continuity of village deity veneration dating back to the Harappan civilization of the third millennium BCE. Each village traditionally has its own specific deity with unique name, mythology, and festival calendar, creating an extraordinarily diverse tapestry of local religious practice. These deities are intimately connected with agricultural cycles, village welfare, and protection from natural disasters and disease

name: Gravfrun
description: Gravfrun (the grave lady) is a female guardian spirit of burial mounds, grave fields, and churchyards in Swedish folklore. She appears as a woman in white or black, sitting on ancient burial mounds at dusk or standing silently among the gravestones. Gravfrun is the protector of the dead — she wards off grave robbers, those who would disturb ancient burials, and anyone disrespecting the dead. She is particularly associated with Bronze Age and Iron Age burial mounds, which were considered sacred places inhabited by the dead and their guardians. Anyone digging into an ancient mound would be stopped by Gravfrun — she might cause the digger to fall ill, send nightmares, or simply appear and drive them away with her terrifying presence

name: Gravso
description: Gravsoen (the Grave Sow), also called Gloso, is a ghostly pig that haunts churchyards and ancient burial grounds in Danish folklore. The oldest recorded account comes from Copenhagen in 1587, where a ghostly sow with glowing red eyes was seen near Sankt Clemens Church. She has razor-sharp bristles along her back and is sometimes headless, sometimes followed by seven or twelve piglets. According to folk belief, the Gravso is the spirit of an unbaptized murdered infant, and the piglets are the ghosts of other unbaptized children. The sow could be laid to rest only if someone found the child's remains and gave them a Christian burial. In Frørup Church in Sjælland, the Gravso is said to guard a hidden treasure beneath the church floor

name: Great Buzzard
description: In the Cherokee account of creation, the Great Buzzard flew over the soft, newly dried earth. Each downward beat of his enormous wings created a valley, each upward stroke a mountain, shaping the rolling landscape of the Cherokee homeland. The story, told in Mooney's 'How the World Was Made', explains the mountains and valleys of Cherokee country.

name: Great Coyote (Mąʼiitoʼí Áłchíní)
description: Great-Coyote-Who-Was-Formed-in-the-Water is a primordial Navajo trickster-creator of the First World. In the Origin Myths of the Navaho he emerged with First Man and First Woman when Black Cloud and White Cloud joined in the East, part of the company that shaped the emerging world and its sacred directions.

name: Great Fisher
description: The Great Fisher (Ojiig) is a heroic animal spirit from Ojibwe mythology who freed the summer birds from the underwater panther Mishipeshu's cave, bringing summer back to the world. Pursued by the enraged Mishipeshu, Fisher was lifted into the sky by spirits and transformed into the constellation known as Ojiig — the Big Dipper. Each year, when the constellation appears in the northern sky, it signals the return of spring. The Great Fisher is remembered as a selfless hero who sacrificed his freedom for the good of all creatures

name: Great Horned Serpent
description: The Great Horned Serpent (Mishiginebig) is a powerful underwater serpent of Anishinaabe mythology, ruler of the underwater world. It is described as an enormous serpent with horns or antlers, often associated with copper, storms, and the depths of the Great Lakes. The Great Horned Serpent is the eternal opponent of the Thunderbirds and the arch-enemy of Nanabozho. In one story, Nanabozho's battle with the Great Serpent caused a great flood that destroyed the world, leading to its recreation from mud brought by the muskrat

name: Great Spirit
description: The Great Spirit is the supreme creator and sustaining power in Comanche religion. According to Comanche creation, the Great Spirit collected swirls of dust from the four directions—north, south, east, and west—and molded them into strong, powerful figures, breathing life into them to create the Comanche people. The Great Spirit cast a shape-shifting demon into a bottomless pit for tormenting the people, but the demon shattered into pieces that became rattlesnakes, scorpions, and spiders. The Great Spirit also caused healing springs to bubble up after battles and provides guidance through visions and dreams

name: Great Turtle
description: The Great Turtle is the immense cosmic turtle upon whose back the earth was formed according to Iroquois and many other Northeastern Woodlands traditions. After the Sky Woman fell from the Sky World, the aquatic animals placed her on the Great Turtle's back. The muskrat brought up mud from the ocean floor, and as the Sky Woman danced in a circle, the mud grew and spread across the Turtle's shell, forming Turtle Island (North America). When the Great Turtle moves, the earth shakes, causing earthquakes

name: Green Knight (Grøn Ridder)
description: The Green Knight (Grøn Ridder) is a figure from the 14th-century Middle English Arthurian poem 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight,' not Danish folklore. He appears as Bertilak de Hautdesert, transformed by Morgan le Fay to test Arthur's court. No independent Danish folk tradition attests a 'Green Knight' as a nature guardian. The Danish name is simply a translation of the Arthurian character.

name: Green Knight Denmark
description: Green Knight Denmark (Unknown). is a human. The Green Knight is a mysterious figure from the 14th-century poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. He challenges the Knights of the Round Table to a beheading game, testing Gawain's honor and courage. Source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (14th century, anonymous)

name: Green Lady
description: The Green Lady is a spirit from St. Kitts folklore who manifests as the legendary Green Flash — a rare optical phenomenon seen at sunset when a bright green light flashes for a brief second over the horizon. According to local legend, the Green Lady was once a beautiful and kind-hearted woman who lived on the island centuries ago but was tragically separated from her true love by societal norms and family feuds. Heartbroken, she sought solace at the island's highest peak, where she would gaze at the setting sun, hoping her love would return. One fateful evening, as she watched the sun dip below the horizon, the heavens heard her sorrow and granted her eternal life as a spirit of nature. She now illuminates the sky with a green flash whenever she roams in search of her lost love. Islanders consider seeing the green flash a rare and auspicious event symbolizing hope and love

name: Grizzly Bear Spirit
description: In the Bear Mother legend shared by the Haida, Nisga'a, Gitxsan and Coast Tsimshian, a young woman who mocked the bears was taken as wife by the son of the Grizzly Bear chief and bore twin bear cubs. Her sons, born of a human and a bear, became ancestors and gave the people the bear as a clan crest and guardian spirit.

name: Grizzly Bear Woman Nuxalk
description: In the Nuxalk Smayusta of Ista, First Born (Patsallht) marries a beautiful woman in a red blanket who builds him a home of hemlock. She often disappears for days, and while away she reverts to her true shape, a grizzly bear. Learning that his wife is a bear, First Born leaves her, and she never again takes human form.

name: Grogoch
description: The Grogoch is a half-human, half-fairy creature from Irish folklore, particularly well-known throughout north Antrim, Rathlin Island, and parts of Donegal. Some traditions say the Grogoch originally came from Kintyre in Scotland before settling in Ireland. On the Isle of Man, similar beings are called phynnodderee. Grogochs are solitary beings that dwell in caves, hollows, or crevices in the landscape, and large leaning stones in the northern countryside are known as "grogochs houses." They possess the power of invisibility and often only allow certain trusted people to observe them. Despite their wild appearance, Grogochs can be quite sociable and may even attach themselves to particular individuals, helping them with planting, harvesting, or domestic chores in exchange for nothing more than a jug of cream. They have a great fear of clergy and will not enter a house where a priest or minister is present, a trait shared with many other fairy beings in Celtic tradition

name: Grootslang
description: The Grootslang, also known as the Grote Slang (Afrikaans for "big snake"), is a legendary creature from South African folklore, particularly associated with the Richtersveld region. According to legend, the gods who created all things made a mistake when they fashioned the Grootslang, giving it incredible strength, cunning, and intellect far beyond any other creature. Realizing their error, the gods split the Grootslang into two separate animals: the elephant and the python. However, one original Grootslang survived and gave birth to more of its kind. These primordial creatures now dwell in deep caves, warm rivers, and lakes, most famously in a cavern known as the "Wonder Hole" or "Bottomless Pit" in the Richtersveld, which is said to connect to the sea some 64 kilometers away. The cave is reputedly filled with diamonds, and local folklore tells of white men who descended into it seeking "stones that sparkled like fire."

name: Gruvrået
description: Gruvrået, also called Gruvfrun or Gruvjungfrun, is the guardian spirit of mines in Swedish folklore, especially in the Bergslagen mining district. She is said to walk the tunnels as an elegantly dressed woman with a ring of keys; her dress color was read as an omen, and she rewarded respectful miners with rich ore while punishing swearing and careless behavior in the workings.

name: Gryphon
description: Gryphon (Greek/Persian). is a hybrid. A powerful hybrid creature with the head, wings, and talons of an eagle and the body of a lion. Source: Greek and Persian mythology

name: Gryphon (Griffin)
description: The griffin (gryps) is a Greek and Near Eastern hybrid of lion and eagle, combining the king of beasts with the king of birds. Aristeas, Herodotus, and Pliny describe it guarding Scythian gold against the one-eyed Arimaspians; scholars link the legend to Protoceratops fossils near Central Asian gold. It became heraldry’s emblem of guardianship and divine power.

name: Gråmannen
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Norwegian source records a mountain spirit called 'Gråmannen' in Trollheimen; the only attested use is the place name Gråmannen, a small summit and viewpoint near Kristiansand in Agder. The troll-guardian narrative in this entry is invented and appears in no ethnographic or folk-tradition source.

name: Grýla
description: Grýla is the monstrous ogress of Icelandic folklore who descends from her mountain cave (Dimmuborgir) at Christmas to hunt naughty children, stuffing them in her sack. Mother of the thirteen Yule Lads, wife of Leppalúði. Documented since the 13th century (Svarfdæla saga) and in Jón Árnason's collections. Originally a generic troll-woman, later specialized as a Christmas disciplinary figure.

name: Grýla
description: Grýla in Faroese tradition is the same ogress as in Iceland, documented in 17th-century Faroese ballads (Grýlukvæði) with specific local caves as her lair. She visits villages at Christmas demanding charity and threatening children. The Faroese version shares the Icelandic core but has distinct ballad tradition. Documented by Hammershaimb and Marianne Clausen.

name: Grýla
description: Grýla (Icelandic). is a ogre. A monstrous ogress who hunts and eats naughty children during the winter. Source: Icelandic folklore, Jón Árnason's collections

name: Gu
description: Gu is a spirit of the Guro people of central Ivory Coast, known as the wife of Zamble, the great mythical being of the Guro, from whom he learned how to appear to humans; her mask dances in Guro masquerades. The entry's attribution to the Mossi of Burkina Faso is mistaken; the attested tradition is Guro, not Mossi.

name: Guabance
description: Guabancex is the supreme storm deity of the Taíno people, the indigenous inhabitants of Puerto Rico, Hispaniola, Jamaica, Cuba, and other Caribbean islands. She is a zemi (deity) of chaos and disorder, controlling hurricanes, storms, volcanoes, and earthquakes. Guabancex is considered the violent and destructive aspect of the mother goddess Atabey, representing natures raw, untamed power. Her name is derived from the Taíno words "guaba" (hurricane) and "cex" (center), emphasizing her connection to the most tempestuous weather phenomena. She is attended by two assistants: Coatriquie, who creates floodwaters, and Guataubá, who controls hurricane winds. Together, these three deities conjure "juracán," the Taíno word for hurricane, which later entered English as "hurricane." The Taíno people recognized her power through elaborate ceremonies and offerings, seeking to appease her and avoid catastrophic destruction

name: Guardian Spirit Iceland
description: Guardian Spirit Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. A guardian spirit from Icelandic folklore protects individuals as an invisible companion.. Source: Icelandic folklore — guardian spirits documented in Icelandic folk belief.

name: Guardian spirits
description: Among the Cheyenne, guardian figures and sacred bundles hold a central place: the culture hero Sweet Medicine brought the Four Sacred Arrows, and Standing-on-the-Ground brought the Buffalo Hat, objects that guard the tribe and are tended by designated keepers. Individuals also acquire personal spirit guardians through vision quests.

name: Gueno
description: Gueno (also spelled Guéno) is the eternal creator god of the Fulani people, the supreme being who existed before all things. He created the universe and entrusted the care of cattle and the land to Koumen, the primordial shepherd. Gueno is associated with the sky, celestial order, and the spiritual essence that animates all life. In pre-Islamic Fulani tradition, Gueno was worshipped alongside 28 lesser deities tied to natural forces. He is a distant, benevolent creator whose presence is felt through the cycles of nature, the movement of herds, and the fertility of cattle. Milk and cattle are considered sacred manifestations of Gueno's creative power

name: Gui
description: Gui is the general Chinese term for ghosts or the spirits of the dead, particularly those who have died unnaturally or have unfinished business that prevents them from moving on to the afterlife. In Chinese folklore and religious belief, heavily influenced by Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism, the gui are souls that have become separated from their bodies and remain trapped in the mortal realm. There are many distinct types of gui, each with specific characteristics and origins: wandering souls who died far from home, hungry ghosts driven by insatiable desire, vengeful ghosts seeking revenge for wrongs suffered in life, water ghosts who drowned, hanging ghosts, and headless ghosts. Chinese ancestor worship traditions emphasize the importance of proper burial rites to prevent the deceased from becoming gui. The Hungry Ghost Festival, held annually, is dedicated to feeding and appeasing these wandering spirits. Gui are traditionally feared as they are believed to cause illness, possession, and misfortune among the living

name: Guije
description: Guije (Unknown). is a water-spirit. Güije (also spelled Jigüe) is a creature from Afro-Cuban folklore, a small, playful, sometimes mischievous black figure that lives near rivers and streams. It is known for splashing water at passersby. Source: Afro-Cuban folklore; Santería tradition-related narratives

name: Guinevere
description: Guinevere (Unknown). is a human. Queen Guinevere is the wife of King Arthur in Arthurian legend. Her love affair with Sir Lancelot ultimately leads to the downfall of Camelot and the Round Table.. Source: Arthurian literary tradition

name: Gullah Frog
description: The Gullah Frog is a trickster figure in Gullah Geechee folklore, smaller and more humble than Br'er Rabbit but equally clever. In many tales, the frog uses his small size and familiarity with the swamp to outwit larger predators. The Gullah Frog appears in stories as a voice of wisdom from the marsh, often offering advice that saves other animals from disaster. His croaking is said to contain messages for those wise enough to understand. The frog is associated with the boundary between land and water, a liminal creature that can move between worlds. In some tales, the Gullah Frog is the keeper of secrets about the swamp — knowing where dangers lurk and which spirits haunt the waterways

name: Gulyabani
description: The Gulyabani is a ghoul-like being of Turkish and Anatolian folk belief, from Persian 'Gul-i Beyabani' ('desert ghoul'). It haunts graveyards, ruins, and lonely roads at night, preying on travelers and those who wander alone after dark. In Turkish tradition it appears as a bogeyman used to keep children indoors, and it features in classical Turkish literature.

name: Gumiho
description: The Gumiho (Kumiho) is a nine-tailed fox spirit from Korean mythology, one of the most iconic and feared creatures in Korean folklore. Unlike the Chinese huli jing or Japanese kitsune, which can be benevolent, the Korean gumiho is almost always portrayed as a malevolent shapeshifter that preys on humans. According to traditional belief, a fox that lives for a thousand years develops nine tails and gains the power to transform into a beautiful woman. The gumiho uses this alluring form to seduce men, then consumes their livers or hearts. It possesses a magical bead called a yeowoo guseul (fox bead) that it uses to absorb human energy through a kiss. If a victim manages to swallow this bead, they gain great knowledge or supernatural powers. In some tales, a gumiho that refrains from eating human flesh for a thousand years may become human. The creature has been featured in countless Korean folktales, including the famous 'The Fox Sister' (Yeou nui), and has become a staple of modern Korean entertainment

name: Gumiho
description: Gumiho is a shapeshifter from Korea mythology. Unlike the Chinese huli jing or Japanese kitsune, which can be benevolent, the Korean gumiho is almost always portrayed as a malevolent shapeshifter that preys on humans. It possesses a magical bead called a yeowoo guseul (fox bead) that it uses to absorb human energy through a kiss. The creature has been featured in countless Korean folktales, including the famous 'The Fox Sister' (Yeou nui), and has become a staple of modern Korean entertainment
