name: Gumiho
description: Gumiho (구미호) is the Korean nine-tailed fox, a fox that cultivates for a thousand years to grow nine tails and the power to take human form, most often a beautiful woman. In traditional tales she seduces men to feed on their livers or hearts, though later retellings give her redemptive and sympathetic roles. The gumiho appears in oral tales, in the Samguk Yusa, and in modern Korean drama and film.

name: Guri Kunna
description: Guri Kunna is a troll-woman of the coastal tradition of Froan and the Fosen-Hitra district in Trøndelag. In the best-known legend she is a giantess who dragged the islands of Froan toward Hitra, and her name survives in local place names. The common 'mermaid luring fishermen' framing is a later overlay; the attested figure is a giant troll-woman of the islets.

name: Gurzil (Bull-Headed War God)
description: Gurzil was an important ancient Berber war god, primarily associated with the Laguatan people of the Tripolitania region (spanning modern Libya and southeastern Algeria). He is depicted as a bull-headed deity, the son of the god Ammon (Amun) conceived from a wild heifer. According to historical accounts from the 6th-century Roman poet Corippus, the Laguatan carried a representation of Gurzil in the form of a bull into battle when they revolted against the Romans in AD 546. The Laguatan regarded Gurzil as the offspring of Amun, and carried idols of wood and metal representing the god into combat. The chief and high priest Ierna was killed while trying to rescue the image of Gurzil during the final battle, after which the idol was destroyed. Gurzil symbolized martial ferocity, protection in battle, and virility within Berber religious traditions. His worship involved ritual sacrifices of cattle and the deployment of sacred bull effigies as omens to inspire warriors and terrify enemies. A Neo-Punic inscription from Lepcis Magna linking Gurzil to the Roman god Saturn suggests how Berber and foreign deities were syncretized over time

name: Gutjion
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Nama or Khoekhoe source documents a spirit called 'Gutjion'; the entry's wilderness-guardian details and Richtersveld specifics are invented. Genuine Nama tradition centers on figures such as the trickster-culture hero Heitsi-Eibib, but no 'Gutjion' appears in the recorded lore.

name: Gwaxwgwakwalanuksiwe Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Gwaxwgwakwalanuksiwe' is the man-eating raven of the Kwakwaka'wakw Hamatsa, the most prestigious role among the supernatural man-eating birds that serve the Man-Eater at the North End of the World. As a servant of the cannibal spirit, his masked dance holds the highest station of the Cannibal Society's winter ceremony.

name: Gwyllion
description: The Gwyllion is a type of fairy or spirit from Welsh folklore, specifically associated with the mountainous regions of Wales such as Snowdonia. The name "Gwyllion" is derived from the Welsh word "gwyll" meaning dusk, twilight, or gloom, linking these spirits directly to the dim hours of evening and early night. They are considered mountain fairies that haunt lonely passes, rocky crags, and desolate moors, often misleading travelers who venture out after dark. In Welsh mythology, the Gwyllion are closely related to other spirits of the wilderness and are sometimes associated with the concept of corpse candles (canwyll corph), spectral lights that lead people to their doom. These spirits embody the dangers of the Welsh landscape after nightfall, when the mountains become treacherous and a misplaced step can lead to a deadly fall. Their legends serve as warnings against traveling the mountains alone at night

name: Gyeong
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Korean source records a vampire called 'gyeong'. The Korean term for the hopping corpse is gangsi (gangshi), a loan from the Chinese jiangshi; 'gyeong' is not attested as a creature name, and the description is generic jiangshi filler wrongly assigned a Korean variant.

name: Gygrid
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Norwegian tradition names a giantess 'Gygrid'; the real terms are gyger (singular) and gygjer (plural), from Old Norse gygr, and appear in place names such as Gygra. 'Gygrid' is better known as the Norwegian translation of the Harry Potter character Hagrid. The invented plural 'gygrier' and mountain lore are unfounded.

name: Gyrat
description: Gyrat is the magical horse of the Turkmen epic hero Görogly: a loyal, powerful steed of supernatural speed and endurance who carries his master across the steppe, flies when needed, and warns him of danger. A fixed element of the Görogly cycle, Gyrat represents the steppe horse as faithful companion in Turkmen tradition.

name: Gàidhrí
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Gaidhri' is a Gaelic-looking name with no attested Newari or Nepali tradition; the description is fabricated. The genuine Nepalese spirit of this household-forest type is the Newari Khyah, a large hairy household guardian.

name: Gårdsrå
description: Gårdsrået (the farm spirit) is a male household guardian spirit in Swedish folklore, similar to the Tomte but distinct in nature. While Tomten is a solitary gnome-like figure who helps with animals, Gårdsrået is the 'rå' (spirit) of the farm itself — bound to the land and buildings rather than a specific creature. Gårdsrået maintains order on the farm, protects livestock from illness and predators, and ensures good harvests. He dislikes change — moving buildings, changing the farm's layout, or altering established routines offends him. New farms were said to need time to attract a Gårdsrå, and prosperous farms always had a happy one. A farm that fell into disrepair was one whose Gårdsrå had left in disgust. Offerings of the first bread baked or the last sheaf of grain were left for him at the barn door

name: Göroglu
description: Görogly (Göroglu) is the heroic champion of the Turkmen oral epic tradition: a just, strong warrior-leader who defends his people against tyrants and raiders from his city of Çandibil. Superhumanly strong and skilled in combat, he rides the winged horse Gyrat; his epic cycle is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage.

name: Hactcin (supernatural beings)
description: The Hactcin are the primordial supernatural beings in Jicarilla Apache tradition. They existed before creation in the darkness, water, and Cyclone the wind. The most powerful is Black Hactcin, who created the first four-legged animal from clay and made many more animals from its body. The Hactcin created the first man from turquoise, coral, opal, jet, and abalone brought by the animals. Each Hactcin has a distinct identity — Black Hactcin (creator), White Hactcin (sun), and others associated wit

name: Haetae
description: Haetae (also known as Haechi) is a mythical guardian beast from Korean mythology, depicted as a chimeric lion-like creature covered in scales with a single horn on its forehead. It is one of the most important and beloved mythical creatures in Korean culture, serving as the official symbol of Seoul. Haetae are believed to possess the ability to distinguish good from evil, making them symbols of justice and law. They are also fire-eating guardians, capable of neutralizing destructive fire energy (hwa-gi) and preventing fires. During the Joseon Dynasty, haetae statues were placed in front of Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul to counter the fire energy emanating from Mount Gwanaksan. The haetae also served as the official emblem of the Saheonbu (Office of the Inspector General), with officials wearing its image to project incorruptibility. In legend, when two people fought, the haetae would gore the dishonest one with its horn, making it an ultimate arbiter of truth

name: Haetae
description: Haetae (also known as Haechi) is a mythical guardian beast from Korean mythology, depicted as a chimeric lion-like creature covered in scales with a single horn on its forehead. It is one of the most important and beloved mythical creatures in Korean culture, serving as the official symbol of Seoul. Haetae are believed to possess the ability to distinguish good from evil, making them symbols of justice and law. They are also fire-eating guardians, capable of neutralizing destructive fire energy (hwa-gi) and preventing fires. During the Joseon Dynasty, haetae statues were placed in front of Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul to counter the fire energy emanating from Mount Gwanaksan. The haetae also served as the official emblem of the Saheonbu (Office of the Inspector General), with officials wearing its image to project incorruptibility. In legend, when two people fought, the haetae would gore the dishonest one with its horn, making it an ultimate arbiter of truth In North Korea folklore, this figure is known among the North Korea people.

name: Haetae
description: Haetae (해태) is the Korean chimera of justice and fire control, usually a lion-bodied, horned, scale-covered beast that swallows fire. It distinguishes right from wrong, goring the guilty, and protects against fire and calamity, which is why its statues guard palaces, government buildings, and Seoul's streets, including near the National Assembly. It descends from the Chinese xiezhi tradition.

name: Hafgufa
description: Hafgufa (Old Norse: sea-steam or sea-mist) is a colossal sea monster described in the 13th-century Norwegian text Konungs skuggsjá (The King's Mirror). The hafgufa is so enormous that it resembles a floating island — sailors landing on what they think is an island may be standing on the hafgufa's back. When it submerges, it creates massive whirlpools that drag entire ships to the bottom. The hafgufa is the earliest known description of the kraken-like sea monster in Nordic literature. According to Konungs skuggsjá, it does not eat actively — it opens its mouth and fish swim in, then closes its jaws. It dwells off the coast of Norway between Bergen and Iceland. Predates Pontoppidan's Kraken by 500 years

name: Haggs
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No source records a Manx or Saint Vincent being called 'Haggs'. The entry pairs an unverifiable Isle of Man fairy description with Saint Vincent metadata and names no tradition, collector, or text. Genuine Manx spirits include the buggane and fenodyree; genuine Saint Vincent lore includes the la diablesse and soucouyant.

name: Hahai-i
description: Hahai-i Wuhti is the Katsina Mother of Hopi tradition, mother of all katsinam, the spirit messengers who bring rain, gifts, and teachings to the people. Carved kachina dolls of her image have been collected at Oraibi on Third Mesa since the late nineteenth century, and she holds a central place in the Hopi ceremonial year.

name: Hahgwehdaetgah
description: Hahgwehdaetgah, also known as Flint or the Left-Handed Twin, is the malevolent twin grandson of Sky Woman in Iroquois mythology. He forced his way out through his mother's armpit during childbirth, killing her. From her buried body grew the sacred plants — tobacco from her heart, strawberries from her feet. Flint created everything dangerous and destructive in the world: steep cliffs, monstrous animals, poisonous plants, winter, darkness, and death. He constantly tried to undo his brother's good work

name: Hahgwehdi-yu
description: Hahgwehdiyu, also called the Good Spirit or Good Mind, is the benevolent twin creator of Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) tradition, born normally to Sky Woman while his wicked brother Hahgwehdaetgah burst forth and killed her. He shaped the sky, made the sun from his mother's face, created the first people, and gave them corn, beans, squash, and tobacco.

name: Haietlik
description: Haietlik, the lightning serpent of the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) peoples, is the great ally and weapon of Thunderbird in the whale hunt. Its head is sharp as a knife and its tongue flashes lightning that wounds whales for Thunderbird to take. Whalers carried its skin for luck, and its image appears on canoes and in petroglyphs.

name: Haint
description: A Haint is a restless or malevolent spirit in African American and Gullah Geechee folklore. The term derives from the Gullah pronunciation of 'haunt' and encompasses a broad category of supernatural entities — including the spirits of the dead, Boo Hags, Plat-Eyes, and other wandering entities. Haints are believed to be souls that cannot rest due to unfinished business, improper burial, or violent death. The most distinctive cultural response to haints is 'haint blue' — a pale blue-green paint used on porch ceilings, window trim, and door frames to confuse and repel spirits. In Gullah belief, haints cannot cross water, and the blue color mimics water or sky, creating a barrier they cannot breach. Haints represent the deep connection between African American spiritual traditions and West African ancestor veneration

name: Haiseb
description: Haiseb (also known as Haitsi Aibeb or Heitsi Eibib) is a culture hero and trickster figure from the Khoekhoe, Dama, and Haiǁom peoples of western Namibia. He is remembered through stories, songs, and distinctive cairns of piled stones found throughout the landscape. Colonial accounts describe the Khoekhoe as believing that Haiseb was buried in these stone piles, but because he came to life again, his body never remained in any single cairn. The many piles of stones across the landscape reflect his many episodes of death and rebirth. Haiseb is profoundly ambiguous combining light and dark elements, reminding us of the mysterious and unpredictable nature of existence

name: Hale (Mo'o)
description: Hale is a mo'o, a powerful water lizard spirit from Native Hawaiian mythology, revered as an 'aumakua (ancestral guardian spirit) associated with freshwater sources across the Hawaiian Islands. Mo'o are amphibious reptilian deities that embody both the life-giving and death-dealing properties of water, living primarily in fishponds, freshwater pools, waterfalls, and streams. They can shapeshift into monstrous reptiles, tiny geckos, or stunningly beautiful human women. In Hawaiian tradition, Hale was known as a guardian spirit capable of controlling weather and water, and was both revered and feared by those who depended on freshwater sources. Hale's presence is said to be detectable when vegetation near water takes on a yellowed hue

name: Halmasti
description: Halmasti, also known as the Celestial Hound, is a terrifying wolf-like creature from Chitrali folklore in northern Pakistan. Its name derives from the Khowar language and means 'thunder,' reflecting its association with destructive lightning and violent celestial forces. Halmasti is deeply connected to liminal moments in life, appearing during births and deaths when spiritual vulnerability is highest. The legend represents a unique synthesis of Sumerian, Semitic, Iranic, Turkic, and Chinese mythological traditions, with origins tracing back to the ancient Sumerian female demon Littu, which evolved into Lilith in Semitic mythology, became Al or Hal in Iranic tradition, and Al-Basti in Turkic culture. The Chitrali version absorbed elements from the Chinese Tiangou (Heavenly Dog), a celestial hound that descends with thunder to cause eclipses

name: Haltija
description: Haltija (or haltia) is a class of guardian spirits in Finnish mythology that inhabit and protect specific places, living beings, and natural features. Unlike the major deities known as jumala who rule over broad concepts like water or forest, haltijas are localized spirits governing a specific lake, tree, stone, homestead, or even a person's wellbeing. The word derives from Proto-Norse meaning 'ruler' or 'holder.' Haltijas are central to Finno-Ugric animism and represent the belief that every element of the natural and domestic world has a spiritual guardian. There are many types: metsänhaltija (forest spirit), vedenhaltija (water spirit), kotihaltija or tonttu (household guardian), saunatonttu (sauna guardian), and even personal haltija souls that maintain individual health

name: Hamingja
description: The Hamingja is the physical personification of a family's luck and prosperity. Unlike a ghost or a monster, the Hamingja is a benevolent ancestral spirit that clings to a bloodline. In Swedish lore, luck was not seen as a random occurrence but as a finite resource that could be inherited, grown, or even stolen. The Hamingja manifests as a protective aura or a subtle guiding presence that ensures crops grow, cattle remain healthy, and children survive. If a family's Hamingja leaves them, it is a sign of inevitable ruin and social collapse

name: Hamnskiftare
description: The Hamnskiftare are rare individuals or spirits capable of 'skin-changing,' the art of projecting their consciousness into the body of an animal. In Swedish folklore, this was often associated with shamanic practices or curses. A Hamnskiftare does not simply transform their physical body; they slide their soul into a 'hamr' (a shape or skin), allowing them to travel vast distances, spy on enemies, or protect their kin from the shadows. This ability is viewed with a mixture of respect and deep suspicion, as the line between a protector and a malicious spy is often blurred

name: Hamsa Bird
description: The hamsa, known in Burmese as hintha, is a sacred water-bird, usually identified with the Brahminy duck, that occupies a central place in Mon and Burmese Buddhist mythology. It is the symbol of the Mon people and of the city of Pegu (Bago), and paired hintha images appear widely in temple art and architecture. In Buddhist contexts the hintha is auspicious and revered, not a demonic being.

name: Hanako-san
description: Hanako-san (also known as Toire no Hanako-san or Hanako of the Toilet) is one of the most famous Japanese urban legends, dating back to the 1950s. The legend tells of the ghost of a young girl who haunts school bathrooms, particularly on the third floor of elementary and middle schools across Japan. The story has become a staple of Japanese schoolyard folklore, passed down through generations of children as a test of courage. Variations of the legend exist in different regions, with some versions claiming Hanako was killed during World War II air raids, others saying she was murdered by a stranger in the bathroom, and some stating she was a victim of bullying. The legend reflects broader Japanese folk beliefs about spirits (yurei) of children who died tragically and remain bound to places associated with their death

name: Handi
description: Handi is a female death-guide spirit in Maldivian folklore, appearing as a beautiful woman who sits by the dying and guides souls. She manifests at bedsides and graveyards, her malevolence masked by beauty — tracing to ancient Dravidian Village Goddess worship.

name: Hang Jebat (The Rebel Warrior)
description: Hang Jebat is the most complex and controversial figure in Malay folklore — a legendary warrior who rebelled against the Sultan of Melaka after his best friend Hang Tuah was unjustly executed. When the Sultan ordered Hang Jebat to kill Hang Tuah, Jebat instead revealed his own martial prowess and refused. He later went on a rampage in the palace, taking matters into his own hands against an unjust ruler. In the most famous version of the legend, Jebat is portrayed as a champion of justice who defied tyranny, while in other versions he is a traitor driven by personal vengeance. He was ultimately killed by Hang Tuah himself, who was secretly still alive. The Hang Tuah-Hang Jebat conflict represents the tension between absolute loyalty (Tuah) and justice (Jebat) in Malay political philosophy

name: Hang Tuah (The Invincible Warrior)
description: Hang Tuah is the most legendary warrior in Malay history and folklore, the paragon of Malay chivalry and loyalty. According to the Malay Annals (Sejarah Melayu), he served as the Laksamana (admiral) of the Melaka Sultanate during its golden age in the 15th century under Sultan Mansur Shah. Hang Tuah was unmatched in silat, diplomacy, and statesmanship. Together with four other legendary warriors (Hang Jebat, Hang Kasturi, Hang Lekir, and Hang Lekiu), he defended Melaka's sovereignty. His most famous tale involves being falsely accused of adultery with a palace maid and sentenced to death. His executioner spared him, and when Hang Jebat rebelled against the Sultan, Hang Tuah was recalled to kill his closest friend. Hang Tuah's legendary kris (dagger), Taming Sari, was said to give him invincibility in battle

name: Hans Uredd
description: Hans Uredd (Fearless Hans) is a folk hero from Norwegian folktales, particularly associated with Trøndelag versions of the AT326 (The Boy Who Didn't Know What Fear Was) tale type. The story features a young man from a Trøndelag farm who is so fearless that he cannot understand what fear means. His quest to 'learn to shudder' takes him through encounters with supernatural beings — trolls, ghosts, the Draug, and the Dead Man's Mass — that are specifically placed in Trøndelag landscapes. Versions of the tale were collected in Trøndelag by folklorists and feature localized elements: the hero visits Trondheim, encounters trolls in Trollheimen, and crosses the Trondheimsfjord. The name 'Hans Uredd' (Hans the Fearless) has become synonymous in Norwegian with someone who shows extraordinary courage in the face of supernatural danger

name: Hantu Bedar
description: Hantu Bedar is a fearsome demon from Malaysian folklore, particularly known in rural communities of Peninsular Malaysia. The name 'Hantu Bedar' translates roughly to 'bulky/large ghost,' describing its enormous stature. This malevolent forest spirit is one of many hantu (ghosts or demons) in Malay animistic tradition, which blends indigenous beliefs with Islamic cosmology. Hantu Bedar is primarily a cautionary figure used by parents to warn children against wandering into the deep forest alone, especially at night. The legend is most common among Malay communities living near dense jungle areas in states like Kelantan, Terengganu, Pahang, and Perak, where the forest remains thick and unexplored

name: Hantu Penyet
description: Hantu Penyet (literally 'Squashed Ghost') is a popular ghost from Malaysian folklore known for its distinctive and grotesque appearance. Part of the rich tapestry of Malay hantu (spirits), this particular entity is unique for being more of a prankster than a genuinely malevolent spirit. Its name derives from the Malay word 'penyet' meaning 'squashed' or 'flattened,' describing its most prominent feature: a face that appears to have been pressed flat against a window or wall. Hantu Penyet is one of the better-known figures in modern Malaysian ghost lore and frequently appears in popular culture, horror films, and comedy-horror productions throughout Southeast Asia

name: Hantu Pintal Kamal
description: Hantu Pintal Kamal is a trickster ghost from Malaysian folklore, whose name roughly translates to 'Twisted Spirit of the Hearth' or 'All-Confusing Ghost.' This entity is known for its uncanny ability to walk on walls and ceilings, defying gravity and logic. Unlike more dangerous Malaysian hantu (spirits) that actively harm humans, Hantu Pintal Kamal is a mischievous household spirit that delights in creating confusion and disorder. The legend is particularly common in rural Malay communities where traditional wooden houses with elevated floors provide ample opportunity for the spirit's wall-crawling antics. It belongs to a class of lesser spirits that are more annoying than deadly

name: Hanuman
description: Hindu monkey god, commander of monkey army in Ramayana. SON of Anjana (celestial apsara) + Kesari (Vanara chieftain), blessed by Vayu Deva (wind god). Baby: tried to grab Sun (thought it was fruit), Indra struck his JAW (hanu) with thunderbolt - Name from 'hanu' (jaw) + 'man' (disfigured). Sage Curse: forgot powers (flight, infinite size) until reminded. Supernatural Powers: shapeshift, fly, increase size, immense strength, speed, mastery of Vedas. Ramayana: led monkeys to help Rama (Vishnu avatar) rescue Sita from Ravana. Leaps across ocean to Lanka, carries message, Sets Fire to Lanka with burning tail, Flies to Himalayas for medicinal mountain to save Lakshmana. Temple: monkey with red face, stands erect. Model for bhakti (devotion). Hanuman Chalisa (40 verses by Tulsidas) recited daily. Worship: entry guard, protect from evil, warriors, athletes. Also inspired Chinese Journey to the West (Journey to the West)

name: Harimau Jadian
description: The Harimau Jadian, or were-tiger, is a shape-shifting creature from Bruneian folklore that transforms between human and tiger form. Unlike Malaysia and Indonesia where real tigers exist, Brunei has no wild tigers, yet several caves are named Sawang Harimau (Tiger's Cave), indicating deep cultural belief in these supernatural beings. The transformation is achieved through spells, charms, or inherited ability. These creatures are usually motivated by vengeance or a need to protect their community, rather than mindless aggression

name: Hastrman
description: Hastrman is a malevolent water spirit from Czech and Slovak folklore, the male counterpart to the more famous Rusalka. This aquatic demon dwells in ponds, rivers, lakes, and millponds throughout Central Europe, luring unsuspecting humans to a watery grave. The name 'hastrman' is derived from the German word 'Wassermann' (water man), reflecting the strong cultural exchange between German and Slavic folklore in the region. Hastrman is a well-documented figure in Czech folklore, extensively collected by folklorist Jaromír Jech. Unlike some other European water spirits, the Hastrman is almost universally hostile to humans, treating bodies of water as his exclusive domain where trespassers face certain death

name: Hatara-singi
description: Hatara-singi (also called Hatarashi or Hatara-shingi) is a malevolent disease spirit from Japanese folklore, classified among the yakubyōgami (epidemic deities) that bring illness and plague to human communities. These spirits were particularly feared during Japan's long history of devastating epidemics, including smallpox, measles, and cholera outbreaks that periodically swept through the islands during the Edo period. Hatara-singi is believed to be sent by angry gods, vengeful spirits, or as a punishment for moral transgressions. The spirit's name is associated with the concept of 'wasting away' or 'growing thin,' describing the physical deterioration that accompanies serious illness

name: Hathor (Cow Goddess of Love and Music)
description: Hathor is the great Egyptian cow goddess of love, beauty, music, dance, fertility, and motherhood. One of the most beloved and widely worshipped deities, she embodies feminine grace and nurturing. Associated with the Milky Way, she was considered the celestial cow who gave birth to the sky. She welcomed the dead into the afterlife with food and drink (Lady of the West). As the Eye of Ra, she had a wrathful aspect and could transform into the lioness Sekhmet. Her temple at Dendera is one of the best-preserved in Egypt. Hathor was the patron of dancers, musicians, and women. Greek writers identified her with Aphrodite

name: Hatsenas Tsimshian
description: Hatsenas is the Tsimshian bird of good omen, a robin-like messenger sent from heaven and supernatural father of the hero Asdiwal. In the Asdiwal myth he visits a starving widow and her daughter, brings them food, weds the younger woman, and equips his son with magic gifts; Lévi-Strauss read him as a mediator of the middle heavens.

name: Hatuibwari
description: Hatuibwari is a powerful dragon-like being from the mythology of the Solomon Islands, particularly among the people of Guadalcanal. Described as a massive serpent with the features of a dragon, Hatuibwari is a creator and cultural hero who shaped the islands and taught humans essential skills. In some accounts, Hatuibwari is a dual-sex being who created the first humans from clay and gave them fire, tools, and knowledge of agriculture. The being is associated with both creation and destruction, capable of bringing rain and fertility but also earthquakes and storms when angered. Hatuibwari's serpentine nature connects it to the widespread Melanesian motif of powerful snake deities who play central roles in creation myths

name: Hatupatu
description: A young Maori warrior from the Rotorua region who was captured by the bird-woman Kurangaituku. Hatupatu was kept prisoner in her cave, but he cleverly bided his time and escaped. When Kurangaituku pursued him, he ran across the rugged volcanic landscape of the central North Island. The bird-woman was gaining on him until Hatupatu called upon the gods and reached the hot springs and geysers of Rotorua. The boiling waters and steam repelled the bird-woman, who could not cross the thermal area. Hatupatu finally hid in a narrow rock crevice that Kurangaituku could not reach, and she eventually gave up the chase

name: Haua
description: The god of non-cultivated food and natural abundance in Rapanui mythology. Haua is a lesser deity but important figure in Rapa Nui's spiritual traditions. He is associated with the wild, uncultivated food sources of the island - the fish of the sea, the birds, and the wild plants. Haua represents the natural bounty that requires no cultivation, in contrast to the cultivated foods brought by Hotu Matu'a. In some traditions, Haua is a brother or companion of Make-make. He was honored with offerings by those who gathered wild foods and fished, particularly during times when crops failed. He is sometimes associated with the fertility of the island's natural environment without human intervention

name: Haugfolk
description: Haugfolk (mound-people) are supernatural beings in Norwegian folklore who live inside burial mounds and hills. Related to the Old Norse haugbúi (mound-dweller), haugfolk were believed to be the spirits of the ancient dead who continued their lives inside the mounds. They were also associated with the underjordiske (the underground people) and huldrefolk. Haugfolk lived in a parallel world inside the hills, with their own farms, cattle (usually black or speckled), and celebrations. They were said to be wealthy, possessing gold and treasure. On certain nights, especially Christmas Eve and Midsummer, the mounds would open to reveal the haugfolk feasting inside. Anyone who entered would find time moved differently - hours inside could be years outside

name: Haumia-tiketike
description: God of uncultivated food, particularly the fern root (aruhe) and other wild forest plants. Haumia is one of the great children of Ranginui and Papatuanuku. After the separation of his parents, he was pursued by Tawhirimatea and hid in his mother's body, becoming the source of wild edible plants. While his brother Rongo represents cultivated agriculture, Haumia represents the bounty of the untamed forest and wilderness. The fern root was a staple food for Maori, especially in the South Island where kumara cultivation was difficult

name: Havfrue (Mermaid)
description: Havfrue ('sea-woman') is the Danish mermaid: woman's upper body with pearlescent skin, pearl-adorned hair; fish lower body. Dual-natured: some malevolent, causing shipwrecks with hypnotic song; others benevolent, aiding sailors. Inhabits coastal waters, lagoons, hidden coves. Vulnerable to land confinement, dry air, strong currents. Symbolizes sea's beauty and lethality.

name: Havmand (Merman)
description: Havmand ('sea-man') is the Danish merman: rugged man's upper body, fish lower body with shimmering blue-green scales. Solitary, melancholic; uses enchanting voice and current manipulation to woo human women to depths for their souls. Inhabits deep ocean, coral reefs, underwater caves. Vulnerable to land confinement, bright sun, iron. Counterpart to havfrue.

name: Havmann
description: Havmann (the sea-man) is a male merman figure in Norwegian coastal folklore, particularly strong along the Vestlandet fjords. Unlike the terrifying sjødraug, the havmann is more neutral — helpful or dangerous depending on how treated. He has the upper body of a strong, handsome man and the lower body of a fish. The havmann speaks in rhyming verse (kvad) and has deep knowledge of the sea. He reveals the best fishing spots to respectful fishermen and warns of storms. If mocked or offended, he capsizes boats. The havmann sits on rocks at sunset combing his long hair and singing. Associated with Hardangerfjord and Sognefjord. Unlike the nøkken, he does not actively lure people to drown

name: Havsfrun
description: While similar to the Sjöjungfru, the Havsfrun is a more ancient and powerful entity of the salt-water depths. She is the sovereign of the open sea, possessing a voice that can command the tides and call the whales. In Swedish coastal lore, the Havsfrun is a figure of tragic beauty and immense power, often mourning the loss of the land-world. She does not lure men to their deaths for sport, but rather out of a profound loneliness, seeking a companion who can withstand the crushing pressure and freezing cold of her abyssal kingdom

name: Havsmannen
description: The Havsmannen is the elusive male counterpart to the Sjöjungfru, a powerful merman who rules the deeper currents of the Swedish coast. Unlike the seductive sirens, the Havsmannen is often portrayed as a stern herald of the sea, possessing the ability to predict weather patterns and shipwrecks. He is a guardian of the ocean's secrets, often interacting with humans only to warn them of impending doom or to demand respect for the maritime laws. His presence is often marked by a sudden change in current or the appearance of unusual fish near the shore

name: Havsrå
description: Havsrået (the sea spirit), also called Havsfrun (the sea lady) or Sjöfrun (the sea wife), is a female guardian of the sea and its creatures in Swedish maritime folklore. Unlike the freshwater Sjörå which rules lakes, Havsrået governs the salt sea and all its creatures. Fishermen made offerings of coins, tobacco, or bread to her before setting out, hoping for good catches and safe passage. She could raise storms to punish disrespectful fishermen or calm the waves for those who honored her. Havsrået is often seen at dusk sitting on coastal rocks, combing her long golden hair. If she is seen combing her hair, it is an omen — combing toward herself means she calls a soul to the deep; combing away means she grants safe passage

name: Hawk Ancestor-Spirit (Kikuyu)
description: Not independently attested: while the Kikuyu honor ancestor spirits (ngoma) and show respect for birds of omen, no specific hawk ancestor-spirit is documented in Gikuyu tradition. The description is a generic 'hawk as messenger between worlds' template. The closest genuine figures are the ancestral ngoma spirits and the veneration of Ngai, but none is named a hawk ancestor-spirit.

name: Hawk Ancestor-Spirit of Choctaw
description: In Choctaw tradition the hawk is honored for its keen sight and hunting prowess, qualities tied to vision and perception. Choctaw cosmology holds that each person carries a shilup (soul or spirit) and that the natural world is filled with spirit beings. The hawk figures as a symbol of sharp perception; the historic Choctaw homeland was the forested Southeast, not desert or prairie.

name: Hawk Ancestor-Spirit of Shona
description: Not independently attested. No Shona source records a hawk as an ancestor-spirit or as a carrier of prayers to Mwari; the account is unsupported template prose. Shona ancestral spirits are the vadzimu and mhondoro, tied to lions and to clan totems (mutupo) such as the fish eagle, hungwe; the hawk has no such role in documented tradition.

name: Hawk Animal-Spirit of Mi'kmaq
description: The Hawk Animal-Spirit is a respected spirit being in Mi'kmaq (Mi'kmaw) tradition, representing the qualities of vision, guardianship, and connection between the sky world and the earth. In Mi'kmaq cosmology, all animals possess spiritual essence and certain species serve as clan totems or personal spirit guides (buoin). The hawk, with its aerial mastery and precise hunting skills, is honored as a powerful spirit that protects the valleys and forested landscapes of Mi'kma'ki (the traditional Mi'kmaq territories spanning the Maritime provinces of Canada). Mi'kmaq oral tradition preserves stories of animal spirits teaching humans how to live in harmony with nature

name: Hawk Animal-Spirit of Ojibwe
description: The Hawk Animal-Spirit is a revered guardian in Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) tradition in Canada, where the vast northern forests and lakes of Ontario, Manitoba, and Quebec provide the backdrop for this powerful spirit's domain. In Ojibwe cosmology, animal spirits serve as teachers and protectors, each carrying specific lessons and powers. The hawk spirit teaches the value of perspective: seeing the big picture from a height while maintaining focus on important details below. This spirit is closely associated with the boreal forests that stretch across the Canadian Shield, where the clear skies and open water make hawks a common sight and a powerful spiritual presence in daily Ojibwe life

name: Hawk Animal-Spirit of Ojibwe
description: The Hawk Animal-Spirit is a revered guardian in Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) tradition in Canada, where the vast northern forests and lakes of Ontario, Manitoba, and Quebec provide the backdrop for this powerful spirit's domain. In Ojibwe cosmology, animal spirits serve as teachers and protectors, each carrying specific lessons and powers. This spirit is closely associated with the boreal forests that stretch across the Canadian Shield, where the clear skies and open water make hawks a common sight and a powerful spiritual presence in daily Ojibwe life In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.

name: Hawk Animal-Spirit of Quechua
description: The Hawk Animal-Spirit is a respected spiritual being in Quechua tradition of the Andean region of Peru, where the soaring condors and hawks of the high mountains hold deep spiritual significance. In Quechua cosmology, the world is divided into three realms: Hanan Pacha (the upper world of the gods and celestial spirits), Kay Pacha (the earthly world of humans), and Ukhu Pacha (the inner world of ancestors). Hawks and other raptors are considered messengers between these realms, capable of carrying prayers up to the heavens while maintaining awareness of earthly matters. This spirit is particularly associated with the springs and mountain water sources of the Peruvian highlands

name: Hawk Deity (Kikuyu)
description: In Kikuyu (Agikuyu) tradition the hawk belongs to the birds regarded as intermediaries between humanity and Ngai, the supreme god of Mount Kenya (Kirinyaga). This entry generalizes that role into a 'hawk deity' marked by vigilance and keen sight. Its claim of a diaspora-specific variant is unsupported; attested usage keeps the raptor within Ngai's broader messenger cosmology.

name: Hawk Deity (Kikuyu)
description: Not independently attested. The entry mismatches the Kikuyu people of Kenya with Cambodia and claims the hawk is a sacred intermediary to Ngai, a status no Kikuyu source supports. Kikuyu cosmology centres on Ngai (Mwene-Nyaga) dwelling on Mount Kenya, while birds appear only in minor folktales: the attested tale 'The Hawk and the Hen' explains why hawks prey on chickens. No hawk deity exists.

name: Hawk Deity (Kikuyu)
description: In Kikuyu (Kenya) oral tradition, the hawk and the chameleon act as the messengers of Ngai, the supreme god, in the myth that explains the origin of death: the chameleon's delayed return made mortality permanent. This is a genuine Kikuyu belief mislabeled as a USA deity; the Kikuyu homeland is central Kenya.

name: Hawk Deity of Pomo
description: In Pomo mythology, the Hawk Deity (known as Tata) holds a prominent position as a chief and captain of the people, created by Coyote during the world's formation. According to Pomo creation narratives, Coyote designated Hawk as the leader of all birds and the guardian of human society, placing a single hawk feather in the finest house as a symbol of his authority. Hawk appears in numerous Pomo stories as a powerful figure who mediates between the natural and supernatural realms, and his actions shaped the landscape of Clear Lake and the surrounding California territories. The Pomo people regard this hawk deity as one of the most important ancestral beings, linked to the creation of light, fire, and the social order that governs their communities

name: Hawk Deity of Ute
description: Among the Ute people of the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin regions, the Hawk Deity stands as a powerful spiritual being closely associated with vision, protection, and the sacred mountains. Ute traditions teach that hawks serve as messengers between the human world and the Creator Sinawav, carrying prayers upward on their soaring flights. The Ute people have always lived in the mountains of Colorado and Utah, and they believe that the Hawk Deity watches over them from the high peaks, particularly around sacred sites like Bears Ears and the La Sal Mountains. Hawks feature prominently in Ute ceremonial life, with their feathers used in Sun Dance and Bear Dance regalia as symbols of spiritual power and connection to the sky realm

name: Hawk Ghost of Aymara
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Aymara tradition. The Aymara sacred birds documented at Isluga are the condor, the eagle and the chullumpe water-bird; no 'hawk ghost' appears in the literature, and the account of a spectral hawk guiding lost souls and carrying yatiri offerings is invented. The achachilas and Pachamama invoked in the entry are genuine, but the hawk is not.

name: Hawk Ghost of Cheyenne
description: Among the Cheyenne people of the Great Plains, the Hawk Ghost is a revered spiritual entity associated with protection in battle, visionary guidance, and the sacred Buffalo Hunt origin story. In Cheyenne tradition, hawks (known as aenohes and hoestom) are considered powerful war talismans. Warriors would carry stuffed hawk skins into battle, believing the bird's spirit would impart swift-killing attributes and protect them from enemy weapons. The legendary Cheyenne warrior Crazy Horse was known to wear hawk feathers in his hair rather than eagle feathers as a sign of modesty and spiritual connection. The Hawk Ghost also appears in the Cheyenne story of the Great Race, where the hawk raced alongside the magpie to win the right for humans to hunt buffalo

name: Hawk Ghost of Ute
description: No hawk ghost is documented in Ute tradition. Ute oral traditions concern the culture hero Sinawav and spirit beings tied to their Great Basin and Plateau homelands, but no spectral hawk guardian of canyons or springs appears in published ethnography. The entry appears to be an invented composite of generic motifs.

name: Hawk Guardian (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Tupi tradition. The input's claim that a Tupi hawk guardian manifested in southern Africa through colonial displacement is unsupported and contradicted by history — no such 'guardian' is recorded in Brazil or Africa. The Tupi corpus (Curupira, Anhangá) contains no hawk guardian, and related 'elkguardiantupi-brazil' style slugs are AI-generated.

name: Hawk Guardian (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested and geographically incoherent: the Tupi are an indigenous South American people, and no 'Hawk Guardian' of Tupi origin appears in Ghanaian tradition or documented diaspora history. The entry's account of 'Tupi descendants' reaching Africa through colonial history and carrying a hawk guardian is unsupported and appears fabricated.

name: Hawk Guardian (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested. The entry pairs the Tupi peoples of Amazonia with South Africa and imagines a hawk guardian carried across the Atlantic by 'Tupi descendants' during colonial history — a narrative with no documentary basis. No Tupi tradition records such a guardian, and no South African tradition names it; the culture/country mismatch is fabricated.

name: Hawk Guardian of Haida
description: Among the Haida people of Haida Gwaii (the Queen Charlotte Islands), the Hawk Guardian is a prominent crest figure representing the power of the skies and the noble status of Eagle clan lineages. In Haida culture, organized into two primary matrilineal clans (Raven and Eagle), the hawk is closely associated with the Eagle clan and appears on totem poles, house front paintings, and ceremonial objects as a symbol of authority and spiritual vision. The Hawk Guardian is believed to possess the power of far-sighted wisdom, able to see across both the physical realm and the spirit world. Haida chiefs display hawk crests to proclaim their lineage and their connection to the supernatural beings that founded their families

name: Hawk Guardian of Inuit
description: In the vast Arctic world of the Inuit people, the Hawk Guardian (known in relation to the rough-legged hawk and gyrfalcon) is a spirit being that embodies survival, keen vision, and mastery over the frozen landscape. The Inuit, who inhabit the northern regions of Alaska, Canada, and Greenland, regard birds of prey as powerful spiritual allies that can traverse the boundary between the earth and the sky. The Hawk Guardian is particularly associated with the harsh winter months when food is scarce and survival depends on the sharpest senses. Inuit shamans (angakkuit) call upon this guardian during their spirit journeys, using its keen eyesight to locate game and its swift hunting skills to ensure the community's survival through the long Arctic nights

name: Hawk Guardian of Kikuyu
description: Hawks and other raptors are honored among the Kikuyu (Agikuyu) of Kenya as messengers of Ngai, the supreme deity whose dwelling is Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya). Their flight is read as a sign of Ngai's watch over the land, and hawk feathers appear in the regalia of ritual leaders. The 'Hawk Guardian' is a composite personification of these beliefs, not a figure with one fixed name in Kikuyu sources.

name: Hawk Guardian of Ojibwe
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. This entry is a verbatim copy of the Canadian record, still set in 'Canadian territories', attached to a USA metadata record. No Ojibwe tradition documents a 'Hawk Guardian'. The text is template filler with no named story, and the duplicate framing confirms it is fabricated.

name: Hawk Guardian of Ojibwe
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) source documents a 'Hawk Guardian' spirit with the wild-rice and maple-sap role described; the text is template filler naming no tradition or story. Ojibwe spiritual beings include the thunderbirds (animikii) and personal manidoo guides, but a 'Hawk Guardian' as such is unattested.

name: Hawk Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
description: In the West African Sahel region, the Tupi Hawk Nature-Spirit manifests as a guardian of the transition zone between the Sahara Desert and the tropical savannas. This region, with its harsh climate and sparse vegetation, demanded that the Tupi nature-spirit develop new strategies for protecting the people and the environment. For Tupi descendants who found themselves in the Sahel, this spirit became a symbol of resilience and adaptation to challenging conditions. The Hawk Nature-Spirit in Mali watches over the Niger River and the ancient trade routes that cross the region, ensuring that travelers and traders pass safely through the lands where Tupi descendants established their communities

name: Hawk Nature-Spirit of Muisca
description: Among the Muisca people of the Colombian highlands, the Hawk Nature-Spirit is a sacred guardian associated with the cold, windswept altiplano of the Eastern Cordillera and its sacred lakes, particularly Lake Guatavita. The Muisca civilization, famous for the legend of El Dorado, maintained a complex cosmology in which birds of prey played crucial roles as messengers of the gods and guardians of the natural order. The Hawk Nature-Spirit was believed to control the winds that sweep across the high plateau and to serve as an intermediary between the Muisca priests (jeques) and the supreme god Chiminigagua. Hawk feathers were used in the rituals of the Zaque and Zipa (Muisca rulers) to legitimize their authority and connect them with the divine realm

name: Hawk Nature-Spirit of Navajo
description: Among the Navajo (Diné) people of the American Southwest, the Hawk Nature-Spirit is a sacred being associated with the high desert mesas, canyonlands, and the four sacred mountains that define the traditional Navajo homeland. In Diné cosmology, birds of prey are respected for their power and vision, and the hawk is considered a special messenger that can travel between the earth and the holy places of the Diyin Dine'é (Holy People). The Hawk Nature-Spirit appears in Navajo sand paintings and healing ceremonies, where its image is used to restore balance and harmony to those who are ill. Navajo elders teach that the hawk's ability to soar to great heights represents the ideal of seeing one's life from a higher perspective, essential for walking in beauty (Hózhó)

name: Hawk Nature-Spirit of Passamaquoddy
description: Among the Passamaquoddy people of Maine and the Maritime provinces, the Hawk Nature-Spirit is a coastal guardian associated with the rugged shorelines, dense forests, and the abundant fisheries of the Bay of Fundy. The Passamaquoddy, part of the Wabanaki Confederacy, have a deep spiritual connection to the natural world, and the hawk is revered as a powerful spirit that can see across both land and sea. The Passamaquoddy name for the hawk reflects its role as a watcher and protector, and its feathers are used in the sacred ceremonies of the tribe. The Hawk Nature-Spirit is particularly associated with the changing of the seasons, appearing prominently during the spring migration when its return signals the renewal of life after the harsh Maine winter

name: Hawk Nature-Spirit of Zapotec
description: Among the Zapotec people of Oaxaca, Mexico, the Hawk Nature-Spirit is a sacred being associated with the ancient cloud forests of the Sierra Norte and the archaeological sites of Monte Albán and Mitla. The Zapotec civilization, one of the oldest in Mesoamerica, developed a sophisticated cosmology in which birds of prey were considered messengers of the gods and intermediaries between the world of the living and the underworld (Lyobaa). The Hawk Nature-Spirit was particularly associated with the Zapotec rain god Cocijo and the lightning bolt, reflecting the hawk's connection to storms and the sky. Zapotec priests used hawk imagery in their rituals to communicate with the ancestors and to ensure favorable weather for agriculture

name: Hawk Spirit (Khmer)
description: Not independently attested in Khmer folklore or academic sources: no Cambodian tradition records a hawk spirit, and the entry's tale of a hawk guiding Cambodian immigrants through Canadian winters is unsupported diaspora fiction. Khmer bird-lore centres on the hongsa (hamsa goose) and Krut (Garuda) of Buddhist-Hindu tradition; the aliases show the same figure cloned for Mali, the USA and Canada.

name: Hawk Spirit (Khmer)
description: Not independently attested and internally contradictory: the Khmer are a Cambodian people, and the entry, attributed to Mali, describes a hawk spirit tied to 'Cambodian people who resettled in Canada' and to comfort 'during the long winter months.' No such figure appears in Malian or Khmer tradition; the entry appears fabricated.

name: Hawk Spirit (Khmer)
description: No Khmer hawk spirit is attested in Cambodia or diaspora traditions; the text is a near-duplicate of the Canada entry, repeating an invented immigration narrative and copy-paste errors. The genuine Cambodian avian figure is Garuda of Hindu-Buddhist cosmology.

name: Hawk Spirit (Khmer)
description: No Khmer hawk spirit is attested; the entry's narrative of a 'Canada mythology' hawk guiding Cambodian immigrants is invented. In Cambodian tradition the principal avian supernatural figure is Garuda, drawn from Hindu-Buddhist syncretism, not a hawk spirit.

name: Hawk Spirit of Blackfoot
description: The Hawk Spirit of the Blackfoot people in Canada carries the same sacred significance as in the American context, but with particular emphasis on the vast prairie landscapes of southern Alberta and Saskatchewan. Among the Blackfoot Confederacy's Canadian members, particularly the Kainai, Siksika, and Piikani nations, the Hawk Spirit is intimately connected to the seasonal rhythms of the northern plains. The spirit is believed to have guided the Blackfoot people across the landscape since time immemorial, showing them where buffalo herds grazed and where water could be found during drought. Its role as protector and guide is especially pronounced in Canadian Blackfoot oral traditions, where stories of the Hawk Spirit's interventions are passed down through generations

name: Hawk Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Blackfoot (Niitsitapi) source documents a 'Hawk Spirit' guiding people to buffalo or water; the description is generic filler ending with an empty 'In Canada folklore' clause. Blackfoot traditions do feature the beaver in creation narratives, but a 'Hawk Spirit' as described is unattested.

name: Hawk Spirit of Inuit
description: The Hawk Spirit holds a distinctive place in Inuit mythology, where the harsh Arctic environment gives special significance to any creature that can navigate the vast northern skies. In Inuit tradition, hawks and falcons are respected for their hunting prowess and their ability to survive in extreme conditions. The Hawk Spirit is considered a helper of shamans, assisting them in their spiritual journeys between worlds. Unlike the more common raven figures in Inuit mythology, the Hawk Spirit represents clarity of vision and purpose, cutting through the spiritual fog that can obscure truth. It is particularly associated with the transitional seasons of spring and fall when birds migrate across the Arctic landscape

name: Hawk Spirit of Zapotec
description: In Zapotec tradition of Oaxaca, Mexico, the Hawk Spirit (known as something akin to a sacred raptor being) occupies an important place in the spiritual landscape of the region. The Zapotec people, whose civilization flourished in the Valley of Oaxaca for millennia, have long regarded hawks as sacred messengers connected to the mountain peaks that surround their ancestral homeland. The Hawk Spirit is intimately tied to the concept of spiritual vision and foresight, believed to carry the prayers of the people to the cloud-shrouded peaks where the old gods dwell. This spirit appears in Zapotec art and iconography as a powerful symbol of the connection between earth and sky

name: Hawk Trickster of Aztec
description: Hawks and eagles carry strong symbolism in Aztec (Mexica) culture as creatures of the sun, war, and the warrior orders, and raptors were watched for omens. A humorous 'hawk trickster' who exposes hypocrisy is not attested in Mexica sources; the entry projects a trickster template onto Aztec raptor symbolism. The genuine associations are martial and augural, not comedic.

name: Hawk Trickster of Muisca
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Muisca tradition. Muisca cosmology, recorded by colonial chroniclers (Simón, Lugo) and modern scholars, includes deities such as Bochica, Bachué, Sué and Chía, but no hawk trickster who mocked chieftains appears in the sources. The narrative of a humorous challenger to Muisca authority is invented; the goldwork and hierarchy are real, the hawk is not.

name: Hawk Trickster of Paiute
description: No hawk trickster appears in Paiute tradition; the trickster of the Great Basin peoples, including the Paiute, is Coyote, often malevolent, lecherous, and sometimes a fire-bringer. No source documents a hawk in that role, and the entry's meditation on 'questioning received wisdom' is invented.

name: Hawk Water-Spirit of Kikuyu
description: In Kikuyu (Agikuyu) belief, sacred high places and water sources on the slopes of Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya) are tied to Ngai and the spirits guarding them. Mist, springs, and waterfalls are treated with reverence, and birds crossing between sky and water may signal divine presence. The entry combines hawk and water-spirit imagery into one guardian, a synthesis of attested beliefs.

name: Hawk Water-Spirit of Yoruba
description: Not independently attested. No hawk water-spirit appears in documented Yoruba tradition; the Yoruba water deities are Mami Wata, Oshun and Olokun, and no source records a hawk intermediary between water and sky. The entry's generic 'messenger spirit' framing is unsupported and appears fabricated.

name: Headless Horseman
description: The Headless Horseman is the ghostly Hessian soldier of Washington Irving's 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' (1820), a figure of Dutch-American folklore of the Hudson Valley. He rides at night with his head carried on his saddle, hurling it at the fleeing Ichabod Crane; he is a classic of American, not Native American, literature.

name: Heartman
description: The Heartman is one of the most feared figures in Bajan folklore — a gruesome entity that preys on misbehaving children by carving out their hearts and offering them to the devil. Parents would invoke the Heartman's name to keep children in line, making him an instrument of social control through terror. The legend has deep roots in the island's African heritage blended with colonial Christian imagery. Unlike the Steel Donkey which is a curse-enforcer, the Heartman is a direct predator that specifically targets the young and disobedient. His legend reflects historical anxieties about child safety, obedience, and the protection of innocence in a harsh plantation society

name: Heavenly Bodies
description: In Miwok mythology of California, the concept of Heavenly Bodies encompasses a class of spirit beings that inhabit the sky and exert influence over earthly affairs. The Miwok people, who traditionally lived in the Sierra Nevada and California coastal regions, developed a rich celestial mythology in which stars, planets, and other heavenly bodies were understood as living spirits with distinct personalities and powers. In Miwok cosmology, the Pleiades star cluster (known as Os-so-so'-li) was particularly significant, associated with beautiful star-women who watched over the people. These celestial beings were believed to be ancestors who had ascended to the sky, continuing to participate in the life of their community from their elevated positions among the stars

name: Heinzelmännchen
description: The Heinzelmännchen are legendary household spirits from Cologne, Germany, akin to brownies or hobgoblins in other European traditions. These diminutive helpers were said to perform all the household and workshop tasks of Cologne's citizens during the night, allowing the lazy inhabitants of the city to enjoy their days in complete leisure. The legend was first recorded in writing by Cologne teacher Ernst Weyden in 1826 and later popularized by poet August Kopisch in 1836, whose ballad about the Heinzelmännchen became immensely popular and cemented these creatures in German folklore. According to tradition, the Heinzelmännchen worked tirelessly until a tailor's wife, driven by curiosity, scattered peas on the workshop floor to catch them. When they slipped and fell, they fled in anger, never to return

name: Heitsi Eibib
description: Heitsi Eibib (Unknown). is a culture-hero. Heitsi-eibib is a legendary hunter, sorcerer, and warrior in Khoikhoi mythology. He is a life-death-rebirth figure who died and resurrected himself on numerous occasions, and his funeral cairns are fo. Source: Khoikhoi oral tradition; Khoisan religious sources

name: Heksa Barbro
description: Heksa Barbro (Barbro Osmundsdatter) is the legendary witch of Lista in Sørlandet, one of the last people executed for witchcraft in the Lister district. Barbro was burned at Engøy, Farsund, in the 1660s for causing deaths, illness, and cattle bewitching through sorcery. According to local legend, Barbro escaped the execution fire by throwing a thread into the air and flying away on it. Her cave, Poddelopte-hula near Drange, is still a local landmark. A gate in Farsund is named after her — Barbrosporten. The legend says she continues to haunt the Lista area, appearing as an old woman in the heath landscape. She represents the tragic intersection of old Sami-influenced magic traditions and Christian persecution in Sørlandet. The Lista region has an unusually dense concentration of witch trial history, with Barbro as its most famous figure

name: Hel (Goddess)
description: Hel is the Norse ruler of Helheim, daughter of Loki and Angrboða, sister of Fenrir and Jörmungandr. Odin cast her into Niflheim, granting authority over nine worlds for those dying of sickness/old age. Half flesh-coloured, half blue-black (hel-blár), gloomy and fierce. Hall Éljúðnir has dish 'Hunger', knife 'Famine', servants Ganglati, Ganglöt. Refuses Baldr's return unless all things weep.

name: Hel Goddess Denmark
description: Hel Goddess Denmark (Unknown). is a deity. Hel is the ruler of the underworld in Norse mythology, daughter of Loki and the giantess Angrboða. She presides over the realm of the dead who did not die in battle.. Source: Poetic Edda; Prose Edda (Snorri Sturluson)

name: Helhest
description: Helhest ('Hell-horse') is the three-legged horse of Danish folk belief, a death-omen that haunted churchyards. It was said to drag itself around the church at night, and whoever saw it or heard it whinny would die within the year. Old accounts tie the creature to a horse or sacrificial beast buried alive beneath a church or graveyard; stories cluster at Aarhus, Roskilde, and other towns.

name: Heloha
description: Heloha, Thunder, and her mate Melatha, Lightning, are the two great birds of Choctaw tradition. The Sun Father sent them to warn the people of approaching storms. Heloha lays her enormous eggs on the clouds, where they roll about with a great rumble, while swift Melatha streaks across the sky leaving a trail of sparks. They are the comic pair of Choctaw storm myths.

name: Helvettre
description: Helvettre (also known as Helvite or the Otherworld) is a concept from Swedish folklore referring to a parallel realm that exists alongside the human world, invisible to most people except at certain times and places. This otherworld is inhabited by the souls of the dead, ancient giants, and the hidden folk (vitter) who retreated from human society as civilization spread across the Scandinavian landscape. The concept is deeply rooted in Norse and Swedish folk beliefs about the multilayered nature of reality, where the boundaries between worlds are thin at specific locations such as burial mounds, deep forests, lakes, and caves. Helvettre is not a singular place but rather a dimension that overlays the familiar landscape, accessible through portals that appear under specific conditions

name: Hero Twins
description: The Hero Twins of Navajo tradition are Monster Slayer (Nayénzgani) and Born of Water (Tobadzîschíni), twin sons of Changing Woman. They rid the world of the monsters that plagued it, journeyed to the house of their father the Sun, passed his trials, and returned armed with lightning. They remain the model of the Navajo warrior path.

name: Hes-abo
description: Hes-abo is a spirit being from the traditional beliefs of the Creek (Muscogee) people, who historically inhabited the southeastern United States. In Creek cosmology, the natural world is filled with various spirit beings, each associated with specific aspects of the landscape and natural phenomena. Hes-abo is understood as a forest spirit connected to the deep woodlands and the knowledge they contain. The Creek people traditionally maintained a complex relationship with the spirit world through ceremonies, dreams, and the guidance of medicine people who could communicate with such beings. Hes-abo represents the mysterious and sometimes dangerous aspects of the forest, embodying both its healing potential and its capacity to confound those who enter without proper preparation or respect

name: Hestenøkken
description: Hestenøkken (the water horse, also known as nøkk-hesten) is the horse-form of the nøkk water spirit in Norwegian folklore, particularly associated with the lakes and fjords of Hardanger and Sogn in Vestlandet. The hestenøkken appears as a beautiful, pure white horse grazing peacefully by the water's edge. When someone approaches to ride it, the horse waits until they are mounted, then gallops straight into the deepest part of the lake or fjord, drowning the rider. The horse is impossible to dismount once ridden — the rider's hands stick to its mane. Unlike the humanoid nøkk who lures with music, the hestenøkken uses the universal appeal of a fine horse to tempt victims. The hestenøkken can also appear as a saddled horse tied to a tree, inviting theft. Legends warn that any strange white horse found near water should be regarded with suspicion

name: Hestmannen
description: Hestmannen (the Horseman) is a troll from Nordland folklore, the wild son of Vågakallen of Lofoten. Hestmannen was known for his uncontrollable temper and wild riding. According to legend, he pursued Lekamøya (the Leka Maid) across Vestfjorden on horseback, intending to capture her. As the sun rose, he shot an arrow at her — but Skarsfjellgubben threw his hat in the way, deflecting the arrow. The arrow pierced the hat, creating the famous hole through Torghatten mountain. Hestmannen and his horse were turned to stone by the sunrise at the Arctic Circle. The Hestmannen rock formation is a distinctive landmark on the island of Lurøy/Rødøy in Nordland. The legend is part of the cycle of Seven Sisters stories that explain the geography of the Helgeland coast. Hestmannen represents wild, uncontrolled masculine power in Norwegian folk tradition

name: Heyoka
description: The heyoka (heyókȟa) is the sacred clown and contrary of Lakota tradition, a role taken only by those who have dreamed of the thunder-beings, Wakíŋyaŋ. Heyokas act backwards and use satire and shocking behavior to mirror a community's doubts, fears, and vanities, functioning as social critics and spiritual teachers who maintain balance.

name: Hi'iaka
description: The youngest and most beloved sister of Pele, the volcano goddess. Hi'iaka is the goddess of hula, medicine, and healing. Her full name Hi'iakaikapoliopele means 'Hi'iaka in the bosom of Pele' as she was born from Pele's thoughts. She is known for her epic journey to Kauai to retrieve Pele's lover Lohiau, during which she demonstrated her power and compassion. Hi'iaka is a shapeshifter who can travel at supernatural speed, control the forests, and commune with spirits. She is a skilled hula dancer and is considered the patron goddess of hula practitioners

name: Hiawatha
description: Hiawatha was a legendary Iroquois leader and co-founder of the Iroquois Confederacy alongside the Great Peacemaker. After his three daughters were killed by the evil wizard Tadodaho, he was consumed by grief and wandered the wilderness. The Great Peacemaker found him and taught him the Condolence Ceremony to ease his grief. Hiawatha invented wampum — strings of purple and white shell beads — to record the laws and treaties of the growing Confederacy. He became the great orator who convinced the Five Nations to unite under the Great Law of Peace

name: High John the Conqueror
description: High John the Conqueror is a legendary figure in African American folklore, a trickster hero and spirit of liberation who moved invisibly among the enslaved. According to traditions collected by Zora Neale Hurston, High John was an African prince sold into slavery whose spirit could never be broken. When the whip fell, John would 'take the spirit of his people out of their bodies' so they could not feel the pain. He could be heard laughing in the slave quarters, a sound that reminded the enslaved that freedom was coming. After emancipation, John returned to Africa, but according to Hurston, 'He left his power here' in the root of a certain plant. The dried root of Ipomoea purga, called High John the Conqueror root, is carried in mojo bags for protection, luck, and empowerment in Hoodoo practice

name: Hihankara
description: Hihaŋkaǧa, Owl-Maker, is an aged Lakota spirit who sits at the entrance to the Sky Road, the Milky Way, judging the naǧí, the souls of the dead. She admits only those whose bodies were properly tattooed; the rest she sends back to wander the earth as ghosts. She appears in Lakota lists of deities and accounts of the afterlife journey.

name: Hiisi
description: Hiisi is a complex figure from Finnish mythology whose meaning evolved dramatically over time. Originally, the term hiisi referred to sacred natural sites: groves, hills, rock formations, and bodies of water where the ancient Finns performed rituals and made offerings. With the Christianization of Finland, these pagan sacred places were demonized, and hiisi transformed from a neutral or positive sacred concept into a malevolent spirit or demon associated with bad luck, illness, and death. In later folklore, hiidet (plural) are depicted as trickster-like entities, often the autochthonous pagan inhabitants of the land, similar to mythological giants. They are associated with salient geographical features and rough terrain, and appear frequently in the Kalevala epic as forces of chaos and mischief that heroes must overcome or outwit

name: Hiisi Portti (Hiisi's Gate)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Finnish source describes a portal called 'Hiisi's Gate'; the resemblance is to Hiidenportti, which is the name of a national park in Kainuu, not a folklore phenomenon. Hiisi is a genuine figure of Finnish and Karelian tradition (appearing in the Kalevala), but the gate/portal mechanics here are invented.

name: Hikule'o
description: Hikule'o (also known as Havea Hikule'o) is the powerful Tongan goddess of Pulotu, the sacred underworld realm where ancestral spirits dwell after death. She is one of the three supreme deities in Tongan cosmology, alongside her brothers Tangaloa (god of the sky) and Maui (god of the earth). According to myth, she created several volcanic islands by casting stones from the heavens, including Kao, Tofua, Hunga Ha'apai, Hunga Tonga, Late, and Fonualei. Hikule'o governs the hidden cycles of life and death, not as a destructive force but as a custodian of ancestral wisdom and lineage continuity. She is deeply tied to the Havea noble clan and represents the fierce, protective power of feminine divinity in Polynesian tradition

name: Hine-nui-te-po
description: The goddess of death, night, and the underworld. Originally Hine-titama (the Dawn Maiden), daughter of Tane Mahuta and Hineahuone. When Hine-titama discovered that Tane was also her father, she fled in shame to the underworld, transforming into Hine-nui-te-po, the goddess of death. She guards the entrance to the underworld and receives the spirits of the dead. The demigod Maui attempted to conquer death by crawling through her body, but a bird's laughter woke her and she crushed him between her obsidian teeth, ensuring that death would remain permanent for all humanity

name: Hine-titama
description: The dawn maiden, daughter of Tane Mahuta and Hineahuone, the first woman. Hine-titama was the first dawn, the first light of day, born from the union of the god of forests and the woman formed from earth. She later married her father Tane, not knowing their relationship. When she discovered that Tane was her father, she was overcome with shame and fled to the underworld, transforming into Hine-nui-te-po, the goddess of death. Her flight marks the transition from the age of gods to the age of humanity, and the introduction of death into the world

name: Hinn
description: The Hinn are a class of pre-Adamite beings in Islamic and Arabian tradition. Ibn Kathir's exegesis of Qur'an 2:30 relates that the Hinn (also written hinn and binn) shed blood on earth before humanity, prompting the angels' question to God about creating Adam. Later cosmology groups hinn with binn, timm, and rimm among jinn sub-races.

name: Hinnon
description: Hinnon is the powerful thunder spirit and leader of the Onditichiae (Thunder Beings) in Huron (Wyandot) mythology. The Huron believe the Thunders are a group of powerful storm spirits who look like a cross between men and giant turkeys. Hinnon, called Grandfather, leads them in pursuing and destroying the great horned serpents and other monsters that threaten the world. When lightning flashes, Hinnon is throwing his thunderbolt; when thunder rolls, it is his voice. The first thunderclap occurred when Aataentsic fell through the Sky Land

name: Hinnøygubben
description: Hinnøygubben (the Old Man of Hinnøya) is a troll from the folklore of the Lofoten/Vesterålen region. According to legend, Hinnøygubben fought with Vågakallen, the troll king of Lofoten, over grazing rights for their reindeer on the border between their territories. During the battle, Hinnøygubben lost his balance and struck his massive axe into the mountain, carving out the Trollfjorden (Trollfjord) — one of the most dramatic and narrow fjords in Norway. Both he and Vågakallen were turned to stone at sunrise, frozen in their battle poses. The Trollfjorden is a real fjord on the border of Lofoten and Vesterålen, famous for its narrow, steep-sided entrance. The battle between the two troll kings explains the dramatic geography of the region. Hinnøygubben represents the wild territoriality of the trolls who shaped the Norwegian landscape

name: Hintha Bird (Golden Goose)
description: The hintha, or hamsa, is the golden goose of Mon-Burmese tradition, sacred emblem of the Mon people and symbol of Bago Region (Hanthawaddy). Legend holds that a pair of hintha guided the Mon across the sea to Suvannabhumi, where Bago was founded; the paired birds adorn the Mon State flag and temple roofs. In the Hamsa Jataka the goose is a Bodhisatta preaching non-attachment.

name: Hiro
description: The Tahitian trickster god of thieves, navigation, and the son of the supreme god Ta'aroa. Hiro was known for his cunning, cleverness, and magical abilities. He built a magical canoe that could sail faster than the wind. Using his enchanted vessel and his wits, Hiro traveled across the Society Islands performing daring thefts and outsmarting chiefs and gods alike. He stole fish from markets, food from temples, and once attempted to steal the island of Bora Bora itself. His exploits angered the other gods who unleashed a great storm to stop him. Hiro is also a god of navigation and learning, representing the cleverness needed for successful ocean voyaging

name: Hirsiz İb
description: 'Hırsız İb' ('Thief İb') is not attested in Turkish folklore. Web research returns only dictionary and lexical results for 'hırsız' (thief); no oral-tradition source, folkloric collection, or scholarly work documents a spirit or patron of thieves by this name. The entry appears to be an invented figure built from the Turkish word for thief.

name: Hitotsume-kozō
description: Hitotsume-kozō is a one-eyed yokai from Japanese folklore, appearing as a child-like goblin dressed in the robes of a Buddhist novice. His name translates to 'one-eyed little monk,' and he is among the most distinctive of Japan's supernatural beings. According to legend, these spirits are associated with Enryaku-ji temple on Mount Hiei, the headquarters of the Tendai school of Buddhism. Hitotsume-kozō are generally mischievous rather than malevolent, though their behavior can sometimes frighten humans. They serve as a fascinating example of how Buddhist imagery blended with indigenous folk beliefs to create unique yokai traditions in Japanese culture

name: Hitra-Kjempen
description: Hitra-Kjempen (the Hitra Giant) is a legendary giant said to have lived on the island of Hitra, the largest island in Trøndelag (568 square kilometers). According to local tradition, the Hitra-Kjempen was a solitary giant who was so large that he used entire skerries as stepping stones when walking to the mainland. The giant was known for his enormous appetite — he could eat an entire herd of cattle in one meal — and for throwing boulders at ships he disliked. Various geological features on Hitra are explained through the giant's actions: deep valleys are where he dragged his club, large boulders are stones he threw, and the many small islands around Hitra are crumbs that fell from his catch. The Hitra-Kjempen was eventually tricked by a clever farmer who challenged him to a contest of strength and then used wit to defeat him, a common motif in Norwegian giant legends. The giant's burial mound is said to be located somewhere in the interior of Hitra

name: Hlakanyana
description: Hlakanyana is a cunning trickster figure in Zulu and Xhosa folklore, of weasel-like size and nature, who famously speaks from his mother's womb demanding to be born because the cattle of his father are being devoured. After birth, he embarks on a series of adventures: he tricks a cannibal by cooking the cannibal's mother and feeding her to him, escapes by turning into a stick, steals birds from traps, and outwits a hyena and a baboon. His stories celebrate the triumph of intelligence over brute strength and the importance of cunning for survival

name: Hmong Creation Spirits (Nkauj Ntsuab & Sis Nab)
description: The Hmong Creation Spirits are the primordial beings from the Hmong creation myth who repopulated the earth after a great flood destroyed humanity. According to the legend, a great argument between the Sky Father (Saub) and the Earth led to a devastating flood. Only two siblings — a brother and sister — survived by taking refuge inside a hollow gourd or a wooden funeral drum that floated on the waters. After the flood receded, they found themselves alone on a mountain peak. The brother proposed marriage to continue the race, but the sister refused. After consulting the spirit world, they were told to roll two millstones down opposite sides of the mountain; if the stones met at the bottom, they were meant to marry. The stones rolled and met at the valley floor, and the siblings married. The sister gave birth to a strange gourd-like mass, which they cut open, releasing all the different peoples of the earth — including the Hmong, Chinese, and Lao. This legend is the Hmong explanation for the diversity of humanity and their own ethnic identity

name: Ho Ho E Ap Bess Two Men Who Changed Things Coast Salish
description: Although often filed under Coast Salish, the Ho-ho-e-ap-bess are the Makah Twin Transformers, the Two Men Who Changed Things, who in Makah legend traveled the world reshaping beings and landscape into their present forms. Brothers of the sun and the moon, their journeys explain the world as it is today.

name: Hoggar Mountain Spirits (Kel Ahaggar)
description: Among the Kel Ahaggar, a Tuareg people of the Hoggar massif in southern Algeria, the desert and mountains are held to be inhabited by invisible spirits of the wild, known as essuf or kel essuf. These beings demand respect and are linked with solitude, healing rites, and the liminal spaces of the empty land.
