The invented specifics (crystal-horned rams, a rain-spirit of Mount Tahat) are removed.

name: Hoklonote
description: Hoklonote is a malevolent spirit from Choctaw tradition, described in 19th-century ethnographic accounts collected by Henry S. Unlike many supernatural beings in Choctaw mythology, Hoklonote is unequivocally evil — a shapeshifting entity with the terrifying ability to read human thoughts. The Choctaw believed that Hoklonote could assume any form it desired, making it nearly impossible to recognize until it was too late. This spirit represents the darker aspects of the Choctaw spiritual world, serving as a cautionary figure about the dangers of trusting appearances and the importance of spiritual vigilance

name: Holy Boy
description: In Jicarilla Apache creation accounts, Holy Boy is the restless spirit of the dark underworld who drove creation forward. When the Black Hactcin had shaped the animals and the world, Holy Boy grew weary of the darkness and pressed for the sun, moon, and light to be made, so that the people could live above in a bright world.

name: Holy People (Diyin Dineʼé)
description: The Diyin Dine'é, or Holy People, are the supernaturals of Navajo tradition who shaped the world and gave the people ceremonies and lifeways. Chief among them is Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé), who created the Navajo from her own skin and a bundle of mountain soil, instructing them to live in balance within the sacred landscape.

name: Home dels Nassos
description: Home dels Nassos (Catalan for 'Man of the Noses') is a traditional Catalan mythological figure associated with New Year's Eve. According to legend, this peculiar being has as many noses as there are days in the year — 365 on January 1st, losing one each day as the year progresses. The trick, of course, is that on December 31st, he has only one nose remaining, meaning any ordinary person on the street could be him. Parents across Catalonia playfully send their children on a quest to find the man with many noses, teaching them to question assumptions and think critically. The tradition likely evolved from the Roman god Janus, the two-faced deity of transitions and beginnings

name: Horagalles
description: Horagalles is the thunder god in Sami shamanism, one of the most powerful deities in the Sami pantheon. His name likely means 'Thor-man' (from Norse Thor and Sami galles 'old man'), showing Norse influence, though he has deep indigenous roots called Tiermes or Dierpmis among eastern and northern Sami. He rules over thunder and lightning, the rainbow (his bow), weather, oceans, lakes, and human life, health, and well-being. He is depicted on shaman drums with a hammer or two crossed hammers — with one hammer he makes thunder and lightning, with the other he withdraws them to prevent harm. Idols of Horagalles were made of wood with a nail or spike in the head and a piece of flint, holding a hammer called Wetschera. He punishes evil spirits (trolls) who haunt rocks and mountains, destroying them with lightning or dashing their brains out with his hammer. In eastern Sami eschatology, he is a heavenly hunter who pursues a celestial elk/reindeer across the sky — when he shoots it with a fiery arrow, the world will collapse in flames, the stars will fall, and the sun and moon will go out

name: Horagállis
description: Horagállis (also Dearpmis, Bajanolmmái) is the Sami thunder god, considered one of the most powerful beings in Sami cosmology. Horagállis controls thunder, lightning, rain, and hail — and through these, life and death on the tundra. He is a parallel figure to the Norse Thor but distinctively Sami in character. Horagállis is both creator and destroyer: his lightning brings life-giving rain but also kills those who disrespect him. Noaidi (Sami shamans) would invoke Horagállis for protection during storms and for victory in conflict. Sacred sites dedicated to Horagállis are marked by unusually shaped stones struck by lightning. Offerings of reindeer antlers and silver were left at these sites. Horagállis was particularly feared and respected in the thunder-prone mountain regions of Troms and Finnmark. The name combines elements meaning thunder and old man

name: Horned Serpent
description: The Horned Serpent and the Tie-Snake (estakwvnayv) of the Muscogee Creek are underwater serpents of the Lower World, sometimes one creature and sometimes two, with the Horned Serpent the larger. It bears a great crystal on its forehead and crystalline scales prized for divination, its stag-like horns were used in medicine, and hunters who ate forbidden food could become such serpents.

name: Horus (Falcon God of Kingship)
description: Horus is the falcon-headed god of kingship, sky, and protection in Egyptian mythology. Son of Isis and Osiris, he was conceived after his father's murder by Set. Isis hid the infant Horus in the Nile marshes to protect him. He grew to challenge Set for the throne of Egypt, a cosmic struggle lasting 80 years. Horus lost an eye in the battle, which was restored by Thoth (the Wedjat or Eye of Horus, a powerful protective symbol). The myth established the divine right of pharaohs, each ruler being the living embodiment of Horus. The four sons of Horus protected the internal organs of the dead

name: Hotu Matu'a
description: The legendary first king and discoverer of Rapa Nui (Easter Island). According to tradition, Hotu Matu'a lived in the mythical land of Hiva, which was sinking beneath the ocean. A prophet named Hau Maka appeared in his dream and directed him to search for a new island called Rapa Nui. Seven explorers were sent ahead, found the uninhabited island, and returned with their report. Hotu Matu'a then sailed with two large canoes carrying approximately a hundred people, including his wife, children, and essential plants and animals. They landed at Anakena Beach. Hotu Matu'a divided the island among his sons, who became the ancestors of the Rapa Nui clans. He is credited with inaugurating the moai carving tradition to honor his lineage

name: Hou Yi
description: Hou Yi (Unknown). is a human. Hou Yi is a legendary archer from Chinese mythology who saved the world by shooting down nine of the ten suns that were burning the earth. He is also associated with the story of Chang'e, the moon god. Source: Classic of Mountains and Seas; Chinese mythological tradition

name: Hounds Iceland
description: Hounds Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. Hounds from Icelandic folklore are ghostly dogs that accompany the Wild Hunt procession.. Source: Icelandic folklore — spirit hounds documented in Icelandic oral tradition.

name: House God (Haashchʼééʼooghaan)
description: House God (Haashchʼééʼooghaan) is a deity in Navajo mythology who guards the home and ensures domestic harmony. He is one of the lesser Holy People tasked with protecting households from evil influences, nightmares, and spiritual intrusion. Haashchʼééʼooghaan is honored during the House Blessingway ceremony, in which the family offers prayers, corn pollen, and sacred smoke to invite his protection. He is associated with the hearth fire and the central fire pit of the hogan, and his presence is believed to keep the dwelling in a state of hózhó (beauty and balance)

name: Hoàng Tử
description: Hoàng Tử is a type of ghost in Vietnamese folklore representing the restless spirit of a prince or noble who died unjustly. These spirits are deeply tied to Vietnam's imperial history, often associated with specific historical figures — such as Hoàng Tử Nhật, the son of Emperor Gia Long who died in exile on Phú Quốc island at age two. Hoàng Tử ghosts are believed to haunt ancient citadels, royal tombs, and abandoned palaces. They embody the Vietnamese belief that those who die with unfinished business or unjust suffering cannot find peace in the afterlife. Depending on how they are treated, these royal ghosts can be either benevolent guardians or vengeful spirits who punish the descendants of those who wronged them

name: Hrosshvalur
description: Hrosshvalur (Horse-Whale) is among the most dreaded of the illhveli (evil whales) in Icelandic folklore. It has a horse-like head with a flowing red mane, a horse's tail, and huge eyes — so large it was sometimes called Monoculus (one-eyed). Hrosshvalur is 15-40 meters long and delights in sinking ships by leaping onto them or whipping up waves with its tail. Eating its flesh is forbidden — it boils away in the pot and cannot be cooked. The Grágás law code banned the eating of hrosshvalur meat. In Kormáks saga, the witch Dorveig transforms into a hrosshvalur to attack a ship. The hrosshvalur neighs like a horse, giving away its presence before it attacks. It represents the uniquely Icelandic classification of whales into edible (nauðvalir) and inedible evil whales (illhveli), a taxonomy found nowhere else

name: Huanca
description: Huanca refers to sacred elongated stone monoliths in Andean tradition, considered living beings with spiritual agency and ancestral power. The term comes from Quechua wanka, meaning 'stone' or 'rock,' and these standing stones served as the physical embodiment of founding ancestors for Andean communities (ayllus). In the animistic worldview of the Andes, huancas were not inert objects but sentient beings that could communicate, protect, and intervene in human affairs. Colonial priests systematically destroyed hundreds of huancas during the extirpation of idolatry campaigns, recognizing them as central to indigenous spiritual resistance. Huancas remain powerful symbols of Andean cultural identity and ancestral connection

name: Hughaman
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Norwegian source records a doppelganger spirit called 'hughaman' or 'hughamar'; the term appears to be built from hug (mind) and ham (shape). The genuine Norwegian traditions of the vardøger (preceding double) and fylgje (attendant spirit) cover this territory under attested names.

name: Hulder (Huldra)
description: Hulder (also called Huldra) is a supernatural female forest spirit in Norwegian folklore. Part of the huldrefolk (hidden people), she is known for her breathtaking beauty and seductive nature. She appears as a tall, fair young woman with long golden hair, but has a hollow back like a rotten tree trunk and a cow's tail that she tries to hide. The hulder lures men into the forest with her enchanting voice and dancing, often seducing them. If a man refuses her, she may kill him or he goes mad (becomes huldrin - bewitched). She can reward kindness, especially to charcoal burners whom she protects. Christian legend says she descended from Eve's hidden children. Related to Swedish skogsrå and Huldra

name: Huldra
description: Scandinavian forest Seductress - 'Huldra' from Old Norse 'huldr' (hidden/covered). Also: Swedish 'Skogsrå' (forest spirit), 'Tallemaja' (pine tree Mary), 'Skogsfru.' Name = 'secret' - conceals true nature. From Front: beautiful young woman, long goldenbirch bark hair, pale luminous skin, forest-green eyes. From Behind: exposes hidden truth - COW'S Tail (most common) or Hollow Back like rotting tree trunk. Symbolizes: forest's duality - enchanting yet dangerous. Can lure men, lead astray forever, drain life force. Protects forest - rewards respectful hunters. Cure: trick into church marriage = tail falls off, becomes human permanently. Christian framework 'civilizes' pagan spirit

name: Huldra Iceland
description: Huldra Iceland (Unknown). is a forest-spirit. The Huldra is a seductive forest spirit from Norse and Scandinavian folklore. She appears as a beautiful woman with long hair, but has a hollow back or a cow's tail that betrays her supernatural natur. Source: Scandinavian folklore; Huldra (hidden folk) are forest spirits documented in Norwegian and Swedish folk records.

name: Huldu-Elder
description: Not independently attested in Icelandic tradition. 'Huldu-Elder' appears a modern invention elaborating on huldufólk ('hidden people') belief. Jón Árnason (1862) describes huldufólk as parallel society in cliffs/valleys, but no distinct 'elder' leader with silver-grey mist-robes and timeless wisdom is documented. Concept of elder council may derive from later literary or neopagan elaboration.

name: Huldufolk
description: Huldufolk (Unknown). is a nature-spirit. The Huldufólk ("hidden people") are elf-like beings in Icelandic folklore who live in rocks and hills. They are nearly identical to humans but invisible to most people, living parallel lives in the Ic. Source: Icelandic folklore; contemporary Icelandic tradition

name: Huldufólk
description: In Iceland, huldufólk ('hidden people') are a parallel race believed to live in rocks and cliffs, largely invisible to humans. They are central to Icelandic folklore, collected by Jón Árnason and others, and were to be treated with respect: building or blasting in their dwelling-places could bring misfortune. The entry's text is corrected from a Faroese copy to the distinct Icelandic tradition.

name: Huldufólk
description: Huldufólk (the Hidden People) are the most pervasive supernatural beings in Faroese folklore — a parallel race living just beyond human sight. Unlike Icelandic hidden folk (often beautiful and slender), the Faroese version is consistently described as unusually large in build, with black hair and somber grey clothing. Their dwellings are in ancient burial mounds (álvheyggjur), the most famous being the elf-mound in Norðstreymoy south of Haldórsvík. The huldufólk keep livestock that graze invisibly among human flocks, and fishermen have reported seeing their boats at sea before they vanish. They hate electricity, church bells, and crosses. Anyone who throws stones at a mound risks their wrath — illness, bad luck, or having their children swapped for a changeling. Road construction in the Faroe Islands has been rerouted around known huldufólk dwellings as recently as the 20th century In Faroe Islands folklore, this figure is known among the Faroe Islands people.

name: Huli Jing
description: Huli jing (狐精) is the fox spirit of Chinese folklore: a fox that cultivates spiritual power over centuries, gaining the ability to shapeshift, usually into a beautiful woman who seduces and drains men's vitality. It appears in tales from the Six Dynasties, including Liaozhai Zhiyi. After a thousand years it grows nine tails, becoming the jiuwei hu; foxes may also be benevolent guardians.

name: Huma Bird
description: The Huma Bird (also known as Homa or Homay) is a legendary mythical bird from Persian folklore and a common motif in Sufi poetry, symbolizing fortune, kingship, and spiritual transcendence. According to tradition, the Huma never alights on the ground but lives its entire life flying invisibly high above the earth — some legends even claim it has no legs. Its shadow is said to bestow kingship upon whomever it falls, making it a powerful symbol of divine right and legitimacy in Persian and Mughal imperial iconography. The Huma is hermaphroditic, possessing both male and female natures, each with one wing and one leg. It is often associated with the bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus), a real bird of prey native to the mountains of Iran

name: Humadapnon
description: Humadapnon is the middle brother among three demigod heroes in the Hinilawod, the epic of the Suludnon people of Panay in the Philippines. Son of the goddess Alunsina and the mortal Datu Paubari, Humadapnon is characterized as a thoughtful strategist and skilled diplomat whose adventures balance his brother Labaw Donggon's brute strength and Dumalapdap's raw courage. His epic cycle covers revenge against those who imprisoned his eldest brother, his quest for the maiden Nagmalitong Yawa, battles against sorceresses and monsters, and a strange love triangle that ends with his wife being magically divided. The Hinilawod epic is one of the longest surviving oral epics in the Philippines

name: Humans Denmark
description: Humans Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. Ordinary humans from Danish folklore and the Molbo stories whose common sense drives comic tales.. Source: Danish folklore — spirit/human figures documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Humbaba
description: Humbaba, originally known as Huwawa in Sumerian, is a fearsome giant and ogre-like figure from Mesopotamian mythology, best known as the divinely appointed guardian of the Cedar Forest in the Epic of Gilgamesh. Appointed by the god Enlil to protect the sacred cedars, Humbaba was a terrifying being whose voice was the Deluge, his mouth was fire, his breath was death. His very presence radiated seven supernatural auras that could paralyze anyone who approached. In the epic, Gilgamesh and Enkidu ventured to the Cedar Forest seeking glory and timber. After a fierce battle aided by the sun god Shamash who unleashed thirteen winds against Humbaba, the heroes defeated the monster. The killing of Humbaba provoked the wrath of Enlil and set in motion the chain of events leading to Enkidu's death

name: Hunabal
description: Hun Hunahpu (also spelled Hun-Hunahpu, meaning 'One Hunahpu') is a central figure in Maya mythology as recounted in the Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya. He is the father of the legendary Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and is widely identified with the Maya Maize God — the deity whose death and resurrection makes human life possible. His story is one of cosmic sacrifice: tricked and killed by the Lords of Xibalba (the underworld), his severed head hung in a calabash tree, where it impregnated the maiden Xquic with his saliva. Hun Hunahpu represents the agricultural cycle of death and rebirth that underlies all of Maya civilization

name: Hundred-Egg Children (Bách Việt)
description: The Hundred-Egg Children (Bách Việt) are the mythical founding ancestors of the Vietnamese people, born from an egg sac laid by the mountain fairy Âu Cơ after her marriage to the dragon lord Lạc Long Quân. According to the creation myth, Âu Cơ gave birth to a sac containing one hundred eggs, which hatched into one hundred sons — the progenitors of all Vietnamese people. Due to the elemental incompatibility between the dragon father (water and sea) and the fairy mother (mountains and sky), the couple separated. Fifty sons followed their father to the coast where they learned fishing, sailing, and tattooing; fifty followed their mother to the highlands where they learned farming, animal husbandry, and forest craft. The eldest son became the first Hùng King, founding the Hồng Bàng dynasty that tradition says ruled for 18 generations. The hundred children became the ancestors of the Bách Việt (Hundred Yue) tribes, explaining both the unity and diversity of the Vietnamese people

name: Huron Wendigo
description: The wendigo (windigo, witiko) is a malevolent cannibal spirit of Algonquian peoples — Ojibwe, Cree, Innu, Naskapi, and Algonquin — not the Huron, whose traditions the entry wrongly implies. Documented first by Paul Le Jeune in 1636, the wendigo is an emaciated, ice-hearted giant whose insatiable hunger warns against greed, isolation, and cannibalism in the winter woods.

name: Huxhukw Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Huxhukw is the supernatural crane-like cannibal bird of the Kwakwaka'wakw Hamatsa ceremony, a long-beaked attendant of the Man-Eater spirit. It cracks open the skulls of men to suck out their brains, and its masked dancer joins the crooked-beak and raven cannibal birds in the winter dance of the Cannibal Society.

name: Hydra
description: The Hydra is a fearsome multi-headed serpent from Greek mythology, most famously known as the Lernaean Hydra that infested the swamps of Lerna in the Argolid. This monstrous water serpent was said to have nine heads, one of which was immortal. Its venom was so potent that even its breath or the scent of its tracks could kill a man. The Hydra was the second of Heracles' Twelve Labors, and its legend has become one of the most enduring monster myths in Western literature. The creature's regenerative ability — growing two heads for every one cut off — has made it a lasting symbol of problems that multiply when confronted directly

name: Hyldemor
description: Hyldemoren (the Elder Mother) is a Danish tree spirit who lives in elder trees (hyld). She appears as a small family of folk — men, women, and children — who emerge from the elder tree at night to help diligent housewives with their chores. They churn butter, spin wool, polish copper, and sweep floors, finishing all work before dawn. The elder tree itself was considered sacred in Danish folklore. Cutting elder wood without asking Hyldemor's permission brings death — numerous legends tell of people who made furniture from elder wood and were haunted by disturbances until the furniture was burned. Andersen immortalized Hyldemoren in his fairy tale 'Hyldemoer' (1845), set in the Nyboder district of Copenhagen, where an old woman living under an elder tree tells stories to a sick boy

name: Hyllemor
description: Hyllemor (Elder Mother) is a protective spirit who lives in the elder tree (fläder). She appears on Christmas Eve, dressed in a green skirt and red bodice with a striped apron, watching over the tree and punishing those who disrespect it. Breaking branches from an elder tree without permission causes 'hylleskåll' — a painful skin rash that only Hyllemor can heal. She is especially offended by anyone who urinates near or on an elder bush. To appease Hyllemor, people would pour milk or beer at the base of the elder tree. In some traditions, she grants wishes if treated with respect. The elder tree was considered sacred in Swedish folklore, and cutting one down required a formal apology to Hyllemor

name: Háldi
description: Háldi (plural Háldit) are nature spirits in Sami animistic belief, the guardians and protectors of specific places, animals, and plants. Each natural location — a lake, a fell, a forest, a stretch of river — has its own háldi who must be respected and propitiated. They are generally benevolent but can cause trouble if offended. Some háldit are associated with sacrificial stones called sieidi. The háldi tradition reflects the Sami belief that all significant natural objects possess a soul. Humans could marry háldi beings — stories tell of men marrying háldi women from invisible parallel worlds, marriages that often came with strict taboos. There are sea háldit (čáhceháldit), forest háldit, and mountain háldit, each governing different domains. The háldi differs from the Ulda in that háldit are tied to specific natural features rather than constituting a separate underground people

name: Hóu-koô-pô
description: Hóu-koô-pô (also known as Hóo-koo-pô, 'Tiger Aunt' or 'Tiger Grandma') is a terrifying figure from Taiwanese folklore — a tiger spirit from the mountains that transforms into an old woman to prey on children. The story is a classic cautionary tale used by Taiwanese parents to teach children about the dangers of trusting strangers and the importance of obedience. With over thirty-two recorded variants across Taiwan, the tale is classified by folklorists as AT type 333C (The Tiger Grandma), related to but distinct from the European Little Red Riding Hood. The most famous version was compiled by Taiwanese writer Wang Shilang and features a quick-witted young girl who outsmarts the man-eating tiger spirit

name: Húlí Jīng
description: Húlí Jīng (Fox Spirit) is a shapeshifting creature from Chinese mythology — a fox that gains supernatural powers through centuries of cultivation. These fox spirits are among the most complex and enduring figures in East Asian folklore, appearing in countless stories, novels, and operas across China, Korea, and Japan. The Húlí Jīng can transform into beautiful women or handsome men after reaching a certain age and level of spiritual attainment. Their moral alignment varies widely — some are benevolent helpers who bring fortune, while others are malevolent seducers who drain human life essence. The most famous Húlí Jīng is Daji, the legendary concubine who supposedly caused the fall of the Shang dynasty

name: Hāmah
description: Hāmah is a mythical creature from pre-Islamic Arabian folklore, described as a flying snake or a screech owl that emerges from the skull of a murdered person. According to Bedouin belief, when a person was murdered, their soul transformed into a Hāmah - an owl-like bird or flying serpent that would endlessly cry out for vengeance, hovering around the grave calling for justice. The Hāmah would not rest until the murder was avenged. This belief was so strong that it functioned as a supernatural justice system, pressuring communities to solve murders. In some accounts, the Hāmah lives in the air as a flying snake. The creature is mentioned in pre-Islamic poetry and early Islamic texts

name: Hızır
description: Hızır (Khidr), the 'Green One,' is the mysterious immortal guide of Turkic and Islamic tradition, revered across Turkmen lands as the patron of travelers and the helper who appears when he is truly needed. On Hıdırellez, the sixth of May, he is honored as the renewer of spring and the bringer of good fortune.

name: Iara
description: Brazilian water mermaid - 'Iara' from Old Tupi 'yîara' = 'water lady.' Origin: based on Tupi-Guarani. Early form: Ipupiara (carnivorous fish-man monster devouring fishermen). Legend: beautiful Indigenous woman betrayed by Brothers who murdered her at night. Fish saved her, turned into Mermaid on full moon. Now Seduces and Drowns all men for revenge. Conflated with African Iemanjá (Yoruba orisha) during colonization. 'Mãe das Águas' = Mother of Waters. Different from Iemanjá: freshwater vs saltwater. Documented by Câmara Cascudo

name: Iara da Praiana
description: Iara da Praiana is a Brazilian coastal variant of the famous Iara legend, specifically associated with the seashores and coastal waters rather than the freshwater rivers of the Amazon. While the Amazonian Iara is a freshwater mermaid who lures fishermen, this saltwater variant sings to sailors and navigators along Brazil's extensive coastline. The Iara da Praiana represents the adaptation of the indigenous Tupi legend to coastal environments, blending elements of European mermaid mythology with local Brazilian folklore. She is particularly associated with the beaches of São Luís, Maranhão, where local legend says her tears formed the Olho D'Água spring

name: Iatiku (Life Bringer)
description: Iatiku (Life Bringer) is one of the two creator sisters in Acoma Pueblo mythology. She and her sister Nautsiti were born underground at Shipapu and guided by Tsichtinako (Thought Woman). Given baskets containing seeds and animal figurines, Iatiku created the mountains, directions, plants, and animals. She created the Corn Mother and the Kachinas. Iatiku's children became the Acoma clans. She represents the life-giving, creative force in Pueblo cosmology and is central to Acoma rituals and clan o

name: Ibeji
description: Ibeji are the sacred twin orishas of the Yoruba, representing the divine spirits of twins. The Yoruba have one of the highest twinning rates in the world, and twins are considered special beings with supernatural powers. The first-born twin is Taiwo ("the one who tastes the world") and the second is Kehinde ("the one who arrives after"). Ibeji are associated with Shango, who is the patron god of twins. They bring prosperity, fertility, and good fortune to their parents but can also punish neglect. When a twin dies, a carved wooden statuette (ere ibeji) is created to house their spirit. Ibeji are the patron spirits of abundance, joy, and protection against evil

name: Ibong Adarna (The Adarna Bird)
description: The Ibong Adarna is a legendary magical bird from Philippine epic poetry whose song has the power to heal any sickness and whose droppings turn anyone they fall upon into stone. It is the central figure of the 19th-century Filipino epic 'Corrido at Buhay na Pinagdaanan ng Tatlong Prinsipeng Magkakapatid.' The story follows three princes sent by their dying king to capture the elusive bird. Each prince falls asleep when the bird sings its enchanting seven songs, until the youngest prince Juan discovers the secret: cutting oneself and applying lemon juice prevents sleep. The Adarna Bird is described as the most colorful bird in Philippine folklore, often associated with the Philippine trogon, and is considered a symbol of healing, magic, and the triumph of perseverance

name: Ibonia
description: Ibonia (Iboniamasiboniamanoro, 'He of the Clear and Captivating Glance') is the great epic hero of Madagascar. Conceived through divine intervention, he began speaking from his mother's womb, demanding betrothal to Iampelasoamananoro ('Girl of Grace'). After birth, Girl of Grace was abducted by Ravato ('Stone Man'). Ibonia defeated the Great Echo in a verbal duel, fought powerful animals including the Crocodile and the Bull, and disguised himself in an old man's skin to infiltrate Stone Man's village. He escaped with his beloved, ruled for ten years, established laws, and died peacefully, promising to return. The epic blends Indonesian riddling traditions with African praise poetry

name: Icarus
description: Icarus (Unknown). is a human. Icarus is a figure from Greek mythology who escaped the Labyrinth of Crete on wings made of feathers and wax by his father Daedalus. Ignoring his father's warning, he flew too close to the sun, meltin. Source: Metamorphoses (Ovid, 8 CE); Greek mythological tradition

name: Ice Giant (Muisca)
description: The Ice Giant is a mythical figure from Muisca mythology, the advanced pre-Columbian civilization of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense in the Colombian Andes. While the Muisca are best known for the legend of El Dorado, their mythology also includes giants and other supernatural beings. The Ice Giant likely relates to the Muisca understanding of their high-altitude environment, where freezing temperatures and paramo ecosystems shaped daily life. Muisca mythology features several giant-like figures, including the monstrous serpent of Lake Tota and various chthonic beings associated with the cold mountain peaks that dominated their landscape

name: Ice Maiden Denmark
description: Ice Maiden Denmark (Unknown). is a human. The Ice Maiden is from Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale about a cold snow spirit who lures a young man to his death.. Source: Danish folklore — the Ice Maiden from Hans Christian Andersen and Danish oral tradition.

name: Ice-Maiden (Isjomfru)
description: Isjomfru ('Ice Maiden') is a Danish winter spirit: pale, translucent skin, frost-haired, ice-gowned. Lures travelers with cold melody to freeze in snow. Inhabits frozen lakes and mountains. Vulnerable to fire, true love, spring sun. Parallels Snow Queen (Snedronningen); both stem from older winter-goddess motifs.

name: Iele
description: The Iele are feminine mythical creatures in Romanian mythology, often described as faeries with great seductive power over men. They possess magic skills and attributes similar to the nymphs, naiads, and dryads of Greek mythology, embodying the untamed and mysterious spirit of the natural world. They are said to inhabit the vast skies, dense forests, deep caves, and isolated mountain cliffs, and are frequently reported to have been seen bathing in sacred springs or guarding mysterious crossroads

name: Ifriqiya (Tunisian Serpent of Wisdom)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Ifriqiya' is the medieval Arabic name of the North African province (from the Roman Africa, named for the Berber goddess Ifri and the Afri people), not a serpent of Tunisian legend. No Tunisian source describes a guardian dragon of that name; the earthquake and 'city built over its head' details are invented.

name: Ifrit
description: The ifrit is a powerful and malevolent class of jinn in Arab and Islamic tradition, famed for brute strength, cunning, and a rebellious nature. The Qur'an names the ifrit of the jinn who offered to carry the throne of Bilqis. In popular tales ifrits appear as enormous winged beings of fire and magic, bound to the underworld and to the spirits of the dead.

name: Ifrit (Powerful Fire Jinn)
description: The Ifrit (plural: Afarit) is a powerful class of jinn in Algerian Islamic folklore, considered among the most dangerous and formidable of supernatural beings. Created from smokeless fire like all jinn, ifrits are distinguished by their immense strength, speed, and malevolent nature. In Algerian tradition, ifrits inhabit desolate places such as ruins, desert wastes, and cemeteries. They are particularly associated with the vast Sahara regions of southern Algeria. Unlike ordinary jinn who may be either good or evil, ifrits are almost always depicted as malevolent, rebellious spirits who actively work against humans. They are known for their incredible speed, ability to lift enormous weights, and their capacity to cause possession, madness, and death. In Islamic scripture, an ifrit is mentioned in the Quran as offering to carry the throne of the Queen of Sheba to King Solomon. In Algerian folk belief, ifrits are especially active at night and are blamed for sudden illnesses, accidents, and unexplained phenomena. Traditional protection involves reciting specific Quranic verses, wearing amulets, and avoiding certain locations at certain times

name: Ifrit (ʿIfrīt)
description: The ifrit, spelled variously ifrit and afrit, is a mighty class of rebellious fire-jinn renowned for guile and supernatural power. It is first met in the Qur'anic tale of the throne of Sheba, where an ifrit of the jinn volunteers to bring it in an instant. Folk tradition pictures the ifrit as a towering winged being of smoke and flame dwelling in ruins and desolate wastes.

name: Igyō no danshi
description: Igyō no danshi (異形の男子), 'the grotesque boy', is recorded in the Edo-period Chikuzen Bakemono Emaki: the armless son of Ōtomo Senzaemon, a retainer of Oka Castle in Bungo Province, born around 1842. He spoke from birth, had a scorching-hot body, breathed fire from his nostrils, and released a hitodama spirit-fire from his mouth — read as karmic retribution for his father's killing of animals.

name: Ijapa
description: Ijapa (Unknown). is a animal-spirit. Ijapa (the Tortoise) is a trickster figure in Yoruba folklore. This clever tortoise uses his wits to survive and thrive, though his schemes often backfire in humorous ways.. Source: Yoruba oral tradition; West African folktales

name: Ijimere
description: Ijimere (Ethiopia). is a demon. malevolent shadow spirits from nigerian folklore who lure victims into the woods with mimicry. Source: Ethiopian folklore — Ijimere shadow demons documented in Ethiopian oral tradition.

name: Ikenga
description: Ikenga is the Igbo alusi of achievement, success, strength, and the right hand. Depicted as a horned anthropomorphic figure holding a sword and a severed human head, Ikenga represents personal power, war, and individual accomplishment. Every Igbo man traditionally owned a personal Ikenga shrine representing his chi (personal god) and his right to achieve. The horns symbolize strength and ambition. A man prays to his Ikenga before important undertakings — trading expeditions, warfare, farming, or legal disputes. When a man dies, his Ikenga is broken to release his spirit. The Ikenga cult reinforces the Igbo values of personal achievement, hard work, and accumulation of wealth through one's own efforts. Three types exist: Ikenga (war), Ikenga Ogu (war), and Ikenga Alusi (deity)

name: Iktomi
description: Iktomi is the spider trickster of Lakota mythology, a complex figure who is both clever and foolish. Born fully grown with the body of a spider and the cunning of a man, Iktomi is known for his clever schemes and predictions. However, his selfishness and mischievous nature often backfire—in one tale he tried to keep fish soup for himself rather than share; in another he angered a boulder and was crushed, only to be freed by bats who were turned into stones. Despite his flaws, Iktomi is considered wise and his stories teach moral lessons about generosity and respect. He is the son of Inyan and is also known as Ksa or the second manifestation of wisdom

name: Iktomi Lakota
description: Iktomi is the spider trickster of the Lakota, Dakota, and Nakota peoples, a wily, foolish being whose schemes usually go wrong. His stories are told as negative models: they show what not to do and teach lessons about pride, greed, and deception through his endless failures, making him one of the best-known figures of Plains oral tradition.

name: Iku-Turso
description: Iku-Turso (Meri-Tursas, Turisas) is a Finnish primordial sea giant in Kalevala. Rises to burn haystack; world oak grows from ashes. Louhi summons him to stop Sampo theft; Väinämöinen seizes him by ears, banishes to ocean depths. Runic songs: father of Väinämöinen (Iku-Turilas) or Meri-Tursas who impregnates Loviatar with diseases. Name from Proto-Germanic *þurisaz 'giant'.

name: Ilmarinen
description: Ilmarinen is the Finnish smith god, eternal hammerer who forged the sky's dome and the magical Sampo. First documented by Agricola (1551) as bringer of peace and air. Runic songs: forges sky in windowless forge, creates fire with eagle feathers, makes iron. Woos Maiden of Pohjola; forges golden bride who proves cold. Equivalent to Sámi Biegga-galles, Udmurt Inmar.

name: Ilmatar
description: Ilmatar (Luonnotar, 'Airess') is the Finnish virgin air spirit in Kalevala, mother of Väinämöinen. Drifts 700 years in primordial ocean until duck lays eggs on her knee; eggs form sky, earth, celestial bodies. Not a creator in pre-Kalevala runic songs; Lönnrot elevated her from White Karelian 'oldest of women'. Sibelius's Luonnotar (1913) immortalized her.

name: Imana
description: Imana is the creator deity in the traditional Banyarwanda and Barundi religion in Rwanda and Burundi and other related ethnic groups, such as Baha in Tanzania and Banyamulenge in the Democratic Republic of Congo. In current-day usage, the term refers to God as found in Christianity. Ancient Banyarwanda and Barundi believed in one god, the creator Imana. In their mythology, Imana was the creator and the supporter of all the Barundi and Banyarwanda people. Imana was seen as almighty and gracious, intervening in one of the legends in an altercation between a man who had always borrowed beans from different people but wriggled out of repaying the debt

name: Imana
description: Imana is the creator deity in the traditional Banyarwanda and Barundi religion in Rwanda and Burundi and other related ethnic groups, such as Baha in Tanzania and Banyamulenge in the Democratic Republic of Congo. In current-day usage, the term refers to God as found in Christianity. Ancient Banyarwanda and Barundi believed in one god, the creator Imana. In their mythology, Imana was the creator and the supporter of all the Barundi and Banyarwanda people. Imana was seen as almighty and gracious, intervening in one of the legends in an altercation between a man who had always borrowed beans from different people but wriggled out of repaying the debt In Rwanda folklore, this figure is known among the Rwanda people.

name: Imana
description: Imana is the supreme creator deity in the traditional Barundi (and Banyarwanda) religion of Burundi and Rwanda. Unlike the many intervening spirits of the Kubandwa tradition, Imana is seen as the almighty and gracious creator who rules all living things but does not normally interfere in the material course of nature. In Barundi mythology, Imana created the world and humanity, then hunted Death itself as a savage wild animal to grant immortality to creation. During this hunt, Imana commanded all people to stay hidden so Death would have no refuge. However, an old woman disobeyed by creeping out to her vegetable garden, allowing Death to hide under her skirt and enter her home. She died, and when her daughter-in-law—who hated her—filled the cracks in her grave with dirt, she sealed humanity's fate, making death permanent. Imana does not intervene directly in daily affairs, leaving that role to the Imandwa spirits led by Kiranga. This theological distinction—a supreme creator who delegates to lesser mediating spirits—demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of divine hierarchy

name: Imandwa Spirits
description: The Imandwa are the collective spirits and initiated members of the Kubandwa spirit cult in Burundi and Rwanda, forming a hierarchical pantheon of approximately forty distinct spirits. This spirit pantheon includes Kiranga (Ryangombe) as the supreme leader, his son and successor Binego, other sons like Ruhanga, legendary heroes like the Rwandan prince Kibogo, and various animal and nature spirits. The Imandwa serve as active intermediaries between the supreme creator Imana and human beings, influencing every aspect of life including agriculture, fertility, health, hunting, marital love, and prosperity. Unlike ordinary ghosts (bazimu) who are mostly malevolent, the Imandwa are a superior order of spirits who can be petitioned through proper ritual. The term 'Imandwa' refers both to the spirits themselves and to living human initiates who have undergone the Kubandwa initiation and can be possessed by these spirits during ceremonies. The Kubandwa tradition represents one of the most sophisticated spirit-medium systems in African traditional religion

name: Imehornets underjordiske
description: Imehornets underjordiske is a supernatural being from the Ime area near Mandal in Sørlandet, famous for offering the legendary Imehornet drinking horn. According to the classic horn legend (ML 6045), two riders passed the Ime farm and were offered a drink by an underground being who emerged from a burial mound. The being offered a magnificent drinking horn. One rider threw the drink over his shoulder — it burned the hide off his horse where it fell. The riders escaped with the horn. The Imehornet is a real artifact now held at the Cultural History Museum in Oslo. The horn likely dates from the 1500s. There are 21 documented Sørlandet variants of this legend, all following the same pattern: a burial mound opens, a being emerges offering a drink, the drink is rejected, and the horn is stolen. The Imehornet variant is the most famous and represents the Sørlandet tradition of mound-dwelling beings

name: Imizimu
description: Imizimu (Burundi). is a ancestor-spirit. Spirits of deceased relatives divided into friendly and harmful categories. Source: Burundian folklore — Imizimu ancestor spirits documented in Burundian oral tradition.

name: Impundulu
description: Impundulu (lightning bird, thekwane) is the Zulu and Xhosa vampiric lightning bird — a human-sized black-and-white bird that summons thunder and lightning with wings and talons. It functions as a witch's familiar, drinks blood, can take human form to seduce women, and is passed down matrilineally. Only fire can destroy it. Documented by Berglund, Werner, and contemporary belief.

name: Imugi
description: Imugi (이무기) is the immature dragon of Korean folklore: a great hornless serpent that failed to achieve full dragonhood, sometimes because it lacked the dragon jewel or could not climb the storm-ladder to heaven, and must wait a thousand years. Tales vary on whether it is benevolent or ominous, and 'imugi' sightings are also folk explanations for lake and river serpents.

name: Ina
description: A beautiful Cook Islands maiden who became the lover of the moon god Marama. Ina is the Cook Islands version of the pan-Polynesian Hina/Sina figure. In the most famous Cook Islands tale, Ina was carried across the ocean on the back of a great shark (Tekea the Great, king of all sharks) to reach her lover Tinirau, the god of the ocean. During the journey, she grew thirsty and cracked open a coconut, drinking its milk. Later she struck a second coconut on the shark's head to open it, hurting the shark badly. The dent on the shark's head remains visible to this day. In some traditions, Ina eventually became the woman in the moon, fleeing from human troubles

name: Ina-Mita (Corn Spirit)
description: Ina-Mita (Mother Corn) is the agricultural spirit of Timor-Leste who, according to Timorese tradition, sacrificed herself to provide corn (maize) to the people during a time of terrible drought. When a severe drought threatened the survival of the highland communities, a poor farmer prayed to the ancestors for help. An ancestral spirit appeared in a dream, instructing him to sacrifice his most prized possession — a single golden earring passed down through generations — and bury it in the driest part of his field. The next morning, a strange new plant sprouted where the earring was buried, bearing golden cobs with kernels like drops of gold. Ina-Mita's spirit resides in every cornfield, and Timorese farmers perform rituals before planting and harvesting to honor her sacrifice

name: Inkanyamba
description: Inkanyamba is a Zulu and Xhosa serpentine water spirit associated with Howick Falls (Umgeni River, KwaZulu-Natal). Its name means "snake cloud" — it causes tornadoes and seasonal storms. Described as a multi-headed serpent with horselike head, dorsal fins, and fish tail. Appeased for rain and fertility; snip angered by corrugated roofs mimicking water.

name: Inkarri
description: The Inkarri myth is one of the most famous legends of the Inca. When the Spanish conquistadors executed the last ruler of the Inca people, Atahualpa, he vowed that he would come back one day to avenge his death. According to the legend, the Spaniards buried his body parts in several places around the kingdom: His head is said to rest under the Presidential Palace in Lima, while his arms are said to be under the Waqaypata in Cusco and his legs in Ayacucho. Buried under the earth he will grow until the day that he will rise, take back his kingdom and restore harmony in the relationship between Pacha Mama and her children

name: Inuarutligaks
description: Not independently attested in Greenlandic folklore. No reliable Greenlandic source records beings called 'Inuarutligaks'; the name resembles a corruption of Greenlandic words for people or giants. The closest attested analogues are the qivittoq, humans who fled to the wilderness and became monstrous, and the dreaded giant spirits of inland Greenland.

name: Invunche
description: Invunche (Imbunche) is a Chilote monster from Chiloé Island, Chile: a kidnapped infant deformed by a brujo (warlock) — leg twisted over back, tongue forked, skin blue, fed on black cat's milk and human flesh. Guards the warlock's cave entrance, acts as advisor and instrument of curses. Created through ritual torture of a firstborn under nine days old.

name: Inyan
description: Inyan is the primordial rock of Lakota creation, the first being who existed alongside Wakan Tanka before the world began. He sacrificed his fluid power and his blood to create Maka, the Earth, and the waters, shriveling into the hard, silent stone that is the foundation of the land; in Lakota cosmology his sacrifice explains why rock and soil remain bound together.

name: Inzoka
description: Inzoka (Rwanda). is a serpent. Snake-like spirits dwelling in lakes and rivers, believed to wield power over droughts and floods. Source: Regional survey of East African indigenous traditions — Kikuyu, Luo, Ganda, Chaga, Malagasy, Maasai, Somali, Ethiopian, and related peoples as documen

name: Ioi
description: Ioi is the sister of Blue Jay in Chinook tradition. Taken as a wife into the land of the dead, she tried patiently to teach her brother the customs of the ghost people, but Blue Jay mocked and mishandled everything and her warnings went unheeded. Her story is a lesson in approaching the supernatural world with humility and respect.

name: Ioi Coast Salish
description: Io'i is not a Coast Salish figure but the sister of Blue Jay, the trickster of Chinookan tales told at the lower Columbia River. Blue Jay and Io'i travel together in adventure stories in which Io'i repeatedly saves her foolish brother from the consequences of his boasting and meddling.

name: Ioskeha
description: Ioskeha is the Good Twin and culture hero of Huron (Wyandot) tradition. With his evil brother Tawiscaron he shaped the world after their mother Aataentsic's death; Ioskeha created the sun and moon, slew monsters, and gave the people corn, tobacco and the arts of living. He is the model of order, light and benevolent leadership.

name: Ippondatara
description: Ippondatara (一本足) is a yōkai of the mountain districts of Kinki and Shikoku, especially Kumano in Wakayama: a being with a single leg and often a single eye that appears on mountain passes and roads during heavy rain, walking with a crashing, staggering gait. It is easily startled and flees when humans shout or throw things, though travelers who panic before it may be frightened to death.

name: Ira
description: Ira are Bijago island ancestor spirits represented by wooden statuettes (iran) placed in family shrines (balobas), maintaining connections between living and ancestors.

name: Irrbloss
description: Irrbloss, meaning "wandering blaze" in Swedish, are ghostly flickering lights seen at night in marshes, bogs, and ancient roads. In Swedish folklore they are most commonly believed to be the restless souls of the dead who were neither good enough for heaven nor evil enough for hell, condemned to wander the earth with only a faint light to guide them. Also called Lyktgubbe (lantern man), they are often described as a small man carrying a lantern who leads travelers astray. The Irrbloss can be either malevolent or helpful depending on how they are treated: offering a coin may earn safe passage home, while following them without permission leads to being hopelessly lost in swamps and marshes. Some traditions hold that they guard hidden treasure, and a clever person can trick them with iron to claim the hoard. In southern Sweden they were said to be the souls of wrongdoers such as farmers who harvested crops on stolen land

name: Irrlicht
description: Irrlicht (will-o'-the-wisp) is the German term for ghostly lights over bogs, called Irrwisch by Luther. Folk belief: souls of unbaptised children or drowned folk leading travellers astray. In Silesia, burying the light's source under a church eave and baptising it with rainwater could redeem the soul. Latin ignis fatuus coined from German in 16th century.

name: Ise-nō
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Japanese folklore. No source documents a nature spirit named 'Ise-nō' associated with Shinto shrine stones and sacred rocks. No matching entry appears in yōkai references, regional folklore collections, or works on stone kami. The recorded traits match no named kami or yōkai and appear to derive from speculation.

name: Isis (Goddess of Magic)
description: Isis is the greatest goddess of Egyptian mythology, known as the goddess of magic, motherhood, healing, and protection. Daughter of Geb and Nut, sister and wife of Osiris, mother of Horus. When her brother Set murdered Osiris and scattered his body, Isis tirelessly searched for the pieces, reconstructed him, and briefly revived him to conceive Horus. She is the greatest magician in Egyptian mythology; she tricked Ra into revealing his secret name, gaining power over all creation. She protects women and children, heals the sick, and guides the dead. Her cult spread throughout the Greco-Roman world, from Britain to Afghanistan. Temples at Philae and Behbeit el-Hagar were major centers of her worship

name: Isokelekel
description: Isokelekel, meaning 'shining noble' or 'wonderful king' in Pohnpeian, is a semi-mythical hero and warrior from Kosrae who overthrew the Saudeleur rulers of Pohnpei. According to legend, Isokelekel arrived at Pohnpei with a fleet of canoes and defeated the tyrannical Saudeleur dynasty that had ruled for centuries from the artificial island city of Nan Madol. Through a combination of military strategy and supernatural aid, he liberated the people from oppressive rule. After his victory, Isokelekel married a local woman and established the Nahnmwarki system of governance that continues in modified form today. He is considered the father of modern Pohnpei and resides in the oral history as the liberator who ended the oppressive Saudeleur regime

name: Ista First Woman Nuxalk
description: Ista is the First Woman of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola) origin account, who descended to the land at the beginning of the world and became mother of the people. Her story, told as a smayusta, explains the beginnings of human life and of Nuxalk society and belongs to the creation narratives of the Bella Coola.

name: Iwin
description: Ìwin are a class of Yoruba spirits, often described as mischievous and elusive forest beings who guard the secrets of the bush and teach wisdom through riddles and illusions. They are said to lure the unwary with playful pranks, and traditional healers may negotiate with them for esoteric knowledge in Yoruba oral tradition.

name: J Tte
description: J Tte (Unknown). is a spirit. Jatte Jattar are giants from Swedish and Nordic folklore, ancient beings who shaped the landscape with immense strength.. Source: Norwegian folklore — the Jøtte giant figure documented in Norwegian oral tradition.

name: Jab Jab
description: Jab Jab (meaning Double Devil in French Creole, from 'Diable Diable') is a central figure in Grenada's Carnival and folklore traditions. Unlike most Caribbean spirits that are purely mythological, Jab Jab is a costumed Carnival character representing the devil — but in a uniquely Grenadian context. Performers cover themselves in grease or paint, wear chains, and carry whips, embodying the spirit of rebellion and freedom. The Jab Jab tradition has roots in the post-emancipation period when formerly enslaved people used Carnival to satirize and invert the power structures of colonial society. The character is both a fearsome mythological figure — a devil spirit that roams during Carnival — and a powerful symbol of Grenadian resistance and cultural identity. The chains represent slavery, and the whipping movements symbolize breaking free from oppression

name: Jack Ball
description: The jack ball is a protective charm of African American Hoodoo and conjure: a red-flannel bundle of roots, herbs, bones, coins, nails, and personal objects bound with string, dressed with oils and 'fed' to maintain its power. Placed to guard a home or carried as a talisman, it descends from Kongo nkisi power objects and parallels the mojo bag.

name: Jack-o'-Lantern
description: In African American folklore, Jack-o'-Lantern (also called Jacky-My-Lantern) is a wandering spirit who carries a flickering light through the swamps at night, luring travelers from the safety of the road into treacherous marshland. According to Uncle Remus tales collected by Joel Chandler Harris, Jacky-My-Lantern was once a man who made a deal with the Devil and was cursed to wander the earth with only a lantern made from a hollowed turnip and a coal of fire, never finding rest. When travelers see the bobbing light and follow it, hoping to reach shelter, they soon find themselves sinking into the bog. The only protection is to carry a Bible, wear a coat inside out, or avoid the swamps at night. The legend blends African American folklore with European will-o'-the-wisp traditions

name: Jackalope
description: The jackalope is a 'fearsome critter' of American tall-tale tradition: a jackrabbit with antelope horns, said to mimic human voices and be lured with whiskey. Popularized in Wyoming in the 1930s by taxidermist Douglas Herrick, it is a 20th-century hoax animal, not a Native American legend.

name: Jacky My Lantern
description: Jacky My Lantern (Unknown). is a spirit. Jacky My Lantern (also known as Jack-o'-lantern or Stingy Jack) is a figure from Irish folklore, a blacksmith who tricked the Devil and was cursed to wander the earth with only a burning coal in a hol. Source: Irish folklore; Halloween tradition; will-o'-the-wisp phenomenon

name: Jade Emperor
description: Jade Emperor (Unknown). is a deity. The Jade Emperor (Yu Huang) is the supreme ruler of Heaven in Chinese folk religion and Taoist mythology. He governs the celestial bureaucracy and decides the fates of mortals.. Source: Taoist canon; Chinese folk religion; Journey to the West (Wu Cheng'en, 16th century)

name: Jade Serpent Spirit
description: Not independently attested as a distinct spirit of Altai folklore. No source confirms a 'Jade Serpent Spirit' with petrifying power in the Altai; searches surfaced only Kosh-Agach area pages with no such serpent legend, and Altai serpent figures are not recorded under this name. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Jaka Tarub
description: Jaka Tarub is the mortal protagonist of a famous Javanese folktale from Central Java. A young hunter, he discovers seven heavenly nymphs (bidadari) bathing in a forest lake and steals the shawl of the youngest and most beautiful, Nawang Wulan, preventing her return to heaven. They marry and have a daughter. Despite their happiness, Jaka Tarub breaks his wife's trust by lifting the cover of her magical cooking pot, shattering her spell. When Nawang Wulan discovers her hidden shawl and returns to heaven, Jaka Tarub is left alone to raise their daughter. According to Javanese tradition, their descendants went on to establish the Mataram Sultanate, one of the most powerful kingdoms in Indonesian history

name: Jambavan (King of the Bears)
description: Jambavan is the king of the bears (rikshas) in Hindu texts, a chiranjivi (immortal being) who has lived through multiple cosmic ages. He emerged from the mouth of Brahma when the creator deity yawned, making him one of the first created beings. He was present at the churning of the ocean (Samudra Manthana) and circled the dwarf avatar Vamana 21 times in a single leap when Vishnu measured the three worlds. In the Ramayana, he was a key advisor to Sugriva and played a crucial role in Hanuman's awakening — it was Jambavan who reminded Hanuman of his dormant divine powers and encouraged him to leap across the ocean to Lanka. He also fought in the war against Ravana, serving as a strategist and healer. In the Mahabharata and Bhagavata Purana, Jambavan fought Krishna for 27/28 days over the Syamantaka jewel before recognizing Krishna's divinity, surrendering the gem, and offering his daughter Jambavati in marriage to Krishna

name: Jann
description: The jann are the primordial fire-born jinn of pre-Islamic Arabia, created from smokeless flame before the coming of Islam. They haunt desert paths and oases, appearing to travellers as whirlwinds of sand or as a beautiful white camel that leads them astray. Capable of every shape, they are as likely to help as to harm, their root name meaning to conceal.

name: Jarjacha
description: Jarjacha is a cursed screaming beast of the Peruvian Andes (Ayacucho, Apurímac, Huancavelica). A human transformed by divine punishment for grave sins (incest, sacrilege), it roams high peaks at night emitting terrifying screams that portent death. Only spiritual cleansing by a healer can free the cursed soul. Documented in Quechua oral tradition.

name: Jembalang
description: Jembalang are earth spirits of Malay folklore, wild and unsociable beings said to haunt hills, forests, and the soil beneath the fields. A jembalang tanah (earth jembalang) can stir landslides and epidemics, and villagers placate it with offerings and shamanic rites; respecting its territory protects a community from its wrath.

name: Jenglot
description: Jenglot are small, fist-sized mummified humanoids of Javanese occult tradition, said to be kept in homes where they are fed blood in exchange for wealth and protection. Modern skeptics note that most jenglot are crafted from preserved monkeys, birds, or calves; even so, the figure thrives as a living example of Indonesian animism and occult commerce.

name: Jengu
description: Jengu (pl. miengu; Bakweri: liengu) are water spirits of the Sawabantu peoples of Cameroon — Duala, Bakweri, Limba, Bakoko, Oroko. They appear as beautiful mermaid-like beings with long hair and a distinctive gap-toothed grin. Miengu mediate between the living and ancestral spirits, bring good fortune, heal illness, and control aquatic fates.

name: Jerff
description: The Jerff (Gulon, 'Glutton') is a beast described in Olaus Magnus's 'Historia de Gentibus Septentrionalibus' (1555), a work of northern European natural history and folklore. It was said to be a gluttonous creature that gorged on carrion until its belly swelled, then squeezed between two trees to vomit so it could eat again; likely an exaggerated account of the wolverine (Gulo gulo).

name: Jhelmaia (Camel)
description: Jhelmaia (Zhel-maya, the 'wind camel') is a legendary camel of Kazakh folklore: an unnaturally fast, tireless steed of the steppe. A tale associates the wind-fast camel with Korkut Ata, who sent it racing across the land; it endures in Kazakh tradition as a symbol of loyalty, endurance, and the speed prized by nomads.

name: Jian (Jian Shu)
description: Under the recorded name 'Jian', Chinese folk tradition documents jian spirits (魙/漸): 'ghosts of ghosts' that arise when dead souls die again into an even lower class of being. The concept, traced to the 13th century, combines the Tang apotropaic jian character with the idea that ghosts are mortal. The input's headless figure matches the separate wútóu guǐ (headless ghost) tradition.

name: Jiangshi
description: Jiangshi (殭屍) is the 'hopping corpse' of Chinese folklore: a reanimated body, often of a person whose breath failed to leave at death or whose grave was disturbed, moving in stiff, leaping bounds with arms outstretched. It drains life energy from the living and is warded off by mirrors, glutinous rice, rooster blood, and talismans.

name: Jinn
description: Jinn (Islamic/Traditional). is a spirit. Jinn is a spirit from Islamic/Traditional folklore in Eritrea, believed to embody the spiritual traditions of the region.. Source: Eritrean folklore

name: Jinn
description: The jinn of Jordan are fire-born spirits, created of smokeless flame, who dwell in abandoned houses, wells, deep caves, and desert wastes. They can take any form and possess the unwary, yet they can be helpful as well as harmful. Jordanians speak of jinn dancing at crossroads and guard against them with prayer, iron, and the rule of never mentioning them at night.

name: Jinn (Gambian)
description: Jinn (or Jinne) are non-human spirit creatures deeply woven into Gambian folklore, existing at the intersection of pre-Islamic African belief and Islamic cosmology. In Gambian tradition, jinn inhabit the world alongside humans — invisible under normal circumstances but capable of interacting with and affecting human life. They are believed to dwell in trees, rivers, rocks, and wilderness spaces, and every village is said to have two guardian jinn: one good and one bad, one male and one female. Gambian jinn are complex beings with their own societies, marriages, and customs. They can form friendships with humans, fall in love, marry, and have children. The famous Wolof folktale 'Mamadou and Anta' tells of a human man who marries a jinn woman and nearly destroys the relationship through broken promises. Jinn can cause illness, madness, or misfortune when angered, but can also serve as protectors and guides when respected. Belief in jinn is nearly universal in The Gambia, and marabouts (Islamic spiritual healers) specialize in negotiating with them. The jinn tradition represents the rich synthesis of pre-Islamic Gambian spirit beliefs with Islamic theology

name: Jinn (Genie)
description: Jinn (Genie) (Djibouti). is a spirit. Supernatural beings of smokeless fire capable of benevolence or malevolence. Source: Djiboutian Islamic folklore — jinn/genie documented in Djiboutian and Horn of Africa Islamic tradition.

name: Jinn of Jerusalem
description: Jinn are supernatural beings of pre-Islamic and Islamic tradition — creatures of smokeless fire, invisible to humans, capable of good and evil. In Jerusalem folklore, jinn are associated with ruins, wells, and thresholds, and are believed to inhabit places where people lived before. They are mentioned in the Qur'an and figure widely in Palestinian and Levantine belief.

name: Jiu Wei Hu (Nine-tailed Fox)
description: Jiǔwěihú (九尾狐), the nine-tailed fox of Chinese mythology, is a shapeshifting fox spirit that gains one new tail each century of cultivation. It often appears as a beautiful woman who seduces and corrupts rulers — famously Daji of the Shang dynasty — yet auspicious nine-tailed foxes also appear as omens in the Shanhaijing. It is the ancestor of the Korean gumiho and Japanese kitsune.

name: Jiuku Tiannu
description: Not independently attested as a goddess of Chinese religion. No source documents a 'Jiuku Tiannu' (救苦天女) who descends during epidemics to cure disease. The name appears to conflate documented figures: Taiyi Jiuku Tianzun (太乙救苦天尊), the Daoist Lord of Salvation, and Jiutian Xuannü (九天玄女). Neither is attested as a plague-curing goddess under this name.

name: John Henry
description: John Henry is the most iconic folk hero in African American tradition, a steel-driving man who raced against a steam drill to prove that human dignity could not be replaced by a machine. According to legend, John Henry worked as a hammer-swinging laborer blasting tunnels through mountains for the expanding railroad. When a salesman brought a steam-powered drill to the worksite, John Henry challenged it to a contest. For hours he swung his nine-pound hammer, driving steel deeper than the machine. He won — drilling fourteen feet to the steam drill's nine — but his heart gave out, and he died with his hammer in his hand. The story, told in the classic blues ballad, became a powerful symbol of the human cost of industrialization and the dignity of Black labor

name: Jok
description: Jok is the all-embracing class of spirits in Acholi belief, covering ancestral shades, nature powers, and the supreme creator. It can strike with illness and misfortune, yet it also grants protection, healing, and prosperity, and is honoured through song. Every clan and place possesses its own jok, weaving the seen and unseen worlds into one order.

name: Jorōgumo
description: Japanese yokai - spider that becomes beautiful woman after 400 Years. Name: '絡新婦' = 'Entangling/Binding Bride' (originally 'whore spider'). Can shapeshift OR IS based on golden orb-weaver spider (Trichonephila clavata). Appears to Prey on handsome young men. Seduction method: beautiful woman lost traveler, widow, or stranger needing help. Invites to home (illusion concealing cave). Offers sake/food/promise of intimacy. Then: binds with Invisible silk threads (strong enough to drop adult), drains life force slowly. Also plays biwa (lute) to mesmerize with music. Near Waterfalls especially - Jōren Falls in Izu famous. Edo period emerged as prominent yokai (1603-1868). Metaphor: dangers of lust, deception, hidden treachery beneath beauty. Represents commercial society's moral hazards

name: Joukahainen
description: Joukahainen is a youthful Finnish warrior who challenges Väinämöinen to a singing contest, loses, and is sung into a mire. Pledges sister Aino as wife; she drowns herself rather than marry the sage. Later ambushes Väinämöinen, killing his horse. In some runic songs he is Väinämöinen's brother or Sampo-quest companion. Name varies widely (Jokkahas, Joukamoinen).

name: Juan Bobo (Puerto Rican Trickster Folk Hero)
description: Juan Bobo (Simple John) is the beloved trickster folk hero of Puerto Rican folklore -- a simple-minded but well-intentioned young boy whose absurd misunderstandings and literal interpretations of his mother instructions create a cascade of hilarious disasters. For over 200 years, Juan Bobo stories have been a cornerstone of Puerto Rican oral tradition and children literature. He is simultaneously a fool and a trickster: his actions are driven by genuine kindness and good intentions, but his complete lack of common sense leads to catastrophes. In the most famous tale, his mother tells him to care for the family pig while she attends church. When the pig squeals, Juan assumes it wants to go to mass too, so he dresses it in his mother finest Sunday dress, puts lipstick and jewelry on it, and sends it to church -- with predictably disastrous results. Juan Bobo stories originated from Spanish picaresque traditions (influenced by Lazarillo de Tormes and Don Quixote) and evolved through centuries of Puerto Rican oral tradition

name: Julunggul
description: Julunggul (Yurlunggur) is the Rainbow Serpent of the Yolngu people of Arnhem Land, a creator being of the Gunapipi ceremony who controls the monsoon and the waters. He swallows and regurgitates initiates to symbolize death and rebirth, and he can bring life-giving rain or destructive floods when angered.

name: Jumbie
description: Jumbie (jumbee) is a generic Caribbean term for malevolent spirits of the dead, widespread across Antigua, Barbados, Guyana, and the Lesser Antilles. Derived from Kongo nfumbi (ancestral ghost) and Akan duppy. They shape-shift into animals, haunt silk cotton trees, and are repelled by shoes, salt, or crossing water. Central to Obeah and Montserrat jumbie dances.

name: Juoksáhkká
description: Juoksáhkká (Bow Woman) is a Sami goddess depicted with a bow on Sami shaman drums. She is one of the three daughters of Máttaráhkká, the origin mother. Her most distinctive power is the ability to change a child's sex from female to male in the womb if given sufficient offerings — an important ability in a culture where sons were valued for hunting. She helps with fetal development and birth, protects children from gunshots and falls, and helps women during menstruation. After a son was born, a small bow and arrow symbol was placed in Sáráhkká's porridge and then placed beside the cradle so the boy would grow into a skilled archer. Her name connects her to the god of hunting Lieaibolmmái (the Alder Man), to whose protection she entrusted baby boys after birth. Like her sisters, she was known only among Scandinavian Sami (Norway and Sweden)

name: Juovlastállu
description: Juovlastállu (Yule Stállu) is the terrifying Christmas giant of Sami folklore, a variant of Stállo who punishes children who misbehave at Christmastime. Unlike the regular Stállo who is primarily a cannibal, Juovlastállu functions as a disciplinary figure — he enforces proper Christmas behavior. He drives a sled (ráidu) pulled by mice or lemmings through the winter landscape. Families must sweep the area around their home clean so the sled doesn't get stuck on woodchips or debris. Water must be left outside for him; if denied water, he becomes enraged and may suck blood from humans. He whistles sharply in the wind and the sound of his pipe can be dangerous to hearing. He is invisible yet everywhere during the Christmas season. He can assume the shape of the moon and enter the tent through the smoke vent in the roof. He demands that people stay inside and remain quiet during Christmas. If children are noisy or naughty, he stuffs them in his sack and abducts them, either eating them or returning them much later. He lives in a large gorge. The tradition connects to the Norse Wild Hunt (Oskoreia/Juleskreia) and the Setesdal tradition of Ståle's journey

name: Jutulkloa
description: Jutulkloa (the Giant's Claw) is a legendary giant associated with a distinctive rock formation on the Fosen coast of Trøndelag. The name combines 'jutul' (a regional variant of jøtul, meaning giant) and 'klo' (claw). According to legend, a jutul who lived in the Fosen mountains reached out his hand to grab a passing ship, but the sun rose and turned him to stone, leaving only his enormous claw-like fingers visible as rock formations along the coast. The jutul was known for terrorizing coastal communities by overturning boats and stealing cattle. Different versions of the legend are told in fishing communities along the Fosen coastline, with varying explanations for the rock formation — some say it is the claw of a sea giant who attacked ships, others say it is the hand of a mountain giant who reached for the sea. The legend is part of a broader Norwegian tradition of giants being turned to stone by sunlight

name: Jábmiidáhkká
description: Jábmiidáhkká (Jabme-akka) is the female ruler of Jábmiidaibmu, the Sami underworld of the dead. She is the major chthonic deity in Sami religion, governing the realm where the dead reside. Jábmiidaibmu was not a place of punishment but resembled the world of the living — the dead continued their lives much as before. However, the dead missed their living relatives, and Jábmiidáhkká sometimes allowed them to cause diseases among the living. If a dead soul managed to catch a living person's soul and drag it to the underworld, that person would fall into a coma or fatal illness. Jábmiidáhkká could permit the soul to return if sufficient offerings were made. Black animals — especially cats and roosters — were sacrificed to her by being buried alive under piles of stones. She was ambivalent rather than evil, a necessary figure governing the cycle of life and death. Christian influence later equated her realm with purgatory and associated her with the Virgin Mary. Finnish scholar Kaarle Krohn compared her to Hel from Norse mythology and Louhi from Finnish mythology

name: Jätte
description: Jättar (giants) are colossal humanoid beings from Swedish folklore, believed to be an ancient race that lived in the land long before humans. The word "jätte" derives from an Old Germanic verb meaning "to eat," reflecting their immense appetites. In Swedish folk tradition, jättar are most famously associated with features of the landscape: glacial erratic boulders called jättekast (giant's throws) were said to have been hurled by angry giants attempting to crush churches, whose bells they could not stand. Mountain formations resembling footprints or cooking cauldrons were also attributed to giants. According to widespread belief, most jättar fled the land when Christianity arrived, but some remained in remote mountains and forests into comparatively modern times. Unlike the wise and ancient jötnar of Norse mythology, later Swedish folklore giants are often portrayed as strong but dim-witted, easily outsmarted by clever humans. Famous Swedish giant tales include "Pojken som åt i kapp med jätten" (The Boy Who Ate Race with the Giant) and the story of Jätten Finn who built Lund Cathedral

name: Jé-rouges
description: Jé-rouges (Lougawou) are Haitian werewolf-like shapeshifters from Vodou tradition, capable of transforming into wolves or other animals to hunt at night. They function as familiars for bokors (sorcerers), characterized by red glowing eyes. Documented in Haitian folklore collections by Simpson (1942) and later ethnographies.

name: Jólakötturinn
description: Jólakötturinn (the Yule Cat) is a gigantic black cat from Icelandic Christmas folklore, the pet of Grýla and the Yule Lads. The Yule Cat roams the Icelandic countryside on Christmas Eve, eating anyone who has not received new clothes before Christmas. The tradition is tied to the Icelandic wool industry — farmers would give new clothes to workers who finished processing the autumn wool before Christmas. Lazy workers received nothing and thus risked being eaten by the Yule Cat. The cat is described as enormous — the size of a house — with glowing yellow eyes. Its first definitive mention appears in Jón Árnason's 1862 folklore collection, and it was popularized by Jóhannes úr Kötlum's 1932 poem Jólakötturinn. The Yule Cat is now one of Iceland's most internationally recognized folklore figures, alongside Grýla and the Yule Lads

name: Jörmungandr (Faroese)
description: In Faroese folklore, the Norse World Serpent Jörmungandr appears in a unique creation myth explaining the origin of the archipelago. After the World Serpent (child of Loki) was defeated in the final battles of the gods, a tooth fell from the dying serpent's enormous mouth into the ocean and became the Faroe Islands. This dramatic origin story connects Faroese identity directly to the great Norse mythological cycle, positioning the islands as a fragment of a cosmic being. An alternative folk explanation claims the islands were formed from dirt that gathered under God's fingernails while He created the world and was flicked away. Both accounts were preserved through Faroese oral tradition and recorded in ballad form. The Jörmungandr version is the more dramatic and poetic of the two, reflecting the deep Norse heritage of the Faroese people who preserved the Old Norse language and mythology in their kvæði (ballads) long after other Scandinavian cultures had Christianized

name: Jøtul
description: Jøtul (also spelled jotne, jotun; plural: jøtuler) is the Norwegian folk term for the giants of Norse mythology and later Norwegian folklore. In Old Norse, the jötnar (singular: jötunn) were the primordial giants, enemies of the gods, living in Jotunheim. In later Norwegian folklore, the jøtul evolved into a mountain-dwelling giant more like a large troll. Jøtuler are enormous - as tall as mountains - and possess immense strength. They throw boulders at each other across valleys (creating scree fields) and turn to stone if caught by sunlight. Many Norwegian landscape features are explained as jøtul activities - boulders they dropped, mountains they shaped, fjords they carved. The Jotunheimen mountain range is named after them. In folk tradition, jøtuler are more primitive and less magical than trolls, but also more ancient and powerful

name: Ka'wimosa (Kachina Maker)
description: Ka'wimosa, the Kachina Maker, is a priestly figure of Zuni origin tradition who led the search for itiwana, the Middle Place. Asked to send his sons in the cardinal directions, he dispatched his eldest, Kiaklo, northward and, when no word returned, his next two sons, the Ánahoho áchi, southward; the journeys founded the kachina cult and brought the Zuni to their homeland.

name: Kaang
description: Kaang (Unknown). is a deity. Kaang (also spelled Khāṅ) is the supreme creator god in the mythology of the San people (Bushmen) of the Kalahari Desert. He created the world, animals, and the first people, and taught them how to li. Source: San (Bushmen) mythology; Kalahari oral tradition

name: Kabouter
description: A small, bearded gnome-like creature from Flemish folklore, equivalent to the Dutch kabouter and similar to the German kobold. Kabouters are benevolent household spirits who live in forests, farms, and sometimes within human homes. They are known for their pointed red caps, long white beards, and helpful nature. A kabouter will secretly perform chores—cleaning, mending tools, caring for animals—while the household sleeps. In return, they expect a small offering of bread, milk, or porridge left in the barn or at the hearth. They are shy and will flee if directly observed or thanked. If treated poorly, they may play tricks or abandon the household entirely

name: Kabouter
description: A small, bearded gnome-like creature from Flemish folklore, equivalent to the Dutch kabouter and similar to the German kobold. Kabouters are benevolent household spirits who live in forests, farms, and sometimes within human homes. They are known for their pointed red caps, long white beards, and helpful nature. A kabouter will secretly perform chores—cleaning, mending tools, caring for animals—while the household sleeps.
