In return, they expect a small offering of bread, milk, or porridge left in the barn or at the hearth. They are shy and will flee if directly observed or thanked. If treated poorly, they may play tricks or abandon the household entirely In Belgium folklore, this figure is known among the Belgium people.

name: Kachikally Sacred Crocodiles
description: The Kachikally Sacred Crocodiles are not ordinary reptiles but are considered spiritual beings and fertility spirits in Mandinka folklore of The Gambia. The sacred crocodile pool of Kachikally in Bakau, Gambia, is one of three such sacred pools in the country (alongside Folonko in Kartong and Berending), each inhabited by Nile crocodiles believed to possess spiritual power. According to Gambian tradition, these crocodiles are sacred manifestations of ancestral spirits and serve as fertility totems for the Bojang clan, who serve as their traditional custodians. Women struggling with infertility visit Kachikally to wash in the holy waters and make offerings, guided by specially trained women of the Bojang lineage. The crocodiles — some up to 100 individuals — are believed to eat only fish offered by the custodians and to never harm those who approach them with proper respect and intention. The Kachikally pool has been a sacred site for over 400 years, and the site includes a museum documenting Gambian cultural heritage. The crocodiles represent the Mandinka belief that fertility, ancestry, and the natural world are deeply interconnected through sacred geography

name: Kachin-mana
description: Kachin-mana is a spirit being in Hopi mythology associated with the initiation ceremonies of young women. She appears as a benevolent figure who guides maidens through the transition to adulthood, teaching them the sacred songs and dances of the Kachina tradition. Kachin-mana is often depicted alongside the other Kachina spirits during the Bean Dance (Powamuya) and the Home Dance ceremonies. She carries a corn husk basket filled with sacred meal and distributes blessings of fertility, health, and harmony to the village

name: Kachinas
description: The Kachinas (Hopi katsinam, Zuni kokko) are the masked spirit beings of the Pueblo peoples of the Southwest who embody ancestors, natural forces, and elements of the cosmos. They live on the San Francisco Peaks and visit the villages during the first half of the year, appearing in dances and carved dolls, and they bring rain, fertility, and instruction.

name: Kaguya Hime
description: Kaguya Hime (Unknown). is a human. Kaguya-hime is the titular princess of The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, one of the oldest surviving Japanese folktales from the 10th century. Found as a tiny glowing infant inside a bamboo stalk, she gr. Source: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter (10th century); Japanese literary tradition

name: Kahausibware
description: Kahausibware is a creator goddess in the mythology of the Mono-Alu people of the Solomon Islands. She is a supreme female deity credited with creating the world, the islands, and all living things. In the beginning, Kahausibware created the land by pulling islands up from the sea. She then fashioned humans from clay and breathed life into them, teaching them how to build canoes, plant gardens, and fish. As a creator goddess, she represents the feminine creative principle and is associated with fertility, growth, and the abundance of the sea and forest. Her worship was central to Mono-Alu religious life, with offerings made to ensure good harvests and successful fishing expeditions

name: Kahp-too-óo-yoo (Corn-stalk Young Man)
description: Kahp-too-óo-yoo, the Corn-stalk Young Man, is a hero of Isleta Pueblo folklore recorded by Charles F. Lummis: a famous hunter, warrior, and wizard who could control the clouds and bring rain. Bewitched far from home and dying of hunger, he was saved by the Little Black Ant, and his story teaches the power of corn and of even the smallest helpers.

name: Kaiamunu
description: Kaiamunu is a powerful dual-natured figure from Papuan mythology with two distinct interpretations. In the Purari Delta, Kaiamunu appears as a towering wicker demon standing 10-12 feet tall, central to male initiation rituals where it symbolically swallows young men who are then reborn as warriors. In other traditions, Kaiamunu is portrayed as a fearsome reptilian predator resembling a giant monitor lizard, capable of climbing rocks and swimming with terrifying speed. The name variations across different PNG language groups reflect the immense linguistic diversity of the region

name: Kaji
description: Kaji are a race of dwarfish master craftsmen in Georgian (Caucasian) folklore. Small and skilled, they live in hidden mountain realms, create magical items, and possess stone-manipulation and house-protection powers. Though helpful, they can be mischievous. Their hidden workshops and magical craftsmanship parallel Norse dvergar and Germanic Wichtel.

name: Kakamora
description: The Kakamora are mythical elf-like creatures in the folklore of Makira and Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands. They are described as small, hairy beings with great strength who live in the deep forests and remote mountains. The Kakamora are shy but mischievous, sometimes stealing food from villages or playing tricks on travelers. In some traditions they are considered forest guardians who protect sacred groves and punish those who disrespect nature. Their small size allows them to move through the forest undetected. Stories about the Kakamora serve as cautionary tales, warning children and adults alike to respect the boundaries between human settlements and the wild, spirit-inhabited forests of the Solomon Islands

name: Kakungu
description: Kakungu is a powerful ancestral spirit of the Suku people of southwestern Democratic Republic of Congo, regarded as the most authoritative figure in the mukanda initiation tradition. Far more than a ceremonial mask or ritual prop, Kakungu is believed to embody an actual ancestral spirit whose presence oversees the transition of boys into adulthood. Entering ritual spaces as a guardian, healer, and symbol of continuity between the living and their ancestors, Kakungu is perceived by the community as an active spiritual being entrusted with the power to protect, discipline, and restore balance. During initiation seasons, the Suku do not see Kakungu as a performer but as the literal embodiment of their most powerful ancestor. His role includes safeguarding initiates during circumcision rites, warding off malevolent forces, and ensuring the survival of those undergoing the symbolic journey of death and rebirth. The name 'Kakungu' refers both to the spirit and the giant mask that represents him

name: Kalai
description: Not independently attested in documented Fijian folklore or academic sources. No dedicated source confirms a trickster shapeshifter named Kalai who steals food, misleads travelers, and helps those who offer kava. The recorded traits resemble general Polynesian trickster themes and appear to derive from modern or speculative retellings rather than a named Fijian figure.

name: Kalala Ilunga
description: Kalala Ilunga is the legendary founder of the Luba Empire, son of Mbidi Kiluwe and Bulanda, and the first sacred king (Mulopwe) of the Luba people. Born with extraordinary strength and mystical gifts, he was said to praise himself for future exploits on the day of his birth. His uncle, King Nkongolo, plotted to kill him by digging a pit filled with spears in the dance hall. The Mbudye priests warned Kalala, and he danced carefully, avoiding the trap. When Nkongolo's warriors attacked, Kalala defeated them, caught Nkongolo, beheaded him, and returned with his head and genitals as proof of victory. The people proclaimed him Mulopwe (Emperor). He expanded the Luba kingdom into an empire, establishing a sacred dynasty ruling for centuries

name: Kalanoro
description: Kalanoro are Malagasy hairy, fanged dwarfs with backwards feet and glowing red eyes, dwelling in Andoboara Cave and rainforests. They kidnap children, steal crops, and serve as clairvoyant familiars to ombiasa (healers/diviners) who communicate through nasal voice possession. Taboos (fady) imparted via dreams. Some identify them with extinct Vazimba.

name: Kalga Jaad (Ice Woman)
description: Kalga Jaad (Ice Woman) is a supernatural being of Haida tradition, counted among the Sgaana Kiidads and appearing in the Raven Traveling narratives recorded by John R. Swanton. She commands ice and winter storms, pairing with Gaayhllga Jaad (Flood-Tide Woman) to represent the balance of seasonal forces in Haida cosmology.

name: Kalga Jaad Ice Woman Haida
description: Kalga Jaad, 'Ice Woman,' is a primordial ancestress of Haida oral tradition, counted among the ancient beings who existed when the glaciers covered the land. She is remembered as one of the very old figures whose presence links the Haida people to the deep past of the world's making.

name: Kaliya (Multi-Headed Serpent)
description: Kaliya is a massive multi-headed serpent (naga) who lived in the Yamuna River during Lord Krishna's childhood in Vrindavan. According to the Bhagavata Purana, Kaliya had fled to the Yamuna from the ocean out of fear of his enemy, Garuda (the eagle deity). The serpent's presence poisoned the river — the water boiled with venom, killing fish, birds, and trees along the banks. The land for half a kos around the river became barren, and the villagers could no longer approach the water. Young Krishna, barely a child, dove into the deepest part of the river to confront the serpent. Kaliya wrapped Krishna in his coils, but Krishna expanded his body, broke free, and began dancing on Kaliya's thousand hoods. As Krishna danced, each hood was crushed under his divine feet until the serpent, bleeding and exhausted, surrendered. Kaliya's wives prayed to Krishna for mercy. Spared but banished, Kaliya and his family were sent to the ocean, and the Yamuna was restored to purity

name: Kallikantzaros
description: The Kallikantzaros is a malevolent goblin-like creature from Greek folklore believed to dwell underground for most of the year, tirelessly sawing at the great tree that holds up the earth. These mischievous demons emerge onto the surface during the twelve days of Christmas, from December 25 to January 6, when they run rampant through villages causing chaos and destruction. According to tradition, just as the kallikantzaroi are about to succeed in felling the world tree, Christmas dawns and they forget their task, coming to the surface to torment mortals by playing pranks, spoiling food, and terrorizing people. They are forced back underground on Epiphany when holy water is blessed, only to find the world tree miraculously restored, forcing them to begin their futile labor anew each year

name: Kalu Devata
description: Kalu Devata, also known as the Black Prince or Kalu Kumaraya, is a fearsome river demon from Sri Lankan folklore, particularly associated with the Sinhalese Buddhist tradition. According to legend, he was originally a prince who attempted to usurp his father throne and, upon failing, committed suicide out of shame. Instead of finding peace in death, he was condemned to remain on earth as a malevolent demon, cursed to prey upon the living. Kalu Devata is considered one of the most dreaded supernatural beings in Sri Lankan culture, especially feared by women and children. He is known to haunt rivers, bathing areas, and dark pathways, lying in wait for unsuspecting victims who venture too close to his domain

name: Kalulu the Hare
description: Kalulu the hare is the foremost trickster of Chewa, Tumbuka and Yao storytelling in Malawi and Zambia: the small, weak animal who outwits hyena, lion and elephant by cunning, collected by Rattray in Chinyanja as early as 1907. In Tumbuka tales he is the clever manipulator whom only the tortoise's wisdom can defeat; his stories teach that intelligence prevails over brute strength.

name: Kalunga-Ngombe
description: Kalunga-ngombe is the Kimbundu god of the underworld in Angola, ruler of Kalunga, the sea and realm of the dead. In the epic of Sudika-mbambi (Chatelain's Folk-Tales of Angola, 1894) he is the otherworldly father whose daughter the hero wins by performing trials, not a monster to be slain as the input claims.

name: Kama-itachi
description: Kama-itachi, meaning "sickle weasel," is a legendary yokai from Japanese folklore, particularly associated with the Koshinetsu region and the mountainous areas of Japan. This supernatural creature is said to ride upon sudden whirlwinds and dust devils, using its razor-sharp front claws to slice human skin with incredible precision. The name combines "kama" meaning sickle and "itachi" meaning weasel, reflecting its distinctive appearance. Victims often feel no pain at the moment of cutting and may not bleed until later, leading to the belief that kama-itachi attacks are supernatural in nature. The kama-itachi is considered both a physical creature and an explanation for strange, painless cuts that appear on hikers and travelers in mountainous regions

name: Kamapua'a
description: Kamapua'a, the 'hog child,' is a Hawaiian kupua, a demigod of dual human and pig nature, born on Oahu to Hina and the chief Kahikiula. Associated with Lono and agriculture, he is defiant and untamed, famous for his shapeshifting between human, hog, fish, and plant forms and for his stormy pursuit of the fire goddess Pele.

name: Kamata
description: Kamata is a culture hero in Vanuatu mythology, particularly among the people of Ambrym and Malekula islands. He is credited with bringing fire, agriculture, and essential knowledge to humanity. Kamata journeyed across the islands performing great deeds, shaping the landscape, and teaching people how to cultivate yams, build houses, and conduct proper ceremonies. He is associated with the volcano spirits of Ambrym, the region known for its active volcanic activity. Kamata's exploits often involve tricking dangerous spirits and defeating monstrous beings. His stories are part of the larger cycle of Melanesian culture heroes who brought civilization to humanity and established the social customs that continue to be observed

name: Kambujanu
description: Not independently attested: no source records a water spirit named 'Kambujanu'. The description instead summarizes the genuine Ronga Chipfalamfula, the 'River-Shutter' of Mozambique's Delagoa Bay — a whale-like or colossal catfish that opens and closes the waters, causing floods and droughts and parting the river for the heroine Chichinguane. The name should be corrected to Chipfalamfula.

name: Kan'du Fureytha (Ocean Demon of Fuvahmulah)
description: Kan'du Fureytha (Ocean Demon) is a malevolent sea spirit from the folklore of Fuvahmulah, the southernmost atoll of the Maldives. According to local legend, this demon emerged from the ocean as a 'pale, large flame looming over the rocks,' terrifying the islanders of Fuvahmulah. It would drag people into the sea, drowning them, and was blamed for numerous disappearances of fishermen and swimmers. The terrified islanders sought help from Edhurutakkaange Mohamed Didi, a renowned fanditha veriyaa (sorcerer) of exceptional power. Despite working his magic for many days at the reef where the demon was most active, the Kan'du Fureytha kept claiming victims. Tormented by his failed attempts, Mohamed Didi cast one ultimate, all-powerful spell that trapped the demon forever within a deserted island. Shortly afterward, the island mysteriously vanished entirely beneath the waves, never to be seen again. A large reef rock called Fureytha Gaa ('Demon Rock') now marks the spot where the island once stood. Local tradition holds that if you prod the stone with an iron rod, it still oozes blood, and will continue to do so forever whenever struck

name: Kanaloa
description: One of the four great gods (ka hā) of Hawaiian religion, Kanaloa is the god of the ocean, ocean winds, and the underworld. He is associated with squid and octopus, and is sometimes called the squid god. Kanaloa is the complementary opposite of Kane, the creator god - together they represent the dual aspects of divine power. Kanaloa is also associated with healing, magic, and the ocean's mysterious depths. In some traditions, he is a rebel god who was bound by Kane for his transgressions. He rules the realm of Milu (the underworld) where souls go after death. He is both feared and respected as the master of the vast, untamable ocean

name: Kanati
description: Kanati is the First Man and great hunter of Cherokee tradition, husband of Selu, the Corn Mother. His name derives from the Cherokee word for 'hunter' (often mistranslated as 'Lucky Hunter'). In the origin story he kept deer and game shut away in a cave and released them into the world, and once his wild son freed the animals, hunting became a necessity for humans.

name: Kane
description: The highest of the four great Hawaiian gods, Kane is the god of creation, life, sunlight, freshwater, and forests. He is the progenitor of all life and the source of divine power. Kane created the first man, Kumuhonua, and the first woman, Ke-oloku. He rules the heavens and represents the supreme creative force. He is associated with freshwater springs, which were considered his sacred domain. Kane is a benevolent god who provides for humanity, but he demands respect for nature and the kapu (sacred laws). He is rarely depicted in physical form as he is considered too sacred for representation

name: Kappa
description: The Kappa, meaning "river child," is one of the most famous yokai in Japanese folklore, considered among the three major yokai alongside the kitsune and tanuki. These water-dwelling spirits inhabit rivers, ponds, and marshes throughout Japan, originating from the belief in debased water deities or suijin that were once worshipped. Kappa are child-sized aquatic humanoids with a complex nature ranging from helpful and mischievous to outright malevolent. They have been both feared as dangerous mankillers that drown people and livestock, and respected as water gods capable of teaching humans bonesetting and medicine. Kappa appear in countless folktales across Japan, and their image has evolved from terrifying water demons to cute mascots in modern times

name: Kapre
description: The Kapre is a towering tree giant from Philippine mythology, one of the most well-known supernatural beings in Filipino folklore. These massive creatures are said to inhabit ancient trees such as acacias, mangoes, bamboo, and balete trees throughout the Philippines. While often appearing frightening, kapre are not necessarily evil, but rather complex beings that can be either benevolent or mischievous depending on how they are treated. The name kapre derives from the Arabic kafir meaning non-believer, introduced by Spanish colonizers who associated the indigenous Aeta people with European mythical giants. Kapre are deeply connected to nature and serve as guardians of the forest, punishing those who disrespect the environment while protecting those who treat nature with reverence

name: Kapua (Tiki)
description: Kapua is a term from Hawaiian mythology referring to demigods or children of gods who are born into mortal families, possessing both human and divine qualities. In the context of carved tiki figures, kapua are believed to be representations of deified ancestors that can come to life as spiritual guardians. These sacred figures are central to Hawaiian spiritual practice, serving as physical manifestations of ancestral mana or spiritual power. Tiki figures are carved from wood or stone and placed at the entrances of homes, villages, and sacred sites to ward off malevolent spirits and attract good fortune. The concept of kapua reflects the Hawaiian belief that the divine and mortal worlds are interconnected, with certain individuals and objects serving as bridges between the two

name: Karakasa
description: Karakasa, also known as kasa-obake or karakasa-kozo, is a tsukumogami from Japanese folklore, a type of yokai formed when an everyday object reaches a certain age and becomes animated by a spirit. Specifically, karakasa are transformed from old Chinese-style oiled-paper umbrellas that have been used and aged for many years. The karakasa is one of the most iconic and recognizable yokai in Japanese culture, frequently appearing in Edo-period art, ukiyo-e prints, and modern media. While not particularly dangerous, these mischievous spirits are known for startling humans with their sudden appearances and unusual behavior. They embody the Japanese belief that all objects possess a spirit and deserve respect, especially as they age and serve their purpose over time

name: Karakoncolos
description: The Karakoncolos is a winter demon of Turkish and Balkan folk belief, known in the Black Sea and northeastern Anatolia and among Bulgarian, Serbian, and Greek neighbors as Karakondžula or similar names. It is said to appear in the coldest midwinter days, imitating human voices to lure people outdoors into the freezing dark. Parents invoked it to keep children indoors at night.

name: Karakondzho
description: Karakondzho is the Bulgarian variant of the Balkan Christmas demon, closely related to the Greek Kallikantzaros and the Turkish Karakoncolos. This malevolent creature is a prominent figure in Bulgarian folklore, appearing during the twelve days of Christmas, from December 25 to January 6, a period known as the Mryasni Dni or "Dirty Days" when supernatural forces are believed to roam freely. According to tradition, the Karakondzho dwells underground for the rest of the year but emerges during the Christmas season to torment humans, entering homes and causing chaos. The creature is deeply embedded in Bulgarian folk tradition and is associated with the Kukeri, ritual costumed figures that perform ceremonies to scare away evil spirits during the winter festival period

name: Karakondzola
description: Karakondzola is a fearsome night demon from Montenegrin and Balkan Slavic folklore, believed to attack people during the Twelve Days of Christmas (between Christmas and Epiphany). It is described as a small, dark, hairy creature with a single eye, sometimes with a long tail. It rides people's backs at night, forcing them to carry it until dawn. It torments sleepers, causes nightmares, and can be particularly vicious during the unbaptized days when the spiritual boundaries between worlds are thin. In Montenegro, Karakondzola is especially feared in rural areas and is associated with the winter solstice period

name: Karakondzula
description: Karakondzula is a winter demon from Balkan folklore, closely related to the Karakondzho of Bulgaria and the Karakoncolos of Turkey. This malevolent spirit is said to appear during the coldest months of the year, particularly around the Christmas and New Year period when the boundaries between the human and spirit worlds are believed to thin. The Karakondzula is part of a broader family of similar creatures found throughout the Balkan Peninsula, all sharing characteristics of hairy, demonic beings that emerge during winter to harass humans. In Serbian and Bulgarian tradition, the Karakondzula is considered one of the most feared supernatural entities, associated with the long, dark winter nights when people huddle indoors for safety

name: Karakondžul
description: Karakondzul is the Serbian variant of the Balkan Christmas demon, closely related to the Bulgarian Karakondzho and the Greek Kallikantzaros. This malevolent creature is deeply rooted in Serbian folk tradition, where it is believed to appear during the twelve days of Christmas, a liminal period when supernatural forces are thought to roam freely among the living. According to Serbian folklore, the Karakondzul dwells in dark, hidden places for most of the year but emerges during the winter solstice season to harass, frighten, and sometimes harm humans. The creature is an important figure in Serbian folk belief and has been documented in various ethnographic studies of Balkan supernatural traditions

name: Karakum Serpent
description: Not independently attested as a distinct serpent of Turkmen folklore. No source confirms a Karakum Desert serpent with earth-shaking power; the Karakum is best known in legend for the Darvaza 'Door to Hell' gas crater and desert water-mirage tales, with no such snake in ethnographic records. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Karanga
description: The Karanga are masked spirits that appear during ceremonial performances in the cultures of Burkina Faso and neighboring regions of West Africa. These sacred figures play an essential role in traditional African religious practices, serving as intermediaries between the human world and the ancestral realm. The Karanga masquerades are deeply rooted in the spiritual traditions of the region, where masked dancers embody the spirits of ancestors, nature deities, and supernatural forces during important community ceremonies. These performances are not merely entertainment but are considered sacred events that maintain the cosmic balance between the living and the dead, ensure agricultural fertility, and transmit cultural knowledge from one generation to the next

name: Karemanua
description: Karemanua is a part-shark, part-human mythical figure from the Eastern Solomon Islands, particularly associated with the Pagewa (Shark) sublineage of Santa Ana Island. According to myth, Karemanua was a man who died in a violent, bloody way and his blood transformed into a wild, uncontrolled supernatural being called ataro wasi. This wild spirit sought to avenge his death by menacing humans, but later voluntarily transformed into a tutelary deity who protects fishermen engaged in fishing, especially the sacred skipjack tuna rites. The myth illustrates the belief that violent death creates dangerous spirits that can eventually become protective deities

name: Karkadann
description: The Karkadann is a legendary beast from Persian and Arabic mythology, often described as the Persian version of the unicorn. This powerful creature was believed to inhabit the grassy plains of India, Persia, and North Africa, and is based on the Indian rhinoceros as described by early scholars. First documented in the 10th and 11th centuries by the Persian scholar Al-Biruni, the Karkadann evolved in later writings from a simple rhinoceros-like animal into a fearsome mythical beast endowed with magical properties. It appears in the famous collection One Thousand and One Nights during the Second Voyage of Sinbad the Sailor, where it is described as a ferocious beast that drives even elephants from its territory. The Karkadann horn is said to have powerful medicinal properties and can neutralize poisons

name: Kasa-obake
description: Kasa-obake, also known as karakasa-obake or karakasa-kozo, is a tsukumogami from Japanese folklore, a spirit that inhabits old, discarded umbrellas that have transformed into supernatural beings after many years of service. This yokai became particularly popular during the Edo period when artists like Toriyama Sekien included it in their illustrated collections of supernatural beings. Unlike many yokai that have extensive oral traditions, the kasa-obake is believed to have originated primarily through visual art and literature rather than traditional folk tales. It represents the Japanese animistic belief that even inanimate objects possess souls and can become animated, especially when treated with neglect or disrespect. The kasa-obake is one of the most recognizable and beloved of the tsukumogami yokai

name: Kashehotapalo
description: Kashehotapalo, 'the woman caller,' is a being of Choctaw folklore that is neither man nor beast, with a small, shriveled old-man's head, a man's body, and the legs and cloven hooves of a deer. It dwells in low, swampy places and delights in creeping up behind hunters and crying out in a woman's voice to frighten them. It does not harm people, though it will warn game or enemies if it is angered.

name: Kataragama Deviyo (Guardian of the Jungle)
description: Kataragama Deviyo is one of the four guardian deities of Sri Lanka and the patron deity of the Kataragama shrine, one of the island's most important multi-religious pilgrimage sites. He is identified with the Hindu god Murugan (Skanda/Kartikeya), the war god and son of Shiva, but in the Sinhalese Buddhist context, he is revered as a powerful guardian deity. According to legend, Kataragama traveled to Sri Lanka from India and fell in love with Valli, a Vedda (indigenous) tribal girl, at Kataragama in the southeastern jungle. Their marriage symbolizes the union between north Indian (Aryan) and indigenous Dravidian peoples. The Kataragama temple complex is unique in Sri Lanka as a site where Sinhalese Buddhists, Sri Lankan Tamils, Vedda people, and even Muslims worship together. He is associated with power, protection, and the fulfillment of vows. Devotees undertake extreme austerities at his shrine — fire-walking, kavadi (burden) dancing, and piercing their bodies with hooks and spears — as acts of devotion and thanksgiving. Kataragama Deviyo is also known as Mahasen Deviyo or Katharagama Deviyo in Sinhalese tradition

name: Katawaguruma
description: Katawaguruma ('broken wheel') is a yokai of Edo-period Japanese ghost lore: a burning wheel rolling through the night, sometimes bearing the tormented face of a woman in its hub. It appears in collections such as the Shokoku Hyakumonogatari and is classed with the fire-wheel apparition wanyudo. Its rolling flame warns against idle curiosity and gossip about the supernatural.

name: Katthveli
description: Katthveli (Cat-Whale) is one of the illhveli (evil whales) in Icelandic maritime folklore, a seal-whale hybrid with cat-like whiskers, hooked claws on flippers, and a terrifying scream. It aggressively attacks boats, ramming and capsizing them. Documented in Jón Árnason's collections and by 19th-century Icelandic naturalists.

name: Katthveli
description: Katthveli in Faroese tradition is the same cat-whale illhveli as in Iceland, attested in Faroese ballads and oral accounts, notably a 17th-century encounter at Suðuroy where it attacked a boat, hissing and spitting like a cat. The Faroese version shares the Icelandic taxonomy of evil whales but has distinct local lair traditions.

name: Kaugjagjuk
description: Kaugjagjuk (also Kaujjarjuk) is a central Inuit legend: a mistreated orphan boy, kicked and humiliated by his community, is taken up by the Moon Man, who rescues him and brings him to the moon, where he becomes a protector of the abused. The tale, documented among Inuit communities and retold in collections of Inuit stories, is not a trickster tale; the prankster framing is corrected here.

name: Kawa-zaru
description: Kawa-zaru, meaning "river monkey," is a lesser-known water yokai from Japanese folklore, considered a weak and cowardly relative of the more famous Kappa. This timid creature inhabits rivers and streams throughout Japan, where it spends most of its time hiding from humans and avoiding confrontation. Unlike its powerful cousin the Kappa, which actively drowns victims and challenges sumo wrestlers, the Kawa-zaru is characterized by its extreme timidity and aversion to contact with people. The creature is named for its simian appearance and its river-dwelling habits, though it possesses the same basic amphibious nature as other Japanese water spirits. In some traditions, the Kawa-zaru is regarded as a degenerate or weakened form of Kappa that lost its power through cowardice

name: Kayeri
description: Kayeri is a seasonal forest spirit from Colombian folklore, particularly associated with the indigenous cultures of the Amazon and Orinoco regions. These mysterious beings are believed to appear during the rainy season when the forest is at its most lush and vibrant. According to tradition, all forest mushrooms are considered to be manifestations or aspects of Kayeri, making these spirits intimately connected with the fungal life of the tropical rainforest. The Kayeri are complex figures in local mythology, both feared and respected for their power over the forest and its resources. They are said to feed on cows and abduct women, making them a source of cautionary tales told to children and young adults about the dangers of wandering alone in the forest during the rainy season

name: Kayra Han
description: Kayra (Kayra Khan, Tengere Kayra Khan) is the supreme creator god of the Altai and broader Turkic peoples, who shaped the sky and earth from primordial water and fathered both the benevolent Ülgen and the underworld ruler Erlik. Supreme and creative, he governs fate and stands first in the Tengrist pantheon, from whom the other chief gods descend.

name: Kazan Serpent
description: The Kazan Serpent, identified with the winged dragon Zilant, is the guardian figure of Kazan: reputedly slain by the Tatar hero and buried on the site of the city's foundation. Prophetic and protective, it was said to have foretold the fall of Kazan, and its image still crowns the city's coat of arms and its foundation legend.

name: Kebo Iwa (Buffalo Toe)
description: Kebo Iwa (meaning 'Buffalo Toe') is a legendary giant and strongman in Balinese folklore, known for his immense size, bottomless appetite, and superhuman strength. According to legend, he was the son of a human mother and a celestial being, and his appetite was so enormous that he could drain entire lakes in a single drink. The villagers of ancient Bali struggled to feed him, but Kebo Iwa repaid their kindness by singlehandedly carving the island's famous rice terraces and irrigation systems using only his bare hands and feet. His finger-shaped footprints are said to have created the deep ravines and valleys of Bali. When neighboring Java threatened war, Kebo Iwa defended Bali by using his incredible strength to reshape the landscape into defensive fortifications

name: Keemse
description: Keemse is an ancestor spirit from the traditional beliefs of Burkina Faso, particularly among the Mossi people of West Africa. These spirits are believed to be the souls of deceased family members who continue to watch over their living descendants from the spirit world. Unlike distant gods or nature deities, Keemse spirits maintain a close, personal relationship with their families, intervening in daily life to offer guidance, protection, and blessings. Ancestor veneration is central to the spiritual practices of the region, with Keemse serving as intermediaries between the living and the supreme creator. The spirits are consulted before important decisions, and their favor is sought through proper rituals and offerings to ensure harmony between the visible and invisible worlds

name: Keeper (Maya)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Maya source documents a guardian spirit called 'Keeper'; the description is a generic 'custodian of sacred places' built from cenotes and jungle-ruin imagery with no named tradition. Maya religion does include specific guardians and deities, but no attested figure corresponds to this entry.

name: Keeper (Maya)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. This record repeats the same fabricated 'Keeper' entry with Mexican metadata and closes with empty filler about the 'Mexico people'. No Maya tradition documents a guardian spirit named 'Keeper'; the entry is template filler with no named source or story.

name: Keiju
description: The keijukainen (modern keiju) are small spirits of Finnish folk tradition, attested since Ganander's Mythologia Fennica (1789) as tiny flying beings connected with the dead — seen near funerals, graveyards, and roads, resembling snowflakes, small dolls, or flames, and counted among the kirkonväki death-spirits. The 'beautiful winged fairy' image is a later literary overlay.

name: Kel Essuf
description: The Kel Essuf (People of the Wild or Solitude) are desert spirits from Tuareg mythology of Niger, particularly the Kel Ewey confederation of the Aïr Mountains. The Tuareg word essuf does not translate cleanly into English - it means solitude, wilderness, and nostalgia simultaneously. The Kel Essuf inhabit deserted places, darkness, and the disorienting spaces encountered during long Saharan crossings. They have their own language and can reproduce. They are not ghosts or demons but the population of emptiness itself. Healers called friends of the Kel Essuf form spiritual contracts with these spirits, using tende drumming and goumaten singing to negotiate with them during possession rituals

name: Kel Tamasheq Spirits (Tuareg Nature Spirits)
description: The Kel Tamasheq (People of the Tamasheq language) nature spirits are a diverse class of supernatural beings in Tuareg belief from the Sahara (Mali, Niger, Algeria, Libya). The most powerful are the Kel Essuf (the Wild Ones), spirits of the uninhabited desert. These beings are neither jinn nor angels but a distinct class of spirits unique to Tuareg cosmology. They inhabit remote plateaus (tassili), dry riverbeds, and solitary mountains. Some are benevolent and guide lost travelers; snip others harass camps and steal milk from goats. They are closely associated with the Tuareg alphabet (Tifinagh) and left inscriptions on rocks. The most dangerous are the Kel Tafukt (Spirits of the Sun), who cause heatstroke. Tuareg oral tradition says these spirits taught the ancestors the Tifinagh script and how to survive in the desert

name: Kellingin
description: Kellingin (The Witch or The Hag) is the petrified wife of Risin, the giant sent from Iceland to drag the Faroe Islands back across the ocean. In the legend, Kellingin climbed Mount Eiðiskollur carrying a heavy rope and attempted to tie the islands together so she could push them onto Risin's back. Her efforts caused the northern part of the mountain to split — a fissure still visible today. After struggling all night, dawn broke and sunlight turned her to stone. She now stands as a 68-meter (223-foot) pointed basalt sea stack closer to shore than Risin, standing with her legs apart. Unlike her husband further out at sea, Kellingin is visibly eroding; geologists note she stands on two legs that may collapse within decades

name: Kelpie
description: The Kelpie is a shape-shifting water spirit of Scottish and Irish folklore, inhabiting rivers, streams, and lochs. Typically appears as a magnificent horse with dripping mane, or a handsome man. Predatory: lures travelers to mount, then skin becomes adhesive and it drags them underwater to drown and devour (except liver). Can be controlled by an iron bridle or learning its true name.

name: Kerepunu
description: Kerepunu is a dangerous water spirit from Papuan mythology, particularly known among the peoples of the Gulf of Papua and the southern coast of Papua New Guinea. This malevolent entity dwells in deep rivers, swamps, and mangrove forests, where it lies in wait for unwary travelers. Kerepunu is known to drag people beneath the water, drowning them, and is especially feared by women and children. The spirit is associated with the darker aspects of the natural world, representing the dangers hidden within seemingly placid waters. Stories of Kerepunu serve as cautionary tales, warning people to respect the boundaries between human settlements and the wild, spirit-inhabited waterways

name: Khan Toolo
description: Not independently attested as a distinct hero of Tuvan folklore. No source confirms an epic hero named 'Khan Toolo' with superhuman strength and horse mastery; Tuvan heroic tales record figures such as the hunters of the Tuvan epic cycle, but no hero by this name appears in published sources. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Khanyapa
description: Khanyapa (Unknown). is a spirit. Khanyapa is a devouring monster from Southern African Sotho folklore defeated by the hero Ditaolane.. Source: Zambian folklore — the Khanyapa is a mythical creature from Zambian oral tradition.

name: Khas-uu
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Mongolian source documents a tiger spirit called 'khas-uu', and tigers are not native to the Khentii or Khangai ranges. 'Khas' in Mongolian tradition refers to the swastika-like eternal symbol (has tamga), not an animal. The entry is a generic animal-guardian fabrication.

name: Khattaf Rafai
description: Khattaf Rafai ('the Snatcher of Women', or simply 'the Snatcher') is a demon of Emirati coastal folklore that takes the shape of a small sailboat drifting toward shore at night. Casting a rope, it snatches young women and children who are alone by the sea; it fears men in groups and flees at Quranic recitation. Parents invoke it to keep the young from wandering at night.

name: Khazyr
description: Khazyr (Khyzyr) is the Turkmen form of al-Khidr, the immortal green prophet-guide of Islamic tradition, honored across Central Asia as a protector of travelers, wayfarers and the fortunate. In Turkmen belief he appears unexpectedly in the Karakum Desert, often as an old man or a guiding light, to lead the lost to water and safety, and he is linked with springs and renewal

name: Khevkher
description: Not independently attested as a distinct deity of Evenki folklore. No source confirms a creator or guardian named 'Khevkher'; the Evenki supreme creator is Buga, with shamanic spirit masters of forest and river, but no figure by this name appears in ethnographic literature. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Khodumodumo
description: Khodumodumo (also Kholumolumo) is the swallowing monster of Basotho mythology in Lesotho; its name, 'great noise' or 'great rumble', echoes its roar and the rumbling of its stomach. The gaping-mouthed beast devoured people, cattle and whole villages until a hero climbed inside and cut his way out, rescuing the swallowed. The myth figures nature's chaos overcome by courage and cooperation.

name: Kholumolumo
description: Kholumolumo (Unknown). is a monster. Kholumolumo is a fearsome monster from Basotho (Lesotho) folklore, a giant lizard-like creature that devoured people and animals alike. It was eventually slain by a culture hero.. Source: Basotho oral tradition; Southern African folklore

name: Khorba Spirits (Berber Ruin Dwellers)
description: In Maghrebi folk belief, jinn and spirits are commonly said to haunt khorba, the ruined or abandoned buildings of North Africa — collapsed granaries, deserted ksour, and old fortifications. These beings are feared for mischief and nocturnal disturbance, and ruins are avoided after dark.

name: Khun Borom (Founder King of the Lao)
description: Khun Borom (Lao: ຂຸນບູລົມ) is the legendary founder-king of the Lao and Tai peoples, sent from heaven by the sky god Phaya Thaen to rule the earthly realm. According to the Nithan Khun Borom chronicle, after a great flood destroyed humanity, three righteous chiefs were preserved in heaven. They returned to earth with a sacred buffalo; when the buffalo died, a bitter gourd vine grew from its nostril, producing gourds from which the new human race emerged — darker-skinned peoples from gourds cut with a hot skewer, and lighter-skinned Tai peoples from gourds cut with a chisel. As the population grew, Phaya Thaen sent his own son Khun Borom to rule. He descended on a royal elephant with crossed tusks to Muang Then (modern Dien Bien Phu). After 25 years of rule, Khun Borom divided his kingdom among his seven sons, who became founders of the Tai kingdoms including Lan Xang (Laos), Lanna, Ayutthaya, and others. The legend establishes Khun Borom as the ancestor of all Tai-speaking peoples and the founder of Lao kingship

name: Kiaklo
description: Kiaklo is the Zuni rain-priest hero who, sent by the kachina priest Ka'wimosa, journeyed to find the Middle Place (itiwana) where the Zuni would settle. According to Zuñi origin myth, Duck carried him to the council hall of the gods, where he learned the story of creation and the sacred dances; his quest brought the kachina ceremonies to the people.

name: Kianda
description: Kianda is the most beloved and widely recognized water goddess in Angolan mythology, a powerful mermaid-like deity who presides over the seas, lakes, rivers, and forests. In the Kimbundu language, 'kianda' translates to a fabulous mythological monster or water god, though she is far more complex than a simple mermaid figure. According to Mbundu tradition, every body of water—every river, lagoon, and coastal area—has its own Kianda, who takes the name of that particular water body. Above them all is the supreme Kianda, queen of all mermaids, the most powerful, loved, and feared. One famous legend tells of Kianda observing a poor, sad man walking alone by the beach of Luanda. In an act of kindness, she revealed a hidden treasure to him. The man grew wealthy but also greedy and selfish, using the money only for himself. Disappointed, Kianda made the treasure disappear, leaving the fisherman with nothing overnight. Kianda is traditionally venerated with offerings of food, drink, and clothing cast into the sea or left at riverbanks, and she is especially associated with the blessing of twins. She continues to be honored in annual festivals like the Luanda Island Feast

name: Kibanda
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Bunyoro or Ugandan source documents a water spirit called 'Kibanda', and 'Lake Bunyoro' does not exist; the python-and-hippo master-of-the-fishery is generic filler. The genuine water-god of the region is Mugizi, associated with Lake Albert and the Cwezi kubandwa spirit cult.

name: Kibati
description: Not independently attested. No documented Guinea-Bissauan or Bijago tradition records a water creature named 'Kibati' in any academic or folklore source; the only web matches are a generic fiction video and country profiles. The description of a feared river-serpent guardian is generic and unverified; the closest documented West African water-dragon is the Gambian Ninki Nanka.

name: Kibuka
description: Kibuka is the fearsome war god of the Baganda people, brother of the lake god Mukasa. According to legend, Kibuka was once a mortal warrior of extraordinary strength and military genius. When Buganda was threatened by Bunyoro invasion, Kibuka led the army, fighting with supernatural ferocity. He became invisible to enemies, raining arrows down from a cloud. The enemy fled in terror. But Kibuka grew overconfident, resting in a fig tree and boasting loudly of his invincibility. An enemy soldier heard him and shot an arrow into the tree, striking Kibuka in the chest. After his death, Kibuka was deified. His shrine at Butikkiro became a national sanctuary where Buganda kings prayed before battle

name: Kiev Ghost
description: The Ghost of Kyiv is a Ukrainian wartime legend that emerged in the first days of the 2022 Russian invasion: a mysterious MiG-29 pilot reportedly downing multiple Russian aircraft over the capital. It became a symbol of resistance and morale before officials clarified that the story was a composite. The entry's medieval 'catacomb haunting' is replaced with the attested modern legend.

name: Kikimora
description: Kikimora is a female house spirit of dual nature — a domestic tutelary when the home is orderly, a malevolent tormentor when neglected. In Ukrainian tradition she has two distinct forms: the house Kikimora who lives behind the stove and the swamp Kikimora (bolotnyana) who dwells in marshes. The house variety is described as a tiny, hunched, ugly old woman with a pointed nose, dressed in rags of moss and grass, who can appear as a deceased family member. The name derives from Proto-Slavic 'mora' (nightmare), connecting her to the universal folklore figure of the night hag who sits on sleepers' chests. She is the wife or companion of Domovyk

name: Kikimora
description: Kikimora is a household-spirit from Slovakia mythology. In Ukrainian tradition she has two distinct forms: the house Kikimora who lives behind the stove and the swamp Kikimora (bolotnyana) who dwells in marshes. The house variety is described as a tiny, hunched, ugly old woman with a pointed nose, dressed in rags of moss and grass, who can appear as a deceased family member. The name derives from Proto-Slavic 'mora' (nightmare), connecting her to the universal folklore figure of the night hag who sits on sleepers' chests. She is the wife or companion of Domovyk

name: Kikimora
description: Kikimora is a household-spirit from Ukraine mythology. In Ukrainian tradition she has two distinct forms: the house Kikimora who lives behind the stove and the swamp Kikimora (bolotnyana) who dwells in marshes. The house variety is described as a tiny, hunched, ugly old woman with a pointed nose, dressed in rags of moss and grass, who can appear as a deceased family member. The name derives from Proto-Slavic 'mora' (nightmare), connecting her to the universal folklore figure of the night hag who sits on sleepers' chests. She is the wife or companion of Domovyk

name: Kilibob
description: Kilibob is a mythical culture hero from northeastern Papua New Guinea whose canoe journey along the northern coast created islands and bestowed gifts upon humanity. He traveled by canoe, creating islands as he went and giving the people fishing nets, canoes, and knowledge of navigation. His travels explain the cultural diversity of Papua New Guinea's coastal peoples, as wherever he landed he left behind different languages and customs. Kilibob and his brother Manup eventually became rivals, and their conflict is said to have created the distinct identities of different language groups. Kilibob represents the archetype of the navigator-hero who brings civilization and maritime knowledge to coastal communities

name: Kilibob and Manup
description: Kilibob and Manup (also Kulbob and Manub) are mythical brothers central to the folklore of northeastern Papua New Guinea, particularly in Madang Province and on Karkar Island. They appear as creator beings whose stories explain the origin of landmarks, trade routes, craft specializations, and material wealth inequality. In the Karkar version, Kulbob is a hunter and carver associated with Mount Kanagioi, while Manub is a fisherman. A quarrel over Manub's wife leads to conflict, and Kulbob eventually sails away in a great canoe loaded with valuable artifacts and people

name: Kilimanjaro Mountain Serpent
description: The Mountain Serpent is a legendary guardian creature of Kilimanjaro in Chaga mythology, dwelling in caves and tunnels beneath the mountain. According to tradition, the serpent was placed by Ruwa to guard the sacred inner chambers where ancestral spirits gather. The serpent is as old as the mountain itself, its body coiling through volcanic tunnels honeycombing Kilimanjaro's interior. During times of great change or danger, the serpent stirs, causing tremors. It is associated with the mountain's water sources -- its movements create springs emerging from the mountain's sides. Only the most powerful Mangi (chiefs) and ritual specialists dare approach its lair, seeking wisdom and guidance. The serpent represents the living spirit of the mountain

name: Killer Whale
description: The Killer Whale, known as Sgaana in the Haida language, is a profoundly significant supernatural being in Haida mythology and the broader Indigenous folklore of the Pacific Northwest coast of Canada. These majestic creatures are not mere animals but are considered powerful spirit beings, the rulers of the ocean, and the ancestors of the Haida people transformed into their present form. In Haida tradition, Killer Whales live in immense underwater villages organized just like human communities, with houses, chiefs, and potlatch ceremonies conducted beneath the waves. They are believed to be the reincarnations of great Haida chiefs and warriors who chose to become protectors of the sea after death. The relationship between the Haida and the Killer Whale is one of deep mutual respect, with the whales serving as helpers, guides, and symbols of clan identity. They feature prominently in Haida art, with their forms carved into totem poles, house posts, and ceremonial objects

name: Killer-of-Enemies
description: Killer-of-Enemies is the chief culture hero of the Lipan and other Apache peoples, son of the Sun and of White Painted Woman (Changing Woman), and brother of Child-of-the-Water, son of the Moon. With his brother he slew the monsters that plagued the people and taught the skills of survival; in Lipan tradition he is identified with the Sun himself.

name: Kim Qui (Golden Turtle God)
description: Kim Qui (literally 'Golden Turtle') is the sacred turtle god of Vietnamese mythology who helped King An Dương Vương build the spiral-shaped Cổ Loa Citadel and forge a magic crossbow that could fire hundreds of arrows at once. According to legend, Kim Qui emerged from the waters and revealed to the king how to construct the citadel's defensive walls, which had kept collapsing until the turtle god explained they were built on a mountain spirit's territory. After appeasing the spirit, the walls stood firm. Kim Qui also gave the king one of his claws to use as a trigger for the magic crossbow, granting the kingdom invincibility. The turtle god later appeared when the foreign prince Trọng Thủy had replaced the claw with a fake, revealing the betrayal to the fleeing king. In the legend of Hoàn Kiếm Lake, the Golden Turtle emerged to reclaim the magical sword Thuận Thiên (Heaven's Will) from Emperor Lê Lợi, declaring that Heaven had lent the sword to expel the Ming invaders and now required its return. Kim Qui remains a powerful symbol of Vietnamese independence, sovereignty, and divine protection

name: Kindoki
description: Kindoki is the complex concept of spiritual power in Kongo belief, referring to the occult force used for either healing or harm. A person with kindoki (called a ndoki) possesses a special intelligence that surpasses ordinary understanding. Kindoki is not inherently evil -- it is a neutral power depending on the user's intentions. Benevolent kindoki is exercised by nganga (spiritual healers) who diagnose illness and combat evil. Malevolent kindoki is wielded by witches who use their power for selfish ends. The concept is intimately connected with nkisi (sacred power objects) and Simbi spirits. Kindoki operates at the fundamental level of reality where physical and spiritual worlds intersect

name: King Lalibela
description: King Lalibela was the 12th-13th century ruler of the Zagwe dynasty of Ethiopia, renowned as a saint and visionary builder of the eleven monolithic rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Born with a swarm of bees around him (meaning his name: 'the bees recognize his sovereignty'), Lalibela made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, and when Jerusalem fell to Muslim forces, received a divine vision commanding him to build a New Jerusalem in Ethiopia. He gathered thousands of workers who carved eleven churches directly from solid volcanic rock, working from the top down. Angels worked alongside humans at night. The largest, Bet Medhane Alem (House of the Savior of the World), remains the largest monolithic church in the world

name: Kinkirsi (Kinkirga)
description: Kinkirsi (singular: Kinkirga) are the powerful nature spirits of the Mossi people of Burkina Faso, invisible beings that inhabit the untamed wilderness beyond village boundaries. According to Mossi cosmology, these spirits are 'as numerous as the stars' and occupy all spaces not inhabited or cultivated by humans — sacred woods, hills, rivers, rocky outcrops, and wild plains. The Kinkirsi are described as small, invisible beings with large heads and long hair, and they play an essential role in human procreation: Mossi tradition holds that a Kinkirga spirit enters a woman's womb during conception, contributing the spiritual essence of the child. Twins (called Kinkirsi themselves) are considered especially sacred as they represent a double spiritual presence. These spirits also claim ownership of wild animals and must be respected by hunters. The Kinkirsi are fundamentally ambiguous — they can be protective ancestors or troublesome tricksters depending on how they are treated. They reproduce an anthropomorphic society in the invisible world, with their own social structures and customs parallel to human Mossi society

name: Kinnara (Celestial Musician)
description: Kinnaras are half-human, half-bird celestial beings from Hindu and Buddhist mythology, renowned as divine musicians and lovers. Described in the Mahabharata, they are eternal lovers who never separate, never bearing children but forever embracing. They come from the Himalayas and are known for their exquisite music, dance, and poetry. In Hindu iconography, they are depicted with a human torso and head atop a bird's lower body, or sometimes as half-horse, half-human centaur-like beings. The Vishnudharmottara describes them as half-man and half-horse, while Buddhist traditions portray them as half-man and half-bird. Kinnaras are gentle, harmless creatures who hop like birds, love music and song, with females beating drums and males playing lutes. Their food consists of flower pollen, their cosmetics are made from flower perfumes, and they dress in garlands. The female Kinnari is a traditional symbol of feminine beauty, grace, and accomplishment across South and Southeast Asia

name: Kinoly
description: Kinoly is a malevolent ghost of Malagasy belief, a variety of the angatra class of the dead. Described with red eyes and extraordinarily long fingernails, it kills by a single touch and tears open its victims. Kinoly haunt sites of violence and death; their stories were recorded in nineteenth-century sources such as The Antananarivo Annual, where they rank among the terrors of the Malagasy night.

name: Kintaro
description: Kintaro (Unknown). is a human. Kintarō ("Golden Boy") is a folk hero from Japanese folklore, a child of superhuman strength who was raised by a mountain witch on Mount Ashigara. He is said to have wrestled bears and befriended wood. Source: Japanese folklore; kabuki tradition

name: Kintogou
description: Not independently attested in documented Mossi (Moose) tradition or academic sources: no collection or record names a water-serpent 'Kintogou' among the Mossi of Burkina Faso. The description of a guardian river-serpent is generic and unverified; the closest documented West African water-dragons are the Soninke Bida and the Gambian Ninki Nanka.

name: Kintu
description: Kintu is the foundational mythological figure and first human in the oral traditions of the Baganda people of Buganda, Uganda. According to legend, Kintu was the only man on Earth, wandering alone with his cow until Nambi, daughter of the sky god Ggulu, descended from heaven via a rainbow and fell in love with him. After proving himself through a series of trials set by Ggulu—including identifying his cow among a vast herd and eating a massive meal without drinking—Kintu won Nambi's hand in marriage. The couple descended to Earth with gifts of agriculture, including millet and banana cultivation, enabling humanity to thrive. However, they were warned not to return to heaven for any forgotten item. When Nambi sent her brother Walumbe (Death) back for grain, he followed them to Earth, claiming their firstborn and establishing mortality as an inescapable force. Kintu's story explains the Baganda origin, the advent of death, and the foundations of agrarian life

name: Kipitaakii
description: Kipitaakii (Old Lady) is the wife of Na'pi and a powerful figure in Blackfoot mythology. She was created alongside Na'pi by Apistotoke and assisted him in shaping the world and creating humans. In the pivotal story of death's origin, Na'pi threw a piece of wood into a river saying if it floated people would die and return after four days; if it sank, death would be permanent. The wood floated, but Kipitaakii rejected this outcome and threw a stone instead, which sank. Na'pi thus decreed permanent death. This story establishes her as the one who determined the final nature of human mortality

name: Kiranga
description: Kiranga is the central figure of the Kubandwa spirit possession cult in Burundi, a revered hero-spirit who bridges the gap between the supreme creator Imana and humanity. According to tradition, Kiranga was originally a mortal prince and accomplished hunter who met a tragic end when he was killed by a wounded antelope during a hunt. Far from simply passing into oblivion, his death transformed him into a powerful spirit who became the leader of the imandwa, the company of hero-spirits who serve as intermediaries between the divine and mortal realms. The Kubandwa cult, which worships Kiranga, is one of the most important spiritual traditions in the Great Lakes region of Africa, incorporating elements of ancestor veneration, spirit mediumship, and therapeutic ritual. Kiranga role is essential for maintaining cosmic order, allowing humans to communicate with Imana and receive divine assistance for healing, fertility, and protection

name: Kirkegrim
description: Kirkegrimmen is the Danish church grim — the guardian spirit of a church created when an animal was buried alive under the church's foundation during construction. In Danish tradition, the Kirkegrim takes the form of the sacrificed animal (lamb, pig, horse, or dog) and protects the church from desecration, thieves, and evil spirits. The Danish Kirkegrim has a unique role not found in other Nordic countries: it fights against the Strandvarsler (strand-wardens) — the spirits of unburied drowned sailors who try to enter the consecrated churchyard. This territorial battle between the Kirkegrim and the Strandvarsler happens at the churchyard wall every night. The Kirkegrim also rings church bells during storms to ward off evil. It is bound to the church until the building crumbles to dust

name: Kirkelam
description: Kirkelamet (the Church Lamb) is a ghostly lamb that appears in Danish churchyards and rural roads as a death omen. Unlike other church foundation spirits, the Kirkelam represents Christ as the Lamb of God, yet its appearance brings ill tidings rather than comfort. The Kirkelam would appear from the churchyard at dusk and run toward a specific house. If it rubs against your leg, you or someone in your immediate family will die within three days. It is silent — its hooves make no sound, and it never bleats. The Kirkelam is considered the gentlest form of church grim, less terrifying than the Helhest or Gravso, but its omen is no less certain. In some traditions, the Kirkelam is the soul of an unbaptized child given animal form, allowed to leave the churchyard only briefly before returning

name: Kishelamakank
description: Kishelamakank (He Who Creates Us By Thought) is the supreme creator god of the Lenape (Delaware) people. According to Lenape tradition, before creation there was only endless darkness. Within this void, Kishelamakank dreamed of the world as it would become — mountains, forests, animals, and people. Upon awakening, he brought his dream into reality, creating helper spirits (the Grandfathers of the directions and Grandmother of the South) who shaped the earth. From a sacred tree the first man emerged from the roots, and when the tree bent and touched the ground, the first woman sprang forth

name: Kishi
description: The Kishi is a two-faced demon of Angolan (Kimbundu/Ambundu) folklore: from the front a handsome young man, from behind the head of a hyena with sharp teeth. He lures young women with charm and courtship, then turns and devours them.

name: Kitchi-Manitou
description: Kitchi-Manitou, also known as Gitche Manitou or Gichi-manidoo, is the Great Spirit in the spiritual traditions of Algonquian-speaking Native American peoples of the United States, including the Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Menominee, and other tribes of the Great Lakes region. As the supreme creative force in the universe, Kitchi-Manitou is understood as the source from which all life, energy, and spiritual power emanate. Unlike the personified gods of many other religious traditions, Kitchi-Manitou represents a more abstract, all-pervasive spiritual reality that connects every aspect of existence in a sacred web of relationships. This concept of the Great Spirit is central to the traditional worldview that governs how people relate to each other, to nature, and to the spiritual realm. Kitchi-Manitou is the ultimate authority behind the Midewiwin or Grand Medicine Society, the traditional spiritual organization that has preserved sacred knowledge across generations

name: Kitchi-Manitou
description: Kitchi-Manitou (Gitche Manitou, Gichi-manidoo) is the Great Spirit of Algonquian-speaking peoples such as the Ojibwe, Potawatomi, and Menominee: the supreme creative power behind all life and spiritual authority, including the Midewiwin (Grand Medicine Society). The entry is condensed to the attested Great Spirit, and the empty filler naming 'the USA people' is removed.

name: Kitsune
description: ONE OF Japan'S 'BIG Three' yokai. Gain powers with AGE - more tails = older/wiser. Up to Nine tails after 1,000 years. TWO Classes: Zenko (善狐, 'good fox') = benevolent, serve Inari. Yako (野狐, 'field fox') = wild, sometimes malicious. Kitsune have supernatural intelligence. Can shapeshift into beautiful women, elderly men, other forms. FOX-Fire (kitsunebi): ghostly blue flames. Nine-Tailed: near-divine, omniscient, can see/hear anywhere. Celestial (tenko): turns white/golden after 1,000 years, flies to heaven. Famous: Tamamo-no-mae (nine-tailed vixen who destroyed dynasty). Inari connection: fox messengers for rice/kami. 32,000+ Inari shrines. Offerings: rice, sake, fried tofu. White foxes ward off evil, black/nine-tailed = good omens

name: Kitsunebi
description: Kitsunebi, meaning "fox fire" in Japanese, are mysterious floating lights that appear in forests and rural areas of Japan, closely associated with the presence of kitsune fox spirits. These ethereal flames are believed to be a manifestation of the kitsune supernatural power, created when the spirits exhale or conjure fire as they move through the darkness. Witnesses describe the kitsunebi as small orbs of colored light that drift silently through the trees, sometimes appearing as a single light and other times as a long procession of flames stretching across the landscape. The phenomenon has been documented in Japanese folklore for centuries and is often cited as an explanation for the will-o-the-wisp or hitodama ghost lights seen in marshy or forested areas. Kitsunebi are deeply woven into the fabric of Japanese folk belief, representing the mysterious and often deceptive nature of the fox spirits that create them

name: Klabautermann
description: The Klabautermann is a water-kobold and ship spirit in Frisian, German, and Dutch maritime folklore — a small, pipe-smoking sailor-specter who resides aboard seagoing vessels from their very construction until their sinking. He is an ambiguous figure, simultaneously a guardian spirit who protects the crew and an omen of doom whose visible appearance foretells certain shipwreck. According to tradition, the Klabautermann enters a ship through its timber: if a stillborn or unbaptized child was buried under a tree later used for shipbuilding, its soul becomes the Klabautermann. By night he works small miracles — repairing broken tackle, pumping out leaks, coiling ropes, and polishing brass — so that sailors wake to a perfectly maintained ship. But if the crew becomes lazy, drunken, or blasphemous, he turns malicious, tangling rigging, hiding tools, and slapping sailors across the face with invisible hands. When the ship is doomed, he reveals himself, then abandons the vessel to its fate

name: Klabautermann
description: The Klabautermann is a ship spirit of German, Frisian, and Scandinavian maritime lore: a small sailor-specter who lives aboard a vessel, working unseen at night — mending ropes, pumping leaks, polishing — and guarding the ship, but who may turn malicious toward a slovenly or blasphemous crew, and whose visible appearance foretells shipwreck.

name: Ko'komiki'somm
description: Ko'komiki'somm, also known as Komorkis, is the Moon in Blackfoot tradition, one of the eldest of the sacred Sky People (Sspommitapiiksi). Wife of the Sun, Naato'si, and mother of the stars, she is the serene ruler of the night whose most important child is the Morning Star, Iipisowaahs; she is also the grandmother of the hero Star-Boy, and watches over lovers and those who travel after dark.

name: Ko'wituma (Twin War God)
description: Ko'wituma (Twin War God) is one of the sacred twin deities in Zuni mythology, the elder of the two warrior brothers who protect the Zuni people from evil spirits and monsters. Together with his brother Pautiwa, Ko'wituma drove the great monsters underground during the time of creation, clearing the world for human habitation. He is associated with the east and the rising sun, and carries a bow of lightning and arrows of flint. Ko'wituma is invoked before hunts and during times of conflict, and his sacred stone images are kept in the medicine kivas

name: Kobold
description: The Kobold is one of the most versatile and widespread spirits in Germanic folklore, inhabiting homes, mines, ships, and natural spaces throughout Germany and surrounding regions. These small, impish beings belong to a broad category of household and nature spirits that can be either helpful or mischievous depending on how they are treated. The name kobold literally means "house dweller" and reflects their close association with human habitation. Kobolds are deeply rooted in Germanic folk belief, with different varieties inhabiting different environments: Hauskobolde (house kobolds), Bergkobolde (mine kobolds), and Schiffkobolde (ship kobolds). They are considered neither fully good nor fully evil but rather morally ambiguous beings whose behavior mirrors the treatment they receive. The English word "cobalt" derives from kobold, as medieval miners blamed the troublesome spirit for contaminating silver ore with unwanted cobalt

name: Kobyl
description: Not independently attested: no Uzbek water-horse spirit named Kobyl appears in sources, and 'kobyła' is the Slavic word for 'mare', suggesting a garbled borrowing. Genuine Central Asian horse lore centers on Tulpar, the winged horse of Turkic epics, and Kambar Ata, the Turkic patron of horses. The description's benevolent horse guardian has no documented Uzbek basis.

name: Kodama
description: Kodama are ancient tree spirits from Japanese folklore, believed to inhabit the oldest and most magnificent trees in the forest. The name kodama literally means "tree spirit" or "echo," reflecting the belief that mysterious sounds heard in the mountains are the voices of these spirits. Kodama are deeply respected in Shinto tradition, where trees are considered living entities with souls deserving of reverence. The spirits are particularly associated with the cedar, camphor, and pine trees that grow in sacred groves around Shinto shrines. Cutting down a tree inhabited by a kodama is considered an act of terrible disrespect that brings curses, illness, and misfortune upon the perpetrator and their family. The belief in kodama reflects the Japanese animistic worldview that sees spiritual presence in all natural phenomena, encouraging environmental stewardship and respect for the living forest

name: Kokopelli
description: Flute-Playing Fertility Deity across Southwest. Different names: Hopi 'Kokopelli' (possibly 'kachina hump'), Zuni 'Ololowishkya,' Tewa 'Neopkwai'i.' Appears in petroglyphs 3,000+ years old. Humpback with flute - may be sack of seeds/trade goods OR insect-like (robber fly connection). Fertility: brings seeds, makes women pregnant, ensures abundant crops. Weather: flute playing Chases Winter, Brings Spring and Rain. Trading: traveling merchant carrying corn in hump. Trickster: playful mischief. May have enormous phallus (fertility symbolism). Associated with snakes, insects, water animals. Hopi: kachina spirit. Zuni: Rain Priest, can make it rain at will. Pueblo: herald of spring. Connected to Paiyatamu (another flautist)

name: Kokopelli (fertility spirit)
description: Kokopelli is the humpbacked, flute-playing spirit of Pueblo and Hopi tradition, a fertility deity who presides over childbirth, rain, and agriculture and appears in petroglyphs across the Southwest. He is also a trickster and spirit of music; his name links the Hopi and Zuni word for deity, koko, with the robber fly, pelli.

name: Kola Sanni Yaka
description: Kola Sanni Yaka is a fearsome demon of disease and spirit possession from Sri Lankan folklore, belonging to the Sanni Yakka pantheon of eighteen demons collectively responsible for causing specific illnesses and afflictions. This particular yaka is associated with severe physical and mental ailments, with its name deriving from kola meaning leaf or herbal medicine and sanni meaning disease or affliction. The Sanni Yakka tradition is deeply embedded in the Sinhalese Buddhist healing practices, where these demons are not considered purely evil but rather as powerful beings that can cause harm when offended or improperly acknowledged. The rituals to appease these demons involve complex exorcisms called tovil, which combine dance, drumming, chanting, and offerings. Kola Sanni Yaka is particularly feared for its ability to cause debilitating conditions that resist conventional medical treatment, requiring the intervention of trained exorcists called edura

name: Kolowa
description: Kolowa is a man-eating ogre of Creek (Muscogee) folklore, a huge, shaggy, humanlike creature covered in thick hair with enormous strength and a foul stench that can be smelled from far away. It lurks in the deep forests beyond the villages, imitates human voices to lure victims, and preys on people who stray too far from home; some modern storytellers liken it to a gorilla.

name: Kolowisi (Horned Water Serpent)
description: Kolowisi, the Horned Water Serpent, is the great serpent of Zuni tradition that dwells in the sacred spring at K'iákime, 'Home of the Eagles,' beneath Thunder Mountain. In Cushing's 'The Serpent of the Sea' it took the form of a child to punish a maiden who defiled the spring's waters, and it brings rain when properly honored.

name: Kolus Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Kolus is the younger sibling of the Kwakwaka'wakw thunderbird Tseiqami, a supernatural bird who wears a coat of thick white down instead of feathers. The down makes him so warm that he sweats, sheds the coat, and becomes human; a Kolus who flew down from the sky and removed his costume became a founding ancestor, and he helps raise ceremonial house beams.

name: Koma
description: Not independently attested as a Dogon spirit. No Dogon shapeshifter named 'Koma' appears in Griaule's ethnography or other sources; the name instead matches the Komo, a powerful secret society of the Bambara (Bamana) and other Mande peoples, whose fearsome helmet-masks invoke nyama. The Dogon masked funerary rites are the Awa society and dama with kanaga masks.

name: Komokwa (Copper-Maker)
description: Komokwa, 'Copper-Maker,' is the wealthy chief of the undersea world in Kwakwaka'wakw and Nuxalk tradition. He lives in a great copper house beneath the sea, its living posts the sea-lions, and rules the ocean's wealth. He tests heroes with dangerous trials, rewarding the worthy with copper, masks and songs; the winter counterpart of the sky Thunderbird, he guards his realm with an octopus.

name: Komokwa (Undersea Chief)
description: In Haida tradition, Komokwa is the powerful chief of the undersea world who controls all the wealth of the sea. He lives in a magnificent house made of copper and abalone shell, surrounded by supernatural beings. Those who drown do not truly die but are taken to live in Komokwa undersea kingdom, where they may acquire great supernatural power. Komokwa controls the movements of salmon, halibut, seals, and whales. He appears as both a generous giver of wealth and a dangerous being who can drown anyone who disrespects the sea

name: Komokwa Copper Maker Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Komokwa (Kumugwe) is the Undersea Chief of the Kwakwaka'wakw, ruler of the ocean world and giver of wealth. He lives in a copper house beneath the sea filled with treasures, owns the salmon and sea mammals, and is the maker of coppers, the most valued wealth of the potlatch; many families trace their riches to him.

name: Kongamato
description: The Kongamato is a legendary flying creature from Zambian folklore, described as a large, bat-like monster that inhabits the swamps and rivers of the remote regions of Zambia, Angola, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The name kongamato means "overwhelmer of boats" in the Kaonde language, reflecting the creatures reputation for attacking and capsizing watercraft. This cryptid has captured the imagination of both local populations and Western explorers, with reported sightings dating from the colonial era through the present day. The Kongamato is often compared to the prehistoric pterosaur or pterodactyl by cryptozoologists who suggest it may be a surviving species of flying reptile. The creature is deeply feared by local communities who avoid its known habitats and report that it attacks without provocation, killing humans and large animals alike with devastating efficiency using its sharp beak and powerful claws

name: Koreisha (Geongumi)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. 'Koreisha' is the Japanese word for 'elderly people', and no Korean ghost tradition uses this name; the aliases 'geongumi' and 'wonhon' conflate invented names with the real Korean concept of wonhon, the resentful spirit of a wronged dead person. The attested figure is wonhon, not 'koreisha'.

name: Korkut Ata
description: Korkut Ata is the legendary sage-musician of the Oghuz Turks, revered across Kazakhstan as a wise, artistic culture hero. His lament for the impermanence of the world is said to have given birth to the kobyz, the bowed Kazakh instrument, granting a kind of immortality through music and story. His legacy survives in the Book of Dede Korkut and the Korkut Ata mausoleum cult.

name: Korkyt
description: Korkyt is the legendary founding father of Kazakh music, a revered sage, composer, poet, and philosopher who is credited with creating the kobyz, an ancient Kazakh stringed instrument, as well as the dombra, the national instrument of Kazakhstan. According to tradition, Korkyt lived for three hundred years, traveling the world to escape death and sharing his wisdom with all who would listen. He is considered the first baksy or shaman-musician, whose kobyz playing had the power to heal the sick, drive away evil spirits, and communicate with the spirit world. Korkyt occupies a unique position in Kazakh folklore as both a historical figure and a mythological hero whose legend has shaped the musical and spiritual traditions of the Kazakh people for centuries. His stories and compositions continue to be central to Kazakh cultural identity

name: Kosen
description: 'Kosen' garbles the attested yokai kosenjobi ('ancient battlefield fire'): ghost-flames rising over old killing grounds from the blood of fallen warriors and horses. Depicted by Toriyama Sekien in the Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki and noted in Edo ghost-story collections, these pale fires drift as unsettled souls; witnesses would chant and withdraw.
