The input's 'dancing ghost woman' is fabricated.

name: Kosenjōbi
description: Kosenjōbi are ghost-fires of Japanese folklore: will-o'-the-wisp flames that appear over old battlefields, said to be the spirits of soldiers and horses killed in war, rising from the ground at dusk. The name is recorded in early modern collections such as the Shūchin-sō (17th century) and depicted in Toriyama Sekien's Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki.

name: Koshari (sacred clowns)
description: Koshari are the sacred clowns in Pueblo tradition, known for their role in ceremonial dances and rituals. Unlike ordinary entertainers, the Koshari serve a vital spiritual function by mocking pretension, exposing hypocrisy, and reinforcing social norms through humor. They paint their bodies with black and white horizontal stripes and wear their hair in two pointed buns. The Koshari have the privilege of speaking and acting in ways that would be unacceptable for ordinary tribe members, using sati

name: Kostroma
description: Kostroma is an East Slavic spring-and-summer fertility figure of Russian folk ritual, honored during Semik as a straw effigy or a disguised girl who is first revered and then burned or drowned to end the season's rites. Her name derives from kostyor, 'bonfire.' The entry's claim that she is a plague goddess is unsupported; her genuine role is seasonal and agricultural.

name: Koumen
description: Koumen is the primordial shepherd of the Fulani, custodian of pastoral initiation, who appears as a child of three to eleven. With his wife Foroforondu he passes the secret knowledge of cattle to initiates (Sile); those who complete the cycle gain mastery of ritual speech as Silatigi. Documented in Griaule and Dieterlen's The Pale Fox.

name: Kowi Anukasha
description: The Kowi Anukasha are the little people of the Choctaw, spirit dwellers of the forests whose name means 'forest dwellers.' Kindly but quick-tempered, they live in the deep woods and under the ground, and they may help hunters and children; the prankster variant, Bohpoli the 'thrower in the dark,' delights in startling travelers.

name: Koyemshi (Mudhead clowns)
description: The Koyemshi, or Mudhead clowns, are the sacred clowns of the Zuni. Their origin myth tells of a father who fathered nine children with his sister and, in remorse, rolled in the mud until his head was covered in bulbous welts; his children were born with the same knobs. Barred from dancing as kachinas, they serve as spokesmen and chorus, opening the Shalako ceremony with comic satire.

name: Koyemsi
description: Koyemsi, also known as the Mudhead or Kachina Clown, is a distinctive figure in Hopi and Puebloan spiritual traditions of the Southwestern United States. These sacred clowns play a vital role in Hopi kachina ceremonies, serving as both entertainers and spiritual teachers who use humor and mockery to reinforce proper social behavior. Unlike the solemn kachinas that represent deities and ancestors, Koyemsi figures are deliberately comical and sometimes crude, using slapstick, mimicry, and parody to convey important cultural lessons. They are considered powerful spiritual beings despite their ridiculous appearance, capable of wielding profound spiritual force precisely because they operate outside normal social constraints. The Koyemsi tradition reflects the Hopi understanding that laughter and humility are essential components of spiritual life, and that the most profound truths can sometimes be conveyed through comedy

name: Krahang
description: Krahang is a malevolent nocturnal spirit from Laotian and Thai folklore, a cursed ghost that takes the form of a shirtless man who flies through the night sky using traditional rice winnowing baskets as makeshift wings. This terrifying apparition is said to be the result of a curse placed upon a man who practiced forbidden dark arts or committed terrible sins during his lifetime, condemning him to wander the night as a tormented spirit. Krahang is considered the male counterpart to the more famous Krasue ghost, and the two are sometimes said to travel together. By day, the Krahang appears as an ordinary villager, indistinguishable from anyone else, but when night falls, the curse transforms him into a flying horror that preys on the living. The belief in Krahang is deeply embedded in rural Laotian culture, where reports of strange flying figures and mysterious nocturnal activities are often attributed to this spirit

name: Krahom
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Cambodian tradition documents a vengeful ghost called 'Krahom'; the Khmer word krahom simply means 'red', and the invented etymology and vengeful-ghost details are filler. Khmer spirit belief does include neak ta (tutelary guardians) and various ghosts, but no attested figure corresponds to this entry.

name: Kraken
description: The Kraken is a legendary colossal sea monster said to dwell off the coasts of Norway and Greenland. Described as a giant octopus or squid-like creature, the Kraken was feared by Norwegian fishermen for its ability to drag entire ships and crews to the ocean depths. First described in detail by Norwegian Bishop Erik Pontoppidan in his work The Natural History of Norway (1753), who portrayed the Kraken as an enormous floating island-like creature with massive tentacles. When the Kraken submerged, it created a powerful whirlpool (mahlstrøm). The creature was said to be so large that fishermen sometimes mistook it for an island and landed on its back. The Kraken's name comes from the Norwegian word krake meaning unhealthy or twisted animal. Now one of the world's most famous legendary sea monsters, appearing in literature from Alfred Lord Tennyson to Pirates of the Caribbean

name: Kraken Iceland
description: Kraken Iceland (Unknown). is a sea-monster. The Kraken is a legendary sea monster of gargantuan size, said to dwell off the coasts of Iceland and Scandinavia. It was described as a massive squid-like creature capable of dragging entire ships un. Source: The Natural History of Norway (Pontoppidan, 1755); Norse legends

name: Krakonoš
description: Krakonoš, known in German as Rübezahl, is the mountain spirit of the Krkonoše (Giant Mountains) on the Czech-Polish border, guardian of the range and its people. He rewards honesty, hard work, and respect for nature while punishing greed and arrogance with wry, inventive retribution; he remains one of the most beloved figures in Czech folklore.

name: Krampus
description: Alpine Christmas Demon from Germanic/Austrian origins (not originally Croatian). 'Krampus' from Old High German 'krampen' = 'claw.' Pre-Christian origin: ancient Pagan winter solstice wild spirit. Rode with Berchta (White Lady) during Rauhnächte (12 mystical nights Dec 25-Jan 6). Christianization: became companion to St. Nicholas, his 'punisher.' Dec 5 = Krampusnacht (Krampus Night). Nicholas Day. 1920s banned by Catholic Church + some political parties. Returns 1960s as 'kitschy folklore,' now massively popular. 50,000+ at Austrian festivals. Chains = Symbol of subjugation to Christian order. Represents winter's brutal honesty predating Christmas softeness

name: Krampus
description: Alpine Christmas Demon from Germanic/Austrian origins (not originally Croatian). 'Krampus' from Old High German 'krampen' = 'claw.' Pre-Christian origin: ancient Pagan winter solstice wild spirit. Rode with Berchta (White Lady) during Rauhnächte (12 mystical nights Dec 25-Jan 6). Christianization: became companion to St. Nicholas, his 'punisher.' Dec 5 = Krampusnacht (Krampus Night). Nicholas Day. 1920s banned by Catholic Church + some political parties. Returns 1960s as 'kitschy folklore,' now massively popular. 50,000+ at Austrian festivals. Chains = Symbol of subjugation to Christian order. Represents winter's brutal honesty predating Christmas softeness In Austria folklore, this figure is known among the Austria people.

name: Krasue
description: Thai floating head Ghost - 'กระสือ' (krase). Head detaches and Flows with trailing Organs (entrails). Famous in Thai horror. Lived normal human life before - became Krasue after death. Active at Night - seeks blood/raw flesh. Whistling cry is signature. Warnings: used to warn pregnant women (fear maternal death). Cursed being - eternally Hungry. Daytime: appears normal, lives normal. Night: transforms. Can appear also in Laos ('Krasue'), Cambodia ('Krasu'). Connected to feminine vulnerability and death

name: Kratt
description: An artificial being of Estonian folklore, the kratt is assembled from hay, straw, old tools or wooden implements and animated by a pact with the Devil, sealed by three drops of blood. It works tirelessly, fetching grain and stealing from neighbors, and must always be given a task, or it turns on its maker. A leak in the roof or a drawn circle forces it to spill its loot.

name: Krishna
description: Krishna is one of the most venerated deities of Hinduism: the eighth avatar of Vishnu and, in Vaishnavism, the Supreme Being in his own right. He is the divine charioteer and teacher of Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita, the cowherd of Vrindavan who charmed the gopis with his flute, the butter-stealing child, the slayer of demons, and king of Dvaraka. His worship spans all of India and its diaspora.

name: Krsnik
description: Krsnik is a vampire hunter from Slovenian and Croatian folklore, a special individual born with supernatural abilities that enable them to see, track, and destroy vampires and other undead creatures. The name krsnik derives from krs meaning cross or baptism, reflecting the Christian folk beliefs mixed with older pagan traditions that characterize these warriors. Krsniks are believed to be born with a caul or born on a Saturday, signs that mark them as chosen for this sacred duty. They operate at the boundary between the human world and the supernatural, possessing spiritual vision that allows them to see vampires in their true forms even when they appear as ordinary people. The krsnik tradition represents a unique blend of Christian and pre-Christian Slavic beliefs about the undead, combining Church-sanctioned methods such as holy water and crosses with older folk magic

name: Kräkl (or Kratt)
description: Krakl, also spelled Kratt or Kraat, is a artificial being from Estonian folklore, a construct created by sorcerers from natural and household materials and animated through dark magic. Like the more common kratt, the krakl is a servitor created to perform tasks for its master, ranging from everyday chores to supernatural theft. However, the krakl is distinguished by its more rudimentary construction and more dangerous temperament, being considered a cruder and less reliable version of the kratt. The belief in such artificial beings is deeply rooted in Estonian and broader Finno-Ugric folk tradition, where the boundary between the natural and supernatural was fluid, and where clever but morally compromised individuals sought to gain advantage through spiritual deals. The krakl legend reflects the cultural understanding that shortcuts to prosperity come with hidden costs

name: Ksapela
description: Ksapela (Little Wisdom) is a minor spirit in Lakota mythology, also known as Gnaski. He is the son of Iya (the destructive storm monster) and Unk (the spirit of contention). Ksapela managed to outwit and perfectly mimic Ksa (the spirit of wisdom) to the point that the two were indistinguishable, earning him the name 'little wisdom.' He appears in the Great Race story as the wise one who proposed the competition between the four-legged animals and the two-legged birds to determine who would eat whom

name: Ku
description: The Hawaiian god of war, politics, and male pursuits. Ku is one of the four great gods of Hawaiian religion. He is the fierce, aggressive god of warriors, rulers, and fishermen. Offerings to Ku included human sacrifices before battle. Ku is associated with the forest (as Ku of the forest) and with the sea (as Ku of the ocean). Different aspects of Ku were worshipped for specific purposes. The war god Kuka'ilimoku was the personal god of Kamehameha I, who built the great heiau at Pu'ukohola to honor him before conquering the islands. Ku represents the masculine principle of power, war, and governance

name: Kukulkan (Plumed Serpent)
description: Kukulkan, the Feathered Serpent, is the Maya deity of wind, rain, and creation, honored from Chichén Itzá to the Yucatán. A culture-bearer who brought civilization, he descends as a serpent on the equinox when sunlight crawls down El Castillo's stairway, forming a snake of light and shadow. He is the Maya form of the pan-Mesoamerican plumed serpent, kin to Aztec Quetzalcoatl.

name: Kukulkan (Plumed Serpent)
description: In the Guatemalan highlands, the plumed serpent is Q'uq'umatz (Gukumatz), the creator deity of the Popol Vuh. With the Heart of Sky he brought the world into being and, in K'iche' cosmology, helped shape humanity from maize. The feathered-serpent identity unites Maya, K'iche', and Aztec traditions, and Q'uq'umatz remains a living symbol of Maya identity today.

name: Kulfre
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Albanian source documents a mountain spirit called 'Kulfre' or a headless dancing phantom of the Albanian Alps; the description appears to be invented. Genuine Albanian tradition includes figures such as the zana (mountain fairies) and orë, but no 'Kulfre' appears in the recorded folklore.

name: Kullervo
description: Kullervo is the tragic antihero of the Kalevala (runos 31-36), sold into slavery, unknowingly seduces his sister (who drowns herself), destroys his tormentor's cattle, and finally falls on his own sword. His story, compiled by Lönnrot from Karelian runic songs, is the darkest in the epic — a shamanic initiate whose power turns destructive.

name: Kulmking
description: A hostile forest spirit of Estonian tradition, the kulmking (linked to Estonian 'külm', cold) is a malevolent being of the woods, bogs and remote wilds, dreaded more than the neutral forest guardians of Estonian nature belief and associated with the unholy dead. It is said to waylay travelers who enter its territory.

name: Kulshedra
description: Kulshedra is a colossal multi-headed female dragon from Albanian folklore, one of the most feared and powerful creatures in Balkan mythology. This monstrous serpentine being is associated with water, storms, and fire, commanding the primal forces of nature and bringing either drought or flood to the land depending on her mood. Kulshedra is the ancient enemy of the drangue, a heroic winged warrior who protects humanity from her depredations. The legend of kulshedra represents the eternal cosmic struggle between order and chaos, with the dragon embodying the untamed, destructive aspects of nature that must be constantly opposed by heroic forces. Her lairs are said to be deep caves near water sources, where she hoards treasure and the bones of her victims. The kulshedra legend is deeply rooted in the pre-Christian Illyrian and Balkan mythological traditions that persisted through centuries of cultural change

name: Kulus (Thunderbird Child)
description: Kulus is the younger brother (or sister) of the Kwakwaka'wakw Thunderbird, Tseiqami, and a founding ancestor of many clans. Lacking the Thunderbird's spiral horns and lightning eyes, Kulus wears a coat of thick white down so warm that he sweats, sheds it, and becomes human. A Kulus who flew from the sky and removed his costume founded a clan; he helps raise ceremonial house beams.

name: Kumakotok
description: Kumakatok is a trio of death-omen spirits from the Visayas (Philippines): a young woman flanked by two elderly men who knock on doors at night, answering the knock portending death within the year. Households paint white crosses above doorways or refuse to answer, for the spirits exploit courtesy. The legend warns against opening doors to strangers after dark.

name: Kuman Thong
description: Kuman Thong is a household spirit from Thai folklore, the animated spirit of a child that has been bound to a golden statue through black magic rituals. The name Kuman Thong means "Golden Child Spirit," and these beings are created through complex and controversial ceremonies performed by traditional sorcerers known as wei monks or ajahn. Originally, the creation of a Kuman Thong involved the remains of a child who died in the womb or shortly after birth, but modern practice typically uses consecrated statues. These spirits are believed to bring good luck, protection, and wealth to their owners if properly cared for, but they can become dangerous if neglected or mistreated. The belief in Kuman Thong reflects the Thai spiritual tradition of animistic household spirits combined with Buddhist and Brahmanic elements, where the spirit world is intimately connected with daily life

name: Kumasi Ghost
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Ashanti (Asante) source documents a 'Kumasi Ghost' as a royal-court messenger spirit; the description is generic ancestor-belief applied to an invented figure. Akan tradition does recognize spirits of the dead such as the saman and the restless atofo, but no attested 'Kumasi Ghost' corresponds to this entry.

name: Kumbhakarna (Sleeping Giant)
description: Kumbhakarna is a powerful rakshasa and the younger brother of Ravana from the Hindu epic Ramayana. Despite his gigantic size and enormous appetite, he is described as a virtuous character and a great warrior. He was born with immense strength, having subdued both Indra and Yama. Fearing his power, Indra manipulated Brahma to curse Kumbhakarna to sleep like the dead. At Ravana's plea, the curse was commuted so Kumbhakarna sleeps for six months and wakes for six months. During his waking period, he wreaks havoc and devours to his heart's content. In the Bhagavata Purana, he is said to be the incarnation of the gatekeeper deity Vijaya, who was sentenced to three mortal lifetimes. Along with his brother Jaya (who became Ravana), Vijaya became Kumbhakarna in his second incarnation. He fought valiantly in the war against Rama, destroying 8,000 vanaras before being slain by Rama's Indrastra arrow, which decapitated him. Despite knowing Rama was divine, he fought out of loyalty and dharma to his brother and kingdom

name: Kumiho
description: The Kumiho is a nine-tailed fox from Korean folklore, a powerful and complex supernatural being that shares characteristics with the Japanese kitsune and Chinese huli jing but possesses distinctively Korean attributes. Unlike its Japanese counterpart, the kumiho is almost always a malevolent or tragic figure, a cursed being that must consume human hearts or life essence to survive or to achieve its goal of becoming fully human. The kumiho is typically depicted as a beautiful woman who uses her appearance to seduce men, but unlike the playful or benevolent fox spirits of other traditions, the Korean nine-tailed fox is driven by hunger, curse, or an obsessive desire for humanity. The kumiho legend explores themes of identity, transformation, and the cost of becoming something one is not, making her a more tragic and ambiguous figure than her foreign cousins

name: Kumvo
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Kwakwaka'wakw source documents a spirit called 'Kumvo'; the description is hedged ('would have been understood') generic spirit-world filler with no named figure or story. The Kwakwaka'wakw do have a rich ceremonial spirit world, but this name is unattested in their recorded traditions.

name: Kunmanggur
description: Kunmanggur is the Rainbow Serpent figure in the mythology of the Murinbata people of the Daly River region in the Northern Territory, Australia. As a powerful creator being, Kunmanggur is associated with the waterholes, rivers, and rain that sustain life in the region. The serpent plays a central role in the Murinbata understanding of the landscape, with its movements creating the waterways and geological features of the Daly River area. Kunmanggur's presence is felt in the deep waterholes that remain throughout the dry season, and the serpent is believed to control the monsoon rains that bring renewal each year. Like all Rainbow Serpent figures, Kunmanggur embodies both creative and destructive powers, requiring respect and proper ceremonial observance

name: Kuntilanak
description: Kuntilanak is a female vampire spirit from Indonesian and Malay folklore, one of the most feared supernatural beings in Southeast Asia. She is the ghost of a woman who died during childbirth or as a virgin, condemned to wander the earth in torment. The kuntilanak shares characteristics with the similar pontianak spirit of Malay tradition, and the names are sometimes used interchangeably across the region. She is a vengeful spirit who targets pregnant women and newborn infants, driven by jealousy and the tragedy of her own unfinished life. The kuntilanak legend is deeply embedded in Indonesian culture, appearing in countless folk tales, films, and urban legends. Unlike many supernatural beings that are purely malevolent, the kuntilanak is sometimes portrayed with tragic depth, a spirit whose evil actions stem from the injustice of her death and the impossibility of finding peace

name: Kuntofengo
description: Kuntofengo is the 'spirit husband' figure in Mandinka folklore of The Gambia, a jinn or spirit being who forms a jealous attachment to a human woman and interferes with her earthly marriage and fertility. In Gambian traditional belief, a woman experiencing infertility, recurrent miscarriages, or the death of infants may be afflicted by a Kuntofengo — a spirit who has claimed her as his spiritual wife and sabotages her human relationships. The Kuntofengo typically begins appearing to a young woman before marriage, manifesting as headaches, dizzy spells, or nightmares. After marriage, the symptoms worsen as the jealous spirit intensifies his attempts to prevent the woman from bearing children for her human husband. The Kuntofengo cannot be addressed by Western medicine; treatment requires intervention from a marabout (a spiritual healer who practices Islamic-influenced traditional medicine) who can negotiate with or exorcise the spirit through Quranic verses, amulets, and holy water. The concept reflects the Mandinka belief that human fertility is subject to negotiation between the visible and invisible worlds

name: Kupe
description: The great Polynesian navigator and chief who discovered Aotearoa (New Zealand) according to Maori tradition. Kupe sailed from Hawaiki in his canoe Matahourua, pursuing the giant octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi which had been stealing his bait. His wife Hine-te-Aparangi was the first to sight land, calling out 'He ao, he ao!' (A cloud, a cloud!) - giving the name Aotearoa (Land of the Long White Cloud). Kupe explored the coastline of New Zealand extensively, naming many landmarks. He returned to Hawaiki with detailed navigational knowledge, providing the first sea charts that guided the later great migration of Maori to New Zealand

name: Kupua
description: In Hawaiian tradition, kupua are shapeshifting demigods and magical beings who can take many forms, with well-known examples such as Kamapua'a (the hog-god) and figures in the epic cycles collected in the 19th century. The description is condensed to the attested shapeshifter-demi god tradition; the invented 'summoned by kahuna' and 'twilight veil' specifics are removed.

name: Kurangaituku
description: A fearsome bird-woman ogre from Maori legend who captured and nearly devoured the warrior Hatupatu. Kurangaituku is described as having sharp claws like a bird, feathers mixed with human features, and a taste for human flesh. She kept Hatupatu prisoner in her cave, intending to eat him, but he cleverly escaped. She pursued him relentlessly across the central North Island before being repelled by the hot springs and geysers of the Rotorua thermal region. Some versions say she was overcome when Hatupatu hid in a narrow rock crevice she could not reach

name: Kurka (Raven Creator)
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Nivkh folklore. No source confirms a raven creator called 'Kurka' among the Nivkh of Sakhalin; the raven creator-god Kutkh belongs to the Chukchi and Koryak, while Nivkh myth centers on sea and taiga masters such as Tolk. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Kurupira
description: Kurupira is a forest spirit from the folklore of Uruguay and the Guarani-speaking regions of South America, a wild and fearsome creature that dwells in the deepest parts of the forest as the lord of all woodland animals. This short, ugly, hairy being is the undisputed master of the wilderness, commanding the animals and plants of the forest according to its will. The kurupira is one of the most important nature spirits in Guarani tradition, serving as both protector of the forest and punisher of those who harm it. Hunters and woodcutters must obtain the kurupira permission before taking anything from the forest, or they risk its terrible wrath. The spirit is particularly associated with the protection of pregnant women and children who become lost in the woods, though its methods of protection are often violent and terrifying to those who do not understand its motives

name: Kurupí
description: Kurupí, fifth of the seven cursed sons of Tau and Kerana in Guarani mythology, is a small, hairy forest being of the Paraguayan monte whose enormous phallus, wound about his waist, marks him as the spirit of desire and clandestine fertility. He abducts women who walk the forest alone, kills men who will not share their hunt, and punishes those who fell trees without need.

name: Kushtaka
description: The Kushtaka, meaning "Land Otter Man" in the Tlingit language, is a shape-shifting creature from the folklore of the Tlingit and Haida peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast of North America. These are hybrid beings with both otter and human characteristics, created when humans are captured and transformed by the Land Otter spirits that inhabit the dense coastal forests. The Kushtaka are among the most complex supernatural beings in Northwest Coast mythology, possessing a deeply dual nature that makes them both terrifying and benevolent, depending on the circumstances. They are closely associated with the boundary between land and sea, between the human world and the spirit world, and between life and death. The belief in Kushtaka reflects the rich spiritual ecology of the Pacific Northwest, where every animal, natural feature, and atmospheric phenomenon possesses spiritual significance and power

name: Kushtaka (Land Otter Man)
description: Kushtaka (Kooshdaa kaa in Tlingit, literally Land Otter Man) are mythical shape-shifting creatures in Tlingit folklore. They can assume human form, otter form, and other forms. In some stories they are cruel creatures who trick sailors to their deaths; in others they save the lost from freezing by transforming them into fellow Kushtaka. They lure victims by imitating baby cries or woman screams. They can be warded off by copper, urine, dogs, and fire. They emit a high-pitched three-part whistle of low-high-low

name: Kushtaka Land Otter Man Tlingit
description: Kóoshdaa káa, the land otter man, is the shapeshifting otter spirit of the Tlingit, a being of the sea edge that appears as a man to lure the drowning and the lost, then transforms them into land otters of its own kind. Related beings appear as 'Watsa among the Tsimshian, and Tlingit hunters treated drowned folk with caution.

name: Kutsutsura
description: Kutsutsura is a malevolent undead entity from the folklore of the Xhosa and Zulu peoples of South Africa. The name Kutsutsura derives from terms meaning 'to be cut off' or 'to be separated,' referring to its nature as a soul severed from the community of ancestors. Unlike benevolent ancestral spirits (amadlozi/izinyanya), Kutsutsura are the restless, corrupted ghosts of evil people, sorcerers, or those who died with unresolved grudges. They are classified as a type of umkhovu (zombie-like animated corpse) and are considered one of the most dangerous spiritual threats in Nguni cosmology, feared even more than ordinary ghosts because of their predatory intelligence and malicious intent

name: Kuutkh (Kutkh)
description: Kutkh (Kuutkh, Kutq) is the great raven-creator of the Chukchi, Koryak, and Itelmen peoples of Siberia: a shape-shifting trickster who appears as raven or man, made the land, rivers, and people, stole the sun, and brought fire to humankind. Protective yet mischievous, he is the central culture-hero of the Chukotkan myth cycle.

name: Kuveni (Yakshini Queen of Lanka)
description: Kuveni (also known as Kuvanna or Sesapati) was a Yakshini (demoness) queen ruling in Lanka when Prince Vijaya arrived from India. According to the Mahavamsa, the ancient Pali chronicle of Sri Lanka, she was a shape-shifting demoness who could assume the form of a beautiful sixteen-year-old maiden. She initially imprisoned Vijaya's men through magical means, but when Vijaya overpowered her, she swore loyalty and helped him conquer the Yakkha city of Sirisavatthu. She bore him two children, Jivahatta and Disala. After establishing the Sinhala kingdom, Vijaya repudiated her saying 'men fear superhuman beings' and sent her away to marry a Pandyan princess instead. When Kuveni returned to her own people, they killed her as a traitor for helping the human invaders. Her children fled to the wilderness of Sumanakuta (Adam's Peak), where they married each other and became the ancestors of the Vedda people, Sri Lanka's indigenous inhabitants. The Vedda venerate her as Maha Loku Kiriammaleththo ('Great Elder Sister')

name: Kuçedra
description: Kuçedra is the multi-headed dragon of Albanian folklore, an enormous fire-breathing serpent of deep caves and mountain peaks that brings storms and chaos. Demanding tribute and battling heroes and spirits alike, it personifies destructive natural forces that saints, weather-lords, and heroes must overcome. The name is an older form of kulshedra, the dragon-queen of Albanian oral tradition.

name: Kvarngubbe
description: Kvarngubbe is a Swedish mill spirit dwelling in water-powered gristmills, helping or hindering the miller. A skilled fiddler like Näcken, strong like a tomte, he maintains mill machinery at night in exchange for respect. The input record incorrectly describes him as a 'mound man' — kvarn means mill, not mound; the mound guardian is a different being (haugbui).

name: Kvernknurr
description: Kvernknurr (also kvernknarr) is a malevolent mill spirit in Norwegian folklore, particularly associated with the water-powered mills of Vestlandet's waterfall-rich valleys. The kvernknurr lives in mill streams and has an enormous gaping mouth — its upper jaw touches the door beam while its lower jaw rests on the threshold of the mill door. When the mill is grinding, the kvernknurr grips the mill wheel mechanism to stop it, causing the millstones to grind slowly or halt entirely. The only remedy is to shoot a gun into the mill race or throw a knife over the mill house. Unlike the fossegrim who is musical and can be placated with offerings, the kvernknurr is purely malicious and delights in ruining the miller's work. The name comes from kvern (millstone/grind) and knurre (to growl or grumble). Closely related to the kvarnvätten of Swedish folklore

name: Kvitormen
description: Kvitormen (the White Serpent) is a magical white snake from the folk belief of Vest-Agder in Sørlandet, particularly the areas of Lyngdal, Bjelland, and Lindesnes. According to tradition, if one could capture a white serpent and place it under the skin of one's arm, the snake would grant supernatural wisdom and healing powers. The person would gain the ability to understand the language of animals, see hidden things, and heal sickness with a touch. However, the white serpent was almost impossible to catch — it was extremely fast, could disappear into the ground, and was protected by supernatural forces. If the white serpent was lost or killed after being implanted, the person would die. The tradition was collected by folklorist Joh. Storaker in the 1800s, who recorded seven variants from Vest-Agder. The white serpent also granted its bearer the ability to find hidden treasure and predict the future

name: Kwanokasha
description: Kwanokasha is one of the Kowi Anukasha, the little people of Choctaw tradition, small cave-dwelling spirits beneath large rocks. He seizes boys who wander off and brings them before three ancient white-haired beings who offer a knife, herbs, and pebbles; the choice foretells a life as warrior, doctor, or one without power. He grants medicine gifts to the respectful but is dangerous to others.

name: Kwatyat Nuu Chah Nulth
description: Kwatyat is the transformer and culture hero of the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka), who traveled the coast in the myth age setting the world right. He changed the ancient beings into the animals, plants, and landmarks of today, and his journeys, recorded by Sapir and Swadesh, explain the shape of the Nuu-chah-nulth world.

name: Kyrkogrim
description: Kyrkogrimen is the guardian spirit of a church, created when an animal was buried alive under the church's cornerstone during construction. The sacrifice bound the animal's soul to the church, creating a protective spirit that would guard the building forever. The animal chosen — usually a ram, dog, rooster, or horse — was believed to give the Kyrkogrim its form and temperament. Kyrkogrimen protects the church from thieves and evil spirits at night, and according to tradition, it chases the souls of the unrighteous from their graves. In Skåne, it was said that the Kyrkogrim would terrify anyone who tried to break into the church, appearing as a spectral animal that could not be harmed. The belief reflects an ancient tradition of foundation sacrifices common across Scandinavia

name: Kyys Debiliye
description: Kyys Debiliye is a warrior heroine of the Yakut (Sakha) olonkho epic tradition: a tall, strong woman famed for archery and combat mastery who battles the heroes of the middle world. Battle-hardened and protective, she exemplifies the female warrior archetype of olonkho and the martial values of the Sakha heroic worldview.

name: Kääk
description: 'Kaak' is not attested in Luxembourgish, Estonian, or Finno-Ugric folklore, and the entry itself mixes an Estonian framing with a Luxembourgish country tag. Genuine Estonian forest spirits (metsavaimud) such as the metsik have documented names; 'Kaak' does not. The name appears invented, and no oral or literary source records it.

name: Kópakonan (Selkie)
description: Kópakonan is the Faroese variant of the selkie legend, a mythical seal-woman who sheds her sealskin to walk on land as a beautiful human. The story comes from the island of Kalsoy in the Faroe Islands, specifically the village of Mikladalur. According to the legend, a farmer from Mikladalur stole a selkie's sealskin while she danced on the shore, forcing her to marry him and bear his children. The term Kópakonan literally translates to 'Seal Woman' in Faroese, and this legend is one of the most enduring and tragic tales in Nordic maritime folklore, deeply intertwined with the Faroese relationship with the sea and its creatures

name: K’eyech
description: K'eyech (also spelled K'eyechi or Kayech) is a rainbow spirit in Maya mythology, particularly among the Tzotzil and Tzeltal Maya communities of highland Chiapas, Mexico. In Maya cosmology, rainbows are not considered benevolent phenomena but are instead dangerous portals or beings associated with illness, misfortune, and the underworld. K'eyech embodies this ambivalent power, serving as both a celestial phenomenon and a spiritual entity that can bring either blessings or calamity. The rainbow in Maya tradition is deeply connected to the Earth Lord (Yahwal Balamil) and the forces that govern weather, fertility, and disease

name: K’’och
description: K''och (also spelled K'och or K'ook) is a star deity in Maya mythology, particularly associated with the Pleiades star cluster (known as Tzab-ek in Yucatec Maya). In the intricate Maya cosmos, stars were living beings with profound influence over human affairs, agriculture, and the calendar. K''och governed the timing of agricultural cycles, particularly the planting and harvesting of maize, the sacred crop that sustained Maya civilization. The Pleiades were especially important because their helical rising and setting marked critical junctures in the agricultural calendar, and K''och served as the divine overseer of these celestial rhythms

name: La Cegua
description: La Cegua (also spelled La Segua) is a terrifying female spirit from Nicaraguan and Costa Rican folklore, known as the 'horse-faced woman' who seduces unfaithful men and drunkards before revealing her monstrous true form. The legend traces its origins to the colonial era of Central America and shares similarities with the Mexican La Llorona and the Venezuelan La Sayona. La Cegua is one of the most feared figures in Central American oral tradition, used by parents for centuries to warn children against wandering alone at night and to caution men against womanizing and drunkenness. The name 'Cegua' is believed to derive from a Nahuatl word meaning 'sleepy' or 'drowsy.'

name: La Ciguapa
description: La Ciguapa (sometimes spelled La Ciguapa or Ciguapa Remadora) is a legendary female creature from Dominican Republic folklore, particularly from the rural Cibao Valley region. She is one of the most iconic figures in Dominican mythology, representing the wild, untamed feminine spirit of the island. The legend likely blends Taíno indigenous beliefs about forest spirits with African and Spanish folk traditions introduced during the colonial period. La Ciguapa is described as a nocturnal creature that inhabits the dense forests, rivers, and mountains of the Dominican Republic, and her story continues to be told throughout the island as a cautionary tale about the dangers of the wilderness

name: La Ciguapa Remadora
description: La Ciguapa Remadora is a regional variant of the Ciguapa legend from the Dominican Republic, specifically associated with the Samaná Peninsula and the northeastern coastal regions. The name 'Remadora' derives from the Spanish word 'remar' (to row), referring to this particular type of Ciguapa that is strongly associated with rivers, lakes, and coastal waters rather than deep forests. While sharing many characteristics with the standard Ciguapa, the Remadora prefers aquatic environments and is more actively predatory toward fishermen, boatmen, and those who travel waterways at night. This variant highlights the adaptation of the core legend to different ecological zones within the Dominican Republic

name: La Culebra Mayor
description: No Bribri or Cabécar source documents a serpent called 'La Culebra Mayor' ('The Greater Snake'). Talamancan mythology does preserve great serpents under other names: ChbekoL, a giant snake that devoured those who broke the incest laws, and Dululba, a snake of justice. The entry's claims of an association with Sibö and the creation of landforms are unattested inventions.

name: La Culebra Vieja
description: Not independently attested as a wise serpent: the genuine figure behind this garbled entry is La Tulevieja (Tulivieja), a feared river hag of Costa Rican and Panamanian folklore rooted in Bribri, Huetar and Cabécar myth (the itsö), who wails for a drowned child, snatches children, and lures men with her inverted footprints.

name: La Diablera
description: La Diablera is a malevolent female spirit from Venezuelan folklore, particularly associated with the Andean regions of Mérida, Táchira, and Trujillo. The name translates to 'The She-Devil' or 'The Diabolical Woman,' reflecting her demonic nature and her role as a tempter and punisher of men. La Diablera is one of the many female specters in Latin American folklore that targets unfaithful husbands and womanizers, placing her in the same category as La Llorona, La Sayona, and La Cegua. However, La Diablera is distinguished by her more overtly demonic characteristics and her association with crossroads and remote mountain passes

name: La Diablesse
description: La Diablesse (Lajables) is a figure of Dominican and wider Francophone-Caribbean folklore: a beautiful, elegantly dressed woman who lures men into the forest at night, revealing a cloven hoof or a withered leg under her long skirt. Dominican accounts describe her as a jumbie to be avoided on lonely roads. The text is corrected from the Saint Lucian version to the Dominican tradition.

name: La Diablesse
description: In Saint Lucia, La Diablesse is a beautiful white demoness usually encountered on bridges or near rivers. She will talk quietly and politely to her victim before using her magical beauty to lure him into the forest. Once enchanted, the victim will be fed on lizards, wood ants, and snakes. Sometimes he is never seen again; if he is lucky, he will awake the next morning in a crevice on some rockface or ravine. She can be recognized by her cloven foot and by the heavy steel fetters glimpsed under her skirts. Making the sign of the cross will make a true Diablesse immediately disappear. Saint Lucian folklorist Kennedy Boot Samuel has documented how the Diablesse legend is still whispered about in rural communities. The legend likely blends French colonial devil imagery with West African spirit concepts, creating a uniquely Saint Lucian cautionary figure about the dangers of temptation In Saint Lucia folklore, this figure is known among the Saint Lucian Creole people.

name: La Diablesse (The Devil Woman of the Road)
description: La Diablesse (French for the she-devil) is a seductive yet deadly spirit in Trinidadian and West Indian folklore. She appears as a breathtakingly beautiful woman -- usually tall, light-skinned, with long flowing black hair and piercing eyes -- wearing a wide-brimmed hat and a flowing white, black, or red dress that conceals her horrifying secret: one leg ends in a cloven cow hoof instead of a human foot. She waits by the roadside at night, particularly near bridges, crossroads, and remote forest paths, and bewitches men (especially those returning from dances or rum shops) with her beauty and perfume. Once she lures a man deep into the forest, she reveals her true form and leads him to his doom -- into a ravine, a river, quicksand, or a cliff. Some say she drinks their blood; others say she simply laughs and vanishes, leaving the man hopelessly lost. She is a cautionary figure, warning against infidelity, lust, and wandering alone at night

name: La Garita del Diablo (The Devil's Sentry Box)
description: La Garita del Diablo (The Devil Sentry Box) is the most famous supernatural legend of Old San Juan, Puerto Rico. The story centers on a solitary sentry box (garita) at Castillo San Cristobal, perched on a rocky cliff above the crashing Atlantic. In the late 1600s, a Spanish soldier named Sanchez, nicknamed Flor de Azahar (Orange Blossom) for his pale white skin, was assigned to the farthest, most isolated sentry box. Sanchez was known for his beautiful guitar playing and his forbidden love for Diana, a local mestiza woman. One night, after the customary watchman calls echoed between the fort sentry boxes, Sanchez voice fell silent. At dawn, his fellow soldiers found his rifle, cartridge pouch, and uniform neatly folded inside the garita -- but Sanchez himself had vanished without a trace. Superstitious soldiers whispered that the devil had taken him. The true story, according to folklore, is that Diana brought him civilian clothes and they eloped together into the Luquillo Mountains. Yet to this day, visitors claim to hear the strumming of a guitar and soft laughter at the Garita del Diablo on windy nights

name: La Lechuza
description: La Lechuza is a terrifying shapeshifting witch from Mexican and Texas border folklore who transforms into a giant owl — seven feet tall with a fifteen-foot wingspan and the face of an old woman. According to legend, she was once a human woman who made a pact with the devil or practiced black magic, gaining the power to become an enormous owl that hunts at night. She preys primarily on drunk men and children, luring victims by mimicking the cry of a human infant or whistling. Her eyes glow like coals in the darkness, and her screech is said to be a death omen. In some versions, she is a witch's familiar serving an evil mistress; snip in others, a wronged mother seeking revenge on those who killed her child. Stories of La Lechuza are particularly widespread in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas and the Mexican states of Tamaulipas, Coahuila, Nuevo León, and Chihuahua

name: La Llorona (The Weeping Woman)
description: ONE OF THE MOST FAMOUS Latin American ghosts — La Llorona ('The Weeping Woman') has pre-Columbian roots in the Aztec goddess Cihuacóatl, who appeared before the Spanish conquest weeping for the fate of her people. During the colonial period, the story syncretized with Spanish folklore of white ladies and became associated with La Malinche, Cortés's interpreter who bore his child — cursed by her people for betraying the Aztec Empire, condemned to wander forever weeping for her mestizo children. In the classic colonial version, a beautiful woman named María discovers her husband's infidelity, drowns her two children in a river, then drowns herself in grief. She now wanders eternally near water, wailing '¡Ay, mis hijos!' In the South Texas borderlands along the Rio Grande, Mexican-American communities tell of La Llorona appearing near irrigation canals and arroyos — sometimes as a protector warning mothers of danger rather than a predator. In New Mexico, the spirits of her drowned children appear as translucent figures playing near rivers at dusk. Chicana feminist writers like Gloria Anzaldúa and Sandra Cisneros have reclaimed La Llorona as a symbol of resistance, survival, and the power of the marginalized feminine voice

name: La Loba
description: La Loba (The Wolf Woman) is a figure from New Mexican and Chicano folklore who protects the wild places and animals of the Southwestern desert. Older than any human, she is the guardian of wolf and coyote spirits. It is said that when a wolf dies, La Loba collects its bones and sings over them until the animal is reborn. She is described as an ancient woman who lives in a cave in the mountains, surrounded by the skulls and bones of animals. Children who get lost in the desert are said to be guided home by her, and hunters who kill for sport rather than need find their guns mysteriously jammed. The figure was popularized by Clarissa Pinkola Estés in her book 'Women Who Run With the Wolves,' which linked La Loba to the archetype of the wild feminine. In Chicano folklore, La Loba represents the deep connection between Hispanic peoples and the land of the Southwest, the wisdom of curanderas, and the power of women as healers and protectors of nature. Her legend connects to the nahual tradition of shapeshifting, as La Loba is sometimes said to transform between human and wolf form

name: La Madre del Monte
description: La Madre del Monte (Mother of the Mountain) is a powerful nature spirit from the folklore of Costa Rica, Panama, and Colombia, particularly among the indigenous Bribri, Cabécar, and Ngäbe peoples. She is the protective goddess of forests, mountains, and wild animals, serving as the guardian of biodiversity and natural balance. La Madre del Monte is one of the most respected and feared spirits in Central American folk tradition because she controls the abundance of game animals, the fertility of the forest, and the safety of those who enter her domain. She represents the feminine principle of nature as both a nurturing provider and a fearsome protector

name: La Malinche
description: La Malinche (Unknown). is a human. Malintzin (also known as Malinche or Doña Marina) is a controversial figure in Mexican history and folklore. She served as interpreter, advisor, and intermediary for Hernán Cortés during the Spanish c. Source: Historical sources; Mexican cultural tradition

name: La Mano Pachona
description: La Mano Pachona is a chilling legend from northern Mexico and the US Southwest about a disembodied, hairy hand that attacks travelers at night. The hand is described as large, dark, and covered in thick hair, with long fingernails. It wanders along lonely roads, scratching at windows and car doors, or reaches up from beneath vehicles to grab unsuspecting victims. Some versions claim the hand belongs to a man who was cursed for his evil deeds, while others say it is the hand of a murdered criminal that continues to seek revenge. In Mexican-American folklore of Texas and California, the story is often told around campfires and at sleepovers, serving as a tale of warning about traveling alone at night. La Mano Pachona represents the fear of the fragmented, disembodied threat — danger that comes not from a whole being but from something partial and inexplicable. The legend taps into the primal fear of being touched or grabbed from below or behind in the dark

name: La Masa
description: La Masa (The Mass) is a bizarre and terrifying entity from Venezuelan folklore, particularly from the central plains (llanos) and Andean regions. The name 'La Masa' literally means 'The Dough' or 'The Mass,' referring to the creature's amorphous, dough-like appearance. Despite its unusual name, La Masa is considered one of the most dangerous supernatural entities in Venezuelan oral tradition, capable of crushing, suffocating, or absorbing its victims into its gelatinous body. The legend likely has mixed origins, drawing from African slave traditions about shapeless forest spirits and indigenous tales of malevolent swamp entities

name: La Pallar
description: La Pallar is a ghostly figure from the folklore of the Canary Islands (Spain), particularly associated with the island of La Palma. The legend of La Pallar is one of the most famous ghost stories in the Canary archipelago, blending elements of romance, tragedy, and the supernatural. La Pallar was a young woman named María de La O or simply 'La Pallar' who lived in the 16th or 17th century and died of a broken heart after her lover abandoned her. Her ghost is said to wander the streets of Santa Cruz de La Palma and the surrounding countryside, forever searching for her lost love and appearing to those who remind her of him

name: La Patonera
description: La Patonera (also known as La Patuda or simply 'Big Foot') is a legendary creature from the folklore of Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil, particularly associated with the vast wetlands of the Esteros del Iberá in Corrientes, Argentina, and the Paraná River delta. The name derives from 'pata' (foot/leg), referring to the creature's most distinctive feature: enormous, oversized feet that leave massive tracks in the mud of riverbanks and swamps. La Patonera is a swamp-dwelling entity that protects wetlands and punishes those who exploit them, sharing characteristics with both the Brazilian Curupira and the North American Bigfoot

name: La Planchada
description: La Planchada (The Ironed One, referring to her perfectly pressed nurse's uniform) is a ghost legend from Mexico City hospitals that has spread through Mexican-American communities in the US Southwest. According to the story, a beautiful nurse named Eulalia worked at Hospital Juárez in the 1930s, deeply dedicated to her patients. She fell in love with a handsome doctor who courted her but ultimately abandoned her to marry another woman. Heartbroken, Eulalia died of sorrow, but her ghost now returns to the hospital where she once worked. Dressed in an immaculately starched white nurse's uniform, La Planchada appears in hospital wards at night, administering medicines, adjusting blankets, and comforting patients. Some patients claim to have recovered miraculously after being visited by her, while others say she only appears to those who are about to die. A key warning states that if you see the hem of her dress or her feet, you will die within days — a version of the classic 'don't look at their feet' motif. La Planchada has been reported in Mexican-American hospitals and clinics along the border, where she is viewed as a benevolent guardian spirit of the sick and dying

name: La Sayona
description: La Sayona is a vengeful female specter from the folklore of Venezuela and Colombia, particularly from the Llanos (plains) region shared by both countries. According to the most popular version of the legend, La Sayona was once a beautiful woman named Casilda who lived in the colonial era. Blinded by jealousy after being told by a rejected suitor that her husband Severiano was having an affair with her own mother, Casilda murdered her husband and infant son by burning their house down, then attacked her mother with a machete. As her mother lay dying, she cursed Casilda to wander the earth forever as La Sayona, punishing unfaithful men for all eternity. The name comes from 'sayal,' the coarse cloth of a colonial-era robe

name: La Siguanaba
description: A BEAUTIFUL WOMAN spirit from Mesoamerican folklore, particularly prevalent in El Salvador, Guatemala, and southern Mexico, with variants told in Mexican-American communities of the US Southwest. The legend has pre-Columbian origins among the Pipil and Maya peoples, where female water spirits were associated with both fertility and danger. La Siguanaba appears as a stunningly beautiful woman with long, flowing hair, seen bathing in rivers or washing clothes. She lures men — especially those who are unfaithful or have been drinking — by appearing as their lover or a beautiful stranger. When the man approaches, she transforms, revealing her true face: that of a horse or a skull, driving him mad with terror. Some versions say she then attacks and kills him. The name derives from the Nahuatl 'cihuatl' (woman) and may be related to Aztec Cihuacóatl. In the US Southwest, the story is told among Chicano communities as a warning against infidelity, drunkenness, and the dangers of trusting appearances — particularly to young men who stray from their commitments

name: La Silampa
description: La Silampa is a legendary white specter from Panamanian folklore, described as a ghostly white sheet-like creature that soars over roads, deserted areas, and fields, blending into the fog. According to legend, La Silampa was originally a beautiful indigenous princess who fell in love with a forbidden warrior. When Spanish soldiers killed her lover and her father murdered him, the spirit of the night entered her body, transforming her into an evil spiritual being. She devoured her father, leaving only his skeleton. Since then, La Silampa roams Panama's roads and fields seeking victims to devour, able to grow several meters tall

name: La Trola
description: 'La Trola' appears only in a single AI-generated Miskito story retelling online; no Nicaraguan folklore source or ethnographic record documents this named figure. Genuine Miskito water-beliefs center on other beings, and Nicaragua's coastal tradition knows figures such as the Cegua and Wihwin-type water spirits, but 'La Trola' has no attestation.

name: La Tulivieja
description: La Tulivieja is one of Panama's most famous legendary figures, a vengeful ghost transformed into a hideous creature. According to the legend, a beautiful young woman had a secret relationship that resulted in pregnancy. To hide her sin, she drowned her baby in a river. As punishment from God, she transformed into a monster with a face full of holes sprouting tangled hair, bat wings, chicken legs, and a distinctive tule hat. She eats carbon and ashes, leaving footprints near bonfires. Under a full moon she regains her original beauty and bathes in the river, but a loud noise reverts her to monster form. Condemned to search eternally for her baby, her breasts are always filled with milk

name: La'ieikawai
description: The legendary Hawaiian princess and heroine of one of the great epic cycles of Hawaiian mythology. La'ieikawai was a beautiful chiefess of legendary status, renowned for her beauty and supernatural powers. The epic of La'ieikawai tells of her birth, her seclusion in a sacred house, her romance with the chief Kauakahi, and her conflict with the jealous sorceress Waka. Protected by her grandmother, the goddess Maile, La'ieikawai possessed the power to call rainbows and command the birds. Her story was memorized and recited as one of the great traditional Hawaiian romances, comparable to the Hi'iaka epic

name: Labaw Donggon
description: Labaw Donggon is the eldest of three heroic brothers in the Hinilawod, one of the oldest and most important epic poems of the Sulod people of Panay Island in the Philippines. This epic, whose name means 'Tales from the Mouth of the Halawod River,' recounts the adventures of the three demigod sons of Alunsina and Datu Paubari. Labaw Donggon is renowned as the mightiest warrior among the three brothers, a figure of superhuman strength and courage who embarked on epic quests to win the hands of beautiful maidens. His most famous adventure involves his journey to conquer Anggoy Doronoon, the goddess of the sea, whom he sought as his wife. The epic showcases the rich pre-colonial mythology of the Visayan people

name: Ladejarlens Gjenferd
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Norwegian source documents a ghost of the Lade Jarls haunting the Lade district of Trondheim; the entry wraps genuine history of the Earls of Lade in an invented spectral-horseman tale with no cited tradition. Trondheim does have attested ghost stories, but the 'Ladejarl's ghost' as such is unattested.

name: Lafaek (The Crocodile Prince)
description: Lafaek (The Crocodile Prince) is a central figure in Timor-Leste's foundational creation myth, explaining why the island of Timor is shaped like a crocodile. According to legend, a young boy discovered a baby crocodile struggling to reach the sea and compassionately carried it to the water. The grateful crocodile promised to repay the boy and invited him to ride on its back. Despite its gratitude, the crocodile fought its predatory instinct to eat the boy. Seeking counsel from the whale, tiger, and water buffalo — all of whom said 'you cannot eat him' — and finally a wise monkey who cursed the crocodile, the crocodile resolved to protect the boy. When the crocodile grew old, it offered its body as a gift, transforming into the island of Timor so the boy and his descendants would have a homeland forever. Timor is often called the 'Land of the Sleeping Crocodile.'

name: Lafaek (The Crocodile Spirit)
description: The crocodile holds profound spiritual significance across East Timor's diverse cultures, appearing in multiple origin myths and as a totemic ancestral figure. In various Timorese traditions, the crocodile is both a creator figure and a sacred ancestor. The island of Timor itself is said by some traditions to be shaped like a crocodile, and the animal is deeply respected as a guardian of sacred waters and ancestral law. Crocodile spirits are associated with lulik potency and are often guardians of specific water sources and coastal areas. Some clans consider the crocodile their direct ancestor

name: Lagahoo
description: The Lagahoo of Tobago is a shapeshifting monster deeply rooted in the island's Afro-Caribbean folklore traditions. Similar to its counterparts in Trinidad and Grenada, the Tobagonian Lagahoo is considered a malevolent spirit that roams the island after dark, embodying the fears and beliefs brought by enslaved Africans and blended with European colonial influences. The creature is a prominent figure in Tobagonian oral tradition, used to warn children and young adults about the dangers of staying out late. The legend varies between communities but consistently portrays the Lagahoo as one of the most feared supernatural beings in the Caribbean

name: Lagarfljótsormur
description: The Lagarfljótsormur, also known as the Lagarfljót Worm, is a legendary lake monster said to inhabit Lake Lagarfljót near the town of Egilsstaðir in eastern Iceland. First recorded in 1345 AD in the Icelandic Annals, this creature is one of Iceland's most famous cryptids, comparable to the Loch Ness Monster. According to the folk tale collected by Jón Árnason in 1862, the worm began as a small heath worm or slug that was placed with gold by a young girl hoping to make it grow. Instead, it grew into an enormous serpent that now terrorizes the lake. The creature is deeply woven into Icelandic folklore and is a significant part of the region's cultural heritage and tourism

name: Lagarto
description: The Lagarto is a dragon-like creature from Portuguese folklore, deeply rooted in the country's medieval mythological traditions. The name derives from the Portuguese word for 'lizard,' and these creatures are often described as large reptilian monsters that dwell in caves, rivers, and remote mountains throughout Portugal. Unlike the fire-breathing dragons of northern European tradition, the Portuguese Lagarto is more closely associated with water and is often depicted as a giant lizard or crocodile-like beast. These legends were particularly common in rural areas where unexplained livestock deaths or mysterious disappearances were attributed to these creatures

name: Laibon Spirits
description: The Laibon (plural: Laiboni or Oloiboni) are the hereditary ritual leaders and spirit mediums of the Maasai people, believed to possess supernatural powers passed down through the Inkindongi clan. Laiboni serve as intermediaries between the Maasai and Enkai, wielding powers of prophecy, rainmaking, healing, divination, and blessing. After death, powerful Laiboni become ancestral spirits who continue to guide and protect their descendants. The position of Laibon is the highest spiritual office in Maasai society. The most famous Laiboni include Subet (mid-19th century), his son Mbatian (the greatest Laibon), and Mbatian's sons Senteu and Lenana

name: Lake Monster (Mapuche)
description: This lake monster variant represents the fusion of Mapuche water spirit traditions with North American lake monster legends, reflecting the growing cultural exchange between North and South American indigenous communities in modern folklore. While the Mapuche people are indigenous to Chile and Argentina, their concept of sacred lake guardians has found resonance with similar beliefs among Native American tribes, particularly those of the Pacific Northwest and Great Lakes regions. This hybrid legend speaks to the universal human fascination with mysterious creatures inhabiting deep, dark waters and the spiritual significance attributed to lakes across cultures

name: Lake Monster (Mapuche)
description: Not independently attested in Colombia. Mapuche lake monsters (Coi Coi-Vilu, Trentren Vilu, serpent of Lake Lanalhue) belong to Chile and Argentina. The Colombian Monster of Lake Tota is a Muisca serpent, not Mapuche. Country attribution is wrong.

name: Lake Monster (Mapuche)
description: The lake monster of Mapuche and Huilliche tradition is the great water serpent called El Cuero or Trelquehuecufe, a flattened, hide-like creature that dwells in the lakes and lagoons of southern Chile. It drags people and livestock underwater to suck their blood and can even slither over land to seek prey, making its waters dangerous to enter.

name: Lakhe
description: The Lakhe is a fearsome demon figure from Nepalese folklore, particularly prominent in the Newar culture of the Kathmandu Valley. Also known as Lakhey, this supernatural being is depicted as a wild, forest-dwelling demon who later became a protector of towns and communities. The Lakhe is central to several traditional Newar festivals, most notably the Indra Jatra festival in Kathmandu, where dancers wearing elaborate Lakhe masks perform ritual dances that are believed to ward off evil spirits. Despite its terrifying appearance, the Lakhe is considered a complex figure that can be both dangerous and protective, representing the untamed forces of nature

name: Lakhey
description: Lakhey (Unknown). is a demon. The Lakhey is a fearsome demon figure in Nepalese folklore, particularly central to Newar culture in the Kathmandu Valley. Dancers costumed as the Lakhey perform during the Indra Jatra festival.. Source: Nepalese folklore; Newar tradition

name: Lamassu
description: The Lamassu is a colossal protective deity from ancient Mesopotamian religion, depicted as a majestic hybrid of a human head, the body of a bull or lion, and the wings of an eagle. Originally a protective goddess called Lamma in Sumerian times, the Lamassu evolved during the Neo-Assyrian Empire (c. 883–612 BCE) into monumental stone sculptures that guarded the entrances of palaces, temples, and cities. These awe-inspiring figures stood up to 14 feet tall and were carved from single blocks of alabaster, strategically placed in pairs at gateways to ward off evil spirits and intimidate human enemies. The Lamassu was believed to combine the intelligence of a human, the strength of a bull, and the freedom of an eagle, embodying the most desirable protective qualities

name: Lamia
description: Lamia is a child-stealing demon from Roman and Vatican-associated folklore. Originally a figure from classical Greek mythology - a lover of Zeus who turned into a monster after Hera killed her children - Lamia was adopted into Roman and later Christian demonology. In Vatican tradition, Lamia represents the demonic forces that threaten innocent souls, particularly unbaptized infants. Medieval Christian writers described Lamia as a female demon who lures and devours children. Augustine referenced Lamia-type creatures in City of God, discussing whether monstrous beings could be saved. In some accounts, Lamia has the upper body of a beautiful woman and the lower body of a serpent

name: Lamia (Italian variant)
description: The Lamia Italian variant in Lebanese folklore represents the fascinating fusion of European and Middle Eastern mythological traditions. Lebanon, with its long history of cultural exchange between East and West, developed its own unique version of the Lamia myth. This version combines the Greek child-devouring monster with Middle Eastern demonic traditions, including elements of the Arabic jinn and the Mesopotamian Lamashtu. The Lebanese Lamia is a shapeshifting female spirit that uses beauty as a disguise to hide her monstrous nature, preying on both children and unwary adults

name: Lamia (Λάμια)
description: The Lamia is a child-devouring female monster deeply embedded in Greek Cypriot folklore, descended from the ancient Lamia of Greek mythology who was cursed by Hera to eat children. In Cypriot tradition, she is a solitary, nocturnal creature who dwells in caves and remote mountain passes, preying on children who wander too far from home. She is said to have the ability to remove her own eyes, which she places in a bowl to sleep — if someone steals her eyes, she becomes blind and helpless until she gets them back. This motif appears in many Cypriot folktales collected in the Troodos villages. The Lamia is also associated with desolate places, old ruins, and deserted wells. Mothers in rural Cyprus, particularly in villages like Kakopetria and Platres, would threaten disobedient children with the Lamia to keep them close to home. In some versions, she is a shape-shifter who can appear as a beautiful woman to lure men before revealing her true horrific form

name: Lampad
description: The Lampad is a spectral figure from Hungarian folklore, described as a ghostly light or swamp spirit that appears as a flickering flame over marshy ground. Known also by various names in Hungarian tradition, the Lampad is similar to the will-o'-the-wisp found in many European folk traditions. These eerie lights were believed to be the souls of unbaptized children, suicides, or other restless spirits condemned to wander between the earthly realm and the afterlife. The Hungarian Lampad is particularly associated with swamps, bogs, and wetlands, where it leads travelers astray

name: Lamya
description: Lamya (lamia) is a female dragon-serpent of Bulgarian and Balkan folklore, a many-headed monster who devours children and drinks blood. She lives in caves, wells, or the sky and causes drought and eclipses; heroes in Bulgarian folk songs kill her to free the waters, reflecting ancient lamia myths adapted to Slavic lands.

name: Landvättir
description: Landvættir are tutelary spirits of specific places in Old Norse and Icelandic tradition, not Swedish. They appear in Landnámabók and Heimskringla as guardians of Iceland's quarters (dragon, eagle, bull, giant) and spirits of hills, stones, and waterfalls propitiated with offerings. The Swedish equivalent is landvättar or rå, but landvættir and its detailed lore are distinctly Icelandic/Old Norse.

name: Landvættir
description: Landvættir (land wights) are the four guardian spirits of Iceland described in Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla. Each guardian protects one quarter of Iceland's coast: a dragon (gríðungur) guards the east, a giant eagle or griffin (gammur) guards the north, a bull (griðungur) guards the west, and a rock giant (bergrisi) guards the south. According to the legend, King Harald Gormsson of Denmark sent a wizard in whale-form to scout Iceland for invasion. The wizard tried to land on each coast but was driven away by the four landvættir — the dragon breathed fire, the eagle tore at his eyes, the bull charged with horns, and the giant smashed him with a club. The wizard returned to Denmark and reported that Iceland could not be conquered. The landvættir are depicted on Iceland's coat of arms and on Icelandic króna coins. They represent the protective power of the Icelandic landscape itself

name: Langgam Harbe
description: Not independently attested in documented Philippine folklore; searches locate no spirit called 'Langgam Harbe,' and 'langgam' is the Tagalog word for ant. The recorded insect-linked traits fit the wider Philippine class of small, mound-dwelling spirits such as the nuno sa punso, spirits of termite mounds and anthills that demand respect and offerings.

name: Latawiec
description: Latawiec (also latawy) is a Polish wind spirit or storm demon, sometimes appearing as a fiery serpent or dragon that flies by night and brings storms, hail, and whirlwinds. In Polish folk belief he can be raised by a sorcerer who keeps him as a familiar, and the same name is given to the kite, the toy that shares his flight.

name: Lauma (Latvian)
description: Lauma (Latvian) (Latvia). is a fairy. Female nature spirit and goddess of fate, childbirth, and meadows in Latvian mythology. Source: Latvian mythology; laumas are female nature spirits and fate goddesses.

name: Lauma (Latvian)
description: Lauma (Latvian) (Lithuania). is a fairy. Female nature spirit and goddess of fate, childbirth, and meadows in Latvian mythology. Source: Lithuanian mythology; lauma are female forest/water spirits.

name: Laumas (plural: Laumės)
description: Laumas (plural: Laumės) (Latvia). is a spirit. Similar to Lithuanian laumė - female forest and water spirits. Source: Baltic folklore; general category of laumė/lauma spirits.

name: Laumė
description: Laumė (Lithuania). is a fairy. Female nature spirit or fairy in Lithuanian folklore. Source: Lithuanian folklore; female nature spirits associated with destiny and childbirth.

name: Lazavik
description: Lazavik (lazovik) is a gentle spirit of Belarusian folklore who lives in the flax fields, guarding the crop and hiding among the fibers. He is described as a small, old, harmless being who flees when the flax is harvested, a personification of the plant essential to Belarusian rural life.

name: Le Zandolite
description: Le Zandolite is a Haitian spectral dragonfly appearing at night. If caught, it grants one wish before disappearing. A wish-granting animal spirit motif in Haitian folklore. Name may derive from French 'zandoli' (lizard/gecko) + diminutive, or creole variation. Not a major figure; minor wish-granting spirit.

name: Leanan Sídhe
description: The Leannán Sídhe ('fairy lover') is a female fairy of the Aos Sí who takes a human lover, granting poetic inspiration but draining their life force so they die young. W. B. Yeats popularized her as a vampiric muse: 'The Gaelic poets die young, for she is restless.' Earlier sources (Lady Wilde, 1887) describe her as a fairy mistress who becomes a slave if refused.

name: Lebe
description: Lebe is an ancestral spirit and earth deity of the Dogon people of Mali. According to Dogon cosmology, Lebe was the first ancestor, who died and was reborn as a serpent and whose body is identified with the earth. Linked with the sacred serpent and cycles of regeneration, he is honoured through offerings and rites in the Dogon ritual year.

name: Legba
description: Legba is the trickster god and divine intermediary in Fon Vodun cosmology of Benin, serving as the essential gatekeeper who opens communication between the human and spirit worlds. No ceremony, prayer, or offering can reach the other Vodun deities without Legba's permission and assistance. He stands at the cosmic crossroads, speaking all human languages, and is the master of doors, pathways, and communication. Legba is a complex figure with both benevolent and malevolent aspects — he can facilitate blessings or create obstacles depending on how he is approached. He is typically depicted as an old man with a walking cane or crutch, wearing a broad-brimmed straw hat and smoking a pipe. Legba is the first spirit invoked at the beginning of every Vodun ceremony, and his role has been carried to the Americas through the slave trade, becoming Papa Legba in Haitian Vodou and Exu in Brazilian Candomblé. Dogs are sacred to Legba, and his offerings include candy, tobacco, and coffee

name: Legendary Warrior Iceland
description: Legendary Warrior Iceland (Unknown). is a human. A legendary warrior from Icelandic saga tradition is a hero of great strength recorded in the sagas.. Source: Icelandic folklore — legendary warriors documented in Icelandic sagas.

name: Legends Iceland
description: Legends Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. Legends from Icelandic folklore are traditional stories preserving the wisdom of the Icelandic people.. Source: Icelandic folklore — general survey of Icelandic folk belief and legends.

name: Lei
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of East Timor folklore; searches locate no figure called 'Lei,' the Tetum word for the grass Imperata cylindrica. The recorded mountain, spring, and rock spirits align with documented Tetum beliefs in mate bein, ancestral ghosts, and lulik, sacred places guarded by land spirits, but no named being matches the entry.

name: Lekamøya
description: Lekamøya (the Leka Maid) is a female troll figure from Nordland folklore, serving as the nanny of the Seven Sisters — the daughters of Suliskongen. According to the legend cycle, when Hestmannen pursued the Seven Sisters, Lekamøya tried to protect them. She fled south from the horseman, leaping across Velfjorden toward Leka island. As the sun rose, she was turned to stone mid-flight. The butter keg she was carrying fell from her hands and became the yellow-colored mountains on Leka island (which are geologically distinct — composed of ultramafic rock with a distinctive yellow-green color). The Lekamøya rock formation is clearly visible on Leka, one of the most famous rock formations in Nordland. The legend explains both the rock formation and the unusual geology of Leka. The island of Leka is located on the border between Trøndelag and Nordland

name: Lemjel
description: Not independently attested as a death spirit of Marshallese folklore. No scholarly source documents a ferryman or soul-guide named 'Lemjel'; the only online reference is an AI-generated content site, and standard accounts of Marshallese religion and the afterlife record no such figure. The entry appears to be an invented death-spirit archetype rather than a recorded being.

name: Lemminkäinen
description: Lemminkäinen is the reckless, handsome hero of the Kalevala who woos Kyllikki, journeys to Pohjola, is killed trying to shoot the Swan of Tuonela, and is resurrected by his mother raking the river of death. His adventures, compiled by Lönnrot from Karelian runic songs, portray a shamanic figure who traverses the boundary between worlds.

name: Lempo
description: Lempo is a malignant forest spirit or devil in Finno-Karelian folklore, documented by Ganander in Mythologia Fennica (1789). Originally a distinct fire/demon entity associated with Hiisi, later conflated with the Christian devil — the Finnish word 'lempo' means 'damn.' Leads travelers astray, causes disease, and personifies destructive passion.

name: Leopard Spirit
description: The 'Leopard Spirit' in Cameroon reflects the historical Leopard Society (Anyoto, Vihokohoko) — secret societies active c. 1890–1940s whose members wore leopard-skin regalia to simulate leopard attacks, often as political resistance against slave traders and colonial rule. Members did not believe they became actual leopards.

name: Leppalúði
description: Leppalúði (Icelandic). is a ogre. Leppalúði is the lazy and gluttonous third husband of the ogress Grýla in Icelandic folklore, father of the Yule Lads, who contributes little to their child-snatching activities.. Source: Icelandic folklore, Jón Árnason's collections

name: Leshy
description: Leshy is the tutelary forest spirit of East Slavic folklore, a shape-shifting guardian of the woods who leads travelers astray, changes his height, and can be befriended with offerings of bread and salt. He speaks with the rustle of leaves and roams with wolves and bears, and hunters address him with respect to avoid his mischief.

name: Lesovik
description: Lesovik (lisovyk) is the Ukrainian variant of the East Slavic forest spirit, a wild old man who guards the woods and their animals. Like the Russian leshy he can change size, herd elk and deer, and lead the unwary in circles, but he also rewards those who treat the forest with respect, protecting hunters who follow his rules.

name: Leszy
description: Leszy (leszek) is the Polish forest guardian, a shape-shifting old man of the woods who herds animals, especially wolves, and plays tricks on those who stray. In Polish folk belief he can be propitiated with small gifts, and woodsmen recognize his territory before felling trees, treating the forest as a living domain with a master.

name: Let-Htau
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Burmese folklore; searches locate no water ghost called 'Let-Htau.' Myanmar's documented spirit world is the nat tradition, which includes river and water nats (such as Amay Yay Yin) and taw saung and taung saung nature guardians, but no figure bears this name, which appears to be a garbled conflation.

name: Letao
description: Letao is the trickster god of Marshallese mythology, a mischievous spirit of winds and ocean currents who delights in confounding navigators and bending the sea to his will. Grandson of the creator Lowa and brother of Jemeliwut, he reflects the ocean's volatility, and his pranks are countered only by the navigational knowledge of Marshallese wayfinding.

name: Leuk (Hare)
description: Leuk is the clever hare trickster of Wolof folklore from Senegal, the embodiment of intelligence triumphing over brute force.
