In countless Wolof tales, Leuk uses his wit, cunning, and patience to overcome larger, stronger adversaries — most often Bouki the Hyena, who is greedy, foolish, and easily tricked. The Leuk-Bouki cycle is the most famous body of Wolof folklore, with Leuk consistently outwitting his larger companion. Leuk represents the Wolof cultural value that intelligence and cleverness are more valuable than physical strength. The character became widely known through the literary works of Léopold Sédar Senghor ("La Belle Histoire de Leuk le Lièvre") and Birago Diop ("Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba"). Leuk is the Wolof equivalent of Anansi the Spider in Akan culture or Brer Rabbit in African American folklore

name: Leyak
description: Leyak (Unknown). is a spirit. Leyak is a malevolent spirit or witch in Balinese mythology. These supernatural beings can fly through the air, having the form of disembodied heads with entrails trailing beneath them, and are believ. Source: Balinese folklore; traditional beliefs

name: Lhamu
description: Lhamu are Tibetan-influenced shapeshifting spirits in Nepali Sherpa/Himalayan folklore. Appear as monks, travelers, or animals in mountain passes, testing or guiding travelers. Related to Himalayan 'lu' (naga) and 'dre' (spirit) classes. Sherpa traditions include mountain spirits (Lha, Lu) that shapeshift. Name 'Lhamu' (Tibetan: Lha-mo) suggests female protective spirit.

name: Libahunt
description: Libahunt (Estonia). is a werewolf. Estonian werewolf from souls of immoral individuals. Source: Estonian folklore; the libahunt is a werewolf created from immoral souls.

name: Libyan Desert Jinn
description: The desert jinn of Libya are wandering fire-born spirits of the Sahara who appear to travellers as guides and lead them astray. Their most famous haunt is Kaf Ajnoun, the Cave of the Jinn near Ghat, a haunted rock fortress where jinn gather, sometimes seen as an uncatchable deer. The Tuareg hold that jinn fear iron, so a blade is carried even to weddings.

name: Lidérc
description: Lidérc is a malevolent demonic spirit of Hungarian folklore, commanded by witches and appearing as a strange animal, a fiery will-o'-the-wisp, or a ball of light. It visits sleepers at night, bringing nightmares and oppression, a menace documented in witch-trial records studied by folklorist Éva Pócs, showing continuity between medieval and early modern belief.

name: Lieaibolmmái
description: Lieaibolmmái, the Alder Man, is the Sami god of hunting, archery, and the forest, his name drawn from the alder wood used for bows. He keeps the wild forest animals as his herds and grants or withholds luck in hunting; the bow goddess Juoksáhkká entrusted newborn boys to him so they would become skilled hunters. Offerings ensured success after reindeer, elk, and small game.

name: Ligaroo
description: The Ligaroo (also spelled Lougaroo) is the male counterpart of the Soucouyant in Grenadian folklore. Unlike the Soucouyant which is typically female, the Ligaroo is a man who has sold his soul to gain the ability to transform into animals — most commonly dogs, donkeys, and fowls — as well as inanimate objects like cakes. The legend has roots in French werewolf (loup-garou) mythology that blended with West African shapeshifting traditions brought by enslaved Africans. In Grenadian culture, the Ligaroo is believed to be a man who practices black magic and uses his transformation powers to torment others and cause mischief. He represents the dangers of making pacts with dark forces and the corrupting influence of power

name: Ligobubfanu
description: Ligobubfanu is the creator goddess in the mythology of Chuuk, Micronesia, and the wife of the god Anulap. She is one of the supreme deities responsible for creating the world and all life within it. As a female creator, Ligobubfanu represents the fertile, nurturing aspect of the cosmos. She created the islands of Micronesia by scattering earth across the ocean and caused the first plants to grow. She is also associated with the tides, the moon, and the reproductive cycles of marine life. With Anulap, she governs the affairs of gods and humans, and their temple was said to exist in the sky world. Her name is invoked in traditional prayers and rituals, particularly those related to childbirth, agriculture, and fishing

name: Lilith
description: Lilith is the great female demon of Jewish tradition, likely descended from a Mesopotamian night-spirit (Lilitu). In the Talmud she preys on men in sleep and threatens newborns; the Alphabet of Ben Sira makes her Adam's first wife, who refused to lie beneath him, fled Eden, and was replaced by Eve. Ever after, amulets and incantations guard infants from her.

name: Lindesnes-varulven
description: Lindesnes-varulven (the werewolf of Lindesnes) is a shapeshifting wolf-creature from the folklore of the Lindesnes region, the southernmost tip of Norway. Unlike the continental European werewolf tradition, the Lindesnes-varulv is more closely related to Norse concepts of hamskifte (shape-shifting) — a person who could transform into a wolf by putting on a wolf-skin belt or by being born under a specific configuration of stars. The Lindesnes werewolf was documented in the Norsk Folkeminnesamling's national sagnkart (legend map) project launched in 2018, which mapped folk legends across Norway's municipalities. The Lindesnes variant is notable for being one of the few documented werewolf traditions in southern Norway — most Norwegian werewolf/lycanthrope traditions come from the central and northern regions. The Lindesnes-varulv was said to haunt the heath and coastal areas around the Lindesnes lighthouse, preying on livestock and lone travelers

name: Lindorm
description: Lindormen is a giant serpentine dragon in Danish folklore, living under churches, in burial mounds, and in lakes. The most famous Danish Lindorm legend comes from Hvalsø Church in Sjælland, where a Lindorm once coiled itself around the entire church, preventing anyone from entering. The beast was defeated by a special bull raised on milk and hazelnuts — the bull charged and disemboweled the Lindorm in a ravine that is still called 'Tyvedskløften' (Bull's Gully). In Danish tradition, Lindormer are associated with curses — some legends tell of princes transformed into Lindormer (the 'King Lindorm' tale type ATU 433B), who can only be restored to human form by a princess brave enough to embrace the serpent. Unlike dragons, the Danish Lindorm has no wings and breathes poison rather than fire

name: Lindorm
description: Lindormen is a giant serpentine dragon in Danish folklore, living under churches, in burial mounds, and in lakes. The most famous Danish Lindorm legend comes from Hvalsø Church in Sjælland, where a Lindorm once coiled itself around the entire church, preventing anyone from entering. The beast was defeated by a special bull raised on milk and hazelnuts — the bull charged and disemboweled the Lindorm in a ravine that is still called 'Tyvedskløften' (Bull's Gully). In Danish tradition, Lindormer are associated with curses — some legends tell of princes transformed into Lindormer (the 'King Lindorm' tale type ATU 433B), who can only be restored to human form by a princess brave enough to embrace the serpent. Unlike dragons, the Danish Lindorm has no wings and breathes poison rather than fire In Denmark folklore, this figure is known among the Denmark people.

name: Lindorm
description: The Lindorm is a colossal, wingless serpent of the earth, often confused with dragons but possessing a distinct, more terrestrial nature. In Swedish folklore, it is a symbol of primal power and hidden danger, often dwelling in deep caves or beneath ancient mounds. Unlike the fire-breathing drakes, the Lindorm's power lies in its immense strength and its ability to influence the land around it, sometimes bringing blight or prosperity depending on its mood. It is often depicted as a guardian of lost treasures or forbidden knowledge, requiring extreme cunning to outsmart

name: Lindworm
description: The Lindworm (Old High German lintrache, Middle High German lintwurm, Old Norse linnormr) is a flightless serpentine dragon of Germanic and Norse folklore. In Swedish tradition, it is a limbless forest serpent with a mane or dorsal fins, spitting blinding milk, swallowing its tail to roll as a wheel.

name: Lindworm
description: The Lindworm is a serpentine dragon from Scandinavian mythology, a massive legless or two-legged reptile that guards treasures, haunts deep forests, and terrorizes rural communities. Unlike the winged dragons of southern Europe, the Lindworm crawls on its belly like a great snake, with iridescent scales and a venomous bite. In Swedish and Norwegian folklore, Lindworms often appear as cursed princes or princesses who can only be freed by a brave knight or a clever maiden. They are associated with ancient burial mounds and the wild, untamed spaces of the Nordic landscape, and stories of Lindworm encounters served as cautionary tales about venturing too deep into the forest

name: Lindworm (Lindorm)
description: The lindorm is a wingless, two-legged serpentine dragon of Germanic and Nordic folklore, dwelling in burial mounds, caves, and deep waters. It guards treasure and can speak. Legends tell of lindorms hatched from eggs laid by a woman or grown from a snake that drank milk. The hero typically kills it by thrusting a spear into its mouth. Attested in Danish and Swedish folktale collections.

name: Lindworm Denmark
description: Lindworm Denmark (Unknown). is a dragon. The Lindworm is a serpentine dragon from Scandinavian folklore, typically depicted as a wingless, legless creature (or with one or two legs). It features in Danish legends involving kings and heroic k. Source: Scandinavian folklore; Danish ballads

name: Lindwurm
description: The Lindwurm is the German variant of the Lindworm dragon, a great serpentine beast that haunts the forests, caves, and river valleys of the Germanic lands. In German folklore, Lindwurms are often depicted as guardians of ancient hoards or as the cursed forms of human beings punished for their sins. The city of Linz, Austria, takes its name from a Lindwurm legend in which a great dragon terrorized the Danube valley until slain by a brave knight. Lindwurms in German tradition tend to be more bestial than their Scandinavian counterparts, lacking the capacity for speech or bargains, and are instead forces of pure destruction that must be overcome through martial valor

name: Liongo Fumo
description: Liongo Fumo (also known as Fumo Liyongo) is the national hero of the Swahili people -- a legendary warrior, poet, and prince who lived on Pate Island (Lamu Archipelago) sometime between the 9th and 13th centuries. A giant of a man, nearly invulnerable except for his navel, a master archer whose bow no other man could draw, and a poet of such skill that his compositions survive as the oldest known Swahili literature. Though the rightful heir, his brother Mringwari usurped the throne, forcing Liongo into exile. He became a heroic outlaw, composing poems and songs still sung at weddings and gungu dances. His death came through betrayal -- his own son stabbed him in the navel with a copper needle. Mortally wounded, Liongo staggered to a well, dying upright with his bow in hand, so fearsome that none dared approach until his mother confirmed his passing

name: Lisa
description: Lisa is the Fon (Dahomey) god of the sun, daytime, heat, strength, and civilization. He is the male counterpart and twin of Mawu, the moon goddess, together forming the dual deity Mawu-Lisa. While Mawu is "cool" (gentle, forgiving, lunar), Lisa is "hot" (fierce, punitive, solar). After Mawu created the earth and retired, she sent Lisa to bring civilization to humanity — teaching them to make tools, clear forests, farm, and live in organized society. Lisa is associated with the chameleon as his messenger and symbol. He represents the active, creative principle of the universe. His priests wear white and his rites involve fire and heat. The name Lisa among the Fon likely derives from the Yoruba "orisha" (lesser deity), and Lisa is considered analogous to the Yoruba Obatala

name: Listasanddjevelen
description: Not independently attested in Norwegian folklore. No scholarly or primary source documents a sand-devil spirit of Lista; the figure appears in a recent Wikipedia article built from real dune-burial history with an invented whirling-sand spirit.

name: Little Black Ants
description: In the Isleta Pueblo tale collected by Charles F. Lummis, the Little Black Ant is a small but heroic helper who assists Kahp-too-óo-yoo (Corn-stalk Young Man), even taking on the sky itself. Though tiny, the ant's diligence and courage save the young man from his enemies, showing that even the smallest creatures can accomplish great deeds.

name: Little Giver
description: Little Giver, also called Fastachee, is the corn spirit of the Miccosukee and Seminole, who usually appeared as a small dwarf and gave the people the gift of corn and of medicine. He was thereafter always honored at the harvest, and the Green Corn Ceremony recalls his generosity.

name: Little People (Cherokee)
description: The Little People (Yûñwï Tsunsdi', 'the Little Folk') of Cherokee tradition are small spirit beings who live in rock shelters and caves in the forests and mountains. They help lost children, teach medicine and song, and punish those who disrespect nature; speaking of an encounter with them is said to bring misfortune, and they can grant good luck or play mischievous tricks.

name: Little People (Cherokee)
description: Not attested as a being of Canadian folklore. The Cherokee Little People (Yûñwï Tsunsdi') belong to the Cherokee of the southeastern United States, whose homeland is the Southern Appalachians, not Canada. This record duplicates littlepeoplecherokee-usa with a mistaken country field; Canada's own traditions feature distinct little-folk such as the Anishinaabe little people.

name: Lizard
description: In Northern Miwok tradition, Lizard (Pe-tā'-le) is a transformer and culture figure who appears in the origin tales of the Sierra; the record's generic 'forest spirit' framing is unsupported. Across California and Southwestern traditions, lizards figure as clever spirit-beings who survive trials and aid humans, and in some tellings Lizard takes part in the theft of fire.

name: Lizard Deity (Tibetan)
description: Not independently attested as a distinct figure of Tibetan folklore. No source documents a named lizard deity guarding treasures and sacred knowledge in Tibet's rivers and lakes. The recorded traits match no specific deity; Tibetan water and underground spirits are the serpentine 'klu' (nāga-like beings), not lizards. The entry appears to derive from conflation or modern invention.

name: Lizard Deity (Tibetan)
description: Not independently attested in Ethiopian tradition. The 'Lizard Deity (Tibetan)' is a Tibetan Buddhist protector (e.g., lizard-headed deity guarding hidden treasures in Dzogchen terma) misassigned to Ethiopia. Ethiopia's traditions include Atete (Oromo fertility goddess), Waaqa (supreme deity), zar spirits—no Tibetan lizard deity.

name: Lizard Spirit (Bhutanese)
description: Not independently attested as a named 'Lizard Spirit' in Bhutanese texts. Bhutanese folklore includes lizard/deity associations (lu/khu spirits in rocks, trees), but no specific 'Lizard Spirit'. The 'protector of the savannas' claim is erroneous — Bhutan has no savannas (Himalayan mountains/forests). Likely a fabricated entry conflating generic nature spirits with incorrect habitat.

name: Ljungrå
description: The Ljungrå is a specialized forest spirit inhabiting the vast, purple heather-moors (ljunghedar) of Sweden. She is a variant of the Skogsrå but more attuned to the open landscapes than the dense pines. The Ljungrå is known for her melancholic nature and her tendency to lead travelers astray by mimicking the voices of loved ones. She is the protector of the heather and the small creatures that dwell within it, and she is known to be fiercely protective of the moorland's silence, punishing those who bring noise and chaos into her domain

name: Loa
description: Lowa (Loa) is the creator of Marshallese tradition who dwelt alone in the primeval sea, who raised the reefs and sandbanks of the atolls from the water and made the birds and plants. Wulleb and Limdunanji, the first people, emerged from a tumor on his leg, and he set gods at the cardinal points to govern the winds. He is the grandfather of the trickster Letao.

name: Lobisomem
description: The lobisomem is the Portuguese werewolf, a person cursed to run out a fado (spell) at night as an animal — in the north a horse, in the south a donkey, dog, or pig. Seventh consecutive sons, children of incest, and the unbaptized were destined for the curse, broken only by drawing the werewolf's blood with steel. The belief is documented in Portugal and carried to Brazil.

name: Lobisón
description: The lobisón is the werewolf of Galician folklore, the regional form of the Iberian lobishome. Its most famous association is Manuel Blanco Romasanta, a nineteenth-century Galician serial killer tried in 1853, who claimed he transformed into a wolf under a curse — a plea that entered Spanish legal and folkloric history. The legend encodes the fear of the man-beast in rural Galicia.

name: Lobizon
description: Lobizon (Unknown). is a werewolf. The Lobizón is a werewolf-like creature from Argentine and Latin American folklore. According to legend, the seventh son born in a family will become a Lobizón, transforming into a wolf-like beast dur. Source: Latin American folklore; Argentine legal tradition

name: Lofa
description: Lofa is a malevolent, ogre-like monster of Chickasaw folklore whose name means 'flayer' or 'skinner,' from his habit of flaying his victims. He appears sometimes as a giant and sometimes as a large, hairy, foul-smelling man; his stench is so overwhelming that it defeats even stronger fighters, and in some tales he abducts women.

name: Lohiau
description: Lohiau was a handsome chief of Kauai loved by the volcano goddess Pele. When Pele saw Lohiau in a dream, she fell deeply in love. She sent her sister Hi'iaka to retrieve him. By the time Hi'iaka arrived, Lohiau had died of grief and heartbreak over Pele's absence. Hi'iaka spent thirty days chanting over his bones, successfully reviving him. The jealous Pele, suspicious of Hi'iaka's long absence, destroyed Hi'iaka's lehua groves, prompting Hi'iaka to embrace Lohiau defiantly at Kilauea's crater. Pele consumed them with flames, but Hi'iaka revived Lohiau once more. Lohiau ultimately returned with Hi'iaka to Kauai to rule as chief

name: Long
description: Long (龍) is the Chinese dragon: a benevolent rain-bringer with a long serpentine body, antlers, four legs, and the power to fly without wings while controlling water, clouds, and weather. It dwells in rivers, lakes, seas, and sky, symbolizing imperial power, yang energy, and good fortune. Dragon dances, dragon-boat races, and rain prayers honor it.

name: Long-Ears
description: Long-Ears is a monster of Seminole tradition, a four-footed, wolf-headed creature the size of a donkey with long, pointed ears and an insatiable hunger. It hunts people in the swamps and forests of Florida, and its great speed, cunning, and tracking ability make it one of the most feared beings in Seminole legend.

name: Lono
description: The Hawaiian god of agriculture, peace, fertility, rain, and music. Lono is one of the four great gods of Hawaiian religion. He is associated with the Makahiki festival, a four-month harvest season dedicated to him when war was forbidden. Lono brings rain to nourish the crops and represents the peaceful, generative forces of nature. His symbol is the mahiole (feathered helmet) and the pulo'ulo'u (a staff topped with woven fiber). During the Makahiki, an image of Lono was carried around the islands collecting tribute. Lono is also associated with the story of Kamapua'a, the pig demigod, who represents Lono's fertilizing and reproductive powers

name: Loogaroo
description: Loogaroo (Lougarou, Ligaroo, Lagahoo) is a Caribbean skin-shedding vampire derived from French 'loup-garou' (werewolf). By day a reclusive woman; by night she sheds her skin (hidden under a silk cotton tree), becomes a fireball, and flies to suck blood to fulfill a pact with the Devil (Bazil). Salt in the mortar destroys her.

name: Loon (Creation Bird)
description: The loon, also called the golden or diving bird, is the creation bird of Altai mythology, small but infinitely courageous, diving into the infinite primordial ocean and risking its life to bring up the mud from which the earth is made. Central to the Altai creation account, the diving-bird motif connects Altaian tradition to the broader family of Siberian and circumpolar earth-diver cosmogonies.

name: Lord of the Gobi
description: The Lord of the Gobi is a desert spirit of southern Mongolia, described as a towering figure of sand and wind, sometimes a dust devil, that can also appear as an old man or a shimmering form in the heat haze. It tests desert travelers for hospitality and worthiness, rewarding the kind with safe passage and hidden water, punishing the cruel, embodying the harsh but just nature of the Gobi.

name: Lorelei
description: The Lorelei is a siren figure of the Rhine Gorge, originating from the 132-meter slate rock at Sankt Goarshausen whose murmuring currents and echo inspired legends. Clemens Brentano (1801) created the tragic Lore Lay, betrayed by her lover, who falls from the rock. Heinrich Heine (1824) transformed her into a golden-haired siren whose song unwittingly lures boatmen to crash.

name: Los Ahuiillas
description: Los Ahuiillas (or Ahuillas) are Peruvian Andean road spirits: ghosts of murdered travelers who appear at night near abandoned houses and mountain paths. They warn or terrify passersby, reflecting colonial-era dangers on highland routes. Documented in central/southern Peru oral tradition.

name: Los Chamos
description: Not independently attested as a folkloric goblin. 'Los Chamos' is a famous 1980s Venezuelan boy band; 'chamo' is Venezuelan slang for 'kid/guy.' The goblin description appears to be a folk-etymology invention punning on the slang term. No Venezuelan ethnography records household goblins by this name.

name: Lost Little Ones (transformed children)
description: The Lost Little Ones are the Zuni children who, crossing the sacred river in the care of the Beloved Twins, fell into the water and were transformed into frogs, lizards, turtles, and newts. In their new forms they learned the Dance of Good (Kókokshi) from the god-priests of Kóthluwalawan, becoming the kachina spirits who return to the village.

name: Lotan
description: Lotan is a seven-headed sea serpent from Canaanite-Phoenician mythology, serving as the servant and animal manifestation of the sea god Yamm. He is one of the most directly identifiable mythical creatures to have survived from ancient Near Eastern mythology into the Hebrew Bible, where he appears as Leviathan. The name Lotan is linguistically identical to the Hebrew Leviathan. In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle, the god Mot taunts Baal: 'When you killed Lotan the fleeing serpent, finished off the twisting serpent, the tyrant with seven heads, the heavens grew weak and drooped.' The Litani River in Lebanon is named after Lotan, believed to be the personification of the coiled serpent god

name: Lotan
description: Lotan is a serpent from Canaanite mythology. He is one of the most directly identifiable mythical creatures to have survived from ancient Near Eastern mythology into the Hebrew Bible, where he appears as Leviathan. The name Lotan is linguistically identical to the Hebrew Leviathan. In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle, the god Mot taunts Baal: 'When you killed Lotan the fleeing serpent, finished off the twisting serpent, the tyrant with seven heads, the heavens grew weak and drooped.' The Litani River in Lebanon is named after Lotan, believed to be the personification of the coiled serpent god

name: Lotan
description: Lotan is a serpent from Canaanite / Ugaritic mythology. He is one of the most directly identifiable mythical creatures to have survived from ancient Near Eastern mythology into the Hebrew Bible, where he appears as Leviathan. The name Lotan is linguistically identical to the Hebrew Leviathan. In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle, the god Mot taunts Baal: 'When you killed Lotan the fleeing serpent, finished off the twisting serpent, the tyrant with seven heads, the heavens grew weak and drooped.' The Litani River in Lebanon is named after Lotan, believed to be the personification of the coiled serpent god

name: Lougarou
description: The Lougarou is a notorious figure in Mauritian folklore, essentially a werewolf that blends French and African mythological influences. It is a human who has the ability to transform into a beast, typically appearing during the full moon. The Lougarou is used as a cautionary figure to scare children into behaving and staying indoors at night. It is believed that the Lougarou brings trouble and chaos to the local population, and the only way to protect oneself is to consult a local sorcerer or witch doctor

name: Lougawou
description: Lougawou is the Haitian Vodou werewolf/shapeshifter. By night, a practitioner (usually female) sends out her soul or transforms into animals (dog, cat, bird) to attack enemies or drain blood. Distinct from the fireball Loogaroo; lougawou emphasizes animal transformation via Vodou ritual. Related to Dominican Galipote (shapeshifter of animals and objects). Feared as a nocturnal predator.

name: Louhi
description: Louhi is the powerful mistress of Pohjola in the Kalevala, a sorceress who steals the Sun, Moon, and Fire, and commissions the forging of the Sampo. She battles Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen, and Lemminkäinen, transforming into a giant eagle in the final pursuit. Lönnrot compiled her from Karelian runic songs where she appears as a shamanic antagonist.

name: Loulou
description: Not independently attested as a Seychellois spirit. 'Loulou' is a French hypocorism and disambiguation term for people (Enver Hoxha, Louise de Vilmorin, Loulou de la Falaise), a 1980 film, a magazine, a children's book. The claim—deriving from Malagasy lolo (spirit) rationalised as le loup (wolf)—has no basis in Seychellois/Malagasy ethnography.

name: Loup-garou
description: In folklore, a werewolf, or occasionally lycanthrope, is an individual who can shapeshift into a wolf or therianthropic hybrid wolf–humanlike creature, either voluntarily or involuntarily due to a curse or other affliction. In modern fiction, especially film, transformations are often depicted as triggered by the full moon and transmitted by a bite or scratch from another werewolf. Early sources for belief in this ability or affliction, called lycanthropy, are Petronius (27–66) and Gervase of Tilbury (1150–1228)

name: Loupo
description: The loupo is the werewolf of Occitan and Alpine French tradition, a loup-garou variant recorded in Savoie and Dauphiné, where belief in human-wolf metamorphosis was widespread. Local accounts describe men who changed shape under a curse and roamed the mountains at night, illustrating pre-Christian shapeshifting belief in southern France, distinct from the northern loup-garou.

name: Lugat
description: Lugat is the vampire of Albanian folklore, an undead blood-drinker that abides in shadows, wells, old ruins, and caves. It flies on the winds, frightens with its visage, and assails victims in their sleep, draining their blood; it can shapeshift and is warded off with salt. The belief reflects anxieties about death, burial, and nocturnal harm shared across Balkan vampire traditions.

name: Luison
description: Luison (Luisõ) is the seventh and most accursed son of Tau and Kerana in Guarani mythology (Paraguay, Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia). A giant dog or werewolf-like being, he haunts cemeteries and burial grounds. The seventh son of a human family is believed destined to become Luison; Argentine presidents historically served as godfathers to seventh sons to avert the curse.

name: Lulik Spirits
description: Lulik is a fundamental spiritual concept in East Timorese cosmology, referring to a potent sacred force that animates the environment and concentrates in specific sites, objects, and persons. Lulik spirits inhabit sacred mountains (foho lulik), waters (bee lulik), lands (rai lulik), and are housed in sacred houses (uma lulik). This animating potency is not inherently good or evil but is transgressive and dangerous. It sustains life yet requires strict prohibitions and rituals to be approached safely. Lulik is similar to the Melanesian concept of mana combined with tapu restrictions

name: Luna
description: Luna is a Walloon (Belgian) lunar spirit — a woman who walks the countryside at full moon, granting blessings and curses. She reflects the moon's sway over human behavior (lunacy). The name comes from Latin luna; the concept echoes Romance/Celtic lunar lore in Wallonia. Not a forest spirit — the input's archetype is wrong. She is a nocturnal wanderer of moonlight and rural paths.

name: Lunar (or L'Ankou)
description: L'Ankou is the Breton/Cornish/Welsh personification of death — a tall, thin man in a black coat and wide-brimmed hat driving a creaking cart (karrig an Ankou) to collect souls. The last person to die in a parish each year becomes the next Ankou. The Walloon (Belgian) variant 'Lunar' reflects Celtic influence in the region. Not a water spirit — the input's archetype is wrong.

name: Lungu (The Great Snake)
description: Lungu is a great mythical snake in Zambian folklore, especially among the Bemba, believed to dwell in the underworld and to command rain, rivers and fertility. Rituals are performed to appease it for rain and good harvests in a region where drought is a constant threat, tying the myth to the community's dependence on water.

name: Lunja
description: Lunja (also Loundja) is a central female figure in Kabyle (Algerian Amazigh) mythology, the beautiful daughter of the ogress Teryel. In traditional tellings, Lunja is described as a maiden of extraordinary beauty — white skin, olive-shaped eyes, long black shining hair — who lives as a captive in her mother's cave. Initially portrayed as passive and silent, scholarly re-examination (particularly from feminist perspectives) has revealed Lunja as a complex trickster figure who uses silence, clever speech, and strategic submission to navigate her mother's tyranny and ultimately achieve freedom. In one famous episode, she tricks the river spirit into letting her cross by claiming Teryel is chasing her. When heroes come to rescue her, she negotiates terms that benefit her while maintaining the appearance of obedience. Lunja represents the Kabyle woman's strategies of survival and resistance within a patriarchal structure — using wit, indirection, and performed submission as tools of liberation. She is sometimes compared to the Greek Psyche figure and appears in tales across Algeria and the wider Maghreb

name: Lupo Mannaro
description: Il lupo mannaro is the Italian werewolf, a person cursed or voluntarily transformed into a wolf to hunt humans, attested since antiquity as lupus hominarius and versipellis ('skin-changer'). Folk tradition distinguished induced, voluntary, and spontaneous lycanthropy, with regional names like lupo menaro and lupunaru. In Basilicata, children born on Christmas night were said to become wolves.

name: Lusca
description: Lusca is the Bahamian sea monster of Andros Island's blue holes. Described as a gigantic octopus, cuttlefish, or half-shark half-octopus hybrid over 75 feet long. Name clipped from Mollusca. Drags swimmers and boats into blue holes. Investigated by Jeremy Wade (River Monsters) as likely a large octopus. Cautionary tale for blue hole divers. Inspired Lusca Fantastic Film Fest (Puerto Rico).

name: Lussi
description: Lussi is a female demon-like figure in Norwegian folklore active on Lussinatten (St. Lucy's Night, December 13), one of the shortest days of the year in the old Julian calendar. On this night, Lussi rides through the air with a host of spirits and demons, punishing anyone who dared to work after dark. All spinning wheels and looms had to be still. Anyone caught working risked being swept up by Lussi's procession or having their work ruined. In Vestlandet, the Lussinatten tradition was particularly strong — no mill could operate, no wool could be spun, and no bread could be baked after sunset. Lussi also punished children who misbehaved. The tradition merged with St. Lucy's Day (Santa Lucia) celebrations after Christianization, but Lussi herself remained a feared figure in rural folklore centuries after. The night was considered extremely dangerous — even animals could speak on Lussinatten, though hearing them meant death for the listener

name: Luus
description: Luus are water-serpent guardians of Mongolian folklore, with iridescent scales, sometimes horns or wings, guarding lakes, rivers, and sacred springs. Benevolent if respected, malevolent if their waters are polluted, they govern the land's fertility. The complex spans Luz/Lusad, terrestrial and subterranean water-spirits, and Luu, heavenly dragon helpers in ritual tradition.

name: Luus Spirits
description: Luus are the dragon-like water spirits of Buryat tradition, serpentine beings with water-shimmering scales, deer-like horns, and glowing green eyes, sometimes appearing as whirlpools or mist. Territorial and mercurial, they may be generous with fish or wrathful with storms, and must be approached with proper ritual. Their veneration reflects the importance of Lake Baikal and its watershed.

name: Luz Mala Gaucha
description: Luz Mala ('evil light') is the Argentine/Uruguayan gaucho name for the will-o'-the-wisp (ignis fatuus): a floating corpse-fire seen over rural plains at night, omen of death or buried treasure. The 'gaucha' variant emphasizes its pampas context. Feared by rural travelers; said to mark where the unbaptized or murdered lie.

name: Lygtemand
description: Lygtemanden (the Lantern Man) is the Danish version of the will-o'-the-wisp — a small being carrying a blue gas-flame lantern that lures travelers into bogs and marshes. According to Danish tradition, the Lygtemand is the ghost of a dishonest land surveyor who moved boundary markers, condemned to wander until all false boundaries are corrected. At Skovby on Falster, the Lygtemand is said to be the spirit of a man who cheated his neighbors on land measurements. At Julstrup near Aalborg, one was seen sitting on a hay wagon, offering to guide travelers home with its lantern, then leading them into the bog instead. The Lygtemand can split into multiple lights, making it impossible to tell which direction is safe. Protection: turning your clothes inside out or carrying a piece of steel

name: Lyktemann
description: Lyktemann (lantern-man), also known as lyktgubbe, is a will-o'-the-wisp ghost light in Norwegian folklore particularly associated with the marshlands and coastal bogs of Vestlandet. The lyktemann appears as a small, dancing light that leads travelers astray into dangerous marshes, bogs, or cliffs. Following the light means certain death — the victim either drowns in a bog or falls from a cliff. The light could not be caught or approached — it always stayed just ahead. In some traditions, the lyktemann is the ghost of a sinful person condemned to wander with a lantern for eternity. Regional variations: in Hordaland it is called lyktemann, in Sogn it is vettelys (spirit light). Some fishermen along the Vestlandet coast believed the lyktemann was a warning of death at sea — seeing one near the shore meant a family member would drown

name: Lyktgubbe
description: Lyktgubben (lantern man) is the Swedish version of the will-o'-the-wisp — a ghostly figure carrying a lantern that lures travelers astray in marshes and forests. In Swedish tradition, the Lyktgubbe is most often the spirit of a dishonest land surveyor who moved boundary markers during his life. As punishment, he is condemned to wander with his lantern forever, endlessly reciting 'this is right, this is wrong' while trying to find the true boundaries. He lures travelers into bogs and marshes by mimicking a friendly light, then vanishes, leaving them lost. However, if addressed politely and asked for help, he will guide the traveler safely home. The Lyktgubbe can be freed from his curse if someone corrects the false boundary markers he obsesses over

name: Lyngbakr
description: Lyngbakr (Heather-Back) is the largest whale in Icelandic folklore, so massive that its back looks like a heather-covered island covered in soil, grass, and small trees. Sailors would land on what they thought was an island only to discover they had landed on Lyngbakr's back. When the whale submerged, the sailors would drown. Lyngbakr appears in Örvar-Odds saga and the Navigatio Sancti Brendani (Saint Brendan's Voyage). The name comes from lyng (heather) and bak (back). According to the legend, Lyngbakr is the second-largest sea creature after only Hafgufa. It feeds only once every three years, opening its enormous mouth to engulf everything in its path. Lyngbakr was believed to live until Ragnarök. The legend likely originated from sightings of whale backs or floating debris fields mistaken for islands

name: Lá
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Vietnamese folklore; 'Lá' is the Vietnamese word for leaf. The recorded mischievous plant spirit of forests and paddies matches the animist veneration of trees and plants found in Vietnamese village religion and upland traditions, but no documented entity named 'Lá' exists.

name: Lạc Long Quân
description: Lạc Long Quân, the 'Dragon Lord of Lac,' is the divine ancestor of the Vietnamese people in the national foundation myth recorded in the Lĩnh Nam chích quái. A dragon prince of the sea, he wed the fairy Âu Cơ, who bore a hundred sons: half followed him to the waters, while half followed their mother into the mountains and became the Hùng Kings.

name: Lạc Long Quân (Dragon Lord of Lạc)
description: Lạc Long Quân (literally 'Dragon Lord of Lạc') is the legendary dragon king and founding ancestor of the Vietnamese people. Son of Kinh Dương Vương and the sea goddess Long Nữ, he ruled the Lạc Việt people along the rivers and coast of what is now northern Vietnam. He taught the Lạc Việt to cultivate wet rice, cook food, and tattoo their bodies with sea-dragon designs so ocean creatures would recognize them. He married the mountain fairy Âu Cơ, and from their union came an egg sac that hatched one hundred children — the ancestors of the Vietnamese nation. As a being of water and sea, he eventually separated from Âu Cơ (a being of the mountains), taking fifty children to the coast while she took fifty to the highlands. Their eldest son became the first Hùng King, founding the Hồng Bàng dynasty. Lạc Long Quân is revered as the father of Vietnamese civilization

name: Ma Dray
description: Not independently attested as a named ghost of Vietnamese folklore; searches locate no spirit called 'Ma Dray.' 'Ma' is the generic Vietnamese word for ghost, and the described wronged-woman revenant fits the widespread female revenge-ghost motif of Vietnamese, Chinese, and Japanese tradition rather than a distinct entity.

name: Ma Sue
description: Mae Sue, Thai แม่ซื้อ ('Mother Buyer'), is a benevolent spirit of Thai animist belief who guards newborn babies. The name reflects a ritual in which the child's soul is symbolically bought back from a wandering spirit to anchor it in the body. Figures and offerings are placed by the cradle until a naming ceremony ends her watch.

name: Ma'heo'o
description: Ma'heo'o (also Maheo, Heammawihio) is the Creator and supreme being in Cheyenne religion, meaning 'sacred power' or 'Great Mystery.' Also known as Heammawihio ('Spider Above'), Ma'heo'o is a divine spirit without human form or attributes. According to Cheyenne creation, Ma'heo'o existed before all things and created the world from mud brought by a waterbird (coot), then formed the earth on a turtle's back. He created plants, animals, and humans, and gave the sacred ceremonies through Sweet Medicine and Erect Horns. He is rarely personified in folklore and represents the ultimate sacred power

name: Ma'i
description: Ma'i is the Samoan spirit of sickness and epidemic: in traditional belief, illness is often inflicted by aitu spirits or by sorcery, and the ma'i is the disease-spirit itself. Such afflictions are understood to punish social or ritual transgression and to be relieved through appeasement, ritual, and the intervention of specialists, linking health to moral and spiritual order.

name: Maadai-Kara
description: Maadai-Kara is the eponymous elder hero of one of the greatest Altai heroic epics, a poem of 7,738 verses, shown in warrior clothing on an argamak winged horse. When Maadai-Kara and his wife are carried off to the underworld by Erlik, their son Kögüdei Mergen, the Heavenly Archer, journeys through all three cosmic worlds to rescue them. The epic was preserved by bard Elbek Kalkin.

name: Maboyo
description: Maboya is the feared evil spirit of the Island Carib (Kalinago), attested since the 1765 Encyclopédie, where Le Romain records that the Caribs of the Antilles dreaded its malign will and carved small grotesque figurines of wood, clay or resin, placed in canoes and huts. The word also came to mean 'evil' generally, and the boyez priest ritually warded the spirit away.

name: Machik Lapdron
description: Machik Lapdron (1055–1153) is the great Tibetan yogini and founder of the Chöd tradition, pictured as a peaceful woman with a slight smile, holding the drum (damaru) and bell, implements of the Chöd practice she founded. Fearless and compassionate, she taught cutting attachment to the self, transforming demonic forces through wisdom, not confrontation. Her Chöd lineage remains a living practice.

name: Mad Computer
description: Not independently attested in any folklore tradition. 'Mad Computer' is a modern internet urban legend/creepypasta — a supposedly supernatural AI haunting outdated systems, causing crashes and whispering in binary. It originates from late-20th/early-21st century digital folklore, not traditional oral tradition.

name: Madremonte
description: Madremonte (Madre Monte, 'Mother of the Mountain') is a Colombian nature spirit protecting wilderness, especially in Andean and Pacific regions. Punishes deforestation, pollution, and harm to nature. Appears as a large woman covered in moss and leaves, with glowing eyes. Blend of Muisca earth goddess traditions and Spanish Catholic influences (Virgin Mary syncretism).

name: Mae Nak Phra Khanong
description: Mae Nak Phra Khanong is the most famous ghost in Thai folklore: a young wife who died in childbirth in Bangkok's Phra Khanong district and returned to keep house for her unwitting husband. Her story of enduring love, loyalty, and tragic revelation has been retold in dozens of films, plays, and novels, and her shrine at Wat Mahabut still draws devotees.

name: Mae Phosop (Rice Goddess)
description: Mae Phosop (Lao: ແມ່ໂພສົບ, Thai: แม่โพสพ, 'Mother of the Rice Kernel') is the ancient rice goddess revered in Lao, Thai, and Isan agricultural traditions. According to legend, she was a beautiful celestial maiden who descended to earth to become the spirit of rice — the essence that sustains all life. In primordial times, rice grew as large as pumpkins and flew directly into granaries by itself. However, a careless woman struck a rice kernel with her broom in anger, and the offended rice spirit withdrew into hiding, causing famine. The people had to perform elaborate ceremonies to call Mae Phosop back. Today, before planting, farmers perform the 'Rice Mother Calling' ritual (riak khwan khao), offering bananas, sugarcane, and flowers. At harvest, the most beautiful rice stalks are selected and dressed in silk as an offering. Mae Phosop teaches that rice is a living spiritual entity deserving of gratitude and respect — an animist belief that coexists with Theravada Buddhism throughout the Lao world

name: Mae Yanang (Boat Guardian Spirit)
description: Mae Yanang (Thai: แม่ย่านาง) is a revered female guardian spirit who protects boats, vehicles, and travelers in Thai, Lao, and Khmer folk religion. She is believed to reside in the prow of every wooden boat, especially those made from Takhian wood (Hopea odorata), which was thought to house benevolent tree spirits. Fishermen and sailors perform elaborate ceremonies before voyages, offering flowers, incense, tricolor cloth, and food to invoke her protection. The prow of a boat decorated with colored sashes and garlands signals her presence. In modern times, belief in Mae Yanang has expanded to include cars, motorcycles, and even airplanes, with drivers offering garlands and incense at dashboards. Her worship derives from ancient matrifocal animist traditions and shares origins with Mae Phosop and Nang Kwak. She is distinctively propitiated at traffic lights throughout Thailand where vendors sell floral garlands to drivers

name: Maganda (The First Woman)
description: In the Tagalog creation myth, Maganda (Beautiful) is the first woman, who together with Malakas (Strong), emerged from a split bamboo stalk. According to the ancient belief, a great bird pecked open a bamboo tube, revealing the first human pair. Maganda represents beauty, grace, and the nurturing spirit of womanhood. She and Malakas became the primordial parents of the Filipino race, teaching their children how to farm, fish, build homes, and honor the spirits of nature. The name Maganda itself means 'beautiful' in Tagalog, reflecting the ideal of inner and outer beauty in Filipino culture

name: Maghwi
description: The Maghwi is a jinn of the night of Gulf and Yemeni coastal folklore. It mimics the voices of friends and loved ones, spies on fishermen before dawn, and lures them into darkness to drown them; it also calls date-palm keepers (nakhlawis) from their companions, the sight of it stopping their hearts. Villagers held no dark night safe until electric lights pushed it back from human settlement.

name: Magic Book Denmark
description: Magic Book Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. The Magic Book is a device from Danish folklore, a tome that reveals knowledge with dangerous consequences.. Source: Danish folklore — spellbook/magic documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Magic Tinderbox Denmark
description: Magic Tinderbox Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. The magic tinderbox summons three giant dogs who grant wishes in Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale.. Source: Danish folklore — magic objects from Hans Christian Andersen and Danish tradition.

name: Magic Trunk Denmark
description: Magic Trunk Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. The Flying Trunk is from Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale, a magical trunk that carries a hero through the air.. Source: Danish folklore — magic objects documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Magical Bird
description: Refers to Grip, the magical talking bird from the Danish literary fairy tale 'The Bird Grip' (Fuglen Grip), collected by Svend Grundtvig and E.T. Kristensen. Grip aids the hero with guidance and warnings. While talking birds appear in Nordic oral tales (e.g., the raven in Icelandic legends), Grip is specifically a literary fairy-tale figure, not a folkloric being with independent tradition.

name: Magical Boy Nuxalk
description: The Magical Boy is the young hero of a Bella Coola (Nuxalk) legend, a child of humble birth who, aided by spirit power, confronts a man-eating monster that has terrorized the people. Where strength fails, his courage and cleverness prevail, and the tale stands as a hero-child story of the Nuxalk.

name: Magician
description: Magician (Unknown). is a human. The Magician is a figure from Western folklore and mythology, representing practitioners of magic who appear across countless tales from the wizard Merlin of Arthurian legend to the cunning folk of vi. Source: European folklore traditions

name: Magpie
description: The magpie (skata) is a bird of Swedish folk belief, regarded as an omen of sorrow or news: its chatter ('skata skriker') and thieving habits were read as signs, and it features in the tale 'The Magpie with Salt on Her Tail' as a clever bird. While not a supernatural being in its own right, it carries genuine omen beliefs in Nordic tradition.

name: Maha Sohona
description: Maha Sohona (Great Cemetery Demon) is a major demon in Sinhala Sri Lankan folklore, king of the Sanni Yakku (disease demons). He dwells in cremation grounds, devours corpses, and spreads plagues. Described as terrifying with red eyes, fangs, and a corpse-strewn form. Can be propitiated by rituals (thovil) but is ruthless. Documented by Wirz, Obeyesekere, and in Kandyan period texts.

name: Maha Sona
description: Maha Sona (the Great Cemetery God) is a fearsome deity in Sri Lankan folklore, a guardian of cemeteries and a spirit associated with death. He appears in ritual exorcism traditions known as tovil

name: Mahagiri Nat (Great Mountain Spirit)
description: Mahagiri Nat (Burmese: မဟာဂီရိနတ်, 'Great Mountain Spirit') is one of the most powerful nats in the Burmese pantheon, the guardian of homes and protector against fires. According to legend, he was originally a mighty blacksmith named Nga Tin De (or Nga Tin Te) who forged weapons of unparalleled quality in the village of Taungbyon. King Thinligyawng of Tagaung, fearing the blacksmith's power, summoned him to the capital and had him burned alive inside a champaca tree. Nga Tin De's sister threw herself into the flames to die beside him, and their spirits were trapped in the tree, terrorizing the region. When King Anawrahta cut down the tree, he ordered the spirits carved into statues and enshrined — the male spirit became Mahagiri Nat, installed at the gates of Pagan's royal palace, while the female became Popa Medaw on Mount Popa. Mahagiri Nat is now the guardian spirit of all Burmese homes, traditionally enshrined at the southeast corner of the house compound

name: Mahaha
description: The Mahaha is a thin, pale-blue demon of Arctic Inuit folklore that hunts solitary people on the ice. It sneaks up on victims and tickles them with long, sharp fingernails until they die of suffocation, leaving their faces frozen in a permanent smile. It captures the dread of isolation and of sudden, absurd death in the winter night.

name: Mahapbi (or Mae Phra Borneo)
description: Not independently attested in documented Bornean folklore; no source names a figure 'Mahapbi' or 'Mae Phra.' The described floating head that trails organs and preys on pregnant women and children is the classic penanggalan–krasue complex of the Malay world, well attested across Malaysia, Sumatra, and Indonesia but not under this name.

name: Mahogany Tree
description: The Mahogany Tree in Antiguan folklore is a sacred tree believed to be the dwelling of protective ancestral spirits. A powerful chief sacrificed himself, transforming into the tree to guard his people. Symbolizes strength, endurance, and protection. Reflects West African tree-spirit beliefs (e.g., Iroko, Silk Cotton) transplanted to the Caribbean.

name: Maiden Of The Rainbow Finland
description: Maiden Of The Rainbow Finland (Unknown). is a human. The Maiden of the Rainbow is a celestial spirit from Finnish folklore associated with the rainbow bridge.. Source: Finnish folklore — maiden figure documented in Finnish oral tradition.

name: Maka
description: Maka is the Earth goddess of Lakota tradition, created from the blood of Inyan, the primordial rock spirit, who sacrificed himself so that she might exist. She is the feminine principle of stability, fertility, and nurture, mother of all life upon her body; when she tried to part from Inyan, the judge Skan bound her to the rocks, which is why rock and soil remain joined.

name: Makara
description: Makara is the legendary aquatic hybrid of Hindu/Buddhist myth — crocodile forequarters, elephant trunk, fish tail, peacock feathers. Mount (vahana) of Ganga and Varuna; guardian of temple thresholds (torana). Appears from 2nd c. BCE (Besnagar pillar) across South/Southeast Asia. Zodiac sign Capricorn. Not specifically 'Bangladeshi' — pan-South Asian.

name: Makemake
description: The supreme creator god of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) mythology. Makemake shaped the world, created the birds, fish, and people, then withdrew to watch over them from the heavens. He is the chief deity of the Tangata Manu (Birdman) cult, which centered at the ceremonial village of Orongo. According to tradition, Makemake gave the Rapa Nui people the Manutara (sooty tern) eggs and established the annual competition that determined the Birdman of the year. Makemake's face is carved on many rocks around the island, depicted as a stylized human face with large eyes. He is associated with seabirds, the ocean, and the life-giving forces of nature

name: Makonde Witchcraft Spirits (Uchawi)
description: Among the Makonde of northern Mozambique, witchcraft (uchawi) is a real and powerful tradition involving spirits deployed by malevolent practitioners and by healers. Belief distinguishes inherited witchcraft, learned sorcery, and spirit-chosen witchcraft; the power is used to harm or to protect, and accusations are adjudicated by traditional courts, maintaining social order.

name: Malahas Nuu Chah Nulth
description: Malahas, the Woman of the Woods in Nuu-chah-nulth tradition, lures children into the forest and is a standing threat to village families. In the myth cycle she steals the children of a woman of the lineage; the hero Andaokut, born from that woman's tears or mucus, later finds her and kills her, returning the children. Malahas is thus central to stories of forest danger and rescue.

name: Malakas (The First Man)
description: In Tagalog creation myth, Malakas (Strong) is the first human man, who together with Maganda (Beautiful), emerged from a split bamboo stalk. According to the myth, the world began as a vast emptiness with only the sky and the sea. A huge bird (believed to be the deity Amihan) grew tired of flying and stirred up the sea, causing an island to emerge. The bird then pecked at a bamboo stalk until it split, revealing the first man Malakas and the first woman Maganda. They became the ancestors of all humanity who populated the Philippine archipelago. Malakas represents strength, masculinity, and the foundational spirit of the Filipino people

name: Malin Kundang
description: Malin Kundang is the tragic protagonist of West Sumatra's most famous folktale, a cautionary story about filial ingratitude. A poor boy from a fishing village, Malin Kundang leaves his widowed mother to seek fortune overseas. After years of hardship, he becomes a wealthy merchant, marries a princess, and returns home in a grand ship. His elderly mother, overjoyed, rushes to embrace him, but Malin Kundang, ashamed of his humble origins in front of his wife and crew, cruelly denies knowing her and orders her driven away. Heartbroken, his mother kneels and prays to God to punish her ungrateful son. A violent storm immediately strikes, and Malin Kundang and his ship are turned to stone. The stone ship remains visible on the coast of Air Manis Beach in Padang, West Sumatra, as a permanent warning against filial disrespect

name: Malina
description: Malina is the Sun goddess of Greenlandic Inuit tradition, sister of Aningaat the Moon. Fleeing her brother's pursuit after he wronged her, she cast seal-oil and soot into his face as she rose into the sky; she became the sun and he the moon, and he still chases her, his face darkened, so that the waxing moon and the racing seasons repeat their flight.

name: Malmkarlen
description: Malmkarlen (the ore man) is a male mining spirit in Swedish folklore, the counterpart to the female Gruvrået. He appears as a small, gray-clad miner with a leather apron and a mining lamp on his cap. Malmkarlen dwells in the deepest shafts and most dangerous passages of iron and copper mines in Bergslagen. Unlike the omen-bringing Gruvrået, Malmkarlen is known for actively helping miners — he knocks on the rock walls to warn of impending cave-ins, leads miners to rich ore veins by tapping his pick, and lights his lamp in places where methane gas has accumulated. However, he also punishes greed: a miner who takes more ore than he needs will find his tools broken or his path blocked. The belief was strongest in Torsåker parish, where many 18th-century miners reported encounters

name: Malsumis
description: Malsumis is the evil twin brother of Gluskabe in Abenaki tradition, born from the divine dust of Tabaldak's hands alongside his brother. From birth, Malsumis resented his brother and plotted to destroy him. He created only evil — dangerous animals, thorns, and crooked rivers that flooded the land. He tricked the animals into revealing Gluskabe's secret weakness (that he could only be killed by a blow from a fern root) and attacked his brother. Gluskabe was saved by Grandmother Woodchuck, eventually defeated Malsumis, and turned him into stone, where he remains as the embodiment of all that is harmful in nature

name: Mama Cocha
description: Mama Qucha (Mama Cocha, 'Mother Sea/Lake') is the Inca goddess of the sea, lakes, and all waters. Wife of Wiraqucha, mother of Inti (Sun) and Mama Killa (Moon). One of four Elemental Mothers with Pachamama, Mama Nina, Mama Wayra. Worshipped by coastal peoples for calm seas and good fishing; snip inland peoples honored her as lake goddess. Inhabits Hanan Pacha (upper world).

name: Mama D'Leau
description: Mama D'Leau, also known as Mama Glo or Mama D'Lo, is the Mother of Water in Dominican and wider Caribbean folklore. She is the wife of Papa Bois and the fierce guardian of rivers, streams, and water creatures. Described as having a beautiful woman's upper body and the lower body of a massive serpent, she uses her enchanting beauty and hypnotic song to lure poachers, trespassers, and those who harm her aquatic domain close before ensnaring them with the powerful coils of her tail. Her name derives from the French Creole 'Maman de L'Eau' meaning Mother of Water. She represents the danger and beauty of Dominica's rivers — islands known for having 365 rivers. Those who respect the water may pass safely, but those who damage aquatic ecosystems face her formidable wrath

name: Mama D'Leau
description: Mama D'Leau is the Mother of Water in Saint Lucian folklore — the wife of Papa Bois and the fierce guardian of the island's rivers and streams. Saint Lucia, like Dominica, is known for its abundant rivers, and Mama D'Leau is believed to watch over each one. She has the upper body of a beautiful woman with long flowing hair, often seen combing it with a golden comb at the water's edge, and the lower body of a massive serpent. She uses her beauty and enchanting song to lure poachers and those who harm her aquatic realm before ensnaring them in the coils of her powerful tail. The legend teaches respect for water resources and the creatures that live within them, blending African, French, and Indigenous Kalinago spiritual traditions

name: Mama Djombo
description: Mama Djombo of Guinea-Bissau is a restless forest spirit that maintains transnational connections through diaspora support and protective shrine worship.

name: Mama Dlo
description: Mama Dlo (Mother of Waters) is the Saint Lucian water spirit, upper body a beautiful woman with long flowing hair perpetually combing, lower body serpentine. Inhabits mountain pools and streams. A Caribbean manifestation of the West African Mami Wata/Mama Wata tradition brought by enslaved Africans. Can grant wealth or drown the disrespectful. Connects to Haitian Simbi and Guyanese Watra-mama.

name: Mama Glo
description: Mama Glo, also known as Mama D'Leau or Mama D'Lo, is the Mother of Water in Grenadian folklore. Of African origin, she is the wife of Papa Bois and the guardian of all rivers and water bodies on the island. She is described as having a beautiful woman's upper body with long hair and a golden comb, and the lower body of a massive snake. She lures people into the rivers where she lives, using her beauty and enchanting presence. Those who encounter her must take off their left shoe, turn it upside down, and walk backwards as fast as possible to escape. She represents the dual nature of water — both life-giving and dangerous — and teaches respect for Grenada's rivers and aquatic ecosystems

name: Maman Brigitte (Queen of the Cemetery)
description: Maman Brigitte is the powerful female lwa of death, cemeteries, and the underworld in Haitian Vodou. She is the wife of Baron Samedi, the master of the dead, and together they rule the Gede family of spirits. She is depicted as a pale-skinned woman with long red or black hair, dressed in black and purple mourning clothes, often wearing a black veil and carrying a broom or shovel. She is fiercely protective of graves and ancestors, and those who defile a cemetery risk her terrible wrath. Despite her macabre domain, she is also a maternal figure who offers comfort to the grieving and protects the souls of the dead. Maman Brigitte is syncretized with Saint Brigid of Ireland, a fascinating example of Celtic-Caribbean syncretism brought by Irish indentured servants in colonial Haiti. Her colors are black, purple, and deep red. Her offerings include black coffee, dark rum infused with hot peppers, and black hens sacrificed at crossroads near cemeteries

name: Mamba Muntu
description: Mamba Muntu (or Mami Muntu, Dona Fish) is the Central African variant of Mami Wata — a mermaid-like water spirit/goddess venerated in Angola, DRC, and Congo. Traced to 15th-century European mermaid depictions, her iconography later absorbed the 1880s Hamburg snake-charmer lithograph of Nala Damajanti and Hindu imagery from Indian traders.

name: Mambabarang
description: Witchcraft has been present throughout the Philippines even before Spanish colonization, and is associated with indigenous Philippine folk religions, where Philippine shamans, who people come to for healing and rituals, are known to counter the magic of Philippine witches, who people fear. Its practice involves black magic, specifically a malevolent use of sympathetic magic. Today, practices are said to be centered in Siquijor, Cebu, Davao, Talalora, Western Samar, and Sorsogon, where many of the country's faith healers reside. Witchcraft also exists in many of the hinterlands, especially in Samar and Leyte; however, witchcraft is known and occurs anywhere in the country

name: Mame Coumba Bang
description: Mame Coumba Bang (Unknown). is a human. Mame Coumba Bang is a legendary figure from Senegal, a beautiful princess associated with the Saint-Louis region. Her story is central to the oral traditions of the Wolof people.. Source: Wolof oral tradition; Senegalese folklore

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata of Liberia appears as a beautiful water spirit who grants wealth, beauty, and luck in exchange for offerings and sexual celibacy. Her cult blends indigenous water deities with Hindu, Islamic, and colonial European imagery, making her one of the most complex and widely recognized water spirits along the West African coast.

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata of Nigeria manifests as a seductive mermaid goddess with long hair and a fish tail, believed to control the sea, storms, and fortune. Her devotees enter trance states and spirit marriage, and her cult is deeply tied to coastal communities, fishing economies, and trade along the Bight of Benin.

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata is a powerful West African water goddess of wealth and beauty who grants prosperity while demanding spiritual devotion and celibacy from her devotees.

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata of Senegal is a seductive mermaid goddess of wealth and the waters, representing both allure and dangerous power in Senegalese coastal communities.

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata of the Gambia is a beautiful mermaid water spirit who grants wealth, luck, and fertility in exchange for offerings and sexual celibacy. She appears in rivers and the sea, holds protective maritime powers, and her cult blends indigenous beliefs with colonial-era imagery along the Gambia coast.

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata of Senegal is a seductive water spirit with wealth-granting powers, reflecting historical tensions between tradition and material aspiration.

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata is a water spirit widely venerated along the Ivory Coast, appearing as a beautiful, seductive woman, often half fish or serpent, who grants wealth, success, and children in exchange for offerings, spirit marriage, and ritual devotion. Her cult blends local lagoon and river deities with imported imagery, making her central to Ivorian coastal religion and healing.

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata is a water spirit widely venerated in Benin, appearing as a beautiful, seductive woman, often half fish or serpent, who grants wealth, children, and fortune in exchange for offerings and ritual devotion. The cult thrives in coastal towns and blends Fon, Yoruba, and imported imagery, with temples serving as centers of healing, spirit possession, and trade protection.

name: Mami Wata
description: Mami Wata is known in parts of Burkina Faso through the spread of the West African water-spirit cult along trade routes, where she appears as a beautiful, seductive woman granting wealth and children in exchange for offerings and celibacy. Her inland temples cluster near rivers and sacred pools of the Volta basin.

name: Mamlambo
description: Mamlambo is a fearsome shapeshifting water deity of the Zulu and Xhosa peoples, often described as a giant serpent with a horse's head or a beautiful woman who lures men to their doom. She controls the waters, causing floods when angered and droughts when she withdraws. Those who seek her for wealth must make terrible sacrifices, and the riches she grants always bring ruin. In 1997, nine deaths near the Mzintlava River were attributed to her, with victims found with their brains sucked out, earning her the name 'brain sucker.' She represents the dangerous seduction of quick wealth and nature's unpredictable power

name: Mammoth (Great Underground Bull)
description: In Yakut (Sakha) tradition the mammoth is the Great Underground Bull, a massive creature with huge tusks, thick shaggy fur, and a body that shakes the earth underground. Solitary and reclusive, it avoids sunlight; when it dies its body causes geological upheaval, and it is linked to tremors and mysterious giant bones. It explains frozen mammoth carcasses emerging from thawing permafrost.

name: Manananggal
description: The manananggal is a vampiric creature of Philippine folklore, a woman by day who at night separates her upper torso, grows leathery wings, and flies out to hunt. She preys especially on pregnant women, extending a long tongue to suck the unborn child, and must rejoin her lower half before dawn. Her night flights warned against night wandering and pregnancy dangers.

name: Manas
description: Manas is the legendary hero who united the scattered Kyrgyz tribes and namesake of one of the world's longest epic poems. The Kyrgyz trilogy 'Manas, Semetey, Seytek,' inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List, tells of tribes united into one nation. Tellers of both sexes and all ages recite it, often after a prophetic dream, in near-trance performances that can run up to thirteen hours.

name: Manasa
description: Manasa is the Hindu snake-goddess worshipped across Bengal for snakebite protection, fertility, prosperity. Daughter of Kashyapa (or Shiva in Mangalkavyas), sister of Vasuki, wife of Jaratkaru, mother of Astika. Central to Manasamangal Kavya (Bengali medieval epics). Worshipped via cactus branch, earthen pot, snake image; festival Nag Panchami. Cult rivals Shaivism; assimilated by 14th century.

name: Manasa
description: Manasa is the Hindu snake-goddess worshipped across Bengal for snakebite protection, fertility, prosperity. Daughter of Kashyapa, sister of Vasuki, wife of Jaratkaru, mother of Astika. Central to Manasamangal Kavya (Bengali medieval epics). Worshipped via cactus branch, earthen pot, snake image; festival Nag Panchami. Cult rivals Shaivism; assimilated by 14th century.

name: Manco Cápac
description: Manco Cápac (Manqu Qhapaq) is the legendary founder and first Sapa Inca of Cusco (c. 1200 CE). In the Ayar brothers legend, he emerges from Paqariq Tampu with a golden staff, disposes of his brothers, and founds Cusco. In the Inti legend, he is the son of Sun god Inti and Moon goddess Mama Killa, sent from Lake Titicaca to bring civilization.

name: Mandinka Forest Spirit
description: The Mandinka Forest Spirit of Gambia tests travelers with tricks while protecting wilderness areas, teaching moral lessons through cunning encounters.

name: Mandukhai Khatun
description: Mandukhai Khatun, 'Mandukhai the Wise,' is the legendary warrior-queen of 15th-century Mongolia, a noble queen in traditional headdress and armor who wields twin swords while riding horseback. A warrior who led armies into battle and a wise counselor in statecraft, she fought to reunify the Mongol nation alongside Dayan Khan and remains a lasting symbol of female power.

name: Mangadhai
description: Mangadhai are the monstrous giants of the Mongolian steppe, destructive ogre-beings of superhuman strength and size who oppose the epic heroes. In tradition they can be countered through wit, strategic traps, and elders' knowledge. Mangadhai is essentially the same figure as the multi-headed mangas of Mongol epic (see mangus-mongol), sharing its hidden, external vulnerability.

name: Mangus (Mangadhai)
description: Mangus (Mangadhai) are the multi-headed chaos-monsters of Mongol epic tradition, gigantic ogre-like beings often bearing 15, 25, or even 100 heads, with iron bodies, fangs, and claws. They devour livestock and people and battle the epic heroes, yet their souls are hidden outside the body in an animal or object, making them nearly immortal until the hidden weakness is destroyed.

name: Mannbjørn
description: Mannbjørn (man-bear) is a werebear in Norwegian folklore — a human who can transform into a bear. In Norwegian tradition, the bear transformation was more common than the werewolf of continental European folklore. The mannbjørn could transform by putting on a bearskin, by drinking a magical potion, or through a family curse. While in bear form, the person retained human intelligence but gained the bear's strength and ferocity. Vestlandet legends tell of men who became bears to fight enemies, protect their farms, or survive in the wilderness. Some mannbjørn were cursed to transform during the winter months and could only be freed if someone recognized them. Unlike the berserkir of the Viking Age (who fought in a trance-like state), the mannbjørn physically transformed. The tradition was particularly strong in the remote mountain valleys of Vestlandet where brown bears were common until the 19th century

name: Mannegishi
description: The Mannegishi (also known as Awwakkule, Nirumbee) are the Little People of Crow and Cree folklore—small, bald humanoid beings with large bulging eyes and tiny tan bodies. They are tricksters who live in rocky areas, along riverbanks, and especially in the Pryor Mountains of Montana. These beings are known for playing pranks, stealing objects, and sometimes more malevolent acts like stealing children. Despite their troublesome nature, they can also confer spiritual blessings (maxpe) to those who seek them through fasting. They are incredibly strong for their size—legends say a Mannegishi can kill and carry off a full-grown bull elk

name: Manticore
description: The Manticore is a man-eating beast of Persian legend recorded by Ctesias and Pliny: a lion's body, a human face, and a tail like a scorpion's stinger that fires poison spines; its three rows of teeth devour humans whole, leaving no bones. The name is the Persian mardkhor ('man-eater'). From Iran it passed into medieval bestiaries as a more beastly cousin of the sphinx.

name: Manup
description: Manup is a mythical culture hero from northeastern Papua New Guinea, the brother of Kilibob. While his brother Kilibob traveled along the northern coast, Manup took a southern route and brought agriculture, domesticated animals, and ceremonial practices to the people. Wherever he landed, he left behind different languages and customs, contributing to the remarkable cultural diversity of the region. Manup and Kilibob eventually became rivals, and their conflict is said to have created the distinct identities of different language groups. Manup represents the archetype of the agricultural hero who teaches settled farming and social ceremonies

name: Mapinguari
description: The Mapinguari is a giant hairy cryptid of Brazilian Amazon folklore (Tupi-Guarani mbaé-pi-guari: 'thing with twisted feet'). Described as monkey-like, bipedal, with backwards feet, a single eye (forehead or belly), a vertical mouth from nose to stomach, and foul odor. Bulletproof except at navel. Devours human heads. Linked to extinct ground sloth (Glossotherium) folk memory by Oren (1993).

name: Mara
description: Mara (Swedish: mara; Old Norse: mara) is a malicious female night-spirit in Germanic and Slavic folklore who 'rides' sleepers' chests, causing suffocating nightmares (Swedish: mardröm) and sleep paralysis. Attested in Ynglinga saga (13th c.) where King Vanlandi is killed by a mara sent by Finnish sorceress Huld.

name: Mara
description: Mara (mora) is a Slavic night spirit who torments sleepers, pressing on their chests and causing nightmares and sleep paralysis. In Ukrainian folk belief she appears as a shadowy woman or animal and can be warded off with prayers, salt, or blessed objects; her name is linked to the crushing motion of the night and to the winter goddess Marzanna.

name: Mara
description: Mara (Icelandic). is a spirit. A malevolent spirit that causes suffocating nightmares by sitting on the sleeper's chest. Source: Icelandic folklore, Nordic mythology

name: Marabout
description: Marabout is an Islamic saint figure venerated across the Sahel, serving as intermediaries between people and spiritual forces with protective amulets.

name: Marawa
description: Marawa is a spider spirit and important figure in Banks Islands mythology of Vanuatu. He appears as the companion and sometimes antithesis of the creator god Qat. While Qat created humans from dracaena wood and brought them to life by playing drums, Marawa grew envious and attempted to imitate Qat's creation. He made his own human figures from different wood, but when he saw them move, he dug a pit and buried them for seven days. When he dug them up, they were lifeless — this is regarded as the origin of death among humans. Marawa represents the archetypal envious rival whose flawed creations introduce mortality and imperfection into the world

name: Mare
description: Maren (the Mare) is the Danish nightmare spirit — a female entity who sits on sleeping people's chests, pressing the air from their lungs and causing terrifying dreams. In Danish folklore, the Mare is a shape-shifter who can take the form of a cat, a dog, an owl, a horse, or even a straw. She is blamed for sleep paralysis, which in Danish is called 'mare-reden' (mare-ride). The Mare creates 'marelokker' (mare-locks) — tangled knots in horses' manes and women's hair, believed to be where she has been braiding at night. Protection against the Mare includes placing steel in the bed, reversing shoes before sleeping, carving a pentagram (called a 'marekors' or mare-cross) over the door, or sprinkling flax seeds on the floor — the Mare must count every seed before she can approach

name: Mare
description: The Mare (Danish: Maren) is the Danish nightmare spirit, a female being who sits on sleepers' chests and presses the breath from them, causing the terror known as mareridt. She can appear as a cat, owl, horse or straw, braids marelokker into manes and hair, and is warded off with steel, reversed shoes, a marekors carved over the door, or scattered flax seeds she must first count.

name: Mare (Germanic)
description: The Mare (Old High German mara, Old Norse mara, Old English mære) is a female nightmare spirit in Germanic and Slavic folklore. She 'rides' sleepers' chests, causing suffocation, sleep paralysis, and nightmares — the word 'nightmare' derives from her (Old English nihtmare, 'mare-ride').

name: Margyge
description: Margyge (also margygr, from Old Norse marr = sea + gygr = ogress) is a grotesque female sea monster in Norwegian medieval literature, first described in Konungs skuggsjá (The King's Mirror, c. The margyge is a hideous sea creature that appears before storms and shipwrecks as a dire omen. Unlike beautiful mermaids of later European folklore, the margyge is monstrous — described with a massive, misshapen body, a face like a hideous old woman with tusks and horse-like ears, clawed hands, and a fish tail. She emerges from the depths before the worst storms, shrieking and thrashing in the water. Seeing a margyge meant imminent danger at sea. She represents the terrifying, destructive power of the sea in the Norse worldview

name: Mari
description: Mari is the supreme goddess of Basque religion, a powerful spirit associated with caves, mountains, weather, and the cycles of nature. She appears as a beautiful woman or a terrible dragon and may bring blessing or destruction, rewarding respect and punishing violation of her taboos. She is the central figure of Basque mythology, with her consort Sugaar beneath her.

name: Maria Makiling (Mariang Makiling)
description: Maria Makiling is the most famous diwata (nature spirit/goddess) in Philippine mythology, the guardian spirit of Mount Makiling in Laguna. She is a breathtakingly beautiful young woman with long black hair and radiant white clothing who protects the mountain's forests, wildlife, and the people who depend on them. Pre-colonially venerated as the goddess Dayang Masalanta, she was sent by the supreme deity Bathala to aid mankind. She rewards those who respect nature and punishes those who harm it. Legends tell of her turning ginger into gold to help the poor, guiding lost hikers, and appearing as a vision of serene beauty to those pure of heart. Her spurned love for mortals who betrayed her is said to be why she now hides from human sight, only appearing as wisps of cloud around the mountain's peak

name: Marid
description: The Marid are the most powerful class of jinn in Arabian tradition — mighty, proud and rebellious spirits of smokeless fire, often bound to water and the sea. Blue-hued giants in the Thousand and One Nights, they can become invisible, shapeshift and grant wishes, but twist them maliciously; some serve as guardians of hidden treasures. They loom large in the Sinbad voyages and tales of the deep.

name: Maring
description: Not independently attested as a forest spirit of Papua New Guinea. The name 'Maring' belongs to a highlands ethnolinguistic group of the Jimi Valley, documented in Roy Rappaport's ethnography Pigs for the Ancestors, not to a spirit being; no source records a 'Maring' tree-spirit. The long-limbed forest being is likely a conflation of the people's name with generic bush-spirit beliefs.

name: Marjatta
