description: Marjatta is the virgin maiden of Kalevala (runo 50) who conceives a son after eating a lingonberry. Her child is presented to Väinämöinen; when he orders the infant killed, the babe speaks and is crowned King of Karelia. Her story, compiled by Lönnrot from Karelian runic songs, marks the Christianized conclusion of the epic, a Marian nativity parallel.

name: Marmennil
description: Marmennil (Marmennilin) is a mischievous merman from Faroese folklore who lives at the bottom of the sea near Elduvík on Eysturoy. Smaller than a human with abnormally long fingers, he delights in teasing fishermen by biting bait off hooks and snagging lines to the seabed. The most famous legend tells of farmer Anfinn (Andfind Jacobsen, born c. 1575), who accidentally hooked Marmennil's hand while fishing and pulled him into the boat. The fishermen made the sign of the cross and brought Marmennil home, where Anfinn kept him by the fireplace for years. Whenever fish were beneath the boat, Marmennil would laugh and play, and the men always caught plenty. But one day in rough surf, the men forgot to make the sign of the cross, and Marmennil escaped into the sea forever. A bronze statue by Hans Pauli Olsen was unveiled in Elduvík on 23 August 2020 to commemorate the legend

name: Marmæle
description: Marmæle (also called marmennil) is a small prophetic merman in Norwegian folklore, first described in Konungs skuggsjá (The King's Mirror, c. This child-sized, half-human half-fish creature was believed to dwell in the deep waters off the coast of Norway, particularly along the Vestlandet fjords. Fishermen who caught a marmæle could force it to foretell the future — it would predict weather, fish catches, and the fates of those present. The marmæle was considered a type of sjøvette (sea wight) and was more benevolent than the sjødraug. It was said to have the upper body of a tiny man with webbed hands and a fish-like lower body. Capturing one was considered bad luck unless it was released after three days. The marmæle tradition appears in Icelandic Landnámabók as well, where a captured marmennil prophesied about the settlement of Iceland

name: Marraco
description: El Marraco is the dragon of Lleida in Catalan folklore, depicted as a wingless green dragon with sharp claws and, in older accounts, linked to the ancient Ilergetes, whose chieftains were said to descend from a dragon deity. Today it appears in the city's festive processions (bestiari), preserving a folk memory of pre-Roman Iberian belief within Catholic celebration.

name: Masalai
description: Masalai are a class of supernatural place-spirits found throughout Papua New Guinea's diverse cultures. Margaret Mead defined them as supernatural beings inhabiting specific locations distinguished by notable natural features such as waterholes, waterfalls, river bends, cliffs, or marshes. They exercise limited jurisdiction over their own territory and manifest as snakes, crocodiles, two-headed creatures, or bizarre hybrid forms. Masalai are neither purely good nor evil. They protect their domain and can either bless or curse humans depending on how they are treated

name: Masauwu (Skeleton Man, Spirit of Death)
description: Masauwu, called Skeleton Man, is the Hopi spirit of death, fire, and the underworld, and owner of the land of the Fourth World. When the Hopi emerged from the lower worlds, it was Masauwu who granted them the earth to dwell upon, and he guards the boundary between this life and the next, appearing with a skeletal, soot-darkened face.

name: Masca
description: Masche are the witches of Piedmontese tradition, women who inherited supernatural powers across generations, able to change into animals, fly, and cast spells. Distinct from Sardinian or Neapolitan witchcraft, their power was held to come from nature rather than the devil. Feared but also consulted for healing, they are remembered in a major festival at Rifreddo.

name: Masewi (Twin War God)
description: Masewi is one of the Twin War Gods in Pueblo (specifically Acoma) tradition, brother to Oyoyewi. These twins are among the most important heroic figures in Pueblo mythology. They were born to a virgin mother who conceived from the Sun. The twins are credited with creating the world and all living creatures, slaying the giant monster that terrorized the Pueblo people, establishing the directions, bringing order to the world, and teaching people how to live. After completing their work, they retur

name: Masmasalanicw (Four Carpenters)
description: Masmasalanicw, the Four Carpenters, are the winged creators of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition who worked in the House of Smayusta at the beginning of time. Led by the eldest, Yulm, they assisted the Creator Alhkw'ntam in fashioning the world; Yulm made Raven from a lump of charcoal, and each carpenter brought a special craft.

name: Masmasalanicw Four Carpenters Nuxalk
description: The Masmasalanicw, the Four Carpenters, are the supernatural craftsmen of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) creation who shaped the world under the direction of the Creator. They made the mountains, rivers, and forests, fashioned the first creatures, and established the pattern of the land that the Nuxalk people know.

name: Matau
description: Not independently attested as a named eel deity of Fijian folklore. While eels (waqawaqa, duna) are widely sacred in Fiji — Degei, the great serpent of Nakauvadra, and the guardian eel of Naqali pool being documented examples — no source records an eel spirit called 'Matau'. The entry appears to generalise the region's sacred-eel beliefs under an unattested name.

name: Mate Bein (Ancestral Ghost)
description: In Tetum cosmology of East Timor, Mate Bein are the ancestral ghosts who occupy a central role in the spiritual world. Unlike malevolent spirits, these ghosts are the transformed souls of the deceased who become agencies for life-affirming fertility after proper ritual action. The soul of a person (klamar mate) transitions through ritual into an ancestral ghost that bestows fertility, sustains life across generations, and maintains the sacred balance between the human and spirit worlds. They are deeply connected to the concept of lulik (sacred potency)

name: Matlose Nuu Chah Nulth
description: Matlose is a hobgoblin of Nuu-chah-nulth tradition, described in early accounts as a Caliban-like spirit of the woods. His head is said to be only half like a man's, his body horrid with black bristles, his teeth monstrous, and his hands armed with bear-like claws. His voice fells listeners, and a single stroke of his claw rends his prey.

name: Matsieng
description: Matsieng is a powerful one-legged giant from Tswana tradition, considered the first ancestor of the Batswana people. According to legend, Matsieng emerged from a waterhole in southeastern Botswana, followed by his people, domestic animals, and wildlife, all sinking their feet into the soft, unformed early earth. Their footprints hardened into stone over millennia, preserved at a sacred site now known as the Matsieng Footprints. The site contains over 170 carvings of human and animal footprints. To this day, the Tswana visit the site for rain-making ceremonies, maintaining the sacred connection between the first ancestor and the living community

name: Matsya
description: Matsya (Fish) is the first avatar of Vishnu in the Dashavatara. In Shatapatha Brahmana, a fish saves Manu from the great flood; later Puranas identify it as Vishnu. Matsya warns Manu, has him build a boat, tows it to Himalayas with Vedas, sages, seeds. In Bhagavata Purana, slays demon Hayagriva who stole the Vedas. Depicted as giant golden fish or half-Vishnu/half-fish. Embodies flood myth motif.

name: Matsyendranath (Karunamaya)
description: Matsyendranath, also known as Karunamaya ('the compassionate one') and Red Machindranath, is one of the most important deities in Nepali Buddhism and Hinduism, revered as the god of rain and compassion. The central legend tells of a devastating 12-year drought that struck the Kathmandu Valley, caused by the demon Bhasmasura (or Bhasmasur). The powerful yogi Gorakhnath had captured all the nagas (serpent gods) in meditation, blocking the rainfall. The people, led by the king of Bhadgaon, traveled to Assam to seek help from Matsyendranath, Gorakhnath's guru. When Matsyendranath arrived in the valley, his mere presence forced Gorakhnath to release the nagas, bringing life-giving rain and restoring the valley to fertility. Matsyendranath is revered as an avatar of Avalokiteshvara (Padmapani), the bodhisattva of compassion. His connection to the revived Red Machindranath chariot festival in Patan — one of Nepal's oldest and grandest processions — involves transporting his towering chariot through the streets of Patan for a month-long festival that is central to Newar cultural identity

name: Matuku
description: Matuku-tangotango is the giant man-eating bird of Māori tradition, a monstrous owl-like creature who swallowed the ancestress Whaitiri and devoured travellers. The hero Tāwhaki slew him and cut open his belly to free his relatives. The name matuku also denotes the bittern, and the ogre's image blends the fearsome night-bird with the taniwha-like predators of old.

name: Maui
description: In Hawaiian tradition, Māui is the trickster demigod and culture hero who fished up the islands with his enchanted fishhook (the constellation Māui's Fishhook), snared the sun to lengthen the day, and drew fire from the depths. The youngest and cleverest of brothers, he used cunning rather than strength to aid humanity, and his exploits explain the shape of land and sky.

name: Maui
description: In Māori tradition, Māui is the great demigod and trickster who fished up Te Ika-a-Māui, the North Island, from the sea with a hook made from the jawbone of his grandmother Murirangawhenua, his canoe becoming Te Waka a Māui, the South Island. He slowed the sun, stole fire from Mahuika, and sought immortality from Hine-nui-te-pō, shaping the human condition.

name: Maui (Polynesian)
description: The great Polynesian trickster demigod and cultural hero whose exploits are celebrated across the Pacific. Maui performed many legendary feats: he fished up the North Island of New Zealand (Te Ika-a-Maui) using a magical fishhook made from his ancestor's jawbone; he slowed the sun to make days longer by capturing Tamanuitera with ropes; he stole fire from his ancestress Mahuika to give to humanity; and he attempted to conquer death by crawling through Hine-nui-te-po. His mother Taranga abandoned him at birth, but he was raised by the gods and given magical powers. He is small, clever, and perpetually mischievous, using his wits to overcome beings far more powerful than himself

name: Maure the Briden
description: Not independently attested in Algerian folklore. Maure the Briden is described as a sea goddess of the Mediterranean who commands storms and shelters coastal villages, a water spirit bound to the shore and offended by pollution of the sea. The garbled name suggests a modern invention conflating the classic siren type with the Amazigh rain rites of Anzar, whose bride ends drought.

name: Mauve Sorciere
description: The mauve sorcière is a witch figure of French folklore identified by Claude Lecouteux, whose name refers to the purple-tinged assemblies of witches, perhaps tied to the Devil's Sabbath. These gatherings at crossroads and isolated places mark the color mauve as the hue of the witches' supernatural realm. The figure condenses the fear of rural witchcraft and the sabbat in French folk belief.

name: Mavka
description: Mavka (plural mavky) are Ukrainian forest spirits, the souls of unbaptized or drowned maidens, who dance in the fields and lure young men into the woods. In Ukrainian folklore and literature they are both beautiful and deadly, vanishing at dawn; the name is linked to the Slavic root for the dead.

name: Mawu
description: Mawu is the supreme creator goddess of the Fon (Dahomey) and Ewe peoples of Benin and Togo. She is the goddess of the moon, night, fertility, and motherhood. Often paired with Lisa, the sun god, they form the dual-sexed creator deity Mawu-Lisa. Mawu created the cosmos, the earth, and humanity. According to Fon cosmology, she created the world while carried on the back of Aido Hwedo, the rainbow serpent, whose winding movements formed the mountains and valleys. Mawu is considered compassionate, nurturing, and forgiving — the "cool" counterpart to Lisa's "hot" nature. As the creator of human souls and ruler of destiny, Mawu's "writing" is called Fa (destiny), revealed through the divination system. She is depicted as an elder female figure with large breasts holding a crescent moon

name: May and Gilan
description: Mayy and Ghīlān are the legendary founding couple of Qatari tradition — a beloved hikâya told for generations about a heroic pair whose story is celebrated as a foundational myth of the peninsula. Cast as brave, protective figures of courage and unity, they embody the protector spirit of the Qatari people in oral storytelling, song and popular memory.

name: Maya Mriga (Golden Deer)
description: The Maya Mriga (Golden Deer) is a pivotal illusionary creature from the Ramayana, created by the rakshasa Maricha at Ravana's command. To enable Ravana's abduction of Sita, Maricha transformed himself into a mesmerizing golden deer with silver spots and jewel-like horns that appeared to be made of precious metals and gems. The deer's magical beauty was so captivating that Sita, seeing it near their forest hermitage, asked Rama to capture it for her. Despite Lakshmana's warnings that such a creature could not be natural and was likely a trick, Rama pursued the deer deep into the forest. The golden deer led Rama far from the hermitage, then, as it died from Rama's arrow, mimicked Rama's voice calling for help — 'O Lakshmana! O Sita!' — a desperate cry that drew Lakshmana away from Sita, leaving her vulnerable to Ravana. The Maya Mriga thus represents illusion (maya) used as a weapon, and its role is the catalyst for the central conflict of the Ramayana

name: Mayohiga
description: Mayohiga (迷い家) is a phantom house of Japanese mountain folklore, recorded in Yanagita Kunio's 1910 Tōno Monogatari. It appears at dusk on remote paths and in deep valleys; those who enter may take food or goods, and some return wealthy, while others who stay too long are never seen again. It is a supernatural dwelling tied to mountain spirits rather than a permanent place.

name: Mazimu
description: Mazimu are ancestral spirits of the Tumbuka people (Malawi, eastern Zambia, Tanzania). They dwell near family graves, monitoring descendants, offering protection or punishment. Elders propitiate them with beer libations at the m'sinda shrine. Term from Tumbuka -zimu (spirit/ancestor). Documented in missionary ethnographies (Rangeley) and oral tradition.

name: Mba-Katrè
description: Mba-Katrè is the hyena of Mossi (Moose) folktales in Burkina Faso, the gluttonous, foolish trickster outwitted at every turn by the cunning hare Mba-Soamba. Published in Folktales from the Moose of Burkina Faso (Langaa, 2010), the paired tales teach children the cost of greed, lack of foresight and unchecked appetite, setting hyena stupidity against hare finesse.

name: Mba-Soêmba
description: Mba-Soêmba is the clever hare trickster figure in Mossi folklore of Burkina Faso, the wise and cunning counterpart to the foolish hyena Mba-Katrè. In the vast oral tradition of the Mossi (Moose) people, Mba-Soêmba represents intelligence, quick thinking, and resourcefulness — consistently using his wits to overcome larger, stronger adversaries. Through clever deception, strategic thinking, and an understanding of human nature, the hare repeatedly triumphs over the hyena's brute force and greed. The stories of Mba-Soêmba serve as a cornerstone of Mossi moral education for children aged 10 to 12, teaching that intelligence and patience are more valuable than physical strength. The hare's cunning is celebrated rather than condemned, as his tricks typically punish greed, arrogance, and foolishness. These tales are traditionally performed by griots and elders during evening gatherings, combining entertainment with cultural education. The Mba-Soêmba figure belongs to a broader West African tradition of trickster hares found across the region, from Ghana to Mali

name: Mbatian
description: Mbatian was the most powerful laibon (spiritual leader/prophet) in Maasai history, a legendary figure of the late 19th century descended from the sacred Inkindongi clan (Oloiboni clan). His prophetic powers were unrivaled -- he could predict droughts, locate lost cattle, communicate directly with Enkai, and control the weather. Mbatian served as the supreme spiritual authority for the Maasai during a period of great upheaval. As he grew old, his younger son Lenana tricked a messenger and usurped his elder brother Senteu's birthright, sparking a rivalry that divided the Maasai. Mbatian died around 1890. His legacy as the greatest laibon endures in Maasai oral tradition

name: Mbe (Tortoise)
description: Mbe the Tortoise is the cunning trickster of Igbo folklore, a small creature who uses his intelligence to overcome larger, stronger animals — and often his own greed leads to his downfall. In the most famous Igbo story, Mbe was once a bird with a beautiful shell who borrowed feathers to fly to a heavenly feast. Through trickery (claiming his name was "All of You"), he ate all the food. The angry birds retrieved their feathers, leaving Mbe stranded in heaven. He convinced the heavenly hosts to throw him down, but his shell shattered on impact — which is why tortoises have cracked, patched shells. Mbe stories teach Igbo values: cleverness is valuable but greed brings ruin. Mbe is the Igbo equivalent of the Yoruba Ijapa the tortoise or the Akan Anansi

name: Mbenga (or Mokèlé-mbèmbé)
description: Mokèlé-mbèmbé ('one who stops the flow of rivers') is a cryptid of the Congo Basin reported since 1913 by German Captain von Stein. Described as a long-necked, herbivorous, elephant-sized creature with smooth skin, it supposedly lives in riverbank caves and attacks canoes.

name: Mbidi Kiluwe
description: Mbidi Kiluwe is the legendary culture hero and founding father of Luba sacred kingship (bulopwe). According to Luba oral tradition, Mbidi Kiluwe was a mysterious prince from the east, distinguished by his refined, dignified manners. He arrived at the court of King Nkongolo Mwamba, the crude and violent red-skinned ruler. Where Nkongolo was barbaric, Mbidi Kiluwe was gentle and wise. He introduced civilizing customs: eating in private, using utensils, speaking softly, covering one's face with dignity. Mbidi Kiluwe married Nkongolo's sister Bulanda, but was forced to flee when Nkongolo's tyranny became unbearable. Before leaving, he prophesied his unborn son would overthrow Nkongolo. Mbidi Kiluwe's refined manners became the model for Luba kingship (bulopwe), establishing sacred traditions defining Luba royal culture for centuries

name: Mbona
description: Mbona is a legendary rain-bringing prophet and martyr from Chewa and Mang'anja mythology of Malawi. Unlike purely mythical figures, Mbona may be based on a historical figure who lived around the 16th century. According to tradition, Mbona possessed extraordinary magic powers: he could bring rain during droughts, create wells of water in sandy lands, cause forests to appear where none existed, and hide from his enemies by transforming into other creatures such as guinea fowls. Mbona's powers made him both beloved by his people and feared by his enemies. Nabbed by his rivals, he was decapitated, but his head continued to speak and prophesy even after his death. His grave became a sacred site, and the Mbona cult remains active in Malawi to this day, with his spirit speaking through mediums. The most famous shrine dedicated to Mbona is at Khulubvi in southern Malawi, where annual ceremonies are held to petition for rain and good harvests. The site is considered so sacred that entry is restricted to certain days and requires specific rituals

name: Mboreví
description: Mboreví (Mborevi) are miniature forest-dwelling nature spirits in Guaraní tradition (Paraguay, NE Argentina, S Brazil). Described as small protective people who guard the forest and its creatures. They punish those who harm nature and can be appeased with offerings. Closely related to Pombero and Kurupi in the Guaraní spirit complex. Documented by Cadogan and Guaraní ethnographers.

name: Mbwiri
description: In Gabon (Fang and related groups), Mbwiri is a possessing spirit that inhabits individuals, manifesting through trance, song, and epileptic-like fits. A shaman builds a hut where the patient and assistants dance to flute and drum for ten days to two weeks; Mbwiri 'abhors good living' and is driven out by the ordeal.

name: Meandash
description: Meandash is the mythic wild reindeer of eastern Sami (Kola Peninsula) tradition, a shapeshifter who is human inside his hut and a reindeer outside. He is the central culture hero of the Ter and Kildin Sami, credited with teaching humans the art of hunting and gifting them the bow. Nearly 30 stories about Meandash have been recorded. He was born to a female noaidi (shaman) who conceived him in reindeer form from a wild reindeer. Meandash lives in a hut made of reindeer skin and bones, separated from the human world by a river of blood with lungs for waves and livers for stones. He marries an earthly girl who crosses this river, and they have children born human. When his wife breaks a taboo by drying urine-soaked reindeer skins in the sun, Meandash transforms permanently into a wild reindeer, and his children become reindeer calves, forming the first wild reindeer herds. In a later act of self-sacrifice, Meandash allows himself to be killed by a Sami hunter so his meat can feed the people, thereby teaching them hunting skills

name: Mechanical Bird Denmark
description: Mechanical Bird Denmark (Unknown). is a bird. The mechanical bird is from Hans Christian Andersen's The Nightingale, a bejeweled artificial nightingale.. Source: Danish folklore — mechanical figures documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Medicine Man
description: The Medicine Man is a recurring human hero figure in Arapaho mythology. In the story of How Medicine Man Resurrected Buffalo, a powerful medicine man saved his starving people by seeking a vision, receiving instructions from the Earth Spirit, and opening a passage to the underground buffalo world. He demonstrates the power of faith, ceremony, and spiritual dedication. Medicine men (also called shamans or holy men) are central figures in Arapaho spirituality who communicate with the spirit world, heal the sick, and maintain the balance between the human and spirit realms

name: Medusa
description: Medusa is the most famous of the three Gorgon sisters of Greek myth, a winged being with living serpents for hair whose gaze turned all who met it to stone. Once a beautiful maiden punished by Athena, she was beheaded by Perseus, and from her neck sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor. Her severed head, the gorgoneion, became an apotropaic emblem on armor and shields.

name: Meiga
description: Meigas are the wise women of Galician folklore, healers and practitioners who communicate with nature and the supernatural and who can cure or harm. Unlike the malevolent witch stereotype, they were knowledgeable community figures consulted for healing and divination. The tradition is recorded in Galician oral tradition and remains part of regional identity.

name: Melatha
description: Melatha is the male lightning spirit of Choctaw tradition, mate of Heloha the thunder bird. Dressed in lightning and rainbows, he races across the sky above the vault of heaven at incredible speed, leaving trails of sparks that flash as lightning, while Heloha's eggs rumble to produce thunder.

name: Mellyng (Mellified Man)
description: The mellified man (miren, 'honey person') is a legendary Arabian medicinal preparation recorded by Li Shizhen in the Bencao Gangmu (16th century): a very old man, fed only honey until death, sealed in a honey-filled stone coffin, and after a century sold in pieces as a remedy for broken bones and wounds. It is folk-medical legend spread along the Silk Road rather than a living creature.

name: Mellyng (Mellified Man)
description: The mellified man (mellified mummy) is a legendary remedy from Arabic and Chinese sources, famously recorded by Li Shizhen in the Bencao Gangmu, in which willing elderly men were steeped in honey until their bodies dissolved into a curative confection. Though almost certainly fanciful, the tale circulated along the Silk Road as an emblem of extreme preservation and folk medicine.

name: Melqart
description: Melqart was the tutelary god of the Phoenician city-state of Tyre (in modern Lebanon) and one of the most important deities in the Phoenician and Punic pantheons. His name means 'King of the City' in Phoenician. Melqart was a complex deity embodying multiple roles: sea god and protector of navigation, a dying-and-rising vegetation god, the divine patron of Phoenician colonization, and a heroic figure identified by the Greeks with Heracles. Every Phoenician colony founded by Tyre included a temple to Melqart as the city's spiritual center. He was depicted riding a winged hippocampus on Tyrian coins, symbolizing his command over the seas. The most famous sanctuary was at Tyre itself, described by Herodotus with its two pillars of gold and emerald

name: Melusine
description: Melusine is a fresh-water spirit of French folklore, often a woman who becomes a serpent or mermaid below the waist, sometimes winged. In the medieval romance she married Raymondin of Lusignan, provided he never saw her on Saturdays; when he broke the oath she fled as a serpent. She is the legendary ancestress of the Lusignan, Anjou, and Luxembourg dynasties.

name: Mendiss
description: Mendiss is a female Serer water spirit who guards the Fatick region coast, controlling tides and protecting maritime communities with guardianship powers.

name: Menehune
description: The Menehune are the legendary dwarf builders of Hawaiʻi, said to have raised temples (heiau), fishponds, roads, and canoes in a single night, working only in darkness and vanishing at dawn if unfinished. The 1820 census of Kauaʻi listed 65 of them. Scholars debate whether they remember earlier settlers (manahune, 'commoners') or are a post-contact invention, but their craftwork lore endures.

name: Menninkäinen
description: Menninkäinen is a Finnish gnome-like forest spirit, small with large head and pointed features, wearing a pointed hat. Originally friendly spirits in isolated places (Ganander), later evolved into goblin-like creatures guarding treasures, enjoying riddles and dominance games (like leprechauns).

name: Merakyat
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Malaysian folklore; searches locate no being called 'Merakyat.' The recorded water spirit of rivers and waterfalls, appearing as a beautiful woman or an old man, matches the attested Malay hantu air (water spirit) and penunggu sungai (river guardian), who demand respect and cleanliness from those who use the water.

name: Merchildren
description: In Danish folk belief, havbørn are the offspring of havmand and havfrue, dwelling in sea caves and kelp forests. They appear in ballads like "Agneta og Havmanden" where a human woman bears a merman's children, caught between sea and land. Unlike literary mermaids, these beings belong to oral tradition and are feared as lurers of humans into the depths.

name: Merger
description: Merger is the foundational epic hero of the Nanai people of the Amur River region, a powerful warrior-shaman in animal-decorated armor who can transform into tiger, bird, or fish. He combines martial prowess with shamanic magic, undertaking spirit journeys across multiple worlds to protect his people. His kind of hero is preserved in the Hezhen Yimakan tradition (UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding).

name: Merlin
description: Merlin (Unknown). is a human. Merlin is the legendary wizard and advisor to King Arthur in British mythology. Possessing prophetic powers and magical abilities, he orchestrates Arthur's birth and guides the kingdom through its gol. Source: Historia Regum Britanniae (Geoffrey of Monmouth, 1136); Arthurian cycle

name: Mermaid
description: Mermaid (Generic). is a mermaid. Aquatic beings with the upper body of a human and the tail of a fish, found in various global folklores. Source: Maritime folklore, global oral traditions

name: Mermaid Denmark
description: Mermaid Denmark (Unknown). is a mermaid. The mermaid of Danish folklore is a sea creature with the upper body of a woman and the tail of a fish. The most famous Danish mermaid is the subject of Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid" . Source: Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales; Danish folklore

name: Mermaids of Black Rocks
description: The Mermaids of Black Rocks are vengeful mermaids said to inhabit the volcanic Black Rocks on the northeastern coast of Saint Kitts. They lure sailors with enchanting songs to drag them to watery graves. A localized Caribbean mermaid belief warning of sea dangers; the rock formation itself is a real landmark. May protect the island in some tellings.

name: Merman Denmark
description: Merman Denmark (Unknown). is a mermaid. The merman is a male sea spirit from Danish folklore who lures human women into his underwater realm through enchanted song.. Source: Danish folklore — Merman figure documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Metsavana
description: Metsavana (Estonia). is a deity. The 'Old Man of the Forest' in Estonian mythology, also called metsataat or metsaisa. Source: Estonian folklore; known as the Old Man of the Forest (Metsavana) in Estonian mythology.

name: Metsänhenki
description: Metsänhenki (Finnish: 'forest spirit' or 'forest self') is not a distinct creature but the animistic concept of the forest's living essence in Finnish tradition. It can manifest as a person, light, or presence, misleads travelers, and is the forest itself — not a being within it. Central to the Finnish relationship with nature.

name: Micipabis
description: Micipabis (Mishipeshu, the Underwater Panther) is the great water being of Anishinaabe and Algonquian peoples: a panther-lynx with horns, copper scales and a spiked tail that dwells in the depths of the Great Lakes, raising storms, whirlpools and floods when angered. It guards copper deposits and must be appeased with offerings; it is the eternal opponent of the Thunderbirds.

name: Micipabis
description: Micipabis (Mishipeshu, the Underwater Panther) is the great water being of Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) and Algonquian tradition: a panther-lynx with horns, copper scales and a spiked tail dwelling in the depths of the Great Lakes, raising storms, whirlpools and floods when angered. It guards the copper of the lakes and must be appeased with offerings; it is the eternal opponent of the Thunderbirds.

name: Midnight Robber (Trinidad Carnival Mas Character)
description: The Midnight Robber is one of the most iconic and beloved traditional masquerade characters of Trinidad and Tobago Carnival. He is a bombastic, theatrical outlaw who combines the swagger of a Wild West gunslinger with the oratory tradition of a West African griot (storyteller). He wears an oversized wide-brimmed hat (often shaped like a coffin or a crown), a flowing black cape decorated with symbols of death and destruction (skulls, crossbones), black satin shirt and pantaloons, and carries a wooden money box shaped like a coffin, a dagger or pistol, and a whistle. His signature feature is Robber Talk -- an elaborate, grandiose monologue delivered in a deep voice, mixing Shakespearean English, biblical cadences, and Creole. He boasts of his invincible ancestry, his terrifying exploits, and his plans for vengeance against his enemies. He stops passersby, holds them at ransom with his eloquence, and demands money before releasing them. The Midnight Robber first appeared in Trinidad Carnival in the early 1900s, drawing from American Wild West imagery and African griot storytelling

name: Migoi (Bhutanese Yeti)
description: The Migoi (from Tibetan 'mi rgod' meaning 'wild man') is Bhutan's indigenous version of the Yeti, a magical wild creature inhabiting the high Himalayan pastures and deep forests. Unlike the more physical Nepali Yeti, the Bhutanese Migoi possesses supernatural qualities: it can become invisible at will, its blood has magical properties used for talismans, and it carries two enchanted objects — the dipshing (a juniper twig that grants invisibility) and the sem phatsa (a special satchel without which it loses all power). Bhutanese folklore distinguishes between two types: the mechume, a smaller ape-like being with reddish-brown hair that inhabits deep forests, and the gredpo (or migoi proper), a huge creature with grayish-black hair said to have a hollow back — a feature associated with dangerous ghosts. The Migoi is considered a bad omen, and only certain spiritually gifted people can see it. Its habitat is so respected that the Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary in eastern Bhutan was established in part to protect the Migoi's habitat, making it possibly the only wildlife sanctuary in the world designated partly for a legendary creature

name: Mimi
description: The Mimi (Mimih) are tall, extremely thin spirit beings of Arnhem Land and Kakadu who live in the rock crevices and escarpments and are so delicate that a strong wind can break them. They are credited with making the first rock paintings, and with teaching Aboriginal people painting, hunting, and cooking. Usually shy, they can be dangerous if their places or pets are disturbed.

name: Minotaur
description: The Minotaur is a monster of Greek myth, a man with the head and body of a bull, born of Pasiphaë and the Cretan bull and known as Asterion. Confined by Daedalus in the Labyrinth beneath Knossos and fed on human tribute from Athens, it was slain by Theseus with the aid of Ariadne's thread. Its story may encode Minoan bull-cult and the palace's intricate architecture.

name: Miraculous Well of Sidi Bou Said
description: The Miraculous Well of Sidi Bou Said is a legendary blessed water source in the famous blue-and-white Tunisian town of Sidi Bou Said, near Tunis. According to local legend, the well was blessed by Sidi Bou Said (also known as Abu Said al-Baji), a 13th-century Sufi saint who lived and taught in the area. The well is said to possess miraculous healing powers, with locals and visitors alike claiming that drinking water from it can cure various ailments, from simple headaches to more serious diseases. The saint, after whom the town is named, was a respected Islamic scholar and mystic known for his piety and miraculous works. The legend holds that he blessed the well so that his followers would always have access to healing water. The well has become a pilgrimage site for those seeking cures and blessings. The story reflects the widespread North African tradition of maraboutism—the veneration of holy figures (marabouts or wali) whose blessings are believed to continue after their death, often associated with specific locations like wells, springs, or trees

name: Mishebeshu
description: Mishebeshu (Mishipeshu, Mishibizhiw) is the Underwater Panther of Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition: a great horned water being, part panther and part serpent, with copper scales and a spiked tail, dwelling in the deeps of the Great Lakes and rivers. It drowns people, causes floods and guards underwater copper; it is balanced against the Thunderbirds, which fight it from the upper world.

name: Mishebeshu
description: Mishebeshu (Mishipeshu, Mishibizhiw) is the Underwater Panther of Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tradition: a great horned water being, part panther and part serpent, with copper scales and a spiked tail, dwelling in the deeps of the Great Lakes. It drowns the unwary, raises floods and guards underwater copper, standing as the eternal foe of the Thunderbirds of the upper world.

name: Mishipeshu
description: Mishipeshu, the Great Lynx or Underwater Panther, is one of the most powerful water beings in Ojibwe and Anishinaabe mythology. It has the head and paws of a giant cat but is covered in scales with dagger-like spikes along its back and tail. It rules the depths of Lake Superior from its home on Michipicoten Island and is master of all water creatures, including snakes. Mishipeshu can cause storms that capsize canoes and is feared as a cause of drownings. It is the eternal opponent of the Thunderbirds and is said to guard vast deposits of copper in the Great Lakes

name: Mishipizheu
description: Mishipeshu, the 'Great Lynx' of the Ojibwe and other Great Lakes Anishinaabe peoples, is the foremost underwater being: a horned, scaled panther with palmed paws and a copper tail dwelling in the depths of big lakes. It stirs waves and whirlpools, breaks winter ice and drowns the careless, yet guards the copper of Lake Superior and can grant healing to those who approach respectfully.

name: Mishipizheu
description: Mishipeshu, the 'Great Lynx' of the Ojibwe and other Anishinaabe peoples of the Great Lakes, is the foremost underwater being: a horned, scaled panther with palmed paws and a copper tail living in deep lakes. It raises waves and whirlpools, breaks winter ice and drowns the careless, while guarding Lake Superior's copper and rewarding respectful travelers with medicine power.

name: Mitsina (Hermit)
description: Mítsina is the Hermit of Zuni folklore, who dwelt all alone in the Canyon of the Pines southeast of Zuni. Because he was unwise and evil in his ways, the gods bade him live apart until, through much happening, he should become worthy to dwell among them; hunters passing by heard the sounds of his solitary gaming.

name: Mmoatia
description: Mmoatia are small forest-dwelling spirits in Akan mythology, often described as dwarf-like beings with backwards-facing feet. They are considered the custodians of the forest under Asase Afua, the fertile aspect of the earth goddess. Mmoatia are invisible to most humans but can be seen by those with spiritual sight, especially children. They are known to be mischievous but can be helpful to those who treat them with respect. In Anansi stories, Mmoatia is one of the creatures that the sky god Nyame demanded Anansi capture as part of the price for the world's stories. Mmoatia is described as an invisible fairy-like being that Anansi caught using a sticky doll (the origin of the "Tarbaby" story motif that spread throughout the African diaspora)

name: Mngwa
description: Mngwa (Swahili 'strange one'), also Nunda ('fierce animal'), is a Tanzanian cryptid: massive grey-fawn cat taller than a lion, leaving no tracks. Swahili tales (Steere 1870, Velten 1907) depict it as a sultan's pet growing into a man-eater—the 'Swallowing Monster' motif (ATU B.11.2.3.1) widespread in Bantu/Malagasy regions. Featured in Lang's Violet Fairy Book (1901).

name: Mnyazi
description: Mnyazi refers to vampiric returning dead in Kenyan coastal (Swahili/Giriama) belief—jealous/greedy ancestors rising as red-eyed blood-drinkers to prey on kin. Protection: iron, garlic, Islamic amulets (hirizi). Term may derive from Swahili nyama (meat) + zi (spirit). Documented in Kenyan coastal ethnography (Lambert) but less widely than Shetani/Popobawa.

name: Mo'o
description: Moʻo are powerful reptilian water deities of Hawaiian tradition who guard freshwater pools, streams, waterfalls, and ponds, and can appear as immense lizards, geckos, or beautiful women. They bless those who honour the waters and punish those who defile them. Many serve as 'aumakua (family guardian spirits), and scholar Marie Alohalani Brown has catalogued some 288 individual moʻo.

name: Mocko Jumbie
description: The Mocko Jumbie is a towering stilt-walking spirit dancer and a central figure in St. Kitts and Nevis Carnival and folklore traditions. The name combines 'Moko' (a West African deity who guards, heals, and delivers retribution) and 'Jumbie' (a Caribbean spirit). Dressed in colorful flowing costumes and balancing on 6-to-8-foot stilts, Mocko Jumbies are believed to be ancestral spirits who walk among the living, providing protection and warding off evil. The tradition was brought to St. Kitts by enslaved Africans and has been preserved for over 200 years. In Kittitian culture, Mocko Jumbies appear during Christmas and Carnival celebrations, and their towering height symbolizes the power of God and the ability to see evil before it reaches the community. The tradition was documented in St. Kitts as early as the late 18th century

name: Modimo
description: Modimo is the supreme deity of the Sotho-Tswana people, the creator of all things, source of life, and controller of destiny. Intangible and all-pervasive, Modimo is addressed by praise names including Mme (Mother) and Lesedi (Light), but also Selo (Monster) for dangerous powers beyond human comprehension. Modimo governs the elements, sending lightning, thunder, rain, or drought. However, Modimo is distant from daily human affairs, and the Tswana approach through the Badimo (ancestors) who act as intermediaries. The Tswana say 'Motho ke modimo' (Man is modimo), expressing the profound interconnection between humans, ancestors, and the divine

name: Mokele-Mbembe
description: Mokele-Mbembe, meaning 'one who stops the flow of rivers' in the Lingala language, is a legendary water-dwelling entity from Bantu mythology of the Congo River Basin. This cryptid is described as a large, reptilian creature resembling a sauropod dinosaur with a long, flexible neck and a single horn or tooth. Stories of the creature have been told for centuries among the Bantu peoples of Central Africa, including the Ba'Aka, whose oral traditions speak of a beast that lurks in deep river pools and swamps. During the early 20th century, European explorers and cryptozoologists brought the legend to global attention, leading to over fifty expeditions searching for evidence. While most scientists believe the stories stem from misidentified rhinoceroses, large snakes, or folk memory of once-extant megafauna, the mokele-mbembe remains one of Africa's most famous cryptids. In recent years, deforestation and habitat loss have led to increased reported sightings as displaced wildlife is mistaken for the legendary creature

name: Mokele-mbembe
description: Mokele-mbembe is a legendary water-dwelling entity believed to inhabit the Congo River Basin, with traditions extending into the Central African Republic among the Bayaka pygmy peoples. The name derives from the Lingala language and translates as 'one who stops the flow of rivers', referring to the creature's supposed preference for nesting in river bends. Descriptions vary widely but commonly depict a large quadrupedal creature with smooth skin, a long neck and tail, and a small head resembling a sauropod dinosaur. In CAR oral traditions, the creature is sometimes described as a spirit rather than a physical animal. The Bayaka people of CAR's southwestern forests have passed down knowledge of this being for generations, describing it as inhabiting remote swampy areas and river systems

name: Mokele-Mbembe
description: Mokele-Mbembe is a dragon from Bantu mythology. This cryptid is described as a large, reptilian creature resembling a sauropod dinosaur with a long, flexible neck and a single horn or tooth. Stories of the creature have been told for centuries among the Bantu peoples of Central Africa, including the Ba'Aka, whose oral traditions speak of a beast that lurks in deep river pools and swamps. During the early 20th century, European explorers and cryptozoologists brought the legend to global attention, leading to over fifty expeditions searching for evidence. While most scientists believe the stories stem from misidentified rhinoceroses, large snakes, or folk memory of once-extant megafauna, the mokele-mbembe remains one of Africa's most famous cryptids. In recent years, deforestation and habitat loss have led to increased reported sightings as displaced wildlife is mistaken for the legendary creature

name: Mokele-mbembe
description: Mokèlé-mbèmbé (Lingala: 'one who stops the flow of rivers') is the same cryptid as mbenga-or-mok-l-mb-mb, here attributed to 'Congolese' culture. Described as a sauropod-like creature in the Likouala swamps, it became a focus of creationist expeditions from the 1980s onward. No specimen, photograph, or trace has been verified.

name: Mokele-Mbembe
description: Mokele-Mbembe is a great water creature of Central African oral tradition, described by Bantu and Ba'Aka peoples as a large, long-necked, reptilian beast that lurks in deep river pools and swamps of the Congo Basin. Local reports later drew dozens of cryptozoological expeditions; science usually explains sightings as misidentified elephants, rhinos, or large snakes.

name: Moko Jumbie
description: The moko jumbie is a towering, stilt-walking ancestral spirit of the Caribbean, and Saint Vincent preserves the oldest written record of the tradition: William Young's 1791 account of 'Moco Jumbies' among the island's Black Caribs, who performed in costumes blending African motifs with women's petticoats and dresses.

name: Momoy
description: Momoy are small, bearded duende-like guardians of water sources, rivers, forests, and agricultural lands in Venezuelan Andean folklore (Mérida, Táchira, Trujillo). Mischievous but protective; snip can summon heavy rains. Leave offerings to gain favor. Blend of indigenous Timoto-Cuica beliefs and Spanish duende traditions. Documented in Venezuelan regional folklore collections.

name: Mon-Daw-Min
description: Mon-Daw-Min is the sacred Corn Spirit of Ojibwe mythology. According to legend, a young boy named Wunzh went into the forest to fast and pray for guidance. After many days, a spirit appeared dressed in green and yellow with feathers on his head. The spirit challenged Wunzh to wrestle. Each day, Wunzh grew stronger. Finally, the spirit revealed himself as Mon-Daw-Min, a gift from the Creator. He instructed Wunzh to kill him, bury his body, and tend the grave. From the spirit's body sprouted the first corn plant — the kernels were his teeth, the silk his hair, and the stalk his body

name: Mong
description: Not independently attested as a spirit of Hopi folklore. No source records a forest spirit named 'Mong' with possession powers. The name almost certainly garbles Mongwa, the Hopi Great Horned Owl katsina, a warrior katsina who disciplines clowns at summer day dances and warns the village to mend its ways. The recorded traits appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Monster Slayer
description: Monster Slayer (Naayéé' Neizghání) is the elder of the Navajo Hero Twins, sons of Changing Woman and the Sun. Armed by his father with flint armor and lightning arrows, he and his brother Born-for-Water slew the Anayé, the unnatural monsters that were killing the Diné, among them the giant Yé'iitsoh, making the world safe for the People. He remains a model of courage for young Navajo today.

name: Monster Slayer (Naayééʼ Neizghání)
description: Monster Slayer (Naayééʼ Neizghání) is the elder of the Hero Twins of Navajo (Diné) tradition, son of Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé) and the Sun. With his younger brother Born-for-Water he travelled the Fifth World destroying the Anaye, the alien monsters that devoured the people, using weapons of lightning; he remains the great protector of the Diné.

name: Moon
description: In Apache tradition the Moon is closely bound to White Painted Woman (Changing Woman), the first being of the Chiricahua and Mescalero accounts, who created the sun and the moon. She carried the Sun's child, Killer-of-Enemies, and the Moon's child, Child of the Water; in Lipan accounts the Moon herself is identified with Changing Woman.

name: Moon (Tłʼéhonaaʼéí / White Shell Girl)
description: Tłʼéhonaaʼéí, the Moon, is the female celestial of Navajo (Diné) tradition, the younger sister and companion of the Sun Jóhonaaʼéí, with whom she was created from the sacred minerals of the universe. She is also known as White Shell Girl, carries the moon across the night sky, and her cycles mark time within the Diné ceremonial year.

name: Moon God (Guarani)
description: This entry conflates Kurupi with a moon deity. Kurupi is a Guaraní forest spirit, one of seven monstrous children of Tau and Kerana, known for his elongated prehensile phallus, backwards feet, and role as abductor/impregnator of women. He is a fertility figure and forest guardian, not a moon god.

name: Moon God (Guarani)
description: The record conflates two distinct Guarani figures. The genuine 'moon' being is Jasy Jatere, 'little piece of the moon,' the fourth of the seven cursed children of Tau and Kerana: a blonde child with a golden staff who sleeps by day and at noon lures children who nap into a trance, guarding yerba mate and the siesta. The Kurupi-like traits recorded belong to a different, unrelated monster.

name: Moon Maiden (Cherokee)
description: Not independently attested as a 'moon maiden' nature-spirit of Cherokee folklore. Genuine Cherokee tradition treats the Moon (nvdo svnoyi ehi, 'night dweller') as the celestial brother of the female Sun; he is addressed as a woman, Age'yaguga, in sacred formulas, and a giant toad, Walosi, is said to swallow him during eclipses. The forest-spirit traits recorded appear to be modern invention.

name: Moon Maiden (Cherokee)
description: Not independently attested in Cherokee folklore, and doubly misattributed: the Cherokee are a Southeastern nation, not Canadian. Cherokee moon tradition concerns nvdo svnoyi ehi, the Moon, brother of the female Sun, whom a giant toad (Walosi) swallows at eclipses, and who is addressed as a woman, Age'yaguga, in sacred formulas. No Cherokee 'moon maiden' nature-spirit exists in any source.

name: Moon Spirit
description: Moon Spirit (Unknown). is a spirit. A moon spirit is a celestial being from world mythology associated with the moon, controlling tides and fertility cycles.. Source: Japanese folklore; moon spirits appear in Kaguya-hime and related Japanese folk tales.

name: Moon Woman
description: Moon Woman is a significant supernatural figure in Haida mythology who features prominently in the Raven cycle. Raven became her son and cried incessantly until she allowed him to play with the moon. When she left, Raven transformed and escaped through the smoke hole with the moon under his wing. He flew to the Nass River where fishermen were taking olachen in total darkness, bargaining with them and offering light. He then broke the moon in half, creating night and day, and scattered fragments as stars

name: Moose Ancestor-Spirit (Ashanti)
description: Not independently attested: moose are not native to West Africa, and no moose ancestor-spirit appears in Ashanti sources. If a deer-like guardian was intended, the closest real analogue is the abosom, nature spirits honored by the Ashanti.

name: Moose Ancestor-Spirit (Ashanti)
description: A garbled entry combining 'Ashanti' with a Canadian moose ancestor spirit; no Ashanti (Ghana) tradition is associated with the moose, a species absent from West Africa. The nearest genuine parallels are Algonquian and Blackfoot traditions in which the moose appears as a provider or spirit being. Not independently attested; flagged as a data-merge error.

name: Moose Ancestor-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Blackfoot (Siksika) folklore. No source records a moose guardian 'of the cliffs' in Blackfoot tradition, whose spiritual life centers on Napi (Old Man), the Sun Dance, beaver bundles and the buffalo. Moose were scarce in Blackfoot plains territory and play no ancestor-spirit role. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Ancestor-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Blackfoot (Siksika) folklore. No source records a moose guardian 'of the cliffs' in Blackfoot tradition, whose religious life centers on Napi (Old Man), the Sun Dance and sacred bundles. Moose were scarce on the northern plains and no such ancestor-spirit appears in ethnographic records; the traits appear derived from speculation.

name: Moose Ancestor-Spirit of Haida
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Haida folklore. Haida Gwaii is a maritime archipelago where moose are not native, and Haida narratives center on Raven, the sea wolf (Wasgo), the killer whale and clan crest animals. No source records a moose ancestor-spirit 'guardian of the hills.' The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Ancestor-Spirit of Kikuyu
description: Not independently attested in Kikuyu tradition. Moose (Alces alces) are absent from East Africa. Kikuyu ancestor spirits (ngoma cia andu a kale) associate with indigenous fauna—elephant, leopard, hyena—or the sacred mugumo fig tree. This entry appears fabricated, conflating North American moose lore with Kikuyu spirituality. Closest analogue: Mugumo tree spirit.

name: Moose Ancestor-Spirit of Miwok
description: Not independently attested as an ancestor-spirit of Miwok folklore. Moose are absent from the California Sierra where the Miwok live, and Miwok traditions center on Coyote the trickster and other animal beings. No source records a moose ancestor-spirit 'guardian of the skies' in their tradition. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Ancestor-Spirit of Zulu
description: Not independently attested in Zulu tradition. Moose are not native to Africa. The record appears fabricated, templated with "guardian of lakes" motifs. No ethnographic source documents a moose ancestor-spirit in Zulu or any Southern African culture. Closest real analogues: eland or antelope ancestral spirits in San/Bantu cosmology.

name: Moose Deity (Inuit)
description: Not independently attested as a deity of Inuit folklore. Moose are absent from most Inuit lands, and no source records a moose god in Inuit cosmology, which centers on beings such as the sea goddess Sedna, the Moon Man (Anningan), Sila and Qailertetang. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Deity of Aztec
description: Not independently attested as a moose deity in Aztec folklore. Moose are not native to Mesoamerica, and no Aztec source records a river-guardian moose god. The closest genuine figures are Mesoamerican deer and water deities, such as the Mazatl deer symbolism of the Aztec calendar and the lake spirits of central Mexico; the moose appears to be a northern animal grafted onto Aztec myth.

name: Moose Deity of Lakota
description: Not independently attested as a deity of Lakota folklore. Moose are not native to Lakota plains and Black Hills territory, and no source records a moose god in Lakota tradition, which reveres Wakan Tanka, White Buffalo Calf Woman (Ptesan Wi), the Thunder Beings and the trickster Iktomi. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Deity of Ute
description: Not independently attested as a deity of Ute folklore. No source records a moose god among the Ute of the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau, whose traditions center on Sinawav, the wolf creator-culture hero, and his brother Coyote. Moose are marginal in Ute territory. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Ghost of Navajo
description: Not independently attested as a ghost of Navajo folklore. Moose are not native to traditional Diné territory, and no source records a moose ghost. Navajo tradition instead tells of the chindi, the lingering ghost of a dead person that can bring illness and requires ritual avoidance and proper burial. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Giant of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in Baloch folklore. Moose are not native to Balochistan (arid Pakistan/Iran/Afghanistan). Baloch oral tradition features tribal heroes (Mir Chakar Rind, Hammal Jiand), desert djinn (Mujna), and mountain spirits, but no moose giants. The record appears fabricated, possibly conflating North American moose mythology with Baloch culture.

name: Moose Giant of Ojibwe
description: Not independently attested as a giant of Ojibwe folklore. No source records a 'moose giant guarding the mountains' in Ojibwe tradition. The closest real figure is the giant Moose of Wabanaki legend, slain by the culture hero Gluskabe; among the Ojibwe the moose (mooz) is a clan animal and symbol of endurance, one of the miigis. The recorded traits appear derived from speculation.

name: Moose Giant of Ojibwe
description: Not independently attested as a giant of Ojibwe folklore. No source records a 'moose giant guarding the mountains' in Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) tradition. The giant-moose tale belongs instead to Wabanaki peoples (Gluskabe's monster moose); among the Ojibwe the moose is a clan animal and symbol of endurance and survival. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Guardian (Mapuche)
description: Not independently attested in Mapuche tradition. Moose (Alces alces) are native to North America and Eurasia, NOT South America. The Mapuche have no moose in their mythology. Their guardians include the Ngen (spirit owners of nature), Pillán (volcano spirits), and animal spirits like the fox (Zorro) or puma.

name: Moose Guardian (Mapuche)
description: Not independently attested as a moose guardian of Mapuche folklore, and wrongly tagged as Mexican. The Mapuche are a southern South American people; their true nature spirits are the ngen, 'owners' of each place and element — Ngen-mapu (earth), Ngen-ko (water), Ngen-wingkul (hill) — created by Pu-am and obedient to Antü. No moose appears anywhere in Mapuche tradition.

name: Moose Guardian of Apache
description: Not independently attested as a guardian of Apache folklore. No source records a moose guardian spirit among the Apache. The real mountain-dwelling guardian spirits of Apache tradition are the Gaan, the Mountain Spirit (Crown) Dancers who appear in ceremony to heal, protect and teach the people. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Guardian of Aymara
description: Not independently attested in Aymara tradition. Moose are absent from South America. Aymara high-altitude mythology (Altiplano) features camelids (llama, vicuña), condors, and fox tricksters, not moose. Lake guardians include the serpent Amaru and mountain deities (Achachila). 'Moose Guardian' is a fabricated template entry.

name: Moose Guardian of Mapuche
description: Not independently attested in Mapuche tradition. Duplicate of mooseguardianmapuche-chile with different habitat description ('undergrounds'). Moose are not native to South America. Mapuche underground spirits are the Ngen-mapu (earth owners) and Anchimayen (little people), not moose guardians.

name: Moose Guardian of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition. Moose are absent from South America. Muisca mythology (Bacatá/ Bogotá savanna) centers on Bochica, Chía, Sué, and lake deities (Sie). No cervid guardians of cliffs exist; snip the spectacled bear (oso de anteojos) is the largest native mammal. 'Moose Guardian' is a fabricated template entry.

name: Moose Nature-Spirit (Mixtec)
description: Not independently attested as a moose nature-spirit of Mixtec folklore. Moose do not inhabit Oaxaca, and no Mixtec source records a lake-dwelling moose spirit. The genuine Mixtec water and rain powers belong to Dzahui, the rain god with a Tlaloc-like goggle mask, and to mountain and spring 'owners' in Ñuu (Mixtec) tradition. The moose appears to be a misplaced northern animal.

name: Moose Nature-Spirit (Mixtec)
description: Not independently attested in Malagasy tradition. Mixtec are Indigenous people of Oaxaca, Mexico—not Madagascar. Moose absent from both Madagascar and Mesoamerica. Malagasy nature spirits include kalanoro (forest dwarf), kokolampo (water spirits), razana (ancestors). Cross-regional fabrication conflating Mexican Mixtec, North American moose, and Madagascar geography.

name: Moose Nature-Spirit (Mixtec)
description: Not independently attested, and geographically impossible: the Mixtec are a Mesoamerican people of Oaxaca, Mexico, where moose do not occur, and this record mislabels them as USA folklore. Mixtec tradition reveres deities such as Dzahui, the rain god, and the earth lord. No moose nature-spirit appears in any source. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Nature-Spirit (Mixtec)
description: Not independently attested as a moose nature-spirit of Mixtec folklore. The Mixtec are indigenous to Oaxaca, Mexico, not Guatemala, and moose are absent from both regions' traditions. No Mixtec or Maya source records a lake-guarding moose spirit. The closest real figures are Dzahui, the Mixtec rain god, and the water-owner ngen-like spirits of Mesoamerican mountain lore.

name: Moose Nature-Spirit of Cheyenne
description: Not independently attested as a nature-spirit of Cheyenne folklore. No source records a moose spirit among the Cheyenne, whose Plains traditions center on Maheo the Creator, the Sacred Arrows, and the buffalo as the people's life-giver. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Nature-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: Not independently attested as a nature-spirit of Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) folklore. No source records a moose spirit on the Northwest Coast, where the forest's wild-man figure is Bukwus, the Wild Man of the Woods, and the great figures are Dzunukwa and Sisiutl. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Nature-Spirit of Shona
description: Not independently attested in Shona tradition. Moose do not exist in Zimbabwe or southern Africa. The record is fabricated, using a template assigning "guardian of lakes" to a non-native animal. Shona water spirits involve mermaids (njuzu) or serpent beings, not moose.

name: Moose Nature-Spirit of Shoshone
description: Not independently attested as a nature-spirit of Shoshone folklore. No source records a moose spirit among the Shoshone of the Great Basin, whose traditions tell of Wolf and Coyote, the creators, and of the dangerous water babies (nu:numbi) of springs and lakes. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Spirit (Zapotec)
description: Not independently attested as a moose spirit of Zapotec folklore. Moose are not native to the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, and no Zapotec source records a cliff- or wilderness-dwelling moose spirit. Genuine Zapotec animal and nature powers belong to the tonas, personal companion-spirits, and to deities like Cocijo the rain god and Pitao Cozobi, god of maize. The moose is a misplaced northern animal.

name: Moose Spirit of Aymara
description: Not independently attested in Aymara tradition. Moose are native to the northern hemisphere and absent from South America; no ethnographic source records a moose spirit in Altiplano cosmology. The closest Andean analogue is the deer or vicuña as herd animal, but no named moose spirit exists.

name: Moose Spirit of Yoruba
description: Not independently attested: moose are not native to West Africa and no moose spirit appears in Yoruba sources. Closest real analogues are bush-cow or buffalo spirits and the wild forces associated with the forest in Yoruba religion.

name: Moose Trickster (Cree)
description: Not independently attested as a trickster of Cree folklore. Cree trickster stories belong to Wîsahkêcâhk, who in one famous tale gives the moose its baggy coat; the moose is a character in his stories, not itself a trickster. No source records a moose trickster in Cree tradition. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Trickster (Cree)
description: Not independently attested as a moose trickster of Cree folklore, and the Mexico country tag is wrong. The Cree are a North American people; their trickster is Wisakedjak (Wesakechak), not a moose. Moose do appear in northern Algonquian stories, but no moose trickster is recorded, and Cree tradition belongs to Canada and the northern US, not Mexico. The record conflates unrelated traditions.

name: Moose Trickster (Cree)
description: Not independently attested: the Cree are an indigenous people of North America, so a Cree moose trickster cannot be a Nigerian figure. The entry combines unrelated traditions and has no real analogue in Nigerian folklore.

name: Moose Trickster (Cree)
description: Not independently attested in Paraguay or Guarani tradition. The Cree are an Algonquian people of subarctic Canada; moose trickster figures (e.g., Wisahkecahk as moose) belong to Cree/Anishinaabe lore, not Paraguay. No moose exist in Paraguay.

name: Moose Trickster of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as a trickster of Blackfoot (Siksika) folklore. The Blackfoot trickster is Napi, Old Man, the bumbling yet powerful being who shaped the world and its customs through his deeds. No source records a moose trickster in Blackfoot tradition. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Trickster of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as a trickster of Blackfoot (Siksika) folklore. The Blackfoot trickster is Napi, Old Man, who shaped the world and its customs through his deeds. No source records a moose trickster in Blackfoot tradition. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Trickster of Kikuyu
description: Not independently attested in Kikuyu tradition. Moose do not exist in Kenya. Kikuyu trickster figures include the hare (mukambi) and spider in some tales, but no moose. Sacred mugumo tree hosts ancestor spirits. This repeats the North American moose fabrication seen in the ancestor-spirit record.

name: Moose Trickster of Shona
description: Not independently attested in Shona tradition. Moose are not native to Africa. This trickster entry repeats the fabricated moose template with "guardian of caves" motif. Shona trickster figures are typically hare (tsuro) or baboon, not moose.

name: Moose Trickster of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as a trickster of Tlingit folklore. The Tlingit trickster is Raven (Yéil), who stole the sun, the moon and the stars and shaped the world through his schemes. No source records a moose trickster on the Northwest Coast. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Trickster of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as a trickster of Tlingit folklore. The Tlingit trickster is Raven (Yéil), who stole the sun, moon and stars and transformed the world. No source records a moose trickster on the Northwest Coast. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Water-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as a water-spirit of Blackfoot folklore. No source records a moose water-spirit among the Siksika; Blackfoot traditions of springs, water and underground beings concern medicine power and the sacred beaver bundle, not moose. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Water-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as a water-spirit of Blackfoot folklore. No source records a moose water-spirit among the Siksika; Blackfoot water and underground traditions concern medicine power and sacred bundles rather than moose. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Water-Spirit of Cherokee
description: Not independently attested as a water-spirit of Cherokee folklore. Cherokee waters belong to beings such as the Uktena, the great horned serpent, the Long Man of the rivers, and the underground panthers of Mooney's tales. No moose water-spirit appears in any source. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moose Water-Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition. Moose are absent from South America; the Muisca of the Colombian Altiplano had no moose in their cosmology. Their water beings include the Monster of Lake Tota (serpent) and lake-dwelling spirits, but no moose.

name: Moose Water-Spirit of Paiute
description: Not independently attested as a water-spirit of Paiute folklore. The real water-beings of Paiute tradition are the dangerous water babies (pit-u-u), long-haired spirits of springs and lakes that lure people to drown and serve as spirit helpers for shamans. No moose water-spirit appears in any source. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Moppet
description: Not independently attested as 'Moppet' in Indian folklore. The description matches Arunachal Pradesh 'Yeti' variants (small hairy forest hominids) reported by Monpa, Sherdukpen, and other tribal groups. 'Moppet' appears to be an invented English name for local wild-man traditions (e.g., Miri 'Mande Barung', Mishmi 'Yeti' variants). Arunachal has numerous hominid cryptids but no canonical 'Moppet'.

name: Mora
description: Mora is a Serbian nocturnal spirit, often female, believed to press on the chest of sleeping people and cause nightmares and sleep paralysis. She may appear as a butterfly, moth, or shadow and can be driven off with a knife, a lamp, or by turning one's pillow; similar mara figures appear across the Balkans.

name: Mora
description: A nocturnal spirit that causes sleep paralysis by sitting on the chest of sleeping victims, suffocating them and draining their life energy. In Slovak belief, mora is not a demon but the soul of a living woman who leaves her body at night while her husband sleeps. She travels invisibly as a shadow or pressure, tormenting neighbors and relatives. Victims wake unable to move or speak, feeling a crushing weight on their chest—a phenomenon now understood as sleep paralysis In Slovakia folklore, this figure is known among the Slovakia people.

name: Morana
description: Morana (Marzanna, Morena) is the Slavic goddess of winter, death, and the harvest's end, honored in spring rituals across Czech, Polish, and Slovak lands. At the end of winter an effigy of Morana is carried to a river, set alight, and drowned to drive out the cold and welcome spring, one of the oldest surviving Slavic seasonal rites.

name: Moremi Ajasoro
description: Moremi Ajasoro was a legendary queen of Ile-Ife who sacrificed her own happiness to save her people from repeated raids by the neighboring Ugbo people. When Ife warriors could not defend against the Ugbo — who were disguised as forest spirits — Moremi allowed herself to be captured. Taken as a slave, she learned their secrets and escaped to reveal them to Ife, enabling victory. As a blood price, her beloved son Oluorogbo was taken by the gods. The Yoruba honor her courage with the annual Edi Festival, celebrating maternal sacrifice for the survival of the people

name: Morgan
description: Morgan (Unknown). is a witch. Morgan le Fay is a powerful enchantress in Arthurian legend, often depicted as King Arthur's half-sister. Her role ranges from healer to antagonist across different versions of the legend.. Source: Arthurian literary tradition; Vita Merlini (Geoffrey of Monmouth)

name: Morning Star
description: Morning Star is a powerful male warrior god in Pawnee mythology, the first being created by Tirawa. Placed in the East, he was commanded to overcome the Evening Star in the West, who resisted the divine plan to create humankind. Morning Star fought and conquered forces in the western sky with his fireball to mate with her, producing the first human. He is associated with warfare, sacrifice, and cosmic order. The Skidi Pawnee performed the Morning Star sacrifice ceremony—a ritual sacrifice of a captive girl to ensure agricultural fertility—reenacting the cosmic battle between Morning Star and Evening Star

name: Morning Star
description: Morning Star is a deity from Australia mythology. Placed in the East, he was commanded to overcome the Evening Star in the West, who resisted the divine plan to create humankind. description: Morning Star is a deity from Crow mythology. Placed in the East, he was commanded to overcome the Evening Star in the West, who resisted the divine plan to create humankind.
