name: Moroi
description: Moroi are the vengeful spirits of dead unbaptized children in Romanian folklore, who return to haunt their families at night, draining life force and bringing illness. As souls denied proper Christian burial, they embody fears around infant death and the power of unfinished rites. The term also names a class of Romanian vampiric undead related to the strigoi.

name: Moskkjerringa
description: Moskkjerringa (the Moskenes Old Woman) is a female troll of Moskenesøy in Lofoten, turned to stone and overlooking the Moskenesstraumen — the famous maelstrom or tidal whirlpool between Moskenesøy and Værøy islands. The rock formation of an old woman sits on the cliffs above the powerful tidal current. Moskkjerringa is said to have been a female jøtul or troll-woman who was fishing when the sun rose, freezing her in place with her fishing line still in the water. The Moskenesstraumen maelstrom is one of the world's strongest tidal currents, described by Edgar Allan Poe in his story A Descent into the Maelström. The Moskkjerringa rock formation warns sailors of the dangerous waters below. The legend ties together the dramatic sea conditions and the rock formation into a single story of a troll-woman caught by the sun while fishing

name: Moso
description: A giant from Samoan mythology who was among the first humans created by Tagaloa on the island of Savai'i. Moso was of such enormous size that he could step from one island to another. His footprint, pressed deep into solid lava rock at the village of Salelologa on Savai'i, remains a sacred site. According to legend, Moso used his foot to push the island of Upolu away from Savai'i, creating the Apolima Strait between them. He owned a legendary war club that could kill hundreds with a single swing. The footprint site is still visible and the story explains the geographical separation of Samoa's two main islands

name: Mosquito Animal-Spirit (Fijian)
description: In Fijian oral tradition the mosquito is explained by an origin legend told at Oneata in the Lau group, recounting how mosquitoes first came to plague humanity. The input's framing of a reef-guarding 'mosquito spirit' is not attested; the documented material is an aetiological tale of the insects' origins rather than a protective animal spirit.

name: Mosquito Guardian (Mari)
description: Not independently attested: no mosquito guardian spirit appears in documented Mari tradition, whose guardian figures center on the forest and household. The entry appears to be an invention; the closest real Mari analogues are the guardians of the sacred groves and the water spirits of the Volga region.

name: Mosquito Nature-Spirit ( Maori)
description: In Māori tradition the mosquito and sandfly (namu) were created from the powdery spores (puanga) of Haumia-tiketike, the atua of uncultivated food, to bite and humble humans. Their stinging presence teaches humility, a lesson often linked to the deeds of Māui. The record's 'protector of rainforests' framing is unsupported; the attested material is aetiological.

name: Moth Ancestor-Spirit (Hausa)
description: Not independently attested in Hausa tradition. No moth ancestor-spirit is recorded in ethnographic sources for the Hausa. Closest real analogues are protective animal spirits and the bori spirit hierarchy of Hausa folk religion.

name: Moth Guardian (Hausa)
description: Not independently attested: no moth guardian spirit appears in documented Hausa tradition, and the claim reads as generic fabrication. If a moth-like protective figure is intended, no real Hausa analogue is recorded.

name: Mothman
description: Mothman is a modern American cryptid of Point Pleasant, West Virginia: a gray, man-sized winged being with glowing red eyes, first reported in Nov 1966 near the abandoned TNT munitions site. About a hundred sightings followed before the 1967 Silver Bridge collapse killed 46 people; John Keel's The Mothman Prophecies (1975) made it a portent of doom. Skeptics cite a misidentified sandhill crane.

name: Mountain Giant (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Tupi-Guarani tradition. Tupi mythology includes forest giants like Curupira (red-haired dwarf), Caipora, and Mapinguari (giant sloth), but no specific 'Mountain Giant' deity by that name. The generic description suggests a conflation of multiple beings.

name: Mountain Giant (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested as a giant of Tupi-Guarani folklore in Canada: the Tupi are a Brazilian people, and this record wrongly assigns them to Canada. Genuine Tupi-Guarani forest beings include the hairy giant Mapinguari, the guardian Curupira, and the serpent Boitatá. No source records a 'mountain giant' among them. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Mountain Sheep
description: For the Southern Paiute, mountain sheep are powerful spirit helpers rather than ordinary game. Shamans (Puha'gants) acquire them through dreams and draw on their power in rain-making ceremonies, and rock art at Delamar Valley shows mountain sheep leading shamans through portals between worlds. A Paiute legend also tells of a mountain sheep that became the North Star.

name: Mountain Spirits
description: Not independently attested as a Navajo spirit-class of 'mountain spirits' who control weather and avalanches. Navajo mountain tradition centers on the Mountainway ceremony (Dsilyídje Qaçàl), whose hero Dsilyi Neyaani was sheltered by Holy People dwelling inside mountains. The Mountain-Spirit dancers (Gaan) belong to the Apache, not the Navajo. The recorded traits appear derived from speculation.

name: Moura Encantada
description: Moura encantadas are enchanted women of Portuguese folklore bound to megalithic monuments, who appear as beauties with golden or black hair combing their tresses and singing beside springs, dolmens, and cromlechs. They guard hidden treasures and may reward or punish those who encounter them. Documented by José Leite de Vasconcelos, these beliefs have guided archaeologists to ancient sites.

name: Mouros
description: Supernatural beings in Portuguese and Galician mythology, believed to be an ancient race that inhabited the land since the beginning of time before being forced underground for unknown reasons. The Mouros work gold, silver, and gemstones in subterranean forges beneath hills and ancient castro settlements, guarding enormous treasures protected by dragon-like cuélebres. They rarely emerge except to obtain food and during special liminal times like Midsummer (São João). Some appear as giants or warriors, while others take tiny forms called Mourinhos or Maruxinhos. The Moura Encantada (enchanted Moor woman) is their most famous manifestation. They are associated with megalithic monuments, and archaeologists have used Mouro legends to locate archaeological sites

name: Mouros
description: The Mouros are supernatural beings in Portuguese and Galician folklore, an ancient race forced underground. They work gold and silver in forges beneath hills and castro ruins, guarding treasure with dragon-like cuélebres, and surface mainly at liminal times such as Midsummer. The Moura Encantada is their best-known form, and their legends have guided archaeology.

name: Mouse Spirit
description: Mouse Spirit is a small but crucial helper spirit in Arapaho mythology. In the story of the Release of the Buffalo, a young man on a vision quest learned from Mouse Spirit that the buffalo were hidden in a cave beneath a mountain, guarded by a powerful spirit. Mouse Spirit revealed the cave entrance to the young man and taught him the songs needed to open the cave. With these songs, the young man opened the cave and the buffalo stampeded out, covering the plains. Mouse Spirit proves that even the smallest creatures possess important knowledge and power

name: Mousso Koroni
description: Mousso Koroni Koundye, 'the Beautiful Little Old Woman,' is the first woman of Bambara (Bamana) myth, created by Pemba from rotten wood and his saliva. Angered by his infidelity, she brought witchcraft and sorcery into the world, taught destructive arts and introduced menstrual taboos — the untamed, dangerous side of feminine creative power.

name: Moán
description: Moán is a Colombian forest spirit of the Pacific/Chocó and Amazon regions who protects wildlife and punishes hunters who break taboos. He appears as an old man or animal (tapir, peccary) and tests humans' ethics. Documented in Chocó and Andean-Amazonian folklore as a conservation-enforcing spirit.

name: Mugumo
description: Mugumo (Mũgumo) is the Kikuyu name for Ficus thonningii, the strangler fig, revered as vessel of Ngai (God) and ancestors. Cutting one invites curse; elders sacrifice roasted lamb beneath branches to call rain. The 2020 presidential decree protecting the Waiyaki Way fig tree exemplifies living sacred status. Central to oath-taking and circumcision rites. The tree itself is the numinous presence.

name: Mujna
description: Mujna (or Mujina) is a desert djinn (jinn) in Pakistani Baloch/Sindhi folklore. Appears to lost travelers in the desert, grants wishes but demands payment (often tragic). Part of Islamic-influenced folk belief in Balochistan and Sindh. Similar to Persian 'Mujina' (badger-shapeshifter) but localized as a desert wish-granting spirit. Documented in regional folk collections and oral accounts.

name: Mukasa
description: Mukasa is the most important of the Lubaale (national deities) of Buganda, the powerful god of Lake Victoria (Nalubaale). According to tradition, Mukasa was a human prince transformed into a lake deity because of his extraordinary wisdom and compassion. He lives in a magnificent palace beneath the lake, surrounded by spirit attendants. Mukasa governs the lake's bounty -- fish, calm waters, and storms. Fishermen make offerings of banana beer, coffee berries, and goat meat at his shrines. Mukasa is also a great oracle revealing the future through his priests (mandwa). The most famous shrine is on the Ssese Islands, where priestesses maintain a sacred fire that must never be extinguished. Mukasa is a merciful god who guides humanity toward wisdom through blessings

name: Muki
description: Muki (Muqui) is an Andean mining goblin of Quechua/Aymara tradition in Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia. A dwarf-like being with blonde hair, pale skin, and hypnotic eyes, he dwells in mines, whistles to warn favored miners, and makes pacts for coca or alcohol. Known regionally as chinchiliku, anchanchu, or jusshi.

name: Muladi
description: Not independently attested as a distinct entity in Brazilian folklore. The name resembles Afro-Brazilian entities (Exu, Pombagira) but no ethnographic source documents 'Muladi' as a specific demon. Likely a conflation of 'mulata' or a garbled Exu epithet.

name: Mulan
description: Mulan (Unknown). is a human. Hua Mulan is a legendary figure from Chinese folklore who disguised herself as a man to take her father's place in the army. Her story appears in the Ballad of Mulan, composed during the Northern Wei . Source: Ballad of Mulan (Northern Wei period); Chinese literary tradition

name: Muldjewangk
description: Muldjewangk is a malevolent water spirit of the Murray River region in Aboriginal tradition, dwelling in deep pools and the lower Murray and Lake Alexandrina. It capsizes boats and drags the unwary under, and the stories warn children against swimming alone in deep waters while some accounts cast it as guardian of the river's secrets.

name: Mumbi
description: Mumbi (meaning 'Molder' or 'Creator') is the first woman and founding mother of the Kikuyu people. According to Kikuyu creation mythology, Mumbi was found by Gikuyu at Mukurwe wa Gathanga, placed there by Ngai as a wife for the first man. Mumbi's name reflects her role as the molder and creator of the Kikuyu people, for she bore nine daughters who became the founders of the nine Kikuyu clans: Wanjiru, Wambui, Njeri, Wanjiku, Nyambura, Wairimu, Waithira, Wangari, and Wangui. These nine daughters form the matrilineal foundation of Kikuyu social organization, known as Nyumba ya Mumbi (the House of Mumbi). Though the daughters married nine men sent by Ngai, the clans are named after the daughters rather than their husbands

name: Mundugumor
description: Not independently attested in Kenyan folklore. Mundugumor is a people and language of the Yuat River, Papua New Guinea—documented by Margaret Mead (1930s) for 'rope' kinship and aggression studies. No cultural link to Kenya. This is a misattribution of the PNG ethnonym. Kenyan highland madness spirits are plausibly Kikuyu 'ngoma' possession or Maasai 'oloi' diviners.

name: Munkholmsånden
description: Munkholmsånden (the Spirit of Munkholmen) is a ghost that haunts Munkholmen island in Trondheimsfjorden. Munkholmen had a Benedictine monastery (Nidarholm) from the 1100s until the Reformation in 1537, when the monastery was destroyed on orders from Danish general Johan Rantzau. The island later served as a prison, a fortress, and an execution site. The ghost is said to be a monk who was killed when the monastery was sacked, or alternatively the spirit of a prisoner executed on the island. The ghost appears as a dark figure walking along the island's shores, sometimes carrying a lantern. Fishermen and sailors in the Trondheimsfjord have reported seeing the ghost for centuries. The spirit is most active on stormy nights and the anniversary of the monastery's destruction

name: Mutiara (The Magic Rooster)
description: Mutiara was a legendary fighting rooster owned by Awang Senuai, nephew of Brunei's first Sultan, Awang Alak Betatar (Sultan Muhammad Shah). The rooster was famed as undefeated in cockfighting. News of Mutiara's prowess reached Raden Angsuka Dewa, King of the Majapahit Empire, who challenged Awang Senuai to a match between Mutiara and his own champion rooster Asmara. During the epic fight, Asmara was fatally wounded and fled into the sea, transforming into Pulau Pilong-Pilongan island. Mutiara, in pursuit, was cursed by the Majapahit king and turned into Pulau Lumut-Lunting

name: Muzimu
description: The Calèche de Lallmatie is a spectral apparition seen in the village of Lallmatie. Local legend describes a ghostly carriage (calèche) drawn by two white horses and driven by two women dressed in white. The carriage is said to appear close to midnight, gliding silently through the streets. It is a classic ghost story that blends the elegance of the colonial era with the eerie nature of the supernatural, serving as a reminder of the island's vanished past In Uganda folklore, this figure is known among the Baganda people.

name: Mvelincanti
description: Mvelincanti (meaning 'He Who Was There from the Beginning') is the supreme creator god in traditional Swazi religion of Eswatini. Unlike the more actively involved deities in some African pantheons, Mvelincanti is considered too remote and transcendent to be directly involved in the daily affairs of humanity. Instead, the Swazi people direct their worship and petitions primarily toward the ancestral spirits known as emadloti, who act as intermediaries between the supreme creator and the living. This theological structure reflects a common pattern in Southern Bantu religions where the high god is acknowledged as the ultimate source of all existence but is too distant for everyday worship. Mvelincanti is credited with creating the world, humanity, and the natural order, after which he withdrew from direct engagement with creation. The Swazi monarchy, particularly the king, traditionally held a semi-divine status as an intermediary between Mvelincanti, the ancestors, and the people, reinforcing the sacred nature of Swazi kingship

name: Myling
description: Myling (Swedish), utburd (Norwegian), or ihtiriekko (Finnish) is the ghost of an unbaptized/murdered child in Scandinavian folklore. Abandoned in forests, the child's soul cannot rest. It weeps at night, revealing the mother's crime. It chases lone wanderers, jumps on their backs demanding to be carried to hallowed ground — growing heavier near the cemetery until the carrier sinks.

name: Myromskåna
description: Myromskåna (the Bog Woman) is a female marsh spirit from Setesdal folklore in Sørlandet. The myromskåna dwells in the extensive bogs and marshes of the Setesdal valley floor and leads travelers astray into dangerous mires. She appears as an old woman dressed in grey rags, often beckoning for help from the edge of the bog. When someone approaches to assist, she leads them deeper into the marsh until they become trapped in the quicksand-like mire. The myromskåna is distinct from the more general Norwegian skrømt in that she is specifically a female bog spirit, not a shapeless apparition. She is also distinct from the hulder — she does not seduce but rather deceives through pity. She was particularly feared by travelers crossing the marshy areas of Setesdal, where the valley bottom is prone to flooding and bog formation. Johannes Skar cataloged myromskåna in his collection of Setesdal folk belief as a distinct being of the wetlands

name: Mythic Animals
description: Not a single attested being: 'Mythic Animals' is a catch-all category, not a figure of Blackfoot folklore. Genuine Blackfoot mythic animals include the buffalo and the Iniskim (buffalo stone), Napi's animal companions, and the underwater people of springs. No source records a Blackfoot entity named 'Mythic Animals.' The recorded traits appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Mythic Animals
description: Not independently attested as a single named being. 'Mythic Animals' is a general category, not a specific figure in any Canadian Indigenous tradition, and the record's 'Blackfoot' label is unsupported. Real Canadian folklore names individual beings such as the Anishinaabe underwater panther Mishipeshu, the Great Horned Serpent, or the Thunderbird, each with its own distinct mythology.

name: Mzé Moya
description: Mzé Moya is the Comorian creator deity who descended from heaven to shape the volcanic islands, bringing water, vegetation, and life. Venerated in Comorian oral tradition (ngoma ya Mzé Moya), he establishes the sacred bond between people and land. Associated with Mount Karthala's fertility. Name from Swahili mzee (elder) + moya (spirit/air). Documented in Comorian folklore collections.

name: Mátsailéma (Evening Star, War God)
description: Mátsailéma is the Zuni god of war and the Evening Star, the younger twin of Áhaiyúta; together the brothers are the Áhayuta, the Twin War Gods of Zuni tradition. In Cushing's tale the pair fared with the Unborn-Made Men of the underworld, and warriors and priests invoke them in the great war ceremonial.

name: Máttaráhkká
description: Máttaráhkká (Origin Woman) is the primordial mother goddess in Sami shamanism, the most ancient of the female divinities. She lives in the ground beneath the goahti, opposite the door in the maadtere (women's sacred space). She is the great ancestress who receives the human soul from Radien-attje and gives it life before passing it to her daughter Sáráhkká who places it in the womb. She makes female humans and animals fertile. Her name literally means 'origin woman' or 'ancestral mother.' According to Christfried Ganander (1789), she receives the child from Radien-attje, breathes life into it, then hands it to Sáráhkká. Some sources give her a husband, Máttaráhttje, but he has a much smaller role and is considered a later addition. She and her three daughters (Sáráhkká, Juoksáhkká, Uksáhkká) form the core group of Sami domestic goddesses. On the Kola Peninsula, the Sami used the word mändir-ähke meaning 'parent's grandmother,' suggesting she was originally a female ancestor buried in the ground and worshipped by later generations

name: Máttaráhkká
description: Máttaráhkká is a goddess from Sápmi mythology. She lives in the ground beneath the goahti, opposite the door in the maadtere (women's sacred space). She is the great ancestress who receives the human soul from Radien-attje and gives it life before passing it to her daughter Sáráhkká who places it in the womb. name: Mô-sîn-á
description: Mô-sîn-á (魔神仔), also romanized mo-sin-a or mosina, are small, hairy, nimble spirits of Taiwanese folklore, pictured as child- or monkey-like beings in mountains, forests, and wild country across the island's ethnic groups. They lead travelers astray, daze victims with illusions, and feed them filth disguised as food; remedies include shouting the lost person's name and making loud noises.

name: Mörksugga
description: Mörksugga (Swedish: 'dark sow') is a legendary pig-like creature from Dalarna, Sweden — a black wild boar with glowing eyes and large tusks, used as a bogeyman to frighten children from staying out after dark. Traditionally fearsome, it was reimagined in modern times (Verner Molin's art, Andrzej Sapkowski's Witcher) as a guardian against darkness.

name: Møllergut
description: Møllergut (mill boy) is a milder, more helpful mill spirit in Norwegian folklore, counterpart to the malicious kvernknurr. The møllergut is a young apprentice spirit who helps the miller with his work — cleaning the millstones, carrying sacks of grain, and keeping the mill race clear of debris. Unlike the kvernknurr who deliberately breaks the mill, the møllergut assists if treated kindly. He expects small offerings — a bowl of porridge left in the mill at night, or a piece of flatbread. If neglected, he becomes mischievous rather than truly destructive — hiding the miller's hat, switching grain sacks, or making strange noises. The møllergut is particularly associated with the smaller farm mills of Vestlandet where a single miller worked alone at night. He represents the more benign, childlike spirits of Norwegian folk belief

name: Māui
description: Māui is the supreme trickster and culture hero of the Māori, a demigod who slowed the sun, fished up the North Island, stole fire from Mahuika, and attempted to conquer death by passing through Hine-nui-te-pō. Shape-shifting and supernaturally strong, he used wit and daring to better the world for humans, becoming the pattern of the Polynesian culture hero.

name: Mộng
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Vietnamese folklore; 'Mộng' is simply the Vietnamese word for dream. The recorded ability to send prophetic or frightful dreams matches the attested Vietnamese belief in báo mộng, a dream message—most often from an ancestor or deceased relative seeking help, atonement, or a ritual act.

name: Mỵ Châu (Princess of Cổ Loa)
description: Mỵ Châu is the tragic princess of the Âu Lạc kingdom in Vietnamese foundation legend. Married to Trọng Thủy, son of the Chinese invader Triệu Đà, she revealed the secret of the magic crossbow built from the Golden Turtle god's claw, and the kingdom fell. Her father King An Dương Vương slew her; her blood became pearls only Trọng Thủy's well-water could cleanse, and he drowned himself in it.

name: N Kk
description: N Kk (Unknown). is a spirit. Nakki is a Finnish water spirit that lures children to drown in lakes and rivers, appearing beautiful from the front but hideous and mossy from behind.. Source: Norwegian folklore — spirit documented in Norwegian oral tradition.

name: Na Kika
description: Na Kika is the giant octopus god of Kiribati (Gilbertese) mythology, child of the primal parents Na Atibu and Nei Teukez. In creation accounts he worked alongside the spider-god Nareau to raise the islands of the Pacific from the sea, his tentacles spreading across the ocean floor. He guards the deep waters and symbolizes the secrets and mysteries beneath the ocean surface.

name: Na'pi
description: Na'pi (Old Man) is the primary culture hero, creator figure, and trickster of Blackfoot mythology. Created by Apistotoke as the first man and demigod, Na'pi shaped the world using mud brought by Turtle during a great flood. He created humans from clay, taught the Blackfoot which plants to eat and animals to hunt, and introduced buffalo. Na'pi is simultaneously wise creator and foolish trickster—he made the land, established the seasons, gave people fire, but also gets into endless trouble through greed, pride, and foolishness. His adventures include the rolling skull, the mossy rock, stealing summer, and the creation of death (when Kipitaakii threw a stone instead of wood into the river)

name: Naato'si
description: Naato'si is the sun deity of the Blackfoot, a name meaning 'holy one' rather than simply 'sun.' Created by the high god Apistotoke, he rules the sky with his wife, the moon Komorkis, and their children are the stars; his son Morning-Star is grandfather to the hero Star Boy (Poia). He is central to the Sun Dance, whose rites and sweat lodge came to the people through his gifts.

name: Nacken
description: Nacken (Unknown). is a water-spirit. Necken is a water spirit from Scandinavian folklore, a skilled male fiddler who lures women and children to watery graves with his enchanting music.. Source: Scandinavian folklore — the Näcken water spirit documented in Nordic folklore.

name: Nafanua
description: The greatest warrior goddess of Samoa, daughter of Saveasi'uleo (god of Pulotu, the spirit underworld) and Tilafaiga. Born a female, Nafanua was hidden in the forest by her mother out of shame at giving birth to a girl. She emerged as a fierce warrior when Samoa was oppressed by tyrannical rulers. She disguised her chest so enemies would not know she was a woman. Nafanua led rebellions that freed the people of Savai'i from bondage, then brought peace after winning the wars between eastern and western districts. She established the matai (chiefly) system of governance and is Samoa's most revered war goddess. After her earthly exploits, she returned to Pulotu, the spirit underworld

name: Nag-drang
description: Not independently attested as a named protective deity of Tibetan Buddhism. No source documents a 'Nag-drang' figure among Tibetan protective deities. The recorded description — fierce or peaceful protectors invoked in rituals — matches the general category of srung ma/dharmapāla protectors, but no specific deity bears this name. The entry appears to generalize these attested categories.

name: Naga
description: Nagas are divine half-human, half-serpent beings in Hindu and Buddhist tradition, children of sage Kashyapa and Kadru. They dwell in Patala (netherworld), guard treasures and waters, and can take human or serpent form. Vasuki served as churning rope in Samudra Manthana; Shesha supports Vishnu. They are eternal rivals of Garuda.

name: Naga (Burmese)
description: The naga is the great serpent being of Myanmar, entwined with Buddhism and royal symbolism: a multi-headed, dragon-like serpent that guards rivers, lakes, and treasures, may appear as friend or foe to humans, and is venerated at shrines and along the Ayeyarwady. Serpent-king tales link the naga to rainfall, fertility, and the protection of the faith; images of it crown pagodas and palace gates.

name: Naga (Burmese)
description: Same naga tradition as the Myanmar entry: in Thailand the naga (phaya nak) is a serpent deity of rivers, lakes, and the underworld, guarding water sources and treasures and appearing with multiple heads. It aids or opposes humans, and is central to Buddhist legends, temple iconography, and the Naga Fireballs. The input duplicates the Burmese figure under a Thai attribution.

name: Naga Berani (Dragon of Brunei Bay)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. No Brunei legend names a 'Naga Berani' guarding Brunei Bay, and the celestial-guardian and sunken-kingdom details are unattested. Naga serpent-dragon motifs are real across Malay folklore and appear in Brunei's epic of Awang Semaun, but not as this specific bay dragon.

name: Nagual (Nahual)
description: The nagual (Nahuatl nāhualli) is a Mesoamerican shapeshifter bound to a person's animal spirit-double. Sorcerers and dreamers transform at night into jaguars, dogs, birds or other beasts; the Maya know the same being as way, written with a glyph of a jaguar-spotted spirit. Good or harmful, the nagual expresses a deep, lifelong link between a person and an animal guardian.

name: Nahual
description: El Nahual (or Nagual) is a shapeshifting witch or sorcerer from Mesoamerican tradition with deep roots in Aztec and Maya cosmology. The belief, originating with the Nahua peoples, holds that certain individuals possess the spiritual power to transform into animals — most commonly jaguars, coyotes, dogs, owls, or turkeys. In Aztec tradition, each person is born with a tonal (animal spirit companion) linked to their birth date, but only those with special power (nagualism) can actually assume the animal's form. The god Tezcatlipoca was the protector of nagualism. During the colonial period, Indigenous shamans were conflated with European witchcraft beliefs. In Mexican-American folklore of the Southwest, nahuales are feared for their ability to cause illness, steal livestock, and harm enemies. In some Indigenous communities, however, the nahual is a respected protector of the people and natural resources. The nagual was popularized in English by Carlos Castaneda's controversial books, but authentic nagualism remains a living tradition in rural Mexico and among Mexican-American communities

name: Nahuelito
description: Nahuelito is a Patagonian lake monster of Nahuel Huapi Lake, Argentina. First reported 1897 by Dr. Onelli; 1910 Garret sighting (5-7m serpent). 1960 Navy 18-day sonar pursuit. 1988 photos in Río Negro newspaper. Described as giant serpent, huge hump, or plesiosaur. Name from Mapuche 'nahuel' (jaguar). Indigenous antecedents likely; cryptozoological status unresolved.

name: Nahurac
description: Nahurac are powerful spirit animals in Pawnee religion upon whom Tirawa conferred miraculous powers. They serve as Tirawa's messengers and servants and can intercede with him on behalf of the Pawnee people. The nahurac had five sacred underground lodges: Pahuk (hill island on the Platte River), Lalawakohtito (dark island in the Platte), Ahkawitakol (white bank on the Loup River), Kitzawitzuk (sacred spring on the Solomon River), and Pahur (guide rock hill). These five lodges were places of spiritual power where the nahurac gathered. Pawnee would visit these sites to seek guidance, healing, and blessings from the animal spirits

name: Nai Tiki
description: Nai Tiki is a forest creature of Fijian mythology, a half-human, half-beast being said to combine animal strength with human cunning. Possessed of extraordinary power and speed, it can command the weather, calling rain and sun over the Fijian wilderness it inhabits. It captures the Fijian understanding of the boundary between the human and animal worlds.

name: Nainas
description: Nainas is a Sami mythological figure associated with the Northern Lights (Aurora Borealis). In Sami tradition, the Northern Lights are sometimes seen as warrior spirits or celestial beings, and Nainas embodies this concept. In the romantic Sami folk tale 'The Daughter of the Moon and the Son of the Sun,' Nainas leads a band of Northern Light warriors who enter an empty house by the sea at dusk. When the Sun sees Nainas and pins him with a heat shaft, the Moon's daughter Niekia shields Nainas and is seized by the Sun. The Moon rescues her daughter, and Niekia ultimately chooses love with the Northern Lights (Nainas) over the Sun's son Peivalke. This story portrays Nainas as a heroic, romantic figure — the personification of the aurora as a beautiful and powerful warrior. In broader Sami tradition, the Northern Lights were treated with both awe and fear — some believed they were the souls of the dead playing ball with a walrus skull, and one should not whistle at them or they would descend and carry you away

name: Naiye' (devouring monster)
description: Naiye' is the devouring giant of White Mountain Apache tradition recorded by Pliny Earle Goddard in 1910. In the tale, the giant swallows the people's world; the twins born to the Sun's maiden then kill the monster, and from the Sun they receive the name Naiyenezgani, 'Monster Slayer.' The story is part of the origin cycle of the White Mountain Apache.

name: Naiyenezgani (Monster Slayer)
description: Naiyenezgani, 'Monster Slayer' or 'Killer of Enemies,' is the elder of the Hero Twins of the Navajo, with a Chiricahua Apache cognate, Naaghéé'neesgháné, often rendered 'Killer of Enemies.' The Navajo hero is a warrior of unmatched strength, while the Apache counterpart is often comic and cowardly. Both twins rid the world of the monsters that plagued the first people.

name: Nakhoda Manis
description: Nakhoda Manis is a central figure in Brunei's most famous folklore, the legend of Jong Batu. He was a wealthy sailor who refused to acknowledge his poor elderly mother when she came to greet his ship upon his return to Brunei. As his mother cursed him for his unfilial behavior, a sudden storm capsized his ship, turning it into a stone outcrop known as Jong Batu in the Brunei River. The rock formation resembles a sinking ship with its bow protruding from the water, serving as a permanent reminder of the consequences of disrespecting one's parents

name: Nakshimo
description: Not independently attested in any recorded Native American tradition. No ethnographer, tribal history, or published collection describes a being named Nakshimo, and the name appears in none of the standard references for North American folklore. The entry appears to be a garbled or invented figure.

name: Nalusa Chito
description: Nalusa Chito, also called Impa Shilup, 'the soul eater,' is the great black shadow being of Choctaw belief. It was said to creep inside a person who let evil thoughts or despair take hold, devouring the soul from within. Many in the Choctaw Nation avoid speaking its name for fear of drawing it, a practice recorded in the tribe's own traditions and in studies of Choctaw mythology.

name: Nalusa Falaya
description: Nalusa Falaya, 'the long black being,' is a feared shadow creature of Choctaw tradition. Usually a tall, gaunt humanoid with small eyes and long pointed ears, it is said to slither like a snake or melt into dusk shadows, frightening children who stay out too late and waylaying lost hunters, sometimes passing on its harmful power with a thorn. Its young drift as small lights along the marsh.

name: Nambi
description: Nambi is the daughter of Ggulu (also known as Mugulu), the sky god in Baganda mythology, and becomes the wife of Kintu, the first man. She plays a crucial role as the bridge between the celestial and earthly realms. According to the creation myth, Nambi and her younger sister first discovered Kintu wandering alone on Earth with his cow. Fascinated by this first human, Nambi approached him and later insisted they return to her father in heaven together. After Kintu passed Ggulu's trials, Nambi married him and descended to Earth, bringing essential gifts of agriculture including millet and banana cultivation. She is revered as the mother of all people and associated with fertility and the earth. However, her decision to send her brother Walumbe back to retrieve forgotten grain from heaven allowed death to enter the human world. Nambi embodies both the nurturing force that enables human civilization and the human error that introduced mortality

name: Namdalsdraugen
description: Namdalsdraugen (the Namdalen Draug) is a sea draug specific to the Namdalen coast and the Namsenfjorden area of northern Trøndelag. Namdalen has a long and rich fishing tradition, and the Namdalsdraugen is the embodiment of the dangers of the Namdalen coast, one of the most treacherous stretches of water in Norway. The Namdalsdraugen is said to be the combined spirit of all those who have drowned in the Namsenfjorden and along the Namdalen coast. Unlike a single draug, the Namdalsdraugen can appear in multiple places at once, a reflection of the many shipwrecks in this area. It appears as a half-human, half-seaweed figure with glowing eyes, sitting on the rocks or floating just beneath the surface. When the Namdalsdraugen is seen, it means someone will drown within three days. The only way to protect oneself is to carry a piece of iron or to draw a cross on the boat's prow. The legend is strongest in the fishing villages of Namsos, Osen, Flatanger, and Vikna

name: Namorroddo
description: Namorroddo are malevolent shapeshifting spirits of Arnhem Land Aboriginal tradition, vampiric beings that strike at night, sinking their claws into sleeping victims and transforming them into new Namorroddos. Tied to the shadows and darkness, they embody the dangers of the night world in Australian Indigenous belief and are invoked in warnings to the unwary.

name: Nana Buluku
description: Nana Buluku (Unknown). is a deity. Nana Buluku is the supreme creator god in the Fon and Ewe cosmologies of Benin and Togo. This androgynous deity gave birth to the twin gods Mawu (moon) and Lisa (sun) who govern creation.. Source: Fon and Ewe cosmology; Dahomean mythology

name: Nanabolele
description: The Nanabolele are horrid, reptilian creatures from Basotho mythology that live underwater and underground in the Lesotho highlands. Their most distinctive feature is their ability to glow in the darkness, giving off a luminous light similar to that of the moon and stars. These creatures are often described as a type of water-dwelling reptile or serpent with bioluminescent properties, making them both beautiful and terrifying. According to legend, the nanabolele skin, which shines in the dark, was highly prized by the Basotho people. The most famous story tells of a brave woman named Thakane who, along with her brothers, hunted the nanabolele, cutting and preparing their glowing skin into clothing, armor, and weapons that would provide light in the darkness. The nanabolele are associated with the dark, cold waters of Lesotho's rivers and mountain streams, and they represent the hidden dangers and mysterious beauty of the underwater world

name: Nanabozho
description: Nanabozho is the trickster-transformer and culture hero of the Ojibwe people, central to their creation stories and oral traditions. As the son of Epingishmook (the West Wind) and a human mother, he was born with great spiritual power and raised by his grandmother Nokomis. He created the world anew after a great flood, formed Turtle Island from mud brought up by the muskrat, gave the people corn and fire, taught them hunting and fishing, and established the Midewiwin society. He is a shapeshifter who can appear as a man or a great hare (Mishaabooz)

name: Nanabush
description: Nanabush, also called Nanabozho, Wenabozho, or Waynaboozhoo, is the great culture hero and trickster of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe, Odawa, Potawatomi) and many Algonquian nations. A shapeshifter born of a mortal mother and the West Wind, he remade the world after a great flood and taught the people how to live. His tales are told in winter and carry both laughter and sacred teaching.

name: Nanabush
description: Nanabush, known in his many nations as Nanabozho or Wenabozho, is the culture hero and trickster of the Anishinaabe and neighboring Algonquian peoples whose lands span the Great Lakes on both sides of the United States-Canada border. Through his adventures he remade the world and taught the people to live. His stories, told when snow covers the ground, mix comedy and sacred instruction.

name: Nanan
description: Not independently attested: no Bajan spirit named Nanan or 'Old Woman of the Woods' guarding Welchman Hall Gully appears in documented Barbadian folklore, which features figures such as the Heartman, Baccoo, Rolling Calf, duppies and Soucouyant.

name: Nanapush
description: Nanapush is a spirit sent by Kishelamakank (the Creator) to restore harmony to the Lenape people after they fell into conflict over a magical bear tooth. Nanapush gathered the warring peoples together at a council fire and introduced the sacred pipe ceremony, teaching them to smoke tobacco as a sign of peace. He declared that no pipe could be lit in anger and that to smoke together was to call the Creator as witness. Nanapush's teachings laid the foundation for Lenape spiritual practices and the use of the sacred pipe in ceremonies

name: Nandi Bear (Chemosit)
description: Nandi Bear (Chemosit) (Kenya). is a cryptid. Large powerful bear-like or hyena-like creature from Nandi folklore. Source: Nandi folklore — the Chemosit werehyena/cryptid documented in Kenyan oral tradition.

name: Nang Kwak (Cat-Calling Prosperity Goddess)
description: Nang Kwak (Thai: นางกวัก) is a benevolent female deity in Thai folklore who brings good fortune, prosperity, and customers to businesses. She is depicted as a beautiful woman in traditional Thai dress, seated with her right hand raised in a beckoning gesture — the 'cat-calling' wave that draws customers and wealth. According to legend, Nang Kwak was a virtuous woman who was granted supernatural powers by the Buddha to attract wealth and abundance. Her origins connect to pre-Buddhist Tai folk religion and spirit traditions of Siam. Nearly every shop, restaurant, and business in Thailand displays a statue of Nang Kwak near the entrance. Her imagery is also linked to Suvannamaccha, the golden mermaid from the Thai Ramakien epic. The legend teaches that prosperity comes not from greed but from kindness, hard work, and generosity

name: Nang Phisuea Samud (Sea Ogress)
description: Nang Phisuea Samud (Thai: นางผีเสื้อสมุทร) is a powerful sea ogress from the Thai national epic Phra Aphai Mani by Sunthorn Phu. She is a giant ogress of the deep ocean who kidnapped Prince Aphai Mani after hearing his enchanted flute playing. Despite her terrifying appearance as a sea monster, she fell deeply in love with the prince and kept him imprisoned in her undersea cave palace for eight years. During this time, she bore him a son named Sin Samudr. The story explores themes of love across boundaries — the ogress loves genuinely but cannot overcome her predatory nature. She was ultimately killed by Aphai Mani's flute magic when she attacked the island where he had taken refuge. Nang Phisuea Samud represents the complex portrayal of non-human beings in Thai literature: monstrous yet capable of deep emotion, loving yet ultimately destructive

name: Nang Tani (นางตานี)
description: Nang Tani (นางตานี) is a Thai female spirit of the banana tree: she appears as a beautiful young woman who haunts wild banana groves, especially under a full moon. Generally kind, she protects those who respect the trees, but may be vengeful if the trees are cut; offerings are made before harvesting. Documented by Thai scholar Phya Anuman Rajadhon, she remains a living village belief.

name: Nang Wanla (Mermaid of Phra Aphai Mani)
description: The mermaid of the Thai epic Phra Aphai Mani by Sunthorn Phu (1822-1844) rescues Prince Aphai Mani from the sea ogress Nang Phisuea Samut, then bears his son Sudsakorn, born on the isle of Ko Kaeo Phitsadan. Unnamed when first met, she is later called Chantawadee and becomes a queen. The tale is taught in Thai schools and memorialized in statues on Ko Samet.

name: Nangona
description: Not independently attested in documented Fijian folklore or academic sources. No dedicated source confirms a forest spirit named Nangona dwelling in banyan or other sacred trees. While Fijian belief does attach spirits to sacred trees and groves, the specific name and protective traits recorded in the input could not be verified.

name: Nanikili
description: Nanikili is a sea demon of Samoan belief, an aitu (spirit of the dead or supernatural being) that lurks in coral reefs and rocky shores, attacking swimmers and fishermen. Tradition holds that it can be slain but returns to life unless it is properly destroyed, and its strikes are invoked to explain drownings and missing fishers. It reflects the perils Samoans associate with the sea.

name: Nanook
description: Nanook is the master of polar bears in Inuit tradition, the great bear who decides whether a hunter succeeds. When a bear is killed, its hide is hung in a place of honor within the igloo and stays there for several days, and small offerings, tools for the bear's soul, are made so that its spirit will return. Such respect keeps the hunting balance between humans and the animals that sustain them.

name: Nara Ga
description: Not independently attested in Sri Lankan tradition as 'Nara Ga'. The name appears to be a garbled transliteration of 'naga' (serpent) or 'nakra' (crocodile). Sri Lankan folklore includes crocodile spirits (kimbula deviyo) and naga traditions from Hindu-Buddhist influence, but no distinct entity called 'Nara Ga'.

name: Narasimha
description: Narasimha (Sanskrit: नरसिंह, 'man-lion') is the fourth avatar of Vishnu, a major Hindu deity — not a folklore creature. He emerged from a pillar to slay the demon Hiranyakashipu and protect the devotee Prahlada, embodying divine intervention beyond normal rules. Worshipped widely in temples with specific iconography (lion head, human torso, claws).

name: Narcissus
description: Narcissus (Unknown). is a human. Narcissus is a figure from Greek mythology, a beautiful youth who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool of water. Unable to leave his own image, he wasted away and was transformed into the na. Source: Metamorphoses (Ovid, 8 CE); Greek mythological tradition

name: Nareau
description: Nareau ('the spider') is the creator god of I-Kiribati cosmology, who emerged in the celestial void and wove order out of chaos, separating the sky from the sea and shaping the first islands. With the aid of beings he created, including the octopus Na Kika, he gave form to the Pacific world. Credited with omniscience, he is the architect of the Kiribati cosmos.

name: Nash Bear
description: Not independently attested in any recorded Native American tradition of the United States. No published ethnography, tribal narrative, or reference work documents a spirit called the Nash Bear, and the entry appears to be an invented or garbled figure. Honoring the bear as a powerful relative, however, is genuinely widespread across Algonquian, Siouan, and Iroquoian nations alike.

name: Nash Bear
description: Not independently attested in any recorded Canadian First Nations tradition. No published collection or tribal account documents a spirit named the Nash Bear, and the entry appears to be invented or garbled. Across Canada, however, the bear is a deeply honored being: a clan ancestor, medicine spirit, and guardian among nations such as the Cree, Ojibwe, and Coast Salish.

name: Nasnās
description: Nasnās is a monstrous creature from Arabian folklore, described as half a human being with half a head, half a body, one arm, and one leg, hopping with agility. According to Arab tradition, the Nasnās was believed to be the offspring of a Shiqq (a half-formed jinn) and a human. In the Hadramaut region of Arabia, Nasnās were said to be eaten by locals who considered their flesh sweet. One was reportedly brought alive to Caliph al-Mutawakkil, described as resembling a man with only half a face located on its chest and a sheep-like tail. In Shia sources, the Nasnās lived on earth before humanity and were replaced by humans due to the destruction they caused

name: Nat
description: Nats are the spirits of Burmese folk religion, a pantheon of 37 official 'great nats' and countless local spirits. Most are souls of people who died violent or unjust deaths, gaining supernatural power, and they inhabit hills, trees, rivers, and death sites. Worshipped with offerings alongside Buddhism, they can bless or afflict; nat mediums (nat kadaw) channel them in trance.

name: Natravn
description: Natravnen (the Night Raven) is the ghost of a wicked person or unbaptized child in Danish folklore, condemned to fly as a raven with holes in its wings until Judgment Day. Unlike the intelligent Valravn, the Natravn is a damned soul trapped in bird form, endlessly flying from west to east trying to reach the Holy Sepulchre before cockcrow. Looking through the holes in its wings means immediate death for the viewer. The Natravn was created when a conjured ghost's term expired — if a 'klog mand' (wise man) summoned a ghost to answer questions, and the ghost failed to return to its grave before the pact ended, it became a Natravn. It cannot cross running water. At Hagensholm in Jylland, a Natravn flew nightly across the same route for decades, always turning back before cockcrow

name: Nats (37 Great Nats)
description: The 37 Great Nats are the official pantheon of Burmese spirit religion, formalized by King Anawrahta in the 11th century. Most were humans who met violent or unjust deaths and became powerful spirits—kings, princes, and commoners—honored through offerings and festivals like Taungbyon. Including Thagyamin (from Hindu Indra) and Mahagiri, their cult coexists with Theravada Buddhism.

name: Nattramn
description: Nattramnen (night raven) is the tortured ghost of an unbaptized child or a suicide victim, forced to wander the night as a spectral raven or crow. The creature was extensively documented by the 19th-century folklorist Gunnar Olof Hyltén-Cavallius in Småland. Nattramnen flies only from west to east, never lower than an ox's yoke, and its wings make a creaking sound like an ungreased wagon wheel. It is doomed to fly ceaselessly until it reaches the grave of Christ — an impossible journey. Anyone who sees or hears a Nattramn is said to receive a warning of death or misfortune. In some traditions, the Nattramn can be freed if someone brave enough catches it and sprinkles holy water over it, or if the unbaptized child is given a name posthumously

name: Nautsiti (Full Basket)
description: Nautsiti (Full Basket) is one of the two creator sisters in Acoma Pueblo mythology, alongside Iatiku. She was born underground at Shipapu and guided by Tsichtinako to the surface world. Nautsiti had more in her basket than Iatiku. She introduced death into the world when she disobeyed a taboo. Despite this, her contributions were essential to the creation of the world and the establishment of human society. She represents abundance, the potential for both creation and destruction, and the dual n

name: Nav
description: Nav (Polish Nawia, Ukrainian Mavka/Nyavka) denotes both the souls of the prematurely dead (tragic deaths, suicides, drowned, warlocks) and the Slavic underworld ruled by Veles. As spirits (nawie), they appear as birds, hostile and jealous of the living. As a place, Nav lies across a living sea or deep underground, guarded by a zmey; souls later reincarnate.

name: Nawang Wulan (Heavenly Nymph)
description: Nawang Wulan is a heavenly nymph (bidadari) from Javanese folklore who descended to earth to bathe in a forest lake with her six sisters. The mortal Jaka Tarub stole her magical shawl, preventing her return to heaven. She married Jaka Tarub and bore him a daughter. Nawang Wulan possessed a miraculous ability: she could cook a single grain of rice into a full meal for the family. She instructed Jaka Tarub never to lift the cooking pot's lid while she cooked. He broke this trust, the magical spell was broken, and Nawang Wulan discovered her shawl that Jaka Tarub had hidden. She returned to heaven, leaving her husband and daughter behind. According to tradition, their descendants founded the great Mataram Kingdom of Central Java

name: Ndi Mmili
description: Ndi Mmili ('people of the water') are powerful Igbo water spirits dwelling in rivers and lakes. They embody life, fertility, beauty, and wealth; invoked for blessings during hardship. Female-centered cult; priestesses mediate. Distinct from Mami Wata though syncretized. Documented in Igbo cosmology and ethnography.

name: Ndundiro
description: Ndundiro (Rwanda). is a giant. Ndundiro is a giant from the folklore and mythology of Rwanda.. Source: Rwandan folklore — Ndundiro giant documented in Rwandan oral tradition.

name: Neak Ta
description: Neak Ta are the guardian spirits of land and village in Khmer popular religion: local deities residing in trees, rocks, mounds, and shrines who protect communities, families, and territory. Documented by scholar Ang Choulean, they receive regular offerings, are integrated with Theravada Buddhism, guard against misfortune, and their worship was rekindled after the Khmer Rouge era.

name: Neang Kay
description: Not independently attested in documented Khmer folklore or academic sources as a female water spirit named Neang Kay. Closest documented figures are the pre-Angkorian nāgī Soma, a serpent spirit of Khmer royal legend, and the Phnom Neang Kong Rei ('Sleeping Lady') legend of a princess who wept herself to death. A river spirit named 'Neang Kay' who lures men to drown was not found in any source.

name: Neang Neak (Queen Soma / Naga Princess)
description: Neang Neak (Khmer: នាងនាគ, 'Dragon Woman'), also known as Queen Soma, is the legendary Naga serpent princess who became the first queen of Cambodia. According to Khmer founding myth, she was the beautiful daughter of the Naga king who ruled the underwater realm. She confronted the Indian Brahmin prince Preah Thong (Kaundinya) on the shore, and after being struck by his magic arrow, fell in love and agreed to marry him. Her father the Naga king blessed the union and drained the ocean to create land for their kingdom — the birth of Cambodia. Neang Neak represents the indigenous, matrilineal, and animist foundation of Khmer civilization. She is considered the matriarch of the Khmer people, and her serpent lineage explains the importance of the naga in Cambodian culture. The tradition of the groom holding the bride's sash during Khmer weddings reenacts Preah Thong holding Neang Neak's tail as he descended to the Naga kingdom

name: Negoogunogumbar
description: Negoogunogumbar is the child-eating giant of the Mbuti (Bambuti) of the Ituri Forest, Democratic Republic of the Congo. In Mbuti oral tradition, documented by Colin Turnbull in The Forest People, he lurks beyond the campfire and devours children who stray, teaching the young the real dangers of the deep forest and reinforcing communal vigilance.

name: Nei Tituaa
description: Nei Tituaa, also recorded as Nei Tituaabine or Titua'abine, is a creator spirit of Kiribati (Gilbertese) mythology, a being of the celestial realm tied to weather and life-giving power. One tradition casts her as a lightning goddess with red skin and blue eyes; another as a tree spirit. She is counted among the first divine beings shaped by Nareau's creative work.

name: Nephthys (Goddess of Protection and Mourning)
description: Nephthys is the Egyptian goddess of mourning, protection, and service. Daughter of Nut and Geb, sister of Isis, Osiris, and Set; snip she was the wife of Set but abandoned him due to his evil nature. She helped Isis search for the scattered pieces of Osiris's body and was a protector of the dead, usually paired with Isis at funerary ceremonies. She is associated with the night and the edge of the desert. She is the 'Mistress of the House' referring to the temple enclosure. In the Osiris myth, she disguised herself as Isis to trick Osiris, conceiving Anubis. Despite being associated with death, she was not a dark goddess; snip she was a loyal protector and healer

name: Nereida
description: Neráïdes are the water nymphs of modern Greek folklore, heirs of the ancient Nereids: beautiful young women in white who sing at springs, wells and seashores and dance in moonlit rings. They can enchant, storm-call and drown the unwary, yet marry mortals under strict conditions. Georgios Megas' folktale collections (Tale Type 400) document their survival into Christian village tradition.

name: Nerstenhornets underjordiske
description: Nerstenhornets underjordiske is a supernatural being from the burial mounds at Nersten farm in Øyestad, near Arendal. According to Andreas Faye's Norske Sagn (1833), a large farmer named Sjur was riding past burial mounds at Lia near Temsevannet when an underground being emerged and offered him a magnificent drinking horn. Sjur threw the drink over his shoulder — the drink burned the hide off his horse. He galloped away with the horn. He was only saved from the pursuing being because he rode over a rye field, which the being could not cross. The horn became known as Nerstenhornet. This legend is one of Sørlandet's 21 variants of the classic horn-stealing legend type. The being from the Nersten mound is distinct from the Ime variant — it emerged specifically from a burial mound near a lake and could not cross a cultivated rye field, reflecting the agricultural landscape of Øyestad

name: New Year Spirit
description: At the Hmong New Year (Noj Peb Caug) a ceremonial address honors Ntoo Xeeb, the titular spirit of the new year, together with four benevolent spirits of the locality. Recorded in an ethnography of the Ban Mae Sa Mai community in northern Thailand, the ceremony combines expiation, supplication, and sacrifice to renew the community's standing with the spirit world at the turn of the year.

name: Nezha
description: Nezha (哪吒) is the fiery third son of the Pagoda-Bearer Li Jing in Chinese mythology, central to Fengshen Yanyi and Journey to the West. Born after three years in the womb, he wields a fire-tipped spear, the cosmic ring Qiankun Quan, and the Wind-Fire Wheels he rides beneath his feet. He rebels, dies, and is reborn from a lotus as a powerful young guardian of heaven.

name: Nga
description: Nga is the Nenets god of death, the malevolent son of the sky god Num and one of the two demiurges of Nenets belief. His domain lies below the earth, where the dead go. In a celebrated myth a shaman journeys to Nga's realm, marries Nga's daughter and becomes the Old Man of the Earth, while Num and Nga together shape the world in a tale of dualistic cosmology.

name: Ngabia Bate
description: Ngabia Bate ('man with horns') is a Chadian cryptid legend from the Mayokebi mountains — a wild man of supernatural wisdom, resembling Bigfoot traditions worldwide. Described as a horned humanoid living in mountainous terrain, it symbolizes stamina, wisdom, and grounding. The legend resonates with global 'wild man' motifs but is specific to Chad's Mayokebi region.

name: Ngai
description: Ngai (Kenya). is a deity. Ngai is a deity from the folklore and mythology of Kenya.. Source: Kikuyu mythology; Ngai is the supreme creator god who dwells on Mount Kenya.

name: Ngai (Mwene Nyaga)
description: Ngai, also called Mwene Nyaga ('Possessor of Brightness') and Mogai ('the Divider'), is the supreme creator god of the Kikuyu (Agikuyu). He dwells on the peak of Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya) and manifests in the sun, moon, rain, thunder, and rainbow. Worship centers on sacred high places and the mugumo (fig) tree, and he created the first parents, Gikuyu and Mumbi.

name: Ngalyod
description: Ngalyod is the Rainbow Serpent creator being in the mythology of the Kunwinjku people of western Arnhem Land, Northern Territory. As a powerful ancestral being, Ngalyod created the landscape, waterholes, and living things during the Dreamtime. Unlike the purely serpentine Rainbow Serpent figures, Ngalyod is a composite creature with features of multiple animals — the body of a snake, the head of a buffalo or crocodile, and the tail of a fish or kangaroo. This composite nature represents Ngalyod's power to transform between different forms and her dominion over all creatures. Ngalyod is depicted in the famous rock art of Arnhem Land, particularly at sites near Gunbalanya. She controls the monsoon rains, creates waterholes, and punishes those who break customary law

name: Ngirngemelas
description: Ngirngemelas is the trickster spirit of Palauan mythology, a shapeshifting figure who uses camouflage and illusion to test and outwit humans. One Palauan account links him to Ngibtal, the boy turned giant clam whose tears made the tides. His mischievous, elusive nature reminds listeners of the unpredictability of the natural world and of the wisdom in humility before it.

name: Ngua
description: Vietnamese tradition mythologizes horses, but not as cosmic steeds pulling sun and moon: the iron horse of Thánh Gióng, the white horse as a sun symbol at Phù Đồng temple, and the White Horse God (Bạch Mã), said to guide Lý Thái Tổ to build Thăng Long citadel. The recorded horses 'whose hooves make thunder' are not independently attested; the entry mislabels real horse-worship as a water spirit.

name: Ngueak (Lao Nāga Serpent)
description: Ngueak is the Lao name for the nāga, the great serpent-deity of the Mekong and guardian spirit of the Lao people. Legend says the river's course was carved by the body of a Ngueak king. Village tales tell of nāga princes wedding mortal women, of protectors of boatmen and hoarders of river treasure; the Rocket Festival (Bun Bang Fai) and longboat races honour them and seek their rain.

name: Nguzunguzu
description: Nguzunguzu is a carved canoe prow figurehead from the Western Solomon Islands that represents a powerful protective spirit. According to Roviana mythology, the figurehead is the transformed head of Tiola, a chief from Nduke (Kolombangara Island) who turned into a dog and whose carved image was placed at the front of war canoes to fight enemies. The nguzunguzu was lashed to the bow of war canoes called mon or magoru to provide protection from Kesoko, a dangerous water fiend who threatened to capsize canoes and devour crews. The figurehead typically features a protruding mouth, pointed nose, and hands cradling a severed head or a bird

name: Nian
description: Nian is the lion-like monster of Chinese folklore said to emerge each Lunar New Year's Eve to attack villages, its wide mouth and sharp teeth terrifying the countryside. Fearless of predators, it is driven away by the color red, firecrackers, and loud noises — the origin of red decorations and fireworks in Chinese New Year celebrations. Its legend anchors the festival's most visible customs.

name: Nica (or Nika)
description: Nica (or Nika) is a Bulgarian water nymph, cognate with Russian rusalka and South Slavic samodiva/vila. Inhabits rivers and lakes as a beautiful young woman with long hair. Can be helpful to fishermen but dangerous if scorned, drowning swimmers. Part of the broader Slavic 'water maiden' complex. The name may derive from 'nica' (water spirit) in Bulgarian dialect.

name: Nidaros-Munken
description: Nidaros-Munken (the Monk of Nidaros) is a famous ghost that haunts Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim. The specter is said to be a Catholic monk from the cathedral's pre-Reformation days who was killed during the Reformation turmoil of 1537. The ghost appears as a tall, hooded figure in a black or brown monk's habit, often with a bloody wound on its neck or head. It has been seen walking silently through the cathedral nave, kneeling at the main altar, and disappearing through stone walls. Some versions describe it as headless, carrying its own head. The ghost is most active during Christmas and on the anniversary of the Reformation. It is considered one of Norway's most famous church ghosts and is well documented in Trondheim's local folklore tradition. The Nidaros Cathedral was the most important church in medieval Norway, making its ghost legend particularly significant

name: Nidelv-Nøkken
description: Nidelv-Nøkken (the Nidelva Nixie) is a localized version of the nøkk (water spirit) that specifically inhabits the Nidelva river in Trondheim. The Nidelva flows through the heart of Trondheim, from Selbusjøen to the Trondheimsfjord, passing under several bridges and through the city center. According to Trondheim folklore, the Nidelv-Nøkken lives in the deep pool beneath Bakke bru (Bakke Bridge), where the water is darkest and deepest. The spirit takes the form of a beautiful horse that emerges from the river at night — the classic bäckahästen (brook horse) tradition — luring people to ride it and then galloping into the deepest part of the river. The Nidelv-Nøkken is also known to appear as a handsome young man playing a fiddle on the riverbank at night, his music irresistible to passersby who are drawn toward the water. The legend was particularly used to warn children away from the dangerous river currents in the city center

name: Nifoloa
description: Nifoloa is a dreaded spirit deity of Samoan tradition, feared especially in the Falelima district of Savai'i, who is said to inflict fatal pricks on intruders and the unwary. The name is bound up with sharp, stinging harm, and the figure is counted among the malevolent forces of Samoan spirit belief. Villagers treat Nifoloa with caution and respect to avoid its deadly touch.

name: Night Marchers (Huakai po)
description: The Night Marchers (huaka'i pō) are the ghostly processions of ancient Hawaiian warriors and chiefs who walk old trails and sacred sites, especially on moon phases tied to the gods Kū, Lono, Kāne, and Kanaloa. Marching with torches, drums, and conch blasts, they demand witnesses lie face down and avoid eye contact lest the spirits strike them down. The belief remains alive in modern Hawai'i.

name: Night Stalker (Cheyenne)
description: Not independently attested in Cheyenne tradition; no recorded Cheyenne narrative describes a 'Night Stalker.' The closest attested beings of the night are the Nightspirits, 'Those Who Walk in Darkness,' of the Ho-Chunk, who spread darkness as they walk and grant war blessings to vision seekers. The entry appears to conflate these figures or to invent a Cheyenne counterpart.

name: Nightingale Denmark
description: Nightingale Denmark (Unknown). is a animal-spirit. This entry appears to reference the nightingale from Hans Christian Andersen's story "The Nightingale," which is set in China. The tale contrasts the beauty of nature with artificial imitation.. Source: Andersen's "The Nightingale" (1843)

name: Nihancan
description: Nihancan (Nih'oo3oo) is the spider trickster figure of the Arapaho tribe. Like Iktomi of the Lakota and Wihio of the Cheyenne, Nihancan is both clever and foolish, wise and ridiculous. His stories range from benign mischief to more violent trickery—in one tale he tricks a bear family and kills the children, in another he encounters a dwarf with a powerful arrow who teaches him humility. Despite his often-antisocial behavior, Nihancan's stories serve as important moral lessons teaching the consequences of greed, selfishness, and disrespect. His name literally means 'spider' in Arapaho, and after European contact was extended to mean 'white man.'

name: Nikommo
description: Nikommo belongs to the little people of Wampanoag tradition rather than to the giants. The attested Wampanoag giants are Maushop and his sons, whose struggles with the dangerous little people of the dawnland are told along the Massachusetts coast. Nikommo is better understood as one of those small, capricious forest beings, akin to the pukwudgies of neighboring Algonquian nations.

name: Nile Water Spirits (Nilotic Folk Belief)
description: Egyptian folk belief holds that spirits and jinn inhabit the Nile and its canals. The best-attested is El Naddaha ('the Caller'), a female, naiad-like spirit who appears near the river at night and calls men by name, hypnotizing and luring them to the water; the tradition was popular in 20th-century rural Egypt. Charms and caution protect fishermen and travellers from such spirits.

name: Nimba
description: Nimba (D'mba) is the Baga (Guinea) great mother headdress spirit, a monumental carved wooden bust worn in harvest dances. She embodies fertility, abundance, and the ideal woman — not a forest guardian. Appears as an elderly woman testing visitors' respect in some narratives. Documented in Baga art and ritual (Smithsonian, Musée du Quai Branly collections).

name: Nina
description: Not independently attested in Sudanese folklore by this name. Nina is described as a Nubian fertility spirit who appears as a beautiful woman or as water itself, protecting mothers and children and honoured in naming ceremonies. The closest documented beings are the Nubian water angels, malayket al-bahr, and the banat el Hur of the Nile, spirits of river, birth, and household.

name: Ninki Nanka
description: Ninki Nanka is the Mandinka (Gambia/Senegal) dragon-like water spirit: a 30-foot reptilian creature with crocodile head, donkey/hippopotamus-giraffe body, mirror scales, and fatal Medusa-like stare. Inhabits swamps and caves; explains river disappearances. Carries a head gem of power. Documented in Mandinka oral tradition and 1906 colonial reports; investigated by CFZ expedition 2006.

name: Nis Puk
description: Nis Puk (also called Puge) is a household spirit from Sønderjylland and the Danish-German border region, a variant of the Nisse but with distinct traits. Nis Puk is short and broad, wears red trousers and a red pointed cap, and lives in the barn or stable of a farm. His special talent is stealing grain and fodder from neighboring farms to enrich his own host farm — a form of supernatural redistribution that made him popular with farmers but feared by neighbors. Nis Puk can carry entire barn-loads of hay on his back and can transform into a cat or a fiery dragon. He also has the power to stop bridal processions and make the horses rear, and wood shavings he scatters turn to gold. Unlike the relatively benign Nisse, Nis Puk is mischievous and demanding — requiring a bowl of porridge with a pat of butter every Thursday evening

name: Nisse
description: Nisse (Swedish tomte, tomtenisse, tomtegubbe) is the Swedish household spirit: small, grey-clad, red-capped, dwelling under farmstead floorboards. Protects livestock, harvests, carpentry; expects Christmas porridge with butter. If neglected, turns vengeful: kills livestock, breaks tools, leaves farm. Shapeshifts (goat, horse). Origin: ancestral ghost of farm-clearer + nature spirit (tomtevätte).

name: Nisse
description: Nisse is the Danish household spirit (husnisse, god dreng, gårdbuk): small, bearded, grey-clad, red-capped, living in barns, lofts, stables. Begins in church but coaxed to farm. Protects animals and property; demands Christmas porridge — especially sweet buckwheat boghvedegrød with butter. Fastidious: missing butter causes cow-killing rage. Danish variant of pan-Scandinavian nisse/tomte.

name: Nisse
description: Nisse (Norwegian tufte, tuftekall, gardvord, fjøsnisse) is the Norwegian farm spirit: small, grey, red-capped, dwelling in barns and stables, especially in Østlandet and Trøndelag. Protects livestock; vengeful if Christmas porridge (rømmegrøt, later risengrynsgrøt) withheld. Shapeshifts. Distinct from Swedish tomte. Christiansen theorized 17th-century Danish introduction; legal tract c.

name: Nisse
description: Duplicate of nisse-denmark (slug #29). The Danish household spirit (nisse, husnisse, tomte): small, bearded, grey-clad, red-capped, dwelling in barns and lofts. Protects farm animals and property for Christmas porridge (especially buckwheat boghvedegrød with butter). Fastidious: missing butter triggers vengeful cow-killing.

name: Nisse
description: Nisse (Icelandic). is a wight. A small household spirit that protects the farm in exchange for porridge. Source: Scandinavian folklore; nisse/tomte are household spirits documented in Nordic folk belief collections.

name: Nisse
description: The Nisse (Tomte, Tomtenisse, Tonttu) is a Nordic household spirit: small, human-like, gray-clad with a red pointed cap, dwelling in farmstead barns, stables, or under floorboards. Performs chores (threshing, animal care, carpentry) in exchange for a bowl of porridge (rømmegrøt or rice pudding) with butter on Christmas Eve.

name: Nix
description: The Nix is a shape-shifting water spirit that inhabits the rivers and lakes of Switzerland. Similar to the Celtic kelpie, the Swiss Nix can assume multiple forms—most commonly a beautiful woman who lures men to watery deaths, but also a horse, fish, or even a log. According to Swiss folklore collected in central Switzerland, the Nix has complete control over water and weather, capable of causing floods or droughts at will. In some tales from Lake Lucerne, the Nix is a malevolent ghost that drowns anyone who pollutes or disrupts its underwater domain. However, in traditions from the Bernese Oberland, the Nix is more ambivalent—sometimes helping fishermen in exchange for offerings of bread or milk. The Nix's song is said to be hauntingly beautiful, heard on misty mornings over still lakes. Fishermen along Lake Zurich traditionally left the first catch of the day as an offering to appease the Nix before it claimed their lives

name: Nix
description: Nix is a water-spirit from Switzerland mythology. Similar to the Celtic kelpie, the Swiss Nix can assume multiple forms—most commonly a beautiful woman who lures men to watery deaths, but also a horse, fish, or even a log. According to Swiss folklore collected in central Switzerland, the Nix has complete control over water and weather, capable of causing floods or droughts at will. name: Nix
description: Nix is a water-spirit from Germanic/Nordic mythology. Similar to the Celtic kelpie, the Swiss Nix can assume multiple forms—most commonly a beautiful woman who lures men to watery deaths, but also a horse, fish, or even a log. According to Swiss folklore collected in central Switzerland, the Nix has complete control over water and weather, capable of causing floods or droughts at will. However, in traditions from the Bernese Oberland, the Nix is more ambivalent—sometimes helping fishermen in exchange for offerings of bread or milk. The Nix's song is said to be hauntingly beautiful, heard on misty mornings over still lakes. Fishermen along Lake Zurich traditionally left the first catch of the day as an offering to appease the Nix before it claimed their lives

name: Nixe
description: The Nixe is the female counterpart to the Nix, a freshwater mermaid of German rivers (Rhine, Danube). Beautiful woman with fish tail, wet hem distinguishes her. Her song lures men to drowning. Nibelungenlied mentions Rhine maidens guarding the Rhinegold. Wagner's Ring adapts them as Woglinde, Wellgunde, Flosshilde. She loves music and dance.

name: Nişançı
description: Not independently attested in Turkish folklore under this name. Nisanci is described as a giant, fifteen to twenty feet tall with a long beard, who works at night shaping the hills and rock fields of Anatolia and hurls boulders at mockers. The tale echoes genuine Anatolian giant lore and the Ottoman court office of nisanci, but no documented folk being bears this name.

name: Nk (or Nkanyin)
description: Nkornkanyin (Nk or Nkanyin) is a Congolese forest guardian spirit (DRC). A tall humanoid with long hair, leaf clothing, and glowing eyes, it can appear as a gorilla or leopard. It enforces forest protocol, cursing overhunters and resource-wasters with disease. Healing and nature manipulation are its powers. It reinforces sustainable hunting and respect for nature.

name: Nk (or Nkanyin)
description: Nkornkanyin (Nk or Nkanyin) is a Congolese forest guardian spirit (Republic of Congo). Identical to the DRC entry — a tall, leaf-clad humanoid with glowing eyes that shapeshifts into gorilla or leopard, curses taboo-breakers, and heals. It watches forest protocol and punishes overhunting. The duplicate slugs reflect the shared culture across the Congo River border.

name: Nkadi
description: Nkadi (also known as Mbumba) is the great rainbow serpent of Kongo mythology, a primordial being dwelling at the boundary between the world of the living and the dead. In Kongo cosmology, Nkadi is a cosmic serpent encircling the universe, its body forming the rainbow bridging the waters above and below. Nkadi is associated with nkisi power objects -- sacred bundles channeling spiritual energy. According to tradition, Nkadi was present at creation, witnessing Nzambi Mpungu's cosmic spark. Nkadi represents the continuity of life, death, and rebirth -- the cycle embodied in the Kongo cosmogram (dikenga). As a rainbow serpent, Nkadi connects the realms of the living (nza yayi) and the dead (nsi a bafwa), separated by a great body of water

name: Nne Miri
description: Nne Miri (literally "Mother of Waters") is the Igbo spirit of rivers, streams, and bodies of water. She is the patroness of fishermen and the guardian of marine life. Closely related to the pan-African Mami Wata figure, Nne Miri is a beautiful but dangerous water spirit who can grant wealth and fertility to those she favors but can also drown those who offend her. She is considered a matron spirit for specific professional guilds, particularly those associated with fishing and water-based trade. Nne Miri is sometimes propitiated with offerings at riverbanks before fishing expeditions or before crossing dangerous waters. She represents both the life-giving and destructive power of water

name: Noaidegažži
description: Noaidegažži (also saivogažži) are the helper spirits of the Sami noaidi (shaman), sent to perform tasks, gather information, and fight other noaidi's spirits. These spirits can take the form of birds (saivoloddi), fish (saivoguolli), or reindeer bulls (saivosarvvát — the strongest form). The noaidegažži assist with healing, finding lost people, predicting weather, locating reindeer herds, and combating evil spirits. They were sent out by the noaidi in trance states, often to great distances. The noaidegažži could be inherited from father to son, sold, or given as dowry. A noaidi's power was measured by the number and strength of his noaidegažži. The most powerful noaidegažži was the reindeer bull form (saivosarvvát), which could fight other noaidi's spirits. The tradition of helper spirits represents the Sami understanding of spiritual power as transferable and competitive

name: Noion
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Tibetan folklore. No source documents a household spirit named 'Noion' tied to Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, who answers questions in dreams. The recorded traits resemble generic depictions of Manjushri, a well-attested figure, but the name and role appear in no Tibetan or scholarly source. Likely a modern invention.

name: Nokomis
description: Nokomis is the wise grandmother of Nanabozho in Ojibwe and Anishinaabe mythology. She raised Nanabozho after his mother died during childbirth. Nokomis is a figure of great wisdom and spiritual knowledge, often providing guidance and counsel to Nanabozho during his adventures. She is associated with the earth, the moon, and the nurturing aspects of nature. In some traditions, she is connected to Grandmother Moon and the cycles of women's lives. Her name simply means 'grandmother' in the Ojibwe language

name: Nokomis
description: Nokomis, 'my grandmother' in Anishinaabemowin, is the wise grandmother of Nanabush in Ojibwe tradition, the elder who raises the culture hero and counsels him through his adventures. Her name and role appear across the Anishinaabe nations of the Great Lakes, and she is a figure of kindness, humor, and steady guidance. Longfellow popularized her as Hiawatha's grandmother.

name: Nokomis
description: Nokomis is the grandmother of Nanabush (Nanabozho) in Ojibwe tradition, her very name meaning 'my grandmother' in Anishinaabemowin. She raises the trickster culture hero after the death of his mother and guides him through his adventures. Cognate grandmother figures include Nukumi of the Mi'kmaq and Grandmother Woodchuck of the Abenaki. Longfellow popularized her as Hiawatha's grandmother.

name: Nommo
description: Nommo (Nummo) are Dogon primordial amphibious ancestral spirits, created by Amma as first living beings.
