Hermaphroditic, fish-tailed humanoids who descended from Sirius in an ark of fire and thunder, created water reservoirs, and sacrificed their bodies to populate the universe with Binu shrines. Masters of Water, Teachers, Monitors. Central to Dogon cosmogony per Griaule's Ogotemmêli interviews.

name: Nonoma
description: Nonoma is the Cheyenne spirit of thunder, a powerful being who controls storms and brings rain to the plains. When Nonoma flaps his wings, thunder rolls across the sky. He is both feared and respected—his storms can bring life-giving rain for crops and buffalo or destructive hail and lightning. The Cheyenne perform ceremonies to honor Nonoma and ask for his blessing. The first thunder of spring signals the time for planting and the Sun Dance ceremony. Nonoma represents the powerful, renewing force of storms that brings life to the plains

name: Noqoilpi (Great Gambler)
description: Noqoilpi is a powerful and malevolent figure in Navajo tradition who challenged all who came to him to gambling contests. He lived at the base of Ch'óol'į́'í (Great Spruce Mountain or El Capitan) and won the possessions, freedom, and even entire nations through his gambling prowess. He grew so powerful that the Holy People intervened, sending a challenger who, aided by divine help, finally beat Noqoilpi at the moccasin game and other contests. Defeated, Noqoilpi departed eastward with his gambli

name: Norns Iceland
description: Norns Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. The Norns are three female beings in Norse mythology who shape or decree the fate of gods and mortals. Their names are Urðr (past), Verðandi (present), and Skuld (future), and they dwell at the base o. Source: Poetic Edda; Prose Edda (Snorri Sturluson, 13th century)

name: Northern Lights
description: The northern lights, called wâwâhtêwak, 'those that go in circles,' in Cree, are seen as spirits dancing across the winter sky. Some nations say they are the ghosts of the departed holding a great dance, and the Cree phrase cîpayak kâ-nîmihitocik, 'the ghosts are dancing,' names the display directly. Whistling at the lights is forbidden, for it offends the dancers and draws them down.

name: Nsenga
description: Nsenga is a Congolese shapeshifter guardian taking forms of lion, leopard, python, or human with animal features — its eyes always remain wise and ancient. It protects sacred locations, tests human intentions, and can be helpful or dangerous depending on treatment. Representing ancestral spirits and nature guardians in Bantu tradition, it appears as a lion to defend sacred places or as a hunter.

name: Ntikuma
description: Ntikuma is the son of Anansi the spider in Akan folklore. Unlike his cunning father, Ntikuma often demonstrates wisdom that surpasses Anansi's schemes. In the famous story "Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom," when Anansi tried to hide all the world's wisdom in a pot at the top of a tree, it was young Ntikuma who pointed out that tying the pot in front made climbing impossible — suggesting instead that Anansi tie it on his back. Angered that his son had outsmarted him, Anansi threw down the pot, shattering it and scattering wisdom across the world. Ntikuma represents the wisdom of youth and the Akan belief that cleverness can come from unexpected sources, including children

name: Ntsomi
description: Not independently attested as a West African creature. Ntsomi is Xhosa (South Africa) women's solo performance art combining storytelling, dance, and song with props — not a monster or forest spirit. Documented by Harold Scheub ('The Xhosa Ntsomi'). The record misattributes a South African performance tradition to West Africa as a creature.

name: Ntxwj Nyog (Spirit of Death and Sickness)
description: Ntxwj Nyog (also Ndu Nyong or Ntxwj Nyug) is the primordial spirit of sickness, death, and evil in Hmong shamanic mythology. According to Hmong creation myth, Ntxwj Nyog emerged from an unburned egg when the original creators failed to properly destroy all evil in the world. He descended to earth and began devouring human souls, causing sickness and death. The high god Yawm Saub sent the first shaman Siv Yis to combat Ntxwj Nyog, beginning an eternal struggle between the shaman and the death spirit. Ntxwj Nyog is cunning and relentless — he once tricked Siv Yis into unknowingly eating his own son's soul. Despite the shaman's efforts, Ntxwj Nyog can only be temporarily defeated, never permanently destroyed, explaining why death and sickness persist in the world. He represents the Hmong explanation for suffering — an active, malevolent force that must be constantly battled by shamans through ritual and sacrifice. His presence justifies the entire shamanic system

name: Nu-u
description: The name nu-u has no independent attestation, but it corresponds most closely to the water babies of Great Basin tradition, known to the Southern Paiute as pit-u-u or paúngaa'a. These small, crying beings guard springs and lakes and aid shamans, but are dangerous to those who approach their waters. Their weeping is a warning, and children are taught to keep away from deep water where they live.

name: Nuckelavee
description: The Nuckelavee (also Nuckalavee, Knucker) is the most terrifying creature in Orkney folklore — a skinless horse-like centaur from the sea whose breath withers crops and spreads disease. Its name derives from the Orcadian Norn 'knoggelvi' meaning devil of the sea. The nuckelavee has the torso of a man fused to the back of a horse-like body, with all its muscles, sinews, veins, and organs exposed because it has no skin. Its single red eye burns like fire and its mouth gapes with no lips. The creature emerges from the sea during prolonged dry spells or when water is polluted, bringing drought, plague, and death to livestock. It is particularly associated with the summer months when it rises from the depths to ravage farmland. The only protection against it is running water, which the nuckelavee cannot cross. Burning kelp (seaweed) on the shore is also said to drive it away. During the Victorian cholera epidemics, islanders blamed the nuckelavee for the outbreaks. The creature was so feared that farmers would leave their fields fallow rather than risk encountering it

name: Nugu
description: Not independently attested in documented Solomon Islands folklore or academic sources. No dedicated source confirms a dwarf or forest people called Nugu who lead travelers astray or mine and craft in the forests. The recorded traits resemble the better-attested Kakamora dwarf-people of Makira, and 'Nugu' may be a conflation of that tradition.

name: Nuku
description: In Samoan spirit belief, Nuku is a ghost (aitu) said to return from death to unfinished business, appearing as a translucent or shadowy figure, sometimes in the form of familiar animals. Encounters bring misfortune, illness, or accidents, and the spirit may be appeased through proper rituals and offerings. Belief in aitu is deeply rooted in Samoan culture.

name: Num
description: Num is the supreme sky god of the Nenets people of Siberia, the good creator of the earth and all living things and the high god of the Nenets pantheon. In Nenets dualistic cosmology he is one of two demiurges whose malevolent son Nga rules the dead below; in one myth a shaman went to Nga's realm, wed his daughter, and became the Old Man of the Earth who upholds the world.

name: Nunnehi
description: The Nunnehi, meaning 'the travelers' or 'those who live anywhere,' are a race of immortal spirit people of the Cherokee, distinct from ghosts and from gods. They dwell in the mountains, forests, and stone houses of Cherokee country, are usually friendly, and sometimes showed themselves to warn of danger. During the Removal they were said to hide Cherokee families in a cave closed by a stone door.

name: Nurarihyon
description: Nurarihyon, the 'Supreme Commander of the Yōkai,' is an elderly aristocratic yōkai of Japanese folklore with a gourd-shaped head and flowing robes. He enters empty homes, makes tea, and acts the master so convincingly that returning residents defer to him. The title 'yōkai no oyadama' is modern, coined by folklorist Fujisawa Morihiko and popularized by Shigeru Mizuki's GeGeGe no Kitarō.

name: Nuribotoke
description: Nuribotoke is a Japanese yōkai appearing as a living Buddhist monk statue with blackened teeth, a long lolling tongue, and an angry face. It manifests to those who misuse temples or neglect worship, cursing the disrespectful or teaching them to show proper reverence for sacred places. The figure embodies a warning against improper religious practice.

name: Nurikabe
description: Nurikabe is the 'wall-spirit' of Japanese folklore, an invisible barrier that blocks travelers on roads and paths at night, sometimes showing an old man's face in the wall. It may be dispelled by knocking three times or reciting a charm, and is occasionally benevolent, shielding walkers from danger. The yōkai explains puzzling detours and getting lost on familiar roads.

name: Nut (Sky Goddess of Egypt)
description: Nut is the Egyptian goddess of the sky and the heavens. She arches over the earth as the starry sky, her body covered with stars. Daughter of Shu (air) and Tefnut (moisture), sister and wife of Geb (earth). Each day she swallows the sun god Ra, who travels through her body at night and is reborn from her womb at dawn. She was separated from her beloved Geb by their father Shu, who holds Nut above the earth. Nut protects the dead; snip the inner lid of coffins were often painted with Nut's image so she could watch over the deceased. The Pyramid Texts describe Nut as providing a ladder for the deceased pharaoh to climb to the heavens

name: Nya-nya Bulembu
description: Nya-nya Bulembu is a Swazi (Eswatini) monster haunting deep pools, described as a massive moss-green beast with fur like living seaweed. It preys on the careless, transforms victims into monsters, and punishes ritual violations. The name suggests a pool-dwelling entity in siSwati. Limited documentation outside local Swazi folklore references.

name: Nyabingi
description: Nyabingi (Rwanda). is a deity. Unmarried woman made immortal by Imana after murder. Source: Rwandan folklore — Nyabingi spirit documented in Rwandan oral tradition.

name: Nyai Roro Kidul
description: Nyai Roro Kidul is the goddess-queen of the Southern Ocean in Javanese and Sundanese belief, appearing as a beautiful woman in royal green robes with a spirit retinue. She rules the waters and is said to draw those who wear green into her undersea kingdom as soldiers. Revered across Java, she is the subject of widespread taboos: hotels, beaches, and courts forbid wearing green in her presence.

name: Nyame
description: Nyame (Onyame) is the supreme god of the Akan people (Ashanti, Fante, Akuapem) of Ghana. Also known as Nyankopon or Odomankoma, Nyame is the omniscient, omnipotent sky deity who created the universe and all living things. The name means "the one who knows and sees everything." Nyame is part of a trinity with Nyankopon (his life-giving power) and Odomankoma (his creative force). According to tradition, Nyame once lived on earth but withdrew to the heavens after being struck by a woman's pestle while pounding fufu. The Adinkra symbol "Gye Nyame" ("I Fear None Except God") is one of the most recognized symbols of Akan culture. Nyame is represented by the sky, and his sacred day is Saturday

name: Nyamgondho (Lady of the Lake)
description: Nyamgondho Wuod Ombare is a legendary lake spirit from Luo mythology who married a poor fisherman on Lake Victoria. The fisherman (whose real name was Julu son of Ombare) pulled a hideously ugly woman from his net. She promised to make him wealthy if he would take her as his wife and never reveal where she came from. The lady of the lake worked tirelessly, and soon Nyamgondho became the richest man in the region. But wealth made him arrogant. One night, drunk and angry, he shouted at her: 'Even you, ugly creature I found in the lake?' Enraged, she walked back into the lake, all his cattle following her until Nyamgondho was left with nothing. After his ruin, he was transformed into a sacred tree at Nyandiwa

name: Nyaminyami (Zambezi River God)
description: Nyaminyami is the most famous river deity in Zambian mythology, the serpent-like god of the mighty Zambezi River. According to Tonga legend, Nyaminyami has the body of a snake and the head of a fish, symbolizing his dominion over both water and land. He is believed to control the flow of the Zambezi River and has the power to either bless or curse the people living along its banks. The legend of Nyaminyami gained international attention during the construction of the Kariba Dam (1955-1959), when the Tonga people warned that damming the river would anger the river god. When the dam faced severe floods and construction delays, many believed Nyaminyami was retaliating. The most dramatic event was the 1957 flood that destroyed the partially built dam wall, an event that entered Zambian national lore. Nyaminyami is still widely venerated by the Tonga people, who hold ceremonies to honor him and seek his protection against natural disasters. The legend represents the deep spiritual connection between the Zambian people and the Zambezi River, one of Africa's greatest waterways

name: Nyang'idi (Lake Serpent)
description: The Nyang'idi is a fearsome serpent monster in Luo mythology said to dwell in the depths of Lake Victoria, a bringer of disease and misfortune. According to tradition, the Nyang'idi was once a servant of Were (the supreme god) who was cast down into the waters as punishment for disobedience. The serpent grows to enormous size and emerges during storms or when the waters are disturbed by human wrongdoing. Its presence is associated with outbreaks of disease, particularly the wasting illnesses that affect fishermen who venture too far into deep waters. The nyawawa (water spirits) are descendants of those drowned in the great flood that created Lake Victoria, and Nyang'idi is their guardian. Fishermen make offerings before launching boats to appease the great serpent

name: Nyenchen Thanglha
description: Nyenchen Thanglha is the great mountain god of Tibet, lord of the Nyenchen Thanglha range and chief of the nyen spirits. A white-clad warrior who rides a white horse, he was a wrathful native deity before he bound himself by oath before Padmasambhava and became a protector of the Buddhist teaching, called upon for protection, good fortune and fair weather.

name: Nyerum
description: Nyerum are Bambara (Mali) water spirits inhabiting seasonal floodplains and ponds. They breathe water, immune to drought, and lure/drown intruders. Part of Bambara animistic tradition alongside Faro (river spirit) and pond genies. Documented in Bambara oral tradition and ethnographic surveys of Niger River communities.

name: Nyi Roro Kidul
description: Nyi Roro Kidul is the legendary queen of the Southern Ocean of Javanese and Sundanese tradition: a beautiful, powerful spirit with long black hair, ruling the waves of the Indian Ocean south of Java. Tied to the fall of the Sunda Kingdom and later to Mataram, she appears in dreams and controls sea creatures, and is appeased with green offerings; wearing green near her waters is taboo.

name: Nyikang
description: Nyikang, son of Kang, is the semi-legendary founder and divine ancestor of the Shilluk people. Said to be born of a human father and a crocodile naiad, he crossed the White Nile into Shilluk country, established the kingship, and later vanished into the river. Shilluk kings are believed to inherit his spirit, tying every reign to his living memory.

name: Nykur
description: Nykur is the Icelandic water horse, a shape-shifting water spirit that lures people onto its back and drowns them. Unlike the Norwegian nøkk who uses music, the nykur appears as a beautiful dapple-grey horse with backward-facing hooves and fetlocks that trail water. It stands quietly by rivers, lakes, or the sea, inviting riders. Once mounted, the nykur gallops into the deepest water and drowns its victim. The nykur has one weakness — if someone says its name (nykur), it will flee in terror. It can also be tamed by throwing steel over its head. The nykur can shape-shift into a salmon, a bull, or a fish. Its whinnying is said to be heard in the cracking of winter ice. In some accounts, the nykur can impregnate regular mares, producing half-breed foals that lie down and refuse to move when ridden through belly-deep water, as if remembering their father's nature

name: Nykur Iceland
description: Nykur Iceland (Unknown). is a kelpie. Nykur is a water horse from Icelandic folklore who lures people onto its back then drowns them.. Source: Icelandic folklore — the Nykur water-horse/kelpie documented in Icelandic folklore.

name: Nykurin
description: Nykurin is the Faroese nix, a dangerous freshwater shapeshifter. Appears as beautiful horse (nykur) on land; touching its tail sticks the victim as it drags them to watery death. Also appears as handsome youth luring women. Calling its true name 'nykur' breaks its power. Can become any quadruped except ram/lamb (cannot form horns).

name: Nyoaty
description: Nyoaty (Tanzania). is a bird. Maasai eagle spirit that carries messages between humans and the divine. Source: Maasai folklore — Nyoaty eagle spirit documented in Tanzanian Maasai oral tradition.

name: Nyonyose Mask Spirit
description: Not independently attested in Mossi (Nyonyose) tradition. The figure appears to be a modern composite or fabrication rather than an authentic element of Mossi (Nyonyose) folklore.

name: Nyurgun Bootur
description: Nyurgun Bootur, 'the Swift,' is the foremost hero of the Sakha (Yakut) epic cycle, the olonkho. A champion of the Middle World, he battles the hostile abaahy demons to defend his people and restore balance to the cosmos, aided by his swift steed and weapons forged by heavenly smiths. His songs were set down in written form by Platon Oyunsky.

name: Nzambi Mpungu
description: Nzambi Mpungu (meaning 'Creator of All') is the supreme god of the Kongo people, the eternal Sky Father and creator of the universe. In Kongo cosmology, the world began as an empty void called mbungi (an empty circle of nothingness). Nzambi Mpungu, with his female counterpart Nzambici, created a spark of fire called kalunga inside the void. The spark grew into an immense force of energy, becoming so hot that it exploded, hurling projectiles that became stars, planets, and all matter. This process is called luku lwalamba Nzambi ('God created and cooked dough'). After creation, Nzambi Mpungu withdrew from the world but still animates natural forces -- thunder, rain, and the growth of crops. His counterpart Nzambici remained closer to humanity, teaching laws and arts

name: Nzazi
description: Nzazi is the powerful spirit of thunder and lightning in Kongo mythology, a fearsome being who patrols the skies during storms hurling bolts of fire at those who break sacred laws. According to tradition, Nzazi was once a man who climbed too high in his ambitions and was transformed into a sky spirit. He patrols the heavens during storms, his flashing eyes creating lightning and his voice thunder. Some traditions describe Nzazi as a canine creature with red or black fur that appears during storms, barks once, and vanishes. Other accounts say Nzazi is accompanied by twelve hounds, with Nzazi representing thunder and the hounds lightning. Trees struck by lightning are said to have been visited by Nzazi's judgment. Survivors of lightning strikes are considered chosen and often become nganga (spiritual healers)

name: Näcken
description: Näcken (Strömkarlen, 'The Stream Man') is the Swedish male water spirit: slender, often naked/elegantly clad, green-haired (foliage), sitting on rocks playing violin, horn, flute in brooks and waterfalls. Music lures women and children to drown; most dangerous Midsummer, Christmas Eve, Thursdays.

name: Näkk
description: Näkk (Estonia). is a water-spirit. Estonian variant of Nordic nixie, a shapeshifting water spirit with subtypes. Source: Estonian folklore; variant of the nixie (näkki) found in Estonian water-spirit lore.

name: Näkki
description: Näkki is the Finnish malevolent water spirit, loaned from Swedish näck. Appears as beautiful woman combing golden hair on rocks, or as old green-skinned monster. Lurks in rivers, lakes, fords, under bridges; drowns night swimmers. Children warned: 'näkki onto the land, me into the water' before swimming. In North Karelia, distinguished from vetehinen (näkki grabs, vetehinen infects).

name: Níðhöggr
description: Níðhöggr ('Malice-Striker') is the monstrous dragon in Norse mythology gnawing Yggdrasil's roots in Niflheim. Wingless, serpentine, dark-scaled, red-eyed, powerful jaws. Creates decay and corruption; awaits Ragnarök to consume all. In Vafþrúðnismál 37 and Gylfaginning 18, Hræsvelgr (eagle-guise jötunn) creates wind; Níðhöggr gnaws roots.

name: Nøkk
description: Nøkk (also known as Nøkken, Näcken, Nykkjen) is a male freshwater spirit in Norwegian and Scandinavian folklore who dwells in dark lakes, rivers, and ponds. One of the oldest mentioned water spirits - first references date to the Viking Age. The nøkk is a master musician who plays violin or harp to lure people into the water to drown. He is also a shape-shifter who can appear as a handsome young man with long hair (to seduce women), as a monster of twigs and seaweed with glowing eyes (Norwegian tradition), or as a pale grey horse. Despite his malevolent nature, he is often portrayed as lonely and sad, lamenting his inability to receive Christian salvation. The nøkken can be appeased with offerings of black animals, three drops of blood, or brandy - in return, he will tune your fiddle to play as beautifully as his own. Water lilies in his pond are called nøkkerose (nøkk's rose)

name: Nøstekatt
description: The troll cat (Norwegian: trollkatt, also nøstekatt) is a witch's familiar in Scandinavian folklore, a supernatural cat sent by a witch to steal milk from neighbours' cows. It may travel in the form of a ball of yarn (trollnøste), and harm done to it is shared by its witch, who must bury it with her. Fisherfolk and farmers feared its milking raids on cattle.

name: Núi
description: Núi is the Vietnamese word for mountain; the country's mountain-spirit tradition centers on documented figures like Sơn Tinh, the Mountain Lord, one of Vietnam's Four Immortals, who battled Thủy Tinh, the Water Lord, for Princess Mỵ Nương. The recorded peak-guardian—a towering figure, part of the mountain itself—echoes this tradition, though 'Núi' is a common noun, not a named spirit.

name: Nûñnë'hï
description: Nûñnë'hï is James Mooney's spelling of Nunnehi, the Cherokee word for a race of immortal spirit people, 'those who live anywhere,' who dwell in the mountains and forests of the old Cherokee country. Usually invisible and kindly, they sometimes appeared to warn their people, and during the Removal they were said to have sheltered Cherokee families in a cave whose door closed against the soldiers.

name: Nāc
description: Nāc is the Lao term for naga, the great river serpent of Lao Buddhist folklore: a huge, usually cobra-hooded serpent, sometimes multi-headed, scales shining, dwelling in the Mekong beneath water palaces. It brings floods or rain by human merit, guards temples and villages, and must be fed and respected. It is bound to the Naga Fireballs phenomenon and the Luang Prabang naak legend.

name: Nāga
description: Nāga is the diacritically-marked Sanskrit form of naga (slug: naga), not a distinct entity. Identical to the naga entry: divine half-human, half-serpent beings, children of Kashyapa and Kadru, dwelling in Patala, guarding waters and treasures, rivals of Garuda.

name: Obambo
description: Obambo (Obambou) is a supernatural being of the Baka and other Central African tribes. It possesses the sick, residing in their bowels until driven out by communal noise-making — singing, dancing, yelling, banging objects. The M'pongwe believed some are born with Obambo, causing innate insanity.

name: Obariyon
description: Obariyon (おばりよん) is a child-sized yōkai of Niigata Prefecture whose name comes from the local dialect phrase for 'give me a piggyback ride'. It leaps onto travelers' backs and grows heavier with every step, and may chew the scalp of its bearer, so some villages wore metal bowls as helmets. If carried home, the burden is found to be a sack of money, rewarding perseverance.

name: Obatala
description: Obatala is the king of white cloth, the oldest of all orishas, and the sculptor of humanity. Sent by Olodumare to create the earth, Obatala descended from heaven on a golden chain carrying a snail shell of sand, a white hen, a black cat, and a palm nut. He poured sand on the primordial waters and the hen scratched it into dry land. He then molded the first humans from clay. Tricked by Eshu into drinking palm wine, he created some imperfect bodies while drunk, and Olodumare decreed that people with disabilities would be sacred and under Obatala's protection. He is the patron of the physically challenged

name: Obayifo
description: Obayifo is an Ashanti (Akan, Ghana) vampire-witch who appears human by day but at night emits phosphorescent light from armpits and anus, flies as a ball of light, and sucks blood/vitality. Known as asiman in Dahomey. Associated with witchcraft (bayi), infant mortality, and food obsession. No defense exists. Documented in Rattray's Ashanti ethnography.

name: Obrigwabibikwa
description: Obrigwabibikwa is a mystical dwarf and shapeshifter from the mythology of the Mbuti Pygmy people of the Democratic Republic of Congo. This enigmatic figure possesses the ability to transform into a reptile, most commonly a lizard, which holds sacred significance in Mbuti cosmology. The lizard is considered the divine messenger of Khonvoum, the supreme creator god of the Mbuti, who uses these creatures to communicate with the mortal world. Obrigwabibikwa plays a crucial role in Mbuti beliefs about death and the soul: when a person dies, their soul (megbe) splits into two parts, with one part inhabiting a totem animal. If the totem is killed or the son fails to inhale the megbe, the soul becomes a wandering spirit. Obrigwabibikwa is said to be responsible for creating these wandering spirits, making him a figure associated with the forces of order and chaos

name: Ocean Spider
description: The Ocean-Spider is a monstrous water creature of Greenlandic Inuit tradition recorded by Hinrich Rink. A kayaker in the firth of Godthaab once found the bottom close beneath him where no shoal was known, remembered the elders' warnings of the ocean-spider, and barely escaped when two monstrous eyes and a gaping mouth opened beside his kayak.

name: Octopus Nuu Chah Nulth
description: In Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) legend, the octopus appears in the tale 'Raven Annoys Octopus,' where Raven pesters the octopus people and learns a lesson in respect. An octopus woman with eight long braids digs on the shore with a stick, and the story teaches listeners about meddling and the boundaries of other beings.

name: Octopus Water-Spirit (Wolof)
description: Not independently attested as a distinct named entity in Wolof tradition. Wolof water spirits (jinés/jinn) inhabit rivers and coasts but no specific 'octopus water-spirit' appears in ethnographic records (Diop, Faye). The octopus motif may reflect Atlantic marine influence but lacks attestation.

name: Octopus Water-Spirit (Wolof)
description: The Octopus Water-Spirit is a Wolof (Senegalese) water spirit, not Cameroonian — the Wolof are a Senegalese ethnic group with some presence in Cameroon. It protects swamps, commands storm calling and weather control, and drowns intruders. Land binding, freezing, and specific rituals counter it. The spirit's octopus form reflects its swamp habitat.

name: Od Iedeh (Fire Spirit)
description: Od Iedeh is the Evenki (Siberian Tungusic) fire spirit, mistress of the hearth. Appears as a face in the flames or an old woman made of fire, sometimes riding a fox. Must be respected with offerings; protects the household, aids cooking and warmth, but burns the dwelling if insulted. Communicates through crackling flames. Central to Evenki shamanic practice.

name: Odin
description: Odin (Odinn), the Allfather, is the highest god of Norse mythology — lord of wisdom, poetry, war, and the dead. He gave one eye to Mimir's well for wisdom and hanged nine nights on Yggdrasil to win the runes. He rides the eight-legged Sleipnir with his ravens Huginn and Muninn, and receives half the battle-slain into Valhalla. He was widely venerated across Norway as chief of the Aesir.

name: Odin
description: Odin (Odinn) is the chief of the Norse Aesir — god of wisdom, poetry, war, and death. Icelandic sources, chiefly the Poetic and Prose Eddas, preserve the fullest accounts of his myths, including his sacrifice of an eye for wisdom and his winning of the runes. He rides Sleipnir, is flanked by ravens Huginn and Muninn, and gathers the battle-slain to Valhalla.

name: Oduduwa
description: Oduduwa is the legendary progenitor of the Yoruba people, first Oba (king) of Ile-Ife, and an orisha of creation. According to tradition, Oduduwa descended from heaven on a chain carrying the materials of creation and completed the work Obatala had begun, creating dry land. His sixteen sons became the founders of the principal Yoruba kingdoms, including Oyo, Benin, Ila, and Ketu. Every crowned Oba in Yorubaland traces their lineage to Oduduwa. The Ooni of Ife is considered his direct descendant and the spiritual head of all Yoruba people. As the initiator of the Ogboni society, he established the sacred authority of Yoruba kingship

name: Ogbanje
description: Ogbanje (Ọgbanje) are Igbo 'spirit children' who cyclically die and are reborn into the same family, causing recurrent grief. They possess a hidden iyi-uwa stone linking them to the spirit world; destroying it ends the cycle. Linked to sickle-cell disease and SIDS in medical anthropology. Documented in Achebe's 'Things Fall Apart' and Igbo ethnography.

name: Ogo (The Cosmic Fox)
description: Ogo (Yurugu), the Pale Fox, is the Dogon trickster. Firstborn of Amma, he rebelled, stole a piece of the sun, and brought death, imperfection, and speech to humanity. His incest with Earth produced first ancestors. Amma restored order by sacrificing his twin Nommo. Ogo's disorder is necessary for a dynamic universe. Per Griaule's Ogotemmêli interviews.

name: Ogopogo
description: Ogopogo is the lake monster of Okanagan Lake in British Columbia, rooted in Syilx (Okanagan) oral tradition, where the being is called n̓x̌aʔx̌ʔitkʷ, the sacred water creature said to demand safe passage of travellers. The name 'Ogopogo' is a 1920s coinage, but the Syilx accounts of a serpentine lake spirit long predate the English nickname.

name: Ogou (Lwa of War and Iron)
description: Ogou is the fierce lwa of war, iron, fire, politics, and justice in Haitian Vodou. He is second only to Papa Legba in importance and is the patron of soldiers, blacksmiths, mechanics, drivers, and all who work with metal. Ogou is descended from the Yoruba deity Ogun (god of iron and war), but in Haiti he evolved into a distinct family of lwa including Ogou Feray (the warrior), Ogou Badagris (the politician), and Ogou Balendjo (the healer). He is depicted as a powerful, muscular man dressed in military uniform -- a general coat with epaulettes, a red sash, and a machete or saber. He rides a horse into battle and smokes a cigar. Ogou is syncretized with Saint James the Greater (Santiago Matamoros), depicted as a Moor-slayer on horseback. In the Haitian Revolution, Ogou was the spirit invoked by the revolutionary leaders, and many Haitians believe Ogou fought alongside Dessalines and Louverture. His colors are red and blue. His offerings include raw rum, cigars, grilled corn, roast goat, yams, and machetes or iron objects

name: Ogress Iceland
description: Ogress Iceland (Unknown). is a ogre. An ogress from Icelandic folklore is a female giant or troll-woman who devours humans and steals children.. Source: Icelandic folklore — ogress figures documented in Icelandic oral tradition.

name: Ogun
description: Ogun (Ògún) is a primordial Yoruba orisha of iron, war, blacksmithing, hunting, and technology. He cleared the path for other orisha to enter Earth with a machete and dog. Patron of warriors, smiths, drivers; oaths sworn on iron invoke him. Venerated across Yoruba, Dahomey, Vodun, Candomblé, Santería. Not a water spirit — his element is earth/iron.

name: Ojalehto (Stream Leaf)
description: Ojalehto ('Stream Leaf') is a small Finnish water spirit of brooks and streams, childlike, greenish-brown with fish scales or gills. Plays pranks but generally harmless; protects water sources and fish. Appears as small child or fish-like creature. In North Karelia, distinguished from vetehinen: ojalehto grabs swimmers, vetehinen infects as illness.

name: Okomfo Anokye
description: Okomfo Anokye (Unknown). is a human. Okomfo Anokye is a legendary priest and co-founder of the Ashanti Empire in present-day Ghana. He is credited with the miracle of bringing down the Golden Stool from the sky, which became the sacred s. Source: Ashanti oral tradition; Ghanaian history

name: Okwa Naholo
description: Okwa Naholo, 'white people of the water,' are supernatural beings of Choctaw tradition who dwell in deep pools and springs. Recorded by Henry S. Halbert in the nineteenth century, they are described with light skins like the underside of a trout, and they seize swimmers, who after three days can no longer leave the water. Some traditions set their home beneath the Abita River.

name: Ol' Hige (Jamaican Vampire Hag)
description: The ol' hige is the Jamaican vampire-hag: an elderly woman bound by a diabolical pact who, by night, sheds her skin, hides it in a mortar or under a tree, and flies as a ball of fire to suck the blood of sleeping victims, often infants.

name: Olapa (Rainbow Serpent)
description: Olapa is the moon goddess of Maasai cosmology, regarded as the wife of Enkai, the sky god and creator. In the best-known myth a quarrel ends with Enkai striking out one of her eyes, which is why the moon wanes each month and then slowly heals. The input's 'rainbow serpent' framing is a mislabel; Maasai tradition knows Olapa as the moon, not as a serpent.

name: Old Man Coyote
description: Old Man Coyote (Isáahkawuattee, Akbaatatdia) is the central creator and trickster figure of Crow mythology. He was alone upon a great ocean when he saw two male ducks and asked them to dive for mud, which he used to build an island that grew into all the lands of Earth. He shaped mountains, rivers, and valleys, then molded humans from clay and created women so they would be happy. Old Man Coyote is simultaneously the world's creator and its most unreliable inhabitant—enormously clever yet occasionally foolish, both source of everything and an ongoing embarrassment. He is still in the world, still making things and making mistakes

name: Old Master
description: Old Master is a recurring character in African American folklore, particularly in the 'trickster slave' narrative cycle. He is the plantation owner (the enslaver) whom clever enslaved protagonists consistently outwit. These stories — collected by Zora Neale Hurston, Julius Lester, and others — portray Old Master not as a benign paternalist but as a figure of arbitrary power who is repeatedly humiliated by the intelligence and wit of those he considers his inferiors. In these tales, the enslaved trickster (often named John or Jack) uses reverse psychology, false deference, and clever wordplay to escape punishment, gain resources, or expose Old Master's hypocrisy. The stories served as coded expressions of resistance, allowing enslaved people to celebrate intellectual triumphs over their oppressors without openly rebelling

name: Old Woman's Water
description: Old Woman's Water is a powerful water spirit in Cheyenne mythology, associated with a sacred healing spring. An old woman who lived by a sacred spring found that her water had healing powers. She shared it with a young wounded warrior who was miraculously healed. The woman then revealed herself as a manifestation of the earth's power. She gave the warrior a buffalo cap made from the scalp of a sacred buffalo, which became the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat) that could summon buffalo herds and protect the people. She taught the rituals needed to care for the cap and warned that neglect would cause the buffalo to disappear

name: Ole Higue
description: Ole Higue (Ol' Higue) is a Guyanese/Caribbean vampire-witch from West African soucouyant traditions. By day an elderly woman; by night she sheds skin (stored in a calabash), becomes a fiery flying orb, and sucks blood from infants. Explains infant mortality. Repelled by scattering rice/salt (must count grains), hot pepper sauce, or finding her hidden skin. Part of Caribbean jumbie/duppy complex.

name: Ole Lukøje (Sandman)
description: Ole Lukøje ('Ole Close-Eye') is the Danish Sandman, a small elderly man in long coat with magic sand bag. Visits children at night, sprinkling sand for dreams: wondrous stories for virtuous, silence for wicked. Created by Hans Christian Andersen (1841) drawing on folk belief in dream-bringers (cf. Norwegian nattravn, Swedish drömmar). Andersen's literary figure became dominant Danish tradition.

name: Ole Lukøje Sandman Denmark
description: Ole Lukøje Sandman Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. Ole Lukøje is the Danish Sandman from Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale. He sprinkles sand in children's eyes to make them sleep and shows them dreams under his magic umbrella.. Source: Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales; Danish folklore

name: Olgoi Khorkhoi
description: Olgoi Khorkhoi (Unknown). is a monster. The Olgoi-Khorkhoi (Mongolian Death Worm) is a cryptid from the Gobi Desert, described as a thick red worm capable of killing with venom or electric discharge. It is one of the most famous cryptids in. Source: Mongolian and Tibetan folk traditions; cryptozoological literature

name: Olifat
description: Olifat is a trickster god in Micronesian mythology, particularly among the islands of Chuuk. He was the grandson of the great god Anulap, born to the god Lugeleng and the mortal woman Tarisso, daughter of the octopus goddess Hit. When Lugeleng's wife tried to prevent the union, Hit danced so lewdly that the wife fainted from arousal and had to be carried back to the sky, allowing Olifat's conception. Olifat is a mischievous and cunning figure who often disrupts the established order with his pranks. He is known for stealing food from the gods, playing tricks on humans, and introducing chaos into the world. Despite his troublesome nature, Olifat's adventures sometimes benefit humanity, as his chaotic actions occasionally lead to useful discoveries and innovations

name: Olobit
description: The olobit, also called the 'sharp-breasted snake,' is a monstrous serpent of the Natchez, a people of the lower Mississippi. Described in John R. Swanton's field research, it is a supernatural reptile closely related to the Uktena of the Cherokee and other great serpents of the Southeast.

name: Olodumare
description: Olodumare is the Supreme Being and ultimate creator in Yoruba religion. Also known as Olorun (Owner of Heaven), Olodumare is the source of all existence, the giver of ase (divine authority), and the architect of the universe. Too vast and transcendent for direct human worship, Olodumare has no shrines, priests, or sacrifices — instead communicating through the orishas who serve as intermediaries. Olodumare created the cosmos, established the framework of existence, and breathed life into the clay figures that Obatala molded. Every orisha is an emanation of Olodumare. The name derives from "O ní odù mà rè" — the owner of the source of creation that does not become empty

name: Olokun
description: Olokun is the Yoruba orisha of the deep ocean, owner of the sea, parent of Ajé (wealth). Androgynous: male in coastal areas, female inland. Grants prosperity to fishermen/traders; withdraws wealth when disrespected. Keeper of subconscious secrets. Imprisoned by Obatala with Ogun's chain after flooding land. Venerated in Lagos festivals and diaspora.

name: Olorun
description: Olorun (Unknown). is a deity. Olórun is the supreme god in the Yoruba pantheon, the owner of the sky and the source of all life force (àṣẹ). He is considered the creator of the universe and delegates authority to the Orishas.. Source: Yoruba cosmology; Ifá tradition

name: Onatah
description: Onatah is the corn spirit of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois), one of the Three Sisters who sustain the people with the bean and squash spirits. A jealous rival, sometimes named Tawiscara, kidnapped her and hid her underground, bringing famine until her sisters freed her. The three crops are still planted together, a living lesson in cooperation.

name: Ondù
description: Ondù is the Alpine water-spirit of Lombardy and Trentino, cousin of the Germanic Nixe and Nordic Nøkken: a pale youth in wet clothing, often playing a violin, sometimes a horse with a drenched mane. He lures listeners with haunting music and drags them under, yet rewards survivors with musical talent. A related Ondina of Lago di Carezza combs her hair on the shore, vanishing at any noise.

name: One Who Walks All Over The Sky Tsimshian
description: A figure of Tsimshian tradition of the Northwest Coast, associated with the origin of the sun and moon. The name describes a being who traverses the sky, and the story belongs to the Tsimshian cycle of sky-world tales that account for the celestial bodies and their movements. Details of the name and narrative vary among Tsimshian and neighbouring peoples.

name: Ongon Spirit
description: The ongon, plural ongod, is the spirit of Mongolian and Siberian shamanism housed in a consecrated idol and tended like a living being. Deceased shamans become ongod, and black shamans summon their spirits up while drumming in trance. Ongod are felt to dwell in liminal places, at river mouths and on the borders between taiga and steppe.

name: Oni
description: Oni (鬼) are the ogres or demons of Japanese folklore: large, fearsome beings with red, blue, or black skin, horns, sharp claws, and tiger-skin loincloths, often carrying iron clubs. They dwell in mountain fastnesses, punish the wicked, and cause disasters, yet also appear in protective roles. During Setsubun, people scatter roasted beans crying 'Oni wa soto!' to drive them from the home.

name: Oniare
description: Oniare is the great horned water serpent of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois), said to lurk in lakes and rivers, capsizing canoes and sending storms against the unwary. The Mohawk word onyare means 'snake,' and Onyarekowa, the great snake, was feared for its poisonous breath. It is the eternal enemy of the Thunderers, and offerings were once made to appease it.

name: Orang Bunian
description: The orang bunian are the invisible 'hidden people' of Malay folklore: beautiful beings who live in deep forests and high mountains, dressed in ancient Southeast Asian style, sometimes said to lack a philtrum. They form families, clans, even kingdoms, befriend dukun, bomoh, and pawang, and are usually benevolent; tales tell of humans intermarrying with them only to find years have passed.

name: Orang Bunian
description: Orang Bunian (Hidden People) are supernatural beings from Malay folklore who are invisible to most humans except those with spiritual sight. They are a parallel race living in another dimension overlapping with the human world, particularly in forests, foothills, and cemeteries. In Singapore, Kubur Kassim Cemetery in Siglap contains tombs specifically dedicated to Orang Bunian. They are described as beautiful beings in ancient Southeast Asian attire, nearly identical to humans but sometimes lacking a philtrum. They are generally benevolent, befriending shamans, but can intermarry with humans with strange time-dilation effects

name: Orang Bunian
description: Orang Bunian (Hidden People) are supernatural beings from Malay folklore who are invisible to most humans except those with spiritual sight. They are a parallel race living in another dimension overlapping with the human world, particularly in forests, foothills, and cemeteries. In Singapore, Kubur Kassim Cemetery in Siglap contains tombs specifically dedicated to Orang Bunian. They are described as beautiful beings in ancient Southeast Asian attire, nearly identical to humans but sometimes lacking a philtrum. They are generally benevolent, befriending shamans, but can intermarry with humans with strange time-dilation effects In Singapore folklore, this figure is known among the Singapore Malay people.

name: Orang Minyak (Oily Man)
description: The orang minyak ('oily man') is a figure of Malaysian urban legend: a man covered head to toe in black oil who creeps in at night to attack women, his oil making him nearly impossible to catch. Publicized in the 1950s by Berita Harian and later in a P. Ramlee film, he is read as a modern moral tale reinforcing sexual morality and fear of strangers.

name: Oriole Spirit
description: The oriole (vàng anh) is a spirit figure of Vietnamese folk narrative, most famously in the tale of Tấm and Cám, where the wronged heroine is transformed into an oriole that sings beside the royal palace and later into other natural forms. The oriole's transformations express themes of death, rebirth, and the eventual triumph of justice in Vietnamese storytelling.

name: Oro
description: The supreme god of war and peace in Tahitian mythology, son of Ta'aroa (the creator god). Oro was the most powerful and revered deity in the Society Islands, particularly on Tahiti and Raiatea. He descended to earth on a rainbow and took a mortal woman as his wife, establishing the Arioi society - a secret religious order of warriors, artists, and priests who spread his cult. The Arioi traveled between islands performing sacred dances, chants, and dramatic performances. Oro's cult was centered at the great marae of Taputapuatea on Raiatea, the spiritual center of Eastern Polynesia. He eventually displaced Tane as the chief god of Tahiti, and his worship involved elaborate ceremonies including human sacrifice

name: Orochi
description: Orochi (Unknown). is a serpent. Yamata no Orochi is an eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent from Japanese mythology. The storm god Susanoo slays the creature after discovering it has been devouring the daughters of an earthly couple.. Source: Kojiki (712 CE); Nihon Shoki (720 CE)

name: Orunmila
description: Orunmila is the Yoruba orisha of wisdom, divination, knowledge, and prophecy. He is the custodian of the Ifá divination system, which contains 256 sacred verses (Odu) that encode the entire knowledge of the universe. Present at creation, Orunmila witnessed everything that would happen and recorded it in the Ifá corpus. He taught humanity the art of divination through Babalawos (fathers of secrets), the initiated priests who interpret sacred palm nuts and the divination chain. Orunmila represents destiny, fate, and the power of knowledge. UNESCO recognized the Ifá divination system as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005

name: Oshun
description: Yoruba river goddess of love, beauty, and fresh water. In Cuban Santeria, syncretized as Ochun (or Oxum in Brazilian Candomble), she is identified with the Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre (Our Lady of Charity), Cuba patron saint. As the most beloved orisha in the Caribbean, she governs rivers, honey, gold, sensuality, and dance. Her devotees wear yellow and amber, and she is renowned for her joyful, flirtatious, yet fiercely protective nature. The annual pilgrimage to El Cobre in Santiago de Cuba honors her as both Ochun and the national patroness

name: Osiris
description: Osiris is the ancient Egyptian god of the afterlife, death, and resurrection. Murdered by his brother Set and restored by his sister-wife Isis, he became ruler of the underworld, judging the dead at the Weighing of the Heart. As a dying-and-returning god he symbolized regeneration, the Nile flood, and the promise of life after death, with his cult center at Abydos.

name: Ossobó
description: Ossobó is a mystical rain-bird in Forro (São Toméan) folklore. Inhabiting cloud forests and mountain peaks, it manipulates weather and heals through sonic powers — its melodic calls bring nurturing energy. A symbol of hope, renewal, and connection to ancestral spirits. The tale 'Gertrude's Bird' features it.

name: Otso
description: Otso ('The Bear', 'Honey-Paw') is the sacred bear spirit, king of the Finnish forest. Divine embodiment of bear, walking upright as man in powerful form. Honored through elaborate peijaiset (bear ceremony): hunters apologized, feasted skull, returned bones to forest. Dozens of euphemisms (otso, mesikämmen, kontio) avoided true name (karhu) to prevent summoning.

name: Owl Ancestor-Spirit (Khmer)
description: Not independently attested in documented Khmer folklore or academic sources as a named 'Owl Ancestor-Spirit.' Owls do carry omen meanings in Cambodia—their calls are often read as ill omens or messages—but no source records a specific ancestor-spirit embodied as an owl and tied to lakes. The entry appears to combine general owl-omen belief with an unattested spirit name.

name: Owl Ancestor-Spirit (Khmer)
description: No owl ancestor-spirit exists in Khmer (Cambodian) tradition, and the Khmer are a Southeast Asian people, not of the United States. Cambodian folklore does regard the owl as an ill omen whose cry foretells death, but no ancestor-spirit, water spirit, or guardian owl is recorded. The entry is a template-generated invention with the wrong country and the wrong people.

name: Owl Ancestor-Spirit of Creek
description: Among the Muscogee (Creek), owls were regarded as vessels for the spirits of the dead: great horned owls and screech owls were thought to be embodied ghosts, restless spirits, or wizards in bird form, and an owl's cry was an omen of death. This is the closest Creek tradition to an owl ancestor-spirit, though no named guardian owl is recorded.

name: Owl Ancestor-Spirit of Dogon
description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon ancestor spirits are the Nommo (amphibious) and Lebe (serpent). Owls appear in Dogon iconography on sanctuary doors but not as named ancestor-spirits guarding valleys. Record appears fabricated from generic 'owl guardian' templates.

name: Owl Ancestor-Spirit of Navajo
description: The Navajo regard the owl as a being of the spirit world tied to death: its hoot is an omen, a dream of an owl foretells death, and owls are linked to witches and to the dead. The most fearsome were 'Those That Kill With Their Eyes' (Binaa' yee aghaanii), monsters slain by the Hero Twins. No guardian ancestor-spirit owl is recorded.

name: Owl Animal-Spirit of Haida
description: The owl holds a place in Haida oral tradition as a crest and spirit being. In the Haida story of Kwel-Kwel the girl married the owl and their children founded the Owl crest; elsewhere the owl appears as a messenger whose cry is an omen, and shamans' familiar spirits could take owl form. It is a spirit animal rather than a forest guardian.

name: Owl Animal-Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition as a named 'owl animal-spirit'. Muisca mythology (Bachué, Bochica, Chía, Sué, Chibchacum, Goranchacha, Monster of Lake Tota) includes no owl guardian of caves. Owls may appear in general Andean bird symbolism but no specific owl spirit is documented in Ocampo López or chroniclers (Simón, Piedrahita, Castellanos).

name: Owl Deity (Guarani)
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. The seven legendary monsters and major deities (Tupã, Arasy, Tau, Kerana, Angatupyry, Pombero, Kurupi, Jurupari, Abaangui) include no owl deity. Owls appear in general Guaraní bird lore but hold no deity status. Entity appears fabricated.

name: Owl Deity (Guarani)
description: No owl deity exists in Guarani religion, and the Guarani are a South American people of Paraguay, Brazil, and Argentina, not of the United States. Guarani and Paraguayan folklore instead cast the great horned owl (ñacurutú) as an evil bird of ill omen and the urutau as a spirit bird; no owl is worshipped or made a god.

name: Owl Deity of Blackfoot
description: No owl deity is attested in Blackfoot religion. The Blackfoot (Siksika, Kainai, Piikani) instead held that owls could be inhabited by the spirits of medicine men, and owl feathers marked warriors and leaders, as in the black-dog society leader's owl-feather bonnet. The owl is a medicine bird, never a god.

name: Owl Deity of Blackfoot
description: No owl deity is attested among the Blackfoot of Canada (Siksika, Kainai, Piikani of the Blackfoot Confederacy). Their genuine owl traditions are the Owl Dance, a social and courtship dance, and the belief that owls may carry the spirits of medicine men. The owl is honored in song and story but is not a deity.

name: Owl Deity of Mi'kmaq
description: No owl deity is recorded in Mi'kmaq tradition. The Mi'kmaq know the owl as kokokwes, a name drawn from the barred owl's calling, and in the celestial story of the stars the Owl is one of the hunters who pursues the Great Bear across the night sky. But the owl is never a god.

name: Owl Deity of Uzbek
description: Not independently attested as a deity of Uzbek folklore. No source records an owl god in Uzbek tradition, and owls are generally birds of ill omen in Central Asian folk belief. The closest real practice is the protective use of owl feathers against the evil eye, a charm best documented among the neighboring Kazakh people rather than in any Uzbek owl cult.

name: Owl Ghost of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. No owl ghost exists in Guaraní mythology (seven legendary monsters, major deities, or spirit categories). Guaraní afterlife concepts involve Luison (death god) and ancestral spirits, but no owl ghost of undergrounds. Entity appears fabricated.

name: Owl Ghost of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. Duplicate of owlghostofguarani-paraguay with Brazil country assignment. No owl ghost exists in Guaraní mythology across Paraguay, Argentina, or Brazil. Entity appears fabricated.

name: Owl Ghost of Maya
description: In Yucatec Maya lore the owl (tunkuluchu) is death's messenger: its hooting near a home foretells a death, and it sings beside the dying. A famous legend explains this — after being humiliated at a noble's banquet, a proud bird was transformed into an owl, and it now cries out whenever someone is about to die, haunting ruins and dark places by night.

name: Owl Ghost of Mi'kmaq
description: No owl ghost is attested in Mi'kmaq folklore. The documented owl traditions of the Mi'kmaq are the celestial Owl, one of the star-hunters chasing the Great Bear, and the name kokokwes for the owl. Owls are not portrayed as ghosts or water spirits in Mi'kmaq stories; the entry is a template-generated invention.

name: Owl Giant of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested as a giant in Kazakh folklore. Kazakh tradition instead holds the owl (üki) sacred: owl feathers are fastened to cradles and headdresses to shield newborns, children and young brides from evil spirits, and to guard akyns, the poet-singers, from harm. No giant owl figure appears in recorded Kazakh tales.

name: Owl Giant of Tlingit
description: No owl giant exists in Tlingit tradition. The documented Tlingit owl figure comes from the story of the Kîksa'dî woman who was turned into an owl after mistreating her mother-in-law; her owl cry thereafter warns of bad weather and bad news. The owl is a transformed woman and omen-bird, never a giant.

name: Owl Giant of Tlingit
description: No owl giant is attested in Tlingit tradition. The Tlingit of southeastern Alaska and British Columbia tell instead of the woman of the Kîksa'dî clan who became an owl as punishment for cruelty to her mother-in-law; her call foretells bad weather and bad news. The owl is a transformed ancestor figure, not a giant.

name: Owl Giant of Yurok
description: No owl giant appears in Yurok folklore. Yurok traditional narratives collected by Kroeber and others center on figures such as the Bear and her fawns, the theft of fire, and the origin of salmon; owls play no giant or guardian role. The entry is a template invention with no basis in Yurok tradition.

name: Owl Guardian (Shona)
description: Not independently attested as a named guardian in Shona tradition. Owls in Shona and wider Bantu culture are widely regarded as omens of death or witchcraft familiars (e.g., goba), not protective guardians of valleys. The entry uses a templated "guardian of valley" description contradicting actual cultural associations.

name: Owl Guardian of Tlingit
description: No owl guardian spirit is attested in Tlingit tradition. The Tlingit tell of the Kîksa'dî woman turned into an owl whose cry announces bad weather and bad news; elsewhere owls are linked to death omens and shamanic spirits. None of this amounts to a guardian owl, and the river-guardian framing is a template artifact.

name: Owl Guardian of Tlingit
description: No owl guardian is attested in Tlingit tradition. Tlingit lore records the woman of the Kîksa'dî clan who was turned into an owl, whose cry warns of storms and ill news, and owls carry associations with death omens. These are the extent of Tlingit owl beliefs; no guardian or tutelary owl exists.

name: Owl Nature-Spirit (San)
description: Not independently attested in San (Khoisan) tradition of Botswana. While /Xam San narratives (Bleek & snip Lloyd) document avian spirits including ostrich and vulture, a specific "Owl Nature-Spirit of the lake" lacks verification. Owls in San folklore are less prominent; snip the entry appears templated.

name: Owl Nature-Spirit (San)
description: No owl nature-spirit exists in San (Bushmen) tradition, and the San are an indigenous people of southern Africa, not of Canada. San mythology centers on |Kaggen, the praying-mantis trickster and creator. The entry pairs an African people with a Canadian country tag and invents an owl lake-spirit that no tradition records.

name: Owl Nature-Spirit of Ashanti
description: Not independently attested in Ashanti (Akan) tradition. Owls in Akan folklore are often witch familiars or omens (e.g., 'koko' owl), not benevolent nature-spirits guarding valleys. No named 'Owl Nature-Spirit' appears in Rattray or Ashanti ethnographies. Record appears fabricated.

name: Owl Nature-Spirit of Haida
description: In Haida tradition the owl is bound up with the spirit world: its call is read as an omen, often of death, and in the story of Kwel-Kwel a girl's marriage to the owl founds the Owl crest of her descendants. As a night-flying spirit being it belongs to the unseen realm, though no generic nature-spirit guardian is recorded.

name: Owl Nature-Spirit of Maliseet
description: Among the Maliseet-Passamaquoddy (Wabanaki) of the Northeast, the owl appears in story as a being of power: in the legend of the Owl Husband a girl marries the great horned owl, and owl figures also take part in Wabanaki tales. The owl is a story-being and omen, though not the forest nature-spirit guardian the entry claims.

name: Owl Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: The Cheyenne hold that owls are spirits of the night: they said only the short-eared owl is a true bird, while all other owls are mista, night spirits, often of a dangerous or deathly kind. Warriors nonetheless wore owl feathers on shields and arms for night vision, and the Contraries society used owl feathers in its regalia.

name: Owl Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: Not independently attested, and likely mislabeled: 'Cheyenne' is a Native American tribe of the Great Plains, not a Myanmar tradition, and no source records an 'Owl Spirit' of Myanmar under this name. The entry's generated filler prose offers no concrete traits. Owl associations in Myanmar relate to the nat pantheon, but no such named owl spirit was located.

name: Owl Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: The Cheyenne recognize owls as night spirits: in their belief only the short-eared owl is a genuine bird, while the other owls are mista, spirits of the night, feared as omens. Owl feathers nonetheless carried protective power, worn by warriors to see in the dark. The same belief holds wherever Cheyenne tradition is told.

name: Owl Spirit of Mi'kmaq
description: The Mi'kmaq know the owl as kokokwes, a name drawn from the barred owl's calling, and place the Owl among the celestial hunters of star-lore: in the Mi'kmaq story of the Great Bear, the Owl is one of the seven hunters who pursue the bear around the northern sky, explaining the turning of the stars.

name: Owl Trickster of Cherokee
description: No owl trickster exists in Cherokee folklore. In Mooney's Myths of the Cherokee the owls appear in 'The Bird Tribes' as embodied ghosts and disguised witches, the dusky horned owl being called tskïlï, 'witch,' with their cries read as omens of death. Cherokee trickster roles belong to Rabbit and Possum, not the owl.

name: Owl Trickster of Mi'kmaq
description: In Mi'kmaq oral tradition the owl appears in stories as a creature of the night, often a messenger or a figure with supernatural associations. The Mi'kmaq culture hero is Glooscap (Kluskap), however, and a specific 'owl trickster' is not independently attested in Mi'kmaq sources; the record likely conflates owl motifs with trickster cycles of other Algonquian peoples.

name: Owl Water-Spirit of Aymara
description: Not independently attested in Aymara tradition. Aymara are highland Altiplano people (Lake Titicaca region); their water beings include lake spirits and amaru (serpent), but no owl water-spirit is documented in Aymara ethnography (Molinié Fioravanti, La Barre, Núñez del Prado). The conflation of owl (highland bird) and water spirit appears fabricated.

name: Owl Water-Spirit of Dogon
description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon water spirits are the Nommo (amphibious ancestors). No owl water-spirit appears in Griaule's documentation of Dogon cosmogony. Record appears fabricated from generic templates.

name: Oya
description: Oya is the powerful Yoruba orisha of winds, storms, lightning, transformation, and the Niger River. Her name derives from "o ya" meaning "she tore." She is the only orisha who can control the Egungun (spirits of the dead), a power granted by Babalú Ayé. Known as the "mother of nine" for her nine stillborn children, Oya guards the gates of the cemetery and escorts souls to the afterlife. She is the goddess of the marketplace, change, and rebirth. Married first to Ogun, then to Shango, she and Shango together represent the full force of the storm — her wind precedes his thunder

name: Oyoyewi (Twin War God)
description: Oyoyewi is one of the Twin War Gods in Pueblo (specifically Acoma) tradition, brother to Masewi. Together, these twins are the most important heroic and protective figures in Pueblo mythology. Born to a virgin mother who conceived from the Sun, they were responsible for creating order in the world, slaying monsters, establishing the directions, and teaching humanity the proper way to live. Oyoyewi and Masewi continue to watch over the Pueblo people from the underworld, and their exploits are cel

name: P 'ban (or Phibaan)
description: Phi Ban, Thai ผีบ้าน, is the guardian spirit of a village or household in Thai and Lao animist belief, propitiated so the settlement stays protected. The input's giant, man-eating ogre traits belong instead to the yak (ยักษ์), the ogre of Thai temple art and the Ramakien—a conflation of two distinct beings of Thai folk religion.

name: Pa'itele
description: Pa'itele is a monstrous sea creature of Samoan legend that terrorized the Apolima Strait, overturning and attacking the canoes that crossed the channel between Upolu and Savai'i. According to oral tradition, the hero Alo eventually defeated the beast, ending its assaults on voyagers. The tale stands as a Samoan hero narrative about courage and the mastery of dangerous waters.

name: Pacific Northwest
description: Not a genuine mythological being. 'Pacific Northwest' is a geographic region, not a creature of Tlingit or any other tradition, and no source names a spirit by this title. The real Tlingit spiritual world is rich with animal guardians, the land-otter people and spirits of forest and coast, but the entity described in this record does not exist.

name: Pacific Northwest
description: Not a genuine mythological being; this is a duplicate of the 'Pacific Northwest' regional placeholder. No First Nations tradition names a spirit 'Pacific Northwest.' The Canadian coastal spiritual world includes real beings such as the Tlingit Kushtaka and the Nuxalk Raven, but the entity described in this record does not exist in any recorded tradition.

name: Pah
description: Pah is the Moon god in Pawnee mythology, placed in the heavens by Tirawa as one of the last divine creations. Along with Shakuru (the Sun), Pah governs the night sky. The Sun and Moon produced a son who was placed on Earth as the ancestor of the Pawnee people. Pah is associated with the night, women's cycles, and the rhythm of time. In some traditions, the Moon is considered female, representing the feminine principle of creation alongside the feminine Evening Star. The Moon's phases mark the timing of ceremonies

name: Pahana
description: Pahana (also Bahana) is the 'True White Brother,' the lost elder brother of Hopi prophecy who left the Hopi people long ago and is destined to return to restore balance and reunite the world. He carries the sacred tablets of the Hopi, and his coming is bound up with the tribe's stories of the four worlds and their migrations.

name: Paiyatuma
description: Paiyatuma, the Zuni Kachina of Dew and Dawn, is the flute-playing spirit who, in Zuni origin myths, brought the people the new music of his flute and led the seven Corn Maidens back to the pueblo after their wanderings. A patron of spring rains and the growing season, he is often cited as the model for the widespread Kokopelli Flute Player.

name: Paiyatuma (god of dawn and music)
description: Paiyatuma (Paiyatamu), the Zuni God of Dew and of the Dawn, is a flute-playing kachina celebrated in Zuni origin myths. He brought the Zuni the new music of the flute and presided over the Corn Maidens, and Zuni belief ties him to the life-giving moisture of morning and spring; scholars regard him as a probable prototype of the Pan-Southwestern Kokopelli Flute Player.

name: Palden Lhamo
description: Palden Lhamo (Śrīdēvī), the 'Glorious Goddess,' is the principal female protector deity of Tibetan Buddhism and the only woman among the Eight Guardians of the Dharma. A wrathful form of Tara, she rides a mule across a sea of blood, bearing a sword and skull cup, guarding the Dalai Lamas and the lineage of the Buddhist teaching.

name: Palo Mayombe
description: Palo Mayombe is not a spirit but an Afro-Cuban religion (Las Reglas de Congo) derived from Kongo traditions. Its spirits are mpungu (deities like Lucero, Sarabanda, Madre de Agua) and nfumbe (dead spirits housed in nganga vessels). The entry misclassifies a religion as a creature.

name: Pamola
description: Pamola is a powerful snow bird spirit who dwells on the summit of Mount Katahdin, the highest mountain in Maine and the most sacred peak of the Penobscot and Abenaki people. Pamola has the body of a man and the head and wings of a giant eagle and makes the cold weather by beating his enormous wings. He fiercely guards the mountain against trespassers, sending blizzards to drive away those who dare approach his domain. According to legend, a Penobscot woman once married Pamola and lived with him on the mountain

name: Pangkarlangu
description: Pangkarlangu are fearsome child-stealing monsters of Warlpiri Jukurrpa (Dreaming) stories from Australia's Western and Central Desert. Huge, hairy beings without necks and with sharp claws, they seize children by the legs and carry them off to eat, and their presence marks dangerous desert places. The tale 'The Pangkarlangu and the Lost Child' teaches children to stay near camp and obey elders.

name: Pangool
description: The Pangool (singular: Fangool) are the ancient saints and ancestral spirits of the Serer people of Senegal, the Gambia, and Mauritania, serving as the central spiritual bridge between humanity and the supreme creator deity Roog. Unlike distant gods, the Pangool are intimately involved in daily life — they are canonized ancestors who have been elevated to spirit status due to their exceptional leadership, sacrifice, or spiritual alignment during their lives. They act as protectors, moral guides, healers, and intermediaries, ensuring balance between human action and cosmic order. The Pangool are associated with specific families, villages, natural features, and sacred geography. Their most recognized symbol is the serpent, often depicted as two coiled snakes, representing spiritual vigilance and continuity. The Serer maintain that the Pangool are not merely historical ancestors but active spiritual forces that respond to proper ritual observance. Sacred groves, ancestral trees, and shrines dedicated to the Pangool continue to be protected across Serer territory, and annual ceremonies invoke their protection during planting seasons and community transitions

name: Panther Ancestor-Spirit (Burmese)
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Burmese folklore; no source documents a 'Panther Ancestor-Spirit.' The underlying idea is real: Karen and Tangshang (Naga) traditions hold that ancestor spirits may appear as big cats, and nats ride tigers, but the big-cat ancestor figures of Myanmar are tigers, and no panther figure bears this name.

name: Panther Ancestor-Spirit (Burmese)
description: Not independently attested as a panther ancestor-spirit in Burmese folklore, and wrongly tagged as Mexican. Burmese tradition venerates nats and ancestor spirits, but no source records a river-guarding panther ancestor-spirit, and panthers do not hold that role in Burmese belief. The record appears to be a generic 'ancestor-spirit' template with a predator animal attached to it.

name: Panther Ancestor-Spirit (Burmese)
description: Not independently attested in Botswana tradition. Panthers (leopards) exist in Africa but "Burmese" ancestor-spirit is a category error — Burmese refers to Myanmar. The entry misattributes a Southeast Asian concept to Botswana. Fabricated templated entry with "river" motif.

name: Panther Deity (Guarani)
description: Partially attested but misnamed. Guarani mythology includes the Celestial Jaguar (Jaguarete, Jaguareté) — a primordial jaguar deity associated with the sky, twins, and ancestral souls — but 'panther' (leopard) is an Old World term. No 'Panther Deity' as distinct entity; the Celestial Jaguar fills this role.

name: Panther Deity (Guarani)
description: Panther Deity (Guarani) (Kenya). is a deity. A panther deity from Guarani tradition that  sky. Source: Regional survey of East African indigenous traditions — Kikuyu, Luo, Ganda, Chaga, Malagasy, Maasai, Somali, Ethiopian, and related peoples as documen

name: Panther Deity (Guarani)
description: Not attested in North American folklore. This entry is a misattribution of Guarani-region material to the United States: no USA tradition records a 'panther deity' of this kind, and no specific panther deity is clearly documented in Guarani tradition either. The closest genuine analogues are jaguar-cult figures of South America and cougar spirits of North American tribes.

name: Panther Guardian (Dogon)
description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon cosmology centers on Amma, Nommo, and the Pale Fox (Ogo); no panther guardian appears in Griaule's or Dieterlen's ethnographies. The closest analogue is the Kanaga mask's antelope symbolism. Record appears fabricated from generic 'forest guardian' templates.

name: Panther Guardian (Dogon)
description: Panther Guardian (Dogon) (Kenya). is a guardian. A panther guardian from Dogon tradition that  ocean. Source: Regional survey of East African indigenous traditions — Kikuyu, Luo, Ganda, Chaga, Malagasy, Maasai, Somali, Ethiopian, and related peoples as documen

name: Panther Nature-Spirit (Yoruba)
description: Not independently attested in Yoruba tradition. Yoruba orisha pantheon includes Ogun, Oshun, Yemoja, and Shango, but no specific panther nature-spirit. Leopards appear as royal symbols and in Egungun masquerades, not as distinct nature-spirits. Record appears fabricated from generic templates.

name: Panther Nature-Spirit (Yoruba)
description: Not independently attested in Lao folklore; no source documents a panther nature-spirit in Laos. The name's internal contradiction—a 'Yoruba' nature-spirit assigned to Laos, a country in mainland Southeast Asia—marks it as an AI-generated placeholder. Lao forest spirits are the phi pa and phi phetu of lowland tradition and the dab spirits of Hmong belief, not panthers.

name: Panther Spirit (Dogon)
description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon spiritual beings are Nommo (amphibious ancestors), Ogo (Pale Fox), and Lebe (serpent ancestor). No panther spirit appears in Griaule's documentation. Record appears fabricated from generic templates.

name: Panther Spirit (Dogon)
description: Not independently attested. The Dogon are a West African people (Mali); panthers (leopards) and Dogon cosmology are absent from Chile. The described 'lake-embodying panther spirit' has no basis in Mapuche or Chilote mythology. Complete cross-continental fabrication.

name: Panther Trickster (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested as a named figure of Lao folklore; searches locate no panther trickster in Lao tradition. Lao oral literature features animal tales, such as the crow-and-peacock legend, and the clever-human trickster Xieng Mieng, but no panther deity or trickster appears in documented sources, marking this entry as an invented name.

name: Panther Trickster (Laotian)
description: Not attested in North American folklore. This entry misplaces a Laotian panther trickster in the United States: no USA tradition records such a being, and the Laotian origin is itself unsupported by any named source. North American trickster roles belong to Coyote, Raven and other animals; a panther trickster is not part of any recorded USA tradition.

name: Papa Bois
description: Papa Bois, 'Father of the Wood' in French Creole, is the guardian of the forest in Saint Lucian and wider Caribbean lore: an old, muscular man with cloven hooves, horns and a beard of living leaves who warns animals with a cow's horn and punishes wasteful hunters, sometimes by shapeshifting into a deer to lead them astray.

name: Papa Bois
description: Papa Bois is a nature-spirit from Trinidad and Tobago mythology. He appears as an ancient, muscular man with cloven hooves, goat-like horns, and a beard woven from living leaves. He can shapeshift into a deer to lure disrespectful hunters into the thickest parts of the woods, where they become hopelessly lost. His name is of French origin ('Papa Bois' meaning Father Wood). In Grenadian tradition, he is married to Mama Glo. He carries a hollowed-out bull's horn which he uses to warn animals when humans approach. Hunters in Grenada traditionally say a prayer or perform a small ritual before entering the forest, acknowledging Papa Bois as the true guardian of the land

name: Papa Bois
description: Papa Bois is a nature-spirit from Caribbean mythology. He appears as an ancient, muscular man with cloven hooves, goat-like horns, and a beard woven from living leaves. He can shapeshift into a deer to lure disrespectful hunters into the thickest parts of the woods, where they become hopelessly lost. His name is of French origin ('Papa Bois' meaning Father Wood). In Grenadian tradition, he is married to Mama Glo. He carries a hollowed-out bull's horn which he uses to warn animals when humans approach. Hunters in Grenada traditionally say a prayer or perform a small ritual before entering the forest, acknowledging Papa Bois as the true guardian of the land

name: Papa Legba (Guardian of the Crossroads)
description: Papa Legba is the foremost lwa (spirit) in Haitian Vodou, serving as the guardian of the crossroads, gateways, and communication between the human world and the realm of the spirits. No ceremony can begin without first invoking Papa Legba, who opens the spiritual gateway. He is an old, wise man who walks with a crutch or cane, often depicted as a humble elder leaning on a staff, wearing a broad-brimmed straw hat and smoking a pipe, carrying a sack or bundle of keys. In Haitian Vodou, he is syncretized with Saint Peter (who holds the keys to heaven) and Saint Lazarus. His origins trace back to the Yoruba deity Elegba/Eshu, but in Haiti he evolved into a gentler, paternal figure who facilitates rather than tests. His colors are red and white, and his sacred day is Monday. Offerings include roasted peanuts, sugarcane, tobacco, coffee, and rum poured at crossroads

name: Papa-Figo
description: Papa-Figo (Papão) is a Brazilian bogeyman: a liver-eating demon that possesses those who eat pork, especially on Fridays or during Lent. Used to frighten children into obedience. Syncretic: African (Quimbanda) pork taboos merged with European 'bogeyman' and Catholic dietary rules. 'Figo' may derive from 'fig' (slang for liver) or be a corruption of 'Papão.'

name: Papatuanuku (Papa)
description: The primordial earth mother in Maori cosmology. Papatuanuku lay embraced with Ranginui (Sky Father) in the beginning, their children trapped between them. After their forced separation, she became the foundation of all life on earth. Her body formed the land, mountains, forests, and waters. All living things are her children. She is the nurturing source of food, shelter, and life itself. The earthquakes are her struggles to turn toward her beloved Rangi, and the mist that rises is her breath. In Maori tradition, humans return to her embrace at death

name: Parikhan
description: Parikhan is the peri-princess of the Tajik fairy tale 'Shahabaskhan and Parikhan.' Left abandoned in the forest by the khan's men, she is saved by the hero Shahabaskhan, and their romance unfolds in the manner of the peri tales of Persianate Central Asian storytelling, in which fairy maidens wed mortal heroes. She is a fairy princess, not a restless ghost.

name: Passadinha
description: Passadinha is a trickster bird in Cape Verdean folklore, known for vocal mimicry and mischief in village gardens and forests. It embodies wit and playfulness, deceiving humans through imitation. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tales alongside figures like Ti Lobo and Chibinho.

name: Pasupata
description: Not independently attested as a distinct demon in Indian folklore. 'Pashupata' is primarily a Shaiva ascetic sect (Pashupata Shaivism) founded by Lakulisha (2nd c. CE), not a demonic being. The record's description ('demonic sect or creature from Tantric traditions, possesses people, causes madness') conflates the sect with left-hand path stereotypes.

name: Patasola
description: Patasola ('single leg') is a Colombian vampire forest spirit.
