She appears as a beautiful woman to lure male hunters deep into the jungle, then reveals her true form: one-legged, one-breasted, fanged, with bovine hoof. She devours flesh and drinks blood. Origin varies: scorned mother, unfaithful wife, or wicked woman mutilated as punishment. Protects forest animals from human predation.

name: Pate Serpent
description: The Pate Serpent is a legendary sea monster said to inhabit the waters around Pate Island in the Lamu Archipelago. According to tradition, the serpent was a guardian spirit placed by the sea gods to protect the ancient city of Shanga (the original Swahili settlement on Pate). The serpent was enormous, its body stretching across the channel between Pate and neighboring islands. It appeared during times of crisis, creating whirlpools swallowing enemy ships. During Pate's golden age, the serpent surfaced at sunset, its scales gleaming gold and green. The serpent is connected to the Liongo Fumo legend -- it is said Liongo himself sang the serpent into a deep sleep to pass through the channel

name: Patsallht First Born Nuxalk
description: Not independently attested under this name in the available Nuxalk (Bella Coola) sources. The name is associated with the Nuxalk origin account of Ista, the First Woman who descended to land, and with the creation of the first people; closer documentation is needed before the figure can be verified.

name: Pattini
description: Pattini (Kannaki) is the Sri Lankan goddess of chastity, healing, fertility — deified heroine of Tamil epic Silappatikaram. After husband Kovalan's execution, she burns Madurai with her anklet, settles in Sri Lanka. Documented by Obeyesekere ('The Cult of the Goddess Pattini'). She walks fire, cures epidemics (smallpox, measles), protects children.

name: Patung
description: Not attested as a Hopi or North American being. 'Patung' is the Indonesian word for 'statue' or 'carved figure,' not a Hopi spirit. The record's claim that a carved figure named Patung guards Hopi villages and patrols boundaries at night matches no documented Hopi tradition; kachina figures are carved, but are never called 'patung.'

name: Patupaiarehe
description: Patupaiarehe (also Tūrehu) are fairy-like people of Māori lore, fair-skinned with reddish-blond hair and no tattoos, dwelling in misty forests and mountains. Nocturnal and shy, they avoid sunlight and cooked food and sometimes lured humans away to bear red-haired children. The subtribe Ngāti Rua is said to live on Mt Ngongotahā, sometimes read as Aotearoa's pre-Māori inhabitants.

name: Pautiwa (chief of Kachinas)
description: Pautiwa (Pawtiwa) is the most important of the Pueblo kachina spirits, a sun deity who rules over all the other kachinas. Chiefly revered among the Zuni, he presides over the kachina priesthood and the kachina village where the spirits dwell, holding the highest position in the Zuni ceremonial world and leading the kachina dancers of the Shalako cycle.

name: Pazuzu
description: Pazuzu is a fearsome demonic deity from ancient Assyrian and Babylonian mythology, best known as the personification of the southwestern wind and king of the lilu wind demons. Unlike purely malevolent entities, Pazuzu held a complex dual role in Mesopotamian religion: he brought famine, locusts, storms, and disease through his control of the destructive southwestern wind, yet was also invoked as an apotropaic protector against other malicious spirits. His grotesque image—a hybrid of canine, human, bird, scorpion, and serpent features—was widely used on amulets and statuettes placed in homes and worn by pregnant women to safeguard infants and mothers, particularly against the child-snatching demoness Lamashtu. He was considered the son of Hanbi, king of the underworld demons, and brother to Humbaba, the guardian of the Cedar Forest in the Epic of Gilgamesh. Pazuzu's image appears in Mesopotamian art from the 8th century BCE through the Seleucid period, and he gained renewed global fame as the possessing demon in William Friedkin's 1973 film The Exorcist

name: Peikko
description: Peikko is the Finnish word for 'troll', a hairy forest being from small to enormous, dwelling in dark woods and rocky ridges. Can shapeshift into stone landscape for centuries. Not a distinct named figure but the generic Finnish troll, cognate with Scandinavian troll. In Kalevala, peikot appear as forest-dwelling obstacles.

name: Peixe Caball
description: Peixe Caball ('horse-fish') is a Cape Verdean mermaid-like being with an equine upper body and fish tail, inhabiting deep ocean and coastal reefs. It appears to sailors as an omen of calm seas and represents the fusion of land and sea in islander identity. Documented in Cape Verdean oral tradition and folkloric collections.

name: Pekapeka
description: Pekapeka is the Māori name for the bat, New Zealand's only native land mammal, a creature of the night tied to omens in traditional belief. In some accounts the night-flying bird hōkioi, whose cry was said to foretell death, is linked to pekapeka, and bats could act as messengers of the spirit world. Conservation efforts now use pekapeka for the two surviving native bat species.

name: Pele
description: Pele is the Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes, fire, lightning, and dance, who dwells in Halema'uma'u crater at Kīlauea. As both creator and destroyer, she builds new land through eruptions and consumes it again, and she is said to produce 'Pele's hair,' the fine threads of volcanic glass found near her vents. Still actively revered today, she is among the most venerated figures of Hawaiian religion.

name: Pele
description: Pele is the Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes, fire, lightning and the hula, who lives in Kilauea on the Big Island and shapes new land through eruptions. A fierce, passionate and sometimes vengeful figure, she is honored with offerings of ʻōhelo berries, and her presence is felt in the lava threads ('Pele's hair') that bear her name. She is still actively worshipped today.

name: Pemba
description: Pemba is the first grain of Bambara (Bamana) creation, which fell to earth and became an acacia tree; from rotten wood and his own saliva he shaped Mousso Koroni, the first woman. His premature, disordered acts of creation let chaos into the cosmos, and the water deity Faro had to descend to restore balance — creation without wisdom.

name: Penanggalan
description: The penanggalan is a vampiric spirit of Malay folklore: by night a woman's head detaches, trailing her lungs and entrails as it flies in search of blood, especially of pregnant women. Vinegar in her body betrays her and thorns snare her guts; the figure has been documented since the 1845 Hikayat Abdullah and Skeat's Malay Magic.

name: Penyimbang Laut (Water Spirit of Brunei)
description: Not independently attested in Bruneian folklore. No scholarly or primary source documents a water spirit called 'Penyimbang Laut'; the figure appears only in a blog source. Brunei's documented river legend is Jong Batu, the tale of a son turned to stone.

name: Pepo (Sea Spirits)
description: Pepo are powerful sea spirits that inhabit the waters around Zanzibar and the entire Swahili coast. According to tradition, the Pepo were the original inhabitants of the coast before humans arrived. These invisible beings can influence human destiny -- bringing good fortune, madness, or illness as they choose. Pepo can possess humans, causing trance states requiring elaborate exorcism ceremonies (kipemba) with specific drum rhythms, incense, and offerings. Each Pepo has a name, personality, and favorite color. The most powerful Pepo are spirits of ancient sultans and warriors who died at sea. Fishermen leave offerings on the shore before long voyages, ensuring the Pepo grant safe passage

name: Pepo wa Bahari (Lord of the Sea)
description: Pepo wa Bahari (the Lord of the Sea) is the most powerful sea spirit in Swahili coastal mythology, ruler of the Indian Ocean depths. Unlike lesser pepo inhabiting specific reefs, Pepo wa Bahari governs all waters from the Lamu Archipelago to the Rovuma River. The spirit controls the monsoon winds driving the dhow trade, fish migrations sustaining coastal communities, and the storms that can destroy fleets. Sailors make elaborate offerings before long voyages -- pouring libations of coconut milk and throwing rice and cloth into the water. The spirit appears during great storms as a towering figure striding across the waves

name: Perchta
description: Frau Perchta (also Berchta, 'the Bright One') is a powerful winter goddess and guardian of moral order in Alpine Germanic folklore, widely regarded as the southern equivalent of Frau Holle. She belongs to the pre-Christian pantheon of continental Germanic peoples and was once venerated as a white-robed deity who oversaw spinning, weaving, and the domestic virtues. During the twelve Rauhnächte (Rough Nights) between Christmas and Epiphany, Perchta roams the countryside entering homes to judge the behavior of children and servants throughout the year. She rewards the industrious with a small silver coin, but the lazy and disobedient face horrific punishment: she slits open their bellies and stuffs the cavity with straw and stones. Her particular concern is spinning — girls who leave their flax unspun by Twelfth Night face her wrath. Despite Church efforts to demonize her (Luther himself railed against 'Fraw Hulde'), Perchta survives in Alpine Perchtenläufe — processions of Schönperchten and Schiachperchten that continue to this day

name: Perchta
description: Frau Perchta (Berchta, 'the Bright One') is a winter spirit of Alpine Germanic folklore, guardian of spinning, weaving and moral order. During the Rauhnächte between Christmas and Epiphany she roams the land inspecting homes, rewarding the industrious with a small coin and punishing the lazy and disobedient, in some tales slitting their bellies and stuffing them with straw.

name: Peri
description: Peri are beautiful winged supernatural beings in Azerbaijani folklore, derived from Persian mythology and deeply integrated into Turkic folk tradition. These enchanting spirits are morally ambivalent but predominantly benevolent, often helping humans in distress and guiding heroes on quests. Peris live in elaborate underground kingdoms with gardens and palaces, organized into societies mirroring human structure. They frequently appear as white doves or gazelles bathing at springs, shedding their animal skins to reveal stunning human forms. If a man steals a Peri's feather garment or animal skin while she bathes, she may be bound to him and can be married. Peris are locked in eternal conflict with their malevolent counterparts, the Divs. They appear throughout the Kitabi-Dede Korkut tales and Azerbaijani fairy tales like 'Malikmammad'

name: Peri
description: Peri are beautiful winged spirits in Azerbaijani folklore, rooted in Persian tradition. Often benevolent but ambivalent, they live in underground kingdoms with gardens and palaces, appear as white doves or gazelles, and can be bound to a man who steals their feather garment or skin. They wage eternal war with the evil Divs and appear in tales such as 'Malikmammad' and the Kitabi-Dede Korkut.

name: Peris
description: Peris are winged fairy-like spirits from Persian mythology, adopted into Pakistani folklore via Persianate influence. Originally ambiguous in pre-Islamic belief, they became beautiful, morally complex beings in mountains and waterfalls. They abduct humans to Peristan and oppose the ugly divs. In Pakistani tradition, they haunt high mountain lakes, sometimes benevolent, sometimes mischievous.

name: Perkūnas
description: Perkūnas (Lithuania). is a god. Thunder god in Lithuanian mythology, comparable to Thor and Zeus. Source: Baltic mythology; Perkūnas is the thunder god, central to Baltic pantheon.

name: Pesta
description: Pesta is the personification of the Black Death (bubonic plague) in Norwegian folklore. She appears as an old woman carrying a rake or a broom. Where she uses the rake, some survive (as the rake's teeth let people through); where she uses the broom, everyone dies. Pesta travels through the countryside visiting farms, and her arrival means the plague will follow. Some traditions say she is the ghost of a woman who survived the actual Black Death in 1349-1350. The name Pesta comes from the Norwegian words pest (plague) and the feminine definite ending -a. Most famous from Theodor Kittelsen's haunting illustrations in his book Sorte Døden (The Black Death, 1900), which shows Pesta as a gaunt old woman in black, carrying her rake or broom through the Norwegian countryside

name: Pet Nat
description: Not independently attested in Bengali tradition as 'Pet Nat'. The name likely conflates 'petni' (female ghost of childbirth/violent death) with generic 'pet' (spirit). Bengali folklore documents petni, pishach, and churail as distinct categories. The record's sudden-death ghost haunting riverbanks matches petni or generic bhoot, not a distinct entity called 'Pet Nat'.

name: Phantom (Zapotec)
description: The Matlazihua ('woman who ensnares') is the female phantom of Oaxaca's Zapotec towns: a beautiful woman in a white dress with long loose hair who appears between one and three in the morning near rivers and empty streets. She lures drunken or lovelorn men into a trance and leads them into thorny thickets and ravines; some versions give her one foot, goat hooves, or a skeletal face.

name: Phaya Nak
description: Phaya Nak (Unknown). is a serpent. Phaya Nak is the Thai name for the Nāga, a serpent-like mythical being that inhabits the Mekong River region. Nāgas are revered as protectors of Buddhism and are associated with waterways and rainfall. Source: Thai and Lao folklore; Buddhist tradition

name: Phaya Nāka (Mekong Serpent King)
description: The Phaya Nāka (Thai: พญานาค) is the great serpent king who dwells beneath the Mekong River in Thai and Lao mythology. As the supreme Nāga of the Mekong, he commands all river serpents and controls the annual Nāga fireball phenomenon (Bang Fai Phaya Nak) that rises from the Mekong each October during the full moon of the 11th lunar month. According to legend, Phaya Nāka releases glowing red orbs ranging from tiny sparks to basketball-sized spheres to honor the Buddha's return from heaven. The Phaya Nāka also created Nong Han lake near Sakon Nakhon by carving the lakebed with his serpentine body. He is believed to protect boatmen, ensure good fish catches, and guard treasures hidden beneath the river. The Nāga fireball phenomenon attracts thousands of pilgrims annually to Nong Khai province

name: Phaya Thaen (Sky God)
description: Phaya Thaen (Lao: ພະຍາແຖນ, also known as Phi Thaen or Phi Fa) is the supreme sky god and creator deity in traditional Lao and Tai folk religion. He is the highest celestial being who rules over heaven (Muang Fa) and is responsible for sending rain, creating the world, and appointing kings. According to the Nithan Khun Borom chronicle, Phaya Thaen destroyed the corrupt first humanity with a great flood, sparing only three righteous chiefs. When they returned to earth, he sent a buffalo to help them cultivate; after the buffalo died, gourds grew and produced the new human races. He then sent his son Khun Borom to rule as the first king. Phaya Thaen controls rain and weather — the annual Bun Bang Fai (Rocket Festival) is performed to signal him to send rain. In Lao Buddhist cosmology, he was syncretized with Indra/Sakra, but retains his distinct identity as the primordial creator in folk practice. His name derives from 'thae' meaning 'truth' or 'real' — making him 'the Lord of Truth.'

name: Phi (ผี)
description: Phi (ผี) is the Thai term for ghosts and spirits, encompassing everything from the malevolent phi tai hong, ghosts of violent death, to household and nature guardians. Scholarly study began with Phraya Anuman Rajadhon's 1954 essay 'The Phi,' which shows that belief in phi shapes Thai respect for ancestors, ritual offerings, and conduct toward the dead.

name: Phi Kam
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Thai folklore; searches locate no 'Phi Kam.' The recorded suicide ghost who haunts the site of a self-inflicted death matches the attested phi tai hong, spirits of those who die suddenly or violently—including by suicide—whose unfinished lives leave them restless, but no documented figure bears this name.

name: Phi Khao
description: Phi Khao, Thai ผีเขา, are mountain spirits of Thai animist belief, guardians of forests and uplands said to appear as an old man or woman. Together with phi pa, the forest spirits, they protect game and groves and are honoured before hunting or clearing land; the Phi Pan Nam range even carries their name, 'the mountains where spirits divide the waters.'

name: Phi Khao Nang
description: Not independently attested in documented Thai folklore or academic sources as a distinct ghost named Phi Khao Nang. The recorded traits—a woman who died in childbirth or unmarried, haunting hills and crossroads, able to appear beautiful or terrifying—overlap generic Thai female-ghost beliefs (such as Mae Nak). No dedicated Thai-language or scholarly reference to this exact name was located.

name: Phi Kret
description: Not independently attested in documented Lao folklore or academic sources as a named goblin or sprite. The recorded traits—a mischievous forest imp that plays pranks but rarely harms, living in forests and rice fields—resemble generic Lao phi (spirit) traditions, but no dedicated source for a spirit specifically called 'Phi Kret' was located.

name: Phi Lam
description: Not independently attested in documented Thai folklore or academic sources as a distinct male ghost named Phi Lam. The recorded description of a water-dwelling male ghost that emerges to grab women or fishermen resembles Thai water-spirit and drowning motifs, but no dedicated Thai-language or scholarly reference to this specific figure was located.

name: Phi Phong
description: Phi Phong (ผีโพง), also called Phi Pao in northeast Thailand, is a ghost born of failed black magic: whoever raises the wan phi phong herb without completing the rite is consumed and becomes a phantom. By day it seems an ordinary person; at night a flame glows from its nose and it feeds on filth—frogs, dung, corpses, afterbirth. Its saliva spreads the condition, and it eludes humans.

name: Phi Phong Ngam
description: Not independently attested in documented Thai folklore or academic sources as a distinct spirit named Phi Phong Ngam. The recorded description—a glowing sphere or humanoid accompanied by fireflies that lures people toward dangerous places or hides treasures—resembles will-o'-the-wisp lore, but no dedicated Thai-language or scholarly source for this exact figure was located.

name: Phi Phrai
description: Phi Phrai is a Thai spirit tied to a woman who died while pregnant or in childbirth together with her unborn child, lingering near forests and water, sometimes described as a water-dwelling, Undine-like being. Tales render it both helpful and harmful; folk practice seeks its oil (namman phi phrai) as a love charm, linking the figure to enduring beliefs about unquiet female spirits.

name: Phi Phraya
description: Phi Phraya (also rendered Phi Phrai, ผีพราย) is a Thai water ghost or water spirit said to live in and control bodies of water—rivers, canals, lakes—and to lure, trouble, or drown people; some believe it is the spirit of a drowned person. Old folk say no one swims at night because a phi phraya dwells in the water. The name can also mean the shimmer on the water's surface.

name: Phi Pom
description: Not independently attested in documented Lao folklore or academic sources as a distinct spirit named Phi Pom. The recorded traits—a pale figure near water that can be protective or vengeful, tied to unfinished business—resemble general Lao beliefs about the restless dead, but no dedicated Lao-language or scholarly source for this exact name was located.

name: Phi Pop
description: Phi Pop (ผีปอบ) is a feared Thai and Lao spirit said to possess people and consume their innards, causing wasting illness and death; it is believed to inhabit a living person and to leave the body at night to feed. Widely discussed in Isan and northern Thailand, it is diagnosed by local healers and expelled through ritual. Anthropologist Ian G. Baird documented the belief among Lao communities.

name: Phi Ta Khon
description: Phi Ta Khon is the ghost of the festival in Dan Sai District, Loei Province, northeast Thailand: a three-day celebration (March–June) within the Bun Luang merit-making ceremony. Participants wear masks built from sticky-rice steamers (huat), coconut-spathe bases, and soft wood, playing ghosts called Phi Tam Khon ('ghosts following people'), a fusion of Buddhist merit-making and animist custom.

name: Phi Tai Hong
description: Phi Tai Hong (Unknown). is a ghost. Phi Tai Hong is a type of ghost in Thai folklore, the spirit of a person who died suddenly or violently. These restless spirits are believed to haunt the place of their death and are particularly fear. Source: Thai folklore; Southeast Asian spirit beliefs

name: Phoenix
description: The phoenix of Egypt is the immortal sun bird, born of the east, that dies in flame and rises renewed from its own ashes. It is linked to the bennu heron of Heliopolis, symbol of Ra and the rising sun, and to the cycle of death and rebirth that sustains all life. Ancient writers set its life span at many centuries.

name: Phoenix
description: The Phoenix is a legendary solar bird first described by Herodotus (Histories 2.73): a golden, purple and crimson bird of eagle size that builds a nest of spices, dies, and is reborn from its own remains, carrying the parent's body to Heliopolis in Egypt. Greeks read it as an emblem of renewal and cyclical time, later of immortality and Christian resurrection; it is linked to the Egyptian bennu.

name: Phoenix
description: Phoenix (Generic). is a bird. A magnificent bird that cyclically regenerates by bursting into flames and rising from its own ashes. Source: Global mythology, Egyptian and Greek sources

name: Piasa
description: The Piasa is a famous painted figure on the limestone bluffs above the Mississippi at Alton, Illinois, long described as a monstrous bird. The legend of a man-eating 'Piasa bird' is a literary invention of John Russell (1836); the original pictograph, later destroyed and repainted, was most likely an Underwater Panther, a cougar with antlers, a scaled body and a prehensile tail.

name: Piasa Bird
description: The 'Piasa Bird' is a man-eating winged monster popularized by an 1836 newspaper account by John Russell, who claimed the Illini called it the 'Piasa.' No genuine pre-contact Illini or Miami tradition describes such a bird; the real pictograph at Alton, Illinois, destroyed in the 1800s and later repainted, most likely depicted an Underwater Panther, which has no wings.

name: Piath
description: Piath is a colossal serpent of Dinka belief, dwelling in the waters of the White Nile and its tributaries. Part of a world of river beings that shape floods and fishing fortunes, it demands care from those who use the water. As a nature spirit it is feared and respected, its moods read in the river's rise and fall.

name: Pichal Peri
description: Pichal Peri (also known as the White Ladies) are Sorbian mythological beings from Slavic folklore in eastern Germany. These water spirits lure people, especially children, into water bodies

name: Pilatus Dragon
description: Pilatus Dragon (Unknown). is a dragon. The Pilatus Dragon is a legendary dragon said to dwell on Mount Pilatus in Switzerland. According to local folklore, the dragon was described as appearing like a bird with a serpent's tail, guarding t. Source: Swiss Alpine folklore; Mount Pilatus legends

name: Pincoy
description: Pincoy is the Chilote sea god of Chiloé Island, Chile: blue-skinned, seal-bodied with human head, son of Millalobo (king of seas) and Huenchula, brother/husband of Pincoya. He herds fish, guides lost sailors, calms or raises storms, and leads drowned souls to the phantom ship Caleuche. Rival to the Caleuche's warlocks.

name: Pincoya
description: Pincoya is a Chiloé water spirit, daughter of Millalobo (king of the sea) and Huenchula. With long blond hair and incomparable beauty, she dances on the shore: facing the sea brings abundant fish, facing the mountains brings scarcity. She and her siblings Pincoy and the Sirena chilota guide drowned sailors to the ghost ship Caleuche.

name: Pipe Spirit
description: In Blackfoot tradition the Medicine Pipe came to the people through a supernatural encounter: a woman appeared to a fasting man with a pipe adorned with eagle feathers and its prayers, or the Thunder spirit delivered it where lightning struck. The pipe mediates between humans and the spirit world, and its keeper observes strict taboos and yearly renewal ceremonies.

name: Pishacha
description: Pishachas are flesh-eating demons in Hindu and Buddhist mythology, created by Brahma or born from Krodha (Anger). They haunt cremation grounds alongside bhutas and vetalas, possess shapeshifting and invisibility, and feed on human vitality. They possess humans causing madness, repelled by mantras or offerings. Described with bulging veins, red eyes, and their own language Paiśāci.

name: Pishacha (Flesh-Eating Demon)
description: Pishachas are flesh-eating demons in Indian religions, appearing in Hindu and Buddhist traditions as malevolent beings often referred to as the very manifestation of evil. According to the Mahabharata, they were created by Brahma, and other legends describe them as sons of Krodha (Anger) or as descendants of Kashyapa and Krodhavasa. They are described as having bulging veins and protruding red eyes. Pishachas haunt cremation grounds along with other monsters like bhutas and vetālas. They possess the ability to shapeshift, become invisible, and feed on human energy. They can possess human beings and alter their thoughts, causing insanity and various maladies. Certain mantras and rituals are prescribed to cure those afflicted by pishacha possession. When burial or funeral rites are not performed properly, the deceased's soul may become trapped in the corpse and transform into a pishacha — unable to eat or drink, blind, and suffering immensely, yet instinctively craving the living

name: Pishacha Bondh
description: Not independently attested in Indian tradition as 'Pishacha Bondh'. The name appears to be a modern compound of 'Pishacha' (flesh-eating demon) and 'bondh' (Bengali for 'bound'). No classical Sanskrit, Pali, or vernacular source mentions this entity. The giant temple guardian description resembles generic rakshasa or kṣetrapāla motifs, not a specific named being.

name: Pishtaco
description: Pishtaco (Quechua: ñakaq; Aymara: kharisiri) is an Andean fat-extracting bogeyman from Peru and Bolivia. Originating in 16th-century conquistador corpse-fat practices, it evolved through priest rumors (nakaq), hacendados, and modern machinery-greasing variants. Victims are waylaid; fat harvested for bells, cosmetics, lubricants. Protection: wayruru beans, garlic, chancaca.

name: Piuchen
description: Piuchen (Mapuche: piwichen, 'dry people') is a Chilote/Mapuche vampiric winged serpent. It flies at night sucking blood from humans and livestock, emitting a deadly whistle or paralyzing gaze. In old age it transforms into a bird or frog-like form. Dwells in alerce forests; tracked by bloody urine trails. Killed by plugging its hollow and burning. Linked to vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus).

name: Pixiu
description: Pixiu (貔貅) is an auspicious chimera of Chinese mythology, usually a winged, lion-like beast with a dragon's head, sometimes split into male (pí) and female (xiū). Because it feeds on wealth and has no anus, it is believed to gather and hold fortune without releasing it, making it a popular talisman for business and prosperity, worn as jade pendants and placed in homes and offices.

name: Plague Spirits
description: Plague Spirits (Unknown). is a spirit. Plague spirits are malevolent supernatural beings believed to bring disease and pestilence in European folklore. They appear in traditions from the Black Death era and are often depicted as spectral f. Source: European folklore; medieval plague traditions

name: Plat-Eye
description: The Plat-Eye is a malevolent shapeshifting spirit in Gullah Geechee folklore, believed to be the restless ghost of a person who was wronged in life and died with unfinished business. Unlike the Boo Hag, which enters homes, the Plat-Eye stays outdoors, lurking in swamps, crossroads, graveyards, and other liminal spaces. It takes various forms — an animal with one large glowing eye, a ball of light, or a shadowy figure — and attacks anyone who intrudes on its territory. To ward off a Plat-Eye, Gullah people carry a small burlap sachet filled with gunpowder and sulfur. The Plat-Eye tradition reflects African beliefs in ancestral spirits who require proper burial rites to find peace, combined with the harsh reality of enslaved people buried in unmarked graves

name: Pocong
description: The pocong is a familiar Indonesian ghost: a corpse wrapped in its white burial shroud (kain kafan), tied at the head and feet, that hops because its legs are bound. It appears in graveyards and lonely places, sometimes asking passersby to untie its shroud, said to arise when the burial knots are not loosened. The figure grounds horror films and folk tales in real Islamic burial custom.

name: Pocong
description: The pocong is a well-known Malay and Indonesian ghost: a corpse wrapped in its white burial shroud (kain kafan), tied at the head and feet, that hops because its legs are bound. It haunts graveyards and empty buildings, especially at night, and is rooted in Islamic burial custom—when the shroud is not loosened, the dead are said to rise. A staple of Malay horror film and urban legend.

name: Pocong
description: The pocong is a ghost of Indonesian folklore: a humanoid figure wrapped entirely in white burial cloth, tied at the head and feet, that moves by hopping or, in some accounts, teleporting because its legs are bound. It appears in cemeteries and abandoned houses, sometimes asking people to untie its shroud, and underscores the importance of completing Islamic burial rites properly.

name: Poliahu
description: The beautiful snow goddess of Mauna Kea who eternally rivals Pele. Poliahu is one of the four goddesses of Mauna Kea's snowcap. She is renowned for her beauty, fair complexion, and cool, serene temperament. She and Pele contested for the affections of a handsome chief, leading to a legendary battle between snow and fire. Poliahu can cover the mountain in deep snow at will, extinguishing Pele's lava flows. Their eternal struggle shapes the Big Island's landscape - volcanic eruptions bringing new land from below, and winter snows cooling the peaks from above. Poliahu's domain represents the cooling, preserving forces of nature

name: Polkan
description: Polkan is a half-human, half-horse hero of Russian folklore, depicted with a human torso and a horse's lower body, who appears in the skazka cycle, most famously in the tale of Bova the Prince. His name derives from the Italian Pulicane, and in the tale he is a mighty opponent who becomes an ally of the hero.

name: Poludnitsa
description: Poludnitsa (Lady Midday) is a Slavic noon-wraith who appears in fields at midday during harvest. She takes the form of a young woman in white, an old hag, or a girl, carrying a scythe or shears. She stops workers to ask difficult questions; failure to answer brings heatstroke, madness, or death. She personifies sunstroke and enforces the taboo against working at high noon.

name: Pombero
description: Pombero (Guaraní: Pombéro, Karai Pyhare 'Lord of the Night') is a Guaraní forest spirit of Paraguay, NE Argentina, and S Brazil. Short, ugly, hairy-footed, moves silently, mimics birds, protects birds from children. Mischievous: releases cattle, steals eggs/honey, frightens horses. Appeased with cigars, rum, honey; then guards property. Linked to unexplained pregnancies.

name: Pombero
description: Pombero (Guaraní: Pombéro, Karai Pyhare 'Lord of the Night') is a Guaraní forest spirit of Paraguay, NE Argentina (Misiones), and S Brazil. Short, ugly, hairy-footed, moves silently, mimics birds, protects birds from children. Mischievous: releases cattle, steals eggs/honey, frightens horses. Appeased with cigars, rum, honey; then guards property. Linked to unexplained pregnancies.

name: Ponaturi
description: A race of hostile, man-eating fairy beings who live under the sea in Maori mythology. The Ponaturi are described as creatures who dwell in a submerged realm, rising to the land at night. They hate sunlight, which is fatal to them. In the stories of Tawhaki and Rata, the Ponaturi are the enemies of humanity who killed Hema, Tawhaki's father. Tawhaki and his brother Karihi avenged their father by trapping the Ponaturi in their house and blocking out all light. They tricked the Ponaturi into thinking it was still night, then suddenly opened the doors to let in the deadly sunlight, killing all but two who escaped

name: Pond Spirit (Guarani)
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition as a distinct 'pond spirit'. Guaraní water beings include Mbói Tu'ĩ (serpent lord of waterways) and Yacy Yateré (water-dwelling culture hero), but no generic 'pond spirit' entity exists in the seven legendary monsters or ethnographic records. The name appears to be a fabricated categorization.

name: Pond Spirit (Guarani)
description: Not attested in North American folklore. This entry is a misattributed Guarani water-spirit template placed in the United States, with no named being and a habitat field garbled as 'Paraguay, USA rivers.' Genuine Guarani tradition has water beings such as Yacy Yateré and the Ypytarã of streams, but no specific 'pond spirit' is documented here.

name: Pontianak
description: The Pontianak is one of the most feared supernatural entities in Brunei, as throughout the Malay world. She is the vengeful spirit of a woman who died during childbirth, transforming into a terrifying undead creature. In Brunei, she is said to inhabit banana groves and dark places near Kampong Ayer. She appears as a beautiful woman with long black hair and a white dress, but reveals her true horrific nature with fangs and sharp claws when she attacks. Her presence is announced by the scent of frangipani flowers and the sound of a crying baby

name: Pontianak (Kuntilanak)
description: The pontianak (kuntilanak in Indonesia) is a vampiric female ghost of a woman who died during pregnancy or childbirth: she appears as a beautiful woman who lures men, revealing her true nature—long claws and a hole in her back—when her disguise fails. She haunts banana trees, swamps, and empty houses, and her cry can reveal her distance. The figure warns of childbirth dangers and mistreated women.

name: Pontianak (Kuntilanak)
description: The pontianak is the famed female ghost of Malay and Indonesian folklore: the vengeful spirit of a woman who died in pregnancy or childbirth, appearing as a beautiful woman whose disguise hides long claws and trailing innards. She lurks in banana groves, swamps, and empty houses, luring men to their doom; her shrieking cry signals danger. She embodies warnings about childbirth and betrayal.

name: Pontianak (Singapore)
description: The Pontianak holds a unique place in Singaporean culture as the most iconic supernatural figure across the island's multi-ethnic population. She is the vengeful spirit of a woman who died during childbirth, depicted with long black hair, a white dress, and a terrifying true form with fangs and claws. The 1957 Cathay-Keris film 'Pontianak' premiered at midnight and ran for nearly three months in Singapore cinemas, becoming a cultural phenomenon that bridged Malay, Chinese, and Indian communities

name: Popa Medaw (Mother of Mount Popa)
description: Popa Medaw (Burmese: ပုပ္ပားမယ်တော်, 'Royal Mother of Popa') is the most important female nat in the Burmese pantheon, the mother of all nats who presides over Mount Popa, an extinct volcano in central Myanmar. According to legend, she was the sister of the blacksmith Nga Tin De (who became the Mahagiri Nat). When King Thinligyawng of Tagaung burned her brother alive in a champaca tree out of fear, she threw herself into the flames to die beside him. Their spirits became trapped in the tree until King Anawrahta had the tree cut down and the spirits carved into statues. Popa Medaw was enshrined on Mount Popa, which became the most important nat pilgrimage site in Myanmar. She is the protector of women, children, and families, and is also associated with flowers, beauty, and prosperity. Her shrine on Mount Popa receives thousands of pilgrims annually, especially women seeking blessings for fertility and family harmony

name: Popa Nat (Guardian of Mount Popa)
description: Mount Popa, the extinct volcano of central Myanmar, is the holiest shrine of the Burmese nat religion, home of the 37 nats under their queen Popa Medaw (the Golden Mother) and her brother the Mahagiri nat, sibling martyrs burned in a champaca tree. Pilgrims climb 777 steps to the Taung Kalat shrine bearing flowers, coconuts and costumes, and nat mediums channel the spirits at festivals.

name: Popobawa
description: Popobawa (Tanzania). is a demon. Popobawa is a demon from the folklore and mythology of Tanzania.. Source: Zanzibari urban legend; the Popobawa is a shape-shifting demon.

name: Porcupine Tsimshian
description: In the Tsimshian tale recorded by Boas, Porcupine is a small, weak animal who turns the tables on Great-Grizzly-Bear. Burned and mocked by the proud bear, Porcupine walks off singing, and his song summons a bitter wind that freezes the land, sealing the bear in his den and killing him. The tale explains why porcupines' backs look scorched and warns against cruelty.

name: Poroniec
description: Poroniec is a Polish demon born from stillborn or unbaptized infants. It haunts crossroads and graveyards, causing stillbirths and infant mortality. If buried under the house threshold, it becomes a protective kłobuk house spirit instead. Related to the Scandinavian myling. Reflects Christian anxiety about unbaptized souls.

name: Poshaiyankya
description: Poshaiyankya is a spirit of the sky associated with the winter solstice in Zuni Pueblo tradition. He figures in kachina religious practice and is connected to the creation of ceremonial life, teaching the people songs and rituals tied to the turning of the year and the renewal of the world.

name: Potkoorok
description: Potkoorok is a water spirit from Aboriginal Australian mythology, particularly known among the peoples of coastal and riverine regions. This freshwater spirit dwells in billabongs, lagoons, and slow-moving rivers, where it is said to create the distinctive bubbling and swirling patterns seen on the water's surface. Potkoorok is generally considered a mischievous but not malevolent spirit, known for playing tricks on people who venture too close to its watery home. It may create ripples to lure curious onlookers or cause floating logs to spin in circles. In some traditions, Potkoorok is a guardian of freshwater ecosystems, ensuring that the water remains clean and that fish and other aquatic life thrive

name: Potopica
description: Potopica is a Serbian water nymph (siren) inhabiting springs and rivers. She appears as a beautiful maiden combing her long hair. If approached respectfully she grants wishes; if rejected she lures men into the water to drown. Part of the broader South Slavic vila/rusalka complex of water maidens.

name: Poverty (Téʼéʼį́)
description: Téʼéʼį́, Poverty, is one of the four lesser monsters of Navajo (Diné) tradition who remained in the world after the Hero Twins destroyed the great monsters. Alongside Old Age (Są́), Cold (Dǫǫh) and Hunger (Báhí), it could not be killed, and the twins decreed that it must be endured; the four mark the unavoidable hardships of mortal life.

name: Povitrulya
description: Povitrulya is a Ukrainian wind spirit from the Carpathian Mountains, daughter of the mountain winds. She appears as a winged, flower-clad maiden who flies without touching ground. She helps lovers and shepherds; a man who steals her wings can marry her, but she will flee if she recovers them. A positive, benevolent spirit of the air.

name: Preah Keo (Sacred Gem)
description: Preah Keo ('Sacred Gem') is one of the two sacred brothers of a famous Khmer legend. His brother Preah Ko took the form of a sacred ox whose belly held precious objects and divine power, while Preah Keo is associated with the sacred gem and the royal line that brings peace and prosperity to Cambodia. The legend is linked to the Emerald Buddha and Khmer royal tradition.

name: Preah Ko (Sacred Ox)
description: Preah Ko ('Sacred Ox') is the sacred ox of Khmer legend, brother of Preah Keo. According to the tale the ox's belly held precious objects and divine power that safeguarded the kingdom, making the brothers bringers of peace and prosperity to Cambodia. The sacred-ox figure is associated with the Hindu bull Nandi, and the legend is tied to the Emerald Buddha and royal tradition.

name: Preah Thaong (Kaundinya I)
description: Preah Thaong (also known as Kaundinya I) is the legendary Brahmin prince from India who founded the Kingdom of Funan, the earliest known Cambodian state, in the 1st century CE. According to the foundational Khmer creation myth, Preah Thong received a divine instruction in a dream to take a magic bow and sail east. He arrived on the coast of what is now Cambodia, where he encountered the Naga princess Neang Neak (Queen Soma) — daughter of the Naga serpent king. After shooting a magic arrow from his bow, the princess agreed to marry him. Her father, the Naga king, drank the ocean waters to reveal land for their kingdom, creating the Cambodian heartland. Their marriage united Indian and indigenous Khmer cultures — introducing Brahmanic traditions, Sanskrit, and Hindu governance — while the Naga heritage provided spiritual legitimacy. Preah Thong symbolizes the foreign element that blended with native traditions to create Khmer civilization. He is considered the founder of the royal dynasty that ruled Cambodia for nearly 2,000 years

name: Prester John
description: Prester John (Latin: Presbyter Ioannes) is a legendary Christian patriarch and king widely believed in medieval Europe to rule a vast Christian kingdom beyond the Islamic world, later identified with Ethiopia. The legend began in the 12th century with a purported letter to Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos describing a magnificent kingdom of riches ruled by a Nestorian Christian priest-king descended from the Three Magi. For centuries, European monarchs and explorers sought Prester John as an ally against Muslim powers. As geographical knowledge expanded, the legend became associated with the Ethiopian emperor. Portuguese explorers in the 15th-16th centuries actively sought Prester John in Ethiopia, merging the legend with Ethiopian Solomonic dynasty traditions

name: Preta
description: Pretas (Sanskrit: प्रेत, 'departed') are hungry ghosts in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and Taoist cosmology — beings reborn in insatiable hunger due to past greed. They have enormous bellies and needle-thin throats. In Hinduism they consist of air and ether; in Buddhism they occupy the Preta Realm among the Six Paths. Families perform śrāddha rites with rice balls for a year to guide them.

name: Prince Sattva (Mahasattva Jataka)
description: Prince Sattva (also known as Prince Mahasattva) is the Bodhisattva in one of the most famous Jataka tales — the story of the starving tigress, from the Jataka-mala (Garland of Birth Stories) by Aryasura. In this past life, the future Buddha was born as Prince Sattva, the youngest son of a king. While wandering in the forest with his two elder brothers, they discovered a starving tigress near a mountain gorge. The tigress was so weak from hunger that she could not nurse her newborn cubs and was on the verge of eating them out of desperation. Overwhelmed with compassion, Prince Sattva sent his brothers ahead on a pretext, then lay down before the tigress to offer his body. When the tigress was too weak even to bite him, the prince cut his throat with a sharp bamboo stick. The scent of blood revived the tigress, who ate his flesh, saving both her and her cubs. His brothers returned to find only his bones. The prince attained a higher spiritual state through this act of ultimate generosity (dana paramita), and his relics were enshrined in a stupa that the Buddha later pointed out to his disciples

name: Prophetic Omens Iceland
description: Prophetic Omens Iceland (Unknown). is a human. Prophetic omens from Norse-Icelandic sagas are supernatural signs that foretell major events.. Source: Icelandic folklore — prophetic omens documented in Icelandic folk belief.

name: Prophetic Spirits Iceland
description: Prophetic Spirits Iceland (Unknown). is a human. Prophetic spirits from Norse-Icelandic tradition foretell the fate of heroes and kingdoms.. Source: Icelandic folklore — prophetic spirits documented in Icelandic folk belief.

name: Protector (Cherokee)
description: Not attested as a specific Cherokee being. Cherokee tradition does record protective spiritual figures, including the Yunwi Tsunsdi (Little People), the spirit helpers of medicine people, and the Red Warrior of the war ceremony, but no single spirit called 'the Protector' exists. The record is a generic guardian archetype with no named Cherokee figure behind it.

name: Psoglav
description: Psoglav (literally Doghead) is a demonic mythical creature from Balkan mythology known in Montenegro and surrounding regions. It is described as having a human body with horse legs, a dog's head with iron teeth, and a single cyclopean eye on the forehead. Psoglavs dwell in caves and a dark underground land rich with gemstones but without sun. They are ghoul-like beings who practice anthropophagy, eating humans and digging up corpses from graves to consume them. Their presence is considered a harbinger of death and misfortune. In Montenegrin tradition, they are particularly feared in remote mountainous and forested areas, representing the dangers that lurk beyond the safety of village settlements

name: Psoglav
description: Psoglav is a monster from Balkan / Slavic Mythology mythology. It is described as having a human body with horse legs, a dog's head with iron teeth, and a single cyclopean eye on the forehead. Psoglavs dwell in caves and a dark underground land rich with gemstones but without sun. They are ghoul-like beings who practice anthropophagy, eating humans and digging up corpses from graves to consume them. Their presence is considered a harbinger of death and misfortune. In Montenegrin tradition, they are particularly feared in remote mountainous and forested areas, representing the dangers that lurk beyond the safety of village settlements
