In Montenegrin tradition, they are particularly feared in remote mountainous and forested areas, representing the dangers that lurk beyond the safety of village settlements In Montenegro folklore, this figure is known among the Montenegrin (Slavic) people.

name: Ptehincala
description: Ptehincala is the sacred Buffalo Calf of Lakota tradition, best known as Ptehincala San Win, the White Buffalo Calf Woman who brought the Lakota the sacred pipe, the Ptehincala hu canunpa, and taught them to pray. She promised to return, and her gift made humans relatives of all creation; white buffalo calves are still revered as her sign.

name: Pugot
description: The pugot is the 'decapitated one' of the Ilocos region: a headless being, usually black and tall, that appears at night in dark places, deserted houses, and under duhat, santol, or tamarind trees. It shapeshifts into hogs, dogs, or humans. Among the Aeta it is a goblin-like forest spirit, a guardian of ancestral treasures; the Ifugao call it Tulud Nimputul. Frightening but not usually harmful.

name: Pugwis
description: Pugwis is an aquatic being of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, described in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology as a sort of sea creature with a fish-like face and large incisors. Dwelling in the coastal waters of the Pacific Northwest, it is counted among the supernatural beings of the sea; the benevolent whale-helper role does not appear in the attested accounts.

name: Puk
description: Puk (Pûks) is a North German/Danish household spirit, cognate with English Puck and the nisse/tomte. Small, red-capped being performing chores for milk and bread, cruel if slighted. The combined Nis Puk unites nisse and puk traditions. Also appears as Drak, a fiery flying shaft bringing grain. Luther recorded a Heintzlein variant.

name: Pukwudgie
description: The Pukwudgie are the little people of Wampanoag folklore, small grey-skinned forest beings of Cape Cod and the surrounding region. Trickster-like and unpredictable, they can be helpful, granting healing or favors, or hostile, leading travelers astray and using fire and magic when offended. Wampanoag stories treat them as beings to approach with caution and respect.

name: Pulotu
description: Pulotu is the Tongan spirit underworld, the realm of the dead and home to the gods. Ruled by Hikule'o, Pulotu is an underwater paradise located to the west beneath the ocean. It is described as a beautiful, bountiful land where spirits of chiefs and nobles go after death, while commoners' souls are believed to be eaten by the goddess of death. Pulotu is also the home of the god Saveasi'uleo (Nafanua's father) and the origin place of many important cultural elements including kava, the chiefly system, and various arts. The entrance to Pulotu is located at Falealupo on the island of Savai'i in Samoa, but the realm itself belongs to Tongan mythology

name: Puma (Sacred Guardian)
description: The puma (kay pacha) is one of three sacred animals of the Inca Trilogy, representing the earthly world (Kay Pacha) with condor (sky) and serpent (underworld). Associated with Inti the sun god, the puma symbolizes strength, vitality, sovereignty. Inca emperor was sun-descended; puma imagery shaped Cusco's layout and royal textiles. A cosmological emblem, not a named spirit.

name: Puteana
description: Not independently attested in documented Italian or Sardinian folklore or academic sources: no legend or record names a creature 'Puteana'. The record appears to be a garbled reference to the Sardinian coga (bruxa), the shapeshifting blood-sucking witch, or to the strega tradition generally — female witches of the night who fly, cast spells and shapeshift, feared yet sometimes consulted.

name: Puteri Gunung Ledang (Princess of Mount Ledang)
description: Puteri Gunung Ledang is a celestial princess and guardian spirit of Mount Ledang (Mount Ophir) in Johor, Malaysia. According to legend, the powerful Sultan of Melaka, Sultan Mahmud Shah, heard of her legendary beauty and sought her hand in marriage. The princess agreed — but only if the Sultan fulfilled seven impossible conditions: build a golden bridge from Melaka to the mountain, build a silver bridge back, provide seven trays of mosquito hearts, a vat of virgin's tears, a bowl of his son's blood, and two cups each of the Sultan's own blood and semen. The Sultan fulfilled six conditions but hesitated at the final ones, realizing the princess never intended to marry him. The princess is considered a guardian spirit of the mountain, appearing only to those pure of heart, and her legend is a timeless lesson in humility and the folly of pride

name: Pwca
description: The Pwca (Púca, Pooka) is a Welsh shapeshifting spirit cognate with the Irish púca. It appears as a horse, goat, or human with animal features, leading travelers on wild rides but doing no lasting harm. Controlled by sharp spurs (cold iron). Associated with Samhain; snip 1 November is 'Pwca's Day.' Regional forms include a goblin in Glamorgan, an eagle in Pembroke, a black goat in Radnor.

name: Pwint
description: Not independently attested in documented Burmese folklore or academic sources as a flower spirit named Pwint. While pwint is a common Burmese name meaning flower, and the padauk is Myanmar's national flower with deep symbolism, no source records a spirit called 'Pwint' living in padauk blooms. The entry appears to blend real flower symbolism with an unverified spirit figure.

name: Pygmalion
description: Pygmalion (Unknown). is a human. Pygmalion is a figure from Greek mythology, a sculptor from Cyprus who fell in love with his own ivory statue of a woman. The goddess Aphrodite brought the statue to life, and Pygmalion married her.. Source: Metamorphoses (Ovid, 8 CE); Greek mythological tradition

name: Pyinsarupa
description: The pyinsarupa is the Burmese chimeric guardian, from Pali pañcarūpa, 'five forms': a composite of the elephant, bullock, horse, white carp, and the tonaya (a horned leo-dragon); some renderings use lion, elephant, water buffalo, white carp, and hamsa. It appears in hsaing waing orchestra finials, on Myanmar Airways' logo, and a royal barge's name, symbolizing unity of diverse powers.

name: Páutiwa (Chief of Kóthluwalawan)
description: Páutiwa is the winter-solstice kachina and the most venerable chief of the Zuni spirit pantheon. He rules Kothluwalawa, the spirit village beneath Kothluwalawa Lake, receives the spirits of the dead, and controls the ceremonial calendar, sending the kachinam to dance at Zuni when the world's rituals require them.

name: Póngo (Circle) Kachina
description: Póngo, the Circle Kachina, is a figure of Hopi tradition. In the recorded Hopi story 'The Circle Kachina and His Wife Become Stars,' the kachina approached a maiden grinding corn and danced at the village kivas; through his actions he and his wife were transformed into stars, a tale about the consequences of heedless courtship and desire.

name: Põrgupõrgu (Hell)
description: Põrgupõrgu (Hell) (Estonia). is a demon. Põrgupõrgu (Hell) is a demon from the folklore and mythology of Estonia.. Source: Estonian folklore; Põrgupõrgu refers to hell-demons in Estonian mythology.

name: Púca
description: The Púca is an Irish shapeshifting spirit (púca, plural púcaí) of Celtic, English, and Channel Islands folklore. It appears as a sleek black horse with golden eyes, or as goat, cat, rabbit, raven, fox, wolf, goblin, or dog—always dark-furred. It entices riders on wild nocturnal journeys but unlike the kelpie does not drown them. Controlled by sharp spurs (cold iron).

name: Púca (or Pook-al)
description: The Púca (or Pook-al) is a regional Irish name for the púca, emphasizing its horse form: a shiny black steed that lures riders, or a goat with long horns, or a dark-haired slightly deformed human. It tangles hair, spits in drinks, steals items, but can also guide travelers. Must be kept fed or it turns angry. Samhain is 'Púca Night.' The name 'Pook-al' reflects the Anglo-Irish pronunciation.

name: Pārī
description: The pari, or peri, is a Persian winged spirit of radiant beauty, born of fire yet gentle and luminous. Early Persian belief classed the paris among the evil spirits of the dark, but in Islamic-period lore they grew into benevolent beings who dwell in hidden, shimmering palaces and mingle with mortals in love and art. They stand in sharp contrast to the ugly, brutish divs.

name: Płanetnik
description: Płanetnik (also chmurnik, obłocznik) is a Polish demonic cloud spirit — the soul of a suicide or sudden-death victim who controls storms and hail. Appears as a tall old man in a wide hat or a small creature. Can be benevolent (warning of storms) or malevolent. Gains favor by throwing flour into wind or fire. Fights storm-dragons in the clouds. Also a term for weather-divining shamans.

name: Pūķis
description: Pūķis (Latvia). is a household-spirit. Pūķis is a household spirit from the folklore and mythology of Latvia.. Source: Latvian folklore; Pūķis is a household spirit often appearing as a dragon.

name: Qals Mink Coast Salish
description: Mink is the trickster of the Coast Salish, told of among the Saanich, Comox, and Lummi. Compared with Raven he is a negative hero, greedy, reckless, and vain, and his adventures — being swallowed by a whale, running across the sky as the Sun's son, tussling with Devilfish — are cautionary tales of how not to behave.

name: Qalupalik
description: Qalupalik (Qallupilluit) is a humanoid sea creature of Inuit tradition that dwells beneath Arctic shorelines and ice floes, waiting to snatch children who wander too close to the water. She carries her victims away in the hood of her amaut parka, and her eerie, ethereal humming lures the curious. The legend teaches children to keep away from dangerous sea ice.

name: Qalupalik
description: The Qalupalik (Qallupilluit) is an Inuit sea creature of Greenland and Arctic Canada that kidnaps children wandering too close to ice floes. Described as green-skinned, slimy, with long hair, webbed hands, scales, fins, wearing an amauti (woman's parka) made of eider feathers to carry victims. Emits a paralyzing shrill sound; snip can shape-shift (pilutitaminik).

name: Qalupalik
description: Qalupalik is the child-stealing ocean spirit told of across the Inuit world, including Greenland. She lives under the ice near the shore, rises silently through cracks to grab children playing alone on the floes, and tucks them into the pouch of her amaut parka. Her soft humming song is said to draw children toward the water's edge.

name: Qamata
description: Qamata (also known as uThixo) is the supreme creator god of the Xhosa people who existed before all things. From a primordial void of darkness and silence, Qamata created the world using Uhlanga (sacred reeds) as the material for all life. He divided existence into three realms: the sky for himself, the earth for humans, and the underworld for ancestors. He defeated the chaos giant Iqungqungqu to bring order to the cosmos, but remains distant from daily affairs, working through ancestors and natural signs with thunder and the sun representing his power

name: Qarakorshaq
description: Qarakorshaq is a monster of Turkic folklore said to lurk in dark hollows, abandoned houses and hidden pits, seizing and devouring anyone who draws near at night. It is driven off by light and noise. Some scholars read the creature as folk memory of large animals now extinct in Central Asia, which explains its shadowy presence in herding lore.

name: Qat
description: Qat is the creator deity and culture hero of the Banks Islands, Vanuatu. He is credited with fashioning the first humans from wood, bringing light by distributing darkness, and establishing many customs. The son of the earth spirit, Qat is generous and clever, often opposed by his foolish older brothers and by the rival figure Tagaro. After finishing his work of creation he departed to the sky or the underworld.

name: Qilin
description: Qilin (麒麟) is the benevolent composite beast of Chinese tradition, with a dragon's head, deer's body, ox's tail, and fish-scale skin, sometimes bearing a single horn. It is said to appear only to mark the birth or reign of a sage and never to tread on living things, symbolizing peace, virtue, and good omens. It passed into Japan as the kirin and appears in Chinese New Year dances.

name: Qori-Ismaris
description: Qori-Ismaris (literally 'the stick-rubber') is a legendary figure from Somali mythology known as the Hyena-Man, the Somali equivalent of the Western werewolf. According to traditional belief, Qori-Ismaris was a man who possessed the dark power to transform into a hyena by rubbing a magical stick on his hindquarters at nightfall. Before dawn, he would repeat the same action to reverse the transformation and return to human shape. Some versions of the legend elevate Qori-Ismaris to an immortal witch-queen who wanders the desert disguised as a beautiful woman, luring travelers into illusions and guiding them to their doom. The figure represents the dangerous boundary between human and animal, civilization and wilderness. Stories of Qori-Ismaris served as warnings about strangers who might not be what they appear, especially those met at twilight—the liminal hour when transformations occurred. The legend reflects deep cultural anxieties about deception, the untamed wilderness, and the animal nature lurking beneath human civility

name: Queen Arawelo
description: Queen Arawelo (Carraweelo) was a legendary proto-Somali queen who established a matriarchal society in the Sanaag region around the 1st century CE. After her husband and children died in clan violence, she was cast out as a widow. Instead of accepting her fate, she gathered other outcast women in the myrrh forests of the northern mountains and formed a warrior sisterhood. Arawelo trained her army to restore peace, believing women must take power to end the cycle of male violence. She instituted a system where women held political and economic control. Some accounts describe her punitive justice against violent men, while others celebrate her as a wise ruler who brought peace. She remains a symbol of female empowerment in Somali culture

name: Quetzalcoatl
description: The Feathered Serpent, key Mexican-American deity. Aztec god of wind (Ehecatl) and the morning star (Venus), he made humanity in Mictlan from his blood and ancestral bones. His name: 'quetzal' (green bird) + 'coatl' (serpent). Tricked by Tezcatlipoca into drunken incest, exiled, he vowed return from the east — a return conflated with Cortés's 1519 arrival. A Chicano symbol of indigenous identity.

name: Quirquincho Vivo
description: Not independently attested in Argentine folklore as a named cryptid. 'Quirquincho' is the Quechua/Spanish word for armadillo (Chaetophractus spp.), and armadillos appear in Andean folk belief as sacred or taboo animals, but 'Quirquincho Vivo' (Living Armadillo) as a specific fortune-bringing/cursing entity lacks ethnographic attestation. May reflect general armadillo taboos.

name: Qutb Shah
description: Not independently attested in Pakistani folklore as a ghost entity. 'Qutb Shah' primarily refers to the Qutb Shahi dynasty rulers of Golconda (1518–1687) or the mythological ancestor of the Punjabi Awan tribe.

name: Qutrub
description: The Qutrub (also spelled Qutrub) is a type of werehyena from Arabian folklore, a shape-shifting creature that combines human and hyena traits. According to the 10th-century scholar al-Mas'udi, the Qutrub was created from a split egg of a female jinn — its counterpart being the Marid (powerful sea jinn). The Qutrub is described as resembling a cat-like creature that haunts graveyards, eating corpses. Pre-Islamic Arabs considered the Qutrub a type of jinn or demon closely associated with death and transformation. Like the European werewolf but with a hyena as its base form, the Qutrub can shift between human and animal form at night. The hyena's scavenging habits, unsettling calls that resemble human laughter, and presence near burial grounds made it a natural candidate for a creature associated with death and deception. The Qutrub is less known than the Ghul but represents an important strand of Arabian shapeshifter mythology tied to specific animals

name: Quỷ
description: Quỷ is the Vietnamese term for ghost and demon, from the Chinese character 鬼, the soul of the dead. In folk belief quỷ are souls unable to reincarnate, wandering the world; in Buddhist cosmology the term includes malevolent beings (Ác quỷ, Ngạ quỷ, yaksha, la sát), and Cao Đài holds vengeful souls transform into them. Hideous and fierce, they harm humans and are warded off by temples and amulets.

name: Qwaxw (Raven)
description: Qwaxw, the Raven of the Nuxalk people of Bella Coola, British Columbia, is the great transformer who freed the light: in the Nuxalk creation account of the four carpenters, Qwaxw released Nusximta, a crystal ball of sunlight held in a container, to light the world. His name echoes his call, and he stands at the center of Nuxalk origin stories.

name: Qwaxw Raven Nuxalk
description: Qwaxw is the Raven of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition, made from charcoal by the youngest of the Four Carpenters, who cried 'qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw' when he came to life. He flew up to Nusmata, tricked the granddaughter of the creator, and carried away the box of daylight, so that the world below gained light, fire, and abundance.

name: Ra (Sun God of Egypt)
description: Ra (or Re) is the supreme sun god of ancient Egyptian religion, the creator of all life and the ruler of the cosmos. He was the most important deity in the Egyptian pantheon for over 2,000 years. Each day, Ra sails across the sky in his solar barque (the Mandjet), bringing light and warmth. Each night, he journeys through the underworld (Duat) in his night barque (the Mesektet), defeating the serpent Apophis to be reborn at dawn. Ra created all forms of life; humans were born from his tears. He was believed to have ruled as the first pharaoh of Egypt. The Pharaohs took the title 'Son of Ra' to legitimize their rule. Ra merged with other major deities over time: Amun-Ra, Ra-Horakhty, and Atum-Ra

name: Rabbit (Mapuche)
description: The record describes the Peuchen (Piuchén), not a rabbit. Peuchen is a Mapuche/Chilote vampiric shapeshifter: a winged serpent that drains blood from livestock and humans, whistles to stun prey, and transforms into birds, bats, or humans. Only the machi (shaman) can defeat it. The 'rabbit' label is a complete misattribution.

name: Radien-attje
description: Radien-attje (also Raedie or Veralden Olmai, meaning 'World Man') is the supreme high god in Sami mythology, the ruler of the cosmos and the celestial father. He is the creator and giver of life, sitting at the head of the divine family trinity alongside his wife Raedieahkka and their son Radien-pardne. In some traditions their daughter Rana Niejta is also included. He is more of an intellectual superior who maintains cosmic order rather than interfering directly — his son Radien-pardne performs practical tasks. His name derives from Old Norse 'ráð' meaning 'rule, governance.' Every autumn, the Sami erected a sacrificial pole symbolizing the world-pillar (Veralden stytto) that connects the earth to the Pole Star, to honor him and prevent the pillar's collapse. He creates human souls and hands them to Máttaráhkká who gives them life. He also takes the souls of the dead back to himself. Some scholars argue that Radien-attje was a later addition to Sami religion, formed from Norse and early Christian influences, while the eastern Sami thunder god Tiermes may have been the original sky god

name: Raedieahkka
description: Raedieahkka (also Radien-akka) is the supreme goddess in Sami mythology, the wife of the high god Radien-attje. Together with her husband, she created the world and the human soul — they are described as the two divinities who jointly created the cosmos. She is the mother of Rana Niejta (the spring goddess) and Radien-pardne (the son who executes his father's will). She forms part of the Sami divine trinity alongside her husband and son. In some traditions, this trinity reflects Christian influence (Father, Mother, Son replacing Father, Son, Holy Spirit), but the concept of a divine couple creating the world together is deeply rooted in Finno-Ugric tradition. Her role in creation of the human soul places her at the very beginning of existence alongside Radien-attje, before the soul is passed to Máttaráhkká and her daughters who handle gestation and birth

name: Ragana
description: Ragana (Lithuania). is a goddess. Ragana is a goddess from the folklore and mythology of Lithuania.. Source: Lithuanian mythology; a goddess or witch figure associated with magic and fate.

name: Rahko
description: Rahko is a Finnish lunar spirit who paints the moon's phases with tar, documented by Ganander in Mythologia Fennica (1789) as a being who covers the moon during eclipses. A marginal figure in runic songs, sometimes identified with the waning moon or a disease spirit. Ganander's account is the primary source; later folklorists treat him as a minor lunar demon.

name: Rainbow Crow
description: In the time before fire, the world was cold and dark. The animals suffered until Kishelamakank placed a great fire atop a high mountain. The crow, who in those ancient days had a beautiful rainbow-colored song and iridescent feathers, volunteered to fetch the fire for the people. He flew to the summit and seized a burning coal in his beak, but the flames scorched his colorful feathers black and the smoke choked his beautiful voice into a harsh caw. Despite the pain, the crow carried the fire down to the people. The Creator honored the crow's sacrifice by declaring that his black feathers would forever shimmer with the rainbow's ghost when the sun catches them at the right angle

name: Rainbow Serpent
description: The Rainbow Serpent is one of the most significant ancestral beings of Aboriginal Australian Dreaming, a vast snake whose travels carved rivers, valleys, and mountains and whose presence brings rain and life-giving water. At once a benevolent creator and a destructive force when angered, it is depicted in rock art across most Aboriginal language groups over some 6,000 years.

name: Rakke
description: Rakke is the supernatural dog of the Stallo giant in Sami folklore. If Stallo is slain, Rakke can lick his wounds and restore him to life, so a hero who defeats the giant must also kill the dog or the victory is undone. Rakke appears in the Stallo tales recorded by Qvigstad, including 'How the Stalos Were Tricked.'

name: Rakshasa
description: Rakshasas are shape-shifting demons in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain myth — fierce, cannibalistic, illusionists (maya). In Ramayana, antagonists (Ravana, Tataka, Maricha) ruling Lanka; some (Vibhishana) righteous. In Mahabharata, Bhima slays Hidimba, Bakasura, Kirmira; Ghatotkacha fights for Pandavas. Not 'guardians' — primarily malevolent disruptors of sacrifices, eaters of humans. Female: rakshasi.

name: Rana Niejta
description: Rana Niejta is the Sami spring and vegetation goddess, the daughter of the high god Radien-attje and his wife Raedieahkka. Her name means 'the green' or 'the fertile fields.' She makes the southern slopes of mountains turn green so hungry reindeer have food after the long Arctic winter. She is one of three divine sisters who together control the seasonal cycle: Sala Niejta (Sun's daughter) ends winter's cold, Rana Niejta brings forth vegetation, and Saivo Niejta governs the underworld. She belongs to the Radien family of spirits — a group of deities who had power over human lives. A bronze statue of Rana Niejta stands in Mo i Rana, Norway, a town whose name some scholars connect to the goddess. Her figure on Sami drums connects her to the fertility of the earth and the prosperity of the reindeer herds

name: Rangda (Demon Queen)
description: Rangda is the terrifying demon queen of the Leyaks in Balinese mythology, the eternal antagonist of Barong. She is the incarnation of Calon Arang, the legendary witch who wreaked havoc in ancient Java during the reign of King Airlangga in the 10th century. Historically linked to the exiled queen Mahendradatta, Rangda leads an army of evil witches and leyaks (black magic spirits) against the forces of good. In the Barong dance, she casts powerful spells that drive warriors to stab themselves with their kris daggers, but Barong's protective magic renders them invulnerable. Despite being the embodiment of evil, Rangda is also worshipped as a form of the goddess Durga/Kali and is seen as a necessary cosmic force representing destruction and transformation

name: Ranginui (Rangi)
description: The primordial sky father in Maori cosmology. Rangi (Ranginui) lay locked in a tight embrace with Papatuanuku (Earth Mother) in the beginning, with their children trapped in darkness between them. Their son Tane Mahuta eventually forced them apart, creating the world of light. Rangi's tears fall as rain, mourning his separation from Papa. The mist that rises from the earth is her longing sighs reaching for him. Rangi and Papa's separation established the cosmic order of the Maori world, with Rangi representing the male, celestial principle overarching all creation

name: Rannamaari
description: Rannamaari is the powerful sea demon of Maldivian mythology — monstrous entity embodying the dangerous ocean surrounding the atolls. In the founding myth, it demanded a virgin sacrifice monthly until the Moroccan scholar Abu al-Barakat Yusuf al-Barbari defeated it by reciting Quran, converting the islands to Islam. Represents pre-Islamic Maldivian fear of the sea.

name: Rannamaari (Sea Demon of the Maldives)
description: Rannamaari is a terrifying sea demon from Maldivian folklore that rose from the ocean each month to demand a sacrifice of a virgin girl. According to legend, before the Islamization of the Maldives in 1153 CE, the Buddhist inhabitants of Malé were terrorized by this demon. Each month, a virgin was dressed in fine clothes and left alone overnight in a temple on the eastern seafront of Malé — by dawn, she was found violated and dead. This practice continued until a Maghrebi Muslim traveler, Abu'l-Barakat al-Barbari (alternatively identified as Yusuf al-Tabrezi from Tabriz, Iran), arrived in the islands. Outraged by the practice, he volunteered to take the girl's place. He spent the night reciting the Quran, and when the demon appeared, the power of the holy verses caused it to flee into the sea, never to return. The king, identified as Dhovemi, was so moved that he converted to Islam along with his court, taking the name Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah. Folklorist Xavier Romero-Frias traces the name Rannamaari to a South Indian goddess, suggesting a pre-Islamic Hindu-Buddhist origin for the belief

name: Ranta
description: Ranta is a monstrous forest creature in Pakistani (Kashmiri/Pahari) folklore — glowing yellow eyes, matted hair, shape-shifter kidnapping travelers in heavy snow, then vanishing. Documented in Kashmir Valley, Pir Panjal oral traditions as winter mountain hazard. Similar to 'Barmanu' (wild man) but more demonic. Part of northwestern Himalayan folk belief, not Baloch.

name: Raróg
description: Raróg is a fire spirit of Slavic folklore, often appearing as a falcon or a fiery whirlwind, associated with the hearth and the sky. In Polish and Czech folk belief Raróg can be summoned or kept as a household familiar, bringing luck or serving its keeper, and some scholars connect his name to the legendary Obodrite stronghold of Reric.

name: Ratcatcher of Hamelin
description: The Pied Piper of Hamelin (Rattenfänger von Hameln) is a German legend from 1284. A multicoloured ('pied') piper lured rats into the Weser River with his magic pipe; when the town refused payment, he returned on Saints John and Paul's day and led 130 children into a mountain cave (Koppenberg/Calvary), never to return. The earliest evidence is a c.

name: Ratovantany
description: Ratovantany is the earth creator god in Malagasy mythology who shaped the physical bodies of all living beings from clay. He worked in partnership with Zanahary, the sky god: Ratovantany molded the forms, but they remained lifeless until Zanahary breathed souls into them. Upon death, the body returns to Ratovantany while the soul ascends to Zanahary. Ratovantany is also credited with shaping the landscape of Madagascar, carving the mountains, valleys and rivers. Under the name Rapeto, he is celebrated as an earth deity and mythical hero who sculpted the physical world with his hands

name: Ratu-Mai-Mbula
description: Ratu-Mai-Mbula is a Fijian god associated with fertility, harvest, and agricultural abundance. As a deity of the land and its bounty, he governs the growth of crops, particularly yams and taro, which are staple foods in Fijian culture. Traditional ceremonies were held to honor Ratu-Mai-Mbula during planting and harvest seasons, with offerings made to ensure fertile soil and abundant yields. He is part of the agricultural cycle that connects the Fijian people to the land, and his favor was sought to prevent crop failures and famine. Together with the sea deity Tui Delaivugalei, he represents the dual sources of sustenance that sustain Fijian life: the land and the sea

name: Rauðkembingur
description: Rauðkembingur (Red-Crest) is the most savage of all the illhveli (evil whales) in Icelandic folklore. It has a distinctive red crest or mane running along its back and is 10-20 meters long, streamlined, and extremely fast in the water. Rauðkembingur attacks ships with unmatched ferocity, ramming them at high speed and leaping across decks. It neighs ominously before attacking. According to one legend, a callous young man was cursed by elves into becoming a rauðkembingur as punishment for his cruelty. The rauðkembingur was considered one of the most dangerous creatures in Icelandic waters, feared even more than the larger illhveli because of its speed and aggression. The name comes from rauður (red) and kembingur (crest/mane). The tradition likely originated from sightings of killer whales (orca), which have distinctive white patches that could be interpreted as a crest

name: Ravana
description: Ravana is the ten-headed demon king of Lanka in the Indian epic Ramayana. A great scholar and devotee of Shiva, he abducted Sita, wife of Rama, leading to the great war in which Rama defeated him. His complex character — learned, powerful, yet doomed by pride and desire — makes him one of the most studied figures in South and Southeast Asian literature.

name: Raven
description: Raven is the great trickster and culture hero of the Pacific Northwest, celebrated among the Haida, Tlingit, Tsimshian and neighboring peoples. A shape-shifter and thief of supernatural powers, he stole the sun, moon and stars from a stingy keeper, letting light into the world, and brought people fresh water and fire.

name: Raven
description: Raven is the great trickster and culture hero of the Pacific Northwest, celebrated among the Haida, Tlingit, Tsimshian and neighboring peoples. A shape-shifter and thief of supernatural powers, he stole the sun, moon and stars from a stingy keeper, letting light into the world, and brought people fresh water and fire.

name: Raven
description: In Greenlandic Inuit tradition the raven (tulugaq) is a culture hero and bringer of light. In an origin tale recorded across the Arctic, a raven-child born of a woman steals the light a selfish being keeps in a box, flying it through the smoke hole and scattering stars and daylight across the sky. Raven also appears in Inuit stories as a creator and transformer.

name: Raven (Nang Kilslas)
description: Raven, known as Nang Kilslas in the Haida language, is the central figure of Haida mythology - the trickster, creator, and culture hero who shaped the world for human habitation. In the time before light, Raven discovered an old chief who kept all the light of the universe hidden in a nested set of five boxes. Raven transformed himself into a hemlock needle and dropped into the river where the chief daughter came to drink. She swallowed the needle and became pregnant, giving birth to Raven-child. The old chief adored his grandchild. Raven cried incessantly until the chief allowed him to open the boxes one by one: first the stars escaped, then the moon, then the northern lights. Finally Raven grabbed the sun in his beak and flew through the smoke hole, releasing light into the world forever

name: Raven Ancestor-Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: Not independently attested in Cheyenne folklore. No source records a raven ancestor-spirit among the Cheyenne; their trickster and transformer is Veeho (sometimes Wihio), a spider who appears as a man and whose foolish, self-serving deeds explain the world. A raven-based ancestor spirit is a modern invention, almost certainly borrowed from the Raven traditions of the Pacific Northwest.

name: Raven Ancestor-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: The Raven is a creator and culture hero of the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl). In the creation account, Raven (Kwekwaxa'we, 'Great-Inventor,' also U'melth) flew over the waters and made islands by dropping pebbles into the sea, then created the trees and grass and, after failed attempts, shaped the first man and woman from wood and clay; he brought the people the moon, fire, salmon and the tides.

name: Raven Animal-Spirit of Aymara
description: Not independently attested as a named Aymara spirit. Aymara cosmology includes animal spirits (fox, condor, llama) but no specific 'raven animal-spirit' guardian of oceans (ravens are rare/absent on Altiplano; condor fills the raptor role). The description borrows Pacific Northwest raven lore.

name: Raven Animal-Spirit of Navajo
description: The raven (gáagii, often not distinguished from the crow) is a genuine figure in Navajo tradition, closely linked with Coyote. In the Diné Bahane', the raven served as a spy for the monster birds, warning Changing Woman's twin sons to keep away, and the obsolescent Ravenway ceremony was connected with Coyoteway. Crows and ravens also figure in Navajo beliefs about skinwalkers and the dead.

name: Raven Coast Salish
description: Raven is the transformative trickster of Coast Salish peoples, a shapeshifting creator-being who brought light, fire, and salmon into the world. His stories are told from the Squamish to the Halkomelem and Nooksack, where he shares the stage with other animal transformers in the tales of the myth age.

name: Raven Deity of Ashanti
description: Not independently attested: ravens do not occur in West African fauna and no raven deity appears in Ashanti (Akan) religious sources. The figure is likely a mistranslation or conflation, possibly with the vulture associated with Nyame or with eagle imagery in Akan royal regalia.

name: Raven Deity of Shona
description: Not independently attested as a deity in Shona tradition. Ravens occur in southern Africa but no ethnographic source documents a "Raven Deity" guarding lakes. The description appears templated. Shona avian spirits include the fish eagle (hungwe) as Mwari's messenger, not a raven lake deity.

name: Raven Deity of Ute
description: Not independently attested in Ute folklore. No Ute deity or guardian is a raven; the culture heroes of Ute tradition are the creator Sinawav (Sinauf) and his brothers Coyote and Wolf, and Coyote is the tribe's great trickster who let the peoples escape from a bag of sticks. A 'Raven Deity of Ute' appears to be a modern invention, likely confused with the Raven traditions of the Pacific Northwest.

name: Raven Ghost of Hopi
description: No 'raven ghost' exists in Hopi tradition, but crows and ravens are genuinely important: the Crow Mother kachina (Angwusnasomtaka) is a chief kachina who leads the Powamu initiation rites and is called mother of all the kachinas, and the crow is a Hopi messenger between the living and the dead. A recorded Hopi tale tells of a Crow who watched the farmers and brought sickness to wrongdoers.

name: Raven Ghost of Kikuyu
description: Not independently attested in Kikuyu tradition. Ravens (Corvus corax) are not native to Kenya; the region has pied crows and white-necked ravens, but no raven ghost tradition. Kikuyu avian spirits involve the sacred mugumo tree and Ngai atop Mount Kenya. Appears fabricated, possibly conflating Norse/Celtic raven lore (Odin's Huginn/Muninn) with Kikuyu spirituality.

name: Raven Giant of Cherokee
description: The raven figure of Cherokee lore is the Raven Mocker (Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï), the most dreaded of Cherokee witches. Withered and old-looking, it flies to the homes of the sick and dying with a rushing sound like a strong wind and a raven's diving cry, robbing the dying of life and eating the heart to gain years. One so recognized by the right medicine dies within seven days.

name: Raven Giant of Cheyenne
description: Not independently attested in Cheyenne folklore. No source records a Cheyenne raven giant or spring-guardian; the Cheyenne trickster and transformer is Veeho (Wihio), the spider, who appears as a man in the tales. A 'Raven Giant of Cheyenne' is almost certainly a modern invention or a mistaken transplant of Pacific Northwest Raven material.

name: Raven Giant of Passamaquoddy
description: Not independently attested in Passamaquoddy folklore. No raven giant appears in Passamaquoddy tradition, whose culture hero is Koluskap (Glooscap); ravens and crows play no major role, the notable birds being Culloo, the giant bird that carries off children, and the Petakiyik thunderers. This entry appears to be a modern fabrication.

name: Raven Giant of Yoruba
description: Not independently attested: ravens are absent from the Yoruba regions of West Africa, and no raven giant appears in Yoruba sources. The entry is a misattribution with no real analogue in the Yoruba pantheon.

name: Raven Guardian (Ashanti)
description: Not independently attested: ravens are not native to West Africa, and no raven guardian figure appears in Ashanti ethnographic or religious records. The entry is likely a conflation; no real Ghanaian analogue is recorded.

name: Raven Guardian (Ashanti)
description: Not independently attested as a raven guardian in Ashanti folklore, and the Guatemala tag is a misassignment. The Ashanti are a Ghanaian people; their celebrated trickster is Anansi the spider, and no raven guardian appears in Ashanti tradition. Ravens figure mainly in northern traditions such as those of the Pacific Northwest and Siberia. The record is an evident cross-cultural mashup.

name: Raven Guardian (Ashanti)
description: Not independently attested: ravens are absent from West African fauna, and no raven guardian appears in Ashanti or Malian tradition. Possible conflation with crow figures in Sahelian folklore; no real analogue is recorded.

name: Raven Guardian of Cheyenne
description: Not independently attested in Cheyenne folklore. No source records a raven guardian of the hills; the Cheyenne transformer and trickster is Veeho (Wihio), the spider, and ravens are insignificant in Cheyenne mythology. The entry appears to be an AI-generated placeholder borrowing the Raven imagery of the Pacific Northwest.

name: Raven Guardian of Ute
description: Not independently attested in Ute folklore. Ute tradition knows no raven guardian of the oceans or the land; its great beings are Sinawav (Sinauf), the Coyote creator who carried the peoples in a bag of sticks, and his brothers Coyote and Wolf. A 'Raven Guardian of Ute' is a modern invention or misattribution, likely from Northwest Coast Raven cycles.

name: Raven Guguyni Nuu Chah Nulth
description: Raven is the great culture hero of the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka), a benevolent transformer and trickster who gave the people fire, light, and the shape of the world. In Nuu-chah-nulth tradition he works alongside the Twin Transformers Kwe'kustepsep, who changed people, animals, and the land into their present forms.

name: Raven Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Raven is the great transformer-trickster of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a being who reshapes the world through appetite and deception. In the tale of Great-Inventor recorded by Boas, Raven tricks the water-woman of Bull Harbor, fills a bladder with stolen water, and urinates to create the rivers. He also works to release daylight and fix the order of things.

name: Raven Mocker
description: Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï, the Raven Mocker, is a malevolent Cherokee witch-spirit that preys on the dying. Ordinary people by day, Raven Mockers fly at night as shadowy birds with sleepless, bloodshot eyes, stealing the remaining years of the sick. Only medicine men and their allies can see them and drive them off with protective rituals, as James Mooney recorded.

name: Raven Nang Kilslas Haida
description: Nang Kílslaas, 'The One Whose Voice is Obeyed,' is the Haida name for Raven, the creator-transformer who shaped Haida Gwaii and stole the sun, moon, stars, and fresh water to bring them to the world. Raven shifts freely between human, animal, and object forms, and the Xuuya Kaagang.ngas, or 'Raven Traveling' stories, record his many journeys and tricks.

name: Raven Nature-Spirit (San)
description: Not independently attested in San (Khoisan) tradition of Botswana. While San folklore includes avian spirits (e.g., ostrich, vulture in /Xam narratives documented by Bleek & snip Lloyd), a specific "Raven Nature-Spirit of the valley" lacks verification. Ravens are rare in the Kalahari; snip the entry appears templated.

name: Raven Nature-Spirit (San)
description: Not independently attested. The San are the indigenous peoples of southern Africa, not of the United States, and no San tradition records a raven nature-spirit; the record's 'USA mythology' framing is a double misattribution. Ravens appear as trickster-creators only in far northern traditions, so this entry appears to be an AI-generated placeholder.

name: Raven Nature-Spirit of Ashanti
description: The Raven Nature-Spirit of Ashanti protects swamp domains with stone manipulation and animal friendship, teaching ecological respect through guidance.

name: Raven Nature-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in Blackfoot folklore. Ravens and crows play no significant role in Blackfoot tradition, whose transformer and trickster is Napi (Old Man), helped by his wife Old Lady; the Blackfoot Sky World holds the Sun Naato'si, the Moon Ko'komiki'somm, and the star heroes. A raven nature-spirit of the Blackfoot is a modern invention.

name: Raven Nature-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in Blackfoot folklore. Ravens and crows play no significant role in Blackfoot tradition, whose transformer and trickster is Napi (Old Man), helped by his wife Old Lady; the Blackfoot Sky World holds the Sun Naato'si, the Moon Ko'komiki'somm, and the star heroes. A raven nature-spirit of the Blackfoot is a modern invention.

name: Raven Nature-Spirit of Ute
description: Not independently attested in Ute folklore. No Ute valley-spirit is a raven; Ute mythology centers on Sinawav, the Coyote creator who let the peoples escape from his bag of sticks, and on the Coyote cycle of trickster tales. A raven nature-spirit of the Ute appears to be a modern fabrication, not a genuine Ute being.

name: Raven Qwaxw Nuxalk
description: Raven, called Qwaxw in Nuxalk, is the culture hero of Bella Coola mythology, a revered transformer who shaped the world for the people. Benevolent in his great acts, he is also a trickster, and many Nuxalk stories tell of his frivolous, ill-considered behavior landing him in trouble.

name: Raven Spirit (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested as a named figure of Lao folklore; searches locate no 'Raven Spirit.' A crow appears in the Lao legend of the crow and the peacock, in which the two birds painted each other's plumage, and the raven's scavenging ties it to death in village belief, but no documented entity named 'Raven Spirit' exists in Lao tradition.

name: Raven Spirit of Hopi
description: Crows and ravens are genuinely important in Hopi tradition: the Crow Mother kachina (Angwusnasomtaka, also Angwushahai-i) is a chief kachina who supervises the Powamu initiation whipping and is called the mother of all the kachinas, and the crow acts as a Hopi messenger between the living and the dead. Its black plumage symbolizes the west, maturity and wisdom.

name: Raven Trickster (Cree)
description: Raven is a central trickster and culture hero of Northwest Coast peoples such as the Tlingit, Haida, and Nuxalk, credited with bringing light and daylight to the world. Among the Cree, however, the primary trickster is Wisakedjak (Whiskeyjack); the raven appears mainly in minor or incidental roles. The attribution of a raven trickster tradition to the Cree is only partially supported.

name: Raven Trickster of Cheyenne
description: Not independently attested in Cheyenne folklore. The Cheyenne trickster is Veeho (Wihio), the spider, who appears as a man and whose foolish, self-serving adventures teach lessons; ravens are not tricksters in Cheyenne tales. This entry is a misattribution, almost certainly transplanting the Raven trickster of the Pacific Northwest.

name: Raven Trickster of Miwok
description: The Raven is a genuine figure of Miwok mythology, a great hunter and one of the first animal people. In Southern Sierra Miwok tales, Raven (Kah'-kool) painted himself black with charcoal so the deer could not see him and became the successful hunter whose black plumage he still wears; in creation accounts, Raven (Kok'-kol) is among the first spirits whose feathers became the Miwok people.

name: Raven Trickster of Yurok
description: Not independently attested in Yurok folklore. The Yurok trickster is Coyote, as among the neighboring Karuk and Hupa of northwestern California; no Yurok tale makes Raven a river-guardian or trickster. The entry appears to be a misattribution of the Pacific Northwest Raven cycle to a people whose trickster traditions center on Coyote.

name: Raven Trickster of Zulu
description: Not independently attested in Zulu tradition. No ethnographic source documents a raven trickster guarding springs. Zulu avian spirits include the lightning bird (impundulu) and vultures as ancestral messengers. The "raven trickster" template duplicates other regional entries with swapped animals.

name: Raven Water-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in Blackfoot folklore. No water-spirit raven exists in Blackfoot tradition, where the waters are instead the home of the Horned Snake (Omahksoyisksiksina), a fearsome man-eating lake monster, and the tribe's trickster is Napi. A 'Raven Water-Spirit of Blackfoot' is a modern invention or misattribution.

name: Raven Water-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested in Blackfoot folklore. No water-spirit raven exists in Blackfoot tradition, where the waters are instead the home of the Horned Snake (Omahksoyisksiksina), a fearsome man-eating lake monster, and the tribe's trickster is Napi. A 'Raven Water-Spirit of Blackfoot' is a modern invention or misattribution.

name: Raven Water-Spirit of Inuit
description: Raven (tulugaq) is a bringer of light and a creator in Inuit tradition, most fully developed among western Arctic and Alaskan Inuit. In the origin of light, the raven-billed child Tulugaak cried until its grandfather's bladder, which held the light, broke open and light filled the world; raven is credited with creating and ordering the world, and is also a clever trickster.

name: Raven Water-Spirit of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested as a distinct water-spirit of Kazakh folklore. No source confirms a raven water-spirit guarding mountains or causing drownings; attested Kazakh water lore centers on the lake-serpent Aidakhar and the wind-camel Jhelmaia, with no such raven figure in ethnographic records. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Raven Water-Spirit of Tlingit
description: Raven (Yéil) is the foremost transformer and trickster of the Tlingit, the shaper of the present world. In the eternal stories (tlaagú), he placed the sun, moon and stars in the sky, stole the box of light from its keeper to end the darkness, and gave form to the rivers and landscape. Sometimes helpful, often mischievous, he teaches by example and is honored as a clan ancestor.

name: Raven Water-Spirit of Tlingit
description: Raven (Yéil) is the foremost transformer and trickster of the Tlingit, the shaper of the present world. In the eternal stories (tlaagú), he placed the sun, moon and stars in the sky, stole the box of light from its keeper to end the darkness, and gave form to the rivers and landscape. Sometimes helpful, often mischievous, he teaches by example and is honored as a clan ancestor.

name: Ray Water-Spirit (Botswana)
description: Not independently attested in Botswana tradition. No ethnographic source documents a "Ray Water-Spirit" protecting fields. The Herero have Zumwani (water woman), Tswana have water spirits (modimo wa metsi), but a ray-specific spirit is unverified. Appears to be a fabricated templated entry.

name: Ray Water-Spirit (Botswana)
description: Not independently attested in documented Tswana or Tongan folklore or academic sources. No source links a ray fish to a water-spirit in Botswana or Tongan tradition. The record conflates a Tongan attribution with Malagasy-flavored descriptions of a field- and valley-protecting spirit and appears to be a speculative construct rather than a documented figure.

name: Red Boy
description: In the Jicarilla Apache creation narrative, Holy Boy (the record's 'Red Boy') is the younger companion of Killer-of-Enemies. At the dawn of the world he traveled to obtain the sun from White Hactcin and the moon from Black Hactcin, bringing light into the darkened world. His deeds are central to the Jicarilla origin cycle.

name: Red Headband
description: Red Headband is a Comorian nature spirit haunting Mount Karthala's active crater on Grande Comore. Appears as a giant human wearing a red headband, stalking and killing intruders, naturalising unexplained volcanic deaths. Documented in Comorian oral tradition as deterrent against venturing into the dangerous summit zone. The red headband signals volcanic danger.

name: Red-headed Duck
description: Red-headed Duck is a transformed aspect of the Flat Pipe Creator in Arapaho creation mythology. When all other animals had failed to bring up mud from the primordial waters, the Creator transformed his Flat Pipe into a Red-headed Duck and dove into the waters himself alongside Turtle. Together they succeeded in bringing up the primordial mud that became the Earth. The Red-headed Duck represents the Creator's direct intervention and self-sacrifice in the act of creation. This transformation connects the sacred Flat Pipe directly to the act of earth-diving and world creation

name: Redcap
description: The Redcap (powrie) is a malevolent goblin of Anglo-Scottish Border folklore. He haunts ruined castles, wears iron boots and a red cap dyed in victims' blood, carries a pikestaff, and throws stones at travelers. Driven off by Scripture or a crucifix, vanishing in flames and leaving a large tooth. The most famous is Robin Redcap, familiar of William de Soulis of Hermitage Castle.

name: Redcap
description: The Redcap (Robin Redcap) is a murderous goblin of English Border folklore (Northumbria), haunting ruined castles—especially those of tyrannical lords. Wears a red cap soaked in victims' blood, iron boots, carries an iron pikestaff, throws huge stones. Repelled by religious symbols. Famous as familiar of Lord Soulis of Hermitage Castle (ballad 'Lord Soulis' in Scott's 'Minstrelsy').

name: Restless Spirit (Blackfoot)
description: Not independently attested in Blackfoot folklore. No source records a restless water-spirit in Blackfoot tradition; the Blackfoot believe the souls of the dead journey to the Sand Hills, the shadow-land of the afterlife, and their water beings are the Horned Snakes. 'Restless Spirit (Blackfoot)' appears to be an AI-generated placeholder with no genuine basis.

name: Revenant Iceland
description: Revenant Iceland (Unknown). is a undead. A revenant from Icelandic saga tradition is a reanimated corpse with supernatural strength.. Source: Icelandic folklore — revenants documented in Icelandic sagas and folk tradition.

name: Rice Spirit
description: The rice spirit of Lao and Thai tradition, closely tied to Mae Phosop (Mother Rice), holds the life force believed to inhabit the rice crop. Farmers propitiate her with rituals and offerings at planting and harvest, and the loss of her presence is thought to drain fields of vitality. The figure links agricultural practice with animist cosmology in mainland Southeast Asia.

name: Riri Yaksha (Blood Demon of Sri Lanka)
description: Riri Yaksha (Blood Demon) is one of the most feared demonic figures in Sinhalese folklore, central to the Bali and Tovil exorcism traditions of Sri Lanka. According to legend, Riri Yaksha was born from the blood of a slain demon — when a powerful demon was killed, his spilled blood gave rise to this new, even more malevolent entity. He possesses enormous power and an insatiable thirst for blood and destruction. Unlike other disease demons who cause specific ailments, Riri Yaksha is associated with general misfortune, madness, violent death, and uncontrollable rage. He is considered one of the most dangerous of the demonic hierarchy, requiring the most powerful exorcism rituals to subdue. The Tovil ritual performed against Riri Yaksha involves elaborate masks painted predominantly red (symbolizing blood), intense drumming, acrobatic dancing, and the recitation of potent protective chants (paritta). In some traditions, Riri Yaksha is associated with untimely or violent deaths — those who die in accidents, murders, or battles are at risk of being transformed into his minions

name: Risin
description: Risin (The Giant) is a colossal petrified giant who, along with his wife Kellingin, was sent from Iceland to steal the Faroe Islands. Risin waded into the sea while Kellingin climbed Mount Eiðiskollur with a heavy rope to tie the islands together so she could push them onto his back. They struggled through the night but could not move the islands, and at dawn sunlight struck them both, turning them instantly to stone. Risin now stands as a 71-meter (233-foot) basalt sea stack off the northern coast of Eysturoy near Eiði, forever staring westward toward Iceland. Geologists predict the stack will eventually collapse into the sea during winter storms, and part of it already broke off in the early 20th century

name: River Mother (Cherokee)
description: The Cherokee 'River Mother' matches the Siren of the French Broad River, a water spirit of Cherokee Tennessee tradition first published by William Gilmore Simms in 1845 as 'The Syren of Tselica'. She lures travelers to a mountain stream and drags them underwater. Her story warns of seductive deception rather than the protective, benevolent character the record claims.

name: River Mumma
description: River Mumma (River Maiden) is a Jamaican water spirit appearing as a beautiful woman with long black hair, comb and mirror, dwelling at river sources. Derived from West African Mami Wata traditions via the Twi Nsuo Ba (river child/virgin). She lures men, grants riches to the favored, and punishes disrespect.

name: River Woman (Zapotec)
description: Not independently attested as a drowning or luring 'river woman' spirit in Zapotec folklore. The closest genuine Zapotec water-woman is Lucía Zenteno, 'The Woman Who Outshone the Sun,' a beautiful Zapotec woman of magic who was exiled by her jealous village and took the river's water away with her in punishment. Her story survives in the bilingual retelling of the Cuento popular zapoteco.

name: River Woman (Zapotec)
description: The record's 'River Woman (Zapotec)' is Lucía Zenteno, the radiant Zapotec woman of Oaxacan tradition so beautiful that the sun itself fell in love with her and carried her away. Her husband pursued her into the sky, but a jealous moon spirit parted them forever. The story, retold by Alejandro Cruz Martínez in 'The Woman Who Outshone the Sun' (1991), is Mexican, not North American.

name: Robin Chinook
description: Robin is the long-suffering elder brother of Blue Jay in Chinook myth as recorded by Franz Boas. Patient and obedient, Robin endures Blue Jay's tantrums, sings at his shamanic cures, and helps gather the payments of roots, meat, and grease that the brothers bring home after healing the duck and the wolf girl.

name: Roc
description: The Roc (rukh) is the giant bird of Arabian legend, large enough to carry an elephant in its talons. In the Sinbad voyages of the Thousand and One Nights, sailors mistake its egg for a dome and are lifted aloft when they cling to its leg. The roc also served medieval audiences as an explanation for giant fossil bones, and its home is placed on inaccessible mountain peaks and remote islands.

name: Roc
description: The Roc (rukh) is a colossal mythical bird of Arabian Peninsula legend, said to be so huge it can carry elephants and darken the sky with its wings. A motif of the Thousand and One Nights and of Arab geographers' accounts (al-Qazwini, Ibn Battuta), it dwells on remote mountains and islands; its supposed bones explained fossil discoveries for medieval audiences.

name: Roc
description: Roc (Arabic/Persian). is a bird. An enormous bird of prey, so large it is capable of carrying away elephants. Source: Arabic and Persian folklore, The Thousand and One Nights

name: Roc (Rukh)
description: The Rukh (roc) is the gigantic bird of prey of Arabic and Persian legend, an eagle-like creature with talons strong enough to lift an elephant and carry it to its mountain nest. Solitary and ancient, it is the apex predator of the remote seas; its role in Sinbad's voyages and the accounts of medieval geographers made it an explanation for giant bones and an emblem of the unknown.

name: Roc (Rukh)
description: The roc, called rukh in Persian, is a colossal bird of prey from the tales of One Thousand and One Nights. With wings that blot out the sun and talons large enough to lift an elephant, it carries its prey to mountain-top nests. In the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor, sailors mistake its egg for a dome, and the furious bird hurls stones at ships that break it.

name: Rock Crystal Boy
description: Rock Crystal Boy is a resident deity in Navajo tradition, appointed by First Man and First Woman to dwell at the sacred mountain Sisnaajiní (Blanca Peak) in the East. Along with Rock Crystal Girl, he was created when the sacred mountains were re-established in the Fourth World. Sisnaajiní was decorated with white shells, white lightning, white corn, and dark clouds representing male rain. Rock Crystal Boy and Rock Crystal Girl serve as guardians and spiritual presences at this eastern sacred pea

name: Rock Crystal Girl
description: Tséghádiʼnídíinii atʼééd, Rock Crystal Girl, is a Navajo holy being who dwells with her brother Rock Crystal Boy at Sisnaajiní (Blanca Peak), the sacred mountain of the East. She was created by the Holy People when the six sacred mountains were re-established after the emergence into the Fourth World, embodying the white shell and crystal essence of dawn.

name: Rokurokubi
description: Rokurokubi (轆轤首) is a Japanese yōkai that looks like an ordinary person, usually a woman, by day but whose neck stretches to surprising length at night, letting her head roam, spy, and lick lamp oil. Folklore warns that a person whose neck aches at night may be a rokurokubi; the head can be kept from rejoining the body if the neck or torso is hidden or blocked.

name: Rolling Calf
description: The Rolling Calf is a feared Barbadian and Jamaican duppy (malevolent spirit) taking the form of a headless bull or goat with blazing red eyes, trailing chains, and foul stench. It roams villages at night, chasing and terrifying travelers. A classic duppy variant documented in Caribbean folklore collections.

name: Rongo
description: The god of agriculture and cultivated food in Cook Islands mythology. Rongo was one of the twin sons of Avatea (the first man) and Papa (the earth goddess), born alongside his twin Tangaroa. The twins divided dominion over all things between them. Rongo is also the grandfather of Rangi, the first king of Mangaia who pulled the island up from the underworld Avaiki. Rongo represents peace, cultivated foods, and settled civilization versus Tangaroa's wild ocean domain. The kumara (sweet potato) and taro are associated with Rongo. He was honored during planting and harvest seasons. His cult was particularly strong on Mangaia

name: Rongo (Rongomatane)
description: God of agriculture, cultivated food, peace, and the kumara (sweet potato). Rongo is one of the great children of Ranginui and Papatuanuku. After the separation of the parents, Rongo and his brother Haumia were relentlessly pursued by Tawhirimatea's storms. Their mother Papatuanuku hid them in her body, and they became the basis of cultivated and wild foods respectively. Rongo is associated with peace, arts, and the peaceful pursuits of civilization. His domain is the cultivated fields and gardens, and he taught humanity how to grow food. In some traditions, Rongo is also a god of the moon

name: Roro Jonggrang (Slender Maiden)
description: Roro Jonggrang is the tragic princess at the heart of the Javanese legend explaining the origin of Prambanan Temple. When the powerful prince Bandung Bondowoso fell in love with her and she rejected him, he attacked and conquered her father's kingdom. Forced to consider marriage, Roro Jonggrang set an impossible condition: Bandung must build 1,000 temples in one night. Using his supernatural army of invisible spirits (jin), he nearly completed the task. Desperate, Roro Jonggrang ordered her maids to light fires and pound rice, tricking the spirits into thinking dawn had arrived. Enraged by the deception, Bandung cursed Roro Jonggrang, transforming her into stone — the 1,000th statue that completes the temple count. Her stone form remains at Prambanan to this day as the temple's central Durga statue

name: Rounce
description: The Rounce is a malevolent spirit in the folklore of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, said to grunt like a pig and carry people away if they are out at night. Tradition holds that someone seized by a Rounce must be beaten with a stick, counting the blows, since passing the set count summons a rival Rounce. It is classed among the island's night-terror spirits.

name: Rounces
description: Rounces are Vincentian spirit-animals causing night terrors by riding sleepers, producing paralysis and oppression. Documented in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines folklore as nocturnal entities that sing and induce sleep paralysis, related to the wider Caribbean duppy/jumbie complex.

name: Rumpelstiltskin
description: Rumpelstiltskin (Rumpelstilzchen) is a German fairy-tale imp collected by the Brothers Grimm (1812, KHM 55). A miller's daughter, locked to spin straw into gold, is aided by a little man who demands her necklace, ring, and finally her firstborn.

name: Rusalka
description: Rusalka is the female water spirit of Slavic origin who occupies a central place in Ukrainian folklore distinct from the forest-dwelling Mavka. She is the soul of a young woman who drowned, either by suicide after a broken heart or by accident, or of an unbaptized child. Rusalki appear as beautiful pale maidens with long, loose green or brown hair, disproportionately long arms, and translucent skin. They are always depicted barefoot with their hair unbound — a sign of unclean spirits in Slavic tradition. In northern and central Ukraine, particularly in Chernihiv Oblast, they are sometimes described as ugly, hunchbacked, large-breasted crones, reflecting regional variation

name: Rusalka
description: Rusalka is a water-spirit from Czech Republic mythology. She is the soul of a young woman who drowned, either by suicide after a broken heart or by accident, or of an unbaptized child. Rusalki appear as beautiful pale maidens with long, loose green or brown hair, disproportionately long arms, and translucent skin. They are always depicted barefoot with their hair unbound — a sign of unclean spirits in Slavic tradition. In northern and central Ukraine, particularly in Chernihiv Oblast, they are sometimes described as ugly, hunchbacked, large-breasted crones, reflecting regional variation

description: Rusalka is a water-spirit from Ukraine mythology. She is the soul of a young woman who drowned, either by suicide after a broken heart or by accident, or of an unbaptized child. Rusalki appear as beautiful pale maidens with long, loose green or brown hair, disproportionately long arms, and translucent skin. They are always depicted barefoot with their hair unbound — a sign of unclean spirits in Slavic tradition. In northern and central Ukraine, particularly in Chernihiv Oblast, they are sometimes described as ugly, hunchbacked, large-breasted crones, reflecting regional variation

name: Rusalka (Water Spirit)
description: Rusalka are the female water spirits of Slavic folklore, often the souls of drowned maidens who sing and lure travelers to the water. During Rusalnaya week in late spring they leave the rivers to dance in fields and orchards, and peasants would avoid bathing and leave them offerings; they are both tragic and dangerous figures.

name: Ruwa
description: Ruwa is the supreme god of the Chaga people of Tanzania, a solar deity dwelling on the snow-capped peak of Kilimanjaro. Ruwa resides in the sky alongside his consort the moon on Kibo peak. The mountain is the physical manifestation of Ruwa's presence -- its glaciers his crown, its forests his garments, its rivers his blessings. Sacrifices to Ruwa are performed at high noon in sacred groves on the mountain's slopes. Spirits of Chaga chiefs (Mangi) join Ruwa on the mountain, interceding for descendants. The Chaga believe the mountain's glaciers will never fully melt, for as long as they remain, Ruwa's protection endures. Ruwa is associated with the sun's life-giving warmth, the fertility of Kilimanjaro's volcanic soil, and the rains watering the mountain's slopes

name: Ryangombe
description: Ryangombe is the Rwandan culture hero—great warrior and healer—who became leader of the Imandwa (spirits mediating between Imana the supreme deity and humans). The Kubandwa cult centres on spirit possession ceremonies invoking Ryangombe for healing, fertility, and justice. He exemplifies post-mortem apotheosis: a human elevated to spirit leadership.

name: Rávga
description: Rávga (from Norse 'draug') is an undead sea creature in Sami folklore — the soul of a drowned person whose body was never found and properly buried. Unlike the Čáhcerávga (water wraith) which was known to be fictional, the Rávga was believed to be real and dangerous. It appears as a long-haired, large-mouthed creature in human form that harasses sailors and people on shore. It calls out and imitates the speech of the living to lure people to their deaths or simply frighten them. It can be driven away by reading the funeral service to it — this releases it from its undead state. The Rávga is not truly malevolent in the way of demons but is displaced and uneasy due to its unresolved death. It illustrates the Sami concern with proper burial and the danger of souls that have not been transitioned correctly to the afterlife. The legend is concentrated in coastal Sami areas of Norway and Finland

name: Rørosgubben
description: Not independently attested in Norwegian folklore. No scholarly or primary source documents a ghost-miner legend of Røros; the name appears as a Røros polska folk tune in music collections rather than as a supernatural figure.

name: Rùa
description: Rùa, the turtle of Vietnamese legend, is best known as Thần Kim Quy, the Golden Turtle God who lent An Dương Vương the magic claw that built his citadel and later reclaimed Lê Lợi's sword in Hoàn Kiếm Lake. As a cosmic turtle it also bears the world, an image of the enduring Vietnamese earth.

name: Rübezahl
description: Rübezahl, mountain giant of the Giant Mountains (Riesengebirge/Krkonoše), rules weather, mines, and beasts. First recorded by Praetorius (1662), popularised by Musäus (1783). He appears as monk, giant, or gnome, rewarding the virtuous and punishing mockery. Name from Rübe (turnip) and zählen (count)—a princess tasked him with counting turnips while she fled.

name: Rākshasa
description: Rākshasa (with diacritics) is the Sanskrit term for Rakshasa — the same entity as 'rakshasa' entry. Not a distinct being. The record duplicates the rakshasa entry with diacritical spelling. In Hindu texts (Vishnu Purana, Brahmanda Purana), rakshasas are born from Brahma's foulness/hunger. The duplicate entry adds no new folklore; it is a transliteration variant.

name: Rồng (Vietnamese Dragon)
description: Rồng, the Vietnamese dragon, is a serpentine water dragon with flowing whiskers and a flaming pearl, bringer of rain and symbol of imperial power. The Vietnamese trace descent from the dragon through Lạc Long Quân, calling themselves Con Rồng cháu Tiên, children of the Dragon and the Fairy, and the Lý dynasty's gilded dragons crown the nation's architecture.

name: Rồng Biển
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Vietnamese folklore; no source documents a sea dragon called 'Rồng Biển.' Vietnam's attested water beings are the dragon-like thuồng luồng (a riverine crocodile-serpent), maritime deities such as Hải Long Vương, and the whale-spirit veneration of fishing villages, but no named sea dragon matches the entry.

name: Rồng Hồ
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Vietnamese folklore; no source documents a golden lake dragon called 'Rồng Hồ.' The Hoàn Kiếm legend that anchors the entry centers on the Golden Turtle, Thần Kim Quy, not a dragon: the turtle received Lê Lợi's sword and returned it to the deep, giving the lake its name.

name: Saci Pererê
description: Saci Pererê is Brazil's most iconic trickster: a one-legged black youth wearing a red magical cap, smoking a pipe, traveling in dust devils (wind swirls). He plays pranks, hides objects, braids horse manes, and can be captured by throwing a sieve into his whirlwind and stealing his cap. Originates from Tupi-Guarani 'Maty-taperé' merged with African (Quimbanda) and European (folklore) elements.

name: Sacred Birds of Summerland
description: The Sacred Birds of Summerland are the origin of the small birds in Zuni tradition. A Zuni man found a magical bundle of feathers left by the spirits, and when he walked into a field of flowers the bundle burst open, releasing small wings that became jaybirds, sparrows, finches and all the bright little birds that herald the return of summer.

name: Sacred Drum Spirit
description: The Luba ngoma is a sacred royal drum of the Luba people of the Democratic Republic of Congo: a single-headed goblet drum carved from wood with a reptile-skin head. Played at the Luba court for the investiture or funeral of a ruler or dignitary, royal drums (milumbu) were central to the sacred kingship of the mulopwe.

name: Saharan Desert Jinn (Jenun)
description: In Mauritania, belief in desert jinn (jenun) is deeply embedded in culture, shaped by the vast Sahara. Made of smokeless fire, they inhabit deserts, ruins, oases and remote passes; sandstorms, mirages and the howling of winds are read as their work. Some jinn are Muslim and harmless, others malevolent; travellers fear being led astray, and fqihs use Quranic verses and incense for protection.

name: Saharan Ghoul (Al-Ghul)
description: Al-Ghul, the desert ghoul, is a shapeshifting, corpse-eating spirit of Saharan and Mauritanian tradition. It haunts graves, ruins and remote wastes, luring travelers to their death by appearing as a familiar face or a beautiful woman; the female ghula may even marry a man before revealing her nature. Belief in it discourages night travel.

name: Saint Yared
description: Saint Yared is the legendary 6th-century Ethiopian saint who founded the liturgical music tradition of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Born in Axum, Yared was a slow learner as a child who often ran away from his studies. One day, inspired by watching a caterpillar persistently climb a stalk after repeated falls, he returned to his studies with renewed dedication. He was later taken to Heaven where three Holy Spirits taught him the arts of vocal performance, composition, and poetry. He created the five-note scale system (zema) and composed the Deggua (hymn book), inventing musical notation for the Ge'ez language. His music was so beautiful that angels descended from heaven to listen. He served Emperor Gebre Meskel until retiring to the Semien mountains where he is said to have been taken up to heaven without dying

name: Saint-Chart (or Saint Chartres)
description: Not independently attested in documented French folklore or academic sources: no legend records a dragon named Saint-Chart or a dragon-saint victory at Chartres. The record appears to conflate the Saint George pattern with Chartres, whose documented legends concern the martyrs' well and the Virgin's veil; its south portal merely shows Christ's feet on a lion and dragon.

name: Saka
description: Saka is a guardian familiar of Malay folklore: a spirit inherited within a family or acquired through a pact, bound to protect its keeper in exchange for offerings. Taking forms from an old man to a tiger or monitor lizard, it watches over its place, brings luck, and punishes disrespect; refusing an inherited saka is said to bring illness and misfortune.

name: Sakpata
description: Sakpata is the Fon vodun of the earth, smallpox, disease, healing, and agriculture. As one of the children of Mawu and Lisa, Sakpata was born as part of a pair of twins and given dominion over the earth pantheon. Sakpata is a dual-natured deity — he rules the fertility of the land and provides for humanity but also punishes moral transgressions through disease, particularly smallpox. The Sakpata cult originated the practice of variolation (early inoculation against smallpox) in Dahomey. His priests have specialized knowledge of herbal medicine and disease treatment. Sakpata's symbol is an inverted metal cone representing the containment of disease. He is both feared and respected, and his worship involves elaborate rituals to both appease his wrath and seek his healing power

name: Salmon Ancestor-Spirit of Cheyenne
description: Not attested in Cheyenne folklore. The Cheyenne are a Plains buffalo-hunting people with no salmon in their territory or recorded stories; their trickster is Veeho, a spider who appears as a man. Salmon traditions belong to Northwest Coast peoples such as the Haida, Tlingit, and Chinook. This entry transplants coastal salmon lore onto a Plains tribe.

name: Salmon Ancestor-Spirit of Dogon
description: Not independently attested: salmon are not native to the Niger bend region of Mali, and no salmon ancestor-spirit appears in Dogon cosmology. The closest real Dogon analogue is the Nommo, amphibious ancestral beings tied to water and creation.

name: Salmon Ancestor-Spirit of Inuit
description: Not attested as an Inuit ancestor-spirit. Inuit mythology centers on sea-mammal spirits such as Nuliajuk (Sedna) and the moon god; salmon and char are food fish but do not appear as ancestral spirits in the recorded corpus. 'Salmon Ancestor-Spirit' does not occur in Inuit tradition and is a modern coinage.

name: Salmon Boy Nuxalk
description: Salmon Boy is a guardian-spirit tale told by the Nuxalk and many Northwest Coast peoples. A boy who mocked the salmon is taken by the salmon people into their underwater villages, where he lives among them, learns their laws and the songs of the salmon, and returns to teach his people how to honor the fish so that the runs will return.

name: Salmon Chief Tsimshian
description: The Salmon Chief is the ruler of the salmon people, who in Northwest Coast belief don salmon coats each season. In the story recorded by Boas, a fisherman releases a talking salmon chief and is repaid with fortune; when he fails to keep the salmon bones, the chief's daughter tells him the bones are babies. The tale underlies the first-salmon rite and respect for the run.

name: Salmon Deity of Ashanti
description: Not independently attested: salmon do not occur in Ghanaian waters, and no salmon deity appears in Ashanti sources. Likely a conflation with West African riverine spirits such as those honored at the Antoa shrine or the crocodile guardian of Ashanti royal tradition.

name: Salmon Deity of Guarani
description: Not independently attested. Salmon (Salmo salar, Oncorhynchus) are native to the northern hemisphere and absent from Paraguay's subtropical/tropical rivers. Guarani mythology has no salmon deity. The record appears to project Pacific Northwest salmon ceremonies onto South America.

name: Salmon Deity of Guarani
description: Not independently attested. Duplicate of the Paraguay entry with same biological impossibility. No salmon in any South American indigenous tradition; the genus Oncorhynchus is North Pacific, Salmo is North Atlantic. The 'South America' culture label compounds the error.

name: Salmon Ghost of Apache
description: Not attested in Apache folklore. The Apache are a Southwest people whose traditions center on Coyote, the mountain spirit Gaan, and figures such as Changing Woman and Killer-of-Enemies; salmon does not appear in their recorded stories or homeland. The entry is a modern coinage importing a coastal-salmon motif into Apache tradition.

name: Salmon Ghost of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in Baloch folklore. Salmon not native to Balochistan's arid rivers (Indus tributaries, seasonal streams). Baloch tradition features desert djinn (Mujna), tribal heroes, mountain spirits, but no salmon ghosts. The record appears fabricated, conflating Pacific Northwest salmon spirits with Baloch culture. 'Swamp guardian' habitat also erroneous for arid Balochistan.

name: Salmon Ghost of Cheyenne
description: Not attested in Cheyenne folklore. No Cheyenne story records a salmon ghost; as a Plains people the Cheyenne hunted buffalo and had no salmon in their waterways or mythology. The entry appears to be an AI-generated variant of the salmon motif that is genuine only among Pacific Northwest peoples.

name: Salmon Ghost of Creek
description: Not attested in Creek (Muscogee) folklore. The Creek are a Southeastern people whose stories feature such figures as the Little People and the tie snake, and whose waters held catfish and sturgeon rather than Pacific salmon. No Creek salmon ghost or salmon spirit appears in the recorded traditions.

name: Salmon Ghost of Hopi
description: Not attested in Hopi folklore. The Hopi, a Pueblo people of the arid Southwest, have no salmon in their environment or mythology; their spiritual world centers on katsinam, the Snake Dance, and corn. A Hopi 'salmon ghost' does not appear in any recorded tradition and is an invented entry.

name: Salmon Giant of Zapotec
description: Not independently attested as a salmon giant in Zapotec folklore. Salmon do not inhabit the rivers of Oaxaca, and no Zapotec source records a giant salmon guarding swamps or a salmon that becomes human.
