Salmon hold a central place in Pacific Northwest and northeast Asian traditions, not Mesoamerican ones. The record appears to be a northern fish motif misplaced onto Zapotec myth.

name: Salmon Guardian of Miwok
description: Not attested as a named salmon guardian in Miwok folklore. Miwok tradition includes a salmon-shaman theme — a shaman empowered to bring or control salmon for the people — but no separate 'salmon guardian spirit.' The input's specific figure does not appear in Central Sierra Miwok records or dictionary materials.

name: Salmon Guardian of Ojibwe
description: Not attested in Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) folklore. Ojibwe water spirits include Mishipeshu, the underwater panther of the Great Lakes, and the memegwesi little people, but salmon was not a traditional Great Lakes fish and no salmon guardian appears in Anishinaabe tradition. The entry transfers a coastal motif to an inland people.

name: Salmon Guardian of Ojibwe
description: Not attested in Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) folklore. Ojibwe water spirits include Mishipeshu, the underwater panther of the Great Lakes, and the memegwesi little people, but salmon was not a traditional Great Lakes fish and no salmon guardian appears in Anishinaabe tradition. The entry transfers a coastal motif to an inland people.

name: Salmon Guardian of Paiute
description: Not attested in Paiute folklore. The Paiute of the Great Basin are known for the waterbaby spirit, the trickster Coyote, and their trout and cui-ui fisheries, but salmon were not native to their waters and no salmon guardian figure appears in their recorded traditions.

name: Salmon Of Wisdom
description: The Salmon of Knowledge (Bradán Feasa) is central to the Fenian Cycle. An ordinary salmon ate nine hazelnuts falling into Connla's Well, gaining all wisdom. Poet Finn Éces fished seven years; his apprentice Fionn mac Cumhaill cooked it, burned his thumb on a drop of fat, sucked it, and acquired omniscience — thereafter accessing it by biting his thumb.

name: Salmon Spirit of Cree
description: Not attested in Cree folklore. While Eastern James Bay Cree have a word for landlocked salmon (uninv), salmon is not a mythic spirit; Cree traditions feature the little people (memegwesi), the wîhtiko, and the trickster Wîsahkêcâhk. No 'salmon spirit' appears in the recorded Cree corpus.

name: Salmon Spirit of Paiute
description: Not attested in Paiute folklore. No Paiute story records a salmon spirit; the Paiute's sacred and trickster beings are Coyote, the waterbaby, and the animal spirits of the Great Basin. Salmon did not inhabit their territory, and the figure is a modern invention.

name: Salmon Spirit of Zapotec
description: Not independently attested as a salmon spirit of Zapotec folklore. No Zapotec source records a desert- or wilderness-dwelling salmon spirit, and salmon are not native to Oaxaca's waters. Zapotec nature spirits are tied to local animals and deities such as Cocijo and Pitao Cozobi. The salmon appears to be a northern animal imposed on Zapotec tradition by a data-generation error.

name: Salmon Spirit of Zulu
description: Not independently attested in Zulu tradition. Salmon (Salmo salar) are not native to southern African waters. The entry is fabricated with templated "guardian of cliffs" motif. Zulu water spirits include the mermaid-like njuzu and the serpent Inkanyamba, not salmon.

name: Salmon Trickster of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in Baloch folklore. Same issues: salmon absent from Balochistan, no trickster salmon in Balochi oral tradition. 'Ocean guardian' habitat erroneous — Makran coast has Arabian Sea fisheries (tuna, sardines), not salmon. Paired entry with 'salmon-ghost-of-baloch' appears fabricated, imposing trickster/ghost duality on a culture without salmon mythology.

name: Salmon Trickster of Maya
description: Not independently attested as a salmon trickster in Maya folklore. Salmon do not occur in Maya lands, and no Popol Vuh or ethnographic source records a salmon trickster. Maya trickster figures derive from local animals, such as the rabbit (the moon rabbit) and the howler monkey. The record is a northern fish motif wrongly assigned to Maya tradition.

name: Salmon Trickster of Passamaquoddy
description: Not attested as a salmon trickster in Passamaquoddy folklore. The Passamaquoddy trickster is Lox, and Leland's Algonquin Legends includes a tale of Lox catching salmon; but no salmon character acts as a trickster. The entry inflates a single episode into a nonexistent trickster figure.

name: Salmon Trickster of Shona
description: Not independently attested in Shona tradition. Salmon do not exist in Zimbabwe. The entry is fabricated with templated "guardian of caves" motif. Shona trickster figures are hare (tsuro) or baboon; snip water spirits are njuzu (mermaids).

name: Salmon Water-Spirit of Navajo
description: Not attested in Navajo folklore. The Navajo world centers on the Holy People, mountain spirits and water beings such as Water Buffalo, but salmon is not a Navajo figure — the Southwest has no native salmon. The entry is a coastal motif mistakenly attached to Diné tradition.

name: Salmon Water-Spirit of Shoshone
description: Not attested in Shoshone folklore. The Shoshone of the Great Basin have no salmon in their territory or mythology; their stories feature Coyote, Water Baby and local animal spirits. No 'salmon water-spirit' appears in the recorded Shoshone corpus.

name: Salt Woman (spirit)
description: Salt Woman is a spirit in Hopi tradition who became angry when people violated taboos involving salt — being wasteful, disrespectful, or using salt improperly during ceremonies. In response, she moved the salt deposits far away to the Grand Canyon and other distant locations. Ever since, the Hopi have had to undertake long, dangerous journeys to gather salt, which is a sacred substance used in ceremonies and daily life. The story teaches respect for natural resources and the consequences of taki

name: Salu'ah
description: The Salu'ah (feminine grammatical form, as opposed to Salu — masculine) is the Arabian she-wolf, a monstrous creature from Bedouin folklore of northern Saudi Arabia. According to Bedouin oral traditions collected by Fatmah Alblui in her anthology 'Salu'ah: Between Fact and Fantasy,' the Salu'ah is a hairy, ugly animal-like woman who hunts primarily men and occasionally children and women. She has sharp teeth, howls like a wolf, and can transform herself into an old woman to approach unsuspecting victims. Unlike the more generic Ghul, the Salu'ah is specifically a monstrous feminine figure — representing the inversion of traditional gender roles. The Bedouins had an ambivalent relationship with wolves, respecting their hunting abilities while fearing their attacks. The Salu'ah myth served to explain disappearances in the desert and reinforce social norms. She represents the terrifying power of female agency in a patriarchal society, the 'monstrous feminine' that devours men rather than serving them

name: Saman Deviyo (Guardian of Adam's Peak)
description: Saman Deviyo (also known as Sumana Saman) is one of the four guardian deities (Catura Varam Deviyo) of Sri Lanka in Sinhalese Buddhist tradition. He is the divine protector of Adam's Peak (Sri Pada), the sacred mountain that is one of the most important pilgrimage sites in Sri Lanka. According to the Mahavamsa, the Buddha, on his deathbed, entrusted the care of Lanka to the god Sumana, who later appeared to Prince Vijaya's followers disguised as a wandering ascetic. Saman is associated with the Sumana Saman mountain range and is considered the guardian of the Buddha's footprint atop Adam's Peak — a footprint revered by Buddhists (as Buddha's), Hindus (as Shiva's), Muslims (as Adam's), and Christians (as St. He is often depicted as a regal figure riding an elephant, holding a lotus flower, and wearing royal white garments. He is considered the most prominent of the guardian deities and is invoked first in most Sinhalese Buddhist rituals. His principal shrine is at Ratnapura, where the Saman Devalaya (shrine) houses his image and receives offerings from pilgrims before they begin their climb

name: Samo (or Samovila)
description: Samovila (samodiva) are the ethereal female spirits of Bulgarian folklore, beautiful maidens with wings who dance in mountain meadows, guard springs and forests, and can heal or curse. They are immune to fire and magic, flee from mortal men's advances, and their songs and dances are central to Bulgarian folk ballads.

name: Samodiva
description: Ethereal woodland nymphs and water spirits (самодива, samodivi) appearing as eternally young maidens with flowing golden/blonde hair, pale glowing skin, and hypnotic eyes. They inhabit deep forests, caves, and remote mountain regions near rivers, springs, wells, and lakes—particularly in the Pirin, Vitosha, Rila, and Rhodope Mountains. Their haunting, melancholic songs are sung at twilight, creating an irresistible compulsion that lures travelers and shepherds to follow them—often to watery deaths by drowning, or to dance until exhausted and die

name: Sampo
description: The Sampo is not a monster but a magical artifact — a wondrous mill forged by Ilmarinen that produces salt, flour, and gold, central to the Kalevala's plot. Stolen by Louhi, fought over, and shattered in the sea, its fragments bring prosperity to Finland. Classifying it as a 'monster' and 'forest-spirit' is a category error; it is a cosmological object in Kalevala mythology.

name: Sand Jinn
description: Sand Jinn are desert spirits in Mauritanian folklore, believed to be made of smokeless fire who dwell beneath the dunes and protect lost travelers or lead them astray. The belief reflects Islamic cosmology adapted to the Sahara, where survival depends on the mercy of the desert and its unseen inhabitants.

name: Sang Kancil (The Mouse Deer)
description: Sang Kancil, the mouse deer, is the most famous trickster figure in Malay folklore. Despite being one of the smallest animals in the jungle, Sang Kancil uses extraordinary intelligence and wit to outsmart much larger and stronger adversaries — crocodiles, tigers, elephants, and humans. In the most famous tale, Sang Kancil tricks a river full of hungry crocodiles into lining up across the river by claiming the king has ordered a headcount of all crocodiles. The mouse deer then hops across their backs to reach the fruit trees on the far shore. When the crocodiles realize the deception, Sang Kancil is already enjoying the fruits of victory. These tales celebrate the triumph of intelligence over brute force and are deeply embedded in Malay cultural identity

name: Sang-ngag (Gökhang)
description: Not independently attested as a named dragon of Tibetan folklore. No source documents a 'Sang-ngag Gökhang' dragon; the name appears to conflate Tibetan terms — 'gsang sngags' (secret mantra) and 'dgon khang' (protector chapel). The recorded form matches the Tibetan dragon 'Druk', a weather-controlling serpent, but the specific name and claimed Bon prominence are unverified.

name: Sangkuriang
description: Sangkuriang is the tragic hero of Sundanese legend from West Java, who unknowingly falls in love with his own mother Dayang Sumbi — a princess blessed with eternal youth by the gods. When Dayang Sumbi recognizes her son by a scar on his forehead (from a childhood wound), she sets impossible tasks to prevent their marriage: he must dam the Citarum River, build a vast lake, and construct a great boat before sunrise. With supernatural help, Sangkuriang nearly succeeds, but Dayang Sumbi tricks him by spreading red cloth in the east to mimic dawn. Enraged at the deception, Sangkuriang kicks the unfinished boat, which forms Mount Tangkuban Perahu (Upturned Boat) — an active volcano near Bandung. He curses Dayang Sumbi before disappearing, never to be seen again

name: Sanni Yakku
description: Sanni Yakku are the 18 disease demons of Sinhala Sri Lankan demonology — each causing a specific illness (fever, madness, skin conditions). Invoked in thovil exorcism rituals where masked dancers (ves) embody them. Documented by Obeyesekere, Wirz, Kandyan medical texts. Not a single demon but a cohort; king is Maha Sohona. Central to Sri Lankan traditional healing (demonology as medicine).

name: Santa Compaña
description: A ghostly procession of tormented souls that wanders rural paths at midnight, wearing white hooded cloaks and carrying lit candles. Known in Northern Portugal as Santa Companha or As da Noite (the Night Ones), the procession is led by a living person from the local parish who unknowingly walks under a supernatural curse every night, carrying a cross or cauldron of holy water. The living leader awakens each morning with no memory but growing exhaustion, and will die within weeks unless they pass the curse to another person during the procession. The Santa Compaña's arrival portends imminent death in whatever home it visits

name: Santa Compaña
description: A ghostly procession of tormented souls that wanders rural paths at midnight, wearing white hooded cloaks and carrying lit candles. Known in Northern Portugal as Santa Companha or As da Noite (the Night Ones), the procession is led by a living person from the local parish who unknowingly walks under a supernatural curse every night, carrying a cross or cauldron of holy water. The living leader awakens each morning with no memory but growing exhaustion, and will die within weeks unless they pass the curse to another person during the procession. The Santa Compaña's arrival portends imminent death in whatever home it visits In Portugal folklore, this figure is known among the Portugal people.

name: Santa Muerte
description: Santa Muerte ('Holy Death') is a folk saint and personification of death venerated in Mexico, blending the Aztec death goddess Mictēcacihuātl with the Spanish Grim Reaper. Her robe colors mark the request — white for purification, red for love, gold for money, black for protection, green for justice. Despite the Church's rejection, her cult grew in the early 2000s, among the marginalized.

name: Santal
description: Malagasy ghost dog that haunts crossroads, graveyards, and dark rural roads. Enormous jet-black spectral hound, the size of a small cow, with eyes blazing like live coals or glowing red embers. Moves in absolute silence, leaving no footprints despite its immense weight. Appears as a death omen, particularly to those who see it at night or near tombs. Its howl portends imminent death. Can be summoned by sorcerers (ombiasy). The creature is a manifestation of ancestral spirits or corrupted dead (angatra) that have slipped from the protective realm of the ancestors

name: Saraswati
description: Saraswati is the Hindu goddess of knowledge, music, arts, speech, learning — consort of Brahma. Originating as Vedic river goddess, she becomes personification of wisdom and arts. Depicted white-clad on lotus, holding veena, book, rosary, water pot. Worshipped on Vasant Panchami; central to Hindu, Jain, Buddhist traditions. Not a 'water-spirit' in folkloric sense but a major deity.

name: Sarki (Daura Serpent)
description: Sarki is the giant serpent that guarded the Kusugu well in the city of Daura, the central antagonist in the foundational legend of the Hausa people. The serpent allowed the townspeople to draw water only on Fridays, terrorizing them the rest of the week. When the prince Bayajidda (Abu Yazid) arrived from Baghdad, he went to the well on a Thursday, unaware of the prohibition. When Sarki attacked, Bayajidda cut off its head with his sword. As reward, Queen Daurama offered him half her kingdom, but Bayajidda instead requested her hand in marriage, ending the tradition of celibate queens. Their descendants founded the seven Hausa states

name: Sasabonsam
description: The Sasabonsam is the vampire-ogre of the Akan and Ashanti of Ghana, a forest spirit with iron teeth, pink or dark skin, long red hair, bat-like wings and iron hooks for feet, which hangs in tall trees and drops on those who venture too deep. Rattray recorded it in Ashanti Proverbs; it polices forest boundaries.

name: Sasabonsam
description: The Sasabonsam (Asanbosam), the 'iron-toothed tree vampire,' is the Akan forest ogre of Côte d'Ivoire, told among the Baoulé, Anyi and neighboring groups. It lives in tall trees, seizes passers-by from above, and is said to have iron teeth, hooked feet and bat-like wings; regional tellings color its skin, hair and limbs differently.

name: Sasabonsam
description: The Sasabonsam (Asanbosam) is the vampire-ogre of the Akan peoples of Côte d'Ivoire, including the Baoulé and Anyi: a tree-dwelling forest predator with iron teeth, pink or dark skin, long red hair, bat-like wings and hooked feet, which drops on travelers and hunters from the canopy. Its legends police forest boundaries and punish excessive hunting.

name: Sasabonsom
description: Sasabonsom is a terrifying giant monster in Akan mythology that dwells in the deepest parts of the forest. Unlike the relatively benign Mmoatia, Sasabonsom is malevolent — a huge, hairy creature with large eyes and long arms that sits on high branches and preys on humans who venture too deep. It is often described as having backward-pointing feet like the Mmoatia but is far more dangerous. Sasabonsom is the enemy of Anansi in some tales, representing brute force and evil that must be overcome through cunning. It is sometimes considered an abosom (deity) of the wilderness but is primarily feared as a monster that eats humans. The name is likely related to the Akan word "sasabonsam" meaning "a giant evil spirit of the forest."

name: Sasq'ets
description: Sasq'ets ('wild man'), of the Sts'ailes (Chehalis) people in British Columbia, is the hairy forest being from whose name J.W. Burns coined the word 'Sasquatch' in 1929. The Sts'ailes hold Sasq'ets in their identity and culture as a genuine, longstanding figure of the mountain forests, distinct from the popularized 'Bigfoot.'

name: Sasquatch (Bigfoot)
description: Sasquatch is the great hairy wild man of the Pacific Northwest woods, attested across many Indigenous traditions under local names such as Halkomelem sæsq'ec, source of the word 'sasquatch.' Usually a huge, ape-like forest dweller who leaves enormous footprints, he ranges from a dangerous man-eater in some legends to a shy forest guardian in others. Modern Bigfoot sightings keep the legend alive.

name: Sasquatch (Bigfoot)
description: Sasquatch is the great hairy wild man of the Pacific Northwest woods, attested across many Indigenous traditions under local names such as Halkomelem sæsq'ec, source of the word 'sasquatch.' Usually a huge, ape-like forest dweller who leaves enormous footprints, he ranges from a dangerous man-eater in some legends to a shy forest guardian in others. Modern Bigfoot sightings keep the legend alive.

name: Sawa (Fonu, I'a Sa)
description: The fonu, the giant sea turtle of Samoan tradition, is a sacred guardian called I'a sa ('sacred fish'), believed to save lost fishermen by carrying them to shore. In the celebrated Turtle and Shark legend of Vaitogi, a neglected brother and sister became turtle and shark, appearing when villagers sing their summoning song. Turtle flesh was reserved for high chiefs, and harming turtles was tapu.

name: Sayad
description: Not independently attested in Yemeni folklore under this name. Sayad is described as a female jinn, tall with long hair, sagging breasts, and donkey legs, who manifests through those who fear her and seizes possession. The figure closely resembles Umm al-Subyan, the child-stealing night demon of South Arabia, and may be a mislabeled variant of that attested being.

name: Schrat
description: The Schrat (plural Schratln) is a versatile and regionally diverse German legendary creature, appearing as either a wood sprite, a domestic kobold, or a nightmare demon depending on location and tradition. The term is ancient, entering Slavic languages as skrat, skrzat (Polish), skřítek (Czech), and even Estonian kratt — a testament to its deep Indo-European roots. In Bavaria and Austria, the Waldschrat is a solitary forest-dwelling spirit, small and mischievous, who plays malicious pranks on woodcutters and hikers. It breaks their axes, fells trees in wrong directions, and leads travelers astray with mocking laughter. In other regions, particularly the Upper Palatinate, the Schrat is a domestic house spirit akin to a kobold, protecting the home and bringing prosperity if respected, but causing chaos if offended. In Switzerland and the Alemannic regions, the Schratteli is an alp-like nightmare demon that causes sleep paralysis and has a unibrow — the telltale mark of those connected to the spirit world. The Schrat is considered the origin of the English term 'scrat' as an archaic word for a devil or goblin

name: Schrat
description: The Schrat is a regionally varied German legendary creature: a wood sprite (Waldschrat) that torments woodcutters in Bavaria and Austria, a domestic house spirit akin to a kobold in the Upper Palatinate, or an alp-like nightmare demon (Schratteli) in Switzerland and Alemannic regions. The old term spread into Slavic as skrzat, skřítek, and Estonian kratt.

name: Scorpion Ancestor-Spirit (Mari)
description: Not independently attested: scorpions do not occur in the temperate forests of the Mari El region, and no scorpion ancestor-spirit appears in documented Mari tradition. The entry appears to be an invention; Mari ancestor and nature worship centers on the forest, the household, and the sacred grove.

name: Scorpion Spirit (Angolan)
description: Not independently attested in Angolan tradition. The input conflates generic 'forest spirit' tropes with the scorpion. The closest real analogue is Angolan veneration of Mami Wata/Mamba Muntu, who sometimes appears as a snake. Scorpions feature in Kongo minkisi as protective medicines, but no named 'Scorpion Spirit' exists in published Angolan ethnography.

name: Se
description: Se is divine law, destiny and cosmic order in Ewe cosmology: the moral and spiritual foundation set by the creator Mawu that governs all existence. Not a personified deity but the underlying balance between the spiritual and physical worlds, Se is honoured through ancestral rites, ethical conduct and respect for the natural order, and violating it brings misfortune.

name: Se'ir
description: The Se'ir is a desert demon known in northern Iraqi folklore, particularly among the Shammar Bedouin tribes. According to descriptions collected by folklorist E.S. Drower, the Se'ir haunts desolate places and ruins, especially the ancient city of Hatra. It appears as an extremely old man with a beard reaching his knees, one eye, very long teeth tipped with iron, and iron toenails. The Se'ir devours human beings and is known to inhabit wastelands and ruins in the desert. The name is connected to the Hebrew 'se'irim' mentioned in the Old Testament — hairy beings or satyrs that haunted waste places. This creature represents the survival of ancient Semitic demonology in modern Iraqi folk belief, blending Mesopotamian, Jewish, and Arab traditions

name: Sea Bear
description: Gunakadeit, the Tlingit sea wolf or sea monster, is the great being of the outer coast who supplies wealth and food. In the story told at Wrangell, a young man gained Gunakadeit's power by wearing its skin and used it to feed his starving village. Related peoples, including the Tsimshian and Haida, tell of the same marine transformer; its name now labels a fossil sea reptile from southeast Alaska.

name: Sea Beast of Raouche
description: The Sea Beast of Raouche is a legendary monster from Lebanese coastal folklore associated with the famous Pigeon Rocks (Raouche) off the coast of Beirut. According to local legend, a fearsome sea monster once threatened the land around Raouche, demanding human sacrifices from the terrified locals. To appease the beast, the people chose to sacrifice the beautiful princess Andromeda. Before the sacrifice could be completed, the hero Perseus arrived, bringing with him the severed head of Medusa. In an epic battle on the coast, Perseus deployed Medusa's petrifying gaze, turning the monstrous sea beast permanently to stone. The Pigeon Rocks that stand today off Beirut's coast are said to be the petrified remains of the monster, weathered by centuries of sea and stone. This legend blends Greek mythology with local Lebanese geography

name: Sea Draugr
description: Sea Draugr (Icelandic). is a undead. The spirit of a drowned man who haunts the coastlines and lures sailors to their death. Source: Norse mythology; draugar are corporeal undead, documented in the Sagas and Norse ethnographic studies.

name: Sea King
description: Sea King (Unknown). is a human. A Sea King (Sjøkonge) is a figure from Norse and Danish folklore, a powerful ruler of the seas who commands the waves and the creatures within them.. Source: Nordic maritime folklore

name: Sea Maid
description: Not independently attested as an indigenous Monegasque folk figure in documented folklore or academic sources. Monaco's documented sea-maid associations are modern: the Little Mermaid statue overlooking Larvotto Beach (2000), a Danish homage linked to Prince Rainier III, and the Grimaldi curse legend of the wronged maiden. No Monegasque siren or 'sea maid' appears in regional folklore collections.

name: Sea Monster
description: In Tlingit tradition the sea monster Gunakadeit, the great sea wolf of the outer islands, appears to lone travelers and can be brought ashore only with the right ritual knowledge. Its supernatural skin grants its wearer power to hunt and feed a community. The figure belongs to the wider Northwest Coast belief in powerful undersea beings.

name: Sea Monster
description: In Tlingit tradition the sea monster Gunakadeit, the great sea wolf of the outer islands, appears to lone travelers and can be brought ashore only with the right ritual knowledge. Its supernatural skin grants its wearer power to hunt and feed a community. The figure belongs to the wider Northwest Coast belief in powerful undersea beings.

name: Sea Monsters
description: Inuit oral tradition tells of several dangerous marine beings, not one named 'Sea Monsters.' Qalupalik lurks beneath the sea ice and snatches children who wander onto thin ice; Arnapkapfaaluk, 'the terrible woman of the sea,' is a form of the Sea Mother who eats hunters. The record is a category label, and its linked Sinbad story is an error.

name: Sea Nymph
description: Sea nymphs are the female sea deities of Greek mythology — the fifty Nereids, daughters of Nereus, and the Oceanids — beautiful immortal maidens who dwell in the Mediterranean and assist sailors, escorting heroes and calming or stirring the waves. They appear throughout Homer and Hesiod and survive in folklore as beneficent sea spirits who guide and rescue those at sea.

name: Sea Serpents
description: Sea-serpent traditions are documented along the Northwest Coast, where the great horned water serpent appears in the art and ceremony of several peoples. The Sisiutl of the Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth and Coast Salish is the classic form: a horned serpent with a head at each end and a central human-like face, whose glance can kill, and whose image protects warriors and house fronts.

name: Sea Serpents
description: Sea-serpent traditions are documented along the Northwest Coast, where the great horned water serpent appears in the art and ceremony of several peoples. The Sisiutl of the Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth and Coast Salish is the classic form: a horned serpent with a head at each end and a central human-like face, whose glance can kill, and whose image protects warriors and house fronts.

name: Sea Troll
description: Not independently attested as a named 'sea troll' (havstroll) in Nordic folklore. Swedish tradition has sjörå (sea rå) and havsfrun (sea lady) as female water spirits, and the Norwegian havtroll appears in Ibsen's literary Peer Gynt. The generic 'sea troll' is a modern categorization, not a specific folkloric entity.

name: Sea-Gull Man
description: Sea-Gull Man is a supernatural figure in Haida creation mythology who plays a crucial role in the formation of Haida Gwaii. In the creation narrative, after Raven fell from the Sky Land, a grebe appeared and summoned him to the underwater house of Sea-Gull Man. There, Sea-Gull Man gave Raven two rocks: a small speckled one that became Haida Gwaii and a larger black one that became the mainland continent. Sea-Gull Man thus holds the primordial land forms and is the source from which the Haida physical world emerged

name: Sedna
description: Sedna is the great sea mother of the Inuit, mistress of the whales, seals and walruses, who lives in Adlivun beneath the ocean. A mortal girl who was thrown from her father's boat, she became the sea animals when her severed fingers were cut away. Hunters keep her favor by obeying taboos; when they fail, the angakkuq (shaman) must journey to comb her hair and free the animals she withholds.

name: Sedna
description: In Greenland, Sedna is known by many names — Arnakuagsak, Arnaqquassaaq, Sassuma Arnaa — the great sea mother who lives at the bottom of the ocean and owns the whales, seals and walruses. She was a mortal girl whose severed fingers became the sea mammals after her father betrayed her.

name: Seer Iceland
description: Seer Iceland (Unknown). is a human. A seer volva from Norse-Icelandic tradition is a prophetess who practices seidr magic.. Source: Icelandic folklore — seer figures documented in Icelandic folk tradition.

name: Segen
description: Segen is the Ethiopian queen of spirits (ayyana), dwelling in sacred peaks of the Simien Mountains, Tigray highlands, and Rift Valley escarpments. She syncretises Oromo fertility goddess Atete with Virgin Mary (Mariam), appearing in rock-hewn church frescoes wearing the golden mitre-crown of Sabaean sovereignty.

name: Sekhmet (Lioness Goddess of War)
description: Sekhmet is the lioness-headed Egyptian goddess of warfare, destruction, plague, and healing. Her name means 'the powerful one'. She was created when Ra sent his fiery Eye to punish humanity for rebelling against him. She descended upon the earth as Sekhmet and began slaughtering humans with such bloodlust that Ra had to trick her by flooding fields with beer dyed red to stop the massacre. She is both a destroyer and a healer; snip she brought plagues but also cured them. Her priests were both warriors and physicians. Consort of Ptah and mother of Nefertem, she formed part of the Memphis Triad. In battle, her fiery breath created the desert winds

name: Selbusjøormen
description: Selbusjøormen is a legendary lake serpent said to inhabit Selbusjøen, one of the largest lakes in Trøndelag. Selbusjøen is located in Selbu municipality and is part of the Nea-Nidelva watercourse. The lake serpent has been reported for centuries by local farmers, fishermen, and travelers. Descriptions vary — some say it resembles a giant eel, others describe a serpent with multiple humps, and some claim it has a horse-like head. The creature is said to live in the deepest parts of the lake, particularly near the areas where the Nea River enters the lake. Sightings are most common in summer when the lake is calm. The Selbusjøormen is part of a broader tradition of lake monsters in Norwegian folklore, similar to the Selma legend in Seljord (Telemark) and Storsjöodjuret in Sweden

name: Selkie
description: Seal folk from Scottish folklore who can shed their sealskin to become human. Found especially in Orkney, Shetland, and the Hebrides. The word 'selkie' derives from the Scots term selchie meaning 'grey seal.' These shape-shifting beings live as seals in the sea but can remove their pelts to walk on land as beautiful humans. Famous tales include 'The Selkie Wife,' 'The Great Selkie of Sule Skerry,' 'Gioga's Son' from Papa Stour, and 'Donald the Seal Hunter' from Shetland. Documented by John Francis Campbell in Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860-1862)

name: Selkie
description: Selkie is a shapeshifter from Iceland mythology. Found especially in Orkney, Shetland, and the Hebrides. The word 'selkie' derives from the Scots term selchie meaning 'grey seal.' These shape-shifting beings live as seals in the sea but can remove their pelts to walk on land as beautiful humans. Famous tales include 'The Selkie Wife,' 'The Great Selkie of Sule Skerry,' 'Gioga's Son' from Papa Stour, and 'Donald the Seal Hunter' from Shetland. Documented by John Francis Campbell in Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860-1862)

name: Selkie
description: Selkie is a shapeshifter from Celtic mythology. Found especially in Orkney, Shetland, and the Hebrides. The word 'selkie' derives from the Scots term selchie meaning 'grey seal.' These shape-shifting beings live as seals in the sea but can remove their pelts to walk on land as beautiful humans. Famous tales include 'The Selkie Wife,' 'The Great Selkie of Sule Skerry,' 'Gioga's Son' from Papa Stour, and 'Donald the Seal Hunter' from Shetland. Documented by John Francis Campbell in Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860-1862)

name: Selkies Iceland
description: Selkies Iceland (Unknown). is a shapeshifter. Selkies are mythological beings from Icelandic and Norse folklore who live as seals in the sea but shed their skins to become human on land. A selkie can be forced into marriage if someone hides its s. Source: Icelandic and Norse folklore; Orkneyinga Saga

name: Selu
description: Selu, the Corn Mother, is the First Woman of Cherokee tradition and wife of Kanati the Great Hunter. By rubbing her body she produced corn and beans from her own flesh, and when her sons discovered her secret she accepted her death, instructing that her body be dragged across the field so that corn would grow where she fell.

name: Semetey
description: Semetey is the son of the great hero Manas in the Kyrgyz epic trilogy: the second generation who must reclaim his father's legacy. Raised in hiding, he grows into a powerful warrior whose righteous fury is turned against the traitors who wronged his father, seeking vengeance while protecting his people across the Manas-Semetey-Seytek cycle.

name: Sennentuntschi
description: Sennentuntschi, the 'shepherd's doll,' is a figure of Swiss Alpine legend, especially Appenzell. Lonely herders fashion a female doll from straw, rags, and wood during the summer on the alps; it comes to life and turns on its creators, often with gruesome violence. The tale works as a moral warning against lust and the mistreatment of women and is among the best-known Alp legends.

name: Sennentuntschi
description: Sennentuntschi, the Alpine shepherd's doll, is best documented in the Swiss Alps, especially Appenzell, where lonely herders build a figure from straw, rags, and wood and it comes to life to punish their sins. Western Austrian variants (Vorarlberg, Tyrol) carry the same motif. The story warns against lust and the objectification of women; this entry is a regional variant of the Swiss legend.

name: Sentient Candle Denmark
description: Sentient Candle Denmark (Unknown). is a object. The Tallow Candle is a sentient candle from a Danish fairy tale that learns its purpose of bringing light to others.. Source: Danish folklore — sentient objects documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Sentient Shadow (Skyggen)
description: Skyggen (The Shadow) is a literary character from Andersen's 1847 fairy tale 'The Shadow,' where a learned man's shadow detaches, gains sentience, and usurps his life. Inspired by Chamisso's 'Peter Schlemihl' (1814). No Danish folk tradition attests sentient shadows as independent beings. The input record misattributes a literary tale to oral folklore.

name: Seri Gumum (Dragon of Tasik Chini)
description: Seri Gumum is a legendary dragon (naga) said to dwell in Tasik Chini in Pahang, Malaysia. According to Orang Asli tradition, a beautiful princess was transformed into a serpentine guardian of the lake's mystical waters. Local folklore holds that Seri Gumum protects the lake, and that harming its environment invokes the dragon's wrath.

name: Serpan
description: Serpan is a Seychellois serpent spirit from Creole oral tradition, capable of shapeshifting into pearl necklaces or children. Associated with forest magic and the supernatural world. Limited English documentation; primarily in Seychellois Creole folklore collections. May relate to Indian Ocean 'Naga' serpent traditions and Malagasy fanahy (ancestor spirits).

name: Set (God of Chaos and Storms)
description: Set is the Egyptian god of chaos, storms, violence, and the desert. He murdered his brother Osiris out of jealousy and fought his nephew Horus for the throne of Egypt for 80 years. Depicted as a mysterious animal with a curved snout (the Set animal), he was associated with the barren desert, foreign lands, and upheaval. Despite being a god of chaos, Set was not purely evil in Egyptian thought; snip he served a necessary role. He stood at the prow of Ra's solar barque each night, using his spear to defeat the chaos serpent Apophis. During certain periods, especially under the Hyksos and Ramesside pharaohs, Set was honored as a major deity. Later, after the Persian conquest, he was demonized and associated with evil

name: Seven Bison
description: Seven Bison are sacred spirit animals in Crow mythology who fought against the monster Bones Together. After breaking their legs against Bones Together's impenetrable bone armor, they were healed through the first Sweat Lodge ceremony performed by their human companion. After this victory and healing, the Creator raised the Seven Bison into the sky to become the Big Dipper constellation, where they can be seen eternally following the seasons. They represent sacrifice, healing, and the celestial connection between earth and sky

name: Seven Rams
description: Seven Rams are magnificent spirit animals in Crow mythology. A Crow man of immense ability and power once encountered them in the mountains. Confident in his own strength, he thought he could overpower them. But the Seven Rams taught him humility—despite his great power, the man learned he must respect the Sweat Lodge and its ceremonies, for the lodge's power was greater than any individual's. The Rams demonstrated that true strength comes from spiritual purity and connection to the Creator, not from physical prowess

name: Seven Sisters
description: The Seven Sisters is a widespread Aboriginal Australian Dreaming story found across many language groups. The story tells of seven sisters who fled across the land and into the sky to escape a persistent pursuer, often a man named Wurrurrumbi or a hunter who wanted to take one of the sisters as his wife. As they fled, the sisters created landmarks, waterholes, and important sites across the Australian landscape. Finally they leaped into the sky, becoming the Pleiades star cluster. The pursuing man became the star Orion or the Moon, still chasing them across the heavens. In different regional versions, the sisters are associated with the arrival of the monsoon season or with ceremonies for girls' initiation. The story encodes practical knowledge about seasonal changes and the movements of celestial bodies

name: SGaana (Supernatural Killer Whale)
description: SGaana are the powerful supernatural killer whales of Haida mythology, considered the most powerful of the undersea beings. They can transform into human form and own houses, territories, and crests just like human chiefs. The SGaana live in magnificent underwater villages with houses made of copper and abalone shell. Those who drown do not truly die but are taken to live among the SGaana in the undersea kingdom, where they may acquire great supernatural power and wealth. The SGaana are the guardians of the sea and control the wealth of the ocean

name: Sgaana Supernatural Killer Whale Haida
description: Sgaana, in Haida belief, are the supernatural beings of the sea, and the killer whale is their visible form in this world. Chiefs among the undersea people, the killer whales live in great houses beneath the ocean, rule the sea creatures, and can take human shape. The word and image figure in Haida crests and in Bill Reid's sculpture Skaana.

name: Shade (Olmec)
description: Not independently attested as a 'shade' or vengeful ghost of Olmec folklore. The Olmec left no textual record of a haunting water-spirit, and scholars identify only a small pantheon of Olmec supernaturals, including the Maize God and a rain/were-jaguar figure. The burial-site and ruin-haunting traits resemble generic ghost templates rather than anything documented for the Olmec civilization.

name: Shade (Olmec)
description: Not independently attested in Colombia. The Olmecs were a Mesoamerican civilization (Veracruz/Tabasco, Mexico, 1400-400 BCE), not Colombian. Colombia's pre-Hispanic cultures include Muisca, Quimbaya, Tairona, San Agustín. 'Shade' as a ghost type is European; no Olmec ghost tradition exists in Colombia.

name: Shade (Olmec)
description: Not independently attested as a USA or North American being. The Olmec were an ancient Mesoamerican civilization of the Gulf Coast of Mexico, and no specific 'Shade' spirit is documented among them; the record's burial-site and battlefield habitat tags are template filler.

name: Shadhavar
description: The Shadhavar is a legendary antelope-like creature from medieval Muslim bestiaries, thought to have originated in what is now Iraq. It resembles a gazelle or unicorn with a single hollow horn containing 42 hollow branches (72 in some versions, 74 in Flaubert's account). When wind passes through these flute-like cavities, the horn produces enchanting melodies so beautiful that all animals gather to listen. When played from the opposite side, the music turns into a mournful dirge that causes deep melancholy. In some stories, the Shadhavar stands six feet tall but appears gaunt, with dark patches on its face that resemble dripping tears. Al-Qazwini described it as native to the country of Rum (Byzantium), while al-Damiri and al-Mustawfi added embellishments, with the latter mistakenly calling it a carnivore

name: Shahmaran
description: Shahmaran (from Persian Shah-i-Maran, 'King of Snakes') is a mythical half-woman, half-snake creature revered in Azerbaijani, Turkish, and Kurdish folklore. She is the immortal queen of all serpents, possessing profound wisdom and magical healing powers. According to widespread legend, Shahmaran dwells in an underground realm beneath the ancient city of Tarsus, where intelligent and compassionate serpents live in peace. In Azerbaijani variants, her legend is known in Nakhchivan, Lankaran, and along the Araz River basin. The most famous tale tells of Cəmşab, a poor woodcutter who discovered Shahmaran's underground kingdom and lived with her for years, learning her secrets. After betraying her location to a sick king, Shahmaran was killed but arranged that her killer would die and her faithful friend would gain all the world's medical wisdom, becoming a legendary healer akin to Luqman

name: Shahmaran
description: Shahmaran ('King of Snakes') is a mythical half-woman, half-snake being revered in Azerbaijani, Turkish and Kurdish folklore: the immortal queen of serpents, keeper of profound wisdom and healing power. In Azerbaijani variants the legend is known in Nakhchivan, Lankaran and the Araz River basin. The tale of Cəmşab recounts how her wisdom passed to a legendary healer.

name: Shahmaran (Kurdish Serpent Queen of Wisdom)
description: Shahmaran is a legendary half-woman, half-serpent figure in Kurdish, Turkish, Persian, and Mesopotamian folklore. The name means 'King of the Serpents' in Persian. According to legend, a young man named Camsab accidentally discovered the underground realm of the serpents, where Shahmaran (the beautiful serpent queen) ruled. She shared her wisdom with him. When Camsab was forced to reveal her location to a tyrannical vizier, Shahmaran accepted her fate. She told Camsab that bathing in her boiled flesh would grant immortality to the vizier, but the first sip would kill him. Camsab tricked the vizier, who drank first and died. Camsab bathed and became immortal. Her spirit lives in the city of Tarsus and in Kurdish cities like Mardin and Diyarbakır. Shahmaran is a symbol of hidden wisdom, secret knowledge, and female power

name: Shaitan (Iblis, the Devil in Islam)
description: Shaitan (Ash-Shaytan), also known as Iblis, is the leader of the devils (shayatin) in Islamic theology. Originally a devout jinn created from smokeless fire, Iblis was elevated to a high station among the angels due to his piety. When God commanded all beings to bow to Adam, Iblis refused out of pride, arguing that he was created from fire while Adam was from mere clay. For this defiance, he was cast out of heaven but granted respite until the Day of Judgment, during which he vowed to lead humanity astray. He whispers temptation (waswasa) into human hearts and commands legions of shayatin (evil jinn). Unlike the Christian Satan, Iblis is not a fallen angel but a jinn with free will who chose disobedience

name: Shakuru
description: Shakuru is the Sun god in Pawnee mythology, one of the last of all gods placed in the heavens by Tirawa. Along with Pah (the Moon), Shakuru is of relatively minor standing in Skidi Pawnee spirituality compared to the more prominent star gods. The Sun and Moon produced a son, a boy who was placed on Earth to be the ancestor of the Pawnee people. Shakuru is associated with warmth, light, and the daily cycle. In Pawnee earth lodge construction, the door faces east to welcome the rising sun, and the smoke hole is aligned to celestial bodies

name: Shalako
description: The Shalako are tall, ten-foot kachina messengers of the Zuni, beings of great spiritual power who appear each winter. During the Shalako ceremony, six Shalako—each the horned, feathered impersonation of a rain-bringing spirit—visit the newly built ceremonial houses, blessing the homes and the people.

name: Shaman
description: Shamans are ritual practitioners, not spirits: among the Tlingit the shaman (íx̲t) gained power from spirit helpers to heal, find lost souls and combat witchcraft; among the Inuit the angakkuq serves the community and speaks with the sea mother Sedna. The record uses 'Shaman' as a generic spirit entry; the genuine figure is the human medicine person of each nation's tradition.

name: Shaman
description: Shamans are ritual practitioners, not spirits: among the Tlingit the shaman (íx̲t) gained power from spirit helpers to heal, find lost souls and combat witchcraft; among the Inuit the angakkuq serves the community and speaks with the sea mother Sedna. The record uses 'Shaman' as a generic spirit entry; the genuine figure is the human medicine person of each nation's tradition.

name: Shango
description: Shango is the Yoruba orisha of thunder, lightning, fire, virility, dance, and justice. Originally the third Alaafin (king) of Oyo, Shango was deified after death and ascended to heaven. He is the patron of twins (Ibeji) and the owner of the double-headed battle axe (oshe), which represents swift divine justice. Shango hurls thunderstones to earth to punish wrongdoers and is known for his fiery temper, powerful drumming, and mastery of the bata drum. His three wives are Oshun, Oba, and Oya. His sacred colors are red and white

name: Shape-shifting Demon
description: The Shape-shifting Demon is a malevolent entity in Comanche creation mythology. It formed in the shadows, envious of the powerful Comanche people created by the Great Spirit. It tormented the Comanche by taking many forms. The Great Spirit cast the demon into a bottomless pit, but before falling, the demon shattered into countless pieces that took refuge in the fangs and stingers of rattlesnakes, scorpions, and spiders, continuing to harm people to this day. This explains the origin of venomous creatures and the existence of evil in the world

name: Sheikh of the Nile (Nile River Spirit)
description: The Sheikh of the Nile is a protective river spirit in Egyptian folk belief, a powerful guardian who inhabits the Nile River. He is a wali (saint) who oversees the river's bounty and dangers, controlling the annual flood, protecting fishermen and sailors, and punishing those who pollute or disrespect the Nile. The figure blends pre-Islamic Nilotic worship with Islamic saint veneration. The Offering of the Bride (Arusa al-Nil) ceremony, an annual ritual, was historically performed to appease him by throwing a decorated doll into the river. This tradition dates back to pharaonic times when a sacrificial offering was made to the Nile's spirit. He is both feared and revered by river communities

name: Shenlha Okar
description: Shenlha Ökar ('Wisdom gshen of white light,' also Shiwa Ökar) is the foremost deity of the Yungdrung Bon tradition of Tibet, counted among the Four Transcendent Lords. Creator of the world with the nine cosmic gods and sambhogakaya emanation of the founder Tonpa Shenrab Miwoche, he embodies supreme compassion, omniscience, and protective guidance in Bon.

name: Shetani
description: Shetani (Swahili, from Arabic shaytan) are malevolent spirits of East African popular belief (Tanzania, Kenya, Mozambique), especially among the Makonde. They appear as distorted, asymmetrical human-animal hybrids—cyclopic, one-limbed, exaggerated orifices. Makonde carve shetani in ebony/blackwood; artist George Lilanga (1934–2005) gained fame for shetani sculptures.

name: Shetani (Spirit Carvings)
description: Shetani (singular and plural in English, mashetani in Swahili) are spirits of East African mythology prevalent in Mozambique, particularly among the Makonde people of the northern Cabo Delgado province. These are mostly malevolent entities that manifest in a bewildering variety of forms with different powers and attributes. Physically, shetani of various types appear as distorted human and animal figures, often with exaggerated features, multiple limbs, or hybrid forms combining human and animal characteristics. What makes Mozambique's shetani tradition particularly distinctive is the extraordinary wood carving tradition that depicts them. Makonde carvers are world-renowned for their intricate representations of shetani in ebony and other hardwoods, creating art that is both aesthetically powerful and spiritually significant. The shetani are believed to inhabit remote forests, baobab trees, caves, and abandoned places. Encounters with shetani are reported cyclically, with specific 'panic' periods generating widespread fear. The word shetani derives from the Arabic shaitan (devil), reflecting the fusion of Islamic and indigenous Bantu spirit beliefs

name: Shichhid
description: Shichhid (or Chichid) is a Himalayan nature spirit in Uttarakhand/Arunachal folklore — smaller, benign Yeti variant inhabiting rhododendron forests. Local names vary by tribe (Monpa, Sherdukpen, Bhotiya). Described as hairy, forest-dwelling, protective of flora/fauna. Not a major deity but a local forest spirit. Documented in Himalayan ethnographies and tribal oral narratives.

name: Shidaidaka
description: Shidaidaka (次第高) is a yōkai reported in Shimane Prefecture and the Chūgoku region of Japan that grows taller and taller the longer a person looks up at it, looming ever higher over the viewer. The folk remedy is to look at it between one's legs, which either reveals it as small and harmless or makes it vanish. It is a classic yōkai that preys on human perception.

name: Shiktur (Erlik)
description: Not independently attested as a distinct demon of Buryat folklore. No source confirms a deceiver called 'Shiktur' associated with Erlik; Buryat tradition knows Erlik (Erlen) as the underworld judge, but no 'Shiktur' appears in published mythology. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Shir (or Sheed)
description: Shir (or Sheed) is the Armenian mythical lion — a giant golden or dusty-brown lion with glowing eyes, often depicted with a solar motif or crown. It guards sacred places in the Armenian highlands, tests human courage, and can be tamed by heroes. Fierce when threatened, it represents strength and nobility. The lion appears on Armenia's coat of arms. The name derives from Persian šīr ('lion').

name: Shiva
description: Shiva (Mahadeva) is a supreme Hindu deity (Trimurti) — god of destruction, transformation, meditation, asceticism. Not a folkloric creature but a major god. Mount: Nandi; abode: Mount Kailash; attributes: third eye, trident, crescent moon, Ganga in hair. Consort: Parvati; sons: Ganesha, Kartikeya. Worshipped across India.

name: Shteli Kherkher
description: Not independently attested as a distinct nature-spirit of Afghan or Pashtun folklore. No source confirms a forest spirit named 'Shteli Kherkher' haunting Afghan woods or meadows; Pashtun lore records mountain spirits and djinn beliefs, but no figure by this name appears in ethnographic literature. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Shtojzovalle
description: Shtojzovalle, the 'moonlight dancers' of Albanian folklore, are beautiful spirit women who dance in moonlit meadows and mountain clearings, enchanting mortals with hypnotic grace. Those who join risk being led astray or bound to the otherworld, and the dancers dissolve at sunrise. They embody the allure and peril of Albanian nature spirits.

name: Shtriga
description: Albania's most feared nocturnal predator—a vampiric witch who drains the 'spiritus vitae' (breath of life) from sleeping infants. By night, she transforms into a flying insect—traditionally a moth, fly, or bee—slipping through keyholes or open windows to hover over her victims. She sucks blood and life force while they sleep, leaving them pale, weakened, and near death. The shtriga lives secretly within the community by day, appearing as an ordinary—though unsettling—elderly woman. Only she can cure those she has drained, and she does so by spitting into the victim's mouth. This paradox is central to the legend

name: Shurale
description: Shurale is the forest spirit of Tatar and Bashkir folklore: a long-fingered, ticklish being with a single horn and leathery skin who lures lone travelers into the woods and tickles them to death. Mischievous and dangerous, he was made famous by Gabdulla Tuqay's verse tale, cementing his place in Tatar national literature.

name: Shurpanakha (Rakshasi)
description: Shurpanakha ('she whose fingernails are like winnowing fans') is a rakshasi (demoness) in the Hindu epic Ramayana, sister of the Lankan king Ravana and daughter of sage Vishrava and the rakshasi Kaikeshi. Her role in the epic, though small, is pivotal — her encounter with Rama and Lakshmana in the Panchavati forest triggered the chain of events leading to Sita's abduction and the great war of Lanka. According to Valmiki's Ramayana, she was widowed when Ravana killed her husband, the Danava prince Vidyutjihva. While wandering the forests, she encountered the exiled prince Rama and became infatuated with him. When Rama and Lakshmana rejected her advances, she attacked Sita, and Lakshmana cut off her nose. Humiliated, she fled to her brother Khara and later to Ravana, whose desire to avenge her led to Sita's kidnapping. Despite her demonic nature, some versions of the epic, particularly the Kamba Ramayanam, portray her as a tragic figure driven by loneliness and love

name: Shuten-dōji
description: Leader of oni in Mt. The most powerful oni in Japan, feared as one of Japan's 'Three Great Evil Yokai' (日本三大悪妖怪) alongside Tamamo-no-Mae and Emperor Sutoku. His name 'Shuten' means 'sake drinker' - he's called the 'King of Drinking' for his legendary love of alcohol. He commanded hundreds of oni from his mountain stronghold, kidnapping young women from Kyoto to serve as his concubines or be devoured at his gruesome banquets. In the 14th-century Ōeyama Ekotoba scroll, he was identified by diviner Abe no Seimei as the culprit behind the disappearances. The Emperor commissioned Minamoto no Yorimitsu (Raikō) to defeat him—disguised as yamabushi (mountain priests), they offered demon-poison sake (jinben kidokusake) given by gods, and beheaded Shuten-dōji during a night raid. Remarkably, his severed head still lived and tried to bite Yorimitsu—only prevented by the hero wearing multiple helmets

name: Shwe Pyat
description: Not independently attested as a named nat or guardian of Burmese folklore; searches locate no spirit called 'Shwe Pyat.' 'Shwe' (gold) prefixes many real nats—Shwe Hpyin Nyidaw and Shwe Hpyin Naungdaw, the Taungbyon brothers, and Shwe Nabay—but the recorded temple treasure-guardian does not match any of them and appears to be a garbled or invented name.

name: Shwe Temperature
description: Not independently attested as a named spirit of Burmese folklore; searches locate no entity called 'Shwe Temperature,' a name with no analogue in Burmese tradition. The recorded golden guardian of temple treasures resembles the attested weikza and nat-guardian lore of pagodas, but no documented figure bears this name, which appears to be a corrupted placeholder.

name: Si'lah
description: The Si'lah (also Sila or Si'lat, plural Sa'aali) is a female shapeshifting jinn from pre-Islamic Arabian folklore, particularly associated with the Bedouin tribes of the Arabian Peninsula including modern-day Saudi Arabia. Unlike the more generic Ghul, the Si'lah is specifically female and known primarily for seduction and shapeshifting. Si'lahs are described as the most intelligent and talented shapeshifters among the jinn, able to perfectly mimic human appearance — unlike the Ghul with its telltale donkey hooves. They prefer living near water sources in remote desert areas and oases. Si'lahs are notably amorous, often seeking human mates and bearing hybrid offspring called 'Bonoo.' In pre-Islamic legend, there was said to be a tribe called Banu Si'lat descended from a human-Si'lah union. The Si'lah represents the archetype of the dangerous seductive female spirit found across world cultures. Al-Qazwini noted that wolves are natural predators of the Si'lah

name: Si'lat
description: The Si'lat is a class of female jinn in Levantine and Arab folklore, a witchlike spirit of fixed appearance, unlike the shapeshifting ghoul. Extremely treacherous, it is linked with madness, leading travellers astray in wilderness areas, and malicious interference in human affairs. Medieval Arabic demonological texts name it alongside the ghoul, the ifrit and the marid.

name: Si'lat
description: In Palestinian folklore the Si'lat is one of the most dangerous kinds of jinn: a female, witchlike spirit of fixed appearance and cunning malice, distinct from the shapeshifting ghoul. Associated with madness and with leading travellers astray in the wilderness, it cannot be reasoned with or placated and delights in causing suffering.

name: Si'lat
description: The si'lat is a shape-shifting female jinn of Palestinian and wider Arab folklore, kin to the ghoul but wickeder and unable to change her limbs. She lurks in abandoned wells, deep caves, and wasteland, appearing as a seductive woman to lure men to their ruin. Those who answer her falsely are lost, while truth-telling and invoking God may break her hold.

name: Si'luwa
description: The Si'luwa is a female water demon from Iraqi folklore that haunts rivers, streams, and caves near running water. She is a variant of the Si'lah (Sila), a type of female jinn known for shapeshifting. The Si'luwa appears as a woman covered in long hair with pendulous breasts so long she throws them over her shoulders when nursing her children, whom she carries on her back. She dwells in rivers and caves near running water, and is known to lure humans, particularly men, as lovers. Like the Si'lah, she is a skilled shapeshifter who can appear as a beautiful woman to seduce victims. In Iraqi tradition, she occupies the same role as the witch or ogress in Western fairy tales and is a common figure in cautionary tales told to children to keep them away from dangerous waters

name: Siagtut
description: The Siagtut (Siasgiut) are lost hunters of Greenland Inuit tradition who froze to death on the Arctic ice and whose souls were placed in the sky, where they now shine as the three stars of Orion's Belt. They serve as an eternal warning to hunters about the dangers of the wilderness, and travelers use the belt to keep their bearings. They can only watch, fixed forever in the night sky.

name: Sidhe (Aos Sí)
description: The supernatural race of Irish folklore - the people of the fairy mounds. The aos sí (pronounced 'ees shee') descend directly from the Tuatha Dé Danann, the divine 'People of the Goddess Danu' who ruled Ireland in pre-mortal times. According to the Lebor Gabála Érenn (Book of Invasions), when the Milesians conquered the Tuatha Dé Danann, they retreated underground into great burial mounds, hollow hills, and ancient forts—becoming the aos sí, the 'hidden people.' The Otherworld (Tir na nÓg, 'Land of Youth') is accessible through the sídhe—ancient burial mounds, passage tombs like Brú na Bóinne, ringforts, often guarded by sacred hawthorn or oak trees

name: Sieidi Spirit
description: Sieidi (also seita) spirits are the spiritual forces dwelling in unusual rock formations, stones, or landscape features considered sacred in Sami religion. Each family or clan had its local sieidi — a naturally shaped stone or rock formation that was the dwelling place of a spirit with power over local animals, fish, and birds. Offerings of reindeer meat, antlers, horns, fish, and metal objects were made at these sites for hunting luck, protection, and general prosperity. Some sieidis were so holy that one had to approach them on hands and knees. In Inari, Finland, there were 17 known seita sites. The sieidi was not itself a god but a place where spiritual power resided; the spirit inhabiting it was a form of háldi. Sieidis were systematically destroyed by Christian missionaries, and shaman drums were burned. Despite this, offerings are still occasionally made at known sieidi sites, showing the persistence of Sami spiritual traditions

name: Sielulintu
description: The Sielulintu is not a bird of flesh and bone, but a luminous projection of the human psyche. It is the ethereal vessel that carries the spark of consciousness from the void into the womb at birth, and guides the exhausted spirit back to Tuonela upon the final breath. To see one's own Sielulintu is an omen of profound transition, often appearing as a shimmering, translucent raptor that weaves through the aurora borealis, singing a melody that resonates with the frequency of the soul's deepest longing

name: Sigbin
description: The sigbin is a creature of Visayan folklore, a hornless, dog-like beast with oversized hind legs and enormous flapping ears that walks backwards with its head between its legs. It emerges during Holy Week to suck blood through shadows and is said to hunt children for their hearts; it is tied to the darker arts of the usar witch tradition.

name: Siguanaba
description: La Siguanaba is one of the most famous figures in Salvadoran folklore — a shapeshifting spirit that appears as a beautiful long-haired woman from behind but reveals the face of a horse or skull when she turns around. According to Salvadoran legend, she was originally Sihuehuet (Beautiful Woman), a peasant girl who used her charms and witchcraft to marry Yeisun, son of Tláloc. After her husband went to war, she had affairs and gave birth to Cipitio. She tried to poison her husband to claim the throne for her lover, but the plan backfired, transforming him into a giant monster. The god Teotl cursed her to wander eternally as the Siguanaba — beautiful at first sight but hideous upon approach. She now appears to unfaithful men, luring them to isolated gorges before revealing her true terrifying face. She is most often seen near rivers, washing clothes or bathing, always searching for her son Cipitio

name: Sihuanaba
description: La Sihuanaba (Siguanaba), 'beautiful woman' in Nahuatl-derived tradition, is a ghost-woman of Guatemalan and Central American folklore. Behind, she seems a lovely long-haired maiden, but turns a horse-like or skull face when approached. She lures unfaithful men to cliffs and rivers, punishing infidelity. Known across El Salvador, Honduras, and Guatemala; a cross or prayer counters her.

name: Sikakokuh's spirit dog
description: In the Hopi story told by Harold Courlander, the boy Sikakokuh owns an extraordinary hunting dog that is no ordinary animal: it tracks game without fail, warns its master of danger, and seems to understand human speech. The tale, 'Sikakokuh and the hunting dog,' shows the dog acting as a spirit helper and guardian, an example of the animal helpers common in Pueblo oral tradition.

name: Silver Fox
description: In Miwok creation stories Silver Fox is a wise creator being who, working with Coyote, shaped the world. Depending on the telling Silver Fox is female or male, but always the quiet, deliberate partner to Coyote's impulsiveness: together they sang and danced the earth into being. Silver Fox appears across northern and central California traditions as a culture hero and a being of the early world.

name: Silver Salmon
description: Silver Salmon (Icelandic). is a beast. A sentient, shimmering salmon that grants wishes and the ability to speak with animals. Source: Icelandic folklore

name: Simbi Spirits
description: The Simbi are powerful water and nature spirits in Kongo mythology, ancient beings existing since before humanity. They inhabit rivers, streams, sacred pools, forests, mountains, and crossroads throughout the Kongo region. They are guardians of esoteric knowledge and natural balance. Simbi take several forms: Simbi d'Maza (Water Simbi) are healers invoked for purification and fertility; Simbi dia Nkita (Land Simbi) guard forests and agriculture; Simbi Nzila (Path Simbi) protect travelers. Simbi may appear as beautiful human figures, snakes, fish, or shimmering reflections on water. Those who respect the Simbi may receive visions or healing. Those who pollute waters incur their wrath

name: Simorgh
description: Simorgh (Unknown). is a mythical-bird. The Simorgh is a benevolent mythical bird in Persian mythology, often described as a massive creature with the head of a dog and claws of a lion. She is said to possess great wisdom and nests on the T. Source: Shahnameh (Ferdowsi, 11th century); The Conference of the Birds (Attar, 12th century)

name: Simurg (Zümrüd)
description: The Simurgh (in Turkmen tales, Zümrüd) is the giant benevolent bird of Iranian and Turkic tradition, adopted into Turkmen folklore from the Persian Simorgh. It nests on a world-tree, knows all that passes in the heavens and on earth, and in hero tales carries the protagonist across vast lands and heals wounds with its feathers.

name: Simurgh
description: Simurgh is a colossal benevolent mythical bird in Azerbaijani folklore, shared with Persian and broader Turkic mythology. This wise and ancient creature possesses profound healing powers and esoteric knowledge. The Simurgh nests atop the mythical Qaf Mountain at the edge of the world and is said to have lived so long that it witnessed the destruction of the world three times. In Azerbaijani tales, the Simurgh appears at moments of greatest despair to rescue heroes trapped in deep pits or remote mountains, carrying them to safety and imparting wisdom. Its feathers have miraculous healing properties. The Simurgh represents the harmony between nature, wisdom, and divine goodness, standing in eternal opposition to dark forces like the Divs

name: Simurgh
description: Simurgh is a colossal benevolent bird in Azerbaijani, Persian and Turkic folklore, keeper of ancient wisdom and healing power. Nesting on mythical Mount Qaf, it rescues heroes trapped in deep pits and remote mountains, carrying them to safety and imparting wisdom; its feathers have miraculous healing properties, and it stands in eternal opposition to dark forces such as the Divs.

name: Sina
description: Sina is one of the most important female figures in Samoan mythology, best known from 'Sina and the Eel,' the story that explains the origin of the coconut. Sina (also known as Hina or Ina in other Polynesian cultures) was a beautiful maiden who discovered a young eel in a pool and kept it as a pet named Tuna. The eel grew unnaturally large and followed her everywhere, eventually revealing itself as the King of Fiji in disguise. When the eel confessed his love and was killed, his head was buried at Sina's instruction, and from it grew the first coconut tree. Sina is also associated with the moon in some traditions and is a central figure in the pan-Polynesian Hina/Sina cycle

name: Singbonga (Supreme God of the Munda)
description: Singbonga is the supreme creator god of the Munda; his name means 'Sun God.' In the creation myth he set a cosmic egg afloat on a primordial sea, from which hatched Horo the tortoise and Karakom the crab. The tortoise brought earth up on its back, and when the land proved too soft, a great spider's web solidified it. He then made the first humans, sun, moon, and stars.

name: Singh Dhan
description: Singh Dhan (Golden Lion/Deer) appears in Rajasthani folk tales as a divine golden deer granting wishes. Related to Hindu 'Mrigashira' motif and golden deer (Mareecha) in Ramayana that lures Rama. Rajasthani folklore includes divine animal helpers (Pabuji's mare, Tejaji's serpent). 'Singh Dhan' may be a local name for a wish-granting forest deity.

name: Singing Well Spirit
description: Not independently attested as a distinct spirit of Uzbek folklore. No source confirms a singing well-spirit prophesying fate in Khiva or Khorezm; the attested Kheyvak well legend involves the boy Shem, not a prophetic singing spirit. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Sint-Holo
description: Sint-Holo is the horned serpent of Chickasaw and Choctaw tradition, a great water serpent who dwells in rivers, lakes and springs. Dangerous to those who disrespect it, it drags careless people to watery deaths, yet it also appears as a spirit guide during fasting, bestowing power and gifts on the worthy; it is the avowed enemy of the Thunder spirits.

name: Sinti
description: Sinti is the Great Serpent of Choctaw tradition, a water monster with a panther's head and horns that dwells in rivers, lakes and whirlpools. One of the three great spirits alongside the creator and the Raven, Sinti is the dangerous being who can overturn canoes and drag people under. He is both feared and honored, with offerings made to keep his waters calm.

name: Sinti Lapitta
description: Sinti Lapitta is the great horned serpent of Choctaw tradition, a giant water snake with two horns on its head, in some accounts a panther head, that lives in the deep waters. It possesses great power and wisdom and was said to visit unusually wise young men, granting them knowledge and strength.

name: Sirdalsjøormen
description: Sirdalsjøormen is a lake serpent or sea monster said to inhabit the connected lakes of Sirdalsvannet and Lundevannet in the Sirdal valley of Sørlandet. The serpent is described as having a horse-like head, a long neck, and a dark body that creates wakes as it moves through the water. It was believed to travel between the two lakes through underground channels. Multiple witness reports have been recorded from the 1800s to modern times, with the last reported observation in November 2016. Local folklorist Berner Eikeland interviewed many informants about their sightings in the 1950s. The Sirdalsjøormen is part of a broader Norwegian tradition of inland lake serpents (like Selbusjøormen in Trøndelag and the Storsjøoddyret) adapted to Sørlandet's specific geography. The serpent was considered generally harmless unless provoked

name: Siring
description: Siring are dwarfs of Philippine lower mythology, tiny green-skinned beings with pointed ears who dwell in nunuk (banyan) trees and forest mounds. In Teduray and Bagobo tradition they watch over the land, may steal or exchange children, yet aid farmers who respect them with offerings—members of the wider class of mound-and-tree spirits of the forest.

name: Sisimito
description: The Sisimito is a bipedal gorilla-like cryptid from Belizean and Honduran folklore, often called the Mexican Bigfoot. It is described as large, covered in black or dark brown fur, with four fingers on each hand and no thumbs, ape-like facial features, and backward-facing feet with no knees. The Garifuna call it Sismidu, and the name derives from the Nahuatl word Tzitzimitl. The Sisimito is said to kidnap human women and feast on humans, though it also eats wild berries and raw meat. It is afraid of water and dogs, and is said to be outsmarted by its lack of intelligence. In Belizean belief, if a man looks it in the eyes and escapes, he will die within a month; snip if a woman does the same, her life will be prolonged

name: Sisimito
description: The Sisimito is a cryptid from Panamanian and Central American folklore, described as a bipedal gorilla-like humanoid with long unkempt fur and a human-like head. In Panama, the creature is known among the Ngäbe and Kuna indigenous peoples of the Darién Gap and the dense forests of western Panama. The Sisimito is a guardian of the deep forest, often associated with the protection of sacred lands and ancestral territories. Legends depict it as shy but dangerous when provoked. Across the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca, elders tell stories of the Sisimito as a warning against venturing too deep into the wilderness alone. The Kuna people of the San Blas islands also have similar tales

name: Sisiutl
description: The Sisiutl is the double-headed sea serpent of the Kwakwaka'wakw and neighboring Northwest Coast peoples, with a serpent head at each end of its body and a human-like face at the centre, all three horned. Seeing it means death to the unprepared, but a warrior who faces it may gain superhuman strength and armor from its blood and hide. Its image guards houses, canoes and warriors.

name: Sisiutl (Double-Headed Sea Serpent)
description: Sisiutl is a supernatural sea serpent of the Kwakwaka'wakw, usually shown as a double-headed snake with two horned serpent heads flanking a central human face, its body marked with crescents. Its glance can turn a person to stone, yet it also grants protective power, and can transform into an invincible war canoe or a warrior's magic belt.

name: Sisiutl Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Sisiutl is the double-headed sea serpent of the Kwakwaka'wakw, a fearsome supernatural creature whose glance can kill or turn an adversary to stone. It can become an invincible war canoe or a magic belt granting strength, its blood gives warriors invincibility, and it is one of the highest-ranking inherited crests of the winter ceremonial.

name: Siv Yis (Shee Yee — First Hmong Shaman)
description: Siv Yis (also spelled Shee Yee or Siv Yig) is the legendary first shaman in Hmong mythology who received shamanic power from the spirit world and taught it to humanity. According to the Hmong creation myth, in ancient times the evil spirit Ntxwj Nyog (Ndu Nyong) brought sickness and death to humanity. The high god Yawm Saub (Yer Shau) sent Siv Yis down to earth to combat Ntxwj Nyog and retrieve stolen souls. Siv Yis learned the sacred rituals, chants, and healing practices from the spirits — how to beat the drum to call spirits, swing the rattle bells (nyiaj cuam) to open gates between worlds, and sacrifice animals to pay the spirit debt. He successfully healed the sick and retrieved lost souls. During a final battle with Ntxwj Nyog, the evil spirit tricked Siv Yis into eating his own son's soul. In grief, Siv Yis left the human world, but before departing, he scattered his shamanic tools across the earth, declaring they would work for those who followed his ways. Today, Hmong shamans call themselves Siv Yis when in trance, channeling his power

name: Själens port
description: Själens port (Soul Door/Gate) is not a spirit but a Swedish folk belief concept: the soul can leave the body during deep sleep, illness, or trance, traveling to other places or meeting the dead. If the body is moved while the soul is away, the person dies. Documented by Ebbe Schön as a framework for dreams, sleep paralysis, and near-death experiences. A belief, not a being.

name: Sjöjungfru
description: Sjöjungfru (Lake Maid) is a Swedish freshwater spirit, a beautiful woman with long wet hair who dwells in deep lakes. She emerges to sing, can grant fishing luck or cause drownings, and may form relationships with land-dwellers. Distinct from the marine havsfrú (Sea Lady) and the more dangerous sjörå. Documented in Swedish folklore collections and place-name legends. The term means 'lake-lady.'

name: Sjöorm
description: The Sjöorm is the general classification for the Great Sea Serpents that haunt the lakes and coasts of Sweden. While the Storsjöodjuret is a specific instance, the Sjöorm is a species of mythical beast characterized by its undulating movement and immense length. These creatures are seen as the 'spirits of the water's flow,' often appearing as a series of humps breaking the surface of the water. They are symbols of the mysteries that remain hidden beneath the mirror-like surface of Sweden's thousands of lakes, reminding the populace that the water is never truly empty

name: Sjörået
description: Sjörået (Lake Ruler) is a powerful Swedish freshwater spirit, guardian of lakes and tarns. Beautiful from the front with long dark hair, but with a hollow back or fish tail. Grants fishing luck for offerings; hangs laundry as storm warning. Unlike Näcken, she does not lure to drown — drownings are punishment for disrespect. Term means 'lake-ruler' (sjö = lake, rå = ruler/warden).

name: Sjødraug
description: Sjødraug (sea-draug) is the Norwegian coastal variant of the draug - the ghost of a drowned fisherman or sailor who returns from the sea. Unlike the inland haugbúi (mound-dweller), the sjødraug is specifically a sea spirit associated with drowning, shipwrecks, and coastal tragedy. The sjødraug appears as a figure with seaweed (tangvase) instead of a head, sitting in half a boat with tattered sails. Seeing or hearing the sjødraug foretells drowning or death at sea. He can also appear as a half-boat or as a stone with seaweed attached (tangstein), which superstitious fishermen would refuse to take as ballast. The sjødraug wails mournfully before a storm and laughs hideously when someone is about to drown. Most stories come from Northern Norway (Nord-Norge) and the coastal islands

name: Skadegamutc
description: Skadegamutc is the ghost-witch of Wabanaki (Abenaki) tradition, the malevolent spirit of a sorcerer who died unquiet. It can change its shape, appearing as a human, a shadow, or an animal, and drifts along forest paths or into villages after sunset, watching unseen. It represents dangerous spiritual power and the warning against misuse of magic.

name: Skan
description: Skan (Taku Skanskan) is the sky spirit and supreme judge in Lakota cosmology as recorded by James R. Walker. Born of the waters that Inyan could not hold, Skan sets motion and law for all things, arbitrates among the four primary Wakan Tanka spirits, and judges souls after death. He is associated with the blue of the sky.

name: Skarsfjellgubben
description: Skarsfjellgubben (also known as Sømnakongen, the King of Sømna) is an old troll king from Nordland folklore who saved Lekamøya from Hestmannen's attack.
