When Hestmannen shot an arrow at Lekamøya as she fled, Skarsfjellgubben threw his broad-brimmed hat into the path of the arrow. The arrow pierced the hat, creating a massive hole through it. Skarsfjellgubben, his hat, the arrow, and Lekamøya all turned to stone at sunrise. The hat became Torghatten — the famous mountain with a distinctive hole through it on Torget island near Brønnøysund. The hole is 160 meters long, 35 meters high, and 20 meters wide. Torghatten is one of Norway's most famous natural landmarks. Skarsfjellgubben represents wisdom and protective elder power in the Seven Sisters legend cycle. His quick thinking saved Lekamøya

name: Skeleton Spirit
description: Skeleton Spirit is a spirit being from Arapaho folklore featured in the story of The Lame Warrior and the Skeleton. A lame Arapaho warrior, unable to fight, was left behind when his village moved. A skeleton approached him and offered to carry him into battle if the warrior would promise to give the skeleton a proper burial afterward. The skeleton carried the warrior to victory, and the warrior performed the burial rites as promised. The skeleton's spirit appeared in a dream, granting the warrior the gift of healing. He became a powerful medicine man. The story teaches the importance of honoring promises and respecting the dead

name: Skeljaskrímsli
description: Skeljaskrímsli (Shell Monster) is a quadrupedal coastal monster from Icelandic folklore, about the size of a bull calf or large horse. Its entire body is covered in a thick coat of shells that rattle loudly as it walks. The creature emits a powerful stench, has reddish eyes, and a phosphorescent glow from its mouth. It has a long tail with a lump or hook at the end. Its blood is toxic. Skeljaskrímsli hauls onto shore on moonless winter nights, attracted to light. It leaves deep gouges in farmhouse doors and walls where it tries to enter. Despite its terrifying appearance, the skeljaskrímsli is not always aggressive — it seems more curious than predatory. However, its toxic blood and powerful stench make it dangerous to approach. The creature is found in Icelandic folklore collections and represents the deep-seated fear of strange coastal creatures washing ashore

name: Skeljungur
description: Skeljungur (Shell-Whale) is a unique illhveli (evil whale) in Icelandic folklore distinguished by being covered in rattling shells and being the only edible wicked whale. Skeljungur is 20-45 meters long, fat-bodied, with short flippers and no dorsal fin. Its body is covered with shells that rattle loudly as it moves — the sound gives it away. It sleeps vertically with its head above water. The shells make it constantly itchy, so it rubs its head against coastal rocks. Skeljungur actively blocks ships and flips them with its fins. Despite being classified as an illhveli (evil whale), its flesh was considered edible, though very dangerous to obtain. Skeljungur has a particular hatred for the sound of iron being filed — it will beach itself to escape the noise, making it the only illhveli that can be driven ashore. Described in Konungs skuggsjá and later Icelandic folk tradition

name: Skeppsrå
description: Skeppsrået (the ship spirit) is the guardian spirit of a vessel in Swedish maritime folklore, analogous to the Tomte on land. Every ship had its Skeppsrå — a small, tomte-like figure who protected the vessel and crew from storms, pirates, and disasters. When a new ship was built, a small hidden compartment or 'rå-rum' (spirit room) was sometimes constructed belowdecks as his dwelling. The Skeppsrå ensured good catches for fishing boats and safe passages for merchant vessels. He demanded respect — swearing on board, poor seamanship, or neglecting the ship's maintenance would anger him, causing lost gear, fouled lines, or worse. A ship whose Skeppsrå had abandoned it was considered doomed; any experienced sailor would refuse to board her

name: Skiapod
description: Skiapodes ('Shadow-Foots') are the one-legged, one-footed people of Greek and Roman paradoxography, placed in the scorched interior of Ethiopia or India. Their single oversized foot is used as a sun-shade when they lie on their backs, leg raised. Ctesias' account, relayed by Pliny (Natural History 7.23), made them a staple of medieval bestiaries, most famously the 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle.

name: Skifting
description: Skiftingen (also called Bytting) is the Danish changeling — a troll or Bjergfolk infant secretly exchanged for a human baby. The changeling is ugly, sickly, never grows, and has an enormous appetite. It cries constantly but also shows unnaturally adult intelligence — it may speak in rhymes, comment on ancient events, or demonstrate knowledge no infant should possess. The most famous Danish changeling story involves a child who, when the mother brewed beer in an eggshell to test it, exclaimed: 'I have seen Rold Forest cut down twice and grow up thrice, but never saw such a long brewing!' giving itself away. The changeling could be forced to leave by: brewing in an eggshell, threatening to slaughter a pig at an unusual hour, or beating the child with a birch rod on Ash Wednesday. The Bjergfolk mother would then return the human child

name: Skimina (Granddaughter of Alhkw'ntam)
description: Skimina is the granddaughter of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola) creator Alhkw'ntam, who lives in the upper world. In the story of how Raven gave light to the world, she unknowingly holds the transforming Raven as he changes into a baby, and her care of the crying child lets him reach the box where the sun was hidden.

name: Skinwalker (Yee Naaldlooshii)
description: Yee naaldlooshii, 'by means of it, it goes on all fours,' is the Navajo term for a harmful witch who can turn into, possess, or disguise itself as an animal, typically by wearing the animal's skin. Skinwalkers are one kind of 'ánti'įhnii, a person who practices evil, the antithesis of Navajo healing values, and are blamed for illness, death and misfortune.

name: Skitters (Merry Dancers)
description: The Skitters (Na Fir Chlis, 'the Nimble Men') are the fairy dancers of the Aurora Borealis in Scottish Gaelic tradition. Seen as multicolored lights or dancing warrior figures in the northern sky, their lively dancing foretells fair weather; snip wild, rapid movement is an ill omen. They are one of three hosts of fallen angels: fairies on land, Blue Men in the sea, and Nimble Men in the sky.

name: Sklavos
description: Not independently attested in documented Albanian folklore or academic sources. No reference describes an Albanian ghost 'Sklavos,' a shrouded figure haunting the living until buried; searches return only Greek σκλάβος ('slave') and the Albanian kukudh, a different undead being. The recorded traits resemble general Balkan burial beliefs and appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Skoffín
description: Skoffín is a deadly hybrid creature in Icelandic folklore, born from the mating of a male Arctic fox and a female tabby cat. The skoffín is partially hairless with bald patches and possesses a deadly gaze — everything it looks at dies instantly. Animals, humans, and even plants wither under its stare. The skoffín changes color with the seasons like the Arctic fox: white in winter, brown in summer. It can only be killed with silver bullets or by showing it its own reflection in a mirror — causing it to die from its own gaze. The creature was considered extremely rare but devastating when encountered. One famous story tells of a skoffín that killed all livestock on a farm before the farmer trapped it and showed it its reflection in a polished silver plate. The skoffín tradition is unique to Iceland and shows how the Arctic environment shaped folklore about hybrid animals

name: Skogmannen
description: Skogmannen (the forest man) is the rare male counterpart to the Skogsrå in Swedish folklore, found primarily in Skåne and adjacent regions. Unlike the female Skogsrå, who is known for luring men, Skogmannen targets women who wander alone in the forest. He appears as a handsome, well-dressed man — often a hunter or a gentleman in green — who approaches solitary women and charms them, only to reveal his non-human nature. His most telling feature is a horse's hoof instead of one foot, a detail he tries to hide. Unlike the hollow-backed Skogsrå, Skogmannen appears fully human at first glance. He is less common in Swedish folklore than the Skogsrå, with most documented sightings concentrated in southeastern Skåne. The belief likely reflects cross-influence from Danish folklore,

name: Skogsfru
description: Skogsfru (Forest Wife/Woman) is a Swedish forest spirit, often another name for Huldra or Skogsrå. Beautiful woman with a cow's or fox's tail, hollow back, dwelling in deep forests. Protects game animals, tests hunters (the 'forest test'), seduces lone men. The name means 'forest-wife' (skog = forest, fru = wife/lady). Regionally conflated with Skogsrå and Huldra. Documented in Swedish folklore.

name: Skogsrå
description: Skogsrå is the paramount Swedish forest spirit, guardian of wildlife and forest. Stunning woman from front, hollow rotting back (or cow/fox tail), sometimes with animal legs. Administers the 'forest test' to hunters: respect brings luck, disrespect brings ruin. Can bear children with humans (often tragic). Embodies sustainable hunting ethics. Term means 'forest-ruler' (skog = forest, rå = ruler).

name: Skookum
description: Skookum, from Chinook Jargon meaning 'strong' or 'powerful,' names the mountain giants and evil spirits of Pacific Northwest tradition. In Chinook folklore the wild man of the woods, called Boqs, Siatco, Sasquatch or Skookum, is a large, hairy forest being, usually a dangerous man-eater though sometimes benign.

name: Skookum
description: Skookum, from Chinook Jargon meaning 'strong' or 'powerful,' names the mountain giants and evil spirits of Pacific Northwest tradition. In Chinook folklore the wild man of the woods, called Boqs, Siatco, Sasquatch or Skookum, is a large, hairy forest being, usually a dangerous man-eater though sometimes benign.

name: Skotta
description: Skotta (meaning Tail) is a specific type of female ghost in Icelandic folklore named for the distinctive tail-like appearance of her headdress hanging down her back. Skotta wears the traditional Icelandic Faldbúningur headdress but backward — the long tail of the headdress hangs down her back like a tail (skott). She wears rust-red headwear, red socks, and is often described sucking her fingers or chewing on her own hair. Skotta attaches herself to specific people, families, or even entire towns, following them and causing misfortune. She is a type of afturganga (one who walks again after death) — a person who was wronged or died under unusual circumstances and returned to haunt the living. Skotta was particularly associated with the Snæfellsnes peninsula and the Westfjords. Unlike the Norwegian ghost traditions, Skotta has specific clothing identifying her as an Icelandic ghost — her backward headdress is the key feature

name: Skrzak
description: Skrzak (or skrzat) is a household spirit of Polish and West Slavic folklore, a small goblin-like being who lives in the home or its garden, brings luck and prosperity while the household is virtuous, and hides or turns spiteful when mistreated. He belongs to the wider Slavic domovoi family of hearth guardians.

name: Skrømt
description: Skrømt (plural: skrømt, from Old Norse: skrimsl meaning ghost or monster) is a general Norwegian term for supernatural apparitions, ghosts, and frightening creatures. Unlike more specific named entities, skrømt is a catch-all category for unexplained eerie phenomena - strange sounds at night, shapeless moving shadows, creepy sensations, or terrifying visions. In Norwegian folk belief, skrømt could be the ghost of a person who died badly, a malicious nature spirit, or simply a manifestation of the wild. The word appears in the compound vetter og skrømt (spirits and ghosts) as a standard phrase in Norwegian folklore studies. Particularly associated with lonely roads, crossroads, and places where violent deaths occurred

name: Skuggabaldur
description: Skuggabaldur (Shadow Baldur) is a hybrid creature in Icelandic folklore, the opposite cross of the skoffín — born from a tomcat and a vixen (female fox). Skuggabaldur has very dark fur, almost black, and sometimes possesses the same deadly gaze as the skoffín. It preys primarily on livestock. The most famous skuggabaldur story involves one that was killed by a farmer. When it was dying, the creature spoke and said: Tell the tomcat at Bollastaðir. The farmer later passed on the message at Bollastaðir farm. When he spoke the words, a tomcat attacked and killed him by biting his throat. This legend illustrates the Icelandic belief that hybrid creatures had supernatural connections and that messages from dying monsters should not be delivered. Skuggabaldur, like skoffín, is part of the uniquely Icelandic tradition of fox-cat hybrids that combines domestic and wild animal traits into supernatural creatures

name: Skunk
description: Skunk appears in Comanche trickster tales as a clever animal who often outwits Coyote. In the famous story Skunk Outwits Coyote, Skunk finds Coyote trying to catch prairie dogs by blocking their holes and waiting with his mouth open. Skunk offers to help, then instead of driving prairie dogs toward Coyote, walks up and sprays him in the face. Coyote runs away howling, and the prairie dogs escape. Skunk proves that even the cleverest schemer can be outsmarted, and that brute force does not always prevail

name: Skvader
description: The Skvader is a Swedish taxidermy hoax from 1918, created by Rudolf Granberg from a tall tale by Håkan Dahlmark (claiming an 1874 hunt). It combines a European hare (front) with a female capercaillie (back/wings). Not genuine folklore but 'fakelore' that entered local culture as a joke — now a symbol of Sundsvall/Medelpad.

name: Sky Father (Cheyenne)
description: The Cheyenne creator Maheo, also called Heammawihio, 'the one who lives above,' is the supreme being who made the world from the void, molding the earth brought by a diving duck into the land. He is a spirit without human form, rarely personified, and in some tellings he first made people immortal before changing death to its present form.

name: Sky People
description: The Sky People are the celestial beings of the upper world in Blackfoot tradition, the Sspommitapiiksi, the sacred family above the earth: Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the star children, foremost Iipisowaahs the Morning Star, who married a mortal and fathered the hero Star-Boy. Sky beings across many peoples descend to teach, marry mortals, and return to homes among the stars.

name: Sky People
description: The Sky People are the celestial beings of the upper world in Blackfoot tradition, the Sspommitapiiksi, the sacred family above the earth: Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the star children, foremost Iipisowaahs the Morning Star, who married a mortal and fathered the hero Star-Boy. Sky beings across many peoples descend to teach, marry mortals, and return to homes among the stars.

name: Sky Spirits
description: Sky Spirits are celestial beings in Arapaho mythology who inhabit the sky world. In the story of The Girl Who Climbed to the Sky, an Arapaho girl climbed a tree that grew taller and taller, carrying her into the sky world where she found a beautiful land populated by these spirits. She married a sky spirit and learned songs and ceremonies from them. Eventually a spider spun a web to lower her back to Earth, where she taught the Arapaho the sky ceremonies she had learned. Sky spirits are associated with celestial knowledge, ceremonies, and the connection between earth and sky

name: Sky Woman
description: Sky Woman (Atsi'tsaká:ion, 'Mature Flower') is the primordial mother of Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) creation. She fell from the Sky World through a hole left by an uprooted tree, landed on the back of the Great Turtle, and with a handful of mud brought up by the water animals the earth was created; her line bore the twins who shaped the world.

name: Slattenpatte
description: Slattenpatte (Saggy-Breast) is a giant elf-woman or troll-woman from Danish folklore, distinguished by her extraordinarily long breasts that she throws over her shoulders or dips into streams to nurse fish and other water creatures. Her most famous depiction is a 1668 woodcarving by Abel Schrøder under the pulpit of Vejlø Church near Næstved, where she stands as a caryatid with her breasts hanging to her knees. According to legend, she was hunted nightly by King Valdemar Atterdag and his Wild Hunt hounds. In 2010, a modern fountain sculpture of Slattenpatte was erected in Næstved town square by artist Bjørn Nørgaard, cementing her status as a unique piece of local folklore. Her name literally means 'flabby-teat' in Danish

name: Sluagh
description: The Sluagh (Sluagh na Marbh, 'host of the dead') are the unforgiven dead in Irish and Scottish Gaelic folklore. They fly in a crescent host like birds, sweeping up souls of the dying—especially those who die unshriven—and carrying them westward over the sea. They cannot cross running water or enter a house with a lighted candle.

name: Snow Queen (Snedronningen)
description: Snedronningen (The Snow Queen) is the titular antagonist of Andersen's 1844 literary fairy tale, ruler of snow bees and ice palace who freezes Kai's heart with a mirror splinter. Inspired by Andersen's unrequited love for Jenny Lind. No Danish folk tradition attests a Snow Queen as a nature spirit. The input record misattributes a literary character to oral folklore.

name: Snåsavettern
description: Not independently attested in Norwegian folklore. No scholarly or primary source documents a water-wight tradition for Snåsavatnet; the lake's genuine supernatural figure is the sea serpent Kudulla, recorded since the 1770s.

name: Sobek (Crocodile God of the Nile)
description: Sobek is the ancient Egyptian crocodile god of the Nile, fertility, military prowess, and pharaonic power. Worshipped primarily in the Faiyum region and at Kom Ombo. He was associated with the pharaoh's strength and authority, as well as the fertility brought by the annual Nile flood. Sobek has a dual nature: as a creator god emerging from the Nile's waters and as a dangerous, predatory force. In the Faiyum, he was worshipped as the supreme deity (Sobek-Ra), and in Kom Ombo he shares a temple with Horus. Sacred crocodiles were kept in temple pools, adorned with jewels, and mummified after death. After death, Sobek could be called upon for protection and healing. Sometimes identified with Set as a god of aggressive power

name: Sodani
description: Sodani is the hero of an Evenki heroic legend recorded in the scholarly series Monuments of the Folklore of the Peoples of Siberia and the Far East as 'The Brave Hero Sodani.' A bogatyr of the taiga who defends his people through strength and courage, he belongs to the Evenki tradition of heroic storytelling rather than to the divine pantheon.

name: Sogolon
description: Sogolon is the mother of Sundiata Keita and a central figure in the Epic of Sundiata. Known as the "Buffalo Woman," she was originally a mysterious and dangerous being — a buffalo that terrorized the land of Do. Two hunter brothers discovered she was a woman transformed by a curse. They captured her, and one brother married her. Sogolon was described as ugly and hunchbacked, and King Maghan Kon Fatta married her on the advice of a soothsayer who prophesied that her son would become a great king. Despite persecution by the king's first wife, Sogolon protected and raised Sundiata. Her strength, patience, and determination shaped Sundiata's character. After fleeing into exile, she pushed Sundiata to fulfill his destiny. The Mandinka saying "the child is worth no more than the mother is worth" reflects Sogolon's importance

name: Son Tinh
description: Son Tinh (Unknown). is a deity. Sơn Tinh (the Mountain God) is a deity from Vietnamese mythology who competed with Thủy Tinh (the Water God) for the hand of Princess Mỵ Nương. His victory over the annual flooding explains the monsoo. Source: Vietnamese mythology; The Legend of Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh

name: Sonangi
description: Not independently attested as a figure of Korean folklore. No source documents a 'Sonangi', a Jeju sea goddess who protects fishermen yet can sink boats. Documented Jeju sea deities include Yeongdeung Halmang, the wind-and-sea goddess honored in the February Yeongdeunggut rites, and Seolmundae Halmang, the giant creator goddess. The recorded traits likely conflate these attested figures.

name: Songa Raudhat
description: 'Songa Raudhat' appears only in a single modern online retelling of a Comorian tale about djinns and a hidden sea garden; the name is unattested in collections of Comorian oral literature. Comorian tradition does preserve djinn and sea-spirit lore, but this named figure has no documented or ethnographic record and reads as a recent invention.

name: Songtsen Gampo
description: Songtsen Gampo, 33rd king and founder of the Tibetan Empire (r. 618/629–650), is revered as the first Dharma King: he introduced Buddhism to Tibet, built the Jokhang, and, by tradition an emanation of Avalokiteshvara, subdued the demoness lying beneath the land by pinning her with 108 temples. His legend guards the Buddhist foundation of Tibetan identity.

name: Sotho Ancestral Ghosts (Matsatsi)
description: In Basotho belief of Lesotho, death is a transition to another realm where the ancestors (badimo) continue to influence the living. Most ancestors are benevolent protectors, but those who died violently, were not properly buried or bear unresolved grievances may wander as restless ghosts (matsatsi). Rituals of animal sacrifice, beer offerings and divination ensure ancestral peace and family bonds.

name: Sotnik
description: Sotnik, meaning hundredman or a Cossack officer, is not documented as a distinct werewolf figure in Ukrainian folk sources. The claim likely conflates a military rank with werewolf folklore or derives from a single local account; no real independent attestation is recorded.

name: Sotuknang
description: In Hopi creation accounts Sotuknang, nephew and helper of Tawa the Sun Spirit, arranged the universes and brought order from the first world onward. When the third world was destroyed by flood, he guided the righteous into the Fourth World through the sipapu of the Grand Canyon, and he continues as a messenger between Tawa and the people.

name: Soucouyant
description: In Antiguan and Barbudan folklore the soucouyant is a blood-sucking hag who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire to enter homes and drain the blood of her victims. A figure shared across the Caribbean, she is warded off with salt in doorways and garlic, and belief in her warns against dabbling in black magic.

name: Soucouyant
description: Soucouyant is a vampire from Trinidad and Tobago mythology. As documented by Charles Day in his 19th-century book 'Five Years in the West Indies' and referenced in the Know Your Caribbean Podcast, Vincentian tradition holds that the Soucouyant sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire. In Saint Vincent, belief in the Soucouyant is intertwined with the practice of Obeah, which remains a powerful force in Vincentian spiritual life. The creature is said to be a reclusive old woman by day who transforms at night to drain the blood of her victims. Vincentians traditionally protect their homes by placing salt in doorways and hanging garlic over entrances. The legend reinforces the importance of community surveillance and the dangers of dabbling in black magic

description: Soucouyant is a vampire from Caribbean mythology. As documented by Charles Day in his 19th-century book 'Five Years in the West Indies' and referenced in the Know Your Caribbean Podcast, Vincentian tradition holds that the Soucouyant sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire. In Saint Vincent, belief in the Soucouyant is intertwined with the practice of Obeah, which remains a powerful force in Vincentian spiritual life. The creature is said to be a reclusive old woman by day who transforms at night to drain the blood of her victims. Vincentians traditionally protect their homes by placing salt in doorways and hanging garlic over entrances. The legend reinforces the importance of community surveillance and the dangers of dabbling in black magic

name: Soucouyant
description: The soucouyant is a blood-sucking hag in Dominican folklore: an old woman by day who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire to enter homes through keyholes and drain blood. A pan-Caribbean figure, she is kept at bay with salt, garlic or scattered seeds, and belief in her is tied to the practice of dark magic.

name: Soucouyant
description: In Saint Lucian folklore the sukuyant is a blood-sucking hag who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire in search of victims, entering homes to drain their blood. A figure shared across the Caribbean, she is warded off with salt in doorways and garlic, and is linked to shape-shifting and dark magic.

name: Soucouyant
description: The soucouyant is a shape-shifting, blood-sucking hag of Vincentian folklore, documented by Charles Day in 'Five Years in the West Indies'. She sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire to drain her victims' blood. Vincentian homes are protected with salt in doorways and garlic, and belief in the soucouyant is tied to Obeah.

name: Soumaoro Kanté
description: Soumaoro Kanté (Unknown). is a spirit. Soumaoro Kante is a powerful sorcerer-king from the Epic of Sundiata, the Sosso ruler whose defeat by Sundiata Keita led to the founding of the Mali Empire.. Source: Mande oral tradition — Soumaoro Kanté is the sorcerer-king of Sosso, the antagonist in the Sundiata epic, documented in Mande griot tradition.

name: Soungoula
description: Soungoula (Seychellois Creole). is a trickster. Soungoula is the most important trickster figure in Seychellois Creole folklore, the clever hare who outwits stronger animals and teaches moral lessons.. Source: Island Hopper Guides - Seychelles Folklore; The Creole Melting Pot; Folklore.unisey.ac.sc; Seychelles Research Journal

name: South Star
description: South Star is a significant celestial deity in Pawnee mythology, ruling the land of the dead. The Pawnee believe that after death, the soul travels along the Milky Way—called the Great Medicine Road or the Path of the Dead—to reach the South Star's dominion in the southern sky. The stars in the Milky Way are the campfires of the dead, and falling stars are souls traveling to their final rest. The dead live in a world much like Earth where they hunt, feast, and dance. The South Star governs this afterlife realm and guides the souls of the deceased to their final home

name: South Wind
description: South Wind is an old man in Chinook tradition who travels north along the coast. Passing the house of a giant old woman, he caught a small whale and, against her warning, cut it crossways; the cut whale turned into a huge bird. Because of this, the Chinook have always slit salmon down the back rather than across the body.

name: Spearfinger
description: Spearfinger, Nûñ'yunu'ï or U'tlun'ta, is a cannibal witch of Cherokee tradition who roamed the mountains of eastern Tennessee and western North Carolina. An old woman armored in stone with a long, sharp forefinger, she cut out the livers of careless travelers and children; only the vulnerable spot on her palm allowed her to be slain.

name: Specter
description: Not independently attested as a named 'specter' entity in Swedish folklore. Swedish tradition has gäst (ghost of the dead), mårtensgås (harbinger), and vättar, but 'specter' is an English generic term. The record's linked stories (Yuletide specters, Fjelkinge specter) refer to gäster or spöken, not a distinct being type.

name: Sphinx
description: The Egyptian sphinx is a guardian of sacred ground, carved with the head of a king or god upon the body of a lion. From the Great Sphinx of Giza to the ram-headed criosphinxes lining temple avenues, it stood watch over tombs and processional ways. It embodies royal power, the horizon god Horemakhet, and the silent strength of the desert edge.

name: Sphinx
description: The Greek Sphinx is a winged monster with a woman's head, lion's body and serpent's tail, sent by Hera to plague Thebes; she devoured all who failed her riddle until Oedipus answered 'Man' and she destroyed herself. Where the Egyptian sphinx symbolized royal power and wisdom, the Greek sphinx embodied dangerous, riddle-guarded knowledge, haunting temple entrances and crossroads.

name: Sphinx
description: The sphinx is a composite guardian creature of Egyptian and Greek tradition, joining a human head to a lion's body. In Egypt it was a colossal, often royal image of divine kingship and solar power; in Greece it became the riddling, man-eating Sphinx of Thebes, a symbol of dangerous knowledge that only a true answer defeats. The hybrid figure recurs across the Near East and Mediterranean.

name: Spider (Maya)
description: Not independently attested as a spider trickster in Maya folklore. No Popol Vuh or ethnographic source records a spider trickster who shapeshifts or commands the wind. The spider in Maya tradition is primarily associated with weaving, as with Ix Chel (Chac Chel), the moon goddess of weaving, textiles, and the loom. The trickster-spider role belongs to figures like Anansi, not Maya myth.

name: Spider Grandmother (Spider Woman)
description: Kokyangwuti, Spider Grandmother, is the Earth Goddess and helper of Hopi tradition, partner to Tawa. She created Huzruiwuhti (Woman of Hard Substances), sealed the righteous in hollow reeds during the great flood, guided clans through their migrations, and aided heroes across many Hopi narratives.

name: Spider Guardian (Amhara)
description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Amhara (Ethiopian) tradition. The 'Spider Guardian of Amhara rainforests' appears generic fabrication. Ethiopian guardians include zar (possession cult), ayyana (like Segen), and Christian saints. Anansi the spider trickster is West African/Caribbean, not Ethiopian. No Amhara-specific spider guardian in ethnographic literature (Levine, Hamer).

name: Spider Man
description: Spider Man is a figure in Navajo tradition who, along with Spider Woman, taught the people the art of weaving in the Third World. He showed them how to shape a spindle wheel and spin cotton thread from planted cotton seeds. He established that spinning must be done toward the body to attract beautiful goods. Spider Man named the spindle "turning around with beautiful goods" while Spider Woman called it "turning around with mixed chips." He instructed that newborn girls should have spider web rub

name: Spider Spirit ( Maori)
description: Not independently attested in documented Māori folklore or academic sources. No spider spirit appears in standard Māori tradition; the closest figures are Punga, a deity associated with ugly, deformed things and ancestor of lizards and insects, and the tree fern ponga. The recorded traits appear to be a generic forest-spirit composite rather than a documented being.

name: Spider Trickster (Mauritian)
description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Mauritian folklore. Anansi the spider trickster is West African (Akan) and Caribbean—absent from Mauritian Creole tradition. Mauritian tricksters include Lougarou (werewolf, from French loup-garou) and Touni Minwi. The 'spider trickster of valleys' entry projects Anansi onto Mauritius due to African diaspora assumptions.

name: Spider Woman
description: Spider Woman is a crucial deity in Navajo tradition who lives near the Crossing of the Waters. She taught the Navajo people the art of weaving, showing them how to construct a rectangular loom frame with warp and weft. She is a wise helper who protects and guides heroes, including the Hero Twins Monster Slayer and Child of the Water during their dangerous journey to visit their father the Sun. Spider Woman protected them from the Sun's deadly tests including a sweat lodge of stone knives and poi

name: Spirit
description: Spirit (Generic). is a spirit. Non-corporeal entities that represent the essence of a person, place, or concept. Source: Comparative mythology, global oral traditions

name: Spirit Beings
description: 'Spirit Beings' is a general term, not a single attested figure: in Salish and other Northwest Coast traditions the world is inhabited by countless spirits dwelling in rocks, trees, waters and winds. These beings must be treated with respect and given offerings, and they can help or harm people depending on how they are treated. The record names no specific spirit.

name: Spirit Beings
description: 'Spirit Beings' is a general term, not a single attested figure: in Salish and other Northwest Coast traditions the world is inhabited by countless spirits dwelling in rocks, trees, waters and winds. These beings must be treated with respect and given offerings, and they can help or harm people depending on how they are treated. The record names no specific spirit.

name: Spirit Helpers
description: Spirit helpers are the benevolent tutelary beings of Hmong shamanic tradition, assisting the shaman during trance journeys and aiding humans in daily tasks and healing. Each shaman relies on personal helping spirits (neeb) gained through initiation and maintained by offerings and respect. Documented in ethnographies of Hmong spirituality, they remain a functioning part of religious life.

name: Spirit Iceland
description: Spirit Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. A guardian spirit landvaettir from Icelandic folklore protects specific places and landscapes.. Source: Icelandic folklore — general spirits documented in Icelandic folk belief.

name: Spirit of the Black Sands
description: Spirit of the Black Sands (Icelandic). is a spirit. A ghostly child who guides the kind and lures the greedy into the crashing waves of the black beaches. Source: Icelandic folklore

name: Spirits of Kerkennah (Enchanted Island)
description: Not independently attested in folklore literature. The sunken-kingdom 'Atlantis' legend of Kerkennah is a modern retelling with no traditional source, and the ghost-inhabitant framing is invented. The real Kerkennah origin stories concern the founding families, notably the Ouled Bou Ali, as studied by Katherine Platt; no sunken kingdom or island-spirit cult appears in the recorded tradition.

name: Spiritus
description: Spiritus (also called Spertus) is a Swedish folk magical creature — a 'drag-being' kept in a box or glass bottle. It was created through a dangerous ritual: one must hatch a rooster's egg or a raven's egg by keeping it in the left armpit (or sitting on it like a hen) until it hatches. The resulting creature — a lizard, large beetle, spider, or tiny skeleton — becomes the owner's servant for life. Spiritus brings wealth, finds stolen property, aids in love affairs, and performs magical tasks. In exchange, it must be fed with a drop of blood from the owner's little finger every Friday. The owner could never be without work, as Spiritus always found new tasks. If the owner died without passing Spiritus on, the creature would haunt the family

name: Splinter Foot Girl
description: Splinter Foot Girl is a miraculous culture hero in Arapaho folklore. A childless woman found a splinter embedded in her foot. To her amazement, the splinter grew and transformed into a baby girl. The girl grew rapidly and possessed supernatural abilities—she could communicate with animals and had the power to heal. She brought good fortune to her family and community, helping them find buffalo and warning them of danger. When kidnapped by a rival tribe, she used her powers to escape and return home. Her story teaches that blessings can come from unexpected places, and even something as small as a splinter can hold great potential

name: Springand-Annbjør
description: Springand-Annbjør (Running Annbjør) is a restless running spirit from Setesdal folklore in Sørlandet. She is described as a female undead or wraith that runs endlessly through the Setesdal valley, never stopping, never resting. The name Annbjør is a female name common in Setesdal, and the legend likely originated as a ghost story about a specific woman condemned to eternal running as punishment for a grave sin. Springand-Annbjør runs along the roads and paths between the farms of the valley, always at night, always alone. Those who see her say she runs with desperate speed, her feet barely touching the ground, her breath coming in ragged gasps. She cannot speak or stop. If someone tries to speak to her, she simply runs past. Seeing Springand-Annbjør was considered an omen — of death, disaster, or simply a reminder of one's own mortality. The spirit is documented in Johannes Skar's supranormal catalog in Gamalt or Setesdal

name: Sri Lanka Naga
description: Naga (serpent deities) in Sri Lankan Buddhist tradition are divine beings inhabiting rivers, lakes, temples — guardians of treasure and Dharma. Distinct from Hindu Naga but syncretized. Prominent in Mahavamsa (Naga kings of Lanka), Kelaniya Temple (Naga king Maniakkhika), Buddhist iconography (Naga guarding Buddha). Sinhala 'Naga' = cobra; revered.

name: St. Sylvester's Dragon
description: Sylvester's Dragon is a legendary dragon from Vatican and Roman Christian tradition that was defeated by Pope Sylvester I (314-335 AD). According to the Golden Legend, a massive dragon dwelled in a deep cave beneath the Roman Forum, and its poisonous breath killed thousands of Romans daily. Emperor Constantine asked Pope Sylvester to deal with the beast. Sylvester descended into the cave, recited prayers, and bound the dragon's mouth with thread, sealing it forever. The dragon is said to have been buried under the steps of the Temple of the Dioscuri, near the Roman Forum. This legend established the Pope's spiritual authority over even the most fearsome earthly powers

name: Stackalee
description: Stackalee (an alternate spelling of Stagolee/Stagger Lee) is the same legendary 'bad man' figure of African American folklore, drawn from the historical Lee Shelton. In the folk tradition, Stackalee shot Billy Lyons in a St. Louis saloon for touching his Stetson hat, was hanged for the murder, but then arrived in Hell and challenged the Devil for control of the underworld. The name 'Stackalee' is particularly associated with early folk recordings and the 'toast' narrative tradition, where long-form oral poems about Stackalee were performed in juke joints, bars, and prison yards across the American South. These toasts elevated Stackalee from a mere murderer to a mythic figure of ultimate defiance

name: Stagolee
description: Stagolee (also known as Stagger Lee, Stackolee) is the quintessential 'bad man' of African American folklore, based on the historical Lee Shelton, a St. Louis pimp who shot William 'Billy' Lyons on Christmas night 1895. In the folk tradition, Stagolee is larger than life — a man so defiant that even Hell could not hold him. After being hanged for murder, he arrived at the gates of Hell still wearing his Stetson hat and carrying his .44 pistol, challenged the Devil himself, kicked him off his throne, and took over the running of Hell. The ballads and 'toasts' about Stagolee became foundational texts in African American folklore, celebrating a figure who fears neither God nor Devil and answers to absolutely no one

name: Stalldemon (Stable Demon)
description: Stalldemon is a generic Swedish term for supernatural beings haunting stables and barns, causing nightmares, livestock distress, and sleep paralysis. Not a single defined entity but a category of stable-haunting spirits (related to mara, cavall). Documented in Swedish folk belief as an explanation for night terrors and animal illness. No specific named stalldemon exists in tradition.

name: Stalo
description: Stalo is a vampire-like creature of Serbian and Croatian folklore, a dead man or woman who returns from the grave to drink the blood of living relatives. It resembles the larger Slavic vampire family, and folk protection included burial precautions, garlic, and the destruction of the corpse by staking or burning.

name: Standing Rock
description: Standing Rock, the stone formation on the Missouri in what is now North Dakota, is a petrified human in Lakota tradition: a young woman turned to stone, in some tellings a jealous Dakota wife. The Arikara, who also lived at the site, told of the Great Spirit turning a woman to rock. The landmark later became a symbol of Indigenous water-rights protests.

name: Star Spirit
description: Star Spirit appears in Arapaho folklore as a celestial being who can take human form. In the Star Husband story, two Arapaho women lay outside their tipi and one wished to marry a star. The next day, a handsome young man appeared—the star in human form, come to claim his bride. She went with him to the sky world, but grew homesick. Told she could return if she did not eat certain food, she broke the taboo and found herself back on Earth. Her star husband appeared no more, but she gave birth to a son who became a legendary Arapaho hero. Star spirits represent the connection between humans and the celestial realm

name: Steel Donkey
description: The Steel Donkey is a terrifying demonic donkey made of metal that roams the back roads of Barbados. Its eyes burn like fire, its mouth emits flames, and it drags heavy chains that clank loudly to announce its approach. The legend dates to the early 20th century and was believed to be summoned by malevolent individuals to carry out curses and inflict torment on enemies. Sightings are often accompanied by inexplicable events like stones pelting rooftops, livestock falling ill, or sudden hoofprints appearing on dusty paths. The creature now haunts places of transformation and decay, such as the Mangrove landfill in St. Thomas parish, evolving from a nightly terror into an emblem of bygone eras

name: Stick People
description: The Stick Indians, also called Cheeplokkeeycum, are malevolent forest spirits of the Salish, Lummi, Yakama and Cayuse peoples of the Pacific Northwest, luring travelers astray with whistles and laughter and capable of paralyzing or harming them. Salish tellers describe them as large, hairy wild men, others as forest dwarves. 'Stick Indians' is an English euphemism for a taboo name.

name: Stihi (or Stihini)
description: Not attested as a Pueblo being. The name 'Stihi' is Albanian, naming a fire-breathing storm demon related to the kulshedra, and no 'Stihi/Stihini' giant appears in Pueblo or New Mexico folklore. The closest real Pueblo giant is Tsahveeyo of the Tewa, a huge being who dwelt on a mesa and preyed on children in the pueblos. The record appears to be a fabricated or mislabeled entry.

name: Stikini
description: The Stikini are dreaded owl-witches of Seminole folklore. By day they look like ordinary people, but at night they vomit up their souls and internal organs and become undead owl-monsters with bloodshot eyes that feed on human hearts. In some communities, saying the name aloud is itself thought to risk transformation.

name: Stiklestadsgjenferden
description: Stiklestadsgjenferden (the Stiklestad Ghosts) are the spectral apparitions said to haunt the Stiklestad battlefield in Verdal, Trøndelag. The Battle of Stiklestad in 1030 was one of the most significant battles in Norwegian history, where King Olav Haraldsson (later Saint Olav) fell. According to local tradition, the ghosts of the fallen soldiers reappear on the anniversary of the battle, reenacting the fight in the mist that rises from the low-lying fields. The phenomenon is most often reported on July 29 (Olsok, the feast of St. Olav) when mist conditions are right. Locals have reported seeing shadowy figures, hearing clashing weapons and battle cries, and feeling an eerie presence in the area. The legend is documented in the Norsk Folkeminnesamling as entry ml4015 (De dødes messe) from Verdal, collected by Anton Røstad

name: Stone Coat
description: The Stone Coats, or stone giants, are terrible giants of Iroquois tradition, taller than any man and covered in a skin of rock-hard scales (native names include Genonsgwa). They wander the winter lands of the Adirondacks and Alleghenies, and heroes defeat them by striking their one soft spot.

name: Stone Giant
description: The Stone Giants (Otneyarhed or Stone Coats) are a race of cannibalistic giants from Iroquois mythology whose skin is as hard as stone, making them nearly invulnerable to weapons. They roll in sand and clay to create their armor-like coating. They are the mortal enemies of humans and were eventually exterminated through the cunning of heroes who discovered their only weakness: the soft spot on the crown of their heads. Associated with winter and frost, they are often described as primordial beings created by Flint (Hahgwehdaetgah)

name: Storjunkare
description: Storjunkare are sacred stone beings in Sami religion — unusually shaped stones or rock formations resembling humans or animals that were set up on mountaintops, in caves, or near rivers and lakes as objects of worship. The term comes from Scandinavian Sami tradition and describes large, sacred stones that were treated as living spirits. Honor was done to them by spreading fresh twigs under them in winter and leaves or grass in summer. They had power over all animals, fish, and birds, and granted good luck to those who hunted or fished for them. Reindeer were sacrificed at these sites, and every clan and family had its own hill of sacrifice dedicated to its local Storjunkare. According to the mid-18th century work Cérémonies et coutumes religieuses de tous les peuples du monde, Storjunkare was the second member of a Sami trinity after Tiermes (the thunder god), with Baivre or Jumala as the third member. Unlike sieidis which were natural formations, Storjunkare were sometimes deliberately set up stones that were then worshipped

name: Stormkäringen
description: Stormkäringen (the storm hag) is a malevolent old woman figure in Swedish coastal folklore who raises storms to destroy ships and drown fishermen. She is associated with the Wild Hunt (Odens jakt / Åsgårdsreien) — the supernatural procession that rides through the sky during stormy nights. Stormkäringen would be seen on rocky headlands during approaching storms, her gray hair whipping in the wind as she chanted or waved her arms, summoning gale-force winds. Fishermen and coastal farmers would leave offerings of bread, fish, or coins at the shore to placate her. The belief was especially strong in the Bohuslän archipelago and along the Baltic coast of Norrland. Some traditions say Stormkäringen was once a human woman who made a pact with the devil for power over the weather

name: Storsjöodjuret
description: Storsjöodjuret is Sweden's most famous lake cryptid, reported in Lake Storsjön (Jämtland) since the 17th century. Described as serpentine, 10-14 meters, with humps, smooth skin, sometimes a long neck. Briefly granted protected species status (1986-2005). A modern cryptid phenomenon with deep roots in local oral tradition, not an ancient mythic being. Major tourist attraction.

name: Strandvaskare
description: Strandvaskaren (shore wanderer) is the ghost of a drowned person whose body was never given proper Christian burial. Unlike a regular ghost, the Strandvaskare is bound to the shoreline where the body washed up, wandering the beach at dusk searching for rest. It leaves wet footprints on dry sand that lead nowhere — no body makes them. The Strandvaskare appears to lonely travelers, sometimes begging for help finding a proper grave, other times trying to drag the living into deep water to share its fate. The creature is most active at twilight, when sea fog rolls in, and is accompanied by the smell of seaweed and salt water. A proper burial of the remains releases the Strandvaskare from its earthly wanderings

name: Stria
description: Stria (striga) is a vampire spirit of Bulgarian and Balkan folklore, sometimes a witch who leaves her body at night to harm the living, sucking blood and bringing illness. Related to the Latin striga and the Romanian strigoi, the stria appears in folk medicine and burial customs designed to keep the restless dead in the grave.

name: Strig (or Štrig)
description: Strig (strigoi) is a vampire or evil spirit of Croatian and broader Balkan folklore, the restless dead who return to drink blood and trouble their families. The term derives from the Latin striga, and folk belief prescribed protections at burial, including poppies, thorns, and the burning of suspected undead.

name: Striga
description: A semi-demonic being with supernatural powers used to harm her community. Unlike the Western concept of a witch, a striga could be born with her powers or acquire them, and she might transform into animals—a cat, toad, or owl—to move unseen. Strigas could summon storms and hail, destroy crops, curse livestock, cause illness and death, raise spirits, and foretell the future. They anointed themselves with magical ointments to fly through the air, especially on solstice nights and early spring, when their sabbats were held

name: Striga
description: A semi-demonic being with supernatural powers used to harm her community. Unlike the Western concept of a witch, a striga could be born with her powers or acquire them, and she might transform into animals—a cat, toad, or owl—to move unseen. Strigas could summon storms and hail, destroy crops, curse livestock, cause illness and death, raise spirits, and foretell the future. They anointed themselves with magical ointments to fly through the air, especially on solstice nights and early spring, when their sabbats were held In Slovakia folklore, this figure is known among the Slovakia people.

name: Strigoi
description: Strigoi are the vampiric undead of Romanian and Moldovan folklore — either the living dead returning to their families or those born with traits marking them for vampirism. They leave their graves at night, causing illness and misfortune, and can be neutralized through exorcism, staking, or burial rites. Documented since the 19th century, the belief helped shape the literary vampire.

name: Strigoi
description: Strigoi are the vampiric undead of Romanian folklore, the restless souls of the unbaptized, the cursed, or those born with a caul, who return from the grave to plague the living. Active mainly at night, they bring illness and misfortune and are countered by garlic, holy objects, exorcism, or staking. Nineteenth-century accounts of strigoi influenced Bram Stoker's literary vampire.

name: Strzyga
description: Strzyga is a vampire of Polish folklore, depicted with two hearts, two souls, and sometimes a bird of prey birthmark, who rises at night to drink blood. Families protected themselves by burying suspected strzygi face down, with a stake or brick under the head, or by planting poppies and buckwheat, which the undead must count before feeding.

name: Stállo
description: Stállo is the most iconic antagonist in Sami folklore — a large, human-like cannibal giant who eats people, especially children. He is evil, strong, and dangerous but also clumsy, stupid, and easily tricked by clever Sami heroes who invariably outwit him using intelligence over brute force. He dresses in dark clothes with gold buttons and carries a rucksack on his back and a sharp knife. Stállo can be created by noaidis (shamans) from earth, wood, or turf, given part of the shaman's own life force, and sent to attack enemies. If killed with his own knife, he gains strength instead of dying. He whistles sharply when approaching, and hearing his pipe or whistle in the wind is a dangerous omen. He lives in mountains near Sami settlements, demanding reindeer sacrifices. The Stállo tradition may originate from historical encounters with Norse Vikings, Karelian raiders, or Russian tax collectors, who wore steel (stål) armor

name: Stállo
description: Stállo is a giant from Sápmi mythology. He is evil, strong, and dangerous but also clumsy, stupid, and easily tricked by clever Sami heroes who invariably outwit him using intelligence over brute force. He dresses in dark clothes with gold buttons and carries a rucksack on his back and a sharp knife. Stállo can be created by noaidis (shamans) from earth, wood, or turf, given part of the shaman's own life force, and sent to attack enemies. He lives in mountains near Sami settlements, demanding reindeer sacrifices.
