name: Stökkull
description: Stökkull (the Jumper) is the most feared of all the illhveli (evil whales) in Icelandic folklore, despite not being the largest. Stökkull has a distinctive rounded body, dark above and white below, 8-20 meters long, with a battering-ram snout. Its most remarkable feature is the flaps of skin (blinders) that cover its eyes — it must leap completely out of the water to see. According to Navigatio Sancti Brendani, Saint Brendan prayed to God to give Stökkull these blinders to limit its destructive power. When Stökkull leaps, it pile-drives ships underneath it, smashing them to pieces. The sight of Stökkull breaching was the most terrifying thing an Icelandic sailor could witness. The jumper whale is unique to Icelandic tradition and represents the danger of breaching whales combined with supernatural malevolence. The blinders motif shows how Christian hagiography adapted native folklore

name: Su Anasi
description: Su Anasy (the Water Mother) is the water spirit of Tatar and wider Turkic folklore: a beautiful woman who dwells in rivers and lakes, combing her long hair on the bank. Territorial and protective of her waters, she may snatch swimmers or reward the kind; her story, including the theft of her golden comb, features in Tatar tales such as Tuqay's.

name: Suliskongen
description: Suliskongen (the King of Sulitjelma) is the troll king of the Sulitjelma mountains in Nordland, and the father of the legendary Seven Sisters — Botnkrona, Grytfoten, Skjeringen, Tvillingene (the Twins), Kvasstinden, and Breitinden. According to legend, Suliskongen sent his seven daughters away from their home in Sulitjelma to the island of Landegode for discipline. When Hestmannen pursued them across the sea, the sisters danced on Alsten island to distract him. They were caught by the sunrise and turned into the seven peaks that form the distinctive silhouette of the Seven Sisters mountain range near Sandnessjøen. Suliskongen himself watches from his throne in the Sulitjelma mountains near the Swedish border. The Seven Sisters mountain range is one of Norway's most famous landmarks, and the legend is the best-known troll story in Northern Norway

name: Sumanguru Kante
description: Sumanguru Kanté is the villainous sorcerer-king of the Sosso people in the Epic of Sundiata. He was a powerful king who seized the remnants of the Ghana Empire and conquered nine neighboring kingdoms, including the Mandinka lands. Sumanguru was a master blacksmith and powerful sorcerer, invulnerable to all weapons except one — an arrow tipped with a white rooster spur. He possessed a magical balafon (xylophone) that could reveal his enemies' secrets. His seven-story tower palace in Sosso was filled with fetishes and magical charms. Sumanguru forced the Mandinka into brutal submission until Sundiata Keita returned from exile. At the Battle of Kirina, Sundiata's magic arrow struck Sumanguru, who fled into the Koulikoro mountains and vanished. The epic portrays Sumanguru as a tyrant whose cruelty necessitated the rise of the Mali Empire

name: Sumbo
description: Sumbo refers to the ritual masks of the Bwaba (Bobo) people of Burkina Faso, which are believed to embody powerful spirits that connect the human world with the invisible realm of ancestors and bush spirits. In Bwaba cosmology, the Sumbo masks represent a complex spiritual system that mediates between two categories of invisible entities: the ancestors and the bush spirits (genies de brousse). The Sumbo tradition includes different types of masks, from the most sacred fresh leaf masks (made from specific species of bush trees and associated with the Do initiatory cult) to fabric masks used in public ceremonies. The leaf masks, made fresh for each ceremony, are considered the most spiritually potent and are intimately connected to the cycle of vegetation. The Do cult, to which the Sumbo masks are linked, is an initiatory society that structures Bwaba social organization into three categories: farmers, blacksmiths, and griots. During ceremonies, the masks serve as the visible manifestation of the spirits, ensuring that proper rituals are observed, ancestors are honored, and the community maintains harmony with the natural and supernatural worlds

name: Sumpurnis
description: Sumpurnis (Latvia). is a shapeshifter. Permanent predator wrapped in dense, shaggy fur - bear-like humanoid with man's torso and dog's head. Source: Baltic folklore; a shaggy humanoid predator from regional myths.

name: Sun
description: In Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache tradition, the Sun is the great creator deity who brought light and order to the world. Their creation story begins with a great flood that destroyed a malevolent world, and the creator, closely linked to the Sun, shaped the world, the gods, and all living things through his power.

name: Sun (Jóhonaaʼéí)
description: Jóhonaaʼéí, the Sun, is a central deity of the Navajo (Diné). A being in human form, he carries the Sun across the sky each day and hangs it on a peg in his home at night. He is the father, with Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé), of the hero twins Nayééneizghani (Monster Slayer) and Tóbájíshchíní (Child of the Water), the slayers of the monsters of the old world.

name: Sun Goat
description: Among the Garap people of Chad, a myth explains the taboo on eating he-goat: a man found daylight personified as a he-goat in the forest but ate it instead of delivering it to the priest. The 'Sun Goat' is a figure in an aetiological tale transmitting moral knowledge about respect for property and authority, not a recurring beast or spirit.

name: Sun Goddess (Muisca)
description: Partially attested but gender is incorrect. The Muisca sun deity is Sué (Xué, Zuhé), a male god, not a goddess. Sué was husband of Chía (moon goddess), worshipped at the Sun Temple of Sugamuxi (Sogamoso). The record's 'Sun Goddess' reflects a common modern error reversing the gender.

name: Sun Goddess (Muisca)
description: Muisca tradition pairs the Moon goddess Chía with Sué (also Sua), the masculine Sun god, both born from the creator Chiminigagua. The zipa of Bacatá claimed descent from Sué's lineage, and the Sun was worshipped with offerings at sacred sites of the Colombian highlands. Modern summaries that call the Sun a 'goddess' likely conflate Sué with Chía; Muisca belongs to Colombia, not the USA.

name: Sun Nuxalk
description: The Sun is a powerful sky deity of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola), who dwells in a celestial house and carries the torches that light the day. He tests his sons-in-law with impossible tasks, and in the origin tale his mortal wife bears a son who takes the sun's course, burns the earth, and is cast down to become the mink.

name: Sun Spirit (Olmec)
description: Not independently attested as a named sun spirit of Olmec folklore. The Olmec pantheon as reconstructed from iconography includes the Maize God, a rain or were-jaguar figure, and a celestial Bird Monster, but no dedicated 'sun spirit' appears in the archaeological record. The record appears to be a generic forest-spirit template rather than a documented Olmec being.

name: Sun Tsimshian
description: In Tsimshian myth the Sun is a celestial chief whose son, Walks-All-Over-The-Sky, carries a burning cedar-bark mask across the heavens each day; sparks from his mouth become the stars and his charcoal-faced brother becomes the moon. In the Asdiwal story the Sun tests suitors for his daughter, who appears on earth as a white bear.

name: Sun Wukong
description: Sun Wukong (孫悟空), the Monkey King, is the trickster hero of the Ming-dynasty novel Journey to the West: a stone-born monkey with a magic staff that can grow to any size, somersault clouds, transformations, and hairs that create copies of himself. After rebelling against heaven, he guards the pilgrim Xuanzang westward, embodying wit, disobedience, and eventual enlightenment.

name: Sundiata Keita
description: Sundiata Keita was the legendary founder of the Mali Empire, the greatest empire in West African history. Born crippled and unable to walk, Sundiata was the son of King Maghan Kon Fatta and the ugly, hunchbacked woman Sogolon. A prophecy foretold his greatness. After his father's death, Sundiata and his mother were persecuted and forced into exile. In exile, he miraculously learned to walk and grew into a powerful warrior. Meanwhile, the sorcerer-king Soumaoro Kanté conquered the Mandinka people. Recalled from exile, Sundiata forged a coalition of kingdoms and defeated Soumaoro at the Battle of Kirina (c. 1235) using a magic arrow tipped with a white cock's spur — Soumaoro's only vulnerability. Sundiata became the first Mansa of the Mali Empire, establishing the Kouroukan Fouga constitution and building an empire that thrived for centuries

name: Sungrasspan
description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Brazilian Cerrado folklore. The name 'Sungrasspan' appears to be an English portmanteau ('sun grass span'). Brazilian savanna spirits include Caipora, Curupira, and local 'encantados,' but no specific 'Sungrasspan' is documented.

name: Suniyam Demon (Sinhalese Sorcery Spirit)
description: Suniyam is the chief demon of sorcery and black magic in Sinhalese folklore, believed to be one of the most powerful and dangerous of the Yaksha spirits. According to legend, Suniyam was once a Yaksha who served the god Vishnu but was cursed for his arrogance or misdeeds, becoming the master of all dark arts and sorcery. He governs all forms of black magic (kodivina), curses (sapa), and bewitchments (vas kavi). In the hierarchy of Sinhalese demons, Suniyam is considered the chief (pradhana) of all disease-bringing and misfortune-causing demons, commanding the other yakshas of the Daha Ata Sanniya (the eighteen maladies). He is associated with madness, epilepsy, chronic illness, business failure, family disputes, and all forms of inexplicable misfortune. When a Sinhalese person suffers a series of unexplained calamities, it is often attributed to Suniyam's influence, believed to have been sent by an enemy through a sorcerer (kattadiya or yaddura). Counteracting Suniyam's power requires the most elaborate and expensive exorcism ceremonies, often involving multiple nights of rituals, food offerings, and the construction of elaborate altars

name: Supay
description: Supay is the Inca/Quechua/Aymara lord of Uku Pacha (the underworld), an ambivalent deity of death, shadows, and mineral wealth. Originally neutral (allisupa = good spirit, mana allisupa = bad), he was syncretized with the Christian Devil. Ruler of the dead's journey, master of mines, honored by miners as 'El Tío.' Brother of Inti, Illapa, Mama Quilla.

name: Supernatural Seal Iceland
description: Supernatural Seal Iceland (Unknown). is a animal-spirit. A supernatural seal from Icelandic folklore is a shapeshifting selkie that sheds its skin to become human.. Source: Icelandic folklore — selkie/seal spirits documented in Icelandic maritime tradition.

name: Suuke (cave-dwelling monsters)
description: The Suuke are cave-dwelling monsters of Zuni tradition, lesser demonic beings who live in the cliffs and caves around Zuni lands. They carry off children in their baskets, and are counted among the dangerous supernatural creatures associated with Atahsaia, the terrible man-eating ogre of Zuni legend.

name: Suv Peri (Water Fairy)
description: Suv Peri (Water Fairies) are mythical water spirits from Turkmen folklore inhabiting the Caspian Sea coast and rivers such as the Amu Darya. According to Turkmen tradition, the Amu Darya mermaids are tender, sweet-voiced, and mysterious, following traditional Central Asian standards of beauty. However, the water maidens of the Caspian Sea and southern rivers are treacherous, dangerous, and have a frightening dark coloration. Suv Peri are guardians of water resources who can permit or forbid fishing and sea travel. They embody the protective role of water spirits in Turkmenistan's arid environment, where water is precious and dangerous

name: Svartalv (Swedish)
description: Svartálfar (black elves or dark elves) are supernatural beings from Norse cosmology who dwell underground in Svartálfheim, the world of the black elves. They are described as the light-avoiding counterparts to the Ljósálfar (light elves) who live in Álfheim. In Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, the svartálfar appear to be synonymous with the dwarves (dvergar), and Svartálfheim is considered interchangeable with Niðavellir (Dark Fields). The svartálfar are renowned as master craftspeople, and among their most famous creations are the Sons of Ivaldi's work: Sif's golden hair, Freyr's ship Skíðblaðnir, and Odin's spear Gungnir. They are described as pitch-black in appearance, turning to stone if exposed to daylight, and dwelling in underground forges and mines. In later Swedish folklore tradition, svartálfar merged with concepts of underjordiska and were sometimes blamed for nightmares — the German word for nightmare, Albtraum, literally means "elf-dream."

name: Swaichen
description: Swaichen (also spelled Swaychen) is a sea-creature of Bahraini folklore that punishes those who steal from the sea, taking from the water without respect. In a 2022 Gulf Weekly feature, Bahraini artist Zainab Almahdi presented it as a towering figure rising from the water that reclaims the thief; the tale is offered as a modern retelling of a traditional maritime warning legend.

name: Swan Maiden
description: The swan maiden (svanejomfru) is a widespread European motif (ATU 400), attested in Danish (Svend Grundtvig), Swedish, and Icelandic collections. A man steals a swan woman's feather cloak, forcing marriage until she recovers it. In Nordic versions, she is often a huldra or elf-woman. The motif is documented but not a specifically 'Swedish' named being.

name: Sweat House
description: The sweat house is a central institution of Yurok life: an earth-covered plank building in every village where men gathered daily, slept and prepared for ceremonies. Heated by fire rather than steam, it was the assembly place of the men and the setting of prayers and purification before the world-renewing dances such as the Deerskin and Brush dances.

name: Sweet Medicine
description: Sweet Medicine (Motsé'eóeve) is the greatest prophet and law-giver of the Cheyenne people. He journeyed to Nóávóse (Bear Butte) in the Black Hills where Ma'heo'o gave him the four sacred arrows (Maahótse)—two for hunting success and two for warfare. He received the structure of Cheyenne government (Council of Forty-Four), the military societies, the legal system, and the Sun Dance ceremony. Beginning as a troublesome trickster figure, he transformed into a wise lawgiver. He invented the hoop-and-stick game (chunkey) and predicted the coming of horses, white men, and the loss of the buffalo

name: Sylph
description: The sylph is the air elemental of Western esotericism, coined by Paracelsus in the 16th century as the airy counterpart of the salamander, undine and gnome. Classically pictured as slender, winged female beings of sky and mountain, they govern winds and weather. The term became a stock figure of alchemical, Rosicrucian and Romantic literature.

name: Syöjätär
description: Syöjätär is a Finnish ogress from runic songs and Ganander's Mythologia Fennica (1789). Mother of snakes, lizards, wolves, wasps, and diseases; her spit births serpents, stones are her 'heart's core'. In folktales she replaces royal children with animals and is burned in a sauna trap.

name: Sárkány
description: The legendary dragon in Hungarian folklore, originating from Turkic roots (Proto-Turkic *sāŕgan meaning 'carp, snake, dragon,' related to Cuman sazagan). Originally conceived as humanoid figures with multiple heads representing souls—a pre-Christian belief where each head embodied a spiritual essence. By the medieval period, evolved into the classic scaly, winged serpentine beast, heavily influenced by Christian demonology. Deeply connected to Slavic zmey traditions through the Carpathian Basin, though Hungarian sárkány remained predominantly malevolent while Slavic zmei could be ambivalent. The word appears first in Hungarian place names from the 12th-13th century (Sárkányosfő in 1262, Sárkányszigete in 1391)

name: Sáráhkká
description: Sáráhkká is the most important birth goddess in Sami mythology, daughter of Máttaráhkká. She lives under the hearth (aernie) of the goahti (Sami tent). She is the most worshipped of the Sami goddesses of childbirth. When Radien-attje creates a soul and sends it to Máttaráhkká who gives it life, Máttaráhkká hands it to Sáráhkká, who places the fetus in the woman's womb and gives it a body. She protects both human women and reindeer during birth, feeling the same labor pains. Before labor, women drank 'Sáráhkká's booze' and after birth ate 'Sáráhkká's porridge.' Wood was split for her to ease delivery — the split pieces were so sacred no one could touch them. A dog was kept during pregnancy and buried alive at labor time as a sacrifice. After successful birth, a female animal was sacrificed (only female animals except roosters). Her cult was so strong that after Christianization, Sami held secret ceremonies consuming 'the flesh and blood of Sáráhkká' before or after going to church, and she was replaced by the Virgin Mary. The modern Sami women's organization Sarahkka (formed 1988) is named after her

name: Sætrevette
description: Sætrevette (seter wight) is a nature spirit that guards the mountain pastures and seter huts in Vestlandet. The sætrevette protects the cattle, goats, and sheep taken to the summer pastures in the high mountains. Every seter (summer mountain farm) had its own sætrevette who ensured the animals were healthy, the milk yield was good, and the cheese-making succeeded. The sætrevette could appear as a small grey woman, a beautiful girl, or an old man. She would help with the milking and cheese-making if treated respectfully, but would sour the milk, hide the cheese curds, or lead the cattle astray if offended. Offerings of the first cheese of the season were left in the seter hut. The sætrevette tradition was particularly strong in the seter pastures of Vestlandet — Hallingdal, Valdres, Jotunheimen, and Hardangervidda. The seter system was central to Norwegian dairy farming, and the sætrevette was its supernatural guardian

name: Sømunk
description: Sømunken (the Sea Monk) is a sea monster reportedly caught in the Øresund in 1546 and presented to King Christian III of Denmark. The creature was described in contemporary sources as being four ells long (approximately 2.5 meters), shaped like a fish but with a monk-like head featuring a tonsure and a body resembling a monk's robe. It was kept alive in the Copenhagen castle moat for three days before dying, after which it was given a Christian burial. This historical event was documented in natural history texts of the 16th century, including Conrad Gesner's Historiae Animalium (1558). The creature was retrospectively identified in 1854 by Danish zoologist Japetus Steenstrup as a giant squid (Architeuthis), which would explain the tentacles that witnesses described as the 'monk's robe' and the head shape as seen from certain angles

name: Søtrold
description: Søtrold (sea troll) is a malevolent fjord-dwelling troll in Norwegian folklore, specific to the deep fjords of Vestlandet. Unlike mountain trolls that turn to stone in sunlight, the søtrold lives permanently in the dark fjord waters and is most active during storms. The søtrold makes terrible bargains with drowning sailors — it saves the ship in exchange for one of the sailors' children. If refused, the søtrold drags the entire ship and crew down. If accepted, the søtrold keeps its word but the child is taken years later. Some versions say it can be outwitted by promising a child that does not yet exist or giving a false name. Associated with Sognefjord (1,308m deep), Hardangerfjord, and Nordfjord

name: Sơn Tinh (Mountain Spirit)
description: Sơn Tinh (literally 'Mountain Spirit' or 'Mountain God') is the powerful deity of the mountains in Vietnamese mythology, specifically associated with Mount Tản Viên (Ba Vì) in northern Vietnam. According to legend, during the reign of the 18th Hùng King, the king's beautiful daughter Mỵ Nương was sought in marriage by two suitors: Sơn Tinh (the mountain spirit) and Thủy Tinh (the water spirit). The king set a challenge — whoever arrived first with the prescribed wedding gifts would win his daughter. Sơn Tinh arrived first with gifts including ivory, gold, and rare mountain treasures, and married the princess. The enraged Thủy Tinh raised floods to destroy the mountains, but Sơn Tinh used his power to raise the peaks higher. Their eternal struggle represents the annual monsoon floods that strike Vietnam's Red River Delta. The myth explains both the region's seasonal flooding and the Vietnamese people's resilience against nature

name: T Qul Tca Coast Salish
description: Not independently attested as the name of the ghost land in the Coast Salish sources consulted. Coast Salish peoples hold documented beliefs in the land of the dead and in soul-loss, and heroes of the myth age visit the spirit world, but the specific name Tqultca requires better sourcing before it can be verified.

name: Tabudo
description: El Tabudo ('Man of Big Knees') is a water-spirit or lake-guardian of Salvadoran folklore tied to Lake Coatepeque in Santa Ana department. Legend says a rich lakeside landowner was dragged beneath the water and returned months later transformed, with swollen knees and a fish-like appearance; he now haunts the lake, sometimes appearing as a fisherman to lure people in.

name: Tagaloa
description: Tangaloa, in Tongan tradition a family of sky-gods headed by the supreme deity, is the great celestial creator of Samoan and Tongan cosmology, dwelling above in the langi (sky-layers) from which the world was ordered and chiefly lineages descended. The input's claim that he 'fished up islands' conflates him with the culture hero Māui, to whom Tongan myth attributes that feat.

name: Tagaro
description: Tagaro is a creator deity and culture hero in Vanuatu mythology, particularly on Ambae Island. In the creation stories, Tagaro is pitted against his twelfth brother Suqe-matua. They shared the work of creation, but whatever Suqe-matua did was wrong — they always disagreed, but the word of Tagaro always prevailed. Tagaro created useful plants, gentle animals, and beneficial customs, while Suqe-matua created weeds, dangerous creatures, and harmful practices. Tagaro made ten human figures from mud and breathed life into them. He then threw a fruit at one of the figures, transforming the man into a woman, thus establishing the two sexes. Tagaro is related to the Polynesian deity Tangaroa, showing the cultural connections across the Pacific

name: Taka-nyūdō
description: Taka-nyūdō ('tall priest') is a yōkai of Japanese folklore, a colossal monk-like figure that appears on mountain passes and roads in the Shikoku and Kinki regions. When a traveler looks up, it grows impossibly tall, higher the longer it is watched, and the only escape is to avert one's eyes. It belongs to the mikoshi-nyūdō class and warns against the taboo of staring.

name: Takhar
description: Takhar is the Serer spirit of absolute justice and inevitable vengeance, enforcing moral retribution and maintaining social order through spiritual law.

name: Talamaur
description: Talamaur is a vampiric figure of the Banks Islands, Vanuatu, described in oral tradition as a blood-drinking, shapeshifting being able to assume seductive forms and to command the spirits of the deceased. Its night-stalking habits and control over the dead set it apart from ordinary sorcerers, linking it to the region's secret-society and ghost lore.

name: Talasac
description: Not independently attested in documented Romanian folklore or academic sources. No reference describes a midnight 'Talasac,' a dog-like beast fetching souls from graveyards to the underworld; searches return only an Occitan place-name and the Bulgarian/Romanian 'talasym' walled-in spirit, neither matching. The input's stated source, Ovid's Metamorphoses, mentions no such creature.

name: Taleju Bhawani (Royal Goddess of the Malla Kings)
description: Taleju Bhawani is a tantric form of Durga and royal tutelary goddess of the Malla kings. Legend says King Jayaprakash Malla played dice nightly with her; when his daughter discovered them, the goddess vanished, but commanded in a dream that he worship a Shakya virgin girl as her living embodiment — founding the Kumari tradition. Her Kathmandu Durbar Square temple was built in 1564.

name: Talking Fish Iceland
description: Talking Fish Iceland (Unknown). is a animal-spirit. A talking fish from Icelandic folklore is a magical salmon that speaks prophecies to fishermen.. Source: Icelandic folklore — talking animals documented in Icelandic oral tradition.

name: Talking Fox
description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Nordic folklore. Talking foxes appear in fairy tales (ATU 370 'The Fox as Shepherd') and fables, but not as a recurring folkloric being with a specific name or role. The closest analogue is the fox as trickster in pan-European tales, not a Nordic-specific spirit.

name: Talking God (Haashchʼééłtiʼí)
description: Talking God (Haschélti, Hastseyalti) is a principal Holy Person of the Navajo, one of the four calling gods of the sacred mountains, mentor and advocate for the People who helped Changing Woman give birth to the Monster Slayer Twins and travels on rainbows. He leads the Night Chant (Yeibichai) ceremony, recorded by Washington Matthews in 1902, and is associated with the white color.

name: Talking Shark
description: Skalugsuak (Eqalussuaq) is the legendary Greenland shark of Inuit lore, said to have been born when an old woman's urine-soaked hair cloth blew into the sea and became the shark; the Igloolik Inuit say it lives in Sedna's urine pot and acts as a helping spirit to shamans. Its flesh, toxic with urea, smells of urine. A 'talking' benevolent shark, however, is not documented.

name: Tamaiti
description: Not independently attested as a distinct spirit of Tongan folklore. The word tamaiti simply means 'child' in Tongan, with cognates across Polynesian languages; no source documents a child-ghost named 'Tamaiti' haunting playgrounds and village commons. The entry is a generic children's-spirit archetype rather than a recorded Tongan figure, and no Tongan child-ghost tradition bears this name.

name: Tamapua
description: Not independently attested as a trickster figure of Vanuatu folklore. No scholarly or ethnographic source documents a shapeshifting trickster named 'Tamapua'; the documented trickster deities of Vanuatu are Kpwet of the Banks Islands and Tagaro in the north, and the name resembles the Hawaiian hog-god Kamapua'a. The recorded traits appear generic rather than drawn from Vanuatu tradition.

name: Tamate (Dancing Spirits)
description: Tamate are mysterious half-divine, half-human dancing spirits from Vanikoro Island in the Solomon Islands. According to Teanu mythology recorded by linguist Alexandre Francois, the Tamate were discovered by a Vanikoro couple who got lost at sea and landed on a mysterious islet called Veluko. The island was inhabited by human-like godly creatures called Tamate who performed beautiful dances. The couple stayed for months, then returned home with five Tamate creatures. They organized a huge dancing festival and revealed the majestic Tamate dances to their people. The Tamate are represented by distinctive ritual headdresses unique to Vanikoro, similar to those found in the Banks Islands of Vanuatu

name: Tamawan
description: Not independently attested in documented Philippine folklore or academic sources. No reference describes a household spirit 'Tamawan'; searches return only Tam-awan Village, a Baguio artist colony and Cordillera living museum, an unrelated proper noun. The recorded house-elf traits resemble Filipino duwende beliefs and appear to derive from conflation.

name: Tane
description: Tāne is the Polynesian god of forests and birds, best known in Māori tradition as Tāne Mahuta, who separated earth and sky and gave humanity the trees of the forest. The record identifies him as a Tahitian forest deity honored through carved wooden figures in temples. Note that the figure belongs to Polynesian, not French, tradition despite the country tag on this record.

name: Tane Mahuta
description: God of forests, birds, and all living creatures within the forest. Tane is the son of Ranginui and Papatuanuku who braced his shoulders against his mother and pushed his feet against his father, forcing them apart and letting light into the world. He then adorned his father's bare body with the stars. Tane created the first woman, Hineahuone, from the earth, and with her fathered Hinetitama. He is the father of all trees, birds, and insects. His domain represents life, growth, knowledge, and the interconnection of all living things. Tane Mahuta is also the god of knowledge and brought the three baskets of knowledge to humanity

name: Tangaroa
description: God of the sea, oceans, rivers, lakes, and all water bodies. Tangaroa is a son of Ranginui and Papatuanuku. After the separation of his parents, Tawhirimatea drove Tangaroa into the ocean depths where he has remained. He is the father of all fish, reptiles, and sea creatures. His descendants include Ikatere (father of fish) and Tu-te-wehiwehi (father of reptiles). When Tane Mahuta offered shelter to the reptiles on land, they abandoned Tangaroa, causing an eternal enmity between forest and sea. The sea forever consumes the shore, and Tane's creatures hide from the ocean's reach

name: Tangaroa
description: The god of the sea in Cook Islands mythology, one of the twin sons of Avatea (the first man) and Papa (the earth goddess). Tangaroa and his brother Rongo shared dominion over all things - with Tangaroa taking everything red. He is a major deity in the Cook Islands pantheon. Tangaroa is also the father of Tinirau, the god of the ocean. In some traditions, Tangaroa rivals his brother Rongo for supremacy. The Tangaroa cult was prominent on Aitutaki and other islands. Fishermen and voyagers offered prayers to Tangaroa for protection and good catches. He is sometimes depicted as a creator figure as well

name: Tangata Manu
description: The Tangata Manu (Birdman) was the winner of the annual competition at Orongo on Rapa Nui (Easter Island). The competition was established by the god Makemake. Each year, representatives of the competing Rapanui clans would descend the sheer 300-meter cliffs of Orongo, swim across shark-infested waters to the islet of Motu Nui, and wait for the Manutara (sooty tern) to lay its first egg. The competitor who successfully retrieved the first egg became the Tangata Manu for that year. He gained supreme temporal power, his clan received special privileges, and he was treated as a living embodiment of Makemake's favor. The winner underwent rituals of purification, shaved his head, and was painted red and white

name: Taniwha
description: Taniwha are supernatural beings of Māori tradition who dwell in rivers, lakes, deep pools, and the sea, guarding tribal waterways and landmarks. Some, like Ngake and Whātaitai, are protective kaitiaki linked to hapū and iwi; others are feared man-eaters who seize travellers. They may appear as giant lizards, sharks, whales, or serpents, their presence marking dangerous waters.

name: Tannin
description: Tannin is the sea-dragon or chaos-monster of ancient Northwest Semitic tradition, appearing in Ugaritic and biblical texts as a raging serpent of the deep, cognate with Lotan (Leviathan). Yahweh crushes the tannin (Isaiah 51:9; Psalm 74:13), a victory over primordial chaos tied to the Levantine coast. The word passed into Arabic (tinnīn) for 'dragon' or 'sea-serpent'.

name: Tannit (Neith-Atheme)
description: Tanit (also Tinnit) was the great goddess of Carthage, a North African deity of sky, fertility and the afterlife, consort of Baal Hammon. Her symbol, a circle above a triangle over a horizontal bar, appears throughout Punic sites. Offerings at the tophet were made to her and Baal Hammon, and she was later identified with Juno Caelestis.

name: Tantal
description: The Tantal is a shapeshifting being of the southern Mesopotamian marshlands, documented among the Marsh Arabs; in Gulf usage the figure also appears in Kuwaiti retellings. It shifts between human, animal, and object forms at night, and individual Tantals are named for the territories they haunt, with Tantal Hafiz described as their ruler. The core lore is Iraqi; the Kuwait framing is derivative.

name: Tantal
description: The Tantal is a shapeshifting spirit of Iraqi folklore, tied especially to the marshlands of southern Iraq and the Marsh Arab (Ma'dan) communities. It is said to change shape at night, appearing as a human, animal, or object, and particular Tantals are named for the marsh territories they haunt, with Tantal Hafiz regarded as foremost among them. Documented in Drower's Folk-Tales of Iraq.

name: Tantal
description: The Tantal (Arabic 'tanṭāl') is a shapeshifting being of Iraqi folklore, particularly among the Marsh Arabs of southern Iraq. It can appear as a human, animal, or object and is active at night; specific Tantals are associated with particular marsh territories, and one, Tantal Hafiz, is named as a chief of them. The figure is documented in Iraqi oral tradition and journalism.

name: Taotaomo'na
description: Taotaomo'na, the 'people of before,' are the ancestral spirits of the ancient Chamorro, told across Guam and the Northern Marianas. Said to be the ghosts of early inhabitants, they inhabit banyan trees, deep jungle, and caves, and can be hostile to those who trespass or disturb ancient sites and bones. Their displeasure is feared, and respect and proper ritual are believed to appease them.

name: Tar-Baby
description: The Tar-Baby is a doll made of tar and turpentine created by Br'er Fox to trap Br'er Rabbit in the most famous African American folktale. Br'er Fox fashions the doll and sets it in the road. When Br'er Rabbit greets the silent figure and receives no reply, he grows angry and strikes it, becoming stuck. Each successive limb he uses — first his paws, then his feet, and finally his head — becomes hopelessly ensnared in the sticky tar. The Tar-Baby has become a powerful metaphor in American English for a problem that grows worse the more one struggles against it. The tale's origins trace to African and Cherokee trickster traditions

name: Tata Duende
description: Tata Duende is one of Belize's most famous mythical creatures — a powerful forest spirit that protects animals and the jungle. Described as a small, bearded man about three feet tall who wears a wide-brimmed red hat, animal skins for clothing, and has his feet pointing backwards. He notably lacks thumbs. Parents warn children never to show Tata Duende their thumbs, or he will break or bite them off. He is known for whistling to mimic his victims, braiding horses' manes, and luring children deeper into the forest. However, among the Yucatec Maya of Belize, he is also known as Nukuch Tat and is seen as a good guardian spirit who protects children in the bush. Offerings are still given to him for protection and help before entering the forest

However, among the Yucatec Maya of Belize, he is also known as Nukuch Tat and is seen as a good guardian spirit who protects children in the bush. Offerings are still given to him for protection and help before entering the forest In Belize folklore, this figure is known among the Maya and Creole people.

name: Tatzelwurm
description: A legendary dragon-like lizard creature from Alpine folklore, also called Stollenwurm, Bergstutz, or Stutzn depending on the region. The Tatzelwurm is described as having the face of a cat with a long serpentine body, four short legs (or sometimes only two forelegs), ranging from one to seven feet in length. Local names in Styria and Tyrol include Bergstutz ('mountain stump'), reflecting its stubby appearance. Reports of encounters date back centuries, with the most famous being farmer Hans Fuchs in 1779 who reportedly died of a heart attack after seeing two of Tatzelwurms. The Tatzelwurm is said to have poisonous breath lethal to humans and animals, and sightings were often believed to occur after humid weather or volatile temperature changes

name: Tatzelwurm
description: Tatzelwurm is a dragon from Germany mythology. The Tatzelwurm is described as having the face of a cat with a long serpentine body, four short legs (or sometimes only two forelegs), ranging from one to seven feet in length. Local names in Styria and Tyrol include Bergstutz ('mountain stump'), reflecting its stubby appearance. name: Tautramunken
description: Tautramunken (the Monk of Tautra) is a ghostly figure that haunts the ruins of Tautra Cistercian monastery on the island of Tautra in the Trondheimsfjord, near Frosta. The monastery was founded in 1207 and was one of the most important Cistercian houses in Norway until it was dissolved during the Reformation in 1532. The ghost is believed to be a monk who refused to leave the monastery when it was closed, or who was killed during the dissolution. The specter appears as a white-robed Cistercian monk walking the ruins at twilight, particularly on misty evenings. Local tradition says the monk can be seen kneeling in prayer where the monastery church once stood. Tautra is also known for its unique natural beauty and bird life, and the ghost legend is an integral part of the island's cultural heritage

name: Tawa (Sun Spirit)
description: Tawa is the primary creator deity in Hopi tradition, the Sun Spirit who existed alone in endless space (Tokpella) before creation. He formed the First World and created Sotuknang, his nephew, who in turn created Spider Woman as a messenger. Tawa divided himself creating Muiyinwuh, God of All Life Germs. He destroyed the Third World in a great flood because of the people's wickedness. Together with Spider Woman (Kokyanwuhti), Tawa represents the creative forces of the Above. He is the supreme cel

name: Tawescaron
description: Tawescaron is the malevolent twin brother of Huron mythology, the younger twin and eternal antagonist of Ioskeha. He created monsters, darkness, winter, and all that is harmful in the world. He constantly tried to undo his brother's good works. Tawescaron represented darkness, destruction, and death. In the great race between good and evil, Tawescaron lost when Ioskeha used buck's horns to defeat him. Though defeated, Tawescaron's spirit declared he would go to the northwest land and condemn death upon the world, establishing the cycle of life and death

name: Tawhirimatea
description: God of winds, storms, clouds, and weather. Tawhirimatea, son of Ranginui and Papatuanuku, was the only one of the children who opposed the separation of their parents. Enraged at the forced separation, he joined his father in the sky and became the god of wind and storms. He unleashed devastating tempests against his brothers, attacking Tane's forests with hurricanes, driving Tangaroa into the ocean depths, and pursuing Rongo and Haumia across the land. He is the father of the various winds, each with its own name and character. His storms represent the ongoing cosmic conflict between the elements

name: Tay
description: Not independently attested in Sudanese folklore under this name. Tay is described as a serpent-like water spirit of the Nile who blesses fishermen with good catches or drags the disrespectful beneath the water. The figure fits the documented river-spirit world of northern Sudan and Nubia, including the banat el Hur and the River Folk, but no source names a being called Tay.

name: Taytoru
description: Taytoru is the magical steed of Semetey in the Kyrgyz Epic of Manas, a sleek, fiery-eyed horse of supernatural speed and endurance. She carried Semetey from Bukhara across the mountains to the Talas valley so he could avenge his father Manas's death. Loyal and shrewd, she is the archetype of the epic hero's faithful mount.

name: Te Ngaru
description: Te Ngaru ('The Wave') is a culture hero of Mangaia in the Cook Islands, whose exploits explain the ocean's power. Grandson of Moko the Great Lizard, he matched himself against the great ocean swell Tikokura and the man-eating shark Tumutearetoka, riding the crests of the sea in a struggle recorded by the missionary William Wyatt Gill and studied in modern scholarship.

name: Te Pusi mo te Ali
description: Te Pusi mo te Ali ('The Eel and the Flounder') is a Tuvaluan creation tale of the lagoon: an eel and a flatfish are bound in a conflict or agreement that shapes the lagoon's life, and eels are regarded as sacred and tapu in Tuvaluan tradition. The story carries the lagoon-based world-view of the atolls.

name: Te Wheke-a-Muturangi
description: The giant octopus that was pursued across the Pacific by the Polynesian navigator Kupe. Te Wheke-a-Muturangi belonged to Muturangi, a chief from Hawaiki. The octopus harassed Kupe's fishing lines and stole his bait repeatedly. Kupe vowed to destroy it and chased it across the Pacific Ocean in his canoe Matahourua. The pursuit of the giant octopus led Kupe to discover Aotearoa (New Zealand). He finally killed the octopus in Cook Strait or at Hokianga Harbour. The immense size of the creature is described in legends as being large enough to wrap its tentacles around whole canoes

name: Tefolaha
description: Tefolaha is the founding ancestor of Nanumea atoll in Tuvalu, a partly divine hero said to have come from Tonga and to have established the island's chiefly lines. His spear Kaumaile is a treasured heirloom of the island, and descent from him is claimed by Nanumea's principal families, making him a central figure of Tuvaluan island-origin traditions.

name: Tek-ko-kui
description: Tek-ko-kui, the 'bamboo pole ghost' of Taiwanese folklore, is said to haunt bamboo groves at dusk, bending a bamboo culm under tension and letting it snap to strike and kill those who pass. Stories place it near the former Kawabata Bridge in Taipei as well as in Yonghe and Chiayi. The legend is used to explain the dangers of dense bamboo forests.

name: Teke
description: Not independently attested in Kyrgyz folklore by this name. Teke, the Turkic word for the ibex, is here described as a guardian spirit of mountain passes and high peaks who protects or misleads according to respect shown. The documented protector of wild game in Kyrgyz and Turkic hunting tradition is Kayberen, guardian of ibex, deer, and mountain herds.

name: Teke Teke
description: Teke Teke (Unknown). is a ghost. Teke Teke is a modern Japanese urban legend about the ghost of a woman who was cut in half by a train. She drags herself on her elbows through the streets, making a "teke teke" sound, and will cut her. Source: Japanese urban legend; contemporary folklore

name: Telematua
description: Telematua is a legendary giant-ancestor of Tuvaluan tradition, a being of colossal size said to have shaped the islands and their channels; his passage or labour is recalled as the origin of the passages (ava) between islets. Sluggish and indifferent to humans in most accounts, he is nonetheless a figure of the islands' ancient founding stories.

name: Temple Guardian (Mixtec)
description: Not independently attested as a named 'temple guardian' figure of Mixtec folklore. No Mixtec source records a stone or jade sentinel guarding temple entrances. The closest real analogue is the deity presiding over the Mixtec Temple of Death at Ñuu Ndeya (Chalcatongo): the skeletal goddess Lady 9 Grass (a Cihuacoatl-like figure) and the Lords of the Underworld who received the dead there.

name: Temple Guardian (Mixtec)
description: In Mixtec (Ñuu Dzaui) belief the ñuhu are sacred beings who guard places: ancient stones, caves and springs are their homes, and hunters, farmers and builders must ask their leave. Temple entrances were watched by carved guardians and by ancestral spirits with clawed hands who seize the disrespectful, as with Lady 9 Grass of the Temple of Death. The US location reflects the modern Mixtec diaspora.

name: Tenga
description: Tenga is the earth goddess of the Mossi (Moose) people of Burkina Faso, wife of Wende, the supreme sky god. She is the guardian of the land, its fields, and its fertility, and authority over the earth belongs to her; humans direct their prayers through Tenga to reach Wende. She is central to Mossi ideas of land, farming, and chieftaincy.

name: Tengbiswem Earth Spirit
description: The Earth Spirit is the invisible guardian of the land, believed by the Mossi to be the true owner of the soil. This spirit governs the fertility of the crops and the overall health of the community. To avoid angering the spirit—which could result in drought, famine, or illness—the community relies on the Tengbiswem (Earth Priests) to perform sacrifices and prayers. The spirit is deeply tied to the ancestors and the physical land, making land ownership a spiritual rather than just a material matter

name: Tengri
description: Tengri is the supreme sky god of the Turkic peoples, the eternal blue sky whose worship long preceded Islam in Central Asia. Creator and sustainer above all spirits, he was honoured by shamans and steppe nomads with open-air rites on high ground. Kazakh reverence for Tengri still echoes in proverbs and in prayerful raising of the hands to the sky.

name: Tengri Khormusta
description: Khormusta, king of the western heavens, is the supreme sky deity of Buryat Tengriism and father of the hero Abai Geser. A radiant warrior-king amid celestial hosts, he wages eternal war against the eastern gods of darkness. His scattering of the slain Atai Ulan's body, meant to prevent resurrection, instead seeded the demons that plague the world.

name: Tengu
description: Tengu are supernatural mountain spirits of Japanese folklore, commonly shown with long noses and magical powers, believed to be reincarnations of the proud. The daitengu are elder masters with red noses and feather fans, and karasu-tengu are crow-like; the daitengu Sōjōbō is said to have taught young Minamoto no Yoshitsune the martial arts. Feared and respected, they guard forests and mountains.

name: Tepuhi
description: Tepuhi is the founding ancestor of Nanumaga atoll in Tuvalu, a spirit who is said to have come from Fiji in the form of a sea serpent and to have established the island's people. Unlike Nanumea's ancestor Tefolaha, who came from Tonga as a half-human hero, Tepuhi's serpent form ties Nanumaga's origin to the ocean and to the spirit world.

name: Termite Animal-Spirit (Komi)
description: Not independently attested: termites do not occur in the boreal forests of the Komi Republic, and no termite ancestor-spirit appears in documented Komi tradition. The entry likely conflates Komi nature guardians with an unrelated insect totem; no real analogue is recorded.

name: Terton (Treasure Revealer)
description: Tertöns are treasure revealers of Tibetan Buddhism: visionary lamas and yogins who discover hidden terma, teachings concealed by Padmasambhava and Yeshe Tsogyal in caves, lakes, rocks, and monasteries. Entering meditative states, they often break convention to retrieve the hidden dharma. The terma system let Buddhist teachings evolve across centuries.

name: Teryel
description: Teryel is the most famous ogress in Kabyle (Algerian Amazigh) mythology — a terrifying female monster with an anthropophagic (man-eating) appetite. According to a foundational Kabyle myth, when humanity was created as fifty men and fifty women, 98 chose to settle and build houses, but one man and one woman chose to live in the wild. The man became a lion (izem) and the woman became Teryel, the first ogress. Teryel represents the untamed, wild feminine that rejects domesticity and social norms. In Kabyle folklore, she lives isolated in caves and wilderness, eating her own children when hungry and devouring anyone who approaches her domain. Despite her monstrous nature, Teryel is also a figure of resistance — she rejects patriarchal society's rules, making her both feared and respected. She is the antithesis of the domesticated Kabyle woman: independent, powerful, and utterly free. Her daughter Lunja plays the role of the beautiful captive in her cave, creating a complex mother-daughter dynamic in Kabyle oral tradition

name: Thagyamin (King of the Nats)
description: Thagyamin is the Burmese name for Sakka (Indra), king of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and head of the 37 nats. King Anawrahta of Pagan placed him atop the nat pantheon in the 11th century to harmonize animism with Buddhism; unlike nats who died violent deaths, he earned his throne by merit. During Thingyan he descends invisibly, recording mortals' fates in a golden book or a dog-hide ledger.

name: Thaman Kyah
description: Thaman Kyah is the weretiger of Burmese folklore, a human who takes tiger form, gaining the beast's strength and stealth in jungles and remote villages. Predatory and secretive, it hunts by night and can only be unmasked by exposure of its true identity, after which its power fails. The figure reflects fear of hidden predators and human duality, a common Southeast Asian weretiger theme.

name: Thanh Gióng
description: Thanh Gióng (Unknown). is a hero. Thánh Gióng is a legendary hero from Vietnamese mythology who grew from a three-year-old boy into a giant warrior overnight to defend the country from foreign invaders. After victory, he flew into the. Source: Vietnamese mythology; The Tale of Saint Giong

name: Thanh Minh
description: Not independently attested as a folkloric creature. In Vietnamese culture 'Thanh Minh' (Qingming) is the grave-sweeping festival of early April, a solar term for honoring the dead, not a wandering ghost of cold months. No source documents such a spirit tempting the living into the cold; the record conflates the festival's name with general beliefs about restless souls.

name: The Chureca
description: The Chureca is a Virgin Islands death-omen spirit appearing as an owl-like creature. Its cry or appearance near a home predicts imminent death in the household. A localized variant of the widespread Caribbean 'owl as death messenger' belief (cf. Jamaican rolling calf, Haitian loogaroo owl form). Not to be confused with La Chureca, the Managua landfill.

name: The Coastal Leviathan
description: The Coastal Leviathan (Somali Maritime). is a beast. A giant sea monster that haunts the Indian Ocean coasts of Somalia. Source: Somali Coastal Oral History

name: The Dandan (World Fish)
description: The Dandan, also known as Bahamut, is a colossal cosmic fish from Arabian and Islamic mythology that supports the structure of the world. According to medieval Islamic cosmography attributed to al-Qazwini and others, the Dandan lies deep beneath the earth, carrying on its back a massive bull named Kuyutha or Kiyuban, upon which stands an angel who shoulders the earth itself. A slab of gemstone sits between the bull and the angel. The Dandan is so immense that all the seas of the world placed in one of its nostrils would be like a mustard seed in the desert. Below the Dandan lies the serpent Falak, waiting in the depths of hell. This cosmic creature appears in the Arabian Nights tale of Abdullah the Fisherman and Abdullah the Merman, where Sinbad encounters it. The name derives from the Hebrew Behemoth via Arabic transmission

name: The Fish-Wife of Lake Toba
description: The Fish-Wife of Lake Toba is the tragic spirit-woman at the center of North Sumatra's most famous origin myth. A poor fisherman named Toba caught a magical golden fish that transformed into a beautiful woman. She agreed to marry him on one condition: he must never reveal her fish origins. They had a son named Samosir, and lived happily for years. But one day, enraged by his son's laziness, Toba shouted 'You son of a fish!' — revealing his wife's secret. The curse was broken. The wife wept, the earth trembled, and a massive flood engulfed the land, forming Lake Toba. The wife disappeared into the waters, and her son became the island of Samosir in the lake's center. She is both a figure of tragic love and a powerful water spirit who created one of the world's largest volcanic lakes

name: The Forest Phantom
description: Not independently attested as a named entity in Ugandan folklore. 'Forest Phantom' / 'Green Shadow' / 'Way-Wanderer' appears to be a generic compilation of widespread Ugandan forest trickster motifs (hare/rabbit, leopard, mimicry spirits in Bwindi).

name: The Goli Spirit
description: The Goli is a spiritual force manifested through an elaborate series of masks and dances among the Baoulé people. Rather than a single creature, it is a composite ancestral entity summoned from the forest to intervene in human affairs. The Goli appears during times of crisis, such as droughts or epidemics, or to celebrate the passing of a great leader. Its presence is believed to cleanse the village of negative energy and re-establish the harmony between the living, the dead, and the natural environment

name: The Great Nile Serpent
description: The Great Nile Serpent is a colossal, iridescent-scaled serpent spirit guarding the Victoria Nile's deep trenches in Ugandan Nilotic/Bantu oral tradition. It emerges during lunar eclipses or ecological crisis, controlling currents and demanding tribute. Associated with Ruhanga (creator) and the underworld ruler.

name: The Great Peacemaker
description: The Great Peacemaker, known as Deganawida, is the legendary founder of the Iroquois Confederacy (Haudenosaunee), the oldest living democracy in North America. Born among the Huron, he crossed Lake Ontario in a stone canoe to bring peace to the warring Iroquois nations. With the orator Hiawatha and the Seneca chief Jigonsaseh (the Peace Queen), he converted the cannibal warrior Hiawatha and confronted the evil wizard Tadodaho. The Great Law (Kaianere'kó:wa) he established the principles of peace, equity, and the power of the clan mothers

name: The Great Whale of Creation
description: In Kemak creation mythology from the Atsabe region of East Timor, a colossal cosmic whale caused a devastating flood that reshaped the world. According to the myth, the immense whale leaped so high from the ocean that when it crashed back down, it drove all the waters to rise to the mountaintops, covering nearly all land. This deluge marked the third great flood in Timorese cosmology. The ancestors survived by climbing to the peak of Mount Ramelau (Lame Lau), where they communed with God. The whale was eventually slain with sacred spears and swords given by God

name: The Helpful Fish
description: The helpful fish of Qatari coastal lore is a benevolent water spirit that guards tide pools and the shallow Gulf waters, guiding honest fishermen to good catches. Often identified with the two-banded porgy known locally as al-fisaikra, it embodies foresight and clear speech, rewarding respect and punishing greed. Tales of the guide fish remain part of Gulf oral heritage.

name: The Kanaga Spirits
description: The kanaga is the great wooden mask of the Dogon of Mali, danced during the dama, the funeral rite that escorts the soul of the deceased from the village of the living to the ancestral realm. Worn with black, red, and white geometric patterns, the kanaga dancer evokes the hand of the creator god Amma and the order of the cosmos, central to Dogon mortuary tradition.

name: The Lion of Njie
description: In Serer tradition of Senegal, the lion is a totemic guardian associated with the Njie (Njai) clan and lineage. Clans hold specific animals as sacred ancestors and protectors, and the lion's strength and dignity mirror the clan's claims to authority. The figure connects the living community with the ancestors and the natural world.

name: The Mantis
description: The Mantis (Unknown). is a animal-spirit. The Mantis (also known as Kaggen or Cagn) is a central trickster-creator figure in San (Bushman) mythology of the Kalahari. He is a praying mantis who possesses great cunning and creative power.. Source: San (Bushman) mythology; Bleek and Lloyd collection

name: The Milkman of Pieter Both
description: According to a popular local legend, the distinctive rock formation at the peak of Pieter Both Mountain is actually a milkman who was turned to stone. The milkman used to sell milk in the surrounding villages and once took a shortcut through the mountain. While resting, he witnessed fairies dancing and singing. The fairies warned him to keep their existence a secret, but the milkman betrayed them by telling his friends. As punishment, the fairies turned him into stone, forever marking the summit of the mountain

name: The Mountain Giant
description: The Mountain Giant (Burundian). is a giant. A colossal stone-skinned giant inhabiting the mountains of Burundi. Source: Highland Oral History Found in L' la highest summits of the Burundi highlands and the Congo-Nile Divide.. Documented in ethnographic records.

name: The Mythical Korp
description: The Korp (Raven) in Swedish folklore is far more than a bird; it is a conduit for prophecy and a witness to the fates of men. Rooted in the legacy of Odin's Huginn and Muninn, the folkloric Korp is seen as a sentinel of the boundary between life and death. These ravens are believed to be the messengers of the underworld, appearing at the site of impending tragedies to collect the souls of the fallen. They are highly intelligent and are said to remember every secret whispered in the forest, making them the most feared and respected spies of the supernatural realm

name: The Night-Walker
description: The Night-Walker (Burundian). is a spirit. A spectral night-spirit that feeds on fear and dreams in Burundi. Source: Rural Burundian Folklore Found in Open valleys and the outskirts of rural Burundian villages during the night.. Documented in ethnographic records.

name: The Pale Fox
description: The Pale Fox (Ogo, Yurugu) is a central figure in the creation mythology of the Dogon of Mali, the trickster twin who rebelled against the creator god Amma, bringing disorder, language, and divination to the world. His wanderings are mapped in the sand drawings of Dogon diviners, and Griaule and Dieterlen devoted a major study, The Pale Fox, to his myth.

name: The Rolling Cauldron
description: The Rolling Cauldron is a Jamaican magical object — a cauldron that rolls along roads and crossroads at night. It contains either treasure or a curse depending on whether one touches it. A road-spirit motif warning against greed and nocturnal travel. Part of Jamaican 'duppy' (ghost) folklore complex.

name: The Saltigue
description: Saltigue (saltigi) are the hereditary priests and priestesses of the Serer people of Senegal, guardians of the traditional religion and its pangool — the ancestral spirits and sacred forces believed to dwell in nature. They conduct rainmaking, healing, and initiation rites, preserve oral history, and maintain the ritual calendar alongside Islam in Serer communities.

name: The Tanganyika Serpent
description: The Tanganyika Serpent (Burundian). is a beast. A silver serpent guarding the depths of Lake Tanganyika in Burundi. Source: Lakeside Oral Traditions Found in The deepest benthic zones of Lake Tanganyika.. Documented in ethnographic records.

name: The Trung Sisters (Hai Bà Trưng)
description: The Trung Sisters — Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị — are Vietnam's most celebrated legendary heroines who led a rebellion against Chinese Han occupation in 40-43 CE. Daughters of a Lạc lord in Mê Linh, they were educated in martial arts and military strategy by their father. When Trưng Trắc's husband Thi Sách was executed by Han officials for plotting rebellion, the sisters raised an army of over 80,000 soldiers, many of them women led by female generals. They stormed 65 Chinese-held citadels, expelled the Han occupiers, and established an independent kingdom with Trưng Trắc as queen — a reign that lasted three years. When the Han Emperor dispatched General Ma Yuan with a massive invasion force, the sisters faced defeat. Rather than be captured, they drowned themselves in the Hát Giang River. Their sacrifice transformed them into national martyrs. Today, temples throughout Vietnam honor them as embodiments of Vietnamese resistance and the indomitable spirit of Vietnamese womanhood

name: The Tuku'uru
description: Not independently attested as a siren or sea spirit of Solomon Islands folklore. No source documents a mermaid-like guardian named 'Tuku'uru' or 'The Tuku'uru'; searches of archives, dictionaries, and scholarship return no such figure, though mermaid and fish-tail beliefs exist regionally. The entry appears to be a generic Solomon Islands sea-guardian archetype rather than a recorded being.

name: The Vao
description: Not independently attested as a ghost of Cook Islands folklore. In Cook Islands Māori, vao means 'bush' or 'wilderness' and does not name a spirit; documented spirits of the dead are tūpāpaku and the tīni, recorded by ethnographers such as Christian Clerk. 'Vao' is also the name of an island off Malekula, Vanuatu. The helpful village-ghost described is not recorded under this name.

name: Thoth
description: Thoth, the ibis-headed god of the moon, is the Egyptian lord of wisdom, writing, magic, and judgement. Scribe of the gods and arbitrator of their disputes, he stands beside Ra's solar barque and records the verdicts of the dead. His cult center was Hermopolis, and the Greeks identified him with Hermes; his name means he who is like the ibis.

name: Three Sisters
description: The Three Sisters are the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) story of corn, beans and squash as three sisters who refuse to be parted. Grown together, the corn gives the beans a pole to climb, the beans feed the soil, and the squash's broad leaves shade it — a planting that nourishes and sustains life; if separated they weaken, and in one telling must be rescued from an evil captor.

name: Three-Fingered Jack (Jamaican Outlaw Hero)
description: Three-Fingered Jack (Jack Mansong or Jack Mantong) was a legendary Jamaican outlaw and folk hero who terrorized the island in the late 18th century (c. A former slave from the western parish of Westmoreland, Jack escaped into the rugged Cockpit Country and formed a band of runaway slaves who robbed plantations, freed enslaved people, and resisted British colonial authority. His name derived from a distinctive physical feature -- he had only three fingers on one hand. Jack became a Robin Hood-like figure in Jamaican folklore, celebrated for his cunning, supernatural invulnerability, and defiance of the colonial system. He was believed to possess an obeah charm that made him bulletproof and gave him the ability to disappear into the forest. After a long campaign of terror, Jack was eventually hunted down and killed by Maroon trackers led by Quashee (or Quashie), but his legend only grew after death. His story was romanticized in 18th-century English ballads, plays, and novels, making him one of the first Caribbean folk heroes to achieve international fame

name: Thunder Beings
description: The Cherokee Thunder Beings (Aniyvdaqualosgi) are sky warriors who command thunder, lightning and life-giving rain and protect people from evil spirits. Though sometimes shown as giant birds, they are usually human in form, the children of Selu the corn mother; in some versions sons of the Great Buzzard, they shaped the mountains while the world was young.

name: Thunder Spirit
description: The Thunder Spirit is a powerful sky spirit in Blackfoot mythology, associated with storms, thunder, and lightning. According to legend, the Thunder spirit gave the Blackfoot the sacred pipe, where lightning had struck a tree and left a beautifully carved pipe. The Thunder spirit instructed the finder to form a society of pipe keepers and taught the songs and rituals for its use. Thunder is associated with the renewal of life in spring and is both feared and respected for its power to bring life-giving rain or destructive storms

name: Thunderbird
description: The Thunderbird is a powerful sky spirit of Wabanaki (Mi'kmaq, Passamaquoddy, and other Wabanaki tribes) mythology. According to tradition, the Thunderbird was once a great chief who loved his people so much that after his death, the Great Spirit transformed him into a giant bird whose wings make thunder and whose eyes flash lightning. He was given dominion over the sky and tasked with hunting the great horned serpent Weewillmekq (Jipijka'm), who lurks in lakes and devours people. The Thunderbird had a nest on the highest mountain peak and its eggs were made of solid lightning

name: Thunderbird (Chinook)
description: In Chinook tradition, Thunderbird began as a whale that Old Man South Wind cut crossways despite the ogress Quoots-hooi's warning, transforming into an immense bird whose wings hid the sun and shook the earth. Flying to Saddle Mountain near the Columbia River it laid a nest of eggs; the ogress broke them, and each egg became a Chinook person. Hence the first salmon is never cut across the back.

name: Thunderbird (Wakinyan/Animikii/Hohoq)
description: Legendary giant bird in Native American mythology—one of the most widespread and spiritually significant creatures. Creates thunder with wing-flaps and lightning from its flashing eyes or beak. Found in dozens of tribes from Pacific Northwest (Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka'wakw) to Great Plains (Lakota, Blackfoot) to Great Lakes (Ojibwe, Menominee). According to Ojibwe, created by Nanabozho to battle underwater spirits. Lakota describes Wakinyan as sacred winged grandson of sky spirit protecting humanity from horned water serpents (Unktehi)

name: Thunderbird (Wakinyan/Animikii/Hohoq)
description: Legendary giant bird in Native American mythology—one of the most widespread and spiritually significant creatures. Creates thunder with wing-flaps and lightning from its flashing eyes or beak. Found in dozens of tribes from Pacific Northwest (Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka'wakw) to Great Plains (Lakota, Blackfoot) to Great Lakes (Ojibwe, Menominee). According to Ojibwe, created by Nanabozho to battle underwater spirits. Lakota describes Wakinyan as sacred winged grandson of sky spirit protecting humanity from horned water serpents (Unktehi) In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.

name: Thunderer
description: The Thunderers (Hadiwennoda:dye's), led by Hino (Hi-nun), are the storm spirits of Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) mythology: mighty bird-men who bring thunder and rain, battle the horned serpent (Oniare) and protect humanity and the crops. In a Seneca tale Hi-nun slew a monstrous serpent in the Niagara River whose thrashing carved out Niagara Falls. They are honored with tobacco offerings.

name: Thunders
description: The Cree Thunderers are great thunderbirds (Piyesiw): immense eagles whose wing-beats roll as thunder, whose flashing eyes strike lightning, and who fight the underwater serpents. They bring the rains of summer storms and are both feared and honored as messengers between the sky world and the earth; offerings are made to keep their goodwill.

name: Thuy Tinh
description: Thuy Tinh (Unknown). is a deity. Thủy Tinh (the Water God) is a deity from Vietnamese mythology who brings annual floods in his eternal rivalry with Sơn Tinh (the Mountain God) for the love of Princess Mỵ Nương.. Source: Vietnamese mythology

name: Thạch Tinh
description: Not independently attested as a distinct Vietnamese nature spirit. No source describes a 'Thạch Tinh,' a being living in rocks and boulders that is helpful or dangerous; searches surfaced the Sơn Tinh–Thủy Tinh legend of the Mountain God versus the Sea God and unrelated game lore, but no stone-spirit entity. The figure likely blends animist beliefs about stones with a misremembered name.

name: Thủy Tinh (Water Spirit)
description: Thủy Tinh (literally 'Water Spirit' or 'Water God') is the powerful deity of waters, seas, and floods in Vietnamese mythology. In the famous legend from the Hùng King period, Thủy Tinh sought to marry the beautiful princess Mỵ Nương but lost to his rival Sơn Tinh (Mountain Spirit), who arrived first with wedding gifts. Enraged by jealousy and humiliation, Thủy Tinh summoned storms, raised the waters, and unleashed floods against the mountains to destroy Sơn Tinh and reclaim the princess. However, Sơn Tinh raised the mountains higher each time. Their eternal conflict continues annually — Thủy Tinh's floods represent the devastating monsoon rains that inundate Vietnam's Red River Delta each year. Though defeated each season, Thủy Tinh never gives up, symbolizing both the destructive power of nature and the inexorable cycle of Vietnamese geography. The myth reflects the ancient Vietnamese struggle to tame their flood-prone landscape through dikes and water management

name: Ti Malice
description: Ti Malice (Little Malice) is the Haitian trickster, a clever hare who repeatedly outwits his greedy, slow-witted uncle Bouki (hyena). Originates from Senegalese Wolof/Fulani tales (Leuk the hare, Bouki the hyena) brought via the slave trade. Manipulates Bouki's greed to steal food, wives, and status. Louisiana equivalent: Lapin and Bouki. Embodies slave resistance through wit.

name: Tibetan Snow Leopard Spirit
description: In Tibetan tradition the snow leopard is a sacred guardian of the high Himalayas, linked to the mountain and wilderness deities of Tibetan Buddhism as a spiritual protector of the highlands. Its solitary, elusive nature lends an aura of purity and spiritual insight, and deities are said to ride it or take its form. The belief reflects deep reverence for the snow leopard across the plateau.

name: Tiddalik the Frog
description: Tiddalik is a giant frog of Gunaikurnai (south-eastern Australian) Dreaming tradition who drank all the water of the world, leaving the land dry and thirsty. To break his spell, the other animals made him laugh; when he did, the waters burst from him to fill the rivers, lakes, and billabongs. His story is told as the origin of the continent's waters.

name: Tide Woman Tlingit
description: Tlingit storytellers recount how Raven made the tides, teaching the ocean to rise and fall. In the tale of how the tides began, the tide-water is kept by an old woman, in some versions Raven's grandmother, and Raven tricks her into releasing the water so the beaches can be walked and the sea fished.

name: Tidzi
description: Not independently attested in Senegalese folklore. No published source records a Senegalese bush spirit named Tidzi; searches return only Tidzi, a rural commune in Essaouira Province, Morocco, and related place names. The claim that a 'Senegalese bush spirit tests travelers' resembles the Rab spirits of Wolof and Lebou belief, but no such entity named Tidzi is documented.

name: Tie Snake
description: The Tie-Snake, also called Water Serpent or Underwater Serpent, is a water spirit of the Muscogee (Creek) and other Southeastern peoples: though the size and shape of an ordinary snake, it possesses immense strength and deadly poison, seizing humans and dragging them under to drown. Some tales describe land monsters that bite their tails and roll like hoops, akin to the Underwater Panther.

name: Tie-Snake
description: The Tie-Snake (u'lax daxgi'ilu in Natchez) is a water spirit common to Southeastern Native American folklore, documented among the Natchez and neighboring peoples. Though the size and shape of an ordinary snake, tie-snakes possess immense strength and can crush victims or drag them into the water. In a Natchez story, a Tie-Snake cut in half becomes two eels that slither away.

name: Tifon
description: No clear attestation of a demon named Tifon in Russian folk tradition; the figure appears to be a borrowing of the Greek Typhon, the storm giant, into Slavic demonology. Without primary documentation the entry cannot be verified, and no distinct Russian folk analogue is recorded.

name: Tigilau
description: A powerful Samoan chief and warrior from ancient legend, Tigilau is remembered for his strength, leadership, and exploits. In Samoan mythology, Tigilau sailed on voyages across the Pacific and was known for his encounters with supernatural beings. He is sometimes associated with the figure of Tinilau, a god or culture hero known across several Polynesian traditions. Tigilau's stories emphasize the values of Samoan chiefship - courage, wisdom, and generosity. He represents the ideal of the Samoan matai (chief) who protects his people, navigates the complexities of politics and war, and maintains the fa'a Samoa (Samoan way)

name: Tihtipihin Nuu Chah Nulth
description: Not independently attested under this name in the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) sources consulted. The input links Tihtipihin to Kwatyat, the Nuu-chah-nulth transformer of the myth age, and to the rescue of their mother; the Kwatyat cycle itself is well documented, but the brother's name requires better sourcing.

name: Tik-tik (or Wakwak)
description: Tik-tik and wakwak are names of the bird-like vampire of Philippine folklore, an aswang form that drinks blood, often attacking pregnant women and sleeping victims. It takes the shape of a large bird or can appear human, and its cry warns of its approach — a loud 'tik-tik' means it is near, a faint one far. Belief in it reinforces taboos around night travel.

name: Tikbalang (Tigbalang)
description: Tikbalang (tigbalang) is the horse-headed, human-bodied demon of Philippine folklore, a tall gaunt being whose long legs bring its knees above its head. It lures travelers in forests and mountains and makes them lose their way, though seizing its mane can bind it to service. Early Spanish accounts describe a forest phantom predating the horse; a Hindu Hayagriva origin has been proposed.

name: Tikoloshe
description: The Tikoloshe (also spelled Tokoloshe or Thokolosi) is a malevolent dwarf-like water spirit found in the folklore of the Nguni peoples of Southern Africa, including the Swazi of Eswatini, Zulu, and Xhosa. This mischievous and often dangerous creature is typically described as a small, hairy humanoid standing between half a meter to one meter tall, with grotesque features including a large head, sharp teeth, clawed fingers, and glowing eyes. According to tradition, Tikoloshe are not naturally occurring spirits but are created by witch doctors (sangomas) to harm enemies or serve their masters. They can become invisible by swallowing a pebble, allowing them to move undetected. Tikoloshe are nocturnal beings that hide under beds, cause illness, steal vitality, and create domestic chaos. Children are warned to behave lest the Tikoloshe get them. The creature reflects traditional Southern African beliefs about witchcraft, spiritual danger, and the importance of maintaining proper spiritual protection through traditional healers

name: Tikoloshe (or Tokoloshe)
description: The Tokoloshe (Tikoloshe) is a Zulu and Xhosa water spirit — a dwarf-like, hairy creature that becomes invisible by swallowing a stone or drinking water. Created by witch doctors to harm enemies, it causes illness, death, and bites sleepers' toes. Protection involves raising beds on bricks. Documented in Nguni ethnography and contemporary South African belief.

name: Tilberi
description: Tilberi (also Snakkur) is a worm-like magical creature created by women in Icelandic witchcraft traditions to steal milk from neighbors' cows. The tilberi was made from a stolen dead man's rib and grey wool, hidden between the woman's breasts and fed with stolen communion wine for three Sundays. Once created, it was sent to suckle from the woman's inner thigh, creating a wart-like mark where it fed. The tilberi would then be sent to neighbors' farms where it stretched its worm-like body to reach both teats of a cow simultaneously, drinking all the milk. It returned to its creator's dairy window crying Full magi, mamma! (Full belly, Mama!) and vomited the milk into her churn. The tilberi could be destroyed by ordering it to count lamb droppings into three piles — the number three was magical and would cause it to burst. The Museum of Icelandic Sorcery and Witchcraft in Hólmavík features the tilberi prominently

name: Timun Mas (Golden Cucumber Girl)
description: Timun Mas (Golden Cucumber) is the heroine of a popular Javanese folktale. Born from a magical cucumber given to a childless couple by the ogre-giant Buto Ijo, she was promised to the giant as his meal when she turned seventeen. As the deadline approaches, a kind hermit gives the parents four magical items: cucumber seeds, needles, salt, and shrimp paste. When Buto Ijo comes to claim her, Timun Mas flees, scattering each item behind her. The cucumber seeds transform into a dense cucumber forest, needles become a bamboo thicket, salt becomes a vast ocean, and shrimp paste becomes a boiling sea of fiery paste that consumes the giant. Timun Mas survives and lives freely, her cleverness and the gifts of nature allowing her to overcome impossible odds

name: Tin Hinan
description: Tin Hinan is the legendary ancestral queen of the Tuareg people, one of the most revered figures in Algerian and broader Saharan folklore. According to legend, Tin Hinan was a noblewoman who traveled from the Tafilalt oasis in the Atlas Mountains, leading her people across the Sahara to settle in the Hoggar Mountains of southern Algeria. Her arrival marked the beginning of the Tuareg civilization in the central Sahara. She is credited with laying the foundations for Tuareg cultural identity, including their unique matrilineal traditions, alphabet (Tifinagh), and social structures. In 1925, a 4th-century CE tomb of a wealthy woman was discovered at Abalessa in the Hoggar, which Tuareg tradition identifies as Tin Hinan's burial place. The skeleton was found with gold jewelry, Roman artifacts, and a funerary couch — evidence of her high status and the far-reaching trade networks of the ancient Sahara. Tin Hinan represents leadership, resilience, and the power of women in Saharan societies. Her legend is a founding myth for the Tuareg nation

name: Tiramakhan Traore
description: Tiramakhan Traore was Sundiata Keita's greatest general, celebrated in the Epic of Sundiata as the military mastermind who conquered the Senegambia region. After the king of Jolof insulted Sundiata by confiscating his horses and sending him ox-hides to make shoes, Tiramakhan marched his army through the Gambia River valley. The greatest battle was against King Kikikor of the Bainuk people in Kaabu (Guinea-Bissau), a powerful sorcerer who could transform into a beast. Protected by Mandinka gris-gris, Tiramakhan killed Kikikor with a spear blessed by Sundiata. Kaabu was annexed into the Mali Empire and became a Mandinka kingdom ruled by Tiramakhan's descendants — the Ñaanco dynasty — for over 600 years until 1867

name: Tirawa
description: Tirawa (Atíʼas Tirawa, 'Our Father Above') is the supreme creator god of the Pawnee people. He created the universe and placed the Morning Star in the East and the Evening Star in the West. The Morning Star, a male warrior god, was created first. The female Evening Star resisted the divine plan to create humankind, so Morning Star fought and overcame forces in the western sky to mate with her, creating the first human (a girl).
