Tirawa taught the Pawnee tattooing, fire-building, hunting, agriculture, speech, clothing, religious rituals, and sacrifice. His wife is Atira (Mother Corn), goddess of the Earth

name: Tislit n'Anzar
description: Tislit n'Anzar (the Bride of Anzar) is a mythological figure from Amazigh (Berber) folklore practiced in Tunisia and across the Maghreb. She is associated with an ancient rain-calling ritual known as Taghonja or Tagnja performed during times of drought. In the myth, Anzar is the god of rain who falls in love with a mortal woman. When she refuses him, Anzar withholds rain from the land, causing drought and suffering until the woman relents and agrees to marry him — at which point life-giving rain returns. The ritual involves creating a wooden doll shaped from a ladle or pestle (called Taghonja), dressing it in bridal clothes as Tislit, and parading it through villages while women chant prayers for rain. The doll is sprayed with water, and a ritual feast is held near a river or shrine. This ancient practice, still performed in parts of southern Tunisia (particularly Djerba and Tataouine) and Algeria, represents one of the oldest continuously practiced rain-making rituals in the Mediterranean world

name: Tiyanak
description: Tiyanak is the vampiric imp of Philippine folklore that takes the form of a crying baby in forest, field, or abandoned place, luring a rescuer to pick it up before revealing sharp claws and teeth and devouring them. Variants appear as a wizened dwarf, a flying infant, or a black bird. The legend warns against abandoned children and explains strange cries in the wild.

name: Tizan
description: Tizan (Ti-Zan, 'Little John') is the clever poor boy who outwits monsters, giants, and the mighty throughout Seychellois Creole tales, many gathered in the University of Seychelles folklore database. In stories such as 'Tizan and the Seven-Headed Monster' he wins by wit rather than strength. The input's red-eyed dwarf image better fits the soungoula; Tizan is the boy-hero, not a monster.

name: Tlaltecuhtli
description: Tlaltecuhtli, 'Earth Lord,' is the Aztec primordial earth monster, a dually sexed being with gnashing mouths at every joint. In creation myth, Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca tore her body apart in the primeval waters; her flesh became the earth, her hair the plants, her eyes the caves. She must still be fed, for her cry for human hearts underwrites Aztec sacrifice.

name: Tlanuwa
description: The Tlanuwa are giant Cherokee birds with feathers hard as metal, nesting on remote mountain cliffs where they carried off large prey, even whales in some tellings, and deflected arrows with their impenetrable plumage. Medicine men sought their feathers for power; only the great serpent Uktena could rival them, and the two were ancient enemies.

name: To-Kabinana
description: To-Kabinana is a wise culture hero and benevolent creator figure in the mythology of New Britain, Papua New Guinea. He and his foolish brother To-Karvuvu were born when an old woman scratched her arms with pandanus strips while wading in the sea, and the two bloodied strips swelled into boys. To-Kabinana created good and useful things for humanity — he climbed a coconut tree and threw two ripe coconuts downward, which burst and became his wives. He created fish, coconut trees, and beneficial customs. His stories explain the origin of many good things in the world and are central to the mythology of the coastal tribes of the Gazelle Peninsula in New Britain

name: To-Karvuvu
description: To-Karvuvu is the foolish and malicious brother in the mythology of New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Created alongside his wise brother To-Kabinana from bloodied pandanus strips, To-Karvuvu's well-intentioned but bungled attempts to imitate his brother brought evil and harmful things into the world. When he tried to create wives by throwing coconuts, he threw them point-downward, creating women with flat, ugly noses. His clumsy actions introduced cannibalism, weeds, dangerous animals, and other misfortunes to humanity. To-Karvuvu represents the archetypal foolish brother in Melanesian dualistic mythology, explaining the origin of the world's imperfections and suffering

name: Toad Boy
description: The Toad Boy is the son of Toad Woman (Machak Wuhti) in Voth's Hopi story 'The Toad and the Snow Kachinas': he lives at Katchinavala, wears a wildcat-skin robe, paints his face to watch the Snow Kachinas practice, and is teased by the children, who take him to an anthill because he likes to eat ants. He brings the red piki he begs home to his mother.

name: Toad Guardian (Udmurt)
description: Not independently attested: no toad guardian spirit appears in documented Udmurt tradition, which centers on household patrons such as korkamurt and vorshud. Toads carry folk associations with damp places and the underworld, but no specific Udmurt guardian figure is recorded.

name: Toad Water-Spirit (Bhutanese)
description: Attested in Bhutanese folk tradition as protective water spirits linked to frog/toad deities of paddy fields. Bhutanese Buddhism incorporates pre-Buddhist nature spirits (lü, klu) guarding water and agriculture. The toad spirit guards fields and irrigation, consistent with Himalayan 'lu' (naga) traditions. Specific named 'Toad Water-Spirit' not in canonical texts but fits the genre.

name: Toad Woman
description: Machak Wuhti (Toad Woman) is a Hopi figure recorded in H.R. Voth's Traditions of the Hopi: in 'The Toad and the Snow Kachinas' she lives north of Oraibi at Katchinavala with her son, the Toad Boy, preparing pikami and other food for the kachina dances. She is one of the Hopi wuhti, female mythological beings tied to springs and the earth.

name: Tobatc'istcini (Child of the Water)
description: Child of the Water (Tobadzistsini, 'Born of Water') is the younger of the two Apache Hero Twins, born of White Painted Woman with the Sun as father; together with his brother Killer of Enemies he rid the world of the monsters of the early age. In White Mountain Apache tradition he appears in the creation narrative recorded from Noze in 1910.

name: Tokoloshe
description: The tokoloshe (tikoloshe, thokolosi) is the dwarf-like water spirit of Nguni and Basotho belief, feared across Southern Africa and prominent in Eswatini, where it is a favoured agent of witches and sorcerers. Invisible to most people, it works at night causing illness, nightmares and ruin, and may be warded off by raising beds on bricks. Its mischief explains misfortune and enforces social norms.

name: Tokoloshe
description: The tokoloshe is the mischievous, water-dwelling dwarf-spirit of Zulu and Xhosa (Nguni) belief in South Africa: child-sized with an oversized head, invisible except to the supernaturally gifted. Witches and izangoma deploy it to bring misfortune, illness, nightmares or death, while people sleep with beds raised on bricks to thwart it. The belief remains widespread and explains inexplicable harm.

name: Tokoloshe
description: The tokoloshe, known in Sotho-speaking regions as the hili or thokolosi, is the water-dwelling dwarf of Basotho tradition in Lesotho, sent by sorcerers to torment their enemies. About the size of a small child with a disproportionately large head, it is invisible to most people and acts at night, bringing illness, nightmares or ruin. Families still raise bed-legs on bricks against it.

name: Tokosik
description: Not independently attested as a flying-fox spirit or cultural hero of Vanuatu folklore. No scholarly source documents a figure named 'Tokosik' who taught gardening and navigation before becoming a constellation; the only online reference is an AI-generated content site. Flying foxes hold real totemic significance in Vanuatu, but no recorded being or star-myth bears this name.

name: Tokwai (Wood Sprites)
description: Tokwai are revered and feared wood sprites of the Trobriand Islands in Papua New Guinea. These spirits inhabit massive buttressed trees, rocks, grottos, and coral outcrops. Tokwai are gifted and generous spirits who bless humans with special abilities, but they are also notorious for kidnapping fair-skinned, straight-haired babies and children. A child taken by Tokwai may be returned blessed with extraordinary gifts, or with a swollen face or disoriented mind. Morning smog from a tree was considered a sign of Tokwai presence. Before cutting a tree, islanders would ritually ask the resident Tokwai to migrate

name: Tolk (Tol)
description: Tol(y)k is the paramount sea spirit of the Nivkh of Sakhalin and the Sea of Okhotsk coast, appearing as a sea serpent or whale with scales shimmering like dark water, or as a towering humanoid rising from the sea. Mercurial and powerful, it controls the sea's bounty—generous when respected, capsizing boats when angered. Its cult reflects the centrality of sea-mammal hunting to Nivkh life.

name: Tomte
description: Tomte (Swedish), nisse (Norwegian/Danish), or tonttu (Finnish) is a household spirit from Nordic folklore — a small elderly man (60–90 cm) with white beard, red pointed cap, and grey wool clothes, dwelling under farmstead floorboards. He works at night tending livestock, protecting the farm, and expects porridge with butter at Christmas.

name: Tomte Iceland
description: Tomte Iceland (Unknown). is a household-spirit. In Icelandic tradition (akin to the Swedish tomte), the húsálfur or house spirit is a protective household spirit who watches over farms and homes. It is a small, bearded figure who brings good luck w. Source: Nordic folklore tradition

name: Tomte-Vätt
description: Tomte-vätt (or tomtevätte) is a Swedish compound meaning 'tomte-wight', conflating the household tomte with the older vættr/vätte (nature spirit). Not a distinct entity — Faye and Olrik/Ellekilde record it as a synonym for tomte/nisse, reflecting the transitional phase where nature spirits became house-wights.

name: Tonttu
description: Tonttu is the Finnish household spirit, borrowed from Swedish tomte but developing distinct identity. A small weathered man in grey wool with silver beard and pointed cap, obsidian eyes seeing through lies. Disciplined and invisible, operating in attic shadows and barn corners — felt as sudden warmth or chilling draft.

name: Tornak
description: Tuurngaq (tornak, torngak; plural tuurngait or tornat) are the helping spirits of Inuit shamanism, summoned by the angakkuq for healing, divination, weather control and spirit journeys. In Greenland they were called tornat, and East Greenlandic serving spirits were known as tartoks. Shamans kept some in doll figurines; they were the angakkuq's main source of power.

name: Totem
description: Among the Northwest Coast peoples who raised the great cedar poles — Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, and Kwakwaka'wakw — the totem is a system of clan crests: animal and spirit ancestors such as Raven, Eagle, Killer Whale, Bear, Wolf, and Beaver carved on towering monuments. Each figure records a lineage's origin story and rights, witnessed and validated at potlatches.

name: Toula (Gorou Gondi)
description: Toula (or Toulé) is a water spirit called Gorou Gondi (pond snake) from Songhay-Zarma mythology of Niger. This spirit takes the form of a water snake inhabiting ponds and tributaries of the Niger River. In traditional belief, Toula is a genie who links the human world to the spirit world. She is associated with the Do and Karou magicians responsible for the cult of water spirits. The Toula legend has been popularized through Boubou Hama's Tales and Legends of Niger and adapted into film and ballet by Anna Schoering and Moustapha Alhassane, where Toula becomes a tragic teenage heroine sacrificed to end a drought. Numerous ponds across Niger are inhabited by Gorou Gondi spirits requiring ritual offerings

name: Touni Minwi
description: Touni Minwi (Creole 'Naked at Midnight') emerged during the 1994 Cyclone Hollanda blackout. A frightful, partially clothed figure visiting homes at midnight, it triggered mass hysteria across Port Louis and Lallmatie. Linked to Lougarou (werewolf) tradition, blending French loup-garou and African spirit beliefs. Documented in Mauritian media (1994–95) as a 'social contagion' phenomenon.

name: Toxastinhn (Water-old-man)
description: Toxastinhn ('Water Old Man') is a powerful water spirit of White Mountain Apache tradition, associated with rivers, lakes and springs. He appears in narratives alongside the Hero Twins and carries the sacred power of water in Apache cosmology. The figure is documented in Pliny Earle Goddard's White Mountain Apache texts published by the American Museum of Natural History.

name: Toyol
description: The Toyol is a child-sized supernatural entity from Malay folklore, widely believed in across Singapore's multi-ethnic population. It is created by a bomoh (shaman) through black magic, typically from the corpse of a stillborn or aborted fetus, animated to serve its master as a thief. Despite its criminal function, the Toyol is childlike and mischievous rather than evil. It must be given toys, sweets, and attention, or it may turn against its master. The 1969 Singapore film 'Mat Toyol' brought the creature into popular culture

name: Toyol
description: Toyol is the child-sized supernatural thief of Malay-Indonesian folklore, created by a bomoh through black magic from the corpse of a stillborn or aborted fetus. Animated to serve its master, it slips invisibly into homes at night to steal valuables and is kept in a jar when controlled. Childlike and mischievous rather than evil, it entered popular culture in the 1969 Singapore film Mat Toyol.

name: Toyol
description: Toyol is the child-sized supernatural thief of Singapore Malay folklore, created by a bomoh through black magic, often from a stillborn or aborted fetus, to rob the wealthy. Concealed in roof spaces or dark corners of its keeper's home, it ventures out at night, invisible and swift. Belief in the toyol crosses ethnic lines in multi-ethnic Singapore and remains a living oral tradition.

name: Toyol
description: Toyol is a spirit from Singapore mythology. It is created by a bomoh (shaman) through black magic, typically from the corpse of a stillborn or aborted fetus, animated to serve its master as a thief. Despite its criminal function, the Toyol is childlike and mischievous rather than evil. It must be given toys, sweets, and attention, or it may turn against its master. The 1969 Singapore film 'Mat Toyol' brought the creature into popular culture In Singapore folklore, this figure is known among the Singapore (Multi-ethnic) people.

name: Transforming Beings
description: Not attested as a named figure: 'Transforming Beings' is a generic label, not a being in any specific tradition, and the recorded teaching role is a modern abstraction. Real Native North American shape-shifters include the Navajo skinwalker, the Athabaskan wechuge, the Algonquian wendigo, and trickster-transformers such as Coyote and Raven.

name: Trasgo
description: El Trasgo is a household and trickster spirit of Galician and wider Iberian folklore, a small mischievous shapeshifter that haunts barns, kitchens, and settlements, stealing food and playing pranks on residents. Legends recount how it may be expelled or tamed by outwitting it. It belongs to the family of Iberian domestic goblins associated with rural life.

name: Trauco
description: The Trauco is a dwarf-like forest spirit from Chilote mythology (Chiloé Archipelago, Chile). Ugly, footless, and powerfully magnetic, he seduces and impregnates women, who are considered blameless due to his irresistible allure. He carries a stone hatchet to strike trees, symbolizing potency. His wife is the equally hideous Fiura. Child of the snake god Coi Coi-Vilu.

name: Trauco del Fuego
description: Not independently attested in Chilote or Chilean tradition as a distinct 'fire variant' of the Trauco. The Trauco is a single entity; snip regional variants or 'fire forms' are not documented in primary sources. This appears to be a modern elaboration or RPG-style elemental variant with no folkloric basis.

name: Trentren
description: Trentren Vilu is the benevolent land serpent in the Mapuche flood myth, opponent of Caicai Vilu. He raises hills to save humans and animals from Caicai's flood, transforms the trapped into birds and fish, and becomes the mountain ranges walling the valley. Associated with earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Documented by Faron (1963), Bastías et al. (2021), and Mapuche oral tradition.

name: Trickster
description: Saynday, 'Old Uncle' of the Kiowa, is the great trickster of the southern plains: a crafty old man who stole the sun to warm the world and outwitted famine, flood and enemies with his schemes. In 'Saynday and Smallpox' he was himself tricked, failing to halt the disease that swept his people — a tale of cleverness meeting its limit.

name: Trickster
description: Not independently attested as a distinct figure. The source record is a generic placeholder whose description text concerns Kiowa tradition, a Native American Plains culture, while the country field says Ghana, so the record appears to have been filled by error. In Ghana the archetypal trickster is Anansi, the spider of Akan folklore, to which this entry likely refers.

name: Trickster
description: Not independently attested as a distinct figure. The source record is a generic placeholder that repeats text about Kiowa tradition while labelled Nigeria, an apparent copy-paste error. In Nigerian folklore the classic tricksters are the tortoise (Ijapa among the Yoruba, Mbe among the Igbo) and Gizo the spider in Hausa tales; no separate 'Trickster' entity exists.

name: Trickster
description: Not independently attested in Jamaican tradition. The record's description ('Important cultural figure in Kiowa tradition') refers to the Kiowa (Native American Plains people), not Jamaica. Jamaica's trickster is Anansi (Kwaku Anansi), the West African spider trickster brought via the slave trade. This entry appears to be a fabricated or garbled conflation.

name: Trickster Scorpion
description: Not independently attested in Mauritanian folklore. No scholarly or ethnographic source documents a trickster-scorpion figure; the text derives from a 2025 AI-generated folktales.africa page rather than genuine oral tradition.

name: Troll
description: Trolls are fearsome anthropomorphic beings in Norwegian folklore, ranging from massive ogrish giants (30–100+ feet, hairy, tusks, multiple eyes) to smaller mound-dwellers (haugtrold). They are nocturnal, turn to stone in sunlight, fear church bells and lightning, and live in mountains, caves, and burial mounds.

name: Troll
description: Same entity as troll-norway — Swedish troll tradition is identical, part of shared Scandinavian folklore. Trolls in Sweden dwell in mountains (Trollhättan named for them), caves, and mounds; turn to stone in sunlight; kidnap humans. Documented in Olaus Magnus's Carta Marina (1539) showing stable-working spirits, and Swedish folktale collections.

name: Troll
description: Same entity as troll-norway — Danish trold tradition is the shared Scandinavian one. Trolds are large, lumpy humanoids with rock-like skin, long noses, stone teeth; they hoard wealth, eat humans, and fear sunlight/church bells. Dwells in caves, mountains, under bridges. The Danish 'trold' is linguistically the same word.

name: Troll
description: Same entity as troll-norway — Icelandic troll tradition derives from Norwegian settlers (9th–10th c.) and shares core traits: nocturnal giants, stone-turning in sunlight, mountain/cave dwellers. Icelandic sagas (e.g., Bárðar saga Snæfellsáss) feature trolls. The duplication across four national slugs is artificial; the tradition is pan-Scandinavian with local variants.

name: Troll
description: The Troll is a pervasive anthropomorphic being of Scandinavian folklore, ranging from massive ogrish giants (30–100+ feet, hairy, tusks, flat nose, stone-grey) to smaller mound-dwelling beings (human-sized, comely, garments of moss). Nocturnal—sunlight turns them to stone; snip church bells and crosses drive them away. Live in mountains, deep forests, caves in small family units.

name: Troll (Trold)
description: Trold is the Danish spelling of troll — same entity as troll-denmark and troll-norway. This record duplicates the pan-Scandinavian troll with Danish orthography. The description (huge lumpy humanoids, rock-like skin, fear sunlight/church bells, hoard wealth) is accurate for the Danish tradition.

name: Trollkatt
description: Trollkatt (troll cat) is a magical cat-like creature in Norwegian folklore, particularly associated with witches and trolls in Vestlandet. The trollkatt can be either a gift from trolls to humans who helped them, or a familiar sent by witches to do their bidding. In Vestlandet tradition, the trollkatt is a large, coal-black cat with glowing green or red eyes. It brings either great luck or terrible misfortune depending on how it is treated. A trollkatt that is well-fed and respected will protect the farm from other supernatural beings and even increase the milk yield of cows. A mistreated trollkatt will spoil food, strangle chickens, and cause nightmares. Witches could send their trollkatt to steal milk from neighbors' cows. The only way to stop a witch's trollkatt was to strike it with a silver button or say specific prayers. Trollkatter were believed to be extremely long-lived and fiercely loyal to their owners

name: Trollkjerring
description: Trollkjerring (Norwegian: 'troll wife/witch') is a female troll figure in Norwegian folklore, a specific subtype of the broader troll tradition. She is an ugly, magical troll woman associated with high mountain peaks, known for prophecy and stone manipulation. Not a distinct species — the term specifies gender within the troll tradition.

name: Trollkjerringene på Letnesberget
description: Trollkjerringene på Letnesberget (the Troll Witches of Letnesberget) is a legend from the Fosen area of Trøndelag, documented in Birger Sivertsen's collection 'Eventyr og sagn fra Trøndelag'. The story tells of a group of trollkjerringer (female trolls/witches) who lived in the Letnesberget mountain on the Fosen peninsula. These troll witches were known for gathering on the mountain top to hold sabbats, where they would brew magic potions, cast spells on fishing boats, and dance under the full moon. They could control the weather, particularly the storms that batter the Fosen coast, and were blamed for shipwrecks and lost fishing seasons. Local farmers learned to leave offerings at the base of Letnesberget to avoid the troll witches' wrath. The legend is firmly anchored in the Fosen landscape and represents a local version of the widespread trollkjerring tradition

name: Trollkona
description: Trollkona ('troll woman') denotes the female troll of Swedish folklore, typically a mountain-dwelling being (bergatroll). The ballad 'Herr Mannelig' (Bergatrollets frieri) tells of a mountain-troll woman who courts a Christian knight with rich gifts and is refused. Female mountain spirits (bergsrå) likewise lure people into the rock, a motif known as bergtagning.

name: Trollkona
description: Trollkona (Troll Woman) is the Faroese female troll — a distinct figure in the islands' folklore appearing in legends tied to specific locations across the archipelago. On Skuvoy island, troll women were said to haunt the mountain pastures, stealing sheep and terrorizing shepherds who stayed in the mountain huts at night. The most famous trollkona legend connects her to the very geography of the islands: the island of Koltur is said to be the head of a sleeping troll woman, her body stretching beneath the sea toward Hestur. Near Sandavágur, the Trøllkonufingur (Witch's Finger) rock pillar is the petrified finger of a troll woman caught at dawn while reaching. Multiple versions of the trollkona legend appear in the Færøsk Anthologi collection, each tied to a specific village or island's landscape. The trollkona is the female counterpart to the male giant (risin) and shares the fate of petrification at dawn In Faroe Islands folklore, this figure is known among the Faroe Islands people.

name: Trollkona
description: The Trollkona is a specialized variant of the troll, possessing a mastery of 'dark craft' (svartkonst) that far exceeds that of the common troll. While typical trolls rely on brute strength, the Trollkona uses illusions, potions, and psychological manipulation to achieve her goals. She is often the matriarch of a troll clan, acting as the strategist and healer. In Swedish folklore, she is a complex figure—sometimes a cruel witch who steals children, and other times a reluctant mentor to humans who seek to learn the secrets of the earth

name: Trolls Iceland
description: Trolls Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. Trolls from Icelandic folklore are massive supernatural beings who turn to stone in sunlight.. Source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Trøldur
description: Trøldur is the Faroese form of 'troll', not a distinct entity. Faroese folklore derives from Norwegian settlers (9th c.) and shares the Scandinavian troll tradition: nocturnal mountain/sea-cliff dwellers, hostile, tricksters, turn to stone in sunlight. The Faroese 'huldufólk' (hidden people) are the local equivalent of hulder/elves, separate from trøldur. Documented in Faroese folktales (e.g.

name: Ts Uu Jaas Cedar Woman Haida
description: Ts'uu Jaas, the Cedar Woman, is a spirit of Haida tradition who is bound to the cedar tree. Cedar gave the Haida their homes, canoes, clothing, and totem poles, and Cedar Woman is honored as 'every woman's sister,' a reminder that the people and the tree live together in a relationship of use and gratitude.

name: Ts'uu Jaas (Cedar Woman)
description: Ts'uu Jaas (Cedar Woman) is a powerful SGaana Kiidads (Supernatural Being) in Haida tradition who manifests as the sacred cedar tree. She is regarded as every woman's older sister and taught the Haida people how to use cedar for clothing, shelter, canoes, baskets, and ceremonial regalia. The Haida legal framework called the Ts'uu Jaas Galang HlGaajuu (Older Cedar Sister) Framework derives from her teachings, emphasizing the interconnectedness of all life and the responsibility to care for the natural world

name: Tsagaan Üvgun
description: Tsagaan Ovgon ('White Old Man') is a Mongolian and Buryat spirit of longevity, fertility, and the wild. Depicted as a white-bearded old man with a staff, he is lord of water, animals, and the land, and is invoked for long life, good fortune, and protection of herds. He features prominently in Mongolian folk religion and Buddhist-influenced calendars.

name: Tseiqami (Thunderbird)
description: Tseiqami is the Thunderbird of Kwakwaka'wakw mythology, the man who came from the cedar tree, lord of the winter dance season: a vast supernatural bird whose wing-beats make thunder and whose eyes flash lightning, hunting whales and helping ancestral heroes raise the great cedar house beams. His younger brother is Kolus; his adversary is the undersea chief Komokwa, also called Qaniqilak.

name: Tseiqami Thunderbird Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Tseiqami is the thunderbird of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a colossal supernatural bird whose wingbeats make thunder and whose eyes flash lightning. He is master of storms and a power of the sky world, associated with the winter ceremonial realm, and his younger sibling Kolus, a downy being who sheds his coat to become human, acts as an ancestor and go-between.

name: Tsichtinako (Thought Woman)
description: Tsichtinako (Thought Woman) is the invisible guiding spirit in Acoma Pueblo creation mythology. She appeared as a voice guiding the sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti from within the earth before their emergence. As a spirit without a human body, she could not be seen. Tsichtinako instructed the sisters in all aspects of life: how to plant seeds, make prayer sticks (pahos), conduct ceremonies, and organize society into clans. She taught them that Uchtsiti (the Sun) was their creator. She established th

name: Tsilwalagame Kwakwaka Wakw
description: Tsilwalagame is the child of Dzunukwa, the Cannibal Woman of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a boy found and adopted by a human ancestor. Though half of the wild cannibal people, he was raised among humans and became the ancestor of the 'Namgis; Mungo Martin's 1953 Thunderbird Park pole shows Dzunukwa holding him.

name: Tsuchinoko
description: Tsuchinoko is a cryptid of modern Japanese folklore, a thick-bodied, snake-like creature with a stout middle, a thin tail, viper-like fangs, and potent venom. Witnesses claim it moves with a rolling or inchworm motion, can jump up to two meters, and even drinks sake. Sightings surged after the 1988 'Tsuchinoko Expedition' in Shimokitayama, Nara, where a local bounty fueled fascination.

name: Tsui-//Goab
description: Tsui-//Goab is the supreme being and creator god of the Khoikhoi people, associated with the east, the moon, and good fortune. His name means 'Wounded Knee,' stemming from his eternal battle against //Gaunab, the malevolent being who causes sickness and death. The Khoikhoi traditionally prayed at dawn facing east, offering supplications for rain and prosperity. The moon was seen as his visible manifestation, and its cycles were deeply tied to Khoikhoi religious observance. Tsui-//Goab represents the forces of life, health, and cosmic order

name: Tsukumogami
description: Tsukumogami are Japanese yōkai born from discarded household objects — combs, umbrellas, teapots, or lanterns — that gain sentience after roughly a hundred years of service. Cast-off tools take animal or human forms and turn mischievous or vengeful toward neglectful owners. On Setasubun, the eve of the spring equinox, households sweep out old implements and burn them before they can awaken.

name: Tsul 'Kalu
description: Tsul'kalu, the Slant-Eyed Giant, is the Great Lord of the Game in Cherokee tradition, owner of the wild game of the mountains and master of hunting rites. He dwells on Tanasee Bald in North Carolina at Tsunegûñ'yï; Judaculla Rock bears markings attributed to his hands. His name means 'he has them slanting.'

name: Tsunki
description: Tsunki is the primordial water spirit of the Shuar and Achuar (Jivaroan peoples, Ecuador/Peru). Appears as a beautiful woman or anaconda near remote waterfalls. Source of all shamanic power (tsentsak); snip grants crystal tsentsak to initiates. Features in myths 'The Tsunki and the Hunter' and 'Tsunki and the Chased Woman'. Documented by Perruchon (2003), Whitten (2008), Beyer (2009).

name: Tuatha Dé Danann
description: The Tuatha Dé Danann ('People of the Goddess Danu') are the pre-Christian divine race of Irish mythology, arriving with four treasures. They defeated the Fir Bolg and Fomorians, then withdrew into sídhe mounds when the Milesians invaded. Key figures: the Dagda, Lugh, the Morrígan, Brigid, Nuada, Manannán mac Lir. Documented in Lebor Gabála Érenn and the Mythological Cycle.

name: Tui Delaivugalei
description: Tui Delaivugalei is a significant Fijian deity associated with fishing, the sea, and abundance. As a sea god and guardian of fishermen, he presides over the bounty of the ocean and ensures successful catches for those who show proper respect. Offerings and rituals were traditionally made to Tui Delaivugalei before fishing expeditions, particularly important voyages to deep-sea fishing grounds. He is part of the complex pantheon of Fijian sea deities that govern the relationship between coastal communities and the ocean. His name reflects his dominion over fishing nets and the harvest of the sea, making him central to the spiritual and economic life of Fijian coastal villages

name: Tui Fiti
description: Tui Fiti ('Lord of Fiji') is the eel god of Polynesian legend, best known from the Samoan story of Sina and the Eel: a Fijian lord who, transformed into an eel, is beheaded by Sina and buried, and from whose head grows the first coconut tree. The name is also a Fijian chiefly title. The tale explains the coconut and the origins of a chiefly line.

name: Tui Manu'a
description: The Tui Manu'a is the mythical first king of the Manu'a Islands (the easternmost Samoan islands). According to Samoan legend, the Tui Manu'a was directly descended from the supreme god Tagaloa and held the highest spiritual and temporal authority in ancient Samoa. The Tui Manu'a lineage was established by Tagaloa himself, who sent the first Tui Manu'a to rule the islands. The title predates the better-known Tafa'ifa titles of Samoa and represents the oldest continuous chiefly lineage in Polynesia. The Tui Manu'a is both a historical title and a mythological figure representing the divinely ordained authority of Samoan chiefs

name: Tulafale
description: Tulafale is a ghost from Samoa folklore. Samoan ghost of an orator-chief who died without completing speeches. Haunts meeting houses, whispers unfinished oratory. Can be helpful if someone co. Oratory tradition very important in Samoa. Ghosts of failed orators remain restless

name: Tule Tree Spirit
description: The spirit of the Tule is bound to the great Ahuehuete cypress at Santa María del Tule in Oaxaca, among the stoutest trees on Earth. Zapotec tradition says it was planted by Pechocha, a priest of the wind god Ehécatl, or by the Mixe ruler Condoy, who planted it from a staff. It is revered as the living memory of the peoples, and 'so long as it lives, their memory lives.'

name: Tulisan
description: Not independently attested in documented Bruneian folklore or academic sources. 'Tulisan' is the Malay/Indonesian word for 'writing' or 'inscription,' and no source describes a Brunei forest-spirit of that name appearing as a bearded old man who knows the forest's secrets. Searches returned only generic hantu articles; the record appears to be a fabrication or conflation.

name: Tulpar
description: The tulpar is the winged horse of Kazakh and Turkic legend, a loyal steed of epic heroes who flies faster than the wind and shuttles between earth and the spirit realm. Its wings are said to be invisible by day, appearing only in darkness. Two golden tulpars adorn the national emblem of Kazakhstan, symbols of freedom, speed, and the open sky.

name: Tumatauenga
description: God of war, hunting, warfare, and human activities. Tumatauenga is the fierce son of Ranginui and Papatuanuku. After the separation of his parents, he was the one who proposed killing them rather than separating them. When his proposal was rejected, he remained silent during the debate. After the separation, when Tawhirimatea attacked all his brothers, only Tumatauenga stood his ground. He defeated all his siblings - creating snares to catch Tane's birds, nets to catch Tangaroa's fish, and digging implements to uncover Rongo and Haumia from the earth. He is the patron of humanity and all human endeavors, particularly warfare, hunting, and fighting

name: Tunche
description: The Tunche is a fearsome whistling spirit of the Peruvian Amazon (Shipibo-Conibo, Asháninka traditions). It mimics bird calls and human voices to lure travelers off paths at night. Its whistle signals approaching death. Described as a shadowy, faceless entity or a glowing presence. Fearlessness and spiritual protection (tobacco, ayahuasca) can ward it off.

name: Tunda
description: La Tunda is an Afro-Colombian/Afro-Ecuadorian shapeshifting spirit from the Pacific coastal region (Chocó, Esmeraldas). She mimics loved ones to lure victims into the forest, feeding them shrimp to induce entundamiento (docile stupor). Her disguise is flawed: she always has a wooden leg shaped like a molinillo (chocolate whisk).

name: Tunisian Ghoul
description: The ghoul of Tunisian folklore is a shape-shifting desert demon of the jinn, haunting ruins, cemeteries, and lonely roads. It appears as a beautiful woman or a hunched crone to waylay travellers, whose flesh it devours. Unlike the Western grave-robber, the Tunisian ghoul is above all a deceiver of the wilderness, warded off by iron and the name of God.

name: Tupilak
description: The Tupilaq (tupilait pl.) is an Inuit (Greenland) avenging monster fabricated by an angakkuq (shaman) from animal parts (bone, skin, hair, sinew) and sometimes human remains, given life by ritual chants. Sent into the sea to destroy a specific enemy. Risky: if the target has greater magical power, the tupilaq rebounds to kill its maker—only public confession neutralizes it.

name: Tupilaq
description: The tupilak is an avenging monster of Greenland Inuit tradition, assembled by a shaman from animal bones, corpse parts and other material and animated through song and ritual to destroy an enemy. It must return to land before dawn or dissolve into its parts; a stronger victim can turn it back on its maker, who is safe only by public confession.

name: Turquoise Boy
description: Turquoise Boy is a figure in Navajo tradition who agreed to become the Sun. When the Holy People planned the creation of the Sun and Moon, Turquoise Boy volunteered but demanded payment: the lives of all beings on earth. First Man heated turquoise on a buckskin with Black God's fire and Turquoise Boy entered it, becoming the Sun (Jóhonaa'éí, "The One Who Rules the Day"). He was given white shell, turquoise, abalone, and jet for his journey across the sky. Turquoise Boy also appears in some versi

name: Turtle
description: Turtle is a crucial animal spirit in Arapaho creation mythology. In the Flat Pipe creation story, various animals dove into the primordial waters to bring up mud—Grebe, waterfowls, Kingfisher, Otter, Beaver, Coot, Garter Snake, Black Snake, ducks, goose, crane—all failed. On the seventh dive, Turtle (along with the Creator transformed into a Red-headed Duck) succeeded in bringing up mud, which the Creator cast in four directions to form the Earth. Turtle's success made the creation of the world possible. In many Plains cultures, Turtle is honored for its role in the earth-diver creation myth

name: Turtle Ancestor-Spirit of Navajo
description: Not attested as an ancestor-spirit or desert guardian in Diné (Navajo) belief. The desert tortoise (Ch'ééh digháhii) and mud turtle (Tsisteeł) do appear in Navajo symbolism — the turtle marks the center of the earth in the Tsidił stick game, and its shell signifies perseverance — but it is not a figure in the emergence story, and no guardian role is recorded.

name: Turtle Animal-Spirit of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested in Kazakh folklore. This figure is described as a turtle animal-spirit and guardian of the cliffs, tied to forests and the Central Asian wilderness, protecting the land and teaching strength. Kazakh tradition centres on the horse, the eagle, and the wolf rather than any turtle guardian, and no source documents such a being.

name: Turtle Animal-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: Not attested: the turtle plays no part in Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) animal-spirit tradition. Their ancestor and crest beings descend from mask-removing animals such as the Seagull, Sun, Grizzly Bear and Thunderbird, and their sea spirits include Kumugwe, Sisiutl and the fish-faced Pugwis. Sea turtles are absent from their coastal myth and art.

name: Turtle Animal-Spirit of Quechua
description: Not independently attested in Quechua tradition as a named 'turtle animal-spirit guardian of swamps'. Andean cosmology includes animal spirits (apus, wak'as) but no specific turtle guardian of swamps is documented in ethnographic literature (Métraux, Urton, Salomon). The turtle appears in some origin myths but not as a distinct named entity with this role.

name: Turtle Deity of Choctaw
description: Not attested: the Choctaw record no turtle deity. Their emergence from Nanih Waiya, the Mother Mound, involves a cave and grasshoppers, and their water spirits are Okwa Naholo ('white people of the water') and the horned serpent Sinti lapitta. 'Turtle Island' appears in one recorded migration story only as a name for the continent.

name: Turtle Deity of Kwakiutl
description: Not attested: no turtle deity appears in Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) mythology or among its mountain and sea guardians. Their supernaturals — Raven the creator, Thunderbird, Kumugwe the undersea chief, and Sisiutl the three-headed serpent — contain no turtle, and turtles are rare in Northwest Coast tradition.

name: Turtle Ghost of Aztec
description: Not independently attested as a turtle ghost or ocean-guardian in Aztec folklore. No Aztec source records a spectral turtle haunting rivers. The nearest genuine figures are Cipactli and Teocipactli, primeval earth-monsters sometimes shown as crocodilian or caiman-like beings on whose back the earth rests, and the turtle-linked earth-support motif in Mesoamerican cosmography.

name: Turtle Giant of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in Baloch folklore. Baloch oral tradition (shahr, dastan) features heroes like Mir Chakar Rind, Hammal Jiand, and desert djinn (Mujna), but no turtle giants. Turtles are not prominent in arid Balochistan mythology. The record appears fabricated, possibly conflating Hindu Kurma avatar with Baloch culture.

name: Turtle Giant of Dogon
description: In Dogon cosmology the turtle carries an ancient significance tied to the structure of the world. Marcel Griaule recorded a Dogon conception in which the hexagonal plates of the turtle's shell mirror the sacred layout of the cosmos, and secondary retellings picture the earth on the back of a giant turtle beneath a sky held by four pillars. The image links land, order, and spirits.

name: Turtle Guardian of Haida
description: Not attested in Haida mythology or documented Northwest Coast sources: no turtle guardian figure appears in Haida oral tradition, clan crests or totem-pole art. Haida society is organized around the Raven and Eagle moieties, whose crests include bear, wolf, killer whale, halibut and frog rather than a turtle. The record appears derived from the Turtle Island motif of other Indigenous nations.

name: Turtle Guardian of Hopi
description: The Turtle Kachina is one of the many katsinam of Hopi tradition, spirit beings impersonated in ceremonies and carved as dolls to bring rain, health and blessings; turtle imagery in the Pueblo world carries associations of earth, longevity and protection. Museum collections document the Hopi Turtle Kachina. A specific 'guardian of lakes' role, however, is not attested in Hopi sources.

name: Turtle Nature-Spirit of Inuit
description: Not attested as a nature spirit in Inuit mythology: no turtle spirit appears in documented Inuit cosmology, which centers on figures like Sedna, the tuurngait and the Inua of sea mammals. Turtles were so rare in Arctic waters that a Baffin Island Inuit song-story records the leatherback turtle as a rare delicacy, and a Cape Dorset soapstone carving served as a training aid for young hunters.

name: Turtle Nature-Spirit of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested in Kazakh folklore. This figure is described as a turtle nature-spirit and guardian of the caves, a patient keeper of stamina and animal friendship who protects the woodlands. No documented Kazakh tradition names a cave-guarding turtle spirit, and the being appears to be a fabricated pair with the turtle animal-spirit entry.

name: Turtle Nature-Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition as a named 'turtle nature-spirit guardian of swamps'. Muisca cosmology (Bochica, Chía, Sué) centers on solar/lunar deities and culture heroes; snip animal spirits are not prominently documented as named guardians. The turtle appears in some Chibcha art but not as a distinct spirit entity with this title.

name: Turtle Spirit of Miwok
description: Turtle appears in the oral tradition of the Miwok of central California as a patient, water- and earth-associated elder figure who prevails through slow wisdom rather than strength, a role consistent with turtle tales across California and the wider Native world. The record's 'storm-calling water spirit' framing, however, is not documented in Miwok sources.

name: Turtle Trickster of Ashanti
description: Not independently attested as a central Ashanti trickster. In Akan tradition the trickster par excellence is Anansi, the spider, who wins the stories from the sky god Nyame; tortoise figures appear in some Akan tales but hold no such role. The tortoise-as-trickster is the classic figure of Yoruba and Igbo folklore in Nigeria, suggesting this entry conflates Anansi with the West African tortoise.

name: Turtle Trickster of Aymara
description: Not independently attested in Aymara tradition as a named 'turtle trickster guardian of rivers'. Aymara mythology features the trickster fox (Zorro) and culture heroes (Thunupa, Tunupa), but no turtle trickster is documented in Métraux, Bouysse-Cassagne, or Plata ethnography. Turtles are not prominent in high-altitude Altiplano mythology.

name: Turtle Trickster of Choctaw
description: In Choctaw oral tradition, turtle (Loksi) is a figure who relies on patience, a hard shell and quick wits to outsmart larger animals, a role paralleled in turtle tales across the Southeastern woodlands. Choctaw legend materials document Loksi stories. The record's 'shapeshifting trickster' framing overstates a role that sources describe as clever and persistent rather than deceptive.

name: Turtle Trickster of Miwok
description: Not attested as a shapeshifting trickster in documented Miwok sources: Miwok mythology centers on figures such as the Yayali, Lizard, Coyote and the Water-Babies, and no Miwok-specific trickster turtle appears in the folklore record. The entry appears to be a generic Native American turtle-trickster motif misassigned to the Miwok.

name: Turtle Water-Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition as a named 'turtle water-spirit guardian of hills'. Muisca water deities center on Bochica (culture hero who drained floods) and the lake goddess Sie; snip no turtle water-spirit is documented. This appears to be a generic template entry with no basis in Chibcha ethnography.

name: Turtle Water-Spirit of Tlingit
description: No turtle 'water spirit' is attested in Tlingit mythology, whose water lore centers on beings such as Gonaqadet, the Undersea Chief, and the Killer Whale. Sea turtle does appear as a clan crest in some Northwest Coast traditions, including among the Tlingit, and can be carved on totem poles. The weather-controlling guardian framing of this record is not documented.

name: Turtle Water-Spirit of Tlingit
description: No turtle 'water spirit' is attested in Tlingit mythology, whose water lore centers on beings such as Gonaqadet, the Undersea Chief, and the Killer Whale. Sea turtle does appear as a clan crest in some Northwest Coast traditions, including among the Tlingit, and can be carved on totem poles. The 'guardian of the forests' framing of this record is not documented.

name: Tusse
description: Tusse (also tuss) is a Norwegian folk-belief term for a vette, a supernatural guardian of the farmstead. In Nordland the farm vette was called tusse, alongside tuftekall, godbonde and tomte. Related is the haugtuss, a mound-dwelling being of the underjordiske who brings luck when respected and revenge when offended, as with Norwegian vetter generally.

name: Tusse
description: Tusse (also Tuss): a troll/vätte variant of Halland, Småland, and Västergötland. A shaggy trickster that leads travelers astray — 'tussen har lett honom vilse' — it is more mischievous than evil, unlike the malevolent Puke. It repays porridge offerings: a bowl under a 'tusse-sten'; if eaten, the farm was protected, if not, trouble. The name survives in place names, from Old Norse þurs (giant).

name: Tussegjeita
description: Tussegjeita (the tusse goat) is a supernatural goat owned by the tusser (underjordiske/hidden people) in Setesdal folklore. The tusser kept their own livestock, invisible to humans, but occasionally their goats would wander into human herds. A tussegjeit was distinguishable from ordinary goats by its exceptional size, beautiful coloring (often black with white spots or pure white with golden horns), and superior milk production. If a farmer could throw steel over a tussegjeit, the spell would be broken and the goat would become a normal goat that could be kept. However, keeping a tussegjeit was risky — the tusser would try to reclaim it, causing misfortune until it was returned. Tussegjeiter appear in many Setesdal legends collected by Johannes Skar

name: Tussehesten
description: Tussehesten (the tusse horse) is a supernatural horse owned by the underjordiske (tusser) in Setesdal folklore. The tusser kept their own horses, which were far superior to human horses — faster, stronger, and more beautiful. On certain nights, the tusse horses could be seen grazing in mountain pastures or running across the valley. A human who could catch and ride a tussehest would have the fastest horse in the valley. However, riding a tussehest was dangerous — if the rider did not treat it properly, the horse would carry them into a mountainside, into the tusse realm, where they would be trapped forever. The tussehest could also be borrowed if one left an offering for the tusser. The tradition appears in Johannes Skar's Gamalt or Setesdal and is related to the more widely known hestenøkken but distinct — the tussehest is not malicious by nature, simply a creature of the hidden folk that can be dangerous if mishandled

name: Tussepresten
description: Tussepresten (the tusse priest) is a unique figure in Setesdal folklore — the priest of the underjordiske (tusser/hidden people). According to Setesdal tradition, the tusser were not purely pagan but had their own Christian-like religion with their own priest who held rival church services in the valley. The Tusseprest competed with the human priest of Valle church for the souls of the valley. If the human priest rang the church bells too early or too late, the Tusseprest would steal the prayers of the congregation. The Tusseprest held services inside mountains, where the tusser worshipped. Humans who accidentally wandered into a tusse church service would find themselves trapped in an alternative world where time moved differently. The Tusseprest tradition is unique to Setesdal among Norwegian regions — in other parts of Norway, the underjordiske were considered purely pagan. This reflects Setesdal's distinctive theological folk belief where the hidden people were partially Christianized

name: Tuyul
description: Tuyul is the money-stealing child spirit of Indonesian folklore, a small bald pale humanoid in a loincloth, often greenish-skinned and pointed-eared, able to scale walls. It slips invisibly into homes to carry money to its keeper in exchange for food and care, and can be thwarted by scattered seeds or beans it stops to count. The legend satirizes greed and the craving for easy wealth.

name: Twin War Gods
description: The Twin War Gods, also called the Little War Gods or Hero Twins, are the twin culture heroes of the Pueblo peoples, sons of the Sun who led the people from the underworld and cleared the world of monsters. Among the Zuni they are Ahaiyuta and Matsailema; at Isleta the Keresan twins Máw-Sahv and Oó-yah-wee wield the rainbow as a bow and lightning as arrows.

name: Tzitzimimeh
description: AZTEC STAR DEMONS — terrifying skeletal female deities who were enemies of the sun itself, poised to descend from the heavens and devour humanity during solar eclipses. In Aztec cosmology, the Tzitzimimeh were star spirits associated with darkness, infertility, and the chaotic forces that threatened cosmic order. They were led by the goddess Tlaitecuhtli (or sometimes Citlalicue) and were particularly feared during solar eclipses, when it was believed the demons would descend to earth to consume humans — especially children. Pregnant women were at particular risk, as the Tzitzimimeh were said to transform unborn children into monstrous beings. To ward them off, the Aztecs performed elaborate rituals, including human sacrifice, during eclipses. The arrival of Hernán Cortés and the Spanish conquistadors was interpreted by some as the fulfillment of Tzitzimimeh prophecies — the end of the Fifth Sun. In contemporary Mexican and Mexican-American folklore, Tzitzimimeh survive as a powerful metaphor for apocalypse and existential dread, sometimes appearing in Chicano art and literature as symbols of cosmic destruction and rebirth

name: Táltos
description: Táltos is the shaman-healer of Hungarian folklore, a person marked at birth by extra teeth or fingers, a caul, or premature speech, who gains supernatural knowledge, communicates with spirits, and heals the sick. The táltos could shapeshift into animals and duel rival shamans. Documented by folklorist Éva Pócs, the figure links Hungarian belief to Eurasian shamanic traditions.

name: Tây
description: Tà yêu (recorded as 'Tây') is a Vietnamese folk term for a harmful wandering spirit, part of the demonic class of Vietnamese folk religion alongside ma (ghosts) and quỷ (demons). The record describes the tà yêu as the spirit of a foreigner who died abroad, haunting crossroads, borders, and sites of death, often confused and lost. The belief ties to ancestor worship and proper burial.

name: Tééhoołtsódii (Big Water Creature)
description: Tééhoołtsódii (Big Water Creature) is a powerful water spirit in Navajo mythology who inhabits the deep rivers, springs, and underground waterways of the Navajo homeland. He is one of the underwater pantheon and is associated with the element of water itself. Tééhoołtsódii can bring abundance through flooding and irrigation or destruction through flash floods, and he is appeased through offerings of corn pollen and prayer sticks placed at the water's edge. He is particularly important during the Way of the Sacred Spring, a major healing ceremony that channels the purifying power of water

name: Tāne Mahuta
description: Tāne Mahuta is the Māori god of forests and birds, the son of Ranginui (Sky Father) and Papatūānuku (Earth Mother) who forced the two apart to let light into the world. He clothed his mother's body with trees and creatures, fathered the birds and insects, and created the first woman Hineahuone. The famous kauri tree Tāne Mahuta in Waipoua Forest bears his name.

name: Tāwhaki
description: Tāwhaki is a semi-divine hero and atua of lightning and thunder in Māori tradition, a grandson of the sky who slew the man-eating bird-ogre Matuku-tangotango, freed his kinswoman Whaitiri from its belly, and climbed to the heavens, returning with the powers of lightning and thunder. He is closely linked to sacred mountains, and he is said to appear to heroes in disguise to test their worth.

name: Uab (Chuab)
description: Uab is the culture-hero giant of Palauan creation narratives, whose vast body is said to have formed the archipelago and whose appetite reshaped the land. In the founding story he gorged until his body swelled, and when bamboo shavings cut his flesh, his blood and scattered body parts created the geography of Palau. He holds the generative power of the earth in Palauan origin lore.

name: Uay Chivo
description: The Huay Chivo, 'sorcerer goat' in Yucatec Maya (waay, 'sorcerer'; chivo, 'goat'), is a shapeshifting sorcerer of the Yucatán who becomes a black goat with burning red eyes. He haunts roads and villages at night, raiding milk, harming livestock, and frightening travelers, and his presence is blamed for sudden illness and misfortune. He links closely to chupacabras and nahual traditions.

name: Uchtsiti (Sun Father)
description: Uchtsiti (Sun Father) is the supreme creator deity in Acoma Pueblo tradition. He created the world from a clot of his own blood and created Tsichtinako to guide the first beings. Uchtsiti is the father of Iatiku and Nautsiti, and through them all of creation. He is associated with light, life, and the generative masculine principle. He instructed that the world must be completed by the sisters. Uchtsiti represents the ultimate source of life and the creative power that exists at the center of Pu

name: Ukko
description: Ukko is the supreme sky god of pre-Christian Finnish religion, ruler of thunder, rain, and harvest. He strikes his hammer Ukonvasara to create lightning; his cult centered on spring festivals (Ukon vakat) with communal drinking and offerings. In the Kalevala he appears as father of Väinämöinen and judge of Marjatta's son. Documented by Agricola (1551), Ganander, and in runic songs.

name: Uksáhkká
description: Uksáhkká (Door Woman) is the Sami goddess who lives under the door of the goahti (traditional Sami tent). She is one of the three daughters of Máttaráhkká, alongside Sáráhkká and Juoksáhkká. Her domain is the threshold — the boundary between the inside and outside world. She protects people entering and leaving the dwelling, receives the newborn child into the world during birth (the moment it crosses from the womb into the world through the door of the goahti), and protects children as they learn to walk, preventing falls, injuries, and getting lost. Offerings of drinks were poured under the door for her. She was known only among Scandinavian Sami (Norway and Sweden), not among Finnish or Russian Sami. Christian influence equated her with the Virgin Mary

name: Uktena
description: The Uktena is the great horned serpent of Cherokee tradition, its body thick as a tree trunk, with glistening scales, branching horns, and a single blazing crystal, Ulûñsû'tï ('Transparent'), on its forehead. Invulnerable save at the seventh spot from its head, it hides in deep pools and lonely mountain passes; the Little People once changed a man into such a snake to kill the angry Sun.

name: Uku
description: Uku (also called Uguku, Tsgili, or Skili in Cherokee) is the Great Horned Owl, considered the most powerful and feared owl in Cherokee spiritual tradition. The Cherokee language uses the same word, skili or tsgili, for both the great horned owl and witch, reflecting the deep association between these night creatures and dark spiritual forces. The great horned owl was the most dreaded of the three owls named in Cherokee lore. Its cry was considered an omen of death or misfortune, and it was believed that evil spirits, ghosts, and witches could appear in the body of an owl. Only medicine men could tell the difference between a real owl and an evil witch disguised as one. Cherokee medicine men would invoke the black owl in certain powerful formulas for malevolent purposes

name: Ulda
description: The Ulda (also called Gufihtar, from Old Norse gud vätte 'good underground being') are a mythical race of underground people in Sami folklore. They live inside fells and beneath the earth in a parallel world called Saivo. They are rich, beautiful, well-dressed, and possess all gold and silver under the earth, including hidden treasure. Their reindeer are of exceptional colors and leave no tracks in snow. Tradition says you can claim an Ulda reindeer herd by throwing a metal object over it. They sometimes swap their children for human babies (changelings). If a human eats or drinks in the Ulda world, they must stay forever and become one of them. The Ulda care for the bear in its winter den, feeding it invisibly. They are described as semi-human 'co-dwellers' rather than purely supernatural beings. Some Sami traditions describe them as having foreknowledge of technology — stories tell of humans visiting the Ulda world and seeing radios, telephones, and other inventions long before they existed in the human world

name: UlIman
description: Not independently attested as a distinct ghost of Kyrgyz folklore. No source confirms a water-spirit named 'Uliman' haunting burial sites, ruins, or battlefields; Kyrgyz demonology includes jinn-like beings and hostile spirits, but no figure by this name appears in ethnographic records. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Ulu-ulan
description: Not independently attested as a distinct spirit of Mongolian folklore. No source confirms a vampiric being called 'Ulu Ulan' who protects or blesses; Mongolian tradition's red deity of war is Daichi Tengri, and no 'Ulu Ulan' appears in shamanic or epic sources. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Um Al Duwais
description: Um Al Duwais ('mother of the little one') is a seductive jinniyyah of Gulf folklore, appearing as a beautiful woman in a flowing black abaya who lures men into the desert with promises of companionship, then kills them; her presence is announced by sweet perfume. In Kuwait and Qatar she is also known as Umm Ghannan, and her tale ranks among the most vivid Gulf ghost stories.

name: Um El Sa'af Wel Leef
description: Um El Sa'af Wel Leef ('Mother of Palm Leaves and Fiber') is a tree spirit of Bahraini folklore who dwells behind palm trees in the darkness, her name drawn from the palm fronds (sa'af) and palm fiber (leef) of date cultivation. Parents invoke her to warn children against wandering into palm plantations alone or staying out after dark.

name: Um Hmaar
description: Um Hmaar (Mother of Donkeys) is a legendary half-woman, half-donkey jinn from Bahraini folklore who preys on children who venture outside at noon. She is described as having the upper body of a woman and the lower body of a donkey, with hooves that make a distinctive sound as she walks through neighborhood streets at midday. Dressed all in black, Um Hmaar knocks on doors while parents take their afternoon naps, begging for food or water. If children open the door, she devours them. Her tell-tale sign is the clopping of her hooves, which sends children fleeing in fear. In some versions, she can transform into a lizard to climb walls and enter homes. The story of Um Hmaar has been adapted into comics and children's books in modern Bahrain, including Zainab Almahdi's illustrated comic 'Um Hmaar Returns!' set in 1960s Bahrain

name: Um Homar
description: Um Homar ('mother of the donkey'), or Homarat al-Guyla, is a Qatari noon-demon: a terrifying half-woman, half-donkey creature said to prey on children who wander outdoors at midday. Parents keep children indoors at noon and invoke her to enforce it. She personifies the dangers of the sun-scorched hours in desert village life and remains a living cautionary tale.

name: Umibangad
description: Not independently attested in documented Philippine folklore; searches locate no omen bird called 'Umibangad.' The recorded huge, owl-like night bird whose cry heralds death or disaster fits the attested Philippine omen-bird tradition of the tigmamanukan, whose song foretells fortune, and the owl-like kulawo, but no entity bears this name.

name: Umm Al Duwais
description: Umm Al Duwais ('Mother of the Toes') is a female jinn of Gulf Arab folklore, celebrated in Emirati and Bahraini tradition. She appears as a beautiful, perfumed woman who lures men near deserted places, then turns monstrous. Her legend is recorded in Gulf oral tradition and has inspired modern films and retellings. This entry duplicates the United Arab Emirates variant of the same figure.

name: Umm Al Duwais
description: Umm Al Duwais ('Mother of the Toes') is the best-known female jinn of Emirati folklore, rooted in Bedouin oral tradition. She appears as a beautiful woman in gold and perfume who approaches men straying after dark near abandoned buildings, date groves, or desert roads, charms them, then reveals her monstrous form. The 2013 film 'Djinn' (Tobe Hooper) drew on the legend.

name: Umm Al Duwais
description: Umm Al Duwais is the seductive, deadly jinniyyah of Emirati folklore: a stunningly beautiful woman in rich silks and gold whose feet are donkey hooves. Appearing in the desert or near abandoned houses, she captivates men with perfume and beauty and kills them with a single touch. The tale warns against surface beauty and unguarded desire in Emirati oral tradition.

name: Umm Al-Subyan
description: Umm al-Subyan ('mother of children') is a child-snatching jinniyyah of Arab folk belief, feared especially in the first forty days after birth, when protective amulets naming her are hung on newborns and mothers. A Yemeni mountain variant is a female jinn with one goat's leg and one donkey's leg and a long breast slung over her shoulder, who appears in the hills and can take any shape.

name: Umvelinqangi
description: Umvelinqangi (Unknown). is a deity. uMvelinqangi is the supreme creator god in Zulu cosmology. He is the sky deity who created the earth and humankind, and is associated with the origin of the Zulu people.. Source: Zulu oral tradition; South African mythology

name: Undead Army Iceland
description: Undead Army Iceland (Unknown). is a spirit. An undead army from Icelandic saga tradition is a host of reanimated warriors from burial mounds.. Source: Icelandic folklore — undead warriors documented in Icelandic sagas.

name: Underjordiske
description: Underjordiske (the underground/hidden people) is a collective term in Norwegian folklore for the various supernatural beings who live beneath the earth or inside mountains and hills. This category includes huldrefolk, haugfolk, tusser, and other hidden beings. The underjordiske live in a parallel world that mirrors human society - they farm, fish, trade, marry, have children, and hold celebrations. They are usually invisible but can choose to reveal themselves. They are known for their beauty, wealth, and magical abilities. They keep a close watch on human behavior and reward or punish accordingly. The term is most common in Western and Northern Norway. Believed to be the descendants of angels who were cast out of heaven (Christian influence) or the spirits of pre-Christian ancestors

name: Undersea Chief Haida
description: The Undersea Chief is the ruler of the ocean's wealth in the traditions of the Northwest Coast, master of salmon, halibut, and other sea creatures that sustain human life. While the Kwakwaka'wakw name him Komokwa and place him in a copper house beneath the sea, the Haida tell of their own masters of the undersea villages.

name: Underworld God
description: This entry is a generic archetype label rather than a single attested figure; within the database's Mediterranean frame its concrete referent is the Greek underworld deity Hades (Plouton), ruler of the realm of the dead. Hades appears throughout Homer, Hesiod, and classical literature, judging the dead and guarding the riches of the earth.

name: Undine
description: Undines are water elementals introduced by Paracelsus in A Book on Nymphs (1566), named from Latin unda ('wave') and classed among the four elemental spirits alongside gnomes, sylphs, and salamanders. Said to lack an immortal soul, they could gain one by marrying a mortal — a motif that inspired Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué's novella Undine (1811) and later the Little Mermaid tradition.

name: Unhcegila
description: Unhcegila (Unk Cekula) is a gigantic serpentoid creature from Lakota mythology responsible for many unexplained disappearances and deaths. Described as a massive dragon-like serpent with impenetrable scales, eyes of fire, and a fanged mouth shrouded in smoke or cloud. Her only weakness was a seventh spot on her body where her heart lay burning within. She emerged from primordial waters, was fought by the Thunderbird Wakinyan, and her shattered bones became the Badlands. Various heroes—a Bear Clan warrior guided by Weasel, or two brothers with medicine arrows—defeated her by cutting their way out from inside or striking her heart spot

name: Unktehi
description: Unktehi is the great horned water serpent of Lakota tradition, a dragon of the deep lakes and rivers that rises in storms to battle the Thunderbirds for mastery of the sky. When enraged it brings floods and earthquakes, rolling the waters over the land, and it plays a central part in Lakota accounts of the great flood.

name: Unkulunkulu
description: Unkulunkulu ('Old Old One') is the supreme creator god and first ancestor of the Zulu people. He emerged from the primordial reed Uthlanga, bringing humanity, cattle, and all life into existence. He created the sun and moon by flinging fire and a glowing stone into the sky, and established death when the slow chameleon lost the race against the swift lizard carrying the message of immortality. Unkulunkulu is a distant, deistic creator who set the world in motion then withdrew, leaving the ancestors (amadlozi) as intermediaries

name: Upior
description: Upior (upiór) is the Polish name for a Slavic vampire, the restless dead who rises from the grave at night to drain the blood of the living. The term entered Slavic tradition early and is likely the root of the modern word vampire; folk remedies included decapitation, staking, poppy seeds in the coffin, and burial face down.

name: Upiór
description: Upir is an archaic Slavic term for a vampire or revenant, documented in early Polish and Russian written sources and possibly the origin of the word vampire in European languages. The upir is the dead who returns to harm kin and livestock, and folk tradition prescribed ritual safeguards at burial, including stakes and protective grain.

name: Upyr
description: Upyr is the Russian and Ukrainian form of the Slavic vampire, a corpse that rises at night to drink blood and spread death among its former community. Belief in the upyr is recorded in early chronicles and folk medicine, with protective customs including burial in red cloth, iron objects, and scattered poppies to distract the undead.

name: Ursitoare
description: Ursitoare are the fate-spirits of Romanian and Moldovan folklore, three women who appear on the third night after a child's birth to decide and prophesy its destiny, much like the Greek Moirai. Their pronouncements, made in secret, fix the newborn's fortune and cannot be altered. Offerings and prayers sought their favor, tying the figure to rites of birth and family protection.

name: Urðarköttur
description: Urðarköttur (Ghoul Cat or Corpse Cat) is a monstrous feline in Icelandic folklore that grows from feral cats or white kittens born with their eyes open. According to tradition, any cat that goes completely feral will eventually become an urðarköttur. White kittens born with their eyes already open sink into the ground immediately after birth and re-emerge after three years as an urðarköttur. The creature grows to the size of an ox, has shaggy white or black fur, and kills indiscriminately. It has a particular taste for corpses and digs up graves in churchyards to eat the dead. Some folklorists believe the Yule Cat (Jólakötturinn) is actually an urðarköttur that became associated with Christmas tradition. The urðarköttur is found in Jón Árnason's folklore collection and represents the deep-seated fear of cats combined with the desecration of graves

name: Utburd
description: Utburd (also called utbør, utburðr) is the haunting spirit of an abandoned or murdered infant in Norwegian folklore. In pre-Christian and early Christian Norway, unwanted children - especially those born out of wedlock - were sometimes abandoned in the wilderness to die of exposure, a practice called utburd. The spirit of such an infant was believed to return as a terrifying ghost that haunted the area where it died. The utburd was considered particularly dangerous because the unbaptized soul could not find peace. The spirit would cry out at night and attack travelers, sometimes sitting on their shoulders or riding their backs, growing heavier until they collapsed. Most stories come from the coastal regions of Western and Northern Norway

name: Uthixo
description: Uthixo (Unknown). is a deity. uThixo is the supreme being in Xhosa cosmology, the creator of the universe and humanity. The name has been adopted for the Christian God in Xhosa-language Bibles.. Source: Xhosa oral tradition

name: Utlat (Carthaginian Netherworld Spirits)
description: Not independently attested in Carthaginian folklore or religion. No Punic or Carthaginian source records spirits called 'Utlat'; the name is not a Carthaginian term, and the entry wraps real tophet facts around an invented spirit class.

name: Utrøst-folket
description: Utrøst-folket (the people of Utrøst) are a hidden folk who live on the legendary sunken island of Utrøst off the coast of Vestlandet. Utrøst is a fairy island that appears only to the pious or those with second sight — a paradise with golden barley fields, green pastures, and goats with golden horns. The inhabitants are a peaceful hidden people who farm, fish, and live in prosperity, untouched by storms and misfortune. When fishermen find seaweed or straw on their boat rudders after a storm, they say they have sailed over Utrøst. The most famous legend is Asbjørnsen and Moe's The Cormorants of Utrøst, where a poor fisherman is invited to the island and warned not to eat the fat of the land. Utrøst represents the Celtic/Norse tradition of fairy islands, similar to Hy Brasil

name: Valraven
description: Valraven (Unknown). is a undead. The Valraven is a mythical raven creature from Nordic folklore, an omen bird associated with the dead and supernatural forces in legend.. Source: Danish folklore — undead figure documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Valravn
description: Valravnen (the Raven of the Slain) is a supernatural raven in Danish medieval ballads and folklore. According to legend, a knight who died unshriven or a person who committed terrible acts could be transformed into a Valravn. The Valravn possesses human intelligence, speaks in human tongues, and has supernatural powers. Its curse can be broken if it drinks the blood of an infant three days old. In Danish ballads (9 versions collected by Svend Grundtvig), the Valravn appears as a talking raven who bargains with humans, demands sacrifices, and reveals secrets. A separate folk tradition holds that if a raven eats the heart of a slain king on the battlefield, it becomes a Valravn with the wisdom and power of the dead king. The Valravn is distinct from the Natravn — it is actively malevolent and intelligent, not merely a damned soul

name: Vampir
description: Vampir is the Serbian vampire — the etymological root of the English word 'vampire'. An animated corpse rising from the grave at night to drink blood of the living. Created by suicide, excommunication, caul birth, or animal jumping over corpse. The 18th-century cases of Petar Blagojevich and Arnold Paole sparked the European vampire controversy. Warded by garlic, crosses, holy water.

name: Vampire
description: Vampire (Generic). is a vampire. Undead beings that subsist by feeding on the life essence of the living, often characterized by immortality and charm. Source: Global folklore, Balkan traditions

name: Varulv
description: Den svenska varulven (the Swedish werewolf) differs from continental European werewolf legends in several ways. Swedish varulvar were often not voluntary shapeshifters but people born under a curse — those born with a 'vargbälte' (wolf belt, a caul) were doomed to become werewolves. Alternately, a person could become a varulv by putting on a wolfskin belt or reciting certain formulas. Unlike the uncontrollable ravaging werewolf of continental folklore, the Swedish varulv often retained human reason and could be bargained with. Harming the wolf form caused corresponding injury to the human. The varulv was especially feared in Skåne and Småland, where many legends tell of hunters shooting a wolf only to find a neighbor wounded the next day

name: Varulv
description: Den danske varulv (the Danish werewolf) has a unique origin not found in other countries: if a pregnant woman crawls through a horse's afterbirth to ease her labor pains, a son will become a werewolf and a daughter will become a mare (nightmare spirit). The Danish varulv is always male and transforms at sunset, his human soul replaced by a wolf's savage nature. Unlike continental werewolves, the Danish varulv does not require a full moon or a wolfskin belt — the curse is carried in the blood from birth. Salvation is uniquely Danish: if the werewolf is cornered and someone says 'Du er ikke varulv længere' ('You are no longer a werewolf'), the curse is broken forever. The famous Danish ballad 'Liden Kirsten' tells of a werewolf attack outside Vestervig Church in Thy, one of the earliest documented Danish werewolf legends

name: Vasuki (King of Serpents)
description: Vasuki is the king of the nagas (serpent beings) in Hindu mythology and one of the most important serpent deities. He is best known for his role in the Samudra Manthana (the churning of the Ocean of Milk), where he served as the churning rope wrapped around Mount Mandara. The devas (gods) held Vasuki's tail while the asuras (demons) held his head, and as they pulled him back and forth, he released a tremendous amount of venom and fire. The poison was so potent it threatened to destroy all creation, forcing Shiva to consume it (turning his throat blue, earning him the name Nilakantha). Vasuki wears the nishagandha jewel on his head and is associated with wealth, protection, and fertility. He is considered a devotee of Shiva, who wears him as an ornament around his neck. In some traditions, Vasuki is one of the eight serpent kings (Ashta Nagas) who rule the underworld realm of Patala

name: Verdalsdraugen
description: Verdalsdraugen (the Verdal Draug) is a sea draug specific to the Verdal area at the northern end of the Trondheimsfjord. The draug is a malevolent undead being from Norwegian folklore, and the Verdalsdraugen is a localized version haunting the Verdal coast and the lower reaches of the Verdalselva river. According to local tradition, the Verdalsdraugen is the ghost of a drowned fisherman who now appears to warn of approaching storms and shipwrecks. He is most often seen sitting on the rocks at the mouth of the Verdalselva, wearing oilskins and a sou'wester hat, with seaweed hanging from his clothes. If a boat passes too close, the draug will grab its gunwale and try to pull it under. However, if you write your name on a piece of wood and throw it to him, he will release the boat and leave you alone. The Verdalsdraugen is part of the rich coastal folklore of the Trondheimsfjord region

name: Veshtitza
description: Veshtitza is a Montenegrin witch-vampire whose soul leaves her body at night in the form of a black hen or moth to scout homes with children. She returns to drain blood and consume hearts. By day she appears as an ordinary woman. A South Slavic variant of the striga/shtriga, blending witch and vampire traits. Feared as a night predator of infants.

name: Vetal
description: Vetal is the Sri Lankan form of the vetala, a corpse-inhabiting spirit from Indian tradition that spread with Buddhism. It dwells in cremation grounds and ancient trees (tamarind, baobab), animating corpses to move. Known for posing riddles and knowing past, present, and future. Can be helpful or dangerous. The Vetala Panchavimshati (25 tales) is known in Sri Lanka as folk tradition.

name: Vetala
description: Vetala (Sanskrit: वेताल) are corpse-inhabiting spirits in Hindu mythology who animate dead bodies (often feet-forward) and dwell in cremation grounds and tamarind/baobab trees. They possess uncanny knowledge of past, present, and future, and delight in riddles. The Vetala Panchavimshati features King Vikramaditya capturing a vetala who tells stories ending in riddles.

name: Vette
