description: Vette (feminine: vetta, plural: vetter, from Old Norse vættr meaning wight/spirit) is a general term in Norwegian folklore for nature spirits and supernatural beings. The vetter are guardian spirits of specific natural places - forests, lakes, rivers, mountains, rocks, and farm buildings. The concept is related to the Old Norse landvættir (land spirits) who protected the land itself. In Norwegian folk belief, every place had its own vette - the skogsvette (forest spirit), vannvette (water spirit), fjellvette (mountain spirit), and husvette (house spirit). Vetter could be benevolent if respected but dangerous if offended. Making offerings at sacred trees, rocks, or waterfalls was a way to maintain good relations with the local vette. The word vette appears in the common phrase vetter og skrømt (spirits and ghosts)

name: Vetāla
description: Vetāla is the diacritically-marked Sanskrit form of vetala (slug: vetala), not a distinct entity. This record duplicates vetala with near-identical data. In Sanskrit texts, vetāla inhabits corpses and trees (baobab/tamarind), knows past/present/future, and features in the Vetala Panchavimshati. The record's 'benevolent' behavior tag is atypical — vetalas are morally ambivalent.

name: Veyis Baba
description: Veyis Baba is the protective spirit (iye) of camels in Turkmen mythology and folklore. Originally based on the historical figure Veysel Karani, a Yemeni Muslim camel herder known for his love of the Prophet Muhammad, Veyis Baba became the mythological guardian of camels among Turkmen and other Turkic peoples. In Turkmen culture, where camels were essential to nomadic life in the Karakum Desert, Veyis Baba is revered as the patron who protects camel herds from disease, predators, and misfortune. Camel herders make offerings and prayers to Veyis Baba before long journeys. The camel itself is a mythological animal in Turkmen culture, symbolizing prosperity, endurance, and the nomadic way of life

name: Viejito del Monte
description: El Viejo del Monte, the 'Old Man of the Forest' (Kiwíkgolo in Miskito), is the ghost of a tireless hunter punished by becoming a shaggy giant with a single eye who now defends the animals of the Nicaraguan bush. He rules over deer and game, thunder and rain, and can ride as a monstrous horseman; hunters must ask his leave before taking any of his creatures.

name: Vila
description: The Vila (plural Vile) are beautiful female nature spirits of South Slavic mythology, deeply embedded in Montenegrin folklore. They are described as eternally young maidens with pale cheeks, long flowing hair, dressed in white, with invisible wings enabling them to fly through the air. There are three kinds: land and forest Vile (zagorkinje/pozemne vile), water nymphs (brodarice/povodne vile), and cloud spirits (vile oblakinje). In Montenegro's rugged mountain landscape, Vile are particularly associated with mountain peaks, springs, and forests. They dance in circles (vilino kolo), ride horses or stags, and possess supernatural healing abilities. They can be both benevolent protectors of heroes and dangerous beings who lure men to their death

name: Vila
description: Vila is a spirit from South Slavic / Illyrian-influenced Mythology mythology. They are described as eternally young maidens with pale cheeks, long flowing hair, dressed in white, with invisible wings enabling them to fly through the air. There are three kinds: land and forest Vile (zagorkinje/pozemne vile), water nymphs (brodarice/povodne vile), and cloud spirits (vile oblakinje). In Montenegro's rugged mountain landscape, Vile are particularly associated with mountain peaks, springs, and forests. They dance in circles (vilino kolo), ride horses or stags, and possess supernatural healing abilities. They can be both benevolent protectors of heroes and dangerous beings who lure men to their death

description: Vila is a spirit from Slavic mythology. They can be both benevolent protectors of heroes and dangerous beings who lure men to their death In Montenegro folklore, this figure is known among the Montenegrin (South Slavic) people.

name: Vindrå
description: The Vindrå is the ethereal spirit of the wind, a volatile and invisible entity that governs the currents of the air. Unlike the grounded rån, the Vindrå is an entity of pure movement and change. In Swedish lore, the Vindrå is responsible for the sudden gusts that blow out candles or the gentle breezes that carry scents from distant lands. She is often sought after by sailors and farmers who wish to influence the wind for their own benefit, though she is notoriously fickle and demands unusual offerings in exchange for her cooperation

name: Vinmara
description: Vinmara (also called Ro-Lei) is a sky maiden from Vanuatu mythology, particularly in the Banks Islands. According to legend, Qat discovered a group of sky maidens who had removed their wings to bathe. He buried one pair of wings, forcing Vinmara to remain behind on earth. She became Qat's wife and was called Ro-Lei. They lived happily until Qat's mother reproached her daughter-in-law, making her cry. Vinmara's tears washed away the earth covering her wings; she put them on and flew back to the sky. When Qat tried to follow, he fell to his death. Vinmara represents the swan maiden archetype found throughout Oceania, where celestial beings are briefly united with humans before returning to their realm

name: Vishap
description: Vishap is the Armenian dragon — a winged serpentine creature closely associated with water (lakes, rivers, mountain springs). Dwelling on Mount Ararat, it causes thunderstorms, whirlwinds, and eclipses by ascending/descending. It steals children, replacing them with evil spirits. Vishap fought Vahagn the Dragon Slayer; a statue of Vahagn slaying Vishap stands in Yerevan.

name: Vishnu
description: Vishnu is a major Hindu deity (not a folklore creature), one of the Trimurti as Preserver. He reclines on the cosmic serpent Shesha in the Ocean of Milk and takes avatars (Rama, Krishna, Narasimha) to restore dharma. Classifying him as a 'water spirit' and 'mythical creature' is a category error — he is a supreme deity in Vedic and Puranic theology.

name: Vitorm
description: Vitormen (the white snake) is a magical serpent in Swedish folklore that guards hidden treasures beneath ancient rune stones, burial mounds, and Viking-age monuments. The Vitorm is distinguished by its pure white or pale golden color and is far larger than ordinary snakes. According to tradition, whoever manages to kill and eat a Vitorm gains supernatural wisdom: the ability to understand the language of animals, insight into hidden things, and knowledge of healing herbs. The white snake's shed skin (vitormsömsk) has protective powers — carrying it wards off evil and brings good luck. The Vitorm cannot be killed by ordinary means; it must be struck with a silver weapon or a branch from a hazel tree that has never borne fruit

name: Vittra
description: Vittra are invisible underground wights of northern Sweden (Norrland), living in parallel cities with livestock. Resemble humans but unseen unless they choose. Peaceful if paths/dwellings undisturbed; cause accidents, illness, livestock loss if buildings block roads. 'Vittra-way' and 'Vitterställe' denote relocated places.

name: Vittra
description: Vittra (Icelandic). is a wight. Invisible underground beings who live in parallel cities and protect their territory. Source: Icelandic and Scandinavian folklore

name: Vještica
description: Vještica is the Croatian/Serbian word for 'witch' (from 'vješti' — to know), not a distinct creature. The record appears to conflate the general term with a specific ogre. Actual Croatian witch beliefs involve night flight on wooden beams, causing storms, illness, and infertility.

name: Vodnik
description: Vodnik (Unknown). is a water-spirit. The Vodnik is a water spirit from Slavic folklore, particularly known in Slovenian tradition. It is said to dwell in rivers, lakes, and streams, and can appear as a humanoid with green hair and webbed. Source: Slavic Folklore: A Handbook (Kononenko, 2007)

name: Vodník
description: Vodník is the Czech male water spirit, ruler of rivers and ponds. He appears as a green-clad man with a dripping coat, or as a frog. Uses colored ribbons to lure victims into water, storing their souls in porcelain pots in his underwater palace. Can be benevolent (helping fishermen) or malevolent (drowning bathers). His wife is frog-like. Friday is his day off from man-snatching.

name: Vodník
description: Vodník is the Slovak water spirit, nearly identical to the Czech Vodník. Inhabits Orava region lakes and rivers. Uses ribbons to lure humans, stores drowned souls in pots. His wife appears as a frog; a widespread tale has a woman serve as godmother to the vodník's frog-wife and free captive souls. Can be helpful to fishermen who offer tobacco.

name: Vodun Spirits
description: Vodun is the Fon/Ewe/Aja religion of Benin/Togo/Ghana venerating hundreds of spirits (vodún) under Nana Buluku and Mawu-Lisa. Key spirits: Legba (crossroads), Sakpata (earth/smallpox), Xêbioso (thunder), Gû (iron/war), Dàn (serpent wealth), Mami Wata (water wealth). Living priesthood tradition; Benin's national religion since 1990s.

name: Vodyanoy
description: Vodyanoy (dedushka vodyanoy) is the East Slavic male water spirit, ruler of rivers, lakes, and millponds. Appears as a naked, green-haired old man with a pot belly, covered in slime and weeds, or as a giant catfish/frog. Demands blood sacrifices (livestock, historically human) when mills are built. Helps fishermen who offer butter; drowns the disrespectful. Rides a wels catfish.

name: Vonde-Åsmund
description: Vonde-Åsmund (Evil Åsmund) is the restless ghost of Åsmund Rygnestad (ca. 1540-1596), a historical outlaw from Rygnestad in the Setesdal valley. Åsmund was a violent, law-defying man who fought as a mercenary in the Dutch war for independence and later built the famous Rygnestadloftet as his fortified storehouse — now a protected historic building. After his death, his ghost was said to haunt the Rygnestad area, unable to find peace due to his violent life. Vonde-Åsmund appears as a tall, dark figure at the Rygnestad farm, particularly near the loft he built. He is sometimes seen riding a black horse along the valley road. The legend says his spirit is bound to the treasure he hid somewhere on the farm. Vonde-Åsmund is a historical figure who has become a local folk legend — the line between history and folklore is blurred in his story

name: Vukodlak
description: Vukodlak (volkolak, vovkulaka) is the Slavic werewolf — a human shapeshifter who temporarily becomes a wolf. Most detailed beliefs among Belarusians, Poles, and Ukrainians; South Slavs conflate it with vampires. Transformation via sorcery (rolling over knives, crawling through horse collar), curse, or birth predisposition. Retains human intelligence but cannot speak.

name: Vungu
description: Vungu (Kenya). is a spirit. Vungu is a spirit from the folklore and mythology of Kenya.. Source: Kenyan folklore — Vungu spirit documented in Kenyan oral tradition.

name: Väinämöinen
description: Väinämöinen is the eternal sage and culture hero of Finnish mythology, central figure of Kalevala. Born ancient after Ilmatar's 700-year gestation, shapes world through magical song. Invented kantele from pike's jaw; forged sky's dome in some runic songs. Battles Joukahainen in song, wins, sings him into mire. Quests for Sampo, stolen words from Antero Vipunen, lost word of creation.

name: Väki
description: Väki is not a discrete spirit but the core Finnish concept of supernatural power residing in natural sites, objects, animals — comparable to mana or orenda. Impersonal force, not universal deity.

name: Vätt
description: Vätt (Swedish, also vätt, vette, vätte) is a household/land spirit synonymous with tomte/nisse, dwelling under houses, barns, rocks, forests. Small, grey-clad, red-capped. Helpful if respected and fed (Christmas porridge with butter); vengeful if neglected. Shapeshifts (goat, horse, goose). Name from ON vættr ('wight'). In Uppland, female gårdsrå parallels it.

name: Vättar
description: Vättar (Unknown). is a nature-spirit. Vättar (singular: vätte) are nature spirits in Swedish folklore that live in rocks, caves, and hills. They are similar to the Icelandic Huldufólk and can be either helpful or malicious depending on ho. Source: Swedish folklore tradition

name: Vågakallen
description: Vågakallen (the Old Man of Vågan) is the troll king of Lofoten, said to sit on his throne 1,000 meters above sea level in the Lofoten mountains. He was the ruler of the Lofoten trolls and the father of Hestmannen (the Horseman). Vågakallen sat on his mountain throne watching over his kingdom — the Lofoten archipelago, Vestfjorden, and the surrounding sea. According to legend, when he was caught by the sunrise, he and his entire kingdom were turned to stone, becoming the dramatic Lofoten mountains. The Vågakallen rock formation is a famous landmark visible from the sea near Henningsvær. The legend is part of the Helgeland/Lofoten cycle of troll stories that explain the dramatic coastal landscape of Northern Norway. Vågakallen represents the ancient power of the troll kings who ruled the land before humans

name: Vård
description: Vård (Swedish 'warden') is a nature guardian spirit of a specific place — sacred tree (vårdträd), rock, spring, forest, field. Personifies land's genius loci. Manifests as white deer, snake, bird, light, or elderly humanoid; often felt as invisible presence. Protects those who respect land and leave offerings; punishes desecrators with misfortune, illness.

name: Völva Iceland
description: Völva Iceland (Unknown). is a witch. A Völva was a female seer and shaman in Norse and Germanic tradition who practiced seiðr magic and prophesied the future. The most famous völva recounts the creation and end of the world in the Völusp. Source: Poetic Edda; Norse sagas; archaeological evidence

name: Waaq
description: Waaq (Somali). is a deity. Waaq is the pre-Islamic supreme sky god of the Cushitic peoples of Somalia and the Horn of Africa, associated with rain, fertility, and the natural forces of the sky.. Source: Somali oral tradition, pre-Islamic Somali mythology, Wikipedia - Somali mythology

name: Wadlim
description: Not independently attested as a Guatemalan water spirit. No source records a jungle river guardian named 'Wadlim' who keeps the fish and drowns offenders; searches surface only Maine surnames and place names. The nearest attested Maya and Central American water beings that punish disrespect for rivers include the Siguanaba and the guardian serpent-spirits of rivers and cenotes.

name: Wagyl
description: Wagyl (also spelled Waugal or Wogal) is the Rainbow Serpent creator being in the mythology of the Noongar people of southwestern Australia. According to Dreamtime stories, Wagyl emerged from the ground and traveled across the land, creating the Swan River, the Avon River, and many other waterways of the southwest. As Wagyl moved, his twisting body carved out riverbeds, and where he rested, waterholes and lakes formed. He is associated with the Derbarl Yerrigan (Swan River) and is considered the guardian of fresh water sources throughout Noongar country. Wagyl can be both benevolent and dangerous — he brings rain and life but also punishes those who break laws with floods. The serpent's journeys explain the unique geology of the Swan Coastal Plain

name: Wairangi
description: Not independently attested in documented Māori folklore or academic sources. No dedicated source confirms a trickster figure named Wairangi associated with forests and villages. Māori trickster roles are dominated by Māui, and the recorded traits appear to be a generic trickster composite rather than a named figure from the tradition.

name: Wakan Tanka
description: Wakan Tanka (Great Mystery or Great Spirit) is the supreme sacred power in Lakota religion, the unified totality of all that is mysterious, powerful, and sacred. Unlike a personified deity in Western traditions, Wakan Tanka is better understood as the sum of all wakan (sacred) forces that permeate the universe. The term encompasses four primary deities: Wi (Sun), Skan (Sky), Maka (Earth), and Inyan (Rock), along with their associates. Everything in creation possesses wakan energy as part of Wakan Tanka

name: Wakinyan
description: Wakinyan is the great Thunderbird of Lakota mythology, a powerful sky spirit associated with thunder, lightning, and storms. His flapping wings create thunderclaps and his eyes flash lightning. When Unhcegila emerged from primordial waters to flood the land, Wakinyan flapped his wings to create a great storm to dry the earth and shot lightning to destroy the serpent's heart. The Thunderbird represents the destructive yet renewing power of storms. Wakinyan is associated with the west direction and is considered one of the most potent spirits, protecting the Lakota against chaos and disorder

name: Wakinyan Lakota
description: Wakinyan is the Thunderer of the Lakota, a powerful sky spirit that dwells in the west and appears as a giant bird whose wingbeats roll thunder and whose eye blinks lightning. Wakinyan brings the life-giving rains and, as the enemy of the evil water monsters, keeps the world in balance.

name: Walumbe
description: Walumbe is the personification of death in Baganda mythology, the brother of Nambi and son of the sky god Ggulu. In the creation myth, Walumbe is forbidden by his father from knowing about Kintu—the first man—and his sister Nambi's marriage. When Kintu and Nambi prepared to descend to Earth, Ggulu warned them to leave immediately without returning for anything forgotten. But Walumbe tricked them, causing Nambi to forget grain for their journey. When Nambi sent Walumbe back to retrieve it, he followed them to Earth, claiming their firstborn child and establishing death as a permanent part of human existence. Kintu attempted to expel Walumbe but failed, and death became inescapable. Walumbe represents the inescapable reality of mortality in Baganda cosmology. He is often depicted as relentless, cunning, and insatiable, always seeking new souls to claim

name: Wamala
description: Wamala is the god of the underworld in Ganda mythology, the third of three powerful divine brothers alongside Mukasa (lake god) and Kibuka (war god). Wamala rules the realm of the dead, a watery underworld beneath Lake Victoria. While Mukasa governs surface waters and life-giving bounty, Wamala rules the dark depths and spirits of the departed. The Baganda believe that when a person dies, their spirit journeys to Wamala's underwater realm to join the ancestors. Wamala is a just but stern deity who ensures cosmic moral order. Those who lived good lives find peace; those who did evil face his judgment. Wamala is also associated with hidden treasures of the deep -- sunken wealth of old Buganda kingdoms

name: Wandjina
description: The Wandjina are powerful cloud and rain spirits in the beliefs of the Wanjina Wunggurr cultural bloc of northwestern Australia, including the Worrorra, Wunambal, and Ngarinyin peoples of the Kimberley region. According to Dreamtime legends, the Wandjina created the landscape and its inhabitants and continue to influence both. When the spirit beings found the place where they would die, they painted their images on cave walls and entered a nearby waterhole. The paintings, dating back about 4,000 years, show figures with large upper bodies, eyes and noses but typically no mouths. The Wandjina can punish lawbreakers with floods, lightning, and cyclones. Aboriginal people repaint these images annually to regenerate their life-force and ensure the coming of monsoon rains

name: Waniwani
description: Not independently attested in documented Māori folklore or academic sources. No source confirms a giant monitor lizard or reptile named Waniwani. Māori tradition does record the taniwha, powerful supernatural beings often pictured as giant lizards or lake monsters, and fossil finds of giant moa-eating eagles may have shaped such stories, but no 'Waniwani' figure was found.

name: Warimu (Kilimanjaro Spirits)
description: The Warimu (singular: Mrimu) are the mountain spirits of Kilimanjaro in Chaga mythology, ancient guardians inhabiting sacred groves (mshitu) on the mountain's slopes. According to tradition, the Warimu were the original inhabitants of Kilimanjaro before the Chaga arrived. They dwell in patches of virgin forest never cut or farmed, where trees are never felled and animals never hunted. Only initiated elders may enter. Within these groves reside spirits of departed Chaga chiefs (Mangi) and ancestors. The Warimu serve as intermediaries between Ruwa and the Chaga, protecting from misfortune, ensuring crop fertility, guarding water sources, and maintaining spiritual health. When a child is born, a tree is planted in the family's grove; when a person dies, their spirit returns to join the Warimu

name: Warlock (Loup-Garou)
description: The loup-garou is the werewolf of French and French-Canadian tradition: a person cursed — often for missing Easter communion seven years running — to become a wolf by night. The curse is broken by drawing blood or by three years of abstinence. The French-Canadian loup-garou, called 'warlock' in some sources, reflects religious guilt, distinct from the Native American skinwalker.

name: Warlock (Loup-Garou)
description: The loup-garou of Acadian and French Canadian tradition is a werewolf, usually imagined as a shaggy dog or bear-like creature rather than a wolf. According to the Canadian Encyclopedia, it was understood as a curse, often the price of failing to perform Easter confession for years, and breakable by drawing its blood. Its tales are a Catholic moral lesson.

name: Wasgo (Sea Wolf)
description: Wasgo, the Sea Wolf, is a Haida supernatural being combining wolf and killer-whale features — wolf head and body with the fins and tail of a whale. A crest figure for Haida clans, he crosses between ocean and forest worlds, and his stories teach the fluid boundaries between animal beings in the Haida worldview.

name: Wasgo Sea Wolf Haida
description: Wasgo, the sea wolf, is a powerful being of Haida tradition that moves between ocean and land, part wolf and part killer whale. Capable of seizing a whale and of storming the shore, it appears in crest carvings and pole legends as a creature of great supernatural strength linking the sea and the forest.

name: Watchman (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested as a named 'Watchman' in Tupi tradition. Tupi/Guaraní guardianship figures include Jurupari (men's secret cult deity), Tupã (thunder/creator manifestation), and forest owners, but no specific 'Watchman (Tupi)' entity. The generic 'shadowy humanoid at forest edge' description appears fabricated. May reflect conflation with Jurupari or general forest guardian concepts.

name: Watchman (Tupi)
description: The Tupi-Guarani forest watchman is Curupira, guardian of the hunt: a red-haired, boy-like being with backward feet and a piercing whistle who defends trees and animals. He misleads hunters who take more than they need, making them lose their way in the deep woods, and punishes those who wound or fell without respect. He is Brazilian in origin, so the Mexico placement is an error.

name: Water Babies
description: Water babies are small, crying beings of Great Basin and Plateau tradition, known among the Southern Paiute as pit-u-u and to other nations by related names. They guard springs, rivers, and lakes; some traditions say they are ghosts of infants who died in a famine, while others know them as spirit guardians who help shamans. Their weeping warns the unwary away from dangerous water.

name: Water Dragon (Olmec)
description: The Olmec Dragon, reconstructed by archaeologist Karl Taube, is a composite water-and-earth deity blending caiman, eagle, jaguar, serpent and human features, with flame-like eyebrows and distinctive L-shaped or trough eyes. Carved at La Venta and San Lorenzo, it is among Mesoamerica's oldest dragon-like beings and foreshadows later Maya and central Mexican dragon and rain deities.

name: Water Horse Iceland
description: Water Horse Iceland (Unknown). is a animal. The water horse from Icelandic folklore is a deadly Nykur that appears as a tame horse near water.. Source: Icelandic folklore — the water horse/kelpie of Icelandic oral tradition.

name: Water Spider
description: In the Cherokee story of how fire came to the people, Water Spider (Dilsdohdi, Kanane'ski Amai'yehi) volunteered when raven, hawk, and the other animals failed. She spun a bowl-shaped web, carried a burning coal across the water on her back, and brought fire to the world; her reddish mark recalls the ember she bore. Recorded by James Mooney.

name: Water Spirits
description: Water spirits form one of the oldest and widest classes of Native American belief in the United States, though no single being bears the plain name 'water spirit.' Each nation has its own: the horned Underwater Panther of the Great Lakes and East, the water babies of the Great Basin, and the Okwa Naholo of the Choctaw. They guard waters, reward respect, and drown those who defy them.

name: Water Spirits
description: Water spirits are a broad, attested class across Canada's First Nations, though each people knows them by its own names. Among them are the horned great lynx of the Anishinaabe, the water babies of the north, and the Naitaka of Okanagan Lake. They rule the rivers, lakes, and ocean, and ceremonies are offered to them for safe passage and for the harvests of the water.

name: Water Sprinkler (Tó Neinilí)
description: Water Sprinkler (Tó Neinilí) is a Navajo Holy Person closely associated with water, rain, and all forms of moisture. He works alongside Talking God and other Diyin Dine'é in the creation narratives, helping to shape the sacred mountains and assisting in the emergence from the Third World during the great flood. He created bowls of white and blue shell that spun open an underwater house to rescue children taken by Big Water Creature. He is considered a life-giving force who brings fertility to th

name: Wats'usi (Twin War God)
description: Wats'usi (Twin War God) is the younger of the sacred twin deities in Zuni mythology, the swift and cunning brother of Ko'wituma. While his elder brother leads the charge against monsters and evil spirits, Wats'usi uses strategy, speed, and clever deception to outmaneuver threats to the Zuni people. He is associated with the west and the setting sun, and carries a shield of obsidian that deflects dark magic. During the Kachina ceremonies, Wats'usi appears as a dancer wielding a bow and a ceremonial knife, performing acrobatic feats that delight the crowds while reminding them of the eternal vigilance required to maintain peace

name: Wee-kin
description: Not independently attested in any recorded Canadian First Nations tradition. No tribal account or published source describes a spirit named Wee-kin, and the name appears to be invented or garbled. It may be a corruption of weyekin, the personal guardian spirit of the Nez Perce, or a generic Canadian entry; either way, no such being is documented in the folklore of Canada.

name: Wee-Tent (or Wee-Tin)
description: Not independently attested under the name Wee-Tent. The Ojibwe and other Anishinaabe peoples do tell of little people, known as Bagwajiwininiwag, 'the wilderness little Anishinaabe,' along with the water-dwelling memengwesi and the mischievous bajiine, but no source names one of them Wee-Tent. The entry appears to be a garbled or invented label for a genuine class of little forest spirits.

name: Wee-Willie-Winkle
description: Wee Willie Winkie is a Scottish nursery rhyme character created by poet William Miller in 1841 ('Whistle-Binkie: Stories for the Fireside'), not a folkloric fairy. The rhyme personifies sleep: 'Wee Willie Winkie rins through the toon... Tirlin' at the window... Are the weans in their bed, for it's now ten o'clock?' It became a bedtime entity alongside the Sandman and Scandinavian Ole Lukøje.

name: Weeget Raven Tsimshian
description: Weeget is the Raven of the Coast Tsimshian, the trickster and creator whose clever thefts gave the people light, fresh water, and salmon. He shapeshifts freely and meddles in the affairs of gods and men, and Tsimshian tellers recount both his world-making deeds and the greed that drives his schemes.

name: Weeget Txamsem Giant Raven Tsimshian
description: Txamsem, also called Weeget, is the great raven of the Coast Tsimshian, the creator and trickster who stole the sun and stars to light the world and brought fresh water and the salmon. A being of immense appetite and endless ingenuity, he both made the world and causes its troubles, and his deeds are told in Tsimshian adaawx.

name: Weeget Txamsem Raven Tsimshian
description: Weeget Txamsem is the raven trickster-creator of the Tsimshian, a shapeshifter whose voracious appetite drives his adventures. He steals the sun to light the world, releases the first salmon, and orders the tides and seasons, while his greed and mischief teach the lessons of the adaawx.

name: Weerwolf
description: Weerwolf is the Dutch werewolf, documented in 16th–17th century witchcraft trials in the Netherlands. De Blécourt and Meder recorded cases of transformation via devil's salve or wolf-skin belt. Dutch cases clustered 1590s–1620s. Word derives from Middle Dutch weerwolf (man-wolf), cognate with Old English werwulf and German Werwolf.

name: Weiße Frauen
description: Weiße Frauen are elf-like spirits in German folklore, derived from Norse Ljósálfar (light elves) per Jacob Grimm. Appear at noon bathing in brooks or combing hair, guarding treasure or haunting castles. Their enchantment symbolises Christianity's ban on older divinities (Holda, Perchta, Ostara). Dutch Witte Wieven (wise women) are cognate, traced to 7th century. Alpine variants: Salige Frauen.

name: Wekufe
description: Wekufe (Mapuche: 'outside being') are malevolent spirits, a category of soulless entities from Minchenmapu (western evil realm). They cause illness, death, misfortune; escaped from cosmic Pillan battle. Controlled by kalku (sorcerers) to harm enemies. Only machi or Pillan can trap them. Represent consequences of breaking admapu (cosmic law). Central to Mapuche spiritual warfare.

name: Well Spirit
description: Well Spirit (Unknown). is a spirit. A well spirit is a guardian entity from European folklore who dwells in springs and wells, protecting the water source.. Source: Polish folklore; well spirit traditions documented in Slavic folk belief collections.

name: Wendigo
description: The wendigo, also spelled windigo, is the cannibal spirit of the Algonquian-speaking peoples, from the Cree and Ojibwe of Canada to the Wampanoag and Pequot of New England. A human possessed by greed and hunger is said to become a gaunt, ice-hearted monster that devours human flesh and never fills its stomach. Scholars read it as a warning against greed and starvation.

name: Wenebojo
description: Wenebojo (also known as Nanabozho) is the great culture hero and trickster-transformer of the Anishinaabe people. Son of the West Wind and a human mother, he was raised by his grandmother Nokomis. He is a shape-shifter, co-creator of the world, founder of the Midewiwin (Grand Medicine Society), inventor of fishing and hieroglyphic writing, and teacher of humanity. His adventures range from the sacred (rebuilding the earth after a great flood) to the humorous (being tricked by greedy geese). He is associated with the Great Hare (Mishaabooz)

name: Were (Nyasaye)
description: Were (also known as Nyasaye) is the supreme creator god of the Luo people. According to Luo cosmology, Were created the world from primordial waters, fashioning the sky, earth, sun, moon, and stars. Were then created the first man and woman from clay, breathing life into their nostrils and giving them cattle, goats, and seeds. Were taught the first people how to live, but they disobeyed a divine command, and death entered the world. After this disobedience, Were withdrew from direct contact with humanity but left ancestral spirits (juogi) as intermediaries. The Luo honor Were through prayers and offerings at dawn and dusk when the boundary between worlds grows thin. Were is associated with the sky, rain, and natural phenomena

name: Werehyena
description: The werehyena is a human-hyena shapeshifter of West, East, and Central African folklore. Said to be people who transform into hyenas by night, they appear in tales from Mali (the bouda), Ethiopia, and elsewhere as sorcerers, grave-diggers, or cannibals. The motif reflects real hyena behavior and the animal's ambiguous place in African symbolism.

name: Werewolf
description: Greek tradition offers the oldest named werewolf: the Arcadian king Lycaon, who tested Zeus by serving human flesh and was transformed into a wolf (Ovid, Metamorphoses). Later Greek belief distinguished the lykánthropos, a man who became a wolf by magic or curse and roamed wild at night. The very words 'lycanthropy' and 'lycanthrope' descend from this Greek root.

name: Werewolf
description: The English werewolf (Old English werwulf, 'man-wolf') appears in medieval chronicles as a human cursed or voluntarily transforming into a wolf. Gervase of Tilbury (c. 1210) wrote that in England men often changed into wolves during lunar cycles.

name: Werewolf
description: In France the werewolf is the loup-garou, a cursed human who sheds human form at night to run as a wolf, often through a pact with the Devil. Documented in medieval chronicles and the great werewolf trials of the 16th century (the Garnier and Gandillon cases), it was read as demonic shape-shifting. The name passed into English as 'loup-garou' and to French Canada with the settlers.

name: Werewolf
description: German Werwolf belief peaked 16th–17th centuries, intertwined with witch trials. Peter Stumpp's 1589 execution sparked panic. Bavaria/Austria persecuted Wolfssegen (wolf-charmers) into early 18th century. Transformation via devil's belt or salve, not full moon (later fiction). Capitulatum Episcopi (9th c.) denied physical metamorphosis; folk belief persisted.

name: Werewolf
description: Werewolf (Generic). is a shapeshifter. A human who transforms into a wolf, either voluntarily or by curse. Source: European folklore, global shapeshifting myths

name: Wewe Gombel
description: Wewe Gombel is a ghost of Javanese folklore said to dwell in tall trees, bamboo groves, and abandoned wells, seizing neglected or disobedient children. Documented by the folklorist James Danandjaja, the figure acts as an instrument of moral education, warning children that misbehavior draws its attention. It relies on the didactic use of supernatural fear in Javanese child-rearing.

name: Whale Ancestor-Spirit of Dogon
description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon are landlocked in Mali's Bandiagara cliffs; whales do not feature in their cosmology. Ancestor spirits are Nommo (amphibious) and Lebe (serpent). The 'whale ancestor-spirit guarding undergrounds' appears fabricated, possibly conflating Nommo's fish-tail with whale imagery.

name: Whale Ancestor-Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition. Muisca are inland highland Andean people (Altiplano Cundiboyacense, 2600m elevation); whales do not exist in their territory or mythology. Muisca beings: Bachué, Bochica, Chía, Sué, Chibchacum, Goranchacha, Monster of Lake Tota (serpent/fish). Whale ancestor-spirit is a fabricated conflation.

name: Whale Ancestor-Spirit of Quechua
description: Not independently attested in Quechua tradition. Quechua/Inca are inland Andean people; whales do not exist in their territory. Inca sacred trilogy: condor (sky), puma (earth), serpent (underworld). No whale beings in Huarochirí Manuscript, Viracocha myths, or Inka animal symbolism. Whale ancestor-spirit is a fabricated conflation.

name: Whale Ancestor-Spirit of Shoshone
description: Not independently attested in Shoshone tradition; the Shoshone, a Great Basin people, have no recorded whale ancestor-spirit, and the description of a guardian of the springs matches no documented being. The real water guardians of the Shoshone are the water babies, known as nu-numbi, who watch over springs and lakes. The entry combines an ocean creature with a desert water spirit.

name: Whale Animal-Spirit of Dogon
description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon animal spirits include the Pale Fox (Ogo), Jackal, and various mask animals (antelope, hyena, monkey); no whale. The 'whale animal-spirit guarding valleys' is fabricated, likely from same Nommo conflation as the ancestor-spirit variant.

name: Whale Animal-Spirit of Mapuche
description: Not independently attested in Mapuche tradition. Mapuche territory includes Chilean coast, but 'whale animal-spirit guardian of deserts' is fabricated — Mapuche are temperate rainforest/Andean, not desert dwellers. Mapuche beings: ngen (nature owners), wekufe, Pillan, Coi Coi-Vilu (sea serpent), Pincoya. No whale spirit in Bacigalupo, Faron, or Guevara.

name: Whale Deity of Aztec
description: Not independently attested: the inland Aztecs had no whale deity, and no such figure guards their lakes. The closest monsters are Cipactli, the primeval crocodilian sea-beast from whose body the earth was made (lured with Tezcatlipoca's severed foot), and Tlaltecuhtli, the ravenous earth-lady. Their lake guardians were water gods such as Tlaloc and Chalchiuhtlicue and the doglike Ahuizotl.

name: Whale Deity of Cherokee
description: Not attested as a whale deity of the Cherokee. The Cherokee tell of the Dakwa, a great fish of the deep waters, whose name was later used in translations of the Bible for 'whale'; Mooney recorded 'The Hunter and the Dakwa,' a tale of a man swallowed and carried by the great fish, told by the storytellers Swimmer and Tagwaddihi. No whale god or cave guardian appears in Cherokee tradition.

name: Whale Ghost of Apache
description: Not independently attested in Apache tradition. The Apache are a Southwestern people whose homelands hold no whales, and no recorded Apache narrative features a whale ghost or desert guardian. The documented supernatural beings of the Apache include the Water Monster and the holy people of their origin stories rather than any sea creature. The entry appears to be an invented figure.

name: Whale Ghost of Miwok
description: Not independently attested in Miwok tradition; the Miwok of California have no recorded whale ghost. The famous whale of California Indian literature is the Wintu tale of the Inland Whale, retold by Theodora Kroeber, a story of a young man swallowed by the great whale, not a ghost and not Miwok. The entry appears to combine a real coastal tale with a wrong tribe and a wrong creature.

name: Whale Ghost of Yoruba
description: Not independently attested in Yoruba tradition. Yoruba water spirits include Olokun (ocean), Yemoja (rivers), Oshun (freshwater); no whale ghost guarding hills. Whales occasionally beach in Nigeria but lack mythological personification. Record appears fabricated from generic 'whale ghost' templates.

name: Whale Giant of Cheyenne
description: Not independently attested in Cheyenne tradition; the Cheyenne, a Plains people, have no recorded whale giant, and no source documents a whale in their mythology. The principal figures of Cheyenne tradition are the creator Maheo and the spider trickster Wihio. The entry appears to be an invented figure, one of a series of impossible whale attributions across desert and Plains nations.

name: Whale Giant of Cree
description: Not independently attested in Cree folklore as a giant whale. The Cree of the plains and subarctic woodlands record no whale spirit; their great water-dwelling monster is the Mishipizhiw or Great Lynx, a dangerous being of deep lakes and rivers who drags people underwater. Where a 'whale giant' is imagined, Cree tradition centers on this underwater lynx and the perils of lakes and rapids.

name: Whale Giant of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. Guaraní are inland people (Paraguay, NE Argentina, S Brazil); whales do not exist in their territory or mythology. Seven legendary monsters include no whale giant. Entity appears fabricated, possibly conflating Teju Jagua (cavern/fruit god, lizard-like) with whale imagery.

name: Whale Giant of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. Duplicate of whalegiantofguarani-paraguay with Brazil country assignment. Guaraní are inland (Paraguay, NE Argentina, S Brazil); no whales in territory or mythology. Entity appears fabricated.

name: Whale Guardian of Maliseet
description: Not independently attested as a whale 'guardian' in Maliseet folklore. Whales do appear in Maliseet stories: in 'Turtle Gets a Whale,' Glooscap directs the boastful Turtle to haul a whale ashore for a feast, and the whale's weight presses the overreaching Turtle down until the other animals cut him free. Whales figure as hunted food and wonders of the sea, not protective guardian spirits.

name: Whale Kwakwaka Wakw
description: In Kwakwaka'wakw belief the killer whale rules the undersea world, attended by sea lions as slaves and dolphins as warriors, and may carry the soul of a deceased chief. In the Siwidi story the ancestor travels the sea kingdom with killer-whale attendants in the copper house of Ḵumugwe; the orca is a high-ranking clan crest.

name: Whale Spirit of Muisca
description: Not independently attested in Muisca tradition. Muisca are inland highland Andean people; whales do not exist in their territory or mythology. Muisca water beings: Lake Iguaque (origin), Lake Guatavita (El Dorado ritual), Monster of Lake Tota. No whale spirit in Ocampo López or chroniclers.

name: Whale Trickster of Dogon
description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon trickster is exclusively Ogo (Pale Fox). No whale trickster exists in landlocked Mali. The 'whale trickster guarding rivers' with flight and storm-calling is fabricated, possibly conflating Ogo's chaos with Nommo's water association.

name: Whale Water-Spirit (Malagasy)
description: Whale Water-Spirit (Malagasy) (Madagascar). is a water-spirit. The whale water-spirit of Malagasy tradition, protector of the valleys. Source: Regional survey of East African indigenous traditions — Kikuyu, Luo, Ganda, Chaga, Malagasy, Maasai, Somali, Ethiopian, and related peoples as documen

name: Whale Water-Spirit (Malagasy)
description: Not independently attested in documented Malagasy or Tongan folklore or academic sources. No dedicated source confirms a whale water-spirit guarding valleys in either tradition. While Malagasy and Tongan mythologies do feature oceanic spirits, the specific whale-valley protector recorded in the input could not be verified.

name: Whale Water-Spirit of Maliseet
description: Not independently attested as a whale water-spirit in Maliseet (Wolastoqiyik) tradition. The whale appears as a great sea creature of the coast, a source of food and a test of strength: in 'Turtle Gets a Whale,' Glooscap has the boastful Turtle haul a whale to camp, where its bulk crushes him until the other animals cut it free. Whale tales teach humility, not a whale-spirit guardian.

name: Whale Water-Spirit of Shoshone
description: Not independently attested in Shoshone folklore. The Great Basin Shoshone had no coastal or whale traditions, and no whale water-spirit appears in their recorded stories. Their dangerous water beings are the Water Babies, eerie spirits of springs and ponds who lure people to watery deaths, along with lake and river serpents. Whale spirits belong to Arctic, Northwest Coast, and maritime peoples.

name: Whirlwind
description: Whirlwind, also rendered Cyclone, is the wind-being of the Jicarilla Apache creation, present before the world began alongside darkness and water. He is one of the primordial forces out of which the cosmos was ordered by the Hactcin, and he remains a power felt in the Southwest winds. The figure is attested in the Jicarilla emergence account.

name: Whiro
description: Whiro is the Māori god of darkness, death, and all evil, one of the children of Ranginui (the sky father) and Papatūānuku (the earth mother). Rival to Tāne, the god of light, he presides over decay, disease, and the underworld, and is said to oppose the forces of life and light. He is regarded as the embodiment of darkness within the Māori pantheon.

name: White Bead Maiden (Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́)
description: White Bead Maiden (Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́), the young form of Changing Woman, was sought in marriage by the Sun, who came disguised as a handsome warrior. After many trials she traveled to his celestial house of turquoise and white shell, where she bore the Hero Twins, then returned to earth and became Changing Woman, the central female deity who governs the cycles of life and the seasons.

name: White Bear Denmark
description: White Bear Denmark (Unknown). is a animal-spirit. The White Bear is a magical bear prince from Danish folklore, transformed by a curse that must be broken by love.. Source: Danish folklore — white bear animal spirit documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: White Beaver
description: White Beaver is a sacred animal spirit in Pawnee mythology, particularly associated with the Chawi band of the South Bands. The White Beaver ceremony served the same purpose as the Skidi Pawnee's Spring Awakening ceremony—renewing life and ensuring fertility. While the Skidi focused on corn and the stars, the White Beaver ceremony revitalized hibernating animals instead. The white beaver was a sacred animal associated with water spirits. The ceremony involved elaborate rituals, songs, and the use of sacred bundles, reflecting the South Bands' reliance on animal spirits as intermediaries with the divine

name: White Buffalo Calf Woman
description: White Buffalo Calf Woman (Ptesan-Wi) is the most revered supernatural figure in Lakota religion, appearing to the people in ancient times when they had forgotten how to pray. She brought the sacred pipe (chanunpa) and taught the Seven Sacred Rites that form the foundation of Lakota spirituality. She appeared as a beautiful woman in white buckskin carrying a bundle, instructed the people in prayer and ceremony, and before departing transformed through four colors—black, red, brown, and white—becoming a white buffalo calf who promised to return when the people need her most

name: White Dove Denmark
description: White Dove Denmark (Unknown). is a spirit. The White Dove is a magical bird from Danish folklore, often an enchanted princess or messenger between lovers.. Source: Danish folklore — white dove spirit documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: White God of the East (Xastc'inilgaiyîn)
description: Xastc'inilgaiyîn, the White God of the East, is one of the directional Hactcin beings of the Jicarilla Apache. In the emergence story he holds the sun in the east and lets it travel across the sky, and with the other Hactcin he raised the great mountain and made reeds grow to build the ladder by which the people climbed into this world.

name: White Hactcin
description: White Hactcin is an important Hactcin supernatural being in Jicarilla Apache tradition. According to Apache mythology, White Hactcin possessed the sun. Holy Boy, guided by Cyclone the wind spirit, went to White Hactcin who gave him the sun, while Black Hactcin gave him the moon. White Hactcin and Black Hactcin held a ceremony with songs, and White Hactcin released the sun into the sky while Black Hactcin released the moon. White Hactcin is associated with light, day, and the celestial forces tha

name: White Lady (Tupi)
description: Not independently attested in Tupi tradition. 'White Lady' is a European ghost archetype (Weiße Frau, Dama Blanca) imported post-contact. Tupi ghosts/spirits include ancestral spirits and Jurupari-related entities, but no 'White Lady' in pre-colonial tradition. The description appears to be a colonial-era syncretic fabrication.

name: White Lady (Tupi)
description: The Tupi water-woman is Iara (Uiara), a beautiful river siren with long dark hair who combs her tresses and sings on the bank, luring fishermen and bathers to drown in her depths. Colonists later blended her with the European White Lady, the Dama Branca, a pale figure in white seen near rivers and roads at night. She is Brazilian, so the Mexico placement is an error.

name: White Lady (Tupi)
description: This record misplaces the being: Iara (or Yara) is the water spirit of Tupi-Guarani lore in Brazil, not of North America. Iara is a beautiful maiden who lives in rivers and sings enchantingly from the water; men who follow her song are drawn beneath the surface and drowned. Some versions describe her with a fish-like lower body. Her homeland is the Amazon and Paraná river basins of South America.

name: White Painted Woman
description: White Painted Woman (Esdzanadehe, also called Changing Woman) is the central culture heroine of Apache tradition. Daughter of the sun, she survived the great flood inside a turquoise mountain and bore the warrior twins Killer of Enemies and Child of the Water, who destroyed the monsters plaguing the world. Apache girls' puberty rites, including the Sunrise Dance, re-enact her power of renewal.

name: White Painted Woman (Changing Woman)
description: White Painted Woman (also known as Changing Woman) is a central deity in Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache tradition. She appeared after a great flood that destroyed a malevolent world. She conceived Child of the Water (Killer-of-Enemies) from the rays of the Sun. White Painted Woman is identified with the Moon and Thunder. The Girls' Puberty Ceremony reenacts her first menstruation, when she received her power from the Sun. The ceremony lasts four days, blessing young women with health, fertility

name: White Reindeer
description: The White Reindeer is the most sacred animal in Sami belief, a spirit creature associated with the sun goddess Beaivi and the mythic reindeer Meandash. Seeing a white reindeer was considered a powerful omen — an encounter with the divine. Its appearance in dreams or visions signaled major life changes. The white reindeer was the most valuable sacrifice to the gods — white reindeer were specifically offered to Beaivi at the winter solstice to ensure the sun's return, and to Bieggolmmái to control the winds. In Sami shamanism, the reindeer was the most important power animal, used for offerings and depicted on shaman drums. The noaidi would wear a coat made from reindeer fur and antlers in rituals to connect with the great reindeer spirit. All parts of the reindeer had magical properties — its skin, fur, meat, hooves, and especially the antlers, which reached toward the sky and connected earth to the universe. The white reindeer specifically was the purest manifestation of this sacred animal, the closest connection between the human and divine realms

name: White Witch of Rose Hall (Annie Palmer)
description: The White Witch of Rose Hall is Jamaica most famous ghost story -- the restless spirit of Annie Palmer, the cruel mistress of Rose Hall Plantation in Montego Bay, who allegedly murdered three husbands and countless enslaved workers through her practice of black magic (obeah). According to legend, Annie Palmer was born in England but raised in Haiti, where she learned voodoo from her Haitian nurse. She came to Jamaica as a young woman and married John Palmer, the wealthy owner of Rose Hall. Dissatisfied with her marriage, she murdered him and then married and killed two more husbands. She also took many enslaved lovers, whose bodies were found in hidden graves across the plantation. Annie was finally killed by an enslaved man named Takoo (or Taku) in revenge for her cruelty. Her ghost is said to haunt the Great House of Rose Hall, appearing as a beautiful woman in a white dress who transforms into a hag, galloping across the plantation on horseback, or wandering the grounds wailing. Visitors to Rose Hall Great House (now a museum) report cold spots, disembodied footsteps, and the sensation of being watched

name: Whowie
description: Whowie (Unknown). is a monster. The Whowie is a fearsome creature from Australian Aboriginal mythology, particularly from the Murray River region. It is described as a giant, six-legged lizard-like monster that emerged from the grou. Source: Australian Aboriginal oral tradition

name: Wi
description: Wi is the Sun god in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan to provide sufficient warmth and light for Maka after Anpo's dawn light proved inadequate. Wi is one of the four primary Wakan Tanka deities and is considered above all other Wakan Tanka in some traditions. He is associated with the supreme power of creation and receives prayers for matters of great importance. In some accounts, Wi is identified as Wakan Tanka Kin (the Great Spirit) itself. The Sun gives life to all growing things and marks the passage of time

name: Wichtel
description: Wichtel are Bavarian/Austrian household spirits akin to Scottish brownies and North German kobolds. Perform nocturnal chores—threshing, cleaning, churning—for milk and bread. Term from MHG wichte (small creature). Variants: Gütel (hayloft spirit), Heinzelmännchen (Cologne's literary gnomes, Weyden 1826, Kopisch 1836 ballad). Gift of clothing drives them away.

name: Wight (or Wraith)
description: In Old English, wiht meant any 'being' (e.g., Grendel as wiht unhaelo). By Middle English, wight narrowed to supernatural beings — ghosts, spirits, or the restless dead — and appears in Chaucer ('sweet wight') and Shakespeare. Modern fantasy 'undead wight' derives from Tolkien and D&D, not medieval folklore. English 'wraith' (Scots) denotes a death-omen apparition.

name: Wight Iceland
description: Wight Iceland (Unknown). is a wight. A wight from Icelandic folklore is a supernatural being connected to a specific place as a land spirit.. Source: Icelandic folklore — wights documented in Icelandic folk belief.

name: Wihio
description: Wihio (Ve'ho'e) is the Cheyenne trickster figure, a spider-like being whose name means 'spider' and is related to the word for 'chief' and the Creator's name Heammawihio. He appears as a man in most tales, both clever and foolish, wise and ridiculous. His stories range from silly antics (losing his eyeballs, falling for obvious tricks) to important cultural tales (releasing the buffalo from the wonderful sack). Wihio teaches Cheyenne values through humor—greed, selfishness, and foolishness always lead to his comeuppance while cleverness and generosity triumph. The name eventually came to mean 'white man' after European contact

name: Wild Hunt Hounds
description: Wild Hunt Hounds (Icelandic). is a spirit. Ghostly hounds of the Wild Hunt that forebode catastrophe and terrorize the night. Source: Icelandic and Nordic folklore

name: Wildcat Ancestor-Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat ancestor-spirit in Cheyenne tradition. The Cheyenne are a Plains people whose culture heroes and tricksters are other beings: the culture hero Sweet Medicine and the spider trickster Veeho (Wihio). No wildcat or bobcat ancestor figure appears in their recorded mythology; this 'Cheyenne wildcat' record is a misattribution.

name: Wildcat Ancestor-Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: Wildcat Ancestor-Spirit (Cheyenne) (Madagascar). is a ancestor-spirit. A wildcat ancestor-spirit from Cheyenne tradition that  river. Source: Madagascar mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Wildcat Ancestor-Spirit of Maya
description: In Maya belief the jaguar is the great guardian of the underworld: each night the sun takes jaguar form to travel through Xibalba, the realm of the dead. Jaguar ancestor-spirits and protectors watch over lineage and territory, and rulers dressed in jaguar pelts and sat on jaguar thrones to claim this night power, as carved at Tikal, Palenque and Naranjo.

name: Wildcat Ancestor-Spirit of Paiute
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat ancestor-spirit in Paiute tradition. Paiute mythology centers on Wolf (Isa), the creator and culture hero, and his younger brother Coyote the trickster; bobcats appear only as minor characters in tales. The wildcat ancestor-spirit is a misattribution. The genuine analogues are Wolf as ancestor-creator and the Water Babies, spirits of springs and ponds.

name: Wildcat Animal-Spirit of Cree
description: The closest attested Cree wildcat being is Mishipizhiw, the Great Lynx or underwater panther, a powerful water monster of Cree and Algonquian tradition who lives in deep lakes and rapids and drags people underwater. It is drawn with catlike features, horns, and a scaly, serpentine body. For the Cree the wildcat of the spirit world is this dangerous water being, not a forest guardian.

name: Wildcat Animal-Spirit of Inuit
description: Not independently attested in Inuit tradition. No wildcats or bobcats live in the Arctic, and no wildcat spirit appears in Inuit mythology, whose animal spirits include the polar bear (Nanook), the wolf (Amarok), the raven, and the whale. The record's forest-dwelling wildcat is a misattribution that ignores Inuit geography and oral tradition.

name: Wildcat Deity (Maya)
description: The Maya jaguar deity, the Jaguar God of the Underworld, is the night form of the sun prowling Xibalba with gleaming eyes and a spotted pelt, bearing fire and war onto incense burners and shields. In highland Guatemala the jaguar still guards caves and mountain shrines, and mountain lords are conceived as jaguars, tying the god to the earth and the deep.

name: Wildcat Deity (Maya)
description: This entry is wrong on two counts: the Maya are a Mesoamerican people, not of the modern United States, and their feline deity is the jaguar, not a generic 'wildcat.' The Jaguar God of the Underworld, associated with the night sun, caves, and the underworld, is a central Maya deity. This record appears to be a jaguar entry garbled and mislabeled as 'wildcat' and 'USA.'

name: Wildcat Deity of Cherokee
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat deity in Cherokee tradition. Cherokee animal lore includes the panther as a powerful being, but no deified wildcat figure is recorded; Cherokee spirit animals are more prominently the bear (whose people became the Yonva bear clan) and the wolf. The record likely conflates a generic feline spirit with Cherokee culture, where no such deity appears.

name: Wildcat Deity of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. No wildcat deity exists in Guaraní mythology (seven legendary monsters, major deities). Wildcats (jaguarundi, margay, ocelot) inhabit the region but hold no deity status. Entity appears fabricated, possibly conflating Kurupi (fertility/sexuality god, sometimes feline-associated) or the Celestial Jaguar myth.

name: Wildcat Deity of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. Duplicate of wildcatdeityofguarani-paraguay with Brazil country assignment. No wildcat deity in Guaraní mythology across Paraguay, Argentina, or Brazil.

name: Wildcat Deity of Shona
description: Not independently attested in Shona tradition. The entry claims a "wildcat deity" guarding oceans — but Zimbabwe is landlocked. African wildcats (Felis lybica) exist but no Shona source documents a wildcat ocean deity. Fabricated templated entry with "guardian of oceans" motif misapplied to landlocked country.

name: Wildcat Deity of Ute
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat deity in Ute tradition. Ute mythology centers on Sinawav (Coyote) as creator and culture hero, and the wolf plays a major role in Ute origin accounts; no wildcat god or goddess appears in recorded Ute stories. The record is a misattribution, likely generated from a generic feline template rather than Ute oral tradition.

name: Wildcat Ghost of Passamaquoddy
description: The closest attested Passamaquoddy wildcat being is Lucifee (also Lusifee or Lucivee), a dangerous malevolent wildcat or lynx spirit of Wabanaki lore shared by the Passamaquoddy and Maliseet. Lucifee is a greedy villain who devours animals and people and must be outwitted; he is a monster of appetite, not a ghost. A genuine wildcat spirit exists, but the 'ghost' framing is inaccurate.

name: Wildcat Ghost of Ute
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat ghost in Ute tradition. Ute folklore records no ghostly wildcat being; its spirit world includes Coyote-Sinawav, the culture hero, and the wolf of creation accounts. As with other Ute 'wildcat' records, this entry appears fabricated, since no wildcat ghost appears in the ethnographic literature on the Ute.

name: Wildcat Giant of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. No wildcat giant exists in Guaraní mythology (seven legendary monsters include no giants). Teju Jagua (cavern lord) is lizard-like; Mbói Tu'ĩ is serpentine. Wildcat giants appear fabricated, possibly conflating feline folklore with giant motifs.

name: Wildcat Giant of Guarani
description: Not independently attested in Guaraní tradition. Duplicate of wildcatgiantofguarani-paraguay with Brazil country assignment. No wildcat giant in Guaraní mythology.

name: Wildcat Giant of Quechua
description: Not independently attested in Quechua/Inca tradition. Inca/Quechua sacred animals: condor, puma, serpent. No wildcat giant in Huarochirí Manuscript, Viracocha myths, or Inka bestiary. Andean wildcats (pampas cat, Andean cat) exist but hold no giant mythic status. Entity appears fabricated.

name: Wildcat Giant of Zulu
description: Not independently attested in Zulu tradition. The entry claims a "wildcat giant" guarding oceans — but KwaZulu-Natal is coastal, yet no Zulu source documents a wildcat giant ocean guardian. African wildcats exist but giant wildcat spirits are unattested. Fabricated templated entry with "guardian of oceans" motif.

name: Wildcat Guardian (Shona)
description: Not independently attested in Shona tradition. The entry claims a "wildcat guardian" embodying oceans in landlocked Zimbabwe. No Shona source documents a wildcat ocean guardian. Fabricated templated entry; snip wildcat guardians appear in South American (e.g., Brazilian curupira) not Shona cosmology.

name: Wildcat Guardian (Shona)
description: Not independently attested in Brazilian tradition. MISATTRIBUTION: The Shona are a Bantu people of ZIMBABWE (Southern Africa), not Brazil. Shona mythology includes Mwari (creator), vadzimu (ancestral spirits), and njuzu (water spirits), but no 'wildcat guardian' in Brazil. Entity appears to be a complete fabrication conflating African and South American elements.

name: Wildcat Guardian of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested as a guardian spirit in Kazakh folklore. The felines that carry mythic weight across the Altai and Turkic world are the lynx, the manul or Pallas's cat, and the snow leopard, dark beasts said in Altai tradition to have been created by the deity of the underworld and surrounded by hunting prohibitions. No specific wildcat guardian appears in Kazakh sources.

name: Wildcat Guardian of Kwakiutl
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat guardian in Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) tradition. The Kwakwaka'wakw of the Northwest Coast have no wildcat guardian figure; their important crests and ancestors include the wolf, raven, killer whale, and bear. In one account the ancestors removed their wolf masks and became human, tying wolf, not wildcat, to origins and chiefly power.

name: Wildcat Guardian of Maliseet
description: The Maliseet wildcat figure is Lucifee (Lusifee or Lucivee), a fierce, greedy wildcat-lynx monster of Wabanaki lore, not a benevolent guardian. Lucifee is a dangerous villain who terrorizes the forest and eats smaller animals and unwary people until a clever being outwits him. The 'guardian' framing misrepresents him; he is among the most feared beings in Maliseet and Passamaquoddy stories.

name: Wildcat Nature-Spirit of Apache
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat nature-spirit in Apache tradition. Apache mythology is built around figures like White Painted Woman and the warrior twins Killer of Enemies and Child of the Water, with animals such as the mountain lion and coyote appearing in tales; no wildcat or bobcat nature-spirit is recorded. The entry appears to be a generic feline misattribution to the Apache.

name: Wildcat Nature-Spirit of Ojibwe
description: The Ojibwe wildcat spirit is Bizhiw (Pishiw or Pizhew), the lynx or bobcat of Anishinaabe tradition, also called the Underwater Lynx or Great Lynx. As a totem, Bizhiw is the animal of the Lynx Clan, and in myth the great underwater lynx is a powerful being of lakes and rapids who battles the Thunderbirds and can drag people beneath the water.

name: Wildcat Nature-Spirit of Ojibwe
description: The Ojibwe wildcat spirit is Bizhiw, the lynx of Anishinaabe tradition, known across Ojibwe communities in both the United States and Canada. The lynx is the totem of the Lynx Clan and appears as the great underwater lynx, a mighty being of deep lakes who clashes with the Thunderbirds and draws swimmers down. As a nature-spirit it embodies both clan kinship and the dangers of northern waters.

name: Wildcat Nature-Spirit of Pomo
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat nature-spirit in Pomo tradition. The extensive Pomo folklore recorded by S. A. Barrett centers on the theft of fire, the earth-diver creation, bear shamans, and Coyote; no wildcat or bobcat nature-spirit appears in these collections. The entry is a misattribution, most likely generated from a generic feline template rather than Pomo oral tradition.

name: Wildcat Nature-Spirit of Uzbek
description: Not independently attested as a nature-spirit in Uzbek folklore. Across the Altai and Turkic world the wild cats, above all the lynx and snow leopard, are mythologized as powerful and untamable beasts hedged about with respect and hunting customs, but no named wildcat nature-spirit is recorded for Uzbek tradition. The claimed water powers are unsupported.

name: Wildcat Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat spirit in Cheyenne tradition. Cheyenne mythology knows no wildcat spirit or deity; its sacred figures are the culture hero Sweet Medicine and the trickster Veeho (Wihio) the spider, along with the spirits of the buffalo, wolf, and eagle. This 'Cheyenne wildcat' record is a duplicate misattribution with no basis in recorded Cheyenne folklore.

name: Wildcat Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: The 'Wildcat Spirit (Cheyenne)' is not attested in Paraguayan or Guaraní tradition. The Cheyenne are a North American Plains people (Montana, Oklahoma) with no historical presence in Paraguay. The closest Guaraní analogue is the Yaguareté-Abá (jaguar shapeshifter) or forest guardian spirits (Yvyraija) documented by Métraux.

name: Wildcat Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: The 'Wildcat Spirit (Cheyenne)' is not attested in Chilean or Mapuche tradition. The Cheyenne are North American Plains people with no presence in Chile. Mapuche tradition features the Ngürü (fox spirit) and ngen (nature owners), but no wildcat spirit matching Cheyenne cosmology. The record appears fabricated.

name: Wildcat Spirit (Cheyenne)
description: Not independently attested in Nigerian tradition. 'Cheyenne' refers to a Native American Plains people (Montana/Oklahoma); wildcat spirits in Cheyenne tradition relate to cave-dwelling guardians. No Cheyenne wildcat spirit exists in Igbo, Yoruba, Hausa, or any Nigerian folklore. Record is a complete cross-continental misattribution.

name: Wildcat Spirit of Dogon
description: Not independently attested in Dogon tradition. Dogon cliff-dwelling culture features mask animals (walu antelope, satimbe woman, kanaga cross) but no named wildcat spirit guarding cliffs. The record's 'central spirit in Dogon mythology' claim is unsupported by Griaule or Dieterlen. Appears fabricated.

name: Wildcat Trickster (Cree)
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat trickster in Cree tradition. The Cree trickster and culture hero is Wisakedjak (Wesakechak), a shapeshifting transformer who rebuilt the world after the flood and whose humorous adventures explain the order of nature; he is not a wildcat. The underwater lynx Mishipizhiw is a Cree wildcat-like being, but it is a dangerous water spirit, never a trickster.

name: Wildcat Trickster (Cree)
description: Not independently attested in Zimbabwe tradition. The Cree are an Indigenous people of North America (Canada/USA). The entry misattributes a Cree wildcat trickster to Zimbabwe. Fabricated cross-continental misattribution; snip wildcat tricksters appear in Cree/Algonquian tradition, not Shona.

name: Wildcat Trickster (Cree)
description: Wildcat Trickster (Cree) (Kenya). is a trickster. A wildcat trickster from Cree tradition that  sky. Source: Kenya mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Wildcat Trickster of Aztec
description: Not independently attested as an Aztec trickster. The Aztecs honored the jaguar and ocelot as warrior emblems, not tricksters, and their trickster roles belonged to the coyote. The nearest shape-shifting trickster god is Tezcatlipoca, whose nagual was a jaguar and whose smoking mirror worked mischief; no wildcat trickster figure appears in the sources.

name: Wildcat Trickster of Dogon
description: Not independently attested in Mali tradition. The figure appears to be a modern composite or fabrication rather than an authentic element of Mali folklore.

name: Wildcat Trickster of Haida
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat trickster in Haida tradition. The Haida trickster and transformer is Raven (Xhuuya), a shapeshifter who stole the sun, moon, and stars and whose adventures shaped the world. No wildcat or bobcat occupies this role in Haida mythology. The record is a generic trickster misattribution, since Northwest Coast trickster lore belongs to Raven, not to any wildcat.

name: Wildcat Trickster of Kazakh
description: Not independently attested as a trickster in Kazakh folklore. The sly-animal role in Turkic Central Asian tales belongs to the fox, while the wild cats of the steppe appear as emblems of strength, power and freedom rather than as tricksters. No wildcat trickster is recorded in Kazakh sources; the claimed shapeshifting traits are unsupported.

name: Wildcat Trickster of Quechua
description: The 'Wildcat Trickster of Quechua' is not independently attested in Quechua tradition. Andean mythology features the fox (atoc) as primary trickster and the puma as a powerful being, but no specific 'wildcat trickster.' The closest analogue is the Andean fox trickster cycle documented by Arguedas and Flores Ochoa.

name: Wildcat Trickster of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat trickster in Tlingit tradition. The Tlingit trickster and culture hero is Raven (Yéil), a shapeshifting transformer whose theft of daylight and other exploits are central to Tlingit oral tradition. Wildcats play no trickster role in Tlingit mythology; the entry is a misattribution, likely generated from a generic template.

name: Wildcat Trickster of Tlingit
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat trickster in Tlingit tradition. The Tlingit culture hero and trickster is Raven (Yéil), the transformer who stole the sun and brought light to the world; no wildcat figure plays this role. This Canada-flagged record is a duplicate of the same misattribution, since Tlingit trickster lore centers on Raven across both Alaska and Canada.

name: Wildcat Water-Spirit of Kikuyu
description: Wildcat Water-Spirit of Kikuyu (Kenya). is a water-spirit. The wildcat water-spirit from Kikuyu tradition, guardian of the mountains. Source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of East Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Madagascar

name: Wildcat Water-Spirit of Paiute
description: Not independently attested as a wildcat water-spirit in Paiute tradition. Paiute water beings are the Water Babies, spirits of springs and ponds who imitate crying infants to lure people into the water, along with great water serpents; no wildcat is associated with water in Paiute lore. The record is a misattribution, possibly confusing the Paiute Wolf creator (Isa) with a feline water being.

name: Wildcat Water-Spirit of Uzbek
description: Not independently attested as a water-spirit in Uzbek folklore. Cats in Central Asian folk belief are domestic creatures whose favor or displeasure is read in omens, but no feline spirit of rivers or lakes appears in Uzbek tradition. The record's ocean habitat and storm-calling powers are modern inventions built on the wildcat's secretive character.

name: Wind
description: Winds figure as living, personified spirits across many Native American traditions. In Navajo belief, Holy Wind (Nilch'i Diyin) is the life-breath that animates all beings; winds guard the four directions at the sacred mountains and appear as spirit people who advise heroes. The Lakota number wind among the aspects of Wakan Tanka, and many Plains peoples revere the four directions.

name: Wind Horse (Lungta)
description: The Wind Horse (lungta) is the sacred steed of Tibetan tradition that carries fortune and the vitality of the living upward to the gods. Its image, a galloping horse bearing a flaming jewel, flies on the five-colored prayer flags of the Himalayas, where the fluttering of the lungta is said to scatter blessings, good fortune and merit across the land.

name: Wind Spirit
description: The Wind Spirit is an elemental force in Comanche mythology. In the creation story, the Great Spirit infused the first people with the spirit of the wind, giving them strength of mighty storms. In the Release of the Wild Animals, a Wind spirit helped a brave warrior open the underground cavern where wild animals were confined, unleashing deer, antelope, elk, bears, wolves, and mountain lions across the plains. The Wind spirit represents freedom, power, and the unseen forces that shape the world. Wind carries prayers and is a messenger between worlds

name: Wind Spirits
description: Wind Spirits (Unknown). is a spirit. Wind spirits appear in the folklore of many cultures as personifications of the wind. In Norse and Icelandic tradition, the wind is associated with supernatural forces, with specific winds believed to. Source: Various folklore traditions

name: Windigo
description: The Windigo is a fearsome cannibalistic ice monster of Ojibwe and Anishinaabe mythology, known throughout the Algonquian-speaking peoples of North America. A Windigo was once human but was transformed through an act of cannibalism or overwhelming greed into a giant, emaciated creature with a heart of ice. It has an insatiable hunger for human flesh and grows larger the more it eats, never satisfied. Windigos are associated with winter, famine, and the cold. They can be killed only by destroying their ice heart or melting it with fire

name: Windigo
description: The Windigo is a fearsome cannibalistic ice monster of Ojibwe and Anishinaabe mythology, known throughout the Algonquian-speaking peoples of North America. A Windigo was once human but was transformed through an act of cannibalism or overwhelming greed into a giant, emaciated creature with a heart of ice. It has an insatiable hunger for human flesh and grows larger the more it eats, never satisfied. Windigos are associated with winter, famine, and the cold. They can be killed only by destroying their ice heart or melting it with fire In United States folklore, this figure is known among the Ojibwe people.

name: Winter Grýla
description: Winter Grýla appears to be a modern seasonal elaboration of the Icelandic ogress Grýla, emphasizing her winter activity. No independent traditional source distinguishes a 'Winter Grýla' as a separate being from the main Grýla figure, who is already intrinsically winter-associated (Christmas). This likely reflects a modern categorization rather than a distinct folk variant.

name: Winter Thunder (Iiʼniʼ Jiłgaii)
description: Winter Thunder (Iiʼniʼ Jiłgaii) is a spirit in Navajo mythology associated with thunderstorms that occur during the cold months. Unlike the summer thunder bringers who release rain for crops, Winter Thunder brings snow, ice storms, and the fierce blizzards that test the resilience of the Navajo people. He is one of the Thunderbird beings and is closely associated with the Thunderbird Mountain in the Chuska range. Winter Thunder is invoked during the Night Chant ceremony to bring clarity and purify those afflicted by illness, and his appearance signals a time of trial and spiritual testing

name: Wise One
description: Not independently attested as 'Wise One' in the standard Apache ethnographic corpus. The Apache monster-slayer is Killer-of-Enemies, with Child of the Water in related traditions; the paired-brothers framing echoes Navajo heroic twins rather than any documented Apache 'Wise One.' The record appears to be a template construct without a firm source.

name: Witch
description: Witch (European). is a witch. Individuals, typically female, who possess supernatural powers, often derived from occult knowledge or demonic pacts. Source: European folklore, occult traditions

name: Witch (Heks)
description: Heks is the Danish witch: practitioner of folk magic (trolldom), from malevolent hag to wise healer. Often withered old woman with crooked nose, warts, familiar (cat, toad), or deceptive beauty. Brews potions, casts curses, bargains with spirits; magic tied to nature and moon. Vulnerable to iron, holy symbols, own greed. Embodies fear/respect for knowledge outside institutions.

name: Witch Bear
description: Not independently attested as a named 'witch bear' in any single Native American tradition, though related themes are widespread. Some tribes tell of bear-women who don a bearskin and become dangerous to their kin, and of bear shamans such as the Pomo Bear Doctors who drew power from bears. The Pawnee Bear Medicine Woman and Cherokee bear-clan stories are the closest genuine analogues.

name: Witch Denmark
description: Witch Denmark (Unknown). is a witch. The Witch is a character from Danish fairy tales who tests heroes with enchantments or aids them with magical gifts.. Source: Danish folklore — witches documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Witch Troll
description: Not independently attested in Nordic tradition as a named hybrid being. Nordic folklore has trolls (trold, jätte) and witches (hejre, klok gumma) as distinct categories; snip 'witch-troll' is a modern descriptive conflation. The closest analogues are trollkonor (troll-wives) who practice magic, or the Finnish hiisi beings blending troll and sorcerer traits.

name: Wodnik
description: Wodnik is the Polish male water spirit, ruler of lakes, rivers, ponds, and millponds. Documented by Oskar Kolberg in Pomeranian and Masovian materials. Controls aquatic creatures; drowns those who disrespect his waters. Fishermen offer tobacco for good catches. Appears as a green-clad man or naked figure. West Slavic counterpart to Czech Vodník and Russian Vodyanoy.

name: Wohpekumen
description: Wohpekumeu is the trickster-transformer and culture hero of the Yurok people of northwestern California, sometimes called 'the Widower.'
