In Yurok mythology he is a shapeshifter who attempts both beneficial and foolish deeds, helping shape the world and teaching people how to live. His exploits balance comedy with the ordering of the world, and he is among the best-known Yurok figures.

name: Wolf Ancestor-Spirit (Kikuyu)
description: Wolf Ancestor-Spirit (Kikuyu) (Kenya). is a ancestor-spirit. A wolf ancestor-spirit from Kikuyu tradition that  swamp. Source: Kenya mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Wolf Ancestor-Spirit (Kikuyu)
description: Not independently attested: the Kikuyu are a Kenyan people with no wolf ancestor-spirit, since wolves do not live in Kenya, and no such figure is recorded in Mexico either. Kikuyu belief centers on the creator Ngai and on animal characters such as the hyena in trickster tales. The record appears to confuse unrelated cultures and animals.

name: Wolf Ancestor-Spirit (Kikuyu)
description: Not independently attested as a Kikuyu or Myanmar ancestor-spirit. The Kikuyu of Kenya worship the high god Ngai (Mwathani) at Mount Kenya under the mugumo fig tree; their documented religion contains no wolf ancestor-spirit. The record mislabels culture and region, combining a Kenyan people with a Myanmar setting; it appears to be a generic spirit template without documentary basis.

name: Wolf Ancestor-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Wolves hold a deep place in Blackfoot tradition as powerful, kinlike beings. In the story of the Wolf Man, a man rescued from murderous wives is adopted by a wolf pack that makes him their brother. The Blackfoot call the Milky Way the Wolf Trail, the road wolves and the dead travel to the sky, and orphaned heroes are befriended by wolves in star legends.

name: Wolf Ancestor-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Wolves are central to Blackfoot (Siksika) tradition on both sides of the Canada-United States border. The Wolf Man story tells of a man saved from his murderous wives and adopted as a brother by wolves, and Blackfoot people call the Milky Way the Wolf Trail, the road wolves follow toward the spirit world. Wolves appear as rescuers and guides in the star legends of the Blackfoot's orphaned heroes.

name: Wolf Ancestor-Spirit of Choctaw
description: The wolf, nashoba in the Choctaw language, is a respected being in Choctaw tradition. Wolf clans (iksa) exist among the Choctaw, and wolves appear in teaching stories such as 'How the Possum Tricked the Wolves.' The name Neshoba, preserved in Mississippi geography, is the Choctaw word for wolf; he is honored as a relative and clan name-bearer rather than a formal deity.

name: Wolf Animal-Spirit of Cheyenne
description: The wolf is a significant being in Cheyenne tradition, most prominently through the Wolf Warriors, a military society renowned for ferocity and courage in battle that scholars such as George Bird Grinnell linked to the Bowstring Men. Cheyenne medicine men rubbed warrior arrows against wolf fur for success in hunting, and the wolf teaches community and loyalty.

name: Wolf Animal-Spirit of Muisca
description: The 'Wolf Animal-Spirit of Muisca' is not attested in Muisca mythology. The Muisca (Altiplano Cundiboyacense, Colombia) had no wolves—wolves are absent from South America. Muisca deities include Bochica, Chía, Sué, Chibchacum, and Bachué; snip animal spirits include the snake and bear-fox Nencatacoa. The record appears fabricated.

name: Wolf Animal-Spirit of Navajo
description: The wolf, ma'iitsoh in Navajo, has two faces in Diné tradition. Gray Wolf is a protector given by Changing Woman to guard the Bitter Water Clan and San Francisco Peaks, and a wolf's howl warns warriors to turn back from a raid. Yet mai-coh, the word for wolf, also means 'witch': skinwalkers are said to wear wolf skins to work evil, so the wolf embodies both protection and misused power.

name: Wolf Brothers Chinook
description: In Wasco (Chinookan) tradition, the Five Wolf Brothers appear as traveling companions in a tale cycle in which Coyote places the stars and orders the sky. Variants tell of rival sets of brothers whose contest produced the winds; the wolf brothers embody the strength of the pack, which Chinookan peoples respected in their storytelling.

name: Wolf Clan Spirits Tsimshian
description: Wolf is one of the four matrilineal clans of the Coast Tsimshian, called Laxgyibuu, and a principal crest whose legend holds that the wolf is the land equivalent of the killer whale. Wolf-clan spirit beings, ancestors who came from the supernatural world, are honored in crest carvings, songs, and potlatch regalia and guard the clan's territory and identity.

name: Wolf Deity (Mapuche)
description: The 'Wolf Deity (Mapuche)' is not attested in Mapuche tradition. Wolves are absent from South America; snip the Mapuche have no wolf deity. Mapuche cosmology features Ngünechen, the ngen (nature owners), wekufe spirits, and animal spirits like the fox (Ngürü) and puma. The record misapplies Northern Hemisphere wolf motifs.

name: Wolf Deity (Mapuche)
description: Not independently attested in South African tradition. The Mapuche are an Indigenous people of Chile and Argentina. The entry misattributes a Mapuche wolf deity to South Africa. Wolves (Canis lupus) are not native to Africa; snip African wild dogs (Lycaon) exist but no Mapuche/South African wolf deity. Fabricated cross-continental misattribution.

name: Wolf Deity of Haida
description: Not independently attested as a wolf deity in Haida folklore. Haida sacred narratives center on the Raven (Xhuuya/Nankil'slas), the culture hero and transformer who shaped the world and freed the sun and the tides; the wolf appears chiefly as a crest and clan emblem carved on poles, never as a worshipped god. The water-spirit archetype is a template artifact.

name: Wolf Deity of Kwakiutl
description: Not independently attested as a wolf deity among the Kwakwaka'wakw. Their central creative and trickster figure is Raven, who made the islands, released daylight, and shaped the first humans from wood and clay; the wolf is a respected hereditary crest figure, not an object of worship. The water-spirit framing is a template artifact.

name: Wolf Deity of Yurok
description: Not independently attested as a wolf deity in Yurok folklore. Yurok tradition is carried by the trickster-heroes Pulekukwerek and Wohpekumeu, recorded by Kroeber, Sapir, and Spott and Kroeber, who put the world in order and bestow power on worthy humans. The wolf is a familiar animal of the Klamath watershed, not a worshipped deity.

name: Wolf Ghost of Choctaw
description: Not independently attested as a wolf ghost in Choctaw folklore. The attested Choctaw spirit beings include Nalusa Falaya, a shadowy figure who slips along trails to attack travelers, and the little forest people Bohpoli and Kowi Anukasha; no wolf specter or wolf ghost appears in the recorded corpus documented by Swanton.

name: Wolf Ghost of Hopi
description: Not independently attested as a wolf ghost in Hopi tradition. The Hopi katsinam include Kweo, a wolf kachina who is a great hunter and pathfinder guiding villages to game, and wolves appear in the world-age account of the second world; a malevolent wolf specter is not part of the ceremonial record.

name: Wolf Giant of Aztec
description: No giant wolf appears in Aztec mythology. The attested wolf-like being is cuetlachtli, described in the Florentine Codex as a woolly, man-faced, wheezing stalker with a bushy tail, whose skin was worn by the 'Old Wolf' priest who tied captives to the gladiatorial stone of Xipe Totec. This is a ritual figure, not a giant.

name: Wolf Giant of Zulu
description: Not independently attested in Zulu tradition. No 'wolf giant' appears in Bantu oral records; wolves are absent from sub-Saharan Africa. The record likely conflates the Zulu river-goddess Mamlambo (a serpentine water spirit) with foreign wolf motifs. Zulu myth features sky spirits like Umvelinqangi and the shape-shifting Nomkhubulwane, but no wolf-beings.

name: Wolf Guardian (Cheyenne)
description: No standalone wolf guardian spirit is attested in Cheyenne folklore; the record inflates a real tradition. The wolf's central Cheyenne presence is the Wolf Warriors, a renowned military society honoring the wolf's wariness and skill, and wolves appear in tales as helpers and teachers. The animal is honored for endurance, not worshipped as a nature-spirit deity.

name: Wolf Guardian of Mapuche
description: The 'Wolf Guardian of Mapuche' is not attested in Mapuche tradition. Wolves never inhabited South America. Mapuche guardianship involves the ngen (place-owners) and machi (shamans) who mediate with spirits. The closest analogues are ngen-wenu (owner of the sky) or ngen-mapu (owner of the land), not a wolf figure.

name: Wolf Guardian of Muisca
description: The 'Wolf Guardian of Muisca' is not attested in Muisca tradition. Wolves never existed in South America. Muisca guardianship is associated with Bochica (civilizer hero), the zipa/zaque rulers, and the sacred lakes (Guatavita, Iguaque). No wolf figures appear in Muisca mythology documented by Ocampo López.

name: Wolf Guardian of Yurok
description: Not independently attested as a wolf guardian in Yurok folklore. Yurok cosmology is carried by the culture heroes Pulekukwerek and Wohpekumeu, who established customs, dances, and the balance of the world as told by Kroeber, Sapir, and Spott and Kroeber; no wolf guardian figure appears in their recorded stories.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit (Tupi)
description: The 'Wolf Nature-Spirit (Tupi)' is not attested in Tupi-Guarani tradition. Wolves are absent from South America. Tupi-Guarani cosmology features the culture hero Mboi-Tatá (fire serpent), the trickster Curupira, and the jaguar (Yaguareté) as a powerful being. No wolf spirits exist in the ethnography of Métraux or Darcy Ribeiro.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Baloch
description: Not independently attested in Balochi folklore as a named entity 'Wolf Nature-Spirit of Baloch'. Balochi oral tradition includes nature spirits, jinns, and animal helpers (e.g., in the epic of Mir Chakar Rind), but no specific wolf spirit by this name. The 'guardian of the swamps' and 'central nature-spirit' description appears fabricated.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as a wolf nature-spirit deity among the Blackfoot. Wolves appear as powerful helpers in Blackfoot tales, most famously in the Wolf Man story, where a pack saves a husband from his murderous wives; wolves are respected allies, but no wolf spirit-deity of nature is recorded.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as a wolf nature-spirit deity among the Blackfoot. Wolves appear as powerful helpers in Blackfoot tales, most famously in the Wolf Man story, where a pack saves a husband from his murderous wives; wolves are respected allies, but no wolf spirit-deity of nature is recorded.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Haida
description: The wolf is a foundational crest figure of the Haida, one of the principal clan emblems along with the Raven, Eagle, and Killer Whale, carved on poles and house fronts. In the legend of Wolf and the Sea, wolves pursue a sea creature underwater and are transformed, giving origin to the killer whales. No separate wolf deity is attested.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Hopi
description: The wolf appears in Hopi kachina religion as Kweo, the wolf kachina, a great hunter, teacher, and pathfinder who helps villages find game and guides hunts. Wolves also figure in the Hopi account of the second world, when the ancestors took the forms of wolves and bears during their migrations. Kweo is a beneficent kachina, not an abstract nature-spirit deity.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Kazakh
description: The wolf (qasqyr, böri) is the paramount sacred animal of Kazakh folklore, a totem descended from the ancient Turkic böri cult. Revered as a protector and as a sign of freedom and strength, the wolf appears throughout Kazakh tales, names and customs; its skin and body parts served as talismans and folk remedies, and the wolf endures as a symbol of the Kazakh people.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: The wolf is a major hereditary crest of the Kwakwaka'wakw. The Dzawada'enuxw recall that their ancestors were four wolves who swam from the mainland and took human form, making the wolf a tutelary ancestor rather than an abstract nature-spirit. Wolves are honored in the winter ceremonial and as clan founders, not worshipped as separate nature spirits.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Miwok
description: Not independently attested as a wolf nature-spirit in Miwok folklore. Miwok creation is carried by Silver Fox, who sang the world into being, and Coyote, the ancestor of the people; the wolf plays no creator or spirit role in the recorded Miwok corpus. The record is a template-generated spirit with no tribal basis.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Muisca
description: The 'Wolf Nature-Spirit of Muisca' is not attested in Muisca tradition. Wolves never existed in South America. Muisca nature spirits are associated with lakes (Guatavita, Iguaque), mountains, and the rainbow (Cuchavira). Animal beings include the snake and bear-fox Nencatacoa. This entry misapplies Northern Hemisphere wolf symbolism.

name: Wolf Nature-Spirit of Paiute
description: Wolf is a creator and culture hero in Paiute tradition, called Isa, who usually appears in human form and made the world and its people in the beginning; Coyote, his younger brother, follows him and brings folly, death, and change. Wolf is the elder and wiser of the pair, respected as the one who set the world in order.

name: Wolf Prince Denmark
description: Wolf Prince Denmark (Unknown). is a animal-spirit. The Wolf Prince is a prince transformed into a wolf by a curse in Danish folklore.. Source: Danish folklore — wolf prince spirit documented in Danish oral tradition.

name: Wolf Spirit
description: The Wolf Spirit is a powerful animal spirit and guardian figure in Comanche mythology. In the story How the Buffalo Were Released, a Wolf spirit guided a young Comanche warrior to the cave where buffalo were hidden, transformed him into a buffalo calf to infiltrate the herd, and taught the people how to hunt the buffalo with respect. In vision quest stories, Wolf appears as a spirit guide granting strength, courage, and tracking ability to warriors who fast and seek visions. Wolf is considered a brother and protector to the Comanche people

name: Wolf Spirit (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested in Laotian folklore: no tradition records a forest wolf spirit. Wolves are not native to Laos, and Lao animist cosmology centers on phi spirits, the protective khwan (thirty-two souls), and tiger- or dog-related shapeshifters (weretigers), with no wolf figure. The description appears to be a generic forest-spirit template applied without documentary basis.

name: Wolf Spirit (Laotian)
description: Not independently attested as a Laotian forest spirit, and wolves are not native to Laos, where folklore features phi nature spirits, nagas and other beings rather than wolf deities. The same mislabeled record appeared in an earlier batch and is a modern fabrication; the Mexico placement compounds the error.

name: Wolf Trickster (Mapuche)
description: The 'Wolf Trickster (Mapuche)' is not attested in Mapuche tradition. Wolves are absent from South America. Mapuche trickster figures include the wekufe (harmful spirits) and the kalku (sorcerer), but no wolf trickster. The fox (Ngürü) appears in some tales but not as a primary trickster. This is a fabricated entry applying Eurasian motifs.

name: Wolf Trickster (Mapuche)
description: Not attested in Mapuche mythology: the Mapuche trickster is the fox (ngürü), whose deceitful adventures fill a large cycle of tales, while no wolf-trickster figure exists. Mapuche tradition includes wekufe, harmful shapeshifting spirits, and the punalka, a wolf-like night creature, but neither functions as a trickster. The record also misplaces this South American figure in Myanmar.

name: Wolf Trickster (Mapuche)
description: Not independently attested in Botswana or Mapuche tradition. Mapuche (Chile/Argentina) mythology features the fox-like trickster Colocolo and the shapeshifting Kalku, but no wolf trickster. Wolves are absent from both southern Africa and Patagonia. The record misattributes a South American culture to Botswana and invents a wolf figure where none exists.

name: Wolf Trickster (Mapuche)
description: Not independently attested: the Mapuche trickster is not a wolf but the fox, ngürü, cast in tales (epew) as a clever and sometimes diabolical 'ñiwa wentru' figure. Wolves do not feature as Mapuche tricksters, and the Mexico placement is mistaken, since the Mapuche live in Chile and Argentina. This duplicates a mislabel found in an earlier batch.

name: Wolf Trickster of Cheyenne
description: Not independently attested as a wolf trickster in Cheyenne folklore. The Cheyenne trickster is Veeho, a spider who takes human form and is both transformer-hero and fool; his name, often misread as 'White Man,' actually means 'Spider.' Cheyenne wolves instead belong to the Wolf Warrior society, an honored order, not trickster tales.

name: Wolf Trickster of Inuit
description: Amaguq is a wolf trickster-spirit in Inuit tradition, able to shape-shift between human and wolf form and known for clever, wily behavior in tales; the name is an Iñupiaq word for the wolf. He is distinct from Amarok, the lone giant wolf-spirit that preys on foolish hunters abroad at night.

name: Wolf Trickster of Kwakiutl
description: Not independently attested as a wolf trickster among the Kwakwaka'wakw. The trickster-creator of their mythology is Raven, who brought daylight, made the islands, and formed the first humans from wood and clay. The wolf is a respected crest and founding ancestor of chiefly lines, not a trickster figure.

name: Wolf Trickster of Maya
description: Not independently attested: wolves never lived in the Maya lowlands, and the Maya trickster and nawal is the coyote, not a wolf. No Maya story features a wolf trickster guarding the hills. The record misattributes a generic wolf-trickster template to the Maya.

name: Wolf Water-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as a wolf water-spirit in Blackfoot folklore. Blackfoot wolves are land animals and helpers, as in the Wolf Man tale, while water is the domain of other beings; no wolf is associated with lakes, rivers, or oceans in the recorded Blackfoot corpus. The water-spirit archetype is a template artifact.

name: Wolf Water-Spirit of Blackfoot
description: Not independently attested as a wolf water-spirit in Blackfoot folklore. Blackfoot wolves are land animals and helpers, as in the Wolf Man tale, while water is the domain of other beings; no wolf is associated with lakes, rivers, or oceans in the recorded Blackfoot corpus. The water-spirit archetype is a template artifact.

name: Wolf Water-Spirit of Inuit
description: Not independently attested as a wolf water-spirit in Inuit folklore. The attested wolf beings are land dwellers: Amarok, a gigantic lone wolf-spirit that hunts hunters abroad at night, and Amaguq, a wolf trickster. Waters are instead the domain of figures such as Sedna of the sea; no wolf spirit is tied to rivers.

name: Woman of the Sea
description: Not independently attested as 'Woman of the Sea' in Haida or generic Canadian folklore. Coastal Northwest Coast traditions do include sea-connected women, such as the Haida Ocean Woman of recent retellings and Property Woman, who grants wealth, but no named 'Woman of the Sea' spirit appears in the ethnographic record. The entry is vague and unattested.

name: Wooden Person
description: Not independently attested as a 'Wooden Person' spirit in Haida folklore. In related Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, Raven fashions the first man and woman from wood and clay, and Haida Raven likewise fashions people; these are episodes within Raven's creation work, not a distinct spirit. The record appears to distill that motif without a tribal basis.

name: Wuriupranili
description: Wuriupranili is the sun woman in Aboriginal Australian mythology, particularly among the peoples of northern Australia. In the Dreamtime, Wuriupranili traveled across the sky each day carrying a burning torch that brought light and warmth to the world. Her torch was so bright that it illuminated everything below. According to tradition, at the end of each day, she would dip her torch into the western ocean, creating the spectacular sunsets that paint the sky with red and orange. She then traveled underground through a tunnel back to the east, emerging each morning to begin her journey again. The red ochre found in the earth is said to be the remnants of her torch. Wuriupranili's daily cycle represents the eternal pattern of day and night

name: Xan
description: Xan (or Khana) is an Azerbaijani ghost — the restless spirit of a murdered person or wronged lover. It haunts the scene of death, family home, or grave until justice is served or bones are properly buried. Nighttime apparitions and haunting are its behaviors. The belief reflects traditional Azerbaijani emphasis on proper burial rites.

name: Xana
description: Xanas are water spirits of Asturian folklore, beautiful young women who dwell in springs, rivers, and caves (cuevas de xanas), often combing their long hair by the water and offering gifts or trials to passersby. Documented by Ramón Menéndez Pidal, the tradition is connected to pre-Roman Celtic belief and the cult of Diana; the name derives from Diana or Jana.

name: Xanaax Atwaayaa Tlingit
description: In the Tlingit story of the Salmon Box (Kudatan Kahidi), Xanaax.atwaayaa is a being who holds a staff tipped with a supernatural octopus tentacle. Raven, disguised, trades him a magic arrow in the form of a magpie and gains the staff, whose power he uses to draw the salmon close to shore and to control their coming.

name: Xbalanque (Jaguar Sun)
description: Xbalanque, 'Jaguar Sun,' is one of the Maya Hero Twins of the Popol Vuh. With his brother Hunahpu he descended into Xibalba, survived its lethal Houses, and defeated the Lords of Death through trickery, rising from the underworld to become the sun and the moon. He is often depicted with jaguar pelt markings, linking him to the night sun of the Maya cosmos.

name: Xe Las Coast Salish
description: Xelas (Xe Las) is the Transformer of Coast Salish oral tradition who walked the world setting it right in the myth age. He and his helpers changed the flawed beings of that time into the animals and landmarks of today, and Coast Salish peoples trace the present shape of mountains, rivers, and creatures to his journeys.

name: Xe Las The Changer Coast Salish
description: Xelas is the great Transformer of Coast Salish tradition, a benevolent culture hero who traveled the Pacific Northwest reshaping the world. He turned the changeling beings of the myth age into their present forms and set the natural order, remembered as Xáays among the Squamish and Xa:ls in Halkomelem.

name: Xhindet
description: Xhindet are the jinn-like trickster spirits of Albanian folklore, beings of illusion and stealth that haunt mountain passes and old ruins. Mischievous and deceptive rather than overtly malevolent, they can be countered with iron or clever riddles. Their stories remind listeners that the world holds unseen forces which must be negotiated with wit, a recurring theme across the Balkans.

name: Xibalba
description: Xibalba, 'place of fright,' is the Maya underworld of the Popol Vuh, ruled by the Lords of Death. Reached through caves, cenotes, or by a river of scorpions, blood, and pus, it is a realm of trial filled with the Houses of Darkness, Knives, Cold, Jaguars, Fire, and Bats. The Hero Twins' descent and escape reveal it as a place both terrible and ultimately conquerable.

name: Xiezhi
description: Xiezhi (獬豸) is the single-horned justice beast of Chinese tradition, usually pictured as a goat-, ox-, or lion-like animal with black fur. In accounts, when disputes were brought before it, it gored the guilty and spared the innocent, making it an emblem of impartial judgment. Its image decorated the robes of imperial censors and judges, and it passed into other East Asian legal symbolism.

name: Xjabil
description: Not independently attested as a named dwarf or guardian spirit of Guatemalan folklore. No source records a Maya mountain-being called 'Xjabil' who guards peaks or restores lost objects. The closest real figures are the Yucatec Maya Xtabay, a forest temptress spirit, and the duende and alux dwarf-helper traditions of Mesoamerican folklore. The recorded name and traits appear to be modern invention.

name: Xnifs
description: Xnifs are mischievous imps of Maltese folklore said to live in ruins and abandoned places, causing minor household troubles and pilfering food. They belong to the broader class of Mediterranean household and ruin-dwelling goblins. The belief is recorded in Maltese oral tradition, though documentation is sparse and largely secondary.

name: Xolotl
description: Xolotl is the Aztec god of fire, lightning, twins, monsters, death, and the evening star, twin of Quetzalcoatl. Dog-headed, he guides the souls of the dead through the underworld as a psychopomp and escorts the sun to its nightly doom. Fleeing the gods who sought to sacrifice him, he hid as the axolotl salamander, which bears his name.

name: Xtabai
description: Xtabai (also spelled Xtabay) is a demonic femme fatale from Yucatec Maya folklore who lures men to their deaths with her incredible beauty. She appears as a stunning woman with long black hair falling to her ankles, wearing a white dress, and combs her hair with the spines of a Tzacam cactus while waiting behind a ceiba tree. According to legend, she was once Utz-colel, a haughty and pure woman who, after death, prayed to evil spirits and became a demon. She lures men deep into the forest, seduces them, then transforms into a poisonous serpent and devours them. In some versions she throws them off cliffs or rips out their hearts. The ceiba tree — sacred in Maya culture as the axis mundi connecting heaven, earth, and underworld — becomes her hunting ground

name: Xác
description: Not independently attested as a named figure of Vietnamese folklore: 'Xác' is the Vietnamese word for corpse. The recorded traits of a reanimated body fit the attested beliefs of ma da, the restless ghost of a corpse, and quỷ nhập tràng, a wandering ghost that seizes a fresh corpse and delays the funeral.

name: Yacumama
description: Yacumama (Quechua: 'mother of water') is an enormous Amazonian serpent spirit, mother of all aquatic life, dwelling in rivers and lakes. She sucks in any living thing within 100 paces; Indigenous boatmen blow conch horns to reveal her presence. Documented across the upper Amazon (Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil).

name: Yacuruna
description: Yacuruna (Quechua: 'water people') are hairy, deformed-footed aquatic beings who inhabit upside-down underwater cities in Amazonian rivers. They abduct humans (especially menstruating women) by transforming into pink river dolphins or handsome men, using aphrodisiacs. Victims gradually transform into Yacuruna. Shamans summon them as familiars for healing knowledge.

name: Yaguarón
description: Not independently attested as a distinct water spirit. 'Yaguarón' is a Paraguayan city named from Guarani 'jaguar-ú' (big dog/jaguar). Guarani myth mentions a primordial giant jaguar/dog, but no named water spirit 'Yaguarón' exists. The record conflates toponymy with mythology.

name: Yagwanggwi
description: Yagwanggwi (야광귀, 'night-light ghost') is a Korean folk spirit said to appear on the night of lunar New Year's Eve (seotdal geumeum), stealing people's shoes or sandals while they sleep. Documented by the National Folk Museum of Korea, the tradition holds that hanging a sieve or mesh by the door keeps the ghost away, because it stops to count the holes and is delayed until dawn.

name: Yaksha
description: Yakshas are nature spirits in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain myth — guardians of treasure, fertility, wilderness. Attendants of Kubera, inhabit forests, sacred trees, mountains, water. Can be benevolent (granting boons) or malevolent (causing illness). Male yakshas; females yakshinis. Prominent in early Buddhist art (Sanchi, Bharhut) as Salabhanjikas. Thirty-six in Uddamareshvara Tantra. Pan-South Asian.

name: Yakshini
description: Yakshinis are female nature spirits in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain myth — attendants of Kubera, linked to trees (ashoka, sal), water, fertility. Can be benevolent (granting prosperity, children) or malevolent (causing illness, madness). Thirty-six with mantras in Uddamareshvara Tantra. Key in early Buddhist art as Salabhanjikas (tree-goddesses). Worshipped as tutelary deities. Pan-South Asian tradition.

name: Yali
description: Yali is a Tamil mythological composite creature — lion body, elephant trunk, horse mane, sometimes goat horns. Prominent in South Indian temple architecture (pillars, stairways) as guardian of thresholds, protector of sacred spaces. Not a 'demonic entity' but a protective guardian. Seen in Chola, Vijayanagara, Nayaka temples (Meenakshi, Srirangam). Symbol of royal power, divine protection.

name: Yam-Nahar
description: Yam-Nahar (literally 'Sea-River') is the god of the sea and rivers in ancient Syrian (Ugaritic) mythology, the personification of the destructive power of the waters. Known as Prince Yam and Judge Nahar, he is son of the supreme god El and the beloved of his father. Yam is depicted as a serpentine deity, often identified with the sea monster Lotan (Leviathan). In the Baal Cycle, Yam challenges the storm god Baal for kingship of the gods, sending messengers to demand Baal's tribute. Baal defeats Yam in cosmic combat using divine weapons crafted by the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis, establishing order over chaos. This Chaoskampf myth is one of the earliest recorded divine combat narratives and directly influenced the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Hebrew Bible imagery of Yahweh's defeat of Leviathan, and Greek myths of Zeus versus Typhon

name: Yamawaro
description: Yamawaro (山童) is a kappa-like mountain yōkai of western Japan, especially Kyūshū and the Chūgoku region, appearing as a small, hairy, childlike figure with a round head and sometimes a water dish on its crown. It is said to descend to rivers in spring and become a river kappa. It helps woodcutters haul logs when given rice cakes, and plays harmless tricks when gifts are withheld.

name: Yamm
description: Yamm is the Canaanite-Phoenician god of the sea, rivers, and primordial chaos. As the deity representing the untamed and destructive power of the Mediterranean, Yamm was especially significant to the maritime Phoenicians of Lebanon's coastal cities. Depicted as consistently tyrannical and angry, he was the brother of Mot and the son of El, the supreme god. His great myth is told in the Ugaritic Baal Cycle where he demands tribute from all the gods and claims dominion over them. Only Baal Hadad, the storm god, dares to oppose him. Armed with two divine maces forged by Kothar-wa-Khasis, Baal fights and defeats Yamm, scattering his body across the sea. This Chaoskampf myth directly inspired the biblical accounts of Yahweh defeating Leviathan

name: Yanauluha (Culture Hero)
description: Yanauluha is a benevolent culture hero in Zuni mythology who brought the arts of medicine and agriculture to the people. After the emergence into the daylight world, he appeared carrying seeds, digging sticks, and sacred objects. He taught which plants were edible and medicinal, how to plant corn and other crops, and how to observe celestial cycles for planting timing. He also taught how to use plants for healing. Yanauluha established the pattern of the agricultural year and the accompanying ce

name: Yara-ma-yha-who
description: The Yara-ma-yha-who is a vampiric spirit from Aboriginal Australian Dreaming legends, particularly in the mythology of the Yuin people of southeastern Australia. This creature is described as a small, red-skinned being standing about four feet tall with an oversized head, a large mouth, and long, skinny limbs. Each of its hands and feet ends in suckers like those of an octopus or frog. The Yara-ma-yha-who lives in fig trees and drops down on unsuspecting travelers, using its suckers to drain their blood. After feeding, the creature swells up and then drops the victim, who wakes up weaker but alive. The process repeats each time the victim passes beneath the tree, and with each encounter the victim grows shorter and redder until eventually becoming a Yara-ma-yha-who themselves

name: Yatoka (Sun Father)
description: Yatoka, the Sun Father, is the Zuni celestial deity, the form taken by Áwonawílona, the All-Container, when he made himself into the sun. From the mist clouds of the Sun Father gathered the Great Waters from which Earth Mother (Áwitelin Tsíta) and Sky Father (Ápoyan Tá'chu) emerged, beginning the Zuni creation.

name: Yawk Yawk
description: The Yawkyawk are female water spirits of the Kunwinjku people of western Arnhem Land, often shown as maidens with fish tails and hair of flowing water-weed who live in freshwater creeks, billabongs, and rock pools. In one account, the girls Likanaya and Marrayka were changed into such spirits after camping near the sacred waterhole of Ngalyod, the Rainbow Serpent.

name: Yawm Saub (God of Creation)
description: Yawm Saub (also Yer Shau or simply Saub — 'The One Who Knows Everything') is the high god and creator in Hmong cosmology. He is the supreme celestial being who created the world and all living things, though he is somewhat remote and delegates daily affairs to lesser spirits. Saub is depicted as polygynous, living in a celestial house with a garden and pigs — very human in his nature yet all-seeing and all-knowing. When the evil spirit Ntxwj Nyog began devouring human souls, Saub sent the first shaman Siv Yis to combat him. It was Saub who advised the surviving siblings after the great flood to marry and repopulate the earth, and who told them to carve the resulting mass into twelve pieces that became the Hmong clans. Saub provided the first seeds for agriculture, caused the first hen to lay eggs, and taught humanity proper rituals. Unlike Ntxwj Nyog who is actively involved in causing harm, Saub is benevolent but distant — he set the world in motion and provides shamans with power but rarely intervenes directly

name: Yeay Lac
description: Yeay Lac is a guardian from Cambodia folklore. Cambodian female guardian spirit of villages and forests. Usually elderly, wise, protects from evil spirits and bandits. Can be summoned by rituals. Village guardian deity. Traditional protection spirit before Buddhism

name: Yei
description: Yei (yé'iis) are the Holy People, the spirit deities of Navajo (Diné) tradition who emerged from the underworld to teach humanity. Chiefs among them are Hasjéyalti (Talking God), Hastséhogan (House God), Hastsézĭni the fire god, and Hastséoltoi the huntress; they appear in masked Yei Bi Chei dances and are painted in sandpaintings, each tied to the cardinal directions.

name: Yeil (Raven)
description: Yeil is the Tlingit name for Raven, the central trickster and culture hero of Tlingit mythology. Yeil is responsible for many fundamental features of the world. He created the tides by making a woman under the earth to control the rise and fall of water. In the Tlingit flood narrative, Raven commanded the tide woman to raise the water. When Raven returned, he turned the remaining people and animals into stone and made new human beings from leaves, explaining why people die in autumn when leaves fall. Yeil is both creator and destroyer

name: Yeil Raven Tlingit
description: Yeil, the Raven, is the great trickster and creator of the Tlingit, who stole the sun, moon, and stars in nested boxes and released them into the sky. He shaped the landscape, brought salmon to the rivers, and gave fire to the people; his lineage, the Raven moiety, is one of the two primary divisions of Tlingit society.

name: Yelmo
description: Yelmo is a nature-spirit from Mongolia folklore. Mongolian wind horse that runs across steppes bringing storms and change. Can be ridden by shamanic spirits. Symbolizes vital energy. Shamanic symbol of life force and change. Important in Mongolian spirituality

name: Yemayá
description: Yemayá is the Yoruba orisha of the sea, motherhood, and fish, brought to Cuba through the transatlantic slave trade. In Santería she owns all waters, governs maternity and fertility, and is syncretized with Our Lady of Regla. She is motherly and protective but destructive when angered, her waters creating rivers and floods.

name: Yemoja
description: Yemoja is the great mother goddess of the Yoruba pantheon, the orisha of the ocean, motherhood, fertility, and the Ogun River. Her name means "Mother whose children are the fish." She is considered the mother of many orishas and the protective spirit of women, children, and sailors. As the primordial ocean from which all life emerged, Yemoja represents the maternal essence of the universe. In times of drought, she emerges from the depths carrying the moon in her womb, bringing tides and rains. Her devotees dress in blue and white and offer her rice, fish, and gourds

name: Yeshe Tsogyal
description: Yeshe Tsogyal, the 'Victorious Lake of Wisdom,' was an eighth-century Tibetan princess and consort of Padmasambhava, revered as a master, consort, and dakini who attained the rainbow body. Credited with concealing the terma treasures with her master, she is invoked for healing and protection and remains a central female figure of Tibetan Buddhism.

name: Yetga-chach
description: Not independently attested as a distinct figure of Kyrgyz folklore. No source confirms a forest spirit named 'Yetga-chach,' described as an old hunter with a huge beard who protects game and trees; searches return only the unrelated Kyrgyz and Turkic word 'chach' (hair) and an unrelated Ukrainian forest deity. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Yeti
description: Yeti (Meh-Teh in Nepali, Dzure in Bhutanese) is the 'Abominable Snowman' of Himalayan folklore — large ape-like creature of high mountains. Rooted in Sherpa, Tibetan, Nepali oral traditions as wild man of snows (Mi-te, Kang-mi). Not a single entity but a class of mountain hominids. Famous globally but locally a spirit-being, protective or dangerous.

name: Yeti (Migoi)
description: The Yeti, known in Tibetan as Meh-teh or Migoi ('wild man'), is a hairy, ape-like being of Himalayan tradition said to roam snow, mountain, and cave. Tibetan lore distinguishes three forms: the giant black Nyalmo, the mid-altitude Chuti, and the small reddish Rang Shim Bombo. Feared yet sometimes revered as a guardian of remote passes, it remains unconfirmed.

name: Yewe
description: Yewe (also known as Hevioso, Xevioso, or Sogbo) is the powerful Ewe god of thunder, lightning, rain, and divine justice. One of the major trɔwo (lesser deities descended from Mawu), Yewe is one of the most feared and respected spirits in the Ewe pantheon. His sacred cult, the Yewe society, is one of the most exclusive and highly developed spiritual organizations in Eweland, with elaborate initiation ceremonies involving seclusion, sacred drumming (Sowu), and ritual dances. Those who offend Yewe may be struck by lightning. His priests (Midawos) serve as intermediaries. Yewe's sacred color is red, and his priests dance in possession trance during annual festivals. Yewe is related to the Yoruba Shango and the Fon Xevioso, reflecting the interconnected spiritual traditions of the region

name: Yggdrasil
description: Yggdrasil (Unknown). is a mythical-tree. Yggdrasil is the immense cosmic tree at the center of Norse cosmology, connecting the Nine Worlds. Its branches extend into the heavens, and its three roots reach to wellsprings that nourish creation.. Source: Poetic Edda, Prose Edda (Snorri Sturluson, 13th century)

name: Yocahu (Taino Supreme God of Fertility)
description: Yocahu (Yucahu Bagua Maorocoti) was the supreme deity and masculine spirit of fertility in Taino mythology -- the greatest of all zemis. His full name, recorded by the Spanish missionary Fray Ramon Pane in 1498, carries multiple meanings: Yucahu means giver of cassava (the staple crop), Bagua means master of the sea, and Maorocoti means conceived without male intervention -- born solely from his mother Atabey, the goddess of fresh water. Yocahu is the supreme creator god who shaped the Earth, created the sun and moon from a cave, and molded the first humans from clay. He is the god of agriculture, peace, and tranquility, representing goodness and order in the Taino universe. His throne is atop El Yunque Peak in Puerto Rico El Yunque National Forest -- the tallest mountain in the reserve, perpetually shrouded in cloud (the Taino called it yuke, meaning White Lands). From there, Yocahu battles the destructive goddess Guabancex, shielding his people from hurricanes. He is also known as the Sleeping Giant (El Gigante Dormido), whose reclining form is visible in the mountain profile

name: Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ (White Shell Girl)
description: Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ (White Shell Girl) is the original form of Changing Woman in Navajo tradition. She was born in the Fourth World and later matured into Changing Woman. She was sought in marriage by the Sun (Jóhonaa'éí), who disguised himself as a handsome warrior. After many trials, she agreed to marry him and traveled to his house in the eastern horizon made of turquoise and white shell. She bore the Sun's children who became the Hero Twins. White Shell Girl later entered the moon to become th

name: Yowie
description: The yowie is a large, hairy, ape-like being of eastern Australian oral tradition, known by many names across language groups — Gamilaraay Yō-wī, 'spirit roaming the earth at night' (recorded 1875), as well as Quinkin and joogabinna in Queensland. In Aboriginal accounts such beings enforce cultural law and warn children not to wander; in modern folklore it is also a Bigfoot-like cryptid.

name: Yuch-Kurbustan
description: Yuch-Kurbustan is a supreme celestial deity of Altai cosmology, a being of pure light in the highest heavens, never shown in human form, only as divine radiance. It wields supreme authority, aids heroes, and judges gods and humans. Apex of the divine hierarchy in Altaian epic, it is invoked in the most sacred narratives—in the Maadai-Kara epic it aids Kögüdei Mergen against Erlik's forces.

name: Yuki-onna
description: Yuki-onna (雪女), the snow woman, is a yōkai of Japanese winter folklore: a beautiful, pale-skinned woman with long black hair and a white or blue kimono who appears in snowstorms. She lures travelers into the cold and freezes them with her breath, yet sometimes spares those who are brave, kind, or handsome. Lafcadio Hearn's retelling in Kwaidan, published in 1904, made her internationally famous.

name: Yul-Chyn (Ice Spirits)
description: Not independently attested as a distinct figure of Nenets folklore. No source confirms ice spirits called 'Yul-Chyn' who strangle travelers; Nenets animism records numerous tundra and river spirits, but none by this name appear in ethnographic literature. The traits recorded appear to derive from modern speculation.

name: Yule Cat
description: Yule Cat (Icelandic). is a monster. A colossal and vicious feline that devours those who do not receive new clothes before Christmas. Source: Icelandic folklore, Jón Árnason's collections

name: Yule Lads
description: The Jólasveinar are thirteen Icelandic troll brothers who visit children on the thirteen nights before Christmas, each with a distinct prank (Clod, Gawk, Stubby, Spoon-Licker, Pot-Scraper, Bowl-Licker, Door-Slammer, Skyr-Gobbler, Sausage-Swiper, Window-Peeper, Doorway-Sniffer, Meat-Hook, Candle-Stealer). Sons of Grýla and Leppalúði. Documented in Jón Árnason's collections and 17th-century poetry.

name: Yule Lads Iceland
description: Yule Lads Iceland (Unknown). is a trickster. The Yule Lads (Jólasveinarnir) are thirteen mischievous figures from Icelandic folklore who visit children on the thirteen nights leading up to Christmas. Each has a distinct personality and prank—fro. Source: Icelandic Christmas folklore; Jón Árnason's collection (19th century)

name: Yulm (First Carpenter)
description: Yulm is the eldest of the Four Carpenters (Masmasalanicw) of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition, the wise and skilled creator who worked in the House of Smayusta with the Creator Alhkw'ntam. In a simple but powerful act he made Raven from a lump of charcoal, and his craft opened the way for the other carpenters to complete the world.

name: Yulm First Carpenter Nuxalk
description: Yulm is the eldest of the Four Carpenters, the culture-hero craftsmen who assisted the Nuxalk creator Alhkw'ntam in shaping the world. His name lives on in the making of the first bird: Yulm molded a qwaxw from charcoal and set it to fly, giving the Nuxalk the origin of birds and of carving.

name: Yum
description: Not attested in Zuni or any North American tradition. This record is a garbled duplicate of the Yumboes, the fairy-like spirits of the Wolof and Lebou peoples of Senegal, as its linked story 'The Yumboes, the Fairy Spirits of Senegal' shows. No being named 'Yum' appears in Zuni ethnography; the entry's Zuni attribution and United States country are both incorrect.

name: Yumboes
description: The Yumboes are supernatural fairy-like beings from the folklore of the Wolof and Lebou people of Senegal, often described as the spirits of the dead. Standing only about two feet tall with pearly-white skin and silver hair, these nocturnal beings live beneath the Paps hills near Gorée Island and emerge to dance in the moonlight. Despite their small stature, the Yumboes are known for hosting elaborate feasts on large tables, waited on by invisible servants whose only visible features are their hands and feet. They are generally benevolent and welcoming, often inviting both natives and foreigners to join their celebrations. The Yumboes are said to eat corn that they steal from humans and fish that they catch themselves. Their name is derived from the Wolof word for 'pumpkin,' reflecting their fondness for stealing human food. The only known source for the Yumboes legend is Thomas Keightley's 1828 book 'The Fairy Mythology,' based on accounts from a woman who lived on Gorée Island as a child and learned of them from a Wolof maid

name: Yunwi Tsunsdi
description: Yûñwï Tsunsdi', 'the Little Folk,' are the Cherokee little people, knee-high beings with perfect miniature Cherokee features and long hair reaching to their waists. They live in rock shelters and caves, help lost children, teach medicine and song, and punish those who disrespect nature; they can grant good luck or cause misfortune depending on how they are treated.

name: Yurei (Edo period)
description: Yūrei are the restless ghosts of Japanese tradition, given their classic form in Edo-period art and kabuki: a woman with long black hair, a white funeral kimono, and trailing sleeves, rendered with pale or blue-tinted skin and no feet. They are souls with unfinished business who died with strong attachment or injustice. Edo woodblock prints, notably Maruyama Ōkyo's, fixed this enduring image.

name: Yurugu (Pale Fox)
description: Yurugu (also called Ogo, the Pale Fox) is the first being of Dogon creation, born prematurely from Amma's flawed creative act. He limps across the Sahel on uneven legs as the living embodiment of disorder and incompleteness. Despite his chaotic nature, Yurugu serves a vital purpose through divination: each night, Dogon diviners draw a rectangular grid in fine sand, and Yurugu walks it, leaving paw-prints that are read at dawn to interpret the future. Because he is the original wound of creation, his tracks reveal truth. This paradox lies at the heart of Dogon spirituality: disorder, read correctly, becomes a map of truth

name: Yééw
description: Yééw is the hyena of Wolof folktales, a greedy and deceptive figure whose schemes always backfire, teaching children moral lessons through comic misfortune. In Senegalese oral tradition Yééw teaches the folly of selfishness while mirroring human weakness in village life.

name: Yéʼiitsoh (Big Giant)
description: Yé'iitsoh, 'Big Monster,' is the first and most powerful of the Anaye, the alien monsters of the Fifth World in Navajo (Diné) tradition. Son of the Sun, he wore four suits of flint armor and made his home at Tsoodził (Mount Taylor), where the Hero Twins, born to Changing Woman, slew him with lightning arrows; his blood became a river of dark, hard stone.

name: Zambur
description: Not independently attested as a scorpion spirit in Tajik folklore. The word zambur (zambūr) simply means 'wasp' in Persian, and no Tajik tale records a desert scorpion spirit by this name. Real scorpion lore in the region is confined to folk warnings about the black scorpion's sting and its place in proverbs and sayings.

name: Zana
description: Zanë are the mountain nymphs of Albanian folklore, beautiful, fierce, and fiercely independent protectors of nature who appear near rivers, waterfalls, forests, and peaks. They guard the wilderness and may aid the worthy, but those who disrespect nature risk their wrath, which can bring madness or harm. Compare with the Greek muses and fairies across the Balkan mountains.

name: Zanahary
description: Zanahary is the supreme sky creator god in Malagasy mythology, the source of all life and spirit. In the creation myth shared across Madagascar, Zanahary and the earth god Ratovantany collaborated to create humanity. Ratovantany shaped physical bodies from clay, but they remained lifeless until Zanahary breathed souls into them from the sky. Upon death, the soul returns to Zanahary in the heavens while the body returns to Ratovantany in the earth. This division underpins the deep Malagasy reverence for ancestors (Razana), who dwell near Zanahary and serve as intermediaries between the living and the divine

name: Zangbeto
description: Zangbeto, meaning 'Men of the Night' in the Goun and Fon languages, are sacred night guardian spirits central to the Vodun faith of Togo and Benin. These towering figures made of raffia and palm fibers spin through villages at night, serving as the eyes of justice in the darkness. According to tradition, Zangbetos are living vessels of ancestral spirits. Believers maintain that no human is inside the raffia structure, only spirit. They function as an unofficial spiritual police force, guarding against thieves and witches. The Zangbeto's hypnotic spinning is believed to cleanse the community of evil

name: Zangbeto
description: Zangbeto is a spirit from Vodun mythology. These towering figures made of raffia and palm fibers spin through villages at night, serving as the eyes of justice in the darkness. According to tradition, Zangbetos are living vessels of ancestral spirits. Believers maintain that no human is inside the raffia structure, only spirit. They function as an unofficial spiritual police force, guarding against thieves and witches. The Zangbeto's hypnotic spinning is believed to cleanse the community of evil

name: Zangbeto
description: Zangbeto is a spirit from Beninese Folklore mythology. These towering figures made of raffia and palm fibers spin through villages at night, serving as the eyes of justice in the darkness. According to tradition, Zangbetos are living vessels of ancestral spirits. Believers maintain that no human is inside the raffia structure, only spirit. They function as an unofficial spiritual police force, guarding against thieves and witches. The Zangbeto's hypnotic spinning is believed to cleanse the community of evil

name: Zankallala
description: Zankallala is a remarkable trickster figure from Hausa folklore, found across the Sahel region including northern Ivory Coast. Despite being only the size of two clenched fists, Zankallala is one of the most powerful beings in Hausa mythology, carrying a snake as a walking stick, wearing a pair of scorpions as spurs, and a swarm of bees as a hat. He rides a jerboa into battle and wherever he goes, he is followed by birds that sing his praises and attack his enemies. The most famous story of Zankallala involves his confrontation with the Dodo, the terrifying Swallower-of-Men. After a boy fleeing from a Dodo encounters Zankallala, the tiny hero allows himself to be swallowed three times, each time emerging unscathed from the monster's body until he kills it from within. This story exemplifies the Hausa tradition of the small and clever triumphing over the large and powerful through wit and courage

name: Zar
description: Zar spirits are genuine in Sudanese folk belief: ambivalent supernatural beings who possess individuals and cause illness and misfortune, and who must be appeased through drumming, dance and trance ceremonies. A zar ceremony involves the possessed person, a healer and the audience; spirits have distinct personalities and demand specific colors, perfumes and foods.

name: Zar
description: Zar spirits are a class of supernatural beings in Eritrean folk belief, particularly among Tigrinya-speaking communities and the broader Horn of Africa region. Unlike the purely malevolent Buda, Zar spirits are ambivalent—they can cause illness and misfortune when angered but may also become protective allies when properly honored through ritual. The Zar possession cult is an important traditional healing system in Eritrea, involving drumming, dancing, and trance ceremonies designed to appease spirits possessing individuals. A person 'ridden' by a Zar spirit may experience physical or mental illness, social withdrawal, or behavioral changes. Diagnosis involves a traditional healer identifying the specific Zar, followed by a ceremony where the spirit is acknowledged, honored, and convinced to reduce its demands. Zar spirits are believed to have distinct personalities, preferences, and demands, often requiring specific colors, perfumes, or foods In Eritrea folklore, this figure is known among the Eritrea people.

name: Zar
description: Zar refers to spirits in the possession cults of Ethiopia, Eritrea, Sudan, and the wider Horn of Africa. A zar is believed to possess an individual, causing illness, misfortune, or altered behavior, and is appeased through drumming ceremonies, song, and offerings led by a sheykha or priestess. The tradition blends indigenous beliefs with Islamic and Christian elements.

name: Zduhać
description: Zduhać (also Zduhač) is a human with supernatural abilities from Montenegrin and Dalmatian folklore, particularly among mountain tribes. Born with a caul (amniotic membrane) on their head, a Zduhać is destined to protect their community from destructive weather. During storms, their spirit leaves their sleeping body to travel through the skies and battle evil forces or other Zduhaći who threaten their village's crops, livestock, and safety. These battles manifest on earth as hailstorms, whirlwinds, and thunderstorms. A Zduhać's physical body remains in a death-like trance during these astral battles, and if disturbed, the spirit cannot return and the person dies

name: Zduhać
description: Zduhać is a human from Slavic mythology. Born with a caul (amniotic membrane) on their head, a Zduhać is destined to protect their community from destructive weather. During storms, their spirit leaves their sleeping body to travel through the skies and battle evil forces or other Zduhaći who threaten their village's crops, livestock, and safety. These battles manifest on earth as hailstorms, whirlwinds, and thunderstorms. A Zduhać's physical body remains in a death-like trance during these astral battles, and if disturbed, the spirit cannot return and the person dies

name: Zduhać
description: Zduhać is a human from Slavic mythology. Born with a caul (amniotic membrane) on their head, a Zduhać is destined to protect their community from destructive weather. During storms, their spirit leaves their sleeping body to travel through the skies and battle evil forces or other Zduhaći who threaten their village's crops, livestock, and safety. These battles manifest on earth as hailstorms, whirlwinds, and thunderstorms. A Zduhać's physical body remains in a death-like trance during these astral battles, and if disturbed, the spirit cannot return and the person dies In Montenegro folklore, this figure is known among the Montenegrin (South Slavic) people.

name: Zelebith
description: Zelebith (Ethiopia). is a bird. Zelebith is a bird from the folklore and mythology of Ethiopia.. Source: Ethiopian folklore — Zelebith bird documented in Ethiopian oral tradition.

name: Zhalmauyz
description: Zhalmauyz (Zhalmauyz Kempir) is the ogress of Kazakh folklore, an ancient cannibal hag who hunts for children to devour. She has seven heads, a single eye and hoof-like feet, and she shifts her shape to deceive her victims. Her name, echoing the steppe word for a child-stealing bogey, is used to frighten the young.

name: Zhar-Ptitsa (Firebird)
description: Zhar-Ptitsa (Firebird) is the Slavic magical glowing bird from a faraway land. Its golden feathers illuminate darkness; a single feather lights a room. Both a blessing and a harbinger of doom to its captor. Central to quest tales (Ivan Tsarevich and the Grey Wolf) where heroes seek it for a tsar. Inspired Stravinsky's ballet The Firebird. Parallel to Armenian Hazaran Blbul and Iranian Simurgh.

name: Zimwi (or Zimwi)
description: Zimwi is a Shona ogre (giant, hairy, man-eating) from Zimbabwe folklore, dwelling in forests and caves. It represents the danger of wilderness and strangers, often depicted with backwards feet to confuse trackers. Heroes outwit it through cleverness. The term zimwi appears in Bantu religion literature as a class of ogre-like beings across southern Africa (amazimu in Zulu, madimo in Sotho).

name: Zin
description: Zin are Hausa water spirits inhabiting the Niger River and lakes in Niger and northern Nigeria. They shapeshift between aquatic and human forms, luring humans to watery domains. Feared as causes of drowning and disappearances. Related to broader West African water spirit complexes (Mami Wata, Ndi Mmili). Documented in Hausa oral tradition.

name: Zin Kibaru
description: Zin Kibaru is a water spirit from Songhay-Zarma mythology of the Niger River region. The term Zin refers to a class of genies inhabiting water bodies, and Kibaru specifically designates a powerful water demon that demands respect and offerings. These spirits are associated with the Holeys, possession dances of the Songhay-Zarma people. Zin Kibaru are believed to inhabit the deepest parts of the Niger River and its tributaries. Fishermen and boatmen must make proper offerings before venturing onto certain waters. The Zin spirits can capsize boats, drown individuals, or bring abundant fish depending on how they are treated. They are served by the Do and Karou priestly lineages

name: Zlydzens
description: Zlydzens (Belarusian zlydni, Ukrainian zlydni) are small, hunchbacked, hazardous stove spirits living under the masonry oven. They wear big boots and earflap hats, resemble cat-dog hybrids. In groups they wreck utensils, spill milk, create chaos; drawn to greedy households. Cowardly alone. The Ukrainian phrase 'zhyty v zlydnyakh' (live in zlydni) means 'to live in poverty.'

name: Zmaj
description: Zmaj is the dragon of South Slavic folklore, including Kosovo, a great serpent or winged, fire-breathing beast dwelling in caves near villages. In Serbian and Kosovan tradition the fiery zmaj is often a guardian of crops who fights storm-demons, though dragons also guard treasure; its presence explains storms and drought. The figure parallels the Bulgarian zmey and Romanian zmeu.

name: Zmaj
description: Zmaj is the Serbian dragon — a winged serpent dwelling in caves near villages. In Balkans lore, unlike the malevolent Russian zmey, the zmaj is often a benevolent guardian who fights the evil ala/lamia (drought demons). Can appear as a handsome man, fire bird, or smoke; takes human lovers (e.g., Tsarina Milica). Symbol of patriotic resistance against Ottoman rule.

name: Zmej
description: Zmej is the Bulgarian dragon — a winged, scale-covered serpent, often with multiple heads (3–12). Unlike East Slavic malevolent zmey, the Balkan zmej is a benevolent guardian who fights the lamia/hala (drought demons). Can appear as a handsome man to woo human women; children of such unions become vampire hunters. Symbol of patriotic resistance. St.

name: Zmeu
description: Zmeu is the dragon of Romanian folklore, a fearsome flying serpent, often multi-headed, that abducts maidens and menaces villages from mountain fastnesses and castles. In the folk ballads a hero must defeat the zmeu, sometimes with the aid of his captive's cunning; the dragon may also appear as a handsome youth. It personifies the dangerous forces overcome by heroic virtue.

name: Zmeu
description: Zmeu is the dragon of Moldovan and Romanian folklore, a flying serpent, often multi-headed, that carries off maidens and plagues the land from mountains and high places, breathing fire and drowning its foes. Folk ballads tell of heroes who overcome it by courage and trickery. The zmeu represents the perilous forces that the human order must triumph over.

name: Zmey
description: In Russian folklore the zmei (zmej gorynych) is a serpent-dragon of skazki and byliny, a fire-breathing monster who abducts princesses and ravages the land. Epic heroes such as Dobrynya Nikitich and Alyosha Popovich slay Zmei Gorynych, and Tugarin Zmeevich appears as a dragon adversary in the oral epic songs.

name: Zmey
description: The zmey is a dragon of Bulgarian folklore, a powerful being that can aid people: male zmey protect villages and battle destructive female lamia or hala in the sky during storms, guarding the wheat harvest. Zmey may take human, serpent or cloud form and fall in love with human women; the forest dragon Zmey Gorianin is a noted figure.

name: Zmey
description: Zmey is a spirit from Macedonian Slavic Mythology mythology. In Macedonian tales and folk songs, Zmey are described as extraordinarily intelligent beings with hypnotizing eyes, possessing a human-like form with a snake's tail and golden wings. They live in caves or on remote mountain tops and are extremely wise. The Zmey has a dual nature: they are territorial guardians who protect villages and fight destructive female Lamia in the skies during storms, yet they also fall passionately in love with human women, often kidnapping them to their mountain lairs. A Zmey can shape-shift into smoke, a spark, a firebird, a snake, a cloud, or a handsome man. In Macedonian belief, a woman may conceive a Zmey after a prolonged pregnancy of 15-20 months, and the child is born with small wings under the arms visible only to righteous people. Zmeys battle Lamia in the sky during storms to protect wheat harvests—the Zmey's spirit astrally projects into the clouds while his body sleeps. A crossbreed between a serpent and a samovila may also produce a Zmey

name: Zmey Gorynych
description: Zmey Gorynych is the iconic Russian three-to-twelve-headed dragon of byliny and fairy tales. Dwells beyond three rivers or in mountain caves. Each severed head regenerates unless cauterized; kidnaps princesses; breathes fire. Slain by bogatyrs Dobrynya Nikitich and Ilya Muromets. A specific named antagonist, not a species. Name means 'serpent of the mountains (Goryny).'

name: Zmora
description: Zmora is a Slavic night demon of Polish folklore, akin to the mare or mara. It is believed to visit sleepers at night, pressing on their chests and causing choking, nightmares, and a heavy feeling upon waking. Zmora were thought to be spirits of the dead or, in some regions, living people whose souls left their bodies at night to torment others.

name: Zombi
description: Zombi (Unknown). is a undead. In Haitian Vodou tradition, a zombi is a reanimated corpse brought back to life by a bokor (sorcerer). Unlike the modern cinematic version, the Haitian zombi is a mindless laborer under the control of. Source: The Serpent and the Rainbow (Davis, 1985); Haitian Folklore (Courlander, 1960)

name: Zonbi
description: The Zonbi is a malevolent spirit or reanimated corpse in Seychellois Creole folklore, linked to dark magic rather than Hollywood-style zombies. A corpse may be animated by sorcery to serve an evil purpose, and Zonbi are associated with abandoned historical sites. Belief in them reflects anxieties about death, the afterlife and the misuse of spiritual power.

name: Zuhri
description: The zuhri is a being of Moroccan belief, born of a human mother and a jinn father, who can see buried treasure beneath the earth. Marked by a slanting gaze, the zuhri is sought by treasure hunters, while the treasures themselves are said to strike the greedy dead. The belief is so potent that it has been invoked in real, violent crimes.

name: Zuleikha
description: The Forty Maidens (Kirk Kiz), here given the name Zuleikha, are a band of warrior women of Turkmen and neighboring Central Asian tradition who defend their stronghold against invaders. The ninth-century fortress of Kirk Kiz at Termez is linked to their tale, told across Turkmen, Karakalpak and Uzbek epic lore and praised for the maidens' courage.

name: Zumwani
description: Zumwani is a Herero water spirit of Namibia, appearing as an exceedingly beautiful woman with reed-like hair wearing colorful cloth, dwelling in rivers, pans, and waterholes. She tests men's character at water's edge: rewarding the respectful with good rains, drowning the disrespectful. Associated with seasonal rains and water scarcity in Herero pastoral culture.

name: Zār
description: The zar is a class of possessing spirits in Sudan, Egypt, and the Horn of Africa, believed to seize people, most often women, causing illness, restlessness, and affliction. Each zar demands its own clothes, jewels, incense, and drumming, met through the healing ceremonies of the zar cult. Seven nations of zar spirits range from holy men to European officials.

name: Áhaiyúta (Morning Star, War God)
description: Áhaiyúta is one of the two Zuni Twin War Gods, the elder of the pair with his brother Mátsailéma; together the 'Twain Little-ones' are the right- and left-hand beings of the Sun, gods of war, chance and games. In Frank Hamilton Cushing's Zuni Folk Tales they descend to the underworld, battle the soft 'unborn-made men', and clear the world of its monsters.

name: Álfar
description: Álfar (elves) are nature-dwelling spirits in Icelandic folklore, distinct from the Huldufólk (hidden people) in several key ways. While Huldufólk are considered to be human-like beings living in a parallel society, álfar are more ethereal, nature-bound beings associated with specific rocks, hills, and cliffs. In Icelandic tradition, álfar are beautiful, graceful, and possess magical powers. They live inside rocks (álfhólar — elf hills) and practice farming in parallel to human farmers. If offended, they can cause illness, misfortune, or accidents. If respected, they bring good luck. Offerings were traditionally left for the álfar at certain rocks. In Norse mythology, the álfar appear in the Poetic Edda and Snorra Edda as a distinct race. Kormáks saga mentions a sacrifice to álfar for healing. Modern Iceland still has a strong álfar belief tradition, with many Icelanders believing in their existence

name: Ápoyan Ta'chu (Sky Father)
description: Ápoyan Ta'chu (Sky Father) is a creator deity in Zuni mythology, regarded as the supreme ruler of the Above World. He is the father of the Sun Priest and the Moon Maiden, and together with Earth Mother (Uchtsiti) he shaped the first beings from cornmeal. Ápoyan Ta'chu instructed the Zuni people in the art of prayer plumes and ritual offerings, and his breath is said to carry the warmth of summer winds. He dwells in the highest reaches of the sky, where the thunderclouds gather before the rainy season, and is invoked during the winter solstice ceremonies to ensure the return of light and fertility to the land

name: Átahsaia (Cannibal Demon)
description: Átahsaia is a giant cannibal demon in Zuni mythology who terrorized the people. He is described as a huge, monstrous being with burning eyes, coarse hair like a buffalo's mane, scales of black and white on his arms and legs, and a mouth filled with crooked yellow fangs. He carried a bow and a great flint knife. Átahsaia would descend from the mountains to raid villages, carrying off victims in a large basket on his back to his cave in the red-gray cliffs. The twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailém

name: Áwitelin Tsíta (Earth Mother)
description: Awitelin Tsita (Áwitelin Tsíta) is the Earth Mother of Zuni creation, formed together with the Sky Father Ápoyan Ta'chu from the mists that lay over the great waters; she conceived all living things in her four-fold womb. In Frank Hamilton Cushing's Zuni Genesis, the All-Father Awonawilona sets this creation in motion. She is a central generative deity of Zuni cosmology.

name: Áwonawílona (All-Father)
description: Áwonawílona (All-Father, Maker and Container of All) is the supreme primordial deity in Zuni creation mythology. In the beginning, only Áwonawílona existed. He made himself into the Sun Father (Yatoka). The mist clouds formed into the Great Waters, from which Earth Mother (Áwitelin Tsíta) and Sky Father (Ápoyan Ta'chu) emerged. Áwonawílona conceived all men and creatures in the four-fold womb of the world. He represents the ultimate source of all existence, the transcendent creator who encompass

name: Âu Cơ (Mountain Fairy)
description: Âu Cơ is the beautiful mountain fairy and founding mother of the Vietnamese people. Daughter of Đế Lai (a descendant of the divine Shennong), she was a tiên (immortal fairy) who lived in the snow-capped mountains and traveled to heal the sick with her medical skills. She married the dragon lord Lạc Long Quân and gave birth to an egg sac that hatched one hundred children — the ancestors of all Vietnamese people. When Lạc Long Quân (a being of water and sea) and Âu Cơ (a being of mountains and sky) realized their elements were incompatible, they separated, each taking fifty children. Âu Cơ settled in the mountainous north with her fifty children, who became the founders of the Hùng King dynasty. She taught agriculture, animal husbandry, and forest survival. Âu Cơ is revered alongside Lạc Long Quân as the dual progenitors of the Vietnamese nation, symbolizing the country's highland and coastal duality

name: Ââ'ototo Kachina
description: Eototo (A'ototo) is a principal Hopi kachina, the chief and 'father' of the katsinam after Angwusnasomtaka, personification of nature and protagonist of the Powamu ceremony. He comes from the red land of the south, belongs to the Bear clan, wears a white cylindrical mask topped with a nest of hair, and draws cloud symbols in cornmeal. He appears in Voth's Traditions of the Hopi.

name: Älvakung
description: Älvakungen (the elf king) is the ruler of the elves (älvor) in Swedish folklore. He leads the elf dance (älvadans) on misty meadows, especially around Midsummer and during the autumn mists. Älvakungen appears as a magnificent but deeply otherworldly figure — handsome, richly dressed, but with an unsettling presence that betrays his non-human nature. Those who join the elf dance, whether lured by the beauty of the music or the king's charm, may dance for what feels like hours only to find that years or centuries have passed in the human world. Älvakungen's realm exists on the boundary between the human world and the otherworld, accessible only at twilight, through mist, or at the liminal times of the year. He is not evil but is dangerously indifferent to human mortality

name: Älvor
description: Älvor in Swedish folk belief are beautiful, human-like beings dwelling in forests, meadows, and mist. They dance in circles (älvadans), causing illness or madness to intruders, and can exchange human children for changelings (bytlingar). Both male and female älvor exist. They are distinct from skogsrå/huldra but regionally conflated. Documented in 17th–19th century Swedish folklore collections.

name: Åland Storm-Witch
description: The storm-witch of Åland is a female practitioner of weather magic who possesses the secret art of tying the wind into knots of rope. Unlike malevolent hags who conjure storms through incantations, the Åland storm-witch operates as a trader of winds: she sells sailors knotted ropes that release favorable breezes when untied. Untying one knot produces a light wind, untying two fills the sails, but untying all three awakens a devastating tempest. This tradition is inextricably linked to Kastelholm Castle, the 14th-century fortress at the heart of the main island, where during the 1665–1668 Kastelholm witch trials storm-witches were among the accused. The practice reflects the deep dependence of Åland’s islanders on safe sea passage — the archipelago’s thousands of islands, skerries, and open Baltic stretches made weather control a matter of life and death. The tradition persists in local memory: even today, some islanders refuse to throw knotted rope into the sea without cutting the knots first, for fear of stirring the winds that should sleep

name: Åmand
description: Åmanden (the River Man) is a Danish male water spirit who rules a specific river stretch and demands an annual human sacrifice. Unlike Nøkken, who lures individuals, the Åmand has a contractual demand: one person per year must drown in his waters, and he calls for his victim on a specific night. His most famous cry echoes through Danish folklore: 'Tiden er kommet, men manden ikke!' ('The time has come, but the man has not!'). In Odense Å, this cry was heard every year at the same hour, and someone always drowned within days. At Vasegård on Bornholm in the 1850s, a man hid from the Åmand's call, barricading himself inside his home, but was found dead in bed by morning. The Bornholm variant is called 'Læsåbobbanj' (the Læså River bump/goblin) and is smaller and more mischievous

name: Ésevone
description: Ésevone is the Sacred Buffalo Hat of the Cheyenne people, one of the two most sacred ceremonial objects of the Cheyenne Nation (alongside the Maahótse Sacred Arrows). Made from the skin of a buffalo cow's head, ornamented with a pair of buffalo horns that have been shaved down, flattened, and decorated. Ésevone represents female power, while the Sacred Arrows represent male power. It was brought to the people by the prophet Erect Horns (or Standing-on-the-Ground). The hat could summon buffalo herds and protect the people. Its keeper must follow strict taboos and perform annual renewal ceremonies

name: Ông Địa
description: Ông Địa is the earth god of the Vietnamese household, depicted as a jovial bald old man with a long beard who resides beneath the home, in gardens, or fields. He protects the family from misfortune and brings prosperity in exchange for offerings and reverence. His cult blends Buddhist practice with indigenous folk religion, and he is among the most widely honored domestic deities in Vietnam.

name: Ölgii-khorkhoi (Mongolian Death Worm)
description: Ölgii-khorkhoi, the 'Mongolian Death Worm,' is the legendary cryptid of the Gobi Desert, a thick, fat worm, bright red or orange, as thick as a man's arm, eyeless and mouthless, sometimes with spikes. Buried in sand and emerging after rain, it is said to kill camels and humans with corrosive spit or electric discharge. Popularized in the West since Roy Chapman Andrews, it remains unconfirmed.

name: Ülgen (Bai-Ülgen)
description: Ülgen (Bai-Ülgen) is the benevolent sky-god of the Altai Turks: the radiant creator dwelling in the sixteenth heaven who made the earth and humanity. Generous, protective, and abundant, he rewards good shamans and watches over rebirth, seated on a golden mountain with a golden staff. His worship anchors Altaian and wider Turkic Tengrist tradition.

name: Čáhcegearpmaš
description: Čáhcegearpmaš, also called Vesikäärme, is a water serpent of the Tornedalen region known to Sami and Meänkieli tradition, a close variant of Čáhcerávga, the Northern Sami 'water rávga' — a malevolent water being, shadow of the drowned, that haunts lakes and streams and pulls people, especially children, beneath the surface. The belief remains alive in Sami-language media.

name: Čáhcerávga
description: Čáhcerávga (Water Wraith) is a fictional creature in Sami folklore, explicitly known to be invented to scare children away from dangerous waters. Unlike the Rávga, which was believed to be a real undead spirit, the Čáhcerávga was recognized as a pedagogical tool. It was described as a long-necked, scary creature that could carry a child away if they went too close to the water. It was said to appear in all bodies of water where children were not supposed to go — lakes, rivers, ponds, and even wells. This belief shows how Sami folklore functioned as practical safety education in the Arctic landscape, where drowning in ice-cold water was a real and constant danger for children. The near-freezing waters of Sapmi meant that falling in could be fatal within minutes, making such scare-stories a matter of survival

name: Čázevulošnieida
description: Čázevulošnieida (the Underwater Girl) is a Sea Sami spirit from the Unjárga/Nesseby region on the Varangerfjord, Norway. She is the daughter of Čáhceháldi (the Sea Guard), a mythical sea ranger who lives in a parallel underwater world. When a Sami fisherman boy encounters her, their meeting reveals how perspectives are completely inverted between the world above the waves and the world below — what is 'up' for one is 'down' for the other. The story originates from the Sea Sami cultural heritage area around Ceavccageađge/Mortensnes, one of the most important Sami cultural heritage sites in Norway. The tale explores themes of parallel worlds, inverted realities, and the meeting of different orders of existence. The story has been adapted into contemporary dance performances and art installations at Black Box teater in Oslo, demonstrating the ongoing vitality of this myth

name: Đào
description: The name Đào (peach) in Vietnamese tradition does connect to documented folklore: in Lĩnh Nam chích quái, peach branches ward off evil spirits, and peach is central to Tết New Year customs. However, the recorded figure of a beautiful mountain fairy named Đào who lures or guides travelers is not independently attested; it appears to be a spirit conflated from real peach-branch symbolism.

name: ǐKaggen
description: ǐKaggen (also Cagn, the Mantis) is the central trickster-creator deity of the San people of southern Africa, including Namibia. A demiurge and culture hero, ǐKaggen can shapeshift into various animal forms, most frequently a praying mantis, but also a bull eland, a louse, a snake, or a caterpillar. He created the world and all living things, with his favorite creation being the eland, which provided meat for the people. ǐKaggen is a complex figure balancing creation with trickery, wisdom with foolishness. His wife ǐHúnntuǓattǓatte̯n (Coti) is the mother of bees and takes the form of a Cape hyrax

name: ǐXue
description: ǐXue is the trickster being of the ǓKun (ǓXung) people of northeastern Namibia, described by scholars as Khoisan mythology's most unrestrained shapeshifter with a trigger-sharp readiness for transformation. ǐXue can transform himself into each and everything conceivable. He has a complicated association with the moon and the hare (one of his most integral animal personas), and is connected to the divinity Huwe and spirit beings ǁgana. ǐXue appears in over 110 stories recorded by Lucy Lloyd from two young ǓKun storytellers between 1879 and 1882. The trickster spirit also engages in a complex dispute with Tamme involving their respective wives
